cards.title: Test suites run in seconds: fix the slow programs, the timeouts and the per-program cost
cards.body:
Owner direction 2026-11-06: suites should finish in seconds or minutes, not take a long time; the golden suite once took about 15 minutes at most.

Measured on vb5 (dev 7f0b3d03ed, s1, 32 cores):
- golden: 4766 rows, about 4 minutes wall, median 0.28 s per row. The 4655 rows under 5 s alone sum to 74 CPU minutes, so per-program cost sets a floor of about 2.3 minutes even with perfect parallelism.
- cases: 4501 rows, about 13.5 minutes wall, median 0.10 s; 284 rows of 5 s or more account for 97 of 131 CPU minutes; 12 rows hit the 60 s wall-clock limit.
- ui: 2412 rows, about 1 minute wall.

Slowest golden programs (all tiers): concurrency/job_queue 248 s, foundations/storage 177 s, foundations/text 161 s, crypto/file_seal_jetc 153 s, game/raylib_indexed 148 s, foundations/realtime 100 s.
Timeouts: cffi/concurrent_bridges_share_one_target_publish_without_racing, cffi/ffi_capability_boundary_is_safe_only_inside_unsafe, ffi_rust/rust_extern_std_round_trip_uses_the_canonical_descriptor, fixtures_crypto_bridge_entropy/jetc_v2_record_boundaries_are_canonical, fmt_project/top_level_jet_fmt_delegates_non_jet_file_to_realized_formatter, jetpack_nix_index/index_backed_nixpkgs_repairs_only_missing_transitive_object, jetpack_nix_index/static_publication_resolves_signed_index_and_nix_objects, jetpack_tool/use_ephemeral_execs_inside_and_outside_project_without_path_projection, repl/repl_tty_prompts_and_reuses_exact_session_tuple, ui_fixes/ownership_ui_fixes_compile_ffi_companions, unsafe_and_runtime/ffi_capability_edge_uses_shared_sentry_prelude, web_dev/embedded_devserver_rejects_hardlinked_source.

For every slow row, first record where the time goes (compile front end, Core/Prelude re-check, code generation per tier, link, the program's own run, or a fixed sleep or timeout in the test), then fix that root. Never raise a limit, drop a tier or move a row out of the default profile to make a number.

log.text: Moved from G1 to G5 by owner ruling 2026-11-07. a0_033 release kit timings (parallel, under load): golden 1479 programs, median 528 ms, 420 at 5 s or more, rows sum 5037 s; cases 4637, median 156 ms, 524 at 5 s or more, sum 8201 s; ui 2252, median 66 ms, 9 at 5 s or more, sum 939 s. c4's shared per-run Core check is compiler work, the same as #6623 and #6647.

c4 progress: MechD-3's 59d955887b (store capacity checks replay a footprint tally instead of scanning every entry) cut golden wall from 1086 s to 118.7 s on fab74a230c s1, all rows passing (4318 PASS, 0 FAIL). The per-program median is 348 ms over 3 tiers, about 0.12 s per tier, against the 0.1 s target. About 90% of each tier is re-checking Core identically for every program; caching checked Core by content key is the remaining c4 lever, and df runs about 6 times per build. c5 still needs a run on the batch machine (118.7 s against the 90 s target).

criteria.text: Each of the six slow golden programs (concurrency/job_queue, foundations/storage, foundations/text, crypto/file_seal_jetc, game/raylib_indexed, foundations/realtime, or their successors after the Examples cutover) runs in under 5 s per tier on the batch machine, with the root cause of its old time recorded on this card. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile golden --filter Each program>` timings in the testkit report.
The 12 cases rows that hit the 60 s wall-clock limit on vb5 are root-caused and each passes, or fails for a recorded unrelated reason, in under 10 s.
criteria.evidence: 85dea10ff4 (TestSystemLead-2). The 12 vb5 60 s rows, rerun at HEAD (release jetpack aaa6331fc067, cargo and bwrap on PATH). Root causes, from reproducing each on 7f0b3d03ed: cffi/concurrent_bridges was a jet check futex deadlock (PASS 3.0 s); ffi_rust/rust_extern_std was an ICE 101 (PASS 2.7 s); fixtures_crypto_bridge_entropy/jetc_v2 was an fsync stall in jbd2 on loaded ext4 scratch (PASS 3.1 s); fmt_project/top_level_jet_fmt was the old jetpack hanging in env -- nixfmt (PASS 0.26 s); jetpack_nix_index static_publication and index_backed_repairs were the old jetpack hanging in env --prep (PASS 4.4 s and 9.5 s); web_dev/embedded_devserver_rejects_hardlinked_source was jet dev watching until the limit (now KNOWN-FAILING #6386, 2.2 s). cffi/ffi_capability_boundary (1.4 s), unsafe_and_runtime/ffi_capability_edge (0.3 s) and ui_fixes/ownership_ui_fixes_compile_ffi_companions (2.6 s) pass; the first two now declare requires tool:cargo/rustc and report SKIP-HOST without cargo. jetpack_tool/use_ephemeral is KNOWN-FAILING #3594 (8.0 s); repl_tty_prompts is KNOWN-FAILING #5949 with its limit lowered to 6 s (6.1 s). Row lists: lanes/TestSystemLead/kf82.txt, kf84.txt, kf85.txt.

criteria.text: Every cases row that took 5 s or more on vb5 (284 rows) runs in under 5 s, or this card records why its work is inherently longer (for example a real network or Nix fetch) and that row moves to a named opt-in profile that the default run does not include. Proof: the testkit report timing table for the cases suite.

Per-program cost: a profile of a typical golden row splits its time into Core and Prelude checking, the program's own front end, code generation per tier, link and run. Any work repeated identically for every program (for example re-checking Core) is done once per suite run and shared, and the median golden row drops to 0.1 s or less. Proof: a committed per-phase profile of a typical golden row and the testkit report median.
On the batch machine the golden suite finishes in under 90 s wall, the cases suite in under 3 minutes and the ui suite in under 30 s, measured on the same commit and recorded with the commit.
criteria.evidence: Merged into #6610 c14: c14 holds the tighter owner budget of 2026-11-04 (about 60 s for all three suites)

criteria.text: The two step timeouts set for #6651 c2 are removed and both rows pass on the default 60 s step limit under full-kit load: Tests/Cases/CompiledWorkloads/compiled_workload_gate_self_check.case (19 s alone; warm 11.6 s splits into contract 2.2 s, synthetic report 2.1 s, 33 check_report calls with about 63 ms of start-up each, then tier, peer, sample and tier-receipt checks) and Tests/Cases/ComptimeSequenceParity/repl_list_and_fixed_list_sequence_methods_are_exact.case (50 REPL turns at about 0.4 s each). Proof: both rows pass in `jet test Compiler --profile cases` with no step timeout in their .case files.

The packages suite on a fresh clone finishes in under 5 minutes wall: the hosted Jetpack engine build overlaps the package runs (2a5ad087af), and the engine unit's claims, which run serially because they share process state, run in under 1 minute. Proof: a timed `jet test Compiler --profile packages` on a fresh clone, committed as a receipt.

Every corpus suite (golden, cases, ui, packages) runs as wide as the machine's cores and memory allow, with no fixed job cap below that. Proof: the job count logged by `jet test Compiler --profile golden` on the batch machine equals its cores-and-memory bound.

Excluding the toolchain fetch, jet test Compiler --profile full on a fresh clone finishes in under 10 minutes on the batch machine. A per-phase timeline is recorded with the commit. Proof: a committed per-phase timeline of the fresh-clone run.
The cold toolchain fetch inside that run (#6592) takes 30 s or less, so the whole fresh-clone run finishes in under 11 minutes. Proof: the fetch phase in the same timeline.

The fresh-clone full profile's startup (building the test runner and assembling before the first suite row; about 4 minutes on 2026-11-07) is measured by phase and cut to under 30 s. Proof: the startup phases in the same timeline.

Mutation testing on by default (#6060): The stock jet test run with mutate: changed and generated rows on stays fast enough to be on by default: a paired cell in the perf manifest compares the default jet test rerun against the matched peers (cargo-mutants plus cargo-fuzz, Go's test cache plus go test -fuzz) under the performance gate. Proof: `node Tools/Gauntlet/Harness/run.mjs --entry mutation-default` shows no loss.
The closed-list guard (#6206) runs in under 5 s (4.2 s measured for the census). Proof: the timed `jet test Tests/Guards --filter closed_lists`.

Owner 2026-11-04: tests take seconds, a minute at most for a few thousand, and never run out of memory unless something leaks. The full ui, golden and cases suites finish in at most about 60 s of wall time on the dev machine, and no test job is killed for memory (today suite.sh gives each job 3 GiB, allows a 6800 s timeout, and cases runs were OOM-killed on 2026-11-04, while hello costs about 180 ms CPU and 15-19 MB). Proof: a testkit report with a per-test wall-time and peak-RSS table for every suite, and a timed full run that meets the budget, committed with the commit.

Running one test costs about that test's own time: the testkit's fixed startup is listed phase by phase (kit build or load, harness compile, corpus scan, Core load, worker start), and a run filtered to one golden entry at --jobs 1 finishes within 0.5 s of that entry's own compile-and-run time (today about 35 s of fixed overhead). Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile golden --filter One entry> --jobs 1` timed against that entry's own `jet run`, in a committed receipt.

Jet's test runner is the fastest of any language: a peer-matched cell runs the same corpus (a few thousand small unit tests plus whole-program goldens) in Jet, Rust (cargo test and nextest), Go, Zig, TypeScript (Bun test and Vitest) and Python (pytest), measuring cold full run, warm full run and edit-one-test-and-rerun in wall time and peak memory, with Jet/peer below 1.00 for every peer and metric. Proof: `node Tools/Gauntlet/Harness/run.mjs --entry test-runner` shows no in-group loss.

Compiler/JetDriver/Tests checks and its tests run in lane-check (on dev 8219108260 CLISeams.jet, RustForeign.jet and SchemaIngress.jet did not compile), so a driver test cannot rot unseen. Proof: `jet test Compiler/JetDriver` passes and lane-check lists it. (was #6637 c21)

cards.title: Import Make, CMake and Cargo builds
cards.body: Importing existing Make, CMake and Cargo projects into Jet build actions. Kept and frozen by owner ruling 2026-11-06; projects declare their build in build.jet meanwhile.

criteria.text: A representative Make project imports into the canonical graph and builds through ActionSpec on the production path, with the same outputs as `make`; no demo, label, stub or sibling claim substitutes. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter Tests/Cases/BuildImport/make_project_builds_through_actionspec`.

An imported build's commands, tools, inputs, outputs, environment, dependencies, resources, cache identity, provenance and resulting actions are all listed by graph inspection. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter Tests/Cases/BuildImport/imported_graph_lists_every_command_tool_input_output_and_provenance`.

Policy denial, undeclared access and path escape in an imported action fail with a registered diagnostic, and no unreviewed fallback command runs. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter Tests/Cases/BuildImport/imported_action_refuses_denied_undeclared_and_escaping_access`.

In CI mode an unreviewed imported command is refused (the CI ban), and a hostile imported project, one whose action writes outside its declared outputs, is refused. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter Tests/Cases/BuildImport/ci_ban_and_hostile_project_are_refused`.

A representative CMake project imports into the canonical graph and builds through ActionSpec on the production path, with the same outputs as the CMake build. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter Tests/Cases/BuildImport/cmake_project_builds_through_actionspec`.

A representative Cargo project imports into the canonical graph and builds through ActionSpec on the production path, with the same outputs as `cargo build`. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter Tests/Cases/BuildImport/cargo_project_builds_through_actionspec`.

An unsupported project construct and a partial import fail with a registered diagnostic naming the construct, and no unreviewed fallback command runs. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter Tests/Cases/BuildImport/unsupported_construct_and_partial_import_fail_without_fallback`.

A failing imported tool and nondeterministic imported output fail with a registered diagnostic naming the tool and the action. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter Tests/Cases/BuildImport/tool_failure_and_nondeterminism_fail_clearly`.

cards.title: `fn build` per-package permissions
cards.body: fn build scope and authority: declared inputs, explicit grants, dependency order and rejection before effects. Moved out of the known-failing card #5454 by owner ruling 2026-11-06.

criteria.text: Each build unit receives only its declared Tier-1 inputs and explicitly named Tier-2 grants, and dependency order, computed package facts, plan, execution, lock and explain output agree.

Unlisted dependency authority, grant escalation, cycles, outside-root paths, read or write failure and stale computed facts are refused before any effect, each with its registered error and UI snapshot.
In a multi-member workspace, grants are not inherited, dependency grants are explicit, order and root-layer boundaries hold, and a failed build rolls back.
The package-default authority floor (#3718) is part of the JetDriver package facts.
`b.include(pkg)` in your `fn build` runs the package's own `fn build` only under that package's authority, and records producer, input and output identity in the Jetpack lock.
Importing a package or using its helpers never runs its build entries or hooks implicitly.
Plan fragments and generated modules from an included build merge transactionally, and a collision or denied effect leaves no partial publication.
Shared preparation can generate the same outputs on non-AOT tiers without misusing `fn build`.
An Examples/ golden of a bindings package used through `b.include` passes on the self-hosted toolchain.

cards.title: core.compute correctness: CPU-oracle parity, checked failures, SIMD kernels and kernel helpers
cards.body: core.compute data integration, tensor meaning, failure checks and CPU-differential proof. Moved out of #5454 by owner ruling 2026-11-06.

log.text: Cleaned 2026-11-15: criteria restated with proofs; c4 now names the failing compute_autodiff golden.
Defect recorded here because #3026 is frozen and design card #3218 is archived as done: ratified D-GPU-HELPER-SCOPE1=A is unbuilt. Report: Docs/audits/2026-11-10-run-where-review.md.

criteria.text: Tensor storage, views, operations, precision, placement, streams, kernels, derivatives and serialization match the CPU oracle: a differential test runs each operation family on every available backend against the CPU result.

Shape, alias, bounds, race, barrier, precision, device-loss, transfer, gradient and unsupported-operation failures are checked at the owning layer and give typed errors, never a fabricated success. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter Compute/failure_` with a negative case per failure.
compute_autodiff runs (no internal compiler error) and prints its expected output on O0, O1, O2 and the AOT build.
criteria.evidence: p238 batch compiler (dev 5bea729463), full collect-all suite: golden Compute/ComputeAutodiff PASS on o0, o1 and o2.

criteria.text: The ufunc and kernel set that must lower to SIMD is listed in Core/Compute, and a scalar-versus-SIMD differential test proves byte-equal results for each.
Runtime dispatch picks the AVX2 or SSE2 path through jet_compute_simd_backend, and both paths give the same results.

D-GPU-HELPER-SCOPE1=A is built: a #Kernel that calls a pure helper (for example a function returning `x * 3`) checks and runs on every applicable tier instead of E1102 at the marker (Sema/Kernel.jet rejects every call edge today), and a rejected helper's diagnostic keeps its span. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile golden --filter Compute/KernelHelper` and `jet test Compiler --profile ui --filter kernel_helper_rejected`.

A handled ComputeError (for example from `compute.eye(-1)`) shows its typed detail through the supported surface, with a golden on O0, O1 and O2; the E0915 suggestion for ComputeError-like types compiles on the next check.

The 2 known-failing rows this card owns (rehomed by #6843 c7) pass and leave Tests/known-failing.tsv: ComputeParity/compute_fixed_vec_and_matrix_aliases_keep_shape_facts_on_the_tensor_substrate, ComputeParity/matrix_shape_measures_match_or_diagnose_inner_sides. Proof: each named test passes in its suite on a batch compiler, and no row of Tests/known-failing.tsv names this card for them.

cards.title: Live hot reload keeps state: #Persist values survive edits and restarts, migrate by rule, and every reset names its reason
cards.body:
Destination: under `jet dev`, editing a running program swaps the code and keeps every #Persist value whose type is unchanged. Type changes follow D-HOTSTATE1=A and D-LIVE-PERSIST1=A: defaults, drops, `migration` blocks, or an announced restart that names the blocking field. Restarts keep #Persist values through the session pipe (D-DEV-STATE1=A). Game state and controls live in the same session (D-DX-GAMELOOP1=A).

Until this card lands, JetDevserver's swap paths (NativeSwap, NativeSwap02, WebModuleSwap) refuse with not-available (#5931, Main's log 2026-11-13). Diagnostic E2210 is registered again with its emitter when this card builds the behavior.

Moved out of #5454 by owner ruling 2026-11-06.

log.text: Cleaned 2026-11-15: proofs added to every criterion. c4 merged into c10 (D-LIVE-PERSIST1) and c13 (the renamed-binding reset), and c7 into c8.

Note (Main): until this card lands, JetDevserver swap paths (NativeSwap, NativeSwap02, WebModuleSwap) refuse with an explicit not-available result instead of using HotSwapDecision and StateRetentionFact; they are restored against the real types when this card lands (#5931).

Main, 2026-11-11, #4260 c29 cleanup (G5DevX-dead-codes-3): diagnostic code E2210 is removed from the registry because nothing emits it, and its known-failing cases go with it. When this card builds the behavior, it registers the code again with its emitter, what/why/fix text and a UI snapshot. The behavior the deleted cases expected: tests/cases/dev_parts_routine/{struct_field,enum_variant,fn_signature}_change_emits_e2210.case: a jet dev edit to a type surface restarts instead of swapping.

criteria.text: On every live edit, each #Persist key's retention comes from its checked type identity, and its payload shape is validated at one Foundation migration boundary. Only unchanged typed values are kept, and changed or unavailable keys record an explicit Fresh or Reset reason, on O0 and O2. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter DevPartsRoutine/persist_binding_survives_hot_swap_and_resets_on_shape_change` on O0 and O2.

Game hot swap runs through the production WatchSession facts and one shared swap kernel. Asset, script and world changes get typed decisions, the resident dev tools apply them, and each is published as an event.

`jet dev` selects the tier, runs the O0 and O2 source paths, watches by content digest, and keeps #Persist semantics in resident live execution across a long-lived session. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter DevPartsRoutine/ul6_native_watch_matrix_budget_and_reconnect` and `--filter dev_parts_routine/persist_example_survives_hot_reload` on O0 and O2.
(was #2504 c2) Published Persist migrations use one shared canonical Shape migration plan; restart and renamed-binding reset policies are implemented (moved from #5454 c69)
criteria.evidence: Merged into #6625 c10: a published #Persist migration through the one Shape migration plan is D-LIVE-PERSIST1=A's step function; the renamed-binding reset is now in c13

criteria.text: A save swaps by default, the explicit session and project restart opt-outs work, existing field values are kept, and each save reports a typed outcome.
Live inspection shows typed pinned #Persist values and their shapes through the ratified live inspect route.
(was #2504 c5) All named live/dev/parity/inspection/diagnostic proof and O0/O2 smoke pass as tests/cases rows on O0 and O2 (#2919, which held them, is gone) (moved from #5454 c72)
criteria.evidence: Merged into #6625 c8: the ported live and dev proofs on O0 and O2 are c8's cases

criteria.text: Under `jet dev`, editing a function body in a running program applies the change and keeps every #Persist value whose type is unchanged, on O0 and O2. The Rust-era tests of #2426 and #765 are ported as cases. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter DevPartsRoutine/persist_` on O0 and O2.

D-LIVE-PERSIST1=A: when a persisted value's type changes and the type is #PublishedSchema with a migration that covers the change, the value migrates in place through the same step function decode uses, and the save line says so. Otherwise `jet dev` announces a restart. A value is never silently reinterpreted. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter DevPartsRoutine/persist_published_schema_migrates_in_place` and `--filter dev_parts_routine/persist_unpublished_change_announces_restart`.
One declared rule decides which state survives an edit. A failed edit never silently repeats external work, and the displayed active revision agrees with the machine diagnostics.

D-DX-GAMELOOP1=A: game state and controls live in the existing resident `jet dev` session. One session owns source and runtime, Canvas routes stay authoritative, and headless and rendered runs share events.

D-HOTSTATE1=A: on a hot swap, an added field takes its declared default, a removed field is dropped, renames and type changes use `migration` blocks, and a renamed binding resets. When no rule applies, `jet dev` restarts and names the field that blocked the swap. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter DevPartsRoutine/hot_state_`, with one case per rule.

D-DEV-STATE1=A: the jet process holds the #Persist store and gives each program child a private pipe through the session. On a stop request, a runtime thread in the child copies every JetPersistCell whole, so #Persist values survive a `jet dev` restart without the store ever being written to disk. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter DevPartsRoutine/persist_survives_restart_through_session_pipe` on O0.

The 4 known-failing rows this card owns (rehomed by #6843 c7) pass and leave Tests/known-failing.tsv: DevPartsRoutine/body_only_edit_is_type_stable, DevPartsRoutine/package_callable_survives_dev_and_run_watch_reload, DevPartsRoutine/persist_binding_survives_hot_swap_and_resets_on_shape_change, DevPartsRoutine/persist_example_survives_hot_reload. Proof: each named test passes in its suite on a batch compiler, and no row of Tests/known-failing.tsv names this card for them.

Live literals (owner-approved greenfield proposal item P27, 2026-11-25): in a jet dev run, an edit that changes only a number, string or colour literal patches the running program in place within one frame, with no reload and no state reset, on every tier jet dev serves.

cards.title: `jet flash`: program a hardware target
cards.body: Programming an external target through a hardware programmer. Moved out of #6418 by owner ruling 2026-11-06 and frozen with the JetOS/embedded work.

criteria.text: (was #2856 c1) Implementation-only closure: jet flash projects an explicit target programmer from canonical TargetMachine facts, binds the exact image digest and programmer invocation into one typed receipt, and reports unavailable or failed programming through the registered command diagnostic path (moved from #6418 c120)
criteria.evidence: Duplicate of #6905 c4 (jet flash programmer from TargetMachine facts, typed receipt, registered command error; proof Flash/receipt_binds_image_and_programmer).

cards.title: Runtime pack and gates build with jet, no jet-env
cards.body: With a jet on PATH, every repo tool, gate, suite and runtime-test driver runs through jet with no Nix and no jet-env. Owner 2026-11-06: like zig, `jet` itself should compile C directly (not only through a separate `jet cc`). Census: ~/jetlanes/handoff/PortsLead-6564-c6-census.md (13 gate/release sites, 6 runtime-test drivers).

criteria.text: With a jet binary on PATH, every repo tool, gate and suite runs through jet directly, with no Nix and no jet-env (owner 2026-11-04). Tools/Agent/jet-env stays only as the bootstrap for a machine with no jet yet, and its environment setup moves into jet as Jet replaces Nix (#3402, #6071). Proof: `git grep -n 'jet-env' -- Tools tests Compiler Jetpack ':!Tools/Agent/jet-env'` prints nothing.
The published native runtime pack has one canonical typed identity, and CLI build receipts record it.

One build function declares jet, the runtime pack, jetpack, the docs site and the release package as targets, so `jet build` builds them concurrently from one graph and the packages suite reuses that jetpack instead of building its own.

The self-host stages and the s2 == s3 byte-identical check are build actions in Compiler/build.jet, each run from cold, and Tools/Agent/Chain.jet is deleted with every caller migrated. Proof: `jet build Compiler` runs the stages and the s2 == s3 check, and `git ls-files Tools/Agent/Chain.jet` is empty.

A runtime source checks on its own: `jet check Compiler/JetRuntime` (and `jet check` of one runtime file such as PerfSamples.jet) checks the sources in their assembled runtime unit (the sources.list the runtime pack builds) and reports exactly that unit's diagnostics, lints included. Today a plain check gives 2710 errors (2010 UnknownName, 698 UnknownFunction, 2 ImmutableAssignment) because each file is checked without the unit, so no worker can check a runtime change or see its warnings before the batch build. Proof: `jet check Compiler/JetRuntime` exits 0 on dev with the same diagnostics as the runtime pack build, and a planted error and a planted warning in a runtime file are each reported once.

cards.title: One receipt kind: test results, goldens, budgets and API snapshots are receipts with one shape, written by shared Prelude code
cards.body:
Destination: every development act (a test run, a golden, a budget or an API snapshot) writes a receipt of one kind: act, locked closure, content-addressed inputs, witness and outcome. Shared Prelude code writes it on every tier.

Decisions: D-ECO-RECEIPT2=A (one connected receipt) and D-FOUND-RECEIPT1=A (typed sections on the one receipt). Start with a design note and an adversarial review of how the existing stores (the #6035 test store, golden files, budget history, API snapshots) map onto the one shape.

Source: #2110, #2112 and #5069, through #6035.

criteria.text: Test results, goldens, budgets and API snapshots are all stored as receipts of one kind.
One receipt record shape exists, with act, locked closure, content-addressed inputs, witness and outcome, and it is the only such shape in the tree.
A development act writes a receipt without the caller asking for one.
A receipt names its inputs by content address, so an identical act over identical inputs is recognisable as the same act.
Shared Prelude code writes the receipt on every tier (I9), with no per-engine re-encoding. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter Receipts/` on O0, O1 and O2 gives identical receipts.

cards.title: Module-graph checking and the per-wave performance gate (moved from #4717)
cards.body: Moved from #4717 on 2026-11-06 because Rust removal is finished: check Compiler/ as a module graph with module-level invalidation, and the per-cell performance gate for the cut-over waves.

criteria.text: Each wave's cutover is proven by golden examples with identical output on O0, O1, O2 and web where applicable (I9), and passes the AGENTS.md performance gate for its cells: Jet/peer below 1.00 for every matched peer, with the ceiling ratio reported only. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile golden` on O0, O1, O2 and web, and `node Tools/Gauntlet/Harness/run.mjs` for the wave cells.

Compiler/ is checked as a module graph, not as one assembled compiler.jet; the assembly entry tooling is retired once replaced, and the sema slice stays under the memory cap. Proof: `jet check Compiler/` under the capped wrapper, plus `git ls-files` showing no assembled-entry tool.

cards.title: WASI random and the Core coverage ratchet (moved from #4717)

cards.title: Reasoning about code: Jet beats every language on how well readers and tools can reason about a program
cards.body: Owner order 2026-11-06: beat all other languages on the ability to reason about code.

criteria.text: A reasoning benchmark defines task families (predict the output, find every effect of a call, show two values never alias, find every caller, find what a change breaks, find where a failure can come from) over matched programs in Jet, Rust, Go, Python, TypeScript, Zig and C++. Proof: `git ls-files "Tools/Gauntlet/reasoning/*"` names the task families and matched programs.

Each task is scored for readers (human or model: accuracy and time) and for tools (what `jet inspect` and the language server answer mechanically versus each peer toolchain). Proof: the committed scored receipt for readers and tools.
End metric: Jet scores best on every task family; every loss names its root on a card. Proof: the same receipt shows Jet best on every family, each loss naming its card.

A seeded repair exercise (a typed CLI error, an invalid external record, a guest failure) records the rejection stage, side effects, edit, check and repair steps and the five quantities against pinned peers. Proof: `node Tools/Gauntlet/Harness/run.mjs --entry repair-exercise`.

Core workflow tasks (imports, errors, lifecycle) are added to the existing runner and measure the five quantities, with no second registry or runner. Proof: `node Tools/Gauntlet/Harness/run.mjs --entry core-workflow`.

cards.title: Concision and builtins: the shortest correct code for common tasks
cards.body: Owner order 2026-11-06: lean toward less code for an equivalent task, with builtins good enough that common scripts are very short.

criteria.text: A matched task corpus of at least 50 common scripting, data, CLI and service tasks has idiomatic solutions in Jet, Python, Ruby, Lua, Go, Rust, TypeScript and Kotlin, measured in tokens and lines. Proof: `git ls-files "Tools/Gauntlet/concision/*"` names the corpus, and its committed receipt gives tokens and lines per solution.

End metric: Jet is shortest or tied on every task family without giving up safety, diagnostics or clarity; every loss names the missing builtin or convenience on a card. Proof: the same receipt shows Jet shortest or tied on every family, each loss naming its card.

For every declared source and ergonomics metric (LOC and tokens included) and every peer in every required gauntlet cell, Jet/peer < 1.00, Rust included; no median, Python-only subset, aggregate, missing or unmeasured row passes. Proof: `node Tools/Gauntlet/Harness/run.mjs` source-metric report shows no loss.

Each of the 36 selected ecosystem and capability cells has a versioned evidence disposition and a specific executable contrast, or a justified non-applicable boundary. Proof: the committed cell table, checked by `node --test Tools/Gauntlet/Harness/measurement-manifest.test.mjs`.

A scripting comparison audit under Docs/Audits compares Jet with Lua, JavaScript, TypeScript, Bash and Python on speed, source tokens and readability (the #5072 c14 checklist); every cell is measured, not estimated, and each cell Jet loses names the card that owns it. Proof: `git ls-files 'Docs/Audits/*scripting-comparison*'` names the committed audit. (was #5949 c14)

log.text: Moved G11 to G13 by Main 2026-11-12 02:25: every open criterion is about expressing and emitting the ceiling techniques, which is the ceiling stage (G13 hill climbing per the owner ruling).

HELD by owner order 2026-11-11 (no small optimizations until the language is mostly stable; architecture and regression fixes go first, per #5479 c5-c8). It stays a horizon card under the 2026-11-08 rule: it blocks no card, milestone, release or gate, and its targets are not pass/fail criteria elsewhere.

criteria.text: Every technique an asm-parity reference uses that Jet code cannot express (SIMD lanes, prefetch, alignment and layout control, branch and cold hints, non-temporal stores, syscall batching and others) is listed with the cells that use it. Proof: `git ls-files "Docs/Research/*expert-techniques*"` names the committed table.

Each missing technique gets an owner ballot with its plain and expert spellings (expert control by explicit opt-in) and a paired two-program cell; it ratifies only when it strictly beats the plain form. Proof: each row of that table names its decision ID and its paired cell.

End metric: every required cell can be written in Jet with its ceiling's technique, and codegen emits that technique. Proof: `node Tools/Perf/AsmParity/AsmParity.mjs --jet $JET --gate` with each required cell written in Jet using its ceiling technique.

Each ratified cache-control surface (D-CACHE-CONTROL1=A: `mem.prefetch`, `mem.stream_store`, the cache-line size fact) has a paired two-program cell against the plain spelling it replaces, recorded in the canonical manifest, and strictly beats it. Proof: `node Tools/Gauntlet/Harness/run.mjs --entry cache-control` shows no loss. (was #6312 c4)

Cache facts distinguish build and exec targets, private and shared caches and unknown values; the acceleration gate uses them without enlarging the scratch budget or worker count; transforms keep output, failure, effect and drop order; the decision ledger reports the facts; and a cache-locality paired entry (nested reuse against a single pass) passes the gate. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter JetirFacts/cache_facts` and `node Tools/Gauntlet/Harness/run.mjs --entry cache-locality`. (was #6312 c13)

cards.title: jetpack: Nix cache admission fails on the dogfood closure and is not checked against tampering
cards.body: Jetpack admits Nix-provided closures (c@nixpkgs deps) into its cache without a test that proves admission is content-checked and fails closed on a tampered or missing path.

criteria.text: A jetpack case realizes a c@nixpkgs dependency into the cache and corrupts the cached entry; the next build refuses it with a registered error and re-admits it only after a clean realize.

The dogfood case gets past Nix cache admission: no 'closure reference discovery: Nix cache object is absent', and the portable Nix CAS bundle has no empty archive path, dangling ld.so symlink or self-reference (found by PortsLead-2 on 2026-11-06 while proving #3590 c162-c165).

cards.title: Transpile Jet to other languages through target libraries that implement one trait (C and Rust first-party, any language by a package)
cards.body:
Owner request 2026-11-07, re-scoped the same day: Jet transpiles a program to another language, and any language can be added as an ordinary Jet library implementing a target trait. Seeding and bootstrapping the compiler are a separate, frozen question on #6683; this card comes first.

Why: interop (Jet code inside C, Rust, Lua or JavaScript projects), reach (platforms with no Jet native writer), and the language-is-a-library priority.

Design: ballot D-EXPORT-TARGET1. The recommended shape: one shared pass makes every meaning explicit, and core.compiler exposes a versioned program view. A Target trait has required operation methods, host leaves and optional idiom hooks. Capabilities are checked first, and `jet test --to <target>` checks every executable example against `jet run`.

log.text: Owner order 2026-11-16: transpiling moves from G6 to G13 for now.

Ballot D-EXPORT-TARGET1 posted and ready. The fresh adversarial review (PortsLead-2, against dev 964e737fcc) broke the first draft's recommendation. Today's IR still leaves exact-Int spill, trap and stop meaning to each writer (X64Select.jet, Web/Select.jet). The runtime's platform layer is 75 #FFI(asm) leaves plus 383 raw x86-64 syscall sites. Comptime and the only native writer are x86-64, so a C seed cannot rebuild itself elsewhere. --target already means a platform. Recommended now: staged A, with a Wasm seed from the existing web writer (C syscall host, evaluator comptime), then a shared pass that makes every check explicit plus jet build --emit c, then third-party emit libraries once the form is declared stable. If ratified, the criteria follow the ruling.

Ballot D-EXPORT-TARGET1 drafted (owner request: challenge, refine, improve). Options: A target libraries over the compiler's final lowered form, with C and WebAssembly first and a C seed every release (recommended); B readable source-level transpilers per language; C WebAssembly seed only (Zig's approach); D prebuilt binaries only. It passes Tools/agent/ballots/Validate.jet except the review pass. Tower needs the adversarial review even for a draft, so the fresh review (PortsLead-2) is in progress, and the ballot is posted once its findings are folded in.

criteria.text: An adversarial design review in Docs/audits tests every claimed strength of the ratified D-EXPORT-TARGET1 design (library-defined targets for any language, one meaning across targets, readable output through idiom hooks, interop) against Haxe with Reflaxe, Fable, Kotlin's shared IR, Nim, Gleam and LLVM targets. Every gap it finds is on a card or ballot.
criteria.evidence: 32ee48040b (batch 47): Docs/audits/2026-11-14-d-export-target1-review.md tests all four D-EXPORT-TARGET1 claims against Haxe with Reflaxe, Fable, Kotlin, Nim, Gleam and LLVM, using code facts from dev 9623399213. Each of its nine gaps is on a card: #6151, #3520 c22 and #6675 c7-c15.

criteria.text: A ratified Tower ballot fixes the command's name and flags, the target-library API (what a target receives from the checked program and how it emits text), and the first-party targets, with same-program alternatives and beginner and expert paths.
criteria.evidence: D-EXPORT-TARGET1 ratified A (2026-11-07): one public core.compiler.target Target trait over the explicit program, with required op methods, host leaves and optional idiom hooks; capability errors before output; jet build --to <target>; jet test --to conformance; C and Rust first-party.

criteria.text: A target is an ordinary Jet library any package can write, using only public compiler-library seams: a third-party test target built outside the repository exports a program as well as a first-party one.

Exporting a program to C and building it with a stock C compiler gives the same stdout, stderr and exit code as `jet run` at O0, O1 and O2 for every executable example, with memory safety, fault reports and error behavior unchanged.

One shared IR pass makes exact-Int spills, fixed-width traps and the stop protocol explicit for every writer: the IR has explicit operations for the inline-Int test and the big-integer spill (jet_int_add, jet_int_sub, jet_int_mul, jet_int_compare, jet_rt_int_clone), for fixed-width traps with their stop texts, and for the stop protocol, proved by an IR dump test. X64Select.jet and Web/Select.jet consume those operations and no longer decide them; `! git grep -n ir_x64_ Compiler/JetWeb/Source/Web/Select.jet`, and the golden and web suites pass. c3 and c4 build on it. (gap from the D-EXPORT-TARGET1 adversarial review, Docs/Audits/2026-11-14-d-export-target1-review.md) Proof: the IR dump test `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter Jetir/explicit_int_traps_stop`, `! git grep -n ir_x64_ Compiler/JetWeb/Source/Web/Select.jet`, and the golden and web suites pass.

The public program view has a version, and a target library built against another version gets a registered error naming both versions before the target runs (adversarial review, Docs/Audits/2026-11-14-d-export-target1-review.md).

An idiom hook may not hand copying, string encoding, Float text or map iteration order to the host unless conformance covers the hosted form: `jet test --to <target>` runs each target with its hooks and again with only the defaults, and both match `jet run` (adversarial review). Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile golden --to c` passes in both modes.

A target implements a closed host-leaf table that replaces the runtime's numbered system calls (168 os_syscall_* sites in 30 runtime files on dev 9623399213); the spec names the table and the code holds it. Builds on #6151 (adversarial review). Proof: `git grep -c os_syscall_ -- Compiler/JetRuntime` reports 0 outside the table's own module, and `jet test Tests/Guards --filter core_declarations` passes.

The program view exposes value ranges the compiler proved (Int ranges, loop bounds, proven-inline operands), so a hook may spell host arithmetic where no spill is possible, and conformance covers it (adversarial review).
A transpile target declares Core/Target MachineFacts, and its capability errors are the existing machine denial rows, with no second capability list (adversarial review).

Transpiled code carries Jet source locations: C output writes #line, other targets write source maps where the language has them, and a fault in transpiled code names the Jet file and line (adversarial review).
A target library runs in the build sandbox and can write only its output directory (ties to #3520's sandbox work; adversarial review).

The interop question the review found (X5) is decided: owner ballot D-EXPORT-INTEROP1, drafted at $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/G6Meta/c3/ballot-D-EXPORT-INTEROP1.json, is reviewed, posted and ratified, and its outcome is added here as criteria. Proof: `tower decision show D-EXPORT-INTEROP1` reports ratified.

cards.title: Test results are reused across runs: the full profile and the admit skip rows whose compiler and inputs are unchanged
cards.body:
Owner direction 2026-11-07: card this; no cached or incremental work now.

Measured: a fresh-clone `jet test Compiler --profile full` took about 2 hours (engine 4 min, cold toolchain fetch 45 min, suites 64 min). The release admit then reruns every suite for the same commit, about 40 more minutes. Corpus rows total 248 CPU minutes (golden 160, cases 79, ui 9).

criteria.text: Test-result reuse is opt-in and off by default: with it on, `jet test Compiler --profile full` and the release admit skip a row only when the compiler identity and every input of that row are unchanged, and each skipped row prints as reused. Not built now (owner direction 2026-11-07: no cached or incremental work now); Main schedules it.

cards.title: The compiler's default thread count is fixed at start from the instantaneous load, so a build started on a busy host runs on one core
cards.body:
Owner direction 2026-11-07: card this; do not build now.

`jet_cli_default_threads` (Compiler/JetCli/Source/Cli/Request.jet) reads procs_running from /proc/stat once at start and drops to one thread when the host is busy. The thread count then never grows. In the full profile, the hosted Jetpack engine build started beside four package runs took about 13 minutes on one core; it took 184 s when it started on a quiet host.

criteria.text: A build's parallel width follows free cores while it runs, instead of being fixed by the load at start.

The hosted Jetpack engine build started beside 8 concurrent package runs finishes within 1.5x of its quiet-host wall time, measured on the batch machine and recorded with the commit. Proof: a committed batch-machine receipt, quiet and loaded.
The quiet-host self-build wall time does not regress (compared on the same machine and commit range as #6527). Proof: the #6527 c1 self-build cell receipt for the same commit range.

cards.title: core.crypto SHA-256 runs at 45-50 MB/s; a scalar native implementation does about 500 MB/s and SHA-NI about 2 GB/s
cards.body:
Owner direction 2026-11-07: card this; do not build now.

Measured on #6592: pure-Jet core.crypto SHA-256 runs at about 45-50 MB/s at O1 and O2, and a hand-unrolled Jet version gives the same speed. The backend has no SHA-NI path. Toolchain install hashes about 450 MB, so hashing alone costs about 9 s per pass on one thread.

log.text: HELD by owner order 2026-11-11 (no small optimizations until the language is mostly stable; architecture and regression fixes go first, per #5479 c5-c8). These criteria stay open and unworked: c1 (owner order 2026-11-11 (no micro-optimization until the language is mostly stable; #5479 c); c2 (owner order 2026-11-11 (no micro-optimization until the language is mostly stable; #5479 c); c3 (owner order 2026-11-11 (no micro-optimization until the language is mostly stable; #5479 c); c4 (owner order 2026-11-11 (no micro-optimization until the language is mostly stable; #5479 c).

Measured on #6592 (PortsLead-2, 2026-11-07): pure-Jet core.crypto SHA-256 at 45-50 MB/s at O1 and O2; a hand-unrolled Jet version is no faster. Parallel hashing of the 442 MB toolchain tree still takes 16.6 s, the largest remaining fetch phase after fsync.

criteria.text: An asm-parity cell under Tools/Perf/AsmParity is the SHA-256 ceiling reference: SHA-NI where the CPU reports it, and the best scalar code otherwise. Proof: `git ls-files Tools/Perf/AsmParity/sha256` names the cell and its ref.S.

core.crypto SHA-256 at O1 and O2 meets that ceiling (Jet/ceiling at most 1.00 in cycles and bytes) on both paths, and beats every gauntlet peer. Proof: `node Tools/Perf/AsmParity/AsmParity.mjs --jet $JET --gate --cells sha256` and `node Tools/Gauntlet/Harness/run.mjs --entry sha256`.
The digest is identical on every tier (O0, O1, O2 and web), held by the existing SHA-256 conformance vectors. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile golden --filter Crypto/SHA256` on O0, O1, O2 and web.

Core crypto expert hashes (#3548): SHA-512, BLAKE2b and Argon2id in Core/crypto/expert.jet run on U64 words with no bigint spill and no per-block list allocation, with hash goldens unchanged and a perf receipt for password_hash. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile golden --filter Crypto/` and the committed password_hash receipt.

cards.title: Portable seed: build a working Jet on a machine that has only a C compiler or a WebAssembly runtime
cards.body:
Owner direction 2026-11-07: seeding and bootstrapping the compiler is a separate question from transpilation (#6675, D-EXPORT-TARGET1) and is frozen for the future. Transpilation comes first.

Goal: a machine with no Jet binary builds a current Jet from what it already has, so a seed never goes stale and a new platform is never stuck.

Candidate plan from the earlier D-EXPORT-TARGET1 draft, which is not ratified: compile the compiler with the existing WebAssembly writer, then turn that .wasm into C with a committed WebAssembly-to-C translator. A small C host answers the runtime's system calls on POSIX, and compile-time code runs on the IR evaluator instead of an x86-64 child. Every release checks that the seed rebuilds the release's own stage-2 bytes. Once the #6675 C target exists, exporting the compiler to C is the alternative route. Trust limit: a seed built from generated output still trusts the compiler that wrote it; only an independent Jet implementation removes that.

criteria.text: An adversarial design review in Docs/Audits tests the seed's claims (durability, onboarding, trust) against existing bootstrap chains: Zig's WebAssembly seed, Nim's generated C, mrustc, and bootstrappable builds. Every gap it finds is on a card or ballot.
A ratified Tower ballot picks the seed route (WebAssembly translated to C, the #6675 C target, or prebuilt binaries only), with same-program alternatives and the trust limits stated.

Exporting the compiler's own source to C (and to Wasm) gives a compiler that, built with only a C compiler (or a Wasm runtime), compiles the same tree to a byte-identical stage-2 compiler: a portable seed for every release, linked with #6186.
Install docs describe building Jet from the exported seed with a stock C compiler, and a fresh machine with no Jet binary follows them to a working jet.

cards.title: The hosted Jetpack engine takes about 3 minutes to build on a quiet host while the whole compiler self-compiles in about 10 s
cards.body:
Owner direction 2026-11-07: Pareto speed work for the fresh-clone full profile.

The packages suite builds the hosted Jetpack engine (Jetpack/Bootstrap/Assemble.jet hosted, then `jet build src/jetpack.jet`, in Compiler/test.jet jetpack_prepare). It took 184 s when it started on a quiet host and about 13 minutes on one core under load. The compiler, a larger codebase, self-compiles in about 10 s (#6527). The ratio points at something specific to the Jetpack build path (the assembled single unit, its optimization level, a pathological function, or a phase that grows superlinearly), not at code size.

log.text: Main 2026-11-07: SpeedLead landed 3412bcf62f (jet build cache entries, locks, leases and touches publish unsynced; reads verify digests, so a lost entry is a miss; the rlib cache, runtime pack, objects and LTO keep their syncs). The store publish tail went from 127.3 s/17.0 s to 8.4 s/5.0 s (fresh store, interleaved), with zero fsync calls during the build (strace). It also landed ef8a3f930d (L0534 copied the 12.5 MB engine module once per block: sema.finalize 149 s -> 5.8 s; sema.bodies 97 s -> 2.7 s; tests/ui_lint/map_group_round_trip.jet still prints L0534 at 10:9). Whole hosted engine build: 168 s -> 33.0 s at load 14 (28.6 s on a rerun); a cache hit takes 16.9 s. Proof by Main is pending (batch).

criteria.text: A per-phase profile of the hosted engine build (front end, sema, lowering, optimization, emission, link) names where the time goes, and it is recorded on this card with the commit.
criteria.evidence: Per-phase traces (jet build --trace; wall s / CPU s; 12 CPUs pinned on the busy 32-CPU host) of jet build src/jetpack.jet in the assembled hosted project (618 sources; one 12.5 MB module). dev eaa085b237: total 156.8-243.9 s wall, of which sema.finalize 98-149 s (sema.bodies 48-97 s wall / 547-928 CPU-s) and the store tail 17-127 s (fsync D-state); the front end 5-7 s, lowering 0.7-1.2 s, ir.opt 2.2-3.5 s, emission 0.7-0.9 s, link 0.15 s. Root cause 1: store fsyncs, fixed by 3412bcf62f (no fsync calls in strace). Root cause 2: the L0534 lint (10ce9aab90) copied the whole module bytes per block, fixed by ef8a3f930d. With both fixes: total 32.95 s wall / 49.7 CPU-s; sema.finalize 5.81 s; store tail 11.8 s under writeback throttling; cache hit 16.9 s. The table and the exact commands are in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/SpeedLead/6684-phases.md.

criteria.text: The root cause is fixed in the compiler or in Jetpack's assembly, and the hosted engine build on a quiet batch host takes at most 30 s, measured and recorded with the commit. Proof: a committed quiet-batch-host receipt of the hosted engine build.
The built engine is byte-for-byte the same program as before the fix, or every packages-suite engine claim still passes. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile packages` passes every engine claim.

cards.title: The Jetpack engine unit's claims all run serially because they share process state
cards.body:
Owner direction 2026-11-07: card the remaining slow phases.

Compiler/test.jet jetpack_engine_rows runs `jet test src/jetpack.jet --serial` over the assembled engine unit (about 559 claims), because the claims share process state. Every claim waits for the one before it.

log.text: Main 2026-11-07, from SpeedLead measurements (hosted engine unit, after #6684 fixes; host busy, load 12-40): `jet test src/jetpack.jet --serial` took 243 s (compile 55 s, claims about 188 s); without --serial 195 s, with the same 807/22/15 and the same 22 known failures. One clean parallel run is evidence that the claims share no state, not proof; dropping the flag means editing jetpack_engine_rows. cards.title: No C: full libc coverage in Jet (census libc against Core and the runtime, then fill every gap)
cards.body: Owner, 2026-11-08: "We should already have a lot of what libc covers just need to fill the gaps." Track full coverage of what a C libc provides (POSIX and C23: memory, strings, stdio and files, time and locale, process, signals, threads and sync, networking and name resolution, math, environment, users and groups, terminal, dynamic memory), as Jet-native Core or runtime surface. Step one is a census: every libc function family, with the Core or runtime API that already covers it, and the gaps. Then each gap is filled through normal Core review (new public API needs a ballot). Math is #6688; threads, syscalls and DNS are #6689 to #6691.

log.text: Burn-down ranking (2026-11-24, by remaining workload; G2Regressions read the open criteria against dev 8a8ea0ee0b): weeks. Every libc census gap filled.

c2 not met (checked 2026-11-21 on dev 24356fa7b8): the libc census names one GAP, msync/mprotect (writable file mappings), and its row cites "ballot D-MAP-WRITE1", which does not exist on the board (`decision show D-MAP-WRITE1` finds nothing). So the gap has neither a ballot nor a ruling. Either a ballot for writable mappings is drafted and filed under that ID, or the census row names the real owning criterion. Deciding that Jet needs no writable mappings, only to close this card, is not an option.

c2 status (p390 tree, `jet Tools/Agent/LibcCensus.jet`, exit 0): one family stays marked GAP, `msync mprotect` (sys/mman.h), citing D-MAP-WRITE1. That ballot is drafted but not posted: its adversarial review (Docs/Audits/2026-11-08-D-MAP-WRITE1-review.md) bars posting it as ready or marking the census rows complete until its blocking gaps G2-G5 are closed (fault recovery, shared atomic layout, durability, one tier meaning). The census accepts a not-needed row only with an owner ruling, and the review names mprotect a separate disposition (HostSpawn.jet already uses it for a guard page). c2 stays open: msync needs the writable-mapping design finished and re-reviewed, and mprotect needs its own census row. All other families are covered, partial, language or owner-ruled not needed.

Owner-wait sweep 2026-11-15 (TowerKeeper-2, for Main): c2 reworded; the text waited on an owner answer that ratified decisions already give, or on a choice within ratified scope; it is recorded as decided (Main's operational authority) and nothing waits.

msync and mprotect rows stay Gap until the D-MAP-WRITE1 ruling (unposted; Docs/audits/2026-11-08-D-MAP-WRITE1-review.md blocks it). Atomic exchange/fetch_sub/and/or/xor and pthread_barrier rows need new public API under D-ATOMIC-WIDTH1: owner ballot. The rwlock try/timed row moves to Covered in GoalsA-1-6696c2-shared-try-guard-r2, queued after gap-rows r2a/r2b.

Batch b6d landed on dev (0073f4fc47): the G1 math rows; CFreeLead-5r2 2f31d91386 (ctype/wctype, memset_explicit, swab, a64l/l64a; group-A NotNeeded), 6r2 9a85b9d141 (Core type-method census checks; openat/renameat/statvfs Covered; ungetc/readv/writev/pathconf Language), 4r3 cd158d6233 (runtime signal hub), 6a3 b901f3c1fd, 7a3 b286f2b414, 8a3 6ad5cee938, 9a2 4b15c1e373, 10a a33b887631 (runtime leaves; their Core surfaces follow in the b parts, in b7). c1 and c2 are still in progress.

D-MAP-WRITE1 adversarial review done (Docs/audits/2026-11-08-D-MAP-WRITE1-review.md, dev 3eed4ae28a): A holds only as a direction; its SIGBUS recovery (Fault.jet is fatal-only, one-shot), shared atomics, durability and tier meaning are unproved, so the ballot is not posted. CFreeLead redesigns to close G2-G8 for a second review. Option E (non-shrinkable backing) was added. The read-only-map defect (G1) is on its own card.

Owner 2026-11-08 ruled A on CFreeLead's c2 gap list: accept all as not needed. (1) locale: *_l variants (124,127,135), setlocale/newlocale/nl_langinfo (346-348), strfmon (167), multibyte locale encodings and legacy iconv charsets (145-148,157); Jet text is UTF-8 and locale-independent. (2) message catalogs gettext/catopen (349-350): a library concern. (3) obsolete or insecure: crypt/encrypt/setkey DES (319-320), ctermid (183), utmpx (318), gethostent/getnetent/getprotoent iteration (330), System V IPC msg/sem/shm/ftok (336-339), aio (223), posix_devctl (224), typed memory objects (230), setbuf/setvbuf (178).
Split 2026-11-08 by Main: CFreeLead owns the non-math gaps; G1Lead keeps the math rows (with #6688 c3) and LibcCensus.jet.

Owner ruling 2026-11-08 (chat, Q18): reach parity coverage. Quote: i dont need to see every api design, just use best practices, idiomatic jet with excellent api, making use of jet s api features appropriately. So the libc gap fill needs no per-API ballot: each gap gets idiomatic Jet surface designed by the lead, using Jet features (effects, Result errors, typed handles, Close) rather than C shapes. New syntax, invariant exceptions and dependencies still go to the owner.
8b040ecdba (G1Lead): the census prints on demand; Docs/audits/libc-census.md is removed, matching the reworded c1. Queued for Main batch verification.

G1Lead landed 6dedd63f5a (Tools/agent/LibcCensus.jet plus Docs/audits/libc-census.md): 261 families, 1,482 functions, every POSIX.1-2024 function once plus the C23 additions; 119 covered, 40 partial, 23 language, 79 GAP. GAP areas: math (rint family, issignaling, Bessel, C23 pi-trig, exp10 and log2p1 family, pown and rootn family, fromfp, fmaximum family, narrowing ops, canonicalize, totalorder, payload); all of fenv; complex elementary functions plus carg and cproj; isblank, isgraph, ispunct, isxdigit, the isw forms, wctype, wctrans and the _l variants; memset_explicit, swab; a64l, l64a; fdopen, fileno, ungetc, setbuf, setvbuf, ctermid; posix_fadvise, fallocate, readv, writev, mknod, statvfs, pathconf; dup family, isatty, ttyname, aio, posix_devctl; mlock and typed memory; posix_spawnattr and sched policy; signal sets and masks, sigwait, sigqueue, sigaltstack, pthread_kill; pthread attributes, mutex and cond attributes, rwlock, spin, once, TLS keys, atfork, semaphores; atomic fences; clock_settime and CPU-time clocks; set-uid and set-gid family, the group database, utmpx, crypt; sendmsg, recvmsg, socketpair, sockatmark, netdb iteration, if_nameindex; mq, shm_open, SysV IPC; tcgetpgrp, tcsetpgrp, pty functions; setlocale, locale_t, nl_langinfo, gettext, catgets, fmtmsg. Which gaps get Jet surface is an owner question (Q18); each new public API needs a ballot.
Assigned to G1Lead 2026-11-08, after #6688 c1 and c2 land: a committed census script listing every C23 and POSIX.1-2024 function family against Jet Core or runtime coverage.

cards.title: No C: a Jet Linux sandbox replaces the bwrap binary shipped in the C toolchain pack
cards.body: Owner order 2026-11-08 (Q8): "B4 BUT that is a longer term card I dont want done now. for the time being, ship bwrap until the sandbox is built PROPERLY in jet, make sure this task is not lost so we dont forget to remove bwrap in the future." Context: #6686 found no bwrap on a NixOS host, so jet cc refused with E1275. The stopgap ships bwrap (a C binary) in the C toolchain pack. This card builds the sandbox in Jet (namespaces plus landlock or seccomp, ratified D-PORTABLE1=A: Jet own sandbox) and removes bwrap. Longer term: not to start before the owner says so. Related: #6687 (Jet depends on no other language), #4268 (authority and sandbox boundaries).

log.text: Owner-wait sweep 2026-11-15 (TowerKeeper-2, for Main): c4 reworded; the owner-only choices are on Main's ballot list (2026-11-15) ($JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/TowerKeeper-2/ballots-needed.tsv); no question for the owner stays on this card.

criteria.text: Process isolation for `jet cc` and every other sandboxed launch is done by Jet code (user, mount, pid and network namespaces, landlock rules or a seccomp filter) with the same confinement bwrap gave. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter Authority/jet_sandbox_refuses_`, one case per refused access.

The bwrap binary is gone from the C toolchain pack and every launch path, with no fallback, and the pack is re-pinned without it. Proof: `jet test Tests/Guards --filter no_bwrap` (git grep finds no bwrap in Compiler, Jetpack, Tools or the pack manifest).
On a host without unprivileged user namespaces, a sandboxed launch refuses with a registered error naming the missing kernel feature.

There is one canonical Core sandbox API: Foundation NativeSandbox.jet (tooling: arbitrary source, output and read-only mounts) and Core ProcessSpec.under (cwd-derived repository grants) become one implementation with one policy and no observable differences. The API shape is the ballot D-SANDBOX-API1, on Main's ballot list (2026-11-15). Proof: git grep finds one sandbox policy implementation, and `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter Authority/sandbox_policy_single_home` passes.
A process spec's `.under(grant)` narrows authority through the shared runtime (`jet_std_process_spec_under` is registered).

Declared filesystem, process, network, environment, device and resource policy is enforced and recorded by the platform backend: a child runs under the native sandbox (Jetpack/Foundation/Source/NativeSandbox.jet, SandboxPolicy.jet) with a declared policy, each denied access fails, and the recorded policy matches. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter Authority/native_sandbox_policy_enforced` on Linux.

A launch's plan, transaction, descendants, limits, outputs and receipt share one policy digest and record the authority actually enforced. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter AgentExecutor/policy_digest_shared` on Linux.

Unsupported enforcement, denied access, an escape attempt, limit exhaustion, cancellation and child-process abuse each fail closed, with no leaked handle, secret or process. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter AgentExecutor/fails_closed_`, one case per failure on Linux.

The known-failing row this card owns (rehomed by #6843 c7) passes and leaves Tests/known-failing.tsv: BuildEntryEpoch4/workspace_build_observes_dependency_order_and_execution_chain. Proof: each named test passes in its suite on a batch compiler, and no row of Tests/known-failing.tsv names this card for them.

cards.title: Core math completeness: correctly rounded results (CORE-MATH grade) and all of C23 math.h
cards.body: Owner 2026-11-08: "it needs to be portable and accurate. we want people to use jet for EVERYTHING including mathematics, simulations". G1Lead audit (musl 1.2.5 worst cases reproduced against MPFR 4.2.2): under 1 ulp: exp .51, exp2 .51, pow .52, log .52, log2 .55, cbrt .67, log10 .81, sin/cos .83, atan .86, log1p .90, expm1 .91, acos .93, asin .98; over 1 ulp: tan 1.01, erf 1.02, cosh 1.03, hypot 1.03, atan2 1.55, atanh 1.80, sinh 1.87, asinh 1.91, tanh 2.22, acosh 2.24, erfc 3.72, exp10 4.14, tgamma 15.9, lgamma 4.4e15 near its zeros, Bessel j0/j1/y0/y1 1e14-1e15 near zeros. Plan: port CORE-MATH (MIT) binary64 and binary32 per function family into Jet, worst gaps first (lgamma, tgamma, erfc, tanh, acosh, exp10, atan2, then the rest), each replacing its musl port in one cutover; Bessel needs its own accurate design (no correctly rounded binary64 implementation exists). Estimate about 150 agent-hours serial.
cards.checkSteps: per function: a committed MPFR-generated corpus (CORE-MATH .wc hard cases plus random inputs) shows 0 mismatches against correctly rounded bits on O0, O1, O2 and web; jet test never calls MPFR; the census marks each function CR

log.text: Burn-down ranking (2026-11-24, by remaining workload; G2Regressions read the open criteria against dev 8a8ea0ee0b): weeks. Correctly rounded f32 and f64 against MPFR, and every C23 math.h function.
Cleaned 2026-11-15: c5 split into the binary64 MPFR corpus, the C23 name census and the musl divergence list.

c5 progress: dev ea1caf0d11 (G3Core-6700-c5-musllist). Every corpus row where musl 1.2.5 differs lists musl's result word: 36,676 binary64 rows and 13,854 binary32 rows. Both core_math_correctly_rounded cases PASS 1 on seed-b14.

c1 status (G1Lead-3, 2026-11-12): F32 exhaustive scan done for 26 of 36 fns, 0 misrounded (rsqrt(-0) convention aside); sinpi 189/256 chunks clean then OOM-killed at 4G and 10G with 16 parallel pipes; not run: rest of sinpi, cospi tanpi asinpi acospi atanpi exp2m1 exp10m1 log2p1 log10p1. Harness and commands: $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/G1Lead-3/HANDOFF-6700.md. Next: find the sinpi memory hold on one chunk, then rerun with -P 4 in the heavy-job slot.
G1Lead-22b2 landed on dev cb6e8c33f6: math.fma is IEEE fused on every tier, hardware FMA3 behind a CPUID probe (c3 progress).

Criteria added from the card body and the slices so far. Landed in b6d: correctly rounded sinpi/cospi/tanpi (d8db0efaec), rsqrt/exp10 and the MPFR-CR harness (f0c28ff1e6). Slices 9-15 are in batch b7. G1Lead-2 owns this card.

criteria.text: binary32: every Core F32 elementary function (exp/log/pow/trig/hyperbolic/inverse, erf/erfc, tgamma/lgamma, cbrt, hypot, the pi variants) is correctly rounded to nearest, proven by an exhaustive scan of all 2^32 inputs against MPFR (f32scan receipts). Proof: the committed f32scan receipts with zero misrounded inputs per function.
binary64: the same functions in F64 are correctly rounded, proven against MPFR on the CORE-MATH worst-case corpus plus at least 10^8 random inputs per function, with 0 misrounded results.
criteria.evidence: dev bcc9c4b023 (CORE-MATH ports, train 1; Core/Math fn bodies identical on 6cea1699f9 except Int abs and Decimal decode, neither scanned): MPFR 4.2.2 scan, $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/G1Lead-3/f32mpfr ./run64.sh over 40 F64 fns (exp..atan2pi), CORE-MATH src/binary64/<fn>.wc corpus + 10^8 seeded random inputs each -> 0 misrounded finite results. Only diffs are conventions, not roundings: rsqrt(-0) = -inf (IEEE 754-2019, CORE-MATH agree; MPFR +inf) and sNaN operands to pow/hypot give qNaN (IEEE; MPFR has no sNaN). Receipt results64/SUMMARY; handoff HANDOFF-6700.md.

cards.title: Native windows in pure Jet: a Wayland client that opens a window and presents frames, no external libraries
cards.body: Owner 2026-11-08: "i want jet to be able to draw to screen immediately with native windows using a full jet native framework/system asap no external dependencies. start with wayland support." Today the static native runtime never opens a window (RouteAGame.jet: the old bridge dlopened libraylib) and core.ui native is headless. Plan: a Wayland client written in Jet (wire protocol over the AF_UNIX socket at $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/$WAYLAND_DISPLAY, wl_registry, wl_compositor, wl_shm with a memfd buffer passed by SCM_RIGHTS, xdg_wm_base/xdg_surface/xdg_toplevel, frame callbacks, wl_seat pointer and keyboard, the compositor keymap parsed in Jet), presenting the existing Jet software rasterizer canvas; then core.game.raylib windows and the core.ui host on top. X11 follows as a separate card.
cards.checkSteps: jet run of an example opens a native Wayland window on a stock compositor (GNOME/KDE/sway), draws animated content from the Jet rasterizer, takes keyboard and pointer input, resizes and closes cleanly; the executable links no external library (symbol census); a headless-compositor case proves it on O0, O1 and O2

log.text: Cleaned 2026-11-15: c3 split into one-implementation, full Wayland and X11 criteria; proofs added.

t15a landed G6LeadC-13 (01b86931e7..8327f5ae47): the Wayland wire part's `net: core.net` broke every web build that imports core.ui (E3304). Fixed at the root: the target socket check judges only the program's own `use`, and ui.open reaches the wire part only under a comptime Linux branch. Proof: cases web_build 31/0, including web_ui_open_answers_no_display.

criteria.text: Ownership makes misuse unwritable: Fd and SharedMemory close on drop (no double close, no use after close, no fd-reuse race across threads), and offsets and lengths are range-typed (Int(lo..hi)) so sema proves bounds before a leaf runs. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile ui --filter fd_use_after_close` and `jet test Compiler --profile ui --filter shared_memory_offset_out_of_range`.

Linux hazards removed by design, each with a case: shared memory is sealed (F_SEAL_SHRINK|F_SEAL_GROW) so a peer cannot SIGBUS us; received fds (keymap) are read with pread, never mapped; MSG_CTRUNC closes every received fd and reports a typed error; every leaf retries EINTR and handles partial sends; every fd is O_CLOEXEC.

cards.title: Prove the runtime OS edge safe: leaf contracts, model checking, fault injection, checked mode
cards.body: Owner direction: find a way to prove the safety of the unsafe runtime layer, holistically. #6701 c4-c6 shrink the trusted base, make misuse unwritable through ownership and range types, and remove Linux hazards by design. This card proves what remains: every runtime syscall leaf against a written contract. Kernel-enforced confinement (a default seccomp allowlist) is a separate owner ballot. A public claim that the edge is proven needs a passing adversarial review per AGENTS.md. Limit: this proves Jet against the kernel documented behaviour, not kernel bugs.
cards.checkSteps: each item has a case or gate that fails when broken

log.text: Cleaned 2026-11-15 by TowerKeeper-1: c1, c3 and c5 split into one outcome each (LEAFPROVE, FAULTINJ, WIREFUZZ, EDGEREVIEW); each criterion names its proof.

criteria.text: Every runtime syscall leaf carries a machine-checkable contract: precondition, postcondition, and frame (which bytes and fds it may touch, with no arithmetic overflow).
The syscall number and argument registers emitted for every runtime leaf at O0, O1 and O2 match a committed table derived from the kernel's syscall_64.tbl, and a mismatch fails.

A pure-Jet model of the fd table and mappings runs at least one million random operation sequences against the real kernel with no divergence. Proof: `jet test Compiler/JetRuntime --filter fd_model_differential` with a committed receipt of the run.

`--checked-alloc` keeps a shadow ledger of open fds and mappings and checks every leaf call against it (owned and open, in range, not after close), and the cases and golden suites pass in this mode. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter CheckedAlloc/fd_ledger_` and a committed receipt of the cases and golden suites under --checked-alloc.

Drift gates: the unsafe-site ratchet can only fall, every leaf has a contract and a proof record, and `jet audit foreign` stays clean. Proof: `jet test Tests/Guards --filter unsafe_site_ratchet` and `jet audit foreign` exits 0.
A symbolic checker written in Jet, with no external solver, proves each runtime syscall leaf's JetIR against its contract, and a leaf without a passing proof record fails the build.
A fault-injection test mode makes every runtime syscall leaf return each documented errno (EINTR, EAGAIN, ENOMEM, EMSGSIZE, truncated control data), and every error path runs.
The Wayland wire and XKB parsers are fuzzed over a fixed seed budget with no hang or panic.

A dated adversarial review in Docs/Audits tries to break the claim that the runtime OS edge is proven, and passes before any public text makes that claim (AGENTS.md). Proof: `git ls-files Docs/Audits` lists the review, and git grep finds no public claim older than it.

A refused carrier thread leaves the pool at the carriers it has, every time: Tests/Cases/FiberLiveness/a_refused_carrier_thread_leaves_the_pool_at_the_carriers_it_has.case errors intermittently (child terminated by signal) in p371, p377, p388 and p389, a race in the refusal path. Proof: the case passes 20 runs in a row under suite load, and the race is named and fixed.

cards.title: Wayland window and ui stack: measured best against every alternative
cards.body: Owner order (2026-11-08): the native Wayland window is good enough for now (the compositor-paced frame loop ran "buttery smooth" at 240 Hz). Land the deterministic functionality first, then hill-climb this card until it is near perfect. The window and ui stack must beat every strong alternative on the same compositor and display, idle and under a full-machine load. The alternatives are GTK4 (frame clock), Qt 6 (QQuickWindow), SDL3, winit with softbuffer, a Chromium/Electron requestAnimationFrame page, and a hand-written C wl_surface.frame + wp_presentation loop as the machine ceiling. The xkb keymap is measured against libxkbcommon. Peer programs stay outside the tree. Each loss is fixed at its root in the runtime leaves or the loop, never by dropping a feature (AGENTS.md performance gate).
cards.plan: Start after the Wayland functionality (frame loop, CSD, HiDPI and fractional scale, cursors, clipboard, multi-window, keyboard) and X11 have landed. Build the same bouncing-square program and a resize/HiDPI/text scene in each alternative, measure every metric in the criteria, rank the losses in Pareto order and fix them.

cards.title: Safe read-only file maps expose bytes another process can change, and fault with SIGBUS when the file shrinks
cards.body: Found by the D-MAP-WRITE1 adversarial review (Docs/audits/2026-11-08-D-MAP-WRITE1-review.md). files.map gives safe code a borrowed byte view of a MAP_PRIVATE read-only mapping. Private mapping is not a snapshot: an external write changed an already borrowed byte from 3 to 9 (probe Current.jet). An external truncate makes the next access of a borrowed byte die with Fault [SIGBUS] and exit 135 (probes Shrink.jet and CFreeLead's MapShrink.jet); the shared flock is advisory and does not prevent it. Safe Jet must not observe a borrowed value changing under it, and an I/O failure in safe code must surface as a typed error or a registered, explained fault, never a raw signal death. This holds whatever D-MAP-WRITE1 decides.
cards.plan: Decide the I1 contract for read-only maps: copy-on-read, or a view the runtime keeps stable (e.g. MAP_PRIVATE plus a seal or lease where the kernel offers one), or an Unsafe-only borrowed view with a safe copying API. Then make the truncation case a typed IOError or a registered fault with what/why/fix text and a UI snapshot, with one meaning on every tier. A choice that changes public API or behavior goes to an owner ballot first.

criteria.text: D-MMAP-STABLE1=A is built (ratified 2026-11-13). files.map gives zero-copy views that another process cannot change: it maps a private file-system clone where the file system can (btrfs, xfs, APFS, ReFS); otherwise it holds the file with a lease on Linux or deny-write sharing on Windows and copies only when a writer arrives; otherwise it copies into an unnamed temp file. Only file systems that cannot be written at all (squashfs, erofs) map directly. mapped.kind() reports Clone, Held or Copy, and an #Unsafe raw map remains for shared live bytes. cards.title: Release cut in 10 minutes or less: faster golden and cases suites
cards.body: Owner order (2026-11-09): the whole seed-cut process (preflight, self-host chain, packs, the golden/ui/cases gates, tag and publish) takes at most 10 minutes of wall-clock time. Today a fresh cut takes about 37 minutes: chain ~3, packs ~2, golden ~10.6, ui ~2, cases ~20 (the suites run one after another with 4 shards x --jobs; the baseline side and the retries add more). Speed it up without weakening the gate. Every row still runs or is soundly reused by content identity; no dropped rows, no easier tier, I9 parity is kept, and timeouts are not hidden as flakes.
cards.plan: 1. Profile one fresh admit: wall time per phase, and per-row cost split by compile, link, run and harness overhead; find the slowest rows and the idle cores. 2. Find the levers: concurrency (shards and jobs sized to cores and memory, the three suites run concurrently), baseline rows reused from the previous seed's recorded evidence instead of rerunning the release side, fine-grained input-hash reuse of candidate rows, compiler start-up and per-row compile cost (cached Core and Prelude artifacts, one compile shared by the O0/O1/O2 rows where the meaning allows), fewer process spawns, and timeout and retry policy. 3. Implement in Tools/release and the testkit, and measure the result on a real admit.

criteria.text: A fresh release admit of a dev commit with no reuse of candidate rows from an earlier admit, on this workstation, runs from the preflight to publish in at most 10 minutes of wall-clock time, with its timestamped log as evidence. Proof: the committed timestamped admit log.

The gate keeps its strength. Nothing is cached or reused between runs and nothing is built incrementally (owner 2026-11-09): every run starts from source. Within ONE run, each test worker may parse and check Core once and share that checked Core in memory across the rows it runs (owner 2026-11-09, the vitest model); each row still compiles and runs its own fresh native program on the candidate. A proof run shows the shared-Core verdicts are byte-identical to per-row cold compiles on every row. OWNER 2026-11-09 (later): the release (previous seed) column runs only on the rows that fail on the candidate, the release's known-failing rows, and rows whose files changed since the baseline commit, with gains and losses judged exactly as before; every candidate row still runs. There are no new skips and no dropped tiers, and the compiler front end itself also gets at least 2x faster cold (owner: both). Proof: the committed diff of shared-Core verdicts against per-row cold compiles is empty, and the admit log shows every candidate row run.

The flaky-timeout rate under the new concurrency is no higher than today's: retried TIMEOUT rows are counted and reported. Proof: the retried TIMEOUT count in the admit log against the prior baseline.

The a0.0.45 known-failing lines for #6717 come off as their fixes land: the plugin route row (Main-a0045-plugin-route), the f32 sema-totality ICE, the JetWeb O1/O2 ICE, the int_converts fraction_stop exit, and the rdtsc and state_arrow streams. No case fails because its neighbours took the memory: the suite's concurrency is bounded by a memory budget per case, or a case that hits its cgroup cap is reported as a resource failure with the cap named, never as the program's own failure.
