cards.title: Run modes: jet run --preview prints a program's plan, --apply PLAN performs exactly it, --undo RUN reverses it
cards.body: Owner approved greenfield proposal item P6 ('Run modes: preview, apply, undo') on 2026-11-25 in chat. Because every effect goes through a provider, the runner can give any program a different world. --preview installs providers that record destructive effects instead of doing them and prints the plan; --apply PLAN performs exactly that plan and refuses if the world changed; --undo RUN reverses what an undo-capable provider recorded. Builds on D-CORE-PROVIDER1 providers; uses the safety classes of proposal item P7 once that item is settled (until then every write effect counts as destructive). Source: Docs/Proposals/2026-11-24-greenfield-language.md, Part 2, item P6; evidence and first review: Docs/Audits/2026-11-24-greenfield-language-review.md (both in the master checkout, not yet on dev).

`jet run --preview FILE` runs the program with recording providers for every write effect and prints a plan that names each effect, its target and its call path, without changing the world.
`jet run --apply PLAN` performs exactly the recorded plan and refuses, naming the difference, when a target changed since the preview.
`jet run --undo RUN` reverses every effect an undo-capable provider recorded, and names the effects it cannot reverse.
Agent and tool runners can request preview mode, and the plan format is a documented, typed Core value.
An executable example with golden output proves the feature on every applicable tier, and the spec, reference pages and editor grammars describe it.

cards.title: Markers apply at every site they declare (value, expression, statement, block, function, …); wrapping policies work on blocks, and Err answers transient()
cards.body: Owner approved greenfield proposal item P13 ('Policies on blocks, and transient failures') on 2026-11-25 in chat. Owner condition: markers were designed to declare every place they can work (a value, a statement or expression, a block, a function and so on), so a wrapping policy on a block should already work. This card makes sure the original idea holds: a marker's declared sites (impl Marker { sites: […], scopes: […] }; the site list at Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/ScopeMembers.jet:83 names Package, File, Module, Function, Method, Block, Statement, Expression, Type, Impl, Trait, Declaration, Constant, Field, Variant, Parameter, Test, Operation, Text, Arm and TypeUse) alone decide where it attaches and how far it reaches, with no per-marker parser or sema special case. #Policy today declares sites Package, Module, Function, Method and Block (Compiler/Prelude/Markers.jet:30-38). Wrapping uses the wrap role of proposal item P2. Source: Docs/Proposals/2026-11-24-greenfield-language.md, Part 2, item P13; evidence and first review: Docs/Audits/2026-11-24-greenfield-language-review.md (both in the master checkout, not yet on dev).

criteria.text: Design review: a dated audit in Docs/Audits attacks the whole mechanism of proposal item P13: it names every place the same fact or operation lives today, the exact cutover list and the copies it deletes, and passes; every gap it finds becomes a row here or a ballot.

Every site kind in the marker site list is parsed, checked and applied from the marker's declaration alone: a marker can be written on each site it declares (a value, an expression, a statement, a block, a function and the rest) and is refused, with a registered diagnostic, on any site it does not; an audit of every Prelude and Core marker finds no per-marker special case left.

A marker's declared `scopes` and inheritance decide how far its effect reaches and how an inner marker adjusts an outer one, with one rule for every marker; an example shows a policy set on a function and adjusted on one block and one statement inside it.

`#Layout(double)` on a store keeps a read copy and a write copy; reads in a step see the previous step's state, writes go to the next, and the step boundary swaps them with no copy.

cards.title: Handles that read like links: relationships held as pool IDs with short, checked navigation instead of stored @T links
cards.body: Owner asked on 2026-11-25 for greenfield proposal item P9 as a ballot of the best-of-both design, with every downside engineered away: keep handles (Pool<T> with generational ID<T>) and views as the one way to hold a relationship, and make navigating them as short as a link. It reopens D-MEMREF1 (live links @T, already built on dev: Spellings.jet:31, Sema/Links.jet, JetIR BuildLinks.jet, runtime Links.jet, Examples/Memory/LiveLinks.jet, and used by the compiler's SemaBodyCheck; open cards #4500, #4756). Owner bar: Jet must be able to do everything any other language can as an end result, easy to reason about and use, with friction in proportion to how often a thing is done. Source: Docs/Proposals/2026-11-24-greenfield-language.md, Part 2, item P9 (master checkout, not yet on dev). Owner direction (2026-11-25, second round): free `@` as a symbol for possible later use, and deliver the best of both worlds with the downsides engineered away; rewriting the compiler's own link code is acceptable (greenfield). Two downsides must be removed, not just mitigated: (1) sharing an object must not require the programmer to make a pool first (today's `alias: hero` case), and (2) a handle to a removed item must not be only a run-time stop. The paused fresh review's findings (in the drafting notes) are also to be engineered away: a handle layout fixed per type rather than by whole-program counting, assignment through `?.` treated as a new feature for every optional place, built-versus-design stated plainly, the superseded rules D-MEMREF1 replaced listed, and the blast radius of a second store of one type. Ballot D-HANDLE-NAV1 posted 2026-11-25 (reviewed by ReviewHandleNav2); its review is Docs/Audits/2026-11-25-handle-navigation-review.md (in the master checkout, to land on dev). If option A is ratified, its sharing story depends on D-SHARED-CYCLE2 (#6066) and D-GC-OPTIN1 (#6295) being built, plus a one-thread Shared cell with no lock (a paired benchmark is owed: a field write through a cell measured about 55 ns against about 1 ns through a pool slot).

log.text: Posted D-HANDLE-NAV1 to the owner; audit draft ready to land on dev.
Owner chose to free @ and require the two downsides engineered away.
Corrected: @T live links are built on dev, not unbuilt (found by the D-HANDLE-NAV1 draft).

criteria.text: Design review: a dated audit in Docs/Audits attacks the whole mechanism of ballot D-HANDLE-NAV1, names every place the same fact lives today with the exact cutover list and the copies it deletes, and passes; the ballot's recorded review cites it.

Ballot D-GLOBAL-SAFE1 posted 2026-11-25 (reviewed by ReviewGlobalSafe1); it decides only what D-MODULE-VAR1=A left open, and its review is Docs/Audits/2026-11-25-global-state-review.md (in the master checkout, to land on dev).

The ratified outcome of D-GLOBAL-SAFE1 is built: each listed downside (test interference, cross-task races, hidden writes in purity and effect facts, hot reload, initialization order) has its ratified remedy with a registered diagnostic where a rule refuses code.

cards.title: Effect classes in plain words: Reads, Adds or Replaces, plus repeatable, checked at routes, retries, transactions and previews
cards.body: Owner approved the reworded greenfield proposal item P7 for ballot D-EFFECT-CLASS1 on 2026-11-25. Each effect operation answers three separate questions: what it does to existing data (Reads: only looks; Adds: makes something new and leaves existing data alone; Replaces: old data is gone afterward), whether calling it twice ends the same as once (repeatable), and whether it can be taken back (the existing irreversible() flag, Compiler/Prelude/Effects.jet:14-15, kept separate: an email Adds and can't be undone, a database delete Replaces and can be rolled back). The words map one to one onto MCP tool annotations (readOnlyHint, destructiveHint, idempotentHint). Source: Docs/Proposals/2026-11-24-greenfield-language.md, Part 2, item P7 (master checkout, not yet on dev). Ballot D-EFFECT-CLASS1 posted 2026-11-25 (reviewed by ReviewEffectClass1); its review is Docs/Audits/2026-11-25-effect-access-review.md (in the master checkout, to land on dev).

log.text: Posted D-EFFECT-CLASS1 to the owner; recorded two effect defects the review found.

criteria.text: Design review: a dated audit in Docs/Audits attacks ballot D-EFFECT-CLASS1's whole mechanism, names every place effect facts live today (Prelude and Core effect declarations, irreversible(), #Transact, manifests, --allow/--deny, reflection) with the exact cutover list, and passes; the ballot's recorded review cites it.
D-EFFECT-CLASS1 is decided by the owner, and every machine and Core effect leaf declares its ratified class and repeatable fact in one place that sema, reflection and tools read.

The checks are built with registered diagnostics and UI snapshots: a GET route that reaches an Adds or Replaces effect is refused, a retry of a call that is not repeatable needs an idempotency key, and #Transact refuses an irreversible effect.
`--preview` lists every Adds and Replaces effect a run would reach and highlights Replaces, and agent tool metadata carries readOnlyHint, destructiveHint and idempotentHint derived from the classes.
An executable example with golden output proves the ratified design on every applicable tier, and the spec, reference pages and editor grammars describe it.

Independent of the ballot: E0746 refuses an irreversible call inside an `on_commit` closure in `#Transact`, the very place its own fix text recommends (probed on jet a0.0.46). A call inside `on_commit` runs after the commit and is accepted; proof is a case that calls an irreversible function from `on_commit` and runs it on every tier.

Independent of the ballot: a `mux.get` route closure that removes a file is accepted although the route handler types (Core/Web/Web.jet:527, Core/HTTP/Server.jet:219) declare `-[Net, FS.Read]>`. Trace the path `mux.get` takes, make the handler row checked at every registration path, and prove it with a UI snapshot of the refused closure.

cards.title: Grammar literals: one Core Grammar type gives typed trees, parse, print and build-time format errors, and serves the checked text heads
cards.body: Owner accepted greenfield proposal item P31 on 2026-11-25, low priority. `Grammar{"""…"""}` is a Core library type using the existing checked-literal form and compile-time code: its rules generate the result types, a parse function, a print function and positioned errors, and an ambiguous grammar is a build error. The owner asked whether it improves the existing checked text heads: today the `check` of SQL (Core/DB/DB.jet:330), Sh (Core/Process/Process.jet:142) and HTML (Core/Text/HTML.jet:115) accepts any text, so a misspelt query or broken markup is found only at run time, and every hole is stringified through Printable. Core holds 246 hand-written parse and lex functions in 104 files; the SQL parser alone is 2,162 lines (Core/DB/Engine/Parse.jet). Source: Docs/Proposals/2026-11-24-greenfield-language.md, Part 2, item P31 (master checkout, not yet on dev). Owner order (2026-11-25): build this immediately, ahead of the epoch order, both the Grammar feature and the grammars behind the existing DSL heads (SQL, HTML, Sh, URL, DateTime); approved directly by the owner in chat, so no ballot is needed. The design review (row 1) still comes first, per AGENTS.md. Owner direction (2026-11-25): Pip's agent produces the design and the build plan only, with no implementation; the owner's orchestrator assigns the implementation. Owner direction (2026-11-25): the rule notation follows industry-standard grammar notation (the shared EBNF conventions of mainstream parser generators), with Jet-only additions kept to field labels, holes and operator precedence; the declaring `Name: Grammar{…}` form, the safe Sh and HTML rules and the Core names are part of the approved feature and need no ballot.

D-SH-ARGV1=A and D-HTML-SCRIPTATTR1=A were decided within the approved P31 scope; the Core bodies record is ruled not a compile cache (design section 14).

## 15. Build order (card-ready items, each at most one hour of code)

Conventions:

- **Crit** is the card #7036 criterion row the item serves. **Deps** lists
  the items it needs first.
- **Proof** is the exact command that must pass. A filter matches row IDs
  relative to the repository root (§1); a filter that selects nothing fails.
- `core F` means `jet test Compiler --profile core --filter Core/Grammar/Tests/F.jet`.
- New cases go under `Tests/Cases/GrammarLiterals/`. `Tests/Cases/Grammar/`
  is Jet's own grammar.
- Each item that adds a code also adds its type to
  `Compiler/Prelude/Diagnostics.jet` and runs
  `jet Tools/Agent/DiagnosticRows.jet --write`. Its proof includes
  `jet Tools/Agent/DiagnosticRows.jet --check`.
- Timed commands (`GrammarPair.jet`, `Throughput.jet`) are run by the
  orchestrator, alone. A worker never runs them.

log.text: Decided (implementation of an approved row, no ballot): the design's §4 row 'Constants: R.RULE: Int, and token-kind constants for sinks' has no Jet form. A type's only static members are trait constants, which are snake_case and can't be declared per grammar. Each grammar instead generates two enums, <Start>Rule (one case per parser rule) and <Start>Token (one case per token kind), whose Int discriminants are the plan's rule and kind numbers, with the to_int/from_int that #Layout enums get. GrammarSink keeps Int rule/kind parameters, since it is shared by every grammar, and a sink matches with <Start>Rule.from_int(rule). Same meaning; Jet's one mechanism for named integer sets; precedent <Start>Slot. G-B9 updates the design doc's row and Sink.jet's doc in the same patch.

Owner order 2026-11-25: P0, ahead of the epoch order. One implementer (GrammarLiterals, Opus) is assigned until done, beside the existing team cap. Order: Phase A (pure Core, proven by the worker with core-profile single-file tests) runs regardless of the gates; then B1..B3g as one change; B4..B7; G-B8a is the hard probe gate (on failure, stop B8b and its chain, record it here, return the design to review). G-P1 runs before any Phase D cutover, G-P2 before Parse.jet is deleted, and every parser deletion needs its GrammarPair pair at least as fast. All timed runs are the orchestrator's, alone in the heavy-job slot.
Design and build plan done and reviewed (ReviewGrammar); plan written here, documents ready to land on dev.
Owner ordered P31 built immediately, ahead of the epoch order; priority raised to P0 and each DSL head given its own row.

criteria.text: Design review: a dated audit in Docs/Audits compares the design with Raku grammars, pest, nom and lark, names every hand-written text-format parser and checked text head in Core with the exact cutover list, and passes.
criteria.evidence: G-0: the review Docs/Audits/2026-11-25-grammar-literals-review.md (with its behavior → source → proof tables) and the design Docs/Proposals/2026-11-25-grammar-literals.md landed on dev 7c91389e6b1 (merged to master b2489523727). Proof on that text: jet Tools/Agent/AgentDocFlags.jet → 'agent-doc-flags: ok (43 documented flag reference(s))'; --policy-only → 'documentation-policy: ok'; neither file trips the personal-information guard. Verdicts: every claim holds or holds within stated limits after repair; pre-registration staging stays unproven until G-B8a (hard gate). One correction to the design: G-C3's proof cell now names AgentDocFlags first, as G-C2 does, so the flag check reads each command's own flags.

criteria.text: `Grammar{"""…"""}` is built in Core: the rules generate typed result types, `parse` with line:column errors and `print`, and a left-recursive or ambiguous grammar is a build error with a registered diagnostic.

The SQL head (`SQL{"…"}`, Core/DB/DB.jet:325-330, whose check accepts any text today) checks its literal at build time against a SQL grammar: a malformed query is a build error with line and column, and each hole is typed and escaped by the position the grammar gives it (a table or column name versus a value).
Every hand-written text-format parser in Core that a grammar can express is replaced by its grammar; the parse-speed pair for each replacement is on #6957.
An executable example with golden output proves the ratified design on every applicable tier, and the spec, reference pages and editor grammars describe it.

The HTML head (`HTML{"…"}`, Core/Text/HTML.jet:115, whose check accepts any text today) checks its literal at build time against an HTML grammar: broken markup is a build error, and each hole is escaped by the position the grammar gives it (text, quoted attribute, unquoted attribute, URL attribute), from the grammar instead of hand-written rules.

The Sh head (`Sh{"…"}`, Core/Process/Process.jet:142, whose check accepts any text today) checks its literal at build time against a command grammar: a malformed command is a build error, and each hole stays exactly one argv item by the grammar, never re-split or globbed.

The URL and DateTime heads (Core/Net/URL.jet:171, Core/Time/Time.jet:1182) replace their hand-written checks with grammars, and every other checked literal head in Core (the Regex head included) is moved onto a grammar or recorded in the design review with the reason it stays hand-written.

Grammar literals cost no compile speed: with every Core head on its grammar, `JET=<candidate jet> jet Tools/Perf/CompileThroughput/Throughput.jet --against <seed jet> --modes check,O0` shows no loss in lines per second against the seed (plan items G-P1 and G-P2), and no grammar is evaluated by a second whole-program compile.
criteria.evidence: Moved to #5479 c43

cards.title: Edit marks at call sites: `^` on every named argument a call changes, never required on receivers, inserted by jet fmt
cards.body: Owner direction on 2026-11-25, to be decided as ballot D-CALLSITE-MARK3 (reopening D-CALLSITE-MARK2=A, card #6586): a call writes `^` before each named argument it changes, as in `grow(^xs)`; a receiver never needs a mark (`xs.push(4)`); a move at a name's last use needs no mark, because it is a backend fact and not a frontend requirement, but a written `^^` is accepted and checked; and `jet fmt` inserts every required mark from checked facts with no manual work at any of the existing call sites. The owner also fully rejected UFCS for now (D-UFCS1=B stands), since pipes give chaining. Sema already computes every site: `jet audit writes` lists them and E0228 carries a Safe edit under #Policy(writes: .Explicit) (Docs/Spec/Reference/cli.md:1425-1436). Owner answers (2026-11-25): a move at a name's last use needs no `^^` but a written one is kept and checked; receivers carry no mark, as in other languages; jet fmt leaves optional marks as written; #Policy(writes: .Explicit) is deleted. Owner confirmed (2026-11-25): every named argument a call changes carries `^`, with no exceptions; a parameter that is already writable (`fn load(buf: ^Buffer) { fill(^buf) }`) is marked like any other argument. Only receivers are unmarked. Ballot D-CALLSITE-MARK3 posted 2026-11-25 (reviewed by ReviewCallMark3); its review is Docs/Audits/2026-11-25-call-marks-review.md (in the master checkout, to land on dev). About 105,000 call sites gain a mark, all inserted by jet fmt.

log.text: Posted D-CALLSITE-MARK3 to the owner; recorded three tool defects the review found.

criteria.text: Design review: a dated audit in Docs/Audits attacks ballot D-CALLSITE-MARK3's whole mechanism, names every place call marks live today (#Policy(writes: .Explicit), E0228, jet audit writes, the parser's call marks, the language server's hints) with the exact cutover list and site counts, and passes.

D-CALLSITE-MARK3 is decided by the owner, and sema requires `^` on every named argument a call changes, with a registered diagnostic whose Safe fix inserts it, never on a receiver, and accepts a written `^^` at a take, checking that the name is not used again.

`jet fmt` inserts every required call mark from the checked compile, as `--explicit-failures` does for failures, and one run over the repository leaves `jet check` clean with no hand edits; a file that does not check keeps its text and reports why.

One greenfield cutover migrates every in-repository call, example, snapshot, doc and editor grammar, and #Policy(writes: .Explicit) is deleted with its E0228 branch and docs, with no parallel rule left.
An executable example with golden output proves the ratified design on every applicable tier, and the spec, reference pages and editor grammars describe it.

Independent of the ballot: the call-mark fix for a slice argument lands in the wrong place (`sort_part(xs[0..2])` became `xs&[0..2]`, which does not compile) because `expr_source_start` has no slice arm (Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/AST/Expressions.jet:809-818, called from CallMarks.jet:122), and `jet fix` still prints "applied 1 fix" in file, package and --dry-run modes because its rollback check misses the new error (Compiler/JetCLI FixCommands.jet:427-456; cause not yet isolated between 47-66 and 102-110). Proof: a case where the slice fix compiles, and a case where a fix that adds an error is rolled back and reported.

Independent of the ballot: `jet fix` makes a binding immutable while a call that may change it is unresolved (with `badsig: fn(n: &Missing)`, it rewrote `k := 2` to `k: 2` although `badsig(k)` may change `k`), and `jet fix` on a file that does not parse prints "no changes made" without naming the parse error (probed on jet a0.0.46). Proof: one case for each.

Independent of the ballot: the refusal of a write through a computed pipe head leaks the internal name `__jet_pipe_174` instead of naming `<>` (Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Ownership/Checks.jet:3540-3570 never checks `pipe_value_is_name`, AST/Expressions.jet:87; location inferred), and E0228 says the callee "reads this input" for takes such as `seal(&&st.buf)` (CallMarks.jet:115, 184-185). Proof: corrected texts with UI snapshots.

cards.title: GPU performance: kernels and the draw path measured against vendor libraries and peers
cards.body: Split from #4731.

criteria.text: Each kernel has a gauntlet cell against the vendor library on the same device
Gauntlet cells measure the GPU path (frame time and draw submission cost) against C with Vulkan and Rust with wgpu, with an asm-parity ceiling reference, per the performance gate.

The 2x2 bias/clamp `Tile<F32>` case (D-GPU-TILE-SCOPE1=B, #3215) has a matched fused benchmark cell that passes the performance gate. Proof: `node Tools/Gauntlet/Harness/run.mjs --entry gpu-tile-fused-bias-clamp`.

D-GPU-INDEXED-RESOURCE1=A (checked multi-write kernel results) has a paired strict-candidate against plain performance cell that wins under the performance gate; the build on its feature card waits for it. Proof: `node Tools/Gauntlet/Harness/run.mjs --entry gpu-indexed-resource-pair`.

cards.title: Build-time values cost no binary bytes: unread build-time data is not emitted and repeated values are stored as pattern plus length (D-COMPTIME-SIZE1)
cards.body: Split from #6769.

criteria.text: Bytes of a build-time value that no run-time code reads are not emitted. In the D-COMPTIME-SIZE1 program (two 50 MB repeats used only for their lengths), the --optimize=full binary holds neither run and is within 10% of the size of the same program reading its size at run time (136,272 bytes on seed-b13). Proof: a case builds it, asserts the binary size bound and the output 100000000, and readelf shows no 50 MB run.

D-COMPTIME-SIZE1=A is built (ratified 2026-11-13). One fixed storage rule applies to every emitted value at O0, O1, O2 and web, with no switch. A value of at least 64 KiB whose bytes repeat one pattern of at most 64 bytes is stored as pattern plus length, and an all-zero value as zero-fill. Item reads, length, loops, slices, comparisons, searches and hashing work on the pattern. print and file or socket writes stream from one reused 64 KiB buffer. A use that needs fixed bytes, such as a [U8] parameter or foreign code, fills it once under a guard into reserved read-only pages. jet inspect decisions lists each pattern value. Proof: identical output digests on every tier, binary size never above raw, the ballot program near 50.1 MB, and a racing-threads fill-once case.

cards.title: Moves never copy: field, parameter, pattern and destructure moves lower to moves in JetIR with no clone
cards.body: Split from #6923.

criteria.text: `s.f.move()` and moves out of struct fields and parameters lower to a move in JetIR, with no clone, and the clone-gate copies the old FieldMove lowering added are removed. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter Moves/field_and_param_move_no_clone` on O0, O1 and O2.

Destructuring an owned temporary (`(program, values) := returned_tuple()`, or a returned struct) moves every field on every tier, with no clone of the fields (D-OUTPUT-RETURNS1=A; frozen #4567 holds the original report). Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter Moves/destructure_returned_tuple_moves_fields` and a paired cell against output parameters.
Pattern payload bindings of owned locals and parameters move at the last use or alias under a stable root, never deep-copy the payload.

The three linear copy residues in Compiler/ (the L1 payload copy, element leftovers and the ref-binding move) use the sema copy decisions, so no copy appears without one. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter Moves/linear_copy_residues` and a lower copy count from `jet inspect choices` over the self-hosted compiler.
The about 64 remaining dead parameter copies at O1 are gone. Proof: the entry-clone count from `jet inspect choices` over the self-hosted compiler is 0 (receipt with command and count).

A `#Static` fixed array is one shared addressable constant, so a hot loop over it (the SHA-256 K table) emits no array copy. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter Moves/static_array_loop_no_copy` on O1 and O2.

A record returned from a call is built in its caller's destination, not in a value slot that is then copied: a hot loop that gets a record from a helper costs no more instructions than one that builds the same record in place. Today on gate-p288 the returned record costs 2.88 G more instructions in the hot loop ($JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/ballot-rework/probes/zipcolumns-r5/ir_*.txt; found 2026-11-18 by the D-ARRAY-ZIPCOLUMNS1 r5 probes). Proof: a paired measurement (the helper record against the in-place record, built at -O2) shows equal instructions within noise, plus a second program that returns a different record shape.

A field of borrowed storage moved into a call (for example `slot.held.move()` or permit.value passed to a && parameter) leaves the moved value unshared: today it stays shared with its source until the source field is written, so every write in the callee deep-copies it (copy-on-write). Found by Lens on #6841 c66: the debugger s held program deep-copied on every print (25 ms per print, 1.8 ms once the slot is emptied before the call), and JetDriver Pipeline jet_driver_held_eval_lend(held.probe.program....move()) likely pays the same. Repro $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Lens/c66held/mv/main.jet (jet run -A at -O0 and -O2): 5.2-5.9 ms per step on 400k strings against 0 us for a local s field. Proof: a case where a moved borrowed field written in the callee costs the same as a moved local field on O0, O1 and O2, with no deep copy (an allocation count of zero per step).

cards.title: Zero unjustified copies: every written and implicit copy is removed or justified in the ledger, ceilings never rise, and copy removal never slows Jet
cards.body: Split from #3836.

criteria.text: Zero unjustified copies (owner order 2026-11-14). Every .copy() in Compiler, Core, Jetpack and Tools is either removed (moved at its last use, borrowed, the owner restructured, or a name made an interned id) or carries a justification row in the copy ledger. A row names the copy site and a paired two-program measurement on the reference machine showing that the copy makes that path faster, in wall time or peak memory, than the copy-free spelling. A copy that is neutral or slower is not justified. Tests/Guards/copy_ratchet.jet fails on any copy without a justified row, and the count of unjustified copies is 0. Baseline 2026-11-14: 6,686 explicit copies in 637 Compiler files, none justified. Proof: `jet test Tests/Guards --filter copy_ratchet` reports 0 unjustified copies.

Implicit copies count too. The compiler reports every deep copy it inserts without a written .copy() as a site list, from jet check --trace or a lint, and the same zero-unjustified rule and guard apply to it. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter Copies/implicit_copy_site_list`, and `jet test Tests/Guards --filter copy_ratchet` counts implicit copies.

No copy ceiling ever rises. No SUB, rebase or lander fix-up raises a ledger ceiling or adds a row without a justification; the guard and the lander refuse it. Main raised SerdeItems.jet to 50 in the stack127 fix-ups on 2026-11-14; that rise is undone. Proof: `jet test Tests/Guards --filter copy_ratchet` refuses a raised ceiling or an unjustified row (a negative-control case), and the SerdeItems.jet ceiling is back below 50.

Removing copies never makes Jet slower. Each copy-removal batch shows the cold self-compile wall time and peak memory, measured on the batch compiler, at or below the batch before it. Proof: each copy-removal batch receipt lists cold self-compile wall time and peak memory, each at or below the batch before it.

decisions.title: Cross-platform executable lease security
decisions.gist: Which existing promise changes so executable packages can work safely on macOS and Windows.
decisions.explainer: Jetpack verifies a package, copies its output into a lease snapshot, and must keep every executable name bound to those verified bytes while a child and its descendants run. Linux does this with a private read-only mount. An unprivileged macOS process has no equivalent immutable named PATH view; Windows file handles can block replacement of files but do not alone protect every descendant name lookup. Today the non-Linux backend returns an error for every lease, even data-only outputs; that empty-output bug is ungated and will be fixed. Executable outputs expose a real conflict among three ratified promises: hostile same-user swaps fail before handoff, Linux/macOS/Windows are tier-1 native, and Jetpack uses no root or daemon. No known design keeps all three. The owner must choose which promise changes.
decisions.story: Mira uses one committed lockfile on Linux, macOS, and Windows. She runs a formatter directly and through jet env. Another same-user process swaps the original package path after verification. Jetpack must execute the verified bytes or refuse; it must never follow the replacement. Beginners need one ceremony-free workflow, while experts need exact audit proof of the native protection used.
decisions.inWild:
$ jetpack run tools:formatter -- src/
formatted 18 files

$ jet env
[jet:dev] $ formatter --check src/
checked 18 files

# A same-user process renames the verified output and replaces it with a malicious symlink tree.
# Jetpack must execute the leased bytes or refuse, never follow the replacement.

options.name: Protected native lease service
options.detail: Keep tier-1 usability and the hostile-race guarantee by narrowly amending the no-root/no-daemon law. Linux keeps its unprivileged private mount. This option also ratifies new macOS/Windows distribution-installer behavior: official Jet installers register a root-owned macOS LaunchDaemon or Windows LocalSystem service after one explicit admin approval; no new Jet command is added. The service independently re-verifies the locked digest and copies executables into an OS-protected lease directory the caller cannot rewrite. It authenticates the local caller, then impersonates that caller and launches the child under the caller UID/session/token with no root/SYSTEM privileges or inherited service handles. The child PATH puts protected lease bins first, followed by the caller's approved inherited/system PATH; privilege-sensitive service variables and handles are removed, and package executable names can resolve only through protected lease dirs. A jet env lease lives through the shell and all descendants, then deletes after the process tree exits. The service has no network access, never resolves packages, and fails closed if stopped, mismatched, or unverifiable. Ordinary run/env use remains ceremony-free and offline.
options.code:
# During the new official macOS/Windows installer flow ratified by A:
Install protected executable lease service? [yes/no] yes
installed jet-lease-service 1.0.0

$ jetpack run tools:formatter -- src/
formatted 18 files

$ jet env
[jet:dev] $ formatter --check src/
checked 18 files
[jet:dev] $ sh -c 'formatter --check tests/'
checked 7 files

$ jetpack doctor
executable leases  protected
service            1.0.0, toolchain-matched
request identity   user, authenticated
child identity     user, no service privileges
handles/env        service authority removed
PATH                protected lease bins, then approved caller/system bins
network             denied
handoff             root-protected verified lease
same-user redirect blocked

$ jet env  # service stopped or version mismatched
error E1292: protected executable lease service is unavailable
fix: repair the Jet installation; no child or shell was started

options.name: Relax the hostile same-user guarantee
options.detail: Keep no-root/no-daemon and tier-1 usability, but explicitly weaken the security law on macOS and Windows. Jetpack uses a private snapshot, restrictive native handles where available, and digest validation immediately before launch. This catches corruption and non-racing swaps, but a hostile process running as the same user can race the final validation and a descendant PATH lookup; post-exit detection cannot undo executed code. Doctor and audit output name the weaker guarantee. This option is an intentional safety downgrade, not an equivalent backend.
options.code:
$ jetpack run tools:formatter -- src/
warning L1292: this host cannot exclude a same-user executable PATH race
why: macos has no unprivileged immutable named PATH view
fix: audit local same-user processes before running executable packages
formatted 18 files

$ jet env
warning L1292: commands in this environment have the weaker macos lease guarantee
[jet:dev] $ sh -c 'formatter --check tests/'
checked 7 files  # a hostile same-user final-lookup race is not excluded

$ jetpack doctor
executable leases  guarded, weaker than linux
same-user redirect not excluded

options.name: Fail closed for non-Linux executables
options.detail: Keep no-root/no-daemon and the full hostile-race guarantee. Fix data-only leases on every platform, but reject leases containing executables on macOS and Windows before any child starts. A new registered diagnostic explains that the platform cannot provide the required immutable handoff. This narrows D-JPK-PLATFORM1: macOS and Windows remain native for data libraries and non-executable package operations, but executable packages are Linux-only until an equally safe unprivileged primitive exists.
options.code:
$ jetpack run tools:formatter -- src/
error E1292: executable leases are unavailable on macos
why: Jetpack cannot create an immutable PATH view without a protected service
fix: run this executable package on Linux; mutable cache paths are never used

$ jet env  # project declares formatter executable
error E1292: this environment needs an executable lease unavailable on macos
no shell was started

$ jetpack doctor
executable leases  unavailable
policy             fail closed

$ jetpack build data:unicode-tables
completed  # data-only leases still work

comparisons.note: Nix protects immutable store objects through privileged ownership and a daemon. Option A uses the same concrete authority boundary, but scopes it to verified executable handoff: no resolution, builds, cache networking, or general store ownership.
comparisons.code:
$ nix-store --verify --check-contents
# protected store paths remain outside user write authority

comparisons.note: Linux supplies a private read-only mount view inside an unprivileged user namespace. Jetpack already uses it to map stable PATH names to inherited descriptors.
CreateFile sharing flags can prevent replacement or deletion of opened executables, but a complete PATH solution must also protect directory/name resolution and child handoff.

decisions.title: Mobile (iOS/Android): compile target scope and who owns signing + store submission
decisions.gist: Whether Jet compiles real iOS and Android apps as first-class targets, and whether signing and app-store submission are first-party Jet commands or someone else's tools.
decisions.explainer:
Glossary first. **Code signing**: Apple and Google refuse to run an app unless its binary is cryptographically signed with a developer key; unsigned apps do not install on a phone, period. **Provisioning profile**: an Apple file that says which developer, which app id, and which devices a signed iOS build may run on. **Keystore**: the Android equivalent — a local file holding the signing key; lose it and you can never update your app again. **App Store Connect / Play Console**: Apple's and Google's web services where builds are uploaded, reviewed, and released; both expose official REST APIs. **Notarization**: Apple's malware scan for apps distributed *outside* the Mac App Store (macOS-side; iOS App Store review replaces it). **NDK**: Google's toolkit for putting native (non-Java) code in an Android app. **.ipa / .aab**: the upload file formats for the App Store and Play Store.

Scope of this ballot: card #480 gates G1 (target scope) and G2 (signing/store ownership), which are coupled — a compile target you cannot sign is a demo, not a product. G3 (the Android/Kotlin widget-interop transport, the JNI parallel to ratified D-FFI-SWIFT1) and G4 (native hot-reload/preview) are **explicitly deferred to follow-up ballots on this card**; every option below is compatible with any G3/G4 outcome. iOS widget access needs no new gate: D-FFI-SWIFT1 (=A) already ratifies the Swift bridge for macOS/iOS.

Ratified frame this must extend: D-NATIVEUI1=A (thin core library over platform widget APIs via FFI, own renderer later), D-NATIVEUI2=B (all platforms simultaneously, one Backend seam), #134's shipped GTK4 backend (same reactive/view/style/component model on every backend — I8), and D-BUILDTOOLCHAIN1=A (toolchains, SDKs, and signing identities are typed jetpack-provisioned handles). Options A and B continue that family; option C knowingly diverges from it and says so.

One hard external fact shapes everything: Apple licenses the iOS SDK for use on Apple hardware only, so *linking* an iOS app requires a Mac with the Xcode SDK present no matter who owns the rest of the pipeline. Every option below handles that with an honest gated error on other hosts (the D-FFI-SWIFT1 precedent). Android has no such wall: the NDK, the .aab bundler, APK signing, and the Play upload API are all fully driveable first-party from any OS.

Trust-boundary note (this is the real long-term cost, and it is a safety question, not an effort question): Apple and Google change store policy and API details continuously. Whatever owns the pipeline inherits that churn forever. In options A and B the churn is contained in jetpack — a separately versioned tool — so the Jet language, compiler, and runtime never change to satisfy a store policy. In option C the churn lands on the user, inside Xcode and Android Studio projects Jet does not see.
decisions.story: Priya built a notes app in Jet. It runs on her Linux desktop today through the GTK4 backend from the same reactive code, and `jet build --target=web` gives her a web version. Her users keep asking for it on their phones. In Swift she would open Xcode, sign in with her Apple account, let Xcode manage certificates, and press Archive → Distribute. In Jet, right now, there is nothing — `--target=ios` does not exist. She wants to know: can she stay in Jet from `notes.jet` all the way to a build her mother can install from the App Store, or does Jet hand her off to Xcode and Android Studio at the finish line? Where that handoff happens (never / at signing / at the whole UI layer / this epoch at all) is exactly this decision.

options.name: Tier-1 mobile targets; Jet owns signing and store submission end to end
options.detail: Core loop: `jet build --target=ios|android` compiles the same reactive app natively, and one first-party command signs it with locally held keys and uploads it to the store — no Apple or Google tool is ever run. iOS/Android become real compile targets through the existing rustc backend (aarch64-apple-ios, aarch64-linux-android via a jetpack-pinned NDK), rendering native widgets per D-NATIVEUI1=A — UIKit via the ratified D-FFI-SWIFT1 bridge, Android views via the G3 follow-up ballot. Signing is implemented first-party (the Ed25519 signing tier D-PKGSIGN1 set this precedent; pure-Rust Apple codesigning is proven ground — see the rcodesign comparison). Submission talks directly to the App Store Connect API and Play Developer API. Users type `jet ship`; jetpack is the engine behind the seam, same dispatch shape as `jet os` — so store-API churn lives in a separately updateable tool, never in the compiler, and signing keys never leave the user's machine (contrast Expo, which holds them in the cloud). Honest gate: iOS builds still require a Mac with the Xcode SDK installed (Apple's license), but Xcode is never opened; Android works from any OS, fully offline until upload. This is the only option under which "no reason to reach for another language" is literally true for mobile.
options.code:
$ jet build --target=android
   toolchain  android-ndk r27 (jetpack, pinned)
   compiled   notes.jet -> aarch64-linux-android
   built      target/android/notes.aab

$ jet ship android
   no signing key found -> created ./release.keystore (BACK THIS FILE UP:
   Google will not let you update the app without it)
   signed     notes.aab
   uploaded   Play Console -> internal testing track (build 1)

$ jet ship ios            # on her Mac
   signed in to App Store Connect (team: Priya Rao)
   created signing certificate + provisioning profile (stored locally;
   keys never leave this machine)
   signed     Notes.ipa (Apple Distribution: Priya Rao)
   uploaded   App Store Connect -> TestFlight build 1

$ jet build --target=ios  # on her Linux desktop
error: building for iOS requires the Apple SDK, which Apple licenses
       only on Apple hardware
  what: the iOS target links against Apple's UIKit frameworks
  fix:  run this on a Mac (or a macOS CI runner) with Xcode installed —
        Jet uses its SDK, you never open it. `--target=android` works here.

options.name: Tier-1 mobile targets; jetpack orchestrates Apple/Google tools for signing and submission
options.detail: Core loop: Jet compiles natively exactly as in A, but `jet ship` drives Apple's and Google's own command-line tools (codesign, Transporter, apksigner, bundletool) under the hood instead of reimplementing them — the fastlane/Tauri shape. The user types the same commands as A and jetpack provisions and hash-pins the vendor tools as toolchain deps (D-BUILDTOOLCHAIN1=A), laundering their errors into Jet diagnostics in the I2 spirit — raw xcodebuild output never reaches the user. What changes versus A is the trust and failure surface: the pipeline is only as correct, as offline-capable, and as scriptable as Apple's and Google's tools of the week; a vendor tool update can break `jet ship` in ways Jet can report but not fix, and iOS signing additionally requires the full Xcode command-line surface installed, not just the SDK. Keys still stay local. The compile-target half of this option is identical to A, so a later verdict could move B→A signing without touching the language.
options.code:
$ jet build --target=android
   built      target/android/notes.aab      # identical to option A

$ jet ship android
   tool       apksigner 35.0 (jetpack, pinned)
   signed     notes.aab (./release.keystore)
   uploaded   Play Console -> internal testing track (build 1)

$ jet ship ios
   tool       Xcode command line tools 17.2
   signed     Notes.ipa (via codesign)
   uploaded   App Store Connect (via Transporter)

$ jet ship ios            # Xcode CLT missing
error: shipping to the App Store needs Apple's command-line tools,
       which Apple does not allow Jet to bundle
  what: signing and upload run Apple's codesign and Transporter
  fix:  xcode-select --install, then rerun `jet ship ios`

options.name: Jet compiles the logic core; UI shells are hand-written in Xcode / Android Studio
options.detail: Core loop: `jet build --lib --target=ios|android` emits the app's state and logic as a static library with generated Swift and Kotlin bindings (the D-FFI-SWIFT1 bridge run in reverse), and the developer writes the screens twice — SwiftUI in Xcode, Compose in Android Studio — with Apple and Google owning signing and submission entirely. This is Kotlin Multiplatform's shape. Be clear about what it breaks: the one reactive/view/style/component model that D-NATIVEUI2=B and #134 built — the same `NotesView` that renders on GTK4, web, and TUI would NOT render on phones; only the data layer crosses. Two UI codebases per app, drifting independently, reviewed in tools Jet does not check — a permanent I8 exception on the two platforms with the most users. KMP itself is the cautionary tale: JetBrains spent years building Compose Multiplatform to escape exactly this split. Included because it is the honest industry-standard fallback shape, not because it fits Jet's frame.

options.name: Ratify deferral: mobile lands in Epoch 4, desktop/web/TUI finish first
options.detail: Core loop: this epoch ships no mobile target, and that becomes a recorded decree with a named landing slot instead of a silent gap. Grounding is sequencing, not effort: the universal-language plan's own dependency order says UL9 native/mobile comes after UL2 + UL3 + UL6, #134's macOS/Windows desktop backends are still open, and native hot-reload (G4) is web-only — mobile shipped now would be the first backend without a complete dev loop behind it. The decree pins three things so the gap cannot silently rot: (1) `--target=ios|android` produce an honest error naming this decision and the epoch, not a parse error; (2) mobile, when it lands, follows D-NATIVEUI1/2 (same widget-FFI pattern, same one UI model — option A or B of this ballot re-raised then); (3) no interim semi-official path (no option-C shells) that would create a second way to mean it before the first exists. Cost: for at least an epoch, "Jet replaces Swift" is claimably false, and the two largest consumer platforms stay dark while Flutter and RN keep shipping there.
options.code:
$ jet build --target=ios
error: iOS is not a supported target in this epoch
  what: mobile targets are scheduled for Epoch 4 (decision D-NATIVEUI3=D,
        after the desktop backends and native hot-reload land)
  fix:  `--target=web` produces an installable PWA your phone can run today

# Board effect: #480 closes as decreed-deferred; #134 proceeds with
# macOS/Windows desktop + native hot-reload unblocked and unsplit.

comparisons.note: Proves the option-A compile half: Dart AOT-compiles to real arm64 on both platforms, no interpreter. But it never owned the ship half — `flutter build ipa` wraps xcodebuild, signing stays Xcode-managed, and submission is delegated to fastlane or Xcode. That seam is where Flutter's one-language story ends and users file toolchain bugs.
comparisons.code:
$ flutter build ipa            # wraps xcodebuild under the hood
$ open build/ios/archive/Runner.xcarchive   # ...and you're in Xcode anyway
$ fastlane pilot upload        # third-party tool for the last mile

comparisons.note: Shows the demand for one-command shipping — and the trust cost of renting it. Bare RN hands you Xcode/Android Studio projects (option C's ergonomics). Expo's answer, `eas build` / `eas submit`, is one command, but builds run on Expo's servers and Expo can hold your signing credentials in its cloud. Option A is that ergonomic loop with keys kept local.
comparisons.code:
$ eas build --platform ios     # builds on Expo's servers
$ eas submit --platform ios    # Expo-managed credentials, cloud-side

comparisons.note: Option C's shape, from its strongest proponent: shared Kotlin logic core, UI written twice in SwiftUI and Compose, Apple/Google tools own everything past the library boundary. JetBrains' own trajectory — years building Compose Multiplatform to render one UI on iOS too — is the evidence that the split-UI compromise does not hold.

The feasibility evidence for option A's ship half: fastlane drives the App Store Connect and Play upload APIs from plain Ruby with no Xcode GUI, and rcodesign (pure Rust, no Apple code) signs and notarizes Mach-O binaries from Linux. First-party signing and submission is proven ground, not speculation — what no language toolchain has done is make it a built-in.
comparisons.code:
$ rcodesign sign --p12-file dist.p12 Notes.app    # pure Rust, runs on Linux
$ fastlane deliver                                # App Store Connect API, no Xcode GUI

comparisons.note: Option B's shape in the wild: `tauri ios build` / `tauri android build` orchestrate xcodebuild and gradle under one CLI. Works, but users must install and maintain both vendor toolchains, and Tauri's issue tracker absorbs every xcodebuild/gradle regression as its own bug — the orchestrator owns the churn without owning the fix.
comparisons.code:
$ npm run tauri ios build      # requires full Xcode installed
$ npm run tauri android build  # requires Android Studio SDK + gradle

decisions.title: Android native-widget and Kotlin interop transport
decisions.gist: How Jet's Android backend reaches native widgets and existing Kotlin libraries without creating a second UI model.
decisions.lesson:
Android applications normally contain Java or Kotlin code running on Android Runtime, plus optional native machine code. The Java Native Interface, or JNI, is Android's standard bridge between those worlds. Jet can compile its application logic to native code, then use JNI to create Android View widgets and receive lifecycle or input callbacks.

Jetpack Compose is Google's newer Kotlin UI toolkit. Compose builds screens from Kotlin functions instead of directly assembling classic View objects. A Compose bridge would generate Kotlin adapters that translate Jet's View tree into Compose calls. That translation must not become a second Jet component model.

The transport matters at two boundaries. Jet's own renderer needs predictable widget creation, updates, events, ownership, and errors. Experts also need access to existing Android libraries whose public APIs are Kotlin or Java. Jet already ratified one `java.*` binder over JNI. This decision chooses whether the Android UI backend uses that common binder directly, adds a Compose-specific adapter, or exposes both behind one backend contract.

For example, a Jet Button remains one Jet Button on every platform. On Android, the chosen transport decides whether its backend creates `android.widget.Button`, calls generated Compose code, or selects either implementation behind the same backend interface. User application code and reactive state remain unchanged.
decisions.story: Mina moves a Jet inventory app from Linux to Android. Its shared screen contains a search field, list, and camera button. She wants standard Android accessibility and lifecycle behavior. Her company also has a Kotlin barcode-scanner library. Mina should keep one Jet screen while still calling that library through a typed, inspectable boundary.

options.name: Direct JNI View backend
options.detail: Jet's Android backend uses generated JNI bindings to Android's classic View toolkit. The same java.* binder projects third-party Kotlin and Java libraries. Every callback crosses one typed boundary with checked ownership and Jet diagnostics. Experts can inspect generated bindings and override provisioned SDK or NDK handles. Compose-only libraries need an explicit Kotlin adapter package.
options.technical: Package a native shared library inside a minimal Android application shell. Generated JNI entrypoints attach to the existing Android Runtime, retain Java objects as opaque owned handles, and lower exceptions to JavaError. UI operations implement the existing JetBackend seam. No second embedded JVM is started on Android.
options.code:
$ jet inspect bind java android.widget.Button
+projected  android.widget.Button -> java.android.widget.Button
+transport  existing Android Runtime via JNI
+
+$ jet build --target=android
+built      target/android/inventory.aab
+backend    android-view / JNI
+
+error: Compose-only type `CameraPreview` has no Android View entrypoint
+  fix: add a Kotlin adapter that exposes a View, or choose the Compose-capable transport

options.name: Generated Kotlin Compose bridge
options.detail: Jet generates a Kotlin layer that renders its View tree through Compose. Existing Compose libraries fit naturally, and Android previews see generated Kotlin components. Classic View libraries require Compose interop wrappers. Experts can inspect and pin generated Kotlin, Gradle, compiler-plugin, and SDK inputs. The generated layer adds a platform-specific translation between Jet and native widgets.
options.technical: Jet emits Kotlin composables plus JNI calls into the native Jet state engine. State identity remains owned by Jet; Compose observes snapshots and returns events. Generated Kotlin is derived output, never an editable source of truth.
options.code:
$ jet build --target=android --android-backend=compose
+generated  target/android/generated/JetInventory.kt
+built      target/android/inventory.aab
+backend    compose / generated Kotlin bridge
+
+$ jet inspect generated android
+JetInventory.kt  hash:7ad2...  source:InventoryView

options.name: One Android backend protocol with View default and Compose adapter
options.detail: Jet keeps one Android backend contract. Its ceremony-free default uses direct JNI Views. A project may select the first-party Compose adapter without changing Jet components, state, events, or accessibility semantics. The same java.* binder handles ordinary Kotlin and Java libraries in both modes. Experts control the backend, generated adapters, toolchain, cache, and audit output through package policy.
options.technical: Define one AndroidBackend implementation contract under JetBackend. AndroidViewBackend is the default. AndroidComposeBackend consumes the identical checked UI tree and event protocol. Conformance tests require matching tree semantics, state identity, lifecycle restoration, accessibility facts, and diagnostics. Backend selection is build policy, not new language syntax.
options.code:
$ jet build --target=android
+backend    android-view (default)
+built      target/android/inventory.aab
+
+$ jet build --target=android --android-backend=compose
+backend    android-compose (same checked View tree)
+built      target/android/inventory.aab
+
+$ jet inspect android --audit
+ui-model   core.ui/View
+transport  JNI + generated Compose adapter
+toolchain  android-ndk r27, Kotlin 2.2, hashes recorded

comparisons.note: Flutter keeps one Dart widget model while platform channels reach Kotlin APIs. Its default renderer owns pixels, unlike Jet's ratified native-widget direction.
comparisons.code:
const channel = MethodChannel('scanner');
+final code = await channel.invokeMethod('scan');

comparisons.note: React Native maps one component model to Android views and also permits native modules. Its generated architecture shows why UI transport and library interop should share typed metadata.

recommendation.why: C preserves the ratified native-widget default while letting Compose ecosystems participate through a conforming adapter. One checked View tree and one java.* binder serve beginners and experts.

whyNot.reason: A makes Compose-only libraries require bespoke wrappers even though a reusable conforming adapter can preserve Jet semantics.
B makes a generated Compose translation mandatory and weakens the direct platform-widget default ratified by D-NATIVEUI1.

recommendation.tradeoff: Two backend implementations require parity enforcement. Shared conformance tests and one checked tree make that duplication an implementation detail, not a second user model.

hybrid.synthesis: C keeps A's direct JNI View path as the default and adds B's Compose access as a selectable adapter over the identical backend protocol. Library calls use the ratified java.* binder in either mode.

harvest.aspect: Direct native View access with one typed JNI boundary.
harvest.use: Use it as the default Android backend and common Kotlin or Java interop transport.

harvest.aspect: Natural access to Compose-only widgets and libraries.
harvest.use: Provide it as a first-party conforming adapter whose generated Kotlin remains derived and auditable.

harvest.aspect: One public UI model across transport choices.
harvest.use: Make backend conformance and identical Jet source the binding rule.

decisions.title: Native UI hot reload and component preview model
decisions.gist: How `jet dev` updates running native apps and previews components while preserving one runtime model.
decisions.lesson:
A native hot reload loop changes a running application after source is saved. A plain restart rebuilds and launches again, losing temporary state. A hot swap replaces checked executable units inside a resident process, then reconciles the existing widget tree with the new View tree.

State identity decides what survives. Jet already ratified `@Persist`: a marked module binding survives `jet dev` reload when its module path, name, and compatible value shape still match. Ordinary local state may reset. Widget identity also needs stable source-derived keys so a changed label updates the existing native widget instead of opening another window.

A component preview renders one component with chosen sample inputs, device size, theme, locale, and accessibility settings. It can run inside a separate preview host or inside the same resident runtime used by the full app. A shared host gives previews the same layout, event, lifecycle, and backend behavior as the application.

This choice controls trust as well as speed. Reloaded code must pass the normal parser, semantic checks, and executable TIR pipeline before entering the process. A failed change leaves the last good app running and shows a Jet diagnostic. No native linker or platform-tool error should leak to the user.
decisions.story: Luis adjusts a checkout screen while it runs on an Android phone and an iPhone simulator. He has already filled a long form. Saving a color change should keep the form values, update both native widget trees, and show the same component under large text. A bad edit should leave the last good screen usable.

options.name: Full-app state-preserving hot reload
options.detail: `jet dev --target=ios|android` runs the complete app in a resident native host. Each valid save swaps changed checked modules and reconciles native widgets. `@Persist` state survives by its ratified identity rules. Beginners use one command. Experts inspect swap units, state migration, backend calls, hashes, timing, and fallback reasons. Component previews are ordinary small applications.
options.technical: Reuse checked TIR and the resident JIT or platform dynamic-loading boundary. Compute a module dependency closure, validate ABI and value layouts before activation, apply the swap atomically, then diff the View tree. Unsupported native changes trigger a diagnosed controlled restart, never partial mutation.
options.code:
$ jet dev checkout.jet --target=android
+ready    Pixel 10 / android-view
+changed  CheckoutView
+checked  18 ms
+swapped  7 ms; widgets reused: 12; created: 1
+state    persisted: cart
+
+error E2204: this edit changes a native boundary
+  what: Scanner.scan now returns a different type
+  fix:  Jet kept the last good app running; press `r` for a controlled restart

options.name: Isolated component preview host
options.detail: `jet preview` runs selected components in a dedicated native host with sample inputs and device traits. Changes reload only the preview graph. This makes themes, sizes, locales, focus, and accessibility states explicit. Full applications still rebuild and restart, so navigation, lifecycle, restoration, and cross-component behavior are not exercised in the fast loop.
options.technical: The preview host loads checked component entrypoints and fixture values. It uses the production backend and renderer, but substitutes lifecycle, navigation, storage, and external effects with declared preview capabilities.
options.code:
$ jet preview checkout.jet CheckoutView --target=ios
+preview  iPhone 17 Pro, light, en-US
+
+keys: d device  t theme  l locale  a accessibility  q quit
+saved    component reloaded; app navigation not running
+
+$ jet dev checkout.jet --target=ios
+note: native full-app changes rebuild and restart

options.name: One resident native dev host for apps and previews
options.detail: `jet dev` owns one resident runtime and checked swap protocol. Full-app mode is the ceremony-free default. A preview selector narrows the root component and adds device, theme, locale, lifecycle, and accessibility controls. Both modes use production backends, identical state identity, and the same diagnostics. Experts control swap policy, restart boundaries, devices, capabilities, scheduling, caches, and audit receipts.
options.technical: Model app and preview as root configurations for one NativeDevHost. Every edit passes parser, sema, TIR validation, ABI checks, atomic activation, View reconciliation, and state migration. Preview capabilities are explicit inputs, not mocks hidden in component code. Device and simulator transports carry signed swap bundles and receipts.
options.code:
$ jet dev checkout.jet --target=android
+mode     app; device: Pixel 10
+saved    swapped 2 modules; persisted: cart
+
+$ jet dev checkout.jet --target=ios --preview=CheckoutView
+mode     preview; device: iPhone 17 Pro; theme: light; locale: en-US
+keys     d device  t theme  l locale  a accessibility
+saved    same swap protocol; widgets reused: 12
+
+$ jet inspect dev --audit
+source  CheckoutView@9f31...
+tir     checked@31aa...
+device  simulator-4A2D
+swap    atomic; fallback:none

comparisons.note: Flutter combines stateful full-app hot reload with widget-focused development. Its resident VM shows the value of preserving state while rebuilding the UI tree.
comparisons.code:
$ flutter run
r Hot reload.
R Hot restart.

comparisons.note: Both provide component previews with device and environment controls. Their previews can differ from full application lifecycle behavior, which argues for one Jet host and protocol.

recommendation.why: C gives beginners one real application loop and gives experts precise preview controls without inventing a second renderer or runtime. It directly fulfills D-PERSIST1 through one checked swap protocol.

whyNot.reason: A preserves real application behavior but treats focused previews as disposable mini-apps without first-class environment controls.
B improves component iteration while leaving the full native application loop restart-only and unable to prove lifecycle parity.

recommendation.tradeoff: The resident host becomes a security and correctness boundary. Mandatory semantic checks, atomic activation, signed device transport, and last-good rollback keep that boundary explicit and auditable.

hybrid.synthesis: C uses A's real full-app resident loop and B's focused environment controls as two root configurations of the same checked native host. Production backends and state rules remain identical.

harvest.aspect: State-preserving edits inside the actual application.
harvest.use: Make full-app hot reload the default `jet dev` mode.

harvest.aspect: Fast component isolation across device and accessibility environments.
harvest.use: Add preview roots and explicit environment inputs to the same host.

harvest.aspect: One swap protocol and one production renderer.
harvest.use: Require app and preview modes to share validation, activation, reconciliation, and audit receipts.

decisions.title: Mobile platform work deferred
decisions.outcome: Defer mobile-native platform work; current burndown focuses the Jet language and Linux support.
decisions.comment: Defer mobile-native platform work; current burndown focuses the Jet language and Linux support.

decisions.title: Where the C compiler behind jet cc comes from
decisions.gist: Whether jet cc ships a C compiler inside Jet, fetches one through Jet's package store, borrows the host's, or is not built.
decisions.lesson:
A C toolchain is the compiler, linker, and standard C library headers needed to turn C source into a program. Cross-compiling means building on one machine for a different kind of machine. The set of target headers and libraries is called a sysroot.

Zig proved a language can win users through its toolchain before its syntax. The zig cc command is a full C compiler that behaves the same on every machine and targets any platform out of the box. Teams adopt it just to build their existing C code, and meet the language later.

Jet today uses whatever clang and cc the host machine happens to have. That works, but every machine behaves differently, and cross-compiling depends on what the user installed. A jet cc that always works identically would be Jet's front door into every C and C++ estate.

This ballot picks how jet cc obtains its compiler. The choice sets the first-run experience, the install size everyone pays, whether two machines produce identical builds, and whether the wedge exists at all.
decisions.story: Marcus maintains a C codebase with a Makefile that predates him. His CI cross-builds four platforms with four fragile container images. He hears one tool can replace all four with CC=jet cc. If the first try works identically on his laptop and in CI, Jet has a champion inside his company.
decisions.inWild:
# unmodified upstream project, cross-built from an x86 Linux laptop:
$ CC="jet cc -target aarch64-linux-gnu" make
$ CC="jet cc -target x86_64-windows-gnu" make

# CI runs the same two lines and produces byte-identical artifacts.

options.name: Bundle clang, lld, and sysroots inside the Jet install
options.detail: Every Jet install carries a complete C compiler and target sysroots, the way Zig does. jet cc works instantly and offline on a fresh machine. Every user pays the download and disk weight even if they never compile C, and the C toolchain can only update when Jet itself ships a release.
options.code:
$ curl -L jet.dev/install | sh   # one large download, everything inside
$ jet cc hello.c -o hello         # works offline immediately

options.name: Jetpack store provisions a pinned toolchain on first use
options.detail: jet cc looks and behaves exactly like option A, but the compiler and sysroots arrive through Jet's own package store the first time they are needed. Every machine gets the identical pinned toolchain, so builds reproduce everywhere. Air-gapped sites preload it with the store's offline bundles. The base Jet install stays small.
options.technical: Toolchain and per-target sysroots become ordinary content-addressed store packages, riding the same provisioning that already fetches nixpkgs C dependencies (CFFI.rs). Offline staging uses the #957 bundle lanes. Keeps compiler seams dependency-free (I6) and one provisioning mechanism (I8).
options.code:
$ jet cc hello.c -o hello
  fetching toolchain clang-19.1 (pinned)...   # first use only
$ jet cc hello.c -o hello                     # instant from then on

options.name: Wrap the host toolchain only
options.detail: jet cc translates flags and shells out to whatever clang or gcc the machine has. Nothing to download. Two machines can produce different binaries from the same source, cross-compiling works only if the host happens to have the right pieces, and works-on-my-machine failures return.
options.code:
$ jet cc hello.c -o hello
  # uses /usr/bin/cc — whatever version this machine has
$ ssh ci 'jet cc hello.c -o hello'
  # different cc, different binary, maybe different bugs

options.name: No jet cc
options.detail: C compilation stays internal to Jet's FFI bridges. C estates get call-in interop but no reason to adopt Jet's toolchain first. The adoption wedge this program exists for is abandoned.
options.code:
$ jet cc hello.c
  error: unknown command "cc"

comparisons.note: Bundles clang, lld, and multiple libcs in one tarball; instant and offline, at the cost of a large install for everyone.
Store-provisioned pinned toolchains; byte-reproducible builds, first use fetches from a cache.
comparisons.code: $ nix develop  # brings the exact pinned gcc/clang

comparisons.note: Downloads toolchains and targets on demand; small base install, per-target additions.

recommendation.why: The experience matches the Zig model from the second invocation onward, and the first invocation is one visible, pinned fetch. Every machine gets bit-identical toolchains — the reproducibility story enterprises audit for. The base install stays small for users who never compile C, and toolchain updates ship on their own schedule. It reuses the store that already provisions C dependencies, keeping one mechanism and the compiler seam dependency-free.

whyNot.reason: Every Jet user pays hundreds of megabytes for a C compiler most never invoke, and a clang security fix must wait for a Jet release.
Host toolchains differ per machine, so the one promise that wins C estates — identical builds everywhere — is broken on day one.
Forfeits the toolchain-first adoption path entirely; C teams get nothing to adopt before the language.

recommendation.tradeoff: The very first jet cc on a fresh machine needs the network or a preloaded offline bundle. Fully air-gapped sites must stage the toolchain bundle in advance.

decisions.title: Migration tier map: which languages get source importers
decisions.gist: Which foreign languages get automatic source conversion into Jet, and which get an explicit call-in-only verdict.
decisions.lesson:
Jet has three ways to meet a foreign codebase. A binder lets Jet call the foreign code where it stands. An overlay replaces one foreign library with a Jet package that must prove identical behavior first. An importer converts foreign source files into editable Jet source with TODO markers, so the team maintains Jet from then on.

The importer contract is already ratified (D-MIGRATE-SRC1): jet import must produce honest, editable Jet, verified by differential tests against the original. Python is the first proof. No other language has a ruling yet.

Conversion quality depends on the source language. Managed languages such as Java or TypeScript have garbage collection and no pointer arithmetic, so their meaning maps cleanly onto Jet's safe surface. C++ has templates, preprocessor macros, and undefined behavior. Faithful conversion of C++ tends to produce machine-shaped output no human wants to maintain.

This ballot decides the wave: which languages get importers, and which get a stated binder-or-overlay-only verdict. Enterprise teams then know the transition story for every pile of code they own.
decisions.story: Elena is an engineering director with 2.3 million lines of Java and 400k lines of C++. Her board approved a five-year modernization. She will only pick Jet if she can show a credible, named path for both piles — even if the two paths differ.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet import java services/pricing/src/main/java
  wrote 214 files under pricing-jet/ (37 TODO markers)
  differential: 1,892/1,892 behavior tests match

$ jet import cpp engine/
  error: C++ has no source importer.
  fix: call it in place instead — use cpp.engine

options.name: Importers for Java, C#, TypeScript/JavaScript, Go, Python; binder-plus-overlay verdict for C and C++
options.detail: The five importer languages cover most enterprise line counts, and each converts into Jet a human would keep. C and C++ get an honest, documented verdict: coexist through the binder, replace module by module by hand, with overlays proving each replacement. No language is left without a named story.
options.code:
$ jet import java src/     # editable Jet + TODOs
$ jet import csharp src/   # editable Jet + TODOs
$ jet import cpp src/
  error: C++ has no source importer.
  fix: use cpp.engine — coexist, then replace by module

options.name: Importers only for scripting languages (TypeScript/JavaScript, Python)
options.detail: Dynamic scripting code converts most cleanly, so only those importers ship. Java, C#, Go, and C++ teams get binders only. The largest enterprise estates — Java and C# — have no conversion story, so a director like Elena cannot present a full modernization plan built on Jet.
options.code:
$ jet import ts web/       # works
$ jet import java src/
  error: Java has no source importer.

options.name: Importers for everything, including a C++ subset
options.detail: Every language gets an importer, with C++ limited to a defined subset. The C++ output would be machine-shaped where templates, macros, or undefined behavior appear, breaking the ratified promise that imported code is editable Jet a team can own. First impressions in the hardest estates would be of generated sludge.

options.name: Stop at Python; every other language is binder-only
options.detail: Only the already-planned Python importer ships. All other languages coexist through binders indefinitely. One scripting importer cannot carry an enterprise migration story; it reads as a demo, not a path, and the tier map this program promises never exists.
options.code:
$ jet import py scripts/   # works
$ jet import java src/
  error: Java has no source importer.

comparisons.note: Won the Java world with a one-click Java-to-Kotlin converter producing idiomatic, editable output — conversion quality drove adoption.
comparisons.code: // IntelliJ: Code > Convert Java File to Kotlin File

comparisons.note: Won JavaScript by making every .js file already-valid input — migration was per-file and gradual.
Transpiles C to Rust but the output is unsafe, machine-shaped Rust that teams struggle to own — the cautionary case for option C.

recommendation.why: It gives every enterprise estate a named, truthful story. The five importer languages convert into Jet a human would keep, which is what makes conversion feel magical rather than burdensome. C++ gets honesty instead of silence: coexist through the binder, replace by hand behind overlay proof. Elena can put the whole plan on one slide.

whyNot.reason: Java and C# are the largest enterprise estates; leaving them binder-only concedes exactly the market this program targets.
A C++ importer would emit unreadable machine-shaped Jet, violating the ratified editable-output contract and poisoning first impressions in the hardest estates.
One scripting importer cannot carry an enterprise migration story; it reads as a demo, not a path.

recommendation.tradeoff: C++ teams are told plainly that conversion is manual behind the binder, and the five importer tracks land over time rather than all at once — some estates wait for theirs.

decisions.title: Command spelling for Jet's C compiler front end
decisions.gist: What the user types to invoke Jet's C compiler: a jet subcommand, a single-word program, both as one mechanism, or a namespaced command.
decisions.lesson:
Jet will ship a built-in C compiler front end (ratified D-ADOPT-CC1=B). Build systems find a C compiler through the CC variable or an explicit compiler path. Whatever spelling Jet picks becomes the string pasted into Makefiles, CMake caches, and CI files across every estate the wedge targets.

There is one practical trap. CC usually holds a single program name. A value with a space, like "jet cc", works in plain make but confuses some tools. Those tools treat the whole string as one file name, cannot find a program by that name, and abort. Zig users hit exactly this with CC="zig cc" and work around it with tiny wrapper scripts in every affected repository.

The spelling therefore decides the first five minutes of adoption on legacy build systems. This ballot picks it.
decisions.story: Marcus, from the toolchain card, pastes CC="jet cc" into his CMake invocation. CMake stores it as a single compiler path, finds no program literally named "jet cc", and aborts. His first five minutes with Jet become a workaround hunt instead of a build.
decisions.inWild:
$ CC="jet cc" make
  # works — make splits the words

$ cmake -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER="jet cc" ..
  CMake Error: Could not find compiler "jet cc"
  # the space is treated as part of one program name

options.name: jet cc / jet c++ subcommands plus jet-cc / jet-c++ alias binaries
options.detail: One mechanism with two spellings. Humans and docs use the subcommand, matching the zig habit and keeping one front door under jet help. Tools that require a bare program name get the installed single-word alias, so CC=jet-cc pastes safely into every build system on the first try. The alias simply re-enters the subcommand — same code path, same behavior, forever.
options.code:
$ jet cc hello.c -o hello        # humans, docs, muscle memory
$ CC=jet-cc cmake ..              # single word — every tool accepts it
# jet-cc re-executes 'jet cc' — one mechanism, two spellings

options.name: Subcommands only: jet cc / jet c++
options.detail: The cleanest single spelling and the exact zig shape. Every space-hostile tool then needs a user-written wrapper script, so the worst first-run experience lands on precisely the legacy build systems this wedge exists to win.
options.code:
$ jet cc hello.c -o hello
$ cat > cc-wrap.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/sh
exec jet cc "$@"
EOF
# every affected repo re-invents this wrapper

options.name: Standalone binaries only: jetcc / jetc++
options.detail: A single word everywhere, so CC always pastes safely. But the compiler leaves Jet's front door. jet help does not list it, typing jet cc gets an error, and the product surface splits into a second command family.
options.code:
$ jetcc hello.c -o hello
$ jet cc hello.c
  error: unknown command "cc"   # muscle memory from zig breaks

options.name: Namespaced: jet toolchain cc
options.detail: Explicit and greppable, and it groups future toolchain verbs under one noun. Three words in CC fail in even more tools than two, and the ceremony reads as policy jargon to the beginner pass. Drop-in adoption is defeated at the paste.
options.code:
$ CC="jet toolchain cc" make
  # breaks wherever two words already broke, plus more

comparisons.note: Subcommand only; CC="zig cc" breakage is a recurring community issue solved per-project with wrapper scripts.
comparisons.code: $ CC="zig cc" cmake ..   # fails in tools that want one word

comparisons.note: A standalone single-word binary designed to be dropped into CC — the paste-safe pattern option A's alias copies.
Everything is a go subcommand; go tool namespaces the long tail — precedent for option D's grouping.

recommendation.why: Drop-in adoption is the entire point of jet cc, so the spelling must survive every legacy tool's CC handling on the first paste.
