decisions.title: Write the full Zstandard decoder in Jet or wrap libzstd
decisions.gist: Should Core decode real Zstandard data with a decoder written in Jet, or through the approved libzstd C library?
decisions.lesson: Zstandard (zstd) is a compression format. Nix caches send packages as zstd files. Core's zstd decoder reads only stored and repeated-byte blocks, so real cache files fail. Rust Jetpack uses libzstd, a C library D-CODECS1 approved as a bridge; I6 calls such bridges temporary. Whichever option wins, Core owes a full streaming decoder, typed errors, a window-size limit, and one result on every run mode.
decisions.story: Priya ports the Jetpack Nix cache client to Jet. A signed package arrives from a Nix binary cache as a .nar.zst file. Her Jet code must unpack it to check its hash, but Core stops at the first compressed block. She needs to know whether Core will parse these untrusted bytes in Jet or hand them to libzstd, the C library Rust Jetpack uses today.
decisions.detail:
Need: card #3596 item 1. The card says: "core.archive.zstd decodes only raw/RLE blocks, whole-buffer, capped at 64 MiB. Store/NixCache.rs streams real zstd NARs. The Jet port needs a full streaming decoder in Core. This is the approved-bridge question for zstd under I6." This ballot answers only who decodes the blocks. The API shape is D-CORE-CODECSTREAM1, and it is the same under both options.

Rust call sites. The product path is Store/NixCache.rs:745-777: a zstd Decoder wraps the counted, hashed HTTP body and feeds the NAR reader, then checks for trailing bytes. Test-only uses are the level-19 encoder at NixCache.rs:427-446 and decode_all at NixCache/Tests.rs:114. NixIndex.rs:2569-2775 hand-writes a stored-block zstd codec and xxh64, which Core already has. Its decoded limit is 256 MiB (NixIndex.rs:23), above the whole-buffer cap.

Dependency facts. crates/jetpack/Cargo.toml:33-34 pins zstd 0.13 with the note "D-CODECS1: owner-approved native standard-cache zstd stream codec". The file crates/jet-jit/Cargo.toml:37-38 pins the same crate, but no zstd:: call exists under crates/jet-jit. The generated FFI bridge reaches zstd only through the parquet feature list (jet-pkg-model/src/FFI.rs:2254).

Ratified law. D-CODECS1=A shipped gzip and zstd through the bridge, with an I6 sign-off per dependency. D-DEP1 says every bootstrap wrap carries a native-ize obligation. D-CORE-SOURCE-AUTHORITY1=A makes Jet source the authority for Core behavior, with only unexpressible operations in a small kernel. D-CORE-COMPRESS1=A keeps zstd a stream codec beside the archive containers. Gzip already went the Jet way: D-CORE-ARCHIVE-BOUND1=A bounds one shared Jet inflater.

The owner's 2026-09-28 rule on #3665-#3670 keeps only policy-free leaves in Rust, such as syscalls and vetted engines. Option B fits that rule as a vetted engine. Option A removes the need for the leaf. Neither option changes the whole-buffer encoder, which stays a stored-block writer. Rust uses a real encoder only in tests, so committed fixture files replace it.

options.name: Decoder written in Jet
options.detail: Core/archive/zstd.jet implements the whole Zstandard frame format from RFC 8878 in Jet. That covers compressed blocks, entropy tables, and checksums. No new dependency is added. The decoder serves both the streaming reader and the whole-buffer calls, so there is one decoder. The zstd crate pin in jet-jit, which has no users, is removed.
options.technical:
Scope is RFC 8878 decoding. It covers frame and block headers, raw, RLE, and compressed blocks, and literals with Huffman tables, including treeless reuse. It also covers sequences with FSE tables in predefined, RLE, compressed, and repeat modes, and repeat offsets. It checks window and content sizes and the XXH64 content checksum, reusing xxh64 in zstd.jet, and skips skippable frames. Frames that need a dictionary fail with IOError.Unsupported naming the dictionary id (D-CORE-FILEERROR1).

Memory is the window plus one 128 KiB block. The window cap and the reader API come from D-CORE-CODECSTREAM1. The decoder is ordinary Core source, so AOT, jet run, the interpreter, and web run the same code (I9, D-CORE-SOURCE-AUTHORITY1).

Proof owed. The RFC 8878 test frames plus committed .zst fixtures made by the reference zstd tool at levels 1, 3, 19, and 22 with long windows. Differential fuzzing compares Jet output to the zstd tool as a development-only oracle, never a runtime dependency. A paired performance cell times decoding one real NAR against Rust Jetpack's libzstd path. Any loss is carded under the strict gate.

options.name: Leaf over libzstd
options.detail: Core/archive/zstd.jet keeps the API, the window limit, error meaning, and messages. A small Rust leaf wraps the zstd crate, which builds libzstd from C source. It turns input chunks into output chunks and returns only numeric status codes. The leaf is linked into the generated bridge, the JIT host, and the interpreter.
options.technical:
Leaf surface: decoder_new(window_log_max) -> handle; decoder_step(handle, input, output_capacity) -> (consumed, produced, status); decoder_free(handle). It calls ZSTD_decompressStream with ZSTD_d_windowLogMax set from the Jet limit. Jet maps each status code to one IOError kind, so no backend text is parsed.

The approval is D-CODECS1 with the existing zstd 0.13 pin. The bridge keeps D-DEP1's native-ize obligation, so a later Jet decoder is still owed. Web builds need libzstd compiled for wasm32. Without that, web needs a named I9 exception.

Proof owed: the same fixtures as A plus a check that the leaf never allocates past the Jet window limit.

comparisons.note: The klauspost/compress zstd package is a decoder written entirely in Go, with no C library. It shows a memory-safe language can own a full decoder. Docs: https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/klauspost/compress/zstd.
comparisons.code:
d, err := zstd.NewReader(body, zstd.WithDecoderMaxWindow(128<<20))
_, err = io.Copy(out, d)

comparisons.note: Python added compression.zstd to its standard library as a wrapper over libzstd, like option B. Docs: https://docs.python.org/3.14/library/compression.zstd.html.
comparisons.code:
from compression import zstd
with zstd.open("pkg.nar.zst") as f:
    data = f.read()

comparisons.note: Rust has both shapes: the zstd crate binds libzstd, while ruzstd is a decoder written in Rust. Jetpack uses the libzstd binding today. Docs: https://docs.rs/zstd/0.13 and https://docs.rs/ruzstd.
comparisons.code:
let d = zstd::stream::read::Decoder::new(body)?;      // libzstd
let d = ruzstd::decoding::StreamingDecoder::new(body)?; // pure Rust

recommendation.why: Cache files come from the network, and safety is Jet's first priority. A Jet decoder keeps that parsing memory-safe, gives every run mode one source, and ends the bridge's temporary status.
gains: Memory-safe parsing of untrusted cache downloads.
One decoder source for AOT, jet run, and the interpreter.

losses.loss: Decoding may start slower than libzstd.
losses.mitigation: libzstd has years of hand tuning; any new decoder starts behind it, and the speed gate measures it.

losses.loss: Core must write and fuzz a large decoder.
losses.mitigation: Real files use entropy-coded blocks; no smaller part of the format reads them.

whyNot.reason: It puts C parsing of network bytes into every Jet program that reads zstd. The dependency law also marks such bridges temporary, so the work returns later.

recommendation.tradeoff: Core takes on a large decoder and must prove its speed, instead of borrowing libzstd's.

decisions.title: Read and write tar archives entry by entry with kind, mode, and link target
decisions.gist: How should a program read and write tar archives entry by entry, seeing each entry's kind, mode, and link?
decisions.lesson: A tar archive is a list of entries. Each entry has a header, then its bytes. The header holds a name, a kind such as file or link, a mode (permission bits), and a size. Today Core's tar helpers work on one whole buffer and return only names and bytes. Whichever option wins, Core owes bounded memory, long names, true sparse-file sizes, and typed IOError failures.
decisions.story: Priya ports the Jetpack source providers to Jet. Before unpacking a LuaRocks or CPAN tarball, Jetpack refuses links, devices, unsafe names, and oversized entries, including sparse files that expand later. It also writes deterministic OCI image layers. Today Rust shells out to tar -tvzf and parses its text, and Core cannot even report an entry's kind.
decisions.detail:
Need: card #3596 item 3, "Streaming tar reader/writer with mode, type and link headers (Store/Archive.rs, Image OCI layers)". One correction: Store/Archive.rs writes Jet's own jet-hangar-archive-v1 format (Archive.rs:24), not tar. It needs no tar API. Its mode, kind, and link needs match this entry shape only by analogy.

Reader call sites. Provider/fetch.rs:274-315 lists entries with tar -tf and -tvf. It refuses unsafe names and non-file, non-directory kinds, and caps the entry count at 4,096. It caps each entry at 64 MiB and the total at 256 MiB (fetch.rs:12-15). fetch.rs:356-423 parses raw tar headers from gzip -dc output, including PAX and GNU sparse logical sizes, to stop sparse bombs.

luarocks.rs:653-692 refuses symlinks and hard links by kind. luarocks.rs:614-633 and script_registry.rs:1048-1132 extract through tar child processes. The test script_registry.rs:2410-2460 builds sparse archives that must be refused by logical size.

Writer call site. Image.rs:1597-1653 builds deterministic ustar OCI layers. It uses file entries with mode, mtime 0, and uid and gid 0. It silently truncates names longer than 100 bytes (Image.rs:1614), a defect a Core writer removes.

Ratified law applied. D-CORE-COMPRESS1=A: core.archive owns containers, so the new calls sit beside tar_add and tar_get with the same tar_ prefix. D-NETIO-CONTRACT1/2: the reader wraps and is an io.Reader, and failures are IOError. F2: next() returns ?TarEntry. D4: kinds are an enum, never flags. D-BYTESDECODE1: non-UTF-8 names fail loudly. L-A: the whole-buffer helpers stay as presets over the stream. Extraction to disk composes this reader with D-CORE-FILEDIR1's Directory handle, which refuses .. and absolute names.

options.name: Entry reader and writer
options.detail: archive.tar_reader(&source) returns a reader. next() returns the next entry header, or None at the end. The reader itself then yields that entry's bytes, and calling next() again skips any unread rest. archive.tar_writer(&sink) adds files, folders, and links with deterministic headers, and finish() writes the end marker.
options.technical:
```text
archive.tar_reader<R: io.Reader>(source: &R) -> TarReader<R>
  next(&self) -> ?TarEntry !IOError
  read(limit: Int) -> [U8] !IOError; chunks(size: Int{65536})   // current entry
archive.tar_writer<W: io.Writer>(sink: &W) -> TarWriter<W>
  add_file(name: String, body: [U8], mode: Int{0o644}, modified: Instant{epoch}) !IOError
  add_directory(name: String, mode: Int{0o755}, modified: Instant{epoch}) !IOError
  add_symlink(name: String, target: String) !IOError
  add_hardlink(name: String, target: String) !IOError
  finish() !IOError
pub struct TarEntry { pub name: String, pub kind: TarKind, pub mode: Int, pub size: Int, pub modified: Instant }
pub enum TarKind { File, Directory, Symlink(String), Hardlink(String), CharDevice, BlockDevice, Fifo }
```

Reading. Formats are ustar, GNU, and PAX. PAX and GNU long names, long link targets, and PAX size and mtime are applied inside the reader. They are never returned as entries. Sparse files in GNU and PAX formats come back as .File. Their size is the logical size, and holes read as zeros. So a size check counts what extraction would write.

Checks. The header checksum is verified. Numbers may be octal or base-256 and are exact Int values. Names and link targets are at most 4,096 bytes and must be UTF-8. One PAX record set is at most 1 MiB. A violation is IOError.InvalidInput. Volume, multi-volume, and unknown type flags are IOError.Unsupported (D-CORE-FILEERROR1).

End and names. next() returns None at the first all-zero header. A source that ends inside an entry is IOError.InvalidInput with cause "truncated". Names are returned as stored. size is 0 for every kind except File, and mode keeps only the 0o7777 bits. Memory is one header, one PAX set, and the caller's read limit.

Writing. Output is deterministic: uid and gid 0, empty user and group names, ustar magic, and mtime from modified, default the Unix epoch. Names over 100 bytes and link targets over 100 bytes use PAX records. Names must be relative with no .. part, the same rule tar_add uses today, or IOError.InvalidInput. Mode must be within 0o7777. finish() writes two zero blocks and does not close the sink.

Presets. tar_add, tar_get, and tar_names_json keep their names and 64 MiB and 4,096-entry caps but run on this reader and writer. tar_add's long names switch from GNU ././@LongLink records to PAX, so one long-name format remains. Defaults table row: tar_writer writes epoch-0 times and owner 0; override with modified:.

options.name: Visitor callback
options.detail: archive.tar_each(&source, visit) calls visit once per entry with the header and a body reader. Unread bodies are skipped. archive.tar_write(&sink, items) writes a finished list of items. Early stop means returning an error from the callback, and results must be gathered in outer mutable state.
options.technical:
```text
archive.tar_each<R: io.Reader>(source: &R, visit: fn(TarEntry, &TarBody) !IOError) !IOError
archive.tar_write<W: io.Writer>(sink: &W, items: [TarItem]) !IOError
```

Format, check, and determinism rules match A. TarItem holds an entry and its bytes, so the writer needs all items in memory before it starts.

options.name: List, then read by name
options.detail: archive.tar_list(path) returns every TarEntry from a plain tar file. archive.tar_read(path, name) opens the file again and returns one entry's bytes. A .tar.gz must first be decoded to a temporary file, because both calls seek. The writer is a list-based tar_write as in B.
options.technical:
```text
archive.tar_list(path: String) -[FS]> [TarEntry] !IOError
archive.tar_read(path: String, name: String) -[FS]> [U8] !IOError
```

Format and check rules match A. The listing holds every header in memory, and the second call re-opens the path.

comparisons.note: archive/tar returns one Header per Next call and exposes Typeflag, Mode, Size, and Linkname. It expands sparse files, reading holes as zeros. Docs: https://pkg.go.dev/archive/tar.
comparisons.code:
hdr, err := tr.Next()
fmt.Println(hdr.Typeflag, hdr.Mode, hdr.Size, hdr.Linkname)

comparisons.note: The tar crate yields entries whose headers carry entry type, mode, and link name, and each entry is a reader. Docs: https://docs.rs/tar/latest/tar/struct.Entry.html.

tarfile has a stream mode, r|gz, that yields members in order without seeking. Python 3.12 added extraction filters because member names are unsafe by default. Docs: https://docs.python.org/3/library/tarfile.html#extraction-filters.

recommendation.why: Jetpack checks each header and hashes each body while the archive streams from gzip. A reader that returns one typed entry at a time does that in bounded memory, like Go and Rust.
gains: Link and device entries are visible before any extraction.
Deterministic image layers from the same entry type.

losses.loss: Name safety is the caller's check.
losses.mitigation: Tar stores names verbatim; only the code that writes files knows the target folder.

whyNot.reason: A callback makes early stop and results awkward, and its writer holds every entry in memory.
It cannot read a gzip stream without a temporary file, and two passes let the file change in between.

recommendation.tradeoff: Callers write a short loop and check names, in exchange for full headers and bounded memory.

decisions.title: Load a sandbox component chosen at run time against a declared interface
decisions.gist: How should a host load a sandbox component chosen at run time, and still call it with checked types?
decisions.lesson: A sandbox component is a WebAssembly file that runs isolated, with only the rights its host lends. Today plugin.load needs the path written in the source, so the compiler can read the component's interface. Jetpack finds build plugins and compiler extensions only at run time. Whichever option wins, Core owes typed calls or errors, fail-closed imports, and today's fuel, memory, and time limits.
decisions.story: Priya ports jetpack-bin to Jet. When a package declares a build plugin, Jetpack verifies the component's digest from a signed manifest, then must run its build export. The compiler also hands Jetpack a compiler-extension path to analyze. Neither path exists when Jetpack is compiled, so today's plugin.load refuses both.
decisions.detail:
Need: card #3598 item 4, "dynamic-path WASM Component instantiation with bounded fuel/memory (core.plugin.load needs a literal artifact)". The users are the compiler-extension and build-plugin hosts in jetpack-bin, which use wasmtime today. This ballot covers the run-time path only. The fuel, memory, and time override is D-CORE-PLUGINLIMITS1.

Rust call sites. crates/jetpack-bin/src/main.rs:20-23 includes the two host files. main.rs:49-128 reads the manifest and component with size caps, checks both digests, and runs the build export. main.rs:133-193 decodes a snapshot and runs analyze. The hosts are jet-pkg-model Prelude/BuildPlugin.rs:52-124 and Prelude/CompilerExtension.rs:99-249. Tests are jetpack-bin/tests/build_plugin_e2e.rs and compiler_extension_e2e.rs.

What both hosts do. They link zero imports, so a guest that asks for any capability fails to instantiate. Each has one export taking list<u8> and returning list<u8>: build or analyze. Limits are 10,000,000 fuel, 16 MiB memory, 10,000 table slots, and 2,000 ms per call (BuildPlugin.rs:13-19; CompilerExtension.rs:39-51). Plugin.rs:52-57 uses the same numbers for application plugins.

The gap study (#3670) calls CompilerExtension.rs "Not Core" and BuildPlugin.rs a jetpack-only leaf. That is right for the protocol: snapshot schema and response validation stay in the Jetpack and compiler model. The owner rule still forbids Jetpack from keeping its own sandbox host. So the Jet port needs Core to load a run-time path, and this ballot adds only that.

Ratified law applied. D-DEP-WASM1=A: Wasmtime 25 runs components, with fuel, epoch, memory, table, wire, and import limits mandatory, and non-plugin builds never link it. D-PLUGIN1=A and D-FOUND-SANDBOX1=A: the guest declares needs, and the host lends one Authority at plugin.load.

D-PLUGIN-EXPORT1 and D-PLUGIN-VERSION1 freeze the literal-artifact interface, and E1257 reports a changed export. D-SCRIPT-PLUGIN-CLOSE1: close(^plugin). D-MODEL-SIGNATURE1 bound a model output to a source trait through models.open<Trait>, the precedent for option A. The spec says there is no dynamic export lookup (Docs/spec/spec.md:3863-3867), which option B would break. D-DX5-HOOK1 keeps the compiler-extension world import-free.

options.name: Declared interface trait
options.detail: plugin.load gains an optional type argument. plugin.load<BuildStep>(path, policy) accepts a path computed at run time. The interface comes from the Jet trait instead of a frozen artifact snapshot. At load, Core checks that the file exports every trait method with the same component type. The literal form, plugin.load("x.wasm", policy), is unchanged.
options.technical:
```text
plugin.load<I>(path: String, authority: Authority, sha256: ?String{None}) -> Plugin<I>
```

The interface. I must be a trait whose methods take self and use exportable shapes: the D-PLUGIN-EXPORT1 scalars, [U8], and closed Component Model shapes (E1260). The expected world is generated from I by the same generator that builds sandbox worlds. Method names map to WIT export names by the existing rule.

The load check. Every method must be exported with the same component type. Extra exports are ignored and cannot be reached. A missing or changed export gives the E1257 message at run time and names the export and trait. If sha256 is given, Core hashes the exact bytes it read and refuses a mismatch before compiling them. This closes the check-then-load race the build host guards against (main.rs:84-99).

Unchanged from plugin.load: path resolution under the lent Authority with the no-follow resource root, import preflight against the guest's declared needs and that Authority, and the failure-reporting contract. A component with no declared needs gets no imports, which gives the build and compiler-extension worlds their zero-import sandbox. Close is D-SCRIPT-PLUGIN-CLOSE1. Limits are today's defaults unless D-CORE-PLUGINLIMITS1 changes them. The effect row stays that of plugin.load.

Without a type argument, a non-literal path stays E1257 at compile time. Its fix text gains "or name an interface trait: plugin.load<Trait>(path, authority)". I4 needs UI snapshots for the compile error and the run-time mismatch. I9: AOT, jet run, and the interpreter share one Core check in Core/plugin/plugin.jet, the home #3670 assigns to plugin policy.

options.name: Call exports by name
options.detail: plugin.load_dynamic(path, policy) returns a DynamicPlugin. call(export, bytes) runs the named export if it takes and returns bytes. No trait is written, but export names are text checked only at run time. This goes against the spec's rule of no dynamic export lookup.
options.technical:
```text
plugin.load_dynamic(path: String, authority: Authority, sha256: ?String{None}) -> DynamicPlugin
DynamicPlugin.call(export: String, input: [U8]) -> [U8] !PluginError
```

Only list<u8> to list<u8> exports can be called. A missing export or another shape is a run-time error. Imports, limits, and close match A. The spec text at Docs/spec/spec.md:3863-3867 must be amended.

options.name: Keep a Rust host
options.detail: Core does not change. jetpack-bin keeps BuildPlugin.rs and CompilerExtension.rs as a Rust Wasmtime host behind its hidden subcommands. Jet code starts that host as a child process and exchanges bytes over stdin and stdout, as the compiler does today.
options.technical: The Rust host stays in crates/jetpack-bin with its own Wasmtime 25 pin. Its limit constants stay copies of Plugin.rs:52-57, the duplicate #3670 flags. Byte pipes to the child need D-CORE-PROCBYTES1. No Core source changes.

comparisons.note: bindgen! generates a typed host type from a WIT world at compile time. instantiate then checks any run-time file against it. Option A is the Jet form of this, with a trait in place of a WIT file. Docs: https://docs.wasmtime.dev/api/wasmtime/component/macro.bindgen.html.
comparisons.code:
bindgen!({ path: "wit/build.wit", world: "build-plugin" });
let step = BuildPlugin::instantiate(&mut store, &component, &linker)?;

comparisons.note: Extism calls plug-in functions by text name with byte input and output, like option B. Docs: https://extism.org/docs/concepts/plug-in.
D-MODEL-SIGNATURE1 already binds a run-time model output to a source trait through a type argument. Option A reuses that shape for components.

recommendation.why: A trait gives run-time paths the same typed calls that literal paths get today. The load checks the file once, so later calls need no string lookups. It follows the model precedent, models.open<Trait>.
gains: Build plugins and compiler extensions run through Core.
Export mistakes in host code fail at compile time.

losses.loss: A wrong file is found only when loaded.
losses.mitigation: The file is chosen at run time, so the compiler never sees it.

whyNot.reason: Text export names move typos to run time and break the spec's rule against dynamic export lookup.
The owner rule forbids working around a missing Core API inside Jetpack, and it keeps duplicate limits.

recommendation.tradeoff: Hosts write a small trait for each component interface, in exchange for typed calls.

surface.lesson: A sandbox component is a WebAssembly file that runs isolated, with only the rights its host lends. Today plugin.load needs the path written in the source, so the compiler can read the component's interface. Jetpack finds build plugins and compiler extensions only at run time. Whichever option wins, Core owes typed calls or errors, fail-closed imports, and today's fuel, memory, and time limits.

current.note: A path held in a variable is refused, because the interface comes from a literal artifact (jet-sema core_call.rs:7714-7735). Read from source; not run.

wild.note: Wasmtime's bindgen! fixes the interface at compile time and loads any file at run time. Docs: https://docs.wasmtime.dev/api/wasmtime/component/macro.bindgen.html.

options.name: Declared interface trait
options.gist: plugin.load<Trait>(path, policy) checks the file's exports against a Jet trait at load time.
gains: Calls stay typed; a wrong export name fails to compile.
One load call for literal and run-time paths.
Optional sha256 pins the exact bytes loaded.
losses: A file missing an export is found only when loaded.

options.name: Call exports by name
options.gist: A dynamic handle calls any byte-to-byte export named by a text string.
gains: No trait to declare.
Matches both Jetpack hosts exactly.
losses: A misspelled export name fails only at run time.
Only one value shape: bytes in, bytes out.
Breaks the rule of no dynamic export lookup.

proposed.code:
// PROPOSED; NOT RUN.
use core.plugin as plugin

policy :: Authority.from_rights(["FS.Read:{component_path}"])
step :: plugin.load_dynamic(component_path, policy)
response :: step.call("build", request) ?? return Err(failed(component_path))
close(^step)

options.name: Keep a Rust host
options.gist: Core stays unchanged; Jetpack keeps its Rust Wasmtime host and runs it as a child process.
gains: No new Core API.
losses: Jetpack keeps private sandbox code outside Core.
Limits and errors stay duplicated in Rust.

proposed.code:
// PROPOSED; NOT RUN.
host :: process.cmd([jetpack_bin, "__build-plugin-host", manifest, component,
    manifest_digest, component_digest]).stdin(.Stream).stdout(.Capture)
child :: host.spawn() ?? return Err(failed(component))
child.stdin.write_all(request)
receipt :: child.wait() ?? return Err(failed(component))

recommendation.why: A trait gives run-time paths the same typed calls that literal paths get today. The load checks the file once, so later calls need no string lookups. It follows the model precedent, models.open<Trait>.
gains: Build plugins and compiler extensions run through Core.
Export mistakes in host code fail at compile time.

losses.mitigation: The file is chosen at run time, so the compiler never sees it.

whyNot.reason: Text export names move typos to run time and break the spec's rule against dynamic export lookup.
The owner rule forbids working around a missing Core API inside Jetpack, and it keeps duplicate limits.

recommendation.tradeoff: Hosts write a small trait for each component interface, in exchange for typed calls.

decisions.title: Let a host set a sandbox component's fuel, memory, and time limits
decisions.gist: How should a host choose the fuel, memory, and time limits for one loaded sandbox component?
decisions.lesson: Fuel counts the work a guest does; when it runs out, the call stops. Today every component gets fixed limits: 10 million fuel, 16 MiB memory, 10 thousand table slots, and 2 seconds per call. The compiler states its own limits for each extension run. Whichever option wins, those defaults stay, and a guest over a limit stops with a typed budget error.
decisions.story: Priya ports the compiler-extension host to Jet. Each snapshot the compiler sends declares the limits that extension may use. The Rust host ignores them and applies its own copies of the defaults. The gap study says to pass the limits in instead, but Core offers no way to set them.
decisions.detail:
Need: card #3598 item 4 asks for component instantiation "with bounded fuel/memory" for the jetpack-bin hosts. The bounds exist today, but only as Rust constants. D-CORE-PLUGINPATH1 covers loading a run-time path, and this ballot covers the limits alone.

Rust call sites. The constants live in Prelude/Plugin.rs:52-57, Prelude/BuildPlugin.rs:13-19, and Prelude/CompilerExtension.rs:44-51, with the same values three times. jet-pkg-model CompilerExtension.rs:148-177 defines ResourceLimits, which every snapshot declares (CompilerExtension.rs:1029-1075). But analyze_with_host (CompilerExtension.rs:865-923) calls the default-limit analyze, so declared limits are checked in the response yet never applied to the guest.

Prelude/CompilerExtension.rs:184-249 already accepts fuel and timeout per call. The e2e test compiler_extension_e2e.rs:240-260 uses a short timeout and huge fuel to prove the timeout path. Card #3670 says to remove the duplicated constants and pass the limits in. That needs a Core way to pass them.

Ratified law applied. D-DEP-WASM1=A makes fuel, epoch, memory, table, wire, and import limits mandatory. D-CORE-DOCTRINE1 D2 requires every magic default to appear in the defaults table with an explicit override. D-AUTHORITY-NAME1=A says an Authority can only be narrowed, never widened, which rules out option B for raises. C2: an uncommon option is a label.

options.name: Limits value at load
options.detail: plugin.load gains an optional limits: label taking a plugin.Limits value. Each field defaults to today's number, so a bare load behaves exactly as now. The limits apply to every call on that component. Fuel is refilled and the timer restarts before each call. Memory and tables are capped for the component's whole life.
options.technical:
```text
pub struct Limits {
    pub fuel: Int              // default 10_000_000; refilled before each call
    pub memory_bytes: Int      // default 16_777_216; at most 4 GiB (wasm32)
    pub table_elements: Int    // default 10_000
    pub timeout: Duration      // default 2000ms; per call
}
plugin.load(path, authority, limits: Limits{Limits.default()})
plugin.load<I>(path, authority, sha256: ?String{None}, limits: Limits{Limits.default()})
```

A field of zero or less, or memory above 4 GiB, is refused before the component is read. That error is the user-error kind. A guest that runs out of fuel, memory, table space, or time stops the current call with the budget-exhausted kind. The error names the limit and the export. The instance, memory, and table counts stay fixed at one each, and so does the 16 MiB wire cap. Those are safety constants, not tuning.

The defaults live once in Core/plugin/plugin.jet, the home #3670 assigns. The three Rust copies are deleted in the same cutover. The build-plugin request and response caps (64 KiB and 4 MiB) stay host policy in Core/build/build.jet. Defaults table row: plugin.load uses the four defaults; override with limits:. I9: one Core value, marshalled to the Wasmtime leaf on every run mode.

options.name: Limits inside Authority
options.detail: Authority gains budget fields set with with_budget. plugin.load reads the limits from the Authority it already receives. Because an Authority can only narrow, a budget can only go down from the defaults.
options.technical: Authority.with_budget(fuel: ?Int, memory_bytes: ?Int, table_elements: ?Int, timeout: ?Duration) -> Authority. A value above the holder's current budget is refused, like widening a right (E0712). The defaults become the root budget. This amends D-AUTHORITY-NAME1's rights-only Authority to also carry resource numbers.

options.name: Fixed limits only
options.detail: The four limits stay fixed Core constants with no override. Hosts cannot apply limits the compiler declares, and tests of the timeout path must wait the full two seconds and burn full fuel.
options.technical: The constants move once to Core/plugin/plugin.jet under #3670. There is no API change. The compiler's declared ResourceLimits become documentation only, or they are removed from the snapshot.

comparisons.note: Wasmtime sets memory and table caps on the store and fuel with set_fuel. Rust Jetpack refills fuel and arms an epoch timer per call. Docs: https://docs.wasmtime.dev/api/wasmtime/struct.Store.html#method.set_fuel.
Extism puts memory pages and a timeout in the plug-in manifest the host passes at load, like option A's single limits value. Docs: https://extism.org/docs/concepts/manifest.

recommendation.why: Defaults stay safe for beginners, and a host that must apply declared limits writes them in one labeled value. Raises stay visible in the source, where review sees them.
gains: Hosts apply the limits the compiler declared.
Timeout tests run fast with a short limit.

losses.loss: A host can raise limits for a guest.
losses.mitigation: Heavier legitimate guests need more, and the raise is written at the load call.

whyNot.reason: Authority can only narrow, so a heavier guest could never get more fuel. Budgets are also not rights.
The compiler-extension host could not apply the limits the compiler declares, and D2 requires an override for every default.

recommendation.tradeoff: Hosts can raise limits, in exchange for applying declared limits without a Rust host.

surface.gist: How should a host choose the fuel, memory, and time limits for one loaded sandbox component?
surface.lesson: Fuel counts the work a guest does; when it runs out, the call stops. Today every component gets fixed limits: 10 million fuel, 16 MiB memory, 10 thousand table slots, and 2 seconds per call. The compiler states its own limits for each extension run. Whichever option wins, those defaults stay, and a guest over a limit stops with a typed budget error.

current.note: The limits are Rust constants with no Jet control (Prelude/Plugin.rs:52-57). Read from source; not run.

wild.note: Wasmtime hosts set fuel and memory on each store; Rust Jetpack does this per call (Prelude/CompilerExtension.rs:195). Docs: https://docs.wasmtime.dev/api/wasmtime/struct.StoreLimitsBuilder.html.

options.name: Limits value at load
options.gist: plugin.load takes an optional limits: value; every field defaults to today's number.
gains: Bare loads keep today's safe limits.
One labeled value sets fuel, memory, tables, and time.
Every raise is visible where the component loads.
losses: A host can raise limits and give a guest more.

options.name: Limits inside Authority
options.gist: The lent Authority also carries fuel, memory, and time budgets.
gains: One value crosses the boundary.
losses: Authority only narrows, so limits could never rise.
Mixes resource numbers into the rights set.

proposed.code:
// PROPOSED; NOT RUN.

decisions.title: Publish the model descriptor, checked model package, and model error in core.models
decisions.gist: Should core.models publish its model descriptor, checked package, and error types, so the compiler, runtime, and tools share them?
decisions.lesson: A model package pins a machine-learning model: its files, their SHA-256 digests, tensor shapes, and meaning. Programs only call models.open<Trait>. The checks behind it live in Rust (jet_rt::model), and the Jet port of the package loader needs the same types. Whichever option wins, the checks move into Jet under Core/models and give one answer at compile time and run time.
decisions.story: Priya ports jet-pkg-model's Model.rs to Jet. It turns a package's .Model output into a checked model package, and it verifies every file's digest. The compiler loader, the JIT host, and generated programs all run that same check today through Rust types. Her Jet port has no Jet type to return and no Jet error to report.
decisions.inWild:
# MLflow: https://mlflow.org/docs/latest/python_api/mlflow.models.html#mlflow.models.get_model_info
info = mlflow.models.get_model_info("models:/search-embedder/3")
# ONNX Runtime reads the tensor contract from a loaded session: https://onnxruntime.ai/docs/api/python/api_summary.html
print([(i.name, i.type, i.shape) for i in session.get_inputs()])
decisions.detail:
Need: card #3598 item 5, "core.models: ModelPackage/ModelDescriptor/ModelError runtime (jet_rt::model) for jet-pkg-model Model.rs." The mapping receipt for Model.rs names the same gap. It says jetpack only re-exports these types, and the real consumers are the compiler and runtime.

Rust call sites. jet-pkg-model/src/Model.rs:9 re-exports jet_rt::model. Model.rs:21-69 builds a ModelPackage from package facts, and Model.rs:127-150 verifies files through the no-follow package-root resolver. jet-driver/src/Loader.rs:79-103 calls from_facts for every .Model output at compile time.

At run time, jet-jit runtime_host.rs:17566 calls ModelPackage::load. jet-codegen MIRRust.rs:4814 emits a ModelDescriptor literal, and MIRRust.rs:5157 checks it with ModelPackage::from_descriptor. The types themselves are jet-rt/src/model/mod.rs:337-355 (ModelDescriptor), 438-446 (ModelPackage), 923-1003 (the check), and 1703-1716 (ModelError, 12 variants).

Why a decision is needed. Core/models/models.jet says the module does not fabricate model handles and has no functions. So any Jet home for these types is new Core surface. The Rust split between ModelDescriptor and ModelPackage is real: one holds declared fields, and the other is the checked result with derived identity. That makes them distinct types (T3), not two spellings.

Ratified law applied. D-MODEL-PACKAGE1=A: models are typed, versioned packages whose identity cannot drift. D-MODEL-BACKEND1=A: ONNX Runtime stays a pinned provider leaf, and nothing here moves it. D-MODEL-SIGNATURE1=A: models.open<Trait> and embed keep their T !Err results, and no core.models.Embedder is added. D-PACKAGE-MODEL1=A: core.compiler owns the typed package view, which can hold a ModelDescriptor for .Model outputs instead of defining another. I9 and the owner's 2026-09-28 rule put validation, limits, and error meaning in Jet under Core/.

options.name: Public read-only types
options.detail: core.models exports three types. ModelDescriptor holds the declared fields of one .Model output. ModelPackage is the checked result, and only models.check can make one. ModelError is a closed enum. check is pure, and ModelPackage.verify(root) hashes the files. models.open<Trait> keeps its ratified shape and runs the same check inside.
options.technical:
```text
pub struct ModelDescriptor { package, output, signature: ?String, version, license,
    graph: ModelFile, weights: ModelFile, tokenizer: ModelFile, adapter: ?ModelFile,
    inputs: [TensorSpec], outputs: [TensorSpec], provider, preprocessing, pooling,
    normalization, meaning, metric, custom_operators: Bool,
    max_context: ?Int, max_batch: ?Int, max_buffer_bytes: ?Int }
pub struct ModelFile { pub path: String, pub sha256: String }
pub struct TensorSpec { pub name: String, pub dtype: TensorType, pub shape: [TensorDim] }
pub enum TensorDim { Fixed(Int), Named(name: String, min: Int, max: Int) }
models.check(descriptor: ModelDescriptor) -> ModelPackage !ModelError
ModelPackage.verify(&self, root: String) -[FS]> !ModelError
```

ModelPackage has read-only fields: name, output, signature, version, license, files (deduplicated), inputs, outputs, and limits. It also has embedding_identity() -> EmbeddingIdentity !ModelError. Its fields cannot be set from outside, so holding one proves the check ran (T2).

ModelError variants carry the same fields as today's Rust enum. They are MissingPackage, MissingOutput, WrongKind, Declaration, Provenance, Artifact, SignatureMismatch, UnsupportedProvider, CustomOperatorsDenied, ResourceLimit, BufferLimit, and Cancelled. Messages follow the what, why, and fix format (F3).

Ownership. Reading a package.jet into a ModelDescriptor stays with the package model, the Jet port of Model.rs and D-PACKAGE-MODEL1's view. Core needs no package parser. The ONNX provider leaf receives a checked ModelPackage and file bytes only. I9: the compiler loader, the JIT host, generated programs, and the interpreter call the same Core/models source. The Rust jet_rt::model checks are deleted in that cutover.

options.name: Private Core types
options.detail: The same types and checks move into Core/models as private code. models.open<Trait> stays the only public door. The Jet compiler and the Model.rs port reach the check through a compiler-only path. Tools read raw .Model fields from the core.compiler package view.
options.technical: Core/models/models.jet gains non-pub ModelDescriptor, ModelPackage, and ModelError plus the check. The Jet port of Model.rs lives outside Core, so it needs a new compiler-only visibility rule to call them, or it keeps its own copy. Failures reach programs only as the text inside models.open's !Err.
options.code:
// PROPOSED; NOT RUN.
use core.compiler as compiler

facts :: compiler.package() ?? return
fields :: facts.outputs["search_encoder"].fields   // raw text fields
print(fields["license"], fields["weights_sha256"])

options.name: Keep them in Rust
options.detail: jet_rt::model keeps the descriptor, package, errors, and checks in Rust. The Jet port of Model.rs sends package fields to a Rust leaf and parses the text result.
options.technical: A new leaf function takes the encoded fields and returns O:<package> or E:<kind>:<message>, the wire shape Plugin.rs uses. This keeps validation, limits, and error meaning in Rust, against the owner's 2026-09-28 rule, and every run mode must link the Rust checks.

options.name: Remove models from Core
options.detail:
Delete `core.models` and every Core hook for model packages. The owner wants AI support as a library, not Core. If checked model loading is still wanted, it ships as a first-party package outside Core. Its name avoids "model", for example `jetpack.inference`.

Cutover: delete Core/models. Remove its Core registry and dispatcher rows (crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Core.jet:17-19,408-410). Remove model sema (ComputeModels.jet:739-790) and the Rust, web, and JIT lowerings. Remove Jetpack CoreImports and PackageModel model projection. Regenerate tables and update tests/conformance/exclusions.tsv:12 and the model fixture. Old `use core.models` gets a teaching error pointing to the package.
options.technical: The package decides whether the `.Model` package output kind survives. Keeping it moves jet_rt/model and jet-pkg-model model code into that package. Dropping it also removes PackageOutputKind.Model and fixture assets. The ML battery (crates/jetpack/batteries/ml) is already outside Core.

comparisons.note: MLflow separates model metadata (ModelInfo and signature) from loading, so a tool can audit a model it never runs. Docs: https://mlflow.org/docs/latest/python_api/mlflow.models.html#mlflow.models.get_model_info.

ONNX Runtime exposes tensor names, types, and shapes only after creating a session. Option A offers the declared contract before any session exists. Docs: https://onnxruntime.ai/docs/api/python/api_summary.html.

recommendation.why: The owner wants AI out of Core. A first-party package keeps checked loading for those who need it without growing Core or overloading "model".
gains: One model check for compile time and run time.
Typed failures a program can match.

losses.loss: Three public types must stay stable.
losses.mitigation: Code outside Core must name them, and only public types can be named there.

whyNot.reason: A grows Core's public surface for a feature the owner wants outside Core.
B still keeps model loading inside Core.
C keeps model checks in Rust inside Core's runtime.

recommendation.tradeoff: Existing model users migrate to a package in exchange for a Core without AI.

decisions.title: Send a child process's output straight into a file
decisions.gist: How should a program send a child process's output and errors straight into files it opened?
decisions.lesson: A child process writes output and errors. Today Jet can pipe them back to the program, capture them in the receipt, or share the program's own terminal. A supervisor that starts a long-running service needs a fourth choice. The service writes into log files directly, with no copy loop in the supervisor. Whichever option wins, the plan and receipt name each file a child writes to.
decisions.story: Ravi ports Jetpack Services. The supervisor starts a database and sends its output and errors into two log files in the service folder. Rust hands the open files to the child. Jet has no output choice that takes a file, so the ported line does not compile.
decisions.detail:
Need: the Jetpack port (#3590) of Services and the JetOS proofs. A child writes output and errors into files the program opened.

Rust call sites that require it:
```text
crates/jetpack/src/Services.rs:3026-3029            service output and errors into log files
crates/jetpack/src/JetOS/vm_proof.rs:127-129         VM phase output into files
crates/jetpack/src/JetOS/nixos_backend.rs:1284-1285  QEMU errors into a file
Jetpack/Services/Source/Supervisor/Lifecycle.jet:192-219  the port already writes .stdout(.File(^stdout))
```

Current Jet surface. ProcessStreamMode has three unit variants: Stream, Inherit, and Capture (crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib/JetStd/CommonTypes.rs:7-10). The checker and the three tiers list the same three names (Codegen/TIR/tir_to_mir_types.rs:2145, crates/jet-jit/src/Process.rs:1791-1801). No choice takes a file.

The only workaround is .Stream plus a copy loop in a task. The port rule forbids working around a missing Core API. The loop also stops when the parent stops.

Beginner path: open the log with files.create and pass it with .File(^log). Expert path: open with files.append, a mode, and links: .Refuse (D-CORE-FILEOPEN1). Two children, or output and errors, can then share one log without overwriting each other.

Related ballots. The ownership rule matches keep_open from D-CORE-PROCINHERIT1: the spec takes the handle with ^. D-CORE-PROCREPLACE1 keeps a .File stream across the replace. D-CORE-FILECLOSE1 makes writers buffered, so the handoff flushes first.

Seen nearby but not part of this ballot: nixos_backend.rs:1284 discards output with Stdio::null(). Jet has no discard choice either.

options.name: A file output choice
options.detail: ProcessStreamMode gains File(FileWriter). The stdout and stderr settings accept it, and the spec takes the writer with ^. Every child the spec starts writes into that file from its first byte. Jet flushes bytes the program already wrote first, so they stay in order. The program's copy closes when the spec is dropped. The receipt text for that stream is empty, as with .Inherit.
options.technical:
```text
enum ProcessStreamMode { Stream, Inherit, Capture, File(FileWriter) }   // Core dot-literal enum
ProcessSpec.stdout(mode: ProcessStreamMode) -> ProcessSpec   // signature unchanged
ProcessSpec.stderr(mode: ProcessStreamMode) -> ProcessSpec   // signature unchanged
```

Ownership. .File(^out) consumes the writer, so the program cannot write to it or close it afterward. The stdin setting rejects .File at compile time. Reading child input from a file is not part of this ballot.

Append or replace comes from how the writer was opened: files.create replaces, and files.append appends. A spec that is dropped without spawning closes the file.

Order. At spawn Jet flushes the writer's buffer before the child starts. A flush failure returns that IOError from spawn, and no child starts.

Limits. output_limit counts only captured streams. A .File stream is not counted, and the file grows as the child writes.

Unix (Linux and macOS). The child receives a duplicate on descriptor 1 or 2 between fork and exec. The parent's descriptor stays close-on-exec, so other children never see it.

Windows. The handle is duplicated as inheritable and listed alone in PROC_THREAD_ATTRIBUTE_HANDLE_LIST. It becomes hStdOutput or hStdError, and no other handle leaks.

Plan and receipt. ProcessPlan and ProcessReceipt name the stream as a file with the writer's path.

Other settings. .detached() keeps the file. .under(authority) follows the rule .Inherit has today: a non-detached authority-bound spec refuses it before spawn with IOError.InvalidInput. Captured output is what the redactor reads (ProcessPolicy.rs:299-313). replace_process keeps the file as the new program's output.

Errors and effects. Failures are IOError from the flush or from spawn; no new error kind. No new effect: spawn already carries Exec, and opening the writer carries FS. One Prelude spawn path serves AOT, the JIT host, and the MIR evaluator (I9).
options.code:
// PROPOSED; NOT RUN.
stdout :: files.create(stdout_path) ?? return
stderr :: files.create(stderr_path) ?? return
spec :: process.cmd(run).cwd(data_dir)
    .stdout(.File(^stdout))
    .stderr(.File(^stderr))
child :: spec.spawn() ?? return
// The service writes both logs itself; no copy loop.

options.name: Core opens the file by path
options.detail: ProcessStreamMode gains Path(String). Core creates or replaces the named file when the child starts. The program never holds the file.
options.technical:
```text
enum ProcessStreamMode { Stream, Inherit, Capture, Path(String) }
```

The file is created or replaced with default permissions and follows links. An open failure is returned by spawn. Append, mode, and link refusal would need their own labels, copying files.create and files.append.
options.code:
// PROPOSED; NOT RUN.
spec :: process.cmd(run).cwd(data_dir)
    .stdout(.Path(stdout_path))
    .stderr(.Path(stderr_path))
child :: spec.spawn() ?? return

options.name: Separate builder calls
options.detail: Add spec.stdout_to(^writer) and spec.stderr_to(^writer). The output choice keeps its three plain words.
options.technical:
```text
ProcessSpec.stdout_to(writer: ^FileWriter) -> ProcessSpec
ProcessSpec.stderr_to(writer: ^FileWriter) -> ProcessSpec
```

A later .stdout(mode) call replaces an earlier stdout_to, and the reverse. The last call wins.
options.code:
// PROPOSED; NOT RUN.
stdout :: files.create(stdout_path) ?? return
stderr :: files.create(stderr_path) ?? return
spec :: process.cmd(run).cwd(data_dir)
    .stdout_to(^stdout)
    .stderr_to(^stderr)
child :: spec.spawn() ?? return

comparisons.note: An *os.File assigned to Stdout is handed to the child directly, with no copy goroutine. Docs: https://pkg.go.dev/os/exec#Cmd. This is the shape A takes.
comparisons.code:
log, _ := os.Create(stdoutPath)
cmd := exec.Command(run[0], run[1:]...)
cmd.Stdout = log
cmd.Start()

comparisons.note: Stdio::from(File) moves the file into the command, like the ^ handoff in A. Docs: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/process/struct.Stdio.html

recommendation.why: A puts the file where every other output choice already lives. It reuses the ^ handoff from keep_open, and the program opens the file with the options it needs.
gains: Output files follow the same handoff rule as keep_open.
The port's existing line works as written.

losses.loss: The program cannot write to that file handle afterward.
losses.mitigation: Two owners of one handle would mix bytes; open the file again to write more.

whyNot.reason: B opens files by name inside spawn, so append, mode, and link rules need a second copy of the file options.
C adds a second way to set output, and the later call silently replaces the earlier one.

recommendation.tradeoff: The output choice carries an owned file, so one setting decides where each stream goes.

decisions.title: Wait for one key press for a limited time
decisions.gist: How should a full-screen program wait for keys: a timed read, keys on a receiver, or both?
decisions.lesson: A full-screen dashboard reads single key presses and redraws between them. #Live already switches the terminal to raw key input and restores it on exit. Inside it, term.read_key() waits forever. A timed read waits a set time, then returns. A reactive read delivers keys as values on a receiver, waited on beside signals and timers. The owner asked for both; this ballot settles how they share input.
decisions.story: Kai ports the bare `jetpack` dashboard. It redraws the store summary while a load runs, quits on q or Escape, and stops on a service stop request. Rust reads keys with a 100 ms limit. In Jet, read_key blocks until someone presses a key, so the screen freezes. Kai wants a plain timed loop, and a loop that stops at once on a stop request.
decisions.detail:
Owner direction (2026-09-30, question on this ballot): "I want to support both reactive & timed." Option A now does that. The earlier timed-only option is C, and the receiver-only option is B. The earlier poll-then-read option is dropped, because A's timed call already returns the key in one step.

Need: card #3598 and the dashboard port (Jetpack/CLI/Source/Dashboard/DashboardSnapshot.jet:93-106, 244-329). The port calls term.enable_raw_mode() and term.read_key_timeout(...). Neither exists.

Raw mode is already covered. #Live { } (D-TERM1, Docs/spec/spec.md:3007-3045) enters unbuffered, no-echo input and restores it on return, error, and panic. The port should wrap its loop in #Live instead of calling enable_raw_mode. So this ballot proposes no new raw-mode API.

The gap is a time limit and a way to wait on keys beside other events. term.read_key() (Core/term/term.jet:111, Prelude/Core/TermKey.rs:230-239) blocks until bytes arrive. At end of input it returns Unknown, so a loop cannot tell a closed terminal from a strange key.

One mechanism (I8). Both spellings in A sit on one key queue in the Prelude. The timed call is the beginner path. The receiver is the expert path, and it uses the same receiver and wait table as D-CORE-PROCSIGNAL1=A signals.

Why one queue matters. crossterm offers both styles, but its docs forbid mixing poll/read with EventStream. Jet removes that trap: every reader takes from the same queue, so mixing styles never loses or steals a key.

Rust call sites that rely on a timed read:
```text
crates/jet-repl/src/Term.rs:32-38                 raw mode "min 0 time 1": reads wait at most 100 ms
crates/jetpack/src/CLI/dashboard.rs:172-278       loop redraws and retries the store between keys
crates/jet-cli/src/Help/Interactive.rs:764-765    Key::Idle drives resize checks
```

Signals. In raw mode Ctrl+C arrives as a key, not as a signal. A stop request still arrives as a signal on the receiver from D-CORE-PROCSIGNAL1.

Beginner path: term.read_key() inside #Live, unchanged, or term.read_key_within(wait) for a redraw loop. Expert path: term.keys() in the wait table beside signals and timers.

options.name: Both, sharing one key queue
options.detail: Add term.read_key_within(wait) for timed loops and term.keys() for reactive loops. Both take keys from the one queue that #Live owns. Each key goes to exactly one reader, so the two styles mix safely. read_key() stays as it is.
options.technical:
```text
term.read_key_within(wait: Duration) -[IO, Time.Wait]> Key? IOError!
term.keys() -[IO]> Receiver<Key> IOError!
```

One queue. Each #Live block owns one key queue. read_key, read_key_within, and every receiver from term.keys() take keys from it. A receiver reads input only while the program waits on it, so it never holds a key that another reader asked for. Each key goes to exactly one reader, in arrival order.

Timed results. Val(key) is one key, decoded by the same table as read_key (Prelude/Core/TermKey.rs). None means no key arrived within wait. A wait of zero checks without waiting.

Reactive results. The receiver yields each Key through receive(), try_receive(), a loop, or a `key, keys ->` arm in the wait table. It closes when its #Live block ends.

Errors. IOError.InvalidInput for a negative wait. Both calls return IOError.InvalidInput outside #Live, or when #Live could not switch the terminal, so a failed #Live is visible. When input reaches its end, read_key_within returns IOError.Closed and the receiver closes. IOError.Cancelled when the task is cancelled during a timed wait.

Linux: poll on descriptor 0 with the time limit, then one read. macOS: select, because macOS poll does not support terminal devices. Windows: wait on the console input handle and skip focus, mouse, and resize records. Both calls use this one kernel.

AOT, the JIT host, and the MIR evaluator call the one key-queue kernel in the Prelude (I9).

options.name: Keys on a receiver only
options.detail: Add only term.keys(). A timed wait is the wait table with an `after` arm. read_key() stays as it is and shares the same key queue.
options.technical:
```text
term.keys() -[IO]> Receiver<Key> IOError!
```

options.name: Timed read only

options.technical:
```text
term.read_key_within(wait: Duration) -[IO, Time.Wait]> Key? IOError!
```

comparisons.note: crossterm has both styles: poll and read for timed loops, and EventStream for reactive ones. Its docs forbid mixing them in one program. A keeps both and removes that rule with one shared queue. Docs: https://docs.rs/crossterm/latest/crossterm/event/index.html

decisions.title: Read a link inside a held folder after its path is gone
decisions.gist: How should a program read a link inside a folder it holds open once the folder's path stops working?
decisions.lesson: A held folder is a Directory handle from files.open_directory. It keeps working after its path is renamed or vanishes. Jet can already list it and inspect entries without following links. It cannot read where a link inside it points. Passing held files to a child is already solved by keep_open with a pinned number. Whichever option wins, the lease check must pass after the helper exits.
decisions.story: Lena ports Jetpack's executable leases. A short helper builds a sealed folder of links in a private mount, and Jetpack holds that folder open. The helper exits, and the folder's /proc path dies with it. Before each launch Jetpack must check that every link still names its pinned file. The port cannot read those links.
decisions.inWild:
# Python: https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#os.readlink (dir_fd)
fd = os.open(root, os.O_RDONLY | os.O_DIRECTORY)
for name in os.listdir(fd):
    target = os.readlink(name, dir_fd=fd)
decisions.detail:
Need: card #3593 and the Store lease port. The brief asked for the descriptor number of an open handle, to build /proc/self/fd/<n> paths for a child.

The child side is already covered. D-CORE-PROCINHERIT1 A pins a handle at a chosen number with keep_open(^handle, at: Val(slot)). The port already does this. It allocates process-unique slots from 64 up and hands children /proc/self/fd/<slot> paths (Store/Source/Reuse/CacheLease.jet:13-33, 57-73, 152-204; Environment/Source/Shell/NixProjection.jet:137-141, 298-306). No parent descriptor number is needed for that.

The remaining gap is on the parent side:
```text
Jetpack/Store/Source/Reuse/LeaseSnapshot.jet:350-360   holds /proc/<keeper>/root<mount>, then the keeper exits
Jetpack/Store/Source/Reuse/CacheLease.jet:598-610      validate lists wrapper.path and reads each link by path
crates/jetpack/src/Store/Reuse.rs:2507-2509            Rust reads through /proc/self/fd/<dirfd> instead
```

After the keeper exits, the /proc/<pid>/root path is gone, so every later lease check fails in the port. Rust avoids that by reading through its own descriptor path.

Current Jet surface. D-CORE-FILEDIR1 gives Directory list, entry_stat, open, create, rename, remove, and fsync, all by relative name without following links. It has no read_link.

Beginner path: files.read_link(path) for ordinary paths, unchanged. Expert path: a held Directory for paths that may move or vanish.

options.name: Read a link through the held folder
options.detail: Add Directory.read_link(name). It returns the text stored in the link named name inside the held folder. It uses the same name rules as the other Directory methods and never follows a link.
options.technical:
```text
Directory.read_link(name: String) -[FS]> String IOError!
```

Names are plain parts separated by slashes. .., ., empty parts, and absolute names are refused with IOError.InvalidInput. Each earlier part is opened without following links. The last part must be a link.

Result: the link text exactly as stored, not resolved. A missing entry is IOError.NotFound. An entry that is not a link, and link text that is not valid text, follow the rules files.read_link has today.

Linux and macOS: readlinkat on the held descriptor after the no-follow walk. Windows: open the entry relative to the held handle with FILE_FLAG_OPEN_REPARSE_POINT and read a symbolic-link target. A junction or other reparse kind is IOError.InvalidInput naming the kind.

No new effect: FS, as for the other Directory methods. AOT and default jet run share one provider (I9).

options.name: A process-local path for a handle
options.detail: Add handle.view_path() on Directory, FileReader, and FileWriter. It returns /proc/self/fd/<n> on Linux or /dev/fd/<n> on macOS. Ordinary path calls then work through it.
options.technical:
```text
Directory/FileReader/FileWriter.view_path() -> String IOError!
```

Windows has no such path and returns IOError.Unsupported (D-CORE-FILEERROR1). The path is valid only in this process and only while the handle is open.

options.name: The raw descriptor number
options.detail: Add handle.descriptor() -> Int. Callers build /proc/self/fd paths by hand, as Rust Jetpack does.
options.technical:
```text
Directory/FileReader/FileWriter.descriptor() -> Int
```

Unix only; Windows returns IOError.Unsupported.

comparisons.note: os.readlink and os.listdir accept a held directory descriptor, so no path is rebuilt. Docs: https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#dir-fd. A gives the same without a raw number.
comparisons.code:
fd = os.open(root, os.O_RDONLY | os.O_DIRECTORY)
target = os.readlink("tool", dir_fd=fd)

comparisons.note: cap_std::fs::Dir::read_link reads a link relative to a held directory, the shape of A. Docs: https://docs.rs/cap-std/latest/cap_std/fs/struct.Dir.html#method.read_link
comparisons.code:
let dir = Dir::open_ambient_dir(root, ambient_authority())?;
let target = dir.read_link("tool")?;

recommendation.why: A adds the one missing Directory method, so the lease check reads links through the held folder. No path or number escapes that could name the wrong file.
gains: The lease check works after the helper exits.
Held folders keep one no-follow name rule.

losses.loss: Only link reading is added; other path-only tools stay out.
losses.mitigation: A general path to a handle names the wrong file in children, so each need gets a method.

whyNot.reason: B hands out a path that silently names the wrong file in a child or after close.
C puts raw numbers in ordinary code, the thing keep_open was chosen to avoid.

recommendation.tradeoff: One more Directory method instead of a general escape hatch.

decisions.title: Remove the helper copy a Windows self-update leaves behind
decisions.gist: How should Jetpack remove the helper copy that a Windows self-update leaves behind?
decisions.lesson: On Windows a running program cannot delete its own file. Jetpack's self-update runs a helper copy of jet.exe that swaps in the new version, then exits. Rust Jetpack asks Windows to delete the helper at the next restart. Windows allows that only for administrators, so per-user installs keep the copy. Whichever option wins, a leftover helper copy never blocks an update.
decisions.story: Amara installs Jet for her own Windows account and runs a toolchain update. The helper swaps in the new jet.exe and exits. Rust asks Windows to delete the helper at restart, fails without administrator rights, and ignores the error. A .jet-update-<pid>.helper.exe copy stays beside jet.exe after every update.
decisions.detail:
Need: card #3593 and the toolchain update port. Jetpack/Recipe/Source/Toolchain/UpdateInstall.jet:6-8 and 460-463 call files.delete_at_reboot(helper), which Core does not have.

Rust flow (crates/jetpack/src/ToolchainUpdate.rs):
```text
1801-1853   copy jet.exe to .jet-update-<pid>.helper.exe beside it and start the helper
2136-2139   the helper swaps in the new jet.exe, then schedules its own deletion
1940-1956   schedule_delete = MoveFileExW(path, NULL, MOVEFILE_DELAY_UNTIL_REBOOT)
```

Microsoft documents that delay-until-reboot needs the administrators group or LocalSystem. A per-user install gets an access error, which Rust ignores. So in the common case the copy is never removed.

Current Jet surface. files.list_dir and files.remove exist (-[FS]>). On Windows, removing a file whose program is still running fails, so a running helper protects its own copy.

Linux and macOS never create a helper: Unix can replace a running program's file. This ballot changes nothing there.

Beginner path: nothing to write; updates clean up after themselves. Expert path: the same sweep function, which tests can call on a scratch folder.

options.name: The next update removes old helper copies
options.detail: No new Core call. At the start of every Windows toolchain update run, Jetpack removes old helper copies beside jet.exe. A copy that is still running refuses removal and is skipped. The helper stops scheduling anything.
options.technical:
The sweep lists the folder that holds jet.exe with files.list_dir. It removes only regular files whose names match exactly: .jet-update-, then digits, then .helper.exe. It never follows a link, and files.remove on a link removes only the link.

Errors from one removal are dropped. A running helper, a locked file, or missing rights leave that copy for the next run. The update itself continues.

Port change: delete UpdateInstall.jet:460-463 and call the sweep before the new helper is created. Effects: FS, already on the update path. No Core change, so AOT and default jet run behave the same (I9).

options.name: A Core call that removes a file at restart
options.detail: Add files.remove_at_reboot(path). Windows deletes the file during the next restart. Other systems refuse. The port renames its call from delete_at_reboot, because Core's verb is remove.
options.technical:
```text
files.remove_at_reboot(path: String) IOError! -[FS]>
```

Windows: MoveFileExW(path, NULL, MOVEFILE_DELAY_UNTIL_REBOOT). Without administrator rights it returns IOError.PermissionDenied. A relative path is IOError.InvalidInput, because the list is read at boot with no working folder.

Linux and macOS: IOError.Unsupported (D-CORE-FILEERROR1). Unix has no restart delete list and can remove a running program's file directly.

Windows deletes by name at restart. A different file placed at that path before restart is deleted instead. One Prelude provider serves AOT and default jet run (I9).

comparisons.note: Rust Jetpack calls MoveFileExW with MOVEFILE_DELAY_UNTIL_REBOOT and ignores the result. Docs: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/winbase/nf-winbase-movefileexw

recommendation.why: A removes the copy for every user with calls Core already has. It keeps an administrator-only Windows request out of Core.
gains: Per-user installs stop collecting helper copies.
Core needs no new call.

losses.loss: One helper copy stays until the next update run.
losses.mitigation: The helper is still running when it finishes, and Windows keeps a running program's file.

whyNot.reason: B fails without administrator rights, the usual per-user install, so copies still pile up.

recommendation.tradeoff: One leftover copy until the next update, instead of a Windows-only Core call.

decisions.title: C header import engine: read real headers with a full C front end
decisions.gist: What should read C headers for Jet bindings, so real libraries like SQLite and SDL import completely?
decisions.lesson: To call a C library, Jet must read its header file: types, functions, constants, and macros. Jet's binder is a small parser of its own that maps simple declarations and skips the rest. Zig reads headers with a full C front end. `jet cc` already ships a pinned Clang in the Jetpack toolchain.
decisions.story: Dev wants to port a game from C to Jet one file at a time. SDL3's headers have unions, callbacks, and macros. Jet's binder skips most of them, so he would hand-write hundreds of declarations before running anything.
decisions.detail:
Interop wedge status: `jet cc` and `jet c++` exist and use the pinned Jetpack toolchain (crates/jet-cli/src/CLI.rs:1333-1349). `#Export(c)` exists. Foreign builds are on #1347, and cross toolchains are on #758, #1058, and #1060. Header import is the weakest link.

Conflicts: I6 governs compiler crate dependencies and new stdlib dependencies. A adds no crate dependency; it runs the toolchain's Clang as a tool, as `jet cc` already does. Binding output stays a generated `#Bindgen` module, checked by ordinary sema before use.

options.name: Pinned Clang reads headers
options.detail: The binder runs the pinned Clang for the chosen target and reads its syntax tree. It maps functions, records, unions, bitfields, enums, function pointers, variadics, and constant-like macros. Anything it cannot map gets a registered diagnostic.
options.technical: Clang JSON AST plus macro expansion for constants; per-target sysroots from the Jetpack toolchain; results cached in jet-store by header digest and target.
options.code: #Import module c.sqlite3 { header: "sqlite3.h" }

options.name: Full C front end in Jet
options.detail: Implement a C preprocessor and parser in Jet, as Zig is doing with Aro.
options.technical: Large new component; must match Clang on real-world headers.
options.code: #Import module c.sqlite3 { header: "sqlite3.h" }

options.name: Keep the focused parser
options.detail: Extend the std-only parser case by case.
options.technical: No change.
options.code: fn sqlite3_open(...) Int = "sqlite3_open"

comparisons.note: translate-c with a full front end; zig cc bundles libc for cross targets.
bindgen generates bindings through libclang.

recommendation.why: A makes real C libraries import completely now, using the Clang that Jet already pins for `jet cc`.

whyNot.reason: B delays complete imports by years to rebuild a C front end.
C leaves SQLite, SDL, and curl to hand-written bindings.

recommendation.tradeoff: Jet leans on its pinned Clang at binding time, so imported C libraries are complete today.

decisions.title: One lane type: exact widths plus a native, scalable width
decisions.gist: Should Jet's twenty named SIMD lane types become one generic type, plus a native type whose width the machine decides?
decisions.lesson: A SIMD lane type holds several numbers that one instruction processes together. Jet has twenty fixed names, like `F32x8`. Code cannot ask for "the widest width here". Arm SVE and RISC-V vector machines choose their width while the program runs. Automatic vectorization of plain loops stays the default whatever wins.
decisions.story: Ines writes an audio filter. On her laptop the best width is eight floats, on the build server sixteen, and on her Graviton host the CPU decides at run time. Today she writes the kernel twice and cannot use the third machine's width at all.
decisions.detail:
Conflicts: D-SIMD1, D-SIMD2, and D-SIMD3=B ratified the twenty named lanes (Docs/spec/reference/core-library.md:1792-1798). A, C, and D supersede that list. They keep auto-vectorization and the `#Scalar` opt-out. Number parameters (#3505, D-CONSTGEN1=A) are required by A and C; today `Packet<4>` is rejected (probe J5).

One meaning across tiers (I9) and D-DEVMODE1: a native width differs between AOT, the Cranelift JIT, and web. `reduce(.Add)` on `Lanes<T>` therefore folds in one fixed logical order, so every tier prints the same bits. An explicit `reduce_unordered(.Add)` trades that guarantee for speed and is visible in review.

Sizeless values: like Arm's `svfloat32_t`, `Lanes<T>` may live in locals, parameters, and returns, but not in struct fields, lists, or `[T#N]`. On fixed-width targets, the build profile's CPU sets its width; D-CPU-DISPATCH1 decides how one binary uses wider units.

Performance gate: ratification needs a paired cell comparing `sum_sq` written with `Lanes<F32>` and the plain auto-vectorized loop, on AVX2, AVX-512, and an SVE host.

Related ratified law (found 2026-10-02): D-FRED1=A already fixes Float reductions to one eight-way pairwise order in every run mode, which settles the I9 reduction concern for lane sums.

options.name: Exact plus native lanes
options.detail: `Lanes<T, N>` takes a fixed-width element type and an exact lane count. `Lanes<T>` is the native vector for the target, with `.count()` known at run time. Lists gain `.lanes()` and `.lanes<N>()` chunk iteration with a masked tail. The ratified operations stay, plus `shuffle` on exact widths.
options.technical: Defined in Core over compiler lane intrinsics (card #4179). `Lanes<T>` lowers to SVE or RVV registers, or to the profile's widest fixed register. Fixed reduction order is part of the Core definition.
options.code: acc := Lanes<F32>.splat(0.0)

options.name: Keep the named family
options.detail: Keep the twenty ratified names and add more, such as F32x16, as hardware needs them.
options.technical: No change.
options.code: acc := F32x8.splat(0.0)

options.name: Scalars are width-one lanes
options.detail: Every fixed-width numeric type is defined in Core as a one-lane `Lanes` value, as in Mojo.
options.technical: Fixed-width scalars become library aliases; diagnostics, layout, and FFI mapping must hide the lane form.
options.code: type F32 = Lanes<F32Bits, 1>

options.name: Native width only
options.detail: Only `Lanes<T>`; no exact-width lane types in source.
options.technical: Like Highway with only ScalableTag.
options.code: acc := Lanes<F32>.splat(0.0)

comparisons.note: `Int = Scalar[DType.int]`; all arithmetic is SIMD methods over pop operations.
Sizeless vector types cannot be struct members or array elements.
Scalable and fixed tags, with dynamic dispatch across targets.
`#simd[N]T` plus array programming; probe O2 found no SIMD instructions for array math at the tested setting.

recommendation.why: A writes a kernel once for every machine, including run-time-width vectors, and keeps exact widths where data layout demands them.

whyNot.reason: B needs a new name and a new kernel for every width, and cannot use SVE fully.
C changes every fixed-width type's identity for a SIMD convenience.
D alone cannot pin a width; A keeps D's native type and adds exact widths.

recommendation.tradeoff: Jet migrates twenty names once, so lane code follows new hardware with no new syntax.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: claude. Adversarial model family: claude-opus. Fresh agent: OpusAdversary. The adversarial review showed a build-time width cannot express SVE, so A became exact plus native lanes with fixed-order reductions for I9.

Arm SVE and RISC-V vector machines choose their width while the program runs. Automatic vectorization of plain loops stays the default whatever wins.

comptime Float32 = Scalar[DType.float32]

`Lanes<T>` values cannot be stored in structs.

options.gist: Twenty ratified names; add names as hardware grows.
gains: No migration.
Each name says its exact width.
losses: One kernel per width.
No way to use run-time-width hardware fully.

options.gist: Mojo style: fixed-width numbers are `Lanes<T, 1>` in Core.
gains: One arithmetic definition for scalars and vectors.
losses: Every fixed-width type's identity changes, in errors, layout, and FFI.
Exact `Int` cannot join, so two numeric families remain.

decisions.title: Using newer CPU instructions safely in one binary
decisions.gist: How should one Jet binary use newer CPU instructions where they exist and still run everywhere?
decisions.lesson: CPUs add instructions over time, such as AVX-512 on x86. Ratified law builds for a baseline CPU, and an advanced build refuses to start on older machines (D-FFI-ASM-CPU1=B). Today's release builds instead target the build machine's own CPU (card #4192). Experts reach new instructions only through audited assembly. Auto-vectorization stays.
decisions.story: Kai ships a search engine to thousands of customer machines, from old laptops to new servers. He cannot ask customers which CPU they have. He wants one binary that uses AVX-512 where it exists and never fails where it does not.
decisions.detail:
Conflicts: D-FFI-ASM-CPU1=B (baseline by default, explicit flags) stays the default for unmarked code. `Compiler/JetCli/Source/Cli/Host.jet:141` passes `-C target-cpu=native` to release builds against that law; card #4192 fixes it whatever wins. D-OSTARGET2=B made `comptime if $build.os` (then spelled `prep if`) the one dispatch primitive for operating systems; A extends the same primitive to CPU levels inside each copy. D-CORE-CALL1 keeps `__core_intrinsic` compiler-only; A and B add a public, typed `core.arch` instead.

Same bits everywhere: D-DET1 says pure code is reproducible, and I9 requires one meaning across tiers. Copies of a multiversioned function must produce identical bits. Intrinsics that round differently, such as fused multiply-add, are allowed only when the function's effect row admits non-reproducible results. The interpreter and JIT run the baseline copy, so they match it exactly.

AVX-512 and SVE intrinsics need D-LANES1's lane types; 512-bit lanes do not exist today. The start-up probe runs once in the Prelude on every tier.

Related ratified law (found 2026-10-02): D-ACCEL1=A covers measured automatic acceleration of proven kernels; per-CPU copies must compose with it rather than add a second selection mechanism.

options.name: Multiversioned functions
options.detail: `#Multiversion(levels...)` marks a function. The compiler builds one copy per listed CPU level. Inside each copy, `$build.cpu` describes that level, so `comptime if $build.cpu.has(.AVX2)` selects typed `core.arch` intrinsics at build time. At start, the Prelude probes the CPU once and binds the best copy.
options.technical: Typed intrinsics are generated from vendor tables per ISA. Calls from inside a copy go to callees compiled for the same level when they are also marked, else to the baseline. The interpreter and JIT use the baseline copy (I9).

options.name: Run-time feature blocks
options.detail: `cpu.has(...)` returns a Bool and records a flow fact. A `#Target(CPU...)` block is legal only where that fact holds; inside it, intrinsics are callable and codegen enables the features.
options.technical: Blocks lower to outlined functions with target attributes. Callees inlined into a block are cloned so features never leak into baseline callers.
options.code: if cpu.has(.AVX2) { #Target(CPU.AVX2) { ... } }

options.name: Baseline plus build flags
options.detail: Keep D-FFI-ASM-CPU1=B: one CPU level per binary, chosen by build flags. Assembly reaches instructions Jet does not expose.
options.technical: No change beyond fixing #4192.
options.code: jet build --cpu=znver4 --features=+avx2

options.name: Compiler clones hot code
options.detail: A build option compiles hot loops for several CPU levels and dispatches once at start, with no source markers or intrinsics.
options.technical: Function multiversioning chosen by profile or loop heuristics.
options.code: jet build --multiversion=x86_64,x86_64_v3

comparisons.note: Per-target compilation with one dynamic dispatch; the model A adopts.
target_clones builds copies and dispatches through an ifunc.
Run-time detection plus unsafe target_feature functions; the guard is not compiler-enforced.
Target queries resolve at build time with comptime if (std/sys/info.mojo).

recommendation.why: A ships one binary that uses each machine fully, gives experts named instructions, and needs no hand-written fallback.

whyNot.reason: B makes experts write every fallback and invents a new run-time proof.
C leaves newer hardware to separate, opt-in fleet builds.
D speeds beginners but gives experts no way to name an instruction.

recommendation.tradeoff: Marked functions grow per CPU level, so one binary uses new hardware safely.
