comparisons.note: One long spelling per flag; a short letter form is the only extra name.

recommendation.why: One rule picks every survivor: the short name that reads right beside its command and partner flags. Removed names teach the kept one, so no script fails silently.
gains: Help lists one name per switch.
Scripts and docs agree on one spelling.
Flags read naturally: --up beside --down.

whyNot.reason: Longer names repeat the command's own word and break the --up/--down pair.
It keeps two names for one switch, against the one-spelling rule.

recommendation.tradeoff: A one-time script update in exchange for one name per switch.

decisions.title: Remove the unused #wire field marker instead of renaming it
decisions.situation: Jet accepts a marker spelled #wire on struct fields, but nothing in the compiler reads it, so writing it changes nothing. It is one of two lowercase markers left, and the owner directed that markers be capitalized. Renaming it would keep a marker that silently does nothing. This vote decides whether #wire is removed, or kept as #Wire with or without a job.
decisions.gist: Should the do-nothing #wire field marker be removed, or kept as #Wire?
decisions.lesson: A marker is a # tag on code, such as #Skip on a field. Jet's registry lists every marker. The data-format markers already exist: #Rename sets a field's outside name per format, and #Skip leaves a field out.
decisions.explainer:
Today #wire is accepted on any field and ignored. No decision defines it and no program uses it. Its only other mention is a zero-use triage entry in a test.

The jobs a wire marker might do already have markers. #Rename("user_id", json: "userId") names a field for each format. #Skip leaves a field out. #Encode, #Decode and #Codable request the codecs. The open casing ballot for outside names builds on #Rename.

Under A, #wire is deleted. Writing it gets the normal unknown-marker error with a did-you-mean, which suggests #Rename or #Skip.

Beginner path: no change, since nobody writes it. Expert path: the existing format markers.
decisions.story: Ana sees #wire in the marker list and puts it on a field she wants sent as JSON. Nothing changes in her output, and nothing tells her why.
decisions.detail:
Code facts, checked 2026-10-05 on the dev worktree.

crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Markers.jet:213 declares marker wire($sites: [.Field]). The same file declares Rename at :126, with per-format names for json, cbor, csv, toml, yaml, xml, args, env, db and layout. It declares Skip at :128, and Encode, Decode and Codable at :79-86.

tests/truthfulness.rs:609 lists wire in the zero-use triage, citing card #1830, which is done. The Core-foundations catalogue (Docs/research/core-foundations-2026-10-04.md, row 31) found no source use, no defining decision and no arguments. The row entered in commit 413ac90b6 without a ruling.

D-MARKER-CASE1=A (2026-10-05) says #allow and the unused #wire get capitals. Owner question q00mjarf (2), from 2026-10-01, asks whether #wire is renamed, given a meaning, or something else. The owner rule of 2026-10-01 says only the owner removes features, hence this ballot.

Open ballot D-WIRE-CASE1 maps Jet names to outside names through #Rename and a package naming key. A second field marker for the same job would give two spellings for one meaning, which I8 forbids.

Research. serde (Rust), System.Text.Json (.NET) and Go's encoding/json each have one per-field rename and one skip mechanism. None ships a marker that is accepted and ignored. Silent acceptance of a no-op tag is the wrong way: users believe it works.

options.name: Remove #wire
options.detail: Delete the marker row, its test entries and its triage line. Writing #wire gets the unknown-marker error, whose did-you-mean suggests #Rename or #Skip.
options.technical: Remove marker wire from Prelude/Markers.jet and the truthfulness zero-use entry. Add wire to the retired-marker teaching table, pointing to #Rename and #Skip. Both compiler halves read the one registry (I9). The #allow to #Allow rename under D-MARKER-CASE1 is unaffected.

options.name: Rename to #Wire, no job
options.detail: Capitalize it as directed and keep it accepted on fields. It still does nothing.
options.technical: Rename the row to Wire. Keep the zero-use triage entry. Writing it compiles and has no effect.

options.name: Give #Wire the outside-name job
options.detail: Make #Wire("userId") set a field's outside name, beside or instead of #Rename.
options.technical: Either a second spelling of #Rename, or a migration of every #Rename use and of the open D-WIRE-CASE1 design to the new word.

comparisons.note: One struct tag per format sets the outside name; a dash skips the field (pkg.go.dev/encoding/json).

recommendation.why: A marker that compiles and does nothing misleads people. Its possible jobs already belong to #Rename and #Skip, so removing it loses nothing and completes the PascalCase cleanup.
gains: No marker silently does nothing.
One way to name and skip fields.
The marker list is fully capitalized.

whyNot.reason: It keeps a marker that compiles and does nothing, which misleads anyone who writes it.
It duplicates #Rename, giving two spellings for one job.

recommendation.tradeoff: Removing an unused name rather than renaming a no-op.

decisions.title: Which characters can a name use, and how Jet warns about look-alike names
decisions.situation: Jet already lets you name things in many languages, but the rule has holes. A Hindi name fails with a confusing error, and so does an accent typed as a separate mark. A Latin a and a Cyrillic a quietly become two different names, and an invisible filler letter is a valid name. You are deciding which characters names may use and how Jet handles look-alikes; we recommend Unicode's standard name rule plus a look-alike warning.
decisions.gist: Which characters may names use, and how should Jet handle names that look identical?
decisions.lesson: A name is the word you give a value, like `total`. Unicode can store one letter as one piece or as a letter plus an accent mark. Today Jet accepts letters and digits, even an invisible filler letter, and keeps no single stored form. Hidden direction marks are blocked by separate work, whichever option wins. Every Jet compiler must read one shared character table.
decisions.story: Asha teaches programming in Pune. Her students name variables in Hindi, the way they think about the problem, and Jet stops partway through नमस्ते with 'doesn't mean anything here'. Her colleague Lukas reviews a pull request where a Cyrillic а sits beside a Latin a; the two names look identical, and Jet says nothing.
decisions.detail:
Exercised 2026-10-05 with release jet $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/candidates/dev-05ea86f65/jet. Probes and outputs are in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/mine/legwork/languages-b/probes/.

Probe A: NFD café gives E0001 'The character U+0301 doesn't mean anything here (yet)'. Its Why text wrongly calls the mark unprintable. Probe C: नमस्ते gives E0001 on U+094D, the virama; vowel signs such as U+0947 are already accepted as alphabetic. Probe D: Latin a and Cyrillic а bind two names and print 1 then 2, with no warning. Probe E: U+202E in a comment and U+2066 in a string literal compile and run.

Source reading: both lexers accept alphabetic or numeric scalars only (Compiler/JetLexer/Source/Lexer/Scan.jet:47-55; crates/jet-lexer/src/Lexer/Scan.rs:772). The self-hosted lexer uses Core's approximate classifier (#4426). So the two compilers can disagree on which names are valid.

Batch witnesses: in CURSED (BiFt4vw1-uM 13:29-24:08) an agent added emoji names by changing only the start and continue tables. The Bun copy then emitted JavaScript that could not run, and the compiler copy segfaulted. A name rule is end-to-end law. DreamBerd (_oiBWfuf0Oo 03:52-04:31) shows the demand for emoji names. D-EXT-EMOJI1=A already rejected an emoji file extension, partly over invisible variation selectors.

Rule-9 research, legwork resources 01-10. Rust RFC 2457: UAX #31, NFC, confusable warning, and the NFC over NFKC rationale. Rust CVE-2021-42574 advisory: deny lints for the nine direction marks in literals and comments. It suggests escapes and found 5 affected crates, none malicious.

Trojan Source paper (Boucher and Anderson, arXiv 2111.00169, section 7.6): ban direction controls in specs and compilers. Use escapes for legitimate text, and keep defenses on by default. PEP 3131: XID with combining marks, normalized to NFKC. C++ P1949R7: UAX #31 and NFC, emoji ill-formed, homoglyphs left to tools.

Go spec: no canonicalization, so accented forms differ. Swift: broad hand-written ranges that include U+200B to U+200D and U+202A to U+202E. Zig #4151: closed for ASCII names plus @"..." quoted names. UAX #31 and UTS #39 introductions.

What worked: UAX #31 with NFC is the converged rule in Rust and C++, and Python uses the NFKC variant. Direction-mark bans shipped in Rust 1.56.1 with negligible ecosystem impact. What failed: hand-made ranges in Swift and pre-23 C++ admitted invisible or accidental characters. No normalization, as in Go and Jet today, makes same-looking names differ.

Evidence gap: no friction data for confusable warnings beyond Rust's note that they stay warnings for forward compatibility. Shared work for any option: one generated character table read by both compilers, the spec.md:47-48 rewrite, registry, grammars and goldens.

Scope change at distill on 2026-10-05. Hidden direction marks in source (probe E, CVE-2021-42574) already have an owner: #3881 criterion [#4204]. That work needs no owner vote, because it follows the ratified UTF-8 source rules. So this ballot drops direction marks, and every option inherits that fix.

Adversarial pass, 2026-10-05, same release; probes in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/mine/legwork/adversary2/. hangul.jet: the invisible Hangul filler U+3164 binds and prints a name today, the trick behind the 2021 'invisible JavaScript backdoor' write-up by Certitude. vs16.jet: U+FE0F after a is E0001 today, yet plain XID_Continue admits it.

subscript.jet: v₀, x² and ⓐ are valid names today and print 13; plain XID rejects all three. So plain UAX #31 would both reopen a hole and break working names.

A therefore adopts two UAX #31 standard profiles added in Unicode 15.1: the Default-Ignorable Exclusion Profile (section 7.3) and the Mathematical Compatibility Notation Profile (section 7.1). UAX #31, fetched from unicode.org/reports/tr31 on 2026-10-05, points to UTS #55, Unicode Source Code Handling, for their use in programming languages. Swift and Julia already accept subscript names.

Only circled letters such as ⓐ remain lost; a repository search found no .jet file using circled, subscript or superscript names. Rust additionally warns on Restricted characters (uncommon_codepoints); A removes the invisible ones at the rule instead.

options.name: Every script, one stored form, look-alike warning
options.detail:
Names follow Unicode's default identifier rule. A name starts with a letter or underscore, then letters, combining marks and digits. So Hindi, Arabic, Thai and accented names all work. Unicode's standard math add-on keeps names Jet accepts today, such as v₀ and x², and adds ∂, ∇ and ∞.

Invisible characters are never part of a name. That closes today's hole where the invisible Hangul filler ㅤ is a valid name, and it keeps out invisible variation selectors. Circled letters such as ⓐ, which Jet accepts today, are not letters under the rule, so they stop being names.

Each name is stored in one normal form. An é typed as one piece and an e plus an accent are the same name. The formatter rewrites names, never text inside quotes, to that one form once.

Different letters that only look alike, such as Latin a and Cyrillic а, stay two names. Two such names in one package get a warning naming both, and so does a single name that mixes scripts to look like another word. Emoji are not names, as in Rust and C++. Invisible direction marks are rejected by separate, already-approved security work in every option.
options.technical:
Identifier = (XID_Start | '_') XID_Continue*, the UAX #31 default identifier, with two UAX #31 standard profiles. The Default-Ignorable Exclusion Profile (section 7.3) removes Default_Ignorable_Code_Point characters such as U+3164, U+115F, U+034F, U+200B-U+200D and U+FE00-U+FE0F.

The Mathematical Compatibility Notation Profile (section 7.1) adds ID_Compat_Math_Start (∂, ∇, ∞ and their styled variants) and ID_Compat_Math_Continue (subscript and superscript digits and signs). No Jet lexer uses those symbols as operators. The Unicode version is pinned with the Core UCD data of #4426.

Identifiers are NFC-normalized at lex time; string and comment contents are never normalized. ASCII names pass the NFC quick check, so ASCII-only code pays no normalization cost. RFC 2457 explains NFC over NFKC: math letters stay distinct, and search tools find NFC text. Field names used as wire keys use the NFC spelling.

The confusable check uses the UTS #39 skeleton per package, also against keywords, plus the UTS #39 mixed-script confusable check for a single name (Rust's mixed_script_confusables). It is a warning only (D-LINTPOLICY1).

One generated table is read by the Rust and self-hosted lexers and by the casing check (D-CASE-LAW1, Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Casing.jet). That check already accepts an uncased first letter for both PascalCase and snake_case (Casing.jet:138-160). It must also count combining marks and math-profile characters as word characters, or Hindi type names and ∂f would fail E0357. Route, registry and file names keep their own rules.

Backends must spell every accepted name in their output. Rust and JavaScript reject math-profile characters, and the Rust emitter only prefixes names with __jet_ (Compiler/JetCodegen/Source/Emit/Context.jet:432-436). So emitted names encode any character outside the target's identifier set; the CURSED witness in detail shows why.
options.code:
café :: 1        // either typing of é is one name
नमस्ते :: 3       // works
v₀ :: 0          // math subscripts keep working
a :: 4
а :: 5           // warning: looks like `a` on line 4

options.name: English letters only
options.detail: Names use A to Z, digits and underscore, as in Zig and early Rust. Text and comments still hold any language. Look-alike names cannot exist, but students and teams who name things in their own language lose that, and existing accented names must be renamed.
options.technical: Identifier = [A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*. No normalization or confusable table needed for names.
options.code:
cafe :: 1        // café as a name: error, use ASCII
naam :: 3        // the Hindi spelling is an error; write naam
print("नमस्ते")   // fine inside text

options.name: Keep today's letters
options.detail: Keep the current rule: letters and digits as Unicode classifies them, with no combining marks, no single stored form and no look-alike check. Scripts that need marks stay broken, and look-alike names stay silent.
options.technical: Status quo: Compiler/JetLexer/Source/Lexer/Scan.jet:47-55 (unicode.is_alphabetic / is_numeric, approximate per #4426) and crates/jet-lexer/src/Lexer/Scan.rs:772 (char::is_alphabetic).
options.code:
café :: 2        // e + accent mark: E0001
नमस्ते :: 3       // E0001
а :: 5           // silent second name

comparisons.note: UAX #31 identifiers with NFC normalization; confusable_idents warns (warn, not deny, so new confusables never break builds); 1.56.1 added deny-by-default lints for direction marks in literals and comments. A crates.io scan found 5 crates with those marks, none malicious. RFC 2457; blog 2021-11-01.
comparisons.code:
let café = 1;
let а = 5;   // warning: confusable_idents

decisions.title: Should unused-name warnings reach fields never read and cases never built?
decisions.situation: Jet already warns about unused imports, unused variables, private functions nobody calls, and exports nobody imports. It says nothing about a struct field that is written but never read, or an enum case that is matched but never created. In a growing app these leftovers mislead new readers about which data matters and can keep costly data moving. You are deciding whether the existing unused-name warnings reach inside types; we recommend yes, with encoding and foreign code counted as real use.
decisions.gist: Should Jet warn about struct fields no code reads and enum cases no code creates?
decisions.lesson: A field is one named part of a struct. A case is one choice in an enum. Today Jet's unused warnings stop at whole names, so a dead field or case stays silent. Whichever option wins, library `pub` items stay exempt and warnings never block a build.
decisions.story: Ravi joins a team whose `User` type has a `nickname` field and whose `Plan` enum has a `Legacy` case. He spends an afternoon preserving both in a refactor before learning that no code reads `nickname` and nothing ever creates `Legacy`.
decisions.detail:
Exercised 2026-10-05 with release jet $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/candidates/dev-05ea86f65/jet on probe $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/mine/legwork/languages-b/probes/F-member-liveness.jet. `jet check` exits 0 with exactly one Warning [L0104] (unused_private_fn) for `unused_helper`. No warning names `nickname` or `Legacy`. `jet run` prints a, 3, free, pro.

Current law: D-STRUCT-LIVE1=A (Docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:7596-7601) warns on unused imports, bindings, private functions and unreachable package or application exports. Warnings follow D-LINTPOLICY1, the repair is delete or `_name`, and library `pub` is exempt. Its recommendation called this one law: every declared name is reachable or carries the `_` mark. Fields and cases are declared names it does not yet reach.

Source witness: the ReScript interview (yKl2fSdnw7w 52:39-60:06). reanalyze finds 'you're never actually reading the name field' and 'this variant you're never constructing'. Teams switch it on, get thousands of findings, and remove old experiments. ReScript-Relay reuses the facts in CI to drop over-fetched GraphQL selections.

Rule-9 research, legwork resources 11-15. Rust 1.57 release notes and PR 85200: derived Clone and Debug no longer count as reads, a compatibility break for deny(dead_code). reanalyze README: the use rules above, @dead and @live annotations, and automatic annotation writing.

Periphery README: index-store analysis misses synthesized Codable, Equatable and Hashable reads, so it needs retain flags. Objective-C dynamic dispatch is unanalyzable. staticcheck U1000: field accesses use fields, and unnamed structs are assumed fully used.

What worked: in-compiler analysis (Rust) sees derives and runs in normal checks. ReScript users report large cleanups. What failed: external tools such as Periphery raise false alarms where they cannot see synthesized code. Counting trivial derived reads hid real dead fields until Rust changed the rule. Evidence gap: no measured false-positive rates; adoption claims are speaker and README testimony.

Design-away in A: Jet's compiler sees its own derives, encoding and reflection, so A counts them precisely instead of offering retain flags. FFI-exported layouts and foreign returns count as use, replacing reanalyze's @live. The existing `_` rename replaces @dead.

options.name: Fields and cases join the unused warnings
options.detail:
Jet's unused-name warnings also cover struct fields that no code reads and enum cases that no code creates. Writing a field does not count as reading it. Matching a case does not count as creating it.

Encoding or decoding, derived equality, hashing or ordering, reflection, and foreign code all count as real use. So data that leaves the program never warns. Derived printing and cloning do not count, because they touch every field by construction.

The fix is the one Jet already teaches: delete it, or rename it with a leading underscore.
options.technical:
Extends the D-STRUCT-LIVE1 liveness pass to members over the closed package or application graph.

A field is live if a field access, a destructuring pattern, encode or decode derivation (Dyn.from, decode<T>), derived Eq, Hash or Ord, reflection (D-METADEPTH1), or an FFI-exported layout reads it. A case is live if an expression, decode, or a foreign return constructs it.

Derived printing and Clone do not make members live, the Rust PR 85200 lesson. Library `pub` members are exempt. The warning class follows D-LINTPOLICY1, the machine fix is delete or `_` rename (D-NAME-SIGIL1), and both compilers give the same verdicts.

options.name: Report only when asked
options.detail: Normal checks stay as they are. A separate check option lists dead fields and cases for cleanup sessions. This is how ReScript's reanalyze and Swift's Periphery work, as tools users run on purpose.
options.technical: Same member analysis as A behind an opt-in `jet check --members` report; no default warnings.

options.name: Whole names only
options.detail: Keep D-STRUCT-LIVE1's four warnings: imports, bindings, private functions and unreachable exports. Fields and cases stay unchecked.
options.technical: Status quo; exercised by probe F (only L0104 fires).

comparisons.note: Built-in dead_code warns 'field is never read' and 'variant is never constructed'. Rust 1.57 (PR 85200) stopped derived Clone and Debug from counting as reads; the release notes warn this broke builds that deny dead_code.
reanalyze is a separate analyzer. A case is dead if never constructed, and matching does not count. A field is dead if never read, and creating does not count. @live marks FFI uses it cannot see.
comparisons.code:
reanalyze.exe -dce-cmt root/containing/cmt/files
// reports dead record labels and variant cases (README rules; output text not captured)

comparisons.note: External indexer finds assign-only properties, but synthesized Codable, Equatable and Hashable code is invisible to it, so it needs retain flags to avoid false alarms.
Field accesses mark fields used; unnamed struct types are assumed to use all fields to avoid false positives.
comparisons.code:
staticcheck -checks U1000 ./...
// reports unused fields of named structs (output text not captured)

recommendation.why: A finishes the rule Jet already teaches: every declared name is used or marked with `_`. Counting encoding and foreign code as use avoids the false alarms external tools suffer.
gains: Dead fields and cases appear where people already look.
No new marker or command.

losses.loss: An older app may see many new warnings.
losses.mitigation: Warnings never block, and each carries a one-step delete or rename fix.

losses.loss: A field kept for later warns until renamed.
losses.mitigation: Renaming it with a leading `_` records the intent and silences it.

whyNot.reason: B hides the finding behind a command most people never run, as ReScript's separate analyzer shows.
C leaves the longest-lived dead code invisible while smaller dead names warn.

recommendation.tradeoff: Jet accepts a one-time burst of warnings in older apps to keep dead data visible from then on.

decisions.title: What a backward range like 10..1 does in a loop
decisions.situation: A range such as 10..1 counts from a bigger number to a smaller one. Today a loop over it runs zero times and nothing warns, so a countdown that forgot its step silently does nothing. A beginner course shows the trap, and the instructor says she makes it often. You decide what it means; we recommend a check error when both ends are written numbers, and an empty loop when the ends are computed.
decisions.gist: When a range's start is bigger than its end, should Jet refuse it, count down, or run zero times?
decisions.lesson: A range names the numbers a loop visits, such as 0..9. A step is the optional third part, as in 0..10, 2. Counting down needs a minus step: 10..1, -1. Today 10..1 without that step quietly visits nothing. A makes that a check error when both ends are written numbers, keeps computed ranges like 0..n-1 empty when n is zero, and writes down what a minus step means. B counts down automatically. C keeps today's silence with an advisory warning.
decisions.explainer:
A range is the list of numbers a loop walks through. In Jet, 0..9 visits 0 through 9, and 0..<10 stops before 10. A third part, the step, says how far each move goes: 0..10, 2 visits the even numbers.

Today a range whose start is bigger than its end, such as 10..1, visits nothing. Nothing reports it. A step of -1 does count down: 10..1, -1 visits 10 through 1. The written rules only describe positive steps, so the minus step works without being stated anywhere.

Option A splits the case by what the compiler can see. When both ends are written numbers, a backward range with no minus step is a mistake. The check reports it and offers the minus step. When the ends are computed, a backward range stays empty, so the common 0..n-1 loop stays correct for an empty list.

A also writes down the minus-step rule. A minus step counts down from the start and includes the end when it lands on it. A step that points away from the end is a check error.

Option B makes every backward range count down. Option C keeps today's empty loop and adds a warning that shows only in the check.
decisions.story: Maya writes a rocket countdown: loop i in 10..1 { print(i) }. The program prints nothing, the check is clean, and she spends ten minutes looking for a bug in print. The fix was one missing step: 10..1, -1.
decisions.detail:
Observed on dev-05ea86f65 on 2026-10-05 (probe p17 and the v3-P2 re-mine). Both loop i in 10..1 and loop j in 0..1, -1 print nothing, and jet check reports no problems. loop i in 10..1, -1 counts down. S19 specifies strides only as a positive source stride and makes a dynamic nonpositive stride E0123. D-RANGE-EXCL1=C says only that a half-open a..<b is empty when a >= b (syntax-decisions.md:574, 590-591).

Inclusive a..b with a > b has no written meaning. Card #4629 currently plans an advisory lint plus a written stride law, which would choose the meaning without a vote.

Sources: Python course 4M87qBgpafk (Boot.dev), the countdown exercise where the instructor says she has made this mistake many times (claims v3-P2:PYB-3, PYB-61, PYB-2; learning-compilers:PY81).

Proven approaches. Python, Rust (10..=1), Kotlin (10..1; downTo counts down), Ruby ((10..1).to_a) and Haskell ([10..1]) all make a backward range empty, silently. Swift's closed range traps at run time when lowerBound > upperBound. That catches the constant mistake but would also crash 0...n-1 for an empty list.

Clippy's reversed_empty_ranges lint (correctness group, deny by default) flags constant backward ranges, because the empty loop is almost always a bug. It does not touch computed ranges. Option A takes the Clippy rule as a check error, Swift's insistence that direction is written, and Python's empty result for computed bounds.

options.name: Written backward ranges are an error; computed ones are empty
options.detail: When both ends are written numbers and the start is bigger, a range with no minus step is a check error that offers the minus step. A step whose sign points away from the end is also a check error. When either end is computed, a backward range is empty, as today. A minus step counts down from the start and includes the end when it lands on it.
options.technical: Sema folds both endpoints and the stride when they are constants. Constant start > end with no stride, or with a positive stride, reports a registered error at the range with a fix edit inserting `, -1`. Constant start < end with a negative stride reports the same error with the reverse fix. S19 gains the negative-stride rule: visit start, start+step, ... while the value stays >= end, inclusive. Runtime ranges are unchanged. One rule for loops, ranges stored as values (D-RANGE-VALUE1) and slices on every tier and in the compile-time evaluator.

options.name: Backward ranges count down by themselves
options.detail: A range whose start is bigger than its end visits its numbers in reverse with no step written. This holds for computed ends too.
options.technical: Range iteration picks the direction from the endpoints at run time. Computed ranges such as 0..n-1 visit 0 and -1 when n is 0, so every index loop over a possibly empty list needs a guard.
options.code:
loop i in 10..1 { print(i) }   // 10, 9, ... 1

loop i in 0..n - 1 { }   // n == 0: visits 0 and -1

options.name: Keep the empty loop, add a warning
options.detail: Backward ranges stay empty everywhere. A new advisory warning marks written backward ranges in the check and the editor. Warnings do not show on jet run.
options.technical: Adds one advisory lint over constant endpoints and writes the negative-stride rule into S19. Runtime behavior is unchanged.

comparisons.note: A backward range is empty; counting down needs a negative step.
A backward closed range stops the program when it is built.
A backward range is empty; Clippy denies written backward ranges by default.

recommendation.why: A catches the written mistake before the program runs, where it is always a bug, and keeps computed loops like 0..n-1 safe for empty lists. Counting down stays one visible step, and the rule for minus steps is finally written.
recommendation.tradeoff: A program that wrote a backward constant range on purpose to skip a loop must delete the loop instead.
gains: A forgotten countdown step is reported before running.
Empty-list loops such as 0..n-1 keep working.
Minus steps get a written meaning.

losses.loss: A deliberately empty constant range no longer checks.
losses.mitigation: Nobody needs a loop that can never run; the error's fix offers the minus step, and deleting the loop says the same thing more clearly.

whyNot.reason: B makes 0..n-1 visit 0 and -1 for an empty list, turning a silent skip into a wrong index.
C keeps the silent empty loop, and its warning is hidden on jet run, where beginners work.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Check that loop i in 10..1 is a registered check error with a fix edit inserting `, -1`. Check that 0..10, -1 and 10..0, 2 are errors with the reverse fix.

Check that 10..1, -1 visits 10 through 1 and that 10..0, -3 visits 10, 7, 4, 1. Check that 0..n - 1 runs zero times for n == 0 on every tier and in the compile-time evaluator.

Check the same rule for stored Range values and list slices. Write the negative-stride rule into S19 and close the reversed-range lint plan on #4629.

surface.gist: When a range's start is bigger than its end, should Jet refuse it, count down, or run zero times?
surface.lesson: A step is the third part of a range, as in 10..1, -1. Without it, 10..1 visits nothing today. A makes a written backward range a check error and keeps computed ones empty. B counts down by itself. C keeps the silence with a warning.

current.note: The loop runs zero times and the check is clean.
current.code:
loop i in 10..1 { print(i) }
// prints nothing, no message

wild.note: Clippy denies a written backward range by default.

options.name: Error when written, empty when computed
options.gist: Written backward ranges fail the check; computed ones stay empty.
gains: A forgotten countdown step is caught.
Empty-list loops keep working.
losses: A deliberately empty constant range fails the check.

options.name: Count down by itself
options.gist: Backward ranges visit numbers in reverse.
gains: No step needed to count down.
losses: 0..n-1 visits 0 and -1 for an empty list.

options.name: Empty with a warning
options.gist: Today's empty loop stays; the check warns.
gains: No program changes behavior.
losses: jet run still prints nothing and says nothing.

proposed.code:
loop i in 10..1 { }
// warning (check only): never runs

recommendation.why: A written backward range is always a mistake, so A reports it with the fix. Computed ranges stay empty, so loops over empty lists stay correct.
gains: Countdown slips are caught before running.
Minus steps get a written rule.

losses.loss: A deliberately empty constant range fails the check.
losses.mitigation: Delete the loop; the fix offers the minus step otherwise.

whyNot.reason: B turns empty-list loops into wrong indexes.
C stays silent on jet run.

recommendation.tradeoff: Intentionally empty constant ranges must be deleted.

designAway.loss: A deliberately empty constant range no longer checks.
attempts: Make every backward range an error, including computed ones. Rejected: index loops over empty lists would stop the program.
Limit the error to constants. Kept: only written numbers can be backward by mistake at check time, and they never need to be.

decisions.title: Whether Jet Learn can run in a web browser with nothing installed
decisions.situation: Jet Learn is Jet's built-in exercise track, and today it runs only inside the installed toolchain. Many beginners meet a language in a browser first: the Python course in the mining run runs Python itself in the page, so learners install nothing. Jet already compiles to WebAssembly, the format browsers run. You decide whether Learn gets a zero-install browser lane; we recommend the same exercises running in the page, with the compiler itself in WebAssembly.
decisions.gist: Should Jet Learn also run in a web browser with nothing installed, and if so, where does the compiler run?
decisions.lesson: WebAssembly is a code format every modern browser runs. A compiles Jet's checker and runner to WebAssembly, so the same Learn exercises run inside the page with no install and no server. B compiles exercises on a hosted server, as the Go and Rust playgrounds do. C keeps Learn install-only.
decisions.explainer:
Jet Learn opens an exercise, asks for a prediction, runs the learner's code and reveals what happened. Jet chose to keep it inside the toolchain and offline, so learning and real work use the same compiler. That choice stays.

The missing piece is the first ten minutes for someone who cannot or will not install a toolchain. Browser-first learning is now common. The course mined on 2026-10-05 runs Python inside the page with Pyodide. The TypeScript playground runs the real compiler in the browser, and Roc ships its whole compiler as about 6 MB of WebAssembly.

Option A adds a browser lane over the same exercises. Jet's checker and runner compile to WebAssembly and load in the page, so nothing runs on a server and the page works offline after its first load. Exercises that touch files or the network get in-memory test doubles, which Jet already uses in tests. Progress can be exported to the installed jet learn.

Option B compiles on a hosted server, as the Go and Rust playgrounds do. Option C keeps Learn install-only.
decisions.story: Nia, a school student on a locked-down laptop, wants to try Jet after a friend's demo. She cannot install anything. The Python course her class uses runs in the browser, so she stays with Python.
decisions.detail:
Current state: D-LEARN1 ships jet learn as an in-toolchain, offline exercise runner, and D-LEARN-FEEDBACK1 fixes predict-then-reveal. Jet has a web target (D-WASM1, D-FREESTAND-WASM1) and source-defined playgrounds (#2464). No record covers a browser lane for Learn (claim v3-P1:PYA-068). Card #4630 owns the zero-experience beginner arc.

Sources: the Boot.dev Python course (4M87qBgpafk), which runs CPython compiled to WebAssembly in the browser (claim v3-P1:PYA-068). Also Roc's in-browser REPL, built as a traffic-proof static page with the whole compiler as about 6 MB of WebAssembly (DzhIprQan68, claim languages-a:R43). And TypeScript's browser-hosted compiler (learning-compilers:AH2).

Proven approaches. Pyodide, the TypeScript playground and Roc run the real toolchain in the page with no server cost and no remote sandbox. The Go Playground, Rust Playground and Kotlin Playground compile on servers. That needs sandboxing, rate limits and uptime, and the Rust playground limits which crates and how much run time a program gets.

The known failure of in-browser toolchains is a large first download. Option A loads lazily, caches across visits and keeps a written payload budget.

options.name: Same exercises, compiler in the page
options.detail: Jet's checker and runner compile to WebAssembly and run inside a static page that loads the Learn track. Nothing runs on a server, and the page works offline after the first load. Exercises that use files or the network run against in-memory test doubles. Progress exports to the installed jet learn.
options.technical: Build the front end, checker and the interpreter or WebAssembly back end for the browser profile (D-FREESTAND-WASM1). Load lazily with a measured payload budget and cache. Learn track content and checks are shared byte-for-byte with jet learn. Effects use D-EFFECT-HANDLE1 scoped replacements.

options.name: Compile on a hosted server
options.detail: The page sends code to a Jet server that checks and runs it in a sandbox and returns the output. The first load is small, but the lane needs servers, sandboxing and rate limits, and it stops working offline.
options.technical: A hosted runner service with per-request sandboxing and quotas. The same track content is served from it.
options.code:
// browser sends source to the Learn service
// server runs jet learn check and returns the report

options.name: Install only
options.detail: Learn stays inside the installed toolchain. The website points beginners to the installer first.
options.technical: No change.
options.code: jet learn   // after installing the toolchain

comparisons.note: CPython compiled to WebAssembly runs courses in the page.
Code compiles on a hosted server with sandbox limits.
The whole compiler ships as WebAssembly for an in-browser REPL.
comparisons.code: // roc-lang.org REPL: about 6 MB of WebAssembly, static hosting

recommendation.why: A removes the install barrier with no servers to run or secure, and learners see the real Jet checker, not a copy. It reuses the WebAssembly target and test doubles Jet already has.
recommendation.tradeoff: The first visit downloads the compiler once.
gains: A beginner can start Learn on any machine with a browser.
No server cost, sandbox or outage.

decisions.title: Does Jet need const or frozen parameters beyond read access?
decisions.situation: In C++ a programmer writes const on a parameter to promise the function will not change it. In Jet every parameter without a mark is already read-only, and the compiler also stops anyone else from changing that value while the call runs. The caller's variable may still be changeable before and after the call. You are deciding whether Jet adds anything on top: a C++ style const keyword, or a frozen parameter that demands a value nobody can ever change. We recommend neither, because read access already gives a stronger promise at no cost.
decisions.gist: Should Jet add a const or frozen parameter kind, or is today's read parameter enough?
decisions.lesson: A read parameter is one with no mark: the function may look but not change it, and nobody else may change it during the call. Frozen means changed by nobody, ever, made with freeze(x). A keeps read as Jet's const and freeze for lasting immutability. B adds a parameter kind that demands a frozen value. C adds a C++ style const keyword.
decisions.explainer:
Jet has three ways to pass a value. No mark means read. &T means exclusive write, and the caller writes & too. ^T means the function takes ownership, and the caller writes ^.

A read parameter is passed as a plain pointer to the caller's value. Nothing is copied, even when the caller's variable is mutable. During the call, no one may change it: passing the same list as read and as write in one call is a compile error, and links that might alias are checked.

That is stronger than C++ const in three ways. It is deep, so fields inside cannot change either. It cannot be cast away. And it also binds every other writer, which is what lets a compiler keep values in registers.

freeze(x) makes a deeply immutable value that stays that way forever. Tasks may share frozen values without locks, and any write through them is a compile error.
decisions.story: Omar comes from C++ and asks whether Jet passes his large mutable list by copy when a function only reads it, and whether he should mark it const for speed. He also wonders whether the function could see the list change halfway through.
decisions.detail:
Owner question 2026-10-05: how does Jet handle const params; what if the values are mutable; do we lose performance?

Current law: D-MEM1 makes an unmarked parameter read, enforced, never elevated. D-MEMREF-EXCL1=A stops any write while a read is live: proven at compile time where possible, checked at run time for aliasing links. D-CONC-FREEZE1=A gives freeze(x) for lasting deep immutability. The memory proposal (Docs/proposals/memory-model-2026-10-05.md sections 4.3 and 4.6) puts read parameters in zero-copy class Z0. It calls their no-alias facts the main speed prize, emitted only after an independent re-proof (card #4619).

Exercised on dev-05ea86f65 (probes in $JET_STATE_ROOT/scratch/OwnerFeedback/sem-probes). p01: a mutable list passed to a read parameter lowers to Rust &Vec<JetInt>, a shared reference with no copy. Rust gives such references LLVM noalias readonly facts. p02: nums passed as read and &nums in one call is E0204. p03: a write through a read parameter is E0202.

p05: a write through a frozen value is E1113. p04: storing a read parameter in a struct field copies it automatically. Returning it as-is is E0120, an inconsistency filed in the report.

Corpus: 34,680 named parameters in Examples, Core and Compiler. 81.7% are read, 17.6% write and 0.7% take. Receivers: 248 read, 89 write, 30 take. Five freeze calls exist, all in Examples.

Other languages: Mojo's default argument convention is an immutable read-only reference, with mut and owned as the marked forms, the same shape as Jet. Swift's default is borrowing with exclusivity enforcement. D has transitive const and immutable. Pony's val means nobody can write. C++ const is shallow and removable with const_cast.

options.name: Read is Jet's const
options.detail: No new keyword. An unmarked parameter keeps meaning deep, call-long, no-copy read access. freeze(x) stays the way to make a value immutable forever. Hover and jet inspect show each parameter's promise in words.
options.technical: No grammar change. Hover and the honest-signature view (D-HONEST-SIG2) print read as "read: nobody changes this during the call". The native backend emits no-alias read facts for read parameters once MIR Lint re-proves them (memory proposal 5.8).
options.code:
fn total(xs: [Int]) -> Int { ... }   // read: no copy, nobody changes xs during the call

nums := [1, 2, 3]
print(total(nums))      // nums is mutable; still no copy
&nums.push(4)

options.name: Add a frozen parameter kind
options.detail: A parameter can demand a value that can never change, written with a new mark. Callers pass freeze(x) or a value already frozen.
options.technical: A fourth access kind beside read, write and take. Sema checks the argument's frozen fact. Useful for long-lived caches and cross-task sharing, which freeze already covers.

options.name: C++ style const keyword
options.detail: Parameters become changeable by default, and const marks the read-only ones, as in C++.
options.technical: Reverses D-MEM1's default. Every read parameter in the corpus gains a keyword.
options.code: fn total(xs: const [Int]) -> Int { ... }

comparisons.note: The default argument convention is an immutable read-only reference; mut and owned are marked.
comparisons.code:
fn total(xs: List[Int]) -> Int: ...     # read by default
fn fill(mut xs: List[Int]): ...

comparisons.note: const is shallow and can be cast away, so it gives no aliasing guarantee.

recommendation.why: Jet's read parameter already does what const promises, and more: it is deep, cannot be cast away, and stops other writers during the call. That costs nothing and copies nothing, even for a mutable caller value.
recommendation.tradeoff: C++ programmers do not see the word const; the hover and the docs say read.
gains: No copy for read parameters, mutable caller or not.
A deeper promise than C++ const, with no keyword.
freeze stays the one lasting immutability tool.

losses.loss: Newcomers may not realize read is enforced.
losses.mitigation: Hover prints the promise in words, and E0202 names the read mark when a write is tried.

whyNot.reason: B forces callers to freeze copies for functions that only read during the call, and adds no speed.
C reverses Jet's safe default and adds a keyword to 82% of parameters.

decisions.checkInstructions: Check that hover and jet inspect describe read parameters in words. Fix the E0202 fix line so it names the parameter's & mark, not a := binding. Confirm the native backend emits no-alias read facts only after MIR Lint re-proof. Keep the probe showing a mutable caller value passed by pointer with no copy.

decisions.title: Automatic WebP images in the Jet web framework
decisions.situation: Photos are usually the heaviest part of a web page, and the WebP format makes them roughly a quarter to a third smaller at the same visual quality. Jet's web framework serves image files exactly as written and has no image pipeline yet. Every major web framework now converts images automatically, but they differ on when they do it. This vote decides whether Jet converts at build time, on first request while running, or never automatically, and which formats are on by default.
decisions.gist: When should the Jet web framework convert page images to WebP: at build, on first request, or never automatically?
decisions.lesson: WebP and AVIF are newer image formats that browsers read; almost every browser supports WebP. Conversion can happen once while building, or on demand while the server runs. Jet's image library is ratified but not built yet. Whichever option wins, original files stay available as a fallback.
decisions.explainer:
Under A, a page writes `web.image("hero.jpg", alt: "Our team")`. At `jet build`, Jet writes WebP versions at up to three widths (640, 1280 and 1920 pixels, never larger than the original), named by content hash so browsers can cache them forever. The page gets a `<picture>` element with a srcset, plus the original file as the fallback. JPEG photos use lossy quality 75, the default of Next.js, Hugo and Squoosh. PNG images use lossless WebP, so graphics never blur.

If a WebP file would be larger than the original, Jet keeps the original. Animated GIFs are left alone.

`jet dev` converts on first request with the same encoder and the same cache, so dev and build output match. AVIF is one setting away (`images: .{ formats: [.AVIF, .WebP] }`) because it encodes several times slower. Images users upload while the app runs are not converted automatically; the image library offers an explicit call for them.

Beginner path: write web.image and get smaller pages. Expert path: set widths, quality, formats, or turn conversion off per image.
decisions.story: Ana builds a portfolio site with twenty phone photos. Each is 4 MB, and the home page takes eight seconds to load on a train.
decisions.detail:
Jet facts, checked 2026-10-05: no image pipeline exists. core.image is ratified (D-CORE-IMAGE1=A) as Jet-owned PNG, JPEG and GIF decode, PNG and JPEG encode, and nearest-neighbour resize under explicit budgets. It has no Core module yet, in Core/ or the CoreLib. Core/net/mime.jet:108 already maps webp. BuildContext lists b.add_asset_bundle in the spec (spec.md:4060, D-BUILDTARGET1) with no implementation. Core/web/web.jet has page and app records but no asset handling.

Framework survey [defaults from current docs; verify at ratification]:
- Next.js next/image. on-demand at request time through /_next/image, Accept-header negotiation, images.formats default ["image/webp"], AVIF opt-in ("AVIF generally takes longer to encode but compresses smaller"). Quality 75, disk cache in .next/cache/images, encoder sharp (Apache-2.0, over LGPL libvips).
- Astro astro:assets: default output WebP; build time for static pages, an on-demand endpoint for server-rendered pages; <Picture formats={["avif","webp"]}> for more; sharp by default.

- Nuxt Image: IPX provider (sharp) on demand in server mode, prerendered for static; NuxtPicture adds WebP with original fallback.
- SvelteKit @sveltejs/enhanced-img: build time; emits AVIF and WebP automatically with the original fallback.
- Gatsby gatsby-plugin-image: build time; formats ["auto","webp"] default, AVIF opt-in.
- Eleventy Image: build time; formats ["webp","jpeg"] by default.
- Hugo: build-time image processing with quality 75 default and WebP output; results cached in resources/_gen.
- Vite: no built-in conversion; plugins (vite-imagetools, vite-plugin-image-optimizer).

Savings. Google's WebP study reports lossy WebP 25-34% smaller than JPEG at equal SSIM, and lossless WebP 26% smaller than PNG (developers.google.com/speed/webp/docs/webp_study, webp_lossless_alpha_study). AVIF typically saves more than WebP versus JPEG (web.dev AVIF article; Netflix tech blog 2020). Browser support: WebP is supported by all current major browsers (Safari since 14/macOS Big Sur), about 95%+ of users; AVIF since Safari 16.4 and Edge 121 (caniuse.com) [approximate shares].

HTTP Archive Web Almanac (Media and Page Weight chapters) reports images as the largest byte share of a median page.

Why build time: Jet's build already knows every referenced image, so there is no server CPU, no writable cache, and static hosting works. Accept-header negotiation needs Vary: Accept, which fragments CDN caches; <picture> lets the browser choose with one cache key per file.

decisions.title: Where the WebP and AVIF encoders come from
decisions.situation: Converting images needs an encoder, the code that turns pixels into a WebP or AVIF file. Jet's image library is planned to be written in Jet with no outside code, but a full WebP encoder is a large piece of work and an AVIF encoder is far larger. Image code written in C has a long record of serious security bugs. This vote decides whether Jet writes its own WebP encoder, wraps Google's open-source library, or wraps libraries for both formats now.
decisions.gist: Should Jet write its own memory-safe WebP encoder, or wrap Google's libwebp and an AVIF library now?
decisions.lesson: An encoder writes an image format; a decoder reads it. libwebp is Google's permissive-license WebP library. Jet accepts outside libraries only by owner decision through a reviewed bridge. Whichever option wins, the web pipeline's settings and output names stay the same.
decisions.explainer:
Under A, core.image gains a WebP decoder and encoder written in Jet: lossless first (used for PNG sources), then lossy for photos. The web pipeline turns WebP on by default for each source type only once its encoder passes a measured gate. Output size within a stated margin of libwebp at equal quality, and speed inside Jet's performance gate. Until lossy passes, JPEG photos stay JPEG, so nothing gets worse.

AVIF is not built now; it returns as its own owner decision if measured demand appears. Owner directive 19 rules out a Rust encoder such as rav1e, so that decision would weigh a Jet encoder against a C library such as libaom.

Why write it in Jet: the 2023 libwebp heap overflow (CVE-2023-4863) was exploited in the wild through every browser and app that bundled the library. A Jet encoder and decoder cannot have that class of bug, needs no new dependency, and runs the same on every tier and target, including the browser build.

Beginner path: no difference. Expert path: the encoder is ordinary Jet code they can read and tune.
decisions.story: Ben's app accepts profile photos. A crafted WebP file in a C library crashes the server, or worse; he never chose that library, a framework bundled it.
decisions.detail:
Jet facts, checked 2026-10-05. I6 (AGENTS.md): compiler and seam crates use path dependencies only; any new stdlib external dependency needs an owner decision and an approved bridge pattern. D-CORE-IMAGE1=A: core.image is Jet-owned with no ambient filesystem or process image library. D-CORE-ARCHIVE-BOUND1: one shared Core inflater for image work. No core.image module exists yet.

Revision by OptionQuality1, 2026-10-07. Owner directive 19 (2026-10-06) removes Rust from the toolchain: host access goes through Jet's own foreign-function surface inside vetted #Unsafe Core internals. The posted B linked libwebp through a Rust bridge crate, and C named rav1e, a Rust AV1 encoder. B and C now bind the C libraries through Jet's own foreign-function surface, and C uses libaom, the C reference AV1 encoder. Their new shared loss is a C compiler or prebuilt per-platform libraries in the toolchain. Options, letters and the recommendation are otherwise unchanged.

Licences and sizes [approximate line counts]: libwebp BSD-3-Clause (Google; encoder sources on the order of 20k lines of C with SIMD paths). Libavif BSD-2-Clause. Libaom BSD-2-Clause plus the AOM patent licence. rav1e BSD-2-Clause (Rust AV1 encoder, on the order of 100k lines; excluded by directive 19). Libvips LGPL-2.1+ (sharp, used by Next.js, Astro and Nuxt, bundles it). image-webp MIT/Apache-2.0 (pure Rust decoder plus lossless encoder; no lossy encoder; cited as precedent only).

Security: CVE-2023-4863 (heap buffer overflow in libwebp's lossless decoder, exploited in the wild, patched across Chrome, Firefox, Electron apps and many Linux packages, September 2023). Google's security blog reports most high-severity browser bugs are memory-safety bugs and documents moves to memory-safe parsers.

Performance gate (AGENTS.md): Jet must beat matched peers per cell; image encoding inside the build is part of the build-time cell for the web workload. The gate in A makes default-on wait for a passing measurement rather than shipping a slower or larger encoder.

Compression evidence for staging: Google's lossless study puts lossless WebP 26% below PNG, so the lossless stage alone delivers savings on PNG-heavy sites.

options.technical: core.image.webp: VP8L lossless encode and decode, then VP8 lossy encode. Gate: size within a stated margin of libwebp at equal SSIM on a fixed corpus, and encode time within the build-time cell comparator. No Rust or C dependency; uses the shared Core inflater where applicable.

recommendation.why: Image codecs parse untrusted bytes, and C codecs have shipped exploited bugs. A Jet encoder needs no dependency, runs on every target, and only turns on by default after it measurably matches libwebp, so users never get a worse default.

decisions.title: Spelling a deliberate copy now that copies are rare
decisions.situation: Today a Jet programmer writes ~x to make an independent copy of a value. The tilde was picked when Jet demanded a written copy almost everywhere, but Jet now moves or shares values by itself. In Jet's own code about 87 of every 100 tildes would then be unnecessary, and the rest keep a snapshot of something that later changes. This vote decides how that rare, deliberate copy is spelled; we recommend the plain method x.copy().
decisions.gist: Should a deliberate copy be written x.copy() instead of ~x?
decisions.lesson: A copy is a second, independent value: changing one never changes the other. Jet moves a value at its last use, and values stored in two places share data until one changes. A local name made with saved :: board is only a live view, so Jet stops board from changing while saved is still used. That snapshot case is the only place you write a copy.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: you almost never write a copy. When Jet stops you because a saved name is still looking at something you change, the error offers one fix: add .copy().

Expert path: under a policy that forbids hidden copies, every copy is spelled .copy(), so a reviewer can search one word. The memory model's cost classes and denials are unchanged.

Shared by every option: the compiler still decides move or share when nothing is written, and an explicit copy still costs nothing until someone writes.
decisions.story: Mia keeps a saved game board while play keeps changing the live one. She writes saved :: board, and Jet says the board cannot change while saved is still looking into it. She wants one obvious way to say make my own copy.
decisions.detail:
Owner feedback, 2026-10-05: the memory proposal suggests ~ is no longer needed as a copy sigil. Consider MyVar.Copy() if copies are rare, freeing ~. Methods are snake_case under the casing law (D-SHAPE-CASE1=C), so the spelling is .copy().

History. D-CAP2/S4 shipped the word copy x on 2026-07-04. At that time D-MEM1 made every copy of a reused value a hard error (E0209). D-SHAPE-COPY1=A replaced the word with ~x on 2026-07-15, by the owner's rule that the rarest marked ownership act gets the last leftover mark. That ballot records that the owner declined a method x.copy() on 2026-07-15, when copies were still written everywhere. This ballot exists because the owner now proposes the method himself, after the premise changed.

D-COPY-DEFAULT1=A later moved the choice to the compiler: last use moves, reuse shares, and the first write copies. The memory-model proposal (section 4.4) says ~x is never needed for speed or for the checker. It only means an independent snapshot. D-SIGIL-ALGEBRA1=B retires ~| exclusive-or, so after both changes ~ has no meaning.

Jet already has the method for some types. Lists, maps, sets, Bits, text and byte buffers have a built-in .copy() today (Collections.rs method tables; Examples/features/collections/set.jet:38 and text/strings.jet:38). A probe on the dev candidate accepts xs.copy() and "jet".copy(), and rejects p.copy() on a plain struct with E0102. So today those types have two copy spellings, ~xs and xs.copy(). Option A makes the method the only one and extends it to every copyable type.

The word copy is still teaching-reserved: copy xs gives E0991, and fn copy(self) gives E0003, so no type can declare a copy method today. Module functions such as files.copy(from, to) and math.copy are not methods. Jet has no uniform call syntax (D-UFCS1 declined), so they keep their names under every option.

Metrics, 2026-10-05. A comment- and string-stripped census covered every .jet file in Examples/, Core/ and Compiler/: 287,354 code lines. The script is $JET_STATE_ROOT/scratch/OwnerFeedback/tilde-classify.mjs. It found 1,927 prefix-~ sites with a name operand: Examples 357, Core 969, Compiler 601. Compiler has 48 more on parenthesized expressions.

Each site was classified by what follows in its function. The copied name is never used again at 790 sites (41%), so a move is identical. It is only read again at 893 (46%), so sharing is identical. It is written again at 236 (12%), where a snapshot may be meant.

That is at most one meaningful copy per about 1,200 code lines, and 8 in the 33,506 lines of Examples. The classifier treats any later write to the root name as meaningful, so 236 is an upper bound.

Live probe on the dev candidate (jet check, 2026-10-05). saved :: board followed by &board.push(4) is E0212, and its fix text already says make an owned copy. Sharing into a struct field without ~ is accepted today.

Other languages. Swift SE-0377 added copy x as a contextual keyword, and the compiler may still remove the copy. Hylo's specification writes a.copy(). Rust writes .clone(). Mojo uses the ^ transfer mark and copies copyable types implicitly. No mainstream language spells copy with a one-character mark.

options.name: The method x.copy()
options.detail: Every copyable value has a built-in copy() method that returns an independent value. Lists, maps, sets and text already have this method today, so A extends it to every type and removes the second spelling. It is owned by the compiler: a type cannot redefine it, and it lowers to the same share-until-write copy as today's ~x. It chains like any method. ~x becomes a teaching error whose fix rewrites it, and the E0212 fix text offers .copy().
options.technical:
Expr::Copy keeps its node; only the surface changes from prefix ~ to a reserved method name resolved before ordinary method lookup. The existing collection, text and buffer copy() rows fold into that one built-in. copy stays teaching-reserved, so fn copy on any type stays rejected; the message changes from E0003 to one naming the built-in, and E0991 (copy x) now points at x.copy(). Module functions such as files.copy(from, to) are not methods and keep their names.

#Policy(copies: .Explicit), !Mem.Copy diagnostics, editor ghost hints and jet fmt --explicit-copies print .copy(). Amends D-SHAPE-COPY1=A, D-ITER-COPY1=A and D-MEM-COPYSEM1=A's spelling only; semantics of D-COPY-DEFAULT1=A and D-MEM-COPYSEM1=A unchanged. One cutover rewrites the 1,975 existing sites with jet fix, and deletes the 87% that the classifier marks as move or share once the share-on-reuse build lands.
options.code:
board := [1, 2, 3]
saved :: board.copy()      // my own snapshot
&board.push(4)
print(saved.len())          // 3

grid := input.copy().rotate()

options.name: Keep ~x
options.detail: The tilde stays the copy mark. It is one keystroke, it is already in every example, and the compiler still decides move or share when nothing is written. Chaining a method needs parentheses. Lists, maps, sets and text keep their existing .copy() method too, so those types keep two spellings unless a later change removes the method.
options.technical: No change. D-SHAPE-COPY1=A stands; the share-on-reuse build still removes most existing tildes. The built-in collection and text copy() rows remain beside ~x.
options.code:
board := [1, 2, 3]
saved :: ~board
&board.push(4)
print(saved.len())          // 3

grid := (~input).rotate()

options.name: The prefix word copy x
options.detail: Bring back the word Jet used before the tilde, as Swift does. It reads as English, but chaining a method still needs parentheses. Lists, maps, sets and text would keep their .copy() method beside the word, or lose it in the same change.
options.technical: Reverses D-SHAPE-COPY1=A to D-CAP2/S4's spelling. copy changes from a teaching-reserved word (E0991) to a live prefix keyword, and E0991 retires.
options.code:
board := [1, 2, 3]
saved :: copy board
&board.push(4)
print(saved.len())          // 3

grid := (copy input).rotate()

comparisons.note: A contextual keyword; the compiler may still remove an unneeded copy.
An ordinary method from the language specification.

recommendation.why: A copy is now a rare, deliberate act, so it gets a readable word that chains like any method and frees the tilde for later use.
gains: Reads as what it does, with no symbol to learn.
Chains without parentheses.
Frees ~ entirely; its only other use, the bit-math mark ~|, is retired by a separate vote.

losses.loss: Seven characters instead of one at each deliberate copy.
losses.mitigation: After the cutover a copy appears about once per 1,200 lines, and the fix rewrites old ones.

losses.loss: A method looks like something a type could redefine.
losses.mitigation: copy is already a reserved word, so no type can declare it today; the cutover keeps that and its error names the built-in.

whyNot.reason: B spends a one-key mark on an act that is now rare, keeps .copy() on lists and text as a second spelling, and chains need parentheses.
C turns a teaching-reserved word back into a live keyword, still needs parentheses in chains, and sits beside the existing .copy() method.

recommendation.tradeoff: A few more keystrokes on a rare act, for a self-explaining copy and a free symbol.

Both lessons now teach that live view, the current code explains :=, :: and &, and the tilde count and ~| wording are fixed.

decisions.title: Where the row policy check and display live
decisions.situation: A row policy is a database rule such as "a user may only see tickets they own". Jet builds that rule with the database library. The only way to test one rule against a user, or to print it, sits in the sync library. That copy shares a type name with an unrelated permission list and is being removed, so programs lose both abilities. The vote picks their new home; we recommend two small functions beside the existing database policy function.
decisions.gist: Where should code check a database row policy against a user and print it?
decisions.lesson: A row policy is a database rule that hides rows a user may not see. The database library already builds one with db.policy. Checking a single row by hand and printing the rule are only possible through a sync library copy that is being removed. Whichever option wins, queries keep enforcing the policy automatically.
decisions.story: Priya writes a help-desk app where each user sees only their own tickets. She builds the rule with db.policy and wants a quick test that alice cannot read bob's ticket, plus a readable print of the rule in her logs.
decisions.inWild:
CREATE POLICY own ON tickets USING (owner = current_user);
-- https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/ddl-rowsecurity.html
decisions.detail:
D-DBPOLICY1=A puts per-row access rules in core.db. There, db.policy compiles a checked RowPolicy, and every query, mutation and live path satisfies it or gets a generated filter.

The core library reference documents the core.sync RowPolicy as a closed allow/deny action policy. The runtime leaves (Prelude/Sync.rs) and the tooling/sync_crdt example instead use an owner == user row policy through core.sync.

Restoring the documented core.sync surface removes that row-policy copy. Then core.db has only policy and policy_audit. GoldenW2b and GoldenFix13 found this on 2026-10-07.

options.name: Two database functions
options.detail: Add core.db.policy_allows(policy, user:, owner:) -> Bool and core.db.policy_show(policy) -> String with the same meaning and output as the current runtime leaves. core.sync keeps only its documented action policy.
options.technical: Move the existing Prelude leaves from core.sync rows to core.db rows; the sync_crdt example imports core.db for the policy lines.
options.code:
print(db.policy_show(policy))
print(db.policy_allows(policy, user: "alice", owner: "bob"))

options.name: Methods on the policy
options.detail: RowPolicy gains a Display form and an allows method.
options.technical: Display impl plus a method row on RowPolicy in both compiler halves.
options.code:
print("{policy}")
print(policy.allows(user: "alice", owner: "bob"))

options.name: Queries only
options.detail: No direct check or display; examples observe policies through scoped queries and policy_audit, and the sync example's expected output changes.
options.technical: Delete the runtime leaves; migrate the example.
options.code: print(db.policy_audit(scope))

comparisons.note: Row policies live with the database; their text is readable from the catalog. https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/ddl-rowsecurity.html

recommendation.why: It keeps every row policy ability in the database library, matches its existing function style, and preserves today's behavior and output exactly.
gains: One library owns building, checking and printing a row policy.

losses.loss: Two new public function names.
losses.mitigation: They replace the removed sync copies one for one, so the total surface does not grow.

whyNot.reason: B mixes method and free-function styles in one library and hides printing inside interpolation.
C removes a simple check people use in tests and forces a database scope for every rule test.

recommendation.tradeoff: Two new names in the database library; the same two names leave the sync library.

decisions.title: min, max and clamp with any number of values, available without an import
decisions.situation: Choosing the smaller or larger of some values, or keeping a value inside a range, is one of the most common small jobs in code. Today Jet has these helpers only inside its math library, they need an import line, and they accept exactly two whole numbers. The vote decides whether min, max and clamp become always-available helpers that take any number of values of any comparable type; we recommend yes.
decisions.gist: Should `min`, `max` and `clamp` work on any comparable values, with no import?
decisions.lesson: The prelude is the small set of names every file can use without `use`. Today `min`, `max` and `clamp` live in `core.math`, take exactly two whole numbers, and need an import. Whichever option wins, they become generic over anything comparable, with one rule for NaN.
decisions.story: Ana writes a small game and keeps the player on screen with `x = clamp(x, 0, width)`. Jet says the name does not exist, then that 2.5 is not an Int.
decisions.detail:
Source: owner scratch note, line 60: Odin has variadic min, max and clamp built in, with no import; ensure Jet has this.

Probe, shared release jet dev-595e0dca3, 2026-10-07. `print(min(3, 1))` is E0102, "Nothing named `min` exists here". `3.min(1)` and `12.clamp(0, 10)` are E0311. Core/math/math.jet lines 21-34 define min, max and clamp for two Int values only, with min_float, max_float and clamp_float beside them.

Ratified. D-TRAIT-OVERLOAD1 lets one `math.max` serve every number type through a `Numeric` trait. Card #4659 makes the two-argument forms generic over Comparable with the NaN rule from #2298: one NaN operand yields the other operand. The prelude is a closed list (D-CORE-PRELUDE1, D-PRELUDE-LAW1), so adding names needs this ballot.

Prelude tests from D-CORE-PRELUDE1. Frequency: min, max and clamp are among the most used numeric helpers in every surveyed language. Total and safe: yes, given at least one value. Names carry no hidden meaning. No better home: the math module stays as the qualified spelling. First-hour coverage: games and scripts need clamp early. Collision-conscious: user names still win, with lint L0510.

Technical. `min(first: T, rest: ...T) -> T` and `max` take one or more values of a Comparable T. `clamp(x: T, lo: T, hi: T) -> T` stops with a registered report when lo is greater than hi. Each call compiles per type, so there is no boxing. Floats use the #2298 NaN rule. `core.math.min` and friends are the same functions, not aliases. Lists keep `list.min()` and `list.max()`, which return an optional for an empty list.

In the wild. Odin provides min, max and clamp as built-in procedures over ordered types. Python's min and max are built-ins over iterables and arguments. Rust uses methods on Ord with two values, plus `clamp`. C++ has std::min with initializer lists.

Why B loses: it keeps an import for a helper beginners reach for in their first hour.

options.name: In the prelude, any count
options.detail: min, max and clamp join the prelude. min and max take one or more values of one comparable type; clamp takes a value and two bounds. The same functions stay reachable as core.math.min and so on.
options.technical: Signatures: `min(first: T, rest: ...T) -> T`, `max` likewise, `clamp(x: T, lo: T, hi: T) -> T`, T: Comparable. Generic and compiled per type. Floats follow the #2298 NaN rule. lo greater than hi is a registered stop. Adds three entries to the closed prelude list with the edition migration lint L2001.
options.code:
print(min(3, 1, 7))       // 1
print(max(2.5, 1.5))      // 2.5
print(clamp(12, 0, 10))   // 10
print(max("ant", "bee"))  // bee
print(clamp(5, 10, 0))    // stop: clamp bounds 10 > 0

options.name: Generic, but still imported
options.detail: The same generic functions, but they stay in core.math and need an import. The prelude does not grow.
options.technical: Same signatures as A inside core.math; the prelude list is unchanged.
options.code:
use core.math as math
print(math.min(3, 1, 7))     // 1
print(math.max(2.5, 1.5))    // 2.5
print(math.clamp(12, 0, 10)) // 10

comparisons.note: Built-in procedures over ordered types, no import.
Built-in functions over arguments or one iterable.
Methods on Ord, two values at a time.

recommendation.why: Picking the larger or smaller value is everyday code in games, graphics and scripts. A removes the import and the two-argument limit while keeping one function per job.
gains: Beginners write `max(a, b)` and it just works.
Experts get the same speed: each call compiles per type.

losses.loss: Three more names every file sees.
losses.mitigation: Your own `min` still wins, with the shadowing warning the prelude already gives.

whyNot.reason: It keeps an import for one of the most common helpers, which is exactly the friction the prelude exists to remove.

recommendation.tradeoff: Three prelude names buy zero-import min, max and clamp for every type.

surface.gist: Should `min`, `max` and `clamp` work on any comparable values, with no import?
surface.lesson: The prelude is the small set of names every file can use without `use`. Today `min`, `max` and `clamp` live in `core.math`, take exactly two whole numbers, and need an import. Whichever option wins, they become generic over anything comparable, with one rule for NaN.

current.note: Without an import the names do not exist; with one, they take two whole numbers only.

wild.note: Odin's built-in procedures take any count of ordered values; no import. See odin-lang.org/docs/overview, Built-in procedures.

print([3, 1, 7].min())    // a list keeps its method

gains: The prelude stays as small as today.
losses: Every script that clamps a value needs an import line.

print(math.min(3, 1, 7))     // 1
print(math.max(2.5, 1.5))    // 2.5
print(math.clamp(12, 0, 10)) // 10

decisions.title: Free memory right after a value's last use, and guarantee tail calls
decisions.situation: When a Jet value stops being used, its memory is still held until the end of the block it lives in. A large value that dies early keeps its memory for the rest of the block. That pending cleanup also stops a recursive call at the very end of a function from reusing its stack space. The vote decides whether Jet frees plain memory right after the last use and promises those final calls never grow the stack; we recommend yes, keeping files and locks on today's rule.
decisions.gist: Should Jet free a value's memory right after its last use, and make tail calls never grow the stack?
decisions.lesson: Cleanup returns a value's memory, or closes its file. Today it runs at the end of the block, even when the value died earlier. A tail call is a call that is the last thing a function does. Whichever option wins, the rule is written down and tested on every engine.
decisions.story: Sam's log tool reads a 1 GB file, counts its lines, then spends a minute on the counts. The machine holds the whole file for that minute. His recursive directory walker also crashes on very deep trees.
decisions.detail:
Source: owner scratch note, line 77: RAII is not great; clean memory up earlier; tail recursion can keep memory alive because it is overwritten before it is cleaned up. Line 70 also asks to beat Rust with tail optimizations.

Jet today. Owned locals are cleaned up at the end of their scope under a drop flag. The header of Compiler/JetCodegen/Source/Codegen/DropFlags.jet says execution order and drop timing are unchanged by its pass. D-FIELD-DROP-ORDER1 cleans fields last-first at scope exit. A last use already moves the value (D-COPY-DEFAULT1), and LastUse.jet computes last uses with one backward liveness pass. No decision mentions tail calls.

The problem. A value that is dead but not moved holds its memory until the scope ends. A call in tail position cannot reuse its frame while any cleanup is still owed after it, so a tail-recursive function grows the stack. This is why Rust cannot promise tail calls without its proposed `become` keyword (RFC 3407).

Evidence. Mojo destroys values as soon as possible after their last use and documents it as a core rule. Swift's ARC does not promise lifetime to the end of scope; `withExtendedLifetime` exists to ask for it. Scheme requires proper tail calls. Zig offers `@call(.always_tail, ...)` as an explicit request.

Option A, memory. A value has visible cleanup when its type has Close, #MustFinish, a lock or guard, or a defer registration. Any other value is freed right after its last use, counting uses through views and borrows, which LastUse.jet already counts. Values with visible cleanup keep the scope-end rule and D-FIELD-DROP-ORDER1.

Option A, tail calls. A call in tail position reuses the frame whenever no visible cleanup is pending after it. When one is pending, an advisory lint names the value that blocks the tail call. The same rule holds at O0, O1 and O2 and in comptime (I9).

Amends D-FIELD-DROP-ORDER1 only for memory-only values; field order among them stays last-first. No syntax changes.

Why B loses: it keeps memory alive after the compiler has proved it dead, and it leaves deep tail recursion able to crash.

options.name: Free at last use; tail calls kept flat
options.detail: Memory-only values are freed right after their last use. Files, locks and other values with visible cleanup still close at the end of their block. A call that is the last thing a function does reuses the frame when no visible cleanup is pending.
options.technical: Move the drop of each memory-only owned value to the point after its last use, as computed by the existing liveness pass, including view and borrow uses. Keep scope-end drops for types with Close, #MustFinish, guards or defer registrations. Emit tail calls as jumps when no visible drop is pending; otherwise report an advisory lint naming the blocker. Debug info records the free point.

options.name: Keep end-of-block cleanup
options.detail: Cleanup stays at the end of each block, as today. The optimizer may still turn some tail calls into jumps, but nothing is promised.
options.technical: No change to drop placement. Tail calls stay an optimizer choice at O1 and O2.

comparisons.note: As-soon-as-possible destruction after the last use.
comparisons.code: var n = len(big)   # big is destroyed here

comparisons.note: Drops at scope end; explicit tail calls are a proposed `become` keyword.
An explicit request for a tail call.

recommendation.why: Jet already knows each value's last use. Freeing memory there costs nothing to write, lowers peak memory, and removes the pending cleanup that blocks tail calls.
gains: Less memory held, with nothing new to learn.
Tail recursion becomes a safe loop.

losses.loss: A debugger shows a dead value as already freed.
losses.mitigation: The debugger names the line where it was freed, so nothing silently disappears.

losses.loss: Freeing order differs from Rust and C++ habits.
losses.mitigation: Values with visible cleanup, such as files and locks, still close at the block end.

whyNot.reason: It keeps memory alive after Jet knows it is dead, and leaves deep tail recursion able to crash.

recommendation.tradeoff: Memory-only values free early; anything with a visible effect keeps its written place.
