decisions.title: Choose a numbered enum's backing integer with #Layout(U8)
decisions.situation: An enum is a list of named cases, and a numbered enum gives each case a whole number so it can be stored in a file or sent over a network. Jet accepts the numbers but cannot say how many bytes the enum takes, and its conversions to and from numbers are not built yet. The vote decides how a program picks the backing integer; we recommend the existing layout marker, as in #Layout(U8).
decisions.gist: Should a numbered enum choose its backing integer type, such as one byte, with `#Layout(U8)`?
decisions.lesson: An enum lists named cases. A numbered enum gives each case a whole number, such as Read = 1. The backing type is the integer that stores the case in memory and in files. Whichever option wins, `Mode.from_int` and `mode.to_int()` get built.
decisions.story: Inez reads a device protocol whose mode field is one byte. She wants `Mode` to take exactly one byte inside her C-layout header and to reject unknown codes.
decisions.detail:
Source: owner scratch note, line 54: Odin lets an enum choose the integer that backs it and assign numbers; can Jet do this, even if only for simple enums?

Jet today. Numbered cases parse, and the numbers may be computed at build time (D-META-CONST1). A checked `Mode.from_int(n)` is ratified for enums whose cases all have explicit unique numbers (D-ENUM-INGRESS1). All values can be read as build-time data (D-ENUM-CASEVALUES1). Packed structs can store an enum field at a bit width (D-BITS1).

Probe, shared release jet dev-595e0dca3, 2026-10-07. `enum Mode { Read = 1  Write = 4 }` checks. `Mode.from_int(4)` is E0107, and `Mode.Write.to_int()` is E0304. No syntax chooses the backing integer.

Option A, technical. `#Layout(T)` on a payload-free enum, where T is a fixed-width integer such as U8 or I32. Every case number must fit T, or the case gets a range error. `#Layout(c)` structs store the enum as T. `Mode.from_int(n)` follows D-ENUM-INGRESS1, and `mode.to_int()` returns the number as Int. A payload enum with `#Layout(U8)` is an error that points to packed structs.

Without the marker, the compiler keeps choosing the representation, and the size stays a build fact (D-LAYOUT-SHOW1).

Evidence. Odin writes `enum u8`. Rust writes `#[repr(u8)]`, an attribute much like option A. C# and Swift write the type after the name. All of them use the choice mainly for files, protocols and foreign interfaces.

Why B loses: it adds a grammar form for something the existing layout marker already expresses.

options.name: `#Layout(U8)` on the enum
options.detail: The existing layout marker takes an integer type for payload-free enums. Case numbers must fit it. Conversions both ways are built.
options.technical: `#Layout(T)` with T a fixed-width integer, payload-free enums only. Out-of-range case numbers are range errors at the case. Storage in `#Layout(c)` and packed structs uses T. `from_int` per D-ENUM-INGRESS1; `to_int() -> Int`.
options.code:
#Layout(U8) enum Mode {
    Read = 1
    Write = 4
}
m :: Mode.from_int(4) ?? Mode.Read  // Write
print(m.to_int())                   // 4
SIZE :: prep { Mode.$layout.size }  // 1

options.name: Type after the name
options.detail: A new grammar form writes the backing type after the enum name, as Odin, C# and Swift do.
options.technical: Parser accepts `enum Name: T { … }`; same checks and conversions as A.

comparisons.note: Backing type after `enum`.
An attribute chooses the representation, like option A.
Backing type after the name, like option B.

recommendation.why: Jet already says how a type is stored with `#Layout`. Reusing it for enums adds one argument, not new grammar, and keeps every storage choice in one place.
gains: One home for every storage decision.
Checked conversions both ways.

losses.loss: The size sits on a marker line, not beside the name.
losses.mitigation: Hover and docs show `Mode (U8)`, the same place `#Layout(c)` already sits.

losses.loss: Only enums without payloads can choose an integer.
losses.mitigation: A payload enum gets an error naming packed structs as the tool for bit layouts.

whyNot.reason: It adds grammar for something the layout marker already says, and puts a type beside a name, which Jet avoids.

recommendation.tradeoff: One more `#Layout` argument buys exact enum sizes with no new grammar.

decisions.title: Number types with a fixed byte order, such as U32be and F64le
decisions.situation: Files, network packets and hardware registers store numbers with a fixed byte order, big-endian or little-endian, while each chip has its own. Jet handles byte order only when it reads or writes raw bytes, so a file header cannot be described as a plain struct and read in place. The vote decides whether Jet adds number types that carry their byte order, as Odin does; we recommend yes, with arithmetic still on ordinary numbers.
decisions.gist: Should Jet add number types with a fixed byte order, such as `U32be` and `F64le`, for files and protocols?
decisions.lesson: Byte order says whether a number's biggest byte comes first (big-endian) or last (little-endian). Files and networks fix the order, while chips differ. Today Jet chooses the order only when reading or writing bytes. Whichever option wins, arithmetic always happens on ordinary numbers.
decisions.story: Kai maps a 2 GB image file whose header and tile index are big-endian. He wants to describe the header once and read fields directly, without copying or converting each one.
decisions.detail:
Source: owner scratch note, line 33: include the primitive types Odin has, such as quaternions, endian types, complex numbers and floats with endian specialization.

Jet today. Byte order lives in codecs: Bytes has typed writes such as write_u32_le (D-CORE-IO-BUF1), the binary pack contract is checked (D-BINARY-CANONICAL1), and bit patterns read and write fields (D-BITS1). Number sizes come from one family definition each (D-CORE-NUMFAMILY1). Files can be mapped as byte views (D-FOUND-VIEW1). No decision adds a byte-order type.

Option A, technical. A byte-order parameter joins the integer and IEEE families, and the standard names are generated: U16le through U128be, I16le through I128be, F32le, F32be, F64le and F64be. They live in core.encoding.binary. They are storage types: reading converts to the native number, and assigning a native number converts back. They have no arithmetic of their own, so mixed-order sums cannot happen. They work in `#Layout(c)` and packed structs, in fixed arrays, and in mapped views.

Cost. On a chip with the other order a read is one swap instruction; with the same order it is a plain load.

Evidence. Odin ships u16le, u32be, f64be and similar. Rust users reach for crates such as zerocopy and byteorder for the same job. Zig and Go pick the order per read call instead.

Why B loses: one order per record cannot describe mixed-order formats or a typed array of big-endian numbers.

options.name: Byte-order number types
options.detail: Storage types with a fixed byte order, generated from the number families. Reading gives a normal number; writing a normal number converts it.
options.technical: Families gain an order parameter; names U16le…U128be, I16le…I128be, F32le/F32be, F64le/F64be in core.encoding.binary. No arithmetic; implicit read and write conversion; valid in C-layout and packed structs, fixed arrays and mapped views.
options.code:
use core.encoding.binary.[U32be, U32le]
#Layout(c) struct Header {
    magic: U32be
    length: U32le
}
fn body_end(h: Header) -> Int { h.length + 8 }  // a normal number
fn stamp(h: &Header) { h.length = 512 }          // stored little-endian

options.name: One order per record
options.detail: A `#Layout(c, order: .Big)` argument fixes the byte order for every number in a struct. No new types.
options.technical: New layout argument; every numeric field converts on read and write.

comparisons.note: Endian-specific basic types.
Byte-order types come from crates.
Order chosen per read.

recommendation.why: The order belongs to the stored number, not to the code that reads it. A lets any field, array or mapped file say its order once, then reads as ordinary numbers.
gains: File formats and protocols read in place, with no hand conversion.
Matches Odin's types one for one.

losses.loss: Many new type names.
losses.mitigation: They come from one family definition, live in one module, and beginners never import them.

losses.loss: A read costs a byte swap when orders differ.
losses.mitigation: It is one instruction, and no swap happens when the order matches the chip.

whyNot.reason: It cannot describe mixed-order records or a typed array of big-endian numbers, which real formats use.

recommendation.tradeoff: A family of storage types buys in-place reading of any binary format.

decisions.title: How Jet learns a target machine's hardware, and how a program can require it
decisions.situation: The owner wants an extensible way to feed target hardware information to Jet, like NixOS hardware description files, and let experts require a GPU or a memory minimum. Current build facts expose CPU information; the supplied records also describe compute capability checks, but no general target-description or requirement API. This vote recommends typed descriptions on the existing fact plane, extensible by packages rather than compiler releases, with requirements checked before ordinary execution.
decisions.gist: How should Jet learn a target machine's hardware, and how should a program require hardware it needs?
decisions.lesson: A hardware description is a Jet file listing a machine's hardware, such as its GPU and memory. A scan can write it, the way NixOS writes hardware-configuration.nix, or you can write it by hand. A requirement is a line saying a program needs some hardware; a machine without it refuses the program with the missing item named.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: no description or requirement is needed for an ordinary local program. The host supplies scanned facts and optional acceleration keeps a fallback. Mandatory requirements deliberately prevent running everywhere.

CPU is the general processor; GPU is a graphics/parallel processor; NPU is a neural-processing accelerator. Memory means main RAM; GPU.memory means device memory. GiB is 1,073,741,824 bytes, not decimal GB. All options need any GPU plus 4GiB main RAM; tensor cores are optional matrix hardware. A 1GiB GPU with 64GiB RAM passes. GPU-memory requirements instead use GPU.memory_at_least(4GiB) under A and .GpuMemory(bytes: 4294967296) under B.

A proposes jet hardware scan --out hardware/workstation.jet, reusing the JetOS scan to write typed source. Import that module in package.jet. Set Target.hardware to workstation.WORKSTATION and SHIP.target to that Target. Cross builds consume the target description, not the build machine. The immutable target view is $build.hardware; $build.cpu is its CPU entry. Code shows this connection.

Requirements are mandatory; uses declares optimization interests, not powers. Shared pure predicates serve $build.hardware.has. Presence is GPU.any(), main-RAM minimum is Memory.at_least, and GPU.feature tests a feature. A conjunction within one GPU requirement must match one device, not combine different GPUs' capabilities.

Core proposes HardwareKind with fn satisfies(self, minimum: Self) -> Bool and fn coarse(self) -> Self. Reflected fields and package-qualified nominal identity supply schema/kind keys. Hardware.require(minimum) returns a HardwareRequirement with that type's checked comparison thunk. Core helpers GPU.any(), GPU.feature(), GPU.memory_at_least() and Memory.at_least() return the same requirement type. The compiler need not know NPU.

Hardware.has accepts that value. Missing kinds return false, not absent-record errors. NPU's example supplies comparison/projection methods and a separately trusted probe.

HardwareProbe carries name and run; run has signature fn(ScanContext) -> [HardwareKind]. The read_int(path) method returns Int? and reads only granted scan inputs. Missing files return None; malformed data is a scan error, never fabricated zero. The example path is an illustrative vendor sysfs contract, not universal NPU hardware.

Packages publish PROBES. The command jet hardware scan --probes vendor_npu names the grant before execution. Copy the full printed identity, review powers, then rescan. The displayed hash is illustrative. Probes never run during compilation or inside apps.

Native builds check the selected description. Startup rechecks actual host requirements before entry. False descriptions cannot authorize unsupported instructions: native CPU dispatch remains mandatory. Hardware-specific binaries refuse hosts incompatible with compiled assumptions; they do not gain portable recompilation.

Portable bundles check granted host facts at install and every launch. Changed code-relevant facts invalidate the copy and recompile before entry. Digests are content identities, not a hardware rescan in one comparison. Acquire a current snapshot first. Cache identity includes kind/probe package identities and privacy grants.

Unknown/withheld required facts refuse, naming the requirement and grant/removal remedy. Unknown optional facts select fallback. Coarse facts are safe lower bounds: memory rounded down to 4/8/16GiB without model/serial identifiers. Exact 6GiB can appear as 4GiB; it cannot satisfy 8GiB.

GPU facts grant no GPU handle. Jobs without that handle are denied by existing compute authority. Free GPU memory is never a build fact; check it before each GPU job, not merely at program launch.
decisions.story: Noor ships a matrix tool. It needs any GPU and at least 4GiB of main RAM. Tensor cores speed it up when present; otherwise its plain GPU path works. A customer adds an NPU unknown to the current compiler, and a package should be enough to describe and use that kind.
decisions.inWild:
# NixOS: generated hardware source feeds system configuration
{ imports = [ ./hardware-configuration.nix ]; }
# Android: required hardware narrows supported machines
<uses-feature android:name="android.hardware.camera" android:required="true" />
decisions.detail:
Owner question q2ufwwsv asks for target-tailored, future-proof hardware inputs and expert requirements. A answers directly: reusable scan, ordinary typed source, Target.hardware selection, extensible Core kinds, shared predicates and pre-entry checks. All newly named API fields, methods and commands below are proposals for this vote, not claims of implementation.

Letters: new A is extensible descriptions; B is the prior fixed-facts option; C is the prior runtime-query option. Their comparison now uses the same GPU-presence plus main-RAM requirement, not different memory resources.

Existing law reused: D-JOS-HARDWARE1 scans to hardware.<host> source and allows shared profiles; D-CONF-PLANE1/READ1/MERGE1/SPLIT1 give typed facts, $build reads, contribution priority and computed contributions in .jet/lock. D-CORE-BOUNDARY1 puts chip knowledge in typed library entries; A generalizes that to kinds. D-CPU-DISPATCH1 and D-CORE-FEATURE-FLOW1 keep CPU dispatch. D-FREESTAND-FACTS1's runtime-service menu stays closed: hardware descriptions do not add allocators, clocks or providers. Facts never grant powers (D-PORTABLE2), and D-COMPUTE-BACKEND1 handles transient resource checks before each GPU job.

Trust and provenance: selected descriptions retain writer/profile/Force provenance under the existing contribution law. Build-time source is an assertion about a target, not launch authority. At launch only host-observed, host-granted facts determine admission and cache validity. Changing a probe package, predicate comparison or privacy projection invalidates the corresponding facts and compiled specialization even if a physical device is unchanged. Denied scans never fall back to running a probe without a grant.

Open-kind transport: generated checked descriptors/thunks retain nominal identity, fields, comparison and projection when kinds are erased into Hardware's device list. A bundle carries the kind package needed for its requirements, while only the trusted host scan can supply observed values. Pure satisfies/coarse methods cannot probe the host. Requirements are evaluated on the actual granted device entries; no package can manufacture its own admission evidence.

B owns a fixed CPU/GPU/main-memory vocabulary and gets the same native and portable checks but requires a compiler release for new kinds. C's runtime record uses that fixed vocabulary too: absent GPU has has(...) == false, and RAM is bytes. It supports an explicit early program guard, not automatic pre-entry refusal; unknown NPU kinds need an API/compiler vocabulary change. All variants ship under C.

A retains more public vocabulary and a scan trust cost. It wins because B lacks package extensibility and C lacks the requested compiler input and declarative admission. No claim that an instruction format inherently cannot access accelerators is needed for this recommendation.

options.name: Extensible hardware descriptions with requirements
options.detail:
A target's hardware is a typed Jet description, written by a scan, by hand, or from a shared profile package, like NixOS's hardware file. It feeds build facts that code reads through $build.hardware. Outputs may list requires: and uses:. Packages can add new hardware kinds without a compiler release.

A native program checks its requirements at build and once at start-up; a portable bundle at install and at each launch, recompiling when hardware changed.
options.technical: Proposes Core Hardware, HardwareKind, HardwareRequirement, HardwareProbe and ScanContext as specified in the explainer. Hardware contains main memory, storage and typed device entries. Target gains hardware; every Output gains target, requires and uses. Package-defined kinds use pure type-owned satisfies/coarse methods; scan probes are separately trust-granted. $build.hardware shares D-CONF's typed fact plane and merge law; $build.cpu remains the CPU entry. Host observations, grants and kind/probe package identities determine launch admission/cache identity, never a producer's asserted facts. Free amounts are checked before each GPU job.

options.name: A fixed set of hardware facts
options.detail: The compiler owns a fixed list of hardware facts: $build.cpu and a new $build.gpu with features and fixed limits. Outputs may list requires: and uses: over that list. Missing requirements are refused before running, and each launch rechecks that the hardware still matches. A new kind of device needs a new Jet release.
options.technical: Fixed $build.cpu, $build.gpu and $build.memory; Output requires/uses over fixed enums. Native build/start-up and portable install/launch checks follow A, as do host-granted facts and privacy. No package-defined kind transport. Free GPU memory is checked before each GPU job.

options.name: Ask at run time
options.detail: A run-time call returns the host's capabilities, and the program branches on them while running. All variants are compiled in, and nothing is refused before the program runs.
options.technical: host.capabilities() returns a fixed CPU/GPU/main-RAM record at runtime. Absent GPU makes gpu.has(...) false; memory is main-RAM bytes. No package kind extension, declarative requirement or automatic pre-entry refusal. The program can guard at its start, then use existing host handles; queries grant no powers.

comparisons.note: A generated hardware file is imported by the system configuration; shared profiles cover known devices.
An app declares hardware it requires or merely uses; stores filter devices by it.

recommendation.why: A gives the compiler hardware knowledge the way NixOS does, from a typed description per target that packages can extend. Experts can require hardware, and it is checked before the program runs.
gains: New hardware kinds arrive as packages, with no compiler release.
One description per target, scanned, written or shared.
Requirements refuse a machine clearly before the program runs.

losses.loss: More to learn: a description type, kinds and requirement forms.
losses.mitigation: Beginners write nothing; the scan writes descriptions, and requires: is optional.

losses.loss: A package-supplied probe runs code on your machine during a scan.
losses.mitigation: Probes run only in the scan, under a jet trust grant, and write plain source you can review.

losses.loss: Hardware facts could help identify a machine.
losses.mitigation: The host grants which facts a bundle sees; by default only coarse classes.

whyNot.reason: B is simpler, but every new kind of device waits for a Jet release.
C ships every variant and checks through program code. An explicit entry guard can fail immediately, but this is not declarative pre-entry admission or compiler target input.

recommendation.tradeoff: A larger hardware vocabulary, for one that packages can extend and experts can require.

decisions.title: Web-style names: camelCase for functions, fields and variables
decisions.situation: Today Jet writes function, field and variable names in lowercase with underscores, such as fetch_user_profile and user_id. You asked for the most practical defaults across fields of work, leaning toward web development, where JavaScript, TypeScript, Kotlin, Swift and Go write these names in camelCase. You already decided that type names keep capital acronyms, such as TaskID, and that camelCase JSON keys write acronyms as words, such as userId. This vote decides how values are spelled in code. We recommend camelCase with acronyms in capitals, userID, so every Jet name follows one acronym rule while web data still reads userId.
decisions.gist: Should Jet values use camelCase, and should acronyms inside them read userID or userId?
decisions.lesson: camelCase capitalizes each word after the first: fetchUserProfile. snake_case joins lowercase words with underscores: fetch_user_profile. An acronym is a word of initials, such as ID or URL. Types keep capital acronyms under every option: HTTPClient, TaskID. camelCase JSON keys write acronyms as words, userId, as you already decided. The choice is how values look in code.
decisions.explainer:
Every option shows the same small program: one record type, one choice type, one constant and two functions. Types, markers, effects and enum cases stay PascalCase with capital acronyms in every option, as already ratified. Constants stay in full capitals. Shared work for A or B: one casing section in the spec, compiler checks with automatic fixes, and one rename of Jet's own code.

Under A, an acronym looks the same in every Jet name: TaskID the type, taskID the field, parseURL the function. Only a leading acronym is lowercase, as in urlText and httpClient, the Swift and Go rule. Two touching acronyms take the underscore type names already use: parseHTTP_URL, like HTTP_API.

JSON keys are computed, not copied. Under A, the field userID sends and reads the key userId, the web's usual spelling, because you ratified word-cased acronyms in data keys. A key spelled userID gets an error naming userId, and jet inspect shapes prints every outside name.

Under B, acronyms in values are written as words: userId, avatarUrl, parseHttpUrl. A field then matches its JSON key letter for letter. But a value and its type spell the acronym differently, taskId: TaskID, which is a second acronym rule. It also reverses your ratified note that Jet code keeps userID.

Under C, values keep underscores, and JSON keys default to snake_case unless a package asks for camelCase.
decisions.story: Kai builds a web service in Jet and its browser front end in TypeScript. The same record travels between them as JSON. He wants Jet names that read like the rest of his web code, one acronym rule to learn, and JSON keys his front end already expects.
decisions.detail:
Revision, 2026-10-10, by BallotPolishA. The owner ratified D-WIRE-CASE1=A and D-WIRE-ACRONYM1=A at 2026-10-07T20:23, about two hours after this ballot was posted. D-WIRE-ACRONYM1=A recommends "writing userId in data keys while Jet code keeps userID". Its option text says "Inside Jet code, acronyms stay fully capitalized." D-WIRE-CASE1=A's examples use camelCase fields with capital acronyms.

The posted A word-cased value acronyms and withdrew D-WIRE-ACRONYM1. That contradicts law ratified since, so the capital-acronym option now leads. Mapping: new A is the posted B; new B is the posted A; C is unchanged. Its detail now states that companion keys are computed under A, so A no longer carries the posted B's loss that a field "differs from common JSON keys" without a remedy.

Replaces D-CASE-LAW2 (OptionQuality1, 2026-10-07). D-CASE-LAW2's C, which also word-cased acronyms in types (HttpClient, Url), stays withdrawn: it reverses the owner's type rule.

Why A leads. D-ACRO-CASE1=A and the owner rule of 2026-09-30 (spec S66) put capital acronyms in every word of every type-like name. D-WIRE-ACRONYM1=A then decided camelCase data keys word-case acronyms while Jet code keeps userID. A completes that pair: one acronym rule for every Jet name, and computed keys for web data. B would give values a second acronym rule and reverse the ratified note.

Irreducible part. Given the owner's type rule and the web's word-cased keys, some pair must differ: either field and key (A) or field and type (B). A keeps Jet code on one rule and lets the ratified projection convert the 1.9% of fields that hold an acronym. The projection is exact in both directions, and a near-miss key names the expected one.

DECISION BOUNDARY

Owner direction, 2026-10-05, given after D-CASE-LAW1=A was ratified the same day. The owner has personal style preferences but ranks pragmatism higher: the best defaults and rules for the most domains at the greatest criticality. The owner added that naming seems most important in web development, so Jet should likely lean toward web conventions. D-CASE-LAW1 is ratified and immutable, so the re-vote is a new decision. Choosing C re-affirms D-CASE-LAW1=A unchanged.

This ballot changes only the case of value-like names. PascalCase stays for types, traits, enum variants, markers including their library part (#Server.Get), effects, unit families and generic type parameters. SCREAMING_SNAKE stays for module-level immutable bindings and compile-time number parameters. The closed acronym lexicon (D-ACRO-LEX1=A) and full-capital acronyms in type-like names (D-ACRO-CASE1=A) stand under every option. Foreign names stay verbatim inside binding modules (D-SHAPE-CASE2=A), so browser names such as innerHTML keep their spelling.

COMPANIONS

D-PATH-CASE2=A, D-WIRE-CASE1=A and D-WIRE-ACRONYM1=A are ratified and work unchanged under A. The path word key already reads userID, user_id and userId alike. Under B, D-WIRE-ACRONYM1's note that Jet code keeps userID would need an amendment. Under C, keys default to snake_case words per D-WIRE-CASE1's detail.

WHAT OPTION A SPELLS

camelCase covers functions, methods, fields, parameters, locals, labels, lint names, import aliases and module path segments. Most module segments are one lowercase word, so core.text.fmt is unchanged. Manifest keys in package.jet are fields, so they become camelCase, as in npm's package.json (devDependencies). Acronyms follow the Swift and Go rule. Inside a name they are fully capitalized: userID, avatarURL, parseURL. At the start they are fully lowercase: urlText, httpClient. Two touching acronyms keep D-ACRO-CASE1's underscore: parseHTTP_URL. Jet's own code has 43 such functions.

WHAT OPTION B SPELLS

Every word of a value, an acronym included, is capitalized like a word: userId, avatarUrl, parseHttpUrl, httpClient, utf8Bytes. No acronym list is consulted for values, and touching acronyms need no underscore. A value and its type then differ: taskId: TaskID.

RESEARCH: WHAT EACH ECOSYSTEM WRITES

TypeScript and JavaScript use camelCase functions, variables, properties and parameters, and PascalCase classes, types and components. Acronyms are split. The browser platform writes innerHTML, URLSearchParams and toISOString, but also getElementById and XMLHttpRequest. Airbnb 23.9 says acronyms are all upper or all lower case. Google's TypeScript guide word-cases them (loadHttpUrl) unless a platform name says otherwise.

JSON keys are camelCase in Google's JSON style guide, JSON:API's recommendation, Microsoft Graph and protobuf's JSON mapping, and those sources write acronyms as words: userId, webUrl. GitHub's GraphQL API sends avatarUrl and databaseId. Stripe, GitHub REST and Slack use snake_case.

Swift and Go write capital acronyms in values: userSMTPServer, appID. Kotlin and Google Java style word-case them: newCustomerId. C# and .NET write Id and Url. Dart word-cases acronyms longer than two letters.

snake_case values: Python (PEP 8), Rust (RFC 430), Ruby, Elixir, the C standard library, SQL by habit, Odin and Jai. Python keeps capital acronyms in class names and lowercase words in values, the same split option A keeps.

Swift's API Design Guidelines say acronyms that are all capitals in English are "uniformly up- or down-cased according to case conventions": utf8Bytes, isRepresentableAsASCII, userSMTPServer. Go's code review comments ask for capital initialisms such as appID and ServeHTTP, and its linters (golint, staticcheck ST1003) report userId.

POPULATION

Stack Overflow Developer Survey 2024: JavaScript has been the most used language every year except 2013 and 2014. [INFERENCE: chart values recalled, not re-read] All respondents: JavaScript about 62%, Python 51%, SQL 51%, TypeScript 38%, Java 30%, C# 27%. Go and Rust are about 13% each, Kotlin 9%, Dart 6% and Swift 5%.

READING STUDIES

Binkley et al., ICPC 2009, 135 subjects: camelCase had 51.5% higher odds of a correct answer and took 13.5% longer. Sharif and Maletic, ICPC 2010, eye tracking, 15 subjects: no accuracy difference, and underscores about 20% faster. Binkley et al., Empirical Software Engineering 2013, 150 subjects: experience shrinks the effect. No study shows a large stable winner; practice dominates.

CENSUS, 7,409 tracked .jet files at 1e300d0af

22,276 function declarations have multi-word names. About 302,000 occurrences of 43,051 distinct snake_case spellings exist, counting call sites, fields, locals and comments. Fields: 13,571 declarations averaging 1.55 words, so most fields are one word and do not change. About 1.9% of fields contain an acronym. Type declarations: 5,396, unchanged under every option.

MIGRATION

Under A or B, one jet fix pass renames multi-word values and every use in one atomic commit between merge waves. A's rename reads each name's words with the shared splitter and lexicon that D-PATH-CASE2 and D-WIRE-CASE1 already use, so it is deterministic. An in-flight branch rebases and re-runs the same pass. The rename commit goes in a .git-blame-ignore-revs file, which git blame and GitHub both honor, so line history skips it.

options.name: camelCase values, acronyms in capitals
options.detail: Functions, methods, fields, parameters, variables and import names use camelCase, as in JavaScript, TypeScript, Swift and Go. An acronym is written in capitals in every Jet name: userID, avatarURL, parseURL, the same as in type names such as TaskID. A leading acronym is lowercase: urlText, httpClient. Two touching acronyms take the underscore type names already use: parseHTTP_URL. JSON keys come out userId, as already ratified. Compiler errors offer the exact fix.
options.technical:
Amends D-CASE-LAW1=A for value-like names only. Functions, methods, fields, parameters, locals, labels, lint names, import aliases, module path segments and manifest keys become lowerCamelCase. E0357 checks the new case. E0358 and the closed lexicon (D-ACRO-LEX1=A) extend from type-like names to values: lexicon acronyms in capitals inside a name, lowercase when leading. Touching acronyms keep D-ACRO-CASE1's underscore. Digits attach to the word before (utf8Bytes). Plural acronyms: userIDs, or urls when leading.

Data keys follow D-WIRE-CASE1=A and D-WIRE-ACRONYM1=A unchanged: userID encodes and decodes as userId, and a near miss names the expected key. Migration: one jet fix pass in one atomic commit, listed in .git-blame-ignore-revs. Foreign names in binding modules stay verbatim (D-SHAPE-CASE2=A).

decisions.title: What a REPL step that fails while running does to earlier variables
decisions.situation: A REPL is the prompt where you type Jet one line at a time and keep variables between lines; notebooks work the same way. Sometimes a line fails while it runs, after it already changed a variable. Today the Jet-written REPL then forgets every variable, while the older Rust REPL keeps them. The vote decides what survives a failed line; we recommend keeping everything that already ran, as Python and Jupyter do.
decisions.gist: When a REPL or notebook step fails while running, what happens to variables from earlier steps?
decisions.lesson: A REPL runs one step at a time and keeps variables between steps. A step can fail while it runs, after it already changed some of them. Jet's Rust REPL keeps earlier variables. The Jet-written REPL currently drops them all. Whichever option wins, a crash of the running program still loses everything.
decisions.story: Mia loads a large data set in a notebook, then spends an hour cleaning it. One cell indexes past the end of a list. She needs to know whether her cleaned data is still there.
decisions.inWild:
>>> items = [1, 2, 3]
>>> items.append(4); items[10]
IndexError: list index out of range
>>> items
[1, 2, 3, 4]
# https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/errors.html
decisions.detail:
Suite revision by BallotSuite1, 2026-10-07. Drafted by ExecHost4 and folded into the suite by BallotSuite1. Checked against the ratified execution and session decisions. D-EXEC3=A runs every level with one meaning, so a REPL turn runs at the quick level and fails with the same report as jet run. D-RESOURCE-LIMIT1=A makes stack and memory exhaustion a stop; option A now says that such a stop restarts the session.

Notebooks. D-DX-CELLS1=A makes Jet notebooks reactive: pure descendants rerun and effectful cells wait for confirmation. Under option A a failed cell publishes no new names, its descendants are marked stale rather than rerun, and earlier cells keep their values. Under C every cell would need rerunning after any failure, which D-DX-CELLS1's bounded live state was meant to avoid. No other open ballot touches the REPL.

Card #4719. Rust REPL (crates/jet-repl) clones pure comptime values per trial step, so a failed step keeps all prior bindings. The Jet REPL port (port/solseams2 a5be604c4, Main-approved 2026-10-06) retires the evaluator machine on a run-time failure and reports that runtime bindings were reset. It does so because owned host handles and shared cells cannot be copied.

Under D-EXEC1/D-EXEC2 the REPL moves to the native session host (#4720): bindings live in typed session slots in one persistent child. A recoverable failure (an error value, cancellation, deadline) returns through MIR cleanup; published slots survive. A panic or trap invalidates the child; the host restarts it with a fresh session and never replays earlier steps.

Static check failures already roll back exactly and are not part of this choice. External side effects are never rolled back under any option.

options.name: Keep what ran
options.detail: Earlier bindings stay after a run-time failure, and changes the failed step made before failing stay. A panic or trap still restarts the session and says which bindings were lost.
options.technical:
Session slots published by earlier turns are untouched; the failed turn's unpublished slots are released without glue (CAbiSession end). Fatal invalidation restarts the child with a fresh session.

Resource stops follow D-RESOURCE-LIMIT1=A. A stack overflow (E3012), a #MaxDepth limit or running out of memory is a stop, so it counts as a fatal invalidation: the session restarts and says which bindings were lost. Output printed before the stop stays on screen, as the prefix rule requires. A failed turn prints the same registered report as jet run, per D-RTFAIL1 and D-EXEC3.
options.code:
>> items.push(4); items[10]
error: index 10 is out of range (length 4)
>> items
[1, 2, 3, 4]

options.name: Undo the step
options.detail: Before each step, copy every binding the step may change; restore the copies if it fails. A step that may change an uncopyable binding (file, socket, shared cell) cannot be undone.
options.technical: Per-turn snapshot of written slots via Clone glue; uncopyable slot types either refuse the turn or are excluded from rollback.

error: index 10 is out of range (length 4)

[1, 2, 3]

decisions.title: Replacing a borrowed field while returning its old value
decisions.situation: A reusable reader stores the current row in a field, then needs to hand that row to its caller and begin the next one. Jet forbids moving a value out of a borrowed field, so today's workaround copies the row and resets the field, adding an allocation each time. A replace operation would put a new value in immediately while returning the old one without that copy. You choose standard replacement, continued copying, or consuming the whole reader; we recommend one standard replacement operation.
decisions.gist: Should Jet add a standard operation to replace a field and return its old value?
decisions.lesson: Borrowing permits access without taking ownership. Moving a field out would leave a borrowed object incomplete. Replacement fills the field while returning its old value. A adds that operation, B copies and resets, and C consumes the whole object. A lets a reader continue without a row copy.
decisions.explainer: The desired operation does not weaken the rule against leaving a borrowed field empty. The replacement is already present before the old value is returned. Consuming an entire object works for final results but not for a reader that must produce another row.
decisions.story: Priya's file reader emits thousands of rows. She wants each finished row handed to its caller without copying its values or giving up the reader she needs for the next row.
decisions.detail: The source ballot identifies an extra allocation per emitted row from copying before reset. mem.replace is proposed Jet API, not an existing function in core.mem. The syntax below uses current Jet borrowing and collection construction; A requires adding the operation's checked move semantics.

options.name: Add standard replacement
options.detail: Add one operation that installs a new value in a writable place and returns the old one. Use it for row handoff instead of copying, without ever leaving the borrowed object incomplete.
options.technical: Proposed mem.replace(&place, new) returns the old value. The write borrow ends before the following statement, and the old value is moved rather than copied.

options.name: Keep copying and resetting
options.detail: Keep the current borrowed-field move rule and add no replacement operation. Reusable readers copy the finished row and reset their field, retaining an allocation for every row.
options.technical: No new Core operation or special field extraction. The copy remains an ordinary allocation.

options.name: Consume the object for its final result
options.detail: Give types a finishing method that consumes the whole object and returns its result. Avoid a general replacement operation, but the object cannot continue producing rows afterward.
options.technical: A consuming finish method moves its payload out and ends the object's use. This fits terminal results such as a hash digest, not repeated handoff from a reusable reader.

recommendation.why: A preserves the borrowed-field rule while giving reusable readers an allocation-free handoff instead of copying each row.
gains: Reusable readers hand off old values without an extra copy allocation.

losses.loss: Users must learn one additional operation and its ownership rule.
losses.mitigation: Document replacement next to existing cell swapping, with one reader example showing the new value remains installed.

whyNot.reason: B keeps a copy allocation on every row even though replacement can preserve the ownership rule.
C fits a final result but consumes the reader needed to produce the next row.

recommendation.tradeoff: Add one explicit ownership-preserving operation rather than pay per-row copies or restrict handoff to final results.

decisions.checkInstructions: Test that replacement returns the old value, leaves the new value installed and ends its write borrow before the next statement. Exercise repeated reader handoff without a copy allocation and verify consuming finish still forbids reuse.

surface.gist: Should a standard replacement operation return a field's old value without copying?
surface.lesson: Moving out of a borrowed field is forbidden. Today the reader copies its row and resets the field. A replaces the field and returns its old value, B keeps copying, and C consumes the whole object. Only A avoids copies while letting the same reader continue.

current.note: Each row is copied before the reader resets its field.
current.code:
row := ~self.fields
self.fields = [String]{}

wild.note: Replacement preserves a complete object without cloning the payload; source is in the long form.
wild.code: let row = std::mem::replace(&mut reader.fields, Vec::new());

options.name: Standard replacement
options.gist: Install a new field value and return the old one.
gains: No row-copy allocation.
Reader can keep producing rows.
losses: One operation and ownership rule to learn.

proposed.code:
// Proposed Jet operation:
row :: mem.replace(&self.fields, [String]{})

options.name: Copy and reset
options.gist: Keep the current workaround and ownership rules.
gains: No new operation.
losses: An extra copy allocation per row.

proposed.code:
row := ~self.fields
self.fields = [String]{}

options.name: Consume at the end
options.gist: A finishing method returns the payload and consumes its object.
gains: No general replacement operation.
No copy for terminal results.
losses: The consumed reader cannot produce another row.

proposed.code:
row :: reader.finish()
// Reader is consumed.

recommendation.why: A avoids the row copy while preserving a complete borrowed object and allowing the reader to continue.
gains: Allocation-free row handoff.

losses.loss: One more ownership operation.
losses.mitigation: Document it beside cell swapping with an example showing the installed replacement.

whyNot.reason: B pays a copy allocation on every row.
C ends the reader instead of letting it produce more rows.

recommendation.tradeoff: Learn one replacement operation to avoid repeated copies without weakening ownership rules.

decisions.title: Unwired CLI files outside the self-hosted compiler build
decisions.situation: The self-hosted compiler is built from Jet source, but some command files and their package-publication dependencies are left outside its assembly. Today package commands such as add are recognized but have empty actions, so users do not get the feature those names suggest. Wiring them would bring roughly 170 additional files into the build and deliberately expand its agreed boundary. You choose continued exclusion, wiring now, or deletion; we recommend keeping the files outside the build until their command wiring is designed.
decisions.gist: Should unwired CLI files stay outside the self-hosted build until their commands are connected?
decisions.lesson: Files can remain in the repository without being built. These package commands have no action today. A retains the files outside the build, B connects the commands and includes their dependencies, and C deletes the callers. A preserves the work but does not make the commands functional.
decisions.explainer: Recognizing a command name is not evidence that the command works. The build boundary and the command wiring are separate obligations; retaining excluded source does not authorize calling unfinished package operations complete.
decisions.story: Priya runs jet add to add a dependency. Today the name is recognized but nothing happens, and she needs the release to state that limitation plainly.
decisions.inWild:
# Cargo supports source retained behind disabled features and optional dependencies.
# https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/features.html
cargo build --no-default-features
# Go build constraints likewise control which source files enter a build.
# https://pkg.go.dev/cmd/go#hdr-Build_constraints
//go:build linux
# These are build-scope precedents, not precedents for silent no-op commands.
decisions.detail: The eight excluded CLI files are Jobs, Package/Bundle, Package/FlashAudit, Package/FlashPlan, Package/NativeBundle, Package/NativeFlash, Supply and ToolchainPin. Dependency.jet also stays outside assembly, with a 162-file fetch closure covering publication, providers, trust, registries and storage. Commands.jet has empty add/remove/fetch/update actions. The sandbox path remains wired through Host.jet:1528 to jet_cli_compile_sandbox. Closure receipt: $JET_STATE_ROOT/scratch/CliR12Fix/fetch-closure.json.

options.name: Keep excluded files until wiring is designed
options.detail: Keep the eight CLI files, Dependency.jet and its publication closure outside assembly while preserving them in the repository. Keep package actions unfinished until separately designed wiring is ready. Explicitly label those commands unavailable.
options.technical: Preserve the pre-merge assembly boundary. Commands.jet actions remain empty and Front.jet recognizes the names; the source files are retained, not deleted.
options.code:
jet add pkg
# Name recognized; action not implemented in this build.

options.name: Wire commands and include the closure now
options.detail: Connect add, remove, fetch and update and the eight CLI files, then include the exact fetch closure. Expand the self-hosted build by roughly 170 files and cross the publication boundary deliberately.
options.technical: Dispatch package dependency commands to jet_cli_package_dependency. Assemble the closure recorded in fetch-closure.json and check the expanded self-host assembly boundary.
options.code:
jet add pkg
# Resolves the package and writes its lock entry.

options.name: Delete excluded callers and commands
options.detail: Delete the eight CLI files and Dependency.jet, remove their command rows and front-end names, and remove caller-specific tests. Do not delete shared Jetpack dependency files that other code may use.
options.technical: Remove package/flash catalog rows depending on these callers. The Jetpack closure itself is not deleted.
options.code:
jet add pkg
# Unknown command after removal.

recommendation.why: A preserves the agreed self-hosted build boundary and retains the source while command wiring is designed separately.
gains: No unexpected assembly growth or loss of retained command source.

losses.loss: Add, remove, fetch and update remain non-functional.
losses.mitigation: Label them unavailable and track their wiring separately with the exact closure receipt, without claiming those commands work.

whyNot.reason: B expands the publication boundary by roughly 170 files in one step before its dedicated review.
C discards existing caller code and removes user-facing commands the owner may still want.

recommendation.tradeoff: Keep the smaller build and retained source while explicitly acknowledging that these package commands remain unfinished.

decisions.checkInstructions: Check the assembly excludes exactly the named callers and dependency closure while retaining the wired sandbox path. Document that recognized package names have no action. Do not count recognition as successful command execution.

surface.lesson: Source can stay in the repository without entering a build. Package command names exist, but their actions are empty. A retains excluded source, B wires it and expands the build, and C deletes callers. A leaves the commands explicitly unfinished.

decisions.title: Every Jai build option as a Jet build option, and pinning options in fn build
decisions.situation: Jai lets a project control dozens of build settings from code, from the target processor to linker arguments and which runtime checks stay on. Jet's build profile has a handful of settings, and its rules say the command line always wins, so a project cannot fix a setting it depends on. Games, embedded programs and plugins therefore cannot be built the way their authors intend. The vote decides which settings Jet adds and whether build code may pin them; we recommend all of them, and pinning.
decisions.gist: Should Jet offer every Jai build setting, and may build code pin a setting the command line cannot change?
decisions.lesson: A build profile is a named group of settings, such as release, written in package.jet. `fn build` is Jet code that registers what to build. Pinning means build code fixes a setting so a command-line flag cannot change it. Today the command line always wins; option A reverses that where a project pins.
decisions.story: Sam ships a game to the web, a desktop build with a custom linker script, and a plugin library. He needs CPU features, linker arguments, a dynamic-library output and dead-code removal set from code, and he needs CI flags never to undo them.
decisions.detail:
Audit rows refer to Docs/audits/jai-parity-2026-10-16.md. Spellings use today's `prep` keyword and `$` fact mark (D-COMPILER-NS1=A, shipped 2026-09-30). The open ballots D-COMPTIME-WORD1 (prep to comptime) and D-META-HASH1 ($ reads to ##) would respell them mechanically. No choice here changes with those outcomes. Words used here. Jai is a systems programming language by Jonathan Blow, built for games, with no guardrails by default. `prep { }` runs Jet code while compiling.

A `$` word such as `T.$fields` reads a fact the compiler knows. A `#Name` marker attaches a rule to the code below it. `package.jet` is a package's settings file. The main package is the one you build directly.

TODAY. The rules list five profile fields: optimize, debug_info, small, panic and settings (D-BUILDPROFILE1). THE CATALOG UNDER A AND B, with Jai names in brackets. Output: the output kind is chosen where it is today, by the package kind and by registration (`b.add_executable`, `b.add_library`). `b.add_library` gains `link: .Static` or `.Dynamic`, `b.add_object` is new, and check-only is `jet check` [output_type]. output_dir and work_dir [output_path, intermediate_path].

Entry name for freestanding targets is the target profile's entry fact [entry_point_name]. Target: os, arch, cpu (native or a name. The existing `--cpu` flag), cpu_features, min_os [os_target, cpu_target, machine_type, target_system_cpu, target_system_features, minimum_os_version]. Code generation: optimize keeps none, basic, full and size, and adds min_size [Optimization_Type]. Inline auto or never. Lto. Split_units. Function_sections. Frame_pointers. Red_zone.

Vectorize, unroll, tail_calls, merge_functions [llvm_options]. Emit ir, bitcode, asm or object [output_llvm_ir, output_bitcode]. Backend_args raw passthrough [llvm_options.command_line]. Fields apply per backend (Jet-native, Cranelift, rustc). A field a backend cannot honour is a registered error naming the backend, never silently ignored. Raw backend_args that make the backend reject the program remain an internal error under I2, and the receipt marks such builds.

Runtime checks: bounds, null and casts take fatal, report or off [array_bounds_check, null_pointer_check, cast_bounds_check]. `off` needs the unchecked_bounds, unchecked_null or unchecked_casts power. overflow sets the build default for `#Arithmetic` (D-WRAP-SCOPE1) and needs no power [math and arithmetic checks]. Per scope, `#Unchecked(bounds, casts, null)` removes named checks on one block or function (Jai #no_abc).

It is legal only inside an `#Unsafe("reason")` scope, the existing I1 gate, so it needs no power. The written reason is the audit record, `policy.unsafe` can deny or confine such scopes, and the build receipt lists each `#Unchecked` site. Today `#Unsafe` keeps bounds checks, and D-OOBPROOF1 elides only proven ones. Debug: debug_info none, lines or full (a Bool today). Debug_format. Stack_traces. Crash_backtrace. Debugger_names.

Step_into_expansions [emit_debug_info, stack_trace, backtrace_on_crash, use_natvis_compatible_types, -debug_for]. Size: dead_code all, packages or none [dead_code_elimination, -no_dce]. Type_info full, reachable or none [runtime_storageless_type_info, #type_info_none]. Max_instance_depth [maximum_polymorph_depth]. Link: link_args, libs, lib_paths [additional_linker_arguments]. Lazy_foreign [lazy_foreign_function_lookups]. A custom link step is D-JAI-EVENTS1's build.link.

Runtime: scratch_size [temporary_storage_size], only if D-JAI-CONTEXT1 adds scratch memory. Diagnostics: diagnostics human, msvc or json. Color. Short_paths. Timings. Quiet [use_visual_studio_message_format, shorten_filenames_in_error_messages, text_output_flags]. Data for build code: typed settings exist [user_data_*]. `jet build -- args` passes strings to fn build as `b.args` [compile_time_command_line].

COMMAND-LINE JAI FLAGS. -run maps to the existing `jet eval`. -add maps to `jet build --add 'decl'` under the raw_code power, if D-JAI-CODE1 passes. -debugger maps to card #5008, which debugs compile-time code. -very_debug maps to the existing hardened profile (D-HARDENED1) with full debug info. -no_jobs is the existing `--threads 1`. -randomize, -seed and -chaos map to `jet build --shuffle[=seed]`, the spelling `jet test` already uses. -report_poly maps to `--report instances` (#5000).

-no_cwd needs nothing. -import_dir maps to path and vendored dependencies, since Jet resolves packages by identity. PINNING (A only). `b.pin(setting, value)` in fn build makes a flag for that setting a registered error naming the pin. This reverses D-BUILDCTX-FLAGS1 ('command line always wins'), which the owner's 2026-10-07 notes digest restates, for pinned settings only, and adopts Blow's rule that program-set options win for reproducibility (OAIqCpqszVw 01:06:25).

INTERPLAY. D-JAI-EXPERT1 names the check powers. D-JAI-CONFIG1 reuses these fields for each profile, so if C wins, CONFIG1's os field comes from `--target` instead.

EVIDENCE. The Way to Jai book/30A, 30B and examples/30/30.4_build_options.jai:50-123. Focus first.jai:23-90. Infinite-pong first.jai:7-33. Cargo's typed profiles succeeded while RUSTFLAGS raw text is a long-standing pain. Zig's typed target query is the closest precedent.

Check fields take `fatal`, `report` or `off`. `off` needs the matching D-JAI-EXPERT1 power. A field a backend cannot honour is a registered error naming the backend.
