decisions.title: Jai workspaces in Jet: may build settings change while an output compiles?
decisions.situation: Jai's build program makes workspaces, separate builds of one game with their own settings, and its message loop can change a few settings while compiling. In Jet each such build is an output, and in every option build code copies settings, shapes outputs and reads the build machine before compiling starts. The vote decides whether settings may change while an output compiles, for example adding a link library once a hook sees the program call Vulkan. We recommend letting compiler hooks change any setting until the first compiler stage that uses it, with every change recorded and only later steps re-run.
decisions.gist: May build settings change while an output compiles, and how?
decisions.lesson: In Jai, a workspace is one separate build; in Jet it is an output with its own settings, shaped by `fn build`. A compiler hook is a function marked `#On(stage)` that Jet calls at a named compiler step. The vote decides whether settings may still change while an output compiles. Hooks could change each one until Jet uses it, a Jai-style loop could, or nothing could.
decisions.story: Tomi's game calls a Vulkan wrapper only in some builds. Their old Jai build program watched compiler messages and added `-lvulkan` to the linker when it saw the call. Tomi wants the same in Jet without a special permission. CI must also show who added the flag and why only the link step re-ran.
decisions.detail:
Round 3, 2026-10-19. The owner wrote: "i dont like that we cant update build settings during a build like jai. why not?" This version answers that. A is new: settings may change until Jet uses them. B is Jai's pull loop, as before. C is the earlier recommendation, where nothing changes once compiling starts.

Rewritten 2026-10-19 on owner instruction: "ensure the ballots are cohesive and aligned, update or remove the jai config ballot accordingly". The update aligns it with card #5069's slate (Tower card c07glrub). The earlier full ballot, with recommendation A and two reader passes, was never ratified and is replaced. This version decides only the Jai-workspace parts the slate leaves open.

Moved to D-TARGET-ONE1: where outputs live, per-output `options:` in data or code, `b.output(name)`, `b.profile(name)`, picking an output by name, and `jet build` building every output. Moved to D-SETTING-ORDER1: whether a flag reaches an output with its own options. That ballot removes the old rule that such an output is built exactly as its code says. `b.pin(.optimize, .Size, output: game_web)` gives the exact build instead.

Moved to D-ENTRY-NAMES1: the name `BuildOptions` for the settings value. Moved to D-ENTRY-SHAPE1: `fn build(b: Build)` with no return value, sealing the plan when it returns, and `b.default(app)`. Words: output means a thing the project makes; target means only the platform, as in `#Target(Web)`.

Letters. The first version's option C let an output list profiles by name and build once per profile. It stays removed, because it contradicts D-TARGET-ONE1 option A and could not edit settings from code. The letter C now holds the earlier recommendation.

Order. D-ENTRY-SHAPE1, D-TARGET-ONE1, D-SETTING-ORDER1, D-ENTRY-NAMES1 and D-DEV-STATE1 are ratified with A, and this ballot uses their spellings. Show it beside D-DEV-SERVICES1 and D-SERVICE-WORD1.

Jai's model. A build program calls `compiler_create_workspace(name)`, edits `Build_Options` with `get_build_options` and `set_build_options`, and adds code with `add_build_file` and `add_build_string`. It then reads that workspace's compiler messages in a loop. Code does not cross workspaces unless done on purpose. Program-set options win over command-line flags (Blow OAIqCpqszVw 01:06:25).

Jai's mid-compile changes. Once compiling starts, `set_build_options_dc` changes only three fields: `do_output`, `write_added_strings` and `append_linker_arguments` (Docs/audits/jai-parity-2026-10-16.md:460, 586). Every other option must be set before compiling. The earlier reason for C, that a cache key would depend on compile order, is weak. A setting matters only to the stages that read it.

Shared, copying settings. `b.options()` returns the command's settings. The command picks its profile as D-BUILD-DEFAULT1=B and the profile row of D-SETTING-ORDER1 say. `b.profile(name)` returns a fresh copy of a package.jet profile; an unknown name is a registered error. An output without `options:` uses the command's settings. Settings values are data, while `b` and outputs are handles to the plan, so their methods take no write mark.

Shared, changing outputs. `b.add_source(out, path)` and `b.set_options(out, opts)` change an output until `fn build` returns. `b.generate(name, value, into: out)` is the typed form of D-BUILD-GENVALUE1=A, scoped to one output. The third argument of `b.add_*` stays the list of build steps the output needs (Core/build/declarations.jet:148); the outputs it depends on are the optional fourth argument (:153).

Precedence. This ballot adds no precedence order. Under A, a hook change sits in the entry-code layer. D-SETTING-ORDER1 gives the one order. Options written in package.jet are the package.jet layer, and options written in code are the entry-code layer. Under the ratified D-SETTING-ORDER1=A, a flag reaches every selected output unless a pin refuses it.

Files and commands, in every option. Today `jet build` names the default programmable output's file after it (`build_artifact_path`, Source/CmdCompile.rs:10302-10318); every other build uses the source-file stem (`bin_path`, :10291).

Every named output now goes to `.jet/build/<output>`, so two outputs built from one `run.jet` never collide. A project with no output list keeps its stem path, so zero-setup projects see no change. D-JAI-BUILDOPT1=A's `output_dir` may move a path. `jet build` builds outputs in parallel, but events and reports arrive in output-name order. A program that cannot run on this machine, such as a web build, makes `jet run` fail with an error naming the output.

Shared, hooks per output. Compiler stages run once per output, and every stage payload gains `.output`. This is the Jet form of Jai's `if message.workspace != w continue`. Results that never read `.output` are shared when outputs share a compiled record.

Shared, build machine. `$build.host` sits beside the platform facts under `$build` (D-BUILD-FACT3=A). A read is a recorded input in the build record and cache key, so a result is never reused on another kind of machine by mistake. `jet inspect build` shows which host facts were read. The open D-META-HASH1 may respell `$` mechanically.

Option A, changing settings from a hook. In every stage payload, `.output` is the handle of the output being compiled. Its setting calls come from the option table, as on `Build`: `d.output.debug_info(.Full)`, `d.output.write(false)`. A list row adds with `d.output.add_link_args([...])`. Handle calls take no write mark, and the payload stays immutable. `d.output.options` reads the settings as they stood when the stage began. Jet collects setting calls as part of the hook's result, so hooks stay order-free (D-HOOK-STAGES1).

Option A, the rule. A setting may change until the first stage that reads it, and each option-table row records that stage. Fixed at a stage means hooks of that stage and every later stage see it read-only. A later change is a registered error naming the setting and the stage. `jet explain build.<setting>` shows the stage, extending the D-CONF-KEY1 explain form.

Option A, records and caching. Every change records the hook, the stage, and the old and new values. It joins the cache key of the stages after it, so only those re-run. A link-argument change re-links only. No expert permission is needed, because changing a setting is not unsafe. Turning a check `off` still needs the D-JAI-EXPERT1 power, from a hook or from `fn build`.

Option A, layers and tools. A hook change is in the entry-code layer of D-SETTING-ORDER1, and a pinned field cannot be changed by a hook.

A hook's list addition (`add_link_args`) is added after every layer merges, the flag included, as Jai's `append_linker_arguments` is; a pin on that row refuses it. When a flag replaces a hook's scalar change, Jet prints the D-SETTING-ORDER1 note naming the hook.

A dependency hook's grant names each settings group it may change as a result power (D-HOOK-STAGES1 grant identity). Dependency hooks may change code-generation fields and add library names; raw `link_args`, `link`, `write` and `output_dir` change only from main-package hooks, like link and write hooks (D-JAI-EVENTS1). `jet inspect build` marks every setting that attached hooks could still change; after a build it names who changed each.

Fixed-at stages, using the compiler's real order. The compiler moves through Parsed, Resolved, Typed, Prepared and Emitted (crates/jet-foundation/src/AST/metaprogramming.rs:29-35). D-HOOK-STAGES1 maps `compiler.parsed` to Parsed, `compiler.declared` to Resolved, `compiler.checked` to after Prepared, and `compiler.emitted` to Emitted. D-JAI-EVENTS1 adds `compiler.imported` per module, `compiler.settled` after `compiler.checked`, then `build.link`, `build.before_write`, `build.after_write` and `compiler.finished`.

Platform fields (`os`, `arch`, `cpu`, `cpu_features`, `min_os`) are fixed when compiling starts. Source markers such as `#Target(Web)` and `$build.os` folds are read while files are read and imports are chosen. So only `fn build`, package.jet or a flag can set them; no hook can.

Check fields (`bounds`, `null`, `casts`, `overflow`) are fixed when compiling starts. Compile-time code already runs during registration and generic-module expansion (crates/jet-sema/src/Sema/Registration/Items.rs:700; Sema/Bundle/GenericModules.rs:1085), so no hook stage is early enough.

Code generation fields (`optimize`, `inline`, `lto`, `debug_info`, `frame_pointers`, `vectorize` and the other backend fields) are fixed at `compiler.emitted`. Code generation runs after the last `compiler.settled` round, so hooks through `compiler.settled` may change them.

Link fields (`link_args`, libraries) are fixed at `build.link`, whose hook receives them as its link inputs. `link: .Static` or `.Dynamic` is the output kind, Jai's `output_type`, and is fixed when compiling starts. Write fields (`write`, `output_dir`) are fixed when the file is written, so a `build.before_write` hook may still turn writing off or move the file.

`write_generated` (Jai's `write_added_strings`) is fixed after the last `compiler.settled` round. Every field not named above is fixed when compiling starts; only a later decision may move a row later.

Fields readable through `$build` (target, profile, `settings:` values and stamps, D-BUILD-FACT3=A) are fixed when compiling starts, because `prep if` folds read them while files are read. So every row's fixed-at stage is static and `jet explain` shows it without compiling.

Improvements over Jai. Jai changes three settings mid-compile (`do_output`, `write_added_strings`, `append_linker_arguments`). A covers them as `write`, `write_generated` and `add_link_args`, and lets every other setting change until its stage. The plan is a value, so tools list every output and its planned settings without compiling. Order is fixed, while Jai's compilation order varied between runs (Blow KHIeP_-Kp00 01:28:00). Every change is recorded with its hook and stage, and outputs are typed, with no 0 for failure.

Not copied from Jai. Changing the platform or check fields mid-compile: files already read and folded for one platform would be wrong. Making workspaces from any compile-time code: only `fn build` makes outputs (D-BUILDENTRY1). Jai's pull loop becomes pushed hooks plus the read-only ordered `compiler.advanced.Session.stages()` (D-JAI-EVENTS1=A), unless B wins.

Option B restated in slate terms. Outputs come from the one list, and `fn build` reads each output's compiler messages in a loop with `b.messages(out)`. It may add code or change settings mid-compile. It needs the D-JAI-EXPERT1 metaprogramming permission. Settings are known only after compiling, so tools cannot list them, and results depend on message order.

Option C. This was the recommendation before round 3. `fn build` shapes every output, Jet seals the plan when it returns, and no setting changes while an output compiles. Hooks may still add code at `compiler.settled`. A library found during compiling can only be added by replacing linking with a `build.link` hook.

Research. Jai: The Way to Jai book/30A:27-67 and examples/30/30.13; Blow OHZwYYW9koI 00:02:01-00:03:01; host-imports workspace LPdMNsL5MgI 00:03:21. Zig's build.zig makes several artifacts, each with its own target and optimize mode. Cargo build scripts read HOST and TARGET as separate variables because scripts confused them. No adoption numbers were gathered.

Design away, loss one: new names. Calling outputs workspaces was rejected, because Jet's workspace already means a group of packages. Keeping file-stem folders was rejected, because two outputs from one source file collide. Result: a porting guide maps each Jai call, and `jet build` prints every output path. Negligible.

Design away, A loss: planned and final settings may differ. Showing only final settings was rejected, because tools must read the plan without compiling. Forbidding hook changes was rejected as option C's cost. Result: `jet inspect build` marks changeable settings and names the hooks, and the build record shows final values and who changed them. Negligible.

Design away, A loss: platform and check fields still fix before compiling. Letting hooks change them mid-compile was rejected, because code already read for one platform would be wrong. Re-running the whole compile after such a change was rejected, because it hides a second build and can loop. Result: Jai fixes them too, and `fn build` sets them from `$build.host`. Negligible.

Design away, host facts. No host facts was rejected, because cross-compiling build code must pick host tools. Result: host reads are recorded inputs, never silently shared across machines. No loss remains. `b.probe(name, "find_program", program)` already finds one host program, but it cannot tell build code the host OS or CPU to choose between tools or settings. `$build.host` covers that and is recorded like a probe.

Amendments in every option. Amends D-CTEFFECT1=A: host identity moves from ambient to a recorded input in its tier table. Amends D-BUILD-FACT3=A: `$build.host` joins the `$build` root. Amends D-HOOK-STAGES1=A: every stage payload gains `.output`, and results that read it are keyed per output. Amends D-BUILD-GENVALUE1=A: `b.generate` gains `into:`.

More amendments in every option. Amends D-BUILDTARGET1=A, beyond the D-TARGET-ONE1 changes: `b.options`, `b.add_source` and `b.set_options` are new. Amends D-JAI-EVENTS1=A: `build.link` runs once per output, and `compiler.settled` items go to the output being compiled.

Amendments if A wins. Amends D-HOOK-STAGES1=A: `.output` is a handle whose setting calls are a new result power beside findings and items, merged per output and field.

Amends D-JAI-EVENTS1=A: payloads stay immutable; only `.output` setting calls record changes, and `Session.stages()` sees `.output` read-only. Amends D-JAI-BUILDOPT1=A: every option-table row gains a fixed-at stage. Amends D-ENTRY-SHAPE1=A and D-TARGET-ONE1=A: the seal at `fn build` return fixes outputs, sources and generated values; each output's settings stay changeable by hooks until their fixed-at stage. `jet inspect build` and `core.build.graph` read planned values; the build record holds final ones.

Amends D-SETTING-ORDER1=A (if A wins): a hook's setting change sits in the entry-code layer. So a flag beats a scalar change (with the usual note naming the hook), and a pinned field cannot be changed by a hook (registered error naming the pin). A hook's list addition such as `add_link_args` is added after every layer merges, the flag included; a pin on that row refuses it.

If B wins: amends D-JAI-EVENTS1=A, which answered Jai's message loop with pushed hooks and a read-only ordered view. `b.messages(out)` adds a pull loop in `fn build` whose `b.add_code` and `b.set_options` change an output mid-compile. It needs the open D-JAI-EXPERT1 permission.

If C wins: no amendment beyond those in every option.

Not changed by this ballot: D-BUILD-DEFAULT1=B, which still picks the command's settings, and D-BUILD-INCLUDE1=A. D-JAI-BUILDOPT1=A is amended by D-SETTING-ORDER1 and D-ENTRY-NAMES1; its fields reach each output through D-TARGET-ONE1's `options:`. D-BUILDENTRY1=B is amended by D-ENTRY-SHAPE1.

Prerequisites and names. `fn build` runs in the compile-time engine, so every part needs the native compile-time host (#5003). Register `b.options`, `b.add_source`, `b.set_options`, `into:`, `.output`, `$build.host`, `HostInfo`, the unknown-profile error, the shared-output-path error and the output-only module error (I7).

Under A also register the `.output` setting calls and the `add_<list row>` form. Register the new `write` and `write_generated` fields (Jai's `do_output` and `write_added_strings`), the fixed-at column, the fixed-setting error and the conflicting-change error. Cutover: `bin_path` names files by output, and `build_session_add_target` in Core/build/declarations.jet:133 takes `options:`.

Review: one fresh combined pass (beginner + adversarial), agent CohesionReview, Claude family, 2026-10-19, per owner directive for one review. Repaired: gist and shared parts, open-sibling wording, D-JAI-EVENTS1 amendment for B, amendment lists, per-output file visibility, `b.options()` timing, output paths, worked example, fourth argument, order. Round 3 (owner feedback): redesigned so settings may change until Jet uses them; review pending. Round 3 review: Round3Review, 2026-10-19; repaired handle calls, dependency-hook powers, seal amendment, static fixed-at stages, write_generated and link kind, list appends, merge identity.

options.name: Change a setting until Jet uses it
options.detail: Build code shapes outputs as in every option. In addition, compiler hooks may change the settings of the output being compiled, through the stage payload. A setting may change until the first stage that reads it, such as link arguments until linking. Every change is recorded with its hook and stage, and only the stages after it re-run.
options.technical:
Shared shaping, as in every option. `fn build` copies settings with `b.options()` or `b.profile(name)` and makes outputs. It changes them with `b.add_source(out, path)`, `b.set_options(out, opts)` and `b.generate(name, value, into: out)` until it returns. It reads `$build.host`. Every hook payload carries `.output`, and each output goes to `.jet/build/<output>`.

Changing settings from a hook. In every stage payload, `.output` is the handle of the output being compiled. Its setting calls come from the option table, as on `Build`: `d.output.debug_info(.Full)`, `d.output.write(false)`. A list row adds with `d.output.add_link_args([...])`. Handle calls take no write mark, and the payload stays immutable. `d.output.options` reads the settings as they stood when the stage began.

Jet collects the setting calls a hook made as part of its result, beside its findings and items. Changes apply when the stage ends, or at the end of each `compiler.settled` round.

The rule. A setting may change until the first stage that reads it. Fixed at a stage means hooks of that stage and every later stage see it read-only. Each row of the option table records that stage. Changing a setting after its stage is a registered error, for example `os is fixed when compiling starts for output game_web; set it in fn build`. `jet explain build.link_args` shows each layer and the stage where the setting is fixed.

Merging, as D-HOOK-STAGES1 already merges results. A scalar field is one merge identity per output for the whole build, across stages and `settled` rounds, so two different values from any hooks are a registered error naming both. A settings change adds no item, so it never starts another `settled` round. List additions, such as `add_link_args`, coexist in a fixed order by hook identity. Equal values deduplicate.

Records and caching. Every change records the hook, the stage, and the old and new values in the build record. The change joins the cache key of the stages after it, so a link-argument change re-links only. The hook result itself is cached as D-HOOK-STAGES1 already caches results.

Layers and authority. A hook change sits in the entry-code layer of D-SETTING-ORDER1. A pinned field cannot be changed by a hook; that is an error naming the pin.

A hook's list addition (`add_link_args`) is added after every layer merges, the flag included, as Jai's `append_linker_arguments` is; a pin on that row refuses it. When a flag replaces a hook's scalar change, Jet prints the D-SETTING-ORDER1 note naming the hook.

A dependency hook's grant names each settings group it may change as a result power (D-HOOK-STAGES1 grant identity). Dependency hooks may change code-generation fields and add library names; raw `link_args`, `link`, `write` and `output_dir` change only from main-package hooks, like link and write hooks (D-JAI-EVENTS1). Turning a check `off` needs the D-JAI-EXPERT1 power from a hook, exactly as from `fn build`.

Tools. `jet inspect build` lists planned values from `fn build` without compiling. It marks each setting that a stage with attached hooks could still change, and names those hooks. After a build it shows final values and who changed each.

Fixed-at stages, using the compiler's real order. The compiler moves through Parsed, Resolved, Typed, Prepared and Emitted (crates/jet-foundation/src/AST/metaprogramming.rs:29-35). D-HOOK-STAGES1 maps `compiler.parsed` to Parsed, `compiler.declared` to Resolved, `compiler.checked` to after Prepared, and `compiler.emitted` to Emitted. D-JAI-EVENTS1 adds `compiler.imported` per module, `compiler.settled` after `compiler.checked`, then `build.link`, `build.before_write`, `build.after_write` and `compiler.finished`.

Platform fields (`os`, `arch`, `cpu`, `cpu_features`, `min_os`) are fixed when compiling starts. Source markers such as `#Target(Web)` and `$build.os` folds are read while files are read and imports are chosen. So only `fn build`, package.jet or a flag can set them; no hook can.

Check fields (`bounds`, `null`, `casts`, `overflow`) are fixed when compiling starts. Compile-time code already runs during registration and generic-module expansion (crates/jet-sema/src/Sema/Registration/Items.rs:700; Sema/Bundle/GenericModules.rs:1085), so no hook stage is early enough.

Code generation fields (`optimize`, `inline`, `lto`, `debug_info`, `frame_pointers`, `vectorize` and the other backend fields) are fixed at `compiler.emitted`. Code generation runs after the last `compiler.settled` round, so hooks through `compiler.settled` may change them.

Link fields (`link_args`, libraries) are fixed at `build.link`, whose hook receives them as its link inputs. `link: .Static` or `.Dynamic` is the output kind, Jai's `output_type`, and is fixed when compiling starts. Write fields (`write`, `output_dir`) are fixed when the file is written, so a `build.before_write` hook may still turn writing off or move the file.

`write_generated` (Jai's `write_added_strings`) is fixed after the last `compiler.settled` round. Every field not named above is fixed when compiling starts; only a later decision may move a row later.

Fields readable through `$build` (target, profile, `settings:` values and stamps, D-BUILD-FACT3=A) are fixed when compiling starts, because `prep if` folds read them while files are read. So every row's fixed-at stage is static and `jet explain` shows it without compiling.

options.name: Jai's message loop
options.detail: A close copy of Jai. Build code makes outputs, then reads each output's compiler messages in a loop while it compiles. It may add code or change settings as messages arrive. The loop needs the expert metaprogramming permission, and the final settings exist only after compiling.
options.technical:
Shared shaping is as in A: `b.options()`, `b.profile(name)`, `b.add_source`, `b.set_options`, `into:`, `$build.host`, `.output` on hook payloads and `.jet/build/<output>`.

`b.messages(out)` pauses `fn build` while that output compiles and hands it each compiler message, in compile order, as D-JAI-EVENTS1 payloads. Inside the loop, `m.output` setting calls and `b.add_code(out, code)` may change the output mid-compile, like Jai's `set_build_options_dc`.

The loop needs the metaprogramming permission of the open D-JAI-EXPERT1. The final settings exist only after compiling, so the cache key includes what the loop did, and results depend on message order.

options.name: Fixed before compiling
options.detail: Build code copies settings, shapes every output and reads the build machine. When `fn build` returns, Jet seals the plan, and no setting changes while an output compiles. Hooks may still add code.
options.technical:
Shared shaping only. `fn build` copies settings with `b.options()` or `b.profile(name)`, makes outputs, and changes them with `b.add_source`, `b.set_options` and `b.generate(..., into:)` until it returns. Then Jet seals the plan, and no setting changes while an output compiles.

Hooks may still add code at `compiler.settled` and may replace linking at `build.link`. A hook that finds the program needs a library can only add it by replacing the whole link step.

gains: Adds link libraries or debug info after seeing the code.
Every setting Jet has not yet used may change, beyond Jai's three.
Each change is recorded with its hook and stage.
Only the stages after a change re-run.

decisions.title: Context parity: readable context, package-owned keys, scratch memory and an assertion handler
decisions.situation: Jai passes a hidden context into every function, holding the current allocator, logger, scratch memory and assertion handler. Jet has a block that sets the allocator, logger or deadline for a region, but code cannot read the context, packages cannot add entries, and there is no scratch memory. Jai games use the context for per-frame scratch memory, swappable logging and data passed through libraries without new parameters. The vote decides how far Jet's context goes; we recommend matching Jai with typed entries owned by packages.
decisions.gist: How far should Jet's context go to match Jai's context, push_context and temporary storage?
decisions.lesson: The context is a small set of values every function can see without parameters, such as the current allocator. `#Context(field: value) { }` changes it for a block. Scratch memory is fast memory cleared all at once, for example every frame. Reading the context is an effect, so it shows in a function's effect list.
decisions.story: Ines writes a game loop. Each frame builds hundreds of short strings and temporary lists, and she wants them all gone at the end of the frame. Her renderer library also needs the frame number for debug overlays, deep inside code that has no frame parameter.
decisions.detail:
Audit rows refer to Docs/audits/jai-parity-2026-10-16.md. Spellings use today's `prep` keyword and `$` fact mark (D-COMPILER-NS1=A, shipped 2026-09-30). The open ballots D-COMPTIME-WORD1 (prep to comptime) and D-META-HASH1 ($ reads to ##) would respell them mechanically. No choice here changes with those outcomes. Words used here. Jai is a systems programming language by Jonathan Blow, built for games, with no guardrails by default. `prep { }` runs Jet code while compiling.

A `$` word such as `T.$fields` reads a fact the compiler knows. A `#Name` marker attaches a rule to the code below it. `package.jet` is a package's settings file. The main package is the one you build directly.

FIELDS UNDER A. allocator, logger, deadline (existing, now readable), scratch, on_assert, print (default formats, Jai print_style), thread (worker index) and trace (stack trace). The `#Context` block stays the only way to change them, restored on every exit (Jai push_context, push_allocator). E0761's field list grows, E0762 types the new fields, and E0760 stays.

KEYS. `#ContextKey pub frame_index: Int{0}` declares a typed key owned by its module (Jai #add_context). It resolves through imports like any name, so two packages' keys never clash (regret, SSVHWrYG974 00:40:00).

EFFECT. Every read of a context field or key adds a `Context` read effect to the function's row, so a function's dependence on context is static and listed. Pure `-[]>` functions and C callbacks, which have an empty row (D-CABI-CALLBACK1), cannot read context. That rule stands unchanged. Who set a value is dynamic and is not claimed.

PROPAGATION. The context belongs to the running task. Function values, generics and trait calls read the caller's current context with no signature change. A spawned task observes the context current when it is spawned (D-NETTASK1). Code entered from C through an exported function starts from the program's root context, which is fixed at load.

SCRATCH. `context.scratch` is an ordinary `mem.Arena`, not a second memory family (D-ALLOC1). A default per-task scratch arena of scratch_size bytes, 64 KiB unless set (D-JAI-BUILDOPT1), exists. `#Context(scratch: a)` swaps in another. Values from scratch are arena views: escape is E0631 and use after reset is E0632 where the arena binding is visible.

Elsewhere each view carries the arena's reset count, checked on every tier at the cost of one compare per read, so a stale read is a located stop, never a garbage read. When scratch is full, the arena's own rule applies (D-ALLOCFAIL1): try_ calls return an error and plain calls stop with a located error. Nothing grows silently. Scratch counts as a declared allocator for L0506.

An unannotated allocation uses context.allocator, which defaults to the program allocator, as today.

HANDLER. on_assert receives the location and message before a failed assertion stops. It may log or show a dialog but cannot resume.

PREP. In prep code, context reads see the build's root context with no scratch unless set. The meaning is the same on every tier (I9).

PREREQUISITE. Defect #5030 (allocator and logger ignored at run time) must be fixed first.

FROZEN CARD. #3502 (context extensions) was frozen when the owner asked what context adds. The owner's 2026-10-16 direction that every Jai feature be supported reopens it for this vote.

EVIDENCE. The Way to Jai book/25A:17-35 lists Context_Base fields. Blow ciGQCP6HgqI shows the context, logger and thread index. SSVHWrYG974 shows temporary storage and #add_context. FCbUV8oSDgI 00:29:00 explains context instead of thread-local storage. Wp9XD5FKZ2c 01:40:06-01:43:44 covers temporary storage. These timestamps come from the mining notes. Odin adopted Jai's context. Zig's explicit allocators are the option C model.

options.name: Jai-level context
options.detail: Code reads typed context fields. The `#Context` block stays the one way to change them for a region. Packages declare typed keys. Scratch memory, an assertion handler, print defaults, the thread index and the stack trace join the fields.
options.technical: Fields context.allocator, .logger, .deadline, .scratch, .on_assert, .print, .thread, .trace. `#ContextKey pub name: T{default}` declarations, set through `#Context(name: v)` and read with `context.get(name)`. Reads add the `Context` effect. Scratch is a `mem.Arena` per task with reset, mark and restore.

options.name: Scratch and handler only
options.detail: The `#Context` block gains on_assert. `context.scratch` is added with A's rules. No keys, and allocator, logger and deadline stay write-only.
options.technical: Fields on_assert and scratch only, with A's scratch, effect and propagation rules.

options.name: Explicit parameters only
options.detail: The ratified block as it is. Frame data, scratch arenas and loggers are explicit parameters, using the existing `&mem.Arena` pattern.
options.technical: No change.
options.code: fn update(frame: FrameData, log: Logger, scratch: &mem.Arena) { … }

comparisons.note: Odin copied Jai's implicit context: allocator, temp_allocator, logger, assertion_failure_proc, user data.
Keys of unexported types avoid clashes by convention.
comparisons.code:
type key int
ctx = context.WithValue(ctx, key(0), traceID)

comparisons.note: Zig rejects ambient allocators and passes them as parameters, the option C model.

recommendation.why: Jai's context lets programs skip threading allocators, loggers and frame data through every call. Typed keys and an effect keep it checked.
gains: Every Jai context field has a home.
Name clashes and library-boundary problems are designed out.

losses.loss: Context reads are hidden inputs.
losses.mitigation: Each read adds the `Context` effect, so signatures and `jet inspect expand --facts context` list it.

losses.loss: Scratch values die at reset.
losses.mitigation: Use after reset is a compile error where visible; elsewhere one counter compare gives a located stop.

whyNot.reason: B gives scratch memory but no context keys, which Jai code uses for frame and request data.
C hides nothing but loses Jai's main convenience, so ported code adds a parameter everywhere.

recommendation.tradeoff: Context reads become a listed effect, for Jai's context power without its clashes.

It found a debug-only stale-scratch guard, an unprovable setter claim and silent callbacks and effects; reads are now an effect and scratch follows the arena rules on every tier.

decisions.title: Should Jet translate C source code into editable Jet?
decisions.situation: Many teams own large C programs and want to move them to a safer language a piece at a time. Today Jet can call C code through checked bindings, but it cannot turn C source into Jet source, so every line must be ported by hand. V offers a translator that converted the whole game DOOM, which is a strong reason people try V. The vote decides whether Jet gains a C translator; we recommend one that writes ordinary safe Jet and leaves anything it cannot prove safe in C.
decisions.gist: Should Jet translate C source into editable Jet, function by function?
decisions.lesson: A binding lets Jet call C code that stays in C. A translator rewrites C code as Jet code you then own. Jet already reads C headers with the Clang compiler to make bindings. Either way, C stays callable through bindings.
decisions.explainer: Jet already has source importers for Python, Java, C#, TypeScript, JavaScript and Go. They convert what they can prove and mark the rest with a JT0101 note. C was left out on purpose. The worry was that pointers, macros and undefined behavior would produce unreadable or unsafe Jet. Option A answers that worry by translating only the functions whose meaning Jet can prove. Every other function keeps running as C behind the same checked binding Jet uses today.
decisions.story: Priya maintains a 40,000-line C image library. She wants new code in Jet without a risky rewrite. With a translator she converts the arithmetic and parsing first, keeps the tricky pointer code in C, and replaces it later.
decisions.inWild:
$ v translate test.c        # V's c2v: writes test.v
$ v -translated test.v      # translated files relax V's safety rules
# https://github.com/vlang/c2v (README), vlang/v doc/docs.md 'Translating C to V'
decisions.detail:
Evidence. V's c2v (github.com/vlang/c2v, read 2026-10-16) reads Clang's JSON AST and writes V. It translated Chocolate Doom's game logic (github.com/vlang/doom) and the Doom 3 engine. V marks such files @[translated], which allows globals, pointer writes without unsafe, and C number conversions (vlang/v doc/docs.md:10990-11014).

The DOOM result still links Chocolate Doom's C platform objects. Its README lists broken sound effects and inlined #define constants.

Jet law today. Docs/spec/reference/migration-tier-map.md:28 makes C binding-only (D-ADOPT-TIER1=A). Importers obey D-MIGRATE-SRC1=A: editable output, JT0101 for omissions, a differential oracle, and byte-stable reruns. C headers are already read by one shared Clang extractor (D-CBIND-UPSTREAM1=A, D-CIMPORT1=A, card #4174).

Why V's relaxed-file model is not offered. It would let generated code use raw pointers outside an audited #Unsafe block. That is an I1 exception needing a full ballot, and it adds a second rule set against I8. Option A needs no invariant change, because a function that cannot be proved safe is not translated.

options.name: Safe translation, one function at a time
options.detail: jet import c converts each C function into ordinary Jet when every construct has a proven safe meaning: integer math, loops, structs, arrays with known lengths, pointers used as array views. A function using something it cannot prove stays in C and is called through the checked binding, with a JT0101 note naming the line and the reason. Translated code follows normal Jet rules; there is no relaxed file mode.
options.technical: Extend the shared Clang extractor (D-CBIND-UPSTREAM1=A) from declarations to bodies. Map pointer+length pairs to slices or views, tagged unions to enums, fixed arrays to [T#N]; fixed-width C arithmetic keeps wrapping semantics through explicit wrapping methods. Each translated function gets a differential fixture against the C original (D-MIGRATE-SRC1). The C row of the tier map changes from binder-only to source importer plus binder.

options.name: Keep C binding-only
options.detail: Keep today's rule. C stays C and Jet calls it through checked bindings. Teams port each function by hand behind the binding when they choose.
options.technical: No change to D-ADOPT-TIER1=A; #4174 continues to deepen header import only.

comparisons.note: Translates whole C projects, then relaxes the language rules for translated files. Source: https://github.com/vlang/c2v and vlang/v doc/docs.md 'Translating C to V'.
comparisons.code:
$ v translate src/doom
$ v -translated -o doom.o doom_v/

comparisons.note: zig translate-c converts C headers and bodies to Zig, keeping raw pointers; output is meant as a starting point. Source: https://ziglang.org/documentation/master/#C-Translation-CLI

recommendation.why: It gives C users the on-ramp V's translator offers without weakening Jet's safety rules, because unprovable code simply stays C behind the binding Jet already checks.
gains: C teams can move code into Jet gradually and keep it safe.
Reuses the Clang reader Jet already ships for bindings.

losses.loss: Pointer-heavy functions stay in C at first.
losses.mitigation: Each JT0101 note names the blocking construct, so teams port those functions by hand in priority order.

whyNot.reason: B keeps every C line manual, so large C codebases have no practical path into Jet.

recommendation.tradeoff: Some functions remain C for a while; all translated Jet is fully checked.

current.note: Jet has no C translator; the tier map sends C users to bindings and hand porting.

# not supported: C is binding-only
$ jet bind sums.h --pkg sums   # call C from Jet instead

$ v -translated test.v

gains: Gradual move from C to safe Jet.

options.gist: C stays C; port by hand behind bindings.
gains: No new tool to maintain.
losses: Large C codebases have no practical way in.
Loses the on-ramp V users value most.

gains: Gradual, safe migration from C.

decisions.title: A new name for the retired word in DataInvalidationCause.Capability
decisions.situation: A data loader in core.data remembers why its cached data went stale, using an enum called DataInvalidationCause. One of its cases is named Capability, meaning the loader's access rights changed. Jet retired the word capability from every user-facing surface and named the access-rights value Authority. This public case is the last place a user still types the retired word in core.data's loader state. We recommend renaming it to Authority, matching the loader's own authority field and Jet's Authority type.
decisions.gist: What should the public enum case DataInvalidationCause.Capability be renamed to, now that Jet has retired the word capability?
decisions.lesson: A data loader marks its cached data stale and records why: the loader changed, an input changed, a credential changed, and so on. One reason is that the loader's access rights changed, and that case is called Capability. Jet's ratified vocabulary retired that word for user surfaces. Renaming a public enum case changes every program that names it, so the new name is the owner's call.
decisions.story: Lena writes a dashboard that reloads data when a user's access is narrowed. She calls `loader.invalidate(&rows, DataInvalidationCause.Capability)`. Everywhere else in Jet, docs and errors say authority for the same idea, and her loader even has an `authority` field. The odd word makes her wonder whether this is a different concept.
decisions.detail:
Source: card #4877 (first real Jet guard run, test11) and Core/data/data.jet:185. Ratified vocabulary: D-AUTHORITY-WORD1=A retires the word capability from user surfaces. D-AUTHORITY-NAME1=A names the value Authority. D-ABILITY-NAME2=A keeps typed Authority handles for experts and plain words in tools.

The case is spelled in four Jet places: Core/data/data.jet:185, Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/Registry/CoreEnumRows.jet:38, and Compiler/JetCodegen/Source/Codegen/Types.jet:1093. The fourth is Compiler/JetBackend/Source/Lower/RuntimeRoutes.jet:7249. The Rust seed (CommonTypes.rs, DataFlow.rs, DataPipeline.rs, CAbiRoutes.rs, tir_to_mir_types.rs) follows by regeneration or dies at the Rust exit.

Under A and B the variant keeps position 6, so the C ABI ordinal mapping is unchanged. As a greenfield cutover there is no alias. A retirements.jet row teaches the old spelling with a machine-applicable fix.

Out of scope, noted for Main: core.data also exports JetDataPlotCapability, which means renderer support, not access rights. It falls under D-AUTHORITY-WORD1's broad rule but needs its own name and card.

options.name: Authority
options.detail: The case becomes DataInvalidationCause.Authority. It matches the loader's own `authority: DataAuthority` field and Jet's Authority type, so the reason reads as the loader's authority changed. The old spelling is a retired name with a fix that rewrites it.
options.code:
use core.data.[DataInvalidationCause]
use core.data.loader as loader

loader.invalidate(&rows, DataInvalidationCause.Authority)
print(loader.status(rows).invalidated_by)    // Authority

// old spelling:
loader.invalidate(&rows, DataInvalidationCause.Capability)
// error: `Capability` was renamed; use `DataInvalidationCause.Authority`

options.name: Permission
options.detail: The case becomes DataInvalidationCause.Permission, a plain everyday word. It does not match the loader's `authority` field or the Authority type, so the same idea has two names inside one loader.
options.code:
loader.invalidate(&rows, DataInvalidationCause.Permission)
print(loader.status(rows).invalidated_by)    // Permission
print(loader.authority(rows).scope)          // the field is still authority

options.name: Fold it into Credential
options.detail: Remove the case and use Credential for both credential and access-right changes. The enum shrinks by one, but a caller can no longer tell a new password from a narrowed permission.
options.code:
loader.invalidate(&rows, DataInvalidationCause.Credential)  // also for access changes
// DataInvalidationCause.Capability: removed, with a fix to Credential

comparisons.note: Zircon names handle access as rights in its API, with constants such as ZX_RIGHT_READ.

recommendation.why: Authority is the name Jet already ratified for this exact idea, and the loader already has an authority field. One word for one idea keeps the loader readable.
recommendation.tradeoff: Programs that name the old case must be rewritten; the retirement row's fix does it automatically.

whyNot.reason: It gives one idea two names inside the same loader.
It loses the difference between a changed credential and changed access rights.

losses.loss: Code naming the old case stops compiling.
losses.mitigation: A retirement row gives a machine-applicable fix to Authority.

surface.gist: What should the public data-loader reason Capability be renamed to, now that Jet retired that word?
surface.lesson: A data loader records why its cached data went stale. One reason, the loader's access rights changed, is still called Capability. Jet retired that word and calls access rights Authority everywhere else. Renaming a public case changes every program that names it.

current.note: The last public use of the retired word in loader state.

wild.note: Zircon calls handle access rights in its API names.
wild.code: zx_rights_t rights = ZX_RIGHT_READ | ZX_RIGHT_WRITE;

options.name: Authority
options.gist: Match the loader's authority field and Jet's Authority type.
gains: One word for one idea.
Matches the field beside it.
losses: Existing code must be rewritten.

proposed.code:
loader.invalidate(&rows, DataInvalidationCause.Authority)
// old spelling: error with a fix to Authority

options.name: Permission
options.gist: A plain everyday word.
gains: Easy to read.
losses: Two names for one idea in one loader.

proposed.code: loader.invalidate(&rows, DataInvalidationCause.Permission)

options.name: Fold into Credential
options.gist: One case for credentials and access changes.
gains: One fewer case.
losses: Cannot tell a new password from narrowed access.

proposed.code: loader.invalidate(&rows, DataInvalidationCause.Credential)

recommendation.why: Authority is Jet's ratified name for access rights, and the loader already has an authority field.
gains: Consistent vocabulary.

losses.loss: Old spelling stops compiling.
losses.mitigation: An automatic fix rewrites it to Authority.

whyNot.reason: Two names for one idea.
Merges two different reasons.

recommendation.tradeoff: A one-time automatic rename for one consistent word.

decisions.title: What an update request means for each command that serves the session on stdio
decisions.situation: A tool such as Jetpack or a third-party build tool can start a Jet command with --listen=- and talk to the compiler over standard input and output. The owner chose that every runnable command gets this flag: check, build, test, run and dev. Zig's build tool works the same way, and its main message, update, means do the work again on the newest files. Jet has not said what update means for each command, or whether a stdio session shares the warm compiler that an open editor already runs. The vote decides both. We recommend that update redoes the command's own work, and that a stdio session joins the workspace's running session when there is one.
decisions.gist: What should an update request do on each command started with --listen=-, and should it share a running session?
decisions.lesson: With `--listen=-`, a command reads requests from standard input and writes answers to standard output instead of to the terminal. `update` is the short request that says: do this command's work again on the newest files. A workspace session is a warm compiler run by `jet dev --serve` or `jet self lsp --serve`; other commands can join it.
decisions.story: Lena writes a build-tool plugin for her team's editor. It starts `jet build --listen=-`, sends update after each save and shows the errors. Her teammate's editor already runs `jet self lsp --serve`, a warm compiler for the same folder. Lena wants to know what update does for build, test and run, and whether her plugin checks every file a second time.
decisions.detail:
Source: compiler-session-protocol-2026-10-17.md in the session-design folder, sections 2.4 and 2.7, and BallotFollowThrough's FOLLOWTHROUGH.md sections 4-9. Ratified: D-SESSION-ENTRY1=C (`--listen=-` on check, build, test, run and dev; each verb must define what an update means). Also D-SESSION-WIRE1=A (NDJSON), D-SESSION-OWNER1=A (`jet dev --serve` and `jet self lsp --serve` may own the workspace endpoint), D-BUILD-SESSION1=A (`--session=auto|off|required`).

WHAT EVERY OPTION SHARES. A `--listen=-` session first sends `hello` with the toolchain identity, then does nothing until asked. It accepts the full request set of section 2.4, such as `check`, `build`, `test`, `query` and `cancel`.

`exit`, or end of input, cancels in-flight work and exits with status 0. A malformed line gets an E2104 report line and the session continues. `--listen=<address>` with anything but `-` is refused with E2104, because sockets stay `--serve` only. `--listen=-` with `--watch` is refused, because `watch{}` is a request. `--listen=-` with `--serve` is refused: one process has one endpoint.

THE UPDATE TABLE (options A and B). `jet check --listen=-`: update is `check{selection}` on the newest revision, for the files or package named on the command line. It returns reports and writes no artifacts. `jet build --listen=-`: update is `build{targets, profile}` from the command line. It returns events and artifact paths; bytes never cross the wire.

`jet test --listen=-`: update is `test{filter}` from the command line. Test output is captured into `test.*` events. `jet run --listen=-`: update builds, then runs the target once with the program arguments. The program's output becomes `run.output` events and never reaches the terminal, and its standard input is empty. An update while the program runs cancels it and starts again.

`jet dev --listen=-`: update is `dev.update{mode: auto}`, a swap or restart under the D-LIVE1 rules. The first update builds and starts the program. Program output becomes `run.output` events.

JOINING A RUNNING SESSION. Under A, a stdio session for check, build, test or run follows the `--session=auto|off|required` rule of D-BUILD-SESSION1. `jet check` gains that flag for this purpose. With the default `auto`, it forwards its requests to the workspace session when one runs, so the editor and the tool share one warm compiler. `off` keeps a private compiler. `required` fails at start with no workspace session.

If the workspace session ends mid-stream, in-flight requests end with a cancelled response. Later requests run on a private compiler, and a `session.detached` note says so. `jet dev --listen=-` never joins, because dev itself may own a session; it keeps its own compiler.

Under B, `--listen=-` with any `--session` value is refused with E2102, and a stdio session always runs its own compiler. Jetpack still attaches to a `--serve` socket directly when one runs, as D-JETPACK-SERVICE1=A says.

OPTION C. There is no `update` request. The command word only sets the default selection, and a client always sends the typed request: `check{}`, `build{}`, `test{}`, `run{}` or `dev.update{}`.

BEGINNER AND EXPERT PATHS. Beginners never type `--listen=-`; tools do. A tool author sends update after each change, as with Zig. An expert sends typed requests with explicit selections, and chooses `--session=off` for an isolated compiler.

Why A over B: B gives a second warm compiler beside the editor's, so every edit is checked twice, which D-SESSION-OWNER1=A was ratified to avoid. Why A over C: C drops the one request D-SESSION-ENTRY1=C's option text assumed, and Zig-style tools would need per-verb logic.

New diagnostics and the `session.detached` event get registry rows with UI snapshots (I4). Implementation lands on #5050.

options.name: Update redoes the command's work; join a running session
options.detail: Update redoes each command's own work on the newest files, as in the table in the detail. Check, build, test and run started with --listen=- join the workspace session when one runs, under the same --session rule as the plain command. Dev keeps its own compiler.
options.technical: Per-verb update mapping as in the detail. `--session=auto` default forwards requests to the D-SESSION-OWNER1 endpoint; `off` keeps a private compiler; `required` fails at hello. Owner loss mid-stream: in-flight requests end `cancelled`, then a `session.detached` event, then local execution.

options.name: The same update table; a stdio session never joins
options.detail: The same update table as A. A --listen=- session always runs its own compiler, and --listen=- with --session is refused. This is the draft in the follow-through notes.
options.technical: As A for update. `--listen=-` plus any `--session=` value is E2102.
options.code:
$ jet build --listen=- --session=auto
error[E2102]: a --listen=- session runs its own compiler; drop --session
$ jet build --listen=-          # private compiler, even with the editor open

decisions.title: May a function borrow a #Persist binding for writing?
decisions.situation: A #Persist binding keeps game or app state across a hot reload, and functions may already write to it with total += 1. Passing it to a helper with bump(&total) is rejected today, and the two compilers even give different wrong errors. The vote decides whether a write borrow of a pinned binding is allowed. We recommend allowing it, because it is the same write the function could already do directly.
decisions.gist: Can `bump(&total)` write to a `#Persist` module binding through a write parameter?
decisions.lesson: A `#Persist` module binding keeps its value when `jet dev` reloads changed code, and a function may write to it directly. A write parameter (`value: &Int`) lets a function change the caller's variable. The question is whether the two combine.
decisions.story: Mia is building a game with jet dev. Her score is `#Persist score := 0`. She moves the scoring code into a helper `add_points(points: &Int, n: Int)` and calls `add_points(&score, 10)`. Today that fails to compile, although `score += 10` in the same place works.
decisions.detail: Fixture tests/ui/static_mutable_borrow.jet. Today the Rust oracle reports E0355 (a policy at a prohibited scope) and the Jet compiler reports E0145 (#Persist on a binding that is not module-level). Both are wrong for this program: the binding is module-level, and D-PERSIST-DEVSTATE1=A makes a #Persist binding writable from a function. No decision says whether a write borrow counts as such a write. Edge cases: a hot reload happens between calls, never while a borrow is live; a borrow of an ordinary module binding stays E0111.

options.name: Allow the write borrow
options.detail: A #Persist binding may be passed to a write parameter. The program prints 1. Ordinary module bindings stay read-only from functions (E0111).
options.technical: Sema treats &persist_binding as a write place like a direct assignment; the borrow ends at the call. The fixture becomes a run example with golden output 1.

options.name: Direct writes only
options.detail: Passing a #Persist binding to a write parameter is rejected with a dedicated error that teaches a direct write or returning the new value.
options.technical: Sema reports one registered diagnostic at the &total argument; the fixture snapshot records it.

comparisons.note: Swift lets a global variable be passed to an inout parameter with &. See https://docs.swift.org/swift-book/documentation/the-swift-programming-language/functions/#In-Out-Parameters

recommendation.why: D-PERSIST-DEVSTATE1 already makes a pinned binding writable from a function; a write parameter is the same write, done by a helper.
gains: Helpers work on pinned state with no special rule.

losses.loss: Module state can change inside a helper call.
losses.mitigation: The & at the call site shows the write, and only #Persist bindings allow it.

whyNot.reason: It adds a second rule for the same write and forces game code to be restructured.

recommendation.tradeoff: A little more reach for pinned state, marked by & at every call.

decisions.title: How diagnostics name Core library types
decisions.situation: When an error mentions a Core library type, Jet prints an internal path such as module:14:source-root:0 followed by the name. Nobody can read that, and it differs between the two compilers. The vote picks one readable naming rule for every message. We recommend the plain name, with the module path added only when two different types in one message share that name.
decisions.gist: When an error message mentions a Core type such as `Secret`, how should it be named?
decisions.lesson: Error messages name the types involved. User types already print as their plain name. Core library types currently leak an internal path such as `module:14:source-root:0::…::Secret` or `<corelib>/core.crypto::Secret`.
decisions.story: Leo reads the raw bytes of a `crypto.Secret` by mistake. The error says the problem is with `module:14:source-root:0::core::crypto::Secret`. He wanted to see `Secret`.
decisions.inWild: expected `HashMap<String, u32>`, found `Vec<u8>`
decisions.detail: Fixtures: tests/ui/crypto_secret_bytes_exposure.jet (E0510), tests/ui/path_builtin_not_core_record.jet (E0112/E0108), tests/ui/ui_facade_single_uinode_identity.jet. The registry templates print `{Type}`, and user types print their leaf name. No decision fixes Core type naming. Edge case: a user type named like a Core type in the same message.

options.name: Plain name, path on a clash
options.detail: Core types print as their plain name. When two different types in one message share that name, each prints as module path plus name, as the user would write it (crypto.Secret).
options.technical: One shared type-display function strips internal module identities and qualifies only names that collide within the message; every diagnostic uses it.
options.code: error[E0510]: reading the bytes of `Secret` needs #Unsafe

options.name: Always the plain name
options.detail: Every type prints as its plain name, with no qualification.
options.technical: The shared type-display function keeps the last path segment.
options.code: error[E0510]: reading the bytes of `Secret` needs #Unsafe

options.name: Always the module path
options.detail: Core types always print with their full dotted module path.
options.technical: The shared type-display function prints the dotted Core module path.
options.code: error[E0510]: reading the bytes of `core.crypto.Secret` needs #Unsafe

comparisons.note: rustc prints the shortest name that is unique in the crate graph ("trimmed paths"), and the full path only when names clash. See https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/73996

recommendation.why: Messages stay as short as user-type messages, and the rare clash still reads unambiguously.
gains: Readable messages with no internal paths, and no ambiguity.

losses.loss: The same type can print two ways in different messages.
losses.mitigation: The longer form appears only when the short one would be ambiguous.

whyNot.reason: It prints two different types the same way when names clash.
It makes every Core message longer for a clash that rarely happens.

recommendation.tradeoff: Rare longer names, in exchange for short messages everywhere else.

decisions.title: A prep value inside a function
decisions.situation: A prep block computes a value while the program is built. A test expects such a block inside a function to be refused with an error saying it is not supported yet, while D-PREP-SURFACE2 says prepared values use ordinary names. Neither compiler gives that error today. The vote decides whether a local prep value is part of the language; we recommend yes, built once and baked in.
decisions.gist: Does `lanes :: prep { calculate_lanes() + 0 }` inside a function compute its value at build time?
decisions.lesson: A `prep { … }` block runs while the program is built, and its last expression is its value. At module level `NAME :: prep { value }` is ratified. A fixture expects a local `lanes :: prep { … }` inside a function to be rejected with E0391, which says the form is not supported yet.
decisions.story: Kai's renderer needs the number of lanes. He writes `lanes :: prep { calculate_lanes() }` inside `run` so the work happens once at build time instead of every run.
decisions.detail: Fixture tests/ui/prep_block_value_unsupported.jet; its comment cites D-PREP-SURFACE2=A and expects E0391. D-PREP-SURFACE2=A: prep is always an expression whose final expression is its value, and prepared values use ordinary names. A 'not supported yet' diagnostic conflicts with the greenfield rule of one canonical current form. Edge cases: the prep body may not read run-time locals; it runs once per build, not per call.

options.name: Supported
options.detail: A local prep binding is computed at build time. The fixture becomes a run example with golden output 8, and E0391 is removed.
options.technical: Comptime evaluates the block once per build; codegen emits the constant. The prep body may not reference run-time locals (existing prep rules).

options.name: Module level only
options.detail: A prep value inside a function is rejected with a permanent error that teaches moving it to a module-level `NAME :: prep { … }`.
options.technical: E0391 is reworded as a permanent rule with a fix; the fixture keeps its snapshot.
options.code:
LANES :: prep { calculate_lanes() + 0 }
fn run() { print(LANES) }

comparisons.note: Zig evaluates a comptime expression inside a function and bakes the value in. See https://ziglang.org/documentation/master/#comptime

recommendation.why: D-PREP-SURFACE2 already says prepared values use ordinary names, and a local value keeps build-time work next to the code that needs it.
gains: One rule for prep values everywhere, with no 'not yet' error.

losses.loss: The compiler must fold local prep values.
losses.mitigation: The same evaluator already folds module-level prep values.

whyNot.reason: It splits one feature by location and turns a 'not yet' into a permanent restriction.

recommendation.tradeoff: A little more compiler work for a uniform rule.

decisions.title: Do method calls into Core count toward the rights a program needs?
decisions.situation: Before a program runs, Jet works out which rights it needs (reading the environment, reading files and so on) and stops with E1803 when the application has not decided them. The self-hosted compiler follows method calls such as `Path.home()` into Core and finds the Env and FS.Read rights they use. The Rust compiler only follows plain function calls, so it never sees those rights. Eleven run goldens (io/path, io/args_spec, dyn/bytes_datetime, io/system_projection and others) expect the program to run with no grants, which matches the Rust result. The vote decides which result is the rule.
decisions.gist: Does `Path.home()` in a program make it need the Env right before it runs?
decisions.lesson: A program's rights are the effects it can reach. Rust's check skips method calls, so a program that reads the home directory through `Path.home()` is treated as needing only IO.
decisions.story: Mia writes a small tool that prints her home directory with `Path.home()`. Under one rule it runs straight away; under the other Jet first asks her to grant Env, because that is what the tool reads.
decisions.inWild: deno run --allow-env main.ts   # Deno asks for the env right whenever Deno.env is reached, however it is called
decisions.detail: Jet: Compiler/JetCli/Source/Cli/Authority.jet:153 walks call edges, method calls included. Rust: crates/jet-pkg-model/src/EffectBudget.rs:638 entry_effects over an effect call graph that records only bare-name calls (crates/jet-sema/src/Sema/OSTarget.rs:503-506). Edge cases: trait method calls through a box, closures passed to Core, generic Core functions. Under A the eleven goldens gain the grant they need in their package.jet (authority.holds) and keep their output.

options.name: Every call counts
options.detail: Method calls into Core count like plain calls. The eleven goldens declare the rights they really use and keep their output.
options.technical: Keep the Jet walk; add authority.holds rows to the eleven golden packages; Rust stays the old route and is not changed.

options.name: Match the Rust compiler
options.detail: Only plain function calls count. The goldens run unchanged with no grants.
options.technical: The Jet walk skips method-call edges into Core, as Rust does.
options.code: fn main() { print(Path.home()) }   // runs with no grant

comparisons.note: Deno checks the env right at the point of use, however the code reaches it. See https://docs.deno.com/runtime/fundamentals/security/

recommendation.why: A right that a method call reaches without being counted is a hole in the check. Any program could read files or the environment through a method.
gains: The rights check sees everything the program can do.

losses.loss: Eleven goldens need a one-line grant in their package.
losses.mitigation: Their printed output does not change.

whyNot.reason: It keeps a known gap in a safety check to match an old compiler's omission.

recommendation.tradeoff: A grant line in a few examples for a rights check with no gap.

decisions.title: In a cross build, which machine do build-time Core calls act on?
decisions.situation: Build code runs on the build machine, but the program it builds may run somewhere else. Today build code can only read the target, through $build.os, and nothing names the build machine. Core is also inconsistent. Most per-OS Core code asks the running machine, but one Core helper folds $build.os, so during a Windows build on Linux it would use Windows path rules on a Linux disk. We recommend one rule: Core calls act on the machine running them, $build always names the target, and $build.host names the build machine.
decisions.gist: When build code cross-compiles, do its Core calls act on the build machine or the target?
decisions.lesson: Build code runs on your machine, while the program it builds may run on another. A file read in build code can only read your disk. The question is whether Core calls in build code follow your machine, and how build code names each machine. Reading a fact never changes its meaning: $build.os always names the target.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: a normal build on one machine changes nothing. The question matters only when you build a program for another operating system.

If you build a Windows program on Linux, a preparation step that lists a directory must answer for one machine. Jet must say which one, every time, so the build is repeatable.
decisions.story: Theo builds a Windows installer on a Linux laptop. His build code lists the assets folder and checks that every file exists. The listing must use Linux path rules, because it reads his Linux disk. The installer itself still uses Windows rules.
decisions.inWild:
Cargo build scripts: cfg!(target_os) inside build.rs describes the build machine, and the target comes from CARGO_CFG_TARGET_OS. Cargo's docs warn about mixing them up. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-build-scripts

Zig: build.zig is compiled for the build machine; b.graph.host names it, and the target is a separate value. Source: https://ziglang.org/learn/build-system/
decisions.detail:
WHAT EXISTS TODAY

Facts are served by Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Expressions/FactReads.jet:641-649. They are $package.name and version, $build.os and profile, the stamps and $build.cpu.cache_line. There is no host fact. Docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:5268 says $build.os is the --target OS, or the host OS when no target is given.

Build code: Docs/spec/spec.md:4888-4935. jet build runs fn build(b: Build) natively at O0 on the build machine, and the spec example uses the FS and Exec effects directly.

Core already asks the running machine in most places. Core/Sys/Sys.jet:897 and Core/Ui/Host.jet:205 pick PathPlatform from core.files.__path_windows(). Core/Files/Files.jet:1105-1109 list_dir calls the runtime's __list_dir_raw, which can only read the disk it runs on.

The one outlier: Core/Service/Service.jet:1455-1465 StatePathPlatform.windows() folds $build.os. In a Linux-to-Windows cross build, a Service state path computed during build code would use Windows rules on the Linux disk.

CARD

Tower card c0rc40yf (Host facts for prep and build-time code) asks for host OS and architecture facts beside $build. It also asks for one stated rule for per-OS Core calls during preparation. Host reads must enter the cache key, and a policy must be able to reject them.

Related rulings: D-BUILD-FACT3=A puts build facts under $build. D-JAI-CONFIG1=A records every host read in the build record and cache key. D-HOST-CAPS1=A says target hardware facts follow the selected target, never the build machine.

HOW A'S DOWNSIDES ARE DESIGNED AWAY

1. A Core call in build code answers for the build machine. Nothing that ships depends on that answer. Shipped names and paths come from b.add_executable, b.add_install and b.action outputs, which apply $build.os rules themselves. Build code that prints or branches on a target fact reads $build.os.

2. Builds reading the build machine. Every option has this, because build actions run on the build machine under all three. A records each $build.host read and host-touching Core call in the build record and cache key (D-JAI-CONFIG1=A). Equal inputs give equal outputs, and a package policy can deny host reads with a registered diagnostic.

No loss remains. Any output call that lacks a target rule today gains one as work owed under A.

WORK OWED UNDER A

Add $build.host.os and $build.host.arch to FactReads.jet and the syntax registry. Change Service.jet:1459 to ask the running machine, like Sys.jet:897. Add a cross-build golden example that prints both facts.

WHY NOT B OR C

B makes build code describe a machine it is not running on. A file listing cannot read the target's disk, so B must ban direct file and process calls in build code. Every read then becomes a declared action. C makes common calls in every cross build carry a side argument, which is noise when only one answer is possible.

options.name: Core calls act on the machine running them
options.detail: A Core call in build code acts on the build machine, the only one it can touch. $build.os always names the target. Build code reads the build machine through $build.host.os and $build.host.arch, and each read goes into the cache key. Everything that ships goes through Build calls such as b.add_executable and b.add_install, which apply the target's rules themselves.
options.technical: Add $build.host.os and $build.host.arch fact reads. Core per-OS code asks the running machine, as Sys.jet:897 already does; Service.jet:1459 moves to that form. Host reads join the build record, and a package policy can deny them. Build outputs (b.add_executable, b.add_install and b.action outputs) take target-relative paths and apply $build.os rules, such as the .exe suffix, with no host call.

options.name: Everything in build code answers for the target
options.detail: Pure Core calls in build code answer as the target would. Because build code cannot touch the target's disk, direct file and process calls in build code are refused, and each such step becomes a declared action.
options.technical: Build code loses the FS and Exec effects. Reads move to b.action steps, which run on the build machine. No host fact is added.

options.name: Refuse calls that do not name a side
options.detail: In a cross build, a per-OS Core call in build code is a compile error unless it names the machine it means.
options.technical: The checker rejects per-OS Core calls in build code under cross-compilation unless a .Host or .Target argument is given. Adds a side argument to those Core calls.

comparisons.note: In build.rs, cfg!(target_os) describes the build machine. The target comes from CARGO_CFG_TARGET_OS. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html
build.zig runs on the build machine. b.graph.host names it, and the target is chosen separately. Source: https://ziglang.org/learn/build-system/
comparisons.code:
const target = b.standardTargetOptions(.{});
const host = b.graph.host;

recommendation.why: A states one rule: a call acts on the machine running it. It is the only answer a file read can give. $build keeps one meaning, the target, and $build.host names the build machine.
gains: Build code reads its own disk with the right path rules.
$build.os means the target everywhere.
Host reads are recorded, so the cache stays correct.
Shipped files get the target's names and paths from the Build API.

whyNot.reason: B makes build code describe a machine it cannot touch, so every file read must become a declared action.
C adds a side argument to common calls in every cross build, though only one answer is possible.

recommendation.tradeoff: A acts on the running machine, and the Build API applies the target's rules to everything that ships.

decisions.title: What the error says when a function can't be a C callback
decisions.situation: Jet lets you pass a function to a C library as a callback, but only a plain one. It must not capture locals, allocate, have effects, be generic, panic or schedule tasks. When a passed function breaks one of these rules, Jet points at the function correctly. The message is wrong, though: it says the callback type is not C-compatible, when the type is fine and the function is at fault. We recommend a dedicated error that names the broken rule.
decisions.gist: When a passed function can't be a C callback, which error should Jet give?
decisions.lesson: A callback type can be fine while the function you pass breaks a callback rule, for example by capturing a local. Those are two different mistakes. The error should name the one you made and the rule it broke, so the fix is obvious.
decisions.story: Omar passes a lambda that adds a local offset to a C library. Jet tells him the callback type is not C-compatible. He checks the type, finds nothing wrong, and is stuck. The real problem is that the lambda captures offset.
decisions.inWild: Rust: a capturing closure cannot be passed where a C function pointer is expected. The error says "closures can only be coerced to `fn` types if they do not capture any variables" and points at the capture. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/types/closure.html
decisions.detail:
TODAY (published base compiler, jet check on each fixture, 2026-11-05)

Six fixtures pass a function that breaks a callback rule: tests/ui/cffi_callback_capture, _allocation, _effect, _generic, _panic and _runtime_handle. Each reports E3203 jet.NonCAbiType at the passed function. The text blames the parameter type, for example "`fn(I32) -[]> I32` is not a C-compatible type". Its Why and Fix talk about stable C layout, which does not apply.

tests/ui/cffi_callback_bound_method reports the same misleading E3203 plus E0302.

tests/ui/cffi_callback_non_c_safe_signature declares cb: fn([Int]) -[]> Int. E3203 at the declaration is correct there, and stays.

The earlier draft said Jet gives E0102 and that the snapshots expect E3203 at the declaration. Both are stale: the snapshots point at the passed function, and E0102 no longer occurs.

CODE

Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Calls/Checking.jet:531-537 runs the callback check before the argument's type check. It reuses sema_checked_foreign_type_error (Registration/Checked.jet:944-949), which produces the type message. sema_call_c_callback_unsafe (Checking.jet:357-374) returns only a Bool, so the broken rule is lost.

E3216 jet.InvalidForeignBoundaryEvidence (Checked.jet:514-516, Items.jet:1991) covers incomplete provider and boundary metadata. It is not about the user's function. Ratified D-FFI-CALLBACK2=A limits callbacks to this plain subset, and D-FFI-CONTRACT1=A requires evidence per obligation. Neither names the diagnostic.

WORK UNDER A

sema_call_c_callback_unsafe returns the first broken rule with its span (the captured name, the allocating expression, the effect). A new registry row jet.UnsafeCCallback gets What/Why/Fix. The seven snapshots are regenerated in the same change. E3203 stays for declared types C cannot call.

WHY NOT B OR C

B keeps E3203. Its name, NonCAbiType, and its More page then cover two unrelated mistakes. C uses E3216, the reference compiler's choice. That code means missing provider metadata, which a user cannot fix in their own function.

decisions.title: Report every error by default
decisions.gist: Should check, build, run and test report every error they find, or stop at the first failing phase?
decisions.lesson: A compile can stop after the first phase that finds an error, so users fix errors one round at a time. A full report shows all of them at once. Run naively, later phases would also report errors caused by earlier ones; the recommended design hides those.
decisions.story: Ana runs jet build on a project with a type error in one file and a bad import in another. Under option A she sees both errors in one run and no output file is written. Under option B she sees the type error, fixes it, and only then learns about the import.
decisions.inWild:
Rust: rustc reports every type error in one pass across a crate, then stops before code generation. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustc/

Go: go build reports up to ten errors per package, then stops. Source: https://go.dev/doc/
decisions.detail:
Owner ruling, 2026-10-09 (card #4914): every phase runs by default for check, build, run and test, with typed traps. No artifact is written when an error occurs. One canonical option is both a CLI flag and a build config setting.

Today the pipeline stops between phases at JetDriver Pipeline.jet:2220 and BodyComptime.jet:221. The full mode exists only behind the compiler-internal JET_KEEP_GOING=1 (Compiler/Bootstrap/Host/Entry.jet:10-128). The card plan keeps JET_KEEP_GOING_SKIP as a developer tool if needed.

No ratified decision found by keyword scan records this default.

Redesign 2026-11-01 (owner: engineer the downsides away). The first version kept two losses: follow-on noise and a longer run. Both are designed away. A failed item is marked failed, and every later phase skips that item and anything whose meaning depends on it. A check that meets a failed type or name stays silent, as rustc does with its error type. So every printed error is a root error, and a later phase does less work, not more.

Follow-on errors are still recorded. The text summary counts them, and --json lists each one with the root it came from. This also settles the owner question about follow-on UI rows: they leave the default output.

options.technical: Remove the stop-between-phases gates at Pipeline.jet:2220 and BodyComptime.jet:221 for the default mode. A failed item carries an error mark; later phases skip it and its dependents, and checks that meet an error type or failed name emit nothing. Keep-going traps stay for lowering. Suppressed diagnostics are kept with a caused_by link for --json. The developer-only JET_KEEP_GOING=1 switch is replaced by the canonical option.
