decisions.title: How the compiler and Jetpack reach Core operations that user programs must not call
decisions.situation:
Jetpack and the compiler need five Core operations that user programs must never call. Two exist today as `files.compiler_with_process_directory` and `files.compiler_link_held`. They are ordinary public functions, and a user program can call them: we checked one with the tree14 compiler and it passed. The other three are blocked because no rule lets the toolchain reach a private Core module.

We recommend one more qualifier in the existing `priv(…)` family, `priv(toolchain) module`. Only Core, the compiler and Jetpack may use such a module. User programs get E0605, as for any private module.
decisions.gist: Should Core operations meant only for the compiler and Jetpack live in a `priv(toolchain) module`, become public documented functions, or be reached through foreign-call glue?
decisions.lesson: Jet marks privacy on modules, not on functions. A `priv module` is usable only by its enclosing module, and a `priv(package) module` by its own package. Neither lets the compiler or Jetpack, which are separate packages, reach a private part of Core.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. The toolchain is the set of packages the Jet distribution ships: Core, the compiler packages and Jetpack, the package manager. A seam is a Core operation that only the toolchain needs, such as running a child process inside a folder that Jetpack already holds open.

A held folder is a `Directory` value that keeps the folder open. Work done through it cannot be redirected by renaming the folder's path.
decisions.story: Omar's app imports `core.files` and sees `compiler_link_held` in completion. He calls it inside an `#Unsafe` block, and the compiler accepts it, because the function is public. Next release the store changes the function's errno rules and his app breaks. Under A the function lives in `core.files.toolchain`, completion never offers it, and his call is E0605 from the start.
decisions.detail:
Source: card #4896 and its four added cases. Five seams need the same answer.

1. Run a child process inside a held folder. Jetpack's TreeHash.jet:562 calls `files.compiler_with_process_directory`.
2. Link an open file into a held folder. Jetpack's TreeHash.jet:738 calls `files.compiler_link_held`.
3. Pass a held lock to a child process, so a child keeps the same lock. Core has no such operation yet.
4. Lower the compiler's `sort_by` to one private Core kernel, so every tier shares one meaning.
5. Let the compiler's build-receipt producer read Core/build's private session.

Today. The double-underscore names were renamed to legal `compiler_` names, so the CLI source parses. But Sema has no caller check on Core calls (Sema core_call, traced by CoreReview5-2-2). A user file calling `files.compiler_with_process_directory` inside `#Unsafe` passes `jet check` on the tree14 compiler (probe ballot/xb/seam.jet). Seams 3 to 5 cannot be written, because a private module refuses every outside package.

The visibility law. Declarations carry no visibility marker; `priv` marks a module or a field. `priv(package) module` is the one qualified form, and any other qualifier is E0414 (syntax-decisions S18). The draft's `toolchain fn` mark broke that law, so A now uses a module qualifier instead.

What A adds. `priv(toolchain) module` is accepted only in a toolchain package; elsewhere it stays E0414. A use from any other package is E0605, the error every private module already gives. A package counts as toolchain when its source root lies inside the Jet distribution that supplied Core. Package names play no part, so a user package cannot claim the status.

Compiler-generated calls. When the compiler lowers `list.sort_by(f)` in a user program to the Core kernel, the call is the compiler's, so it passes. A call written in the user's source still gets E0605.

Safety. Seams 1 and 2 become typed functions that return `IOError`, with no raw errno tuple and no `#Unsafe` marker. Seam 1 has the same body as the public `Directory.pass_to`, which needs no gate. The `#Unsafe` blocks at Jetpack's two call sites go away.

A side question in the draft, whether diagnostics can read text without copying it, is not a privacy question. Borrowed text is ordinary public Jet, so it needs no seam.

options.name: One `priv(toolchain) module` in Core for all five seams
options.detail:
Core gathers the seams into private modules marked `priv(toolchain)`, such as `core.files.toolchain`. Core, the compiler and Jetpack may use them. Any other package gets E0605, and completion and the reference never list them.

The qualifier joins the existing `priv(…)` family and is accepted only inside a toolchain package. User code can never write it. Calls the compiler generates, such as the `sort_by` kernel, pass. The seams take typed arguments and return `IOError`, so their callers need no `#Unsafe` block.
options.technical:
Parser: `priv(toolchain)` is accepted before `module` when the file's package is a toolchain package, else E0414 as today. Sema: the E0605 check in Calls/Core.jet:354 and Expressions/Places.jet:790 admits a toolchain-private module in two cases. The caller's package root lies inside the distribution root that supplied Core, or the call is compiler-generated.

Core: move the two `compiler_` functions into `priv(toolchain) module toolchain` in Core/Files as `run_in` and `link_into`. Add `pass_lock`, the sort kernel and the build-session readers to toolchain modules beside their owners. Jetpack drops both `#Unsafe` blocks. Syntax-decisions S18 gains one line.

options.name: Make each seam a public, documented Core function
options.detail:
Each seam becomes a public function with documentation, such as `spec.run_in(folder)`, `reader.link_into(folder, name)` and `lock.pass_to(spec, at)`. The sort kernel and the build-session readers become public too.

Anyone may call them, and each becomes a promise Core must keep stable across releases.
options.technical: Rename the two `compiler_` functions to public methods and remove the `#Unsafe` markers. Add `AdvisoryLock.pass_to`. Export the sort kernel from core.collections and the build-session readers from core.build, which turns a read-only query surface into one with mutable session state.

options.name: Reach the runtime directly through foreign-call glue
options.detail:
Jetpack declares the runtime symbols itself with `#Import(c)` and calls them, as C code would. Core adds nothing.

Seams 4 and 5 are Jet functions, not runtime symbols, so glue cannot reach them and they stay blocked.
options.technical: Jetpack adds `#Import(c)` declarations for `jet_process_spec_with_directory_raw` and `jet_files_link_reader_at_raw`, and keeps their argument layouts in step with the runtime by hand. The Core checks in `process_directory` (slot range, closed folder, slot taken) are skipped.

comparisons.note: A module may export a package only to named modules. java.base exports `jdk.internal.misc` to a fixed list of JDK modules, and other code cannot use it. Source: JLS 7.7.2, qualified exports.

A package under `internal/` can be imported only by code rooted at its parent. Since Go 1.23 the linker also refuses new `go:linkname` pulls into the standard library. Source: go.dev/doc/go1.23, Linker.
comparisons.code: import "internal/poll"   // only the standard library may

comparisons.note: The standard library marks internal items unstable with no tracking issue, so stable user code cannot call them. The compiler's own crates opt in with `rustc_private`. Source: rustc-dev-guide, Stability attributes.

recommendation.why: A protects all five operations with the privacy rule Jet already has: one module qualifier and the existing E0605. User programs can no longer reach compiler-only operations, and the three blocked ones can be written.
gains: User programs cannot call compiler-only operations.
One rule for all five operations, with no new declaration marker.
Jetpack's two `#Unsafe` blocks go away.

losses.loss: A third-party package manager cannot use the operations Jetpack uses.
losses.mitigation: An operation useful to everyone moves out of the toolchain module into a public typed API, as `Directory.pass_to` did.

whyNot.reason: Every compiler-only operation becomes a public promise, and the build session gains public mutable state.
Glue skips Core's checks, any user can write it too, and two of the five seams stay blocked.

recommendation.tradeoff: One more `priv(…)` qualifier that only toolchain packages may write. In return, compiler-only operations are closed to user programs and all five seams have a home.

A is now a module qualifier keyed on the distribution root, with generated calls admitted and typed seams; the one remaining loss is stated.

decisions.title: What an HTTP body value is once the Rust code is gone
decisions.situation: When a Jet program downloads something, the data arrives as an HTTP body. Jet's reader for that body was written in Rust, and that code is now deleted. Jet's own Body is a plain value that cannot hold a download still arriving, so Jet's package manager cannot download anything yet. The vote decides what a body is; we recommend a file-like reader, which keeps the large-download streaming you already approved.
decisions.gist: When a program receives an HTTP body, should it get a file-like reader, or a plain value?
decisions.lesson: A body is the data inside a web request or response, such as a downloaded file. Jet's body() reader used to live in deleted Rust code. Jet's own Body today is a plain value with three cases: empty, text or bytes. A plain value cannot hold a download that is still arriving. Whichever option wins, Jet's HTTP client must then be written in Jet.
decisions.story: Mia's build script downloads a 300 MiB package archive with Jet. She wants it streamed to disk under a size cap, not loaded into memory, and she wants the same body methods on her small server.
decisions.inWild:
resp, err := http.Get(url)
defer resp.Body.Close()
data, err := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 1<<20))
// https://pkg.go.dev/net/http#Response
decisions.detail: Code: Core/http/http.jet:87 defines the Body enum with Empty, Text(String), and Bytes([U8]). A shared, one-shot native body cannot be held there. Option A makes Body opaque with a private shared carrier and constructors and inspection methods. Option B adds a hidden fourth case. Option C reads the whole body on access, which conflicts with the ratified streaming cap. The public carrier for the native body is decided in a separate card, which this ballot depends on.

options.name: A file-like Body
options.detail: Body becomes a closed Core type with private fields. Programs build one with Body.empty(), Body.text(s) or Body.bytes(b). They read one with text(limit), bytes(limit), json(limit), chunks() and copy_to(^writer), each a single pass. The size cap you approved in D-CORE-HTTPBODYLIMIT1 applies to every read. Client and server use the same type.
options.technical: Core/Http/Http.jet: Body becomes a struct with a private shared one-pass reader state (the connection, the remaining framing, a consumed flag) or an in-memory payload. body_as_text and body_as_bytes, the only matches on the cases today, move to the read methods. Calls/Http.jet keeps the same method names and results. No example matches on the cases.
options.code:
text :: resp.body().text(1024 * 1024) ?? panic("body")
resp.body(limit: 2.gib).copy_to(^file)
reply :: Body.text("ok")

options.name: Hidden fourth case
options.detail: Body keeps its Empty, Text and Bytes cases and gains a private Stream case that programs cannot name. Every match on Body then needs an else arm, which runs for streamed bodies.
options.technical: The enum gains a private variant carrying the shared reader state. The checker would need a new rule for a variant that is hidden from user matches.

options.name: Read it all on arrival
options.detail: The client reads the whole body into memory before it returns the response, so Body stays a finished three-case value. Streaming large downloads to disk is no longer possible.
options.technical: send() reads to the end of the framing and stores Body.Bytes. This contradicts D-CORE-HTTPBODYLIMIT1, which ratified a one-pass streamed body with its own cap.
options.code:
resp :: http.get(url) ?? panic("get")
text :: http.body_as_text(resp.body())

comparisons.note: net/http gives Response.Body as an io.ReadCloser that the program reads once: https://pkg.go.dev/net/http#Response.
reqwest reads the body through methods on the response (bytes, text, chunk), not through an enum: https://docs.rs/reqwest/latest/reqwest/struct.Response.html.

recommendation.why: Only a reader can stream a large download under a cap, and Go and Rust clients make the same choice.
gains: Keeps the approved streaming rule and one meaning for Body.

losses.loss: Code can no longer match on .Text or .Bytes cases.
losses.mitigation: Only Core's own helpers do this today, and they move to the read methods.

whyNot.reason: B makes every match carry an else arm that quietly mishandles streams.
C breaks the streaming you already approved and can exhaust memory on big downloads.

recommendation.tradeoff: Body loses pattern matching; reading it uses the same methods everywhere.

decisions.title: How each linked part is spelled, defaulted and reported
decisions.situation: Native Jet programs are fully static today. The GPU driver must load from the user's system, and a static process cannot load it. Each linked part needs its own linkage, because tools and graphics programs differ. We recommend per-part settings in the build function, with defaults that need no annotation in most programs. Tools stay one file.
decisions.gist: How should a program choose static or dynamic linking for each part it uses?
decisions.lesson: A program often mixes parts that must stay static with parts the system must load. One setting per program cannot serve both.
decisions.story: Eli builds a small command-line tool and a game. The tool should stay one file. The game must load the system's graphics driver at run time.
decisions.inWild: go build ./game   // static unless cgo uses a system library
decisions.detail:
Source: card #5088 log, 2026-10-21 owner amendment. Linkage is decided per linked item: Jet runtime and libc, system libraries such as libGL, bundled C libraries, and foreign closures. Defaults: pure Jet and bundled C static; OS driver and system libraries dynamic. CLI --linkage stays a whole-program override. Still open: exact spelling, the full defaults table, and per-item reporting in jet inspect. Ratified D-JPK-VARIANT1 (D) sets the axes.

Redesign 2026-11-01 (owner: engineer the downsides away). The first version listed testing two linkage modes as a loss of A. It is shared work: any design where a graphics program runs needs dynamic loading, and any design where a tool stays one file needs static linking. B and C carry the same test work, so it is not a reason to choose between them.

The test matrix is generated from one list of cells, each run in its required mode. jet inspect shows each part with its linkage and why, so a wrong default is visible at once. A program that names no dynamic part stays one static file, exactly as today.

options.name: Per-part settings in the build function
options.detail: Each linked part has its own linkage. Defaults: pure Jet and bundled C static; OS driver and system libraries dynamic. The build function changes any part. jet inspect lists each part with its linkage and its source.
options.technical: The build function returns a per-item linkage map; the linker resolves each item separately and rejects impossible combinations as diagnostics.

options.name: One setting for the whole program
options.detail: The build command or manifest picks one linkage for everything.
options.technical: One linkage value passes to the linker; no per-item map.
options.code: jet build --linkage=dynamic game.jet

options.name: Separate link file
options.detail: Linked parts are listed in a linking file beside the package.
options.technical: A second input file is parsed and checked against the package's imports.
options.code: link.jet: gpu = dynamic

comparisons.note: Go builds static binaries and links dynamically only when a system library is needed.

recommendation.why: Each part gets the linkage its platform needs, from a default table, so most programs write nothing. Tools stay one static file and graphics programs load the system GPU driver.
gains: Static tools stay single-file.
Graphics programs work out of the box.
jet inspect shows each part’s linkage and its reason.

whyNot.reason: One setting cannot keep tools static and graphics programs working.
A second file adds a place to forget a setting.

recommendation.tradeoff: None remaining: testing both modes is shared work every option needs.

surface.gist: How should a program choose static or dynamic linking for each part it uses?
surface.lesson: A program often mixes parts that must stay static with parts the system must load. One setting per program cannot serve both.

current.note: Every native program is fully static with a private libc. Graphics drivers cannot load into that process.
current.code: jet build game.jet   // one static file; the GPU driver cannot load

wild.note: Go builds static binaries, and links dynamically only when a program needs a system library.
wild.code: go build ./game   // static unless cgo uses a system library

options.name: Per-part settings in the build function
options.gist: Each part has its own linkage, with a default table, set in the package's build function.
gains: Pure Jet and bundled C stay static.
System drivers load from the OS.
Most programs write nothing.

options.name: One setting for the whole program
options.gist: Choose static or dynamic once in the build command or manifest.
gains: Simplest to explain.
losses: A static program cannot use the GPU, and a dynamic one loses single-file output.

proposed.code: jet build --linkage=dynamic game.jet

options.name: Separate link file
options.gist: List each linked part in a separate linking file next to the package.
gains: Build code and link settings stay apart.
losses: A second file must be kept in step with the package.

proposed.code: link.jet: gpu = dynamic

recommendation.why: Each part gets the linkage it needs from a default table, so tools stay one file and graphics programs just work.
gains: Single-file tools and working graphics.

whyNot.reason: One setting cannot serve tools and graphics.
A second file is a place to forget a setting.

recommendation.tradeoff: None remaining; testing both modes is shared work.

decisions.title: Nixpkgs packages come in as native Jet packages, with no Nix
decisions.gist: Should Nixpkgs packages be translated into native Jet packages stored only in Hangar, with no Nix program or store at all?
decisions.lesson: Jetpack can use Nixpkgs packages, but today it can call an installed Nix as a fallback. Jetpack can instead read each Nixpkgs recipe itself and run its build steps inside Hangar, so every package installs with no Nix at all.
decisions.story: Ravi installs a tool that exists only in Nixpkgs. Under option A Jetpack translates its recipe into a native Jet package, and the install needs no Nix on his machine. Under option B Jetpack calls his installed Nix when the translation is missing, so the install depends on a Nix he never chose.
decisions.inWild:
Guix: a package manager with its own store and recipes, separate from Nix. Source: https://guix.gnu.org/manual/en/html_node/Invoking-guix-package.html

Nix: packages are built into /nix/store by the Nix daemon. Source: https://nixos.org/manual/nix/stable/
decisions.detail:
Owner requirement, 2026-09-13 (card #3402): ingest Nixpkgs through an adapter that translates definitions into the native Jet package model. Jetpack owns resolution, builds, installation, updates and removal. Hangar is the only store. No separately installed or bundled Nix package manager, daemon, profile or store is permitted, including hidden or mounted stores. Native Jet packages bypass the adapter. Jet and Jetpack code is MIT; the adapter must not depend on Nix executables, libraries, daemons, services or storage.

The card records that D-NIX-UPSTREAM1 was superseded unratified, so this requirement is not a ratified decision.

Conflict: ratified D-JPK-SNIXREUSE1 (2026-08-25, option A) keeps a local Nix import on a miss, and D-JPK-NIXSTORE1 (2026-07-10, option D) uses a projected Nix store. Both predate the 2026-09-13 requirement and conflict with it. The card's current state: crates/jetpack/src/NixFallbackPolicy.rs and Jetpack/Nix/Source/Fallback/FallbackPolicy.jet still call nix build.

Redesign 2026-11-01 (owner: engineer the downsides away). The first version translated packages one by one, so an untranslated package failed until someone converted it. Now Jetpack translates at the level every package shares. NixEval, Jet’s own Nix-language evaluator, reads the recipe and yields its build plan: sources, dependencies, build script and environment.

Jetpack then fetches the sources by hash and runs that plan in its own sandbox, storing the result in Hangar under Jet’s own paths. That is generic, so any package Nixpkgs can build installs without per-package work, and no Nix program, daemon or store is used.

What can still fail is a recipe that uses a Nix language feature NixEval lacks. That failure names the feature, and one evaluator fix unblocks every package using it.

options.name: Build Nixpkgs recipes natively in Hangar
options.detail: Jetpack reads each Nixpkgs recipe with its own evaluator, fetches the sources by hash, and runs the recipe’s build steps in its sandbox. Hangar stores the result. The installed-Nix fallback is deleted. Native Jet packages skip this path.
options.technical: Delete the fallback files and the JETPACK_NIX_FALLBACK_POLICY variables. NixEval evaluates the attribute to its build plan; the realizer fetches fixed-output sources, runs the builder with the recorded environment in the Hangar sandbox, and rewrites output paths to Hangar paths. Upstream provenance is kept so updates re-evaluate. Unsupported evaluator features become named, tracked diagnostics.
options.code: $ jetpack install ripgrep-nix   # translated; stored in Hangar; no nix on PATH

options.name: Keep an installed-Nix fallback
options.detail: Native packages come first. When a Nixpkgs package has no translation, Jetpack calls an installed Nix.
options.technical: Keep Fallback/FallbackPolicy.jet and the nix build path behind the policy variable.
options.code: $ jetpack install postgres-nix   # falls back to installed nix build --json

comparisons.note: Guix keeps its own store and recipes, separate from Nix. Source: https://guix.gnu.org/manual/en/html_node/Invoking-guix-package.html
Packages are built into /nix/store by the Nix daemon. Source: https://nixos.org/manual/nix/stable/

recommendation.why: The owner required one native store and no Nix on the install path. Building recipes natively meets that for every package at once, instead of one translation at a time.
gains: One store, Hangar, for every package.
An ordinary install needs no Nix.
Any package Nixpkgs can build installs, with no per-package work.

whyNot.reason: B brings an installed Nix back as a dependency, which the owner requirement forbids.

recommendation.tradeoff: None remaining: every Nixpkgs package installs, and Nix is never installed.

surface.gist: Should Nixpkgs packages become native Jet packages stored only in Hangar, with no Nix at all?
surface.lesson: Today Jetpack can fall back to an installed Nix for Nixpkgs packages. Should it build those recipes itself, with no Nix at all?

current.note: A missing translation falls back to an installed Nix.
current.code: $ jetpack install postgres-nix   # calls nix build --json

wild.note: Guix keeps its own store and recipes, separate from Nix. Source: https://guix.gnu.org/manual/en/html_node/Invoking-guix-package.html
wild.code: guix install hello

options.name: Build Nixpkgs recipes natively in Hangar
options.gist: Jetpack reads each recipe and runs its build steps itself; Hangar stores the result.
gains: No Nix on any install path.
Every buildable package installs.

proposed.code: $ jetpack install ripgrep-nix   # built in Hangar; no nix on PATH

options.name: Keep an installed-Nix fallback
options.gist: Untranslated packages call the installed Nix.
gains: More packages install today.
losses: A Nix dependency remains on the install path.

proposed.code: $ jetpack install postgres-nix   # installed nix

recommendation.why: Building recipes natively removes Nix from every install path and needs no per-package translation.
gains: No Nix, and every package installs.

whyNot.reason: B keeps Nix as a dependency, which the owner forbade.

recommendation.tradeoff: None remaining.

decisions.title: A built-in exit for expected failures
decisions.situation: Command-line scripts stop with a message when input is wrong. Today each script defines a four-line helper that prints to stderr and exits. The alternative returns an error from the entry function, which prints a framed report. We recommend a built-in fail that takes a message and an exit code. It prints the message, runs scope cleanup, and exits with no frame. Panic stays for program bugs.
decisions.gist: Should scripts get a built-in way to stop with a message and an exit code?
decisions.lesson: Scripts that stop on bad input need a four-line helper. A built-in call would print the message and exit with no frame.
decisions.story: Ana writes a tool that needs one file name. When the name is missing, she wants one line of usage text and exit code 64, not a crash report.
decisions.inWild: fn fail(message: String) -> Never { term.eprint(message); process.exit(1) }
decisions.detail: Source: card #5085, item B6. Four ported scripts each defined this helper. Ratified D-FAIL-EXIT1 makes errors report and exit 1, and keeps exit 101 for the compiler. Ratified D-PANICROOT1 places panic in the effect table. Ratified D-CORE-PRELUDE1 governs what the readable prelude may hold. The exit code parameter is a literal in the card's signature, so the type should be checked before ratification. Savings are per script.

options.name: Built-in fail with an exit code
options.detail: `fail(message, code)` writes the message and a newline to stderr, runs scope guards, and exits with the code. It prints no frame. `panic` remains for bugs.
options.technical: Prelude function returning Never. Uses the existing exit path, so guards run before exit as they do for a normal return.
options.code: fail("usage: tool FILE", 64)

options.name: Return an error from run
options.detail: The entry function returns an error value. The runtime reports it and exits. The report carries a frame.
options.technical: Uses the existing error-result path. No new surface.
options.code: return Err(UsageError("usage: tool FILE"))

comparisons.note: A script writes to stderr and exits with a status code.

recommendation.why: A usage error is expected, so it should exit with a message and no frame. A built-in call removes the helper each script repeats.
gains: Four fewer lines in each script.

losses.loss: A second way to stop with an error.
losses.mitigation: Built-in fail is for expected failures only. Bugs still use panic, and the docs place them side by side.

whyNot.reason: It prints a framed error report for a plain usage mistake, which reads as a crash.

recommendation.tradeoff: A new prelude name, in exchange for one call in place of a helper.

surface.gist: Should scripts get a built-in way to stop with a message and an exit code?
surface.lesson: Scripts that stop on bad input need a four-line helper. A built-in call would print the message and exit with no frame.

current.note: Each script defines its own helper that prints to stderr and exits.

wild.note: A script stops with a message on stderr and a nonzero status.
wild.code: echo "usage: tool FILE" >&2; exit 64

options.name: Built-in fail with an exit code
options.gist: `fail(message, code)` prints the message, runs cleanup, and exits, with no frame.
gains: No helper in each script.
Expected failures print no compiler frame.
losses: One more built-in name in the prelude.

proposed.code: fail("usage: tool FILE", 64)

options.name: Return an error from run
options.gist: Declare an error type and return it from the entry function.
gains: Uses the existing error path.
losses: Prints a framed report for an ordinary usage error.

proposed.code: return Err(UsageError("usage: tool FILE"))

recommendation.why: A usage error is expected, so it should print a message and exit without a program frame. A built-in call removes the helper every script repeats.
gains: Four fewer lines in each script.
Cleanup still runs before the exit.

losses.mitigation: Built-in fail is for expected failures only. Bugs still use panic, and fail is documented beside it.

whyNot.reason: It prints a framed error report for a plain usage mistake, which reads as a crash.

recommendation.tradeoff: A new prelude name, in exchange for one call in place of a helper.

decisions.title: Text search returns a character index
decisions.situation: `find` on text returns a byte offset, and -1 when the text is absent. Slicing takes character positions. On accented text the two disagree, and a slice can cut inside a letter. Ports carry a helper to convert between them. We recommend returning a character index, or nothing when absent. Byte search stays available through the bytes methods. The change is one cutover across every caller.
decisions.gist: Should `find` return a character position instead of a byte offset?
decisions.lesson: Text search returns a byte offset, but slicing takes characters. Accented text then cuts in the wrong place.
decisions.story: Lee cuts a comment off a line. On a line with an accented letter before the comment, the slice keeps one character too many.
decisions.inWild: at :: line.find("//")
decisions.detail: Source: card #5085, item B3. Today `find` is in Core/Text/String.jet:83, returns a UTF-8 byte offset, and returns -1 when absent. A probe showed `"héllo // c".slice(0, "héllo // c".find("//"))` prints `héllo /`. Ratified D-ITER-REMAINDER1 already reports byte offsets explicitly for char-offset observations. Ratified D-CHAR-SCALAR1 notes no String method decodes a character at a byte position. The card counts 103 lines of byte helpers across ports. The savings figure is an estimate.

options.name: Character index, optional result
options.detail: `find` and `rfind` return the character index of the first or last match, or nothing when there is no match. The result composes with slice, len and the regex match positions.
options.technical: Signature changes from Int to Int?. Implementation counts scalars up to the byte match. One cutover migrates every caller in Core and the ports.
options.code: code :: line.slice(0, line.find("//") ?? line.len())

options.name: Keep byte offsets, add a byte slice
options.detail: `find` keeps its byte offset and -1 sentinel. A new helper slices by byte positions.
options.technical: Adds one builtin that slices on byte bounds, with a boundary check.
options.code: code :: slice_bytes(line, 0, line.find("//"))

options.name: Document the split form only
options.detail: `find` keeps its current result. The docs teach `split_once` for splitting at a pattern.
options.technical: Documentation change only.
options.code: code, _ :: line.split_once("//")

comparisons.note: `str.find` returns a character index, and -1 when the text is absent.

recommendation.why: A character index matches the slice and length methods, so a found position works directly. One unit removes the byte helper from every text port.
gains: Found positions compose with slice and len.

losses.loss: Every existing caller of find changes at once.
losses.mitigation: One cutover migrates every caller, and byte search stays available through a bytes method.

whyNot.reason: It keeps two position units, and each port still writes the helper.
It fixes one call shape and leaves the same mismatch in other searches.

recommendation.tradeoff: A breaking change to find, in exchange for one position unit across text.

surface.gist: Should `find` return a character position instead of a byte offset?
surface.lesson: Text search returns a byte offset, but slicing takes characters. Accented text then cuts in the wrong place.

code :: if at < 0 -> line else -> byte_slice(line, 0, at)

options.gist: Keep the byte offset and add a helper that slices by bytes.
gains: No change to existing callers.
losses: Two position units stay in the language, and the -1 sentinel remains.

options.gist: Keep byte offsets and teach `split_once` for the common case.
gains: No API change at all.
losses: Other position searches still return byte offsets.

gains: Found positions compose with slice and len.
The -1 sentinel becomes an absent value.

losses.loss: Every existing caller of find changes at once.
losses.mitigation: One cutover migrates every caller, and byte search stays available through a bytes method.

It fixes only one call shape and leaves the mismatch in every other search.

recommendation.tradeoff: A breaking change to find, in exchange for one position unit across text.

decisions.title: Check whether a file is executable
decisions.situation: A deployment script checks that a binary is executable before it runs. Today it starts the shell test command and reads the exit code. That needs process authority, for one question about one file. We recommend a file function that reports whether the path names a regular file the process may execute. A failed probe returns false, as the existing file check does.
decisions.gist: Should Jet check whether a file is executable without running a shell command?
decisions.lesson: Checking a file's executable bit today starts a child process. A file check can answer it directly.
decisions.story: Lee's script checks a helper binary before a build. The check starts a child shell and needs process permission, only to ask whether one file is executable.
decisions.inWild: process.cmd(["test", "-x", "{root}/{JET_ENV}"]).run()
decisions.detail: Source: card #5085, item B8. The card's example is WebBundleCheck. Ratified D-CORE-PATH1 makes Path accepted wherever a string is. The file module already has a file check, and this ballot follows its failure rule. Ratified D-CORE-FILEOPEN1 covers opening files, not permission checks. The card saves no lines; the gain is one fewer process and no process authority.

options.name: A file-system check
options.detail: `files.is_executable(path)` returns true when the path names a regular file the current process may execute. It returns false for a missing path or a failed probe.
options.technical: Reads file metadata and checks the execute bit for the current user. Declared with the file-system effect. No child process.
options.code: if !files.is_executable(path) -> fail(...)

options.name: Keep the shell test
options.detail: The script keeps running the shell test command and reads its exit code.
options.technical: No change. The process effect stays in the script.
options.code: process.cmd(["test", "-x", path]).run()

comparisons.note: A permission check reads the file mode, with no child process.

recommendation.why: The question is about one file, so a file check should answer it. The check then needs only file access.
gains: No process started for one permission check.

losses.loss: A failed probe reads as false, which can hide a permission problem.
losses.mitigation: The function documents that false covers both missing and non-executable paths.

decisions.title: Check fixed regex patterns while building
decisions.situation: Scanner code often compiles a fixed pattern at run time and wraps the result in a panic branch. For a fixed pattern that branch never runs. A typed regex literal is checked when the program compiles, but four ports in the review never used it. We recommend that the compiler check and compile every fixed pattern while building, whichever form it is written in. Users get the literal’s safety and speed with no warning and no rewrite.
decisions.gist: Should Jet warn when a constant regex pattern is compiled at run time?
decisions.lesson: A fixed pattern compiled at run time needs a panic branch for a bug that cannot happen. A literal is checked when the program compiles.
decisions.story: Sam ports a scanner from another language. Every line it compiles a fixed pattern and handles a failure that can never occur, and the code is longer than it needs to be.
decisions.inWild: re.compile("\\d{2}:\\d{2}") ?? panic("bad pattern")
decisions.detail:
Source: card #5085, item B10. Evidence is in the port review: 873 lines of scanners across four ports, with no literal form used. Ratified D-REGEX-LIT1 makes a bare string never a regex, and makes the typed literal Regex{...} the checked form. The lint code is the next free code, to be assigned. The card's speed figures are from the rewritten scanners and are a single measurement set.

Redesign 2026-11-01 (owner: engineer the downsides away). The first version recommended a lint, whose loss was a warning that can be ignored. A lint only asks people to rewrite code. Folding needs nothing from them: a constant string passed to the run-time compile call is compiled while building. A bad pattern then fails the build at the call, and a good one is stored compiled, so the failure branch is provably dead and removed.

This follows the ratified rule for constants: pure work on constant input folds while building. The typed literal stays the one documented form, so no second mechanism is added.

options.name: Check fixed patterns while building
options.detail: A constant string passed to the run-time compile call, or to its flag form, is compiled while building. A bad pattern is a build error at the call, naming the problem. A good pattern is stored compiled, and the dead failure branch is removed. Nothing changes for patterns built at run time.
options.technical: The checker marks a compile call whose pattern argument is a constant with no interpolation. Lowering evaluates it at build time with the same Core regex compiler. An error becomes a diagnostic at the argument span; success becomes a static compiled value, and the Result’s error arm is dropped as unreachable. Same meaning on every tier, because the same Core code runs.
options.code:
rx :: re.compile("\\d{2}:\\d{2}") ?? panic("bad pattern")
// checked while building; the panic branch is removed
re.compile("(\\d") ?? panic("x")
error: this pattern is not valid: unclosed group at 1

options.name: No lint
options.detail: Constant patterns compile at run time with a failure branch, and no warning is shown.
options.technical: No checker change.
options.code: re.compile("\\d{2}:\\d{2}") ?? panic("bad pattern")

comparisons.note: A regex in a constant is built once and checked by the regex crate's macro.

recommendation.why: A fixed pattern cannot fail at run time, so the compiler can prove it while building. Users get the literal’s compile-time check and speed without changing their code or seeing a warning.
gains: Every fixed pattern is checked when the program builds.
Dead failure branches are removed automatically.
Existing code benefits with no rewrite.

whyNot.reason: It keeps unchecked fixed patterns and dead failure branches in every port.

recommendation.tradeoff: None remaining: checked, fast fixed patterns with no user action.

decisions.title: Where the running program and this code live: `$program.dir` and `$here.dir`
decisions.situation: A program that loads files beside it uses the current directory as its root, so running it from another folder reads the wrong files. Any program can need this, not only scripts. Jet already gives code facts about itself through `$` roots: `$here.line` and `$here.function` (ratified D-JAI-SITE1) and `$build.os`. This ballot adds where the code is and where the running program is to that same family, instead of a script-only function.
decisions.gist: How does any program find its own file and directory?
decisions.lesson: Programs that load sibling files assume the current directory. Running them from elsewhere reads the wrong files.
decisions.story: Ana's repository tool reads a config beside its script. Run from a subfolder, it reports missing files, because the working directory is not the repository root.
decisions.inWild: root :: files.cwd()
decisions.detail:
Source: card #5085, item B9. The owner asked on 2026-11-01 for metadata like function, line and build data, not a script-only function. Regular programs also need their own file and directory.

Two questions hide in one. Where is this code written? That is a fact about the source, the same kind as `$here.line`. Where is the program that is running now? That is a fact about the run. Option A gives each its own member in the existing `$` family, so neither one has to stand in for the other.

`$here.file` and `$here.dir` are package-relative (`tools/gen.jet`, `tools`), the same text `$here` already prints in `app.jet:12:5`. So a built binary holds no build-machine path and stays reproducible.

`$program.path` and `$program.dir` are read when the program starts, never stored at build time. Under `jet run`, `jet dev` or a shebang script they name the entry source file, which matches the owner's 2026-10-23 ruling that a script run in memory reports its script path. A built program gets its own executable from the operating system (/proc/self/exe on Linux). In compile-time code, the running program is the file being compiled, so `$program.dir` is that source's directory.

Edge cases: a deleted or moved executable keeps the path the OS reports at start. A program loaded as a library (`jet build --lib`) reports the host executable, as dladdr-free runtimes do. The web target has no file, so `$program.path` is the page URL path.

options.name: Location facts: `$program.dir` and `$here.dir`
options.detail: `$program.path` and `$program.dir` are the file that is running and its directory: the source file under jet run or as a script, the executable when built. `$here.file` and `$here.dir` are where the code is written, package-relative, beside the ratified `$here.line` and `$here.function`. Both are Path values and work in every program.
options.technical: `$program` is an already-registered fact root, and `$here` is ratified (D-JAI-SITE1). The new members are registered in Syntax (I7). `$program.path` is set once by the runtime at start: jet run passes the canonical entry source, as it already passes arguments, and a built image reads /proc/self/exe. Nothing goes in the build record. `$here.file` is a per-site constant relative to the package root. Misuse, such as assigning to a fact, uses the existing fact diagnostics.
options.code:
config :: $program.dir.join("config.toml")
log.info("{$here.file}:{$here.line} in {$here.function}")

options.name: Only `$here.dir`, absolute
options.detail: One fact: the absolute directory of the source file, recorded when the program is compiled.
options.technical: SourceLocation.file becomes absolute, and `$here.dir` folds to a constant string in the binary.
options.code: config :: $here.dir.join("config.toml")

options.name: Keep the working directory
options.detail: The program keeps reading the current directory. Each run needs the caller to start in the right folder.
options.technical: No change.
options.code: root :: files.cwd()

The source location is a compile-time builtin; the running executable comes from the OS at run time.

recommendation.why: It answers both real questions with the metadata family Jet already has: where this code lives, and where the running program lives. It is not script-only, works from any folder, and stores no build-machine path.
gains: Any program finds its own files from any working directory.
Same `$` family as `$here.line` and `$build.os`, so there is nothing new to learn.
Builds stay reproducible: no absolute build path is stored.
An installed program finds data installed beside its executable.

whyNot.reason: It embeds the build machine's path, so builds stop being reproducible, the path leaks, and an installed or moved binary looks in the wrong place.
Every program then depends on the caller's folder.

decisions.title: Compound update of a list slot
decisions.situation: Jet rejects `xs[i] += n` on a list element. The error teaches the total update, which reads the element and stores it again. Maps already have a one-step form: a starting value in the brackets, as in `counts[w, or: 0] += 1`, makes the slot sure to exist. A list element that is in range is just as sure to exist. We recommend one rule for both: a compound update works on any slot that is sure to hold a value.
decisions.gist: Should Jet let `xs[i] += n` update a list element in one step?
decisions.lesson: Updating a list element takes the element twice today. A compound form would write it once, with one bounds check.
decisions.story: Sam tallies rows into buckets. Each update repeats the bucket name twice, and a typo in one copy quietly updates the wrong bucket.
decisions.inWild: loads[lightest] += row.weight
decisions.detail:
Source: card #5085, item B2. Today's rejection is E0164, "Compound assignment can't target an indexed slot". Ratified D-MEM-INDEXMUT1 keeps compound arithmetic rejected on indexed slots, because it hides a default-value question. That reason covers maps only, so this ballot asks whether lists are different. Lists have no default value, and an out-of-range index stops the program. Maps stay on E0164 under either option, as D-MAP-SLOT1 requires.

Redesign 2026-11-01 (owner: engineer the downsides away). The first version listed "maps still need the longer form" as a loss. That is not so: ratified D-MAP-SLOT1 A already gives maps `counts[w, or: 0] += 1`, where the starting value makes the slot exist.

The rule is now stated once for both: a compound update needs a slot that is sure to hold a value. A list element is (an out-of-range index stops before any write); a map slot is when it names a starting value. A bare `m[k] += 1` keeps E0164, whose fix text shows the `or:` form, as D-MAP-SLOT1 requires.

options.name: Compound update on any slot sure to hold a value
options.detail: `xs[i] op= v` works for a mutable list and an Int index, for every compound operator the element type supports. The index is checked once, and a bad index stops before any write. Maps keep their ratified form with a starting value; a bare map slot keeps E0164, whose fix shows that form.
options.technical: Lowered to one bounds check, then a read-modify-write of the slot in the same IR function. No new runtime call.
options.code:
loads[lightest] += row.weight
counts[w, or: 0] += 1

options.name: Keep the error and the total update
options.detail: Compound assignment on any indexed slot stays rejected with E0164. Users read the element, change it, and store it back.
options.technical: No checker or lowering change.
options.code: loads[lightest] = loads[lightest] + row.weight

comparisons.note: `+=` works on an index expression of a Vec, with one bounds check.

recommendation.why: One rule covers every indexed slot: a compound update needs a slot that is sure to hold a value. A list element in range always has one, and a map slot has one when it names a starting value. So list updates become one step, and lists and maps follow the same rule.
gains: Shorter list updates with one bounds check.
Lists and maps share one rule for compound updates.

whyNot.reason: It keeps the repeated name in every list update, with no safety gain on lists, and leaves lists behind maps.

recommendation.tradeoff: None remaining: one rule for lists and maps, with one-step updates on both.

decisions.title: How type names are quoted in error messages
decisions.situation: Jet's error messages quote some type names and not others. A named type gets backticks, as in `WebForm`. A built-in type prints bare with a short explanation, as in String (text). For a generic type, only the head is quoted, as in `Cell`<Int>. Readers cannot tell where the code ends and the prose begins. We recommend one rule: the whole type is quoted as code, and the plain explanation stays outside the backticks.
decisions.gist: Should every type in an error message be quoted whole, with its explanation outside the quotes?
decisions.lesson: In an error message, backticks mark text you could type in your program. A type is something you type, so it gets backticks, all of it. The friendly explanation, such as (text), is prose about the type, so it sits outside them.
decisions.story: Priya passes a string where a web form is expected. The error says the call wants `WebForm`, but this is String (text). A later error mentions `Cell`<Int>. She copies `Cell` into her search box and loses the <Int> part.
decisions.inWild: Rust quotes the whole type in its messages, generics included, for example: expected `HashMap<String, u32>`, found `Vec<u8>`. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/error_codes/E0308.html
decisions.detail:
TODAY

Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Diagnostics.jet:389-414 sema_type_show builds every type name in type errors. Named types are quoted: .Named gives `WebForm`. Built-in scalars are bare with a gloss: String (text), Int (a whole number), I32 (a 32-bit whole number, ...). Generic types quote only the head: .Apply gives `Cell`<Int>.

The earlier draft said three web snapshots expect bare WebForm and fail. That is stale. I ran the published base compiler on tests/ui/web_suite_forms_type_mismatch, _query_ and _router_. Each prints "`field` wants `WebForm` for argument 1, but this is String (text)", and the committed snapshots match.

Scope of a change: 95 committed test outputs contain a bare built-in with its gloss, and 26 contain a head-only quoted generic (git grep over tests, 2026-11-05).

RULINGS

D-DIAG-CORE-NAME1=A decides how Core type names are spelled, not quoting. D-CASE-PROSE1=A decides case. Docs/spec/proof-replay-decisions.md:602-604 says code is quoted in backticks in every diagnostic. No ruling covers types in particular. The plain gloss after built-ins is kept under every option.

HOW A'S DOWNSIDE IS DESIGNED AWAY

About 120 snapshots change. They come from one function, so one edit to sema_type_show changes them all. The regenerated diff only moves or adds backticks, and a script can check that claim over the whole diff before it lands.

WHY NOT B OR C

B removes all quotes. Multi-word messages then run type names into the prose, as in "wants WebForm for argument 1". C keeps today's mix, so readers keep guessing where code ends.

decisions.title: Zero leaks in the native compiler
decisions.gist: Must the native compiler report zero leaks, double frees and use-after-free across its full test corpus?
decisions.lesson: A leak is memory the compiler never frees. Small leaks grow into large use, so the compiler slows and then fails on big inputs. A zero rule catches each leak, but the current harness still reports some.
decisions.story: Omar compiles a large project and memory keeps climbing. Under option A the leak harness fails on the exact phase that keeps the memory, so it is fixed before the self-build. Under option B the same leak is listed as a known class and shows up again on the next large build.

Rust: Miri detects leaks and use-after-free in test runs. Source: https://github.com/rust-lang/miri
decisions.detail:
Owner order (card #5014): the memory-safety release plan requires a zero-leak result.

State recorded in the card: the lircheck harness reports LEAK 0, DOUBLE 0, UAF 0, SHELL 0 as of 2026-10-17. Still open: a mixed probe at 1.89 MB, 89 static LEAK reports, and a full 129-program corpus sweep. Tools live under $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/discovery/memverify/.

No ratified decision found by keyword scan records a zero-leak rule for the compiler. D-MEM-GUARANTEE1 and D-MEM-HARDEN1 concern Jet programs.

options.name: Zero leaks, double frees and use-after-free
options.detail: The native compiler must report zero leaks, zero double frees and zero use-after-free on the lircheck harness and the full 129-program corpus. Static leak reports are cleared or proven false.
options.technical: Keep the lircheck counters at zero in CI. Clear the 89 static LEAK reports and the mixed 1.89 MB probe. Run the 129-program sweep before each cutover.
options.code:
$ tools/memverify lircheck
LEAK 0  DOUBLE 0  UAF 0  SHELL 0

options.name: Zero leaks on the probe set only
options.detail: The rule covers the lircheck probes. Static reports and corpus leaks are tracked as known classes.
options.technical: Keep counters on the probe set. List the static reports as known classes with owners.

LEAK 0  DOUBLE 0  UAF 0  (corpus: 3 known classes)

comparisons.note: The test allocator reports leaked memory with the allocation site. Source: https://ziglang.org/documentation/master/#Memory
Miri detects leaks and use-after-free while tests run. Source: https://github.com/rust-lang/miri

recommendation.why: A compiler that leaks cannot be trusted on large inputs. The owner made zero leaks the release condition.
gains: Each leak is found by the harness, not by a user.

losses.loss: Release waits for the 89 static reports and the corpus sweep.
losses.mitigation: Each static report is listed by name, so each has an owner.

whyNot.reason: B leaves corpus leaks known but unfixed, which the release plan does not allow.

recommendation.tradeoff: Slower release, for a compiler that frees all its memory.

decisions.title: Typed row handles for add-only column tables
decisions.situation: Large programs such as compilers, games and databases keep huge tables of small records and refer to one record by its row number. In Jet that row number is a plain Int, so a node number can be used on the type table by mistake and silently read the wrong record. Jet already stores tables as packed columns and can share frozen data with tasks; only a safe row name is missing. The vote decides that name; we recommend an add-only table that hands out a typed row handle for each record.
decisions.gist: How should a program name one row of a large add-only table of records?
decisions.lesson: A column table keeps each field of a record in its own packed list, so a scan of one field is fast. Jet already has this as Columns<T>, and it already has freeze for sharing data with tasks. What it lacks is a safe name for one row. Today a row is a plain Int, so a node number can index the type table by mistake.
decisions.story: Priya writes a compiler in Jet. Her syntax nodes, types and functions each live in a big table that only grows. She once passed a node number to the type table, and the program printed a wrong type for an hour before she found it. She wants the compiler to catch that mix-up.
decisions.detail:
Already settled, so not on this ballot. Column storage is Columns<T> with field views such as ps.y (D-SOA-SITE1=A). Every tier shares one column store (D-SOA-TIER1=A). Read-only sharing with tasks is freeze(x) (D-CONC-FREEZE1=A). Tables that delete rows use Pool<T> and ID<T>. This ballot decides only the handle for tables that only grow.

Why now: the S3 compiler core (card #5073, D-ARCH-IR1) stores the syntax tree, sema results and flat IR as add-only tables. Those tables are keyed by u32 ids (RustOut-4 s3-design.md, O0Speed-3 flat-ir.md). RustOut-4 proposed a library IdTable<T>, merged here as option A. It is renamed Rows<T> and Row<T> for two reasons. Id<T> next to Pool’s ID<T> differs only in case. The spec also rules out a public Table<T> (D-QUERY-RETAIN1=A).

Measured on the HEAD self-compile (seed a0_017), with one Int-indexed list per IR field. Copies in jet_ir_unique are 13% of ir.opt CPU. Freeing the IR takes about 0.1 s of main-thread time after object writing. The IR merge spends another 0.06 s on duplicate drops. Allocator self time is 9-19% of every phase.

Research. The Rust compiler uses IndexVec with a typed u32 index per table, and push returns the new index. Cranelift uses PrimaryMap, an add-only table with typed u32 keys. Its SecondaryMap side tables reuse the same keys, which is the S3 side-table pattern. Zig’s MultiArrayList stores columns but indexes with a plain usize. The Zig compiler then wraps those indexes in its own enum types, the per-program wrapper that option C leaves to users. No widely used system uses a run-time flag like option B.

options.name: Add-only Rows<T> with Row<T> handles
options.detail: Rows<T> is a Core collection for any struct T, laid out exactly like Columns<T>. It has add, len, index by Row<T>, iteration, field column views and freeze. It has no remove, insert, sort or other reordering, so every handed-out Row<T> stays valid for the table's life. A Row<T> from one table cannot index a table of a different T.
options.technical: Row<T> is a 4-byte copyable u32 index; Row<T>.index() returns it as Int for printing and hashing. add panics past 4,294,967,295 rows. Rows<T> shares the column store and field-view lowering of Columns<T>, so it adds a type and methods, not a second layout. Indexing is bounds-checked like list indexing. freeze(rows) gives tasks lock-free reads. A side table is a [U] indexed by row.index().
options.code:
nodes := Rows<Node>{}
id :: nodes.add(Node{kind: .Call, line: 3})
print(nodes[id].line)
nodes[id].line = 4
kinds :: nodes.kind          // column view
shared :: freeze(nodes)       // tasks may read

options.name: Columns<T> hands out rows itself
options.detail: Columns<T> gains add, which returns a Row<T>. Once any row has been handed out, remove, insert and sort panic at run time because they would move rows under existing handles.
options.technical: Each Columns<T> carries a 'rows handed out' flag set by add and checked by every reordering method. The compiler cannot prove the flag statically, so misuse is a run-time panic.
options.code:
nodes := Columns<Node>{}
id :: nodes.add(Node{kind: .Call, line: 3})
print(nodes[id].line)
nodes.remove(0)   // panics: rows were handed out

options.name: Keep plain Int rows
options.detail: No new API. Programs index Columns<T> with Int. Each program that wants safety writes its own wrapper struct per table.
options.technical: No compiler or Core change.
options.code:
nodes := Columns<Node>{}
nodes.push(Node{kind: .Call, line: 3})
id :: nodes.len() - 1
print(nodes[id].line)

comparisons.note: IndexVec with a typed u32 index per table: https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/nightly-rustc/rustc_index/vec/struct.IndexVec.html.
comparisons.code:
let id: NodeId = nodes.push(node);
let line = nodes[id].line;

comparisons.note: PrimaryMap is add-only with typed keys; SecondaryMap adds side tables: https://docs.rs/cranelift-entity/latest/cranelift_entity/struct.PrimaryMap.html.
comparisons.code:
let block: Block = blocks.push(BlockData::new());
let data = &blocks[block];

comparisons.note: MultiArrayList stores columns but indexes with usize: https://ziglang.org/documentation/master/std/#std.MultiArrayList.

recommendation.why: Most big tables only ever grow. A separate add-only type turns that fact into a compile-time rule, so handles stay valid and cannot cross tables.
gains: Wrong-table and stale-row bugs become compile errors.
Small handles keep large tables compact.

losses.loss: One more collection type next to Columns<T>.
losses.mitigation: Rows<T> is Columns<T> without remove or insert; the docs show it beside Pool<T> and ID<T>.

losses.loss: At most about 4 billion rows per table.
losses.mitigation: add panics with a clear message past the limit; larger tables use Columns<T> with Int indexes.

whyNot.reason: B catches a removal only when it runs, and only after some row was handed out.
C keeps the wrong-table bug and leaves every program to write its own wrapper.

recommendation.tradeoff: Tables that must delete rows keep using Pool<T> or Columns<T>; add-only tables get checked handles.

decisions.title: Unfinished dev server: delete and rebuild lean, or finish the copy
decisions.situation: Jet has a dev server that is meant to show live app previews, browser devtools and the editor helper that powers code completion. It was copied from the old Rust compiler but never finished, so it does not compile and every one of those commands refuses to run. Plain jet dev, which reruns your program on save, already works without it. The vote decides whether to delete the copy and rebuild the editor helper fresh, or to finish the copy.
decisions.gist: Should Jet finish the half-ported dev server, or delete it and rebuild only the editor helper fresh?
decisions.lesson: The dev server is the part of Jet that hosts live app previews, the browser devtools and the editor helper. It was copied from the old Rust compiler but never finished, so all of those commands refuse to run today. Plain jet dev, which reruns a program when you save, already works without it. Whichever wins, the editor helper must work again.
decisions.story: Mia opens a Jet project in her editor and gets no completions, because the editor helper depends on the unfinished dev server. She just wants completions back; she has never used live previews.
decisions.inWild:
$ gopls version
golang.org/x/tools/gopls v0.x
# https://go.dev/gopls
decisions.detail: Census by O0Image-3 on 2026-10-24 ($JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/O0Image/g3/CENSUS.md): Compiler/JetDevserver is a 15.4k-line port of the deleted crates/jet-devserver with 1626 check errors, outside the build. Callers that refuse with E2104: jet dev --canvas, jet run --app/--share, jet self devtools, jet self lsp (JetLSP depends on it). Core/Web/Devserver.jet declares jet_devserver_* routes with no runtime implementation. JetCanvas and JetDebug are orphaned if it is deleted. Card #5931.

options.name: Delete and rebuild lean
options.detail: Delete Compiler/JetDevserver and the jet_devserver_* routes. Rebuild JetLSP so it no longer depends on the dev server. File one card each for live preview (canvas), app sharing and devtools, to be rebuilt on the Jet runtime later.
options.technical: JetLSP is cut loose from JetDevserver; the dead E2104 refusals are replaced by honest not-built-yet errors tied to cards.
options.code:
$ jet self lsp
# starts the editor helper; no dev server needed
$ jet dev --canvas app.jet
Error: live preview is not built yet (tracked card)

options.name: Finish the copy
options.detail: Keep Compiler/JetDevserver and fix it until it type-checks and builds, add the missing jet_devserver_* runtime routes, then switch each refusing command back on.
options.technical: Requires clearing 1626 check errors in Rust-shaped code and implementing the runtime routes.
options.code:
$ jet dev --canvas app.jet
# opens the live preview again
$ jet self lsp
# starts the editor helper through the dev server

comparisons.note: Go keeps its editor helper, gopls, as its own small program, separate from any preview server. See https://go.dev/gopls.

recommendation.why: Nothing works today either way. A fresh, small editor helper returns the most-used feature soonest, and previews get a design that fits Jet instead of the old Rust shape.
gains: The editor helper returns without waiting for previews.

losses.loss: Live previews and devtools stay off for a while.
losses.mitigation: Each gets its own card with a plan, so it is rebuilt when a lane is free.

whyNot.reason: B spends far more work reviving a Rust-shaped design and keeps the editor helper blocked behind it.

recommendation.tradeoff: Previews return later, but on a clean design; the editor helper returns first.

decisions.title: Where the lock file lives
decisions.situation: A lock file records the exact library versions a project uses, so every computer builds the same program. Today Jet keeps it inside a hidden folder that also holds throwaway build output, and new projects tell git to ignore it. Teammates and CI can then build with different library versions, and deleting the hidden folder silently drops the lock. The owner decides where the lock lives; we recommend a committed file at the project root, so the hidden folder is always safe to delete.
decisions.gist: Where should the lock file live so it is committed and the build folder stays disposable?
decisions.lesson: A lock file records the exact versions a project builds with, so every machine gets the same result. Today Jet keeps it inside `.jet/`, the folder for generated files, and `jet new` tells git to ignore it. The lock also stores a build time, which must move out whichever option wins.
decisions.story: Ben clones a teammate's project and gets a different library version than she tested with, because her lock was never committed.
decisions.inWild:
my-app/
  Cargo.toml
  Cargo.lock   # committed
  target/      # ignored
# Cargo keeps Cargo.lock at the project root and commits it for applications; build output goes to target/. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/cargo-toml-vs-cargo-lock.html
decisions.detail: Audit 2026-10-28 LAY-02, LAY-06: generated .gitignore lists .jet/build/ .jet/lock .jet/cache/ (Compiler/JetCli Host.jet:1478); the lock carries [build.stamp]. Related: D-LOCK1 (spec: commit the lock for executables), D-GENERATED-STORAGE2=B (one top-level .jet), #3421.

options.name: Root jet.lock
options.detail: Move the lock to `jet.lock` at the project root and commit it; `.jet/` holds only throwaway files. Gains: `.gitignore` is one line: `.jet/`. Deleting `.jet/` is always safe. Losses: One more file at the project root.
options.technical: The lock path becomes <root>/jet.lock; [build.stamp] moves to .jet/build/stamp; jet new writes a one-line .gitignore.
options.code:
hello/
  package.jet
  jet.lock     # committed
  .jet/        # ignored, safe to delete

options.name: Cleaned .jet/lock
options.detail: Keep `.jet/lock`, remove machine state from it, and commit it. Gains: No new file at the root. Losses: `.jet/` mixes kept and throwaway files. The `.gitignore` needs exceptions.
options.technical: The lock stays at .jet/lock without [build.stamp]; .gitignore ignores .jet/* except .jet/lock.
options.code:
hello/
  package.jet
  .jet/lock    # committed
  .jet/build/  # ignored

options.name: Never commit the lock
options.detail: Keep the lock as a local file that is never committed. Gains: No lock changes in commits. Losses: Two machines may build different versions.
options.technical: Reverses the spec rule that executables commit their lock.
options.code:
hello/
  package.jet
  .jet/        # ignored, lock rebuilt per machine

comparisons.note: Cargo keeps Cargo.lock at the project root and commits it for applications; build output goes to target/. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/cargo-toml-vs-cargo-lock.html
comparisons.code:
my-app/
  Cargo.toml
  Cargo.lock   # committed
  target/      # ignored

recommendation.why: A root lock is the common habit and makes `.jet/` safe to delete, which is the simplest rule to teach.
gains: Builds repeat across machines, and cleanup is one safe delete.

losses.loss: One more file at the project root.
losses.mitigation: It is one small file, the same habit as Cargo.lock or go.sum.

whyNot.reason: Keeps a committed file inside a folder people delete.
Gives up repeatable builds.

recommendation.tradeoff: One visible root file in exchange for a folder that is always safe to delete.

decisions.title: Optimization flags versus profile settings
decisions.situation: A build profile is a named group of build settings, such as debug or release. Jet already has a profile flag and a release shortcut, and it also has separate flags that change optimization and inlining one at a time. Users meet three ways to ask for a fast build, and the help page grows longer for each. The owner decides whether the separate flags stay; we recommend moving those settings into profiles in the project file and keeping only the profile flag and the release shortcut.
decisions.gist: Should optimization and inlining stay as build flags, or become profile settings only?
decisions.lesson: A profile is a named set of build settings, such as debug or release. Jet already has `--profile` and the `--release` shortcut. It also has `--optimize`, `--opt-level` and `--inline`, which change the same settings one at a time. Whichever option wins, `--release` stays.
decisions.story: Kim wants a fast build and finds three different flags in help. She is unsure which one the team uses.
decisions.inWild:
# Cargo.toml
[profile.release]
opt-level = 3
$ cargo build --release
# Cargo offers --release and --profile; optimization level lives in profile settings. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/profiles.html
decisions.detail: Audit 2026-10-28 CLI-03, CLI-04: jet --help is 419 lines and 249 flags. Ratified: D-CONF-WORD1 and D-BUILD-DEFAULT1 (--profile plus --release sugar); the audit's "--release only" variant would reopen D-CONF-WORD1 and is not offered. Host #4913 (short help). Exact profile field spelling follows the manifest rules.

options.name: Profile settings only

decisions.title: A dataframe in Core or in packages
decisions.situation: A dataframe is a table of named columns that you can filter, group and join, like a spreadsheet inside a program. Jet has decided how files are read into columns, but it has no table type, so analysts loop over rows by hand. Data analysis is a goal for Jet, and every peer language offers a table type. The owner decides whether Core ships one; we recommend a lazy table type in Core built on the shared column format and compute operations.
decisions.gist: Should Core ship a dataframe for table data, or leave it to packages?
decisions.lesson: A dataframe is a table of named columns you can filter, group and join. Jet has decided how files are read into column batches but has no table type to work with them. Whichever option wins, tables run on Jet's shared compute operations rather than a second engine.
decisions.story: Rosa has a sales CSV and wants monthly totals for one region. In Jet today she writes the loop and the grouping herself.
decisions.inWild:
pl.scan_csv("sales.csv")
  .filter(pl.col("region") == "EU")
  .group_by("month").agg(pl.col("amount").sum())
  .collect()
# Polars offers a lazy dataframe over Arrow memory. Source: https://docs.pola.rs/
decisions.detail: Audit 2026-10-28 domain gaps (B12 dataframe half). Ratified context: D-COMPUTE1=D (dataframes integrate through the operation family), D-COLUMNAR-BOUNDARY1, D-DATA-READER1 (scan into column batches). The AI/ML half of B12 is replaced by D-ACCEL-LIB1. Snippets use illustrative method names.

options.name: Dataframe in Core
options.detail: Ship a lazy table type in Core over the shared column batches. Gains: Data analysis works with no extra package. One table type shared by every data package. Losses: Core grows a large API to maintain.
options.technical: core.data.frame wraps the Arrow import and ColumnBatch; operators lower to core.compute operations; evaluation is lazy until print or collect.
options.code:
sales :: data.frame("sales.csv")?
by_month :: sales.filter(region == "EU").group_by(month).sum(amount)
print(by_month)

options.name: Packages only
options.detail: Core keeps column batches; table types come from packages. Gains: Core stays small. Losses: Competing table types that do not work together. Analysts must choose a package first.
options.technical: Core exposes ColumnBatch only.
options.code:
use some_frames
sales :: some_frames.read_csv("sales.csv")?
print(sales.filter(...).group_by(...).sum(...))

comparisons.note: Polars offers a lazy dataframe over Arrow memory. Source: https://docs.pola.rs/

recommendation.why: One shared table type makes data work possible out of the box and lets packages interoperate instead of competing.
gains: Analysts start working without choosing a package.

losses.loss: Core grows a large API to maintain.
losses.mitigation: Start with filter, group, join, sort and select, and measure each against Polars.

whyNot.reason: Splits the ecosystem into table types that cannot work together.

recommendation.tradeoff: A bigger Core in exchange for data analysis that works on day one.

decisions.title: Order for bringing build targets back on the self-hosted compiler
decisions.situation: A build target is a kind of machine or runtime a program can be built for, such as a web browser or a phone chip. On the current compiler, asking for any target other than the local machine fails. Each target is a large piece of work, so the order decides which users are served first. The owner decides that order; we recommend web assembly first, then the ARM chips used by phones and modern laptops, then small embedded boards.
decisions.gist: In what order should build targets return on the self-hosted compiler?
decisions.lesson: A target is the kind of machine a program is built for. On the current compiler, every non-native target answers "not built yet". Earlier support was proven on a compiler that has been retired. Whichever order wins, each target returns with tests that run the built program.
decisions.story: Lin wants to ship a small web service as a WebAssembly component, but `jet build --target` fails today.
decisions.inWild:
$ GOOS=wasip1 GOARCH=wasm go build -o app.wasm
# Go builds for another platform by setting two environment variables. Source: https://go.dev/doc/install/source#environment
decisions.detail: Audit 2026-10-28 TIER-01: --target answers E2104 on the self-hosted CLI; #1914 criteria proven on the Rust path are reopened by draft 12. Order: wasm32-wasip2 (#1914), then aarch64 (#4136), then embedded; e13 Cross Platform is recorded only and not touched here.

options.name: Web, then ARM, then embedded
options.detail: WebAssembly first, then ARM64, then embedded boards. Gains: Web services and browsers are served first. ARM64 covers phones and modern laptops next. Losses: Embedded users wait longest.
options.technical: wasm32-wasip2 (#1914) -> aarch64 (#4136) -> embedded.
options.code:
$ jet build --target=wasm32-wasip2    # first
$ jet build --target=aarch64-linux    # second
$ jet build --target=thumbv7em        # third

options.name: ARM first
options.detail: ARM64 first, then WebAssembly, then embedded boards. Gains: Native phone and laptop builds arrive sooner. Losses: Web deployment waits.
options.technical: aarch64 (#4136) -> wasm32 (#1914) -> embedded.
options.code:
$ jet build --target=aarch64-linux    # first
$ jet build --target=wasm32-wasip2    # second
$ jet build --target=thumbv7em        # third

comparisons.note: Go builds for another platform by setting two environment variables. Source: https://go.dev/doc/install/source#environment

recommendation.why: WebAssembly serves the web and server-side component users first, and an earlier version of it already worked.
gains: The broadest audience gets a working target first.

losses.loss: Embedded users wait longest.
losses.mitigation: Embedded keeps its own card and starts once ARM64 lands.

whyNot.reason: Delays the target with the widest reach.

recommendation.tradeoff: Web first, native ARM second.
