decisions.title: New GPUs and accelerators arrive as libraries
decisions.situation: An accelerator is a chip, like a graphics card, that runs number-heavy work much faster than the main processor. Today every accelerator family Jet can use is wired into Jet itself, so supporting a new chip means changing the language. New AI chips appear every year, and users of those chips cannot wait for a language release. The owner decides how new hardware support arrives; we recommend a public interface so a library can add a new device, checked against the main-processor result.
decisions.gist: Should a library be able to add support for a new GPU or accelerator?
decisions.lesson: An accelerator is a chip, like a GPU, that runs number-heavy work fast. Jet's own code knows each GPU family today. The Mojo language lets a hardware maker add a chip by shipping a library. Whichever option wins, results on any device must match the main processor's result.
decisions.story: A startup ships a new AI chip. Its engineers want Jet programs to use it next month, without waiting for a Jet release.
decisions.inWild:
from gpu.host import DeviceContext
var ctx = DeviceContext()
ctx.enqueue_function[scale](input, grid_dim=1, block_dim=64)
# Mojo targets accelerators through libraries written in Mojo, so new hardware support ships as library code. Source: https://docs.modular.com/mojo/manual/gpu/basics
decisions.detail:
Owner direction 2026-10-28: this replaces the audit's "restore AI/ML / re-scope #3955". It builds on ratified D-CORE-BOUNDARY1=A: CPU chip instructions are Core library entries (#4565). It also builds on D-HOST-CAPS1=A: packages add hardware kinds (#4195). D-GPU-PACKAGING1=A, D-COMPUTE1=D and D-COMPUTE-BACKEND1=D apply too. Core owns the compute contract with a CPU reference. Related: #3026, #3028, #4731, #4762, #3955. Snippet names are illustrative.

FutureAudit 2026-10-28 (FUTURE.md T25) refines option A; owner direction folds its D-KERNELIR1 here, no separate ballot. The provider interface covers caps, lower, load, launch, alloc and copy over a public, versioned kernel IR (a subset of the compiler IR). MLIR was weighed and rejected (I6; research avoid-list).

A typed Device value from D-HOST-CAPS1 replaces the string devices in Core/Compute/Solve.jet:83-84; #Kernel stays the restricted subset with a CPU reference (D-COMPUTE-KERNEL-SURFACE1=B). First providers are mined from the Rust-era CUDA, Metal and Vulkan/WebGPU backends (#1144-#1146). Per-vendor backends inside the compiler would contradict D-CORE-BOUNDARY1=A.

options.name: Public device interface
options.detail: A package adds a device by implementing a public interface; it must pass the CPU-reference tests. Gains: New chips arrive without a Jet release. Built-in GPUs use the same interface. Losses: The interface becomes a public promise.
options.technical: A provider interface covers code generation for kernels, memory transfer and launch; providers declare their hardware kind (D-HOST-CAPS1) and must pass the CPU-reference conformance suite before selection.
options.code:
use acme_npu                        // package adds the device
device :: compute.select(.npu)?
out :: device.run(scale, input)?    // checked against CPU result

options.name: Fixed list in Core
options.detail: Core keeps the list of supported device families; new ones need a Jet change. Gains: Full control over every device path. Losses: New chips wait for a Jet release. Core grows with every device family.
options.technical: Status quo.

options.name: Foreign libraries only
options.detail: New chips are reached only by calling their vendor libraries through FFI. Gains: No new interface to design. Losses: No shared compute model or result checks. Every program wires each vendor by hand.
options.technical: Vendors are reached through FFI bindings only; core.compute does not see them.
options.code:
use c.[acme_npu_sdk as npu]
npu.launch("scale", input)

comparisons.note: Mojo targets accelerators through libraries written in Mojo, so new hardware support ships as library code. Source: https://docs.modular.com/mojo/manual/gpu/basics

recommendation.why: A public device interface lets hardware makers add chips themselves, while the CPU-reference tests keep every device's answers correct.
gains: Hardware support grows without waiting for Jet releases.

losses.loss: The interface becomes a public promise.
losses.mitigation: Version the interface, and port the built-in GPUs to it first to prove it.

whyNot.reason: Every new chip waits for a Jet release.
Gives up the shared compute model and its correctness checks.

recommendation.tradeoff: A public interface to maintain in exchange for hardware support that scales with the industry.

decisions.title: Teaching the Jet spelling for words from other languages
decisions.situation: Newcomers type words from languages they already know, such as let, for, while or match. Jet used to answer with a message naming the Jet word to use, but that teaching was paused, so these lines now get a generic error that points the wrong way. Every newcomer meets this in the first hour. The owner decides whether to restore the teaching now for a small fixed set; we recommend restoring it, with every message coming from one table.
decisions.gist: Should Jet now teach the Jet spelling for common words from other languages?
decisions.lesson: Newcomers type words such as `let`, `for`, `while` or `match`. A teaching message names the Jet form to use instead. That work was paused, so these lines get a generic error today. Whichever option wins, any teaching comes from one table with a tested message per row.
decisions.story: Omar types `let x = 5` on his first try. The error tells him to use the value, which does not help.
decisions.detail:
Audit 2026-10-28 DIAG-01: let/for/while/match lines give E0003 "This line computes a value but doesn't do anything with it". Comma enums give "Expected a name for a variant name". This reopens the spec pause D-S14-PAUSE. It applies ratified D-TEACH-FOREIGN1=A to a fixed set. The set is let/var/const, for, while, match/switch, comma enums and `x: T = v`.

It also covers null/nil, println/console.log, fn main/def/func and import/#include. D-S14-PAUSE is not a Tower record; its 135 retired rows sit in Compiler/Prelude/Diagnostics.jet:13-33.

options.name: Teach a fixed set now
options.detail: Restore teaching for about ten common words, from one table. Gains: The first-hour errors name the right Jet form. One table, one tested message per row. Losses: The table must be kept small and current.
options.technical: One foreign-spelling table in the syntax registry feeds one parser recovery rule; each row has a UI snapshot.

options.name: Keep the pause
options.detail: Keep the pause and only improve the generic error text. Gains: No new rows to maintain. Losses: Newcomers still get advice that points the wrong way.
options.technical: E0003 text lists the three common statement forms.

comparisons.note: rustc recognises a common word from another language and names the Rust keyword to use instead. Source: rustc parser diagnostics; try it with any current Rust compiler.

recommendation.why: A message naming the right Jet form is the cheapest fix for the most common first-hour errors.
gains: Newcomers learn the Jet form from the error itself.

losses.mitigation: Each row needs a tested snapshot, and the set is fixed at about ten words.

whyNot.reason: Generic text still leaves users guessing which form applies.

decisions.title: Keep inline C as the one inline shape, beside header bindings for libraries
decisions.situation: Jet can call C, so programs can reuse C libraries and write small fast helpers. There are two ways in. A Jet function can hold a C body written inline. Or a C library is read through its header file. An audit proposed removing inline C bodies, so each tool handles one way. A check of today's compiler changes the picture. Inline C builds natively, and Jet writes its C prototype from the Jet signature. So the C compiler catches a mismatch. Reading a header does not yet work in the new compiler. The vote decides whether inline C stays.
decisions.gist: Should a Jet function still be able to hold an inline C body?
decisions.lesson: Yes: your own few lines of C go inline, and a C library uses its header.
decisions.story: Ana writes a script with a three-line C helper inline. It stays one file, and it builds.
decisions.inWild:
Option          Inline C   Inline asm   Like
A keep          yes        yes          Go, Nim
B no inline C   no         yes          Rust, Zig, D
C no inline     no         no           Swift
decisions.detail:
WHAT WE BUILD
- No language change. Keep D-FFI-INLINE1=A as ratified for c, cpp and asm.
- Docs: spec "Inline native functions" (spec.md:2785) states the split: inline for a few lines of your own C, header binding for a library.
- Header import on the self-hosted compiler stays card #4174; jet cc (#1344, D-ADOPT-CC1=B) serves both forms.
- Separate bug card: a plain call to inline C checks without E3103 though the spec requires it.

EVIDENCE
- Compiler/JetCli/Source/Cli/ForeignLink.jet:273-291: Jet writes `ret name(types);` from the Jet signature before the body, so the C compiler rejects a body that disagrees.
- ForeignLink.jet:293-350: each inline body is one translation unit; one strict link refuses unresolved symbols. Compiler/JetBackend/Tests/test-native-inline-c.mjs builds and runs a native inline C program.
- Header import: a probe (deps c@"c", use c.[add as m]) gave E0102; Examples/features/lowlevel/cbind fails check with E1002 and E0067 (bd6, earlier audit).

- Inline C without #Unsafe on the declaration gives E3215 (bd6).

IDS
Keeps D-FFI-INLINE1=A, D-FFI-RAWBODY1, D-FFI-ASM1, D-FFI-CPP1, D-FFI-UNIFY1=A. Audit FFI-01. Host card #4174. Related: D-FFI-UNSAFE1.

options.name: Keep inline C
options.detail: Inline bodies stay for C, C++ and assembly. A C library comes in through its header. Gains: Scripts with a C helper stay one file. The path that builds today stays. One inline shape for every language. Losses: Two ways to bring in C, split by size.
options.technical: No language change. Jet writes the C prototype of each body from the Jet signature. So the C compiler rejects a mismatch. Each body compiles as its own C unit, and one strict link refuses unresolved symbols. Header import is finished on the new compiler as already planned. Docs teach the split: your own few lines inline, a library through its header.

options.name: No inline C
options.detail: C lives in its own files, read through a header. C++ and assembly keep inline bodies. Gains: One way to bring in C. Losses: Removes the C path that builds today. A three-line helper needs two extra files.
options.technical: Removes the inline C form. `jet fix` moves each body into a C file with a header. It also adds the package dependency and the use line. It can land only after header import works on the new compiler.

options.name: No inline bodies at all
options.detail: Remove inline bodies for C, C++ and assembly. All foreign code lives in files. Gains: One way for every language. Losses: Removes working inline C and assembly. Even tiny helpers need separate files.
options.technical: Removes the whole inline tier for every language. Each body moves to a file through `jet fix`.

comparisons.note: cgo compiles C written in the comment above `import "C"`. Source: https://pkg.go.dev/cmd/cgo
The emit pragma places raw C into the generated code. Source: https://nim-lang.org/docs/manual.html#implementation-specific-pragmas-emit-pragma
No inline C; C builds through a build script. Inline assembly is built in. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/inline-assembly.html
C comes in through a header, and the build adds C files. Source: https://ziglang.org/documentation/master/#cImport
ImportC compiles a C file as a module. There is no inline C. Source: https://dlang.org/spec/importc.html

recommendation.why: Inline C is the C path that builds today, and its prototype is checked. Removing it costs scripts a file split and gains no safety.
gains: Small C helpers stay next to the Jet code.
Nothing working is removed.
C, C++ and assembly share one shape.

losses.loss: Two ways to bring in C.
losses.mitigation: The split is by size, as in Go: a few lines inline, a library by header.

whyNot.reason: It removes the working path for the unfinished one, and only for C.
It removes working inline assembly too, which Rust and Zig both keep.

recommendation.tradeoff: Two ways to bring in C, for single-file programs that keep working.

decisions.title: Publishing runs every doc example; coverage is shown, not forced
decisions.situation: A package page helps most when each function shows a working example. In Jet, an example is a code block in a doc comment. `jet test --docs` runs it as a test. The registry already checks gates before it publishes, such as the signature and the name. It checks nothing about examples. So a package can ship with no examples, or with examples that no longer run. The vote decides what publishing checks about examples.

decisions.title: Checking grows in a straight line with expression size, held by a test
decisions.situation: A type checker works out the type of every expression. In some languages that work explodes on long expressions. Swift can give up on one line of arithmetic. There, one operator can mean many things, chosen by the type its result must have. Jet avoids that design today. But no rule keeps it that way, and no test measures it. A probe found a different limit. Adding up 200 copies of `a` crashes the checker with a stack overflow. The vote decides whether straight-line checking becomes a rule with a test.
decisions.gist: Should checking work grow in a straight line with expression size, as a tested rule?
decisions.lesson: Yes: checking time and depth grow in a straight line, proved by a test.
decisions.story: A generator writes a 5,000-term sum. `jet check` passes in a blink, because a test on every compiler change keeps it so.
decisions.inWild:
Option          Long expression   Result-type picks   Like
A rule + test   checks, linear    never               Go
B best effort   may crash         not ruled out       most compilers
C budget        refused past N    allowed             Swift, TS, Rust
decisions.detail:
WHAT WE BUILD
- Spec: the rule beside D-INFER-LEVEL1 (one pass; expected type read where present; no choice by result type).
- Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Expressions.jet: check left-nested operator chains without recursion depth per term (sema_expr_check_binary :3948, sema_expr_decimal_literal_operand :3825).
- Host gate #4601: a corpus of 1..10,000-term expressions; work counters and stack depth must grow linearly.

EVIDENCE (r14, ballots2/redo/probe/)
- plain_150.jet (150 x `a +`) and lin_150.jet: `jet check` ok.
- plain_200.jet, lin_200.jet and larger: `Stop [E3012]: Stack overflow` in sema_expr_check_binary or sema_expr_decimal_literal_operand, exit 70. This is a compiler crash, which I2 forbids.
- Check time stayed near 100-500 ms up to the crash; the risk shown is depth, not time.

IDS
Consistent with D-INFER-LEVEL1=A and D-TRAIT-OVERLOAD1=A. Does not reopen D-COMPILE-SPEED1 (#4999). FutureAudit 2026-10-28, FUTURE.md T08. File a bug card for the 200-term crash.

options.name: Straight-line rule with a test
options.detail: Checking takes one pass and never picks a function by its result type. A size test runs on every change. Gains: Long and generated code always checks fast. Finds crashes like the 200-term one before users do. Losses: Rules out picking a function by its result type.
options.technical: Expression typing is one pass that reads the expected type where it exists. No function or operator is chosen by the type its result must have. The checker handles long operator chains without deep recursion. The compiler speed gate adds a corpus of expressions from 1 to 10,000 terms. Its work counters and stack depth must grow in a straight line.

options.name: Best effort
options.detail: No rule and no test. Slow or crashing cases are fixed when someone reports them. Gains: No new test to keep. Losses: Nothing stops a later feature from breaking it. Crashes like the 200-term one wait for a user.
options.technical: Today's state. The crash is fixed as an ordinary bug.

options.name: A size budget
options.detail: Past a size or depth budget, the checker stops and asks for a split. Swift and TypeScript do this. Gains: A clear error instead of a crash. Losses: Valid long code is refused. The budget hides slow growth below it.
options.technical: The checker counts steps or depth per expression. Past the budget it reports an error with a fix.

comparisons.note: Result-type overloads make some literal expressions time out. Source: https://www.cocoawithlove.com/blog/2016/07/12/type-checker-issues.html
Deep type instantiation stops at a fixed limit with error 2589. Source: https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/release-notes/typescript-4-5.html
Go has no overloading, so each expression checks in one pass. Source: https://go.dev/doc/faq#overloading
Rust uses result-type inference through traits and sets recursion limits. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/attributes/limits.html

recommendation.why: Jet already avoids the designs that explode. A tested rule keeps it that way. Its first run would have caught the 200-term crash.
gains: Fast checking for any size of code.
Generated code never hits a hidden limit.
Uses the existing compiler speed gate.

losses.loss: Rules out picking a function by its result type.
losses.mitigation: Traits already give one function per operation, and generic calls still read the expected type.

whyNot.reason: It waits for users to find crashes the test finds today.
It refuses valid code instead of checking it.

recommendation.tradeoff: No result-type overloading, for checking that never explodes.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude. Adversarial model family: Claude. Fresh agent: BallotReview. I attacked whether the rule is complete, whether its loss is real, and each peer row; the probes confirm the 200-term crash. Rust caps checking with recursion limits, which is option C's budget, not best effort, so the table now places it there; A still wins.

decisions.title: Remote builds speak Jet's own signed protocol, with adapters for existing farms and web stores
decisions.situation: Big teams speed up builds two ways. They share a cache of build results, and they run build steps on a farm of machines. Most farms speak one open protocol, first defined by Bazel. You asked whether Zig copied it. It did not: Zig's build protocol is its own, and it only runs on one machine. Jet's spec already defines signed records for remote results, which that open protocol cannot carry. No wire protocol is chosen yet. The vote picks how Jet talks to remote builders and caches.
decisions.gist: Should remote builds speak Jet's own signed protocol, with adapters for existing build farms?
decisions.lesson: Yes. Jet's protocol carries signed results and Jet's own step names. Existing farms and plain web stores work through adapters, and every result still comes back signed.
decisions.story: Ana's team shares a cache in an ordinary web bucket, because every record is signed and checked on her machine. Later her company's existing farm runs Jet steps through a relay the team runs beside it. Each result comes back signed by that relay, naming the farm.
decisions.inWild:
Option              Core protocol       Existing farms        Like
A Jet's own         signed Jet records  via signing relay     Zig (own), Nix (signed)
B the open protocol Bazel's REAPI       direct                Bazel, Buck2, Pants
C cache only        plain web requests  cache only            Gradle, Turborepo
decisions.detail:
OWNER QUESTION (q3u6bcmb)
Zig made its own. Its compiler server (lib/std/zig/Server.zig) is a small binary message protocol over stdin and stdout between the build runner and the compiler. Messages include error bundles, emit digests, test results, file inputs and timing reports. The build runner adds `--watch`, `--webui`, `--fuzz` and `--time-report`. Zig has no remote cache and no remote execution, and none of this is Bazel's Remote Execution API.

WHY OUR OWN
The open protocol names steps as opaque commands and trusts the farm. Jet's spec (spec.md:4660-4679) requires worker identity and receipts bound to a credential. A stock farm cannot sign those. Copying it would make Jet's typed steps and receipts second-class.

WHAT WE BUILD
- Protocol library `core.build.remote` on the public build-session API: content-addressed blobs, Jet step keys, signed request, result and receipt envelopes (spec.md:4620-4679). `jet remote serve` is a thin command over it.
- Web store adapter: any HTTP or S3-style store holds blobs and signed records. Records are verified locally, so the store needs no trust.

- Farm adapter: `jet remote serve` on a host the team controls, beside an existing farm, relays steps to it over Remote Execution API v2. Each action runs Jet's worker, uploaded as an input blob, so no special farm image is needed.
- The relay holds its own credential and signs every receipt. The receipt names the farm as the trust domain, as D-JPK-REMOTE1=D grants require. So no result reaches a client unsigned.

- `harden: true` can further require receipts from Jet-run workers only; `jet audit` lists which trust domain built each output.
- Adapters are ordinary packages, so anyone can add a peer for another farm or store.

WHY A HAS NO REAL LOSS
- The old loss was unsigned results from farms without Jet's worker image. The relay uploads the worker with each action and signs every receipt, so every farm returns signed, attributed results.
- The relay is one more process only for teams that keep an existing farm; teams on Jet's own servers never run it.

EVIDENCE
- spec.md:4620-4639 defines HMAC-SHA256 request, result, cache-record and CAS-blob envelopes and worker receipts, but no wire protocol.
- `jet remote` exists in r14 help ("manage host-owned remote builders").

IDS
Unchanged: D-JPK-REMOTE1=D (#422: build.remote grants, jet remote bind, no endpoint flags), D-NEST-REMOTECACHE1. Uses D-BUILD-REUSESET1 (`--cache=off` rebuilds locally). FutureAudit 2026-10-28, FUTURE.md T22.

options.name: Jet's own protocol, with adapters
options.detail: Jet's signed records are the wire format, served by `jet remote serve`. Adapters reach plain web stores and existing farms; the farm adapter is a relay that signs every receipt. Gains: every result carries a signed Jet receipt; a cache can live in any web bucket, with no trust in it; teams keep the farm they already run. Losses: none.
options.technical: The protocol is a Core library on the public build API. It moves content-addressed blobs and signed step records keyed by Jet's own step keys. `jet remote serve` runs it on a machine or beside a farm. The web store adapter keeps blobs and records in any HTTP or S3-style store; records are checked locally, so a leaked bucket cannot forge a result. The farm relay speaks the open protocol, ships Jet's worker as an action input, and signs each receipt naming the farm.
options.code:
$ jet remote bind cache s3://corp-builds/jet          # any web store
$ jet remote bind farm jet+grpcs://relay.corp:8980    # relay to the farm
$ jet build --builder farm
1204 steps: 1180 cache hits, 24 run remotely, all receipts signed

options.name: The open protocol at the core
options.detail: Jet speaks Bazel's Remote Execution API directly, for cache and remote steps. Gains: works with existing farms with no adapter. Losses: stock farms cannot sign Jet's receipts; Jet's steps become opaque commands.
options.technical: Jet becomes a client of Remote Execution API v2. Each step becomes a command and an action, named by content hash. A farm is trusted as the trust domain its grant names. Signed receipts ride in result metadata only when the worker is Jet.
options.code:
$ jet remote bind farm grpcs://build.corp:8980
$ jet build --builder farm
1204 steps: 1180 cache hits, 24 run remotely

options.name: Shared cache only
options.detail: Jet shares build results over plain web requests, as Gradle does. It never runs steps remotely. Gains: small and easy to secure. Losses: no remote steps, so cold builds stay slow.
options.technical: Results are stored and fetched by content hash with plain web reads and writes. No remote execution.
options.code:
$ jet remote bind cache https://cache.corp/jet
$ jet build --builder cache
1180 cache hits, 24 built locally

comparisons.note: Its own binary protocol between build runner and compiler, on one machine. Source: https://github.com/ziglang/zig/blob/master/lib/std/zig/Server.zig
comparisons.code:
# Zig: local build runner, its own protocol
$ zig build --watch --webui
$ zig build --time-report

comparisons.note: Defined the Remote Execution API; one flag points at a farm. Source: https://bazel.build/remote/rbe
comparisons.code:
# Bazel
$ bazel build //app --remote_executor=grpcs://farm:8980
INFO: 1180 remote cache hit, 24 remote.

comparisons.note: Meta's build tool speaks the same protocol to the same farms. Source: https://buck2.build/docs/users/remote_execution/
Its own protocol; binary caches are signed, so any web store can host one. Source: https://nix.dev/manual/nix/stable/command-ref/conf-file#conf-trusted-public-keys
comparisons.code:
# nix.conf: a signed cache in a plain web store
substituters = https://cache.corp.example
trusted-public-keys = corp:3k8...=

comparisons.note: The build cache is plain HTTP; there is no remote execution. Source: https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/build_cache.html

recommendation.why: Jet's steps and signed receipts are its own, so its protocol should carry them natively, as Zig and Nix do. A signing relay keeps existing farms usable with no unsigned results. The protocol and every adapter are ordinary libraries.
recommendation.tradeoff: Nothing is given up: existing farms work through a relay, and every result stays signed.
gains: Every result carries a signed Jet receipt.
A cache can live in any web store, with no trust in it.
Teams keep the farms they already run.

whyNot.reason: Stock farms cannot sign Jet's receipts, and Jet's steps become opaque commands.
No remote steps, so cold builds stay slow.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude. Adversarial model family: Claude. Fresh agent: BallotReview. I attacked the trust loss, the cache-only rival and the cited decisions. The build list cited D-JPK-REMOTE1=C, which is the per-command endpoint option; the ratified answer is D, now fixed, and A still wins on reuse of existing farms.

decisions.title: Publish packages with short-lived identities, never stored tokens
decisions.situation: To publish a package, a tool must prove it may publish under that name. Most registries use a long-lived secret token, and in 2025 a worm spread through npm by stealing such tokens. Trusted publishing replaces the token with a short-lived identity that a build service issues for one job. The owner decides whether Jet's registry accepts only short-lived identities. We recommend that, with an interactive login that expires within an hour for people publishing from their own machine.
decisions.gist: Should Jet's registry refuse long-lived publish tokens and accept only short-lived identities?
decisions.lesson: To publish a package you prove you own its name. A long-lived token is like a password that works for months, so a thief can reuse it. A short-lived identity comes from a build service for one job and expires within minutes. Signing and the public publish log are already decided.
decisions.story: A worm steals Ana's saved publish token from her laptop and publishes a poisoned version of her package overnight.
decisions.inWild:
permissions:
  id-token: write
steps:
  - run: npm publish   # identity from the CI job, no NPM_TOKEN
# npm trusted publishing lets a GitHub Actions or GitLab CI job publish with an OIDC identity and no token. Source: https://docs.npmjs.com/trusted-publishers
decisions.detail: FutureAudit 2026-10-28, FUTURE.md T15 option B. Already ratified and not reopened: transparency log, sparse TUF metadata and transactional publish (D-JPK-REGISTRY1=D, #423); signing (D-PKGSIGN1); keyless --no-sign (D-PKGSIGN-NOSIGN1=A); trust root (#2199). This ballot is only the upload credential. Short-lived identity = OIDC tokens from configured CI issuers (GitHub, GitLab) bound to repository and workflow, or a device-code login with expiry of at most one hour. Snippet flags are illustrative.

options.name: Short-lived identities only
options.detail: A CI identity or a login that expires within an hour; stored tokens are refused. Gains: Nothing long-lived to steal. The publish log records which job published. Losses: Publishing from a laptop needs a login each session.
options.technical: The registry accepts OIDC tokens from configured issuers, bound to repository and workflow. Each one is recorded in the transparency log. Device-code login issues a credential of at most 1 h; no long-lived API tokens are issued.

$ jet registry publish                  # in CI: job identity

decisions.title: Infrastructure as typed Jet code
decisions.situation: Teams describe servers, databases and networks in tools like Terraform, then apply that description to a cloud. Those tools use their own languages, keep secrets in a state file, and make plans hard to test. A Jet package could describe infrastructure in ordinary typed Jet, with the plan as a value that tests can check. The owner decides whether Jet ships such a package and whether it reuses Terraform's existing provider plugins. We recommend both, after the HTTP library is finished.
decisions.gist: Should Jet ship a first-party infrastructure package that reuses Terraform's provider plugins?
decisions.lesson: Infrastructure as code means you write which servers and databases you want, and a tool makes the cloud match. Terraform does this with its own language and thousands of provider plugins, one per cloud service. Reusing those plugins would give Jet the same reach. Writing the plan in Jet makes it typed and testable.
decisions.story: Raj changes one database setting in a Terraform file. The mistake only shows when apply fails halfway, after two servers have already changed.
decisions.detail: FutureAudit 2026-10-28, FUTURE.md T24. Sequenced after the HTTP client and server (audit card 3: #3665, #4957). Plan = pure value; apply under Net and Secret authority; state = content-addressed lock; Secret values never serialized. The Terraform/OpenTofu plugin protocol is gRPC (tfplugin5/6); licensing of the protocol must be verified [INFERENCE: OpenTofu is MPL-2.0]. Fleet and OS deployment are e9 and out of scope. Related #4195, #5696.

recommendation.why: A typed plan that tests can check fixes the worst infrastructure failures, and reusing existing providers gives full cloud reach without writing thousands of them.
gains: Services and their infrastructure live in one checked language.

losses.loss: An outside plugin protocol to follow.
losses.mitigation: Pin the protocol version and test providers against recorded plugin replies.

whyNot.reason: Writing a provider for every cloud service would take years.

recommendation.tradeoff: Dependence on a plugin protocol in exchange for full cloud coverage from day one.

decisions.title: The REPL can use packages, with the same pins and permissions as a script
decisions.situation: A REPL is the prompt where you type code and see each result at once. Jet's REPL is not built yet. The current plan limits it to the standard library. Then nobody can try a package at the prompt. IPython, Deno, Julia and Elixir all allow it. Data work and API exploration mostly happen at such a prompt. The vote decides which packages the REPL may use, and how they are pinned and allowed.
decisions.gist: Should the REPL (the interactive prompt) import packages, like a script can?
decisions.lesson: Yes, with the same version pins and permission prompts a script uses.
decisions.story: Dee types `use textkit#1.4` at the prompt. Jet fetches it once and pins it. `:save slug.jet` writes a script that runs the same tomorrow.

A script rules    fetches, asks once            yes           Deno
B standard only   refused                       n/a           no peer
C project only    only inside a project         project lock  Elixir
Elixir Mix.install and Rust evcxr also fetch at the prompt.
IPython: %pip installs into the whole environment, unpinned.
decisions.detail:
WHAT WE BUILD
- The REPL itself is card #4720 (not built; `jet repl` gives E2104).
- Reuse the inline-dependency resolver (Compiler/JetCli/Source/Cli/ScriptDeps.jet) for each `use` line; fetching is card #4833.
- A session lock in the cache (Compiler/JetCli/Source/Cli/ScriptCache.jet).
- Docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:4217: replace "`jet repl` stays std-only" with this rule.
- Deleted: the standard-library-only gate in the REPL plan.

EVIDENCE
- Probe (commit 8fbf094): `jet repl` gives E2104 "`jet repl` is not built yet".
- `textkit` stands for any registry package.

IDS
Narrows D-REPL18 (syntax-decisions.md:4217). Reuses D-JPK-SCRIPTDEP1=A (inline `use pkg#ver`) and the #5949 ask-once prompt.

options.name: Same rules as a script
options.detail: `use pkg#ver` fetches, pins and asks for permissions once. `:save` writes a pinned script. Gains: Try any package at the prompt. A saved session runs the same later. Losses: A first import waits for fetch and compile. Each session keeps a small lock file in the cache.
options.technical: Each prompt entry is a script body, and bindings carry over. `use pkg#ver` uses the same resolver as a script's inline dependency. The pin goes into a session lock in the cache. Inside a package folder, its locked dependencies import, read-only. A package's permissions join the session through the ask-once prompt. The prompt names the package. `:save` writes the entries and their pins to a file. Offline, only cached packages import.

> textkit.slug("Hello World")

decisions.title: Script mode: a `#!` first line makes a file a script
decisions.situation: A script is a small file you run to do one job. Today every Jet file that runs needs `fn run() { … }`. A three-line script with no wrapper fails with three errors. A `#!` first line also grants every permission today, silently. A new owner ruling ends that: scripts will ask once instead. The owner proposes one switch for both problems: a `#!` first line turns on script mode. In script mode, the statements form the body of `fn run`. The vote decides whether this is the right switch, and what it may change.
decisions.gist: Should a `#!` first line turn on a script mode where statements run without `fn run`?
decisions.lesson: Yes: in a `#!` file, statements become `fn run`, and permissions live on that line.
decisions.story: Ana's script starts with `#!/usr/bin/env jet` and has three lines. Jet asks once to read `name.txt`, then remembers. When the script grows, `jet fix` wraps it into `fn run`.
decisions.inWild:
Option                Hello script   Mode shown by    Like
A #! script mode      2 lines        first line       Deno (#! flags)
B statements anywhere 1 line         nothing          Python, Ruby, C#
C jet script command  1 line         the command      no peer
D .jets extension     1 line         file name        Kotlin, Elixir
E fn run everywhere   4 lines        n/a              Go, Rust, Zig
Every option keeps the same types, checks and imports.
decisions.detail:
WHAT WE BUILD
- One test for script mode: jet_cli_is_script (Compiler/JetCli/Source/Cli/Authority.jet:56), shared by the checker and the CLI.
- Entry: in script mode, build `fn run` from the statements instead of E0621 (Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/CheckProgram.jet:8245-8260; E0621 at :8254). E0620 for imported files (:8253) stays.
- Parser: in script mode, lower-case file-scope bindings join the body in order (Compiler/JetParser/Source/Parser/Entry.jet:850-867). The formatter already interleaves body and items (Compiler/JetParser/Source/Formatter/Formatter.jet:1631-1650).

- Permissions: delete the silent allow-all (Authority.jet:60-67). Flags on the `#!` line apply as typed. The ask-once prompt and its memory are the 2026-10-28 ruling (#5949).
- Fixes: E0621 offers "add a `#!` line" and "wrap into `fn run`". The wrap also moves `#!` permissions into package.jet (Compiler/JetCli/Source/Cli/LspFixes.jet:18).
- Docs: rewrite Docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:349-364; one example showing both shapes.

EVIDENCE
- ballots2/probe/script_today.jet (the program above): `jet check` reports E0621, E0357 and E0622.
- Authority.jet:53-67: a `#!/` file runs as if `-A` were typed.
- Bench (scripting/bench, 15 programs): the `fn run` wrapper and indent are 783 of 6,954 bytes. Python totals 4,420.

IDS
Reopens D-ENTRY-EXPLICIT2=A (#3122) for `#!` files only; all other files keep explicit `fn run`, and #3122 skips `#!` files. History: D-ENTRY-SCRIPT1=B (implicit `fn run`) was built in the Rust era (#1808, #1809); the owner walked it back on 2026-09-13 (idea bksxea84), keeping notebook cells (D-ENTRY-SCRIPT1=C, syntax-decisions.md:349-364). Folds in #5949 (no grant from `#!`; ask once) and sits beside D-SCRIPT-DESIGNATE1 (#6010). #5085 B5 drafted this item. Option letters changed from the earlier draft: old A is now B, old B is now E, old C is now A.

options.name: Script mode by `#!`
options.detail: A `#!` launch line on line one makes a script. Its statements form `fn run`; its permissions live on that line. Gains: A script is as short as Python, and still fully checked. Line one tells every reader the file runs top to bottom. Fixes the silent allow-everything bug in the same design. Losses: Without `#!`, a bare `print("hi")` file is still an error. A function cannot read a variable from the script body.
options.technical:
Script mode starts when line one begins with `#!/`. Jet already detects this line today. In script mode, statements outside functions form the body of `fn run`. They run in file order. `fn`, `struct`, `use` and ALL_CAPS constants stay declarations. A lower-case `name :: …` is a local of the body. A function cannot read it; the error offers an ALL_CAPS constant or a parameter. A script may write `fn run` itself instead, but not both. Permissions: a `#!` line no longer allows everything.

Flags on that line apply as if typed, as in `#!/usr/bin/env -S jet -A`. Otherwise Jet asks once in a terminal and remembers the answer for this exact code. `jet fix` writes a chosen permission onto the `#!` line. In a normal program, permissions live in package.jet instead. Script mode never changes types, checks, effects, failures or exit codes. The body is `fn run`, so it means the same on every tier.

An imported file still may not hold statements, so imports never run code. To grow a script, delete the `#!` line or import the file. Jet then reports the loose statements. `jet fix` wraps them into `fn run` and moves the `#!` permissions into package.jet. The code itself does not change.

options.name: Statements in any file you run
options.detail: Any file given to `jet run` may hold statements, with or without `#!`. Gains: No first line needed, so hello is one line. Same as Python and Ruby. Losses: Nothing in the file says it runs top to bottom. Reopens the explicit-entry ruling for every file.
options.technical: The file you run may hold statements; imported files still may not. Permissions follow the new ruling, with flags as their only home.
options.code:
// B: any file you run may hold statements
use core.files as fs
name :: fs.read("name.txt").trim()
print("hi {name}")

options.name: A `jet script` command
options.detail: `jet script hi.jet` allows statements; `jet run hi.jet` does not. Gains: Normal files never change. Losses: One file means two things, chosen by the command. `./hi.jet` still needs `#!` to pick the command.
options.technical: The command, not the file, picks the mode. A `#!` line would have to name `jet script`.
options.code:
# C: the command decides
$ jet script hi.jet     # statements allowed
$ jet run hi.jet        # error: needs fn run

options.name: A script file extension
options.detail: A `.jets` file may hold statements, like Kotlin's `.main.kts` files. Gains: The file name shows the mode. Losses: Growing a script means renaming it, and every reference to it. Every tool must learn a second extension.
options.technical: Kotlin (`.main.kts`) and Elixir (`.exs`) work this way.
options.code:
# D: the extension decides
$ cat hi.jets
print("hi")
$ jet run hi.jets

options.name: Keep `fn run` everywhere
options.detail: Every file that runs keeps `fn run() { … }`, as today. Gains: One file shape everywhere. Same as Go, Rust and Zig. Losses: The wrapper and its indent are 11% of our benchmark scripts. The `#!` permission fix lands as a separate change.
options.technical: Today's rule. The new permission ruling still lands, on its own.

comparisons.note: A single file runs with statements and `#:` lines for packages. `dotnet project convert` turns it into a project. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/sdk/file-based-apps
Flags on the `#!` line grant permissions. Without them, Deno asks at run time. Source: https://docs.deno.com/runtime/fundamentals/security/
Only `.main.kts` files hold statements. A growing script is rewritten with `fun main`. Source: https://kotlinlang.org/docs/custom-script-deps-tutorial.html
Importing a file runs it, so files guard their script part. Source: https://docs.python.org/3/library/__main__.html
Single-file cargo scripts still need `fn main`. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/3424-cargo-script.html
Every program needs `package main` and `func main`. Source: https://go.dev/ref/spec#Program_execution

recommendation.why: One visible switch fixes script length and the permission bug together. It reopens the explicit-entry ruling, but only for `#!` files.
gains: Scripts as short as Python, still fully checked.
The `#!` line now marks the mode and holds the permissions.

losses.loss: Without `#!`, a bare `print("hi")` file is still an error.
losses.mitigation: The error offers one fix: add the `#!` line.

losses.loss: A function cannot read a variable from the script body.
losses.mitigation: The error offers two fixes: an ALL_CAPS constant, or a parameter.

whyNot.reason: Nothing in the file would say it runs top to bottom.
One file would mean two things, chosen by the command.
Growing a script would mean renaming it everywhere.
Scripts keep a wrapper that Python, Ruby and C# dropped.

recommendation.tradeoff: A second file shape, marked on line one, for scripts as short as Python.

C# allows statements in a file with or without `#!`, which is B's model, so the table moves it; A still wins because the file says how it runs.

decisions.title: Implicit context: scratch memory that cannot dangle, plus the context name, keys and fields
decisions.situation: Jai and Odin give every function a hidden context: the allocator, the logger, and scratch memory that is freed all at once. Jet ratified that context (D-JAI-CONTEXT1) and must now settle how it works. The hard part is scratch memory. Jai frees it with one reset per frame, and a value kept past the reset reads garbage. This vote picks how Jet frees scratch safely, together with the name, key and field rules.
decisions.gist: Should scratch memory rewind when its block ends and move out what leaves, or be reset by hand as in Jai?
decisions.lesson: Scratch memory hands out space by bumping a pointer and frees everything at once. A frame's temporary text and lists then cost almost nothing. In Jai, code resets scratch once per frame, and a value still held after the reset points at reused memory. Jet must rule that out without putting lifetimes in signatures, which D-REGION1 already rejected.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: nothing new to learn. Code that never names scratch allocates as it does today. A library reads `context.allocator` or `context.logger` like any other name.

Expert path: wrap a frame in `#Context(allocator: context.scratch) { ... }`. Everything the frame builds, inside any library, comes from scratch. When the block ends, scratch rewinds. A value that left the block, such as a line pushed onto an older log, was moved into the log's own memory as it was pushed.
decisions.story: Ren writes a game loop. Each frame builds a few hundred labels and throws them away, and one function also pushes a line onto the game's log. In Jai that line would dangle after the reset. Under A it moves into the log as it is pushed, and the labels vanish together at the closing brace.
decisions.detail:
WHAT IS ALREADY RATIFIED
- D-JAI-CONTEXT1=A: code reads typed context fields, packages declare typed keys, reads add the `Context` effect, and scratch is a per-task arena. D-CTX1: `#Context(field: value) { ... }` changes fields for one block and restores them on exit.
- Today only `deadline` takes effect. The allocator and logger are checked and dropped (Compiler/JetIR/Source/BuildTransact.jet:223-228, defect #5030). The task-owned context record landed with #5025 ctx0 (commit 36825b7a15).

THE QUESTION
- The five earlier context ballots (CONTEXT-NAME1, KEYS1, ALLOC1, FIELDS1 and SCRATCH1) are one design, so they return as this one vote. Main withdraws the five when this one goes live.
- Four of their rules have one clear answer, shared by both options below. The real choice is how scratch memory is freed safely.

SHARED: THE NAME AND THE EFFECT
- `context` is a short name for a new Core module, `core.context`, like `print` and `time` today. A local named `context` hides it by the ordinary scoping rule, and `core.context` always reaches it.
- The repository has 1,009 lines declaring something named `context` (query on dev 479d6936df). None needs renaming. A reserved word would force all of them to change.

- Reads add `Context` to the function's effect row. Packages never need it granted, because a read touches no file, socket or device. A budget may still deny it with `!Context`.

SHARED: KEYS
- A package declares a key with a required default, written like a field default: `#ContextKey frame_index: Int{0}`. An optional key writes `#ContextKey user: User?{None}`.
- The ratified spelling had `pub`. That word was removed from Jet (E0411), so the form above drops it.

- A key is an ordinary name. Another package's key is imported with `use game.[frame_index]` and renamed with `as`, like any import, so no dotted labels are needed.
- `#Context(frame_index: n) { ... }` sets it, and `context.get(frame_index)` reads it. A key may not reuse one of the eight field names, so a label never means two things.

SHARED: FIELD TYPES
- `allocator: mem.Allocator` (default: the program allocator). `logger: log.Handler` (Core/Log/Log.jet:382). `deadline: Int?` in epoch milliseconds. `thread: Int`, read-only.
- `on_stop: fn(debug.Stop)` runs before every stop: assert, panic, and bounds or key checks. It replaces the ratified `on_assert`, which covered failed assertions only, so the name says what it does.

- `trace: [debug.Frame]` is captured when read, so it costs nothing until used. Frame names follow `debug_info`, exactly as crash reports already do (spec.md:3722-3725).
- `print: term.PrintStyle` shapes `print` only. String interpolation never reads context, so `-[]>` functions stay pure.

OPTION A: A SCRATCH BLOCK OWNS WHAT IT ALLOCATES
- `#Context(allocator: context.scratch) { ... }` sends every allocation made in the block's extent to scratch, including inside libraries. When the block ends, scratch rewinds to where the block began.
- Nested blocks are nested marks. So `reset`, `mark` and `restore` are not needed, and there is nothing to forget.

- Scratch is one contiguous range of address space per task, reserved on the task's first scratch block. Its pages cost memory only once touched.
- An allocation past the reservation comes from the program allocator. That stays correct, because a heap value never needs to move.

- A value is newer than the block when it lies in scratch above the block's start, or in a stack frame entered after the block began. Each test is one subtract and compare on an address.

A: THE EXITS
- A newer value leaves only by being stored into older data: a binding declared before the block, a global, a link, or anything reached through a `&` parameter.
- It also leaves by `return` from inside the block, by being handed to a task, or inside a closure that outlives the block.

- The block is a statement, not an expression, as `#Context` is today (probe q/b4/ctx/expr.jet gives E0003). A result therefore leaves only through one of these exits.
- At each exit the value first moves into the destination's allocator. It is moved, never duplicated, so the program means what it would without scratch.

- Stores in the block's own text are resolved by the compiler. A store inside a library, such as a callee pushing onto a list passed with `&`, runs the address test.

A: GROWING OLDER CONTAINERS
- A container grows in the allocator that owns it, not the one in context. `&game.log.push(x)` inside the block grows `log` from the program allocator, because `log` is older than the block.
- The owner is read from the container's own address by the same test. No container gains a word, so `[T]` and `String` keep their current size.

- Dropping a scratch value frees nothing. Programs with a reachable scratch block use a free entry that makes the same address test first. Other programs keep today's entry.

A: OTHER RULES
- An installed arena is borrowed for reading until the block ends. So `&arena.reset()` inside the block is the existing E0204 conflict, found at compile time.
- `@` link boxes and their contents always use the program allocator, because a link has no lexical lifetime. Tasks spawned inside the block get the program allocator and their own scratch (D-ALLOC1).

WHAT A COSTS, MEASURED
- Moving one short label out of a block cost 18 ns. Building and freeing the same label on the heap cost 170 ns (q/b4/ctx/cost.jet, `jet run --release`, 1,000,000 labels).
- A moved list moves every element. Relocating a 10,000-label list took 0.11 to 0.12 ms, about 12 ns per label. Building it took 2.3 to 2.7 ms (q/b4/ctx/deep.jet, three runs).

- Jai and Odin code pays the same copy by hand, with `copy_string` or `strings.clone`, when it keeps a temporary. A does it at the exit and never misses one.
- `jet audit copies` lists each exit that can move a value out of scratch, with the value's type. A list exit is marked as moving per element.

- The address test was measured as a proxy: ten million `String` stores through a `&` parameter, with and without one extra compare and branch.
- Over four runs the difference was +77, -32, -90 and -38 ms on about 1,580 ms. That is inside run-to-run noise (q/b4/ctx/store.jet).
- A program with no reachable scratch block emits no test. The build already proves reachability per effect, as E0749 does for denied effects.

A: THE EXPERT WAY OUT
- Code that must never move a value uses an explicit `mem.Arena` and `arena.alloc(v)` views. Views never move, and E0631 and E0632 keep them inside the arena's life at compile time.
- `&arena.reset()` then frees by hand, as Jai's reset does, with zero copies. The cost is managing that lifetime yourself, with no block to do it.

OPTION B: JAI'S RESET, STOPPED IF A VALUE SURVIVES
- The same block sends allocations to scratch, but nothing moves and nothing rewinds. The program calls `&context.scratch.reset()` once per frame, as Jai calls `reset_temporary_storage()`.
- `mark()` and `restore(m)` give nested resets.

- Scratch counts its living values. Each allocation adds one, and each free of a scratch value subtracts one. A reset while any value is alive stops the program and names where that value was made.
- A value meant to outlive the frame must be built outside the block, as in Jai. E0632 catches a read after a reset where the compiler sees both; the rest are run-time stops.

WHY NOT A FULLY STATIC DESIGN
- Rust's bumpalo ties each value to its arena in the type, so every function that returns or stores one needs a lifetime parameter.
- D-REGION1 ratified that such lifetimes never appear in Jet syntax. `arena.alloc(v)` views keep that compile-time rule (E0631, E0632) as the zero-copy expert rung, unchanged in both options.

EACH RULE'S WAY OUT (REWORK item 7)
- A's move at an exit: the expert way out above, at the cost of managing the arena by hand.
- Links and tasks using the program allocator: install an arena inside the task, or hold `arena.alloc` views. Nothing extra is paid.

- A key that repeats a field name: rename it on import with `as`. Nothing extra is paid.
- E0204 on resetting an installed arena has no way out. It is a soundness rule (I1), because the reset would free values the block still uses.

RATIFIED TEXT TO AMEND (flag for Main)
- D-JAI-CONTEXT1=A SCRATCH says scratch has reset, mark and restore, and that scratch values are arena views. Under A, scratch is used only by installing it, and the block replaces all three.
- D-JAI-CONTEXT1=A HANDLER names `on_assert` for failed assertions. Both options rename it `on_stop` and run it for every stop.
- D-JAI-CONTEXT1=A KEYS writes `#ContextKey pub`. `pub` no longer exists (E0411).
- D-CTX1: under A, a block that installs an arena also rewinds it on exit.

PROBE
- q/b4/ctx/pA3.jet is A's program with a local `mem.Arena` in place of `context.scratch`. It runs on dev today and prints the six labels and a log length of 3.
- With `context.scratch`, the only error is E0107 for `context`. With the key declaration, the only errors are E0003 at `#ContextKey` and E0761 for the key label. Those are the features themselves.

IDS
- Builds on D-JAI-CONTEXT1=A, D-CTX1, D-DEADLINE1, D-ALLOC1, D-ALLOC2, D-REGION1, D-MEM-COPYSEM1 and D-ALLOCFAIL1. Card #5025.

options.name: Scratch blocks; what leaves moves out
options.detail: A `#Context(allocator: context.scratch)` block sends every allocation in it to scratch, including inside libraries. Scratch rewinds when the block ends. A value stored into older data, from the block or from any callee, first moves into the destination's own memory. There is no reset call, no mark to forget, and no stop.
options.technical:
Install with `#Context(allocator: context.scratch)` or with any `mem.Arena`. Every arena is one contiguous address reservation per task, with pages committed on touch. The block borrows the arena for reading, so `&arena.reset()` inside it is E0204. Exit rewinds the arena to its entry point, and nested blocks are nested marks.

A value is newer than the block if it lies in the arena above the block's mark, or in a stack frame entered after the block began. Each test is one subtract and compare. Exits are stores into older places, `return`, task hand-offs and escaping closures. The block is a statement, so it has no result value. At an exit the value moves into the destination's allocator, element by element for a list.

An older container grows from its owner's allocator, found by the same address test, so no container gains a word. Dropping a scratch value frees nothing. Stores in the block's text are resolved by the compiler. Stores in callees, and the free entry, run the test only when a scratch block is reachable. Links use the program allocator. The expert way out is `arena.alloc` views with `&arena.reset()`.

options.name: Jai's reset, stopped if a value survives
options.detail: The same block sends allocations to scratch, but nothing moves. The program resets scratch by hand once per frame, as in Jai. Scratch counts its living values, and a reset while one is still alive stops the program and names where it was made. Values to keep are built outside the block.
options.technical: Install as in A, with no rewind on exit. `&context.scratch.reset()`, `mark()` and `&context.scratch.restore(m)` free scratch. Each scratch allocation adds one to a live count; each free of a scratch value subtracts one. A reset or restore with a live value made after that point is a located stop, or E0632 where the compiler sees it. Shared fields, keys, name and effect are as in the detail.

comparisons.note: Temporary storage is freed by `reset_temporary_storage()`, usually once per frame. Nothing checks for a value kept past it. (The Way to Jai, ch. 25A)
comparisons.code:
label := tprint("% at %", name, tick);
reset_temporary_storage();

comparisons.note: `context.temp_allocator` is freed with `free_all`. Nothing checks for a kept value. https://odin-lang.org/docs/overview/#allocators
comparisons.code:
label := fmt.tprintf("%v at %v", name, tick)
free_all(context.temp_allocator)

comparisons.note: An arena is passed explicitly and freed with `deinit`. Nothing checks for a kept value. https://ziglang.org/documentation/master/#Choosing-an-Allocator

recommendation.why: A keeps Jai's frame pattern and its speed, and a kept value can never dangle. The block is the mark, so there is no reset to call or forget. Moving a leaving value costs about a tenth of building it.
gains: No value can outlive its scratch memory, and nothing stops at run time.
Libraries allocate from scratch with no change to their code.
No reset, mark or restore to write or forget.

whyNot.reason: B turns a kept value into a run-time stop, found only by running that path, and makes authors build kept values outside the frame by hand.

recommendation.tradeoff: A value that leaves a scratch block moves once: 18 ns for a short label, against 170 ns to build it on the heap. A list moves per element, about 12 ns each. Programs without scratch blocks pay nothing, and `arena.alloc` views never move.

surface.gist: Should scratch memory rewind when its block ends and move out what leaves, or be reset by hand as in Jai?
surface.lesson: Scratch memory frees everything at once, so a frame's temporary text costs almost nothing. In Jai, a value kept past the reset reads reused memory. Jet must rule that out without lifetimes in signatures.

current.note: The allocator is checked and then ignored, so this block still uses the heap.

wild.note: One reset per frame. A string kept past it dangles.
wild.code:
label := tprint("% at %", name, tick);
reset_temporary_storage();

options.gist: Scratch rewinds when the block ends, and a value stored into older data first moves to that data's memory.
gains: No value can dangle, and nothing stops at run time.
No reset or mark to write or forget.

options.gist: Code resets scratch by hand each frame, and a reset while a value is still alive stops the program.
gains: Exactly Jai's shape.
Nothing is ever moved.
losses: A kept value is a run-time stop.
Kept values must be built outside the frame.

Libraries use scratch unchanged.

decisions.title: `package.jet` is the one project file: `members:` and `environments:` are its fields
decisions.situation: A Jet project describes itself in up to three files. package.jet holds the package. workspace.jet lists member packages, and env.jet lists developer tools. package.jet already accepts the same `members:` and `environments:` fields, so the same fact has two spellings and two places. The env file even uses different words, `packages:` where package.jet says `tools:`. The vote decides whether workspace and environment facts live in package.jet or in their own files. We recommend package.jet alone.
decisions.gist: Should a project's member packages and developer tools live in package.jet, or in their own files?
decisions.lesson: Every Jet project has a package.jet that names it and lists what it needs. A project with several packages also lists its members, and many projects list the tools developers need. If those lists are fields of package.jet, there is one file to read, one shape to learn, and one parser for every tool.
decisions.story: Sam adds `nodejs_22` to the dev tools in package.jet. The team's env.jet still lists the old tools under `packages:`, and that file wins. Sam spends an hour finding out why nothing changed.
decisions.inWild:
# Cargo: one Cargo.toml holds the package and its workspace.
[workspace]
members = ["packages/*"]
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Card c05i2uiq. This is the one-file question from the D-PROJECT-FILE1 package, asked alone. Test profiles are D-TEST-PROFILE1. Growing loose files is D-LOOSE-GROW1. Confirms D-ECO-FILEROOT1=A; overrides the sentence "env.jet and workspace.jet stay canonical" in D-JPK-LEGACY1=A, flagged for the owner.

Probes, in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/bd/probe/proj, with the dev jet. one/: a named package.jet with `members:` and `environments:` checks clean, and `jet run packages/shop` prints "shop". root/: a package.jet with no `name:`, holding only `members:` and `environments:`, checks clean today. three/: the same project with workspace.jet and env.jet also checks clean, so both spellings are live.

Counts (git ls-files on dev): 159 env.jet and 22 workspace.jet. 154 of the 181 sit in folders with no package.jet and become 152 nameless root files. 27 merge into 25 existing package.jet files. 78 env.jet files use `packages:`. The largest merged file would be the repo root at 61 lines. The median is 4.

Local values stay out. Secrets are declared by name only; values come from `.env` (allow-listed by `dotenv:`), the shell, or `--set`. Personal tools belong in a developer's own shell setup. A Config listed in `configs:` may hold environments but never `members:` or `build:` (PackageParse.jet:234-240), so each build fact has one owner.

options.name: One package.jet
options.detail:
Members and environments are fields of package.jet. A root folder that only groups packages has a package.jet without `name:`, like Cargo's virtual manifest.

A large team can still split a part out: `configs:` lists other files that hold environments. Editing an environment never invalidates a build.
options.technical: PackageParse.jet:188-217 already parses `members:`, `environments:`, `build:` and `configs:`. env.jet words join `Environment`: `sources`, `languages`, `dotenv`, `imports`, `files`; `packages:` becomes `tools:`. Build keys hash build fields only. `jet fix` moves 181 files (159 env.jet, 22 workspace.jet). A leftover file is an error naming its field.

options.name: Keep three files
options.detail:
Each file keeps one job, as Go splits go.mod and go.work.

To end the duplication, package.jet must stop reading `members:` and `environments:`, and every tool keeps three parsers.
options.technical: Removes the package.jet fields (PackageParse.jet:188-217) and keeps ConfigEval.jet and Host.jet env.jet readers.

options.name: Fold the workspace only
options.detail:
The workspace becomes a package.jet field, but developer tools keep their own file.

The tools list still has its own shape and word, and package.jet loses a field that works today.
options.technical: Retires 22 workspace.jet files; keeps 159 env.jet files and their readers.

comparisons.note: Cargo.toml holds package and workspace; tools live elsewhere. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/workspaces.html
One deno.json holds workspace members, tasks and imports. Source: https://docs.deno.com/runtime/fundamentals/workspaces/
go.mod per module and go.work for the workspace: two files. Source: https://go.dev/ref/mod#workspaces

recommendation.why: A uses fields package.jet already reads, so the project has one file, one vocabulary and one parser. Teams can still split a large part into a listed config file.
gains: No duplicate facts.
One shape to learn.

whyNot.reason: B keeps three shapes and must remove fields that work today.
C keeps the second vocabulary for developer tools.

recommendation.tradeoff: `jet fix` moves the 181 old files once.

decisions.checkInstructions: Use the dev jet from $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/discovery/base/latest with JET_TOOLCHAIN_ROOT set to the dev worktree. In probe/proj/one and probe/proj/root run `jet check`; both pass. In probe/proj/one, `jet run packages/shop` prints "shop".

surface.gist: Should a project's member packages and developer tools live in package.jet, or in their own files?
surface.lesson: Every Jet project has a package.jet that names it and lists what it needs. A project with several packages also lists its members, and many projects list the tools developers need. If those lists are fields of package.jet, there is one file to read, one shape to learn, and one parser for every tool.

current.note: Today the same facts can be written in two places with two vocabularies.

wild.note: Cargo keeps the workspace in Cargo.toml; a root with only `[workspace]` is a virtual manifest. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/workspaces.html
wild.code:
[workspace]
members = ["packages/*"]

options.name: One package.jet
options.gist: workspace.jet and env.jet retire; their facts become package.jet fields it already reads.
gains: One file and one vocabulary.
Every tool reads one parser.
Nothing new to learn: the fields already parse.

options.name: Keep three files
options.gist: workspace.jet and env.jet stay; package.jet stops accepting the same fields.
gains: Each concern has its own small file.
No migration of the 181 files.
losses: Three shapes: fields, `module workspace` and `module env.dev`.
package.jet's working fields are removed.

options.name: Fold the workspace only
options.gist: Members move into package.jet; env.jet stays as the developer tools file.
gains: Build facts in one file.
Developer tools stay apart from the build.
losses: Two files and two vocabularies remain.
`environments:` in package.jet must be removed.

recommendation.why: A uses fields package.jet already reads, so the project has one file, one vocabulary and one parser. Teams can still split a large part into a listed config file.
gains: No duplicate facts.
One shape to learn.

whyNot.reason: B keeps three shapes and must remove fields that work today.
C keeps the second vocabulary for developer tools.

recommendation.tradeoff: `jet fix` moves the 181 old files once.

decisions.title: `jet init` grows loose files into a package: it writes package.jet and rewrites path imports, showing every edit
decisions.situation: Loose files import each other by path, such as `use "./app/report" as report`. Inside a package all files share one namespace, so path imports are an error there. Adding a package.jet to a folder of loose files therefore breaks every import at once. `jet fix` makes no changes, and `jet init` is not built yet. The vote decides how a folder of loose files becomes a package. We recommend `jet init` doing the whole move, showing every edit and asking about name clashes.
decisions.gist: How should a folder of loose script files become a package?
decisions.lesson: Jet starts small: a few loose files that import each other by path. When a project grows, it becomes a package, and files in a package see each other's names directly. Growing should be one command that writes package.jet and rewrites the imports, never a pile of errors to fix by hand.
decisions.story: Ana's three-file script grows into a tool her team uses. She adds a package.jet, and every file now fails with an import error. She deletes the package.jet and keeps the scripts loose.
decisions.inWild:
$ cargo init
     Created binary (application) package
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Card c0cwk90x. This is the growing question from the D-PROJECT-FILE1 package, asked alone. The default for a package with no name stays split out to #6058.

Probes, in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/bd/probe/proj. loose/: the loose files run and print "sales up". grown/: the same files beside `name: "news"` give E0623 "`use \"./app/report\"` imports a file, but this file belongs to a package". `jet fix --all .` prints "no changes made". In loose/, `jet init --check` is E2104 "`jet init` is not built yet".

Reads with the related ballots. Under D-MANIFEST-ONE1 A the written package.jet is the one project file. D-TEST-PROFILE1 adds nothing to `jet init`.

options.name: `jet init` does the move
options.detail:
`jet init` writes package.jet, removes each path import and turns `report.headline()` into `headline()`. It prints the whole plan first; `--check` prints it and writes nothing.

If two files declare the same name, nothing is renamed silently. The plan proposes a name and a terminal asks to accept or type one. Scripts pass `--rename` or `--yes`.
options.technical: Front.jet `jet init` (E2104 today). Rewrites use the compiler's public rename API, the one the editor uses. E0623 and E0624 gain the same fix. Imports captured by a local binding, or `../..` paths outside the root, stop with the line named. Keeps D-ECO-FILEROOT1=A's fold of retired manifests.

options.name: Path imports stay legal
options.detail:
A path import inside a package stays legal, so adding package.jet changes nothing.

But a package now has two ways to reach the same name, which the one-namespace rule was made to remove.
options.technical: Retires E0623 and overrides the 2026-09-30 owner ruling (card #3862) that files of one package share one namespace.

options.name: Rewrite by hand
options.detail:
The user adds package.jet, reads each E0623 error and edits the files.

A larger project meets every broken import together, and clashing names surface only as later errors.
options.technical: Today's state: E0623 with a prose fix; `jet fix --all .` makes no changes.

comparisons.note: `cargo init` turns a folder into a package. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-init.html
`go mod init` writes go.mod; imports then use the module path. Source: https://go.dev/ref/mod#go-mod-init
Deno keeps relative imports everywhere, so nothing changes on growth. Source: https://docs.deno.com/runtime/fundamentals/modules/

recommendation.why: A makes growing a project one safe command. It shows every edit first and never renames a clash without asking.

decisions.title: A run's own temp folder is free: files inside the folder `fs.temp_dir` made need no grant
decisions.situation: Many scripts need scratch space: they make a temp folder, write a few files and read them back. Today that is a file write like any other, so a loose script stops with an authority error off a terminal, or asks on one. The folder is new, private and removed at exit, so nothing the user owns is at risk. The vote decides whether a run's own temp folder needs a grant. We recommend it is free, while deny rules still win.
decisions.gist: Should a script need permission to use the temp folder it just made for itself?
decisions.lesson: Jet scripts must be allowed to touch files. But a temp folder made with `fs.temp_dir` is brand new, private to this run and deleted when the run ends. Reading and writing inside it cannot touch anything you own, so Jet can allow it without asking.
decisions.story: Mia's script renders thumbnails into a temp folder. In CI it fails with an authority error about writing files. She adds `-A`, which also lets the script reach the network and her home folder.

Provenance. Card c0w8kkg9. Split from D-SCRIPT-DESIGNATE1 with Main's approval; that ballot covers paths the user typed. Builds on owner ruling #5949 (ask once, `-A`, basics free).

Probes, in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/bd/probe/proj. tmp.jet is the beginner script. Off a terminal it is E1803 "Application authority is undecided for `FS, FS.Read, FS.Write`". With `--allow=FS` it prints "draft". `fs.temp_dir` returns a TempDir with a `path` field today.

Reads with D-SCRIPT-DESIGNATE1 A: typed paths and the run's own temp are the two narrow grants, and both yield to deny rules.

options.name: Own temp is free
options.detail:
When `fs.temp_dir` or `fs.temp_file` makes a folder or file, the run may create, read and write inside it with no grant. The folder sits under a private root for this run and is removed at exit.

Only paths this run made are free. `--deny=FS.Write` or a package `authority.deny` still refuses them. Signatures do not change: `fs.write` still says it writes files.
options.technical: The run records each temp path it creates; the authority preflight (files8_preflight, Core/Files/Files.jet:1631-1656) allows FS.Read and FS.Write beneath a recorded path. Links leaving the folder are refused. `jet inspect rights` shows "own temp" beside each such use. D-AUTHORITY-DENYROW1=A and `--deny` (E1803) are unchanged.

options.name: A grant, as today
options.detail:
Nothing changes. A script that only uses scratch space still needs a file grant.

That grant covers every file the user owns, not just the scratch folder.
options.technical: Today's E1803 path and the `--allow` flag (owner ruling #5949).

options.name: A free `FS.Temp` effect
options.detail:
`fs.temp_dir` and new `TempDir` methods carry `FS.Temp`, which is free by default.

But the ordinary `fs.write` on a temp path still needs FS.Write, so scripts must switch to the new methods.
options.technical: Adds the leaf `FS.Temp` under the D-EFFTREE1 tree and `write`/`read` methods on TempDir (Files.jet:194). `-[!FS]>` still forbids it by subsumption.

comparisons.note: Android apps own their cache folder without permission. Source: https://developer.android.com/training/data-storage/app-specific
Sandboxed macOS apps get their own temporary directory. Source: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/foundation/filemanager/temporarydirectory

No new API or effect.

whyNot.reason: B pushes scratch-only scripts to grants that cover all user files.
C adds a second set of file methods for one folder.

decisions.title: A path the user typed for a `Path` argument may be read without a prompt; deny rules still win
decisions.situation: A loose script that reads files must be allowed to read them. Off a terminal it stops with an authority error, and on a terminal it asks once. But when the user typed the file name as the script's input, the question is already answered: they chose that file. Desktop systems treat a file picked in an open dialog the same way. The vote decides whether a path the user typed grants access to it. We recommend that a typed `Path` argument grants reading exactly that path, and an `#Output` one grants writing.
decisions.gist: Should a file path the user typed as a script argument be usable without asking again?
decisions.lesson: Jet scripts must be allowed to touch files. When you run `wc.jet --input notes.txt`, you already chose `notes.txt`. If the script declares that argument as a `Path`, Jet can let it read exactly that file and nothing else. Your own deny rules still win.
decisions.story: Bo runs `wc.jet --input notes.txt` in a CI job. It fails with an authority error about reading files, though the only file it reads is the one Bo named. He adds `-A`, which allows everything, including the network.
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Card c0w8kkg9. The private temp folder question is split out as D-SCRIPT-TEMP1, approved by Main. Builds on owner ruling #5949 (ask once, `-A`, basics free) and D-SCRIPT-CONFIRM1=A; neither is reopened.

Probes, in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/bd/probe/proj. wcp.jet is the beginner script with `input: Path`. `jet run wcp.jet -- --input notes.txt` off a terminal is E1803 "Application authority is undecided for `FS.Read`". With `--allow=FS.Read` it prints 3. `Path` is accepted as a `#CLI` field and by `fs.read` today.

Why a marker for writing, not a type. `#CLI` fields already take their CLI facts as markers: `#Doc`, `#Env` and `#Short` (Examples/features/cli/typed_entry_args.jet). `#Output` is one more of those. Core has no write-capable path type; Core/Files/Path.jet has only `Path`. A new `OutPath` type would have to be accepted by every `fs` call that takes `String | Path`, and would mean nothing outside entry arguments.

Reads with the related ballots. D-EFFTYPE-GRANT1 A has `jet add` write what a dependency may do; this ballot grants one run one path. Both keep deny rules first. With `--deny=FS.Read` the probe gives E1803 "Application authority denies `FS.Read`".

options.name: Typed paths are granted
options.detail:
After parsing, each typed `Path` argument grants reading exactly that path, or anything under it for a folder. An `#Output` path also grants writing it. Defaults grant nothing; only values the user typed do.

Deny rules always win: `--deny=FS.Read` or a package `authority.deny` still refuses the read. Every other path keeps today's ask-once rule.
options.technical: Entry decode for `#CLI` resolves each `Path` field, following links and `..`, and adds an exact FS.Read grant before `run` starts. `#Output` adds FS.Write and create on that path; `--help` marks it "(written)". An `authority.deny` entry is still a compile-time prohibition (D-AUTHORITY-DENYROW1=A), and `--deny` still wins at run time (E1803). `jet inspect rights` lists each grant with its argument. Builds on owner ruling #5949 and D-SCRIPT-CONFIRM1=A (c06jij4v).

options.name: Ask, naming the argument

options.technical: Today's E1803 and prompt, plus the argument name in the prompt text.

options.name: Grant on the launch line

The flag grants reading any file, which is wider than the one file the user meant.
options.technical: Today's E1803 path and `--allow` flag (owner ruling #5949).

comparisons.note: macOS grants sandboxed apps the files a user picks. Source: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/security/accessing-files-from-the-macos-app-sandbox
Permissions are flags; `--allow-read=notes.txt` narrows to one path but must be typed. Source: https://docs.deno.com/runtime/fundamentals/security/

Scripts work in CI without `-A`.

whyNot.reason: B still stops in CI and asks a question the user already answered.
C grants every file to read just one, which pushes users to `-A`.
