decisions.title: Whether an explicit para_map limit may exceed host parallelism
decisions.gist: When a program writes `para_map(f, limit: 32)`, should Jet run up to 32 items at once even on a machine with fewer cores?
decisions.lesson: A parallel map runs several items at the same time. The limit says how many. For waiting-heavy work such as web requests, more items in flight than cores is faster.
decisions.story: Ana fetches 100 web pages with `urls.para_map(http.get, limit: 32)`. Her laptop has 8 cores, so only 8 requests run at once, and each waits on the network. Bun keeps 32 in flight and finishes 1.46 times faster.
decisions.inWild: Bun, Node and Python's thread pools let the caller set any concurrency. Rayon caps at the core count, because it targets compute work.
decisions.detail:
spec.md:2715-2716 says the worker count never exceeds available host parallelism, so an explicit limit above the core count is silently lowered. Compute-heavy work gains nothing from more workers than cores. Waiting-heavy work, such as network calls, does.

Without a limit, nothing changes under either option.

Memory grows with the written limit under every design that keeps n items in flight; Bun keeps the same per-item state. A waiting item costs only the stack pages it touched.

options.name: The limit bounds items in flight; waiting items hold no thread
options.detail: A written `limit: n` lets up to n items be in progress at once. An item that waits on the network, a sleep, a child process or a file read parks its own small stack and frees its worker for another item. Workers never exceed the cores, and waiting items hold no thread.
options.technical: spec.md:2716 changes: workers stay bounded by host parallelism, and an explicit limit bounds items in flight. The runtime runs each item on its own stack. A host wait submits the operation to io_uring and switches to another item. Where io_uring is unavailable, network and timer waits use epoll, timerfd and pidfd, and regular-file reads go to one shared I/O helper thread. Nothing in the language changes, and the same runtime serves every tier. Chunk boundaries stay stable, so results and order are unchanged.
options.code:
pages :: urls.para_map(http.get, limit: 32)   // 32 in flight on any machine
sums :: rows.para_map(score)   // no limit: at most one worker per core

options.name: Keep the core-count cap
options.detail: The limit can only lower the worker count below the core count. Waiting-heavy work stays bounded by cores until an asynchronous I/O path exists.
options.technical: No spec change. ScriptBench w11 keeps losing to Bun on wall and CPU.
options.code: pages :: urls.para_map(http.get, limit: 32)   // 8 in flight on an 8-core machine

comparisons.note: The caller sets any concurrency.
The pool is capped at the core count.

recommendation.why: The program gets the concurrency it wrote, computing work never oversubscribes the cores, and waiting costs no threads.
gains: Network maps keep up to the written limit in flight, as Bun does.
Compute maps never run more workers than cores, so a large limit is harmless.
A waiting item holds no thread, only the stack pages it used.

whyNot.reason: B silently ignores what the program wrote and keeps waiting-heavy maps slower than peers.

recommendation.tradeoff: Running work stays within the cores; waiting work reaches the written limit.

recommendation.tradeoff: Compute within the cores; waiting up to the limit.

decisions.title: How should Jet offer both ways to take a value out of a place it writes?
decisions.situation: Both of your answers are kept. The old manual option is now the manual form, and the old call option is now the beginner form. The new A and B only decide where the calls live. This revision makes the two forms one mechanism with two spellings. The beginner calls are written with the manual form, and one rule checks both. Only one choice is left: whether the beginner calls need an import.
decisions.gist: Should swap and replace work with no import, or only after use core.mem?
decisions.lesson: A parameter marked & lends the caller's place to the function, which may change it; the caller still owns it. ^x moves a value, leaving the old place empty. swap(&a, &b) exchanges two places, and replace(&place, value) puts in a new value and returns the old one.
decisions.story: Mia is new to Jet and writes swap(&d.front, &d.back) and replace(&self.head, None). Her teammate Raj writes the same moves by hand in a hot loop. Both compile to the same moves, and neither copies a list.
decisions.inWild:
Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Expressions/Places.jet:193-199 refuses ^ on every read or write parameter at a binding (E0201).
Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Calls/Checking.jet:583-584 lets a write parameter's field move into a call whose result refills it. That path closes the value twice when the call stops (probe stop_refill.jet).
Compiler/JetCli/Source/Cli/AdaptiveTable.jet:103-107 already refills before anything that may stop, by hand, on a local.
Docs/spec/spec.md:1534-1535: Cell.replace(value) returns the old value, the spelling replace follows.
Rust: std::mem::swap, std::mem::replace, Option::take; the take_mut crate aborts the process on a panic inside the gap.
decisions.detail:
WHAT IS ALREADY RATIFIED

The mark ^place is the exact move, and any later use of the moved place is E0121. The same mark on borrowed storage is E0201 (D-COPY-DEFAULT1 A). &place is the exclusive write window, and the caller keeps ownership (D-SHAPE-PLACE1 A). The mark sits on the place, as in swap(&d.front, &d.back) and &s.pop_all() (D-CAP-RECEIVER1 D).

A stop runs the cleanup of every frame it leaves (D-FAIL-EXIT1). A function can deny Panic with -[!Panic]> (D-NOPANIC1 D). A task's join can report that the task stopped, so code after the group still runs (D-TASK-WINDOW1 A).

```jet
struct Deque {
    front: [Int]
    back: [Int]
}

fn flip(d: &Deque) {
    t :: d.front.copy()      // today: a copy, because ^d.front is E0201
    d.front = d.back.copy()
    d.back = t
}

fn run() {
    d := Deque{front: [1], back: [2, 3]}
    flip(&d)
    print(d.front.len())
}
```

THE OWNER'S ANSWER

Both forms are valid. The call is the beginner form, and the move and refill written out is the manual form.

ONE MECHANISM, TWO SPELLINGS

core.mem gains swap(&a, &b) and replace(&place, value), which returns the old value. Both are ordinary Jet functions whose bodies use the manual form, so a call and the hand-written moves are the same moves. The compiler checks one rule, for both.

```jet
// In Core (core.mem): the beginner calls are written with the manual form.
fn swap<T>(a: &T, b: &T) -[!Panic]> {
    t :: ^a
    a = ^b
    b = ^t
}

fn replace<T>(place: &T, value: ^T) -[!Panic]> T {
    old :: ^place
    place = ^value
    old
}
```

THE RULE FOR THE MANUAL FORM

^ on a & parameter, a field below one, or a named write window opens a gap. The function must put a value back before anything can see the gap. Inside the gap, a read of the place is E0121, as today.

A return, break, next, ? or ?? exit inside the gap is E0201 at the exit, with a note at the move. Both arms of an if or match must refill, or neither. A loop body closes its own gap in the same pass.

STOPS INSIDE THE GAP

A stop is a panic, a trap, or a cancellation at a wait. If one comes while the moved value is still whole in a local, the stop path moves it back first. Then the cleanup and any defer run, so the caller finds a whole value.

If the moved value is no longer whole in a local when something can stop, nothing is left to put back. That is E0201 at that point, as at a call that takes the value with ^. The fix offers two ways out. One is to put a stand-in first, as in old :: replace(&self.conn, .Idle). The other is to mark the callee -[!Panic]> with no wait in it.

WHAT EACH FORM GUARANTEES

The call never leaves a place empty. The manual form copies nothing, and the compiler proves every exit is refilled. After a stop, the caller always holds a whole value.

THE BEGINNER FORM IS THE DEFAULT

The tour and jet explain E0201 teach the calls first. When the manual form is refused, the fix rewrites it to swap or replace. The manual form needs no opt-in line. The ^ mark is the explicit opt-in, at the exact place, as D-COPY-DEFAULT1 defines it. A gate would refuse a safe program, and the owner's #6066 direction says only #Unsafe opts out.

PLACES THAT MIGHT OVERLAP

swap needs two places that cannot be one place. Two fields, two locals, or two fixed list positions such as rows[0] and rows[1] work today. The same place twice, two list positions picked at run time, or two map keys are E0204.

The way out is the list's or map's own swap, which this ballot adds: &rows.swap(i, j) and &m.swap(a, b). They check at run time, and the same position twice does nothing. The E0204 fix writes that call. Lists have no swap method today (E0311).

PINNED PLACES

While a pin into node is live, swap(&node, &other) is E0220, and the fix says to go through the pin. A Pin<Node> is not a Node, so swap(&pinned, &other) is E0112. Fields still swap through a pin, as in swap(&pinned.payload, &other.payload), because the address stays put. The manual form ^node beside a live pin stays E0219. The rule changes none of these.

WHY NOT METHODS

A value method a.swap(&b) would have to exist on every type. A replace method would clash with the replace that String, Regex, LocalDate and Cell already have. Free functions keep one meaning per name.

A BUG THIS RULE FIXES

Today self.r = next(^self.r) on &self is accepted. If next stops, the value is closed twice (probe stop_refill.jet prints "close a" twice on O0 and O1; #6066 c10). The gap rule refuses it unless next cannot stop. A repo scan finds 8 sites of that shape to check.

COST

The normal path is unchanged: a call is the same moves, and at O0 it is one call. Only stop paths inside a gap gain a move back. Existing programs keep compiling, except the 8 sites above if their callee can stop.

THE QUESTION

Should the beginner calls work with no import, as swap and replace, or only after use core.mem, as mem.swap and mem.replace?

options.name: swap and replace need no import
options.detail: Both forms are valid. The beginner calls swap(&a, &b) and replace(&place, value) are ambient, with no import. They live in core.mem and the prelude names them, as it names read_file and channel. A user function named swap or replace still wins, so existing code keeps compiling.
options.technical:
core.mem gains swap<T> and replace<T>, both -[!Panic]>, with the manual form as their bodies. The prelude adds pub use core.mem.[swap, replace], two names on the closed list of D-PRELUDE-LAW1. #NoPrelude files write mem.swap after use core.mem. List and Map gain swap(i, j) and swap(a, b) as Core methods.

Sema tracks each gap in the moved-place state behind E0121. An exit inside a gap is E0201, and so is handing the value to a call that can stop. Each E0201 fix offers swap or replace. IR gives every stop path inside a gap a move back from the local that holds the value.

options.name: swap and replace come from use core.mem
options.detail: Both forms are valid, with the same rule and the same guarantees as A. The beginner calls are written mem.swap and mem.replace after use core.mem. The prelude does not change. The E0201 fix adds the import line when it is missing.
options.technical: As A, without the prelude alias. core.mem is also the module behind the low-level rung, so the import puts a beginner one line from Ptr and the allocators. Ptr and the allocators still need #Unsafe for their operations (E3101).

recommendation.why: A gives the beginner form with no ceremony, which makes it the easy default. One rule checks both forms, because the calls are written with the manual form. It fixes today's double close too.
gains: A beginner swaps or takes with one call and no import, and never sees an empty place.
An expert writes the moves by hand with no copy, and the compiler proves every exit is refilled.
A stop inside a gap leaves the caller a whole value, which also fixes today's double close.

losses.loss: Two names join the ambient prelude.
losses.mitigation: A user function with the same name wins, so no existing program breaks. In such a file the E0201 fix writes mem.swap.

losses.loss: Two list positions picked at run time cannot both go to swap, because they might be one place (E0204).
losses.mitigation: &rows.swap(i, j) checks at run time and does nothing when i equals j. The E0204 fix writes it.

losses.loss: By hand, the moved value cannot go to a call that can stop while the place is empty.
losses.mitigation: This cannot be removed: the stop runs cleanup that can see the place, and nothing is left to put back. The fix writes a stand-in with replace, or the callee denies Panic.

whyNot.reason: B makes the beginner form need an import from the low-level memory module, which works against it being the default.

recommendation.tradeoff: Two ambient names, in exchange for a beginner form with no import beside an expert form with no copy.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude. Adversarial model family: Claude. Fresh agent: Main, reviewing Prep's draft, because the owner caps agents at three. Findings were E0204 for two elements of one list, unprobed pinned places, a stale probe compiler and the old-to-new option mapping, and all are fixed.

surface.gist: Should swap and replace work with no import, or only after use core.mem?
surface.lesson: & lends a place to a function. ^ moves a value out. Both forms are now valid: a call, or the moves written out.

current.note: Today the value must be copied.

wild.note: Rust offers only the calls, because a &mut place may never be empty.

options.name: swap and replace need no import
options.gist: The calls are ambient; the manual form is valid beside them.
gains: No import for the beginner form.
losses: Two new ambient names.

options.name: swap and replace come from use core.mem
options.gist: The calls need use core.mem; the manual form is valid beside them.
gains: The prelude does not change.
losses: The beginner form needs an import.

recommendation.why: The beginner form needs no ceremony, and one rule checks both forms.
gains: One call, no import, never an empty place.
The manual form copies nothing.

losses.loss: Two new ambient names.
losses.mitigation: A user function with the same name still wins.

losses.loss: By hand, no call that can stop may take the moved value.
losses.mitigation: The fix writes a stand-in with replace.

losses.loss: Two run-time list positions cannot both go to swap.
losses.mitigation: The list's own swap(i, j) checks at run time.

whyNot.reason: An import for the beginner form.

recommendation.tradeoff: Two ambient names for an import-free beginner form.

decisions.title: Can tasks in a task group write separate parts of one list?
decisions.situation: A task.group waits for all of its tasks before its block ends. Today a task in the group cannot capture a write window into a local list, even when the two windows do not overlap. So splitting work across tasks means copying each half out and writing the results back. The program is safe when the windows do not overlap and the group ends before the list does. The vote decides whether such tasks may write their window directly.
decisions.gist: May each task in a group write its own, separate part of a list the block owns?
decisions.lesson: &v.split_write(mid) gives two write windows, left and right, that cannot overlap. task { … } starts work that the enclosing task.group joins before its block ends. Today a task may only capture owned values, so a window is refused with E0631.
decisions.story: Lee splits a pixel buffer in two and wants one task to brighten each half in place. Today Jet makes him copy both halves into owned lists, run the tasks, and copy the results back.
decisions.inWild:
Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Expressions/Lambdas.jet:2171-2184 refuses a view capture that is a write window or cannot be materialized (E0631).
Compiler/JetIR/Source/BuildExpr.jet:6297-6300 already holds a written alias by address so a scoped task's writes land on the owner.
Rust: std::thread::scope with split_at_mut gives each thread one &mut half.
decisions.detail:
WHAT IS ALREADY RATIFIED

One crossing prover answers every concurrent boundary, and each refusal names what cannot cross, the boundary and the fix. A task.group joins every task before its block ends. split_write returns two non-overlapping write windows.

```jet
task.group g {
    { left: a, right: b } :: &v.split_write(2) ?? panic("split")
    left :: task { a[0] = a[0] + 1 }   // today: E0631
    right :: task { b[0] = b[0] + 1 }
    ^left.join() ?? panic("left")
    ^right.join() ?? panic("right")
}
```

THE QUESTION

Should a task in a group be allowed to capture a write window, or a read view, whose owner outlives the group?

options.name: Tasks in a group may write windows into a list that outlives the group
options.detail: A task inside a task.group may capture a read view or a write window when the owner of the storage lives longer than the group. Two live tasks may not hold overlapping windows where either writes, and nothing outside the tasks may touch the owner until the group ends. The element type must still be sendable. Callers do not change.
options.technical: The crossing prover admits a view or window capture into a task whose innermost group scope ends inside the owner's scope. The capture becomes a loan held until the group's join, so the existing loan-conflict checks (E0204, E0212) refuse a second overlapping write window and any use of the owner inside the group. IR holds the window by address, as it already does for written aliases.

options.name: Tasks keep taking owned values
options.detail: No change. A task works on an owned copy and returns its result, which the block writes back.
options.technical: No change.

recommendation.why: A accepts a safe and common parallel pattern without copies, and the existing loan checks keep overlapping writes out. The group's join is what makes it safe, and the group is already required.
gains: Parallel in-place work on one buffer, with no copy in or out.
No new syntax; split_write and task.group already exist.

losses.loss: The crossing prover gains a scoped case to reason about.
losses.mitigation: The case is one rule: the group ends inside the owner's scope; everything else reuses loan checks.

whyNot.reason: B copies both halves in and out, for a program that is already safe.

recommendation.tradeoff: One scoped rule in the prover, for zero-copy parallel writes.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude. Adversarial model family: Claude. Fresh agent: Main (separate from the author, Prep). Renamed A: it is the list storage, not the window, that outlives the group. Checked that overlapping writes and outside access during the group stay refused.

surface.gist: May each task in a group write its own, separate part of a list the block owns?
surface.lesson: split_write gives two windows that cannot overlap. A task.group joins its tasks before the block ends.

current.note: Today a task must take owned copies.
current.code: left :: task ^a { bumped(a) }

wild.note: Scoped threads may borrow disjoint halves.

options.name: Tasks in a group may write windows into a list that outlives the group
options.gist: Each task writes its own window in place.
gains: No copies.
losses: One more prover case.

proposed.code:
left :: task { a[0] = a[0] + 1 }
right :: task { b[0] = b[0] + 1 }

options.name: Tasks keep taking owned values
options.gist: Copy out, compute, write back.
gains: Nothing new.
losses: Two copies per half.

proposed.code: left :: task ^a { bumped(a) }

recommendation.why: Safe parallel writes without copies; loan checks keep windows apart.
gains: Zero-copy parallel work.

losses.loss: One more prover case.
losses.mitigation: It reuses loan checks.

whyNot.reason: Copies a safe program's data twice.

recommendation.tradeoff: One scoped rule for zero-copy parallel writes.

decisions.title: Can a function return a write window onto one map value?
decisions.situation: A function can already return a write window onto one list element, written &lib.books[i..i], and the caller edits it through the window. There is no such window onto one map value, so a helper that finds or creates a map entry and hands it back for editing cannot be written. The vote decides whether &map[key] can be returned as a one-value write window.
decisions.gist: May &map[key] be returned as a write window, like &list[i..i]?
decisions.lesson: ViewMut<T> is a write window over values of type T in some owner. &books[i..i] is a window over one Book. from map in the result type names the owner the window points into. While the window is live, the owner cannot change shape.
decisions.story: Sam keeps groups of ids in a map and wants slot(&groups, key) to return the list for a key so callers can push into it. Today the return is refused, so every caller repeats the lookup.
decisions.detail:
WHAT IS ALREADY RATIFIED

A returned view uses View or ViewMut with public provenance and no lifetime syntax, and there is no second view mechanism. A one-element list window is written i..i. A live window blocks any change to its owner's shape (E0212).

```jet
fn edit_at(lib: &Library, i: Int) -> ViewMut<Book> { &lib.books[i..i] }

fn run() {
    dune :: edit_at(&lib, 0)
    dune[0].pages += 10
}
```

THE QUESTION

Should &map[key] at a ViewMut<V> destination be a one-value window onto that map entry?

options.name: &map[key] is a one-value window
options.detail: Where a ViewMut<V> is expected, &map[key] is a window over that one map value, used as w[0] like a one-element list window. A missing key fails the same way map[key] does. While the window is live the map cannot gain or lose entries.
options.technical: Sema types &map[key] at a ViewMut<V> destination as a window with provenance on the map, and records the loan that the list window records, so E0212 covers adds and removes. IR builds the window header from the entry's value address with length 1, the same shape as ir_list_window.

options.name: No map windows; pass the map and the key
options.detail: No change. A helper takes the map and the key and does the edit itself.
options.technical: No change.

recommendation.why: A extends the ratified window to the one owner that lacks it, with the same spelling and the same loan rule, so entry-style helpers can be written.
gains: Find-or-create helpers that hand back an editable value.
One window rule for lists and maps.

losses.loss: A map entry window is written w[0], like a list window.
losses.mitigation: It is the same rule as &list[i..i], which the example already teaches.

whyNot.reason: B forces every edit into the helper, so callers cannot keep a handle to the value.

recommendation.tradeoff: One more owner kind for windows, for entry-style helpers.

decisions.title: Can += and the other compound updates target a list or map slot?
decisions.situation: Today counts[key] += 1 and xs[0] += 1 are refused with E0164, while counts[key] = counts[key] + 1 and xs[0] = xs[0] + 1 are accepted and mean the same thing. The refusal was meant to stop a read of a missing map key, but the long form does that same read. The vote decides whether compound updates may target an indexed slot.
decisions.gist: Should xs[i] += 1 and counts[key] += 1 be allowed, meaning the same as the long form?
decisions.lesson: x += 1 means x = x + 1. Reading map[key] stops the program when the key is missing, and reading xs[i] stops it when i is out of range. map.get(key) ?? 0 reads a key that may be missing without stopping.
decisions.story: Ana counts words with counts[w] += 1 and gets E0164, then writes counts[w] = counts[w] + 1, which compiles and fails the same way on a missing key.
decisions.inWild:
Docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:259-265 S17: direct indexed compound updates remain E0164 (copy, update, then store).
prep/c6066/bal/idx_a.jet today: E0164 at 4:11 and 5:7; prep/c6066/bal/idx_c.jet (long form) runs: 2, 2.
Rust, Python, Swift and C# accept v[i] += 1 and m[k] += 1.
decisions.detail:
WHAT IS ALREADY RATIFIED

Compound updates work on mutable names, & parameters and fields, including fields reached through list elements. Direct indexed compound updates are E0164. An indexed read stops on a missing map key or an out-of-range index.

```jet
counts := [String: Int]{"a": 1}
counts["a"] = counts["a"] + 1   // accepted today
counts["a"] += 1                 // E0164 today
```

THE QUESTION

Should a compound update on an indexed slot be allowed, with the meaning of the long form?

options.name: Allow it on lists and maps
options.detail: xs[i] op= v and map[key] op= v mean xs[i] = xs[i] op v and map[key] = map[key] op v, with one lookup. They stop where the long form stops. E0164 is retired.
options.technical: Sema checks the slot as a write place of the indexed collection and lowers to one element address, then a load, the operator and a store. The missing-key and out-of-range stops are the ones the indexed read already has.

options.name: Allow it on lists only
options.detail: xs[i] op= v is allowed. A map slot keeps E0164, so a count that may start missing is written with get(key) ?? 0.
options.technical: As A for lists. E0164 stays for map slots, with its total-update fix.

options.name: Keep E0164
options.detail: No change. Indexed slots use the long form.
options.technical: No change.

recommendation.why: The refusal does not prevent the stop it was meant to prevent, because the long form it suggests does the same read. A removes a rule that only costs keystrokes and matches every mainstream language.
gains: The shortest form works on every place.
One lookup instead of two.

losses.loss: counts[w] += 1 on a missing key stops at run time.
losses.mitigation: The long form already does; map.get(w) ?? 0 remains the total form, and a lint can suggest it.

whyNot.reason: B keeps a map rule that the accepted long form already bypasses.
C refuses a safe program for no safety gain.

recommendation.tradeoff: A run-time stop on a missing key, the same as the long form, for the short form everywhere.

decisions.title: Ask whether a Pool id still names a live entry: pool.has(id)
decisions.situation: A Pool is Jet's box for game objects such as monsters. Adding a monster gives you an id, a small ticket for its spot in the box. A monster can remember its target by id. When the target dies and is removed, reading through that old id stops the program, and today there is no way to ask first. We recommend pool.has(id): it answers yes or no, copies nothing, and the read after it still checks, so an old id can never reach the wrong monster.
decisions.gist: Should Pool answer whether an id still names a live entry?
decisions.lesson: An id holds a spot number and a count. Removing an entry bumps the spot's count, so an old id never reaches a new monster that reuses the spot. Reading through an old id stops the program. A yes-or-no check lets a chasing monster forget a dead target instead.
decisions.story: Ana's imp chases a target it holds by id. Between two game ticks the target dies and is removed. On the next tick the imp must hit the target if it still exists, or else forget it. Every option runs the same program and prints 90, then true. No option may hit a new monster that took over the old spot.
decisions.inWild:
Rust's slotmap crate, a widely used generational arena, offers contains_key(id) -> bool beside indexing. Source: https://docs.rs/slotmap/latest/slotmap/struct.SlotMap.html#method.contains_key

In C the same check is written by hand: the spot number is in range and the spot's count matches the id's count.
decisions.detail:
RATIFIED RULES

Docs/spec/spec.md:1569-1576 and Docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:2848-2856 (D-POOLID-API1) give Pool add, indexing, ids and remove. Ids are copyable and comparable. Indexing a stale id stops the program; remove returns an optional value. add, remove and pool[id] = v need a writable pool: a := binding or a & parameter. D-HAS-VERB1=A makes has the membership word for lists, sets and map keys. 

D-FNVAL-WRITE1=A lets a function type carry & and ^ input marks, which makes option B's write callback legal. D-WRITE-TAKE1=A gives replace(&place, value) and swap on any place, including pool[id].

WHAT THE CODE DOES TODAY

Compiler/JetIR/Source/BuildPools.jet:111-129 (ir_pool_find) computes one live bit: the spot number is below the pool length and the spot's count equals the id's count. remove (:133-155) and indexing (:192-217) both use that bit. Indexing stops with 'this ID no longer refers to a live value — its pool slot was removed' (:207). Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Calls/SharedOwner.jet:378-429 checks add, remove and ids; has is unknown, E0102.

Probes, rechecked on 2559996f at O0 and O2: opus_pool_today prints 60, then stops with E3001 after removal. opus_pool_has_today fails with E0102. opus_pool_reuse shows a stale id still stops after a new entry takes the spot, and removing it again returns None. opus_pool_shape runs every line of option A except has and prints 90, then true.

HOW A'S DOWNSIDES ARE DESIGNED AWAY

The earlier draft listed two losses for A and a third caveat. Each now has a concrete answer.

1. Two checks (has, then index). has returns the same live bit that indexing computes, so the extra cost is one length compare and one count compare on a spot just read. It never reads or copies the monster. Code that already knows an id is live indexes directly.

2. The answer could go stale before the read. Only code that holds the pool for writing can remove an entry (spec.md:1574-1576). So between has and the read, only code written on that path can remove it. If it does, the read still checks and stops. It never reaches a newer monster in the same spot.

3. Ids carry no pool identity. In review61_edges an id from one pool read 300 from another. This is true of indexing and remove today and of every option. It is shared, not a cost of A. A pool stamp in ids would fix it for all options and needs its own card.

WHY B CHANGED

The earlier B returned a copy. A copy cannot write the target back, costs a full copy and does not work for entries that cannot be copied. With D-FNVAL-WRITE1=A, the honest alternative is a write callback, which removes A's two-step gap. So B is now that design.

KNOWN DEFECTS, NOT VOTES

review61_id_eq fails with E0312 even for id == id, against the comparable-id rule; option C needs it fixed. review61_edges removes an entry through a read-only Pool parameter, against spec E0202. That defect weakens A's staleness argument until fixed and needs a defect card whatever the vote.

STALE IDS AND REUSE

has(id) is false exactly when remove(id) would return None: spot out of range or count mismatch. Reusing a spot never makes an old id live again. The count is a 64-bit number, so wraparound needs 2^63 removals of one spot.

BEGINNER AND EXPERT

Beginners call has right before indexing. Experts who know an id is live index directly and keep the safety check. Proposed examples use the ratified name-first declaration spelling (D-DECL-BINDING1=B); probes use the current spelling.

options.name: pool.has(id) -> Bool
options.detail: Ask whether the pool still has a live entry for this id. Read and write the entry with pool[id], as today. The read still checks, so a stale answer stops the program and never reaches the wrong monster.
options.technical: has returns the live bit that indexing already computes: spot in range and matching count. It is false exactly when remove(id) would return None. It neither reads nor copies the entry. Sema gains one Pool method beside add, remove and ids; the lowering reuses ir_pool_find.

options.name: pool.edit(id, action) -> Bool
options.detail: Run an action on the entry if it is live, and return whether it ran. Check and write happen in one step. While the action runs, the pool is busy, so the action cannot touch other monsters in it.
options.technical: action has type fn(&T), allowed by D-FNVAL-WRITE1=A. edit checks once, lends the entry to the action and returns true, or returns false for a stale id. The pool is borrowed for writing during the call, so a lambda that also uses the pool is refused. It adds a second way to write an entry beside indexing.

options.name: No new API: search pool.ids()
options.detail: Take a fresh list of live ids and compare the target with each one. Pool gets no new method.
options.technical: Uses only ratified operations. It needs id == id, which fails today with E0312; that bug fix needs no vote. Each check builds a list and scans it, so a tick with many chasers does work that grows with chasers times entries.

comparisons.note: slotmap pairs a yes-or-no check with indexing, and indexing a removed key panics. Source: https://docs.rs/slotmap/latest/slotmap/struct.SlotMap.html
The same check written by hand over a spot table.

recommendation.why: A asks one yes-or-no question with the word maps and sets already use. It copies nothing, keeps pool[id] as the one way to read and write, and the read still checks, so the worst case is a clear stop.
gains: A dead target is forgotten instead of stopping the game.
No copy, no callback, no new way to write.
The same has word as maps and sets.

losses.loss: The check and the read are two steps.
losses.mitigation: Only code you write between them can remove the entry. If it does, the read stops clearly, never reaching the wrong monster.

losses.loss: has and the read both check the id.
losses.mitigation: The second check is two number compares on the spot just read. Code that knows an id is live indexes directly.

whyNot.reason: B closes the two-step gap, but the action cannot touch other monsters and every write needs a callback.
C needs no new method, but every check builds and scans a list of all monsters each tick.

recommendation.tradeoff: A adds a small check and keeps one way to read and write. B joins check and write but locks the pool inside a callback. C adds nothing but scans.

decisions.title: Preserve write and move parameters in stored function types
decisions.situation: A function value is a function kept in a variable or table, like the action in each Doom monster state. Today a stored function may only read its inputs. A function that changes its input, such as chase spending a monster tic, cannot be stored. So a Doom-style action table cannot hold its actions directly. Programs must return a changed copy of the monster, or store an enum and switch on it. You are deciding whether stored functions may keep write and move inputs, which changes an earlier ruling. We recommend A: a function type uses the same input marks as a declaration.
decisions.gist: May a stored function change or take over its input, as a directly called function can?
decisions.lesson: A function value lets a table pick which code runs. A plain input is read-only: it is lent, not copied. An input marked & is lent so the function can change it in place. An input marked ^ is handed over for good.
decisions.story: Ana has a monster table with two states, Look and Chase, each holding an action. Look heals the monster by 1, and Chase spends one tic. Three steps from state 0 must print 62 7 1. Every option runs this same program. It is a small model of the Doom table, not a line-for-line port.
decisions.inWild: C stores a function pointer taking a monster pointer. Rust stores fn(&mut Mobj), which preserves exclusive write access in the pointer's type. These are comparisons of parameter passing, not claims that Jet has C's pointer layout or Rust's callable representation.
decisions.detail:
RATIFIED RULES

S47 in syntax-decisions.md:467-483, with spec.md:881-887 and 927-930, governs function values; D-MEM-PARAM1 defines parameter marks. The spec records D-CALLVALUE1=B for .call; Tower ratifies D-LAMBDA-SHAPE1=C and D-DECL-BINDING1=B. A and D amend S47 on purpose. They do not treat the current rejection as a bug.

WHAT CHANGES IN S47

S47 has three parts. Part 1: fn(T1, T2) -> R, where an unmarked parameter is read-only. Every option keeps it. Part 2: a named function becomes a value only when every parameter is read-only. One with & or ^ stays direct-call-only, and a callback that must change a value returns the new value instead. Part 3: capture rules, closure copying and the invocation lock. Every option keeps it.

A replaces part 2. Function types may mark parameters with & or ^, and a function becomes a value when its marks match the type. Returning a new value becomes one choice, not the rule. D replaces part 2 for & only; a function with a ^ parameter stays direct-call-only. B and C leave S47 unchanged. Under A or D, spec.md:881-887 and 927-930 and the syntax-surface.jet:444-446 comment change too.

CHECKED TODAY

Written against 0ccdff27 and rechecked on 2559996f at O0 and O2. opus_fnval_return and opus_fnval_enum each print 62 7 1. opus_fnval_ref fails with E0003 at fn(&Mobj), and opus_fnval_move fails with E0003 at fn(^Mobj). review61_return_read shows that returning an unmarked m unchanged is E0120; m.copy() works. Parser/Types.jet:424-470 parses parameter types without marks.

DEFECTS FOUND, NOT VOTES

opus_fnval_coerce stores chase, which takes &Mobj, in a fn(Mobj) slot. Sema accepts it, then the backend fails with an internal compiler error at O0 and O2. S47 requires a user diagnostic there. That needs a defect card whatever the vote. Lambdas also cannot spell a marked parameter today: (m: &Mobj) -> is E0003 in opus_lambda_write.

THE PROPOSAL

A accepts fn(&T) and fn(^T), mixed with unmarked parameters. The requirement survives assignment, fields, lists, generics and returned function values. A function needing & never fits fn(T). A move slot consumes its argument as a direct call does; using it afterward is an ownership error. D permits only the & part. Effects, labels, parameter zones and returned-view contracts remain obligations.

LAMBDAS

Under A and D a lambda takes marks like a named function: (m: &Mobj) -> { m.tics -= 1 }. Where the slot fixes the type, m -> { m.tics -= 1 } takes its mark from the slot. The caller still writes .call(&m), so no write happens without the caller mark.

ALIASING

A stored call must enforce the same exclusivity as a direct call. Two write arguments must not overlap, including paths through Pool ids or shared links. Known overlap is rejected; uncertain linked overlap follows the D-MEMREF-EXCL1=A runtime checks. A captured write path that overlaps an explicit argument is a conflict too. A function value cannot erase those checks.

CAPTURES

Passing &m lasts for the call; it does not authorize storing a writer to m in an escaping closure. The S47 capture ownership and lifetime checks still apply. Mutable closure environments keep the S47 invocation lock. That lock protects the environment, not explicit arguments or another closure captures. Move parameters transfer arguments on each call; they do not make every function value a one-shot callable.

BEGINNER AND EXPERT

Beginners keep plain parameters until they need to change an input. A stored writer uses the same & at declaration, type and call. Experts can pass ownership with ^ under A. No action-table speedup, unchanged call layout or allocation saving has been measured. The proposal avoids rebuilding Mobj in source, not every cost of function values.

EXAMPLES AND I8

Full options use ratified name-first bindings, which 2559996f does not build yet. B and C were run after translating only declaration heads to the current spelling. A and D reuse parameter marks and the existing .call mechanism; they add no special action-table or mutable-callback type. Changing S47 needs this explicit owner amendment.

options.name: Function types preserve both & and ^ parameters
options.detail: A function type may mark inputs with & (write) or ^ (move), the same marks a declaration uses. A function or lambda fits only when its marks match. Calls write the same mark: .call(&m). Read-only types and calls do not change.
options.technical: Access mode is part of the callable contract at every storage boundary. Reuse direct-call ownership checks and preserve effects, labels, zones and view provenance. Do not assume that the existing call representation already carries addresses correctly: lowering must implement marked arguments without copying the lent T.

options.name: Keep S47: return the updated monster
options.detail: Actions read the original and return an owned replacement. The caller assigns the result. This is useful when actions are deliberately value transformations, not just a workaround.
options.technical: Read access does not copy the input. Each call builds a new Mobj, and the caller assigns it back. Whether the optimizer removes that work is unmeasured. Forgetting to assign the result drops the update.

options.name: Keep S47: store an enum and call actions directly
options.detail: The table stores an Action case. One dispatcher makes direct calls with &. It is a good fit when the application controls a fixed set of actions.
options.technical: No replacement Mobj is required. The enum and dispatcher must be edited when an action is added; a new module cannot register an arbitrary function without changing that set. This can make the action list easy to audit. Dispatch speed is unmeasured and may be optimized differently from an indirect call.

options.name: Add write parameters only: fn(&T)
options.detail: Permit fn(&T), but keep functions with move parameters direct-call-only. This solves the action-table example with a smaller amendment. It does not authorize fn(^T).
options.technical: Write-argument alias and capture checks are exactly those required by A. Keeping ^ out reduces this ballot's ownership-transfer scope, but leaves function values unable to preserve one existing parameter mode. It creates no separate writer-callback mechanism.

comparisons.note: A small state-table model changes the monster through a function pointer; not a quotation from Doom.
The pointer type preserves exclusive write access to the argument.

recommendation.why: A uses one rule: a function type carries the same input marks as a declaration. There is no second kind of callback and no exception to explain. D also fixes this program, but keeps move inputs as a special case that stays direct-call-only.
gains: In-place actions without reconstructing Mobj.
Write and move obligations survive storage.
One set of parameter access rules.

losses.loss: This reverses part of an earlier ratified ruling on function types and adds ownership checks at stored calls.
losses.mitigation: Approve the amendment explicitly; require overlapping-argument, capture, move-after-call and nested-storage proofs before implementation is accepted.

losses.loss: The vote includes move callbacks beyond this monster example.
losses.mitigation: D is an explicit write-only choice if the owner wants the narrower scope.

whyNot.reason: A fair design when actions really are transformations. For an in-place edit, every action must rebuild the whole monster, and forgetting to assign the result loses the change.
A strong choice for a closed game. It does not allow independently supplied action functions without editing the dispatcher.
Solves the demonstrated need with less scope, but keeps one parameter mode unavailable in function values, an exception users must learn.

recommendation.tradeoff: A preserves all access modes; D adds only writing; B and C keep the current callable restriction and change application design.

surface.lesson: A plain input is lent read-only; it is not copied. A stored writer must keep the same exclusive access a direct call has, including against captured values. This vote changes an earlier ruling; it is not a bug fix.

current.note: This value-returning pattern runs today. Returning the unmarked m itself is E0120, so actions rebuild or copy it.

wild.note: A state can hold an action that changes its argument.

options.name: Preserve & and ^ in function types
options.gist: Use the existing parameter modes through stored calls too.
gains: In-place actions.
Ownership transfer is expressible too.
losses: Changes an earlier ruling for write and move inputs.

options.name: Return the changed monster
options.gist: Keep read parameters; apply an owned replacement.
gains: No new callable rules.
Useful value-transform design.
losses: Must construct or copy a replacement.
Caller must apply the returned value.

options.name: Store an enum; dispatch direct calls
options.gist: Keep a closed, auditable action list.
gains: No replacement record.
No callable language change.
losses: Adding an action edits the enum and dispatcher.

options.name: Add only fn(&T)
options.gist: Solve stored writers now; keep moves direct-call-only.
gains: Same in-place chase.
Smaller amendment than A.
losses: Stored functions still cannot take ownership.

recommendation.why: Preserve the existing parameter modes in the existing function-value mechanism. Choose D instead if this vote should authorize only the demonstrated writer case.
gains: One access contract survives storage.

losses.loss: More scope than this example needs.
losses.mitigation: The write-only alternative is explicit; no call-layout or speed claim is assumed.

whyNot.reason: Good for transformations, less direct for an in-place update.
Good for a closed action set, not arbitrary supplied functions.
Smaller, but leaves ownership-taking callbacks unavailable.

recommendation.tradeoff: A is the full access contract; D is the narrower writer-only amendment.

decisions.title: How a test asks to be rerun with its tasks taking turns differently each time
decisions.situation: Some bugs only happen when two tasks take turns in one unlucky order. For example, both tasks read a counter before either writes it back, so one increase is lost. Today jet test runs such a test once, so it passes almost every time and the bug ships. This vote picks how a test asks to be rerun many times, with the tasks taking turns differently each time. We recommend writing reruns: 100 on the test line.
decisions.gist: How should a test ask to be rerun many times, with its tasks taking turns differently each time?
decisions.lesson: When two tasks run at once, their steps can interleave in many orders. A bug may appear in only one order. Rerunning the test many times, in a different order each time, finds it. Every rerun must pass, and Jet never retries a failure. Each order has a number, so a failing order can be replayed exactly.
decisions.story: Priya writes a counter that two tasks increase. Her test passes every time on her laptop. In production one increase is lost once a week, and nobody can make it happen again. She wants jet test to find the bad order for her and print a command that replays it.
decisions.inWild:
Shuttle (Rust) reruns a test body 100 times in random task orders, in its README example: shuttle::check_random(|| { ... }, 100). Source: https://github.com/awslabs/shuttle

Loom (Rust) reruns a test in every possible task order: loom::model(|| { ... }). Source: https://github.com/tokio-rs/loom
decisions.detail:
WHAT CHANGED FROM THE LAST DRAFT

The word is now reruns, as you suggested, and the ballot is rewritten in plain words. Schedules named the machinery, not what you see. Following your rule that every flag is also a setting, the count can also be set in a test profile and in fn test.

TODAY

A test that starts two tasks runs once, in whatever order the machine picks. Jet already records task order so a run can be replayed (D-REPLAY-ORDER1=A). That recorder must move into the Jet runtime under every option.

Card #6012 asks for: a rerun count, a report per order, two planted bugs found within the guide's count, and replay of a failing order three times in a row.

PRECEDENTS

- expected_fail: true is already an argument on the #Test line (D-TEST-XFAIL1=A).
- Counts and seeds are plain whole numbers (D-TEST-COUNT1=A).
- jet test already takes --seed=<n> (Docs/spec/reference/cli.md:215).

WHY THE WORD RERUNS

Some tools use rerun to mean trying a failed test again until it passes, such as pytest-rerunfailures. That hides bugs. Jet has no such retry: here every rerun must pass, and the report says so. B and C use the same word, so the vote is only about where it is written.

HOW A'S DOWNSIDES ARE DESIGNED AWAY

1. Time. Reruns are independent, so they run side by side on the profile's workers. Sleeps and timers use simulated time during reruns. A small test stops after its few possible orders. A passing test whose inputs did not change is reused from the test cache (D-TEST-READS1=A).

2. Missing a bad order by chance. A small test is rerun in every possible order, so its bug cannot slip through. A large test samples orders, and a deep run raises the count.

3. A hidden default. The count is always written, as D-TEST-COUNT1 asks of counts. The guide's first example writes reruns: 100, the same number as Shuttle's README.

EDGE CASES

- A test that never starts a second task runs once and says so: 1 run (no tasks take turns).
- expected_fail: true with reruns: expects some rerun to fail. If all pass, that is an unexpected pass.
- A property test, which already runs many generated inputs, cannot also take reruns:. The error's fix moves the task part into a plain #Test, so the two counts never multiply silently.

- A blocking file read or a child process counts as one step that no other task can interrupt.
- The profile's time_limit applies to each rerun.
- --reruns=<n>, reruns: and t.reruns(n) change the count only for tests that already ask for reruns. They never turn reruns on for other tests.

WHY 100 IN THE GUIDE

For the two-task lost update, about half of all orders fail, so 100 random reruns miss it with odds near 2^-100. A two-lock deadlock fails in about one order in four, so 100 reruns miss it with odds below 10^-12. Both planted bugs also have few enough orders to be checked completely. These are estimates, not measurements.

WHY NOT B OR C

B reruns only when someone passes a flag, so a plain jet test on your machine still hides the bug, and the code never says which tests need it. C reruns only a block inside the test. Values made before the block carry over from one rerun to the next and cause failures that are not real bugs.

options.name: reruns: on the test line
options.detail:
Write reruns: 100 on the #Test line, beside expected_fail:. The value is a whole number of at least 1. Without it, a test runs once, as today. A value below 1 is a compile error with a registered code and a UI snapshot.

What happens. jet test runs the test 100 times, and each time the tasks take turns in a different order. The order is chosen wherever a task can pause. Those points are starting or joining a task, a lock, a channel send or receive, a shared read or write, and yielding.

Small tests. If a test has fewer possible orders than its count, Jet runs each possible order once and stops. The report then says all 6 orders, so a small test is checked completely, not by chance.

Report. A pass prints one line, such as pass counter keeps every increment (100 reruns). A failure prints which rerun failed, its order number, each step in order with its source line, and the command that replays it. A deadlock, where every task waits on another, names who holds what and who waits.

Replay. jet test FILE "name" --seed=<n> replays exactly that order. --seed is a flag jet test already has.

Deep runs. The count is also a setting, as every flag must be. reruns: in a test profile and t.reruns(n) in fn test set it for a whole run. --reruns=<n> sets it for one command. They apply in that order, as build settings do.

Beginner path: add reruns: 100, run jet test, and copy the printed replay command. Expert path: pick a count per test, raise every count in a deep profile, and replay one order under jet debug.
options.technical: The typed #Test argument path parses reruns:, and sema checks the count. The generated test entry loops reruns and hands them to the profile's workers. The runtime gains a seeded one-worker scheduler whose choice points are the replay recorder's switch points. A depth-first walk over the same choices covers small tests completely. TestProfile and the Test value of fn test gain reruns, layered profile, then fn test, then the flag.

options.name: A flag only
options.detail: jet test --reruns=<n> reruns every test that starts a second task, n times each. The code does not change. A plain jet test runs each test once, so reruns happen only where someone passes the flag, usually on the build server. The code never shows which tests need reruns, and every such test pays the same count. Replay uses --seed=<n>, as in A.
options.technical: The flag and its matching profile and fn test settings set the count for the harness. Whether a test starts a second task is found while it runs. The scheduler is the same as A's.

options.name: A block inside the test
options.detail: reruns(100) { ... } inside a test reruns only that block. Code before the block runs once, so every rerun shares its values. A change made in one rerun carries into the next and causes failures that are not real bugs. jet test learns about the reruns only while the test runs, so it cannot list them first. It also adds a second place for test options beside the #Test line.
options.technical: Needs a rerun boundary inside the harness and a new Core testing call. The scheduler is the same as A's.

comparisons.note: Reruns the body in random task orders; its README example uses 100. A failure replays exactly. Source: https://github.com/awslabs/shuttle
Reruns the body in every possible task order. Source: https://github.com/tokio-rs/loom

recommendation.why: The test itself says it needs reruns, every plain jet test does them, and a failure prints the command that replays it. It is written like expected_fail:, which people already know.
gains: These bugs are found on every plain jet test, not only in special runs.
Small tests are checked in every possible order.
A failure prints the order number and the exact replay command.

losses.loss: A test with reruns takes longer than one run.
losses.mitigation: Reruns run side by side on simulated time, small tests stop early, and unchanged passing tests are reused.

whyNot.reason: A flag nobody passes on their own machine leaves the bug hidden, and the code never says which tests need it.
Values made before the block carry between reruns and cause false failures, and it adds a second place for test options.

recommendation.tradeoff: A spends a little test time, spread across cores, to find these bugs on every plain run.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: claude (TestProfiles, rewritten by Main). Adversarial model family: claude. Fresh agent: Main. The pass kept the count a plain Int, added complete checking of small tests, and made the flag also a setting.

wild.note: Shuttle reruns the body in random task orders, 100 times in its README (github.com/awslabs/shuttle).

decisions.title: Run normal exit cleanup before process replacement, with an explicit skip setting
decisions.situation: Process replacement hands the running program over to another one, like a shell's exec. The approved call skips cleanup, and the seed does not implement that call yet. Running cleanup first would finish logs and restore the terminal, but cleanup cannot be undone if startup fails or deletes an input file. We recommend normal cleanup by default with an explicit skip setting, while stating that irreversible cost without calling it rare.
decisions.gist: Should process replacement run normal cleanup first, with an explicit opt-out for resource-sensitive handoffs?
decisions.lesson: Every option hands the same launcher to sh, which exits 3. A prepares the command, then runs normal exit cleanup before handing over. Checks can catch errors early, but cannot guarantee startup. One cost remains: cleanup is irreversible, including deleted temporary inputs. Use explicit kept handles or .cleanup(.Skip) when the target needs those resources.
decisions.story: Priya's launcher records a tool choice and leaves a full-screen picker before handing over. She wants its log finished and terminal restored without writing a second cleanup path.
decisions.inWild:
# POSIX shell; source and exercised results are in detail.
exec sh -c 'exit 3'
# Same process, exit 3; the old shell's EXIT trap does not run.
decisions.detail:
WHAT THIS AMENDS

D-CORE-PROCREPLACE1=A ratified spec.replace_process(), skip-cleanup and a Windows waiting stand-in. A changes default cleanup and post-cleanup errors; B keeps that approval. Retain -[Exec, Time.Wait]> Never IOError!, admitting Exec before preparation or cleanup. D-JAI-DEFER1=A supplies one reverse-order cleanup list; D-TERM-COMMANDS1=A supplies terminal restoration. Reuse the ordinary exit boundary, not a second cleanup mechanism.

PREPARE, THEN COMMIT

Reject ratified incompatible settings before side effects: Capture/Stream, terminal, detached, timeout, output_limit and under. Retain cwd, environment, supported limits and explicit keep_open ownership under D-CORE-PROCINHERIT1=A. Unset stdin stays closed. Pin launch data and kept handles outside frames cleanup destroys. Resolve using the spec's PATH/cwd and check what can be validated without changing the caller. Preparation failure returns IOError without exit cleanup.

After preparation, A commits to normal cleanup and terminal restoration. Launch data and kept handles survive; flush writers without closing transferred handles. Start only after cleanup succeeds. A reported startup failure after commitment prints once and exits 127 for missing program/interpreter, otherwise 126, without repeated cleanup. Cleanup failure follows existing exit-failure policy and never starts the target. Cleanup can remove files or cancel work; it cannot be rolled back.

NO AUTOMATIC TEMPORARY RETENTION

The prior draft scanned argument strings and cancelled temporary-path deletion. That misses --input=path, script/config dependencies, environment references, symlink aliases and arbitrary deferred deletes. It also changes ownership and can leave unowned files. Remove that mechanism: temporary owners keep normal deletion semantics.

Targets needing temporary content use existing explicit keep_open ownership and an open-handle path where supported, or .Skip when the original pathname must survive. No new file-lifetime API is hidden here.

PREFLIGHT IS NOT A PROOF

Opening an executable protects that file against replacement/unlinking, not its interpreter, loader, libraries or later permission/resource checks. Path-based starts and scripts have different constraints. Do not substitute a script interpreter manually and claim unchanged semantics. Linux execveat of a script with a close-on-exec descriptor can fail ENOENT; inheriting it can leak a descriptor. Use the approved launch and kept-handle contracts, not a prescribed syscall trick. No Jet measurement establishes failure frequency.

SKIP AND FAIR B

spec.cleanup(.Skip).replace_process() keeps skip-cleanup behavior: no defers, resource cleanup or exit handlers; output still flushes. This suits deliberate terminal/resource inheritance. A defaults to .Run. The setting applies to replacement, not run/spawn.

B keeps skip as the sole contract. Callers can finish resource scopes and restore the terminal explicitly; not every launcher needs to duplicate all cleanup. Ordinary reported launch errors return as approved. Neither option can recover from kernel failure after the old image is already destroyed.

ONE COST REMAINS

Cleanup is irreversible: late startup failure ends the launcher, and cleanup may delete inputs the target needs. Use explicit kept handles where suitable or .Skip for resource-sensitive handoffs. This is not engineered away or proven negligible for every launcher.

WINDOWS AND TIERS

Keep Windows start/wait/exit with the child's status. A cleans once before start; B skips. Add no descendant-killing policy. One runtime contract covers O0/O1/O2, memory execution and file fallback under D-EXEC-RELAUNCH1=A and D-EXEC-NOEXEC1=A. Web refuses Exec before cleanup.

Future acceptance covers rejected settings, normal cleanup/defer order, terminal restoration, kept writers/handles, temporary-path deletion, scripts, missing interpreter/loader, cleanup failure, late startup failure, signals and the Windows stand-in. These are not completed checks.

CHECKED EVIDENCE

exec_now.jet ran a child and exited 3; exec_replace.jet failed E0102. HostProcess.jet:72-85 uses a root stop for cleanup. RouteAFiles.jet:694-698 describes last-owner temporary-file deletion. ProcessExecutionPrepare.jet:192-278 contains relaunch and argv/env preparation, not the old draft's complete preflight. Shell probes skipped EXIT traps on successful exec (3) and missing executable (127).

PRIMARY SOURCES

Linux execve documents permission, interpreter, I/O, resource and format failures, including failure after image teardown: https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/execve.2.html. execveat documents script-descriptor limitations: https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/execveat.2.html. No proposed replacement implementation or late-failure rate was exercised.

options.technical: ProcessSpec.cleanup(ProcessCleanup), .Run default and .Skip, applies only to replacement. Preserve existing explicit kept-handle ownership.

options.name: Keep the approved contract: no cleanup
options.detail: Keep the approved replacement contract. Callers finish resource scopes and restore modes themselves when needed.

comparisons.note: Replacement keeps the process; the old shell's EXIT trap is skipped. Source and executed results are in detail.
comparisons.code:
trap 'echo cleanup' EXIT
exec sh -c 'exit 3'
# Exits 3 without printing cleanup.

recommendation.why: A reuses the normal cleanup path for logs and terminal restoration. Resource-sensitive launchers explicitly choose skip instead of relying on guessed file retention.
gains: Normal cleanup is the beginner default.
Expert skip preserves deliberate handoff behavior.

losses.loss: One cost remains: cleanup is irreversible, including deleted inputs and late startup failures.
losses.mitigation: Use explicit kept handles for temporary content, or .cleanup(.Skip) when the target needs the original resource state.

whyNot.reason: B preserves useful low-level semantics, but makes safe cleanup an explicit caller responsibility rather than the default.

recommendation.tradeoff: One cost remains: cleanup cannot be undone; early checks and explicit skip reduce, not remove, that risk.

decisions.title: Transpile Jet to any language through a target trait that a library implements
decisions.situation: Transpiling means writing a Jet program as the same program in another language, such as C, Rust, JavaScript or Lua. You asked for targets that anyone can add: each target is an ordinary Jet library that implements one trait. The hard part is keeping Jet's meaning. Overflow checks, bounds checks, cleanup and error stops must behave the same in every language. You are asked what a target library receives from the compiler, what it must implement, and how much of the output it may shape. Seeding and bootstrapping the compiler are a separate, later question on their own card.
decisions.gist: What does a transpilation target implement, and what does it receive from the compiler, so that a library can add any language while the program keeps one meaning?
decisions.lesson: A target can only keep Jet's meaning if every check is already an explicit step when it receives the program. A target that receives the source tree must re-implement every check itself, and that is where languages drift apart. Haxe is the known example: its Int behaves differently on different targets.
decisions.story:
Ana's team has a Lua game engine and wants her Jet pathfinding code inside it. She adds the community `lua` target package to her project and runs `jet build --to lua path.jet`. She gets `path.lua` plus `jet_runtime.lua`, and the engine loads them like any other module.

An overflow in her code stops with the same message in Lua as in `jet run`, because the target spelled checks the compiler had already made explicit. Ben writes that `lua` target in about 2,000 lines of Jet. He implements the required trait methods, then overrides the hooks for records and loops so the output reads like ordinary Lua. `jet test --to lua` runs every executable example through his target and compares the output with `jet run`.
decisions.inWild:
Haxe compiles one language to JavaScript, C++, C#, Java, Python, Lua and PHP. Reflaxe lets a library add a target from Haxe's typed syntax tree (https://github.com/SomeRanDev/reflaxe). Integer width and overflow differ between Haxe targets (https://haxe.org/manual/types-basic-types.html).

Fable compiles F# to JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, Rust and Dart from the typed tree. Its documentation lists behavior that differs per target, such as numeric types and reflection (https://fable.io/docs/).

Kotlin lowers every platform from one shared IR, and its JVM, JavaScript, Wasm and Native back ends consume that IR (https://kotlinlang.org/docs/multiplatform.html).

Nim, Gleam and Scala.js each ship a fixed set of first-party back ends, and third parties cannot add a language (https://nim-lang.org/docs/backends.html, https://gleam.run/documentation/).

LLVM lets anyone add a machine target by implementing its target classes. Emscripten and wasm2c turn low-level code into JavaScript or C that is correct but hard to read.
decisions.detail:
WHAT VOTING A INCLUDES

1. One trait. `core.compiler.target.Target` is a public, versioned trait. A target is any Jet package with a type that implements it. First-party targets are ordinary implementations with no special access.

2. What a target receives. It receives the checked program after one shared pass that makes every meaning explicit. That covers overflow checks, big-integer spills, bounds checks, cleanup, error stops and the stop protocol. Jet's own runtime (Prelude and Core) arrives the same way and is transpiled by the same target.

3. What a target must implement. Required methods spell a closed list of explicit operations (arithmetic, memory, calls, branches, loops and returns). A small set of host leaves gives the target language's system calls, clock, memory and threads. Each operation has a conformance test.

4. Idiom hooks. Optional hooks let a target spell records, enums, functions, loops, strings and errors in the target language's own style. Each hook receives the already explicit form and has a default built from the required methods. A target can therefore start plain and grow idiomatic, and a hook can never drop a check.

5. Capabilities first. A target declares what it can spell, such as threads, 64-bit integers, tail calls or SIMD. A program that needs something missing gets a registered error naming the target before anything is written.

6. One meaning. `jet test --to <target>` runs every executable example through the target and compares stdout, stderr and the exit code with `jet run`. A target is listed as conforming only when that passes.

7. Command. `jet build --to <target> file.jet` writes the program's files. `c` and `rust` are the first-party targets; any other name is a target package listed in the project's dependencies.

8. Order. The shared explicit pass and the public program view land first, because today the x86-64 and web code writers still decide some meaning themselves. Then the trait and the C target, then Rust, then third-party targets.

WHAT VOTING A DOES NOT INCLUDE

Seeding and bootstrapping the compiler, which are on their own frozen card. Native code writers for new machine architectures. Speed claims for transpiled code.

EDGE CASES

Languages without fixed 64-bit integers, such as JavaScript or Lua, spell `Int` through host leaves, so overflow still stops at the same values. Garbage-collected languages still run Jet's cleanup at the same points, because cleanup is an explicit step. C's undefined behavior is avoided because the C target spells only operations C defines exactly. A target without threads rejects programs that spawn them, with the capability error. Compile-time code runs in the compiler before transpiling, and only its results are written.

options.name: A trait over the explicit program, with optional idiom hooks (recommended)
options.detail: A target implements required methods for a closed list of explicit operations and host leaves, and may override idiom hooks that shape readable output. The runtime is transpiled through the same target. Conformance runs every executable example.
options.technical: Prerequisite: one shared IR pass moves exact-Int spills, fixed-width traps and the stop protocol out of the x86-64 and web selectors. Then core.compiler exposes a versioned, read-only program view. Target: trait has required op methods, a host-leaf table and hooks with defaults. Capabilities are registered diagnostics checked before any output. `jet test --to` drives the example corpus.

options.name: A trait over the checked source tree (Haxe with Reflaxe, Fable)
options.detail: A target receives the typed, checked syntax tree and writes idiomatic code directly. Each target re-implements Jet's checks, cleanup and error behavior. The conformance suite catches what it gets wrong.
options.technical: core.compiler exposes the checked tree and its types. Target: trait has one method per syntax node. Prelude and Core are transpiled from source by the same target, so every target re-spells overflow, bounds and stop semantics.

options.name: A trait over the explicit program, with no idiom hooks
options.detail: Like A, but a target spells only the explicit operations. Output is correct and portable but reads like machine code, as Emscripten and wasm2c output does.
options.technical: Same prerequisite and program view as A, with no hook layer. Target: trait has the op methods and host leaves only.

options.name: First-party targets only, with no public trait (Nim, Gleam)
options.detail: The compiler ships C and Rust writers. Nobody outside the compiler can add a language.
options.technical: The C and Rust writers live in Compiler/ beside the x86-64 and web writers and read the internal IR directly.

recommendation.why: It is the only option where any language can be added by a library and the program still keeps one meaning. Every check is explicit before a target sees it, and idiom hooks cannot remove a check.
gains: Any language can be added by an ordinary Jet package.
Overflow, bounds, cleanup and error stops behave the same in every target, proven by the example corpus.
Targets can start plain and become idiomatic one hook at a time.

losses.loss: Targets wait for the shared explicit pass and the public program view.
losses.mitigation: Both also remove duplicated meaning from the x86-64 and web writers, so the work pays off even before the first target.

losses.loss: The trait is a public contract that changes as the compiler grows.
losses.mitigation: It is versioned with the compiler library, and first-party targets change in the same commit, so breakage shows up at once.

losses.loss: Output without hooks reads like low-level code.
losses.mitigation: The C and Rust targets ship with hooks for records, enums, functions and loops.

whyNot.reason: Every target re-implements Jet's checks by hand, so meaning drifts between languages, as it does in Haxe and Fable.
It keeps the meaning but gives up readable output, which is much of why teams want transpiled code.
It rules out the library-defined targets you asked for.

recommendation.tradeoff: A delays third-party targets until the explicit pass and the public program view exist, in exchange for one meaning in every language.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude. Adversarial model family: Claude. Fresh agent: PortsLead-2. It reviewed the earlier seed draft and found that each writer still decides exact-Int, trap and stop meaning; fixing that is option A's first step. A fresh review of this re-scoped revision is pending and is the build card's first criterion.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Claims checked against dev 964e737fcc.

Compiler/JetIR/Source/X64Select.jet header: x86-64 selection decides exact-Int inline and spill paths (jet_int_add) and the slow paths.

Compiler/JetWeb/Source/Web/Select.jet header: WebAssembly selection re-gives each IR instruction the x86-64 selector's meaning (exact-Int fast paths, big-integer routes, fixed-width traps and stop texts, stop protocol). It also imports jet_ir X64 tables, so IR is not yet a fully decided form.

Compiler/JetWeb/Source/Web/Leaf.jet: the web target re-spells the Linux layer's #FFI(asm) leaves and makes every atomic a plain read-modify-write.

Compiler/JetWeb/Source/Web/Host.jet: the JavaScript host answers the runtime's Linux system calls and the C library calls the runtime makes.

Compiler/JetBackend/Source/OS/Linux.jet: 75 runtime leaves, os_syscall_i64 a raw Linux x86-64 syscall; 383 raw syscall sites across 58 runtime files use x86-64 numbers.

Compiler/JetBackend/Source/Image/SessionHost.jet: compile-time code runs in a child process that loads x86-64 code under seccomp.

Compiler/JetBackend/Source/X64/FaultReport.jet: the fault report is an x86-64 code blob; Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/Fault.jet reads Linux x86-64 ucontext offsets.

Compiler/JetCli/Source/Cli/Front.jet jet_cli_build_options: `--target web` sets the build option `os: web`.
