decisions.title: Background tasks still alive when run returns: cancel them with a short grace, keep today's rule, forbid them, or end the process at once
decisions.situation: A background task is work a program starts with detach() and does not wait for. When run returns, such a task can still be alive. Today a waiting task, such as a ticker that sleeps between ticks, stops the program with error E3013 and exit status 70. A task stuck in a loop that never waits keeps the process alive forever. Past 4,096 tasks, waiting ones are not even cleaned up. This matters for servers, tickers and anyone who wants a clean, prompt exit. You are asked what happens to background tasks when run returns. We recommend cancelling every one, giving them one second to clean up, and then exiting with run's own status.
decisions.gist: When run returns, what should happen to background tasks: cancel with a grace, today's rule, forbid them, or exit at once?
decisions.lesson: A background task is work started with detach() that nobody waits for. When the main function run ends, some of that work may still be going. Jet must stop it cleanly, treat it as an error, forbid it, or simply end the process. This vote picks one rule.
decisions.explainer: Words used here. A task is work that runs alongside the rest of the program. detach() lets a task go on without anyone waiting for it. Cancel asks a task to stop, and a task notices only at its next wait, such as a sleep, a channel read or a network read. Cleanup is the code that runs as a value goes away, such as closing or flushing a file.
decisions.story: Kai starts a ticker task that wakes every second to refresh a cache, and detaches it. When run finishes, the program prints run returns. Today it then stops with E3013 and exit status 70. Under A the ticker is cancelled at its sleep, cleans up and the program exits 0 at once. Under B Kai must keep the handle, cancel it and join it. Under C, detach() is gone, so he must do the same. Under D the process ends the moment run returns, and the ticker's cleanup never runs.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. What the runtime does with detached tasks that are still alive when run returns.

Today, parked tasks. After run returns, main_exit_cleanup in Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/Main.jet looks for tasks parked on a wait. If it finds any, it reports E3013 (Parked tasks remain at process exit). It cancels the tasks it can reach so they unwind, and the process exits 70. Tasks past the registry cap (OBSERVE_TASK_CAP, 4,096) are neither reported nor unwound. A seed run of the ticker program prints run returns, then E3013 with the ticker blocked on its sleep, and exits 70.

Today, running tasks. If no task is parked, jet_scheduler_drain_after_exit waits until no task is queued or running. A seed run of a program whose detached task runs `loop { n += 1 }` never exits; it was killed after 10 seconds.

Cancellation reaches only waits. In spec.md, cancellation is preemptive at wait points: channel send and receive, time.sleep, join, select and I/O. There is no check on loop back-edges. A seed run that cancels and then joins a task looping on `n += 1` also never returns. tasks.yield_now() is a wait point, so a loop that calls it can be cancelled.

The rest of the spec. A cancelled task unwinds and runs Drop-backed cleanup. #Shield defers cancellation until its block exits. Dropping a handle without joining or detaching is L1101, so every detach is an explicit choice.

Why it matters for memory. #6567's leak witness counts live allocations at exit. A task that is not unwound keeps its frame and captures, so the witness must either see every task unwound or leave task frames out.

options.name: Cancel every background task, wait up to one second, then exit
options.detail: When run returns, the runtime cancels every task still alive. A waiting task stops at its wait at once, runs its cleanup, closes its files and frees its memory, with no cap on how many. The exit waits until every cancelled task has unwound, or for one second, whichever comes first. A task still running after that second is in a loop that never waits. It is abandoned, the process exits, and the system takes its memory back. The exit status is run's.
options.technical: Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/Main.jet: after run returns, cancel every live task through the task registry, with no OBSERVE_TASK_CAP limit. Drain until no task is queued, ready or running, or until 1 s of monotonic time has passed, then exit. Retire E3013's exit report: its registry row, explainer page and runtime_e3013 ui snapshot, which becomes a case that exits 0. The leak witness counts after the drain and names each abandoned task instead of counting its frame. spec.md gains the rule.

options.name: Keep today's rule and close its gap
options.detail: A waiting background task still stops the program with E3013 and exit status 70, after it is cancelled and cleaned up. A task in a loop that never waits still keeps the process alive forever. The 4,096-task cap goes, so every waiting task is reported and cleaned up. A program with a ticker keeps its handle, cancels it and joins it before run returns.
options.technical: Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/Main.jet and Observe.jet: lift OBSERVE_TASK_CAP from the exit report and unwind. No other change; E3013 stays.

options.name: No task may outlive run
options.detail: detach() is removed. Every task handle is joined, so every task ends before the function that started it returns. A ticker is kept, cancelled and joined. A server that serves each connection in its own task joins those tasks through a group. A joined task in a loop that never waits still never ends.
options.technical: Remove Task.detach from Core and the sema rule that lets it discharge L1101. Retire the detach forms of E1103 and E1106, and migrate every detach() caller (Core/Http/Server.jet and others) to task groups. spec.md D-DETACH1 is superseded.

options.name: End the process the moment run returns
options.detail: This is the model of Go and of Rust's standard threads. When run returns, the process exits at once with run's status. Background tasks stop where they are, without cancelling and without cleanup, and the system takes their memory back. Nothing can hang the exit, and nothing waits.
options.technical: Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/Main.jet: after run returns and the main task's own cleanup, flush stdout and exit without draining the scheduler. Retire E3013's exit report and the exit unwind. The leak witness leaves every live task's frame and captures out of its count. spec.md gains the rule.

comparisons.note: When main returns, the process ends; goroutines stop at once and their deferred calls do not run.
When main returns, the process exits; spawned threads stop without running their destructors.
Runtime shutdown drops spawned tasks at their await points and runs their destructors; a task that never awaits blocks a blocking shutdown, so shutdown_timeout bounds it.
asyncio.run cancels the tasks still pending when main returns and waits for them to unwind.

recommendation.why: A gives every program a clean exit with run's status. Every task that waits, which is almost every background task, cleans up and frees its memory at once. A loop that never waits can delay the exit by at most one second, so nothing hangs. It is Tokio's shutdown_timeout as the default.
gains: A ticker or server task no longer turns a normal exit into status 70.
Every waiting task's cleanup runs at exit, with no 4,096 cap.
No exit hangs: a loop that never waits costs at most one second.
No new syntax; detach() keeps its meaning of not waiting.

losses.loss: Background work still in progress at exit is cut short.
losses.mitigation: Join the task when its work must finish, or put that work in #Shield, which finishes before the cancel lands.

losses.loss: A loop that never waits is abandoned after one second without its cleanup.
losses.mitigation: Its memory goes back to the system and the leak witness names the task. Calling tasks.yield_now() in the loop makes it cancellable.

losses.loss: E3013 no longer reports a background task stuck on a wait at exit.
losses.mitigation: A task whose end matters is joined, and L1101 already forces that choice.

whyNot.reason: B keeps stopping normal programs with ticker or server tasks with status 70, and a loop that never waits still hangs the exit.
C removes detach(), which servers and tickers use, and a joined loop that never waits still hangs.
D is fastest, but it skips every background task's cleanup, so files go unflushed and connections unclosed, and the leak witness cannot see task memory.

recommendation.tradeoff: Up to one second of exit for a loop that never waits, in exchange for cleanup in every task that waits.

decisions.title: Mapped files: keep borrowed bytes stable by cloning the file, else holding it, else copying it; copy always; copy on every read; or let the bytes change
decisions.situation: A mapped file is a file the program reads as if it were already in memory. files.map(path) gives Jet code a borrowed view of the bytes with no copy. Today another program can change those bytes while the view is borrowed, and a probe saw a borrowed byte change from 3 to 9. If the other program shrinks the file, the next read kills the process with SIGBUS. Safe Jet promises a borrowed value does not change under you. The owner asked whether A's downsides can be engineered away. Most can: A now asks the file system for a free private clone of the file first, and only holds or copies the file where no clone is possible. We recommend A.
decisions.gist: When another program writes a file Jet has mapped, should borrowed bytes stay put through a clone, hold or copy, be copied first, be copied per read, or change?
decisions.lesson: Mapping a file lets a program read a huge file without loading it first: the operating system brings in each page when the program touches it. The bytes still belong to the file, so another program can change them while Jet is reading. Jet's rule is that a borrowed view never changes under you. This vote picks how mapped files keep that rule.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A view is a borrowed window into bytes someone else owns; it is not a copy. A clone, or reflink, is a new file that shares the original's disk blocks. It costs no time and no space until one side writes; the writer then gets fresh blocks and the clone keeps the old ones.

A lease is a Linux promise to the program that holds it: before another process may write or shrink the file, the kernel tells the holder and makes the writer wait. Copying means reading the bytes into new storage, which costs time and space equal to the file's size.
decisions.story:
Mia's log tool maps a 2 GiB log and scans it for errors. One night a rotation script truncates the log mid-scan. Today her tool dies with SIGBUS. Under A, on her btrfs laptop or her Mac, Jet mapped a clone, so the script never waits and the scan finishes. On an ext4 server the script waits about 0.7 s while Jet copies the 2 GiB.

Under B every map first copies 2 GiB. Under C each read copies and two reads can disagree. Under D her scan sees whatever the file says at each moment.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. What a safe borrowed view from files.map sees when another process writes or truncates the file, and where zero-copy mapping lives.

The owner's question (q3huikf3). The posted A held the file with a lease and copied where it could not. Its five costs were real: writers stalled, a 45 s deadline could stop the program, many hosts copied, a signal was reserved, and Windows refused writers. This version removes most of them by trying a clone first. The costs that remain are named in the recommendation with their price and their best mitigation.

Today's map. Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/CompilerMapped.jet jet_std_files_map opens the file read-only, takes a shared flock (advisory, so non-Jet writers ignore it), and calls mmap with PROT_READ and MAP_PRIVATE. A private mapping is not a snapshot on Linux: pages not yet copied show the file's current bytes.

What the card says. #6706 c1: a safe borrowed view must not observe a byte change made by another process after the borrow, or the safe API no longer hands out such a view. c2: a truncation during safe access gives a typed error or a registered fault, never a raw SIGBUS.

The clone probe. clone_probe.py clones a file into an unnamed temp file on the same file system, maps the clone, then overwrites and truncates the original. On btrfs, a 64 MiB clone took 0.06 ms and a 1 GiB clone 0.10 ms. The mapping still read the old byte at the old length. On ext4 and tmpfs the clone call failed with ENOTSUP, which is the signal to fall back.

Where a clone works. Linux btrfs, xfs (reflink is the default since xfsprogs 5.1), bcachefs, and OpenZFS 2.2 with block cloning on. macOS APFS through fclonefileat. Windows ReFS, including Dev Drive, through FSCTL_DUPLICATE_EXTENTS_TO_FILE. FreeBSD ZFS through copy_file_range. NFS 4.2 and SMB servers that support a server-side clone. Ext4, tmpfs, f2fs and NTFS cannot clone. [INFERENCE] Clone time grows with the number of extents, so a heavily fragmented file clones slower than the probe's fresh file.

Disk space. A clone shares blocks only until the original changes. If another program rewrites or truncates the file while it is mapped, the clone keeps the old blocks, so the space is not freed until the map is dropped. A fallback copy needs free space equal to the file. When the temp file cannot be written, files.map fails with its IOError, as it does today when the file cannot be opened.

The other probes. lease_probe.py shows the lease path: a writer waited 18-32 ms while a 64 MiB map was copied, and lease_probe.py stall shows the kernel's 45.2 s deadline. copy_cost.py shows a 1 GiB map opens in 0.05 ms at 32 MiB RSS, while a copy took 0.36 s and 1056 MiB RSS.

Sources. Linux ioctl_ficlone(2): man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/ioctl_ficlone.2.html. fcntl(2) Leases: man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/fcntl.2.html. macOS clonefile(2). Windows: learn.microsoft.com/windows/win32/api/winioctl/ni-winioctl-fsctl_duplicate_extents_to_file. memmap2: docs.rs/memmap2/latest/memmap2/struct.Mmap.html. Java MappedByteBuffer and Go syscall.Mmap, as in the comparisons.

options.name: Stable map: map a clone where the file system can, hold the file where it can't, copy as the last resort
options.detail:
files.map keeps zero-copy views and makes them stable. First Jet asks the file system for a private clone and maps that, so another program's writes never reach the view and never wait. Where no clone is possible, Jet holds the file with a lease on Linux or deny-write sharing on Windows, and copies only when a writer arrives. Otherwise it copies into an unnamed temp file, so even files larger than memory map.

Beginner path: write files.map(path); nothing else changes. Expert path: mapped.kind() reports Clone, Held or Copy, and an #Unsafe raw map remains for shared live bytes.
options.technical:
Map time, in order. A file system that cannot be written at all, such as squashfs or erofs, maps the file directly. A read-only mount alone does not count, since a bind mount or a network server can still write the file. Next, clone into an O_TMPFILE in the file's own directory or another writable directory on the same mount. Linux uses FICLONE, macOS fclonefileat with an unlink, Windows ReFS FSCTL_DUPLICATE_EXTENTS_TO_FILE and FreeBSD copy_file_range. Any refusal falls through.

On local Linux ext4, tmpfs and f2fs, take the posted lease: F_SETSIG SIGRTMAX, F_SETLEASE F_RDLCK. At a break, copy into an unnamed temp file on the same mount and map it over the same address with MAP_FIXED. NTFS opens without FILE_SHARE_WRITE.

A lease is taken only for a file that copies well inside lease-break-time, about 4 GiB at 100 MB/s and the 45 s default. Larger files, refused leases and other hosts copy at map time into an unnamed temp file. Truncation can no longer fault a safe view, which meets c2.

options.name: The safe map is a copy; zero-copy mapping moves behind #Unsafe
options.detail: files.map(path) reads the whole file into the program's memory, as files.read_bytes does, and keeps the MappedFile API (window, lines, len). Views are stable because they borrow the copy. Zero-copy mapping becomes an expert call inside #Unsafe that hands out raw reads, never a safe view.
options.technical: jet_std_files_map reads the file into an owned buffer instead of calling mmap; the drop frees the buffer. Add an #Unsafe raw map in core.files whose reads go through checked raw access and whose truncation fault is c2's registered stop. Web gets the same copy.

options.name: VolatileBytes: no borrowed views; every read copies
options.detail: files.map returns a map that never lends a view. mapped.read(start, count) copies the bytes it asks for at that moment, and lines() yields copied lines. Searching and counting run inside the runtime over the live pages. Two reads can disagree if another program wrote in between. A read past a shrunk end stops with a registered message.
options.technical: MappedFile loses window, window_len and the View<U8> lines iterator; it gains read(start, count) -> [U8] !IOError, a copying lines() and runtime scan kernels (find, count, checksum). c2's registered SIGBUS stop is required.

options.name: Keep views and let them change: a mapped view is shared with other programs
options.detail: files.map keeps today's zero-copy views. The spec states that another program may change a mapped file's bytes at any time, so a mapped view can read different values at different moments. The compiler never assumes a mapped byte stays the same between reads. A read after a shrink stops with a registered message.
options.technical: No API change. Sema marks map views as externally mutable, so no optimization reuses a loaded mapped byte. c2's registered SIGBUS stop is required. Card #6706 c1 is rewritten to accept change.

comparisons.note: memmap2 marks every file-backed map constructor unsafe, because the map is undefined behavior if the file is modified in or out of process; the caller must prevent that.
comparisons.code: let map = unsafe { Mmap::map(&file)? }; // UB if the file changes

comparisons.note: syscall.Mmap returns a plain byte slice that shows other processes' writes. A read after truncation crashes the program unless debug.SetPanicOnFault turns the fault into a panic.
comparisons.code:
m, _ := syscall.Mmap(fd, 0, size, syscall.PROT_READ, syscall.MAP_SHARED)
first := m[0] // may change later

comparisons.note: MappedByteBuffer documents that its content can change at any time when the file changes, and that touching a truncated region throws an unspecified exception, possibly later.
comparisons.code:
MappedByteBuffer buf = ch.map(MapMode.READ_ONLY, 0, ch.size());
byte first = buf.get(0); // may change

comparisons.note: cp --reflink=auto clones where the file system can and copies otherwise. A uses the same clone-else-copy rule, at map time. Source: www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/html_node/cp-invocation.html
comparisons.code: cp --reflink=auto big.log snapshot.log   # instant on btrfs, xfs

recommendation.why: A keeps both the promise and the speed. On file systems that clone, the map is zero copy, never makes a writer wait and has no deadline or reserved signal. Elsewhere it holds the file or copies with the same meaning. The remaining costs apply only on file systems that cannot clone.
gains: A borrowed mapped byte never changes, on every host.
On btrfs, xfs, APFS and ReFS, a 1 GiB map is a 0.10 ms clone and no writer ever waits.
A shrink by another program can no longer fault a safe view.
Copies go to an unnamed temp file, so files larger than memory still map.

losses.loss: On ext4, tmpfs and f2fs, the first writer waits while Jet copies: 18-32 ms for 64 MiB, and non-blocking opens fail once.
losses.mitigation: It happens once per map. A program that must never stall a writer reads with files.read_bytes.

losses.loss: On those file systems the runtime reserves signal 64, and storage slower than 100 MB/s can still miss the 45 s deadline.
losses.mitigation: Big files copy at map time instead; a miss is a located stop while the writer still waits.

losses.loss: Hosts without clone or hold copy at map time, and NTFS refuses other programs' writes while the map lives.
losses.mitigation: The meaning is the same everywhere. A file already open for writing on NTFS is copied instead.

losses.loss: A clone or copy holds disk space: a rewritten or truncated original frees nothing until the map is dropped, and a copy needs space equal to the file.
losses.mitigation: Space returns when the map is dropped. A map that cannot get its copy fails with IOError, and files.read_at reads a part without either.

whyNot.reason: B copies every map on every host, even where a free clone gives the same stability with no copy.
C removes borrowed views from maps, so every line a program keeps is a copy, and two reads can disagree.
D gives up Jet's promise that a borrowed value doesn't change under you.

recommendation.tradeoff: On file systems that cannot clone, a short writer wait or a map-time copy, for stable zero-copy views everywhere a clone exists.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude Opus. Adversarial model family: Claude Opus. Fresh agent: BallotReview-3. The review checked the clone probe and today's map. It removed the unsafe read-only-mount shortcut and named the disk space a clone or copy holds.

decisions.title: F32 remainders: give rem_quo, remainder and fmod an F32 result under their own names, add _f32 names, or keep the Float results only
decisions.situation: rem_quo divides one number by another and returns two parts: what is left over, and the whole number of times it went in. For 6.5 and 2.0 that is 0.5 left over and 3. Today the left-over part is always a Float, a 64-bit number, even when both inputs are F32, a 32-bit number. math.remainder and math.fmod also answer a Float for two F32s. Floor, hypot, frexp, modf and most other math functions answer in the argument's width. The math card asks for C's float forms remquof, remainderf and fmodf. This vote decides how a program gets them. We recommend A: these three follow the width rule too.
decisions.gist: Should math.rem_quo, remainder and fmod give an F32 remainder for F32 inputs, as most math functions do?
decisions.lesson: A Float is a 64-bit floating-point number and an F32 is a 32-bit one. Most math functions answer in the width you give them: math.floor of an F32 is an F32. The three remainder functions, rem_quo, remainder and fmod, answer with a Float today. This vote picks how an F32 program gets an F32 remainder.
decisions.explainer: Words used here. rem_quo divides a by b and rounds the quotient to the nearest integer, ties to even. It returns what is left over plus that integer's low 31 bits and sign, as musl's C does. remainder returns the left-over part alone. fmod cuts the quotient toward zero. Widening an F32 to a Float is always exact. F32{x} narrows a Float back. It stops the program when x is a NaN or an infinity, which are values outside every number range.
decisions.story: Mia reduces an F32 angle into one turn and needs to know which quarter it fell in. Under A she writes math.rem_quo(angle, quarter) and gets an F32 remainder, as math.floor(angle) gives an F32. Under B she must know to write math.rem_quo_f32(angle, quarter). Under C she widens both inputs and narrows the remainder with F32{}. Her program then stops on the first angle that is a NaN, where C's remquof hands the NaN back.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. How a program gets C's remquof, remainderf and fmodf, which card #6700 c5 requires as the float forms of every C23 math.h function. frexpf and modff are not on this ballot. Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/Registry/CoreSignatures.jet already gives frexp and modf generic rows over the argument's float type (lines 369-379).

Today, run on the seed compiler. With two F32 arguments, math.rem_quo, math.remainder and math.fmod each answer a Float (probe f2). CoreSignatures.jet line 405 types remainder and fmod as Float only, and rem_quo is a Float source function. Passing the result where an F32 is wanted is E0112. Most other functions keep the width: math.floor of an F32 is an F32 (probe f1).

How the other functions keep the width. sema_call_try_core_math_f32 in Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Calls/Core.jet widens two F32s, calls the Float source and rounds the result once to F32. That rounding never stops: a NaN stays a NaN.

Why that round trip is exact here. The remainder of two binary32 values is itself a binary32 value, and widening is exact. So computing in Float and rounding once gives exactly remquof's remainder, and the quotient is the same integer. A zero divisor or an infinite dividend gives a NaN, as C specifies. No new F32 source is needed.

Narrowing in a program. F32{x} stops with E3010 on a NaN or an infinity (probe f3), and F32.from_float returns an Err for them. Jet has no public narrowing that passes them through.

Why no new record type. The result is an anonymous named tuple, (rem: Float, quo: Int), not a record. A tuple with an F32 field needs no new type declaration.

Beginner and expert paths. A beginner under A writes math.rem_quo(a, b) and gets a remainder in their width, with no conversion to learn. An expert who wants a Float remainder widens first, the same under every option. An expert porting C maps remquof, remainderf and fmodf to their Jet names under A, and to three _f32 names under B. Under C each becomes two widens, the call and a guarded narrow.

options.name: Same names, F32 remainder
options.detail: math.rem_quo, math.remainder and math.fmod follow the rule most core.math functions follow: two F32 arguments give an F32 result. rem_quo's quotient stays an Int. Float arguments keep today's Float results. No new public name.
options.technical:
Signatures for two F32s: rem_quo -> (rem: F32, quo: Int), remainder -> F32 and fmod -> F32.

CoreSignatures.jet: line 405's Float-only row for fmod and remainder becomes generic over the float type, and rem_quo gains a generic tuple row like frexp's. Calls/Core.jet: sema_call_try_core_math_f32 adds remainder and fmod to its member list, and rounds only the rem field of rem_quo. The round trip is exact, so no F32 source port is needed.

docs/core-library.md and Tools/agent/LibcCensus.jet name the F32 forms. Proof: the F32 exact corpus case gains rows for all three against musl 1.2.5's remquof, remainderf and fmodf on O0, O1, O2 and web.

options.name: Separate _f32 names
options.detail: Three new public functions, math.rem_quo_f32, math.remainder_f32 and math.fmod_f32, return F32 results. The plain names keep returning a Float for two F32s. A program picks the width by the name, as C picks remquo or remquof.
options.technical: Signatures: rem_quo_f32: fn(a: F32, b: F32) -> (rem: F32, quo: Int), and remainder_f32 and fmod_f32: fn(a: F32, b: F32) -> F32. Each uses A's exact round trip. Compiler/Prelude/Core.rows exports them in both core.math rows, and docs/core-library.md gains three rows. New public Core API: three names.

options.name: No F32 form; widen and narrow
options.detail: Nothing new. A program widens both F32s to Float, calls the Float function and narrows the remainder with F32{}. The narrowing is exact for every finite remainder, but F32{} stops the program on a NaN, so a program that may see one checks math.is_nan first. The card's c5 text is amended to say the three remainder functions have a Float form only.
options.technical: No Core or compiler feature. Tools/agent/LibcCensus.jet notes that remquof, remainderf and fmodf are the Float calls on widened arguments. Card #6700 c5 text: these are not separate forms. This program runs today on the seed compiler (probe f1).

comparisons.note: One function per width; the quotient comes back through a pointer.
comparisons.code:
int quo;
float rem = remquof(a, b, &quo);

comparisons.note: No remquo in std; the libm crate has one function per width.
One float width; math.remainder gives no quotient.

recommendation.why: A gives the three remainder functions the rule most core.math functions already have, frexp and modf included: F32 in gives F32 out under the same name. The result is exact, no public name is added, and a NaN passes through as in C.
gains: One rule: the remainder has the argument's width, as floor, hypot and frexp do.
No new public names; remquof, remainderf and fmodf map to the names a program already uses.
The F32 result is exact and a NaN passes through, with no guard to write.
No new F32 source: the exact round trip reuses the Float functions.

losses.loss: The result's width comes from the arguments, so a reader must know their types to know the remainder's.
losses.mitigation: Most core.math functions already work this way; the editor's hover shows the type, and widening first asks for a Float.

whyNot.reason: B adds three public names for a choice most core.math functions make by the argument's type, so F32 code has two styles.
C makes F32 programs write three conversions per call, and F32{} stops on a NaN where remquof returns it.

recommendation.tradeoff: The remainder's width follows the arguments, as for most math functions, for one rule and no new names.

The fresh review probed the seed and found remainder and fmod also answer a Float for F32s, so A now covers all three. It showed the Float round trip is exact, removing the port cost.

decisions.title: How the web package puts its app on a network port: one serve call in core.http, a public route table, the app kept in Core, or HTTP in the package
decisions.situation: The web toolkit, the code behind web.app(), is moving out of Jet's built-in library into an installable package called web. A package may use only the public parts of the built-in library. Today the app builds its route table and starts its server through 15 hidden calls in the HTTP module. The build of an earlier vote, one route table on web.app(), also removes every public way to start a server. So once the move lands, the web package has no public way to listen on a port. You are asked which small public door the HTTP module keeps. We recommend A: one call that serves one handler, a ready handler for a folder of files, and a route pattern whose match alone tags a request with its route.
decisions.gist: Once web.app() moves into the web package, what is the best public door for that package to start a server?
decisions.lesson: A web app needs two things: a route table that picks the code for each address, and a server that listens on a port. The route table is moving into the web package. The server stays in Jet's built-in HTTP module. This vote picks the public calls that join them.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. Core is Jet's built-in library. A package, or battery, is an installable library outside Core; the web package is one. A public call is one any program may use. A private name starts with two underscores, and only Core itself may use it.

A route table maps an address, like GET /hello/:name, to the code that answers it. A handler answers one request with one response; Core's handler type is HTTPHandler, and a function written where an HTTPHandler is expected becomes one. Listening means opening a network port and waiting for requests.
decisions.story: Ana writes a small app: web.app(), one app.get route, then app.bind and serve. Under A, B and D her program is the same. Under A the web package serves her table through one Core call, server.listen. Ana can also serve a folder with no package at all: server.listen with server.static_dir("public"). Under B the package wraps a public Core route table, server.mux(). Under C her pages move to a second value. Under D the package parses HTTP itself.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. The public Core calls the web package uses to serve its route table once core.web leaves Core.

The gap. Card #6445 moves core.web, router included, into the web package under D-WEB-HOME1=A; core.http and core.net stay in Core. D-WEB-RUNTIME-API1=A says that package uses public Core calls only, with no new general primitive, and that its compiler rules become markers it declares. A double-underscore name is refused outside Core with E0067.

D-ROUTE-ONE1=A makes web.app() own the one route table and removes server.mux(). Its build, the #6055 c2 submission, also removes server.serve, server.bind, serve_once, serve_once_listener, static_files, cors, request_id and http.serve. On dev today, core.http.server already has no mux, bind or serve, and HTTPServer keeps local_addr, serve, wait and shutdown(grace:).

What the app uses today. Core/Web/Web.jet calls 15 private core.http.server names, 36 times. Building the table uses __mux_new, __route_add, __route_add_dynamic, __route_add_custom, __handler and __layer_add. Its options use __static_files, __cors_handler and __request_id_handler. OpenAPI uses __mux_routes, __route_parse and __route_openapi_path. Serving uses __bind, __serve_once and __server_on. __server_on is how app.serve tells a busy port from other failures before it tries the next port.

The routing code also writes two private request fields, the path values and the matched route, which request.param and server.access_log read. Route registration stops with E2804, E2805 and E2808 through core.rt.__coded_stop, which is private too.

What stays public under every option. The helpers response, response_body, json, static_file, static_file_range, tls, sse, cors_policy and the access log helpers. HTTPServer with its methods. HTTPHandler with handle; a function written where one is expected becomes one, and the compiler checks its captures as handler captures. The #Server.Get route markers.

How A removes the earlier downsides. serve_once is a method on the server listen returns, as Python's handle_request is. static_dir returns a handler, as Go's FileServer and Deno's serveDir do, so a folder needs no package. Only Core's RoutePattern.match tags a request with its route, so no code can forge one. Literal routes keep E2804 at check time; only a computed pattern meets the run-time stop.

Is A's server.listen a general primitive? No. D-WEB-RUNTIME-API1=A turned down process-wide shared state, a publish reachable from anywhere and the startup environment. Its rule is that a host power stays in the Core module that owns it. Listening on a port is core.http.server's own job. listen holds no route table, so it is not the second builder D-ROUTE-ONE1=A removed.

Sources. Deno.serve and serveDir: docs.deno.com/api/deno/~/Deno.serve, jsr.io/@std/http/doc/file-server. Go ListenAndServe, FileServer, StripPrefix and Request.SetPathValue: pkg.go.dev/net/http. Python socketserver handle_request: docs.python.org/3/library/socketserver.html. Node http.createServer: nodejs.org/api/http.html. Bun.serve: bun.sh/docs/api/http.

options.name: core.http.server serves one handler and answers a folder; routing, CORS and request ids move into the web package
options.detail:
Core keeps a server that answers every request with one HTTPHandler. The web package owns everything about routes: the table, matching, the 404, 405 and OPTIONS answers, middleware, CORS and request ids. web.app() hands its table to Core as one handler. Core keeps what belongs to one request and its connection: framing and limits, TLS, WebSocket upgrade, the status for a handler error, and the safe answer for files under a folder.

Beginner path: web.app(), app.get, then app.bind or app.serve(), unchanged. A folder of files needs no package: server.listen("127.0.0.1:8080", server.static_dir("public")). Expert path: server.listen with any handler, for a health probe or a proxy, with TLS and graceful shutdown the same way.
options.technical:
core.http.server gains two functions, one HTTPServer method and one small type, RoutePattern. Each replaces a private call.

listen: fn(on: String | TCPListener, handler: HTTPHandler, *, tls: HTTPServerTLS?{None}, deadline: Duration?{None}) -[Net]> HTTPServer HTTPError!
It replaces __bind on an address and __server_on on a bound listener. So app.serve still sees a busy port from core.net.tcp_listen and tries the next one. A failed bind or a bad TLS identity is HTTPError, as app.bind reports today.

HTTPServer.serve_once: fn(self) HTTPError! -[Net, FS.Read, Time]>
It answers the next connection, for tests, replacing __serve_once. It sits beside serve, wait and shutdown on the server listen returns.

static_dir: fn(root: String, *, prefix: String{""}, index: Bool{true}, dotfiles: Bool{false}, follow_links: Bool{false}) -> HTTPHandler Never!
Its handler is today's static mount answer: the dot-dot, dotfile and symlink checks, index.html, content type, ETag, 304 and byte ranges. It drops prefix from the path first. The web package's app.static_files routes {prefix}/* to it, so the folder escape checks keep one home.

RoutePattern is an opaque type with three operations.
route_pattern: fn(text: String) -> RoutePattern HTTPError!
match: fn(self, request: HTTPRequest) -> HTTPRequest?
overlaps: fn(self, other: RoutePattern) -> Bool.
 A pattern that does not parse is an Err worded as E2805. match returns the request tagged with the path values and the template only when the path really matches. So request.param and server.access_log work on routed requests, and no code can set a tag that did not match. overlaps is the clash test.

HTTPHandler stays in core.http.server. The package wraps its table in a function written where an HTTPHandler is expected, so the compiler's handler capture check still applies. A probe stores route functions in a list and wraps them this way. A handler's Err becomes a status in Core, as today: BodyTooLarge 413, InvalidFraming 400, UnsupportedEncoding 415, anything else 500.

Into the web package go HTTPMux, the table and its order, the 404, 405 with Allow, OPTIONS * and HEAD answers, middleware layers, CORS, request ids, route input decoding and OpenAPI. The one-pattern parser and matcher stay in Core behind RoutePattern, a narrow amendment to D-WEB-HOME1=A, which moves the router. The custom method check uses the public http.valid_method and http.method_parse.

Which clashes are found when. A route whose pattern is a literal or a constant gets E2804, E2805 and E2808 at check time, keyed on the #RouteTable marker the package declares. A probe shows two literal app.get rows refused with E2804. A pattern computed while the program runs is not seen by the check; the same probe with a computed pattern passes it.

That computed route is checked when it is added: overlaps finds the clash, and route_pattern's Err finds a bad pattern. The package words each through its own Diagnostic type, so the stop text carries the code, what, why and fix. The stop itself is a panic, E3001, because the coded stop is private to Core.

options.name: server.mux() and its HTTPMux route table become public again; the web package wraps it
options.detail:
Core keeps the route table type, HTTPMux, public with its get, post, mount, middleware, static_files, cors, request_id, bind and serve_once methods. web.app() builds one and adds pages on top.

Beginner path: web.app(), unchanged. Expert path: server.mux() builds a route table with no web package. That is the second builder D-ROUTE-ONE1=A removed, so two tables can again hold routes for one address.
options.technical:
core.http.server exports mux: fn() -> HTTPMux Never! again. HTTPMux's methods become public: the verbs get, post, put, delete, patch, head, options and custom, plus mount and middleware. static_files(prefix, root), cors(policy) and request_id() are public too. HTTPMux also lists its rows publicly, because web.openapi reads them.

Serving is mux.bind(address, tls:, deadline:) -[Net]> HTTPServer HTTPError! and mux.serve_once(listener) HTTPError! -[Net, FS.Read, Time]>. The web package's App holds an HTTPMux and forwards to it. Route stops stay coded, because the table stays in Core.

A route a program puts on its own mux is not in the app's table. So E2804 cannot see a clash between the two tables, and jet explain --routes lists only the app's rows. The compiler lowers route rows twice: once on HTTPMux in Core and once on #RouteTable in the package. This reverses part of D-ROUTE-ONE1=A.

options.name: The app type and its route table stay in Core under core.http.server; pages, forms and their markers move to the web package
options.detail:
The App type, with routes, binding and serving, stays in Core with its private calls. The web package keeps pages, forms, islands and the build steps. A package can add methods only to its own types, so pages cannot be App methods: they go on a second value, web.Site, that adds rows to the App.

Beginner path: a program with routes only is unchanged; a program with pages writes site: web.site(app) and site.page(...), two values for one app. Expert path: core.http.server.app() works with no web package.
options.technical:
App moves from Core/Web/Web.jet into Core/Http as core.http.server.App. It keeps its route table and its bind, serve, serve_once, static_files, cors, request_id and middleware methods, and its private calls stay private because it is in Core.

An external inherent method must be in the module of its type (spec, methods), so page, layout, loader, action, the render modes and assets move to web.Site. web.Site adds GET and POST rows to its App through App's public methods, so one table still holds every row.

#RouteTable is declared by Core, not by the battery, so the battery declares three of D-WEB-RUNTIME-API1=A's four markers; the rule stays keyed on a marker. C amends D-WEB-HOME1=A, whose card #6445 moves the router out of Core.

options.name: No serve call in Core for the package: the web package reads and writes HTTP itself over core.net
options.detail:
Core keeps its HTTP client and helpers but no server entry the package uses. The web package accepts TCP connections from core.net.tcp_listen, reads HTTP/1.1 requests, applies limits, runs TLS and writes responses.

Beginner path: web.app(), unchanged. Expert path: a program with no package has no server; it uses the web package or writes HTTP over core.net itself.
options.technical:
The package needs new public Core calls for what is private today. The server side of TLS is core.net.tls.__server and __server_context. A WebSocket upgrade uses the socket number and an upgrade cell: core.net.__tcp_fd, http.__upgrade_cell and http.__upgraded. Requests and responses are built by http.__server_request and http.__response.

A public socket number lets any code act on a connection the server owns. That is a general primitive of the kind D-WEB-RUNTIME-API1=A turned down. HTTP/1.1 framing then has two homes: core.http's client in Core and the server in the package. HTTPServer and its shutdown report leave Core.

comparisons.note: ListenAndServe takes one Handler. FileServer is a Handler for a folder. Request.SetPathValue (Go 1.22) lets any code tag a request; A lets only a real match do it. Its ServeMux panics on a clashing pattern at registration. Source: https://pkg.go.dev/net/http
Deno.serve takes one handler; routers such as Hono are libraries above it. The std serveDir answers a folder for a request. Source: https://docs.deno.com/api/deno/~/Deno.serve
http.server serves one handler class; socketserver's handle_request answers one request on a bound server, the shape of serve_once. Source: https://docs.python.org/3/library/socketserver.html
http.createServer takes one request listener; Express builds its router on top and adds no request id by default. Source: https://nodejs.org/api/http.html

recommendation.why: A gives the web package one public door, the shape Go, Deno, Node and Python ship. Each part stays with its owner: connections, TLS and file safety in Core, routes in the package. One table holds every route, as D-ROUTE-ONE1=A asks. The package needs no private Core call, and a folder of files needs no package at all.
gains: The web package serves through public Core calls only.
Route matching has one home, so E2804 sees every clash.
A program with no package serves one handler or a folder, with TLS and graceful shutdown.
Middleware keeps Core's HTTPHandler and the compiler's handler capture check.
The folder escape checks keep one home in Core.
Literal routes keep E2804 at check time; a computed route's clash still prints E2804 with its why and fix lines.
Only a real match tags a request with its route, so no code can forge path values.

losses.loss: Core gains four public items: server.listen, server.static_dir, HTTPServer.serve_once and the RoutePattern type.
losses.mitigation: Each replaces a private call that does the same job, and none holds a route table.

losses.loss: A route whose pattern is computed while the program runs and clashes stops as a panic, E3001, with E2804's text inside.
losses.mitigation: Literal and constant routes, the common case, are refused at check time with the full E2804 report.

whyNot.reason: B brings back server.mux(), a second route builder, so a clash across two tables escapes E2804 and jet explain --routes, and the compiler lowers route rows in two places.
C keeps the router in Core against D-WEB-HOME1=A, and splits one app into two values, because a package cannot add page methods to Core's App.
D makes a socket number public for WebSocket upgrades, a general primitive D-WEB-RUNTIME-API1=A turned down, and gives HTTP/1.1 framing two homes.

recommendation.tradeoff: Four small public items in Core, for a web package with no private Core call, one route table and a file server without a package.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude Opus. Adversarial model family: Claude Opus. Fresh agent: Main. The reader asked that the forgeable route tag and the run-time clash be engineered away. v3 r2 mints the tag only by a real match and keeps literal clashes at check time.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Read Core/Web/Web.jet on dev for the 36 calls to 15 private core.http.server names. Among them are __handler, __route_add, __layer_add, __static_files, __mux_routes, __bind, __serve_once and __server_on. rt.__coded_stop raises the route stops.

Read Core/Http/Server.jet. HTTPHandler is at line 154, HTTPServer at 278 with local_addr, serve, wait and shutdown(grace:). __serve_once is at 568, __static_files at 607 and __static_serve at 1832.

Read Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Expressions/Lambdas.jet:1474, where a function becomes an HTTPHandler, and Calls/Http.jet:400-423 for the handler capture check.

Probes on the batch-8 compiler. b6445/wrap: a list of stored route functions, wrapped in a function where an HTTPHandler is expected, answers a parsed request. b6445/diag: a package-declared Diagnostic type prints E2804 with What, Why and Fix in a run-time stop.

b6445/clash: two literal app.get("/a/:id") rows are E2804 at check time. b6445/clash_computed: the same clash with one pattern built at run time passes the check. Validate this payload with Tools/agent/ballots/Validate.jet.

decisions.title: Amending D-CORE-FILE-ADAPTERS1=A: on every Core stream the plain name takes text and the _bytes name takes bytes, and Writer is write_bytes plus flush
decisions.situation: You ratified D-CORE-FILE-ADAPTERS1=A: the JSON, CBOR, CSV and XML writers write through the Prelude's Writer trait, and the screen's Stdout and Stderr are Writers too. Two facts block that as written. Writer's write takes bytes, but Stdout's write takes text, and one type cannot have two methods named write. And Writer has no flush, so a log watched with tail -f shows nothing until the program ends. We recommend A. Every Core stream follows the rule core.files already uses: the plain name takes text and the _bytes name takes bytes. Writer becomes write_bytes, which writes every byte or fails, plus flush.
decisions.gist: Which names do Core's streams and the Writer trait use, so the screen, files, sockets and codecs fit one rule?
decisions.lesson: A codec turns values into JSON, CSV, CBOR or XML bytes, and under the ratified plan it writes through a Writer. Core names its write methods two ways today. Files and the screen say write for text and write_bytes for bytes. A child's stdin, a TCP socket and the Writer trait say write for bytes, write_all for every byte, and write_text for text. Writer also has no flush.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. Bytes are a list of U8 values, written [U8]; text is a String. A trait is a named set of methods; a type that has them implements the trait, and generic code can accept any such type. The Prelude is the part of Core every program sees without a use line. A default body is a method body the trait itself supplies, which a type may replace.

A buffered writer collects bytes in memory and hands them to the operating system in large pieces. Flush means: hand over whatever is collected now. tail -f is a Unix command that prints the lines a file gains while another program writes it.

A partial write takes some of the bytes, maybe not all, and returns how many it took. The caller must loop until every byte is taken.
decisions.story:
Ana's service logs events to a JSONL file, prints a summary on the screen, and sends frames to a peer over TCP. Her teammate watches the log with tail -f.

Under A her screen line stays out.write("summary"). She calls log.flush() after each event, and tail -f shows each event as a whole line. Her socket code says conn.write_bytes(frame), which sends every byte or fails. She can point a JSONL writer at term.stdout() or at the socket.

Under B a codec cannot write to the screen. Under C she writes out.write_text for the summary, and conn.write(frame) may send part of the frame. Under D her teammate sees records only in bursts. Under E her own writer type needs two impl blocks.

Under F she hands term.stdout().binary() to a codec. Under G a buffering writer she forgets to give flush still compiles, and the log stalls. Under H conn.write(frame) still means a partial byte write while out.write means text.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. The write and read method names on Core's streams: Stdout, Stderr, FileWriter, FileReader, a child process's pipes, TCPStream and UnixStream. It also decides the methods of the Prelude's Writer and Reader traits. It amends D-CORE-FILE-ADAPTERS1=A and changes nothing else that vote decided.

Core's first naming rule. core.files says read(path) and write(path, text) for text, and read_bytes(path) and write_bytes(path, bytes) for bytes (Core/Files/Files.jet:954-992). Stdout and Stderr say write(text), write_line(text), write_bytes(bytes) and flush (Core/Term/Term.jet:113-152).

Core's second naming rule. A child's stdin says write(bytes), which takes what the pipe accepts and returns the count, then write_all(bytes) and write_text(text). The sources are ProcessHandles.jet:516-545 and core-library.md:2988-2989. TCPStream has the same three, and its read(n) gives bytes while read_text(n) gives text (NetworkHandles.jet:102-114). The Writer trait has write(bytes) returning a count, and write_all (Compiler/Prelude/Traits.jet:249-253).

The trait's partial write is used by no one generically. FileWriter implements Writer.write by writing every byte and returning the length (Files.jet:430-436), so its write is never partial. The codecs only ever write whole buffers and flush.

Partial writes are a known trap. Rust's write may take part of a buffer, and Clippy denies ignoring its count as a correctness lint, unused_io_amount. Jet's own code falls in it: Doctor.jet:116 and Repl.jet:620 call child.stdin.write(bytes) and drop the result. A body larger than the pipe takes would be cut short with no error.

Go removed the trap at the contract. io.Writer's Write must return an error if it writes fewer bytes than given (src/io/io.go), so generic code never loops. A gives write_bytes that same contract.

Default bodies work. Probe r3 runs on the seed-b17 compiler. A user trait declares write_bytes and flush, with default bodies for write(text) and write_line(text). Counter implements only the two required methods. Screen replaces write with its own. A generic function calls all four through the bound and prints counter bytes 11 flushes 1, then screen texts 1 bytes 7. The Prelude's trait rows carry no default bodies today (OwnedTraitRows.jet:45-48), so A adds that.

Flush today. Each codec writer's flush calls the file's flush directly, at CborStream.jet:694, Csv.jet:729, Stream.jet:1525 and :2001 and Xml.jet:304. Under D-CORE-FILE-ADAPTERS1=A a codec holds a generic W, so it can call only the trait's methods. FileWriter buffers its writes (Files.jet:400-401). Without a trait flush, nothing reaches the file until the buffer fills or the program ends.

The held-back line end. The JSONL and CSV writers hold back each record's line end until the next write or finish (Stream.jet:1955-2013, Csv.jet:660-671). Probe p4 shows that after each flush the file holds one whole line fewer than the records written. Every option with a codec flush, all but D, has the codec's flush write the pending line end first. A finished file's bytes stay the same as today.

The missing last line end was never a mark. JSON Lines calls a final line terminator strongly recommended but not required (jsonlines.org). RFC 4180 section 2 says the last CSV record may or may not have an ending line break. So no reader can take a missing last line end to mean an unfinished file.

The beginner path. The core.term reference teaches out.write("done") (core-library.md:2260). It keeps working under A, B, F and H, and is E0112 under C. Today's E0112 fix line for bytes passed to a text write says to use interpolation (probe p3), which is the wrong advice.

One write for both kinds cannot work. A method whose parameter is String | [U8] does not satisfy a trait method taking [U8]: review probe r1 gets E0907. Review probe r2 shows an impl may add -[IO]> to a trait method that declares no effect, so Stdout's IO methods can implement Writer.

Size of the change, which weighs for no option. census-v3.mjs over the 20,620 .jet files at dev 8e1c67443b counts 195 write_all calls, 53 write_text and 80 read_text. It lists 137 lines for a hand read of byte reads and partial writes. Under A, Stdout's and Stderr's call sites do not change.

options.name: One rule on every Core stream: the plain name takes text, the _bytes name takes bytes; Writer is write_bytes, which writes every byte or fails, plus a required flush
options.detail:
Every Core stream says write(text), write_line(text) and write_bytes(bytes), as core.files and the screen do today. On the read side, read gives text and read_bytes(limit) gives up to limit bytes. Stdout and Stderr keep every name they have and implement Writer.

The trait. Writer requires write_bytes(bytes), which writes every byte or returns an error, and flush. It supplies write(text) and write_line(text) as default bodies over write_bytes, so a user writer writes two methods. Reader's read(limit) becomes read_bytes(limit); read_into is unchanged.

A partial write is no longer in the trait. A child's stdin, TCPStream and UnixStream keep it as write_some(bytes), which returns the count taken, for code that must stop at a deadline. The name says it may stop early.

Beginner path: out.write("hi") is unchanged, and so is the reference example. A file writer and a socket now take text the same way. Expert path: generic code over W: Writer writes text or bytes, and flush pushes a codec's records to the file.

Edge cases. Code written with Rust or Go habits, conn.write(frame) with bytes, is E0112, and the fix line names write_bytes. A codec's flush writes the record's pending line end first, then flushes its writer. A cut log ends on a whole line, which JSON Lines and CSV already treat as a complete file.
options.technical:
Compiler/Prelude/Traits.jet and OwnedTraitRows.jet:45-48: Writer becomes { write_bytes: fn(&self, bytes: [U8]) IOError!; flush: fn(&self) IOError!; write: fn(&self, text: String) IOError! { self.write_bytes(text.bytes()) }; write_line: fn(&self, text: String) IOError! { self.write_bytes("{text}\n".bytes()) } }. The Prelude's trait rows gain default bodies, using the rule user traits already follow (Examples/Modules/Library.jet:10-17; probe r3). Reader becomes { read_bytes(limit); read_into(buffer, limit) }.

Core/Term/Term.jet: Stdout and Stderr keep write, write_line, write_bytes, flush and is_tty, and wrap write_bytes and flush in impl Writer { }. Their own write and write_line replace the defaults with stdio_write. StdinHandle and the cursor reader rename read to read_bytes.

Core/Files/Files.jet: FileWriter's write_all becomes write_bytes, and its fake partial write at :433-436 is deleted. It gains write(text) from the default, and keeps write_line, flush and fsync. FileReader's read(max) becomes read_bytes(max).

The handle rows follow. In ProcessHandles.jet:516-545 a child's stdin write becomes write_some, write_all becomes write_bytes, and write_text becomes write. The child's stdout and stderr read becomes read_bytes. NetworkHandles.jet:102-133 does the same for TCPStream and UnixStream, and read_text(n) becomes read(n). In StreamHandles.jet:160-171, FileWriter's write_all row becomes write_bytes and FileReader's read row becomes read_bytes.

E0112 gains a fix line for a [U8] argument passed to a text write that names write_bytes. Each codec's flush writes its pending line end, then calls the trait's flush. The renames run as one cutover with every call site, sized by census-v3.mjs.

options.name: Names stay as they are; Stdout and Stderr do not implement Writer; Writer gains flush
options.detail:
Every stream keeps today's names. Stdout and Stderr keep write(text) and write_bytes(bytes) and are not Writers, so no codec can write to the screen. Writer keeps write(bytes) returning a count and write_all, and gains flush. The codec flush behaves as in A.

Beginner path: unchanged. Expert path: to stream records to the screen, encode a batch to text with jsonl.to_string and write it. That builds the whole batch in memory, outside the codec's size limits. A Linux or macOS program can open /dev/stdout as a file; Windows has no file path for a redirected stdout.

Edge cases: the two naming rules stay, so write means text on the screen and on files but bytes on a socket. The partial write stays in the trait.
options.technical: Core/Term/Term.jet is unchanged. D-CORE-FILE-ADAPTERS1=A's list of Writer types drops Stdout and Stderr. Traits.jet's Writer gains a required flush, and the codec flush changes are A's. No call site changes.
options.code:
out := term.stdout()
out.write("logging to events.jsonl\n")
log := jsonl.writer(files.append("events.jsonl"))
log.write(record)
log.flush()
// jsonl.writer(term.stdout()) is refused: Stdout is not a Writer.
out.write(jsonl.to_string(records))
conn.write_all(frame)

options.name: Byte-first names, as Rust: write and write_all take bytes and write_text takes text on every stream, Stdout included; Writer gains a required flush
options.detail:
Stdout and Stderr read like a child's stdin and a TCPStream: write(bytes) returns the count taken, write_all(bytes) writes every byte, and write_text(text) writes text. write_bytes goes away. FileWriter gains write_text. Writer gains flush.

Beginner path: out.write("hi") is E0112, and the reference example moves to out.write_text("hi"). Expert path: as in A, with write, write_all and flush in a user writer.

Edge cases: the plain name write takes part of the bytes, so code that forgets the count can lose bytes silently, as Doctor.jet:116 does today. core.files keeps write(path, text) for text, so files and streams still use two rules.
options.technical: Traits.jet: Writer { write: fn(&self, bytes: [U8]) -> Int IOError!; write_all; flush }. Term.jet: Stdout and Stderr gain write(bytes) and write_all, rename write(text) to write_text, and delete write_bytes. FileWriter gains write_text. The codec flush changes are A's. About 60 text writes and 18 write_bytes calls on the screen change.
options.code:
out := term.stdout()
out.write_text("logging to events.jsonl\n")
log := jsonl.writer(files.append("events.jsonl"))
log.write(record)
log.flush()
conn.write_all(frame)
files.write("notes.txt", "text")   // the file function still takes text

options.name: Names as in A, but flush stays on the concrete writers only; codec writers lose flush, and finish hands the writer back
options.detail:
The names follow A. Writer requires only write_bytes. Codec writers lose their flush method, since a generic codec cannot reach its writer's flush. finish ends the line, writes the closing bytes and hands the writer back, so the program can flush and close it.

Beginner path: write records, then file := log.finish() and file.flush(). Expert path: as in A without flush.

Edge cases: nothing a codec writes is certain to reach the file before finish. A long-running log fills FileWriter's buffer before any bytes appear, so tail -f sees records in bursts. A crash loses the last buffer.
options.technical: Traits.jet: Writer { write_bytes; write and write_line by default }. Every codec writer's flush (Cbor.jet:23, Json.jet:252, Jsonl.jet:33, and the four push types) is deleted. Each finish returns W instead of nothing. The renames are A's.
options.code:
log := jsonl.writer(files.append("events.jsonl"))
log.write(record)
// no flush: tail -f sees records only as the file buffer fills
file := log.finish()
file.flush()

options.name: Names as in A, with flush in a separate Prelude trait, Flush, and codec writers ask for both
options.detail:
The names follow A. A second Prelude trait, Flush, holds flush. Each codec writer takes W: [Writer, Flush], so its flush works as in A.

Beginner path: identical to A. Expert path: a user writer implements two traits to reach a codec; one with only Writer is refused at the constructor.

Edge cases: as in A. Jet has no where clause, so a codec cannot offer flush only to writers that have it. Every writer passed to a codec needs Flush, so the two traits always appear together.
options.technical: Compiler/Prelude/Traits.jet gains Flush: trait { flush: fn(&self) IOError! }. FileWriter, Stdout, Stderr, TCPStream and a child's stdin implement both. The codec constructors and types take <W: [Writer, Flush]>. OwnedTraitRows.jet opens Flush as a bound user code can name. Every other change is A's.
options.code:
writer: fn<W: [Writer, Flush]>(output: &&W) -> JSONLWriter<W> EncodingError!
// A user writer: impl Writer { write_bytes } and impl Flush { flush }.

options.name: Stdout and Stderr keep text names only; out.binary() returns a byte Writer over the same buffer, as Python's sys.stdout.buffer
options.detail:
Stdout and Stderr keep write(text), write_line(text), flush and is_tty. Bytes move to a view: out.binary() returns StdoutBytes, a Writer over the same stdout buffer. Writer gains flush, and the codec flush works as in A. Other streams keep today's names.

Beginner path: out.write("hi") unchanged. Expert path: jsonl.writer(term.stdout().binary()) streams records to the screen.

Edge cases: text and bytes share one buffer, so they keep call order. The name write means text on Stdout but bytes on its own binary view, a child's stdin and TCPStream. Each screen stream needs a second type.
options.technical: Core/Term/Term.jet gains StdoutBytes and StderrBytes, each holding the fd, with write, write_all and flush routed to stdio_bytes and stdio_flush, and impl Writer. Stdout.binary() and Stderr.binary() return them. write_bytes is deleted; its callers write out.binary().write_all(bytes). The codec flush changes are A's.
options.code:
out := term.stdout()
out.write("logging to events.jsonl\n")
screen := jsonl.writer(term.stdout().binary())
screen.write(record)
screen.finish()
conn.write(frame)   // bytes, and may send part of them

options.name: As A, but Writer's flush has a default body that does nothing, as Java's OutputStream
options.detail:
As A, except Writer declares flush: fn(&self) IOError! { Ok() } as a default body. FileWriter, Stdout and Stderr write their own flush; a user writer may leave it out.

Beginner path: as in A. Expert path: a user writer implements write_bytes alone, and adds flush only if it buffers.

Edge cases: a buffering user writer that forgets flush compiles. Its codec's flush then returns Ok without pushing bytes, so a tailed log stalls with no error.
options.technical: Compiler/Prelude/Traits.jet: Writer as in A, with flush: fn(&self) IOError! { Ok() }. Every other change is A's.

options.name: The trait renames its partial write to write_some, Stdout keeps write for text, and a child's stdin and TCPStream keep write for bytes
options.detail:
Writer becomes write_some(bytes) returning the count, write_all(bytes) and flush. Stdout and Stderr keep write(text) and write_line(text), rename write_bytes to write_all, and gain write_some. FileWriter gains write_some. A child's stdin and TCPStream keep write, write_all and write_text.

Beginner path: out.write("hi") unchanged. Expert path: a user writer implements three methods, one of them a partial write.

Edge cases: the name write means text on Stdout and Stderr but bytes on a child's stdin and a TCPStream. Moving code from one to the other gives a type error, not wrong output. The partial conn.write trap stays.
options.technical: Traits.jet: Writer { write_some: fn(&self, bytes: [U8]) -> Int IOError!; write_all; flush }. Term.jet: write_bytes renamed write_all; write_some added; write(text) kept. FileWriter gains write_some. The codec flush changes are A's. A child's stdin and TCPStream need write_some as a second name for their write before they can implement Writer.
options.code:
out := term.stdout()
out.write("logging to events.jsonl\n")
out.write_all(bytes)
child.stdin.write(bytes)   // bytes, and may send part of them
conn.write_text("hello\n")

comparisons.note: io.Writer has one method, and its contract forbids a silent short write: Write must return an error if it writes fewer bytes than given. Generic callers never loop. A's write_bytes takes this contract. Flushing lives on bufio.Writer and the optional http.Flusher. Source: https://github.com/golang/go/blob/master/src/io/io.go
comparisons.code: n, err := w.Write(frame) // n < len(frame) implies err != nil

comparisons.note: Write::write may take part of a buffer, and write_all takes all of it; flush is required. Clippy denies an ignored write count as a correctness lint, unused_io_amount, because the short write is a common bug. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-clippy/master/index.html#unused_io_amount
A text stream's write takes text, and sys.stdout.buffer is the byte stream beneath it, sharing its order; the shape of F. Source: https://docs.python.org/3/library/sys.html#sys.stdout

Writer takes text and OutputStream takes bytes, two type families; OutputStream's flush has a body that does nothing, the shape of G. Source: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/io/OutputStream.html#flush()

recommendation.why: A extends the rule files and the screen already use to every Core stream: write takes text and write_bytes takes bytes. So out.write("hi") keeps working and one name never means two kinds. Writer's write_bytes writes every byte or fails, as Go's io.Writer does, so the short-write trap Rust lints against is gone. A required flush with a line-ending codec flush lets a tailed log show each record.
gains: write, write_line and write_bytes mean the same on files, the screen, pipes and sockets.
The beginner's out.write("hi") and the reference example are unchanged.
No generic write can silently send part of a buffer.
A user writer joins every codec with two methods.
Codecs stream straight to the screen with their limits, and a tailed log shows each flushed record.

losses.loss: Pipes, sockets, FileWriter and Reader rename their byte methods, so Rust or Go habits like conn.write(frame) with bytes are E0112.
losses.mitigation: It fails at compile time, never at run time, and the fix line names write_bytes. The renames land in one cutover with every call site.

losses.loss: Every Writer must write flush, even one with no buffer.
losses.mitigation: It is one line, flush: fn(&self) IOError! { Ok() }. A default body, option G, would let a buffering writer forget it and pass silently.

losses.loss: Generic code over a Writer cannot write part of a buffer and stop at a deadline.
losses.mitigation: Pipes and sockets keep write_some for that, on the concrete type. No codec needs it, and Go's io.Writer makes the same choice.

whyNot.reason: B keeps two naming rules and leaves the codecs unable to write to the screen except through a whole batch in memory.
C breaks the beginner's out.write("hi"), keeps a plain write that may send part of the bytes, and still disagrees with core.files.
D cannot show a record before the file buffer fills, so a tailed log stalls and a crash loses the last buffer.
E puts flush in a trait that every codec, Core's only generic writer user, asks for anyway, so a user writer needs two impl blocks.
F needs a second type per screen stream, and write still means text on the screen but bytes on pipes and sockets.
G lets a buffering writer that forgets flush compile, and its codec's flush then pushes nothing, with no error.
H keeps write meaning text on the screen but bytes on pipes and sockets, and keeps a partial write in the trait.

recommendation.tradeoff: Pipes, sockets and FileWriter rename their byte methods once, and every writer writes flush, for one naming rule across Core, no silent short writes, and logs that show each flushed record.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude Opus. Adversarial model family: Claude Opus. Fresh agent: Main, which did not write this rework. The pass attacked A on unbounded text reads, short writes at a deadline, a required flush on unbuffered writers, and text names on sockets. Each holds: read_bytes(limit), write_some, a one-line flush, and E0112 with a fix line naming write_bytes.

decisions.title: Should Jet try a fully data-parallel compiler design?
decisions.situation: Most compilers handle code one piece at a time: look at this node, then its children. A data-parallel compiler instead runs each pass as operations over whole tables at once, like a spreadsheet formula applied to a whole column. That can use wide vector hardware, and graphics cards, which normal compilers cannot. It has been shown for small languages, not yet for a language as rich as Jet. Jet's speed plan reaches its 30-million-lines-per-second goal on ordinary processor cores, so this is about going past the goal or rescuing a step that falls short. You are asked whether, and when, to explore it. We recommend A: one bounded prototype of one pass, started once the plan meets its goal or a step stalls, with a bar it must clear.
decisions.gist: Should Jet fund one bounded prototype of a compiler pass written as whole-array operations, and when?
decisions.lesson: A new shape of algorithm can use hardware the usual one cannot, but it must beat the usual one on every core.
decisions.explainer: A pass is one step of the compiler, such as name resolution. A column is a flat list of values, one per node. SIMD means one instruction working on many values at once. A GPU is a graphics card used for general computing. Wall time is the time on the clock from start to finish.
decisions.story: Even with 32 threads, a one-node-at-a-time compiler hits a ceiling. Vector instructions handle many values per step, and a graphics card has thousands of small cores, but both help only if the work is written as whole-column operations.
decisions.inWild: Co-dfns and Pareas are research compilers. No production compiler for a large language works this way.
decisions.detail:
Prior art: Co-dfns, Aaron Hsu's APL compiler (thesis, 2019), runs its passes as array operations on a GPU. Pareas (Voetter and others, 2022) lexes, parses and generates code on a GPU.

The plan's exit (#5479 c3, 30M lines/s) is budgeted inside 32 CPU threads: step 6 (#5479 c9) allows at most 1 µs of CPU per line. Jet has no general GPU compute path today; `GPU` is an effect root for graphics and game operations. The plan's steps 0 to 5 are staffed by one agent.

Under A, the prototype starts once #5479 c3 lands, or earlier if a plan step stalls below its gate. One pass is rewritten as array operations over #6793's flat columns: name resolution, or type propagation for a subset. It runs on CPU vector instructions, and on a GPU only if Jet has a GPU compute path by then. The bar to continue: at least 4x less wall time than the scalar pass running on all 32 threads, on the c1 corpus, with identical results and diagnostics.

Below the bar, the prototype is recorded as evidence and stopped. Under D, the same prototype starts as soon as #6793 lands.

decisions.title: Should 'checking time grows in step with the code' be a language rule?
decisions.situation: Some language rules can make the compiler's work grow much faster than the code: doubling a file can quadruple, or worse, the time to check it. Swift's slow type inference on long arithmetic and Rust's trait solver on deep generic code are known examples. Jet already has a scaling test that fails when a compiler step grows too fast on its sample programs. But no language rule says every rule must keep pace, so a rule that no sample exercises can still blow up on someone's code. You are asked whether 'checking keeps pace with the code' becomes a language rule. We recommend A: adopt the rule, audit today's rules once, add a scaling sample per rule, and ballot only real language changes.
decisions.gist: Should every language rule check in time that grows in step with the code, with one audit of today's rules?
decisions.lesson: Compile speed is partly a language-design property: a rule that can blow up will eventually blow up on someone's code.
decisions.explainer: 'Proportional' (linear) means twice the code takes about twice the time. The rule allows a little more, N log N, the cost of sorting a list, which is what Jet's scaling test already accepts. 'Super-linear' means much more, such as four times. Type inference is the compiler working out types you did not write. A trait solver finds which implementation of an interface a call uses.
decisions.story: A generated file has a 20,000-arm choice. If the checker's work grows with the square of the arms, the file takes minutes and gigabytes to check, and nothing warned anyone in advance.
decisions.inWild: Go was designed for fast compiles, with simple inference and no overloading. Swift's expression type checker is known for 'expression too complex' errors. Rust's trait solver can be slow on deep generics. Zig and Jai keep inference local.
decisions.detail:
Today: Tools/perf/scaling (Tower #4319, #4601) compiles generated program shapes at growing sizes. It fails when a compiler phase or work counter grows faster than k * N log N, but it covers only the shapes it generates. #5910 c61 (open) adds one shape: a 20,000-branch chain must check with peak memory growing at most linearly from 1,000 to 20,000 branches.

One audit candidate is visible in code. The ownership last-use query reads the rest of a body's statements at a use (Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Ownership/LastUse.jet). That may be quadratic in a long body with many moves; it is not measured.

Under A, the rule is written in Docs/spec: checking takes at most N log N time and memory in the program's size. Compile-time code a user writes is excluded, because it is the user's own program.

One audit in Docs/audits lists every rule whose cost can grow faster: inference, overload and trait resolution, exhaustiveness, flow typing, ownership, generic instantiation depth and compile-time evaluation. Each finding gets a shape in Tools/perf/scaling. A finding that is only slow checking code is fixed under a card like any bug. A finding that needs the language to change gets its own ballot.

options.gist: Checking keeps pace with the code (at most N log N). One audit lists today's exceptions; slow code is fixed as a bug, and only language changes get ballots.
