decisions.title: Should the compiler keep a syntax tree, and in what form?
decisions.situation: A syntax tree is the compiler's in-memory outline of a program, one entry for each piece of code, built while reading the text. Jet builds it from many small boxes; in one measured run, copying and freeing such boxes, with similar compile-time values, took a fifth of the busy time. The tree is not where the finished program gets faster: every optimization runs later, on a lower form of the code. We recommend A: keep one compact outline per file, a flat list that the checker, formatter and editor all share.
decisions.gist: Should Jet keep one compact syntax list per file, drop the syntax tree, or keep today's tree of small boxes?
decisions.lesson: Keep the outline, but make it a flat list: the cost was the boxes, not the outline.
decisions.explainer:
A syntax tree, also called an AST, is the outline the parser builds from source text. The checker reads it to find errors. It then writes a checked body for each function. The lowering step turns the checked body into IR, a simple instruction list. The optimizer and the machine-code generator work only on IR.

A flat list stores the outline as a few plain arrays: kind, position and size per entry, children before their parent. It needs no boxes and no pointers, so it is cheap to build, copy and free.
decisions.story: Priya's team has 200,000 lines of Jet. Every `jet build` and every editor keystroke reads all of it into small boxes, copies some of them, and frees them. A compact list per file removes that waste without taking anything away from the formatter, the editor or the optimizer.
decisions.inWild: Zig parses each file into one flat node list (std.zig.Ast: tokens, nodes and extra_data arrays). zig fmt, the compiler and the language server read that list. Carbon's toolchain stores its parse tree as one flat array in postorder (toolchain/docs/parse.md). Rust checks ownership on MIR with liveness, not on syntax (RFC 2094). Tiny C emits code while parsing, with no tree, but has no generics, ownership or formatter to serve.
decisions.detail:
Where optimization happens. All 17 optimizer passes run on IR (Compiler/JetIR/Source/Opt.jet:97, IR_OPT_PASS_NAMES). JetIR, JetBackend and JetEval never name the parser's types: their `.Expr` matches are variants of the checked body (BodyLambdaBody.Expr). So the outline's form cannot change the finished program. Rust (MIR), Go (SSA), Swift (SIL) and Zig (AIR) also optimize on a lower form, never on the syntax tree.

What it costs today. The parser builds boxed payload enums (Expr 51 variants, Stmt 35, Item 24, Pattern) in Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/AST. Clones and drops of these trees and comptime values were 20.5% of busy samples on the measured slice and 7.8% on `check main.jet` (Docs/research/fast-compiler-architecture-2026-09-30.md, line 83). The ownership last-use query walks the remaining statements' trees by name for each question (Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Ownership/LastUse.jet). The driver's route and plugin scans walk the trees too (Loader.jet, PluginFacts.jet).

Under A, the parser writes one flat postorder record per file into the file's arena. It holds the lexer's token columns plus node columns: kind tag, span, subtree size, first token and payload. This is #6793 S4. The Expr, Stmt, Pattern and Item enums and the Func struct are deleted, and every reader uses accessors. The checker, formatter, language server, semantic index and driver scans read the same record.

Generic and compile-time bodies keep their node ranges for later use. The rest of a file's record is freed once its bodies are checked (#6793 S7). The ownership last-use rule moves to one backward liveness pass over the checked body, so the checker no longer walks syntax ahead. The proof is #6793's: the self-host fixed point, byte-identical ui snapshots and cases, and the c1 throughput cell (#5479 c1).

options.name: One flat syntax list per file, shared by every tool
options.gist: The parser writes a compact list per file. The checker, formatter and editor read it, and ownership moves to the checked body.
options.detail: No boxes, no clones, one parser. Generic and compile-time bodies keep their slice of the list. The rest is freed after checking. The optimizer is unchanged, because it already runs on IR. The list keeps every token with its byte span, comments and blank lines included, so jet fmt stays lossless. Code a compile-time splice generates is written as rows of its own generated file. An editor change re-reads only the edited file.

options.name: Keep today's tree of small boxes
options.gist: Every piece of code stays its own box, copied and freed as today.
options.detail: No change to the parser or its readers. The per-function pipeline (#5479 c8) still fuses later steps.

options.name: No stored syntax for ordinary code
options.gist: The parser feeds the checker directly. Generic bodies are re-read from text, and the tools get their own parser.
options.detail: Ordinary bodies go straight from parser notes to the checked body. Generic and compile-time bodies are re-parsed for each use. The formatter and editor keep a separate tree-building parser.

recommendation.why: A removes the measured cost, the boxes and their copies, and keeps everything the outline is for. The finished program is unchanged, because optimization runs on IR.
gains: No per-entry boxes or copies, part of a measured fifth of busy time
One parser and one list for the checker, formatter and editor
Optimization of the finished program is unchanged

losses.loss: Generic and compile-time bodies keep their part of the list after checking.
losses.mitigation: Only those bodies' slices stay. They are flat arrays with no boxes, and every other entry is freed once its file is checked.

whyNot.reason: B keeps the boxes and copies that, with compile-time values, took a fifth of busy time in one run, for no gain.
C needs a second parser for the tools, re-parses generic bodies for every use, and saves little over a flat list.

recommendation.tradeoff: Generic bodies keep a small flat slice after checking, in exchange for no boxes, one parser and an unchanged optimizer.

decisions.title: How far should the compiler go in tuning operating-system costs?
decisions.situation: When a compiler handles a gigabyte of code per second, small operating-system costs add up. Examples are each new page of memory the system hands out, each separate file read, and each step of writing the output. These are fixed costs every compile pays. Linux offers ways to pay them in bulk; other systems offer different ones. Fast paths can also backfire: Jet's memory allocator turns large pages off today, because on a busy machine they can stall every thread. You are asked how far Jet's compiler should go. We recommend A: per-system fast paths inside the shared runtime, each kept only where a measurement shows a gain, with identical output everywhere.
decisions.gist: Should the compiler use operating-system fast paths such as large memory pages and batched file reads, and where?
decisions.lesson: At high speed fixed costs dominate, so pay them in bulk, but only where a busy machine measures a real win.
decisions.explainer: A memory page is the unit the system hands out, usually 4 KB. A large page is 2 MB, so far fewer hand-outs are needed, but each is slower to set up. Pre-faulting means asking for the pages up front. io_uring is a Linux way to submit many file reads at once. An arena is a block of memory a compiler step fills and then frees all at once. The program image is the runnable machine code the compiler produces.
decisions.story: `jet run hello.jet` compiles a tiny program, yet it still pays these fixed costs: memory handed out a page at a time, and each file read on its own. With bulk paths those costs shrink for every compile, large or small.
decisions.inWild: The mold linker pre-sizes its output file and spreads its work over every core. Zig's compiler once never freed memory until exit and dropped that policy as compile-time work grew. Most compilers use the general allocator and plain reads.
decisions.detail:
Today: `jet run` and `jet dev` link the program image and run it from memory (jet_cli_launch in Compiler/JetCli/Source/Cli/Host.jet). They write a file under `.jet/build` only when the system refuses executable memory.

The runtime allocator deliberately keeps 4 KiB pages: alloc_region_map in Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/Alloc.jet sets MADV_NOHUGEPAGE. Its reason: a first touch of a huge page zeroes 2 MiB, and an advised huge region compacts memory on fault. That stalls every allocating thread on a loaded host. The runtime has no io_uring or other batched read path.

Under A, the compiler's phase arenas (#6793 S7) may use large pages and be pre-faulted in one call. That holds only where the size is known up front and the c1 throughput cell (#5479 c1) shows a gain on both an idle and a loaded host. The general allocator keeps its 4 KiB pages. Source files are read in one batch: io_uring on Linux, plain reads elsewhere. The runtime and precompiled Core (#6328 c22) sit at fixed places in the image, so each compile only patches its own code.

All of it lives in the shared runtime (I9) and changes timing only, never output. Each fast path has the plain path as its tested fallback. Arenas are freed in bulk at phase end, so nothing is left for process exit to clean up (I1).

options.gist: Large-page arenas, batched reads and a pre-laid-out image wherever the system offers them and a measurement shows a gain; identical output everywhere.
options.detail: Fast paths live only in the shared runtime; a system without one uses the plain path. Each is kept only where the c1 cell shows a gain on an idle and a loaded host. Proof: identical goldens on every system, timings reported per system.

hello

options.gist: No system-specific fast paths.
options.detail: One plain path on every system.

options.name: Linux fast paths only
options.gist: Tune Linux and leave other systems on the plain path.
options.detail: Fast paths on Linux only.

options.name: Never free compiler memory; let exit release it
options.gist: Skip freeing during a compile and let the system reclaim everything when the compiler exits.
options.detail: The compiler's own memory is never returned while it runs. Each compile saves the cost of freeing, but peak memory grows with everything the compile ever held. It needs an exception to I1, which says safe Jet cannot leak.
options.code:
$ jet run hello.jet
hello
# nothing freed until the compiler exits

recommendation.why: A cuts fixed per-compile cost wherever a system allows it, keeps only measured wins, and never changes output.
gains: Lower fixed cost for every compile
No output differences
No regression on loaded machines

losses.loss: More runtime code for each system's fast path.
losses.mitigation: Fast paths sit behind one runtime interface, the plain path is the tested fallback, and a path that measures no faster is dropped.

whyNot.reason: B leaves fixed costs that dominate small compiles.
C leaves other systems slower for no design reason.
D trades unbounded memory growth for a small saving that arenas freed in bulk already give.

recommendation.tradeoff: Some per-system runtime code in exchange for lower fixed cost everywhere.

decisions.title: May a fast vector scan skip clean code before the compiler's checks?
decisions.situation: Before Jet builds a program, it checks the code for mistakes, one small piece at a time. Processors have vector instructions that look at 16 to 64 pieces in one step, which could speed up the common case of code with no mistakes. The risk is two versions of a check that disagree, or error messages that change. We recommend A: a fast vector scan only marks stretches that might hold a mistake, and today's precise check alone writes every message and answer.
decisions.gist: Should a fast vector scan mark which stretches of code need checking, while today's checks still write every message?
decisions.lesson: Use the fast path only to decide where to look; let one precise path decide what to say.
decisions.explainer: A vector instruction, also called SIMD, does the same small test on 16 to 64 values at once. A diagnostic is an error or warning message with its place in the source. A filter is a quick test that answers either 'certainly fine' or 'maybe not'. A 'maybe' only sends that stretch to the precise check, so a cautious filter costs a little time and never changes a message.
decisions.story: Sam saves a 5,000-line file and the editor rechecks it. Almost every line is fine. A vector scan clears most of the file in a few steps, and the precise check looks only at the stretch around Sam's typo. Sam sees the same message, in the same place, as before.
decisions.inWild: simdutf's validate_utf8_with_errors checks text 64 bytes at a time with vector instructions. When a block fails, it rewinds and runs its scalar validator from there to report the exact error position (src/generic/utf8_validation/utf8_validator.h). simdjson finds structure with vectors and parses values with scalar code. Most compilers check node by node with no vector filter.
decisions.detail:
Today every check after lexing is scalar: it looks at one token or node at a time. The optimizer already turns a plain counting loop over bytes into SSE2 vector code (JetIR OptReduce.jet:190 calls Compiler/JetBackend/Source/X64/Count.jet). Jet's lane types, such as U8x16 and U8x32, define each operation as the scalar operation applied lane by lane. So the same source runs on every machine (Docs/spec/reference/core-library.md, SIMD lanes; D-SIMD3=B).

Under A, the scalar check stays the only code that writes diagnostics or computes results, such as which declaration a name means. A vector filter runs first over blocks of 64 tokens or nodes. It answers 'certainly clean' or 'maybe' per block. Each 'maybe' block, with its neighbors at the edges, goes to the scalar check. A filter tests a simpler, wider condition than its check, for example 'any token of these kinds'.

Filters are written in plain Jet with lane types or loops the optimizer turns into vector code, never with unsafe processor intrinsics. A machine without vector units runs the same code lane by lane. A differential test runs every check over all test corpora and generated inputs twice, with filters on and with filters off. Diagnostics must be byte-identical and results equal. A filter lands only where the throughput cell (#5479 c1) shows a gain. It depends on #6793's flat columns (S4); the lexer's own vector classifier is #5910 c6.

options.name: Vector scan marks the spots; today's check writes every message
options.gist: A portable vector filter clears clean blocks. The existing precise check runs on the rest and alone writes messages and answers.
options.detail: One implementation of each rule. The filter only chooses where the check looks. A test with filters on and off must give byte-identical messages and equal results. A filter may clear a block only by a rule that is conservative by construction: every byte in it belongs to a class the precise check accepts without context. Generated inputs and fuzzing run the on/off differential.

options.name: Scalar checks only
options.gist: Every check keeps looking at one piece at a time.
options.detail: No change. Checks of clean code cost the same as today.
options.code:
// A misspelled name; every token is checked one at a time.
show: fn(name: String) { print("hello {nmae}") }

options.name: Full vector checks that write their own messages
options.gist: Each chosen check is rewritten in vector form, which reports errors itself, with a coarser place or order.
options.detail: A second implementation of each rule. Messages may point at a block instead of the exact token, or come in a different order.

recommendation.why: A speeds up checking of clean code, which is almost all code, while one precise implementation still writes every message and answer.
gains: Clean code is cleared many pieces per step
Messages and answers come from one implementation
Same code on every machine, no unsafe intrinsics

losses.loss: A filter bug could call a block clean and hide a mistake.
losses.mitigation: Filters test a wider, simpler condition than the check. The on-and-off test over every corpus and generated input fails on any difference.

whyNot.reason: B leaves the speed-up for clean code unused, with no gain in correctness over A.
C keeps two versions of each rule that can drift, and makes messages less exact.

recommendation.tradeoff: A small filter beside each chosen check, guarded by an on-and-off test, in exchange for faster checking with unchanged messages.

decisions.title: C library features Jet leaves out on purpose: floating-point flags, thread attributes, signal masks and message queues
decisions.situation: The C standard library is the toolbox every C program on Linux uses. Jet is replacing it with its own Core library, and a census lists each C function and the Jet call that does its job. Thirteen groups still have no Jet counterpart, because C threads, signals and arithmetic work differently from Jet's. For example, C sets a hidden overflow flag after a multiplication, while Jet shows the overflow in the result itself. Someone porting a C program meets these gaps first. You are asked whether Jet should copy these thirteen groups or say plainly that Jet does not need them, naming the Jet way for each. We recommend naming the Jet way and not copying them.
decisions.gist: Should Jet copy thirteen C library groups that clash with how Jet works, or say they are not needed and point to the Jet way?
decisions.lesson: A new kitchen does not need a part for every gadget of the old one. If the new oven has a built-in timer, the old clip-on timer is not missing. Jet does many C jobs in another place: an overflow shows in the value itself, and a task is stopped by cancelling it. This vote decides whether those old parts are copied anyway.
decisions.explainer: Words used here. libc is the C standard library. A census is a list of every libc function and its Jet counterpart. A task is Jet's unit of concurrent work, like a C thread. A signal is a message the operating system sends to a process, such as Ctrl-C. A mask blocks some signals for a while. A floating-point flag is a hidden note C keeps when arithmetic overflows or loses precision.
decisions.story: Ravi ports a C tool that checks an overflow flag after a long calculation, and that stops a worker thread with pthread_kill. Under A the census row for fetestexcept says to check the result with math.is_inf or math.is_finite. The row for pthread_kill says to call cancel on the task. Ravi writes those two lines. Under B Ravi finds core.sys.fenv and a per-task kill call, which only some machines support, and the rest of Jet never sets or reads them.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. The owner's 2026-11-08 rule (Q18) is parity coverage: each libc gap is either filled with idiomatic Jet, or carries an owner ruling that Jet does not need it. Tools/agent/LibcCensus.jet lists 277 families; 33 are GAP. This ballot covers the thirteen whose C shape clashes with a Jet rule. The other GAP families are being filled: complex and Bessel functions, run-once, task-local storage, semaphores, read-write locks, descriptor duplication, terminals, sockets, shared memory, fences and pthread_atfork.

The thirteen families follow, each with the Jet way its row would name.

1. fenv.h exception flags (feclearexcept and six more). There are no sticky flags: the result carries the fact (math.is_inf, math.is_nan, math.is_finite), and checked integer arithmetic stops on overflow.

2. fenv.h rounding and environment (fegetround, fesetround and eight more). Jet fixes round-to-nearest-even; directed rounding is math.floor, math.ceil, math.trunc and Decimal's rounding modes.

3. pthread_attr_*. A task takes no attributes; stack and placement belong to the runtime.

4. pthread_getschedparam, pthread_setschedparam and pthread_setschedprio. There is no per-task priority; the scheduler is fair.

5. pthread_mutexattr_*, the prioceiling calls and pthread_mutex_consistent. Jet has one lock kind (tasks.lock), with no robust, priority-ceiling or process-shared locks.

6. pthread_condattr_*. Deadlines use the monotonic clock, and conditions are not shared between processes.

7. pthread_spin_*. Use tasks.lock; whether to spin is the runtime's choice.

8. pthread_kill. A task handle's cancel() stops one task.

9. sigprocmask and the sigset family (sigaddset through sigaltstack). Signals arrive as values through process.signals, so nothing needs blocking.

10. posix_spawnattr_getsigmask and setsigmask. These follow item 9.

11. mqueue.h. Use channels inside a process, and pipes or sockets between processes.

12. fmtmsg. Use core.log.

13. gethostid. core.sys.hostname and core.sys.uname name the machine; libc's 32-bit host id is neither stable nor unique.

pthread_atfork is not in this ballot, because core.sys.fork exists.

Under A each row becomes coverage NotNeeded, with a note citing the owner ruling on #6696 and naming the Jet way. LibcCensus.jet already checks that a NotNeeded note cites the ruling.

options.name: Say not needed, and name the Jet way
options.detail: The thirteen groups stay out of Jet. Each census row says not needed and names the Jet call that does the job.
options.technical: In Tools/agent/LibcCensus.jet, set coverage .NotNeeded on the thirteen GAP rows (fenv x2, pthread_attr, schedparam, mutexattr, condattr, spin, pthread_kill, sigset, spawnattr sigmask, mqueue, fmtmsg, gethostid). Each note cites 'owner ruling on #6696' and names the Jet API. No Core change.

options.name: Copy them into Core
options.detail: Core gets a floating-point flag module, thread attribute records, signal masks and message queues, with the C names translated.
options.technical: Add core.sys.fenv (test, clear, raise, round mode), task attribute records, a per-task signal call, sigset values with process masks, and POSIX message queues as runtime rows on Linux. Every engine must save and restore the floating-point state around task switches, and the web engine has none of them.

comparisons.note: std has no fenv, no signal masks and no thread priorities; the libc crate exposes raw calls.
No floating-point flags, goroutines take no attributes, and os/signal delivers signals on a channel.

recommendation.why: Each of these jobs already has one Jet way, and copying the C shape would add a second mechanism that most engines cannot honour.
gains: One mechanism per job: overflow in the value, cancel for tasks, signals as values.
Every census row still names where the job is done.

losses.loss: A C program ported line by line has no same-named call for these thirteen groups.
losses.mitigation: The census row for each C name prints the Jet call to use, so the porter finds it from the C name.

whyNot.reason: B adds hidden global state and second mechanisms, Linux-only rows the web engine cannot support, and task-switch costs for every program.

recommendation.tradeoff: No same-named C calls for thirteen groups, in exchange for one Jet way per job on every engine.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Use the Jet repository at 81b426cf46. Run JET=<jet> jet Tools/agent/LibcCensus.jet from the root and read its Gaps by area section. The thirteen families are the GAP rows at LibcCensus.jet lines 120, 121, 257, 281, 284, 296, 297, 301, 304, 306, 334, 359 and 376.

Check that Compiler/Prelude/Core.rows exports core.math is_inf, core.tasks lock, core.process signals, core.log, and core.sys hostname, uname and fork. A task handle's cancel() is used at tests/run/Concurrency/StopBoundaries.jet:82. Option A's program prints overflowed. Validate this payload with Tools/agent/ballots/Validate.jet.

surface.gist: Should Jet copy thirteen C library groups that clash with Jet, or name the Jet way instead?
surface.lesson: C keeps hidden flags, thread settings and signal masks. Jet does those jobs elsewhere: an overflow shows in the value, and a task is stopped by cancelling it.

current.note: Today the census lists these groups as gaps with no answer.

wild.note: Go has no float flags and delivers signals on a channel.
wild.code: signal.Notify(c, os.Interrupt)

options.name: Name the Jet way
options.gist: Each group is marked not needed, with the Jet call to use.
gains: One way per job.
Works on every engine.
losses: No same-named C calls.

proposed.code:
if math.is_inf(big) -> print("overflowed")
worker.cancel()

options.name: Copy them
options.gist: Core gains flag, attribute, mask and queue calls.
gains: C code ports name for name.
losses: Hidden global state.
Linux-only calls.

recommendation.why: Each job already has one Jet way, and the copies would be second mechanisms most engines cannot honour.
gains: One way per job.
The census still names each answer.

losses.loss: No same-named C calls for these groups.
losses.mitigation: Each census row names the Jet call.

whyNot.reason: Hidden state, second mechanisms and Linux-only calls.

recommendation.tradeoff: No C names for thirteen groups, for one Jet way everywhere.

decisions.title: How an app declares and uses a typed database table: a table value with a key function, a marker on the row type, or SQL checked against the migrated schema
decisions.situation: A database table is a list of rows on disk that a program reads and changes. In a Jet app today, a programmer writes the SQL text for every table by hand and turns each result row into a struct with a decode call. Nothing ties a table to its row type or its key, and nothing checks the SQL against the tables. Live screens refresh a whole table after any write. This vote picks how an app names a table, its key and its row type, and how a change to the row type reaches the stored table. It also fixes the rule that each method that writes runs as one transaction. We recommend A: a typed table value made from the row type and a key function.
decisions.gist: Should an app's tables be typed values with a key function, a marker on the row type, or SQL checked against the migrated schema?
decisions.lesson: A table holds rows of one shape, and each row has a key that finds it. When the language knows the shape and the key, it can check reads and writes, keep secrets out of answers, and refresh only the screens a write touched.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A row type is the struct one row holds, such as Task. A key is the value that finds one row, such as a task's ID. A composite key is a key made of two or more fields, such as a project and an account together.

A transaction is a group of reads and writes that happens all at once or not at all. Serializable means the result is the same as if the transactions ran one after another. A row policy is a rule that decides which rows a caller may read or change.

A migration is a step that changes the stored tables when the row type changes. A full scan reads every row of a table. A read set is the list of rows a query looked at, so a later write can tell which live queries it changed.
decisions.story:
Mia builds a task board. A Task has an ID, a title, a status and a version number. A Member is found by its project and its account together.

Under A she writes one line per table: store.table("tasks", key: task_key). Her method move_task reads a task with get, checks its version and writes it back with put. Two people move the same task at once. One call wins, and the other gets Conflict, because the method is one serializable transaction.

Later she adds a due date to Task as an optional field, and jet check records the new column on its own. She renames title to name next. jet check now stops with an error naming Task.title, and its fix line is the one migration step to add.

Under B she marks the Task struct with #Table and writes the key field names in the marker. Under C she writes CREATE TABLE in a migration and every SELECT by hand, and jet check verifies each query against the migrated schema.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides: how a service declares a typed table, its key and its row type, and the methods get, add, put, delete, query and search. It also fixes, for every option, the transaction rule of a method that writes.

Current code. Core/Db/Db.jet has a connection (DBConnection), a policy scope (DBScope) and an open transaction (DBTransaction). A scope runs checked SQL through query and query_one, which need DB.Read, and execute, which needs DB.Write. The SQL type checks its holes, not the tables. live binds one SELECT as a live query, refreshed when its table is written.

More current code. transaction runs SQL steps in one transaction, and migrate records SQL steps and their checksum in a ledger. db.decode turns a row and a list of column names into a struct. A row policy (RowPolicy, made by db.policy(table, expr)) accepts only true and owner == user. There is no table type. The data library's Query<T> filters, sorts, groups and collects into an ordinary list; its public Table<T> carrier was retired.

The transaction rule, the same for every option. A method of a mounted service whose effects include DB.Write runs in one serializable transaction. On SQLite that is BEGIN IMMEDIATE, so writers take turns. On a server database it is the SERIALIZABLE isolation level. A method called from another method joins the caller's transaction. A method that only reads runs on one consistent snapshot.

move_task's read, version check and write rely on this: no other writer can change the task between them. A serialization failure or a busy database retries the whole method, up to 5 attempts with a short random wait. After the last attempt the method returns DBError.Busy. A client call that ends in Busy gets 503 with Retry-After, which the client maps to app.CallError.Unreachable with a retry time.

A retried method must not repeat work outside the database. So a Net, FS.Write or Exec effect inside a method that writes is a compile error that names the call. The program queues such work with app.after_commit(fn), which runs once after the commit, or starts a job.

Out of scope: the full-text index syntax and live-query transport, which have their own cards.

options.name: A table value: db.Table<K, T>, made by store.table(name, key: fn(T) -> K)
options.gist: The row type and the key function make a typed table; queries return the data library's Query<T>.
options.detail:
A service's field is a table: tasks: db.Table<TaskID, Task>. The server opens it with store.table("tasks", key: task_key), where task_key is a function from a row to its key. A composite key is a struct key, such as MemberKey with project and account.

The key function must be pure and deterministic. It has no effects, reads only its row, and calls only functions that do the same. Each field of K is stored as a key column, and the primary key is those columns. A key function that reads a clock, a global or anything but its row is a compile error at key:, naming the read.

get(key) returns the row or None. add(row) inserts a row whose key must be new, and answers Exists or Denied. put(row) inserts or replaces. delete(key) removes a row. query() returns the data library's Query<T>, so filter, sort_by, group_by and collect mean what they mean on a list.

Filters. A filter made of field comparisons joined by && and || becomes SQL. Any other filter needs a full scan, and A makes that explicit. A filter the compiler cannot turn into SQL is a registered warning at the filter, naming the part it could not read. Writing .scan() before it says the full scan is meant and silences the warning.

Secrets and policies. The row is stored with its storage codec, which keeps #Secret fields. Answers to a client use the wire codec, which drops them. A table attaches a row policy with .guard(policy), the typed form of the ratified row-policy rule. Each query records its read set and each write its write set, so a live query refreshes only when a write touched its rows.

Schema changes. The row type is the schema, and Jet writes the steps it can prove safe. Each table's layout is kept in a schema snapshot beside the package, the way a published wire shape is pinned. jet check compares the row type and the key type with that snapshot.

A new field with a default, or an optional field, is recorded as one generated step, applied when the table opens. A removed, renamed or retyped field, or a changed key type, is a compile error naming the table, the field and the change. Its fix line is the SQL step to add, which the program lists with store.table(..., migrate: [steps]). Each step runs once and is recorded in the migrate ledger.

Edge case: renaming Task.title to name. jet check reports that tasks lost title and gained name, and suggests SQL{"ALTER TABLE tasks RENAME COLUMN title TO name"}. After the step is listed, open applies it once.

Beginner path: one line per table and plain methods. Expert path: the same store still runs checked SQL, and a scope that runs as the system can bypass a guard on purpose.
options.technical:
Proposed, not implemented. Core/Db gains Store (db.open) and Table<K, T> with get, add, put, delete, query, search and scan. It gains Who (Account, System) and Op (Read, Insert, Update, Delete), and DBError gains Denied, Exists and Busy. Query<T> gains limit and count. T and K are #Codable; K is #Comparable. The table keeps key columns from K and one column per top-level scalar field of T for filters.

New diagnostics: an impure key function, a filter that needs a full scan (a warning), and a row type that changed without a migration step.

Proof: an example with a db.Table holding a #Secret field prints its stored and wire forms on O0, O1 and O2. A case shows a query's read set refreshing a live query after a write. A UI snapshot shows the effect error for a put without DB.Write. A case runs two concurrent move_task calls and prints one Ok and one Conflict.

options.name: A marker on the row type: #Table(name:, key:) on the struct, and db.Table<T> fields
options.gist: The row struct says which table it lives in and which fields are its key.
options.detail:
The row struct carries #Table(name: "tasks", key: [id]). A composite key lists two fields: key: [project, account]. The service field is tasks: db.Table<Task>, and store.open<Task>() binds it. get takes the key fields in order, as a tuple: self.members.get((project, account)).

The methods, the storage codec, the guard, the filter warning, the read sets and the schema changes work as in A. The key is a list of fields, so it is pure by construction. The difference is where the table is declared: on the row type, once, instead of where the table is opened.

Beginner path: one marker per row type. Expert path: as A.

Gain: the table name and key sit beside the fields they name. Loss: a row type can live in only one table, so an archive table of old tasks needs a copy of the Task struct. The key is a list of field names inside a marker, so a renamed field breaks the marker, and the key has no type of its own to pass around.
options.technical: Proposed, not implemented. A new #Table marker, declared by core.db, with name: String and key: a list of field names checked against the struct. db.Table<T> derives its key type as a tuple of the key fields' types. The rest is as in A.

options.name: SQL checked against the migrated schema: no table type; jet check verifies each query, like sqlx
options.gist: The program writes the migrations and every query in SQL; jet check proves each query against the schema the migrations build.
options.detail:
The service holds a database scope. A migration creates each table with SQL. jet check replays the package's migrations into a schema and checks every SQL text against it. Each table and column must exist, and the selected columns must match the struct db.decode fills. A method reads with query_one, decodes the row, and writes with execute.

Schema changes are migrations the programmer writes. A struct field with no column, or a query naming a dropped column, is a compile error at the query.

Read sets come from the parsed query: the table and the columns its WHERE clause compares. A write names its table and the key it changes, so a live query refreshes only when a write could match it.

Beginner path: learn SQL first. Expert path: full control of every statement, joins and indexes included.

Gain: what runs is exactly what is written, every query is checked, and no new table surface is taught. Loss: every table and every query is written by hand, so a get-by-key is three lines of SQL and decode. A composite key, a row policy and a #Secret column are the program's job in SQL text, and a policy stays limited to true and owner == user.
options.technical: Proposed in part. Core/Db has query, query_one, execute, migrate, decode and live today. New: a schema built from the package's migrations at check time, a check of each SQL text against it, and statement-level read sets. The transaction rule above applies. Proof: the same move_task case written in SQL, and a UI snapshot of a query naming a dropped column.

comparisons.note: A table is a value built from a name and typed columns, and queries are typed by it: the shape of A. Migrations are generated from the table values by drizzle-kit. Source: https://orm.drizzle.team/docs/sql-schema-declaration
comparisons.code: export const tasks = sqliteTable("tasks", { id: text("id").primaryKey() });

comparisons.note: One schema file is the source of the typed client and of generated migrations; a rename needs a hand-edited migration. Close to A's schema story. Source: https://www.prisma.io/docs/orm/prisma-migrate/workflows/customizing-migrations
A schema macro on the row module names the table and its fields, the shape of B; migrations are written by hand. Source: https://hexdocs.pm/ecto/Ecto.Schema.html

A table! description, printed from the migrated database, types every query at compile time; migrations are SQL the programmer writes. Between A and C. Source: https://diesel.rs/guides/schema-in-depth.html
comparisons.code: table! { tasks (id) { id -> Text, title -> Text, } }

comparisons.note: Plain SQL text, checked at compile time against the migrated database or its saved description: the shape of C. Source: https://docs.rs/sqlx/latest/sqlx/macro.query_as.html
comparisons.code:
let task = sqlx::query_as!(Task, "SELECT id, title FROM tasks WHERE id = ?", id)
    .fetch_one(&pool).await?;

comparisons.note: Each mutation is one serializable transaction that the platform retries on conflict, and side effects go to scheduled functions: the transaction rule here. Source: https://docs.convex.dev/database/advanced/occ
comparisons.code: export const move = mutation(async (ctx, { id }) => { await ctx.db.patch(id, { status: "done" }); });

recommendation.why: A gives each table a typed key and row with one pure function, writes the schema steps it can prove safe, and reuses the data library's Query<T>. B ties a row type to one table and puts the key in field names. C checks every query, but leaves every table, key, policy and secret to hand-written SQL.
gains: A table, its key and its row type are declared once and checked at every get, put and query.
#Secret fields stay in storage and never reach a client answer.
Live screens refresh only when a write touched the rows they read.

losses.loss: New public names in core.db: Store, Table, Who, Op, and three DBError cases.
losses.mitigation: They replace hand-written CREATE TABLE, SELECT and decode code, and the query side adds no carrier: query() returns the existing Query<T>.

losses.loss: A filter the compiler cannot turn into SQL needs a full scan.
losses.mitigation: Such a filter is a registered warning naming the part it could not read, and only an explicit .scan() silences it.

losses.loss: A retried method could repeat work outside the database.
losses.mitigation: The compiler refuses Net, FS.Write and Exec effects inside a method that writes, and app.after_commit runs such work once after the commit.

losses.loss: A renamed or removed field, or a new key type, needs a migration step the programmer adds.
losses.mitigation: jet check finds the change before the app runs, and its fix line is the SQL step to add; safe additions are generated.

whyNot.reason: A row type can live in only one table, and the key is a list of field names with no type of its own.
Every query is checked, but each get-by-key is hand-written SQL and decode, and composite keys, policies and secrets stay the program's job in SQL text.

recommendation.tradeoff: A typed table costs a handful of new core.db names in exchange for checked keys, guarded secrets, generated safe migrations and precise live refresh.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude Opus. Adversarial model family: Claude Opus. Fresh agent: Main. Main's review found five gaps (a checked-SQL option, schema evolution, the full-scan filter, isolation and Busy, and the key function's purity), and every one is fixed in this payload.

decisions.title: Where a streamed page splits into regions: at each read's Loading branch, at an explicit deferred wrapper, or nowhere with the client finishing slow reads
decisions.situation: When a server builds a web page, some data comes back fast and some comes back slow. Today a Jet server waits for every read to finish before it sends any of the page. One slow read makes the whole page late, and the person sees a blank screen. Streaming sends the parts that are ready first, with a loading state in place of the slow parts. Each slow part then arrives on the same connection when its data is ready. This vote picks where a page splits into those parts, which we call regions, and in what order they appear. We recommend A: each read that a screen matches on is its own region, and its Loading branch is what shows until the data arrives.
decisions.gist: Should a streamed page split at each read's Loading branch, at an explicit deferred wrapper, or should the client finish slow reads itself?
decisions.lesson: A page is ready in pieces. If the server knows which piece waits on which read, it can send the ready pieces at once and fill in each slow piece the moment its data arrives.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A read is a call a screen makes for data, such as app.state(app.live(fn() { crew.board(id) })). A screen matches on its state: Loading, Failed or Loaded. The Loading branch is the code that draws the screen while the data is on its way.

The shell is the first part of the page the server sends. A region is a part of the page that the server may send later. Streaming means sending one HTTP answer in several pieces over one connection.

Layout shift is the page jumping when a late part appears with a different size. Resuming means the browser picks the page up where the server left it, without running the screen code again.
decisions.story:
Sam opens a project board. The page has a header, the board and a members panel. The board's read takes 300 ms; the header and the members panel are ready in 10 ms.

Under A the app graph says .stream(after: 50ms). At 50 ms the server sends the header, the members panel and the board's spinner, which is its Loading branch. At 300 ms it sends the board, and the spinner is replaced in place. Sam's programmer wrote no new code; the spinner was already there.

Under B the programmer also wraps the board in ui.deferred with a fallback, and an unwrapped slow read still holds up the whole page. Under C Sam sees the spinner at 50 ms too. But the browser then asks the server for the board in a second request, so the board arrives one round trip later.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides: where a page streamed by .stream(after:) splits into regions, in what order they appear, and what each region carries. The graph spelling .stream(after: 50ms) is already in the web app shape.

Current code. Core/App/App.jet's state reads a live binding and returns Loadable: Idle, Loading, Failed or Loaded. On the server it runs the read at once and waits for it. App.stream is a stub in the shape proposal and is not built.

The same for every option. Without .stream the page is sent whole, after every read, as today. A page whose reads all finish before after: is sent whole too, with no swap code. A screen cached with .cache(.Public) is always sent whole, so a shared cache never keeps a page with Loading regions.

HTTP status, the same for every option. The status code and the head are fixed when the shell is sent. A 404 from a bad link comes from the route decode, which runs before the shell. A read whose Failed branch shows the graph's not-found or error view decides the status, so it holds the shell until it finishes. Any other read that fails after the shell draws its Failed branch under the 200 already sent.

Placing a late piece, for A and B. Each later piece is HTML in a template tag plus a short inline script that moves it into place. A browser with scripts off keeps the Loading branch. Requests from known search crawlers get the whole page, as Next.js does for bots.

Resume, the same for every option. Each piece carries its read's encoded result in the page's resume state. The browser never runs the read or the screen code again for that region.

Out of scope: the head and sitemap builders, install and assets, which have their own cards.

options.name: Each read is a region, and its Loading branch is the fallback
options.gist: A screen that matches on app.state is one region; no new code.
options.detail:
Each app.state read on the server starts its source on its own task. When after: passes, a read still running draws its Loading branch inside a marked region. The server then sends the shell. When the read finishes, the server draws that region's Loaded branch and sends it. A read that fails after the shell draws its Failed branch the same way.

Concurrency. A page runs at most 8 reads at once; the rest wait their turn in page order. The reads belong to the request's task group, so they stop when the browser disconnects or the request times out.

Reveal order. A region inside another region appears only after its parent. Sibling regions appear in page order: one that finishes early waits for the regions above it. Reveals are batched every 300 ms, so the page moves a few times at most, top to bottom.

Layout shift remains when a Loading branch and its Loaded branch differ in size. A Loading branch drawn at the size of its content, such as a placeholder of the board's height, avoids it.

Beginner path: add .stream(after: 50ms) to the graph; the spinners already written become the fallbacks. Expert path: a screen that must arrive whole reads its data with a plain call instead of app.state. jet inspect choices lists each region with its read.
options.technical:
Proposed, not implemented. app.state gains a server mode that returns Loading when the stream deadline passes and records the region. The web server writes the response in chunks and bounds each page's reads at 8. The renderer marks each region's root node and orders reveals. No new public names beyond the shape's App.stream.

Proof: a case with two reads, one fast and one slow, shows the shell with the slow read's Loading branch and then its Loaded HTML. A second case shows a read that fails after the 200 status drawing its Failed branch.

options.name: An explicit wrapper: ui.deferred(fallback:, content:)
options.gist: Only code wrapped in ui.deferred streams; every other read holds up the shell.
options.detail:
A region is written by hand: ui.deferred(fallback: kit.spinner(), content: fn() { board(crew, view) }). The server sends the fallback in the shell and the content later. A read outside any ui.deferred holds up the shell until it finishes. Concurrency and placing are as in A; reveal order follows the wrappers, which can group several reads into one reveal.

Beginner path: wrap each slow part. Expert path: choose exactly which parts stream and which appear together.

Gain: a reader sees each region in the code, and grouping is explicit, as React's Suspense and SuspenseList give. Loss: two ways to say loading, the Loading branch and the fallback, and a screen needs both. A slow read that nobody wrapped makes the whole page late, which is the problem streaming is meant to fix.
options.technical: Proposed, not implemented. A new ui.deferred function in the ui package. The rest is as in A.

options.name: No server streaming: send the shell at the deadline, and the client finishes slow reads
options.gist: The server stops waiting at after:; the browser runs each unfinished read itself.
options.detail:
At after: the server sends the whole page with each unfinished read's Loading branch and closes the answer. The browser resumes the page, sees the unfinished reads and calls the server for each one.

Beginner path: as A. Expert path: as A.

Gain: the server sends one plain answer and needs no chunked writer. Loss: each slow region arrives one round trip later than in A. The server's work on that read is thrown away and done again. A browser with scripts off keeps the Loading branch, as in A, and crawlers get whole pages, as in A.
options.technical: Proposed, not implemented. app.state gains the same deadline as in A; the client runs unfinished reads through app.Remote after resume. No chunked response.

comparisons.note: Explicit Suspense boundaries mark regions, the shape of B, and SuspenseList controls reveal order. React throttles reveals to limit layout shift, and Next.js sends whole pages to bots. A borrows the ordering, throttling and bot rule but places boundaries at reads. Source: https://react.dev/reference/react/Suspense

A loader returns a deferred promise and the page awaits it inside Suspense, with its own error element. Each deferred value is chosen in the loader, closer to B. Source: https://remix.run/docs/en/main/guides/streaming

An await tag streams in order with no script, or out of order with client-reorder. A only streams out of order, so A needs a script that Marko's in-order mode does not. Source: https://markojs.com/docs/await/
Suspense boundaries over resources stream out of order, and a resource read outside a boundary suspends the nearest parent. Source: https://docs.solidjs.com/reference/components/suspense

assign_async loads data after the first render, and the template matches on loading, failed and ok, close to A's Loading branch. It updates over the live socket, not one streamed HTML answer. Source: https://hexdocs.pm/phoenix_live_view/Phoenix.LiveView.html#assign_async/4

recommendation.why: A streams every slow read with the Loading branches screens already have, so there is one way to say loading and no slow read can hold up the page by accident. B adds a second loading form, and C makes each slow region a round trip late.
gains: Turning streaming on is one line on the app graph; screens do not change.
Every slow read streams, so no forgotten wrapper makes the page late.
Each region resumes from its own result, with no second render in the browser.

losses.loss: A screen cannot ask for one read to hold up the shell while the rest stream.
losses.mitigation: It reads that data with a plain call instead of app.state, and jet inspect choices lists every region with its read.

losses.loss: A read that fails after the 200 status cannot change the status code.
losses.mitigation: A read whose Failed branch shows the not-found or error view holds the shell, and a 404 from a bad link comes from the route decode first.

losses.loss: Late regions can make the page jump.
losses.mitigation: Regions appear in page order, batched every 300 ms, and a Loading branch drawn at its content's size does not shift.

losses.loss: A browser with scripts off keeps the Loading branch of a late region.
losses.mitigation: Known search crawlers get the whole page, and a cached public page is always sent whole.

whyNot.reason: It needs both a fallback and a Loading branch for one wait, and a slow read nobody wrapped still makes the page late.
Each slow region costs one more round trip, and the server's work on it is done twice.

recommendation.tradeoff: A gives up a per-read hold-the-shell switch and explicit grouping in exchange for streaming that needs no screen changes.

decisions.title: How a program makes an HTTP body: free functions in core.http, renamed Body constructors, or one name for both a constructor and a reader
decisions.situation: An HTTP body is the payload of a web request or response: some text, a form or JSON. Today a program can make one in two ways. It can call http.body_text("hi"), or it can call http.Body.text("hi"). The second form reuses the name of the method that reads a body back, body.text(limit). Jet does not let one type have two members with one name, so the compiler checks those Body calls with about 1,000 lines of special code. No library can use that code, which breaks the rule that Core is ordinary Jet. You are asked how a program should make a body. We recommend the free functions that already exist, http.body_text and its family, and removing the Body.* forms.
decisions.gist: Should HTTP bodies be made with http.body_text(...) and its family, with renamed Body.of_text(...) constructors, or should a type allow a constructor and a method with one name?
decisions.lesson: One thing should have one name. When making a value and reading it back share a name, either the language needs a special rule or the library needs special compiler help. Neither is needed if the maker has its own name.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A body is the payload of an HTTP message. A constructor is a function that makes a new value of a type. A static member is a function written inside a type and called through the type's name, such as Body.text("hi"). An instance member, or method, is called on a value, such as body.text(5), which reads the body back as text of at most 5 bytes.

A free function is one written at module level, called through the module, such as http.body_text("hi").

The compiler-side checker is code inside the compiler that knows these HTTP calls by name. Any library that wanted the same shape could not have it.
decisions.story:
Ada writes a small client. She builds a JSON body, sends it, and reads the answer as text.

Today she finds two ways in the docs: http.body_text("hi") in the core library table, and http.Body.text("hi") in the HTTP example. Both work. Later she writes her own Message type and tries the same trick, a text constructor next to a text method. Jet stops her with E0105, a duplicate definition. Core could do it only because the compiler helps Core.

Under A she sees one way: http.body_text, http.body_form and http.body_json. Her own library can use the same pattern with no special help.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides: one spelling for making an HTTP body, and whether a type may have a static and an instance member with one name.

Current code, checked on dev 963b9fbd76. Core/Http/Http.jet declares Body with the reading methods bytes(self, limit), text(self, limit) and json<Target>(self, limit). It also declares the free functions body_empty, body_text and body_bytes. The spec's core library table lists those as the constructors (Docs/spec/reference/core-library.md, line 1614).

The Body.* forms are not declared on Body at all. They are Body.empty(), Body.bytes(b), Body.text(t), Body.text(t, media_type), Body.form(fields), Body.multipart(fields), Body.json(value) and Body.reader(reader) with an optional length.

Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Calls/Http.jet recognizes them by type and member name. It calls hidden helpers: __body_typed_text, __body_form, __body_json, __body_reader and __body_reader_sized. The same file handles Headers.new and Client.new, which have no name clash and become ordinary static members under every option.

A user type cannot copy this shape: a struct with text(words: String) and text(self) is E0105, a duplicate definition.

Callers of the Body.* forms: 8 code sites, plus 2 rows in the core library table. Seven sites are in Examples/Network/HTTP/HTTPMessageValues.jet and one in tests/ui/print_lazy_iter_view.jet. Callers of the free functions http.body_empty, body_text and body_bytes outside Core/Http: 30 sites in 8 files.

This ballot leaves out the route checks in Sema/Calls/HttpRouting.jet, which move to library markers in a separate design.

options.name: Free functions in core.http: http.body_text, http.body_form, http.body_json and the rest
options.gist: Extend the free functions that already exist and remove the Body.* forms.
options.detail:
core.http keeps body_empty, body_text and body_bytes. It adds body_typed_text(text, media_type), body_form(fields), body_multipart(fields) and body_json(value). It also adds body_reader(reader) and body_reader_sized(reader, length). Each one is an ordinary public function with its own declared signature and effects. The Body.* call forms are removed, and the compiler's HTTP body checker is deleted with them.

Beginner path: type http.body_ and the editor lists every way to make a body. The core library table already teaches this spelling.

Expert path: the same functions; a library with its own message type writes the same free-function family with no compiler help.

Cost: 8 code sites and 2 table rows change. The 30 existing free-function callers do not change.

Edge cases: a missing Body.text("hi") call gets the ordinary missing-member error, whose fix names http.body_text. Two-argument forms that differed only by count get their own names (body_typed_text, body_reader_sized), because Jet has no overloading.
options.technical:
Proposed. Core/Http/Http.jet: the hidden __body_* helpers become public body_typed_text, body_form, body_multipart, body_json<T: Encode>, body_reader and body_reader_sized with today's bodies. Headers.new becomes an ordinary static new on Headers next to headers(), and Client.new an ordinary static new on Client. Sema/Calls/Http.jet's static-constructor path is deleted.

The missing-member error E0102 gains a fix that names the free function. It applies when the type's module declares a function named for the type in lower case, an underscore and the member. Proof: the HTTP example and a ui case for the fix text.

options.name: Rename the constructors: Body.of_text, Body.of_json, Body.of_form, Body.of_reader
options.gist: Constructors stay on Body under names that differ from the reading methods.
options.detail:
Body declares static members of_empty, of_bytes, of_text, of_typed_text, of_form, of_multipart, of_json, of_reader and of_reader_sized. The compiler's checker is deleted.

Beginner path: type http.Body. and the editor lists the makers next to the readers.

Expert path: the same members.

Cost: the 8 Body.* sites and 2 table rows change. The 30 free-function callers must also move to Body.of_*, or the free functions stay as a second spelling of the same thing, which breaks the one-way rule.

Edge cases: none new; of_ is a new naming pattern that no other Core type uses today.
options.technical: Proposed. Body gains nine static members; body_empty, body_text and body_bytes are removed with their 30 callers. Sema/Calls/Http.jet's static-constructor path is deleted.

options.name: Let a type have a static and an instance member with the same name
options.gist: Body.text("hi") makes a body and body.text(5) reads one, by a new language rule.
options.detail:
A type may declare one static member and one instance member with the same name. Resolution rule: a call through the type's name, Body.text(...), picks the static member; a call on a value, body.text(...), picks the instance member. Two static or two instance members with one name stay E0105.

Edge cases. Reading Body.text without parentheses where a function is expected gives the static member, since a method is bound only on a value. A trait that declares both forms must be implemented with both. A generic call T.text(...) on a type parameter picks the static member. A name used with both forms gets a new registered error when one call could match either, such as a future form that passes the receiver explicitly.

Beginner path: today's code keeps working. Expert path: the same.

Cost: no caller changes. The free functions stay, so a body still has two spellings unless the 30 free-function sites move too.
options.technical: Proposed. Registration keeps a static slot and an instance slot per member name. Method lookup on a type name reads the static slot; on a value, the instance slot. Body declares its constructors as static members; the free functions either stay or are removed with 30 callers. Sema/Calls/Http.jet's static-constructor path is deleted. One new diagnostic code for an ambiguous call.

comparisons.note: Bodies are made with free constructors of readers, such as strings.NewReader, and passed to http.NewRequest; reading is a method on the response body, the shape of A. Source: https://pkg.go.dev/net/http#NewRequest
Body is made through From and read through methods with other names, the shape of B. Source: https://docs.rs/reqwest/latest/reqwest/struct.Body.html

Static and instance members may share a base name, told apart by the receiver and argument labels, the shape of C. Source: https://docs.swift.org/swift-book/documentation/the-swift-programming-language/methods/
comparisons.code: struct Note { static func text(_ s: String) -> Note { ... }; func text() -> String { ... } }

recommendation.why: A keeps the spelling the spec already teaches and 30 callers already use, removes the second spelling, and needs no new language rule. B renames 38 call sites to reach one spelling, and C adds a rule for a single type.
gains: One way to make a body, the one the core library table already lists.
Only 8 code sites and 2 table rows change.
About 1,000 lines of compiler-only HTTP checking are deleted.
A user library can copy the pattern with no compiler help.

losses.loss: Typing http.Body. in the editor no longer lists the makers.
losses.mitigation: Body's doc comment names the body_ functions, and a call such as Body.text("hi") gets an error whose fix names http.body_text.

losses.loss: Forms that differed only by argument count need two names.
losses.mitigation: Each name says what it takes, body_reader and body_reader_sized, as Jet does everywhere it has no overloading.

whyNot.reason: To reach one spelling it renames all 38 sites, including the 30 that already use the spelled-out free functions, and it adds an of_ pattern no other Core type uses.
It adds a language rule and an ambiguity error for one library type, and it leaves two spellings for one body unless 30 sites move anyway.

recommendation.tradeoff: A gives up listing makers under Body. in exchange for one spelling, no language change and the smallest migration.

decisions.title: How an app gives each row a checked ID
decisions.situation: A row ID is the text that names one row, such as one task. Offline apps let the device make the ID itself: a UUIDv7, a random text that also records the time, so a task made on a train opens at once. The server must refuse IDs a client made up. Today a request with the ID "t1" is stored as is, because the decoder sees an ID type as a String. The vote decides how an app declares ID types and makes new IDs. We recommend one line per table and nothing per new row.
decisions.gist: How should an app declare and make row IDs, so they are checked UUIDv7 text with the least code?
decisions.lesson: An ID names one row. Offline apps make IDs on the device, so the server must refuse made-up ones like "t1" with 422 (bad input) before any method runs. The options differ in what an app writes for each table and each new row.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: the app writes one line per table, TaskID: distinct app.ID, and nothing else. On the client, TaskID.from_id(app.new_id()) makes a new ID. A crafted request with "t1" gets 422 at the id field, and the method never runs. The ID prints as its text, travels in JSON as a plain string, and is stored as one text column.

Expert path. Code can build an ID only from app.new_id() or by decoding checked text, so no TaskID ever holds "t1". A generic function can ask for any ID through the wrapped type. A legacy key that is not a UUIDv7 stays a plain distinct String, and an integer key stays Int. Neither option changes those.

Some things stay the same under every option: the ID's text, the 422 answer, the JSON string and the SQL text column. Passing a ProjectID where a TaskID belongs is a compile error under all three.
decisions.story: Ana's TaskList app makes a task on the train and gives it a fresh ID. Later Leo writes a script that sends {"id":"t1","title":"Ship it"} straight to the server. Today the server stores a task named t1, and the next client that makes its own t1 collides with it. Ana needs the server to refuse t1 before her code runs.
decisions.detail:
Code is truth, checked on today's dev with the gate jet. Each probe below is a file in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/inbox/Speed-3-ballot-app-id/.

jet run gap.jet prints "accepted id t1". A distinct String decodes any text.

jet run core_id_and_row_id.jet prints "A: t1 refused: [at `id`: expected a UUIDv7]". A struct with a hand-written bare-text codec already refuses t1. It also prints "A: uuid accepted, encodes {\"id\":\"0193a5e0-7c1a-7000-8000-000000000001\",\"title\":\"x\"}", so the ID travels as a plain string. Its last line, "C: x", shows that a generic struct whose parameter only names a row compiles today.

jet run distinct_over_struct.jet fails with E0311: "`TaskID` has no matching static method `from_id`". A distinct type over a struct does not derive its codec yet. That is a gap in D-CODABLE-DISTINCT1=A (a distinct type codes as its base), and A must close it.

The proposal (D-WEBAPP-SHAPE1=A, Docs/proposals/2026-11-13-web-app-framework-shape.md, sections 3.2 and 4.8) writes TaskID: distinct String. It requires that an ID type's decoder accept only UUIDv7 text, with a test sending "t1". It never says what marks an ID type.

app.new_id() -[Rand, Time]> String is in Core/App/App.jet (SUB Speed-3-c6-server). It makes the text through core.crypto.uuid.v7, and its return type follows this vote. The same SUB makes Table.add on a taken key answer Exists or Denied, by whether the caller may read the row. Card #6867 c6.

options.name: A distinct ID with a fresh default
options.detail:
Core adds app.ID, whose decoder accepts only canonical UUIDv7 text and answers anything else with FieldError{path: "id"} and 422. Each table declares its own ID type in one line, TaskID: distinct app.ID, so a ProjectID can never be passed where a TaskID is expected. A distinct type codes as its base (D-CODABLE-DISTINCT1=A), so TaskID gets the check.

app.ID has one constructor, fresh(), which makes a new UUIDv7. A distinct type gets its base's constructors, typed as itself and made through its own conversion, the same path decoding takes. So the field default id: TaskID = .fresh() means a new row needs no ID code: Task{title: "Ship it"}.
options.technical:
Core: app.ID in Core/App/App.jet with Encode, Decode, Display, Equatable, Comparable and fresh(). Language: a distinct type forwards each static constructor of its base that returns the base, through its own conversion. A base whose conversion can fail, such as a range type, forwards none.

The generated codec fills a missing id from the default, so a request without one gets a server-made ID. The request key (#6867 c2) makes a retry return the first result instead of a second row. Under the app test host, fresh() draws from the test's seeded clock and random source, so tests stay deterministic. The derived codec of a distinct type over a struct base is fixed (today E0311).

decisions.title: Where a growing value lives when the code does not say
decisions.situation: Every Jet program keeps its lists, text and other growing values somewhere in memory. Today a value the code does not place goes to the general heap, which finds room for it and frees it piece by piece. The Goose language shows a faster way for values that end in the reverse order they began: stack them, and free a whole scope in one step. The vote decides whether Jet's compiler does that on its own, keeps it an explicit choice, or makes it the only default. We recommend the compiler choose, and use the heap whenever it cannot prove the order.
decisions.gist: Where should Jet put a growing value, like a list or text, when the code does not say where?
decisions.lesson: A scope stack hands out memory by moving one pointer and frees a whole scope in one step. It only works when values end in the reverse order they began. Today Jet uses the heap unless code picks an arena. Any winner still needs an adversarial review and measurements before it ships.
decisions.story: Noor writes a log tool that splits each line into words, counts them and drops the list. Each word and the list are separate heap requests and frees today. She will never write an arena, and her tool runs on servers and in the browser.

options.name: The compiler chooses
options.detail:
One rule decides, and a reader can apply it: a growing value goes on a scope stack unless it is stored in something that outlives it or sent to another task. A value a function returns is built on its caller's stack, so builder functions qualify too.

Each growing value gets its own stack, as in Goose, so it is freed at its last use with one pointer reset, not at its scope's end. Everything the rule leaves out uses the default heap of D-ALLOC-DEFAULT1 and costs exactly what it costs today. An allocator named by #Context (D-ALLOC-SITE1) always wins. No syntax, diagnostic or API is added; `jet inspect placement` names each heap value and the rule that sent it there.
options.technical:
Placement is a sema fact (I3), so O0, O1, O2 and the web place every value the same way (I9). Threads reserve address ranges for their stacks. Tasks and the web use chunked stacks instead, taken from the thread's pool on a task's first stacked value. So a task that stacks nothing costs nothing, and thousands of tasks reserve no address space. A task's stacks belong to the task, so a stacked value survives a wait.

Growth already compares length with capacity on the heap path; a chunked stack reuses that check, extending in place when the value is on top. A recursive function's growing locals use the heap, so recursion stays unrestricted (contrast goose-048). Scope stacks are separate from the native call stack, so Mem.Stack budgets are unchanged. #6469, stack slots for small boxes that never escape, is the scalar end of the same placement ladder.

options.name: Explicit only, as today
options.detail: Every value uses the default heap unless code names an allocator with #Context(allocator:), as D-ALLOC-SITE1=A ratified. The compiler keeps only the small, invisible optimizations it does today, such as stack slots for small boxes that never escape (#6469).
options.technical: No sema placement fact. Arena, Bump and Pool stay the explicit route (Docs/spec/spec.md, Allocator families).

options.name: Stacks by default, heap by hand
options.detail: Goose's model becomes Jet's default. Every growing value lives on a compiler-assigned stack. Some values have lifetimes that do not nest: a map of lists, a cache, a value kept past its scope. Code must place those on the heap explicitly, and the compiler refuses the stack-only forms with a diagnostic.
options.technical: C inherits Goose's restrictions. Each stack has one growing value on top, and growing values cannot be array elements (goose-023, goose-024). Recursion is restricted so the stack count stays constant (goose-048). Specialization is whole-program by root (goose-051), and web growth is checked (goose-143). About 60% of Goose's rejection tests are lifetime errors (goose-220), and Jet's beginners would meet them.

comparisons.note: Data stacks with a bump pointer, freed by one store at scope exit; growing values are restricted to keep the model sound. https://github.com/aardappel/goose rev 94cc64da; claims goose-001, goose-023, goose-024, goose-048, goose-143, goose-173.
comparisons.code: var scratch: u8[>..] = [];  // grow-only, pointer bump

comparisons.note: Region inference (ML Kit) later added a garbage collector for what regions leaked; Cyclone kept LIFO arenas only where callers know lifetimes (goose-144). Lesson: inferred stacking needs a heap fallback.
comparisons.code: (* ML Kit: regions inferred, plus a collector for the rest *)

recommendation.why: It gives stack speed to the common shapes with no new syntax, and the rest costs no more than today.
gains: No new syntax and no new errors.
The fast path reaches code nobody tuned.
One stated rule says which values are stacked.

losses.loss: Values stored in a longer-lived container stay on the heap.
losses.mitigation: They pay exactly today's cost, and `jet inspect placement` names each one and the rule that sent it there.

whyNot.reason: B is simplest but leaves common temporaries on the slower heap unless authors tune them.
C is fastest where it fits but rejects everyday code like maps of lists, and slows the web.

recommendation.tradeoff: Placement becomes a compiler decision users can predict and inspect but never write.

wild.note: Goose keeps every growing value on compiler-chosen data stacks. Source: the README of https://github.com/aardappel/goose.

losses: Values kept in longer-lived containers, like maps of lists, keep today's heap cost.
