decisions.title: Preload from navigation intent and live user input through one bounded executor
decisions.situation: Following declared links can prepare likely navigation, but it cannot predict a search query or a route selected by live input. The owner needs both pages and their content ready before the user opens them. We recommend one typed preload operation, fed by link intent and explicit input-driven hints. It shares foreground loading and caching, while bounding speculative work and making offline coverage visible.
decisions.gist: Preload likely pages and content from links and live input, using one loader.
decisions.lesson: Preloading is speculative loading, not a promise that every future input works offline. The same request and cache must serve both paths.
decisions.explainer: Beginner: links can hint on hover or tap; a search box can submit the latest typed query to preload. Opening that same typed view consumes the same cache entry. Expert: shared read dependencies, assets and code participate in one cancellable loading plan; authentication, freshness and budgets are part of the key and execution policy.
decisions.story: Maya types a customer name, then opens the matching page. Its content can already be loading before the navigation, even though no static link contained her query.
decisions.inWild: await preloadData('/search?q=' + encodeURIComponent(query));
decisions.detail:
gate-p260 probes/app.jet imports app, configures app.new(title:...).offline(.Queue), and runs successfully. probes/app-missing.jet reports E0102 for app.preload and app.phase. Core/App/App.jet:2212 configures offline mode; no claim about network interception or arbitrary unopened pages was established by that configuration probe. The proposed API is new.

SvelteKit's link options document hover and tap preload, code preload, Save-Data suppression and staleness risks. Its public preloadData can be called from input handling and reuses the route load path; static link traversal alone is therefore not a fair strongest-alternative comparison. Sources: https://svelte.dev/docs/kit/link-options and https://svelte.dev/docs/kit/$app-navigation.

One executor must power both explicit preload(view) and compiler-generated link hints. It loads the selected page's code, required assets and declared read content, not just HTML. It must not execute render bodies or mutating handlers to discover dependencies. Unknown dynamic dependencies require the same typed read-loader path used by foreground loading.

No language can prefetch an unbounded input space within a finite offline budget; the UI must expose which content is actually ready. Full dataset synchronization is a real competing design for locally searchable bounded datasets, not a free consequence of page warming.

options.name: One loader, automatic and input-driven hints
options.detail: Combine link intent with explicit typed preload calls from input events. Share foreground loading, caching and dependency tracking.
options.technical:
Proposed app.preload(view) returns a cancellable Preload handle with observable Queued, Loading, Ready, Partial, Failed and Cancelled states. It schedules the same typed page read-loader used by opening view; it does not rerun UI bodies or submit writes. Hover/tap hints invoke this exact operation. Search handlers debounce configurable input, cancel obsolete handles and keep the newest input generation separate, so a late old response cannot replace current content. Cancellation is best effort for I/O; correctness depends on identity and generation, not cancellation arriving in time.

Cache identity includes page, normalized arguments, user/tenant authority, locale, content version and dependency freshness. A hint never broadens authority. Recheck authorization on use; logout, revoked authority and relevant writes invalidate entries. Share in-flight reads, evaluate loaders once per request identity, prioritize foreground requests, and bound request count, bytes, CPU, dependency depth and retention. Respect metered/save-data policy. Reclaim obsolete work without cancelling a foreground consumer that joined it.

The compiler may enumerate known links and pure dependencies, but cannot claim complete reachability across arbitrary input. Ready means that particular page/input snapshot has its declared required content. Partial coverage and expired or uncached queries remain visible offline; do not show missing data as an empty successful search. Persisted entries follow the same authority and freshness contract. Unavoidable speculative traffic is capped, observable and suppressible.

options.name: Explicit preload only
options.detail: Expose the same shared loader but require application code to issue every hint, including links.
options.technical: This is a strong choice for apps where prediction quality matters more than automatic coverage. It has A's cache, security, cancellation and offline rules, without automatic link discovery. It avoids speculative link traffic but requires every feature author to wire navigation hints. Input-driven preloading is still first-class, not omitted.
options.code:
pending: app.preload(SearchView{query: text})
// Link hover and tap handlers call preload explicitly too.

options.name: Synchronize declared datasets for local queries
options.detail: Download an authorized, bounded dataset and run supported searches locally instead of predicting each query.
options.technical: This gives arbitrary input over the synchronized subset genuine offline answers, often stronger than query preloading. It requires declared query semantics, local indexes, authority-filtered replication, freshness and deletion propagation. Page code and assets still need the shared loader. Large or server-only queries cannot be represented as fully synchronized without an explicit storage and security cost. Do not promise semantic parity with arbitrary remote search.

comparisons.note: Link intent and programmatic preloadData both reuse route loading; save-data can disable automatic speculation.
Hover/tap policy balances latency against speculative traffic; preload is not unconditional freshness.

recommendation.why: It directly covers input-selected pages and content while retaining useful link prediction, without creating a second loading system.
gains: Input and navigation share content, code and cache.
Authority, freshness and cancellation remain consistent.

losses.loss: Unused predictions spend bandwidth and work.
losses.mitigation: Debounce input, enforce resource budgets, prioritize foreground work and honor save-data settings.

losses.loss: Finite storage cannot cover every future query offline.
losses.mitigation: Expose per-input coverage and use declared dataset synchronization where complete local search is required.

whyNot.reason: It is equally capable, but every link needs manual hint wiring that A can generate through the same operation.
It is stronger for bounded local datasets, but not a general replacement for arbitrary remote page loads.

recommendation.tradeoff: Responsive speculation is bounded and honest about coverage, not advertised as universal offline availability.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude Opus. Adversarial model family: OpenAI GPT. Fresh agent: BallotRework. Replaced static-only warming with one input-driven and link-driven executor, correcting unexecuted offline claims and the unfair SvelteKit comparison. Added latest-input correctness, authority, budgets, visible coverage and the stronger bounded-dataset alternative; A is recommended within those limits.

decisions.checkInstructions: Replay app.jet and app-missing.jet on gate-p260. Implementation acceptance: input changes before completion, shared foreground request, logout and revocation, write invalidation, metered connections, resource exhaustion, no mutating preload, dynamic dependency and offline partial-coverage behavior. Proposed snippets do not work today.

    .sync(Customers.for_user(user))

gains: One cache and authority model.

losses.mitigation: Debounce, cap work, prioritize navigation and respect save-data.

losses.loss: Unseen inputs may lack offline content.
losses.mitigation: Show coverage; synchronize datasets when complete local querying is required.

whyNot.reason: Same capability, more repeated wiring.
Strong for bounded data, not all remote queries.

recommendation.tradeoff: Bounded responsiveness, not impossible universal preloading.

designAway: Combined automatic and explicit hints behind one foreground loader.
Specified generations rather than relying on perfect cancellation.
Named finite offline coverage and speculative traffic as physical costs, with concrete limits.

decisions.title: Whether a predicted write may queue a job
decisions.situation: A predicted write updates the screen at once, before the server answers. D-OPTIMISTIC1 predicts a write only when it "has no other effects". Many writes also queue a job, such as telling the assignee about a task, with app.enqueue. The job runs on the server, and only after the write commits. You decide whether queuing a job stops a write from being predicted. In Crewboard, 6 of its 12 writes are predicted if it doesn't and 2 of 12 if it does. We recommend that it doesn't: the job still runs once, on the server, and only after the commit.
decisions.gist: May a write that queues a job still update the screen at once?
decisions.lesson: A prediction runs the write on the device's own copy of the rows and shows the result at once. The server then runs the same write, and its answer replaces the guess. A job queued with app.enqueue never runs on the device. It runs on the server after the write commits, and never runs if the write is refused. So the question is only whether the screen waits for the server.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: the app writes update_task once, with its app.enqueue line. Under A, the edit shows at once and the assignee is told after the server commits it. Under B, the edit shows a busy state until the server answers, unless the app moves the job into a second call.

Expert path: under both options, the job runs only on the server, once, after the commit (#3709 jobs). A refused write queues nothing. jet inspect choices lists each method as predicted or waiting, with the fact that decided it.

Under both options, a method that reads the clock or randomness, calls the network or writes files is never predicted.
decisions.story: Ana assigns a task to Leo on the train. Under A, the card shows Leo at once, and when Ana's phone reaches the server, the write commits and Leo gets his notification. If the server refuses it (Leo left the project), the card goes back and Ana sees why, and Leo is told nothing. Under B, the card spins until the phone reaches the server.
decisions.detail:
Code read on dev 77f7729b72. app.enqueue is `fn(call: Int, job: &&CallJob) Never!` in Core/App/App.jet:919, and it carries no effect. A job runs after the commit and never after a rollback (Tests/Cases/WebApp/job_runs_after_commit_and_never_after_rollback.case).

Crewboard (Docs/Proposals/2026-11-13-web-app-framework-shape.md) has 12 writes a client can call. create_task and update_task queue tell_assignee through after_assign (line 1543). remove_member queues the unassign job, and leave calls remove_member. move_task and set_role queue nothing. The other six read the clock or randomness, write files, or make their ID on the server, so they wait under both options.

The count is in Docs/Audits/2026-11-16-d-optimistic1-review.md, claim 13 and the second re-review. The review's D8 has the client also run named row policies. Until member_policy stops reading the clock, set_role, remove_member and leave wait too. That makes the counts 3 of 12 under A and 1 of 12 under B. The ratio between the options stays the same.

options.name: Predict it; the job waits for the commit
options.detail: A write that queues a job is predicted like any other write. The device runs the method on its copy and skips the app.enqueue line. The server runs the method, commits, then runs the job once. In Crewboard, 6 of 12 writes update the screen at once: create_task, update_task, move_task, set_role, remove_member and leave.
options.technical: Prediction treats app.enqueue as a compiler-known call it skips, as it skips row policies. No new syntax. jet inspect choices says "predicted (queues tell_assignee after commit)".

options.name: Queuing a job makes the method wait
options.detail: A write that queues a job is not predicted. The screen shows the busy state until the server answers. In Crewboard, 2 of 12 writes update the screen at once: move_task and set_role. To get an instant edit, the app moves the job into a second method that the screen calls after the reply.
options.technical: Eligibility refuses a body that reaches app.enqueue. No new syntax. jet inspect choices says "waits (queues tell_assignee)".

comparisons.note: The client mutator updates the screen; server-only work runs in the server mutator after the client's guess is shown. This is A's shape.
A method stub runs on the client and skips server-only calls with isSimulation; the server sends the mail. This is A's shape.
The guess is hand-written in onMutate; whatever the server does after is invisible to it. Neither option's question arises.

recommendation.why: The job never runs on the device and runs on the server only after the commit, so a refused guess sends nothing and a committed one sends once. What the ballot's "no other effects" protects against, an outside effect before the server agrees, cannot happen. A predicts three times as many of Crewboard's writes with the same code.
gains: Crewboard: 6 of 12 writes are instant instead of 2.
No code is moved to get an instant edit.
A refused write still tells no one.

losses.loss: It widens the ratified "no other effects" to allow one effect that is deferred until after the commit.
losses.mitigation: jet inspect choices names the queued job beside each predicted method; the opt-out (D-PREDICT-PIN1) keeps any method waiting.

losses.loss: The screen shows the edit before the notification goes out, so for a moment the screen is ahead of the job.
losses.mitigation: That is true of every committed write too: a job always runs after the commit.

whyNot.reason: It makes 4 of Crewboard's 6 predictable writes wait. Its workaround, a second call after the reply, is more code and loses the job if the app closes between the calls.

recommendation.tradeoff: One deferred server effect allowed inside a prediction, for three times as many instant writes.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Under A: the case WebApp/client_id_create_is_predicted (#6555 c7) creates a task with an assignee and shows the card at once. decisions.title: How a write method opts out of prediction, or pins it
decisions.situation: D-OPTIMISTIC1 predicts each write the compiler can predict, so the screen updates before the server answers. It promised an opt-out per action, spelled optimistic: false on app.action(...). The web app shape has no app.action. A write is a method of a service, marked #App.SignedIn or #App.Public, and those markers already take arguments, as in #App.Public(limit: 30, per: 1min). You decide how a method says "never predict me" (the opt-out) and "always predict me, and fail the build if you can't" (the pin). Most methods write neither. We recommend one argument on the marker: predict: .Never or predict: .Always.
decisions.gist: How does a write method say "never predict" or "must be predicted"?
decisions.lesson: With nothing written, the compiler decides, and jet inspect choices shows the decision and why. The opt-out keeps a method waiting for the server, for example a payment or logic the app wants to keep off the device. The pin is for experts: it fails the build when a change makes the method unpredictable, so an instant screen can't silently become a slow one.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: write nothing. A method the compiler can predict is predicted; one it can't waits. jet inspect choices lists each with the fact that decided it, for example "move_task: predicted" or "invite: waits (reads the clock)".

Expert path: the opt-out and the pin are each one argument on the access marker the method already has. A pinned method that stops qualifying fails the build with a diagnostic naming the fact, such as the line that reads the clock.

Under every option the default is the compiler's choice, and no option adds a marker to methods that don't use it.
decisions.story: Ana's Crewboard predicts move_task, so a card moves the moment it is dropped. Later Leo adds a timestamp to move_task with time.now_utc(). Without a pin, the card quietly starts to spin. With the pin, Leo's build fails at that line and he passes the time in as an argument instead. Separately, Ana's pay method must never show a paid state before the bank agrees, so she opts it out.
decisions.detail:
Code read on dev 77f7729b72. Marker arguments exist on the access markers: #App.Public(limit: 30, per: 1min) (Core/App/App.jet:58; Tests/Cases/WebApp/MethodRateLimitAnswers429.fixture). #App.Job(retries: 2) and #App.Webhook(path:, signature:, key:) also take arguments.

The ratified D-OPTIMISTIC1 example is app.action("pay", pay, optimistic: false). The shape (Docs/Proposals/2026-11-13-web-app-framework-shape.md) has no app.action and no spelling for the opt-out. jet inspect choices (Compiler/JetCLI/Source/CLI/InspectChoices.jet) has no prediction kind yet; #6555 c3 adds it. The review is Docs/Audits/2026-11-16-d-optimistic1-review.md, claim 11 and D6.

options.name: predict: .Never / .Always on the marker
options.detail: The access marker takes one more argument, predict:, with two values. predict: .Never keeps the method waiting for the server. predict: .Always pins it: the build fails if the method can't be predicted, naming the fact. With no argument, the compiler decides.
options.technical: One argument name, predict, on #App.SignedIn and #App.Public, typed by a two-case Core enum app.Predict { Never, Always }. One diagnostic for a pin that fails, and one for predict: on a method that can't write (a #App.Query).

options.name: optimistic: false / true on the marker
options.detail: The ratified ballot's word, carried to the marker as a Bool. optimistic: false keeps the method waiting. optimistic: true pins it, with the same build failure as A. With no argument, the compiler decides.
options.technical: One argument name, optimistic, on #App.SignedIn and #App.Public, typed Bool. The same two diagnostics as A.

options.name: Two markers of their own
options.detail: Two new markers stack beside the access marker: #App.Wait keeps the method waiting, and #App.Predicted pins it. With neither, the compiler decides.
options.technical: Two marker rows, App.Wait and App.Predicted, legal only beside #App.SignedIn or #App.Public, plus a diagnostic for both on one method and the same pin diagnostic as A.

Prediction is hand-written per mutation in onMutate; leaving it out is the opt-out.

decisions.title: Offer F32 complex values without requiring generic default syntax
decisions.situation: Complex currently stores two Float components. Signal buffers may need F32 components to reduce component storage and match other F32 data. The draft proposed Complex<T> while allowing plain Complex to mean Complex<Float>. That is also a public generic-default and literal-typing decision, not just a struct edit. We recommend one shared implementation with concrete Complex and Complex32 aliases. An explicit public generic family remains a strong alternative, with its language costs stated honestly.
decisions.gist: How should Jet offer a complex number with F32 components?
decisions.lesson: Complex32 here means two F32 components, not 32 bits in total. Sharing an implementation does not require exposing generic defaults to every caller.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: existing Complex code keeps Float components. Complex32{real: 3.0, imaginary: 4.0} asks for F32 components explicitly. Context supplies each literal's component type. No new imaginary literal inference rule is approved.

Expert path: share arithmetic and every existing Complex math method over an internal component parameter restricted to F32 or Float. Expose destination-owned from_complex conversions for both concrete aliases, using scalar conversion policy for each component. Narrowing is explicit and fallible; do not silently select a type from the operand values or promise twice the throughput.
decisions.story: Em edits a long signal buffer. F32 components halve the payload bits compared with two Float components, before considering padding or container overhead. She measures numerical error and actual throughput instead of treating smaller components as a universal speedup.
decisions.detail:
Core/Math/Math.jet:40404-40406 fixes both components to Float. :40414-40487 contains the full current arithmetic and elementary method surface, which any new precision must cover. missing.jet rejects Complex<F32>{...} with E0104. edges.jet rejects the audit's call-shaped Complex<F32>(...) with E0803, not its older E0119. Current z.abs() prints 5.0 and z*z prints -7 + 24i. The review does not infer successful F32 support from generic syntax or from another language.

D-SHAPE-CONVERT1=A requires destination-owned source-named conversion. D-ARRAY-CONJ1 is an open companion ballot, not a ratified prerequisite or a current method. Public generic defaults and complex literal inference are not licensed by merely adding F32 storage. B explicitly requests a default type argument for this family and thus needs full syntax review. A needs no such default and must migrate compiler-protected Complex handling to the shared representation in one cutover, without a hidden legacy type.

options.name: Concrete aliases over one implementation
options.detail: Keep public Complex as the Float specialization and add Complex32 as the F32 specialization of one internal generic implementation. Both have identical operations at their own precision.
options.technical: The internal generic family is not a second public construction path. Preserve existing Complex meaning and literal behavior. Complex32 fields are F32, with normal aggregate alignment rather than a packed-ABI guarantee. Generate or share implementations for all existing methods, including transcendental functions, without silently calculating in Float then narrowing. from_complex infers the source specialization; widening is lossless and narrowing follows the established scalar fallible conversion policy. No implicit precision change.

options.name: Public Complex<T> with Float default
options.detail: Expose Complex<F32> and Complex<Float>, with bare Complex denoting the Float specialization. This is the original recommended model, with the default rule made explicit.
options.technical: Approve omitted component arguments for this family, not a general default-argument feature by implication. Explicitly annotated fields receive T; unannotated imaginary literals keep today's Float behavior rather than gaining value-driven inference. Restrict T to F32 or Float. Supply the full A operation and conversion set. Migrate every compiler identity check and existing caller; do not preserve an old non-generic Complex beside the new family.

options.name: Two concrete nominal types
options.detail: Keep today's nominal Complex and add a distinct Complex32 struct with F32 fields. Share private generic helpers or generated methods instead of duplicating algorithms by hand.
options.technical: Same mathematical coverage, conversion and precision rules as A. This avoids converting the existing protected type into an alias, but creates two nominal declarations and associated compiler registrations. It does not inherently double handwritten math. I8 permits implementation sharing; do not ship multiple public mechanisms for the same precision.

options.name: Float computation with F32 boundary pairs
options.detail: Keep Complex unchanged. Store compact buffers as fixed F32 pairs, widen components when reading, compute with Complex, and explicitly narrow when writing.
options.technical: A complete same-program route for storage-oriented work; it does not supply F32-precision complex arithmetic. Conversions and pair indexing remain caller code. This may be enough when buffer size matters more than F32 computation throughput, without a second complex API.

comparisons.note: complex64 has two f32 components; the name counts total bits. Odin also has complex32 and complex128, so Jet's Complex32 name must explain its different convention.
Complex<T> offers reusable generic algorithms; Complex32 and Complex64 aliases make common precisions easy. Layout compatibility does not guarantee by-value C calling convention compatibility.
Complex is parametric; ComplexF32 and ComplexF64 are concrete aliases. Promotion provides convenience beyond Jet's explicit conversion rule and has its own complexity.
SIMD's scalar parameter reuses vector algorithms across precisions. It is a representation example, not a claim that a two-lane SIMD value has complex multiplication semantics.

recommendation.why: Concrete aliases keep the beginner surface small and share one implementation. Public generic defaults and new complex literal inference are unnecessary to offer F32 components.
gains: One implementation across precisions.
Existing Complex meaning stays stable.
No public generic-default rule.

losses.loss: Two public precision names.
losses.mitigation: Document component widths explicitly, including the difference from Odin's total-bit names.

losses.loss: No public component-generic complex family.
losses.mitigation: Choose B if cross-precision generic APIs are a requirement, accepting its explicit default-type decision.

whyNot.reason: Strong for public generic numeric code, but couples the precision feature to omitted type arguments and compiler identity migration.
Avoids alias migration, but keeps two nominal declarations even when all operations share one implementation.
Sufficient for compact storage with Float math, but not F32-precision complex computation.

recommendation.tradeoff: Convenient concrete precisions now, without implicitly approving a broader generic-default feature.

Measure actual buffer layout and kernels before promising ABI size or speed; compare execution tiers.

decisions.title: Add Complex.conj without adding a synonym
decisions.situation: Jet has a Complex value with real and imaginary parts, but no conjugation method. A program can construct the conjugate by copying the real part and negating the imaginary part. The free math.conj currently accepts a Float and returns it unchanged. The approved quaternion API uses conj. We recommend the same short method name for Complex, without also adding conjugate. Extending the existing free function is a serious alternative for generic numeric code.
decisions.gist: Should complex conjugation use conj, conjugate, or the existing free function?
decisions.lesson: Conjugation keeps the real part and negates the imaginary part. It does not compute magnitude, inverse, transpose or a matrix adjoint.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: z.conj() returns a Complex. For 3 + 4i the result is 3 - 4i. This is a value operation; the receiver does not change.

Expert path: use the existing scalar negation on the imaginary component, including signed zero, infinities and NaNs. Do not replace a norm calculation with z*z.conj() under an exact floating-point identity: overflow and non-finite values can invalidate that shortcut. If both complex precisions are approved, the method preserves the receiver's component type.
decisions.story: Ivo needs the conjugate in a signal calculation. A named operation avoids repeating the two-field construction. His quaternion code uses the same operation name, but the quaternion surface is approved work, not an API demonstrated by today's compiler.
decisions.detail:
Core/Math/Math.jet:40404-40406 declares Float components; :40414-40487 gives magnitude, elementary methods and arithmetic, with no conj. :37547-37552 defines real/imag/conj for Float; conj returns its input. missing.jet reports E0102 for z.conj(), confirming audit Q4. current.jet prints z*z as -7 + 24i, magnitude 5.0, and real conj 3.0.

reference.jet's manual conjugate prints 3 - 4i and product 25 + 0i. Its reciprocal of conjugated positive imaginary zero prints -inf. These are finite and signed-zero witnesses, not a universal floating-point norm identity.

D-ARRAY-QUAT1=A ratifies quaternion conj(); it does not prove an implementation exists. D-ARRAY-COMPLEXT1 is a separate open precision question. This ballot approves scalar Complex conjugation, not complex matrices or automatic elementwise broadcasting. I8 does not inherently prefer methods to free functions; do not add both conj and conjugate for the same receiver.

options.name: Complex.conj
options.detail: Add conj() to Complex, preserving its component precision. Keep the approved quaternion operation name. Do not add a conjugate alias.
options.technical: Return Complex{real: self.real, imaginary: -self.imaginary} using ordinary scalar negation. No allocation, mutation, conjugate-transpose or norm shortcut is included. The existing Float free conj remains a real-number identity; this ballot adds no second Complex call path.
options.code:

c: z.conj() // proposed: 3 - 4i

options.name: Complex.conjugate
options.detail: Use the full English method name. Amend the approved quaternion name at the same time, avoiding two synonymous methods.
options.technical: Same value and special-value semantics as A. Rename the quaternion operation in its approved spec and all implementation callers when landed; do not keep conj as a compatibility alias. Costs are the amendment and migration, not an intrinsic inability to write clear math.
options.code:

q2: q.conjugate()

options.name: Extend math.conj
options.detail: Extend the existing free function to Complex. Use one generic numeric entry point alongside the current real identity.
options.technical: No Complex method is added. This is attractive for code handling real and complex numbers under a shared function constraint. Existing overload and owning-package rules still apply. Quaternion method naming need not change because it is a different receiver surface; this does not automatically authorize a second Complex spelling.
options.code:

r: math.conj(Float{3.0})

options.name: Use explicit fields
options.detail: Add no API. Write the complete same-program operation using today's fields and scalar negation.
options.technical: Useful when conjugation is rare and requires no protected-type method work. Repeated field construction is less recognizable than a single named operation. Same numerical behavior as the proposed method, including signed-zero negation.
options.code: c: Complex{real: z.real, imaginary: -z.imaginary}

comparisons.note: The built-in conj operation works on complex values and the overview also documents quaternion conjugation. One mathematical name can serve multiple number families.
num-complex exposes conj as a method; nalgebra supports matrix conjugation separately. Scalar conjugation need not also approve matrix adjoints.
Free conj is familiar in numerical code and numpy applies it elementwise. numpy also has a conjugate alias, which Jet need not copy.

recommendation.why: The method fits Complex's existing numeric methods and the approved quaternion name. The free-function alternative is stronger for generic numeric code, not a semantic error.
gains: Matches existing Complex method style.
Matches the approved quaternion name.

recommendation.tradeoff: Prefer the existing numeric method style while acknowledging the generic-function advantage.

decisions.title: Braces convert whole arrays through the existing From mechanism
decisions.situation: A shader wants four F32 values, but the application has four Int counts. Explicit scalar construction works; passing the whole fixed array to its destination constructor fails. The owner wants braces to construct or convert one supplied value, rather than a second source-named conversion family. This vote decides aggregate conversion while retaining literal and nested-element meanings.
decisions.gist: Should a whole array convert through destination braces and From?
decisions.lesson: Braces construct a destination from the information supplied. A whole value or one nested element keeps its existing meaning; otherwise a single applicable From converts. Element conversion remains exact unless a named policy explicitly requests loss.
decisions.explainer: Answer to q0xqu5fn: yes, [F32#4]{counts} is a whole-array conversion, not a literal containing one incorrectly typed element. It uses the same From system as scalar conversion.
decisions.story: A tile engine converts counts for a shader without writing four scalar conversions or a new method name for every source type.
decisions.inWild: The useful competing design is an ordinary element map: it can transform, validate or selectively handle each element rather than only convert a type.
decisions.detail:
Replayed gate-p275 probes/a1.jet: explicit scalar conversions print 4.0, nested-list construction prints 1, and existing matrix helpers run. probes/a2.jet fails E0963 for [F32#4]{counts} and E0303 for Mat4{m}. The latter is important: today's parser treats a bare identifier as shorthand even when it is not the matrix's field name.

r1's claim that only a local named lanes collides was false. The proposal changes this failing dispatch path; it is not already supported. probes/f2.jet also establishes two scalar From keys, not aggregate From support.

D-CONVERT-TRAIT1 supplies one From mechanism, exact braces, label-only policy options and source/destination-module ownership. D-DOTCTOR3's earlier literal-only description must be read with that amendment. D-IMPL-COND1 forbids concrete specialization and overlapping conditional impls: r1's implied blanket plus customizable aggregate override is not legal. D-LANES1 and D-ARRAY-WINDOW1 govern lane sizes and input windows. D-COPY-WORD1 requires .copy(), not ~.

A is retained. B is the strong existing map alternative, not a second conversion mechanism merely because it writes a function. r1 C's new source-named conversion system is removed: it contradicts the ratified single-From choice and is not an ordinary eligible option. Ratified specialized APIs such as from_complex are not silently removed by this ballot. No comparative speed, allocation-count or general in-place-conversion claim remains.

options.name: Whole-value braces through From
options.detail: When a supplied value is neither the destination nor one accepted element, convert the aggregate through From. Equal nesting and fixed extents stay intact.
options.technical:
Dispatch Head{e}: retain labelled fields, spreads and multiple-element literals. For one unlabelled expression, first preserve valid existing field shorthand, then a whole value of Head, then one accepted element. Otherwise select exactly one Head.From(type-of-e); do not search conversion chains. A bare identifier that does not name a field must reach this path instead of today's E0303. A name that does name a field keeps shorthand and its normal field-type diagnostic; its explicit conversion repair is Head.from(name). Do not silently reinterpret a failing real field initializer.

Provide one generic structural From row per corresponding family, conditional on the scalar T.From(S). The rows are [T#N] from [S#N], an owned [T] result from [S] input, and sized Lanes<T,N> from Lanes<S,N>. These are the sole structural rows, not blankets plus concrete overrides.

Resolve and reject overlap under ordinary coherence before use; no override precedence, trait-disjointness guess or concrete specialization. Recursive element selection handles equally nested arrays; a source fitting as one destination element remains one element rather than being flattened. Fixed length mismatch is a compile-time error at the relevant nesting level, including zero. Native sizeless lanes retain D-LANES1 restrictions.

Evaluate e once, traverse in index order and write each converted element directly into destination storage. Fixed arrays and sized lanes require no extra heap container; their elements may themselves allocate or fail. Different element widths generally require distinct destination storage, not in-place rewriting of the source.

An owned list result reserves for the known length without repeated container growth; do not promise one allocator call for arbitrary element conversions. Ownership follows the selected From parameter: ordinary read parameters borrow, consuming parameters move, and .copy() is explicit duplication. A borrowed source is never overwritten.

Exact numeric checks and scalar typed failures retain their existing meaning. checked around the aggregate catches exactly the same numeric-check failures as checked around scalar braces; it does not swallow a user From error or AllocError.

On any failure drop the initialized destination prefix exactly once, preserve borrowed input, and clean moved input exactly once according to its ownership. Labelled rounding/overflow options on .from apply to each scalar conversion, evaluated once before traversal. Reject a policy not supported by the selected scalar impl. No hidden deep copy or implicit lossy conversion.

options.name: Explicit element map
options.detail: Keep aggregate braces literal-only and convert with a scalar constructor inside map. Mapping is more general and allows per-element recovery or transformation.
options.technical: A shape-preserving fixed-array/lane map must be specified rather than falsely claimed demonstrated here. Each nested level maps separately. A map returning optional elements is not the same as checked whole-array conversion: the former keeps per-element outcomes, the latter yields one absent aggregate on the first numeric failure. Scalar exactness, typed errors and allocation failure remain unchanged. This alternative avoids aggregate dispatch work but does not follow the owner's requested direct conversion syntax.
options.code:
// PROPOSED fixed-shape mapping contract
weights: counts.map(fn(n) { F32{n} })

comparisons.note: Stronger than type conversion for arbitrary transforms and per-element recovery; not an illegitimate competing conversion trait.

recommendation.why: Directly answers the owner and extends the ratified conversion mechanism without a parallel family of names.
gains: Destination braces express whole-array conversion.
Nested elements, ownership and failures keep one defined dispatch order.

losses.loss: A lone source identifier can coincide with a real field name.
losses.mitigation: Keep genuine shorthand priority and offer explicit Head.from(name); do not reinterpret a field initializer.

losses.loss: An element conversion that allocates or fails does so inside the array too.
losses.mitigation: Fixed arrays of numbers write straight into the destination with no heap. Any failure is the element conversion's own declared failure, so the aggregate adds no new failure.

whyNot.reason: Flexible and familiar, but adds a map at each nesting level and withholds the direct whole-value conversion the owner requested.

recommendation.tradeoff: Conversion is concise; arbitrary transformation still belongs in map.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude Opus. Adversarial model family: GPT. Fresh agent: BallotReview. Verdict: ready to post as an aggregate From proposal that keeps literal and field precedence, with no blanket no-heap or speed claim.

decisions.checkInstructions: Implementation acceptance covers dispatch precedence, including real and nonfield identifier collisions, and fixed or nested length errors. It also covers one coherent generic row per family, zero extents, and the exact, checked, user-error and AllocError distinction. Further cases: borrowed and moved inputs, prefix cleanup, list reservation, and no extra container allocation for fixed arrays of nonallocating elements. No implementation or performance gate was run here.

surface.gist: Should a whole array convert through destination braces and From?
surface.lesson: Braces can construct or convert. Existing whole-value, field and nested-element meanings keep priority; otherwise one From handles conversion.

decisions.title: Add lane-scalar arithmetic through typed hooks, not broader mirroring
decisions.situation: A lane value currently needs an explicit splat before arithmetic with a scalar. Vec3 already supports a scalar on the right, so the two families feel inconsistent. We recommend scalar arithmetic on either side of exact lanes, using ordinary typed hooks. The draft incorrectly relied on D-OPMIX1 mirroring for fixed-width F32 and integer scalars. That rule mirrors only Int, Float and Decimal. Explicit reverse hooks can supply the feature without changing the mirror rule or adding a special broadcast parser.
decisions.gist: Should exact lane values support scalar arithmetic without an explicit splat?
decisions.lesson: A scalar is repeated across the lanes for +, -, * and /. Preserve operand order and scalar arithmetic policy; this is not a general array broadcast feature.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: lanes * gain means lanes * LaneType.splat(gain), where gain has the lane element type. gain - lanes means subtract each lane from gain, not the reverse. Scalar operands are evaluated once, in source order.

Expert path: add L.Add<E>, L.Sub<E>, L.Mul<E> and L.Div<E> for operations L already supports. Add the corresponding E hooks for a lane on the right in the owning Core package. Existing direct hooks win before D-OPMIX1 fallback. Exact lane type and element type remain unchanged; normal literal context applies, with no new cross-width coercion.
decisions.story: Kai changes brightness with a runtime F32 gain. He no longer writes a manual splat at every arithmetic site. He does not assume that a literal-only example proves a stored Decimal variable can silently narrow to F32.
decisions.detail:
Core/Math/Math.jet:40675-40686 gives F32x4.splat and adapters; :41486-41515 gives I32x4's four vector arithmetic operations. missing.jet reports E2511 for F32x4 * 2.0. current.jet runs explicit F32x4.splat(10.0) and Vec3 * 2.0; its earlier scalar-left Vec3 expression failed E0133. Ratified mixed operators are therefore not fully working today. Audit S3's gap is real.

D-OPMIX1=D ratifies typed hooks and mirrors only + and * from Int, Float or Decimal on the left. It does not automatically mirror F32, I32 or U8. Direct hooks win; operands evaluate left-to-right once. An unconstrained 2.0 is Decimal, not Float.

D-LANES1=A replaces the current named structs with exact generic lanes. A adds library hooks under existing rules; it does not amend lookup or extend fixed-array arithmetic. No performance identity is asserted without code-generation evidence.

options.name: Typed hooks on both sides
options.detail: Support +, -, * and / between an exact lane value and its element scalar, on either side, whenever that lane-lane operation exists. Implement each direction with ordinary owning-package hooks.
options.technical: Do not depend on fixed-width scalars entering D-OPMIX1's mirror set. Reverse subtraction and division retain source order. Match explicit splat arithmetic for overflow, division by zero, signed zero and NaN behavior. Receiver and scalar evaluate once, left-to-right. No comparison, mask, bitwise, shift, arbitrary array or sizeless-lane feature is included. Compound assignment follows existing direct-hook rules rather than gaining an automatic mirror.
options.code:
gain: F32{0.8}
bright: pixels * gain
inverted: F32{1.0} - pixels
ratio: F32{2.0} / pixels

options.name: Scalar on the right only
options.detail: Add lane-owned typed hooks, but no scalar-owned reverse hooks. Left-scalar expressions use an explicit splat.
options.technical: A smaller implementation and a visible direction for broadcasting, without a new lookup mechanism. Existing D-OPMIX1 mirroring still applies only where its actual permitted types and hooks match. Do not teach that every literal or fixed-width scalar automatically mirrors. Noncommutative reverse operations are written explicitly.
options.code:
bright: pixels * gain
inverted: F32x4.splat(F32{1.0}) - pixels
ratio: F32x4.splat(F32{2.0}) / pixels

options.name: Explicit splat only
options.detail: Keep the current representation conversion visible at every arithmetic site. This is a complete equivalent program with no new mixed hooks.
options.technical: Evaluate a stored scalar once, splat it to the exact lane type, then use existing lane-lane operators. This is Zig's strong explicit baseline, not an inherently slower program. Avoid claiming redundant machine copies without checking lowering for the actual target and optimization tier.
options.code:
bright: pixels * F32x4.splat(gain)
inverted: F32x4.splat(F32{1.0}) - pixels
ratio: F32x4.splat(F32{2.0}) / pixels

comparisons.note: Scalar operands are convenient for SIMD arithmetic and array programming. Jet can offer that convenience through existing typed operator hooks rather than a general broadcast rule.
Vectors and scalars cannot be mixed directly; @splat is explicit and exposes the repeated value. Its optimized cost need not exceed mixed-operator syntax.
Float SIMD supports scalar arithmetic on both sides. Integer SIMD deliberately rejects ordinary checked +, - and * in favor of wrapping operators; its overflow policy differs from Jet's.
Scalar-vector component arithmetic is familiar in shader expressions. That convenience does not settle CPU overflow or Jet's typed-hook ownership rules.
Broadcast syntax and array operations cover broader shape combinations. They solve more than exact-lane scalar arithmetic, at the cost of a larger shape and dispatch model.

recommendation.why: Ordinary typed hooks provide the requested convenience on both sides. Explicit reverse hooks preserve D-OPMIX1's narrow mirror set and ordered subtraction and division.
gains: Less repeated splat notation.
Both operand orders are supported.
No new operator lookup rule.

losses.loss: More hook instances to maintain.
losses.mitigation: Share elementwise implementations and test each supported direction against explicit splat.

losses.loss: Broadcast is less visible at the call.
losses.mitigation: Restrict it to exact element scalars and document the equivalent splat expression.

whyNot.reason: Smaller, but left-scalar subtraction and division remain asymmetric.
Strong explicit baseline with potentially identical code; A favors readability in repeated lane arithmetic.

recommendation.tradeoff: More Core operator instances in exchange for simpler expressions, without a compiler broadcast mechanism.

Do not expand the mirror set or fixed-array rules here.

decisions.title: Direct matrix conversion, with explicit cropping and defined reshape order
decisions.situation: The owner wants Matrix<2,8>{grown}, not a matrix-to-array-to-matrix adapter chain. Matrix conversion needs a clear distinction between preserving coordinates, reshaping all cells and discarding cells. Existing Mat3/Mat4 helpers already provide useful operations, so their absence is not the reason for this vote. The remaining question is which shape changes destination braces choose by default.
decisions.gist: Should matrix braces grow coordinates or reshape equal cell counts, with cropping explicit?
decisions.lesson: Growth preserves coordinates; reshape preserves a stated traversal; cropping discards cells. All alternatives use From for conversion and .copy() for explicit duplication. A window makes discarded coordinates visible.
decisions.explainer: Answer to q13p1rdp: direct Matrix<2,8>{grown} is part of A. No array adapters are required, and ~ is never copy syntax. This proposal deliberately rejects silent cropping, rather than claiming scalar conversion law already decides matrix shape policy.
decisions.story: Grow a 3x3 rotation to a 4x4 transform, then reshape its sixteen cells to two rows. Extracting a 3x3 region is a visible window before conversion.
decisions.inWild: Eigen offers layout parameters and storage-order-aware operations. Traversal order and physical representation are separate questions; neither makes all reshapes free.
decisions.detail:
A remains A. B is repaired to be a coherent named-operation alternative; C requires explicit .from policies for every shape change. r1 incorrectly treated D-CONVERT-TRAIT1's exact scalar rule as already forbidding matrix cropping. The no-silent-crop rule here is a proposed shape policy and its rationale must stand on its own. It also incorrectly called an equal-count reshape a free storage move. Inline values may require byte movement, borrowed sources require a new owned result, and element type or layout changes may require work.

Replayed gate-p275 probes/a1.jet: existing Mat3.new/from_array/to_array/transpose and Mat4.identity().determinant execute; probes/a2.jet rejects Mat4{m} with E0303. These probes establish current helpers and the brace-dispatch gap, not generic Matrix implementation or no-copy performance. Source inspected in Core/Math/Math.jet includes Mat2's fixed lanes and Numeric's zero/one requirements in Compiler/Prelude/Traits.jet.

Ratified: D-ARRAY-MATOPS1 already selects Matrix<R,C,T=Float,Layout=.ColumnMajor>; D-ARRAY-MAT21's small names remain aliases under that family. D-MATRIX-INDEX1=E defines coordinate indexing and matrix windows. D-CONVERT-TRAIT1 provides the one From conversion mechanism and labelled options; D-COPY-WORD1 fixes .copy(). The aggregate dispatch/failure rules are shared with D-ARRAY-CONVERT1, including actual field shorthand priority. The old answer's implied Mat3{grown} contraction is superseded by explicit Mat3{grown[0..<3,0..<3]}; direct equal-count Matrix<2,8>{grown} is retained exactly. This is explained rather than hidden in a footnote.

options.name: Direct growth and equal-count reshape
options.detail: Braces preserve coordinates at the same shape, reshape equal cell counts in logical column order, or grow both axes with identity fill. Cropping must first name a window.
options.technical:
Precedence has four steps. First, an identical shape preserves coordinates while converting element type or layout. Second, a different shape with an equal total cell count reshapes the logical column traversal. Third, when every destination extent is at least the source extent, source coordinates stay at the top left and new coordinates fill from identity. Fourth, anything else is rejected with a window-first repair. This ordering settles mixed shrinking/growing equal-count shapes: they reshape, not crop/pad. Shape multiplication must be checked at compile time without overflow.

Default identity fill requires the element type's zero and one through the existing Numeric contract. A nonnumeric element type needs explicit .from(source, fill: value), evaluated once and reused only under ordinary copyability rules; do not duplicate a move-only fill value. For move-only cells use an explicit fill function taking row and column, invoked once per new coordinate. Reuse the existing array from_fn callback convention rather than inventing an identity sentinel in the cell type. Reject unavailable defaults with the explicit-fill repair.

.from(source, order: .Rows) selects logical row traversal for equal-count reshape; order on other shape changes is rejected as irrelevant. .from(source, fill: value) or fill_fn: changes only growth fill. Labels follow the existing From options rule; no second conversion trait. Cropping remains a window under every alternative, not an option that silently drops cells. Preserve logical coordinates independently of physical layout.

Equal zero counts reshape to an empty matrix. Zero-axis growth preserves no source cells and generates only coordinates inside the target. Same-shape empty conversion does not invoke element conversion or fill. Evaluate source/options once; exact scalar checks, checked, typed errors, AllocError and prefix cleanup follow aggregate From rules. Borrowed sources stay unchanged; ownership follows the selected parameter.

Storage: construct directly in final destination, without an intermediate array. When count, element representation, alignment and physical sequence match and ownership permits last-use reuse, no cell permutation is needed; byte moves or allocation behavior still follow ordinary value representation. A live borrowed source requires copying its values into the owned result.

Changed traversal/layout/type may require visiting every cell; write once into final storage rather than allocating a repacking buffer. No universal zero-copy/no-heap assertion: element operations can allocate. Window .copy() creates an owned matrix under the ratified view rule. Genuine shorthand names retain priority; a nonfield bare identifier must reach From, repairing today's broader E0303 path.

options.name: Named resize and reshape
options.detail: Use explicit resize/reshape operations rather than matrix-to-matrix braces. The two names advertise coordinate preservation versus traversal.
options.technical: Same shape, failure, ownership and explicit-crop semantics as A. resize permits growth, not implicit cropping; reshape requires equal cell counts and names traversal. These operations replace the corresponding brace conversion rather than coexist as conversion aliases. This is a genuine readability advantage, but declines the owner's requested direct destination constructor.

options.name: Name every shape-change policy
options.detail: Braces convert only identical shapes; .from must name order for reshaping or fill for growth. This keeps one From mechanism but makes every shape change explicit.
options.technical: Use the same rules as A with no inferred identity-fill or column-traversal default. Use the existing Numeric identity operation through an explicit fill function, not an invented .Identity cell value. Same-count source/destination shape changes always require order:. Cropping is still an explicit window.
options.code:
// PROPOSED; reshape policy always explicit.
flat: Matrix<2,8>.from(grown, order: .Columns)

comparisons.note: Optional storage order exists; changing storage order may reorder cells, and performance depends on traversal.

recommendation.why: Provides the owner's direct constructor without an array round trip, while separating coordinate growth, traversal and explicit data loss.
gains: Matrix<2,8>{grown} is direct.
One From/ownership/failure protocol; no silent cropping.

losses.loss: A nondefault traversal or fill needs a label.
losses.mitigation: Defaults cover column traversal and numeric identity growth; labels are local and evaluated once.

losses.loss: Owned results from borrowed or differently ordered sources need cell work.
losses.mitigation: Each cell is written once, straight into final storage, with no intermediate array or repacking buffer. A last-use source with matching layout needs no cell reordering.

whyNot.reason: Names explain the operation well, but withhold the direct destination conversion the owner asked for.
Maximum local explicitness, but repeats the same default policy at every ordinary growth or reshape.

recommendation.tradeoff: A fixes deterministic defaults; it does not promise every reshape is a zero-copy operation.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude Opus. Adversarial model family: GPT. Fresh agent: BallotReview. Verdict: ready to post as a deterministic shape policy with direct Matrix<2,8>{grown}, explicit cropping windows and .copy(), not as a performance claim.

decisions.checkInstructions: Implementation acceptance: ordered shape dispatch, equal-count mixed extents, zero/overflow extents, numeric and nonnumeric fills, move-only fill functions, explicit cropping, borrowed ownership, element/AllocError cleanup and direct construction. Inspect physical movement separately; no universal no-copy test.

surface.gist: Should matrix braces grow coordinates or reshape equal cell counts, with cropping explicit?
surface.lesson: Growth keeps coordinates; reshape uses a traversal; cropping discards cells. Direct conversion uses From. Explicit copies use .copy(), never ~.

losses.mitigation: Each cell is written once, straight into the result; a matching last-use source needs no reordering.

Needlessly repeats defaults.

decisions.title: Pick slots by number with shuffle, without promising one instruction
decisions.situation: A swizzle picks slots to make a new row, such as rgb to bgr. Jet currently supports letter swizzles on selected vector types, not fixed arrays or every lane type. Letters cannot name slot 7 or 15. Programs can already write indexed elements out by hand. We recommend shuffle with constant indexes on fixed arrays and exact lanes, sharing the operation name ratified for lanes. This chooses the call and result rules, not a machine-instruction count.
decisions.gist: How should arrays and exact lanes pick slots by number?
decisions.lesson: Write the source indexes in result order. Indexes may repeat; compile-time bounds checking does not imply that hardware can perform every permutation in one instruction.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: a.shuffle(2, 1, 0) produces those three slots. Fixed arrays return [T#K], where K is the argument count. The source is evaluated once. Existing letter swizzles remain available where supported.

Expert path: accept compile-time Int expressions, including named constants, rather than literal tokens only. Reject negative and out-of-range indexes. Exact lanes return Lanes<T, K> only when K is a legal exact width; otherwise report the unsupported width and show the fixed-array adapter. This does not add dynamic gather, two-source selection, writes or sizeless-lane shuffle.
decisions.story: Sam reverses the channels in a 32-byte pixel block. He lists all 32 destination picks, not just eight. A pick of 32 is out of bounds; 9 is valid. The target may need several instructions, especially across register sublanes.
decisions.detail:
Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Expressions/Places.jet:1448-1491 limits letter reads to Vec2/3/4, F32x4 and F64x2, using x/y/z/w. Core/Math/Math.jet:40695-40706 makes a three-slot F32x4 letter read a Float Vec3, not three F32 lanes. Numeric shuffle deliberately preserves the source element type. Literals.jet:1120-1122 and :1164-1167 establish bounds diagnostics E0965.

missing.jet reports E0311 for the audit W8 method; edges.jet gives E0302 for fixed-array letters. Planned #6177 c3 is not current support. D-LANES1=A ratifies shuffle on exact widths, but not this argument syntax or an instruction guarantee. The generic family replaces the current twenty names rather than preserving another family.

Numeric and letter forms must share selection semantics where their result types agree. This ballot needs full syntax review because it introduces constant-argument and result-shape rules, despite using ordinary method tokens.

options.name: shuffle with constant arguments
options.detail: a.shuffle(2, 1, 0) returns picks in that order. At least one constant Int argument is required. Arrays preserve T and return length K. Exact lanes preserve T and require a legal result width.
options.technical: Bounds are 0 <= i < N. Constants may be expressions. Evaluation reads an unchanged source once; repeats are allowed. Non-copy element types are rejected rather than duplicated or implicitly moved out of a read place. Empty calls are errors, without inventing a Random API fix. Reuse the same selector lowering as letter projections; code generation chooses a legal instruction sequence.

options.name: swizzle with constant arguments
options.detail: Exactly A, named swizzle. This aligns numeric calls with letter-swizzle terminology and Odin.
options.technical: Amend D-LANES1's shuffle operation name in the same cutover. Do not ship both method names. All A bounds, copy, width and evaluation rules apply.
options.code:
bgr: rgb.swizzle(2, 1, 0)
picks: eight.swizzle(7, 6, 5, 4)

options.name: Explicit indexed construction
options.detail: Add no numeric method on arrays. Build the result from indexed reads; fixed-array helpers can use a constant index table for reusable picks.
options.technical: D-ARRAY-INIT1=A already ratifies from_fn. A typed index table and result length make a same-program alternative without a new selector API. The lane shuffle remains independently required by D-LANES1.

options.name: shuffle with a constant index array
options.detail: Pass one fixed array of indexes instead of a variable number of arguments. This makes selection tables reusable and generated masks natural.
options.technical: The mask must be known at compile time, with [Int#K] and K > 0. All A bounds and result rules apply. This is a competing signature, not an additional overload; it avoids a new scalar argument count for every result length.

decisions.title: Complete one generic matrix algebra family, with measured performance requirements
decisions.situation: Jet already has small Float matrices with identity, determinant and fallible inverse, but scalar scaling and several basic operations are missing. The owner asks for a stronger design than a narrow list of helpers and unsupported superiority claims. We recommend one element-generic matrix family covering real, integer and complex algebra, views and core decompositions. Performance and numerical quality become explicit acceptance requirements, not promises inferred from short syntax.
decisions.gist: Complete generic matrix functionality without duplicated types, aliases or unsupported fastest claims.
decisions.lesson: Adjugate is transposed cofactors, not conjugate transpose. Integer algebra, numerical inversion and element-wise masks have different valid domains.
decisions.explainer: Beginner: m * scale scales cells; trace adds the diagonal; u.outer(v) constructs a possibly rectangular matrix. Expert: use inverse()?.transpose() for inverse transpose and transpose().conj() for conjugate transpose. These compositions must fuse where safe, not acquire redundant method aliases. Factorizations and solves belong to the same numerical family, not a separate unfinished promise.
decisions.story: Ines transforms normals after uneven scaling, while another program needs cofactors of a singular matrix. A third solves a rectangular system and must not be told that a four-by-four inverse replaces a numerical library.
decisions.detail:
gate-p260 probes/matrices.jet successfully executes Mat2.identity().determinant(), Mat4.identity().inverse(), Mat3 transpose and array-mediated scaling. probes/missing.jet reports E2511 for Mat3 * Float and E0102 for trace, adjugate, minor and Vec3.outer. The original ballot's claims that Mat2, identity, determinant, inverse and a private adjugate helper were absent are false on this gate. Core/Math/Math.jet:39471-39793 contains them, including mat4_adjugate at 39744. Its matrix_singular predicate at 39533 uses an absolute epsilon, not a scale-invariant numerical guarantee.

D-ARRAY-MAT21 already ratifies a generic Matrix destination for Mat2-4 aliases. This proposal makes the element and optional layout parameters consistent with the other matrix ballots: Matrix<R,C,T=Float,Layout=.ColumnMajor>. D-MATRIX-MUL1's operand-pair rule must be amended narrowly to admit plain matrix/scalar and scalar/matrix scaling while preserving matrix composition and its existing cell operator. No dotted call broadcasting is reintroduced.

Odin's overview lists scaling, determinant, adjugate, inverse transpose, Hermitian adjoint, trace and minor; its linalg source implements generic outer product and square complex conjugate transpose. Eigen and nalgebra also supply views, factorizations and solves; Julia documents fused element-wise expressions, and Eigen documents aliasing temporaries. A proposal lacking those capabilities cannot honestly claim blanket superiority. The recommended delivery includes the listed baseline and comparative acceptance; it does not claim Jet already beats mature libraries or replaces their entire dynamic, sparse, GPU or scientific ecosystems.

options.name: One complete generic matrix family
options.detail: Use shared scalar-constrained algorithms for fixed rectangular matrices, including integer and complex elements, common operations, views, factorizations and solves.
options.technical:
One Matrix<R,C,T=Float,Layout=.ColumnMajor> family owns shape checking, aliases, indexing, conversion, views and layout. Mat2-4 become aliases with shared implementations, not wrappers or duplicate formulas. Multiplication requires matching inner dimensions and compatible element types; no implicit element widening. Integer operations retain scalar overflow checks. Bit masks remain element-wise integer operations, not invented integer inverses. Scalar division requires the element's ordinary division domain; scalar/matrix division is rejected.

Required coverage includes scalar multiplication in both orders, matrix/scalar division and square trace. Add square minor(row,col), returning the determinant after deleting that row and column. Add cofactor-based adjugate valid even when singular, arbitrary-length outer product and element-wise complex conjugation. The adjugate of 1x1 is [1]; the empty determinant is one and empty adjugate empty, where the scalar supplies zero/one.

Integer determinant and adjugate use exact, overflow-checked algorithms, not Float round trips. Complex conjugate transpose is transpose().conj(), with no adjoint alias. Inverse transpose is inverse()?.transpose(), with no inverse_transpose alias.

Include LU with pivoting, QR, SVD, rank and square/least-squares solve in this delivery, using reusable factor objects rather than recomputing a decomposition per right-hand side. Restrict inverse and decompositions to supported real/complex field types; integer callers must explicitly convert. Define rank tolerance relative to scale, expose nonconvergence/singularity/nonfinite errors, and never return identity on failure. Small inverse fast paths must satisfy the same error contract as the shared kernel; replace the current absolute-cutoff divergence at alias cutover.

No hidden heap allocation for fixed-size elementary operations. Borrow strided views rather than copying them; preserve overlap correctness through dependence analysis and a bounded temporary when needed, never an unchecked noalias default. Fuse safe composed cell transforms.

Shared work for every API option includes numerical residual tests, scale extremes, allocation inspection and representative paired measurements against applicable Odin, Eigen and nalgebra operations. Publish a faster claim only for a measured matched workload and contract. Specialized code size and robust numerical work are real costs; prune unused combinations and reuse factor objects. This is not a vote to duplicate their entire sparse/dynamic/GPU ecosystems.

decisions.title: Iterator next propagates failure; results() keeps per-item recovery
decisions.situation: The tested file-lines loop stops the program on invalid UTF-8 even inside a function that returns IOError, while explicit read_line returns the error normally. The Iterator trait currently requires an infallible next. Directory and HTTP cursor sources instead declare failure inside their items. This vote chooses one predictable fallible-iteration boundary without losing deliberate per-item recovery.
decisions.gist: Should a failing next propagate from the loop header, with results() for per-item recovery?
decisions.lesson: End means no item; failure means the next operation failed. They are different outcomes. A propagating loop stops at failure; results() yields that failure as an item so the body may decide what to do.
decisions.explainer: Ordinary loops propagate next's error like an ordinary call. results() explicitly requests error-as-data. Fusion concerns None exhaustion, not whether an iterator may continue after an error.
decisions.story: A damaged log must not be reported as a complete successful read. A repair tool may instead handle each damaged record and keep advancing when its source supports that behavior.
decisions.inWild: Rust BufRead::lines returns Result items. A loop can use ? to propagate, handle each Result, collect them, or pass them onward; it does not necessarily unwrap in every body.
decisions.detail:
A remains A. r1 removed associated-type default syntax but incorrectly suggested that deriving Error from next adds no machinery. It is a new conformance-inference rule, specified below. B is repaired to remove stop/silent-end behavior rather than offer it as acceptable. C is the strong Rust-style error-as-data option, not a straw man that every consumer must unwrap.

Executed on gate-p275: probes/review-lines.jet prints 'loop got alpha', then exits 70 with E3001 and the invalid-UTF-8 read message. The second function in that program cannot run after the stop. Isolated probes/review-steps.jet prints 'step got alpha', then 'steps err invalid input during read ... stream did not contain valid UTF-8', exiting 0. These are the independently reproduced current behaviors. The author's it1/it2 sources referenced another scratch path, so this review created self-contained probes using this folder's bad.txt.

Compiler/Prelude/Traits.jet:299-310 declares Iterator.next -> Item? Never! and infallible Iterable.iter. Compiler/JetIR/Source/CoreReach.jet:279-310 contains named reader routing. Core/Process/Process.jet:887-896 was inspected: read_bytes is handled with ?? [U8]{} and empty pieces set done. No actual failing process pipe was injected, so this review does not claim an observed pipe-failure result. Core/Files/Files.jet:2066 and Core/HTTP/HTTP.jet:548 declare cursor items carrying failure; those declarations, not a live HTTP/walk failure, were inspected.

D-ITER-FUSED1 concerns permanent None, not post-Err continuation; r1's citation for resumability was wrong. D-ITER-BORROW1 distinguishes borrowed and owned cursors: leaving a loop must not close an externally owned borrowed resource. D-ITER-SELECTION1 and D-ITER-COLLECT1 preserve errors through adapters/collection, and D-ITER-SIZE1's bounds do not predict future success. D-ALLOC-FAIL1 governs adapter allocations. D-LANG-MIGRATE1 forbids calling intentional panic-to-error behavior changes Safe rewrites. The Rust BufRead documentation was read; no comparative speed claim is made.

options.name: Propagate from next; adapt errors into items
options.detail: Allow next to fail and propagate that failure from the loop header. results() turns failures into items for explicit recovery without changing the underlying source.
options.technical:
Proposed Iterator has associated Item and Error, with next returning Item? Error! and carrying its ordinary declared effects. Error is explicit or inferred from the implementation's declared/inferred next failure channel, Never for an actually infallible next. Infer before conformance checking; do not invent default associated-type syntax or claim this inference already exists. An explicit Error and next signature must agree under ordinary failure conversion rules. Existing infallible implementations retain Error=Never; they do not acquire a new runtime failure branch merely to satisfy the trait.

The loop header is the next call site: propagate by ordinary function failure/effect rules and From conversions. If the surrounding contract cannot carry the error, use the ordinary propagation diagnostic with two manual choices: widen/convert the error channel or select results(). Do not assume a particular diagnostic number without a fixture. No further next call occurs in that propagating loop after failure. Clean up loop-owned iterators and temporaries on every exit; borrowed iterators/resources remain under their owner's scope and may be used again when loans permit.

results() has Item equal to the ordinary result type carrying the source Item or Error and has Error=Never for next itself; it retains the source's effects. Each source success becomes Ok(item), each source error becomes Err(error), and None stays None. It does NOT latch errors as exhaustion or invent a resumability marker: a later adapter next calls source next again.

A terminal source must update its own state so its next call ends; a recoverable source may advance after an error. Normal loops still stop at None; only the separately ratified fuse behavior latches None. An endlessly failing source can yield endless Err items, just as any iterator may be infinite; results() must not silently discard or stop them.

Map/filter/collection propagate upstream failures through the same channel as ordinary calls and preserve selected error-as-data items. Callback failures require an ordinary common declared error conversion, not a newly invented implicit union; reject incompatible channels with a conversion diagnostic. results() wraps state without duplicating elements or imposing a heap allocation. Iterable.iter stays infallible: opening/constructing a potentially failing source is an explicit call before iteration.

Migrate file/stdin/process lines and chunks, directory walk and HTTP chunks to ordinary Core iterators with failure in next. Delete equivalent named-reader routing only when those paths are covered. Preserve old Result-item clients by adding results() at their sources before retaining their existing bodies.

Never remove recovery code based on a guess. A current panic/silent-end to returned-error change is an intentional behavior correction, not a Safe fix; surface it explicitly and require a selected migration. Only mechanically equivalent rewrites qualify as Safe. Resource-close and error-construction paths must remain valid under allocation failure.

options.name: Explicit stepping for fallible sources
options.detail: Keep Iterator infallible; remove infallible adapters over sources that can fail. Call read_line/read_bytes explicitly in an ordinary loop.
options.technical: This is the smallest trait change and matches the isolated successful read_line error probe. It must not retain silent truncation or panic as the default failure protocol. Existing error-as-data cursor families can still use C's ordinary Item mechanism, but callers who want automatic propagation must step explicitly. Source-specific stepping methods remain API surface to learn.

options.name: Failures are Result items
options.detail: Keep next infallible and make every fallible source yield Result items. Consumers choose propagation, recovery, collection or forwarding.
options.technical: No new associated Error or failure inference. This is a strong compositional choice and already appears in inspected Core cursor declarations. Ordinary map sees a Result item; success-only adapters must explicitly preserve and pass errors rather than silently dropping them. A propagating consumer needs an error-aware boundary, but a consumer retaining outcomes need not unwrap each item. Migrate line/process adapters to the same model instead of retaining panic/end behavior.

comparisons.note: BufRead::lines yields io::Result<String>; callers may propagate, recover, collect or forward outcomes.

recommendation.why: Ordinary failure propagation should not change merely because repeated calls are expressed as a loop; results() keeps deliberate error-as-data processing.
gains: No panic/end conflation for fallible next.
Per-item recovery remains explicit without changing the source type's error contract.

losses.loss: The trait gains associated failure inference and adapter plumbing.
losses.mitigation: One failure channel follows existing call/conversion rules; Never implementations erase it. No new default syntax, implicit error union or resumability capability.

losses.loss: Loops that crashed or ended early on bad input now return the error.
losses.mitigation: The migrator lists every loop whose crash or early end becomes a returned error. Each needs a selected edit, and .results() keeps per-item handling where wanted.

whyNot.reason: Simple and correct, but fallible sources lose ordinary adapter/loop composition.
Strong for outcome-processing pipelines; propagation-first consumers need explicit handling at an error-aware boundary.

recommendation.tradeoff: A makes propagation the default and error-as-data explicit; C makes the opposite default.

Every migrated source runs with injected failures, and explicit migration is told apart from Safe migration. No suite was run.
