decisions.title: Package formatting returns String, with ordinary style traits
decisions.situation: Jet prints built-in numbers with selectors such as :Hex(4), but rejects the same selector on a package wrapper. The owner rejected a public output argument, and ratified law requires returning newly produced text. Both alternatives therefore return String and use the existing String execution contract. The remaining choice is ordinary traits for the existing style families or extending keyed-trait dispatch.
decisions.gist: Should package styles use ordinary per-style traits or extend keyed-trait dispatch?
decisions.lesson: A selector chooses how a value becomes text. Implement only the styles your type actually supports. Both options return String: no output argument, public writer, builder type or separate streaming trait.
decisions.explainer: Answer to q5xewxmx: the output argument is gone from every alternative. A HexFormat method returns the hexadecimal text. Allocation and destination handling follow the already ratified String rules, not a new promise about hidden return storage.
decisions.story: A package wraps an integer ID. It deliberately implements hexadecimal formatting by delegating to its integer field, without exposing that field at each call site.
decisions.inWild: Rust's LowerHex is one trait for hexadecimal and writes to Formatter; Python's __format__ returns str and interprets a style specification. They demonstrate two real extension designs, not equivalent allocation costs.
decisions.detail:
r2 changes the recommendation, so r1 B (ordinary traits) becomes A and r1 A (keyed Format) becomes B. The owner chose no output argument, not a keyed trait. r1 correctly removed the public writer but incorrectly called keyed support existing general machinery: probes/f3.jet rejects an arbitrary Styled(Int), listing only Add/Sub/Mul/Div/From.

Reusing those special cases is compiler work, not proof that an arbitrary style key and its coherence/bounds already work. Ordinary traits are the stronger low-mechanism alternative and should not be dismissed as seven implementations every user must write. A user implements only the desired family.

Executed on gate-p275. The probe f1.jet prints 21.5, 31 m and 001f. The probe f2.jet executes two From source keys and prints 24.5 and 9. The probe f3.jet fails E0003 for a user keyed trait.

The probes f4.jet and f5.jet fail E0112 for Hex on a distinct Printable ID and a struct wrapper. These establish current built-in selectors and the extension gap, not either proposed trait's implementation. Compiler/Prelude/Traits.jet:218-235 declares current String-returning Display/Debug; Core/Text/Fmt.jet contains String-returning numeric helpers.

D-OUTPUT-RETURNS1 requires the public result signature. D-EFF-FORMAT-WRITER1 already specifies which String-building bodies and immediate destinations avoid a whole-result temporary, and explicitly retains an ordinary wrapper for saved values and unlisted bodies. A hidden return pointer alone does not eliminate a String's backing allocation.

Reuse that exact closed rule, including alias, effect, padding, failure and separate-compilation behavior; do not replace it with 'every return appends to the caller'. D-ALLOC-FAIL1=C requires recoverable allocation failure, including implicit text allocation; neither new trait may assert Never! merely because today's Fmt helpers do. No allocator-call count or performance superiority was measured.

D-PRINTSTYLE1's inherited print settings remain separate from per-type style implementations. Distinct #Printable currently supplies default text, not Hex; neither option silently re-exposes all numeric styles on semantic wrappers. Explicit impls let a units type reject a misleading style. The comparison sources were read: Rust std::fmt::LowerHex and Python's datamodel __format__ (which must return str).

options.name: Ordinary traits for the existing style families
options.detail: HexFormat, BinFormat, OctFormat, FixedFormat, GroupedFormat, SciFormat and PercentFormat each return String. A package implements the families it supports; Core numbers use those same traits.
options.technical:
Declare ordinary Prelude traits with distinct methods hex, bin, oct, fixed, grouped, sci and percent. Hex and decimal-style methods take the existing selector's Int count; Bin and Oct have no count. Preserve each selector's current argument validation and numeric behavior. New traits' effect/failure contracts permit the allocation route required by D-ALLOC-FAIL1; implementations may narrow it when proven. No output-only parameter and no public writer trait.

Resolve each existing numeric selector to its ordinary trait requirement. Evaluate the value once, then its selector arguments once in source order. A missing implementation is E0112 naming the requirement and showing a manual impl template; never silently use Display or fail at runtime. Generic code uses ordinary single-trait bounds.

Concrete calls resolve statically; trait-value calls use the normal trait call path. No extra style-key column, trait parser exception or per-style compiler helper-name routing survives. Register the selector-to-trait mapping in the existing owned selector registry rather than a second hidden list. This ballot covers the seven existing families, not arbitrary new selector syntax.

Display, Debug, Pretty, padding, Unit and computed selector counts keep their own existing meanings. Padding wraps produced text; it is not a numeric style conformance. Distinct wrappers and structs both opt into each supported style explicitly, following ordinary trait coherence and visibility. Default #Printable does not authorize all base styles.

Core migration is one cutover: move existing numeric behavior behind these same traits, delete equivalent type gates/helper dispatch, preserve signs, widths, zero/negative counts, nonfinite values and padding byte for byte. Use D-EFF-FORMAT-WRITER1's existing String lowering and fallbacks, including preserved effect/error order. A saved result remains an ordinary String and may allocate. No universal no-allocation or one-allocator-call guarantee is added.

Style-polymorphic code needs no keyed trait. A function bound by one style trait names it directly. A function choosing the style at run time takes `fn(T) -> String`, and each style fits it, such as `fn(x: T) -> String { x.hex(4) }`. Function values of that shape work today: probes/fmt-fnvalue.jet passes `fn(x: Int) -> String { "{x:Hex(4)}" }` and prints 001f on gate-p277.

options.name: One trait keyed by a style type
options.detail: Format(fmt.Hex) and Format(fmt.Fixed) share a method returning String. Typed style values bundle options and generic code can abstract over the style key.
options.technical:
This is a genuine alternative, especially for generic style-polymorphic libraries. It must extend keyed-trait parsing, conformance identity, orphan checks, bounds, diagnostics and dynamic dispatch to Format rather than calling the existing From/arithmetic exceptions general support.

Each concrete pair of value type and style type has one impl; selectors construct the corresponding typed option value and resolve exactly that pair. The same ordinary String failure and lowering contract as A applies. No independent per-style writer API. This ballot does not claim generic keyed traits already compile, or that adding a style metadata flag is cost-free.

comparisons.note: LowerHex is a separate style trait and writes to Formatter; its no-temporary path is a strong design, but the owner rejected that public signature for Jet.
__format__ returns str. Its open string specification is flexible but does not statically prove a type supports a style.

recommendation.why: Use ordinary traits for today's distinct style families; do not add keyed conformance merely to avoid several trait names.
gains: Direct answer to the owner: returns text, never an output argument.
Package and Core formatting use the same trait path and existing String execution law.

losses.loss: Several named style traits instead of one style-polymorphic key.
losses.mitigation: Completion lists only the selected family's requirement; implement only supported styles. Generic code requesting Hex needs one ordinary bound, not all seven.

losses.loss: Generic code cannot take any style as one type parameter.
losses.mitigation: Code that must choose a style at run time takes a text function such as fn(x: T) -> String { x.hex(4) }. Every style fits that one shape, with no new trait machinery.

whyNot.reason: Useful for style-polymorphic code, but requires extending specialized keyed dispatch; the probe does not establish that machinery for arbitrary traits.

recommendation.tradeoff: B offers more generic style abstraction; A minimizes new conformance machinery. Neither makes allocating String results free.

decisions.title: Library-written built-in methods use ordinary Core traits, not hidden routing
decisions.situation: Package traits can already add methods to String, while a plain impl String is rejected. Some built-in method rows route to library bodies by compiler-known module/member names. Simply saying Core owns String does not supply an ordinary declaration or prove ownership from its bundle location. The remaining choice is ordinary traits for library-written methods, authentic declaration ownership, or scoped open extensions.
decisions.gist: Should Core use ordinary traits for library-written methods on built-in types?
decisions.lesson: Machine primitives stay behind the ratified jet_builtins boundary. Library-written methods should use the same declaration, lookup and conflict rules as package methods. Keeping a method's name and body does not by itself preserve its lookup behavior.
decisions.explainer: A moves Core's library methods onto the trait route that package code already uses. Existing call spellings remain through Prelude imports. A duplicate name is a real conflict, not a special built-in tidy warning that still runs.
decisions.story: A library helper moves between source modules without editing a compiler routing row. A package method with the same name is diagnosed using the same conflict rule as an ordinary user type.
decisions.inWild: Rust separates owner-only inherent implementations from trait implementations. Inherent ownership is based on a real defining crate, not merely two modules shipping in the same distribution.
decisions.detail:
r2 changes the recommendation completely: r1 B (traits for everyone) becomes A; r1 A (Core-owner inherent methods) becomes B; C remains scoped open extensions. The fresh review disagrees with the claim that A's ownership problem was already engineered away. D-CORE-BUILTINS1 says jet_builtins ships in the Core bundle and declares compiler-provided operations/storage.

It does not establish that every built-in surface type has an ordinary nominal declaration owned by the Core package. Registering 'Core owns these names' would recreate a privileged compiler list. The ordinary trait route is the strongest demonstrated alternative and needs neither that assertion nor a new ownership binding.

Replayed gate-p275 probes/bm1.jet prints 8 and [alpha] using a String trait and the existing helper. bm2.jet rejects plain impl String with E0301, whose repair does not teach traits. bm4.jet prints [a]: the package trait's first_lines is silently shadowed by the built-in method. bm3.jet reports E0105 and E0772 for the analogous user-type collision. These observations disprove r1's assertion that keeping names/bodies guarantees unchanged lookup.

Inspected Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/Registry/BuiltinMethods.jet, including CoreSource routes in the string/regex rows. This ballot does not rely on an unverified census or claim that every other row is intrinsically unexpressible. Inspected Sema/Registration/Items.jet:2785-2812, :2921-2937 and :3087-3135: nominal owner identity and package-member attachment are explicit, while unregistered builtin impl targets have special refusal teaching. Sema/Registration/BuiltinOwners.jet describes Task/Receiver/Sender identity facts, explicitly not invented source nominal declarations; it does not establish ordinary String ownership.

D-EXTEND-ARCH1 requires library extension through ordinary declarations, not hidden library-name powers. D-CORE-BUILTINS1 keeps genuinely compiler-provided operations at one typed kernel door; D-CORE-SOURCE-AUTHORITY1 keeps expressible behavior in source. D-TEXT-FIXED1's public String verbs and D-BOUND-METHOD1's expected-function-type rule must survive lookup migration. D-NO-WARNINGS1 does not justify a built-in-only ambiguity severity: r1's tidy conflict preserves precisely the unequal lookup mechanism this cutover should remove. Rust's implementation reference was read; no Rust cost or Jet speed-equivalence claim is made.

options.name: Ordinary traits for Core library methods
options.detail: Core declares traits for its library-written built-in methods, implements them normally and re-exports them through the Prelude. Package traits use the same lookup path; no CoreSource routing remains.
options.technical:
Group related library methods into ordinary public Core traits; do not create a trait per individual method without a semantic reason. The declaring Core module owns each trait and can implement it for a built-in type under the local-trait rule demonstrated for String. Prelude supplies the traits so existing call spellings need no extra imports. Genuine primitive operations remain typed jet_builtins operations; source methods call them through the ratified boundary. Do not keep a hidden compiler method alias beside the trait.

String support is demonstrated, not every generic family. For lists and fixed arrays, extend the ordinary impl target reader to structural type heads: proposed impl [T].SequenceTools and impl [T#N].SequenceTools. The canonical built-in family declares its parameter roles/order (T is a type, N a compile-time extent); these names bind in the target exactly as parameters of a nominal conditional impl. Bounds attach to those parameters under D-IMPL-COND1; concrete-head specialization and overlapping impls remain illegal.

This is public, registered impl-target grammar available to any local trait owner, not a Core-only owner list or a claim that structural impls already parse. Sized lanes and other canonical families use their existing type-head parameter order; native sizeless restrictions remain in force. Register structural targets and fixture every supported family before removing its library route. Bytes retains its own type identity, never silently becomes a list alias.

Migrate every CoreSource method with its exact parameter/result/effect/failure/default and visibility contract, then delete that enum case and each backend/reachability routing branch. Audit other rows by source-expressibility under the existing source-authority law rather than assuming not-CoreSource means machine-only. The remaining kernel list may describe machine operations, not destinations in Core library code. Root ordinary trait bodies through ordinary reachability in every tier; docs and definition links point at the source declaration.

Use the ordinary user-type duplicate/ambiguous-member rule for all built-in and user methods. Report both declarations before execution; no built-in-only tidy severity, silent builtin precedence or second suppression mechanism. Resolve conflicts by explicit source changes such as renaming the local trait method; do not advertise an unverified qualified-call spelling. Existing ambiguous programs need an explicit migration decision.

Today the built-in method wins, so renaming the shadowed package trait method and its references preserves every current call. The migrator offers that rename as one selectable edit. Matching names/bodies are insufficient: fixtures must pin receiver resolution, defaults, imports, generic bounds and bound-method values. Safe edits fix only a proven equivalent resolution, never guess intended behavior.

E0301 for a package's plain impl builtin explains the local-trait path and offers a named-trait conversion as a selectable rewrite only after collision checks and preserving method contracts. Public helper trait names become API and need stable documentation. No claim that generated calls are byte-for-byte identical or that metadata costs zero bytes; concrete dispatch follows ordinary trait rules and delivery compares actual outputs, effects and emitted footprint.

options.name: Authentic owner declarations and inherent methods
options.detail: Bind each built-in surface type to an actual source owner, then use ordinary owner-only inherent methods. Packages still use traits.
options.technical:
Strongest benefit: inherent library methods require no additional public helper traits and look like ordinary methods of a source type. But the owner must be a real declaration/identity in the resolved graph, not 'belongs to Core because bundled'. Kernel storage in jet_builtins and a public facade are different roles; a complete typed declaration binding must preserve primitive representation, generic families, exports and ownership without a name whitelist.

This is additional design/implementation, not established by the current E0301 probe. No independently maintained owner list or per-method routing may survive. Same hard conflict rule and migration requirements as A. Until such declarations exist, do not describe impl String inside arbitrary Core modules as ordinary code that already works.

options.name: Scoped open extensions
options.detail: Any package may extend an imported type; imported extensions are considered at calls. This avoids Core ownership privilege and can be pleasant for local helpers.
options.technical: Would amend the present builtin impl restriction. Define extension visibility by explicit imports; diagnose multiple matching members before execution using the same ambiguity mechanism. Needs a concrete disambiguation/migration design before selection, not a vague promise that qualification will solve every collision. It is not recommended here because ordinary local traits already support extensions while giving them an explicit semantic contract.

comparisons.note: Owner-only inherent impls and trait impls are distinct; source ownership must actually exist.

recommendation.why: Use the ordinary extension mechanism that is demonstrated to work, rather than invent an ownership fact from a bundle path.
gains: Core and packages share trait lookup and conflict handling.
Library destinations disappear from the compiler's method-routing table.

losses.loss: Core helper trait names become public API.
losses.mitigation: Group by real contracts, re-export through Prelude to preserve calls, and document stable traits rather than expose a second hidden dispatch path.

losses.loss: Existing silent builtin/trait collisions become hard errors.
losses.mitigation: The error names both declarations, with the same rule for all types. Renaming the shadowed package method keeps today's resolution, so the migrator offers it as one selectable edit.

whyNot.reason: Attractive once authentic owner declarations exist; current evidence does not establish them and a bundle is not a declaration.
Convenient local syntax, but adds import-sensitive open-member resolution when ordinary traits already provide extensions.

recommendation.tradeoff: A adds explicit helper contracts; B needs genuine type ownership. Neither earns a free lookup-preservation claim.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude Opus. Adversarial model family: GPT. Fresh agent: BallotReview. Verdict: ready to post with Prelude-imported Core traits as A and hard, uniform collisions, as a lookup cutover, not a binary-cost win.

It covers ordinary trait bounds, bound-method values, all tiers and source definition links. It also requires deletion of CoreSource routing, honest primitive and source classification, and an emitted-footprint comparison. No build or suite was run.

decisions.title: Declare compiler and build services through phase-checked imports
decisions.situation: Compiler queries and build operations already run through invocation-owned host services. The checker recognizes some services through library names, and a runtime call to a compiler query is correctly rejected. This vote chooses a declarative host boundary without weakening that phase or authority separation. We recommend the same checked import family as runtime leaves, with provider-declared availability and invocation-owned capabilities.
decisions.gist: How should compiler and build host services declare their boundary?
decisions.lesson: Compile-time availability is not permission to inspect another invocation or access undeclared files. Phase, effects and authority are separate checks.
decisions.explainer: Beginner: compiler queries still belong in build or compile-time code, not runtime. Expert: provider imports carry schema, phase and effects; every host handle is checked against its active invocation and every observable input follows the existing build rules.
decisions.story: Eli writes a build tool that inspects checked declarations. A saved handle from an earlier build must not let it read the next build's private state.
decisions.inWild:
resource session;
schema: func(value: borrow<session>) -> string;
decisions.detail:
Card #6852 c10 asks for declaration-owned compiler/build leaves. Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Calls/CompilerServices.jet:48-56 recognizes member names; :143-151 enforces compile-time availability. On gate-p261, probes2/compiler-service.jet gets E0956 at runtime, while probes2/compiler-comptime.jet uses #run and prints schema checked. probes2/provider-compiler.jet rejects a proposed bodyless import with E0081; this does not separately establish provider-name checking.

Compiler/JetDriver/Source/Driver/BuildAdapter.jet:66-98 checks active session ownership and dispatches by member prefixes. These source checks must survive declaration routing. Compiler/JetDriver/Source/Driver/RuntimeInterface.jet:1-12 already exposes generated host declarations through ordinary module imports. The corresponding existing-leaf probe runs; extending that generator across phases is a real implementation path, not permission to expose arbitrary compiler internals.

Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Registration/Checked.jet:490-635 already carries artifact identity, authority, effects, assumptions and boundary obligations. Extend it with phase/invocation facts for these services; do not introduce an independent compiler-service certificate. WIT borrowing illustrates call-lifetime handles, not invocation expiration, reproducible builds or authority. Those are additional checked/runtime obligations, not guarantees obtained from a resource declaration.

options.name: Phase-checked provider declarations
options.detail: Extend the same import/generated-interface contract used for runtime leaves with provider-owned phase and invocation authority.
options.technical:
The shown #Import(jet.compiler,symbol:) and jet.build forms are proposed import-family extensions. Generated service modules and handwritten declarations bind to the same extended checked foreign-provider carrier. Validate symbol/signature, exact artifact, target, version, effects and evidence. Provider policy, not a user marker, determines permitted phases and capabilities. Wrong-phase calls are checking errors, not runtime fallbacks; keep ordinary library wrappers and public call spelling.

Read-only compiler-query authority and effectful build authority remain distinct exports. Every context-bearing host operation checks active invocation identity, including calls through saved function values. Live handles are nonforgeable, nonserializable and expire on completion or cancellation. Snapshot values and generated code are ordinary checked outputs, not live capabilities. Never cache invocation handles across builds; cache immutable snapshots only with the existing complete input/receipt identity.

Preserve declared filesystem/environment/network inputs, output effects, query limits and receipt rules. Binding a host operation grants no ambient access to compiler state. Unsupported evaluator/target availability is rejected before execution. Retain assumption and evidence classifications; a complete metadata record alone does not prove determinism or safe host behavior.

Generate checker, evaluator and inspection facts from the one carrier. Migrate every prefix/name-based route, keep semantic implementations and session checks, and remove obsolete aliases/routes in the same cutover. Provide diagnostics naming service, required phase, missing authority and expired invocation. All supported evaluators must implement the selected export or explicitly reject it; no no-op service.

options.name: Typed capability-specific gateways
options.detail: Expose typed request/reply gateways grouped by authority rather than an imported leaf per operation.
options.technical:
Use request variants, never string commands, and separate read-only queries from effectful build capabilities. This can give a compact stable ABI with generated ergonomic wrappers; users need not manually unpack every reply. The same phase, invocation, declared-input and evidence checks as A apply.

A statically known request exposes its exact effects. A dynamically selected request must carry the union of possible effects/authority rather than hiding them under a broad permit. Central request schemas evolve with the service, but that is not inherently a performance penalty. Generate gateway and wrappers from one provider authority, not an independent compiler command protocol.
options.code: reply: compiler_service.call(query_session, .Schema)

comparisons.note: Borrowed resources model call-lifetime handles; invocation expiration and reproducible build authority need additional enforcement.

resource session;
schema: func(value: borrow<session>) -> string;

recommendation.why: Reuse checked provider declarations and the existing generated-interface approach, while preserving operation-level phase and authority rather than compiler member-name exceptions.
gains: One host-binding/evidence family across phases.
Operation effects remain directly visible.

losses.loss: Cross-evaluator migration needs complete phase/authority metadata and retained session checks.
losses.mitigation: Generate bindings from one carrier and require wrong-phase, stale-handle and receipt cases before deleting old routes.

losses.loss: Invocation checks still cost host calls and cannot be replaced by schema matching.
losses.mitigation: Keep ownership checks at context-bearing operations; cache only immutable, fully keyed snapshots.

whyNot.reason: A compact viable ABI with generated wrappers, but central request evolution and dynamic-request effect unions add another public protocol.

recommendation.tradeoff: Shared binding machinery, never shared unrestricted authority.

surface.lesson: Phase, authority, reproducible inputs and active invocation ownership are separate checks. Matching a schema does not prove them.

gains: Compact ABI; ergonomic wrappers are possible.
losses: Request-schema evolution; dynamic requests carry effect unions.

recommendation.why: Share existing binding machinery while keeping each operation's phase, authority and effects explicit.
gains: No compiler member-name exceptions.

decisions.title: Keep or revert direct whole-store SQL for scripts
decisions.situation: A script can already query its database Store directly without constructing a row policy. That convenience landed before this owner vote, so the choice is whether to keep it or require the existing explicit all_rows step. Neither spelling makes database handles safe to give untrusted code, and current scopes have known confinement gaps. We recommend keeping the owning-script convenience without claiming that this vote fixes authorization.
decisions.gist: Should an owning script query Store directly or explicitly request all rows?
decisions.lesson: Effects are not row authorization, and DBScope is not a sandbox today. Both options concern trusted owning code.
decisions.explainer: Beginner: a script may use the supported SQL methods on its Store. Expert: with_policy returns a filter-bearing scope without revoking Store, and public scope state currently allows reconstructing the owner; do not rely on that type for confinement.
decisions.story: June writes a database migration. She owns the database and does not want to invent a user row policy just to inspect its schema.
decisions.inWild:
con = sqlite3.connect("app.db")
rows = con.execute("SELECT name FROM sqlite_master")
decisions.detail:
Card #6822 c6 records that direct Store Driver methods landed before approval. On gate-p261, probes2/sql.jet queries select 1, prints 1 and closes with true. Core/DB/DB.jet:906-948 defines with_policy/all_rows and implements Store Driver through all_rows. Query uses DB.Read and execute uses DB.Write. This proves supported query convenience, not unrestricted arbitrary SQL: policy_apply at :724-748 still rejects schema/control statements outside the migration path.

The original ballot falsely said a DBScope cannot recover Store. Store.state and DBScope.state are public at :906-908 and :959-962. probes2/scope-escape.jet reconstructs Store from scope.state, queries successfully and prints 1/true. Source :753-762 also explicitly leaves other-table queries unchanged. Main has recorded both gaps as criteria on the typed-tables card. This vote must not present either as fixed, nor advertise scopes as safe authority confinement.

The existing all_rows method is the strongest explicit alternative: it creates a visible review/search point for broad access. Its benefit is auditability, not a sandbox. Python sqlite3 documents direct connection execute as an implicit cursor convenience. Both options preserve the same SQL engine, binding, errors, effects and existing migration/transaction restrictions; no row-security redesign is bundled into this ergonomic vote.

options.name: Keep direct Store methods
options.detail: Ratify supported Store Driver operations as trusted owning-code convenience.
options.technical:
Keep query/query_one with DB.Read and execute with DB.Write through the same existing all_rows Driver path. Do not interpret broad ownership as permission for every SQL statement: migration-only schema/control checks and current transaction operations remain unchanged. with_policy returns another scope and does not revoke or narrow the Store.

Callers must not treat DBScope as a security boundary today. Its public state escape and other-table behavior are known, separately tracked gaps. Keep executable SQL and database handles inside trusted application code; expose narrowly implemented application operations to untrusted callers, not raw query capabilities. Neither option fixes this by spelling alone.

Direct Store calls omit a conspicuous all_rows review point. Document broad access at Store Driver methods and show the resolved receiver/authority in editor information. Preserve parameter binding, typed DB errors, policy filters on their documented table and identical close/transaction semantics. No second engine, script detection, ambient policy or no-op restriction is introduced.
options.code:
store: db.open_memory()
rows: store.query(db.SQL{"select 1 AS value"}) ?? panic("query failed: {err}")
print(rows.len())
print(store.close())

options.name: Require explicit all_rows
options.detail: Remove direct Driver methods from Store and migrate owning code through the existing unfiltered scope.
options.technical:
The explicit all_rows call is a useful audit/search point for broad access. Any Store holder can request it, and current DBScope state also escapes; this is acknowledgment, not confinement. It preserves the same supported statements, errors, parameters, effects and transaction/migration behavior as A.

Remove the Store Driver implementation and migrate every caller, including examples, generated helpers and generic Driver use, to all_rows or a policy-bearing scope. Do not keep forwarding aliases or introduce another broad-scope type. Closing the owning Store and existing scoped transaction controls must remain coherent. The cost is one explicit construction step and a real source/caller migration, not a mandatory runtime penalty.
options.code:
store: db.open_memory()
scope: store.all_rows()
rows: scope.query(db.SQL{"select 1 AS value"}) ?? panic("query failed: {err}")
print(rows.len())
print(store.close())

comparisons.note: An owning connection can execute a query directly; this does not provide per-row application authorization.
comparisons.code:
con = sqlite3.connect("app.db")
rows = con.execute("SELECT name FROM sqlite_master")

recommendation.why: Keep simple trusted owning code concise. The same SQL path already exists, and authorization gaps require actual capability enforcement, not another spelling.
gains: No fabricated row policy for scripts.
One existing SQL execution path.

losses.loss: Broad access is less conspicuous than an explicit all_rows call.
losses.mitigation: Document Store Driver authority and expose resolved receivers in tooling; audit database operations in trusted application code.

losses.loss: Existing scopes do not confine untrusted code.
losses.mitigation: Keep handles in trusted code and expose narrow application operations; retain the tracked scope-confinement criteria as unresolved.

whyNot.reason: Its explicit broad-access review point is valuable, but it costs a caller migration without fixing current confinement.

recommendation.tradeoff: Concise owner code, not a row-security approval.

Proved public scope.state reconstructs Store and removed every sandbox claim, linking both known confinement gaps to their tracked criteria. Added all_rows auditability, migration/schema restrictions and real caller/tooling costs while retaining the owning-code recommendation.

The schema-creation probe stopped at the existing migration-only restriction and proves no other-table runtime claim. decisions.title: Import typed runtime leaves, including retained callbacks
decisions.situation: The event library already reaches runtime operations that accept generic typed callbacks. Those calls rely on compiler-known library identities instead of a declaration that another package can check and use. This vote chooses the runtime function boundary, including callback lifetime and generic handle binding. We recommend extending the existing import family with a validated runtime provider rather than inventing a second host-call marker. This extends the ratified D-HOST-LEAF1=E (Core declares the runtime functions it calls with a checked #Import) to generic typed callbacks and handle binding; it does not reopen it.
decisions.gist: How should packages bind runtime functions that accept Jet callbacks?
decisions.lesson: A retained callback needs checked storage, destruction and concurrency rules. A plain C bridge can do this with a context pointer; a token lookup is not mandatory.
decisions.explainer: Beginner: a runtime leaf is a checked bodyless import, not a fake Jet wrapper body. Expert: provider metadata validates effects, generic type descriptors, callback retention and handle ownership; every execution mode consumes the same contract.
decisions.story: Paz publishes a scoped event package. A retained callback must live until the subscription ends, without a use-after-free when its original stack frame returns.
decisions.detail:
Card #6852 c7 asks for declarative generic runtime leaves. Core/Event/Event.jet:61-75 reaches private constructors; gate-p261 probes2/event.jet runs a scoped Event<Int> handler and prints 7. This proves present event capability, not public managed imports. probes2/provider-runtime.jet rejects the proposed bodyless import with E0081; that result does not isolate provider-name checking.

Existing generated jet.runtime modules are a stronger starting point than a new host-call system. Compiler/JetDriver/Source/Driver/RuntimeInterface.jet:1-12 describes their #Import(c) bindings; :38-72 excludes generic and some ownership-shaped signatures. probes2/runtime-interface.jet successfully calls a public generated leaf. Extending managed signatures therefore requires real generator/checker changes, not merely exporting another symbol.

Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Registration/Checked.jet:490-635 already has the artifact-bound foreign-provider carrier, handle cleanup and callback/effect obligations. All proposed runtime/type/phase imports must extend that authority rather than create another descriptor registry. Trusted assumptions remain assumptions. WIT resources do not prove generic Jet closure support. Rust's Nomicon gives the stronger callback alternative: a function pointer plus direct opaque context, with unregister-before-destroy obligations for asynchronous callbacks. It requires neither a token table nor a lookup per call.

options.name: Checked managed-provider imports
options.detail: Extend the existing import/generated-interface family to validate managed callbacks and generic handle contracts.
options.technical:
A proposed #Import(jet.runtime,symbol:) binds through the existing checked foreign-provider carrier extended for managed signatures. Generated jet.runtime modules expose those same declaration facts, not another dispatch authority. Validate complete signatures, ordinary effects/errors, ownership, target, ABI version and exact loaded-artifact evidence. A user's annotation cannot certify unsafe native behavior.

Generic handles use the imported-type contract and checked per-instantiation runtime identities. Intern immutable type/drop/layout descriptors rather than allocate them per call. No erased cast can mix unrelated instantiations. Code-size and descriptor metadata grow with used instantiations; deduplicate structurally shareable adapters without collapsing type identity.

Retained callbacks move/copy their captures into provider-owned scoped storage under the ordinary ownership rules. Call-borrowed callbacks cannot escape the call. Retained borrows cannot outlive their referents; that relation must be checked, not inferred from a parameter named scope. Descriptor evidence states allowed threads, reentrancy, invocation effects, dispatch snapshots and cancellation behavior. Async/thread-crossing callbacks require corresponding ordinary bounds. Lifetime inference and generated adapters are new work, not implemented by writing this signature.

Closing a subscription must prevent new callback entries and keep captured storage alive until in-flight calls finish. Define reentrant close without waiting on the closing callback itself; defer final reclamation until the last entry exits. Provider failure/cancellation releases retained state exactly once. Generate adapters, diagnostics and reachability from one authority; migrate all existing leaves and delete identity routes. Unsupported targets/modes fail at build time, never turn callbacks into no-ops.
options.code:
// Proposed provider contract retains handler until scope close.
#Import(jet.runtime, symbol: "events.attach")
attach: fn<T>(point: Event<T>, scope: Scope,
    handler: fn(value: T)) Never!

options.name: Typed C context/trampoline bridge
options.detail: Use a C function pointer and opaque context pointing directly to checked callback storage.
options.technical:
Generate one typed trampoline per required callback shape. The opaque context refers directly to stable Jet-owned capture storage; no registry, token lookup or per-call allocation is inherently needed. Type-erased pointers never cross without generated type/drop contracts. Existing imported-handle evidence owns unregister, cleanup, thread and effect obligations.

This can preserve A's retention and generic identity guarantees through generated wrappers, without treating closure layouts as C structs. It has the same storage and in-flight-call lifetime problem as A, including reentrant close. A small explicit C ABI can be interoperable and efficient; the cost is generator/adapter work and exposing a C-shaped provider surface, not unavoidable token overhead. Use one general bridge generator rather than per-library registries.

comparisons.note: The Nomicon passes a typed object behind an opaque callback context; asynchronous callbacks require unregister-before-destroy guarantees.
Owned resources illustrate cleanup, but not generic Jet closures or reentrant cancellation.

recommendation.why: Expose managed semantics directly in checked declarations while reusing the existing import and boundary-evidence family. A C adapter may implement that boundary internally.
gains: One provider authority for types and functions.
Callback retention and effects visible at declaration checking.

losses.loss: Adapters, capture storage and instantiation metadata are real implementation/runtime costs.
losses.mitigation: Generate shared adapters and intern descriptors; allocate retained storage only when capture lifetime requires it.

losses.loss: Concurrent or reentrant close makes destruction nontrivial.
losses.mitigation: Stop new entries, retain in-flight state, and reclaim after the final exit without self-deadlocking.

whyNot.reason: An efficient interoperable solution without mandatory lookup, but keeps a C-shaped public surface and requires equivalent checked adapter machinery.

recommendation.tradeoff: Managed public contracts, not a claim that C bridges are slower.

decisions.title: Join and split Columns without element copying; performance evidence still required
decisions.situation: The owner wants a readable column join with maximum performance by default, not a choice between borrowing and efficient ownership. Columns<T> is already ratified, but the tested compiler does not recognize that type. Joining existing field buffers can avoid rebuilding rows, provided length checks, sharing and failure recovery are defined. This draft repairs that design but cannot establish the required performance advantage on the available compiler.
decisions.gist: Should Columns join owned buffers and borrowed windows without rebuilding elements?
decisions.lesson: A join groups equally long field buffers into one logical row collection. Owning adopts buffer owners; borrowing retains checked loans. Splitting returns the current buffers and row count, not necessarily the original allocations after growth or copy-on-write.
decisions.explainer: Answer to q4f453bp: A includes both owning and borrowed joins, transactional validation and explicit .copy(). It does not pretend that shared inputs are unique or that independent buffers become one allocation.
decisions.story: A parser already owns positions and velocities as separate lists. It wants row indexing without copying those elements, and must recover every input if lengths differ.
decisions.inWild: Odin's documented soa_zip/soa_unzip borrow slices into a structure-of-arrays view and recover those slices. A plain struct owning Vec fields is also a strong safe design; adopting separate vectors does not inherently require raw-parts tricks.
decisions.detail:
A is retained, B is a real borrowed-view alternative, and r1 C's separately named copying constructor is removed: explicit duplication is .copy() under D-COPY-WORD1, not a second named copy mechanism. r1 used Columns in its 'current' example and said rows could be rebuilt that way today. Replayed probes/review-columns.jet on gate-p275: E0119, no type called Columns. All new API examples below are proposed.

D-SOA-SITE1=A selects compiler-provided Columns<T> and specifically retains correctness/performance gates, including comparison with the automatic-column path authorized by D-ACCEL1. D-ARRAY-COLUMNS1 supplies field views and coordinated length changes; later D-COPY-WORD1 replaces its old ~ copy spelling. D-COLUMNS1 selects add-only Rows handles separately; it does not make Columns add-only. D-RECORD-BRACE1 supplies record spelling. D-ALLOC-FAIL1 requires unchanged logical collection contents on failed growth and bounded nonallocating error/cleanup paths.

r1's zero-field split discarded row count, and telling the caller to inspect len first was not a fix. A now returns count in every split result. r1 also blurred a borrowed join's error with an owning error, promised validation before ownership transfer, and implied rollback of capacities after failed growth. Transfers happen at the call boundary; validation precedes committing a joined table. Rollback preserves lengths and values, not necessarily capacity or address.

Posting remains BLOCKED: no candidate implementing Columns/adoption is available in the allowed published compiler, so no paired throughput, allocation or footprint evidence can establish the owner's maximum-performance claim or the inherited D-SOA-SITE1 gate. The single-file availability probe was run; no repository build or suite was attempted. The design below removes unsupported speed claims instead of treating no-element-copy as proof of fastest execution. The Odin overview's soa_zip/soa_unzip section was read; it supports borrowed grouping, not Jet ownership or mismatch behavior.

options.name: One collection, owning and borrowed joins
options.detail: from_columns consumes a record of field lists; view_columns borrows field windows. Both validate lengths without copying elements. into_columns consumes the owner and returns count plus all current field buffers.
options.technical:
Each struct field has one labelled column, matching its declared field type and order. from_columns accepts a consuming record of owning lists. Omitted, duplicate or mistyped fields are compile-time errors. Evaluate arguments once in source order, transfer their owners at the call boundary, inspect all lengths before committing the Columns value, and never truncate to the shortest. With no fields require an explicit count; with fields infer count from their common length, rejecting an inconsistent explicitly supplied count. Negative or unrepresentable counts fail before constructing a table.

On length mismatch return a typed owning join error containing the entire transferred record and inline fixed-per-field length information, allowing recovery without element copying or allocating error storage. No partial adoption and no loss of move-only elements. Shared lists follow ordinary copy-on-first-write semantics: adoption transfers descriptors without eagerly copying elements; later writes may detach, and are not advertised as zero-copy. Unshared last-use inputs are the unique-owner fast path. .copy() explicitly requests independent duplication; no hidden deep copy merely to make the join succeed. Multiple fields referring to shared backing storage remain ordinary shared owners, with the same write isolation as lists.

view_columns takes read-only windows, not ownership. It returns the ordinary borrowed-view form with loans to every source; mismatch returns only bounded length metadata, never owning buffers or escaping references. The view cannot grow or mutate. Source growth/mutation obeys the existing loan rules. Moving-only elements can be viewed and iterated without copying. Requesting an owned copy requires ordinary element copyability and .copy(); a borrowed-only design is not incapable of reading move-only data.

into_columns returns a record with count and a nested field-record containing every owning list, including count when the field-record is empty. It consumes the collection. With no intervening detachment/growth the allocations are the adopted ones; otherwise they are the current allocations. This does not promise the historical originals. Borrowed field windows already provide extraction without consuming the owner.

Growth checks size overflow and reserves needed capacities before committing lengths or inserting values. A later reservation failure preserves all previous logical values/lengths, but earlier successful reservations may change capacities and addresses. Existing loans forbid invalidating growth. Argument ownership follows the normal fallible push contract; clean uncommitted values once. Never publish a row length until every field is initialized. Owning/splitting moves buffer descriptors; it need not allocate or copy element buffers, though ordinary control metadata and growth must still follow AllocError law. No reflection-based user implementation or new layout marker: extend the already ratified compiler-provided collection.
options.code:
// PROPOSED; positions and velocities transfer ownership.
ps: Columns<Particle>.from_columns(x: positions, v: velocities)
parts: ps.into_columns()
print(parts.count)
xs: parts.fields.x
vs: parts.fields.v

options.name: Borrow existing columns only
options.detail: Only create read-only joined windows. Owners stay separate; code that wants an owned Columns builds it explicitly.
options.technical: Same field/length/count validation and checked loans as A. Strongest benefit: no new owning recovery payload, split operation or ownership-adoption API; a plain owning record of lists can often serve the application. Borrowed traversal supports move-only elements. Limitation: the joined collection cannot itself grow or outlive its inputs; converting it to owned storage requires copyable elements or a separate explicit ownership transfer design. Do not claim Rust's safe struct-of-Vec alternative needs unsafe reconstruction.

comparisons.note: soa_zip groups slices and soa_unzip recovers them; this is a borrowed-view precedent, not an owning transactional guarantee.

recommendation.why: The design supports readable borrowing and efficient ownership in the same ratified collection, but performance readiness has not been established.
gains: Unique-owner adoption avoids rebuilding elements.
Mismatch recovers all moved buffers; zero-field splitting preserves count.

losses.loss: Shared inputs can detach on later mutation and separately adopted buffers stay separate allocations.
losses.mitigation: Use ordinary copy-on-write, expose that cost, and preserve the unique-owner fast path. Compare against ordinary owning records and the automatic-column path before claiming superiority.

whyNot.reason: Smaller and sufficient for read-only work, but cannot by itself provide an independently owned growable joined collection.

recommendation.tradeoff: Agree with A's ownership contract, not an unmeasured fastest-default claim. Posting is blocked on inherited performance evidence.

decisions.title: Function copies copy their captures; resource-owning callbacks are Unique
decisions.situation: A function value is code plus captured data, and copying it is refused today. We prefer ordinary capture-wise copying for eligible callbacks. Proposed plain fn types promise copying; resource-owning repeatable callbacks instead use Unique<fn>. Explicit-record models support the direction, but actual erased callable conversions, topology and crossing proofs remain open.
decisions.gist: Should copying a function value give it its own captures, share them, or stay refused?
decisions.lesson: Copy eligible captures by their ordinary rules. Lists get independent contents when written; Shared still shares. A unique resource may belong to a repeatable callback without making it copyable.
decisions.explainer:
Proposed plain `fn(Int) -> Int` promises a copy; each captured value follows its own copy law. List and map contents detach on writes; Shared still shares.

Unique<fn> would preserve repeatable resource owners without forcing Shared. Moving a repeatable callable into OneShot would weaken its invocation permission. These are proposed callable capabilities, not implemented generic ownership wrappers.

Copying is not a crossing proof. Hidden Shared, Cell, nested callbacks and ownership edges must still satisfy the ratified crossing and cycle checks.
decisions.story: Mia copies a Button to make a second toolbar. Each toolbar should keep its own click list, unless she deliberately gives both one Shared history.
decisions.inWild: Rust closure Clone depends on capture kinds and Clone implementations; non-Clone closures can remain repeatable. C++ std::function requires a copyable target and copies it, including shared pointers. Swift closures have reference semantics.
decisions.detail:
Independent gate-p289 runs: copy-cleanup preserves separate list/map mutations and shared strong-owner counts, then closes its Shared resource once. This is an ordinary Env record, not a function-value copy. copy-crossing gives explicit record copies to two tasks, prints 201 and 202 on this run, and preserves the creator's list. Their lock acquisition order is not guaranteed.

unique-callback runs 2, 3, 4, 5 and closes once; unique-callback-copy fails E0211. The model is Unique<E>, exposing E, with an ordinary fn field. Today's fn field itself refuses copying, so the model does not prove unconditional Unique noncopyability after plain fn becomes copyable.

fnval-fc1 and fc9 still fail E0211; fc8 fails E0121. None demonstrates implemented callback copy, erased public capability conversion, hidden-capture cycle checking or the complete #6048 creator/task regression. Independent real closure receipts remain required.

The shared_owner_topology oracle has not been derived for A. Copy-related strong counts and cleanup must come from the implemented program, not predicted replacement numbers.

Preserve D-COPY-WORD1, D-FNVAL-WRITE1, D-SHARED-CYCLE2 and D-CONC-CROSS1. I8 requires Unique and OneShot to express capabilities in the same callable mechanism and existing ownership laws, not introduce independent generic wrappers or duplicate runtimes.

options.name: Copies copy captures; Unique never copies
options.detail: A function value copies by copying its captures under the ordinary copy law. Callbacks owning a resource with no copy have type Unique<fn(…)>, which moves but never copies. Shared captures stay shared.
options.technical:
Proposed type contract: plain fn promises capture-wise copying; Unique<fn> is repeatable but noncopyable even with copyable captures; OneShot<fn> has consuming invocation and is also noncopyable. Permit only capability weakening, never recovery of repeatability or copying. Specify inference and conversion for lambdas, named functions, fields, returns, collections and separate compilation before approval.

Copyable captures follow their ordinary laws, including COW detachment and Shared strong-owner retention. A resource-owning lambda must remain usable in a noncopyable repeatable slot without forced Shared. Read-borrowed unique repeatable callbacks and scoped OneShot adaptation need consistent signatures across both ballots.

I8: implement these as capabilities of one callable family using existing copy, ownership, invocation, lifetime and crossing facts. They are not general Unique<T> ownership containers, do not stack into nested competing wrappers, and do not add another copy spelling or runtime refusal. The explicit Unique<E> record is only a model.

Crossing and cycles must preserve complete hidden-environment summaries through copying and erasure, including Shared, Cell and nested callbacks. Fresh ordinary contents do not remove shared edges or prove race freedom. A task's copy remains subject to the same ratified checks.

Migration retypes every affected plain fn slot and preserves input modes, effects and results. Copy costs follow capture storage, allocations, COW and retained owners; copying is not a deep snapshot. No real callable conversion or generated-copy receipt exists yet.

options.name: Share the environment
options.detail: copy() makes another handle to the same captures. Calls through either handle advance the same state.
options.code:
// PROPOSED; same maker and calls
counter: make_counter()
alias: counter.copy()
print(counter(1)) // 101
print(alias(2))   // 202
print(counter(3)) // 303
options.technical:
A shared environment preserves action identity without copying unique resources. Its invocation lock can serialize mutation, with contention and reentrancy costs; it is no crossing-safety exemption.

B explicitly amends D-COPY-WORD1 so fn copy aliases, like Shared. E0204 says a stored lambda owns its captures; that alone does not forbid later aliases. Added handles retain captures and add ownership edges. Complete hidden-environment cycle and crossing proofs remain required.

options.name: Refuse function copies
options.detail: Keep callbacks and aggregates containing them uncopyable. Share explicit state between newly made callbacks when two menus need one action.
options.technical:
Retain E0211 and repair E0121's misleading copy hint. Two menus that share an action need a maker taking Shared state; shared-capture.jet prints 101, 202, 303 today.

Costs: any struct holding a callback stays uncopyable, so a Button cannot be copied. The topology oracle's copy scenario must be replaced by an explicit-state witness.

comparisons.note: A closure is Clone when all its captures are, and cloning clones each capture. Shared state is written as Rc or Arc.
Copying a std::function copies its target, including value captures; reference or shared-pointer captures still share.
Closures are reference types: assigning one to another name aliases the same captured state.

recommendation.why: Prefer capture-wise copy law with statically represented callable capabilities, but the new erased type contract still needs implementation and adversarial proof.
gains: Buttons and other callback holders copy.
Copy refusal is decided from types while compiling.
Ordinary copied contents separate on mutation; shared captures retain their existing checks.

losses.loss: Slots holding resource-owning callbacks must be retyped Unique.
losses.mitigation: The refusal names each capture and proposes the Unique type.

losses.loss: Copied Shared captures still share and may contend.
losses.mitigation: Keep guards short and release copies promptly; use independent ordinary state where sharing is unnecessary. Retention and later COW allocation remain capture-dependent costs.

whyNot.reason: Preserves action identity, but aliasing fn copies amend copy law and need invocation synchronization, cycle and reentrancy design.
Refuses copies even when every capture copies, so Buttons never copy.

recommendation.tradeoff: One more function type name, Unique, against blanket refusal or aliasing copies.

losses.mitigation: The refusal names the capture and proposes the type.

decisions.title: One #Once mark on function types, for helpers, fields, returns and tasks
decisions.situation: A lambda that moves a capture may run at most once. Jet checks that locally (E0121) but cannot pass such a lambda on: no helper, field, return or task can say "I call this at most once". r3 (owner, 2026-11-18) drops the OneShot<F> wrapper type: the owner asked why a named marker cannot do the job, whether a type is the best carrier, and disliked the name. A marker can. The fact must belong to the function's type, as its effect row does, but it needs no wrapper type. Jet already writes a marker before a type (`#PII String`), and the p294 compiler parses `#PII fn(Int) -> Int` as a parameter, field, return, list element and type argument today. #Once uses that spelling at its own marker site for function types, so value tags keep their one meaning.
decisions.gist: Should a #Once mark on a function type carry run-once callbacks through helpers, fields, returns and tasks?
decisions.lesson: A function type marked #Once may run zero times or once. The mark travels with the value: helpers, fields, returns and tasks can hold it, and calling it uses it up, exactly as Jet already checks for a local one-shot lambda. Any function fits a #Once slot; only a #Once value is limited to one call.
decisions.explainer:
`done: #Once fn(Int) -> Int` is a function type with the compiler-known #Once mark. It is written where value tags are written, but registered at its own function-type site. It is part of the function's type, as the effect row is, not an erased dataflow tag, so #Scrub cannot remove it. The mark follows the value through parameters, fields, list elements, type arguments, returns and task captures; a lambda gets it by inference.

Calling a #Once value moves it, so the second call, a call after forwarding, and a call in a loop are the existing use-after-move errors. Calling one needs ownership: a field is called by the holder's owner, and a list element by draining the list. An optional #Once field reached through edit access is fired with `.move()`, which leaves None.

Parameters keep Jet's ordinary modes. A plain `done: #Once fn(...)` parameter is call-scoped: the helper may call it once or pass it to another such parameter, but cannot store, return or send it (E0120). A lambda passed there captures as for any read parameter today: it borrows locals and moves only what it moves. A helper that keeps the callback takes it with `&&#Once fn(...)`, the ordinary take, and its lambda owns its captures like every escaping lambda.

Any function value fits a #Once slot, since running at most once is a promise only the receiver makes. A repeatable function passed to a call-scoped parameter is lent, so the caller keeps it; into a taken slot it moves, as every function value does today. A #Once value passed anywhere is used up. No conversion object, adapter type or runtime flag exists. An unused #Once value drops its captures once; #SingleUse captures keep their must-consume duty.
decisions.story: Ravi's helper finishes a job and hands the job's Log to keep. Later he queues jobs with their completion callbacks, builds callbacks in a factory function, and runs a job on a task. He writes #Once in the signatures that hold a callback, adds && only where a helper keeps one, and writes nothing at the call sites.
decisions.inWild: Rust's FnOnce is one trait for one-shot closures in parameters, fields and threads (Option::map, Box<dyn FnOnce>, thread::spawn). Swift and Kotlin mark the call contract on parameters only (Kotlin's callsInPlace AT_MOST_ONCE), so stored callbacks cannot carry it. Jet's #Once is FnOnce's reach with Jet's marker spelling instead of a trait bound or wrapper type.
decisions.detail:
r3 answers the owner question of 2026-11-18 ("Downside not engineered away. Why can't named markers work as the recommended option? Is a type really the best way? I don't like the proposed name for the type.").

1. Markers work. The run-once fact must travel with the value, so it is part of the function's type, as the effect row is, with no wrapper type. Probes on the p294 compiler (dev 3c593a7f16) parse `#PII fn(Int) -> Int` as a parameter, field, return, list element and nested return. They also parse it as a type argument (`Box<#PII fn(Int) -> Int>`) and after a take (`&&#PII fn(Int) -> Int`). An optional callback needs parentheses, `(#Once fn(Int) -> Int)?`, which parses and type-checks.

2. Calls on a marked function type are refused today (E0803); that is the build work. Spec section "Computed fields, tags, and applied rules" defines a .TypeUse marker as an erased dataflow value tag with a required #FX row (E0734) that #Scrub removes. So Once gets its own function-type site rather than joining that site.

3. The r2 downsides are engineered away. "Helper signatures name &&OneShot<F>": a helper that only calls the callback writes `#Once fn(...)`; only a helper that keeps it writes &&, the ordinary take. "A temporary adapter cannot outlive its retained callback": there is no adapter, and a call-scoped parameter lends a repeatable function. Probe readparam.jet passes a lambda over a kept function to a read parameter and keeps it (prints 12, 6, 13). Probe kept.jet shows the same lambda refused by a taken parameter (E0120, E0121).

4. The name: OneShot is gone; A is #Once, B the same design spelled #RunOnce.

Still true from r2 (gate-p289 probes once-r5): today's explicit-record models close a resource twice when the callback runs (owner-pass, owner-branch, places-field-return-task). That is defect #3645 c14-c16 (I1, function-value double close). It is a build prerequisite for every option here, not a cost of the spelling.

options.name: #Once on function types
options.detail: A compiler-known mark on a function type: parameters, fields, list elements, type arguments, returns and task captures. Calling a #Once value uses it up. A plain #Once parameter is call-scoped; `&&#Once` takes it for keeping. Any function fits a #Once slot; lambdas infer it.
options.technical:
Register Once in Compiler/Prelude/Markers.jet with sites [.FunctionType]. That new site accepts only a function type and makes the mark part of the type: assignability, type arguments and identity. Once is compiler-known like SingleUse. It is not a value tag: it has no #FX row, is not erased, and #Scrub(Once) is refused.

Sema: a marked function type is callable, and its call is a move of the callee place. So second-call, forward-then-call and loop errors are the existing E0121. A plain #Once parameter is call-scoped: one call or one pass to another plain #Once parameter. Storing, returning or sending it is E0120, and lambdas passed to it capture as for any read parameter. `&&#Once fn` is the ordinary take.

Assignability adds the mark and never removes it; a type mismatch (E0113) names the one-call promise. A repeatable argument to a call-scoped parameter is passed as a lent handle whose drop does nothing. The callee drops an uncalled handle at exit. `.move()` on an optional #Once field through edit access leaves None. Closure layout and calling convention are unchanged. Prerequisite: #3645 c14-c16 exactly-once cleanup.

options.name: The same, spelled #RunOnce
options.detail: Identical meaning to A; only the word differs. It says what is limited (running) where #Once leaves it implied.
options.technical: As A, with the marker registered as RunOnce.

options.name: #Once on parameters only
options.detail: A parameter mark: the callee may call or forward it at most once, during this call only. Fields, returns and tasks cannot hold a run-once callback.
options.technical: Marker site .Parameter. This is A's call-scoped parameter alone. Job, enqueue, later and the task in A's program have no spelling, so queued or deferred callbacks still need explicit state (D).

options.name: Keep explicit state
options.detail: No new surface. Pass the Log as a taken argument to a reusable callback, or branch on an optional before moving it.
options.technical: Works today (once-on3b prints 8). Payload types spread through every callback API, and a queued job must carry its payload beside its callback.

comparisons.note: FnOnce is one trait for one-shot closures as parameters, boxed fields and thread bodies. A call-scoped `impl FnOnce` may hold borrows; a kept `Box<dyn FnOnce + 'static>` may not, which is A's plain versus && parameter. `&F` lends a repeatable closure, and Option::take fires a stored one from `&mut self`. Thread handoff separately needs Send.
callsInPlace with AT_MOST_ONCE promises a synchronous call count; it cannot describe stored callbacks.
move_only_function is move-only, but calling it does not use it up, so a second call is not prevented statically.

recommendation.why: The run-once fact has to follow the value, so it belongs to the function's type, as the effect row does. A mark carries it with no wrapper type, adapter or runtime flag, and parameters keep Jet's ordinary read and take modes.
gains: One mark for every position a callback can live in.
Second calls, forwarding twice and loop calls are existing use-after-move errors.
Helpers that only call a callback write no &&, and lambdas passed to them borrow as today.
No new type name, no adapter, no runtime cost; value tags keep their one meaning.

whyNot.reason: Same design; #RunOnce is longer, and fields and returns read as nouns ("done: #RunOnce fn") less naturally than "done: #Once fn".
It is A's call-scoped parameter alone, so fields, returns and tasks have no spelling and queued callbacks still need explicit state.
Works today, but threads payload types through every callback API.

recommendation.tradeoff: One compiler-known mark on function types, against a parameter-only mark or payload plumbing.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude Opus. Adversarial model family: Claude Opus. Fresh agent: Lens. A holds after repair: the implicit take broke r3's own loan claim (probed E0120, E0121), and sharing the value-tag site broke the erased-tag rule; both are fixed. Every probed position parses on gate-p294, the FnOnce gaps are closed (call-scoped versus kept, firing from an edited object, lending), and the losses are now empty.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Build card first criteria: #3645 c14-c16 closed. Then at O0, O1 and O2: the program of option A prints 8, 9, 2 and 6 and closes each Log once.

Positive cases: a lambda over a loan passed to a plain #Once parameter, and a repeatable function lent and used after. An optional #Once field fired through edit access with `.move()` leaves None. A list of #Once callbacks is drained and each runs once.

Negative cases each give their registered error with a UI snapshot. They are: second call, forward twice, loop call, and a #Once value into an unmarked slot (E0113). Also: a plain #Once parameter stored, returned or sent (E0120), a #Once value called through a read borrow, and #Scrub(Once). An uncalled #Once callback drops its captures once on return, error, panic and cancellation.

surface.lesson: A #Once function runs at most once. The mark rides on its type, so helpers, fields, returns and tasks can hold it; calling it uses it up.

losses: Longer in every signature.

recommendation.why: The run-once fact has to follow the value, so it belongs to the function's type. A mark carries it with no wrapper type, adapter or runtime flag, and parameters keep their ordinary modes.
gains: One mark for every callback position, no wrapper type or adapter.
Helpers that only call a callback write no &&.

No stored, returned or task callbacks.

designAway: No wrapper type: the fact is a mark that is part of the function type, as the effect row is.
No shared marker site: Once has its own function-type site, so type-use markers stay erased value tags and #Scrub(Once) is refused.
No implicit take: a plain #Once parameter is call-scoped (one call or one forward, never stored); a helper that keeps the callback writes the ordinary &&#Once.
No adapter or conversion object: any function fits a #Once slot, and a call-scoped parameter lends a repeatable function so the caller keeps it.
No runtime once flag: all checks are static moves; the callee drops an uncalled handle it was given, and a lent handle drops nothing.
Firing a stored callback from an object you edit: `.move()` on an optional #Once field leaves None, the shape of Rust's Option::take.
Exactly-once cleanup (#3645 c14-c16) is a build prerequisite, proven before the feature is claimed.

decisions.title: A typed worker address reaches the worker's current route on every call, and a refusal hands the message back
decisions.situation: A typed worker address remembers a route generation, so a handoff makes it stale, and a refused call consumes its message. We recommend one stable address that finds the worker's current route on every call, with refusals that hand the message back. A prototype on today's Core does both: a stopped worker returns the identical message, and route changes after admission keep the answer. Durable delivery, cancellation and restart remain unproved.
decisions.gist: How should a caller reach its typed worker after a route handoff, without losing its message?
decisions.lesson: Stable identity avoids manual local refresh. Delivery must either admit its message to the permitted queue or return ownership before admission. After admission, an uncertain result cannot guarantee safe repetition.
decisions.explainer:
Proposed stable typed identity avoids manual local refresh. Delivery resolves the permitted route, reserves room, then publishes the message; before publication a refusal returns ownership, after publication an uncertain outcome is Ambiguous.

The prototype exercises those sequential paths. It does not prove atomic admission against every route change, cross-process coordination or cancellation.

Delivery and maintenance should use one identity resolver with distinct liveness policies, so a partitioned worker can still be reconciled without widening authority.
decisions.story: Lena upgrades a pricing worker while checkout tasks keep its typed address. Every checkout must keep reaching prices through the upgrade, and a checkout that is refused must keep its order.
decisions.inWild: Erlang gen_server accepts a registered name or a process id; name-based calls avoid manual pid refresh but can fail. Tokio SendError returns an unsent value. Orleans references preserve logical identity across activations, not unconditional availability.
decisions.detail:
Independent gate-p289 rerun: the four PROBE5 tests pass in a scratch Core overlay containing the author's Actor.submit and service helpers. Stopped inbox returns [unsent]; room counts are 4 before and after. Answered port 1 and refused port 2 each close once. Admission before handoff answers 10; before drain answers 20; later calls return their payload.

Partitioned delivery returns [a, b], reconciliation then permits answer 2, foreign authority fails, and resolving the old id permits drain. This is a private resolver plus explicitly rewritten maintenance calls, not migration of every public dispatcher.

exclusive-tree fails E1101 for two tasks using current service.call and handoff_generation. It does not call admit5, exercise its internal stages, or prove coordinated admission across all handles and processes. call5 retains its &ServiceTree parameter while waiting for the reply; splitting admission into a helper does not itself release that function's exclusive borrow.

Actor.submit is marked Time.Wait and uses Sender.send on the actor's unbounded channel. It avoids waiting for the reply, but the prototype does not prove cancellation-free, nonblocking publication; request construction is arbitrary callable code in that API. Remove the blanket non-waiting and atomicity claims.

The public Core generic Refused<Q> lowering remains unproved and tracked as #6048 c9; the model uses existing SendError<Q?> instead. Durable commit, cancellation and replacement/discovery paths are still missing.

D-SERVICE-IDENTITY1 preserves discovery authority/freshness; D-SERVICE-UPGRADE1 preserves pinning. A explicitly amends D-SERVICE-REPLY1's error signature. No automatic lossless retry is promised after admission.

options.name: One address; delivery finds the current route
options.detail: A typed address names a worker, not a route generation. Each call resolves its permitted current route. Before admission a refusal returns the message; maintenance shares the identity resolver but has its own policy.
options.technical:
Proposed contract: Endpoint<Q,R> retains authority-bound worker identity. One canonical resolver checks authority, tree and worker; delivery adds current route, pin, liveness and drain checks, while maintenance uses its own policy. Restart must replace the dead transport without widening authority.

Admission linearizes route validation, reservation and publication against handoff, rollback, drain, partition and revocation. Before that commit, refusal returns Q and any reservation exactly once; after it, the queue owns Q and an uncertain result is Ambiguous. Cross-process admission coordinates with rollout authority. Keep coordination restricted to admission, never across reply waits; full-mailbox and handler-reentry progress must be demonstrated. The current exclusive-borrow helper proves only sequential cases, not that implementation.

Refused<Q> holds the reason and optional original Q. Cancellation or allocation failure must leave exactly one owner and no leaked reservation at every boundary. A durable operation commits at the journal's durable admission point, not the prototype's volatile send; retained receipt/key scope must suppress documented retries, while nontransactional external effects remain potentially ambiguous.

These are stated implementation limits with real coordination, journal and recovery costs. Prove them in the build card's first criterion before claiming support. Migrate every public delivery and maintenance path through the canonical resolver and public Core Refused<Q>; preserve discovery freshness and pinning with no shim. The public generic lowering gap is #6048 c9.

options.name: Refresh the address explicitly
options.detail: Keep today's generation-bearing address and its Stale refusal. Add `tree.current(api)`, which returns the same worker at its current allowed generation.
options.technical:
current<Q,R> refreshes the same authority-bound worker's route snapshot. Earlier probes exercised handoff, rollback and pins. Another handoff can stale it again.

B can use A's returned-message error: recovery is independent of address policy. Its real costs are refresh work and coordinated route validation at admission. Stale diagnostics can suggest refresh, but cannot eliminate that caller work.

options.name: Resolve with a typed witness
options.detail: Pass the retained typed address with the directory name. The signed entry selects a current route, while the witness proves its message and reply types. Reject an entry naming another worker.
options.technical:
Typed-witness resolution validates the signed entry and matches authority, tree and worker against Endpoint<Q,R>. No runtime type identity or journal schema change is required.

C can return unsent payloads just like A and B. Its real costs are alias registration, a witness, directory availability and refresh work. Register during setup; acquire a new typed capability explicitly if an alias changes worker.

comparisons.note: gen_server:call accepts a registered name, so callers reach the current process without fetching a new pid. Calls may still fail or time out.
mpsc::error::SendError<T> holds the value that could not be sent, so the sender gets its message back.
A grain reference names a logical interface and key, independent of where or when the grain is activated.

recommendation.why: Prefer stable authority-bound identity and payload-preserving refusal, but the passing sequential prototype does not establish the complete admission and lifecycle contract.
gains: No refresh after a local handoff.
A message never queued comes back identical, with its mailbox place.
Delivery and maintenance share one resolver.

losses.loss: A queued message whose worker then fails has an unknown outcome.
losses.mitigation: Ambiguous says so; reconcile effects, and use idempotency keys for duplicates.

losses.loss: Admission coordination, durable journaling and lifecycle recovery add work; only sequential volatile paths are prototyped.
losses.mitigation: Keep coordination out of reply waits, scope duplicate-suppression keys explicitly, and prove durable/cancellation/restart receipts in the build card's first criterion before shipping.

whyNot.reason: Every holder must refresh, and a later handoff stales it again.
Needs an alias, a witness and refresh work per worker.

recommendation.tradeoff: Resolution at every call, against addresses that pin a generation.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude Opus. Adversarial model family: GPT. Fresh agent: BallotReview2. Holds within stated limits: sequential recovery passes; coordinated admission, lifecycle protocols and public migration require first-build proof, with generic Core lowering a prerequisite.
