The build card's first criterion proves the stated limits and compiler prerequisite. Rerun the four PROBE5 tests in the scratch overlay; then port stopped-inbox and unique-payload tests to the actual public Refused<Q> API. Compile Core exports and every error-matching caller. Do not run a script that edits the repository.

Cover full mailboxes, handler reentry and cross-process coordination without holding registry coordination across reply waits. Migrate all maintenance APIs through the identity resolver with distinct policies.

decisions.title: What a two-name loop over a list of records binds
decisions.situation: A loop with two names, `loop (a, b) in xs`, binds the index and the item. A record here is a value written in braces with named members, such as `{package: "a", name: "b"}`. Over a list of records with members called a and b, a reader may expect each name to get its member. Since 2026-11-11 the compiler does that whenever either name is a member, although the ratified rule said two-name loops stay index and item. You decide the rule. We recommend writing the destructure in braces, as every other record destructure is written.
decisions.gist: Should `loop {a, b} in pairs` destructure each record, with `loop (a, b)` always meaning index and item?
decisions.lesson: Destructuring takes a record apart into named bindings. In Jet a record is written in braces, and a binding destructures it with braces too: `{x, y}: pair`. A loop with two names in parentheses binds the index and the item.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: `loop (i, row) in rows` gives the index and the row, as today. To take each record apart, write `loop {name, price} in items`, the same braces a binding uses. A paren loop whose first name is a member of the record is an error that shows the brace spelling, because that name would only ever hold the index.

Expert path: renames work as in a binding, `loop {name: n, price: p} in items`. Struct items use the struct pattern a binding writes, `loop Item{name, price} in items`. Maps keep `loop (key, value) in map`. The brace head lowers to an ordinary loop plus a destructure binding, so every tier runs the same code.
decisions.story: Ana loops `loop (package, name) in deps` over records with package and name members. Under the ratified rule `package` silently held the index, and her printed list showed numbers. Under the recommendation she gets an error at `(package, name)` that shows `loop {package, name} in deps`, and her program is right on the first run.
decisions.detail:
Today: sema destructures when either name is a member of the item's named-tuple type. The code is at Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Statements.jet:3458-3488 and 10257-10265. It came in commit d3c7589954, for #6281 c185.

Struct items never destructure: the trigger reads only `Type.Tuple` items (Statements.jet:3463). Names that name no member keep the index and item. A wrong member name is E0313, so `loop (i, name)` over records with a `name` member is an error today. A wrong count is E0315. The spec states the current rule (Docs/Spec/spec.md:708-714).

Ratified around it: S73 named records only, and D-RECORD-BRACE1=A writes records in braces. S74 destructuring reuses bracket conventions. It says two-binding loops such as `loop (i, item) in xs` are unchanged (Docs/Spec/syntax-decisions.md:1384-1387). D-RANGE-EXCL1=C makes `loop (i, item) in xs` yield index then item (syntax-decisions.md:2150-2151). The shipped rule overrode those two lines without a ballot.

Parser: `loop {` opens the infinite loop (Compiler/JetParser/Source/Parser/Statements.jet:1285), and the brace binding patterns live at Statements.jet:1581-1615.

Row: #6895 c7 (TowerKeeper ballot list, 2026-11-15).

options.name: Braces destructure, parens bind index and item
options.detail: `loop {a, b} in xs` destructures each record by member name, with renames as in a binding; struct items take the struct pattern, `loop Dep{a, b} in xs`. `loop (a, b) in xs` always binds index and item. A paren head whose first name is a member of the item record is an error that offers the brace spelling. `loop (i, name) in deps` stays index and item, with no error.
options.technical: The parser accepts a binding's brace or struct pattern in a loop head. `loop {` opens an infinite loop today. The parser tells the two apart by an `in` after the matching `}`. A loop body is never followed by `in`, because `in` cannot start a statement. Sema lowers the head to the hidden-row loop plus the existing destructure binding. The name-trigger in Statements.jet becomes the first-name error check.

options.name: Names decide (the current behavior)
options.detail: `loop (a, b) in xs` destructures named-tuple items when either name is a member; otherwise it binds index and item. Struct items always bind index and item.
options.technical: Shipped in d3c7589954, against the S74 line that keeps two-binding loops unchanged. One spelling, whose meaning depends on the record's member names.

options.name: Refuse the ambiguous loop
options.detail: A paren loop whose first name is a member of the record is an error. Destructuring takes two lines: `loop dep in deps` then `{package, name}: dep`.
options.technical: No new loop form. The name-trigger becomes an error.

options.name: Always index and item
options.detail: Return to the ratified rule: two names in parentheses always bind index and item, with no diagnostic.
options.technical: Remove the destructure path from Statements.jet. This is the S74 and D-RANGE-EXCL1=C rule as written before d3c7589954.

comparisons.note: Braces in the loop head destructure an object by property name, which is A's spelling.
Parens destructure a tuple by position; the index needs enumerate(). Records by name need attribute access.

recommendation.why: One mark should mean one thing. Braces already mean a record in Jet, so braces in a loop head destructure one, and parens keep their single meaning, index and item, whatever the member names are.
gains: A loop's meaning never depends on the record's member names.

The old trap becomes an error with the fix in it.

It brings back the trap #6281 found, which stays silent whenever both names still type-check, as in string interpolation.

decisions.title: A wait cycle among tasks stops the program and names the cycle
decisions.situation: Two tasks that each wait for the other hang forever. Today a Jet program in that state prints nothing and never exits; a probe of two tasks receiving from each other's channel ran until it was killed. The runtime owns every channel, lock and join, so it can see a cycle of waiting tasks the moment the last one blocks. You decide what happens then. We recommend that each task in the cycle fails as a panicking task does, with a message naming each task, what it waits on and where. Other tasks keep running.
decisions.gist: When tasks wait on each other in a cycle, should those tasks fail and name the cycle?
decisions.lesson: A deadlock is a set of tasks where each waits for another in the set, so none can ever move. Go reports one only when every goroutine is stuck. Java finds lock cycles when asked. Jet's runtime sees every wait, so it can find a cycle as soon as it forms.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: if two tasks wait on each other, each one fails the way a task that panics does. Whoever joins them gets the failure, with a message listing each task, what it waits for, and the line where it waits. If the main task is in the cycle, the program stops. Under jet debug, the failure is a breakpoint, and `tasks` shows the cycle.

Expert path: the scheduler keeps a wait-for edge for each blocked task: the lock's holder, the joined task, or the tasks that still hold a sender for an empty channel. A sender held outside any task, such as in module storage, gives no edge. When a task blocks, the scheduler walks edges from it, bounded by the number of blocked tasks.

A wait under a deadline is never in a cycle, since it can still end. Neither is a wait on I/O, a timer or an FFI call, so there are no false failures.
decisions.story: Sam's pipeline has a reader task and a writer task joined by two channels. Under load, the writer waits for the reader's reply while the reader waits for room on the writer's channel. Today the service just stops answering. With A, both tasks fail, and the log shows both tasks, both channel lines and both stacks, and the test fails at once instead of timing out.
decisions.inWild:
// Go: only when every goroutine is blocked
fatal error: all goroutines are asleep - deadlock!

goroutine 1 [chan receive]:
main.main()
	/app/main.go:12 +0x5c
decisions.detail:
Probe deadlock.jet on the p294 compiler (dev 3c593a7f16): two tasks each receive from the other's channel; `jet run` printed nothing and was killed by `timeout 45` (exit 124). Fact F1 in the review.

Code: Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/Channel.jet:181 (channel_receive), Sync.jet:419 (sync_park) and Fiber.jet:134 (fiber_park) park tasks without recording what they wait on. #6841 c7 already records the awaited task for joins.

A task that panics fails its join with `.Panicked(reason)` and does not stop other tasks (Docs/Spec/spec.md:4603-4604), so A delivers a deadlock the same way. Knowing which tasks hold a channel's senders means counting sender handles per task when they move. The cited review Docs/Audits/2026-11-18-best-debugger-profiler.md (axis D8) is not on dev.

options.name: Fail the tasks of any wait cycle, in every build
options.detail: When the last task of a cycle blocks, each task in it fails as a panicking task does: its join returns `.Panicked` with the cycle, and its scope unwinds. The message names each task, its wait and its line. If the main task is in the cycle, the program stops. Partial cycles are found while other tasks run.
options.technical: Wait-for edges kept by the scheduler for locks, joins and channels; a bounded walk on each block. Channel edges need a per-task count of sender handles, updated when a sender moves between tasks. Waits under a deadline give no edge. The failure goes through the task panic path, so `context.trace`, `.Panicked` and jet debug's stop all apply.
options.code:
deadlock: tasks wait on each other
  task 2 (reader)  waits to send on `replies`   pipeline.jet:41
  task 3 (writer)  waits to receive on `jobs`   pipeline.jet:58
  task 2 holds the only sender of `jobs`
  task 3 holds the only receiver of `replies`

options.name: Report only when every task is stuck
options.detail: Like Go: when no task can run, the program stops with a deadlock message. A cycle among some tasks while others run is not reported.
options.technical: A check when the run queue empties and no timer or I/O wait is pending.
options.code:
deadlock: no task can run
  task 1 waits to receive on `done`  main.jet:12

options.name: Show cycles in the debugger only
options.detail: The program behaves as today. `jet debug` and `jet inspect live` show waits and mark cycles when asked.
options.technical: The same edges, read only by tools.
options.code:
(Jet) tasks
  2 reader  blocked  on send `replies`  (cycle with 3)
  3 writer  blocked  on receive `jobs`  (cycle with 2)

comparisons.note: Fatal error only when all goroutines block; partial deadlocks hang. This is option B's shape.
comparisons.code: fatal error: all goroutines are asleep - deadlock!

comparisons.note: ThreadMXBean finds monitor and lock cycles when called; nothing stops on its own. This is option C's shape.

recommendation.why: A wait cycle with no deadline never ends by itself, so failing its tasks loses nothing and turns a silent hang into a named bug. Servers usually deadlock in part while other tasks keep running, which only A catches, and the rest of the server keeps serving.
gains: A hang becomes a stop that names the tasks and lines.
Partial deadlocks in servers are caught, not only whole-program ones.
Tests fail at once instead of timing out.

losses.loss: Every sender move updates a per-task count, a small cost on channel-heavy code.
losses.mitigation: c6's gauntlet measures it; a sender that never leaves its task costs nothing.

losses.loss: A cycle hidden behind a sender kept in module storage is not caught.
losses.mitigation: `jet inspect live` still shows every blocked task and its wait.

whyNot.reason: A server with one idle listener never has every task stuck, so its deadlocks still hang silently.
Production hangs stay silent until someone attaches a tool.

recommendation.tradeoff: A short walk of wait edges on each block, for named deadlocks instead of hangs.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Under A: `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter Tasks/wait_cycle_stops_with_the_cycle` covers a channel cycle, a lock cycle and a join cycle at O0, O1 and O2. Each fails both tasks with `.Panicked` naming both, while a third task keeps running and finishes.

A task waiting on a timer, or a receive under a deadline, is never reported. A cycle that includes the main task stops the program. Under B: the same program with the third task hangs, and without it stops. Under C: the program hangs and `tasks` marks the cycle.

Evidence labels: the hang is measured (probe deadlock.jet). The walk's cost is inferred, bounded by the number of blocked tasks; c6's gauntlet measures it.

surface.lesson: A deadlock is tasks waiting on each other forever. Today a Jet program in one hangs silently. The runtime sees every wait, so it can spot the cycle when it forms.

options.name: Fail the cycle's tasks
options.gist: Each task in the cycle fails like a panicking task, naming its wait and line.
gains: Hangs become named failures.
Catches deadlocks while other tasks still run.
losses: A small cost when a sender moves between tasks.

  task 2 (reader)  waits to send on `replies`  pipeline.jet:41
  task 3 (writer)  waits to receive on `jobs`  pipeline.jet:58

options.name: Only when all are stuck
options.gist: Stop only when no task at all can run, as Go does.
gains: The simplest check.
losses: Servers with an idle listener still hang.

proposed.code: deadlock: no task can run

options.name: Debugger only
options.gist: The program hangs as today; tools mark the cycle.
gains: No change to running programs.
losses: Production hangs stay silent.

  2 reader  blocked  (cycle with 3)

recommendation.why: A wait cycle with no deadline never ends, so failing its tasks costs nothing and names the bug. Only A catches partial deadlocks, and the rest keeps serving.
gains: Named failures instead of silent hangs.
Partial deadlocks caught.

losses.loss: A small cost when senders move.
losses.mitigation: The overhead gauntlet measures it.

whyNot.reason: Misses deadlocks while any task still runs.
Production hangs stay silent.

recommendation.tradeoff: A short check on each wait, for named deadlocks.

decisions.title: The debugger and profiler window is Canvas, grown to RemedyBG's panels and one timeline
decisions.situation: The best native debuggers show source, stack, locals, watches and threads at once, and the best profilers draw a timeline you can zoom. Jet already has one graphical surface, Canvas, opened with jet dev --canvas in a browser. Its debugger view can step, show locals, evaluate named watches, print and list up to 32 stack frames. It has no task list, no replay controls and no profile timeline. You decide where the full debugger and profiler window lives. We recommend growing Canvas, so Jet keeps one graphical tool. The other paths are a separate native window or a terminal interface. r2 (owner, 2026-11-18): Canvas is meant to run natively or in a browser, whichever the user prefers, so option A now includes both hosts.
decisions.gist: Should the full debugger and profiler window be Canvas, grown, rather than a second graphical tool?
decisions.lesson: RemedyBG and the RAD Debugger show every debugger panel at once in a fast native window. Tracy and Superluminal draw a zoomable timeline of every thread. Jet's Canvas already shares one live session between its editor, preview and debugger views, so a debugger panel there sees the same source and edits.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: run `jet dev --canvas app.jet`. The Debug view shows source with breakpoints, the call stack, locals, watches and the task list together. The Profile view opens a trace and draws samples, zones, waits and I/O on one zoomable timeline. A crash dump or a recording opens in the Debug view.

Expert path: the views read the existing Canvas session and debug documents, extended with watches, tasks, frames and replay positions. The Profile view reads the canonical trace. The console and DAP stay for terminals and other editors. Canvas sends source edits through its checked transactions, so a fix made while stopped goes through the same path as any edit.
decisions.story: Noor stops her game at a breakpoint in Canvas. The stack, locals and the task list sit beside the source. She opens last night's trace in the Profile view and sees one task's waits line up with the long frames. She edits the function in the same window and the preview picks it up.
decisions.inWild:
# RAD Debugger: one native window, every panel docked
$ raddbg --auto_run game.exe
# source, watch, call stack, threads, disassembly, memory panels
decisions.detail:
Today: `jet dev --canvas` serves Canvas to a browser (Docs/Spec/Reference/canvas-protocol.md). Its debug session (canvas-protocol.md:288-330) runs under Jet's own native debugger. It takes step, next, continue, finish, locals, print and backtrace, plus named watches evaluated at the stopped frame. Each command is one HTTP request.

The bounded limits are 32 live sessions, 64 commands, 128 breakpoints, 32 watches, 32 call-stack frames and 128 trace entries (canvas-protocol.md:326-327).

D-PERF-MEMORY1=A already adds a Memory metric to Canvas's code map from a saved trace. D-PROGRAM-FORM1=A makes Canvas a co-editor of the program. Core also has a native UI stack (Core/UI, with a Wayland backend) and a terminal UI library (Core/TUI).

The cited review Docs/Audits/2026-11-18-best-debugger-profiler.md (axis D11) is not on dev.

options.name: Grow Canvas
options.detail: Canvas's Debug view gains every panel at once: source, stack, locals, watches, tasks, and replay controls. A Profile view draws the trace timeline. Dumps, recordings and traces open there. No new command. Canvas runs in a native window or in a browser, whichever the user prefers; both hosts show the same views from one session.
options.technical: Extends the Canvas debug document with tasks, frames and replay positions, and raises its watch and stack bounds or pages them. Adds a profile document over the canonical trace, which the server reduces to the zoom level shown, so a large trace never ships whole to the browser. The console and DAP remain.

A native profiler window with a zoomable timeline, separate from the debugger.

recommendation.why: Jet already has one graphical tool that shares a live session between editor, preview and debugger. Growing it gives the debugger and profiler the same source and edits, with no second window to keep in step.
gains: One graphical tool for editing, debugging and profiling.
Debugger and profiler share one session and one timeline.
No new command; Canvas already exists.

losses.mitigation: Both hosts render the same Canvas documents from one session, so a view is written once.

losses.loss: Each step is an HTTP round trip, slower than a native debugger's in-process redraw.
losses.mitigation: Canvas is served from the same machine, so each round trip stays local and short.

losses.mitigation: The grown document pages frames and watches instead of cutting them.

whyNot.reason: A second native tool would drift from Canvas; Canvas's own native host already gives a native window.
A terminal cannot draw a zoomable timeline well, and the console already covers terminal use.

recommendation.tradeoff: A browser-hosted window, for one graphical tool that edits, debugs and profiles.

decisions.title: The jet debug console words for conditions, logpoints, watches, frames, tasks, attach and fix
decisions.situation: The jet debug console has step, next, continue, finish, break by line number, locals, print, backtrace, help and quit, most with one-letter short forms. The everyday workflow also needs conditional breakpoints, logpoints, watches, a breakpoint list, frame selection, a task list, attach and a fix command. Each new word is a user surface and needs a ballot before it is built. You decide how the words look. We recommend gdb's short words where gdb has one, plain new words where it has none, and Jet expressions after them.
decisions.gist: What words should the jet debug console use for conditions, logpoints, watches, frames, tasks, attach and fix?
decisions.lesson: A debugger console reads one command per line. Most people who use one learned gdb or lldb. gdb uses short words such as `break`, `watch` and `frame`. lldb uses longer noun-then-verb commands, with short aliases. Jet's console already uses gdb's words and one-letter forms for stepping, so the question is whether the new commands follow them.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: `break cart.jet:88 if total < 0` stops only when the condition holds, and `break 88` still means line 88 of the current file. `log cart.jet:88 "total={total}"` prints and keeps going. `watch order.total` stops when that value changes. `breaks` lists breakpoints and watches with their numbers, and `delete 2` removes one. `tasks` lists every task, and `frame 2` selects a caller.

Expert path: every expression is a Jet expression, checked by the compiler in the stopped scope. Expressions must be effect-free, so evaluating one cannot change the program. Conditions run inside the program as compiled code, so a false condition costs a call, not a debugger stop.

On x86-64, `watch` uses the CPU's four debug registers first, then page protection. `jet debug --attach PID` attaches to a process the user owns. `fix` applies an edited function, under the checks #6919 sets. `jet debug -O2 app.jet` builds at the level the user ships.
decisions.story: Leo's game loses health points at random. He types `watch player.hp` and continues. The debugger stops at a line in the poison system, shows 40 becoming 35, and names the task. He edits the poison rate, types `fix`, and the running game picks up the new code on the next frame.
decisions.inWild:
# gdb
(gdb) break cart.c:88 if total < 0
(gdb) dprintf cart.c:88,"total=%d\n",total
(gdb) watch order->total
(gdb) info breakpoints
(gdb) frame 2
(gdb) info threads
decisions.detail:
Ratified: D-DBG2/3 names step, next, continue and finish with s, n, c and f, and the locals dump (Docs/Spec/syntax-decisions.md:7514-7516). break, print, backtrace and help ship in the console without a recorded decision. D-DBG-DAP1=A ships the full DAP profile: conditions, hit counts, logpoints, attach and read-only bounded Jet expression evaluation (syntax-decisions.md:7519-7533).

The #6841 c36 criterion lists the workflow: break by line and by function, conditions, logpoints, step in, over and out, finish, backtrace, frame select, print and watch expressions, and attach. #6919 c5 plans a checked transactional fix. #6841 c40 holds native expression evaluation unbuilt until a redesign answers a failed review. So `print`, conditions and watch expressions under every option wait on it. That proposal and its review are not on dev yet.

Code at dev 3c593a7f16, unchanged on dev since: the console words live in Compiler/JetDebug/Source/Native.jet:405-441. They are s/step, n/next, c/continue, f/finish, b/break, locals, p/print, bt/backtrace and h/help. `break` takes a line number of the current file only (Native.jet:411-425). `print` reads locals only (Native.jet:1153-1158). `jet debug` always builds at -O0 (Native.jet:1066-1067).

A second argument is refused with E2104, so program arguments cannot be passed (Compiler/JetCLI/Source/CLI/Debug.jet:39-42). The cited review Docs/Audits/2026-11-18-best-debugger-profiler.md is not on dev; the landed reviews are Docs/Audits/2026-11-14-debugging-profiling-review.md and 2026-11-17-debug-latency-vs-lldb.md.

options.name: gdb's short words with Jet expressions
options.detail:
gdb's words where gdb has one: `break <line|file:line|function> [if <expr>]`, `watch <expr>`, `delete <n>`, `frame <n>`, `up`, `down`. Plain new words where gdb has none: `log <file:line> "<text with {expr}>"` for gdb's `dprintf`, `breaks` for `info breakpoints`, `tasks` and `task <n>` for `info threads` and `thread <n>`, and `fix`.

`break 12` keeps meaning line 12 of the current file. The existing one-letter forms stay; new words get none. `jet debug --attach PID` attaches. `jet debug` takes `jet build`'s `-O` level and passes the words after `--` to the program.
options.technical: One parser for every command's expression: the compiler's, in the stopped scope, effect-free only, as DAP's read-only evaluation already is. The same words run live, on a dump and in a replay. DAP maps each to its standard request, including hit counts.
options.code:
(Jet) break cart.jet:88 if total < 0
(Jet) log cart.jet:90 "total={total} items={items.len()}"
(Jet) watch order.total
(Jet) breaks
  1 break cart.jet:88 if total < 0
  2 watch order.total
(Jet) tasks
  1 run       running   main.jet:20
  3 discount  blocked   on lock cart.jet:60
(Jet) frame 2
(Jet) fix

options.name: lldb's noun-then-verb commands
options.detail: `breakpoint set --file cart.jet --line 88 --condition 'total < 0'`, `breakpoint list`, `watchpoint set expression order.total`, `thread list`, `frame select 2`, with short aliases such as `b` and `w`.
options.technical: Each command has a long form with flags and a short alias. The existing stepping words stay as they are, so the console mixes two styles.
options.code:
(Jet) breakpoint set --file cart.jet --line 88 --condition 'total < 0'
(Jet) watchpoint set expression order.total
(Jet) breakpoint list
(Jet) frame select 2

options.name: Keep the console small; editors get the rest
options.detail: The console keeps its current words and adds only `frame`, `up` and `down`. Conditions, logpoints, watches, tasks and fix are reached through an editor over the ratified DAP profile.
options.technical: No new console parser. DAP already carries conditions, hit counts and logpoints; watch, tasks and fix are built as DAP requests only.

comparisons.note: Short words; `dprintf` is the logpoint and `info breakpoints` the list.
comparisons.code:
(gdb) break cart.c:88 if total < 0
(gdb) watch order->total
(gdb) info breakpoints

comparisons.note: Noun-then-verb, with aliases such as `b` and `w`.
comparisons.code:

decisions.title: An always-on flight recorder and typed crash dumps that jet debug opens
decisions.situation: When a Jet program stops on a panic in production, it prints a trace and exits. Nothing is left to open in a debugger, and nobody knows what the program did in its last seconds. The runtime could keep a small ring of recent events, such as samples, task waits and file or network results. On a stop it could write a dump with every task's stack and typed values. You decide whether that recorder is on by default and where dumps go. We recommend it on in every build, with a measured cost and a build setting to turn it off.
decisions.gist: Should every Jet program keep a small flight recorder and write a typed dump that jet debug opens when it stops?
decisions.lesson: A crash dump is a snapshot of a program at the moment it failed, opened later in a debugger. A flight recorder keeps the last few seconds of events in a fixed-size ring, so the dump also shows what led up to the failure. Windows minidumps and Go's flight recorder each do half of this.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: when your program panics, it writes a dump file and prints its path. Run `jet debug crash-2026-11-18T10-04-12.jetdump` to see every task's stack and values, with the same commands as a live session. `jet perf attach PID` reads the same recent events from a running program.

Expert path: each thread keeps a ring of recent samples at a low rate, sync events and chokepoint results, in memory reserved at start. On a stop, the panic path writes the dump from reserved memory: every task's stack, values reachable from those frames to a byte budget, and the rings. Values tagged #Secret or #PII are written as redacted, by the same rules the log uses. The default rate must fit the profile-overhead budget, which the gauntlet measures.
decisions.story: Priya's service panics once a week in production. Today she gets a trace and a guess. With the recorder, the panic leaves a dump. She opens it with jet debug on her laptop, walks the failing task's frames, and reads the last twenty file and network results before the panic. The cause is a truncated reply from one upstream server.
decisions.detail:
Today: a stop prints context.trace (Docs/Spec/spec.md:4473) and exits; there is no dump file and no way to open one. `jet perf attach` and `jet inspect live --attach PID` (Compiler/JetCLI/Source/CLI/Inspect.jet:115-136) work only on a process started with observe enabled (#6841 c18-c20).

Ratified around it: D-OBSERVE-LIVE1=A defines `jet inspect live` (Docs/Spec/syntax-decisions.md:5990). D-DENY-COST1=A lets code forbid hidden costs such as allocation and locks with a compile error, so a recorder event written from such code must allocate nothing and take no lock. The value tags `#Secret` and `PII` are in spec.md:1145-1205.

The cited review Docs/Audits/2026-11-18-best-debugger-profiler.md (axes D9 and P10) is not on dev.

options.name: On in every build; dumps on every stop
options.detail:
Every program keeps the recorder at a low default rate. A stop, a panic or a fatal signal, writes a typed dump and prints its path. Dumps go to `.jet/dumps/` under the working directory, or to a directory a setting names when that one is not writable.

The directory keeps the newest few dumps, so a crash loop cannot fill the disk, and each file is readable by its owner only. `jet debug <dump>` opens it; `jet perf attach` drains the rings live. A build setting turns the recorder off, or keeps stacks and drops values.
options.technical: Per-thread rings in memory reserved at start; an event write allocates nothing and takes no lock, so code under D-DENY-COST1 denials stays legal. The dump writer runs on the panic and signal paths from reserved memory. Redaction follows the value tags. The overhead gauntlet measures the default rate against c6's budget.

panic: index 12 out of range for a list of 12 (cart.jet:71)
dump written: .jet/dumps/orders-2026-11-18T10-04-12.jetdump
$ jet debug .jet/dumps/orders-2026-11-18T10-04-12.jetdump

(Jet) events --last 20

panic: index 12 out of range (cart.jet:71)

options.name: Dumps on request only
options.detail: No ring. A user attaches jet debug to a running or stopped process and writes a dump by command.
options.technical: A `dump` console command; no runtime change.

(Jet) dump orders.jetdump

comparisons.note: A crash writes a minidump that a debugger opens with full types; there is no event history.
Keeps the last seconds of the execution trace in memory and writes it on demand; no dump of values.

recommendation.why: The failures that need a dump are the ones nobody expected, so the recorder must already be running. A measured low rate and redaction by value tags make it safe to keep on.
gains: Every production panic leaves a dump jet debug can open.
The dump shows the last events, not just the final state.

losses.loss: Every program spends a little memory and CPU on the ring.
losses.mitigation: The overhead gauntlet measures the default rate against c6's budget; a build setting turns it off.

losses.loss: A dump holds values that were never tagged secret, such as customer records.
losses.mitigation: Dumps are owner-only files with a byte budget, and a setting keeps stacks and events but drops values.

losses.loss: A crash loop or a read-only working directory could lose or flood dumps.
losses.mitigation: Only the newest few dumps are kept, and a setting names another directory.

whyNot.reason: Programs are rarely started with observation on, so the surprise failure leaves nothing behind.
A crashed process is gone before anyone can attach, and there is no history.

recommendation.tradeoff: A small measured cost in every program, for a dump of every failure.

`--filter Perf/attach_drains_flight_ring` attaches to a running program started without flags. A function under `!Mem.Alloc` and `!Lock` still compiles with the recorder on. `node Tools/Gauntlet/Harness/run.mjs --entry profile-overhead` reports the default cost. Under B: the same cases pass only with observation on. Under C: the dump case attaches before the stop.

Evidence labels: nothing here is built; the cost is to be measured.

decisions.title: A causal profile lens that predicts which line is worth speeding up
decisions.situation: A sampling profiler shows where time is spent, but not what would get faster if that code got faster. In a program with many tasks, speeding up the hottest line often changes nothing, because another task is the real bottleneck. Causal profiling answers the right question. It briefly slows everything else down to simulate speeding up one line, then measures the effect on throughput. Jet's scheduler owns every pause, and its capability chokepoint sees every finished request. So it can run these experiments without source changes. You decide whether jet perf gets a causal lens. We recommend it.
decisions.gist: Should jet perf predict how much faster the whole program gets if one line gets faster?
decisions.lesson: A causal profiler pretends a line is faster by pausing the other tasks a little each time that line runs. If throughput rises, speeding up that line for real would help. The answer is a ranked list of lines with their predicted gain. Coz introduced the method in 2015; it needs a marked progress point.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: run `jet perf run --lens=causal server.jet` under a realistic load. `jet perf view` lists lines with their predicted gain, such as "speed this line up 20%, the program gets 9% faster", each with a confidence range. Lines with no effect are listed too, so you know what to leave alone.

Expert path: during the run, the profiler picks a line and a virtual speedup. Each time a sample lands on that line, the scheduler delays every other task at its next pause point. Progress points are found automatically: every zone that closes, every request the capability chokepoint answers, and every task that finishes.

A `perf.progress("name")` call adds one by hand. Each progress point is ranked on its own, so cheap health checks never stand in for real requests. A task running foreign code cannot be delayed until it returns to Jet, so its delay is charged when it does, as Coz charges a blocked thread. The lens refuses to rank when the run was too short for the experiments to be significant.
decisions.story: Lena's image service has a hot resize function at 40% of samples. She is about to rewrite it. The causal lens says making resize 30% faster gains 1%, while the upload parser, at 8% of samples, gains 12% if made 30% faster, because every worker waits on it. She fixes the parser instead.
decisions.detail:
Today: jet perf has cpu, alloc and tasks lenses (D-PERFSESSION1) and a memory lens (D-PERF-MEMORY1=A); none predicts the effect of a speedup. Peer: Coz (SOSP 2015, dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/2815400.2815409), which also measures latency between a begin and an end point; this ballot covers throughput only.

The scheduler's pause points are its stop polls, placed after calls, at loop turns and at recursive entries (Compiler/JetIR/Source/IR.jet:184-194). Zones and `perf.progress` belong to the Core perf API that D-PERF-ZONES1 proposes, so the zone progress points of A exist only if that ballot passes.

The cited review Docs/Audits/2026-11-18-best-debugger-profiler.md (axis P6) is not on dev.

options.name: A causal lens with automatic progress points
options.detail: `jet perf run --lens=causal` runs the experiments. Progress points are found automatically: closed zones, answered requests and finished tasks. `perf.progress(name)` adds one by hand. The view ranks lines by predicted gain with confidence ranges.
options.technical: The scheduler inserts the delays at its pause points. The lens changes timing, so it runs alone and refuses to combine with other lenses. The view refuses to rank lines whose interval is too wide.
options.code:
$ jet perf run --lens=causal images.jet -- --port 8080
$ jet perf view images.jettrace
If this line were 30% faster:
  upload.jet:52  parse_part     +12%  (9% to 15%)
  resize.jet:118 resize_rows     +1%  (0% to 2%)
  progress: 41,200 answered requests

options.name: A causal lens with hand-written progress points only
options.detail: The same experiments, but the program must call `perf.progress(name)` where a unit of work ends, as Coz requires.
options.technical: As A, with no automatic progress points.

options.name: No causal profiling
options.detail: Users read samples and wait times and judge the bottleneck themselves.
options.technical: No change.
options.code: $ jet perf view images.jettrace   // samples and waits only

comparisons.note: Virtual speedups by pausing other threads; progress points by hand. This is option B's shape.
Samples and blocking profiles only; the bottleneck is inferred by the reader. This is option C.

recommendation.why: It answers the question profiles are opened for: what to fix. Automatic progress points remove Coz's main setup step, because the runtime already sees every finished request and task.
gains: Ranks lines by real predicted gain, not by time spent.
No source change needed to get a first answer.
Shows which hot lines are not worth fixing.

losses.loss: A useful run needs realistic load for minutes, and runs alone.
losses.mitigation: The lens refuses to rank a short run and says how long it needs.

losses.loss: Tasks inside foreign code are delayed late, which skews results.
losses.mitigation: Their delay is charged when they return, and the view marks lines that ran mostly in foreign code.

losses.loss: Zone progress points depend on D-PERF-ZONES1.
losses.mitigation: Answered requests, finished tasks and `perf.progress` still work without zones.

whyNot.reason: Most users never add a progress point, so the lens would sit unused.
Users keep optimizing hot lines that do not move throughput.

recommendation.tradeoff: One more lens that runs alone, for predictions of what to fix.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Under A: `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter Perf/causal_profile_predicts_speedup` runs a fixture where a less-hot line is the real bottleneck. The lens ranks it first, and a hand-sped version of that line lands within the predicted interval. The case passes at O0, O1 and O2. A short run is refused with the reason, and two progress points are ranked apart. Under B: the same fixture needs `perf.progress` added. Under C: no case.

Evidence labels: nothing here is built; prediction quality is inferred from the Coz paper's results.

decisions.title: Typed heap snapshots, their diffs and retention paths, inside the existing alloc lens
decisions.situation: When a Jet program's memory keeps growing, the tools today show only how much it allocated in total. They cannot say which types are alive, which line made them, or what keeps them alive. The allocator counts blocks and bytes but does not record a block's type, so the compiler would add a type and line record for each allocation while a profiler is recording. You decide where heap snapshots live in the tool. We recommend adding them to the existing alloc lens of jet perf, with a Core call to mark a moment and a diff in jet perf compare.
decisions.gist: Should the alloc lens of jet perf take typed heap snapshots, diff them, and show what keeps a block alive?
decisions.lesson: A heap snapshot lists every block of memory still in use at one moment. Comparing two snapshots shows what grew between them, which is how leaks are found. A retention path is the chain of references from a global or a task's stack to a block, which shows why it was not freed.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: run `jet perf run --lens=alloc app.jet`. At exit, and wherever the program calls `perf.heap_mark("after-load")`, the trace keeps a snapshot. `jet perf view` lists live memory by type and by the line that allocated it. `jet perf compare` shows what grew between two snapshots, and `jet perf view --retained-by <type>` shows the shortest chain keeping one alive.

Expert path: under the alloc lens, each allocation also records its type and line in a side table through the allocator's existing observe hook; other runs pay nothing. Retention paths walk references using a layout table the compiler emits for each type. The snapshot is taken in a forked copy-on-write child on Linux, so the program keeps running; pages the program writes meanwhile are copied, so memory can briefly grow.

Arena, bump and pool storage is expanded through the same records or marked opaque. `jet perf attach PID --lens=alloc` sees only allocations made after it attached. Memory held only through FFI pointers is reported as unreachable from Jet roots, never guessed.
decisions.story: Omar's chat server grows by 200 MB a day. He adds `perf.heap_mark` after each hourly cleanup and runs a day of traffic under the alloc lens. The compare shows 1.9 million live Message values allocated at room.jet:88. The retention path runs from the room list through a history ring that is never trimmed.
decisions.inWild:
// Go heap profile: sampled live bytes by allocation stack, no types or retainers
$ go tool pprof -sample_index=inuse_space http://localhost:6060/debug/pprof/heap
(pprof) top
      flat  flat%   sum%
  180.5MB 62.1% 62.1%  main.(*Room).append
decisions.detail:
Today: `.jettrace` carries an allocation total, shown as the alloc delta in `jet perf compare` (Compiler/JetCLI/Source/CLI/Perf/Command.jet:243-322). The heap allocator takes a size and an alignment, never a type (Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/Alloc.jet:2585). Its facts are six counters: allocations, requested, live, high-water, cap and mode (Alloc.jet:1706-1707).

It has an observe hook for each allocation and free (Alloc.jet:2910). Arena, bump, pool and fixed storage live beside it (Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/MemStorage.jet). #6841 c17 adds allocation counts per line. There is no snapshot, retention path or diff.

Ratified around it: D-PERFSESSION1 defines the lens list (cpu, alloc, tasks); D-PERF-MEMORY1=A adds the memory lens the same way. `perf.heap_mark` joins the Core perf API that D-PERF-ZONES1 proposes.

The cited review Docs/Audits/2026-11-18-best-debugger-profiler.md (axis P4) is not on dev.

options.name: Snapshots in the alloc lens
options.detail: `--lens=alloc` keeps a typed snapshot at exit and at each `perf.heap_mark(name)`. `jet perf view` shows live memory by type and line, `--retained-by <type>` shows retention paths, and `jet perf compare` diffs snapshots. `jet perf attach PID --lens=alloc` snapshots a running program.
options.technical: Under the lens, the compiler passes each allocation site's type and line to the allocator's observe hook, which fills a side table; a per-type layout table lets the snapshot follow references. Snapshots are taken in a forked copy-on-write child and stored in the canonical trace. No new command; one Core call and one view flag.
options.code:
use perf: core.perf

loop {
    serve_hour(rooms)
    cleanup(rooms)
    perf.heap_mark("after-cleanup")
}

$ jet perf run --lens=alloc chat.jet
$ jet perf view chat.jettrace
live at after-cleanup #24   1.9M Message  412 MB  room.jet:88
$ jet perf view chat.jettrace --retained-by Message
rooms -> Room.history -> Ring<Message>.items[17]

options.name: A separate jet heap command
options.detail: `jet heap snapshot PID`, `jet heap diff a b` and `jet heap retain` form their own family with their own file format.
options.technical: A second artifact beside the trace, with its own reader and viewer.
options.code:
$ jet heap snapshot 4242 -o a.jetheap
$ jet heap diff a.jetheap b.jetheap

options.name: Sampled allocation profile only
options.detail: Like Go: sample live bytes by allocation stack at a fixed byte interval. No types, no retention paths.
options.technical: A sampled counter in the allocator, shown in `jet perf view`.
options.code:
$ jet perf run --lens=alloc chat.jet
live (sampled)  412 MB  room.jet:88

comparisons.note: Heap snapshots show typed objects, comparisons between snapshots and retainer paths. This is A's view, for a garbage-collected heap.
comparisons.code: // Memory panel: Take snapshot, then Comparison view, then Retainers

comparisons.note: Allocations marks generations and shows growth between them by allocation stack; sizes, not Swift types, for raw allocations.
comparisons.code: // Allocations instrument: Mark Generation, then compare generations

recommendation.why: Leaks are found by asking which type grew, where it was made and what holds it. A answers all three inside the tool users already run, with one trace format.
gains: Live memory by type and allocation line, with no guessing.
Snapshot diffs and retention paths find leaks directly.
No new command or file format.

losses.loss: Every build carries a layout table for its types, so retention paths can be followed.
losses.mitigation: The table is emitted beside the debug information and stripped with it.

losses.loss: Recording type and line per allocation slows allocation-heavy code under the lens.
losses.mitigation: Only lens runs pay; c6's gauntlet reports the cost, and other runs use the hook-free path.

losses.loss: Attach sees only allocations made after it attached, and a fork can briefly grow memory.
losses.mitigation: `perf.heap_mark` under `jet perf run` covers the whole run, and the view says when a snapshot is partial.

whyNot.reason: A second command family and file format for what is one more view of the alloc lens.
It says where memory was allocated but never why it is still alive, which is the leak question.

recommendation.tradeoff: One Core call and one view flag, for typed leak hunting inside jet perf.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Under A: `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter Perf/heap_snapshot_types_retention_and_diff` leaks a typed list at a known line between two marks. The view names the type and line, the compare shows the growth, and the retention path names the holding field, at O0, O1 and O2. A run without the lens shows the same allocation speed as today. Under B: the same checks through the jet heap commands. Under C: the view shows sampled bytes at the line, with no type or path.

decisions.title: A topdown lens that says why each hot line is slow on the CPU
decisions.situation: A profile says which lines take the time, but not why the processor is slow on them. Modern processors can split their cycles into four causes: useful work, wrong branch guesses, waiting for instructions, and waiting for data. Intel's VTune made this method standard, and AMD and Arm chips now publish the same split. It tells a programmer which kind of fix to try. You decide whether jet perf reports it and how it is asked for. We recommend a topdown lens beside the memory lens, which works the same way and says unavailable, with the reason, where counters are refused.
decisions.gist: Should jet perf say why each hot line is slow on the CPU, using the processor's own counters?
decisions.lesson: The top-down method sorts every cycle into one of four buckets. They are retiring (useful work), bad speculation (wrong branch guesses), front-end bound (waiting for instructions) and back-end bound (waiting for data or execution units). Level 2 splits each bucket once more. The biggest bucket tells you which kind of change helps.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: run `jet perf run --lens=cpu,topdown app.jet`. `jet perf view` adds four columns to each hot function and line. If back-end bound is high, the code is waiting on memory; if bad speculation is high, a branch is unpredictable. Where the machine refuses counters, the lens prints why.

Expert path: the lens reads the CPU's published top-down events through perf_event_open, per thread, in user mode, on the same path as the memory lens. Per function the split comes from counts; per line it comes from samples, so a line with few samples is marked low confidence rather than shown as exact.

Levels 1 and 2 use the formulas for the detected CPU model, stored in the trace. On a chip with two core types, each type has its own formulas and its rows say which type ran. An unknown model, or a virtual machine without counters, reports unavailable rather than guessing. Rows are attributed through the compiler's own line table at -O2, with no symbol step.
decisions.story: Kai's parser spends 35% of its time on one loop. The topdown lens shows that line 62% bad speculation. A branch on each byte's class is mispredicted. He replaces the branch with a table lookup, and the loop runs twice as fast.
decisions.inWild:
# Linux perf, which needs the perf tool and gives whole-program numbers
$ perf stat --topdown ./parser

   31.2%        38.5%            9.1%          21.2%
decisions.detail:
Today: no perf_event_open path is on dev (no Compiler or Core source names it). #6841 c13-c16 (owned by another lane) add cache, TLB and page-fault counters per line under the memory lens (D-PERF-MEMORY1=A), and c16 requires "unavailable with a reason", never zeros. D-PERFSESSION1 defines the lens list. This ballot adds one lens on the same counter path.

The example machine, Raptor Lake, mixes performance and efficiency cores whose top-down events differ, so per-core-type formulas are part of the design, not an extra. The cited review Docs/Audits/2026-11-18-best-debugger-profiler.md (axis P5) is not on dev.

decisions.title: Profiler zones, frame marks and plots, and one marker that profiles every function
decisions.situation: The sampling profiler shows where time goes, but a game or server also wants named regions: this frame, this request, this physics step. Jet's only timed region today is a log span. It needs the Log effect, so a pure function cannot use it, and it allocates its name. You decide how programs mark profiler regions, frames and plotted values. You also decide how one line profiles every function. We recommend a small Core API that needs no effect, plus a marker built from the compile-time program kit. The regions cost nothing until a profiler turns them on.
decisions.gist: How should a program mark profiler regions, frames and plotted values, and profile every function in one line?
decisions.lesson: A zone is a named region of code whose start and end the profiler records, like a stopwatch around a block. A frame mark tells the profiler where one frame or request ends, so it can line frames up. A plot records a number over time, such as entity count. Instrumenting every function means adding a zone to each one without editing them.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: write `_z: perf.zone("physics")` at the top of a block. The zone closes when the block ends. Call `perf.frame()` once per frame and `perf.plot("entities", n)` for a number. Put `#Profiled` on a function, or on a package to profile every function in it. Then `jet perf run game.jet` shows the zones on the timeline with the samples.

Expert path: the API carries no effect, as `debug(value)` carries none. A zone writes only to the profiler's per-thread ring, which the program cannot read. A zone name is a string literal kept in the site table, so nothing allocates. Each site compiles to a short patchable no-op until `jet perf run` or `jet perf attach` turns zones on.

Because zones are not effects, the optimizer may still fold, merge or memoize a pure call, and that call's zone then appears once or not at all. `#Profiled` is a compile-time program over the compiler's events that wraps each body in a zone; users can write their own. `core.log.span` writes the same ring, so there is one timing mechanism.
decisions.story: Ana's game drops a frame every few seconds. She adds `#Profiled` to the physics package and runs `jet perf run`. The timeline shows each frame mark, and the long frames all contain one `broadphase` zone that takes 9 ms when the entity plot passes 4000. She never edited a physics function.
decisions.detail:
Ratified around it: D-PERFSESSION1=D defines the `jet perf` family and its one `.jettrace` timeline (Docs/Spec/syntax-decisions.md:8210). D-DBG1=A makes `debug(value)` an observation that adds no effect, the precedent for an effect-free zone (syntax-decisions.md:9053-9061). That precedent also rejects any remaining `debug` in a shipped artifact or release compile (E3405), which is option B's shape. So option A departs from it on purpose: a zone is off and silent until a profiler attaches.

#6841 c2 requires a ratified ballot for the instrumentation hook and marker. c3 proves a user-written compile-time program instruments every function. c6 measures the cost when off and when on.

Code at dev 3c593a7f16: Core/Perf/Perf.jet has only a fidelity knob. Core/Log/Log.jet:141 makes `span` need the Log effect and allocate its name. Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/PerfSamples.jet writes closed log spans for the profiler. `meta.events` and `meta.rewrite_body` exist in Compiler/JetBuildSession/Source/Session.jet. The cited review Docs/Audits/2026-11-18-best-debugger-profiler.md (axis P2) is not on dev.

options.name: An effect-free zone API and a #Profiled marker, off until attached
options.detail: `perf.zone(name)` opens a zone that closes at the end of its block; `perf.frame()` marks a frame; `perf.plot(name, value)` records a number. Names are string literals. None needs an effect. `#Profiled` on a function or package wraps each body in a zone. Every site is a patchable no-op until `jet perf run` or `jet perf attach` turns zones on, in any build, including shipped ones.
options.technical: The compiler emits a short patchable sequence at each site and a table of sites. The runtime patches them on attach; where the system forbids rewriting code pages, a site tests one flag instead. Zones write a per-thread ring; `core.log.span` writes the same ring. A zone site is not an effect, so it never blocks folding or memoizing a pure call. `#Profiled` is a Core compile-time program using meta.events and meta.rewrite_body.

options.name: The same API, compiled in only for profiling builds
options.detail: The API and marker are the same. Zones exist only in builds `jet perf run` makes; other builds drop them entirely. A running production program cannot turn zones on.
options.technical: The compiler removes zone sites unless the build is a profiling build. Attach sees samples only.

options.name: Use log spans
options.detail: No new API. Programs time regions with `core.log.span`, which needs the Log effect and allocates its name. Pure functions cannot be timed. There are no frame marks or plots.
options.technical: No change.

recommendation.tradeoff: A few bytes per zone site in every build, for zones you can turn on in production.

decisions.title: Step backward by line through any recorded run, threads included, and ask where a value came from
decisions.situation: A recorded run can be replayed in the debugger. The ratified plan steps backward only between recorded events, refuses programs that use threads, and defers asking where a value came from. Safe Jet code has no data races. So a run is fixed by what its inputs returned and the order its tasks used shared things: channels, locks, shared values, joins and atomic cells. Recording just those lets a replay run on real threads, at any optimization level. Stepping backward then works by line, as forward stepping does. You decide whether to widen the ratified plan this way. We recommend it: it would put the debugger ahead of rr and Pernosco.
decisions.gist: Should the debugger step backward by line through any recorded run and say where a value came from?
decisions.lesson: A recording keeps what the program could not compute itself: clock readings, random numbers, file and network results, and the order tasks met at channels and locks. Replaying runs the program again and feeds it those answers, so it does the same thing. Going backward means replaying from a saved point to just before where you are. Asking where a value came from means replaying a short stretch while watching that value's memory.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: run `jet run --record=r1 app.jet`, then `jet debug --replay=r1`. Stop where the value is wrong and type `why total`. The debugger names the line that wrote it and the value it replaced. `reverse-next` goes back one line.

Expert path: the recording logs every result the capability chokepoint returns and the order of every synchronization: channels, locks, `Shared` values, joins and `Atomic` operations. Safe code is data-race free, so this fixes every shared read. Replay enforces the order on real threads.

The log has no instruction counts, so a recording made at -O2 replays at -O0, where every local is visible. A deadline is replayed where it was delivered, by source position and count. Reverse moves re-run from the nearest checkpoint. Unsafe code that writes shared memory outside the order is caught by a digest at each sync event, and replay names the first divergence.
decisions.story: Mia's order service sometimes charges a negative total. It runs eight tasks and the bug shows once in fifty runs. She records runs with `--record` until one fails, opens it in jet debug, stops at the charge and types `why total`. The answer is a discount line in another task that ran before the cart was locked. Under the ratified plan she could not have recorded the run at all, because it uses tasks.
decisions.inWild:
# rr with gdb: record once, then step backward and watch a value
$ rr record ./server
$ rr replay
(rr) break charge
(rr) continue
(rr) watch -l order->total
(rr) reverse-continue
# stops at the write that set total
decisions.detail:
Ratified today: D-RUN-RECORD1=A adds `--record=` on run, dev and test and `jet debug --replay=`. Two of its clauses are reopened here: "Refused programs stay refused; they are Epoch 6 scope" and "Reverse-step stays deferred per D-TIMETRAVEL1=C". D-TIMETRAVEL1=C defers per-variable history to Epoch 6; it is reopened.

D-TIMETRAVEL2=B ships jump with the recorder. It makes `back N` a thin verb counting recorded events ("back 3 from event 11 is jump 8"). Its event granularity is reopened; its re-execution from recorded values is kept. #Track (D-TRACK-ORIGIN1=A) is a compile-time origin fact and stays. #6919 c3-c4 plan retained write transitions and say replay "never re-executes"; option C is that plan.

Safe Core has lock-free `Atomic<T>` cells with sequentially consistent operations (D-ATOMIC-WIDTH1=A, Docs/Spec/syntax-decisions.md:4773-4782). Their order is not fixed by channels or locks, so A logs each atomic operation as a sync event.

Code at dev 3c593a7f16: Compiler/JetCLI/Source/CLI/Debug.jet:27-28 returns not-ported for --record and --replay. Stop polls deliver deadlines (Compiler/JetIR/Source/IR.jet:184-194), so the recording keys them by source position and count. That works across tiers only where the recording tier's poll sites are also poll sites at the replay tier. The cited review Docs/Audits/2026-11-18-best-debugger-profiler.md (axis D2) is not on dev.

options.name: Record inputs and order; step back by line; ask why
options.detail: The recording logs every capability result and the order tasks met at channels, locks, `Shared` values, joins and `Atomic` cells. Any safe program records, threads included. Replay runs on real threads at any optimization level. In replay the debugger adds reverse-step, reverse-next, reverse-finish and reverse-continue, plus `why <expr>`, which names the write that set a value. `jump` stays; `back N` becomes `reverse-next N`.
options.technical: The runtime appends chokepoint results and sync order, including each `Atomic` operation, to the recording. Replay enforces sync order and forks checkpoints every N sync events. Reverse moves re-run from the nearest checkpoint. `why` re-runs the window with write tracking on the value's place. DAP gets stepBack and reverseContinue. A digest per sync event detects divergence from unsafe code, and replay at another tier runs on a stack large enough for that tier's frames.

$ jet debug --replay=r1
(Jet) break cart.jet:88
(Jet) continue
(Jet) why total
total = -4, set at cart.jet:71 in apply_discount (task 3)
  before: 12
(Jet) reverse-next
71 |     total -= discount        <- here

options.detail: Replay jumps between recorded events and `back N` counts events. Programs the recorder refuses, including those with threads, stay refused until Epoch 6. There is no `why`.
options.technical: As D-TIMETRAVEL2=B and D-RUN-RECORD1=A stand. Time is the only safe input recorded.

options.name: Record every write
options.detail: The recording keeps every write to memory, as WinDbg's time travel does. Replay never re-runs the program; it reads the log. Stepping back and `why` are lookups.
options.technical: Every store goes to a per-thread log with its sequence number. This is #6919's plan of retained write transitions.

comparisons.note: rr records system calls and timing on one core, then replays; gdb steps backward. Threads run one at a time while recording.

recommendation.why: Safe Jet has no data races, so inputs plus the order of syncs and atomic operations fix a run. That makes recording cheap, threads included, and lets replay run where every value is visible. Stepping backward by line and asking why answer the question users actually ask.

A deep recursion that fits at -O2 replays at -O0 without overflowing. `--filter Debug/replay_reverse_` covers the four reverse moves over the console and DAP. `--filter Debug/replay_why_` names the last write and shows an optimized-away local.

decisions.title: How `jet perf compare` takes repeated captures
decisions.situation: `jet perf compare base.jettrace head.jettrace` compares two single captures, and only as whole-run totals. #6841 c56 makes it report each function's and each line's change, with a verdict on whether the change is real. A verdict needs several captures of each side, because one capture can't tell a real change from run-to-run noise. You decide how a user hands compare several captures of each side. We recommend that each side may be a folder of traces: `jet perf compare base/ head/`.
decisions.gist: How does a user give `jet perf compare` several captures of each side?
decisions.lesson: The same program, run twice, takes a different number of samples on each line. On the PerfView fixture's hot loop, five runs took 581 to 598 samples, a 3% spread. With one capture a side, a smaller change can't be told apart from that noise, so compare shows the deltas and refuses a verdict. With several captures a side, it tests whether the two groups differ by more than each varies inside itself. It then says `faster`, `slower` or `no significant change`.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: run each build a few times, then compare. Under A, run `jet perf run prog.jet --out base/1.jettrace` four times, changing the number. Do the same into `head/`, then run `jet perf compare base/ head/`. Under B, make the same runs, then name each with `--base` or `--head`. Under C, run `jet perf run prog.jet --repeat=4 --out base.jettrace` once per side. Then run `jet perf compare base.jettrace head.jettrace`.

Expert path: every option uses the same verdict test. The captures must share a toolchain and hardware fingerprint, or pass `--override-identity`. `--json` gives each function's and line's per-capture samples, means, delta and verdict. The two-trace form `jet perf compare base.jettrace head.jettrace` keeps working under every option. It prints the per-line deltas with `verdict: none (one capture each; capture each side at least 4 times)`.
decisions.story:
Mia speeds up a parser's tokenizer and wants to know if `next_token` really got faster. Under A, she runs `jet perf run parse.jet --out before/$i.jettrace` in a loop of five on main. She runs the same loop into `after/` on her branch. Then `jet perf compare before/ after/` prints `parse.jet:88 next_token 412 -> 301 samples (-27%) faster (p=0.008)`.

Under B, she types ten paths, or a shell glob, after the repeated flags. Under C, she runs `jet perf run parse.jet --repeat=5` on each branch and compares the two files.
decisions.inWild:
# Go benchstat: each side is one file holding repeated runs (go test -count=10).
$ benchstat old.txt new.txt
        │   old.txt   │              new.txt               │
        │   sec/op    │   sec/op     vs base               │
Parse-8   412.0µ ± 2%   301.0µ ± 1%  -26.94% (p=0.000 n=10)
decisions.detail:
Code read on dev be8e6a353e. `jet_cli_perf_compare` (Compiler/JetCLI/Source/CLI/Perf/Command.jet:284) takes exactly two paths. It prints whole-run `wall`, `cpu` and `alloc` deltas, the receipt deltas and a #241 budget line, and always exits 0. The audit's F14 (Docs/Audits/2026-11-14-debugging-profiling-review.md) is that gap. A trace's per-line CPU samples are its `cpu` profile rows, the per-line table of `jet perf view`.

The verdict is the same under every option. Per function and per line, it is a two-sided Mann-Whitney U test over the per-capture sample counts, at p < 0.05, as benchstat does. It assumes nothing about the noise's shape, and one outlier capture moves it little. It can reach p < 0.05 only from 4 captures a side: 4 against 4 gives a smallest p of 0.029.

So with fewer than 4 a side, compare shows the deltas and refuses the verdict, naming the count. A file on one side and a folder of 4 on the other is 1 against 4, so it gets no verdict either. The 0.029 figure assumes no ties. Tied counts are ranked as halves and judged against the no-tie distribution, which only makes p larger. A line that a capture never sampled counts 0 samples in that capture.

Many lines means many tests. At p < 0.05, about 1 in 20 unchanged lines would be flagged by chance. So compare judges only rows holding at least 1% of a side's samples. Colder rows show their deltas with `too few samples to judge`. Within each table it then applies Benjamini-Hochberg at a 5% false discovery rate.

A row is called faster or slower only if it passes that. At 4 a side the smallest p is 0.029, so a verdict holds when the changed row is the only judged row, or when most judged rows changed. A change confined to one of m judged rows needs more than 4 captures a side once m ≥ 2.

options.name: A side may be a folder of traces
options.detail: Each of compare's two arguments is a `.jettrace` or a folder; a folder stands for every `.jettrace` directly in it. `jet perf compare base/ head/`. Two single traces work as today.
options.technical: No new flag. `jet perf run --out base/3.jettrace` already makes the folder's files. A folder with no trace is refused, naming it. A file on one side and a folder on the other is one capture against the folder's: compare shows the deltas and refuses the verdict, as with one capture each.
options.code:
for i in 1 2 3 4; do jet perf run parse.jet --out before/$i.jettrace; done
# switch branches
for i in 1 2 3 4; do jet perf run parse.jet --out after/$i.jettrace; done
jet perf compare before/ after/

options.name: Repeat a flag per capture
options.detail: `--base <trace>` and `--head <trace>` each name one capture and repeat. The two-path form stays as shorthand for one of each.
options.technical: Two new repeatable flags on compare. Every capture is named on the line, so no stray file joins a side.
options.code:
jet perf compare --base before/1.jettrace --base before/2.jettrace --base before/3.jettrace --base before/4.jettrace \
  --head after/1.jettrace --head after/2.jettrace --head after/3.jettrace --head after/4.jettrace

options.name: One trace holds repeated runs
options.detail: `jet perf run --repeat=N` runs the program N times and writes one trace holding N captures; compare takes two such traces.
options.technical: A new run flag and a trace schema change: the profile carries one row set per run. Each side is one self-contained file, easy to share, with no stray capture to join it.
options.code:
jet perf run parse.jet --repeat=4 --out before.jettrace
# switch branches
jet perf run parse.jet --repeat=4 --out after.jettrace
jet perf compare before.jettrace after.jettrace

comparisons.note: One file per side holds repeated runs from `go test -count=N`; a Mann-Whitney U test, and `~` for no significant change. This is C's shape.
comparisons.code:
go test -bench=Parse -count=10 > old.txt
benchstat old.txt new.txt

comparisons.note: Each benchmark samples itself many times and saves a named baseline; the next run reports `Performance has improved` with a p-value. The repeats live inside one run, as in C.
comparisons.code:
cargo bench -- --save-baseline before
cargo bench -- --baseline before

comparisons.note: Runs each command N times and prints mean ± σ and the ratio; no significance test.
`-diff_base` subtracts one profile from another, with no repeats and no verdict.

recommendation.why: A adds no flag and no schema: the files `jet perf run --out` already writes are the captures, a folder is the natural group, and the two-trace form is unchanged. Like B, it lets the two sides' captures be interleaved in time, which cancels slow machine drift. C can't interleave, since each side's runs come back to back.
gains: No new flag or trace field.
Base and head runs can be interleaved, as under B, so drift cancels.
Adding a capture is one more file in the folder.

losses.loss: The user writes the loop that makes the captures.
losses.mitigation: The refusal names the command to run, with `--out <folder>/<n>.jettrace`; the docs give the loop.

losses.loss: A stale trace left in the folder joins the group.
losses.mitigation: Compare lists each side's traces by name and refuses a group whose toolchain or hardware fingerprints differ.

whyNot.reason: Every capture is named on the line, so no stray file can join a side. But ten captures means ten flags, and a glob after a repeated flag works only by accident of shell quoting. A gets the same interleaving with a short command, and lists each side's traces so a stray one shows.

One self-contained file per side is easy to share and can't pick up a stray capture. But it needs a new flag and a trace schema change, and each side's runs come back to back, so drift between the sides is not cancelled.

recommendation.tradeoff: A shell loop and a folder that could hold a stray trace, for no new flag, no schema change and a short command.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Under A, the case Perf/compare_per_line_with_significance captures the PerfView fixture 4 times at 20M rounds into `base/`. It captures it 4 times at 40M rounds into `head/`. Then `jet perf compare base/ head/` names `main.jet:11 spin_hot_loop` slower with BH-adjusted p < 0.05 (within the 5% FDR). `jet perf compare base/1.jettrace head/1.jettrace` prints the same line's delta and `verdict: none (one capture each; capture each side at least 4 times)`.

Under B, the same case uses `--base` and `--head` flags. Under C, it uses `--repeat=4`.

Evidence labels: the PerfView spread (581 to 598 samples on main.jet:11) is from five `jet perf run`s on this machine with the gate-p298 jet. No option's compare is built.
