decisions.title: What the debugger does with calls the compiler works out ahead
decisions.situation: Jet works out some values while it compiles. When a program writes `first: count_up(1000000)` and count_up only computes, the compiler runs count_up during the build and the program just holds the answer. That is fine for `jet run`, but it surprises the debugger. Today `jet debug` accepts `break count_up`, says "Breakpoint set", and the program finishes without ever stopping, because count_up never runs. A logpoint inside it is accepted and logs nothing. Beginners feel this most: their first breakpoint on a small test function silently does nothing. You decide what `jet debug` does about calls the build computes ahead. We recommend that the program `jet debug` builds keeps those calls. An image built elsewhere computed the call and dropped the function. With debug info, it then refuses such a breakpoint and says why, instead of answering "No function".
decisions.gist: When the compiler works out a call ahead of time, what should a breakpoint inside that function do?
decisions.lesson: Jet runs a pure call with fixed arguments while compiling and keeps only its answer. The program then never runs that function. A breakpoint or logpoint in it is set but never fires. The choice is whether debug builds keep those calls, or the debugger explains why it cannot stop there.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: write the program, run `jet debug prog.jet`, type `break count_up` and `c`. Under A it stops in count_up with n = 1000000, as the code reads. Under B the break is refused, naming the line that was computed and the fix. Under C the break is set with a note, and the program finishes without stopping.

Expert path: an expert who wants the exact release program builds it with `jet build -O2`. They open the image with `jet debug <image>` or `--attach`. That image computed the call ahead and dropped count_up, so today `break count_up` answers "No function `count_up`". Under A and B the break is refused with E2239 (Jet.DebugNeverCalled), naming the computed line and the fix.

That needs the image's debug info. Built with `--debug-info=false`, or with its side `.debug` file gone, it answers "No function" as today. Putting `#Runtime(.NoEager)` on a function keeps its calls in every build, today and under every option.
decisions.story: Sam is learning Jet and writes count_up with a test call, `first: count_up(1000000)`. He wants to watch the loop, so he runs `jet debug prog.jet` and types `break count_up`. Today the debugger answers "Breakpoint set", and the program prints its total and ends. Sam decides the debugger is broken.
decisions.detail:
Code read on dev 3e8d443247 and checked with the gate-p310 jet. JetSema computes an immutable local `name: value` whose initializer calls only pure code while compiling, and the program holds the value (Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Comptime/LocalValues.jet). The language promises this never changes what a program prints (Docs/Spec/Reference/metaprogramming.md). It is a checked fact, so -O0, -O1 and -O2 compute the same locals. `#Runtime(.NoEager)` on a function, method or block turns it off there.

`jet debug prog.jet` builds with `jet build -O0 --dead-code=keep` (JetDebug Native.jet native_debug_build_argv). So count_up stays in the image with no caller. With the program above, on gate-p310: `break count_up` and `break prog.jet:5` answer "Breakpoint set" and never stop. `log prog.jet:5 "s{step}"` says it runs in the program and logs nothing. A break after line 11 shows `first = 2999997`, and `watch first` works. The same program with `#Runtime(.NoEager)` on run stops in count_up with n = 1000000.

The placed-logpoint case met this: its loop never ran until its count came from the program's arguments.

Images built elsewhere, re-checked on the gate-p392 jet (dev f768b6597e). `jet build -O0 prog.jet` (and `-O2`) drops count_up, because nothing calls it at run time. `jet debug .jet/build/prog` then answers "No function `count_up`" to `break count_up`. It answers "No code on prog.jet:5" to `break prog.jet:5`.

A breakpoint that is set and never stops arises only where dead code is kept. That is jet debug's own `-O0 --dead-code=keep` build (Native.jet native_debug_build_argv). `jet debug --replay=NAME prog.jet` builds through that same build (jet_cli_debug_launch). A replay of a .jet file is a jet debug build. A replayed image is treated like any built image.

options.name: Debug builds keep the calls
options.detail:
The program `jet debug` builds computes no local while compiling in the workspace's own packages. It is as if every function there carried `#Runtime(.NoEager)`. So every call in a local the user wrote runs, and its breakpoints, logpoints and watches work.

A function called only from a constant, `#run` or `@` still never runs; its breakpoint is refused with E2239. There E2239 says that code always runs while compiling, and its fix moves the call into a local. For an image built elsewhere, the fix also adds `#Runtime(.NoEager)`. Constants, `#run`, `@` and Core keep computing while compiling. `jet run` and `jet build` are unchanged.

An image `jet debug` did not build (`jet debug <image>` or `--attach`) still computed the call. Unless it kept dead code, it dropped the function. So today `break count_up` answers "No function `count_up`". Under A it is refused with B's E2239 instead, naming the computed line and the fix. A replay of a .jet file is a jet debug build, so it runs the calls. A replayed image is treated like any built image.
options.technical:
`jet debug` builds in a separate `jet build` child (native_debug_build_argv). The policy reaches it as one new build-option row, `eager`. Its values are `on`, the default, and `off`: the workspace's own packages compute no local while compiling, the policy `#Runtime(.NoEager)` sets. Jet debug passes `--eager=off` beside the `--dead-code=keep` it already passes.

The row in the build-option table (Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/Registry/BuildOptions.jet) is a Choice. Its `stock_build` and `stock_run` are both `on`. It has `shapes_image: true`, which names the value in the options' cache key and compile identity (build_options_key).

By the table's one naming rule the row brings four spellings. They are the profile field `eager: off`, the flag `--eager=off`, the method `b.eager(.Off)` and the pin `b.pin(.eager, .Off)`. It adds no syntax. An expert can also use it for a built image that runs every call.

The image's debug info records each workspace function the build computed ahead and never calls at run time. It covers functions kept with dead code and functions dropped. Each record holds the name, the declaration line and the line that computed it. The record costs debug-info bytes only, which a release build keeps in its side debug file.

The debugger reads that record for E2239, and DAP returns the breakpoint unverified with the same message. An image with no record answers "No function `count_up`" as today. That is an image built with `--debug-info=false`, or a split image whose side `.debug` file is gone.

The image's debug info records its `eager` value, as it records its level. `print` and `why` read it there, and native_debug_build_argv takes it as an argument. So `why` recovery builds of a built image keep that image's policy, and recovered frames match it. JetCanvas's debug session builds through the same function and gets `--eager=off` too.

The `print EXPR` evaluation compile builds with its own arguments (jet_cli_debug_eval_argv in Compiler/JetCLI/Source/CLI/DebugCompile.jet). It passes the image's `eager` value too. So an expression computes ahead exactly what the image computes ahead. Output is unchanged on every tier, so I9 holds; only when the work runs differs.
options.code:
// jet debug prog.jet builds with the call kept:
(Jet) break count_up
Breakpoint set  count_up
(Jet) c
Breakpoint hit  prog.jet:2  in count_up()
Locals:  n = 1000000
// jet run and jet build still compute it ahead.

options.name: Refuse, and say why
options.detail:
Builds stay as they are. A breakpoint, line breakpoint or logpoint in a function the image never runs is refused with a new error, E2239, Jet.DebugNeverCalled. It names the computed line and gives the fix: put `#Runtime(.NoEager)` on the calling function and start the debugger again. When the only call is in a constant, `#run` or `@`, E2239 says that code always runs while compiling. Its fix moves the call into a local and puts `#Runtime(.NoEager)` on that local's function.

In a default build the function is already dropped, so this replaces today's "No function" answer with the reason. In jet debug's own build, which keeps dead code, it replaces a breakpoint that never stops. A function that is also called at run time somewhere is accepted as today. A watch on the computed local works, as it does today.
options.technical: The compiler records in the image's debug info each workspace function with no run-time call, no taken address and no export. It records kept and dropped functions, each with its name, its declaration line and the line that computed it. The console refuses; DAP returns the breakpoint unverified with the message. The same holds for -O1 and -O2 images. An image with no record answers "No function `count_up`" as today: one built with `--debug-info=false`, or a split image whose side `.debug` file is gone.
options.code:
(Jet) break count_up
Error: Jet.DebugNeverCalled: `count_up` never runs in this build.
  Its only call, `first: count_up(1000000)` at
  prog.jet:11, was computed while compiling.
  Fix: put #Runtime(.NoEager) on `run`, then
  run `jet debug prog.jet` again.

options.name: Accept, with a note
options.detail: Builds stay as they are. The breakpoint or logpoint is set, and a note says this build never runs the function, names the computed line and gives the same fix. The session goes on, and the program finishes without stopping there. A default `jet build` drops the function, so there is no code to set a breakpoint on. There the note replaces today's "No function" answer, and no break is set.
options.technical: The same image record as B, read as a note, not an error. DAP returns the breakpoint unverified with the note. No new error code; the note is plain text.
options.code:
(Jet) break count_up
Breakpoint set  count_up
Note: this build never runs `count_up`: its only
  call (prog.jet:11) was computed while compiling,
  so this breakpoint will not be hit.
(Jet) c
total 2999997

comparisons.note: A call runs while compiling only when code asks with comptime, so a Debug build runs every other call and a debugger stops in it. https://ziglang.org/documentation/master/#comptime
comparisons.code: const ahead = comptime countUp(1000);  // only this is computed ahead

recommendation.why: The program a beginner debugs runs the code they read, so their first breakpoint stops. Output stays the same, and built images that carry debug info explain themselves.
gains: Every breakpoint in a call the program runs stops; the rest say why.
No new syntax or step for a beginner; jet debug passes the option itself.
Built images with debug info refuse with the reason and the fix.

losses.loss: A function that computes a big value ahead runs slower under jet debug.
losses.mitigation: Only the workspace's own locals move to run time; Core, constants and #run still compute ahead.

losses.loss: The debugged program differs from jet build -O0 in when work runs.
losses.mitigation: Output is the same by the language's promise; a built image is still debuggable as it is.

losses.loss: One new build option, `eager`, in four spellings.
losses.mitigation: Jet debug passes it; a beginner never types it.

whyNot.reason: B explains the problem but makes the user edit the code and restart to see what they asked for.
C accepts a breakpoint it knows will never fire, and the note is easy to miss.

recommendation.tradeoff: jet debug builds compute the workspace's locals at run time, so the code the user reads is the code that runs.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Under A: a Debug case uses the placed-logpoint fixture with a literal count. `jet debug prog.jet` with `break count_up` stops with n = 1000000. A logpoint on the loop logs each hit. The same program built with `jet build -O0` and opened with `jet debug <image>` refuses `break count_up` with E2239, naming prog.jet:11. Today that image answers "No function `count_up`" (re-checked on gate-p392). A case also checks that `jet build --eager=off` changes the build cache key.

Under B: both runs refuse with E2239. Under C: `jet debug prog.jet` sets the break with the note and finishes. The `jet build -O0` image answers the note instead of "No function" and sets no break.

Under A and B, the same image built with `--debug-info=false` answers "No function `count_up`". Under A, `print` of an expression calling count_up at the stop computes what the image computes, with `eager` passed to the evaluation compile. Nothing here is built yet.

surface.lesson: Jet runs a pure call with fixed arguments while compiling and keeps only its answer. The function then never runs, so a breakpoint in it is set but never fires. Debug builds could keep such calls, or the debugger could explain itself.

decisions.title: How a program under jet debug reads its input from a file or pipe
decisions.situation: Under the Jet debugger, a program cannot read any input today: its first read finds nothing. The debugger takes its own commands from the same place, called stdin, so a keyboard can be shared one line at a time, and that part is already being built. A file or pipe cannot be shared, because the program reads ahead and would swallow the debugger's commands, and an editor already uses that channel for itself. The vote decides where a user names the program's own input: in a launch flag and editor setting, at the debugger's prompt, or by moving the debugger's commands to a file.
decisions.gist: How should a program under `jet debug` get its input from a file or a pipe, when the debugger reads its own commands from stdin?
decisions.lesson: A program reads its input, called stdin, from a keyboard, a file or a pipe. Under `jet debug`, stdin also carries the debugger's commands. A keyboard can be shared one line at a time, and that part is already being built. A file or pipe cannot be shared, because the program reads ahead and would swallow commands. So the program's input needs its own name. This vote picks where that name is written.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path. On a terminal, `jet debug echo.jet` needs nothing new: the program reads what you type while it runs, and the prompt reads what you type while it is stopped. With a file, the beginner writes `jet debug echo.jet --stdin=input.txt`. The prompt stays on the keyboard and the program reads the file. A beginner who writes `jet debug echo.jet < input.txt` gets an unknown-command message that names `--stdin=FILE`.

Expert path. An agent pipes the debugger's commands and names the program's input with the flag, as in `printf 'break 5\ncontinue\n' | jet debug echo.jet --stdin=input.txt`. A live producer goes through the shell's process substitution, as in `--stdin=<(producer)`. An editor sets `"stdin": "input.txt"` in the launch settings. A nested session of the compiler itself runs as `jet debug ./jet --stdin=inner.txt -- debug echo.jet`, with the outer commands piped, and `inner.txt` holding the inner session's commands.
decisions.story:
Ana writes a small program that reads lines and prints them. It works with `jet run echo.jet < input.txt`. One line comes out wrong, so she runs `jet debug echo.jet < input.txt`. The debugger answers ``Unknown command `apple` `` for each line of her file. Then the program finishes without printing anything. Her input became debugger commands, and the program saw empty input.

Under option A, the first unknown command tells her to use `--stdin=input.txt`. She runs `jet debug echo.jet --stdin=input.txt`, types `break 5` and `continue`, and `print line` shows `apple`. In her editor she adds `"stdin": "input.txt"` to the launch settings and gets the same run with a click.
decisions.inWild:
gdb shares its terminal with the program by default. For other input it applies shell redirection to its `run` command, as in `run < input.txt`, or points the program at another terminal with `tty`. Its manual says only the program's input is affected; gdb's input still comes from the terminal. Batch runs read commands from a file with `-x` and `-batch`.

lldb names the file when it launches the program: `process launch -i input.txt` (long form `--stdin`), with sibling options for stdout and stderr, and `--tty` for a fresh terminal. The setting `target.input-path` names the file once for every later launch. Batch runs use `lldb -b -s steps.txt`.

Delve redirects at startup with `dlv debug -r stdin:input.txt`, and its `restart` command can change the redirect, as in `restart <input.txt`. The Go extension for VS Code exposes the same thing as the `stdinFrom` launch field. Its manual says the editor captures output but not stdin, and points users who need typed input to the `console` setting.

CodeLLDB has a `stdio` launch list for descriptors 0, 1 and 2, where a string is a file, pipe or terminal path, as in `"stdio": ["input.txt", null, null]`. The Debug Adapter Protocol hands a program a terminal through the `runInTerminal` reverse request.

rr records the program's reads, so `rr record ./echo < input.txt` followed by `rr replay` needs no input file at replay time.

Sources follow, one per line.
gdb: sourceware.org/gdb/current/onlinedocs/gdb.html/Input_002fOutput.html
lldb: lldb.llvm.org/use/map.html, the `process launch` options in lldb/source/Commands/Options.td, and `input-path` in lldb/source/Target/TargetProperties.td
Delve: github.com/go-delve/delve/blob/master/Documentation/usage/dlv_redirect.md and Documentation/cli/README.md, `restart`
vscode-go: github.com/golang/vscode-go/blob/master/docs/debugging.md
CodeLLDB: github.com/vadimcn/codelldb/blob/master/MANUAL.md
DAP: microsoft.github.io/debug-adapter-protocol/specification, RunInTerminal
rr: github.com/rr-debugger/rr/wiki/Usage
decisions.detail:
Code read on master 6f3f982eec. The program starts in `x64_trace_spawn` in Compiler/JetBackend/Source/Image/Loader.jet. Its comment says the program's standard input reads /dev/null, and the helper process duplicates a /dev/null descriptor onto descriptor 0. Output goes to a scratch file that the session relays.

The console loop is `jet_cli_debug_commands` in Compiler/JetCLI/Source/CLI/Debug.jet. It reads one line at a time from the debugger's own stdin and echoes each command when stdin is not a terminal. The end of stdin acts as `continue`.

The program starts before the first prompt. `jet_cli_debug_console` opens the session, which runs to the start of `run`, or to the first `--break` stop. Only then does it read commands.

The console commands are listed in `NATIVE_DEBUG_HELP` in Compiler/JetDebug/Source/Native.jet. They are step, next, continue, finish, the reverse commands, jump, back, events, break, log, watch, why, breaks, delete, frame, up, down, locals, print, backtrace, tasks, fix, help and quit. There is no run, restart or stdin command. An unknown word answers ``Unknown command `word` `` followed by the help line.

The flag registry is Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/Registry/CLICommands.jet. Debug has `--raw-frames`, `--dap`, the repeated `--break`, `--attach`, `--record`, `--replay` and `--deep-checks`; there is no `--stdin` or `--commands`. The nearby `--stdin-path` belongs to `jet fmt -` and only labels diagnostics, so option A's help line must say the program reads that file.

The editor adapter is Compiler/JetCLI/Source/CLI/DebugDap.jet. Its `launch` and `restart` requests read only `stopOnEntry` and `args`. The VS Code extension in Tools/Editors/Vscode declares `program`, `args`, `cwd`, `env`, `stopOnEntry` and `showRawFrames`, and no input field. It starts the adapter in the workspace folder.

The ratified editor decision, D-DBG-DAP1, speaks the protocol over the adapter's stdio and rules out reverse requests. So `runInTerminal` is unavailable, and a file path is the only way to give an editor-launched program a file's or pipe's input.

The ratified D-DBG-AUTH1=B treats every path an editor session opens as a capability. Paths are confined to the workspace or the approved working directory, and anything else gets that decision's E2242 refusal, which is not built yet. Its launch preview lists them. An editor `stdin` path joins that list under every option, so it is shared work, not a loss of one option. The terminal flag is typed by the user and needs no preview.

The terminal-sharing change already being built on this card, which adds no new surface, gives `x64_trace_spawn` an input path that the debugger opens before the fork. It also gives the session an `input_path` that defaults to /dev/null and becomes /dev/stdin when the console's stdin is a terminal. Each start of the program reopens that path. Option A only lets the user set it.

The runtime fills one shared stdin buffer of up to 65536 bytes per read (Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/TerminalInput.jet, `TERM_INPUT_CAPACITY`). That is why a shared pipe would swallow later commands. The console reads its own stdin through the same kind of buffer.

Recording already covers stdin. Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/ProveJournal.jet says a replay answers stdin from the recording. Reverse commands rerun the program only in a replay. So `--replay` must refuse `--stdin`, while `--record` with `--stdin` keeps the file's bytes in the recording.

Edge cases under option A. A missing or unreadable file is refused before the build with E2105, as ``couldn't open `input.txt` for the program's stdin``. A named pipe opens when the program starts, and the session says it is waiting for a writer, as a shell's `<` would.

A path that names the console's own pipe or file, such as /dev/stdin under a pipe, is refused with E2102. The check compares the opened file with the console's stdin. On a terminal the same path just shares the keyboard, which is the default being built. Process substitution works because jet debug opens the path itself, before the helper closes its other descriptors.

A terminal plus a file splits cleanly: the console keeps the keyboard, and the program reads the file and sees no terminal. `--attach` refuses `--stdin` with E2102, because a running process keeps its own stdin. `--dap` refuses the flag with E2102, as it refuses `--break`, and the editor sets the `stdin` launch field instead.

In an editor, a relative path resolves against the launch's `cwd`. The adapter does not read `cwd` yet, a gap D-DBG-DAP1 already owns, so until then that is the workspace folder. `restart` reopens the file from its start; a named pipe or a process substitution gives only what is left. Without the field, an editor-launched program still reads end of input, because the protocol owns the adapter's stdin.

The unknown-command hint has a limit. A redirected file whose lines are all valid commands, such as `n`, `c` or `q`, runs them and prints no hint. The `jet debug` help and the flag's help line still name `--stdin`.

The nested case runs `jet debug ./jet --stdin=inner.txt -- debug echo.jet` with the outer commands piped, where `./jet` is an unoptimized build of the compiler. The pty case uses keyboard sharing at both levels.

options.name: A launch flag and an editor launch field that name the input file
options.detail:
`jet debug echo.jet --stdin=input.txt` starts the program with the file as its stdin. The debugger keeps reading commands from its own stdin, whether that is the keyboard or a pipe of commands. In an editor, the launch settings take `"stdin": "input.txt"` with the same meaning. Without the flag, a keyboard is shared as already planned, and a file or pipe leaves the program with empty input.

A live producer uses the shell's process substitution, `--stdin=<(producer)`, or a named pipe. When the debugger's stdin is not a keyboard, the unknown-command message adds that `--stdin=FILE` gives the program input.
options.technical:
The terminal-sharing change in flight gives `x64_trace_spawn` an input path, opened by jet debug before the fork and duplicated onto descriptor 0, and gives `NativeSession` an `input_path`. Option A sets that path. Because jet debug opens it before the helper closes its other descriptors, /dev/fd paths from process substitution work.

CLICommands.jet gains `--stdin` with a value, scoped to debug. Each start of the program reopens `input_path`, including the adapter's `restart`. DebugDap.jet reads `stdin` in `launch` and `restart` under the D-DBG-AUTH1 path law, and the VS Code package.json declares it.

Refusals: E2105 for a path that cannot be opened. E2102 for a path naming the console's own pipe, and for `--stdin` with `--attach`, `--replay`, a crash dump or `--dap`. For an editor path outside the workspace or approved working directory, D-DBG-AUTH1's E2242, which is not built yet.
options.code:
$ jet debug echo.jet --stdin=input.txt
(Jet) break 5
(Jet) continue
Breakpoint hit  echo.jet:5  in run()
(Jet) print line
line = "apple"

// editor launch settings
"stdin": "input.txt"

options.name: A prompt command that restarts the program with an input file
options.detail:
`stdin input.txt` at the prompt starts the program again from the beginning, reading that file, and keeps the breakpoints. Later restarts keep the file. This is gdb's `run < input.txt` and lldb's `process launch -i input.txt` in the console's own words. A piped transcript starts with that line.

Jet has no prompt before the program starts. The program has already run to the start of `run` with empty input, so the command must restart it.
options.technical:
Adds a restart path to the console in Native.jet next to `command()`, plus an input descriptor on `x64_trace_spawn` as in A. The word `run` is not used, because it is also the entry function's name, and `break run` already means a breakpoint there.

The editor protocol has no prompt, so editors still need a `stdin` launch field. That makes two spellings for one setting.

$ jet debug echo.jet
4 |     loop line in io.stdin().lines() {        <- here
(Jet) stdin input.txt
Restarted, reading input.txt
4 |     loop line in io.stdin().lines() {        <- here
(Jet) continue
got apple

options.name: Debugger commands from a file, so stdin goes to the program
options.detail:
`jet debug echo.jet --commands=steps.txt < input.txt` reads the debugger's commands from steps.txt, and the program inherits the debugger's own stdin. A plain shell pipe then reaches the program: `producer | jet debug echo.jet --commands=steps.txt`. This follows gdb's `-x`, lldb's `-s` and Delve's `--init`.

When the commands file ends, the program runs to its end, because stdin belongs to the program. Without the flag, today's piped commands keep working.
options.technical:
Adds `--commands` to CLICommands.jet, and `jet_cli_debug_commands` reads lines from that file instead of the terminal. The program inherits descriptor 0 in `x64_trace_spawn`.

Under the editor protocol, the adapter's stdin carries the protocol, so editors still need a separate `stdin` launch field. Debug cases would split between `stdin:` command transcripts and commands-file fixtures. A restart cannot re-read a pipe that the program has already drained.
options.code:
$ jet debug echo.jet --commands=steps.txt < input.txt
(Jet) break 5
(Jet) continue
Breakpoint hit  echo.jet:5  in run()

$ producer | jet debug echo.jet --commands=steps.txt

(lldb) process launch --tty
$ lldb -b -s steps.txt ./echo

One launch list for descriptors 0, 1 and 2; a string is a file, pipe or terminal path, and null keeps the session terminal.
The recording keeps the program's reads, so a replay needs no input. Jet's `--record` and `--replay` already behave this way for stdin.

recommendation.why: An editor-launched program can only get input from a path, because the protocol owns the adapter's stdin and reverse requests are ruled out. A flag on the command line and a field with the same name in the launch settings give the terminal and the editor one answer. The flag leaves today's piped command transcripts untouched, so the existing Debug cases and agent sessions keep working. A file can be reopened on restart, and Delve with the Go editor extension already ship this shape.

decisions.title: When narrowing an Authority to a right it doesn't hold is reported
decisions.situation: An Authority is a value that carries a list of permissions, such as reading the repo folder or writing build output. Calling with on it makes a smaller Authority that keeps one permission the list already covers. Today, asking for a permission it doesn't cover is found only while the program runs. The program then stops with a generic panic that points into the standard library, not at the line that asked. In the example, Authority.workspace() holds only two folder-scoped file rights, so with("FS.Write"), which asks to write anywhere, stops the run. You decide when this mistake is reported and with which exit code. We recommend refusing it before the run whenever the compiler can see both the list and the request, and otherwise stopping at the asking line with the same named report.
decisions.gist: When should Jet report narrowing an Authority to a permission it doesn't hold?
decisions.lesson: An Authority is a list of rights a program hands to a child process or a plugin. authority.with(right) returns a smaller Authority holding just that right, and only when a right in the list covers it. A folder-scoped right, like writing to .jet/build, never covers the bare one, writing anywhere. One function decides coverage, and the compiler and the running program already share it. So whenever the compiler knows both the list and the request, it can give the same answer the run would give.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: Mia writes the example program below. Under A, jet check, jet run and her editor flag the with line before anything runs. The report lists what the authority holds and suggests the scoped right. Under B and C, the program runs until that line, then ends there: with exit 1 under B, and exit 70 under C.

Expert path: Theo builds an Authority from a config file and narrows it to a right named at run time. The compiler can't know either one, so under every option the check happens when the line runs. Under A and C that is a stop at his line with exit 70, like a failed bounds check. Under B it is exit 1, the code an unhandled returned error gets.

Edge cases under A. Generics: rights are not part of the Authority type, so a generic function's Authority parameter is unknown and checked at run time. A generic body is checked once, never per caller. Closures: a lambda that captures a `:` binding sees the same value, so its rights stay known; a lambda's own parameter is unknown. Comptime: a #run Authority is a constant whose rights are known, so a #run narrowing outside them is refused at check time.

Effect rows: with and without have no effects, so no row, callback bound or function value changes the answer. An Authority passed through a function value is simply unknown. A `:=` binding, a struct field, a function result and an if that picks between authorities are unknown too. without never fails. A misspelled right such as FS.Wrte is covered by nothing, so it is refused like any other.
decisions.story: Mia copies an example that hands a build step the workspace authority. She narrows it to FS.Write so the step can write its output. Under A, jet run refuses before building anything: the report points at her with line, lists the two rights the workspace holds, and suggests FS.Write(".jet/build"). Under B, the program does its earlier work, then ends at that line with exit 1. Under C, it does the same work, then stops at that line with exit 70.
decisions.detail:
Code read on dev f2cf0a8324. Sema's narrowing check (Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Calls/Methods.jet:234-261) checks only the argument count and that the right is a String. It records an empty effect row (line 253). The runtime's jet_authority_with (Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/Authority.jet:271-285) keeps the request when a held right covers it. Otherwise authority_narrow_failure (lines 256-269) raises the shared panic.

The row's case was run on the gate compiler. It exits 70 with `Stop: Jet.Panic: panic: Jet.EffectWithoutAuthority: authority cannot narrow to FS.Write outside its held rights`. The report points at <core.prelude>:0, not main.jet. Authority.workspace() holds FS.Read("repo") and FS.Write(".jet/build") (Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/ProcessGrants.jet:3-7 and 37-44). A scoped right never covers the bare one (Docs/Spec/spec.md:2993-2995).

One covers rule answers for the checker and the runtime (spec.md:2988-2991). Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/Policy/EffectScope.jet:139-143 calls the runtime's covers. The runtime's from_rights sorts and dedups the raw text without respelling it (Authority.jet:32-55). The compiler's CanonicalAuthority.from_rights respells (Policy/Authority.jet:256-260). So A's check must compare the raw text, as the runtime does, or the two could disagree.

Precedent: E1003 and E0123 are registered with stage [.Sema, .Runtime] (Compiler/Prelude/Diagnostics.jet:15287-15306 and 2400-2419). A constant is refused at check time, and a run-time value stops with exit 70. See Tests/Cases/FailureTierParity/runtime_e1003_is_a_stop_with_exit_70_on_every_hosted_tier.case and Compiler/JetIR/Source/BuildLazy.jet:2030-2044. Effect rows treat a constant file path the same way (spec.md:2997-3021).

The exit law is spec.md:1897-1904: program-side stops exit 70, and an unhandled entry error exits 1. E0712 is registered today for #FX regions only (Diagnostics.jet:9760-9783, a sema row). It is reported from Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Effects/Checks.jet:4268. Docs/Spec/syntax-decisions.md:4115-4118 gives it the wider meaning: an effect without a backing grant.

The Rust original (tests/authority.rs before commit 845a39cdce) asserted only that the JIT run's stderr held E0712, with no exit code. Its erased-scope test counted one compile-time E0712 in a file that also narrows workspace() to FS.Write twice. That case, erased_authority_scope_does_not_survive_erasure, passes today (run on the gate compiler). Under A it would count three, so its assertion moves to the region report's own text.

Every other narrowing in the repository asks for a right its #FX head holds. About thirty fixtures write authority.with("IO") inside #FX(authority: IO). So A refuses nothing else that checks today. without has no failure path (Authority.jet:287-309).

options.name: Refuse it before the run when the compiler can see it
options.detail: When the compiler knows both the Authority's rights and the requested right, an uncovered right is E0712 at check time. jet check, jet build and jet run refuse with exit 1, and nothing runs. Anything the compiler can't see is checked when the line runs, as today. That run-time stop now names E0712 and the asking line, with exit 70.
options.technical:
Known rights come from Authority.workspace(), Authority.from_rights with a list of constant strings, a named #FX head, and a #run constant. They also come from with or without, with a constant right, applied to a known Authority held in a `:` binding. Sema asks the runtime's covers on the raw text.

E0712's registry row gains stage [.Sema, .Runtime], like E1003. Its meaning widens from #FX regions to any effect or right with no authority behind it. The runtime failure becomes a registered `Stop: Jet.EffectWithoutAuthority` at the caller's line instead of Jet.Panic at <core.prelude>:0.

options.name: Check it at run time and exit 1
options.detail: The compiler adds nothing. When with fails while the program runs, the runtime prints `Error: Jet.EffectWithoutAuthority` at the asking line, runs cleanup and exits 1 instead of 70. The row keeps its exit 1 and becomes a run-time case.
options.technical: The runtime gains a program-side stop that exits 1. The exit law in spec.md, where program-side stops exit 70 and exit 1 means an unhandled entry error, gains an exception for this report. E0712 gains stage .Runtime with moment .Run.

options.name: Check it at run time and stop with exit 70
options.detail: The compiler adds nothing. A failed with stops the program with `Stop: Jet.EffectWithoutAuthority` at the asking line and exit 70, like every other program-side stop. The row's case changes its exit from 1 to 70.
options.technical: Only the runtime report changes: the registered stop replaces Jet.Panic at <core.prelude>:0. E0712 gains stage .Runtime. The case row rewrites its exit line.

comparisons.note: A literal that can't fit its type is a compile error, and a run-time value is checked when it runs. This is A's shape.
comparisons.code:
let a: u8 = 300;           // error: literal out of range for `u8`
let b: u8 = n.try_into()?; // checked at run time

comparisons.note: Duplicating a handle may only keep rights the original has. Asking for more fails when the call runs, as a returned status. This is a run-time check, like B and C.
comparisons.code:
zx_status_t s = zx_handle_duplicate(h, ZX_RIGHT_READ | ZX_RIGHT_WRITE, &out);
// s == ZX_ERR_INVALID_ARGS when h lacks ZX_RIGHT_WRITE

comparisons.note: Permissions are granted with flags and checked when an operation runs. Nothing is checked before the run, as in B and C.
comparisons.code:
// deno run --allow-write=.jet/build main.ts
await Deno.writeTextFile("/etc/x", "y"); // throws when the run lacks write access there

recommendation.why: Jet already refuses constants it can see and checks the rest at run time: an out-of-range number, a constant loop step, and a constant file path outside an effect row. A applies that rule here. The mistake is found before anything runs, at the line that made it. Its run-time half is C, so A gives up nothing C has.
gains: A wrong request the compiler can see never reaches a run.
Every report, at either moment, names E0712 and the asking line instead of the standard library.
Exit codes keep one meaning each: 1 for refused before the run, 70 for a stop.

losses.loss: The same mistake is reported at two moments: at check time when the compiler can see it, and at run time otherwise.
losses.mitigation: Both reports share one name, one text and the asking line, and jet explain describes both, as it does for out-of-range numbers.

losses.loss: A narrowing in code that never runs is still refused.
losses.mitigation: Every check-time report works this way. The fix is one edit, and #Off already removes code that should not be checked.

losses.loss: One passing case, erased_authority_scope_does_not_survive_erasure, would count three E0712 reports instead of one.
losses.mitigation: Its assertion moves to the region report's own text, which is what the case is about. No other check in the repository changes.

whyNot.reason: It finds the mistake only after the program has done its earlier work. It also gives exit 1 a second meaning: a tool reading exit 1 could no longer tell a mid-run stop from an error the entry returned.
It keeps the exit law, but it waits for the run even when the compiler can see the mistake, and the line may sit in a branch that rarely runs. A's run-time half is exactly C.

recommendation.tradeoff: A second report moment for one rule, in exchange for catching every visible wrong request before the program runs.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Under A, Tests/Cases/Authority/authority_with_outside_held_rights_is_e0712.case passes as written: exit 1 with Jet.EffectWithoutAuthority, before the run. A new case narrows a parameter's Authority to a right named at run time and expects `Stop: Jet.EffectWithoutAuthority` at the caller's line with exit 70. erased_authority_scope_does_not_survive_erasure counts the region report's text.

Under B, the same row passes with the run-time report and exit 1. Under C, the row's exit becomes 70.

Evidence labels: today's stop (exit 70, pointing at <core.prelude>:0) and the passing erased-scope case were observed by running those cases on the gate compiler at f2cf0a8324. No option is built.

surface.gist: When should Jet report narrowing an Authority to a permission it doesn't hold?
surface.lesson: An Authority is a list of permissions you can hand to a child process. with(right) makes a smaller one, and works only when the list already covers that right. Today a wrong request is found only while the program runs. Its report then points into the standard library, not at your line.

options.name: Before the run, when visible
options.gist: Refuse it at check time when the compiler sees both sides; otherwise stop at the line.
gains: Found before anything runs, at the asking line.
Same rule Jet uses for constant numbers and file paths.
losses: Two report moments for one rule.

options.name: At run time, exit 1
options.gist: The program runs until that line, then ends with an error report and exit 1.
gains: The compiler doesn't change.
losses: Found only when the line runs.
Exit 1 would mean two different things.

options.name: At run time, exit 70
options.gist: The program runs until that line, then stops with a named report and exit 70.
gains: Exit codes keep their meaning.
Smallest change: one runtime report.
losses: Found only when the line runs.

Every report names the asking line.

losses.mitigation: Both share one name, one text and the asking line, as out-of-range numbers do.

It waits for the run even when the compiler can see the mistake.

recommendation.tradeoff: A second report moment, for catching every visible wrong request before the run.

current.note: Today the run stops with a generic panic and exit 70, and the report points into the standard library.

wild.note: A literal that can't fit is a compile error; a run-time value is checked when it runs.
wild.code:

designAway.loss: A reports one mistake at two moments.
attempts: Check only at run time (C): rejected, because it gives up the check-time catch.
Refuse every narrowing the compiler can't see: rejected, because a right from a parameter or a config file is legitimate and can't be known.
Use one name, one text and the asking line at both moments, as E1003 does: kept.
designAway.result: The two moments read as one rule; only the time it is found differs.

designAway.loss: A refuses a wrong narrowing in code that never runs.
attempts: Skip code the compiler proves unreachable: rejected, because no other check-time report does, and #Off already removes code that should not be checked.
designAway.result: Negligible: the fix is one edit, and the code was wrong.

designAway.loss: B gives exit 1 a second meaning.
attempts: Make with return `Authority AuthorityError!`, so an unhandled failure exits 1 under the existing law: rejected, because every existing call (about thirty in the repository) would need ? or ?? for a failure that can't happen.
designAway.result: Not removable under B; a reason to prefer A.

decisions.title: A live timeline: watch a running program's work as it happens
decisions.situation: A timeline is the picture a profiler draws of what a program did over time: which work ran, how long it took, and what it waited on. Today Jet draws it only after a recording ends, in jet perf view or in Canvas's Profile view. A game that stutters every few seconds must be recorded, stopped and reopened before you can see why. Tracy, the best-known game profiler, draws its timeline while the game runs. You decide how Jet's timeline becomes live, under D-PERF-ZONES1's rule that zones stay idle until a profiler attaches. We recommend that jet perf attach --follow and Canvas's Live switch be an attach that stays open, reading each event from memory the program shares with its owner.
decisions.gist: Should Jet's timeline draw a running program's work as it happens, through an attach that stays open?
decisions.lesson: An observed program is one started with jet run --observe. It keeps a flight ring: a fixed-size buffer of its latest events. The events are CPU samples, task waits and wakes, and file and network transfers. Today each event is one write call, and a helper thread saves the buffer to a private file every 100 ms. Zones are named, timed pieces of work marked with perf.zone. They cost 1.8 ns while idle and 26 ns once jet perf run or attach turns them on.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: run jet dev --canvas live.jet, open the Profile view and press Live. Canvas starts the program under the profiler, as jet perf run does, so zones are on from its first instruction. The lanes scroll as it runs: zones, frames, waits, I/O and the hottest lines. Press Stop and the run so far stays open as an ordinary trace you can zoom.

In a terminal, start jet run --observe live.jet, then run jet perf attach --follow in another. With one observed program of yours running, no process id or source path is needed. The follower first shows what the flight ring holds: samples, waits and I/O from before it attached. Zones start when it attaches, because D-PERF-ZONES1 keeps them idle until then.

Expert path: jet perf attach PID --follow --out run.jettrace follows one process by its id. A follow is today's attach whose window stays open until Ctrl-C or the program's end. While it stands, zones are on and samples run at 8 kHz, as an attach with --zones= does today. When the last attach leaves, zones go idle again at 1.8 ns a site.

In a terminal the follower redraws the last 5 seconds as events arrive. Piped, it prints one line per event on stdout, as jet perf view's timeline does. On stop it writes the followed window as a .jettrace, prints its path on stderr and exits 0. Its memory stays bounded: it saves records as it reads them, and its copy holds at most 256 MiB.

To watch a program on another machine, run ssh devbox jet perf attach 48213 --follow --stream | jet perf view -. The far side saves what it reads to its own trace and sends from there, so a slow link delays the view but loses nothing. The near side checks every length in the stream, as it does a local file, and draws it with the same reader. Nothing in the program listens on a network; ssh does the login.

Canvas's profile request takes pid or live in place of trace, plus an optional host, and answers the same lanes with the program's end and losses. For a host, Canvas runs ssh itself, and refuses a host name that starts with a dash or holds a space, so a request can't add ssh options.

Refusals name their diagnostic. A process that publishes no events, or is not yours, gets Jet.AttachTargetNotObserved and exits 1, with the jet run --observe command that fixes it. No observed program of yours, or several and no id, gets Jet.AttachWhichProcess and exits 2; it lists each pid with its source. --follow beside --zones= or --lens=alloc gets the conflicting-flags refusal, exit 2, because those are one-time captures.

A follow costs the program what an attach with --zones= costs today: zones on, samples at 8 kHz, and its buffers. A point attach without --zones= still turns nothing on. Two followers, or a follower and a point attach, share one window, so none turns zones off under another. Up to 64 MiB behind, nothing is lost unless a thread tops 870,000 zones a second; beyond, gaps are counted. A program killed while followed keeps every event its buffers held, and the follower says it ended without an exit.

A program paused in jet debug draws nothing new until it resumes. A build whose zones are stripped shows a zones lane that says so.

On the web tier, a jet dev page sends each span to the dev server as one beacon. The dev server writes them to its owner-only relay file every 40 ms. Following the dev server's pid, or pressing Live on a web entry, reads that file as it fills, so web spans show about 40 ms after they end. The relay keeps its newest 4096 rows instead of stopping there. Rows a watcher missed, and beacons the dev server's full queue refused, show as counted gaps.
decisions.story: Mia's game hitches about every three seconds. She opens Canvas, presses Live in the Profile view and keeps playing. On the next hitch she sees a load_level zone 40 ms long, beside a file read the frame waited on. She presses Stop and zooms into that frame, which is still there as a trace. The game she ships keeps its zones idle until someone attaches.
decisions.detail:
Code read on dev e2069b5709, and probed on 2026-11-20 with a compiler built from it. jet perf attach is a point capture (Compiler/JetCLI/Source/CLI/Perf/Session.jet:341). It copies the published ring <home>/jet-flight-<pid>.samples and the program's 53 MB image on every attach (jet_cli_perf_attach_flight, line 569). Home is $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/jet, else jet-<uid> in the temp directory, owner-only, or Jet.PerfDirectoryNotPrivate (line 692).

Without XDG_RUNTIME_DIR, as in many ssh, cron and container sessions, home is in the temporary directory, which may be on disk. Where logind makes XDG_RUNTIME_DIR, it is a memory file system capped at 10% of RAM by default. A killed program's files are removed by the next jet perf run or attach (jet_cli_perf_sweep, line 744).

Jet.AttachTargetNotObserved exits 1 and Jet.AttachWhichProcess exits 2 (lines 825 and 832). A conflicting flag gets the CLI's conflicting-flags refusal, exit 2, today named Jet.UnknownFlag (Docs/Spec/observability.md:765-771); its final name lands separately. Each renders by its name, with no error number (Tests/Cases/Perf/attach_names_each_refusal.case).

Each wait, wake, spawn and I/O record allocates, walks up to 32 frames, sends one datagram to a nonblocking socket, and frees. See perf_samples_wait (Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/PerfSamples.jet:2891) and perf_samples_io (line 3033). A socket's wait also asks the kernel for both its addresses (perf_samples_sockaddr, line 2934). Each sample is one write too (perf_samples_put_one, line 1215), and a refused send is counted lost (perf_samples_send, line 1238).

A ping-pong probe ran 100,000 channel turns, five runs each way. Observed, it made about 400,000 write calls, counted from /proc/self/io: one per wait and wake. Observing cost 0.34 µs a record at best-versus-best (576 ms against 710 ms), and 0.58 µs at the medians.

The observation writer turns every 100 ms (Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/ObserveLive.jet:596). Each turn, perf_flight_publish (PerfSamples.jet:4887) drains the socket into the 256 KiB ring and writes it into the owner-only file. A full ring keeps its newest half (perf_flight_keep, line 4754). At exit, perf_flight_end (line 5077) drains once more, writes the ended tally and removes the files. A killed run loses what the socket still held, up to one 100 ms turn.

A zone closes with two time-stamp reads and plain stores into a 64 KiB ring per thread, with no lock (perf_zone_ring_put, line 1870). The record copies the zone's name, so a short name makes it 40 bytes. Fibers borrow their carrier's ring before the switch (perf_zone_ring_lend, line 1921; Fiber.jet:256). Each publication drains the rings into a spans file bounded at 16 MiB (PERF_SPANS_FILE_BYTES, line 2075).

With --zones=WINDOW, attach leaves <ring>.zones, waits the window, removes it, and copies <ring>.spans 250 ms later (Session.jet:672). Jet emits only x86-64 code at e2069b5709, where sync_store is a plain store that x86's ordering makes a release store (JetBackend OS/Linux.jet:411).

Probe p2 ran zones.jet at -O2, 2,000,000 calls, best of seven. A plain call took 6.60 ns and one with an idle zone site 8.38 ns, so an idle site costs 1.8 ns. Under jet perf run, a call with its zone recorded took 32.48 ns. That is 25.88 ns over the plain call; the redesign reported 25.76 ns.

This review reran p2 the same day at load 16 to 20. Under jet perf run a plain call took 6.95 ns and a zoned one 33.66 ns, 26.7 ns a zone.

The 2026-11-19 review measured 59.25 ns before the per-thread rings. Tracy's manual measures 37.7 ms more for 16,777,216 zones on 12 parallel threads, which it states as 2.25 ns a zone. If all 12 threads ran at once, that is about 27 ns of each thread's time. Tracy's zone stores a pointer to a static source location; Jet's copies the name.

The sampler's and counters' handlers are one function, installed with an empty signal mask (PerfSamples.jet:508 and 3212). So a counter's signal can interrupt a sample's record today; each handler claims its own record buffer to cope (perf_samples_claim). The timer's signal comes from a POSIX timer, whose missed expiries the kernel counts as overruns (perf_samples_periods, line 4438). A crash dump's capture signal shares the handler but writes only the dump's page (perf_flight_capture, line 5426).

In the 8 kHz probe, a sample's kernel delivery took 2479 ns and its handler about 911 ns. The flight recorder samples each thread 100 times a second (PERF_FLIGHT_INTERVAL_US, line 4467). Attach uses no ptrace; it reads files, so kernel.yama.ptrace_scope does not limit it. Like today's attach, a follow needs the same user, not a debugger's ptrace permission. A inherits that and does not widen it; matching D-PERF-ZONES1's debugger permission is a separate defect.

Canvas's profile request (Docs/Spec/Reference/canvas-protocol.md:375-402) draws one finished .jettrace, or profiles the entry with jet perf run. Its lanes are spans, zones, waits and io, reduced to the width shown.

A jet dev page sends each span as one beacon (Compiler/JetDevServer/Source/WebHost04.jet:169). The dev server queues at most 256 and answers the rest 503, uncounted (WebHost03.jet:106). Its clock writes the queue to the relay every 40 ms (LIVE_RELOAD_POLL_MS). The relay is an owner-only file in the temporary directory, which stops at 4096 rows after one marker (BrowserTrace.jet:13).

This ballot is the 2026-11-19 review's gap G37, owned by #6841. D-OBSERVE-LIVE1=A made live attach opt-in with --observe, D-OBSERVE-FLIGHT1=B made the flight ring, and D-DBG-UI1=A made Canvas the one profile window.

D-PERF-ZONES1=A keeps zones idle until jet perf run or attach turns them on, in every build that keeps them, shipped ones included. Every option here keeps that rule unchanged: a follow is an attach, so zones are on only while it stands. #Profiled sites stay idle at 1.8 ns in every unwatched run, and D-OBSERVE-FLIGHT1=B's observed runs in production are unchanged until someone attaches.

Today's attach request, rechecked on dev ba5711569a: attach leaves <ring>.zones and renews it every 250 ms. A request not renewed within 1 s is removed as one a dead attach left (perf_flight_zones, PerfSamples.jet:6301; PERF_FLIGHT_LEASE_NS, line 5712). The writer's 100 ms turn sees it, turns zones on and opens the zones window.

In that window each thread samples at 8 kHz, as under jet perf run (perf_flight_window_open, line 5723). A thread's zone ring is made on its first zone, so an unwatched run holds none (perf_zone_ring, line 3101). A point attach removes the one request file as its window ends, so a second holder's zones would go off with it.

Sources for the comparisons: Tracy's manual, sections Performance impact and On-demand profiling (github.com/wolfpld/tracy, manual/tracy.tex). Superluminal's documentation on Start analyzing (superluminal.eu/docs). Instruments Help on deferred mode (help.apple.com/instruments). Go's runtime/trace FlightRecorder (pkg.go.dev/runtime/trace). perf top's manual page.

options.name: Follow: an attach that stays open, read from shared memory
options.detail: jet perf attach --follow and Canvas's Live switch are today's attach with a window that stays open until they stop. While it stands, zones are on and samples run at 8 kHz, as an attach with --zones= does today. Each thread writes its events straight into memory it shares with its owner, and the follower reads them as they fill, here or over ssh. When the last attach leaves, the program is again exactly an unwatched observed run. Stopping writes the window as an ordinary .jettrace.
options.technical:
Turning on. <ring>.zones stays the one trigger, and an unwatched turn makes today's one lstat of that fixed name. Each follow, and each point attach with --zones=, also leaves its own lease, <ring>.zones.<pid>, written before the trigger. It renews both every 250 ms under today's 1 s lease. A point attach without --zones= leaves neither, as today.

Only while the trigger stands does the 100 ms turn list the holders' leases. Ending, an attach removes only its own lease. The turn removes the trigger once no lease stands, and zones go idle. So no attach turns zones off under another. One arriving as the last leaves recreates the trigger at its next renewal, within 250 ms.

While a window is open, the program keeps one owner-only live file, made as the window opens and removed as it closes. Its header holds the run's start time, the slot count, two clock pairs and the run's end. A slot holds three buffers, 384 KiB in all: 256 KiB for zones, frames, plots and log spans, 64 KiB for waits, wakes, spawns and I/O, 64 KiB for samples.

Each thread claims a slot at its first record in the window, in its own context, never in a signal handler. The claim reserves the slot's pages with fallocate, so no later store can fault on a full file system. A thread whose claim fails keeps today's path for the window and is counted in the header. Until its claim, a thread's records also take today's path.

As the window closes, each thread drops its slot at its next record, and the file's pages are freed once its readers close it. An unwatched observed run claims no slot and keeps today's datagram socket, flight ring and 100 ms publication, which point attach and crash dumps read.

The file lives on a memory file system, so no store waits on disk writeback. That is the private directory when it is one, else jet-<uid> under /dev/shm, made and checked the same way. Where neither exists, the window keeps today's path, and attach --follow says it can only show each turn.

A record is written as a zone is today: plain stores past the head, then one store of the new head, with no lock, allocation or system call. Before overwriting, the writer moves the buffer's tail past whole records, so it keeps its newest. Each record carries a sequence number, which makes a short-named zone 48 bytes. Fibers borrow their carrier's buffers before the switch, as zone rings do today.

While a thread holds a slot, a socket's two addresses are asked once per socket and kept, so its waits make no system call.

Samples come from a signal handler, so they get their own buffer, and an interrupt never shares one with the code it interrupted. The sampler's and counters' handlers block each other's signals while they run. A timer signal that arrives meanwhile is counted in its overrun, which perf_samples_periods already reads. A counter's signal waits in the kernel's queue until the sample is whole. So no handler interrupts another's record, and no batch is needed.

On x86-64, Jet's only target today, stores reach other cores in program order and loads are not reordered with loads. So a reader that sees a head sees the record before it. An arm64 port needs a release store of the head, a store fence after moving a tail, and the reader's load fences.

Readers use pread on an open descriptor, never a mapping, so a file cut short can't crash them. The heads sit in a table at the file's start, one cache line each, so a poll is one read. A reader reads the heads every millisecond, copies new records, then rereads the tails. Records overwritten meanwhile are a gap counted from the sequence numbers, never garbage. A buffer the last poll found more than half new is read again at once.

The follower's copy loop runs on a thread of its own, doing only pread and appends to memory. Drawing, disk saves and the ssh pipe work from that copy, so a slow disk, terminal or link never laps the program's buffers. The copy holds at most 256 MiB; past that the loop waits, and the spare chunks below take the backlog.

Spare chunks. Each follower writes its read positions into its own row of the live file's header each poll; a row not renewed for 1 s is ignored. As a writer's head enters the next quarter of a buffer, it checks those rows. If that quarter holds records a follower has not read, it links in a spare chunk instead of overwriting.

The per-record path is unchanged: the check sits where the writer already wraps. The writer only compares those numbers, so a bad row can cost spare chunks, never a wrong store. The helper thread reserves spare chunks with fallocate. When the follower catches up, the helper punches their pages out.

While a follower stands, the helper keeps one 4 MiB spare reserved ahead for each thread with a slot, so a sudden stall never waits for its turn. It refills a taken spare on its next turn, within 100 ms; 4 MiB covers a turn's 2.9 MB at 600,000 zones a second. Chunks for a lagging follower stay within 64 MiB per program.

64 MiB holds about 1.4 million short zones, over 2 s at 600,000 a second, against 9 ms without spares. Past the cap, or in a thread writing over 4 MiB a turn, 870,000 short zones a second, the writer keeps its newest records and counts the gap, as before. The spares are the program's memory, charged to it: 4 MiB a thread while followed, and up to 64 MiB more while a follower lags.

A reader trusts nothing in the file or the stream, since a buggy program can scribble on its own buffers. Every length, offset and count is checked against its buffer, and a record that fails is drawn as a damaged gap. Names are drawn with control characters escaped.

The program refreshes its clock pair each 100 ms turn: it writes the spare pair, then stores which pair is current, so no reader sees half of one. Readers turn time-stamp counts into the run's nanoseconds with it.

At exit the program stores its status in the header and removes the file's name; a reader holding it open reads to the end. A program killed while followed loses nothing its buffers held, since the pages belong to the file. The one record a thread was writing has no head store yet, so no reader sees it. A killed program's live file stays until attach with its pid reads it, or the leftover sweep finds it a day old.

attach --follow --stream saves what it reads to its own trace on that machine and sends from that file, so a full pipe never stops its reading. The stream opens with its format's name and version. Framed parts follow: the header and clock pairs, each buffer's new records unchanged, each address's function and line the first time it appears, lost counts, and the end.

Names come from the program's image on that machine. jet perf view - reads the stream with the same reader and checks. Another version or a broken frame is Jet.DriverOperationFailed, and so is --stream to a terminal.

attach's pid becomes optional: with exactly one live observed program of this user, it is that one. --source defaults to the source the run published (ObserveLive.jet observe_env_key), resolved against its working directory. --zones=WINDOW keeps its meaning, a point attach of that length. jet.canvas.profile gains pid, live, host and stop in place of trace, and its answer gains live {pid, ended, exit, lost}. Canvas's Live starts the entry as jet perf run does.

The dev server's relay becomes a fixed ring of its newest 4096 rows, each with a sequence number. Each beacon its full queue refuses is counted, and the count is written with the next rows.
options.code:
// live.jet: each turn runs a `tick` zone, plots `sum`, marks a frame,
// then sleeps 10 ms (Tests/Cases/Perf/AttachTurnsZonesOn.fixture).
$ jet run --observe live.jet &        # zones idle until an attach
$ jet perf attach --follow | cat      # piped: one line per event

options.name: Repeat today's one-time capture
options.detail: No new command. To watch a program, repeat jet perf attach --zones=1s in a loop and reopen the newest trace each time. Canvas reloads a trace path when asked again. Each picture is one finished second, drawn after that second ends.
options.technical: No runtime or protocol change. Each pass copies the whole 256 KiB ring and the program's image, 53 MB for live.jet in the probe. It turns zones on for its window by request, then off, and waits 250 ms more for the rows, so a 1 s pass takes about 1.3 s. A zone that spans two windows is cut at the edge, and each pass rewrites its trace file. Records still leave the program by one write call each.

options.name: Stream to a connected viewer, Tracy's way
options.detail: Every observed program also listens on a private socket. jet perf attach --follow and Canvas's Live switch connect to it, and the program's helper thread sends each new event down the connection. Connecting turns zones on, as an attach does. The view looks the same as A's, a helper thread's turn behind.
options.technical:
A Unix socket per observed program, owner-only, beside the published ring. A connection turns zones on, as an attach does, and the last one leaving turns them off. Each turn, the writer sends the new records and zone rows to every connected viewer, so its work grows with each viewer. A slow viewer either holds the writer up or loses records. A kill loses what the writer had not sent.

Point attach, crash dumps and jet debug keep reading the published ring, so the same records leave the program two ways. ssh can forward the socket to another machine.

$ jet perf attach 48213 --follow --source live.jet

comparisons.note: Tracy's client queues each zone, and a helper thread streams it over TCP to the profiler window. Its manual states 2.25 ns a zone, as wall time over 12 parallel threads: about 27 ns of each thread's time. By default it records from before main and never drops an event; unsent events wait in memory. Its on-demand mode records only while connected, as D-PERF-ZONES1 and A do. C is Tracy's socket shape; A has no listener but drops what a stalled watcher misses.

recommendation.why: A gives Tracy's live picture through the attach Jet already has, so zones stay idle until someone watches, as D-PERF-ZONES1 ratified. A watcher sees each event within a millisecond, and an unwatched run is unchanged.
gains: A stutter is seen while it happens, in the terminal, in Canvas, or from another machine over ssh.
D-PERF-ZONES1 holds unchanged: zones and #Profiled sites idle at 1.8 ns until an attach, in every build that keeps them.
An unwatched observed run is exactly today's, with no new memory or cost.
While followed, a native event shows within the reader's 1 ms poll, with no write call, and a kill loses nothing the buffers held.
One request rule for point attach and follow, so no attach turns zones off under another.
The watched window is kept as a normal trace, and beginners need no id or path.

losses.loss: While followed, the program pays what an attach with --zones= pays today: 26 ns a zone, 8 kHz samples costing 2.7% of each busy thread's CPU, and 384 KiB a thread.
losses.mitigation: Only while someone watches. The memory is freed when the last follower leaves, and an unwatched run holds none and samples at 100 Hz.

losses.loss: A follower stalled past 64 MiB of unread records, over 2 s at 600,000 zones a second, loses the oldest it had not read. So can a thread writing over 870,000 zones a second, between refills of its spare.
losses.mitigation: The gap is counted, and the program never waits. A copy thread that only reads keeps a slow disk, terminal or link from lapping it.

losses.loss: While followed, a 4 MiB spare stands ready for each thread; while a follower lags, the program holds up to 64 MiB more.
losses.mitigation: Only while someone watches: the spares go as the window closes, and lag chunks as the follower catches up. Where the memory is not there, the writer keeps its newest records and counts the gap.

losses.loss: A terminal follow has no zones from before it attached.
losses.mitigation: That is D-PERF-ZONES1's rule, kept. The follow opens with the flight ring's samples, waits and I/O from before it, and Canvas's Live starts the program with zones on.

losses.loss: A watcher's reads move cache lines the program writes; not yet measured.
losses.mitigation: Any reader on another core pays this, Tracy's in-process one too, and a check measures ours against an unwatched run.

losses.loss: On the web tier, spans show about 40 ms after they end, and a flood past 256 beacons a turn is lost.
losses.mitigation: That is the dev server's existing turn, and each refused beacon is now counted, so no web loss goes unseen.

whyNot.reason: Each picture arrives more than a second late and copies the program's 53 MB image again. A zone across two windows is cut in half, and zones are off between passes. The stutter that prompted the look can fall in a gap.

It needs a listening socket in every observed program, and a helper thread whose work grows with each viewer. The same records leave the program two ways, the view trails by a turn, and a kill loses what was not sent. A reaches other machines over ssh without a listener.

recommendation.tradeoff: While someone watches, the cost of an attach with --zones=, 384 KiB and a 4 MiB spare a thread, for a live timeline that leaves unwatched runs and D-PERF-ZONES1 unchanged.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Under A: a new case, Perf/attach_follow_draws_zone_before_exit.case, starts live.jet with jet run --observe. It runs jet perf attach --follow piped and receives a live.jet#tick line before live.jet prints done. It interrupts the follower, which exits 0 and names a trace whose jet perf view shows zone tick.

Zones rule: under jet run --observe with no attach, probe p2's zones.jet costs the idle site, within 0.5 ns of a run without --observe. The private directory then holds no live file, and under strace each 100 ms turn makes today's calls: one lstat of <ring>.zones and no directory read. While followed, a zone costs at most 1 ns more than under today's jet perf run. Within 1.5 s of the follower's end, zones are idle again and the live file is gone.

Two holders: a point attach that ends while a follower runs leaves the follower's tick lines unbroken. Delay: a fixture does one file read and one task wait, then blocks on a pipe for ten seconds. The follower prints both lines within 5 ms of each, while the program is still blocked. Kill: a followed program killed after its 1000th tick shows 1000 tick zones in the follower and a later attach.

Write calls: the ping-pong probe, followed, adds under 100 write calls for 100,000 turns, by its /proc/self/io count. Loss: at 600,000 zones a second, a follower stopped with STOP for one second, then resumed, prints no lost line, and the program's memory returns to its size before the stop. Stopped for five seconds, it prints a lost line whose count equals the gap in sequence numbers. Signals: the 8 kHz sampler and the counters together for ten seconds leave no torn record.

Faults: a followed program with more threads than a small memory file system holds runs to its end, and attach counts the threads that got no slot. A fuzz case flips bytes in a live file and in a stream: the reader draws damaged gaps and never crashes. A stream of another version gets Jet.DriverOperationFailed.

Remote: ssh localhost jet perf attach PID --follow --stream | jet perf view - shows the same tick lines as a local follower. A viewer that pauses its pipe for two seconds loses no record. Refusals: two observed programs and no id give Jet.AttachWhichProcess and exit 2. A sleeping process gives Jet.AttachTargetNotObserved and exit 1, and --follow with --zones= gives the conflicting-flags refusal and exit 2.

Canvas: a protocol case posts jet.canvas.profile with pid and gets a zones lane with marks and live.ended false; a host that starts with a dash is refused. Web: a case follows a jet dev page past 4096 rows, and a burst past the dev server's queue shows a counted gap.

Under B: the first case can only show tick lines in a finished one-second trace. Under C: the first case, with the follower connected over the socket.

Evidence labels: current behavior is read from code on dev e2069b5709, and the attach request, window and zone ring were rechecked on dev ba5711569a. Probe p2 and the ping-pong probe ran on 2026-11-20 with a compiler built from e2069b5709, at load 5 to 9 on 32 cores. No option is built, and no option's output was run. A watcher's cache cost and remote bandwidth are not measured.

surface.lesson: An observed program, started with jet run --observe, keeps a flight ring of its latest events. Zones stay idle until jet perf run or an attach turns them on, as ratified. Today an attach copies the ring once and the timeline is drawn afterward. A keeps the attach open and reads shared memory, B repeats the one-time copy, and C streams over a socket.
