designAway.loss: The posted A recorded zones from the start of every observed run, overruling D-PERF-ZONES1.
attempts: Record zones from each observed run's start: rejected. It overrules D-PERF-ZONES1 and charges unwatched runs 26 ns a zone, #Profiled ones on every call.
Make a follow an attach that stays open, so its request turns zones on, as D-PERF-ZONES1 says: kept.
designAway.result: Removed: zones and #Profiled sites idle at 1.8 ns until an attach, in every build that keeps them. Watching costs what an attach with --zones= costs today.

designAway.loss: A's view trails the program by a helper thread's turn.
attempts: Turn the writer every 20 ms while someone watches: rejected. Samples and waits still trail by a turn.
Write every record straight into a shared per-thread buffer, ending with one head store: kept. A record is readable the moment it is written.
Readers poll each buffer's head every millisecond, one read of a head table: kept. Polling costs the reader, not the program.
designAway.result: Removed while followed: the program adds no delay, and a watcher draws each event within its 1 ms poll. Web spans still wait for the page's beacon and the dev server's 40 ms turn.

designAway.loss: Each thread of an observed run reserved 384 KiB as it started, watched or not.
attempts: Commit each slot as its thread starts: rejected, every unwatched observed run would pay.
Commit pages as they are first written, without fallocate: rejected, a full file system would raise SIGBUS inside a handler.
Claim a slot at a thread's first record in a follow window, and free the pages as the window closes: kept.
designAway.result: Removed for unwatched runs, which hold no slot. Remaining while followed: 384 KiB and a 4 MiB spare a thread, freed when the last follower leaves.

designAway.loss: Two watchers, or a follower and a point attach, turn zones on and off under each other.
attempts: Keep today's one request file: rejected, the first attach to end removes it under the others.
One request per attach, which the program lists every turn: rejected, every unwatched turn would then read the directory.
Keep <ring>.zones as the one trigger, and read per-attach leases only while it stands: kept. An unwatched turn makes today's one lstat.
designAway.result: Removed: no attach ends another's window, and an unwatched run's turn is exactly today's.

designAway.loss: The hottest-lines lane settled over about a second, at 100 samples a second per thread.
attempts: Raise the rate for every observed run: rejected. A sample costs 3.4 µs measured, so 8 kHz takes 2.7% of a core in unwatched runs.
Sample at 8 kHz while a window stands, as an attach with --zones= does today: kept. It costs about 2.7% of each busy thread's CPU, only while followed.
designAway.result: Removed: a followed run samples as an attach with --zones= does, and unwatched runs keep 100 Hz.

designAway.loss: Each record leaves the program by a write call, which a full socket or a kill loses.
attempts: Batch records per thread and flush each turn: rejected. A batch is a delay, and a kill loses it.
Plain stores into per-thread buffers in the shared file while followed: kept. The ping-pong probe's write calls, 0.34 µs a record, go for the window.
Ask a socket's two addresses once per socket while followed: kept, so a socket wait asks the kernel nothing.
Back the buffers with a file on a memory file system, not private memory: kept, so the pages outlive a kill.
designAway.result: Removed while followed: a kill loses nothing still in the buffers. Unwatched runs keep D-OBSERVE-FLIGHT1's path, which a kill can cut by one 100 ms turn, as today.

designAway.loss: A store into a file's page can fault: a full memory file system, a file size limit, or a disk's writeback can stop or kill the program inside a zone or a signal handler.
attempts: Map pages as they are first written: rejected. A full file system would raise SIGBUS inside a handler and kill the program.
Reserve each slot with fallocate when its thread claims it, in its own context: kept. A failed claim keeps today's path for that thread and is counted.
Keep the file on a memory file system, under /dev/shm when the private directory is on disk: kept, so no store waits for writeback.
Where no memory file system exists, keep today's path and say so: kept.
designAway.result: Removed: no store into the buffers can fault once a slot is claimed.

designAway.loss: A signal handler writing into a thread's buffer could tear a record the thread was writing.
attempts: One buffer per thread, with a busy flag and a slot that parks the handler's record: rejected, a parked record is a batch.
A separate sample buffer per thread, written only by the handlers: kept.

The sampler's and counters' handlers block each other's signals: kept. A blocked timer signal counts in its overrun, which perf_samples_periods reads, and a counter's signal waits in the kernel's queue.
A crash dump's capture signal shares the handler but writes only the dump's page: checked, it needs no block.
designAway.result: Removed: no batch anywhere, and every record is whole when its head is stored.

designAway.loss: A reader could see a head before its record, half a clock pair, or a file cut short under it.
attempts: Rely on x86-64's ordering, Jet's only target: kept. Stores reach other cores in order and loads are not reordered with loads, so the head store publishes the record.
For an arm64 port, a release store of the head, a store fence after moving a tail, and load fences in the reader: kept as a port requirement.
Two clock pairs and one store of which is current: kept.
Read with pread, never a mapping: kept, so a shortened file can't crash Canvas or a follower.
designAway.result: Removed: every record a reader accepts was whole when published, and no reader can fault on the file.

designAway.loss: A scribbled file or a hostile stream could crash or fool a reader.
attempts: Trust the writer: rejected. A buggy program can scribble on its own buffers, and a stream crosses machines.
Check every length, offset and count against its buffer, draw failures as damaged gaps, and escape control characters in names: kept.
Open the stream with its format's name and version, and refuse another with Jet.DriverOperationFailed: kept.
designAway.result: Removed: a reader shows what it could check and marks the rest, and never crashes on input.

designAway.loss: Feeding watchers could add a second way out and work that grows with each watcher.
attempts: A file per watcher that the writer appends to each turn, capped at 64 MiB: rejected. It is a second exit, the writer's work grows with each watcher, and point attach would read a different file.
One shared file that every reader reads at its own pace: kept. Beyond the attach's window, no instruction in the program runs for a watcher.
designAway.result: Removed: the program's work does not grow with watchers. Remaining cost: a watcher's reads pull cache lines from the writing core, at most one per 64 bytes written plus the head table once per poll. The observer-effect check measures it.

designAway.loss: Lost events could go unseen.
attempts: In a window, the writer never refuses a record, since its records bypass the socket: kept.
Count the threads that got no slot in the header: kept.
Count the records a lapped reader missed, from each record's sequence number, and a reused slot's unread records by its generation: kept.
designAway.result: Removed: every record a watcher missed is drawn with its exact count.

designAway.loss: A stalled watcher, a slow link, or a burst between polls falls behind the program.
attempts: Make the program wait for its slowest watcher: rejected, a watcher could then stall the program.
Grow the buffers without bound: rejected, a stalled watcher would cost the program memory without limit.
Spill to disk on the far side: kept for a slow link, but a disk save comes after the copy, so it cannot save what a stalled reader never copied.
Let the program spill to disk itself: rejected. Its helper turns every 100 ms against a 9 ms buffer, and keeping up would be program work for a watcher.
Bounded spare chunks while a follower lags, reserved by the helper with fallocate, up to 64 MiB per program and freed on catch-up: kept. A lag covered goes from 9 ms to over 2 s.
Reserve spares only once a follower lags: rejected. The helper turns every 100 ms and a buffer laps in 9 ms, so a sudden stall would lose up to a turn.
Keep one 4 MiB spare a thread reserved ahead while a follower stands, refilled each helper turn: kept. A sudden stall never waits for the helper.
A copy loop on its own thread that only preads and appends to memory: kept. Only that thread being descheduled can lap, never a slow disk, terminal or link.
Reread at once a buffer that the last poll found more than half new: kept, at the reader's cost.
Past the cap, keep the newest records and count the rest as lost: kept.
designAway.result: Reduced to a follower stalled past 64 MiB of unread records, over 2 s at 600,000 zones a second, or a thread writing over 4 MiB a turn. It loses the oldest records it had not read, as a counted gap, and the program never waits.

designAway.loss: Another user could read a program's events, or a request could steer ssh.
attempts: Keep the file owner-only in the user's private directory, or a private directory under /dev/shm, made and checked as dev e2069b5709 does: kept.
Watch other machines only through ssh's login, never a listener: kept.
Canvas refuses a host name that starts with a dash or holds a space, so a request can't pass ssh options: kept.
designAway.result: Removed: only the program's owner reads its events, here or remotely.

designAway.loss: A follow reaches only programs on the same machine, unlike Tracy's TCP.
attempts: A listening socket in the program: rejected, as in C.
attach --follow --stream over ssh into jet perf view -, a versioned stream of the same records, read by the same reader: kept.
Resolve names and lines on the program's machine, once per address: kept, so the viewer needs no copy of the image.
designAway.result: Removed: any machine ssh reaches, with no listener in the program. Remaining cost: jet must be installed there, at a version whose stream this side reads.

designAway.loss: Beginners must find a process id and repeat the source path.
attempts: Follow the one live observed program of this user when no id is given, and list them when there are several: kept.
Skip files left by a program that no longer runs, so a killed run's file waits for attach with its pid: kept.
Default --source to the source the program published, resolved against its working directory: kept.
Canvas's Live button starts the program as jet perf run does, with zones on from its first instruction: kept.
designAway.result: Removed: jet perf attach --follow, or one button in Canvas.

designAway.loss: A terminal follow has no zones from before it attached.
attempts: Record zones always: rejected, it overrules D-PERF-ZONES1.
Open the follow with the flight ring's samples, waits and I/O from before it: kept.
Let Canvas's Live start the program under the profiler, zones on from the start: kept.
designAway.result: Remains by the ratified rule. A beginner's Live run has every zone, and a terminal follow opens with the flight ring's recent samples and waits.

designAway.loss: On the web tier the relay stops at 4096 rows, and beacons a full queue refuses are lost uncounted.
attempts: Make the relay a fixed ring of its newest 4096 rows, each with a sequence number: kept.
Count each beacon the dev server's full queue refuses, and write the count with the next rows: kept.
Write beacons as they arrive instead of each 40 ms turn: rejected, the dev clock is the dev server's one writer.
designAway.result: Removed for loss: a web page is followed with counted gaps, as a native program is. Remaining cost: web spans show about 40 ms after they end.

decisions.title: Machine code in Jet's own tools: list a function's instructions in jet debug and give each its samples in jet perf view
decisions.situation: Machine code is the list of instructions the processor actually runs. Jet writes that code itself, but none of its tools shows it. At a stop, jet debug shows the source line and has no command that lists the instructions under it. jet perf view says line 7 of fib.jet takes most of the time, and cannot say which instruction of that line does. A developer chasing a slow loop has to reach for gdb or Linux perf, which Jet's rules allow on Jet code only as a recorded stopgap. You decide where Jet shows its machine code. We recommend a disassemble command in jet debug and the editor adapter, plus an --instructions view in jet perf view, both reading one x86-64 decoder.
decisions.gist: Where should Jet show the machine code it compiled, with each instruction's source line and its share of the samples?
decisions.lesson: A disassembler turns code bytes back into readable instructions, such as add rax, rbx. Jet's image keeps a line table: for each instruction address, the source line it came from. A sampling profiler notes which instruction was running, up to 8,000 times a second of CPU time. Annotating prints each instruction with the share of those samples it took, under its source line. That is what Linux perf annotate shows.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: run jet debug fib.jet, stop on a line, and type disassemble (or disas). The listing shows the function's instructions in address order. Each run of instructions sits under the source line it came from, and an arrow marks where the program stopped. In a profile, run jet perf run fib.jet, then jet perf view TRACE --instructions. That opens the hottest function, each instruction with its share of the function's samples.

Expert path: disassemble NAME lists a Jet function by the name break takes, or any other symbol in the image, such as a runtime routine or a linked C function. A name several functions share lists each in turn. disassemble FILE:LINE or FILE:A-B lists only those lines' instructions, including pieces the optimizer moved away. --bytes adds the encoded bytes.

jet perf view --instructions=fib.jet:7 opens one line, --instructions=fib one function, and --json gives the rows. Editors get the Debug Adapter Protocol's disassemble request, so VS Code's Disassembly view opens at the stop.

Stepping one instruction (stepi) and breaking at an instruction are not on this ballot. The criterion asks to see the code. Stepping changes how a stop is reached, which touches placed conditions, replay and fix, so it needs its own ballot.

Every native level works the same way. jet debug builds a source file at -O0. A built -O1 or -O2 image is debugged as it is, through its side debug file when the release profile split one out. jet perf run takes -O0, -O1 and -O2. Crash dumps, replays and attached programs list code too, since each holds its image.

Refusals are named. A browser trace has no instruction samples, so --instructions on one gets Jet.PerfNoInstructions, which says to profile the native build. A line with no sampled code, or a function whose code the trace cut, gets the same name and lists the trace's hottest lines. --instructions beside --retained-by, or on a pprof or OTLP export, gets Jet.UnknownFlag, as --retained-by does today. Each exits with status 2.

In the console, a name that matches nothing prints No function, and a line without code prints No code on, as break does.

What the listing shows is the program's own code. A breakpoint's trap byte is shown as the instruction it covers, marked with the breakpoint's number. A condition that runs in place, through a jump to code the debugger placed, is marked the same way. The debugger's own code, a placed condition's or the room an evaluation runs from, is never listed as the program's; the adapter names it [debugger]. After fix, the listing shows the new code that runs and says where the old entry now jumps.

A zone site is shown as it is now: test while zones are off, jmp to its stub while a profiler records them. A crash dump keeps the image, not the live code, so it shows each site as the image holds it.

In an inlined frame, disas lists the function the code was inlined into and marks the inlined run. The header names where each local lives at the stop, from the image's location lists. Runtime routines and linked C code with no Jet line are listed by symbol and offset alone.

An image built with debug_info false has no line table, and jet debug refuses it today with Jet.DebuggerUnavailable; that stays. A trace keeps the code that ran. So a trace whose program was rebuilt still lists the old code, and its source lines carry the note the view prints today when a file changed since the capture.

On the web tier the browser compiles the WebAssembly module to machine code that Jet never sees, and no Jet debugger runs there. Chrome DevTools lists the module's WebAssembly instructions through the source map Jet already writes. This is tooling, not a language meaning, so it needs no I9 exception.
decisions.story: Mia's fib.jet is slower at -O2 than she expected. jet perf view says line 7 takes most of the time, so she runs it again with --instructions=fib.jet:7. Most of the line's samples sit on the two calls, and a few on the overflow check after the add. She opens jet debug on the built image, breaks on line 7 and types disas. The listing shows the line's code with her breakpoint marked, and both calls are still real calls.

// gdb: stop in fib, then list its code under its source lines.
(gdb) break fib
(gdb) run 35
(gdb) disassemble /s
// Linux perf: record the run, then annotate the hottest function.
$ perf record ./fib 35
$ perf annotate --stdio fib
decisions.detail:
Code read on dev f2cf0a8324. Probed on 2026-11-20 with the gate-p345 compiler on Tests/Cases/JetPerfTracePartsCaptureRun/Fixtures/Fib/fib.jet. The console's commands are NATIVE_DEBUG_HELP (Compiler/JetDebug/Source/Native.jet:5806), and a crash dump's are NATIVE_DUMP_HELP (NativeDump.jet). None lists code: disassemble and disas both print Unknown command (probe). break NAME finds a function in the image's line table only (break_in, Native.jet:582), and prints No function or No code on when it finds none (Native.jet:2682, 2693).

The adapter advertises no disassemble support (Compiler/JetCLI/Source/CLI/DebugDap.jet:178). D-DBG-DAP1 records disassembly as truthfully unsupported, and its default projection shows no addresses (Docs/Spec/syntax-decisions.md:7545-7550); A replaces that line for the disassemble request. Only showRawFrames frames carry an instructionPointerReference (DebugDap.jet:751).

The image's .debug_jetline gives each function's code range and its address-to-line rows (Compiler/JetBackend/Source/Image/Jetline.jet). NativeFacts.jet reads the DWARF's inlined runs, call sites and .debug_loclists. The release profile's debug_info split writes them and the symbol table to <image>.debug and .jet/symbols/.build-id/ (Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/Registry/BuildOptions.jet:65-71).

jet debug reads that side file (native_image_load, Native.jet:401). An image with no Jet debug information is refused with Jet.DebuggerUnavailable (Native.jet:552). A .jetdump holds the whole image (Compiler/JetDebug/Source/NativeDump.jet).

The debugger already decodes instruction lengths, to move the instructions a placed condition's 5-byte jump covers (native_decode, Compiler/JetDebug/Source/NativePlace.jet:251). It reads legacy and VEX forms and gives up on EVEX, 3DNow!, 16-bit branches, loop and jrcxz. It names no instruction. Jet's WebAssembly side keeps one instruction table that its decoder, text reader and validator all read (Compiler/JetWasm/Source/Wasm/Opcodes.jet).

The encoder writes the integer and control subset, SSE and VEX FMA forms (Compiler/JetBackend/Source/X64/Encoder.jet). Only its ALU and shift groups are checked, while the compiler builds, against the template assembler's 53 mnemonics (Encoder.jet:21-23, Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/Facts/InlineAssembly.jet:284).

Images also hold code Jet's encoder never wrote. The fault report is bytes assembled from report.S (Compiler/JetBackend/Source/Image/StaticLink.jet:1553-1557). The asm leaves of X64/IntSum.jet, Fill.jet and Count.jet are written as bytes. link_args admits .a archives built by a C compiler (BuildOptions.jet:883-888). Fifteen files under Tests run objdump on Jet's code today, such as Tests/Cases/Debug/objdump_disassembles_main_from_text_section.case.

The session keeps the program's own byte under every trap byte and placed jump (originals, Native.jet:1566). fix maps changed functions into a debugger region and makes each old entry jump to its new code (NativeFix.jet). Evaluations run from a room the session maps in the program (NativeEval.jet). A zone site is test eax, imm32 in the image, and the runtime turns it into jmp while zones record (Compiler/JetIR/Source/X64Select.jet:1912-1923).

A perf session reads raw program counters and an image copy, resolves them to lines, then deletes both (Compiler/JetCLI/Source/CLI/Perf/SourceSampling.jet:406). The trace keeps one row per function and source line (TraceProfileRow, Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/Trace/Carriers.jet:52), at most 4096 rows, and no code.

The trace format is version 2, and the reader refuses any other (Trace/JetTrace.jet:6, 80-88). The text view shows at most 24 line rows (Perf/Command.jet:1855) and notes a source that changed since the capture (Perf/LineCosts.jet:58). Every jet perf view refusal is Jet.UnknownFlag with exit 2 (jet_cli_perf_error, Perf/Command.jet:69).

The receipt names the sampler and its skid (SourceSampling.jet:532). IBS and PEBS name the instruction that ran, and the runtime picks one only where perf_event_paranoid is at most 1 (Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/PerfSamples.jet:10-13). Otherwise the task clock or the timer lands on the instruction it interrupted, which skids past the slow one. The timer asks for a sample every 125 microseconds of CPU time (PerfSamples.jet:79). jet perf run takes -O0, -O1 and -O2 (Tests/Cases/Perf/game_frame_events.case).

A web build writes a WebAssembly module with a source map (Compiler/JetWeb/Source/Web/Build.jet:117-129). A browser trace holds timed spans of class event, wasm or dom, and no samples (Perf/BrowserCapture.jet:133). Canvas's profile answer lists at most 64 hot lines (Docs/Spec/Reference/canvas-protocol.md:375-402), and Canvas's native tier speaks the same console (Native.jet:5802).

jet emit prints the AST and the O0 IR (Compiler/JetCLI/Source/CLI/Emit.jet); its -O2 is refused with Jet.UnknownFlag, exit 2 (probe). Under A a built image's code at any level is listed with disas NAME at the entry stop, so emit gains no --asm. IR at -O1 and -O2 is a gap of jet emit, outside this criterion. This ballot is c95 of #6841.

options.name: List code in the debugger and annotate it in the profile view
options.detail: jet debug gains disassemble (disas), and the editor adapter answers the disassemble request. jet perf view gains --instructions. All read one x86-64 decoder and the image's line table, through one listing builder. Listings show the live program, with breakpoints marked over the program's own instructions. Profiles keep the code of their hottest sampled functions, so the view needs no image later. Nothing steps by instruction.
options.technical:
Decoder: one x86-64 decoder table in JetBackend covers the user-mode legacy, VEX and EVEX encodings. The encoder and the template assembler are unchanged. A test decodes every form the encoder's tests write, every template-assembler mnemonic, the asm leaves' bytes and the fault report's bytes. It checks each against its own name.

The same test compares every table row's text with objdump -M intel's, when the tool is present, as fifteen test files run objdump today. The placer's native_decode becomes a call into the decoder, so the debugger keeps one decoder, and the placer's tests pass unchanged. Bytes that decode to nothing show as (bad), one byte at a time, as objdump does.

Listing: one builder turns code bytes, the line table, the symbol table and the marks into rows. A row holds the address, offset, bytes, text, the symbol a call or jump reaches, the source line and the marks. The console, the adapter, jet perf view and Canvas only format these rows.

Console: disassemble [NAME | LINE | FILE:LINE | FILE:A-B] [--bytes], also disas, in jet debug and in a crash dump's console. With no operand it lists the selected frame's function and marks that frame's pc with =>. A line header repeats each time the line changes in address order, as gdb's /s does.

Call targets are named, such as <fib> or <jet_int_add>. Bytes are read from the program, with originals() put back under trap bytes and placed jumps; a crash dump reads them from its image. NAME is looked up as break looks it up, then in the image's symbol table. Answers: No function `NAME`, and No code on FILE:LINE.

Adapter: supportsDisassembleRequest becomes true, and every Jet frame gets an instructionPointerReference. disassemble answers address, bytes, text, symbol and the source line. An address outside any code answers presentationHint invalid, as the protocol asks; an address in the debugger's own code answers its rows under the symbol [debugger]. Stepping granularity and instruction breakpoints stay unsupported, so VS Code steps by line from its Disassembly view.

Trace: the format becomes version 3, with an instructions section. It keeps each sampled function, hottest first, up to 1 MiB of code per trace. Each keeps its symbol, level, link address, code bytes and address-to-line rows. It also keeps the names its calls and jumps reach, and one row per sampled instruction: offset, samples and counter events. A function past the cap is marked cut.

Data, strings and values are never kept, pprof and OTLP exports carry no code, and the receipt counts the functions and bytes kept. A version 2 trace is refused as an older format, as the reader refuses old versions today, and the seven committed fixture traces move with it.

View: jet perf view TRACE --instructions[=NAME|FILE:LINE] [--json|--html]. The value takes =, since a bare word after the flag is the trace path; bare, it opens the hottest function. Shares are each instruction's share of its function's samples, as perf annotate gives them, with a column per counter the memory lens captured.

The header names the sampler. Under the task clock or the timer it says the shares skid, and that precise samples need perf_event_paranoid at most 1. Jet.PerfNoInstructions is registered with its what, why, fix and snapshot. Canvas's debug console accepts disassemble, since it speaks the same console, and its profile request takes instructions with a line or function and answers the same rows.

options.name: One inspect command outside the debugger
options.detail: A new jet inspect asm lists a function or a line of a source file or built image, with its source lines. Given a trace, it adds each instruction's share. For a web build it lists the WebAssembly module's instructions. jet debug and the editor adapter gain nothing, so a stopped program's code is read from its image in another terminal.
options.technical:
jet inspect asm <file.jet|image> [NAME|FILE:LINE] [-O0|-O1|-O2] [--target web] [--trace T.jettrace] [--bytes] [--json]. A source file is built at the level given, -O0 by default. The same x86-64 decoder as A and the same instructions section in the trace are needed, since a trace must keep sampled code to annotate it.

For --target web it prints the module through Jet's WebAssembly instruction table, each instruction under its source-map line. It reads the image file, never a running program, so trap bytes, fix and live zone sites are not shown, and no pc is marked. The adapter keeps disassembly unsupported.
options.code:
// fib.jet, unchanged. Illustrative.
$ jet inspect asm fib.jet fib -O2
fib  fib.jet:5-8  -O2  76 bytes
fib.jet:6   if n < 2 -> return n
    +0    push   rbx
    ...
fib.jet:7   fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)
    +14   call   fib
    ...
$ jet inspect asm fib.jet fib.jet:7 -O2 --trace .jet/perf/1795089901-a41b55f6.jettrace
  33.1%   +14   call   fib
$ jet inspect asm fib.jet fib --target web
fib.jet:7
    local.get 0
    i64.const 1
    i64.sub
    call 3 <fib>
// At a jet debug stop: run it in a second terminal on the same image.
// It cannot mark the stop or show the debugger's breakpoints.

options.name: A compiler listing from jet emit
options.detail: jet emit, which prints the AST and IR today, gains --asm. It prints each function as the compiler's emitter writes it, with source-line comments, like Compiler Explorer or gcc -S. For a web build it prints the WebAssembly text. Nothing runs, so no stop is marked and no samples are shown. The debugger, the profile view and the adapter gain nothing.
options.technical:
jet emit --asm <file.jet> [--fn NAME] [-O0|-O1|-O2] [--target web] [--json]. The encoder already logs part of what it writes for one function (JET_X64_EMIT_LOG: jumps, calls, memory operands, divisions and string copies). --asm extends that log to every instruction and prints every function's rows after branch relaxation, with local labels for jump targets. No decoder is built: the emitter names what it writes.

The asm leaves (X64/IntSum.jet and its siblings) are written as bytes, so they print as .byte rows. The runtime pack, the fault report and linked C archives are not listed, since the program's compile never emits them. jet emit --ir must take -O1 and -O2 too, for the levels to match.
options.code:
// fib.jet, unchanged. Illustrative.
$ jet emit --asm -O2 fib.jet --fn fib
fn fib  fib.jet:5
  ; fib.jet:6  if n < 2 -> return n
  push   rbx
  mov    rbx, rdi
  cmp    rdi, 2
  jl     .L2
  ; fib.jet:7  fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)
  lea    rdi, [rbx-1]
  call   fib
  ...
$ jet emit --asm --target web fib.jet --fn fib   # the WebAssembly text
// No sample shares, and no listing at a jet debug stop.

comparisons.note: disassemble lists the current frame, a function by name or an address range, with --mixed for source lines and -b for bytes. It decodes every x86-64 form through LLVM, and its VS Code adapter answers the disassemble request. This is A's shape in the debugger; lldb has no sample shares.

disassemble /s interleaves source lines in address order and marks the pc with =>. /r adds bytes, and layout asm keeps the code on screen while stepping with stepi. Its decoder covers the whole instruction set on many architectures, and record lets it step back by instruction. A's listing follows /s; A adds no instruction stepping.

It prints each instruction's share of a function's samples, with source lines when the binary has DWARF, and its TUI follows jumps and calls. Any hardware event can be annotated, such as cache misses, on any binary on the machine, the kernel included. It needs the binary at report time, through its build-id cache. A's trace keeps the sampled code instead, and annotates Jet programs only.
comparisons.code:
$ perf record -e cycles:pp ./fib 35
$ perf annotate --stdio -s fib

comparisons.note: Its source view opens a function's assembly beside the source, with sample counts per instruction and arrows for jumps. It adds per-instruction latency and throughput from uops.info tables, and decodes with Capstone. That cycle-cost column is something A does not offer.
comparisons.code:
// Tracy: click a hot zone, then Source > Assembly.
ZoneScopedN("tick");

comparisons.note: Its source and disassembly view shows per-line and per-instruction sample shares for the function you select, after the capture ends. It is A's profile half in a desktop window.
comparisons.code: // Superluminal: open a function, then Source & Disassembly.

comparisons.note: A fast Windows debugger whose disassembly window interleaves source and steps one instruction while that window has focus. It is A's debugger half; it has no profiler.
comparisons.code: // RemedyBG: View > Disassembly; F10 steps one instruction there.

comparisons.note: It compiles a snippet with many compilers and flags and colors each source line with its assembly. Its best case is comparing two compilers or levels side by side, viewing the optimizer's passes, and sharing a link. It never runs your program under a debugger or shows samples. This is C's shape.
comparisons.code:
// godbolt.org: paste fib, pick a compiler and -O2.
int fib(int n) { return n < 2 ? n : fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2); }

recommendation.why: A puts machine code where the questions are asked: at the stop and on the hot line. It gives gdb's listing and perf annotate's shares through one decoder, one line table and one listing builder. Because the trace keeps the sampled code, a profile can be annotated later on any machine, even after a rebuild.
gains: The code at a stop is listed in place, with the stop and breakpoints marked.
A hot line's instructions carry their sample shares, as perf annotate gives them.
VS Code's Disassembly view works through the adapter.
One decoder serves the debugger's placed conditions and both listings, and the encoder is untouched.
Every native level, crash dumps, replays and attached programs list code the same way.

losses.loss: A full x86-64 decoder is a large table to write and keep correct.
losses.mitigation: The encoder stays as it is. A test decodes every form Jet writes back to its own name and compares every row with objdump's text, so a wrong row fails Jet's tests before it reaches a listing. The placer's length decoder is replaced, so the debugger still has one decoder.

losses.loss: Traces grow by the code of their hottest functions, and the trace format moves to version 3.
losses.mitigation: At most 1 MiB of code per trace, hottest first, with a cut marked. The trace then needs no image to annotate, which perf needs its build-id cache for. Old traces are recaptured, as each format change already asks.

losses.loss: A shared trace shows the machine code of its hot functions.
losses.mitigation: Only code is kept, never data, strings or values: bytes the built image already holds. pprof and OTLP exports carry none, and the receipt counts what is kept.

losses.loss: With the task clock or the timer, a share can land on an instruction after the slow one.
losses.mitigation: PEBS or IBS is used whenever the kernel allows it. Otherwise the header says the shares skid and how to allow precise samples. Line shares are unchanged.

losses.loss: The web tier gets no listing.
losses.mitigation: The browser compiles the module itself and samples none of it for Jet, so no Jet listing could be true there. Jet.PerfNoInstructions says so, and DevTools reads Jet's source map.

whyNot.reason: It cannot list the code of a stopped program, mark the stop or show breakpoints, which is half of the criterion. It still needs A's decoder and trace change, and adds a second place to look.

It shows what the compiler meant to write, not what runs: no runtime, no fault report, no linked C code and no samples. It answers Compiler Explorer's question and neither of the criterion's. Under A, -O2 code is read without running anything past the entry stop: build, open jet debug on the image, and disas NAME.

recommendation.tradeoff: One decoder table and a bounded bigger trace, for machine code at every stop and on every hot line, in Jet's own tools.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Under A: a new case, Debug/disassemble_marks_stop_and_breakpoint.case, builds fib.jet at -O0, -O1 and -O2. At a breakpoint on line 7 it runs disas, then checks the => line, the b1 mark and a fib.jet:7 header. With --bytes it checks that no cc byte appears at b1's address, and disas nope prints No function `nope`.

A second case lists disas jet_int_add, a runtime routine, by symbol and offset. A third opens a .jetdump and checks disas lists the stopped function from its image. A decoder test decodes every encoder form, the template assembler's mnemonics, the asm leaves and the fault report's bytes, and checks no (bad) row appears. It also compares every table row with objdump -M intel when the tool is present.

A perf case runs jet perf run -O2 fib.jet, then jet perf view --instructions=fib.jet:7. It checks that the shares of the line's instructions sum to the line's share of fib within rounding, and that the sampler line is present. A browser trace checks Jet.PerfNoInstructions and exit 2, and a version 2 trace the older-format refusal. An adapter case sends disassemble at a stop and checks the instruction at the frame's instructionPointerReference.

Under B: the same perf case through jet inspect asm --trace. Under C: jet emit --asm -O2 fib.jet --fn fib prints a fib.jet:7 comment.

Evidence labels: current behavior is read from code on dev f2cf0a8324. The Unknown command answers and jet emit's -O2 refusal are from 2026-11-20 probes. No option is built, and every listing and share shown is illustrative. The decoder table's size, the trace growth and how much the 1 MiB cap keeps are not measured.

surface.gist: Where should Jet show the machine code it compiled, with each instruction's source line and sample share?
surface.lesson: A disassembler turns code bytes back into instructions such as add rax, rbx. Jet's image says which source line each instruction came from. Its profiler notes which instruction was running, thousands of times a second. Today no Jet tool lists instructions. A lists them in jet debug and annotates them in jet perf view. B adds one inspect command. C prints the compiler's own listing.

designAway.loss: A decoder written for x86-64 is a second description of the instruction set beside the encoder.
attempts: Decode only the forms Jet's encoder writes: rejected. The fault report's bytes come from report.S, and linked C archives hold any instruction, so a hot loop there would show as bytes.

Make the encoder and the template assembler read the decoder's table, as Jet's WebAssembly decoder, text reader and validator share one: rejected. The criterion needs no encoder change, and rebuilding the compiler's emitter around a table risks its speed and its code for nothing a user sees.
Generate the table from Intel's XED data files at build: rejected, it adds an outside data dependency.

One decoder table, with a test that decodes every form the encoder and the template assembler write back to its own name and compares every row with objdump's text: kept. Encoder and decoder stay inverses, checked against each other.
Make the placer's native_decode call the new decoder: kept, so the debugger keeps one decoder.
designAway.result: One decoder in Jet, checked against every form Jet writes and against objdump, with the encoder untouched.

designAway.loss: A profile could not be annotated once the image it ran is gone.
attempts: Keep the image path in the trace and read it at view time, as perf's build-id cache does: rejected, the session deletes its image copy, and a rebuilt image would not match.
Keep the whole image in the trace: rejected, it grows every trace by the program's size.
Keep the code bytes, line rows and reached names of each sampled function, hottest first, up to 1 MiB: kept. A function past the cap is marked cut.
Keep only code, never data, strings or values, and leave it out of pprof and OTLP exports: kept, so a trace shows no more than the image already ships.
designAway.result: Any trace is annotated anywhere, from the bytes that ran, at a bounded size.

designAway.loss: Debugger edits to the code could appear in the listing as if they were the program's.
attempts: Read the image file instead of the program: rejected, it would miss fix and live zone sites.
Read the program, and put the session's originals() back under each trap byte and placed jump: kept.
Mark each such instruction with its breakpoint's number, and list the debugger's own code only under [debugger]: kept.
designAway.result: The listing shows what the program runs, with the debugger's changes named, not shown as code.

designAway.loss: Timer samples skid, so a share lands on a later instruction.
attempts: Hide shares under the timer: rejected, the user loses the rough picture the line view already gives.
Move each timer sample back one instruction: rejected, the skid is not always one instruction, so the share would be wrong as often as right.
Use IBS or PEBS when the kernel allows, and otherwise name the sampler, its skid and how to allow precise samples in the header: kept.
designAway.result: With precise samples each share is charged to the instruction that ran; otherwise every share is labelled as skidded.

designAway.loss: Optimized code is hard to read: a line's code is scattered and locals move between registers.
attempts: Repeat the line header each time the line changes, as gdb's /s does: kept.
Name inlined code with the line it was inlined at, and in an inlined frame list the function it was inlined into: kept.
Name where each local lives at the stop, from the image's location lists: kept.
designAway.result: An -O2 listing reads as the -O0 one does, with the optimizer's moves named.

designAway.loss: VS Code's Disassembly view steps by line, not by instruction.
attempts: Add stepi, nexti and instruction breakpoints to A: rejected here. The criterion asks to see code; stepping changes how a stop is reached, which touches placed conditions, replay and fix, so it needs its own ballot.
Answer the disassemble request alone, so the view lists code and VS Code steps by line, as it does for any adapter without stepping granularity: kept.
designAway.result: The listing ships whole; instruction stepping stays a separate choice.

designAway.loss: The web tier gets no listing.
attempts: List the module's WebAssembly with sample shares: rejected, a browser trace holds no samples, so no share could be true.
Refuse with Jet.PerfNoInstructions, naming the native build to profile: kept.
designAway.result: The web tier is refused by name; DevTools lists the module through the source map Jet writes.

decisions.title: How jet perf measures any command or built program, not only a .jet file
decisions.situation: `jet perf run` builds a Jet program and samples it from inside, 8,000 times a second, with tasks and waits. `jet perf test` reads the tests' live records. `jet perf attach <pid>` watches a running process jet perf did not build. It reads what the process offers: its browser relay, or its runtime's live records under `--observe`. When the process publishes nothing, attach samples its threads' CPU from outside, 1,000 times a second for one second. No form starts a built program or a jet command and counts its work or lists its system calls, its requests to the operating system. So the repo still runs Linux `perf`, GNU `time -v` and `strace` in 19 places. You are asked how a user names that job. We recommend that `jet perf attach` also start a command given after `--`, with two new lenses, `counts` and `syscalls`.
decisions.gist: How should `jet perf` count the work of, and list the system calls of, a built program or a jet command?
decisions.lesson: `jet perf run` and `jet perf test` watch a Jet program from inside. `jet perf attach` watches a running process it did not build. None of them starts a built program or a jet command and counts its work or lists its system calls. Those jobs still use Linux `perf stat`, GNU `time` and `strace`.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path. To see how much work a built program does, write `jet perf attach --lens=counts -- .jet/build/hash data.bin`. The view prints `counts instructions:u=... cycles:u=... cpu_ns=... peak_rss_bytes=...`. To see which files it opens, write `--lens=syscalls` instead. To profile a Jet program's own code, `jet perf run hash.jet` stays the tool, as today.

Expert path. A gate writes `jet perf attach --lens=counts,syscalls --out run.jettrace -- jet build Compiler` and reads `jet perf view run.jettrace --json`. The counts are the whole command's totals, and every call has its pid, arguments and result. `jet perf compare` compares two such traces' counts.
decisions.story:
Sam wants to know whether a change made `jet build Compiler` do more work. Today the speed gate runs Linux `perf stat`, which the dogfood rule allows only as a named gap. Under option A, Sam writes `jet perf attach --lens=counts -- jet build Compiler`. The view prints the instructions and cycles of the whole build, every helper process included.

Later a test fails because `jet run` opened its own file twice. Sam writes `jet perf attach --lens=syscalls -- jet run main.jet`, and the view lists both opens with their paths.
decisions.inWild:
$ perf stat -e instructions:u,cycles:u -- jet build Compiler
$ strace -f -e trace=openat -o run.trace jet run main.jet
$ /usr/bin/time -v jet build Compiler
decisions.detail:
The code was read on dev 2e2ac929c1 and re-read on 97d2a287ab. The command `jet perf run` is the function `jet_cli_perf_session` in the file Compiler/JetCLI/Source/CLI/Perf/Session.jet. It always spawns `jet run --observe` with the user's words. The words after `--` go to the program. So no spelling today names a built program or a jet command, and `--` cannot be reused for that.

The lenses are `cpu`, `memory`, `alloc`, `topdown` and `causal` (`jet_cli_perf_session_lenses`). The runtime opens the memory and top-down counters with perf_event_open on the program's starting thread only (Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/PerfSamples.jet). The runtime also counts the calls that pass through `host_call` in HostProcess.jet, by number and Jet stack, without arguments. Thread starts, the allocator's munmap, the open of /proc/self/exe and the sockets go around it through raw syscalls. Children and the loader are never seen.

Two kinds of users wait on this. Tools/Perf/CompileThroughput/Throughput.jet runs each compile under `perf stat -x , -e instructions:u,cycles:u` to count its work. Seven cases run strace. CLICompilerSpeed checks the clone and openat calls of `{jet} run`, twice. ControlAndData checks the munmap calls of a built program at exit. Report checks the network calls of `{jet} build`. TaskgroupStack checks the clone calls of a built program. JetpackJetOS runs it twice, and Tools/Perf/CoreStrace once.

The engine is the same under every option. Counts use perf_event_open with `inherit` set, so every thread and child adds into the total, user mode only. Calls use ptrace on the target, which follows fork, vfork, clone and exec. JetDebug's Native.jet already drives ptrace for `jet debug`. A Jet program also gets the Jet line that made each call, from its debug info.

The call decoder covers the whole file class: open, mkdir, the chmod family, rename, unlink, stat and their *at forms, with paths and modes. It also decodes clone flags, munmap ranges, write and writev, and the socket calls. JetpackJetOS needs the file class whole. Its case orders mkdir against the protected chmod-class calls (nixos_migration_protects_stage_before_writing_inputs.case).

Edge cases, the same under every option. A machine may have no counters: a virtual machine without them, or perf_event_paranoid above 2. Then `counts` is reported `unavailable` with the kernel's errno and the paranoid level, and the line names the sysctl to change. The command still runs.

Ptrace may be refused: Yama ptrace_scope 2 without CAP_SYS_PTRACE, or 3, or a seccomp sandbox. A child the command itself traces, as `jet debug` does, cannot be traced again. Then `syscalls` is reported `unavailable` the same way, with the errno and the ptrace_scope. E2124 (Jet.AttachTargetNotObserved) keeps its meaning for the pid form alone.

A setuid program runs without its privilege under ptrace, as under strace, and the view says so. The command's exit code is passed through. A child still running when the command ends is listed by pid and detached; its counts so far are kept. Each call row keeps at most 4096 bytes of decoded arguments. Past 65536 calls the rest are counted per name.

How attach watches today (Session.jet, jet_cli_perf_attach): three ways, chosen by what the target offers, not by a lens. A devserver program is read through its browser relay. A process that publishes a live snapshot is read from its runtime's own records, with `--source`. Those are the flight ring, the `--zones=` window and the heap. A process that publishes nothing is sampled from outside (Outside.jet).

Attach takes no `cpu` lens: any `--lens=` but `alloc` is refused. Its window is a fixed second (JET_CLI_PERF_OUTSIDE_WINDOW_MS). `--for=<duration>` is ratified (D-PERF-ATTACH-WINDOW1 = A) and being built.

options.name: `jet perf attach` can start the command
options.detail:
Attach is the verb for a process jet perf did not build. Today it takes a running pid and chooses how to watch it by what it offers. That is a browser relay, the runtime's live records, or, when the process publishes nothing, the outside sampler.

Under A it also takes a command after `--`. It starts the command and watches it for its whole life. A launched process is read through its browser relay or sampled from outside. Live records, zones and `alloc` need `--source`, which only the pid form takes. With no `--lens`, attach keeps today's CPU view; no `cpu` lens word is added.

Two lenses join it, both read from outside whatever the process publishes. `counts` gives the whole command's user-mode instructions and cycles, CPU time and peak memory. `syscalls` lists every system call with its process, arguments and result.

Following children is new work. Today jet_cli_perf_outside_family (Outside.jet:503) reads each thread's /proc `children` once, when sampling starts, at most 64 processes. A process started later is never sampled. `jet build` and `jet test` start their compile and link children later, so the command form must follow them as they start. The pid form keeps today's read: children started after the attach are missed, and this ballot leaves that.

The command's exit code is passed through. The pid form is unchanged. Its window is `--for=<duration>` (D-PERF-ATTACH-WINDOW1, ratified A, being built); until that lands it is a fixed second.

`jet perf test` is unchanged. It profiles the tests' own code from inside. `jet perf attach --lens=counts -- jet test x.jet` measures the whole command: compile, test binary and helpers. Those are two jobs, so nothing is spelled twice.

The compiler compiling Compiler, the compile-speed profile, stays on `jet perf run Compiler/JetCLI/run.jet -- build Compiler`. That runs the compiler from source under the inside engine, with phases and tasks. Attach of `jet build Compiler` is the quick look at an installed jet, for the whole run. It samples 1,000 times a second with frame-pointer stacks. It names functions from the image's symbols and declaration lines. Compile-time code counts as `unnamed`, and phases come from the package split.
options.technical:
Session.jet jet_cli_perf_attach: words after `--` are the command. It is spawned stopped, the engines open on its pid before it runs, then it runs.

New child following, with its costs. The outside sampler today opens per-thread task-clock events (x64_sampler_open) on the threads of the family read at open. The command form opens one sampling event per CPU with `inherit` on the stopped command instead. Inherited sampling events cannot keep today's per-thread ring, so samples arrive through one ring per CPU, tagged by pid and tid.

`counts` opens instructions:u and cycles:u with `inherit` before exec. Every thread and every child process then adds into one count, read once when the command ends. Counting needs no ring, so that inherit is cheap.

It gives the whole command's totals, not one row per process. With `inherit`, a child's count folds into its parent's at exit, and the counter reads only the sum. CPU time and peak memory come from the command's own reap (wait4). Its rusage folds in every descendant the command waited for. Its peak memory is the largest any one process reached, not a sum.

Per-process counts would need one counting event and ring per CPU (inherit_stat, with read, fork and exit records). Or they would need ptrace to follow every fork. This ballot offers neither; a later one may add them.

The pid form refuses `counts` and `syscalls` with E2102 (Jet.UnknownFlag), whose fix is the `--` form: a count or call list missing the start would mislead. The command form refuses `--for=`, `--source` and `--zones=` the same way.

Receipt delta. The `syscalls` section (JetPerfSyscalls) exists: `jet perf run` counts each host call by number and Jet stack (HostProcess.jet host_call). Its rows have no arguments, no pid and no result. Children and the compile are never seen. Runtime calls that bypass host_call are missed too. The command form fills the same section, adding `pid` to each row and a `calls` list: pid, tid, name, decoded arguments, result.

The bypass count. `git grep -c -E '^\s*[^/ ].*os_syscall_i64\(' f768b6597e -- Compiler/JetRuntime/Source` with HostProcess.jet and PerfSamples.jet excluded prints 153 lines in 30 files. It counts call lines only. Comment lines are excluded, and so are host_call itself and the perf hook. The definition is in Compiler/JetBackend/Source/OS/Linux.jet:390 (393 at f768b6597e), outside that path. The plain `git grep -c os_syscall_i64` there prints 180 lines in 33 files, comments included.

The `instructions` section (JetPerfInstructions) also exists. It keeps the sampled machine code, not run totals, so it is unchanged. One new section, `counts` (JetPerfCounts), holds the totals: `instructions_u`, `cycles_u`, `cpu_ns`, `wall_ns`, `peak_rss_bytes`, for the whole command.

Refusals. No new diagnostic code is needed. A kernel without counters makes `counts` `unavailable`, with the errno and the perf_event_paranoid level. The memory and topdown lenses already report a counter they cannot open this way. The memory lens prints `unavailable errno=N`; topdown prints `unavailable: <reason>` (Docs/Spec/observability.md:301, :576). The paranoid level appears today in the sampler's JSON and its reason (SourceSampling.jet:622, :651). `counts` adds it to its line.

A refused ptrace makes `syscalls` `unavailable`, with the errno and the Yama ptrace_scope. The command still runs. E2124 (Jet.AttachTargetNotObserved) keeps its meaning for the pid form alone. A refusal instead would need a new code. E2127 is free, but a new code needs its registry row, UI snapshot and diagnostics.md entry.
options.code:
$ jet perf attach --lens=counts -- jet build Compiler
counts instructions:u=81204417733 cycles:u=29511803012 cpu_ns=31877000000 peak_rss_bytes=5120000000
$ jet perf attach --lens=syscalls -- jet run main.jet
syscalls calls=412 processes=2
  4251 openat(AT_FDCWD, "main.jet", O_RDONLY|O_CLOEXEC) = 3
$ jet perf test hash_test.jet        # unchanged: the tests' code
$ jet perf run Compiler/JetCLI/run.jet -- build Compiler   # inside: the compiler's own phases

options.name: `jet perf run --exec`
options.detail:
`jet perf run` keeps its .jet form and gains `--exec`. Every word after it is the command. The engine, lenses, receipt and refusals are option A's: the outside sampler, `counts` and `syscalls`. That includes A's new work of following children the command starts later, with its costs. `jet perf attach` stays for running pids, missing children started after it attaches, as today.

`jet perf test` refuses `--exec`; `jet perf run --exec jet test x.jet` measures the whole command. For the compiler compiling Compiler, `jet perf run Compiler/JetCLI/run.jet -- build Compiler` stays the inside route. `jet perf run --exec jet build Compiler` is the outside one, with option A's detail and costs.
options.technical: Session.jet jet_cli_perf_session ends its flags at `--exec` and spawns the rest without `jet run --observe`, under the engines of option A. Run then takes targets it did not build, so it needs attach's per-process choice of how to watch (relay, live records or outside sampler), and both verbs carry that choice. Its traces come from the inside engine at 8,000 samples a second or from outside at 1,000. The receipt's `capture.sampling` names which. Outside sampling is reachable from both run and attach.
options.code:
$ jet perf run --lens=counts --exec jet build Compiler
$ jet perf run --lens=syscalls --exec .jet/build/hash data.bin
$ jet perf attach 4242

options.name: New verbs `stat` and `trace`
options.detail:
Like Linux `perf stat` and `strace`, `jet perf stat <command>` prints the counts and `jet perf trace <command>` the calls when the command ends. `--out` also writes a trace. The engine, receipt and refusals are option A's, including its new work of following children the command starts later, with its costs.

The perf family then has six verbs that run something: run, test, attach, stat, trace and view. `jet perf stat jet test x.jet` and `jet perf test x.jet` both measure a test run, from outside and from inside. The compiler-compiling-Compiler route is as in A.
options.technical: Two verbs join the perf family in the command registry. Each spawns its command under option A's engines and prints a text report on stderr. The CPU view of a launched command has no verb of its own in this option, so `jet perf attach` would still need a launch form for it.
options.code:
$ jet perf stat jet build Compiler
$ jet perf trace --calls=openat jet run main.jet

comparisons.note: `perf stat` and `perf trace` take a command; `-p` takes a running pid. https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man1/perf-stat.1.html
One tool takes a command or `-p` a pid, `-f` following children. https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man1/strace.1.html
One capture dialog either launches a program or attaches to a running one. https://superluminal.eu/docs/documentation.html
comparisons.code: Run > Launch Process... | Attach to Process...

recommendation.why: Attach already watches processes jet perf did not build, choosing how by what each one offers. Letting it start the process and follow its children covers the whole run with no new verb.
gains: Run and test watch what they build; attach watches what it did not build.
No new verb and no change to run or test.
Retires the listed perf stat, time and strace uses; two remain as named work.

losses.loss: Users of `perf stat` and `strace` may not look under attach.
losses.mitigation: `jet perf stat` and `jet perf trace` answer with the attach line to paste.

losses.loss: Following children started later is new engine work with costs.
losses.mitigation: Counts follow children cheaply. The CPU view costs a buffer per CPU; ptrace runs only under `syscalls`.

whyNot.reason: B makes run take targets it did not build, so run and attach both carry the choice of how to watch.
C adds two verbs, and `jet perf stat jet test` overlaps `jet perf test`.

recommendation.tradeoff: Attach's name stretches to a process it starts; each verb keeps one rule.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Census: git grep on f768b6597e, re-checked on 97d2a287ab, with Docs and Tower excluded. Every option retires the same rows: all three use the same counting and tracing code.

Retired by `counts`, each matching its old figure within 1% on one revision. Wall time is the command's run window (`wall_ns`), and the exit status is the command's own. Tools/Perf/CompileThroughput/Throughput.jet runs perf stat (Throughput.jet:680). Its --batch form does not run GNU time -v itself. It reads time.txt, which the batch build harness outside the repository writes (Throughput.jet:93-98, :1255-1268). So retiring time -v there changes that harness as well.

Tools/Gauntlet/Harness/run.mjs runs perf stat cycles:u over the process tree, named in standings.mjs and measurement-manifest.json. Tools/Perf/AsmParity runs perf stat in AsmParity.mjs and run.jet. Tools/Release/Admit.jet runs perf stat in the speed gate.

Also retired by `counts`: Tools/Perf/Selfhost/Run.mjs runs /usr/bin/time. Tools/Perf/HelloCompile/Bench.py, Tools/Perf/JetcProfile/Startup/run.jet and Tools/Perf/UnicodeLiteral/Run.jet run time -v.

Retired by `syscalls`, each checking the same facts from `jet perf view --json`. The strace cases are CLICompilerSpeed (two), ControlAndData, Report, TaskgroupStack and JetpackJetOS (two). Tools/Perf/CoreStrace/run.jet takes its strace -c table from the section's per-name totals. Tools/Perf/StdoutBuffer/run.sh counts write and writev.

Partly: Tools/Perf/Scaling (Profile.mjs, Gate/Source/Profile.jet) uses perf record and perf script for timed samples by phase. Outside samples carry no time today (X64Samples: thread, depth, frames). So it moves to the inside route, `jet perf run Compiler/JetCLI/run.jet`.

Not this ballot. Jetpack/CLI/Source/Jobs/AccessTrace.jet runs strace for the cached-job access proof, and Jetpack/CLI/Tests/JobRunner.jet:122 tests it. It is product code that would call the ptrace engine as a library, so it needs its own card row. Tools/Perf/ReadInto (Memory.jet, memory.mjs) runs gdb at exit, #6995 c15.

Kept as named comparisons under #6995 c1's allowlist. Tools/Perf/DebugLatency compares with lldb. Tests/Cases/ToolInterop reads Jet output in lldb (four cases) and perf record and report (one). Tools/Perf/Scriptbench runs hyperfine, a peer timing harness. The dev shell (flake.nix) keeps perf and lldb only for those.

Further cases: counters unavailable (the PerfRun NoCounters seccomp seam), ptrace refused, the exit code passed through, a child left running, and the refused `jet perf stat` hint.

Fixtures that stand in for `perf` move with their tools. AsmParity's is Tools/Gauntlet/Entries/AsmParity/Fixtures/fake-perf. Scaling's is ScalingProfile/Fixtures/fake-perf in the same tree, named in ScalingProfile/entry.json.

JetpackJetOS's strace rows retire only once `syscalls` decodes the whole file class, which the detail names. Its case nixos_migration_protects_stage_before_writing_inputs.case runs `strace -f -s 4096 -e trace=%file` (lines 8-24).

decisions.title: How long `jet perf attach` samples a process that publishes nothing
decisions.situation: `jet perf attach <pid>` with no `--source` samples from outside, by the kernel's task clock, for a fixed second. The window is JET_CLI_PERF_OUTSIDE_WINDOW_MS in Compiler/JetCLI/Source/CLI/Perf/Outside.jet. The compiler profile JetcProfile sampled for as many seconds as it was given, 20 by default, before it moved to attach. A second of a compiler's run is about 1000 samples per busy thread. That is too few to split a long check by phase or to read a flame graph's narrow towers. You decide how the user sets the window. We recommend a `--for=<duration>` flag, the duration written as `--zones=` already writes one.
decisions.gist: How does the user say how long an outside attach samples?
decisions.lesson: An outside attach reads nothing the program publishes. The kernel interrupts each of its threads once per millisecond of CPU time and records the stack, and jet names the frames from the program's own executable. More time means more samples. The error of a share falls with the square root of the count: about 3 points at 1000 samples and about 1 point at 10,000.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: `jet perf attach 4242` samples for one second, as it does today. `jet perf attach 4242 --for=10s` samples for ten. The attach ends early if the process exits, and the trace says so.

Expert path: the window goes in the `functions` section as `window_ms`, and `jet perf view` prints it. The value is checked like `--zones=`: a whole number of `ms` or `s`, at least 1 ms, at most 10 minutes. `--for=` with `--source` is refused, since a published flight ring is read at once and `--zones=` is that path's window.
decisions.story: A user's `jet check` of the compiler takes 40 seconds, and they want to know which phase holds it. They start it and run `jet perf attach $(pgrep -n jet) --for=20s`. They get 20,000 samples split by package (JetSema 46%, JetIR 31%, JetBackend 12%), with a flame graph of the same window.
decisions.inWild:
# Linux perf: the window is the command it runs beside the process.
perf record -g -p 4242 -- sleep 20

# Go: the window is a query parameter.
curl -o cpu.pprof 'localhost:6060/debug/pprof/profile?seconds=20'

# py-spy: an explicit duration flag.
py-spy record --pid 4242 --duration 20
decisions.detail: Code read on dev 6c1c887a39. Session.jet jet_cli_perf_attach takes `--zones=<duration>` through jet_cli_perf_attach_window, which accepts `500ms` and `2s`. Outside.jet jet_cli_perf_outside_sample(pid, window_ms) already takes the window as a parameter; only its caller fixes it at 1000. No other attach path samples over time: the flight ring and the heap snapshot are read once, and the zones window has its own flag.

options.name: `--for=<duration>`
options.detail: `jet perf attach <pid> --for=20s` samples for 20 seconds. Without it the window stays one second. The duration is written as `--zones=` writes one.
options.technical: jet_cli_perf_attach parses `--for=` with jet_cli_perf_attach_window and passes it to jet_cli_perf_outside_sample. With `--source` it is refused (E2102 family, naming `--zones=`). The receipt section keeps `window_ms`, and the view prints it.
options.code:
$ jet perf attach 4242 --for=20s
functions samples=19874 processes=2 threads=9 window_ms=20000 lost=0 unnamed=12
  phases: JetSema 46.1%  JetIR 31.0%  JetBackend 12.4%  ...
Trace: .jet/perf/20261120-1530-4242.jettrace

options.name: Sample until the process exits or Ctrl-C
options.detail: There is no flag. An outside attach samples until the process exits or the user presses Ctrl-C, as `perf record -p` does.
options.technical: jet_cli_perf_outside_sample loops until /proc/<pid> is gone or SIGINT arrives. A script or a test that wants a bounded window has to send the signal itself or wrap the attach in `timeout`.
options.code:
$ jet perf attach 4242
Sampling 4242 until it exits; Ctrl-C ends the window.
^C
functions samples=20311 processes=2 threads=9 window_ms=20431 lost=0 unnamed=12

comparisons.note: The CPU profile endpoint takes `seconds=N` and defaults to 30. This is A's shape.
`record --duration N` bounds the window; without it the tool records until Ctrl-C. This is A's flag with B's default.
`perf record -p` samples until Ctrl-C or until a command run beside it ends. This is B's shape.

recommendation.why: A window is a number the user knows before starting, and scripts, tests and the compiler profile need a bounded one. A adds one flag that writes a duration the way `--zones=` already does, and today's one-second default is unchanged.
gains: `jet perf attach <pid> --for=20s` gives a compiler profile JetcProfile's 20-second window, with nothing but jet.
A case or a script bounds the window without signals.
The trace records the window it asked for and the one it got.

losses.loss: One more flag on `jet perf attach`.
losses.mitigation: It applies only to the outside sampler and is refused elsewhere with a fix that names `--zones=`.

whyNot.reason: An unbounded window needs a signal to end. A test or a script cannot rely on one, and a long-running server would be sampled until someone remembered it.

recommendation.tradeoff: One flag for a bounded, scriptable window.

decisions.checkInstructions: Under A: the case Perf/attach_gives_the_jetcprofile_facts (#6995 c22) attaches to a busy `jet check` with `--for=3s`. It reads window_ms=3000 with more than 1000 samples. `--for=3s --source x.jet` is refused, naming `--zones=`. Under B: the case ends the attach by its target exiting.

decisions.title: What context.thread reads in Jet code that runs outside the task pool
decisions.situation: Jet code can ask which thread it runs on by reading context.thread: 0 is the main thread, and 1 up are the task pool's threads. Programs use that number to give each thread its own slot in a list, such as one counter per thread. A Ctrl-C handler and a realtime audio callback run on threads of their own, outside the pool, so the vote decides what they read. We recommend -1, which keeps pool numbers within the list and makes a missed check stop at the bad index.
decisions.gist: What should context.thread read in Jet code that runs outside the task pool?
decisions.lesson: context.thread numbers threads: 0 is the main thread, and 1 up are the task pool's threads. A Ctrl-C handler and a realtime callback run on threads of their own. C callbacks are settled already: they cannot read the context. Under every option, handlers stay on their own thread, so Ctrl-C still works while every pool thread is busy.
decisions.story: A program keeps one hit counter per thread in a list sized for main plus the pool. It adds a Ctrl-C handler that counts too. The handler's number came from start order, so it landed past the list's end and the program stopped.

options.name: Outside threads read -1
options.detail:
Only the main thread (0) and the pool's threads (1 up, dense, in start order) get numbers. Any other thread that runs Jet code reads -1. Those are the Ctrl-C dispatcher that runs on_interrupt handlers, and a realtime stream's callback thread. Threads the runtime starts for its own work, such as the timer and the poller, run no Jet code.

Beginner path: read context.thread in tasks; a handler checks for -1 or keeps its own variable. Expert path: size the list for the pool plus 2 and index context.thread + 1. Slot 0 is then shared by every outside thread, so guard it with an atomic or a lock.

The program prints `main counted 1, task on 1`, and Ctrl-C prints `handler on thread -1`.
options.technical:
Built as the interim by the context-thread numbering fix. The main thread claims 0 once, and each pool carrier takes the lowest free index from 1 under the scheduler lock. Every other thread starts at -1. A missed check was probed on gate p382: counts[-1] stops with Jet.ArithmeticOrBoundsFailure "position -1 doesn't exist" and shows at = -1.

Interrupt handlers stay on the dispatcher thread under every option. Each handler runs under its own stop boundary, and a stop's report goes to stderr while later handlers still run. After the last handler, the first stopped handler's exit code ends the process; process.exit ends it at once.

A move onto the pool was weighed and dropped. The dispatcher would join each handler as a task, and a join that finds its task unstarted runs it on the joining thread. A busy pool would also delay Ctrl-C.

Lending outside threads the next number above the pool was dropped too. A lent number overflows a list sized for the pool. The pool's numbers also stop being dense once it grows past a lent one.

Each option's program passes jet check and jet fmt --check on the p380 compiler. Option C was checked through a stand-in function returning Int?.

options.name: A second count, downward
options.detail: Pool numbers stay as in A. Each outside thread that runs Jet code takes the next number of a second count: -1, -2, -3, freed when the thread ends. A handler and a stream started later read -1 and -2. Beginner path: the same check as A, since every outside number is negative. Expert path: a second list indexed by -thread - 1, sized by the number of handlers and streams the program starts.
options.technical: Needs a second lowest-free allocator under the scheduler lock for outside threads that run user code. It also needs a way to tell those threads from the runtime's own helpers when they start.

options.name: An optional number
options.detail: context.thread becomes Int?, as context.deadline already is: Val(i) on main and pool threads, None on any other thread. Indexing a list needs an unwrap first, so a missed check is a compile error. Beginner path: write `at: context.thread ?? return` and index with at. Expert path: the same; a fallback such as ?? 0 compiles too, and then sends outside threads to the main thread's slot.
options.technical: Changes the field's type in the checker's context row and the runtime read, where -1 becomes None. Every existing read migrates: the context examples and the Context, NestedJoin, HTTP and WebApp test fixtures. The compile-time build-root read becomes Val(0).

comparisons.note: current_thread_index() returns Some(index) on a pool worker, stable for the thread's life, and None on any other thread. https://docs.rs/rayon/latest/rayon/fn.current_thread_index.html
thread::current().id() is an opaque ThreadId, unique and never reused, but no list index. https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/thread/struct.ThreadId.html
Go gives goroutines no ID on purpose, so code cannot key state on the thread. https://go.dev/doc/faq#no_goroutine_id
comparisons.code: // no goroutine or thread index; pass state in explicitly

comparisons.note: Thread.threadId() (getId() before Java 19) is unique per thread for its life but not dense, so it does not index a list. https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/Thread.html#threadId()
omp_get_thread_num() is 0..team size - 1 inside a parallel region and 0 outside one. https://www.openmp.org/spec-html/5.0/openmpsu113.html

recommendation.why: Pool numbers stay small and dense, so per-thread lists fit. Outside threads are rare and get one plain marker, and a missed check stops loudly at the bad index.
gains: A list sized for main plus the pool always fits.

losses.loss: Code that indexes a list must check for -1 first.
losses.mitigation: A missed check stops with "position -1 doesn't exist" and shows at = -1, so the fix is plain.

whyNot.reason: B adds a second list and negative indexes for threads few programs have.
C makes a missed check a compile error, but every pool task unwraps a None it never sees, and a quick ?? 0 hides outside threads in main's slot.

recommendation.tradeoff: A missed check is caught when it runs, not when it compiles; in return, the common read in pool tasks stays a plain Int.

surface.lesson: context.thread numbers threads: 0 is the main thread, and 1 up are the task pool's threads. A Ctrl-C handler and a realtime callback run on threads of their own. C callbacks are settled already: they cannot read the context. Under every option, handlers stay on their own thread, so Ctrl-C still works while every pool thread is busy.

current.note: Before the interim fix, a handler's number came from start order and could land past the list. The interim build reads -1, which stops at the list.

wild.note: Rayon's current_thread_index() is Some(i) on a pool worker and None on any other thread. Source: https://docs.rs/rayon/latest/rayon/fn.current_thread_index.html

options.gist: Only main and pool threads get numbers; any other thread reads -1.
gains: Numbers stay within main plus the pool, so lists fit.
A missed check stops at the bad index, naming -1.
Already built as the interim; reads stay a plain Int.
losses: Code that indexes a list must check for -1 first.

options.name: A second count, downward
options.gist: Each outside thread gets its own number: -1, -2, and so on.
gains: Each outside thread can keep state of its own.

losses: A second list, sized by outside threads nobody can count ahead.
