decisions.title: How Jet's own tools list a built program's symbols, segments and code without running it
decisions.situation: A built program is a file of named pieces of code and data, called symbols, laid out in memory blocks called segments. Jet's tests and speed tools check that file: a hot loop keeps its locked count updates, a feature adds no code when it is off. Today they ask the outside tools objdump, nm and readelf, which Jet's rules allow only as a recorded stopgap. You decide where Jet itself lists a program's symbols, segments and code without running it. We recommend that the jet debug console answer these from the file, before it starts the program, with a one-line form for scripts.
decisions.gist: Where should Jet list a built program's symbols, segments and code, without running it?
decisions.lesson: A symbol names a function or a data word in the program file. A segment is a block the system loads, such as the code block. The jet debug console lists code with disas, but only after it starts the program. It cannot list symbols or segments. Under every option, the listing reads the file and runs nothing.
decisions.story: A contributor changes how reference counts are updated. Their test must prove a multi-threaded program still uses the locked form. The test machine has no objdump, so the test is skipped there and the change lands unchecked.

options.name: The debugger answers from the file first
options.detail:
jet debug IMAGE reads the file before anything starts. symbols, segments and disas NAME answer from the file alone. A command that needs a running program, such as continue, bt or locals, starts it first. It then stops at the first line, as today. An interactive session looks the same as today: it still starts the program and stops at the first line.

New surface: the console words symbols and segments, and the repeatable flag --do 'COMMAND'. With --do, jet debug runs each command in order and exits. It prints only their output: no prompts, and no stop banner unless a command starts the program. The exit code is 0, or 1 when a command is refused or the program ends badly. The same words work at a stop and in a crash dump. disas rows keep disas's format.

symbols prints one row per defined symbol, in address order, then name order. Each row holds the address in hex (a column of 20), the size in bytes (a column of 10), the kind and the name. The kind is function, object, thread, label or other, in a column of 10. segments prints one row per program header, in file order. Each row holds the type, then offset, address, file, memory, flags and align, each named. Tests parse these rows, so columns change only with a decision.

Stripped images: symbols come from the side debug file the image names when it keeps none. With neither, symbols prints `IMAGE` keeps no symbol table and exits 0. disas NAME then prints No function `NAME`. Plain disas of the whole code lists each executable segment whole, as segment 0, segment 1, and so on.

Beginner path: jet debug IMAGE --do 'disas NAME'. Expert path: --do symbols to find a specialized name, then --do 'disas THAT'.
options.technical:
Not built yet. The reader and rows exist in the held filing Errors3202-image-list (Compiler/JetDebug/Source/NativeImageList.jet). It reads the ELF symbol table, the .gnu_debuglink side file and the program headers. It builds code rows with NativeListing.jet, the same builder disas uses. A file-only session is the crash dump's session over the image's own bytes (NativeDump.jet), so the commands join NATIVE_DEBUG_HELP and NATIVE_DUMP_HELP. The process starts lazily on the first command that needs one.

Today, probed on gate p383 with Tests/Cases/SingleThreadRc/AReachableTaskSpawnKeepsCountsLocked.fixture: piping disas then quit into jet debug IMAGE starts the program and stops at entry. It then lists entry with its three lock inc rows. disas main.run__entry prints No function; symbol lookup is D-DISASM1's ratified expert path and lands without this decision.

Users moved: CodegenCeiling, the Perf zone cases and hot.sh, AllocatorFamilies (symbols, segments, disas NAME). SingleThreadRc x6 and SimdWitness move to piped disas sessions now.
options.code:
// Not built. Segment sizes are illustrative.
$ jet debug .jet/build/main --do segments --do 'disas nosuch'
LOAD         offset 0x3000      address 0x402000            file 412160    memory 412160    flags r-x align 4096
No function `nosuch`
$ jet debug stripped --do symbols
`stripped` keeps no symbol table

options.name: A listing mode of jet debug
options.detail: jet debug --listing=symbols|segments|code|code:NAME IMAGE reads the built program, prints, then exits 0. It never starts the program and has no console. code:NAME lists what disas NAME lists. The output contract and stripped-image rows are A's.
options.technical: Built in the held filing Errors3202-image-list (base 5a72afd74a). Parity: Tools/Perf/CodegenCeiling.jet --check on the listing matched all 9 golden rows, and --update left golden.tsv byte-identical. The symbol, function and source columns of its listing file matched the objdump-made file.
options.code:
// Segment sizes are illustrative.
$ jet debug --listing=segments .jet/build/main
LOAD         offset 0x3000      address 0x402000            file 412160    memory 412160    flags r-x align 4096
$ jet debug --listing=code:nosuch .jet/build/main
No function `nosuch`

options.name: A new jet inspect image command
options.detail: jet inspect image IMAGE [--symbols|--segments|--code NAME] reads the file and prints A's rows. jet debug keeps disas for stops only.
options.technical: A new InspectPlane action in Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/Registry/CLICommands.jet, calling the same reader and listing builder. jet inspect build reads source targets today and refuses a program file as not UTF-8 (probed on gate p383).

comparisons.note: target create loads a file without starting it; image dump symtab and image dump sections list it, and disassemble -n lists a function. -b with -o runs commands and exits. This is A's shape.
gdb -batch -ex runs info functions, maint info sections and disassemble on a file it never starts, and starts it only on run. Also A's shape.
nm lists symbols, readelf -l segments, objdump -d code: three tools, each file-only, one command per view. This is B's and C's shape.
go tool nm and go tool objdump list a built binary's symbols and code through the toolchain itself, apart from its debugger, Delve. C's shape.
comparisons.code:
$ go tool nm ./main
$ go tool objdump -s main.main ./main

recommendation.why: A keeps one console with one set of words for a file, a stop and a crash dump, as lldb and gdb do. Its script form also drives stops, which no other option offers.
gains: Tests and speed tools drop objdump, nm and readelf.

losses.loss: Commands that need a running program must start it first.
losses.mitigation: Such a command starts the program itself and stops at its first line, as jet debug does today.

whyNot.reason: B is smaller, but it spells disas a second way and leaves scripted stops to piped input.
C splits code listings across two commands, which the machine code decision chose not to do.

recommendation.tradeoff: A adds two console words and a flag where B adds one flag; in return, files, stops and dumps share one console.

decisions.title: How Jet's own tools show a counting allocator's totals when a program ends
decisions.situation: A program can count its memory use with allocator: mem.Counting.over(mem.Heap). The runtime keeps the number of allocations and the most bytes live at once. Nothing shows those totals when the program ends. Jet's read_into memory check stops the program at its end in gdb and reads the totals from memory, which Jet's rules allow only as a recorded stopgap. You decide which Jet tool shows the totals instead. We recommend that jet debug show them when it stops at the program's end.
decisions.gist: Which Jet tool should show a counting allocator's totals when the program ends?
decisions.lesson: A counting allocator keeps three totals: allocations made, bytes asked for, and the most bytes live at once, called the high water. They live in the program's memory and vanish when it ends. Under every option, the totals are the runtime's own counts.
decisions.story: A contributor makes reading from a socket allocate less. The memory check must show fewer allocations per read. The test machine has no gdb, so the check cannot run there, and the gain goes unmeasured.

options.name: jet debug shows them at the program's end
options.detail: When the program's allocator counts, jet debug stops it at its end, before it is gone, whatever its exit status. The end report gains one line, Allocator: counting, N allocations, high water N bytes, ahead of Program finished. A program without a counting allocator shows no such line. The memory check builds each arm at -O2 with the counting allocator, runs it under jet debug, and reads that line. It pipes continue and quit today, and uses D-DEBUG-LISTING1's --do once that lands.
options.technical: Not built. Today jet debug pauses at a nonzero exit only; a zero exit is reported after the process is gone (Native.jet, Program finished). The memory check measures each arm's -O2 build. D-PERF-TARGET1 decides how jet perf run names a built program; with it, B runs that build directly, as shown here with its option A spelling. Without it, jet perf run needs a new -O flag.
options.technical: Receipt rows are an existing named list that the view prints and compare diffs (Command.jet, jet_cli_perf_receipt_lines). The new part is the row's fields. Today jet perf run builds its own way. Probe of the same counted surface arm: an -O2 build made 17,389 to 18,084 allocations with a high water of 148,640 to 152,664 bytes. Under jet perf run it made 82,761 to 83,299, high water 85,880 to 88,584.

options.name: The program prints its own totals
options.detail: Core's mem module gains program_allocator_totals, which returns the allocations, bytes asked for, live bytes and high water. Any program can call it in any run, with no tool and no ptrace, so a server can report its own memory in production. The memory check adds a print of them to the end of each arm's run, then reads it.
options.technical: The runtime already keeps the totals behind a private export (Alloc.jet, jet_rt_program_allocator_fact). A Core call wraps it. Printing at the end of run misses any allocation during teardown, which gdb at exit counts.

comparisons.note: catch syscall exit_group stops a program at its end, before it is gone, so its memory can still be read. This is A's shape.

runtime.ReadMemStats lets a program read its own allocation counts. This is C's shape.

runtime.ReadMemStats(&stats)

whyNot.reason: B needs a new build flag on jet perf run, and the profiler's own work may change the counts.

decisions.title: One shape for a compiler error in every machine-readable output
decisions.situation: When Jet finds a mistake in a program, it describes it for tools as a record: code, message, location, file and the exact text it read. Today three outputs build that record with separate code, and their fields have drifted. For one `x++` error in main.jet, `jet inspect compiler parse` gives a repair but no file in the span. `jet inspect compiler check` gives the file but no repair. `jet check --json` gives a graded repair, calls the message `what`, and never says which text it read. A tool that merges them must special-case each command. We recommend one record, written in one place, that carries its graded repairs, so no output loses information.
decisions.gist: Should every machine-readable compiler error be one record, written in one place, with its graded repairs inside?
decisions.lesson: A compiler diagnostic is Jet's record of one problem in a program. Jet code reads it as a CompilerDiagnostic value. `jet inspect compiler` prints that value as JSON. `jet check --json` prints a report with more members. The editor protocol converts at the edge. The vote decides whether the value and the report are one record, and whether repairs belong to it.
decisions.story: A build script runs `jet inspect compiler parse`, `jet inspect compiler check` and `jet check --json` on main.jet and merges errors by location. The same `x++` error arrives three times, each with different fields. One has a repair and no file in its span, one has the file and no repair, and one calls its message `what`. The script reports the error three times. It can't tell whether main.jet changed between the commands.

options.name: One record with its graded repairs
options.detail:
The typed CompilerDiagnostic is the one record. It gains `fix_edits`: every repair the compiler knows, each with its safety grade. One writer prints it in `jet inspect compiler lex`, `parse` and `check`. The same writer prints the first members of each `jet check --json` report.

A file the command read is named in `span.file` and `origin.path`, such as "main.jet". Text that Jet code hands to `compiler.check` names no file: `span.file` is "" and `origin.path` is null. The digest is always the SHA-256 of the exact bytes checked.

Beginner path: read `code`, `message`, `span` and `fix_edits` from any output; they mean the same everywhere. Expert path: match reports across commands by `origin.source_digest`, and apply only the repair grades you accept.
options.technical:
The record moves to version 3: JET_COMPILER_SERVICES_SCHEMA_VERSION goes from 2 to 3 (Compiler/JetEval/Source/CompilerServices.jet:186). Its Jet types:

```jet
CompilerDiagnostic: struct {
    code: String, severity: String, message: String, why: String, fix: String,
    span: SourceSpan?, origin: CompilerDiagnosticOrigin?,
    fix_edits: [CompilerFixEdit],
}
CompilerFixEdit: struct { span: SourceSpan, new_text: String, safety: String }
```

`safety` is one of the report's words: formatting, behavior-preserving, api-changing, target-changing or needs-review (Compiler/JetCLI/Source/CLI/Report.jet:165). Each edit's `span.file` names its own file. The rows go in CoreRecordRows.jet and the sema host-value lists.

One writer: `jet_eval_compiler_services_diagnostic_value` (CompilerServices.jet:296). The hand-written inspect writer is deleted (Compiler/JetCLI/Source/CLI/Inspect.jet:1065-1095). Every inspect path prints the value through `jet_cli_compiler_checked_value` (InspectCompiler.jet:54).

The report moves from jet.report/v3 to jet.report/v4 (Report.jet:31). `jet_cli_report_json_with` (Report.jet:401) prints the record through the same writer, then appends the declared report extension. jet.report/v4 means CompilerDiagnostic version 3 plus that extension, so one string names both. Member by member:

```text
stay      code, why, fix
stay      severity: error | lint (the record's words)
renamed   what -> message
moved     file -> span.file
moved     fix_edits -> into the record; fix_edits[].file -> fix_edits[].span.file
added     origin {path, source_digest}
extension schema, moment, name, applicability, detail, denial_kind, call_chain,
          scope_chain, nearest_granting_scope, line, col, no_fix_reason, cause,
          labels, clears, reason, operation, expected, actual, build_error
extension tier: warning | tidy, on a lint (v3 spelled it in severity)
```

The language server builds its protocol diagnostic from the internal `Diagnostic`, not from the record (Compiler/JetLSP/Source/LSP/Diagnostics.jet:118). It recomputes severity (:119), the URI (:83-91) and the range from the held text (:121, :219). It reads causes for relatedInformation (:150).

Under A, the server converts the record and the extension's `cause` at the edge. Severity comes from `severity` and `tier`. The URI comes from `origin.path` against the checked root. The range comes from `span` over the text whose SHA-256 is `origin.source_digest`.

Multi-file: a cause in another file carries its own span and origin, in the report and as LSP relatedInformation. A repair in another file names it in its own `span.file`. Nothing borrows the primary's file.

No span: `span` and `origin` are null. The report then has no `file`; today it inherits the batch file, which D-BIG-DIAGORIGIN1 forbids. `line` and `col` are null. The LSP places it over the whole document, as today (:122).

Changed file: the digest comes once from the bytes the check held, never from a re-read. A consumer whose current text hashes differently knows the report is stale. The LSP already publishes a version only when the open text equals the checked text (:217, :175); A keys that test by digest.

Package-model schemas are untouched. Proof cases assert one field set across Jet code, inspect lex, parse and check, the v4 report and LSP routing, for a read file and for handed text.

options.name: One record, repairs stay in the report
options.detail:
The typed CompilerDiagnostic stays at version 2 and is the one record. One writer prints it in `jet inspect compiler lex`, `parse` and `check`, and as the first members of each `jet check --json` report. A file the command read is named, such as "main.jet". Text handed at compile time names none: "" and null.

Repairs stay a report-only member, so inspect lex and parse lose their `edit`.

Beginner path: read `code`, `message` and `span` from any output. Expert path: match by `origin.source_digest`, and take repairs from the check report.
options.technical:
One writer as in A, without `fix_edits` in the record. The typed version stays 2. The report moves from jet.report/v3 to v4 (Report.jet:31), meaning CompilerDiagnostic version 2 plus the report extension. Member by member:

```text
stay      code, why, fix
stay      severity: error | lint
renamed   what -> message
moved     file -> span.file
added     origin {path, source_digest}
extension fix_edits (each item's file moves into its span.file)
extension every extension member A lists, and tier
```

The LSP fix and the edge cases are as in A, except that repairs are not in the record.

options.name: Keep separate writers
options.detail:
Each output keeps its own writer. Inspect lex and parse, and a check that fails early, print a span without `file`, plus `edit`. A checked result prints the typed value with the file and no repair. `jet check --json` keeps v3: `what`, a top-level `file`, graded `fix_edits`, and no digest.

Beginner path: learn which command prints which fields. Expert path: merge outputs with per-command rules.
options.technical: Leaves Inspect.jet:1065-1095 beside InspectCompiler.jet:54. Report.jet:401 stays its own encoder at jet.report/v3. The LSP keeps converting from the internal Diagnostic.

comparisons.note: --error-format=json prints one Diagnostic record type for every consumer. Suggestions ride in the span with an applicability grade. https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustc/json.html
tsc and tsserver both start from one ts.Diagnostic record; the editor protocol converts it at the edge. https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/wiki/Using-the-Compiler-API
comparisons.code:
const d: ts.Diagnostic = program.getSemanticDiagnostics()[0];
console.log(d.file?.fileName, d.start, d.length, d.code);

comparisons.note: An analyzer reports one Diagnostic whose SuggestedFixes carry their TextEdits; gopls converts it at the edge. https://pkg.go.dev/golang.org/x/tools/go/analysis#Diagnostic
comparisons.code:
pass.Report(analysis.Diagnostic{Pos: pos, End: end, Message: msg,
    SuggestedFixes: []analysis.SuggestedFix{{TextEdits: edits}}})

recommendation.why: One writer can't drift from itself, and the ratified origin record becomes the one origin every output names. Only A loses no information and leaves no ungraded repair.
gains: A new record field appears in every output at once.

losses.loss: Jet callers move to version 3; report readers move to v4.
losses.mitigation: Version 3 only adds `fix_edits`. Every report rename is listed, and the schema string names the shape.

whyNot.reason: B reaches one record but drops the repair from inspect lex and parse.
C keeps three shapes and a report that can't name its text.

recommendation.tradeoff: Jet callers and report readers each take one version step. In return, every output prints one record with its graded repairs.

decisions.title: What the 2% profiling-cost promise covers at 8,000 samples a second
decisions.situation: A sampling profiler stops a program thousands of times a second to see where it is, and each stop costs a little CPU time. Jet promises its profiler costs under 2% of the program's CPU time at the default 8,000 samples a second with whole call stacks. On a quiet machine it costs 1.74%; on a busy test machine it cost 2.2% to 3.3%, so the test failed five suites in a row. About three quarters of that cost is the Linux kernel's own work for each sample, and no design we measured got it under 2% on a busy machine. You are asked what the promise should cover. We recommend it cover Jet's own share, under 1%, and that every profile print the kernel's share beside it.
decisions.gist: At 8,000 samples a second, profiling costs a busy machine over 2%, mostly in the kernel. What should Jet's promise cover?
decisions.lesson: A sampling profiler stops a program thousands of times a second to note where it is. Each stop costs CPU time. Part is Jet's own code, which collects the samples. Part is the Linux kernel's, which takes each stop and walks the call stack. Jet controls only the first part.
decisions.story: Dana profiles a service on the team's CI box while other builds run. The profile is right, but the receipt says sampling cost 2.7%, over the 2% Jet promised. She cannot tell whether Jet got slower or the box was busy.
decisions.inWild:
$ perf record -F 8000 -g ./burn
# perf reports no cost of its own; when the sampling interrupt runs long the kernel logs
# "perf: interrupt took too long (10658 > 10533), lowering kernel.perf_event_max_sample_rate to 18000"
# (seen in this machine's journal, Nov 16-19)

options.name: Promise Jet's share, show the kernel's
options.detail:
Nothing changes in how you profile. `jet perf run` still samples 8,000 times a second with whole stacks. The receipt keeps its total, overhead_ns. It adds two parts that sum to it exactly. overhead_runtime_ns is what Jet's runtime spent, measured: its handlers, its ring drains and the signals it asked for. overhead_kernel_ns is the kernel's time taking and writing the samples, estimated from timed samples.

`jet perf view` prints both as shares of the CPU time sampled: `overhead=measured runtime=0.54% kernel=1.42%`. The promise becomes: Jet's share stays under 1% at the default rate. The kernel's share has no bar, but it is always shown.

The kernel's estimate is not yet validated against a direct timing on the same runs. On similar runs it read lower than the probe's direct timing. Quiet, it charged 1.85 us a sample against the probe's 2.3 us. Busy, it charged 1.7 to 2.7 us against 2.4 to 4.0 us. Those were different programs and runs, so the share may read low.

Beginner path: run `jet perf run` and `jet perf view` as today. The profile line says what the profile cost and who paid. Expert path: read the two fields from the .jettrace JSON. overhead_kernel_ns over the sample count gives the kernel's estimated nanoseconds per sample on that machine.
options.technical:
Receipt: the profile section of every .jettrace, attach traces included (SourceSampling.jet). overhead_runtime_ns = handler_ns + signals x delivery_ns. Under a perf event the drain timer's signals are already inside handler_ns. overhead_kernel_ns = ring_ns, the PERF_SAMPLES_RING_PS tally, an estimate. Each drained sample is charged the median of the last five kernel timings plus its callchain entries. overhead_ns is their sum, unchanged in meaning.

Under the CPU-timer sampler (no perf event) overhead_kernel_ns is 0. Both fields are absent exactly when overhead_ns is (overhead_status not_measured). overhead_reason keeps its text, and no other field changes.

The case Perf/receipt_reports_measured_overhead asserts five lines. overhead_status is "measured". overhead_runtime_ns is at least 1 and at most 20000000, 1% of the 2 s sampled. overhead_kernel_ns is at least 0. overhead_ns equals the two parts' sum, by captures. overhead_reason still names its share.

Basis: Jet's share was 4.8 ms quiet and 9.7 to 12.0 ms in three runs at load 163 to 166. So the 1% bar leaves 1.7x headroom over the worst run seen.

Criteria: c44(d) would read: "Every receipt states the overhead in two parts, the runtime's share measured and the kernel's estimated from timed samples. The runtime's share is under 1% on fib at the default rate." c68's last sentence follows c44(d). c105 closes when the case passes three suites in a row.

options.name: One looser total
options.detail:
Nothing changes in the receipt or the tools. The promise moves from 2% to 4% of the CPU time sampled at the default rate. Quiet machines still show about 1.7%.

Beginner and expert paths are as today: one total in the receipt, and its parts only in the reason's text.
options.technical: The case's bar becomes overhead_ns <= 80000000, 4% of 2 s; its other lines stay. Basis: p387 to p391 gave 62641683, 58226414, 43276664, 66153400 and 50262488 ns. Three runs at load about 165 gave 39169587, 53652503 and 54463836 ns. The worst, 66.2 ms or 3.3%, leaves 1.2x headroom. c44(d) and c68 read 4% for 2%.

options.name: Slow down when the machine is busy
options.detail:
The runtime keeps the total under 2% itself. When the measured cost per sample would pass 2% at 8,000 a second, it spaces the samples out just enough. When the machine calms down, it speeds back up. The receipt states the rate used and why. Each sample then stands for more CPU time, and the profile weighs it so.

Beginner path: nothing to set; the profile line says when the rate was lowered. Expert path: read rate_status and rate_reason, and each sample's count in the samples file.
options.technical:
Every 1024 drains the runtime recalibrates and sets the sampling period. The period is 125 us, or fifty times the measured cost of one sample (kernel plus runtime) when that is longer. It applies the period to every live sampler with PERF_EVENT_IOC_PERIOD. Each sample's weight is its period, read from its count word (the stack-id samples format).

Receipt: new rate_status ("held" or "lowered") and rate_reason fields; capture.sampling.interval_us becomes the mean period. The case keeps overhead_ns <= 40000000 and asserts rate_status.

How it squares with c68: its rate sentence would read "8 kHz while the measured cost allows it within 2%, else the highest rate within 2%, named in rate_reason". Four fib tasks still keep 90% of the nominal samples at the rate used. At the measured 3.0 us a sample under load, the rate falls to about 6,700 a second.

comparisons.note: perf record states no cost of its own; the kernel throttles the rate when its sampling interrupt runs long (perf_cpu_time_max_percent). https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man1/perf-record.1.html
The parity target of #6841 c68: 8 kHz sampling with whole stacks by default. https://superluminal.eu/docs/documentation.html

recommendation.why: Jet should promise what Jet controls and show the rest. No design we measured gets the kernel's part under 2% when busy.
gains: A slowdown in Jet's sampler fails the test at once.
The full cost stays visible, in two named parts.
The default rate and whole stacks stay as c44 and c68 ratified.

losses.loss: The program still pays the kernel's share at 8,000 samples a second.
losses.mitigation: Every profile prints it, estimated from timed samples, so nobody mistakes it for Jet's cost. Any perf-event profiler pays it [INFERENCE].

whyNot.reason: B hides a doubling of Jet's own cost inside a loose total.
C drops the rate on busy machines, where noise is worst, and makes profiles hard to compare.

recommendation.tradeoff: The 2% promise narrows to Jet's share; the kernel's share is shown, not bounded.

recommendation.tradeoff: The 2% promise narrows to Jet's share; the kernel's share is shown, not bounded.

designAway.loss: At 8,000 samples a second with whole stacks the total passes 2% on a busy machine (2.2-3.3% in p387-p391).
attempts: Measured first where the time goes. Quiet (gate-p391 jet, burn.jet): 34.9 ms total = 4.8 ms Jet's handlers and drains + 30.1 ms the kernel writing 16269 samples (1.85 us each). At load ~165 (gate-p392 jet, three runs): totals 39.2, 53.7, 54.5 ms; Jet's share 10.8, 12.0, 9.7 ms; the kernel's 28.4, 41.7, 44.7 ms (1.7-2.7 us a sample). The kernel's part is 72-82% of the cost.
User-only callchain, kernel frames never walked: already shipped. perf_precise_open sets exclude_kernel and exclude_callchain_kernel (flags 35651681), so no kernel-side walk is left to cut.

The kernel's floor: a sample with no stack at all (ip and time only) costs 1102 ns quiet (the median in every quiet round of cost4.txt and cost5.txt) and a paired median 1503 ns less than the shipped sample busy (9 rounds, load 186 falling to 29). At 8 kHz that interrupt alone is 0.9% quiet and 1.2-1.8% busy, before any stack.

Rejected as a fix: it loses the caller of a frameless leaf function (Perf/unwinds_without_frame_pointers), and even with it the kernel's part is about 2.6 us a sample busy, 2.1% at 8 kHz.

Rejected: a stack deeper than the copy loses its outer frames (c44 requires every sample's whole stack), each record grows to 4 KiB (32 MB/s of ring per thread, raising Jet's drain share), and the kernel's part is still about 2.3 us busy, 1.8% at 8 kHz.

Hardware cycles (the PMU overflow interrupt) instead of the task clock: busy paired median +571 ns, worse, and it counts cycles, not CPU time.

Keep a calling-context id in a register, kept by the compiler on every call, so the kernel copies one register instead of walking: rejected without a build. A fib(16) chunk (3,193 calls) takes about 4.4 us quiet in the probe, so 1 ns more per call slows the program itself by about 70% [INFERENCE].
Take whole stacks on one sample in eight and the program counter on the rest: rejected, it breaks c44's whole stack on every sample.

A fixed lower default rate, 4 kHz with whole stacks, halves the kernel's share (about 0.9-1.4% busy at the measured 2.3-3.0 us a sample) and would meet 2% in total. Excluded here: c68 ratified 8 kHz parity with Superluminal, and changing the default rate is a separate owner choice.

Option A bounds Jet's share and prints the kernel's; B and C trade it differently. decisions.title: How a package turns on an optional part of a package it depends on
decisions.situation: A dependency is a package your package uses, and it often has optional parts: TLS support, a faster backend, a louder logger. Jet already has typed package settings, declared as `settings: { tls: Bool{true} }` in package.jet, read in code as `#build.settings.tls`, and set by a build profile or `--set`. Today they work only in the package being built. A probe on the gate compiler shows a dependency's own `settings:` block is ignored, and its code reads the root package's setting of the same name instead. You are asked how a package chooses a dependency's optional part. We recommend the settings Jet already has, written on the dependency's entry in package.jet, with no new concept.
decisions.gist: How does a package choose an optional part of a dependency, and where does the build record that choice?
decisions.lesson: A dependency often has optional parts, such as TLS support or a loud logger; Rust calls them features. Jet packages already declare typed settings with defaults in package.jet, and code reads them as `#build.settings.<name>`. Today those settings reach only the package being built, never its dependencies.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path. A dependency's optional parts are the `settings:` block in its package.jet, each with a type and a default. Keeping the defaults takes nothing. To change one, add it to that dependency's entry: `tool: { path: ../tool, settings: { loud: true } }`. A misspelled name or a wrong type is an error at that line, and it lists the settings the dependency declares.

Expert path. The value climbs the same rungs as the root's own settings. The dependency's default is lowest, then the entries other dependencies write, then your own entry, your build profile, your `build: fn` (`b.contribute("tool.loud", true)`) and `--set tool.loud=true`. The most explicit rung wins. Two dependencies that disagree, with nothing from you, are an error naming both lines. `jet explain` lists every writer, and the build receipt records each package's values.
decisions.story: Ana's app uses a package `tool` that prints a quiet or a loud greeting. Its author declared `settings: { loud: Bool{false} }` and branches on `#build.settings.loud`. Ana adds `settings: { loud: true }` to tool's entry in her package.jet, and writes no build function. When she types `lound`, the error points at her line and lists tool's `loud`. Later her library `report` also sets `loud: false` for tool. Ana's own entry outranks it, and `jet explain` shows report's value as overridden.

options.name: Package settings, set on the dependency's entry
options.detail:
A dependency declares its optional parts as ordinary package settings, with a type and a default. Its code branches on them with `#if #build.settings.loud == { … }`, as a root package does today. A depending package sets a value inside that dependency's entry in package.jet.

Every writer goes through the one contribution law settings already use. From least to most explicit, the rungs are the dependency's default, the entries other dependencies write, the root's own entry, its profile, its `build: fn` and `--set`. Dependencies only suggest; the package being built decides.

When dependencies suggest different values, any value from the root decides, and `jet explain`, the receipt and the lock list the overridden lines. With no value from the root, the build stops and names both lines. Each build checks every branch of the dependency's code, so no combination of settings ships unchecked.
options.technical:
Works today and is reused: the settings parser (JetDriver Loader.jet `jet_driver_parse_package_settings`) and the `#build.settings` read and `#if` fold (JetSema FactReads.jet, Statements.jet). So are the writer chain (BuildFactChain.jet `jet_driver_setting_writers`), its E3521 report and `jet explain`'s writer list. The contribution law (PackageModel FactLaw.jet `pkg_fact_resolve`) is reused and extended in parts two and three below.

New work, one card, in five parts. First, settings are read per package, not from the root alone. That also ends today's leak of a root setting into a dependency. A dependency entry takes the record form for every source, with a `settings:` block; path entries gain `{ path: … }`, which the gate compiler refuses today.

Second, the law gains two layers between the default and the profile: dependency entries, then the root's entry. `jet explain`, the receipt and the lock name them. Today nothing sits between Declaration and OptimizationBundle (FactLaw.jet `ContributionLayer`).

Third, the conflict rule. Today the law refuses a same-layer disagreement on any layer, even when a more explicit writer decides (FactLaw.jet lines 411-420). For the dependency-entry layer only, a disagreement stands when a more explicit writer decides, and is E3521 when that layer decides. Every other layer keeps today's strict rule.

Also, every build reports a refused chain. Today it does so only when the build has a `--set` (BuildFactChain.jet line 165); otherwise the last writer silently wins. That is a current bug, filed with the settings work.

Fourth, names and checks. `--set`, `b.contribute` and a profile's `settings:` accept a dependency's setting as `tool.loud`. All three refuse it today. Loading the manifest checks each entry's setting names and types against the dependency's declarations. E0302 is then reported at the entry's line and lists the declared settings; today E0302 is raised only where code reads a setting.

Fifth, the receipt records each package's resolved values and their writers, and each package's `check` nodes take them as inputs. `jet build --set` reaches a package with a `build: fn`; a probe shows the gate compiler ignores it there today.

Declarations use the ratified brace default `Bool{false}`; the dev parser still reads the older `= false` until that migration lands.

options.name: Typed arguments to a build function, as today
options.detail:
A dependency offers a choice as a typed parameter of an exported build function. The depending package calls that function from its own `build: fn`. This works on dev today for a dependency that generates code.

A probe on the dev compiler changed the ProvenanceBuild fixture's `install` to take `loud: Bool` and add one of two greetings. The program printed the loud one, and the receipt named the handoff from main.jet:5.
options.technical:
Keying. The depending file's `check` node digests its bytes, which hold the argument. The generated module's `check` node digests the code the argument chose. The `compile` node is keyed by every `check` key, and `link` by `compile`. So two choices give two compile and link keys, with no new receipt field.

Limits. Only code a metaprogram adds through `meta.add` can vary; an ordinary library's own functions cannot. Every user must write a `build: fn`, and the receipt names the call's line, not the value. Nothing lists the choices except the function's signature, and no rule covers two packages passing different values.

options.name: Manifest features, as Cargo
options.detail: Like Cargo, a dependency's `package.jet` gains `features: { loud: [] }`, and a dependency entry gains `features: ["loud"]`. Code tests a feature at compile time. Every feature turned on anywhere in the graph is on for everyone, so features only add. The receipt gains a `features` row per package.
options.technical: New manifest vocabulary beside `settings:` (DepSpec in Jetpack PackageModel Manifest.jet has Path, Git, Registry and Foreign today, none with features). It also needs a compile-time fact for code to read, union rules across the graph, a receipt field and new diagnostics. Jetpack's Variant.features (PackageModel Variant.jet) is for foreign provider packages and stays separate.

comparisons.note: Features are named in the manifest and unified across the graph, so one crate's feature turns on for every user. https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/features.html

A dependency declares typed options with defaults in its build script, and the user passes values when adding it. Option A is the same idea, declared in the manifest Jet already has. https://ziglang.org/learn/build-system/

recommendation.why: Jet already has typed package settings, profiles, `--set` and `jet explain`. A carries that one mechanism down to a dependency's entry. It needs two new law layers, qualified names and an entry check, but no build function, feature list or new word.
gains: One mechanism with names users already know: `settings:`, `#build.settings`, profiles, `--set`, `jet explain`.
The beginner writes one line in package.jet; no build function.
A typo or wrong type is an error at the entry's line, listing the declared settings.
Every branch is checked in every build, so no setting combination ships broken.
Disagreement is never silent: the root decides, and `jet explain` and the receipt name every writer.

losses.loss: A setting has one value for the whole build, as a Cargo feature does.
losses.mitigation: A library that needs several variants in one program offers a generic module with a value parameter, such as `cache<Int>(64)`, which Jet already has. Each instance then takes its own value.

losses.loss: Code behind an off setting is still fetched and checked, along with any dependency it uses.
losses.mitigation: The program carries none of its bytes: a probe found the off branch's text absent from the image. The lock fetches it once per machine. A heavy optional part can ship as its own package.

whyNot.reason: B lets only code-generating dependencies vary, and makes every user write a `build: fn` for a one-word choice. It is a second way to vary a dependency beside settings, and its receipt names a line, not the value.
C adds a feature list beside the settings block, a second mechanism for one meaning. Its features add up across the graph, so one package's choice silently changes another's build.

recommendation.tradeoff: One value per setting for the whole build, and off code still fetched and checked, in exchange for one checked, explainable mechanism with no new concept.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Proof for A uses a CompilerAPI fixture: `tool` declares `loud: Bool{false}` and branches on it, `app` sets `loud: true` on tool's entry, and library `report` sets `loud: false`. The image prints the loud greeting, and `jet explain` shows report's writer shadowed. With app's entry removed, `jet run` with no `--set` fails with E3521 naming both entries; adding `--set tool.loud=true` builds and prints the loud greeting.

Writing `lound` fails with E0302 at app's entry line. Under a `build: fn`, `jet build --set tool.loud=false` prints the quiet greeting, and `b.contribute("tool.loud", false)` does too. A release profile that writes `tool.loud: false` prints the quiet greeting with `--profile release`. The two builds have different compile and link keys, and each receipt records tool's value and its writers.

A root setting named `loud` no longer changes tool. A profile that writes one root setting twice with different values fails with E3521, with or without `--set`.

decisions.title: Let Jet code read the state graphs, fact registry and derivations of a checked index
decisions.situation:
Jet code that calls `compiler.check` gets a semantic index. It can read the index's definitions, references, calls, structural nodes, effects, arithmetic and outputs. The same index also holds three more lists: state graphs, the fact registry and derivations. `jet inspect compiler check` prints all three in its JSON. Jet code cannot name them, because the CompilerSemanticIndex record has no such members. So the typed value and the CLI JSON disagree on what an index is.

You decide whether the record gains the three members, or whether the CLI JSON drops them. We recommend adding them: the compiler already builds every value, and the JSON already prints it.
decisions.gist: Should Jet code read the same three index lists the CLI JSON already prints?
decisions.lesson: A semantic index is the compiler's record of what a checked program means. Jet code gets it from `compiler.check`, and `jet inspect compiler check` prints it as JSON. Three lists appear only in the JSON. State graphs list each typestate's states and the operations between them. The fact registry lists every fact name: effects, states and tags. Derivations say how each item's facts were established and whether they are still current.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: under A, a build step can loop over `index.state_graphs` to list each typestate's states. It can also check that every tag in the fact registry denies Net. Under B, it cannot. The fact registry leaves every CLI output. `jet inspect semindex` keeps state graphs and the program's own derivations, as JSON a build step would have to run and parse.

Expert path: under A, every member has the same name and value in Jet code and in `jet inspect compiler check`. So a tool written against the JSON and a build step written in Jet agree. The values are built once, by the producer that builds the other seven lists. Nothing new is computed; the three lists become nameable.
decisions.story: Mia writes a build step that refuses a release if any typestate has an unreachable state. Under A she reads `index.state_graphs`, finds a state whose `reachable` is false, and calls `b.error` at its span. Under B she shells out to `jet inspect compiler check`, parses its JSON, and maps spans back by hand. Her step breaks the day the JSON changes.
decisions.detail:
Code read on dev 49abf9184a. The producer is sema_compiler_semantic_index_from_checked (Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/SemanticIndex.jet:2106). It already writes the three lists into the CompilerSemanticIndex value, at lines 2267, 2268 and 2269.

`jet inspect compiler check` prints that value whole, through jet_cli_compiler_checked_value in InspectCompiler.jet. So its JSON carries the three lists.

The public record is its rows in Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/Registry/CoreRecordRows.jet:190-198. They are schema_version, source_digest, definitions, references, calls, structural_nodes, effects, arithmetic and outputs. Typed code checks member reads against those rows, so `index.state_graphs` does not type-check.

Take a 24-line typestate program (Tests/Cases/Typestate/Fixtures/CorrectLifecycleOk). Its JSON holds one state graph: Reservation, with Pending, Confirmed, CheckedIn and three transitions. It holds 19 fact-registry rows: 14 effect roots, Reservation.State and the 4 built-in tags Credential, Input, PII and Secret. It holds one derivation per checked item, Core's included.

The case CompilerAPI/typed_consumers_match_cli_json compares typed and JSON values for source_digest, definitions, references, calls and effects. Its header says the other three are not compared, because typed code cannot read them.

options.name: Add the three members and their records
options.detail: CompilerSemanticIndex gains state_graphs, fact_registry and derivations, with the records they hold. Each is named and shaped exactly as the JSON prints it today. Jet code and `jet inspect compiler check` then read one value with one set of members. The semantic-index schema_version stays 20, because the JSON does not change.
options.technical:
New CoreRecordRows: CompilerSemanticIndex.state_graphs [CompilerStateGraph], .fact_registry [CompilerFactDeclaration] and .derivations [CompilerDerivationRecord].

CompilerStateGraph {owner: String, module: String, states: [CompilerStateNode], transitions: [CompilerStateTransition]}. CompilerStateNode {name: String, terminal: Bool, reachable: Bool?, span: SourceSpan}. CompilerStateTransition {operation: String, from: String?, to: String}.

CompilerFactDeclaration {kind: String, name: String, members: [String], deny: [String], from: [String]}.

CompilerDerivationRecord {id, subject, claim, producer, method, rule: String, premises: [String], identity, assumptions: [String], disposition: String, observation?, payload?}. Its identity is CompilerDerivationIdentity {source, build, run, target: String}. Its observation is CompilerDerivationObservation {counterexample: String?, event: String?}. Its payload is CompilerDerivationPayload {kind: String, json: String}.

The eight record names join ir_host_value_name (RuntimeHandles.jet) beside the other index records. Typed code that reaches them then lowers. The JetIR guard host_value_fields_reach_only_lowerable_records covers them. The producer is unchanged.
options.code:
use compiler: core.compiler

INDEX: #run { (compiler.check(compiler.parse(embed_file("main.jet")) ?? panic("parse")) ?? panic("check")).semantic_index() ?? panic("index") }

STATES: #run (loop g in INDEX.state_graphs -> "{g.owner}: {(loop s in g.states -> s.name).join(",")}").join("\n")
TAGS: #run (loop f in INDEX.fact_registry -> (if f.kind == "Tag" -> "{f.name} denies {f.deny.join(",")}" else -> "")).join("")
STALE: #run (loop d in INDEX.derivations -> (if d.disposition != "current" -> d.subject else -> "")).join(" ")

options.name: Drop the three lists from the CLI JSON
options.detail: The record keeps its nine members. `jet inspect compiler check` stops printing the three lists, so the typed value and the JSON agree by both lacking them. Under B the fact registry leaves every CLI output. `jet inspect semindex` keeps state graphs and the program's own derivations. That command is built by a separate index producer, from documentation modules, and has its own shape.
options.technical: InspectCompiler writes the index without the three fields, or the producer stops building them. The semantic-index JSON of `inspect compiler check` changes, so its schema_version moves from 20 to 21. The open criterion asking typed code to read these lists could not be met. It would be reworded.
options.code:
// Jet code cannot read the facts; a build step runs the CLI instead.
// jet inspect semindex main.jet --json | jq '.semindex.state_graphs'

comparisons.note: Analyzers read the compiler's semantic model through typed APIs; the compiler's own tools use the same model.
comparisons.code:
var model = compilation.GetSemanticModel(tree);
var symbol = model.GetDeclaredSymbol(node);

comparisons.note: The `ide` crate's typed API and the LSP JSON are produced from one HIR; the LSP layer converts at the edge.

recommendation.why: The compiler already builds the three lists inside the index value, and the CLI already prints them; only the public record leaves them out. A makes the record match the value it already is, so the typed result and the JSON are one shape. B removes facts users can see today. It also sends Jet code to a second producer with a different shape.
gains: Jet code and `jet inspect compiler check` read one index with the same ten list members.
Build steps can check typestates, tags and derivation freshness without running a command.
No new computation: the producer is unchanged, and the JSON and its schema_version stay as they are.

losses.loss: Eight more public record names in core.compiler.
losses.mitigation: Each is the exact shape the JSON already prints, so no new concept is taught. The names follow the existing Compiler* index records.

losses.loss: Derivation method and disposition, and fact kind, are strings, not enums; payload.json is JSON text.
losses.mitigation: The other index records already use strings for such words, such as CompilerArithmeticOperation.policy. The JSON prints the same words. Turning them into enums later is one change for both readers.

losses.loss: Derivations include Core's items: the 24-line example sees 176 records, most of them Core's.
losses.mitigation: Each record names its target (identity.target), so a reader keeps its own package's records in one filter. The JSON already holds the same list.

whyNot.reason: It deletes facts users read today from the JSON, and bumps the index schema for that removal. It leaves Jet code no way to read typestates, the fact registry or derivations. The only route left is running a CLI and parsing a second producer's different shape.

recommendation.tradeoff: Eight more public record names, for one index shape across Jet code and the CLI.

surface.lesson: A semantic index is the compiler's record of what a checked program means. Jet code gets it from `compiler.check`, and `jet inspect compiler check` prints it as JSON. Three of its lists, state graphs, the fact registry and derivations, appear only in the JSON. Jet code cannot name them. The vote decides whether Jet code gains them or the JSON loses them.

current.note: Observed on the current compiler for a small typestate program.

wild.note: Analyzers read the compiler's semantic model through typed APIs, the same model the compiler's own tools use.

options.gist: Jet code reads the same three lists, with the same names and values, as the JSON.
gains: One index shape in Jet code and the CLI JSON.

The JSON and its version stay unchanged.

proposed.code:

    "{g.owner}: {(loop s in g.states -> s.name).join(",")}").join("\n")
TAGS: #run (loop f in INDEX.fact_registry ->
    (if f.kind == "Tag" -> "{f.name} denies {f.deny.join(",")}" else -> "")).join("")
STALE: #run (loop d in INDEX.derivations ->
    (if d.disposition != "current" -> d.subject else -> "")).join(" ")

Jet code still cannot read them.
The index schema version moves for a removal.

// Jet code cannot read the facts; a build step runs a command instead.
// jet inspect semindex main.jet --json | jq '.semindex.state_graphs'

Reuse the ProgramInfo records StateInfo and TransitionInfo for state_graphs: rejected. StateInfo has no span, and TransitionInfo.from is a StateRef that cannot be absent, so a constructor (book: no state to Pending) has no honest row. Reusing them would also change the JSON the CLI prints today.
