decisions.title: Choose what runs a plugin whose path is known only at run time
decisions.situation: Today `plugin.load` takes only a literal path, and the compiler translates that plugin into the program's own machine code at build time. The ratified decision D-CORE-PLUGINPATH1 adds `plugin.load<Trait>(path, policy)`, whose path is computed while the program runs. A built program holds nothing that can run a component it never saw, so that load needs an engine, and this ballot picks one. The main users are Jetpack's build-plugin and compiler-extension hosts. The owner ruled that a guest escaping its sandbox is unacceptable, even when the translator has a bug. So the recommendation translates in a child process, then a separate checker proves the machine code safe before it may run. The code then runs behind guard pages and, on CPUs that have them, hardware memory keys that lock the program's memory. One cost is physical and stays: a program that translates plugins must carry the translator, at least 2.5 MB.
decisions.gist: When a program loads a plugin whose path it learns only at run time, what runs that plugin's code?
decisions.lesson: A plugin is a WebAssembly component: portable code that a host runs inside a sandbox. Something must turn it into work the processor does. An interpreter reads each instruction and acts on it, so it is small but slower. A translator turns the whole component into machine code before the first call, so calls run at full speed, but the translator must be present at load. The sandbox is the promise that the plugin's code never touches the program's own memory.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: the code is the same under every option. A user declares a trait, calls `plugin.load<Analyzer>(path, policy)`, and calls `tool.analyze(bytes)`. A missing or mistyped export is refused at load under every option. Under A nothing else is written or shipped: no helper file, no second limits value, no setting and no sandbox switch.

Expert path: the expert passes the ratified `limits: plugin.Limits{...}` and handles each `PluginError`. To bound how long a load may take, the expert uses Jet's one deadline mechanism, `#Deadline(5s)` or `task.timeout`. Under A the load returns the expiry as `Budget(.Time)`, as a network read returns its timeout. Code the checker refuses fails the load as `Defect`, naming the file and the function.

Under A and E the guest runs the same translated code as a literal-path plugin, with the same fuel, time, memory, table and bounds checks and the same frames. Under A, D and E every guest, literal or loaded at run time, also runs behind the same checker, guard pages and memory keys. Under B that code runs in a child process. C and D add a second way of running guest code, so each must repeat the fuel, time and frame rules exactly.

Every option bounds a load's work with the same fixed safety caps, as the wire cap and frame count are fixed today. A function body over 1 MiB, control nested over 10,000 levels, or translation memory past its cap fails the load. The cap is 1 GiB, or half the memory the process can still claim if that is less. A, D and E map new code from a sealed in-memory file, never from writable memory.
decisions.story: Ravi ships a log tool that loads customer-written filters from a folder named on the command line. Under A he ships one file, and each filter runs at native speed once loaded. A filter without `analyze` is refused at load. A filter crafted to trip a translator bug fails its own load at the checker, and the tool keeps running. Under B or E he must also ship an engine helper beside his tool. Under C his tool is at least 3.5 MB smaller, but filters run slower.
decisions.detail:
Code read on dev 49abf9184a, and on 97d2a287ab for the sandbox walls. Measurements used the compiler at commit 628e9695aa on x86-64 Linux, one small program at a time. The wall probes are C programs, run on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X3D under Linux 7.2.8 while the machine was heavily loaded.

Literal loads today: the plugin link step (Compiler/JetPlugin/Source/Plugin/Link.jet) reads each literal artifact while the program is built. It decodes it with JetWasm and translates every core function into the program's own JetIR functions (Translate.jet). The runtime host (Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/PluginHost.jet) calls that code in process. At load, pg_load only compares the file's bytes with the copy embedded at build time.

Fuel is spent at function entry and at loop heads, in slices of 4096. The deadline is checked when a slice runs out, so a call past its deadline fails as Budget(.Time) and the plugin keeps serving calls. Memory and table growth go through runtime checks against the load's caps.

Sandbox today: each heap access is checked against the memory's limit in the translated code (Translate.jet `address`). The memory is mapped at its cap with no guard region (PluginHost.jet `pg_mmap`). Guest code runs on the host's stack and writes its fuel and depth words in the instance record, a host heap block. So the checks are the only wall, and a translator bug that drops one is an escape.

Guest code calls 34 runtime helpers (Translate.jet `PLUG_RUNTIME_NAMES`). 15 of them, the bit counts and float helpers, take only values and return a value.

A computed path does not type-check today. `jet check` on a host that calls `tool.analyze(41)` after `plugin.load("{name}.wat", policy)` reports `Plugin export \`analyze\` has no Component interface`.

Same-program size, built with `jet build` (O2). Both programs build an Authority, read `process.args()` and print one number:

```text
without a plugin                            179,832 bytes
with one literal plugin and one call        265,592 bytes
the plugin host code adds                    85,760 bytes
```

Call speed. One million calls of a one-instruction export took 54 to 66 ms over several runs. So a call costs about 55 to 65 ns.

What the optimizer is worth. A guest loop that makes a call, a load and a store each iteration ran 60 calls of 2 million iterations. Process user time, in two builds of the same host:

```text
                    build 1          build 2
guest built at O0   462 to 470 ms    439 ms
guest built at O2   313 to 320 ms    303 ms
O0 time / O2 time   1.47             1.45
```

So O2 runs such a guest about 1.45 times faster. A three-instruction loop settles nothing. Its O0/O2 ratio was 1.96 in one build and 0.82 in the other, from code layout alone.

Load cost and memory, as upper bounds. Each row is a whole `jet build` of a host that loads one literal plugin and calls it. So it includes the front end, the WAT reader and the link, and the translation alone costs less. These builds don't use the build store: an empty store gave the same times and stayed empty. The large guests have one generated function body of arithmetic with a branch every 16 steps:

```text
guest code                    peak RSS        wall time
none (the host alone)          82 MB          0.04 s
SandboxMathKit, 17 KB          101 to 109 MB  0.07 to 0.09 s
one 247 KB body                174 to 178 MB  0.42 to 0.55 s
one 1,012 KB body              454 to 466 MB  2.07 to 2.15 s
```

O0 and O2 differ by under 5 percent in each row. Under heavy machine load, another run took 0.38 to 0.75 s for SandboxMathKit, also with no store use. Memory and time grow about linearly with the code: about 380 bytes of memory per byte of guest code.

The largest function body in the WebAssembly the repository ships is 94,691 bytes, in the site's 796 KB HarfBuzz module. The largest in a shipped component is 6,352 bytes, in the Zed extension.

Sandbox walls, probed:

```text
keys register written in and out, per call   16.3 to 17.0 ns at best
                                             19 to 48 ns under load
protection keys one process can allocate     15
8 GiB no-access reservation, 64 KiB opened   9.2 us each
reservations that fit one address space      16,382
guard fault caught and resumed               2.6 us
fault through the exit landing, keys on      3.1 to 4.1 us
guest read of host memory, guest key only    faulted (SEGV_PKUERR), 20,000 of 20,000
process start and reap, 265 KB Jet program   0.37 ms at best, 3 ms mean under load
process start and reap, 504 MB jet binary    0.65 ms at best, 4 ms mean under load
x86-64 decoder at O2, 2.6 MB of code         3.4 MB/s, 0.85 us an instruction
checker prototype, every loadable component  452 functions, 125,754 instructions,
  at O0, O1 and O2                           none refused
checker prototype, hand-made unsafe changes  74 of 74 refused; 8 safe ones accepted
signal to guest code, own stack, guest key   handler ran, process went on
the same, handler without its own stack      process died (SIGSEGV)
64 KiB frame near a 4 KiB stack guard        no fault; the page below overwritten
64 KiB frame near a 1 MiB stack guard        faulted at the guard; page untouched
task parked in an import, resumed elsewhere  keys follow the task; nested and outer
                                             host reads trapped; chain unwound
40 guests through 14 keys, 400 calls         15,600 cross-guest reads, all faulted;
                                             1.24 key re-tags per call
14 guests parked in imports, then a 15th     15th took a parked guest's key; all
  guest's call that releases them            finished; 406 cross reads all faulted
```

Three conditions surfaced in those probes. With the host's memory locked, a signal is delivered only to a handler on its own stack. Jet's fault and profiler handlers already use one, but its process-signal and SIGSYS handlers don't yet. With glibc's rseq registration on, a trap during guest code ended the process. So did plain preemption of a thread in guest code. With it off, every probe returned, and Jet's runtime registers no rseq area. And a guest stack guard smaller than the largest frame can be stepped over.

Why a child process: an in-host task contains a panic, but not a stack overflow or an allocation failure. Probed: a task indexed past a list's end returned `.Panicked` to its joiner and the program went on. A task recursing without end stopped the whole program (Jet.StackOverflow, exit 70). An allocation failure aborts the process (JetRuntime Alloc.jet).

Machine code in the jet binary, summed from its symbol table by source file:

```text
JetWasm decoder, validator, component, opcodes    about 0.35 MB
JetWasm WAT text reader (Text.wat_*)               353,630 bytes
JetPlugin translator, link, descriptor, interface  about 0.25 MB
JetIR x64 selection, allocation, module, SSA, IR  1,534,065 bytes
JetBackend x64 encoder                              45,788 bytes
JetBackend x64 decoder (Decoder.*, 31 functions)    97,861 bytes
JetBackend in-memory linker (MemoryLink)           158,381 bytes
JetIR optimizer passes (Opt*)                    1,931,419 bytes
```

So A's translator needs at least 2.18 MB of code at O0, for binary `.wasm` only. Linking in memory adds an estimated 0.16 MB, taking MemoryLink as the stand-in. An O1 or O2 host adds the optimizer, about 1.93 MB more. The decoder and a checker on it add an estimated 0.2 MB.

These are lower bounds. JetPlugin also depends on JetFoundation and on more of JetIR than the rows above. A user host links no compiler code, so it shares none of that. It would link only the part the translator reaches, which is not measured. In `jet`, JetFoundation's functions total 13.9 MB and JetIR's 13.6 MB. JetWasm depends on nothing, so C and D carry none of this. The gap between A and C is therefore larger than the table shows.

Size per host and per option. The A column sums the measurements above, so it is a lower bound. The C, D and E columns are estimates. B's helper is an estimated 4.5 MB file, shipped once:

```text
host                               A (min)  B             C        D        E
jet run program (O0)               +2.5 MB  +helper file  +0.6 MB  +1.0 MB  +0.4 MB
jet build program (O2)             +4.5 MB  +helper file  +0.6 MB  +1.0 MB  +0.4 MB
jetpack build-plugin and
compiler-extension hosts           +4.5 MB  +helper file  +0.6 MB  +1.0 MB  +0.4 MB
the same hosts moved into `jet`    +0.1 MB  +0            +0.6 MB  +1.0 MB  +0.1 MB
```

The jetpack binary today links only the compiler front end (Jetpack/Bootstrap/sources.list), so its hosts pay A's full size. The design note plans to run them inside `jet`, which already links the translator, back end and decoder. Then they pay only the checker under A. For scale, the nixpkgs build of libwasmtime.so 48.0.0 is 50,449,344 bytes; a trimmed embedding is smaller.

Pipe round trip: a Python loop writing 8 bytes to a native `cat` child and reading them back took 6.4 to 6.6 microseconds. Python's own write and read cost 1.1 microseconds, so a native round trip is about 5 microseconds. That is roughly 60 to 90 times one in-process call, with or without memory keys.

Web tier: `plugin.load` needs the `Exec` effect, and the web target denies it. Building the plugin host with `--os=web` fails today with `Jet.TargetDeniedEffect: run uses Exec, which target wasm32-unknown-unknown denies`. No option changes that. Native code generation is x86-64 only today, so every option serves Linux x86-64 hosts.

Systems that forbid new machine code: SELinux with deny_execmem, and PaX MPROTECT, refuse anonymous memory that becomes executable and private mappings made executable after a write. A, D and E map their code shared from a sealed memfd, read and execute, which is neither. Not probed, since no SELinux or PaX system was at hand: deny_execmem does not refuse it. The policy must still let the domain execute its own in-memory files, and where it doesn't, the load is refused with the named error.

So a policy that refuses executable in-memory files still refuses run-time loads under A, D and E. That is physical: such a policy forbids exactly what any translating engine must do. B maps code only in its helper. C maps no code. Literal-path plugins are built into the program, so they work under every option.

Jet's image loader already fills memfds and maps them (JetBackend Image/Loader.jet `loader_memfd`). It creates them with MFD_EXEC, to start images; A does not use that flag. A creates its memfd with MFD_NOEXEC_SEAL, which a kernel set to refuse executable memfds still allows, since mapping code needs no exec bit.

Saved work: none for a host today. Reuse is a compile-time constant of the compiler, off on dev (JetFoundation BuildOptions.jet `BUILD_REUSE_SAVED_WORK`). The store code lives in JetCLI, which no host links.

Caps: the ratified `plugin.Limits` has fuel, memory_bytes, table_elements and timeout, all per component or per call (Core/Plugin/Plugin.jet). The wire cap of 1,048,576 bytes and the 32-frame fault limit are fixed constants beside them (spec, plugin budgets).

The design note Docs/Proposals/plugin-wasm-engine-2026-10-29.md leaves a run-time path in a user program out of scope until a ballot asks for one.

options.name: Translate in a child, check the code, run it fenced in the host
options.detail:
A program that calls `plugin.load<T>` links the WebAssembly decoder, the plugin translator, the code generator's back end and a code checker. At load, Core reads the bytes once and checks the optional sha256. It starts a copy of the program itself as a translating child and pipes it those bytes. The child checks every trait method against the exports and translates at the host's own level. So the guest runs the same code as a literal-path guest.

The host seals the child's code, then a separate checker follows every value through every instruction. It proves the code can reach only its own memory, stack and guest page, its own functions and fixed entry points. Anything else fails the load as `Defect`, so a translator bug is caught, never run.

The code then runs behind guard pages, on its own stack. On CPUs with memory keys, the program's memory and every other plugin's memory are locked while guest code runs. A crash, stack overflow or memory blow-up while translating ends only the child. A run-time path names a binary `.wasm` file, as a run-time `exec` path names a built program.
options.technical:
Reused: the link step's translation (Compiler/JetPlugin Link.jet, Translate.jet), the descriptor and PluginHost. Fuel slices, the per-call timeout, memory and table caps, and frames are unchanged. The ratified `plugin.Limits` value is unchanged, and no second limits value is added. Code read on dev 97d2a287ab. Probes ran on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X3D under Linux 7.2.8, on a heavily loaded machine.

The rule. Guest code may touch only its own memory, its own stack and its own guest page. It may read its own read-only page. It may call only its own functions, its dispatchers and a fixed list of runtime entry points. Three walls enforce the rule, and none of them trusts the translator.

Wall 1, the checker. It is new code, written apart from the translator, on the existing x86-64 decoder (JetBackend X64/Decoder.jet). The host runs it on every translated function after the code is sealed and before it is mapped executable. So the bytes checked are the bytes that run.

The checker is a dataflow abstract interpreter over registers and frame slots, as VeriWasm is. It takes the shared back end's output as it is, at every level, and asks nothing of it. Each register and frame slot holds one abstract value:

```text
const c, bnd B    a known integer, or an integer in 0..B; a 32-bit write
                  or `and` with a mask gives bnd
inst              the instance pointer: rdi of guest functions, rsi of entries
area              the export's argument and result area: rdx of an entry
outp              a results pointer: rsi of a guest function, rdx of a dispatcher
memtab, tables    the read-only rows: [inst+0x30] and [inst+0x38]
heap B            a memory's base plus an offset in 0..B, loaded from a row
stack d           rbp plus d, in this function's own frame
entry r           the caller's callee-saved register r, until restored
top               anything else; never used as an address
```

Values move through `mov`, `lea`, `add`, `sub`, `and`, shifts and frame-slot spills and reloads. At a join the values merge. A bound or heap offset that grows round a loop widens to its cap, then to `top`, so every load settles or is refused. The rules it enforces:

```text
heap      [heap B + bnd C * scale + disp] with disp >= 0 and
          B + C * scale + disp + size within the 8 GiB reservation
stack     a slot of this frame, never at or above the saved rbp;
          frames at most 64 KiB
slots     a slot keeps a value only after a full-width mov to its
          exact offset; any other write over its bytes (ALU, SSE,
          setcc, pop, xchg, a narrow or unaligned store) forgets it;
          a call forgets every slot below rsp
guest page   the trap, fuel and depth words, globals below the
          module's global count, the area within its 512 bytes, and
          the dropped flags; fuel is only ever lowered, so a guest
          can't outrun its budget
read-only page   reads only, and only rows below the module's
          memory and table counts
results pointer   [outp + d], d >= 0; each caller passes a range of
          its own live frame, and forgets what that range held
calls     direct only, to a function's first byte: guest functions
          and dispatchers with rdi = inst, and the fixed runtime entry
          points; no indirect call or jump
returns   rsp back at entry and rbx, rbp, r12 to r15 restored, at ret
          and at every tail jump
code      every jump lands on an instruction decoded in that function;
          no syscall, int, WRPKRU, XRSTOR, segment write or far jump;
          only an allowlist of instructions; every access has a size
```

The counts come from the decoded module, which the host also uses to build the read-only page, so a row past them is never read.

A refusal fails the load as `Defect`: couldn't load plugin `x.wasm`: the translated code breaks the sandbox rule in `f` at +0x1a4. That is a translator bug caught at load, never a guest run. Literal-path guests pass the same checker when the program is built. The fuzzer runs every translation through it, so a refusal there is a translator bug found.

Probed with a 873-line Python prototype of these rules, reading the disassembler's text. It ran over every component that loads today, at O0, O1 and O2, with each module's own counts. That is SandboxMathKit, 13 plugin test fixtures and a review probe guest: 452 functions and 125,754 instructions. It refused none of them.

Two more plugin fixtures are meant to fail at build, with `Jet.ArgumentCountMismatch`, so they have no code. The Zed extension and the site's HarfBuzz module don't load through `plugin.load` today. The extension's exports return Unit, which the plugin surface refuses, and HarfBuzz is a core module, not a component.

The prototype also refused every unsafe change made by hand to real output: 74 of 74. On the review probe's O2 guest it refused these 25:

```text
heap        a dropped zero extension, a negative displacement, an index
            past the reservation, a base from a forged spill slot
read-only   writes to the memories row and to a limit
calls       an indirect call, a forged instance, a jump out, a host call
code        syscall, WRPKRU, an image-data read, an fs store
frames      a store over the return address, a 128 KiB frame, three
            broken returns
instance    a reused instance register, a replaced area pointer, an
            indexed instance store
fuel        the fuel word raised by a constant, set from a guest value,
            or raised in place
```

The review probe's own set added 10 changes and a loop, all refused. They change a spilled heap base by a 4-byte store, `add`, `movq` and `pop`, and swap a slot with `xchg`. They read rows past the module's counts and store past its globals. They call or jump into a function's middle. The loop grows a heap pointer without end.

A further 25 changes, all refused, cover the other write forms over a slot. Those are `setcc`, `xor`, `or`, `neg`, `movsd`, narrow and unaligned stores, a store through a copied frame address, and both `xchg` orders. They also cover a spill below rsp across a call, and a `pop` to an rsp-based operand.

The rest of those 25 are row 1 of one memory, row 0 of no tables, global 0 of no globals, and two area overruns. Then come an index grown round a loop, a heap pointer stepped back, a sizeless operand, a fuel swap, and two wrong branch addresses.

The multi-value fixture gave 7 of 7 results-pointer changes refused. They cover a write below the pointer and a write into saved registers. They also cover a pointer into the caller's caller and one over saved registers. A guest integer, the instance or a dispatcher's slot passed as the pointer were refused too. The guest-side code below gave 6 of 6 refused.

Eight safe variants were accepted, so the rules don't refuse sound code. They are a re-masked table slot, a 64-bit copy cursor, a removed copy check, a plain spill and reload, and a register swapped twice. The others are an index re-extended inside a loop, a slot rewritten after a narrow store, and a store at the area's last word.

The size of the Jet checker will be close to the prototype's logic, without its text parsing. No line count is claimed before it is written.

Wall 2, guard pages. Each guest memory is an 8 GiB reservation with no access, and only its current size is open. A 32-bit index plus a 32-bit offset can't leave it, so a dropped bounds check lands in the guard. The explicit checks stay, so traps keep today's meaning; the guard is the backstop. Memory64 is refused at decode today (JetWasm Decode.jet, the limits flags), and that refusal stays, since the guard relies on it.

The runtime's fault handler sees a fault from guest code at a guard or guest-stack address. It points the guest at the exit gate's landing, and the call fails as a trap with frames.

Probed: reserving 8 GiB and opening 64 KiB took 9.2 µs per memory, and 16,382 reservations fit one address space. A fault in a guard was caught and resumed in 2.6 µs. A reservation takes address space, not memory.

The guest stack. Each guest gets its own stack, reserved at the depth limit times the largest frame the checker found, plus the largest pure helper frame. Below it sits a 1 MiB guard: more than the 64 KiB frame cap plus the red zone. Jet emits no stack probes, so one frame may skip up to 64 KiB; the 1 MiB guard still catches it. The depth limit stays 1,000 calls, and it traps before the stack runs out.

Probed with a C stand-in for a guest frame: a 64 KiB frame plus pushes near the bottom of a stack. Over a 4 KiB guard, no fault came, and 8 bytes of the page below now held the guest's word. Over a 1 MiB guard, the fault came at the guard and the page below was untouched.

Wall 3, memory keys. On x86 CPUs with protection keys, guest memory and the guest stack carry the guest's key. The host's own memory keeps key 0. The entry gate opens only the guest's keys and switches to the guest stack; the exit gate restores the host's keys and stack.

The instance splits into three pages, so each word sits under the right key. Today it is one 120-byte host block (PluginHost.jet `PG_INST_*`, Translate.jet `PLUG_INST_*`):

```text
guest page, read-write, guest key    trap, fuel and depth words; globals;
                                     the export argument and result area;
                                     data and element dropped flags
read-only page, shared read key      memory rows (base, limit), table rows,
                                     the pointer to the host record
host record, host key                trap message, frame count and frames,
                                     descriptor, plugin, fuel reserve,
                                     deadline
```

The export area moves into the guest page. The entry gate passes its address in rdx, and the checker binds the area to that argument alone. The read-only key is write-disabled while guest code runs, so the bounds and bases can be read but never changed.

Each gate writes an absolute value to the keys register and compares it before going on. So a jump into a gate's middle can't open host memory. While guest code runs, host memory refuses every access, even if walls 1 and 2 both failed. Pure helpers, the 15 bit-count and float helpers that take only values, run without leaving the guest. The build checks that their code touches only the stack; any that fails goes through the gates.

Probed: with only the guest's key open, a read of host memory faulted with SEGV_PKUERR. The host's handler ran and the host word stayed unchanged, 20,000 times in 20,000. A trap through the exit landing cost 3.1 to 4.1 µs. A gate pair cost 16.3 to 17.0 ns at best and 19 to 48 ns under heavy load. So a call costs about 72 to 82 ns instead of 55 to 65 ns.

Helpers. Guest code calls 34 runtime helpers today, and 19 are host code that would run with host memory open. Under A they shrink to six behind the exit gate. The translator emits the rest as guest code, which the checker checks and the guest's key confines:

```text
guest code     memory.fill, copy and init; data.drop; table.get, set,
               fill, copy, init and size; elem.drop; call_indirect's
               lookup; trunc's range check
exit gate      memory.grow, table.grow, the fuel slice end, trap,
               frame, and host imports
```

Guest copies use the same checked form: two bounds checks against the limit, then 8-byte and byte loops. Each step re-extends its 32-bit cursor, so the heap rule holds. Large copies may run slower than the host's memmove; that was not measured.

call_indirect becomes guest code too. Each table's entries sit in their own reservation, sized to the table cap rounded up to a power of two. An entry is the function id plus one, and its signature. The lookup checks the index against the size, masks it to the reservation, and reads the entry. A zero id traps as an uninitialized element, and another signature traps as a mismatch. It then calls the signature's dispatcher directly.

Today a dispatcher's default case returns zero, since the host helper checked first. Under A it traps as a signature mismatch. So even a forged entry can only reach a function of the right signature. call_indirect no longer crosses a gate at all; its lookup cost was not measured.

The six exit-gate helpers stay host code. They take integers and guest addresses, and they read and write guest memory only through one accessor. It forms each address as base plus a 32-bit pointer plus a 32-bit length, inside the reservation. So a missed bounds check in a helper still lands in the guard. A logic bug elsewhere in those six is one wall, not three. Every in-process engine has the same seam, Wasmtime's runtime calls included.

Signals. While host memory is locked, a signal can only be delivered to a handler on its own stack. So every runtime sigaction gets SA_ONSTACK. Today three handlers lack it. Two are the process-signal handlers (JetRuntime ProcessSignal.jet lines 39 and 337, flags 0x14000000). The third is the SIGSYS handler (ComptimeServe.jet line 107). A guard test asserts the flag on every runtime sigaction.

The entry gate refuses a thread with no alternate stack. Fault.jet `fault_stack_start` returns 0 when it can't map one, and the runtime records that in a thread flag. The first load's key test, in the child, sends a non-fault signal while in guest code, besides the fault.

Probed: a thread spinning in guest code, on the guest stack with only the guest key open, got SIGUSR1. With SA_ONSTACK and an alternate stack, the handler ran once and the process went on. Without SA_ONSTACK, as ProcessSignal.jet installs today, the process died with SIGSEGV.

Keys need one more thing: no rseq area. With glibc's rseq registration on, a thread preempted in guest code died with SIGSEGV from the kernel, with no trap and no signal of its own. A trap with rseq on ended the process too. With it off, every probe returned. Jet's runtime is static musl and registers none, and a guard test asserts that.

Re-entry and thread moves. A host import may call back into a guest, and a task may park in an import and resume on another thread. So each task keeps a chain of gate contexts in host-key memory: host stack, guest stack, the previous context and the keys value. The gates find it through the current task, not the thread. Fiber switches happen only in host code, and every gate writes absolute keys.

Probed with a C model of that chain on a ucontext fiber. A task started on one thread, parked in an import and resumed on another, whose own keys were the host's. A nested re-entry then trapped on host memory, and the chain went back to the outer call. The outer guest, now on the second thread, wrote its own memory and then trapped on host memory. The chain ended empty and the host word was unchanged.

Many guests. One process can allocate 15 keys, and one stays for the read-only pages. So 14 guests hold keys at a time, and any number may be loaded. A guest without a key has its pages tagged key 0 and closed. When it next runs, it takes the least recently used key and the old holder's pages are re-tagged to key 0.

A key held by a guest that is running is never taken. A guest parked in a host import is not running, so its key may be taken. The import's return path takes a key and re-tags before guest code resumes. So a fifteenth guest running at once waits only until another leaves guest code, which every fuel slice end and every import does. No two guests ever share a key, and one guest reading another is the same fault as reading the host.

Probed: 40 guests and 400 calls in random order through 14 keys, with 240 steals and 494 re-tags, 1.24 per call. Each guest read its own memory every time, and 15,600 cross-guest reads all faulted. The steal cost was not timed.

Probed again with fourteen guests parked in imports, each waiting on work only a fifteenth guest's call does. Each guest is its own thread. Under this rule the fifteenth took a parked guest's key, and all fifteen finished. The 406 cross-guest reads all faulted, and every own-memory read succeeded. When parked guests kept their keys instead, the fifteenth found no key in 2 s, and nothing would ever free one.

Keys need three things. The CPU must have them: Intel servers since 2017, Intel desktops and laptops since about 2019, and AMD since 2020, per vendor documents; this machine has them. The kernel must deliver signals as above, which Linux 7.2.8 did. And no rseq area may be registered. At the first load the child runs a one-shot key test, so a failing kernel costs only the child.

Without keys. Walls 1 and 2 still hold, and the guest behaves identically: same results, traps, limits and frames. An escape would then need a translator bug and a checker bug that agree. Calls cost 55 to 65 ns. The gates have two bodies, since WRPKRU faults on a CPU without keys. So an internal runtime switch, not a user surface, forces the keyless gates. The plugin test cases run both ways in CI, so neither body ships untested.

Hardware isolation without keys means a process per guest, which is option B: a second mechanism under I8, at about 5 µs a call.

Side channels. Base plus a masked 32-bit index keeps even speculative heap and table reads inside the guest's own reservation. That covers bounds-check bypass. Branch-target and return-stack poisoning inside one process are not covered: a guest could steer the host's speculation and read host bytes through cache timing. That is a leak, not a write, and it stays a named residual. Only a process per guest closes it, which is B.

Multi-memory. Each memory gets its own reservation and its own row. The checker ties each base to the row it was read from, so an index meant for one memory can't reach another. A copy between memories checks both, as above.

Translation in a child. The host starts itself again through /proc/self/exe with a translator entry, so no helper file ships and versions always match. It passes the bytes and the addresses to link against over a pipe. The child decodes, validates and translates, writes the code into a memfd the host made, and replies with the descriptor. Untrusted bytes never reach a decoder in the host, which checks the descriptor against the trait.

The child runs under an address-space limit at the memory cap, and an OOM score that makes the kernel kill it first. A system-call filter lets it use only its pipe, its memfd and memory calls. A panic, stack overflow, allocation failure or OOM kill ends only the child: `Defect` or `Budget(.Memory)` in load. One translation runs at a time.

Probed: starting and reaping a 265 KB Jet program took 0.37 ms at best, and 0.65 ms for a 504 MB binary. Under heavy load the means were 3 and 4 ms. The child replaces the earlier in-host task with its heap budget and 16 MiB stack, so that runtime work is dropped.

Memory. Translation memory is capped at the smaller of 1 GiB and half the memory the process can still claim, read at load start. That room is free memory, lowered to each enclosing cgroup's memory.max less its use, and the address-space limit less the mapped size. The compiler already reads the first two this way to size its threads (JetCLI Request.jet).

The code generator holds the whole module until it finishes, so memory is not freed per function (JetIR X64Module.jet). The worst peak measured was about 660 MB for a 1 MiB body at O2, so 1 GiB holds about 1.6 MiB of body. A code-size cap would never bind, so there is none. A function body over 1 MiB fails the load: 11 times the largest the repository ships.

Time. Today a 1 MiB body of 69,000 nested blocks, each with a branch out, takes 20 s at O2, 18 s of it in the x64 code generator. Each block end scans every pending forward jump of the function (JetIR X64Select.jet `ir_x64_end`), so time grows with the square of the depth.

At 50,000 levels that pass took 10.7 s for nested blocks with the branch. It took 0.3 s for nested blocks without it, for nested ifs and for flat blocks with it. New code generator work keeps each open block's pending jumps with that block, so an end patches only its own. Deeply nested Jet programs compile faster too.

A 1 MiB body of nested ifs builds in 2.6 s at O2. Run-time loads stay off until every probed shape, nested branches included, builds a 1 MiB body in under 3 s. The memory cap holds 1.6 to 2.2 MiB of body by shape, so that bounds a load to about 5 to 7 s.

Deadline. A caller that wants a tighter bound wraps the load in `#Deadline` or `task.timeout`. New runtime work makes the load a typed-error wait on the child, like a network read. At expiry the host kills the child and returns `Budget(.Time)` in load. The load joins no task, so the E3003 end of a late join can't happen. Jet code gains no new call; the deadline stays the one mechanism.

Mapping. The host makes a memfd with MFD_NOEXEC_SEAL and hands it to the child, which writes the relocated code and exits. The host seals it against writes and resizing, checks it, and maps it shared, read and execute. Probed earlier: after sealing, a write and a writable map were refused, a read-execute map ran its code, and a change to read, write and execute was refused.

So no page is ever writable and executable. SELinux was not probed: deny_execmem does not refuse it. The policy must still let the domain execute its own in-memory files, and where it doesn't, the load is refused with the named error.

Reuse. Loads of the same sha256 in one process translate once and share the code, each with its own limits and its own key. Across runs: none today. The checker would make a disk cache safe to read, since planted code must pass it too. A later ballot that ratifies saved-work reuse must say how a deployed host opts in and count the store code's size.

Required work, all in the plugin translator, runtime and code generator:

```text
checker          the rules above, on X64/Decoder.jet, run at build and load
guard pages      8 GiB memory reservations, table reservations, the
                 fault-to-trap path, guest stacks with a 1 MiB guard
instance split   guest page, read-only page and host record; new
                 PG_INST_* and PLUG_INST_* offsets; the area moved
guest helpers    bulk memory and table operations and call_indirect's
                 lookup emitted as guest code; dispatchers trap by default
host helpers     six behind the exit gate, guest memory through one
                 reservation accessor
gates            absolute keys, a per-task context chain, the key
                 manager with least-recently-used steal
signals          SA_ONSTACK on every runtime sigaction, the alternate-
                 stack flag, the guard tests, the no-rseq test
keyless switch   internal; plugin cases run with and without keys
child            the translator entry, its limits and filter, the typed wait
code generator   per-block pending jumps
tests            a WebAssembly spec-test runner and a fuzzer of mutated
                 components, which cover literal-path guests too
```

Run-time loads stay off until the spec suite's core tests pass, the fuzzer runs with no open crash or checker refusal, and the time check holds.

Size: at least 2.5 MB in an O0 host and 4.5 MB in an O1 or O2 host. That is the translator's 2.3 or 4.3 MB, plus the decoder and checker, an estimated 0.2 MB. Calls: about 72 to 82 ns with keys and 55 to 65 ns without; literal-path calls pay the same gates. Web: refused at build, as today, because `plugin.load` needs `Exec`. I9: one code generator on every level, and the checker generates no code, so no exception.

```text

bad module        Guest in load: couldn't load plugin `x.wasm`: not a WebAssembly
                  Component: magic header not detected (at byte 0)
missing method    Guest in load: couldn't load plugin `x.wasm`: x.wasm does not
                  export `analyze` required by Analyzer
.wat path         Guest in load: couldn't load plugin `x.wasm`: a run-time path must
                  name a binary .wasm component
load race         one read; the sha256 and the child use that buffer
translator bug    the checker refuses the code: Defect in load, naming the function
                  and offset; the guest never runs
missed check      an access past the bounds lands in the guard: the call traps as
                  out of bounds memory access; the plugin keeps serving calls
deep frames       a guest stack overflow hits the 1 MiB guard: the call traps
host memory       with keys, any guest access to it faults: the call traps
other guests      each running guest holds its own key; another's memory faults
                  as host memory does; a fifteenth running guest waits for a key
signals           every runtime handler runs on its own stack; a thread with no
                  alternate stack is refused at the entry gate
re-entry          an import that calls back nests a gate context; a task that
                  moves threads takes its keys with it
forged table      a guest-written table entry reaches only functions of the
                  right signature; others trap as a signature mismatch
translator crash  a panic, stack overflow or allocation failure ends the child:
                  Defect in load: the translator failed: <its report>
compile bomb      a body over 1 MiB or nesting over 10,000 levels: Guest in load;
                  memory past the cap: Budget(.Memory) in load; past the caller's
                  deadline the child is killed: Budget(.Time) in load
OS memory kill    the child's OOM score makes it the kernel's first choice
concurrent loads  one translation at a time; a waiting load returns Budget(.Time)
                  at its caller's deadline
no /proc          Guest in load: couldn't start the plugin translator
no keys           no CPU flag, a failed key test or a registered rseq area: walls
                  1 and 2 only; same behavior, calls 55 to 65 ns
address space     a limit with no room for an 8 GiB reservation: Budget(.Memory)
                  in load: no room for the plugin's guard pages; literal plugins too
no new code       a policy that refuses executable in-memory files: Guest in load:
                  this system refuses executable in-memory files
memory64          refused at decode, as today: the guard needs 32-bit addresses
side channels     heap and table reads stay inside the guest's reservation even
                  speculatively; branch-target and return-stack poisoning are a
                  named residual
```

options.name: Translate and run in a helper process
options.detail: The host starts an engine helper, `jet-plugin-engine`, for each loaded plugin. The host reads the bytes, checks the sha256 and pipes those exact bytes to the helper. The helper never opens the path. It decodes, checks and translates the component, then runs each export on request over two pipes. A crashing guest or translator cannot touch host memory. The helper ships beside the program or with the Jet toolchain.
options.technical:
The helper holds A's code as its own executable, an estimated 4.5 MB or more, shipped once. The host grows only by its start and pipe code. Each call becomes a pipe round trip of about 5 microseconds, measured as an upper bound through Python.

Limits: the helper's translated code checks fuel, deadline, memory and tables exactly as A does. A call past its deadline returns Budget(.Time) and the plugin keeps serving calls. The host stops the helper only if it does not answer within the deadline plus one second. That call then fails as Defect, and so do later calls. Web: refused at build, as today. I9: one code generator, so no exception. Literal-path plugins still run in process, so guests run two ways.

Edge cases:

```text
guest trap        the helper sends the fault and frames; the host builds the same PluginError
bad module        the helper's decoder refuses it; same Guest in load message as A
load race         the host hashes and pipes the bytes it read; the helper never reopens the path
concurrent loads  one helper per load; nothing shared
translator defect the helper exits; that load or call fails as Defect, the host lives
compile bomb      the helper applies A's caps: Guest in load past 1 MiB a body or
                  10,000 levels of nesting, Budget(.Memory) in load past the memory
                  cap; the host stops it past the caller's deadline: Budget(.Time)
                  in load
no runtime code   works once the helper alone is exempted; the host maps no code
missing helper    Guest in load: couldn't load plugin `x.wasm`: the plugin engine
                  `jet-plugin-engine` was not found
untrusted bytes   reach only the helper; the host parses replies only
```

options.name: Interpret the component in the runtime
options.detail: The shared runtime gains an interpreter beside the WebAssembly decoder. At load it decodes and checks the component. Each call then steps through the guest's instructions one at a time. Nothing ships beside the program, and loading does no translation. Guest code runs slower than translated code.
options.technical:
Size, an estimate: the decoder is about 0.35 MB measured, plus an interpreter of 0.1 to 0.3 MB. Wasm3, a C interpreter, needs about 64 KB of code. So C saves at least 3.5 MB against an O2 host under A. Speed: on CoreMark, wasm3 ran 4 times slower than an optimizing wasmtime and 12 times slower than native code. Those numbers are from 2019 and 2020.

Limits: the interpreter must spend fuel at function entry and loop heads, in slices of 4096, and check the deadline at each slice end. Then Budget(.Fuel) falls at the same point as in translated code. Memory and table growth call the same runtime checks. These rules become a second copy of the translator's checks. Web: refused at build, as today; C would be the only option able to run in a browser later.

I9 forbids an interpreter on any level. So C needs this ratified exception:

"Excluded from I9 on O0, O1 and O2: a plugin guest loaded by `plugin.load<T>` runs in Core's WebAssembly interpreter, not the Jet code generator. Literal-path guests are unchanged. The web tier has no `plugin.load`."

Edge cases:

```text
guest trap        frames come from the interpreter's own call stack; offsets must match A's
bad module        same decoder; same Guest in load message as A
load race         one read, as A
concurrent loads  no shared state
interpreter defect stops the host, as A
compile bomb      none; loading only decodes and validates, under A's caps and
                  the caller's deadline
no runtime code   works; the interpreter maps no code
untrusted bytes   reach the decoder, validator and interpreter inside the host
```

options.name: Single-pass WebAssembly compiler in the runtime
options.detail: The runtime gains a baseline compiler that turns each WebAssembly function straight into x86-64 code in one pass. Loading is fast and the compiler is small. Calls run in process. It is a second code generator beside Jet's own, with its own copy of the bounds, fuel and deadline checks.
options.technical:
Size, an estimate: the decoder is about 0.35 MB measured, plus a one-pass emitter of 0.3 to 0.6 MB, plus A's decoder and checker, an estimated 0.2 MB. No comparable Jet code exists to measure. Speed: on the same CoreMark table, Wasmer's single-pass compiler ran about 1.6 times slower than its Cranelift compiler. Those numbers are from 2019 and 2020.

Limits: the emitter must spend fuel at function entry and loop heads, in slices of 4096, and check the deadline at each slice end. Memory and table growth call the same runtime checks. A's checker, guard pages and memory keys apply to its code too, so escapes stay closed. But its fuel, deadline and frame rules are a second copy to keep equal to A's. Web: refused at build, as today.

I9 forbids a second code generator. So D needs this ratified exception:

"Excluded from I9 on O0, O1 and O2: a plugin guest loaded by `plugin.load<T>` is compiled by Core's single-pass WebAssembly compiler, not the Jet code generator. Literal-path guests are unchanged. The web tier has no `plugin.load`."

Edge cases:

```text
guest trap        frames come from the emitter's own frame records; offsets must match A's
bad module        same decoder; same Guest in load message as A
load race         one read, as A
concurrent loads  one compile at a time, as A
compiler defect   fails one load as Defect if the emitter is Jet code, as A
emitter bug       A's checker refuses the code: Defect in load
compile bomb      linear in size; A's caps and the caller's deadline apply
no new code       as in A: mapped from a sealed memfd
untrusted bytes   reach the decoder, validator and emitter inside the host
```

options.name: Translate in a helper at load, run in the host
options.detail: At load the host pipes the bytes it read to an engine helper, `jet-plugin-engine`, a separate file. The helper translates them with A's translator and returns native code tagged with the bytes' sha256. The host checks the tag, runs A's checker over the code, and runs it in process behind A's guard pages and memory keys. So a steered translator bug fails the load, as in A. The host stays about 4 MB smaller than under A. The helper must ship beside the program and match its Jet version exactly.
options.technical:
This is Wasmtime's precompile route, done by a helper at load, with A's checker in the host. Size: the host adds a loader of an estimated 0.2 MB, with MemoryLink as the stand-in, plus A's decoder and checker, an estimated 0.2 MB. The helper is an estimated 4.5 MB or more, shipped once. Calls: as A, about 72 to 82 ns with memory keys and 55 to 65 ns without. Load: a process start plus A's translation and check.

Limits, frames, the three walls and the web tier behave as in A. I9: one code generator, so no exception. The only difference from A is where the translator lives: a second file instead of the program itself.

A disk cache keyed by sha256 would skip repeat translations. It is left out, as in A. With the checker, planted code must still pass it, so a later ballot could allow one.

Edge cases:

```text
guest trap        same PluginError and frames as A
bad module        the helper's decoder refuses it; same Guest in load message as A
load race         the host hashes and pipes the bytes it read; the reply must carry that sha256
concurrent loads  one helper per load
translator defect the helper exits; the load fails as Defect, the host lives
translator bug    A's checker refuses the code: Defect in load; the guest never runs
compile bomb      the helper applies A's caps; the host stops it past the caller's
                  deadline: Budget(.Time) in load
missing helper    Guest in load: couldn't load plugin `x.wasm`: the plugin engine
                  `jet-plugin-engine` was not found
version mismatch  Guest in load: the plugin engine is from another Jet version
untrusted bytes   reach only the helper; the host reads its code and descriptor
no keys           as in A: the checker and guard pages hold
no new code       as in A: the host maps the reply from a sealed memfd
```

comparisons.note: Compiles a component to machine code when it loads, inside the host process, with Cranelift or the single-pass Winch. It can also precompile ahead and map the result, which it marks unsafe.
An interpreter of about 64 KB of code. It loads quickly, and its guest code ran 4 times slower than an optimizing compiler on CoreMark in 2019.
Compiles WebAssembly at load with a single-pass compiler, then recompiles hot functions with its optimizing one.

recommendation.why: A runs run-time-path plugins with the same translator as literal-path plugins. A separate checker proves each load's code safe before it runs. It passed every component that loads today, and refused all 74 unsafe changes tried. Guard pages catch any stray heap address, and memory keys lock the host's and other plugins' memory where the CPU has them. It needs no helper file, no new limits value and no I9 exception.
gains: A translator bug alone cannot let a guest escape: the checker refuses unsafe code before it runs, and guard pages and memory keys back it up.
Calls cost about 72 to 82 ns with memory keys and 55 to 65 ns without, 60 to 90 times faster than a pipe.
One file to ship; a translator crash, stack overflow or memory blow-up ends only the translating child, never the host.

losses.loss: Hosts that use `plugin.load<T>` grow by at least 2.5 MB at O0 and 4.5 MB at O2.
losses.mitigation: This is physical: a program that translates must hold a translator. Only those hosts pay; literal-path programs are unchanged, and hosts inside `jet` pay about 0.1 MB.

losses.loss: On CPUs with memory keys, each call pays about 17 ns to lock and unlock the host's memory.
losses.mitigation: Only the way in and out pays; work inside the guest runs at full speed, and pure helpers run without leaving the guest.

losses.loss: Without memory keys, safety rests on the checker and guard pages alone.
losses.mitigation: The checker is small, written apart from the translator, and fuzzed on every translation. Behavior is identical with or without keys.

losses.loss: Each new component is translated and checked before its first call: about 2.6 s per MiB of body, once the code generator fix lands.
losses.mitigation: Loads of the same sha256 in one process translate once. The memory cap bounds a load to about 5 to 7 s, and `#Deadline` returns `Budget(.Time)` sooner.

losses.loss: A system that refuses executable mappings of in-memory files refuses run-time loads.
losses.mitigation: This is physical: such a policy forbids what any translating engine must do. The error names the cause, and literal-path plugins still work.

losses.loss: Six runtime helpers stay host code: memory and table growth, fuel, traps, frames and host imports. A logic bug in them has one wall, their own checks.
losses.mitigation: Every guest address they use is formed inside the guest's reservation, so a missed bounds check still faults. Bulk memory and table work moved into checked guest code.

losses.loss: Branch-target and return-stack poisoning inside one process could leak host bytes to a guest through cache timing.
losses.mitigation: It is a leak, not a write, and heap and table reads stay inside the guest even speculatively. Only a process per guest, option B, closes it.

losses.loss: With more than 14 plugins running guest code at once, the next one waits for a memory key.
losses.mitigation: Any number may be loaded. A plugin gives up its key at every fuel slice end and every host import, so the wait is at most one slice.

whyNot.reason: Every call pays a pipe round trip of about 5 microseconds, roughly 60 to 90 times an in-process call. A helper must also ship beside each program.
Guest code runs several times slower, and the interpreter repeats the fuel, time and frame rules in a second place. It also needs an I9 exception.
It is a second code generator whose fuel, deadline and frame rules must be kept equal to A's. It needs an I9 exception, and its code is slower than the translator's.
It differs from A only in where the translator lives: a version-matched helper file instead of the program itself. That saves about 4 MB per host, for a second file to ship and keep matched.

recommendation.tradeoff: At least two and a half to four and a half megabytes in hosts that load plugins at run time, and about 17 ns per call for the memory keys. Two residuals stay named: six host helpers and speculative leaks. In return: a sandbox no translator bug alone can break, native-speed calls and one file to ship.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude. Adversarial model family: Claude. Fresh agent: Lens. Lens rejected the first revision on nine claims and the second on the checker's frame-slot, count and loop rules and a key-wait deadlock. This revision answers each with a probe, and Lens reviews it against the owner's ruling that a guest must never escape.

surface.gist: When a program loads a plugin whose path it learns only at run time, what runs that plugin's code?
surface.lesson: A plugin is a sandboxed WebAssembly component, translated at build time, so its path must be in the source. A run-time path needs an engine at load: a translator in the program, a helper, or an interpreter. That engine may have bugs.

designAway.loss: A translator crash, stack overflow or allocation failure ended the host.
attempts: Translate in a helper and run in the host: this is option E, which needs a version-matched helper beside every program.
Run the translation as a Jet task: rejected. A probe shows a task contains a panic, but a task's stack overflow stopped the whole program, and an allocation failure aborts the process.

Translate in a child started from the host's own program file with a translator entry: kept. The child gets the memory cap as its address-space limit and is first in line for the kernel's out-of-memory killer.
designAway.result: Removed: any translator failure ends only the child. The load fails as `Defect`, or as `Budget(.Memory)` past the cap, and the host runs on.

designAway.loss: The 1 GiB memory cap ignored cgroup and address-space limits.
attempts: A setting for the cap: rejected, a knob each host would have to tune.
Cap at the smaller of 1 GiB and half the room the process can claim, read at load start from free memory, the cgroup chain and the address-space limit: kept.
designAway.result: Removed: the cap follows the environment with no setting. The compiler already reads the cgroup chain this way.

designAway.loss: A deadline around the load ended the host, since a join past its deadline raises E3003.
attempts: Add a join with a timeout to Jet code: rejected, a second way to bound a wait beside `#Deadline`.
Make the load a typed-error wait, as a network read is: at expiry it kills the child and returns `Budget(.Time)`: kept, as new runtime work.
designAway.result: Removed: `#Deadline` and `task.timeout` bound a load and the host runs on.

designAway.loss: Translation time grew with the square of nesting depth: a 1 MiB body took 20 s.
attempts: A smaller body cap: rejected, it only scales the square down and refuses real code.
Keep each open block's pending jumps with that block, so a block end patches only its own: kept, as code generator work that Jet programs share.
designAway.result: Removed once that fix lands: run-time loads stay off until every probed shape builds a 1 MiB body in under 3 s.

designAway.loss: Untrusted bytes reach the decoder, validator and back end inside the host process.
attempts: Move them to a helper process that also runs the guest: that is B, which pays 60 to 90 times per call.
Decode, validate and translate in the child: kept. The host reads only the child's code and descriptor, and checks both before use.
designAway.result: Removed from the host: untrusted bytes reach only the child, and nothing the child returns runs until the checker passes it.

designAway.loss: Each new component is translated before its first call, on every build and every `jet` start.
attempts: Cache translated code on disk under a rule of its own: rejected, a second store and a second reuse rule.
Translate each sha256 once per process: kept.
Keep translated code in the machine store `jet build` uses: not today. No host links the store code, and no ratified switch reaches a deployed host.
designAway.result: Reduced to once per process. The child's start adds 0.4 to 0.7 ms, and the check reads code at 3.4 MB/s or faster. Across runs: none today.

designAway.loss: Memory keys cost each call about 17 ns, and up to 48 ns under heavy load.
attempts: Skip the keys: rejected, the owner ruled that a guest escape is unacceptable.
Gate every helper call: rejected, it doubles the cost for bit counts and float helpers.
Let helpers that touch no memory run without leaving the guest: kept. If one ever touched memory, the keys would trap it.
designAway.result: Reduced: only entering and leaving the guest, and helpers that touch memory, pay.

designAway.loss: Machines without memory keys, or hosts that register glibc's rseq area, cannot use the key wall.
attempts: Fall back to running the guest in another process: rejected here. That is option B, a second mechanism that I8 would have to allow.
Run with the checker and guard pages alone, with identical behavior: kept.
Turn keys off when the CPU lacks them, a one-time test in the child fails, or rseq is registered: kept.
Force the keyless gates with an internal switch and run the plugin cases both ways: kept, so the keyless body never ships untested.
designAway.result: Reduced: two walls hold on every machine, and the third is added where the CPU and kernel allow. Jet's runtime registers no rseq area.

designAway.loss: A signal during guest code, with the host's memory locked, could end the host.
attempts: Run every handler on its own stack and open all keys before it reads the interrupted state: kept. The process-signal and SIGSYS handlers gain SA_ONSTACK, and a guard test asserts it on every runtime sigaction.
Refuse guest entry on a thread with no alternate stack: kept.
Send a non-fault signal in the first load's key test: kept. Probed: with its own stack, a signal to guest code ran its handler and the process went on; without one, the process died.
designAway.result: Removed: a trap or signal in guest code lands in the host as a `PluginError` or a handled signal, as today.

designAway.loss: Run-time loads failed where new machine code is forbidden, such as SELinux deny_execmem.
attempts: Write anonymous memory, then make it executable: rejected, deny_execmem and PaX MPROTECT refuse it.
Map the code shared from a memfd made with MFD_NOEXEC_SEAL and sealed, never writable: kept. Probed: writes and a writable map were refused, and the read-execute map ran.
designAway.result: Reduced, not probed under SELinux: deny_execmem does not refuse it. A policy that refuses executable in-memory files still refuses the load, by name; that is physical for any translating engine.

designAway.loss: A second limits value, `plugin.LoadLimits`, sat beside the ratified `plugin.Limits`, sharing field names with other meanings.
attempts: Add load fields to `plugin.Limits`: rejected, they would do nothing on literal loads.
Bound loads by fixed safety caps and the caller's `#Deadline`, which Jet already has: kept.
designAway.result: Removed: one limits value, as ratified, and Jet's one deadline mechanism.

designAway.loss: The checker's rules described code the back end doesn't emit, and the export area and instance mixed guest and host words.
attempts: Make the shared back end emit fixed forms for the checker: rejected, a second code generator mode.
Check the back end's output as it is, with a dataflow interpreter over registers and frame slots: kept.
Forget a frame slot on any write over its bytes but a full-width mov, and bound rows, globals and the area by the module's own counts: kept.
Split the instance into a guest page, a read-only page and a host record, with the export area in the guest page: kept.
designAway.result: Removed: the prototype accepts all 452 functions that load today, at every level, refuses all 74 unsafe changes, and binds the area to the entry's own argument.

designAway.loss: Runtime helpers ran as host code with host memory open, behind one wall.
attempts: Gate every helper and trust its checks: rejected, one wall for 19 helpers.
Emit bulk memory and table operations and call_indirect's lookup as checked guest code: kept.
Form every guest address the remaining helpers use inside the reservation: kept.
designAway.result: Reduced: six helpers remain host code. A missed bounds check in them still faults, but any other logic bug in them is a single wall, a named residual.

designAway.loss: A 64 KiB guest frame could step over a one-page stack guard.
attempts: Stack probes in the back end: rejected, it changes code every Jet program shares.
A 1 MiB guard under every guest stack, more than the 64 KiB frame cap: kept. Probed: a 4 KiB guard was stepped over; a 1 MiB guard caught the same frame.
designAway.result: Removed: any admitted frame that overruns the guest stack faults in its guard and traps.

designAway.loss: Imports that re-enter a guest, and tasks that move threads, had no defined gate state.
attempts: One saved host context per thread: rejected, a parked task can resume on another thread.
A per-task chain of gate contexts in host memory, and absolute keys at every gate: kept. Probed with a task that moved threads and re-entered.
designAway.result: Removed: each gate restores exactly the context it saved, on whichever thread the task runs.

designAway.loss: Past about 13 live guests, guests shared memory keys, so one could read another behind two walls.
attempts: Share keys past the limit: rejected, the owner's bar counts a cross-guest read as an escape.
A process per guest past the limit: rejected, that is option B.
Give each running guest its own key, taking the least recently used one and closing its old holder's pages: kept. Probed with 40 guests and 14 keys.
Count a guest parked in a host import as not running, so its key may be taken; it takes one again on return: kept. Probed with fourteen guests parked on a fifteenth.
designAway.result: Removed: no two guests ever share a key, and parked guests can't starve a running one. A fifteenth guest running at once waits at most one fuel slice.

designAway.loss: Branch-target and return-stack poisoning inside one process could leak host bytes.
attempts: Mask every heap and table index: kept, which stops speculative reads outside the guest's reservation.
Fill the return-stack buffer at the exit gate: not adopted. It doesn't cover branch targets, and its cost was not measured.
A process per guest: that is option B.
designAway.result: Remains as a named residual: a leak through cache timing, never a write. Every in-process engine shares it.
