decisions.title: Registers, memory and machine code at a stop: three panels in the Canvas Debug view, with the same words in the console and the editor adapter
decisions.situation: At a stop, the Canvas Debug view shows six panels at once: Source, Call Stack, Locals, Watches, Tasks and the Debug Console. RemedyBG and the RAD Debugger also show the registers, a memory window and the machine code around the stop. Jet's view shows none of the three. jet debug can list machine code with disas, but Canvas only prints it into the console transcript. The console has no word for registers or memory. The VS Code adapter shows only a runtime frame's pc and cfa, under [raw] Locals, and reads no memory. You decide how the three panels look, how a user opens and aims each, how the console spells them, and how memory is shown. We recommend three always-present panels fed by two new console words and the existing disas listing, so the console, Canvas and VS Code show the same facts.
decisions.gist: How should the Canvas Debug view show registers, memory and machine code at a stop, and how does a user open, aim and read each?
decisions.lesson: A register is one of the processor's few named slots, such as rax or rsp; rip holds the next instruction's address. Memory is the program's bytes, read at an address. A memory panel prints them in rows of 16, as hex and as text, or as numbers of a chosen type. Machine code is the instructions the processor runs, which disas already lists. Optimized code keeps many locals in registers, so these panels show where a value really is.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: open the Debug view in Canvas and stop at a breakpoint. Three new panels, Registers, Memory and Disassembly, join the six the view already shows at once. Each panel's header folds it, and the page keeps that choice for the next session. Disassembly shows the selected function as disas lists it, scrolled to an arrow on the next instruction. Registers lists the general registers, each with the local it holds. In Locals, Show memory on a value opens Memory at its bytes.

Expert path: the console gains registers [--all] and memory WHERE [COUNT] [as TYPE]. WHERE takes three forms. The first is a place, as watch takes it: a local, a field path under it, and at most one index at the end, such as order.lines[2]. The second is a hex address, such as 0x7f3a1c002010. The third is a register, such as $rsp. Any of the three may end in + or - and a number of bytes, as $rsp+16.

TYPE is a Jet number type. U8, the default, shows hex bytes and text. Int, I64, I32, I16, I8, U64, U32, U16, Float and F32 show one number per item; I64 reads as Int. A TYPE that is not a number type, such as String, is refused, naming the number types. COUNT counts items of TYPE, and defaults to 64 bytes' worth. Canvas and the adapter call the same two session calls, so a panel and the console never disagree.

A place shows its own bytes: a stack slot's, or a String's or List's header. Show memory on a List opens on its buffer, as its element type when that is a number type. In Memory, every aligned 8-byte word that points into the program's mapped memory is underlined. Clicking it follows the pointer, and Back returns. Bytes that belong to a local of the selected frame carry its name above them, as the RAD Debugger labels them. A List's buffer is labeled by index.

Disassembly reuses the ratified D-DISASM1 listing rows, so call targets open their function and breakpoint marks match the console. Stepping from Disassembly steps by line, since the ratified D-DISASM1 adds no instruction stepping.

Registers label two kinds of fact, drawn apart. A local's name, such as total, means the image's location lists place that local in the register at this pc. An arrow, such as -> items[0], means the register's value is the address of a local's bytes or of an item in its buffer. That second label is a match the debugger found, not a location fact.

The panels follow the selected task and frame. In an outer frame, rip and rsp are that frame's, and the registers the call saved are recovered from the image's call frame information. Any other register reads not saved, as gdb prints it, instead of a guess.

A parked task resumes with only rip, rsp, rbx, rbp and r12 to r15 saved, so its other registers read not saved. A task running on another runtime thread shows that thread's registers; every thread is stopped at a stop. A queued task that never ran has no registers, and Registers says so.

The register set is the same at -O0, -O1 and -O2: rax to r15, rip and rflags, 18 rows with the flags spelled out. --all, or All in the panel, adds xmm0 to xmm15 as hex and as two Floats, mxcsr, fs_base and gs_base. The level changes the labels. At -O0 locals live in stack slots, so few registers name one; at -O2 the image's location lists put many in registers.

A register whose value changed since the previous stop of the same task and frame is highlighted. In a replay, the previous stop is the one shown before, in either direction. After selecting another task or frame, nothing is highlighted until that task's or frame's next stop.

Edge cases are named, never guessed. A local the image cannot show answers <Unavailable>, and a parameter not kept answers unavailable (not kept at this point), as Locals prints them today. A local held in a register names that register, since it has no address, and offers the register's word to follow.

A stop inside the runtime or linked C code lists its code by symbol and offset, as disas does. Its registers carry no local labels. With a runtime frame selected, a place in WHERE resolves in the nearest Jet frame outward, and the answer names that frame.

Memory is read page by page against the program's memory map. A live or replayed program's map is the kernel's for that process, and a dump's map is its own region list. So a range that starts in unmapped memory shows ?? there and the mapped bytes after it.

Over code, Memory puts the program's bytes back under the debugger's trap bytes and placed jumps, as disas does. The debugger's own code, its evaluation room and a placed condition, reads [debugger], and pointers into it are not offered to follow. After fix, the old entry's bytes are the jump fix wrote, labeled with where it goes. A huge range is read 4 KiB at a time as the panel scrolls. A console answer stops at 4096 bytes, naming where it cut.

Each tier shows what it holds. A live run and a replay show everything above. A dump holds the stopped thread's general registers, only the registers it marked for other tasks, no xmm registers, and only the memory regions it kept. Its #Secret bytes, and every copy of them, were zeroed when the dump was written. Memory shows ## over a Secret local's own bytes, and other zeroed bytes read 00; the panel says the dump was redacted.

Canvas's live and replay sessions build the entry at -O0, as they do today. So in Canvas, -O2 code reaches the panels only through a dump of an -O2 build. jet debug -O2, and VS Code through the adapter, show the panels' facts at any level. jet debug --attach shows the same words with the same rules; Canvas has no attach session.

The panels exist where Jet's native debugger runs, on x86-64 Linux. The register table lives in the loader, so another native host brings its own rows. A web build runs in the browser, where no Jet debugger stops it; DevTools' memory inspector reads its linear memory.

Everything is read-only. Writing a register or a byte changes the program under the user's code, touches replay and fix, and needs its own ballot.
decisions.story: Theo's -O2 build prints a wrong total. He runs jet debug -O2 and stops in the loop of sum. locals says i is <Unavailable>. disas shows the add reading [r12+rcx*8]. registers shows rcx is 2, and marks r12 -> items[0]. He types memory $r12 3 as Int, and it prints 12, 29 and -5. A negative price had slipped into the list. In Canvas the same panels show it at -O0, where items sits in its stack slot and Show memory opens its buffer.
decisions.inWild:
// gdb: registers, 16 bytes in hex at the stack pointer, then the code.
(gdb) info registers
(gdb) x/16xb $rsp
(gdb) disassemble /s
// lldb: the same three.
(lldb) register read
(lldb) memory read --size 1 --count 16 $rsp
(lldb) disassemble --frame --mixed
decisions.detail:
Code read on dev 50aae50f71. The console's commands are NATIVE_DEBUG_HELP (JetDebug Native.jet:6558). They include disassemble (disas), symbols and segments, and no word for registers or memory. disas dispatches at Native.jet:2784. Listing rows are NativeListedRow (JetDebug NativeListing.jet:303), cut to a window around an address by native_listing_window (NativeListing.jet:337). Bytes no instruction covers become native_listing_invalid rows (NativeListing.jet:382).

The loader reads the stopped thread's registers with PTRACE_GETREGS (JetBackend Image/Loader.jet:2119, 2831-2840). That is the kernel's 27-word user_regs_struct, X64_TRACE_REGISTERS (Loader.jet:2185), including fs_base and gs_base. No ptrace read of the SSE registers exists; only the evaluation room saves them, with xsave, inside the program.

Memory is read through x64_trace_read (Loader.jet:2779). It returns the bytes up to where a mapping ends, and None when the first byte is unmapped. Stops are all-stop: every other thread is stopped too (Native.jet:3953-3955).

A parked task's registers come from native_task_registers (Native.jet:6921). It fills rip, rsp and the six registers the fiber switch saves, and copies the rest from the stopped thread, so those must read not saved. A dump marks which registers it knows for each task (native_dump_known, NativeDump.jet:366). Outer frames unwind callee-saved registers by the image's call frame information, with a mask of known registers (unwind_from, Native.jet:5764-5804).

The watch command reads its place with debug_place (JetDebug Debug/Expression.jet:74, used at Native.jet:3257): a local, a field path, and one index at the end. Its refusal names the grammar. Watches use the CPU's debug registers, DR0 to DR7, which are the debugger's own state. Locals prints <Unavailable> (NATIVE_DEBUG_UNAVAILABLE, Native.jet:6583) and unavailable (not kept at this point) (NATIVE_DEBUG_NOT_KEPT, Native.jet:6587).

The adapter answers initialize with supportsDisassembleRequest true and no readMemory support (JetCLI CLI/DebugDap.jet:191). Its scopes answer Locals for a Jet frame, and [raw] Locals with presentationHint registers for a runtime frame (DebugDap.jet:289). That scope shows the frame's pc and cfa (DebugDap.jet:1235-1243). The ratified D-DBG-DAP1 records memory features as absent until a later ballot adds them; A adds readMemory only.

The Canvas protocol's debug commands already include disassemble (Docs/Spec/Reference/canvas-protocol.md:307). Its listing goes into the transcript that the overlay's trace field shows. The overlay carries locals, watches, call_stack, trace and source (canvas-protocol.md:316, 360). Its limits include 32 call-stack frames and 128 trace entries (canvas-protocol.md:355). The native and native-recorded tiers build the entry with jet build -O0 (canvas-protocol.md:319-321).

The page's six panels are Source, Call Stack, Locals, Watches, Tasks and the Debug Console (JetCanvas CanvasAssets/HTML.jet). The Debug view shows every debugger panel at once (debug-profile.js:1-3), and has no Panels menu. Every tier runs under Jet's own native debugger: native for jet dev at -O0, native-recorded for a replay and native-dump for a crash dump (canvas-protocol.md:357, 366-369).

A dump is written through perf_flight_redacted (JetRuntime PerfSamples.jet:6937). secret_redact (Secret.jet:228-234) zeroes every Secret run and every copy of one, and the dump keeps no list of where. NativeDump redacts locals by their type (NativeDump.jet:421-426, 680). A live session shows #Secret values.

The audit's surfaces check, in the 2026-11-19 debug and profile audit, measured a painted stop in 56.8 ms at a load average of 26, with six panels. Its verdict is that the view lacks three of RemedyBG's panels.

options.name: Three always-present panels fed by console words, in Canvas, the console and the adapter
options.detail: The console gains registers [--all] and memory WHERE [COUNT] [as TYPE]. Canvas gains Registers, Memory and Disassembly beside the six panels it already shows at once; each header folds its panel. Memory has a type selector, from bytes to Int or Float. Disassembly shows disas's rows for the selected function. The adapter gains readMemory and a Registers scope. One engine answers all three surfaces, and nothing writes to the program.
options.technical:
Engine: NativeSession gains registers(task, frame, all) and memory(where, count, type). registers reads the 27 words it already reads at each stop, or the selected task's saved registers. For an outer frame it unwinds callee-saved registers as bt does, and marks the rest not saved. --all adds one PTRACE_GETFPREGS read in the loader, for xmm0 to xmm15 and mxcsr. A parked task and a dump read those as not saved.

DR0 to DR7 are never listed: they hold the debugger's watches, which breaks lists. Each register carries the local the image's location lists place in it at that pc. A register whose value is the address of a local's bytes, or of an item in its buffer, carries an arrow label instead.

memory resolves a place with debug_place, as watch does, and refuses with its refusal text. An unknown $register is refused with the register names. A COUNT of 0, a negative COUNT or one that is not a number is refused: COUNT is a positive number of items. A TYPE that is not a number type is refused, naming the number types. A place in a register has no address: memory answers with the register and its value.

gdb's words point to these. As the ratified D-DBG-VERBS1 has it, an unknown gdb word answers with its Jet word. So info registers answers with registers, and x/16xb $rsp answers with memory $rsp 16.

Bytes are read page by page against the memory map: the kernel's for a live or replayed program, and the region list for a dump. Unmapped bytes print as ??. Originals go back under trap bytes and placed jumps, and the debugger's own code reads [debugger]. After fix, the old entry's jump is labeled. The console prints at most 4096 bytes per command, saying where it cut.

Canvas: the overlay gains registers, the selected task's and frame's 18 register rows with labels and a changed flag. It also gains disassembly, the 16 listing rows around the pc from native_listing_window. A folded panel's field is not sent.

The request gains a reads list, such as {kind: memory, where, count, type} or {kind: disassembly, function, from}. The answer gains a reads field: the address, the bytes, a mapped mask and the labels, or more listing rows. Reads stay out of the transcript, so scrolling never fills the Debug Console. This is a protocol addition, as B's is, but it calls the console words' session calls. The page keeps at most 64 memory pages, and fold state in its local settings.

Adapter: supportsReadMemoryRequest true, a memoryReference on each variable with an address, and a Registers scope whose variables are the register rows. On a runtime frame, the Registers scope joins [raw] Locals, which keeps its pc and cfa. Writes stay unsupported.

// Canvas Debug view, every panel present:
// Source | Call Stack | Locals | Watches | Tasks | Registers | Memory | Disassembly | Console

options.name: Canvas-only panels
options.detail: Canvas gains the same three panels, fed by new overlay fields and a new memory request in the Canvas protocol. The console and the adapter gain nothing. RemedyBG's layout is matched in Canvas alone.
options.technical: The overlay gains registers and disassembly as in A, and the protocol gains a memory request {address, count} answered with bytes. The session code that builds them is called by the Canvas service only. The console keeps disas and no register or memory word, and the adapter keeps memory unsupported. Memory takes a place, an address or a register, resolved by the session as in A, since the Canvas service already holds a NativeSession.

options.name: Console words only, shown in the transcript
options.detail: The console gains registers and memory, and Canvas shows their answers in the Debug Console transcript, as disas works in Canvas today. No new panel is drawn, and the adapter gains nothing.
options.technical: The same registers and memory session calls as A, printed as text. Canvas sends them through the commands field, and the answers land in the overlay's trace, capped at 128 entries. Nothing stays on screen as the user steps: each stop needs the words typed again. Following a pointer is typing memory with the next address.

options.name: A without the adapter change
options.detail: A's panels in Canvas and A's two console words, with the adapter as it is. VS Code keeps [raw] Locals for runtime frames. It reports memory as unsupported, as the ratified D-DBG-DAP1 profile has it.
options.technical: The engine, console and Canvas halves of A, unchanged. The adapter answers initialize with no readMemory support, and sends no memoryReference and no Registers scope. VS Code's debug console evaluates expressions only, so it gets no registers or memory.

options.name: A with panels opened from a new Panels menu
options.detail: As A, but the three panels are hidden until the user opens each from a new Panels menu in the Debug view. The six panels stay always present.
options.technical: The Debug view gains a Panels menu, which it does not have today, listing Registers, Memory and Disassembly. An unopened panel's overlay field is not sent. The open set is kept in the page's local settings. Show memory in Locals opens Memory without the menu.

options.name: A with gdb's spellings
options.detail: As A, but the console words are gdb's: info registers [all] for registers, and x/COUNT FORMAT WHERE for memory. The format takes gdb's size letters b, h, w and g, for 1, 2, 4 and 8 bytes. It takes gdb's display letters x, d, u, f and c, for hex, signed, unsigned, float and character.
options.technical:
The engine and the panels are A's. The console parses gdb's format letters after x/ into COUNT and TYPE. So x/16xb $rsp is memory $rsp 16, and x/3dg $r12 is memory $r12 3 as Int. info registers rip rsp names registers.

The ratified D-DBG-VERBS1 rule is gdb's words where gdb has one, and plain words where it has none. For gdb's info subcommands it chose plain words: breaks for info breakpoints, and tasks for info threads. A reads the rule that way for info registers. x is one gdb word, but its meaning lives in a format language no other Jet word uses. A spells the same choices as a Jet type; F keeps gdb's letters.
options.code:
// Illustrative.
(Jet) info registers
rbx 0x0000000000000029  41   total
(Jet) x/16xb $rsp
0x7ffd5e3a1f40  29 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 ...
(Jet) x/3dg $r12
0x7f3a1c002010  12  29  -5

options.name: A with a bytes-only memory view
options.detail: As A, but memory shows only hex bytes and text, 16 to a row. There is no as TYPE, and the panel has no type selector.
options.technical: memory WHERE [COUNT], COUNT in bytes. Show memory on a List opens on its buffer as bytes. Reading the third Int of a List is reading 8 little-endian bytes at offset 16 by eye. Labels and pointer following are A's.
options.code:
// Illustrative.
(Jet) memory $r12 24

decisions.title: A built program's sections: their sizes and a named section's bytes, from jet debug's file-first console
decisions.situation: A built program file is cut into named sections: .text holds the code, .rodata the constants, .data the values the program changes. Two Jet checks still ask binutils about them. The Core battery cost report reads every section's size with size -A. A build test proves a folded 50,000,000-byte string left no bytes behind, by reading .data and .rodata with readelf -x. The ratified D-DEBUG-LISTING1 lists symbols and segments, but no sections. You decide how Jet lists sections and shows one's bytes. We recommend a sections word that owns both, whatever the open debugger-panels ballot decides.
decisions.gist: How should jet debug list a built program's sections and show a named section's bytes, so Jet's own checks drop size and readelf?
decisions.lesson: A section is a named run of bytes in a program file, such as .text for code or .rodata for constants. A segment is what the loader maps into memory, and one segment can hold several sections. On a Jet image, the read-only segment holds .rodata and .eh_frame together, so a segment's size cannot say how big .rodata is. Debug info and the symbol table are sections that no segment loads.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: jet debug IMAGE --do sections lists every section of the program file, in file order, without starting it. Each row holds the name, the type, then offset, address, size, flags and align, each named, as segments names its fields. The flags are readelf's letters, all of them, in readelf's order. W is written, A loaded and X code; M, S, I, L, O, G, T, C and E follow. So .tbss shows WAT.

Expert path: sections NAME... lists only the named sections, in the order given. When the file holds two sections of one name, it lists both, in file order. sections NAME... --bytes prints each listed section's bytes under its row. Each byte row holds an address, 16 bytes in hex, and the same bytes as text, with a dot for each byte that does not print. That is the look of the byte rows the open debugger-panels ballot proposes, and of readelf -x's text column.

The bytes always come from the file, since sections lists the file. So a section no segment loads, such as .symtab or .debug_info, prints its bytes as well. With --bytes, every section row ends with from the file: before a start, at a stop and in a dump alike. A row listed without --bytes carries no such words. A program's own memory is the memory word's job, if the panels ballot passes one.

Size: at the interactive console, --bytes prints at most 4096 bytes of each section. The cap is per section, unlike the panels ballot's per-command cap, so sections .data .rodata --bytes can print 8192 bytes. Where it cuts, the console prints cut at ADDRESS: 4096 of SIZE bytes shown; --do prints the whole section. To see the rest, run the same sections command with --do.

A --do command prints every byte, since a script asked for it, so the build test reads the whole section. This rule belongs to sections; it does not change the panels ballot's memory word.

Scripts read these rows, so their columns change only with a decision, as the ratified D-DEBUG-LISTING1 set for symbols and segments.

Edge cases are named. A name the image lacks is refused with No section `NAME`, so --do exits 1. A section that takes no file space, such as .bss, prints its row, then (no bytes in the file). The reader checks the type before it reads any bytes.

An image with no section headers prints `IMAGE` has no section headers and exits 0, as segments does for program headers. A file with more than 65,279 sections keeps its real count in the first header, and the reader takes it from there. The null header that opens every table is not listed.

A stripped image lists its own sections. When it names a side debug file, sections prints that file's name under its rows, as debug info: main.debug. To list the side file's sections, run jet debug on the side file itself; its code sections print (no bytes in the file), since the side file keeps only debug info.

The reader takes 64-bit little-endian ELF files, Jet's or not, as symbols does. So the cost report can list the C stand-ins its tests build. A file that is not a 64-bit ELF is refused as symbols refuses it: `X` is not a 64-bit ELF image. A big-endian ELF is refused: `X` is a big-endian ELF image. A web build's wasm sections are out of scope, as jet debug does not run on the web.

The two users move with it. The cost report reads sections for each section's size. The build test reads sections .data .rodata --bytes. It checks that no row is sixteen 78 bytes, the letter x, or sixteen 79 bytes, the letter y. That is the same fact its readelf check proves today.
decisions.story: Mia adds a JSON import to a program and its release build grows by 40 KB. She runs jet debug on both builds with --do sections and compares the rows. .text grew by 3 KB; .rodata grew by 37 KB. She runs sections .rodata --bytes and finds a whole Unicode table that a fold left in. She never left Jet's tools, and the cost report reads the same rows on every battery.
decisions.detail:
Code read on gate p407, dev 50aae50f71; dev b946c4dfc4 has no JetDebug change since. The file-first console is native_image_command (JetDebug NativeImageList.jet:237). It answers symbols, segments, disassemble and help from the file, and returns None for anything else, which starts the program. A stop answers symbols and segments at Native.jet:2787, and a dump at NativeDump.jet:651, both through native_image_listing (NativeImageList.jet:62). The help line is NATIVE_DEBUG_HELP (Native.jet:6558).

The reader already walks the section header table. native_image_symbols reads it to find .symtab (NativeImageList.jet:97-127), and native_elf_header and native_elf_section find a section by name (NativeFacts.jet:302-315). native_elf_section does not check the type, so the reader tests for NOBITS before reading.

native_image_bytes refuses a file that is not ELFCLASS64 (NativeImageList.jet:80). It never reads the data-encoding byte, so a big-endian file would be misread today; the new refusal closes that. native_image_side finds the side file through .gnu_debuglink (NativeImageList.jet:88). Segment rows are native_image_segments_text (NativeImageList.jet:191), pinned by its test (NativeImageList.jet:317).

The memory word is not built. The open debugger-panels ballot proposes it, as memory WHERE [COUNT] [as TYPE] under its recommendation and as gdb's x/COUNT FORMAT WHERE under its option F. Under its option B the console gets no memory word. Its byte rows show hex bytes and text, and it caps a console answer at 4096 bytes. A here does not depend on which of these passes.

Probed on gate p407 with a two-line program built at -O2. segments lists a read-only LOAD of 7,588 bytes, an executable LOAD of 33,839 and a writable LOAD of 1,620. The section headers, read with a 20-line script, list 18 sections. .rodata is 2,415 bytes and .eh_frame 4,884, both in the read-only LOAD. .text is 33,839, and .data 1,592.

Eight .debug_ sections, .symtab, .strtab, .shstrtab and .jet_command load in no segment. jet debug IMAGE --do sections answers Unknown command `sections`, after starting the program and stopping at its first line.

The cost report is Tools/Perf/CoreActivation.mjs and its Jet twin CoreActivation/run.jet. It runs size -A and reads each section's name and size (run.jet:284-293). Its deltas are .text bytes, .rodata bytes and defined symbols (run.jet:217-219). A pending change moves its defined-symbol count to the rows of symbols, which list what nm --defined-only lists.

The cost report's Gauntlet entry builds stand-in programs with a fake jet. In that change, the fake jet's debug answers carry the rows jet debug printed for the same stand-in images, and the entry's expected output pins their counts. Under A the fake jet gains sections rows, taken the same way.

The build test is Tests/Cases/BuildEntry/a_folded_string_read_only_for_its_length_costs_no_bytes.case. It requires tool:readelf, runs readelf -x .data -x .rodata on the -O2 image, and checks that no row reads 78787878 78787878 78787878 78787878, or the same with 79.

options.name: A sections word that owns its byte rows; a memory word, if one passes, also takes a section name
options.detail:
The file-first console gains sections [NAME...] [--bytes]. Plain, it lists every section in file order. With names, it lists those, in the order given. --bytes prints each listed section's bytes from the file under its row, 16 to a row, as hex and text. The same word answers at a stop and in a crash dump, as symbols does, and reads the file there too.

If the debugger-panels ballot passes a console memory word, under either spelling, that word also takes a section name as its place. It then reads the section's loaded bytes from the program. If that ballot passes no console word, nothing more changes here.
options.technical:
NativeImageList.jet gains native_image_sections, which walks the section header table it already reads for .symtab, and native_image_sections_text, which pads the columns as segments does. Types are named as readelf names them: PROGBITS, NOBITS, SYMTAB, STRTAB, NOTE, RELA, DYNAMIC, INIT_ARRAY, FINI_ARRAY and others; any other type prints as hex. --bytes reads the file at the section's offset, and every section row it prints ends with from the file.

The interactive console prints at most 4096 bytes of each section. Where it cuts, it prints cut at ADDRESS: 4096 of SIZE bytes shown; --do prints the whole section. To see the rest, run the same sections command with --do, which prints every byte.

A section name in the memory word names the section's loaded address and size. memory .rodata reads from the section's start, and COUNT, when given, stops at the section's end and says so. Under gdb's spelling, x/16xb .rodata prints the first 16 bytes; x with no COUNT reads one item, as gdb does. A byte offset works as for a register, as .rodata+16, and as TYPE works as for any address.

Two sections of one name are refused in memory: Two sections are named `.data`, at 0x40bdc0 and 0x40c400; give memory an address. A section no segment loads is refused: `.symtab` is not loaded; sections .symtab --bytes shows it. As for every word but the listing words, memory starts the program first when none runs, so it always reads a program. Its cap and default COUNT stay the panels ballot's.

options.name: A new jet inspect image command
options.detail: jet inspect image IMAGE --sections lists A's rows, and --bytes NAME prints one section's bytes. jet inspect's --json gives the rows as JSON. The debugger keeps symbols and segments, and gains nothing.
options.technical: Inspect.jet gains an image plane that calls the same reader as A. Its rows and refusals are A's; --json emits name, type, offset, address, size, flags and align per section. It reads only files, so it has no stop or dump to disagree with.

options.name: sections for sizes, and gdb's find for a byte search instead of a dump
options.detail: sections lists rows as A does, with no --bytes. A second word, find BYTES [in NAME...], prints each address where the bytes occur in the named sections, or Not found. BYTES is a quoted text or hex bytes.
options.technical: find scans the section bytes in the image file and prints at most 100 hits, naming how many more. gdb's find takes a start address and a length; this form takes section names instead.

options.name: A, with readelf -x's byte rows
options.detail: As A, but --bytes prints rows as readelf -x does: the address, four groups of four bytes, and the text. Checks written for readelf carry over unchanged.
options.technical: Only the byte row format differs from A. Each group is four bytes in file order, written with no spaces between bytes.

options.name: sections lists the rows; only the memory word shows bytes, and reads the file before a start
options.detail: sections lists A's rows, with no --bytes. The console memory word the panels ballot proposes takes a section name and prints its bytes. Before a start it reads the file; at a stop, the running program; in a dump, the dump's memory. F stands only if that ballot passes a console memory word.
options.technical:
memory becomes a file-first word: with no session it answers from the file, for a section name or an address inside a loaded section. An unloaded section, such as .symtab, reads from the file before a start, and is refused at a stop as not loaded. Rows gain the text column, as that ballot's byte rows have it. COUNT, offsets, as TYPE and duplicate names follow A's rules for memory.

Under A: a new case, Debug/sections_list_an_image_and_its_bytes.case, builds a small program at -O0 and -O2. It checks that --do sections lists .text with flags AX and .rodata with flags A. The size of .text must equal the executable LOAD's file size from segments. It checks that sections .rodata --bytes prints rows of 16 bytes in hex and text, whose first row holds the program's first constant.

The case checks that sections .nope exits 1 with No section `.nope`, and that .bss prints (no bytes in the file). sections .symtab --bytes prints the file's bytes. At a stop after a global is written, sections .data --bytes still shows the file's first value, and its row ends with from the file. The answer is the same in a crash dump.

At the interactive console, sections .text --bytes stops after 4096 bytes with cut at ADDRESS: 4096 of SIZE bytes shown; --do prints the whole section. Two sections each get their own 4096. The same command under --do prints it whole. A section named twice lists both.

It checks the refusals: a text file is not a 64-bit ELF image; a big-endian ELF fixture is a big-endian ELF image. On a release image with a side file, sections prints debug info: NAME under its rows. jet debug on that side file lists its code sections with (no bytes in the file).

If the panels ballot passes a memory word, its case gains rows. memory .data 16 at a stop shows the written value, and memory .symtab is refused as not loaded. .rodata+16, a COUNT past the end and a name used twice behave as stated, with the stated texts.

The build test drops requires: tool:readelf, and reads jet debug .jet/build/constant --do 'sections .data .rodata --bytes'. Its two checks become a row of sixteen 78 bytes and a row of sixteen 79 bytes. The cost report runs sections instead of size -A, in both twins, and its fake jet answers sections with the rows jet debug prints for its stand-ins. Both users then run with no size or readelf on the path.

Under B: the same case through segments and disas .rodata. Under C: through jet inspect image. Under D: the sizes, and find for the build test. Under E: A's case with readelf's rows. Under F: A's case through memory, with the file read before a start.

decisions.title: How a called function learns where its returned value goes
decisions.situation:
The ratified D-PLACE-DEFAULT1 builds a growing value that a function returns, such as a list or text, on its caller's scope stack. When the caller stores that value in something older or sends it, the value goes to the heap at today's cost. So every call has to tell the callee one fact: stack or heap.

A direct call can say it. But function values, closures, runtime kernels, C exports, plugin guests and the debugger's evaluator reach the same code without knowing which function they call. The vote picks how the fact travels. We recommend one hidden argument that the runtime checks, with one builder body.
decisions.gist: How should a called function learn whether the list or text it returns goes on its caller's stack or the heap?
decisions.lesson: A function that returns a list has to build it somewhere. Under the ratified placement rule the caller decides: its scope stack when the list stays local, the heap when the list is stored or sent. The callee must learn that choice at every call, even through a function value, where the compiler does not know the callee. Nothing changes in what users write.
decisions.explainer:
A call's destination is one word: heap, which means the current allocator, or stack, which means a fresh scope stack of the calling task. The caller's placement rule picks it at each call, and sema records the pick. So O0, O1, O2 and the web pass the same word at the same call (I9).

Heap is 0. It sends the callee to the allocator it would use today, #Context's or the default. Stack is the address of the fresh scope stack the caller opened. Cyclone passes a region handle; this word is an address the runtime's page map already knows.

Trait calls dispatch by a type test, then call directly; every option treats them as direct calls. The options differ in how the word reaches the callee through function values and closures. A passes it as one hidden argument that the runtime checks, and keeps one builder body. B compiles two bodies. C passes it only on direct calls. D sends no word and copies afterward. E keeps the word in the task's context record.
decisions.story: Noor's log tool splits each line with a splitter it picks at startup, so the call goes through a function value. The list of words stays in the loop, so the rule puts that list on a stack. Each word was stored into the list, something older, so the words stay on the heap, as today. Her tool keeps the word lists of error lines for the whole run, so those lists go to the heap. One function serves both calls and must build each list in the right place.
decisions.detail:
Rules every option shares. The caller's rule picks the destination at each call: stack when the result stays local, heap when it is stored in something older, sent or captured by a task. Inside a #Context(allocator:) block every call passes heap, which means that allocator, so a named allocator still wins as ratified.

Only the returned value itself is placed. Its elements follow the stored-in-older rule: an item pushed into the list being built is stored in something older than itself, so it goes to the heap, as today. The list's fixed header keeps today's home: the caller's frame through a return slot (JetIR OptReturnSlot.jet), else a box.

A value carries its home. Today a value made under #Context goes back to the allocator that served it, through a header word below its address (JetRuntime Context.jet). A stacked value records its stack the same way. So a caller frees whatever it receives correctly, even a parameter or field the callee hands back.

Forwarding, f() { g() }, passes f's destination on to g and makes no new offer. When a function can return one of two values, each candidate grows where the destination says, so none is stacked under heap. Under stack, the first to grow claims the offered stack, and the others grow on the heap. The one not returned is freed at its last use. After ? or an early return, a partly built result is dropped like any local.

Recursive calls the compiler can see pass heap, as the ratified rule puts a recursive function's growing locals on the heap. The function's own result still follows its caller. Recursion through a function value cannot be seen, so such a call passes its destination as usual, and each level that gets stack takes its own fresh stack, in chunks.

A destination never crosses a task: a task's result reaches others by a send or a join, which the rule places on the heap.

A generic function, fn<T>() -> T, takes the word only in the instances where T grows, since each instance is compiled apart. Trait methods are called directly after a type test, so each implementation takes the word only if its own result grows.

Foreign entries pass heap. They are the C export thunk, whose Text result C frees with jet_text_free, and plugin guest exports, whose results the host copies. Runtime kernels and JavaScript callbacks that call a Jet function pass heap too. The spec says collection result builders cross a native kernel as host callbacks (spec.md 1752), so map, split and partition builders are called from runtime code. JavaScript exports on the web and the debugger's evaluator entry pass heap.

Each such entry passes a constant, so it needs no row of its own in the probe. On the web, trait calls and closures take the same shape as natively. Every function value already passes one hidden argument, its closure record, through a generated adapter (JetIR BuildExpr.jet).

Hot patching. jet dev restarts a native program on each change (JetCLI Host.jet). The debugger's fix accepts changed parameters only when no live frame would pass the old ones (NativeFix.jet native_fix_types). Under A and C the word comes or goes only when a function's result starts or stops growing. That changes its result type, so the same frame check refuses it while an old caller's frame is live.

The first probe, Docs/Audits/PlaceDefault20261121/Probes/returns.jet with returns.sh and returns.log, measures what each convention adds to a call. Every list there comes from today's heap, so a row differs from plain only by its convention. The trait row is a type test, then a direct call. The log prints the one-minute load beside every run: 1.3 to 6.0, median 2.1. Each row is the fastest of five runs that alternate with the other conventions.

These figures come from returns.log at dev commit b66642b8bc: 5 rounds per row at machine load 1.3 to 6.0, median 2.1.

O2, a call returning a two-item list, ns per call (plain, argument, test, branch, context word, copy): direct 21.9, 22.0, 22.1, 27.0, 41.6, 37.8. Function value 23.1, 22.6, 22.8, 26.5, 40.4, 38.5. Trait 30.7, 29.6, 29.4, 33.9, 47.8, 45.6. Closure 29.5, 29.9, 30.4, 35.3, 48.2, 45.2.

The argument is within 1.1 ns of plain at O0, O1 and O2 on every form. The context word adds 16 to 20 ns at each of them, and the copy 14 to 18. On the web under node, plain, argument, test and context word cost 49.9, 49.5, 50.0 and 80.6 ns direct. Through a function value they cost 51.8, 51.0, 51.4 and 82.4.

The branch row merges two lists into one variable, so O2 keeps the list in memory. That costs 3 to 6 ns over plain at O2, and nothing measurable at O0 and O1.

The copy grows with the value. At O2 direct, 16 items cost 54.1 ns plain, 83.9 with one sized copy (1.55 times) and 109.2 with the probe's push-by-push copy (2.02 times). 1,000 items cost 1,118, 1,929 (1.73 times) and 2,444 (2.19 times). So a sized copy costs about 1.5 to 1.8 times plain, and a push copy 2.0 to 2.2.

The second probe, place.jet with place.sh and place.log beside returns.jet, measures A as revised. Its arm row passes the word and keeps a whole second body for the stack, never taken. Its place row is one body whose list lives in storage the caller names, so each growth asks the runtime's place lookup which allocator owns it. Its local row has the same call and caller but grows its own list, with no lookup.

So place less local is the lookup alone, the step a stacked result adds to each growth. Plain less local is returning a list's header rather than a length. The arena row makes the place calls inside a #Context(allocator: arena) block, so the same body grows its list in the arena.

place.log times a call that builds a two-item list, in ns per call, the fastest of five runs. Its rows are plain, argument, arm, local, place and arena. O2 direct 22.1, 22.3, 22.6, 21.8, 27.9, 50.6. Function value 22.9, 22.8, 23.3, 22.8, 23.9, 49.8. Closure 29.7, 30.0, 32.8, 29.0, 29.4, 67.1.

On the web, direct: 50.0, 49.3, 49.9, 46.7, 45.5, 65.8. Through a function value: 51.3, 50.5, 51.6, 49.2, 49.9, 68.3. These figures come from place.log at dev commit 71c563d975: 5 rounds per row at machine load 1.5 to 8, median 3.

Across O0, O1, O2 and the web, the argument is within 1.6 ns of plain, and the never-taken arm within 3.1. The lookup, place less local, costs -0.8 to 6.1 ns natively and -1.3 to 0.8 on the web. Returning the list's header instead of a length, plain less local, is 0.1 to 4.5 ns. The arena row costs 18.4 to 37.7 ns more than place. There the lookup finds the arena's carrier, and the list grows in the arena.

The O2 symbol table: build 1,749 bytes, build_to 1,765, build_arm 3,736, build_into 1,658 and build_local 2,153. Their function-value adapters are 75, 79, 79, 475, 79 bytes. The debugger lists dest, i, items and out in build_to, and i, items and out in build.

The same log runs convention.mjs and register.py. convention.mjs writes a wasm module byte by byte and runs it under node. Its builder is called through call_indirect with no word, with one more i32 parameter, and with a mutable global set first. The fastest of nine runs: 2.15 ns with no word, 2.26 with the parameter and 3.61 with the global.

register.py writes x64 machine code byte by byte and runs it through Python. Its call goes through a register with no word, the word in rdx as a third argument, and the word in RAX. The fastest of nine runs: 0.89 ns with no word, 0.89 in rdx and 0.89 in RAX.

The scope-stack path does not exist yet, so no row measures a stack's own gain. The review's ceiling is 12 to 13 ns per short-lived value (alloc.jet). That is what a value returned to the heap instead of a stack gives up.

options.name: A hidden destination argument, checked by the runtime, and one builder body
options.detail: Each function whose result grows takes one hidden argument, the destination: the next argument register on x64 and one more i32 parameter on the web. Jet types do not change. The callee hands the word to the runtime calls that grow its result, as their place. The runtime honors a stack word only when it names the task's newest offer, still unclaimed; any other word means heap. Each builder keeps one body.
options.technical:
The word is one IR argument of every call to a function whose result grows, so the verifier checks it at every call. Each back end lowers it as a real argument, right after the declared ones. On x64 it takes the next argument register. Once the declared ones fill all six, it takes the next stack argument slot, as a seventh argument would. On the web it is one more i32 parameter.

A return-slot address (JetIR OptReturnSlot.jet) stays last, after the word. The grow path, the frame-free prefix, tail calls and adapters already keep arguments (JetIR X64Select.jet).

Every function of one Jet type takes it or none does, since the result type decides. So a function value's adapter, which already adds the closure record, adds the word too, and call_indirect checks one wasm type. In the probes, the word costs no measurable time a call on x64 and 0.11 ns through call_indirect on the web.

A word cannot misplace a result. Heap is 0 and takes today's path unchecked. Offers nest like calls: a call that offers a stack pushes it on its task's offers. Its return withdraws the offer if it is still unclaimed, and a claim takes the offer off the task's offers, as a return does for an unclaimed one. A stack word is honored only when the page map names the task's newest offer, still unclaimed. The first growth claims it, and a missing, stale or garbage word means heap.

A compiler that passed its own caller's offer to a call whose result it stores would still be honored. So the IR verifier checks where each call's word comes from: heap, a fresh offer, or the function's own word when it returns that call's result.

One body. The runtime already grows a list from the allocator that owns a place it is told (JetRuntime Alloc.jet alloc_grow_carrier, through alloc_owner). Place 0 means the current allocator, which a builder's own list passes today, so the heap path runs today's code. Text growth (alloc_grow_bytes) takes no place today, so it gains the same argument. A scope-stack word is a place alloc_owner resolves through the page map, written once in the runtime. 

In the probe, the lookup costs -1.3 to 6.1 ns a call at two items.

The builder grows 16 bytes at O2 in the probe for keeping and using the word, and has no test and no arm. A whole stack arm, as the first draft of A carried, measured 1,971 bytes.

The debugger sees nothing new. The word is no source variable, so the debug info records none for it, and Locals and the frame list read as today. The evaluator's compiled entry passes heap like any foreign entry, and calls inside an expression follow the rule like any Jet code.

options.name: Two bodies, chosen by destination
options.detail: The compiler builds each such function twice: a body that builds on the heap and one that builds on a fresh stack. A direct call, a trait call after its type test included, picks a body. Function values and closures hold both entries, so an indirect call picks too. Foreign entries take the heap body.
options.technical: It needs no word and no test of a word. Each builder's code doubles: 1,749 more bytes for the probe's builder at O2. A stack body calls stack bodies when it forwards. Each function value needs a second entry word. The debugger sets a line's breakpoint in both bodies, and the profiler merges two symbols into one function. On the web, both bodies and both table entries exist. I9 holds, as specialization is a sema fact.

options.name: The heap at every indirect call
options.detail: Direct calls pass the destination as a hidden argument, and so do trait calls, which call directly after a type test. A call through a function value or closure always gets heap, because its adapter passes heap. Function types stay as they are today. The placement report names such values as returned through an indirect call.
options.technical: A call through a function value or closure costs exactly today's call and today's heap. It gives up the stack's gain on every value returned through one, up to the review's 12 to 13 ns ceiling per value. The census the review asked for has a row for that rule, so its share will be known.
options.code:
words := trimmed(lines)  // direct: passes stack
split: if wide -> trimmed else -> squeezed
more := split(lines)     // indirect: always the heap

options.name: The result's stack moves with it
options.detail: No destination at all. A callee builds the value it returns on a fresh stack of the task, as for any local, and hands that stack over with the value. When the caller's rule says heap, the caller copies the value onto the heap, as a value leaving a #Context block moves today.
options.technical: Zero cost at the call, direct or indirect, and no change to any signature. Every stored or sent result pays a copy: 14 to 18 ns more at two items. A sized copy costs about 1.5 to 1.8 times plain at 16 and 1,000 items; the probe's push copy, 2.0 to 2.2 times. Today such a result is built on the heap once, so this breaks the ratified promise that the heap path costs what it costs today.
options.code:
words := split(lines)    // the list's own stack comes back with it
kept.push(split(lines))  // the caller copies it onto the heap

options.name: A destination word in the task's context
options.detail:
The caller writes the destination into a word of the current context record, where #Context's allocator lives, right before the call. The callee reads and clears it on entry. No signature changes.

Why not the context: Jet's context is reached today through the thread's control block (one load of the current record's pointer), not passed as an argument. It holds settings that last across many calls (allocator, deadline, print). The destination changes at every call. In the context it needs a store before each call and a load and clear in the callee. It also needs a save around nested calls and task switches. Option A's register argument needs none of that.
options.technical:
The probe kept the word in a module global written under #Unsafe. At O2 that cost 17 to 20 ns more per call on every form. It cost 16 to 19 at O0 and O1 and 31 to 31 on the web, and grew the builder by 395 bytes. A context word adds a thread-base load to the same store, load and clear; the probe does not show how much of the gap it keeps.

The word waits in memory from one call to the next. A missed write leaves the previous call's word, a real stack, which misplaces the result unchecked. The debugger's evaluator must save and restore the word.

comparisons.note: Passes a result's data stack as a hidden argument and specializes every function by its roots and stacks over the whole program (goose-051, goose-064). https://github.com/aardappel/goose rev 94cc64da.
comparisons.code: // the compiler passes the result's data stack to the callee

comparisons.note: Region-polymorphic functions take their regions as extra arguments. A function used as a value has its regions fixed where the value is made, not where it is called. Tofte and Talpin, Region-Based Memory Management, Information and Computation 132(2), 1997.
comparisons.code: (* f [r1, r2] at r3: regions passed when the closure is made *)

comparisons.note: A function's result defaults to the heap region, because a separately compiled caller can't know the callee's regions. Code that wants another region passes a region handle explicitly. Grossman et al., Region-Based Memory Management in Cyclone, PLDI 2002.
comparisons.code: list_t<`r> copy(region_t<`r> h, list_t l);  // rnew(h) builds in h

comparisons.note: A large result travels through a hidden pointer to the caller's slot, LLVM's sret argument, and C++17 guarantees it is built there. Only the fixed part is placed; a vector's buffer still comes from the heap.
A variadic call already passes one hidden fact outside the parameters: AL holds the number of vector registers used, and no prototype names it. System V AMD64 ABI, section 3.5.7.
comparisons.code:

It calls the builder directly, through a function value, a trait and a closure. jet inspect placement reports the result stacked in all four, and heap when it is pushed into an older list. The case also maps a list with a closure that returns text, at O1; the closure's result reports heap, because a runtime kernel calls it.

Under B: the same cases, plus a symbol check that each builder has two bodies. Under C: the indirect calls report heap. Under D: the stored result reports a copy. Under E: the probe's context word rows.

The claim check and the stack's own gain are not measured, since the scope-stack path does not exist yet. The 12 to 13 ns ceiling is the review's alloc.jet figure.

decisions.title: Zero-copy borrowed pieces for String.split and String.rsplit
decisions.situation: Splitting a line into fields is one of the most common loops in scripts, CSV parsers, and compilers. Today, String.split and String.rsplit return a lazy iterator that still allocates a fresh heap string for every single piece. That adds millions of small allocations to idiomatic text loops and pushes fast code down to manual byte offsets. This vote decides whether split and rsplit yield zero-copy borrowed pieces tied to the source string; we recommend borrowing pieces by default and copying only when stored.
decisions.gist: Should String.split and String.rsplit yield zero-copy borrowed pieces instead of copying every piece?
decisions.lesson: Both split and rsplit already return a lazy iterator of String values. Borrowing each piece straight from the source string avoids heap copies while keeping plain String types for beginners. Storing a piece into a list or field still copies it automatically.
decisions.story: Devon writes a CSV and log analyzer using line.split(","). He wants the plain high-level loop to run with zero per-field heap allocations rather than rewriting it with manual byte offsets.

options.name: Zero-copy pieces by default
options.detail:
`String.split(sep)` and `String.rsplit(sep)` keep their `Iter<String>` signature and yield zero-copy slices into the source string while the iterator lives. The source string holds a read loan until the loop ends (`E0212` on conflicting mutation). Storing a piece into an owning slot copies it automatically, or asks for `.copy()` under `#Policy(copies: .Explicit)`.

Rust `str::split` and Zig `std.mem.splitScalar` avoided per-piece allocation from day one. Go shipped allocating `strings.Split` first and later added `strings.SplitSeq` in Go 1.24 to cut loop allocations. Jet avoids that two-API split by borrowing on the existing `Iter<String>` methods. `String.lines()` returns `[String]` (`BuiltinMethods.jet:191`) and stays separate so this vote avoids a breaking return-type change.
options.technical: Per `Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/Registry/BuiltinMethods.jet:187-188`, `String.split` (`TBuiltinOp.Split`) and `String.rsplit` (`jet_iter_string_rsplit`) both return `Iter<String>`. In `Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Ownership/`, track iterator provenance from the receiver place onto the `Iter` binding. Mark loop items drawn from a borrowed-string iterator as local string views (`SemaScopeBinding.string_view = true`), emitting `MaterializeView` at owning destinations (`Docs/Spec/spec.md:2210,2310,2322`). In `JetIR` and `JetRuntime`, yield borrowed `(ptr, len)` slices from the iterator cursor instead of calling `rt_text_copy` per item.

options.name: Separate split_views methods
options.detail: Keep `String.split(sep)` and `String.rsplit(sep)` allocating fresh owned `String` pieces on each step, and add `split_views(sep)` and `rsplit_views(sep)` for zero-copy iteration. This lets callers mutate the source string during a plain `split` loop, but repeats Go's two-API split (`strings.Split` vs `strings.SplitSeq`) and leaves the default spelling allocating on every field.
options.technical: Keep `TBuiltinOp.Split` and `jet_iter_string_rsplit` allocating owned strings; register two new builtin iterator methods returning borrowed-view iterators.

options.name: Always allocate owned pieces
options.detail: Keep `String.split(sep)` and `String.rsplit(sep)` allocating an owned `String` for every yielded piece with no borrowed-view iterator. Mutating the source string inside the loop stays allowed, but every yielded field pays a heap allocation (or inline copy), keeping idiomatic split loops slower than byte-offset scanners.
options.technical: Leave `TBuiltinOp.Split` and `jet_iter_string_rsplit` unchanged, calling `rt_text_copy` for each yielded piece.

comparisons.note: str::split yields borrowed &str slices with zero heap allocation; https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.str.html#method.split.
comparisons.code: for field in line.split(',') { total += field.len(); }

comparisons.note: std.mem.splitScalar yields zero-copy []const u8 slices into the source buffer; https://ziglang.org/documentation/master/std/#std.mem.splitScalar.
Go 1.24 added strings.SplitSeq after eager strings.Split proved an allocation bottleneck in hot loops; https://pkg.go.dev/strings#SplitSeq.
comparisons.code: for field := range strings.SplitSeq(line, ",") { total += len(field) }

recommendation.why: Borrowing pieces by default makes idiomatic split loops zero-allocation while keeping one small text API.
gains: Removes per-field heap copies in parsers, CSV tools, and scripts.
Matches Jet's existing zero-copy behavior for trim, after, and before.

losses.loss: The source string cannot be mutated while iterating its split pieces.
losses.mitigation: Call line.split(",").to_list() before mutating line, matching Jet's existing read-loan error.

whyNot.reason: B duplicates the split API and leaves the default spelling allocating.
C keeps a heap allocation on every piece and pushes fast code off String.

recommendation.tradeoff: Mutating the source string mid-loop requires collecting with .to_list() first.

decisions.title: Struct and record update syntax with trailing ...base
decisions.situation: Updating one or two fields of a struct while keeping the rest unchanged is common in configs, web state, and compilers. Today Jet requires repeating every unchanged field by name, or copying into a mutable variable and assigning fields one by one. Repeating ten fields hides the one field that actually changed and copies fields you meant to replace. This vote decides whether Jet adds struct update syntax; we recommend trailing three-dot spread syntax matching Jet's existing expression spread.
decisions.gist: How should Jet build an updated struct or record when only a few fields change?
decisions.lesson: A struct or record holds named fields. Jet already uses three dots (...) to spread lists and call arguments in expressions, and two dots (..) for ranges and pattern rests. Every option keeps field visibility and ownership rules unchanged.
decisions.story: Sam builds HTTP and compiler configuration records with twelve fields. When overriding just a port or timeout, Sam wants an immutable one-liner that highlights the changed field without copying fields being replaced.
decisions.inWild:
let next = Config { port: 9090, ..base };
// Rust Book ch05-01 (https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch05-01-defining-structs.html#creating-instances-from-other-instances-with-struct-update-syntax)

options.name: Trailing ...base spread
options.detail:
Allow one trailing `, ...base` after at least one explicit field or pun in a struct literal (`Config{port: 9090, ...base}`) or unnamed record (`{max: 100, ...bounds}`). Requiring at least one explicit field forbids `{...base}` and `Config{...base}`, preserving Jet's brace-record rule with zero block ambiguity and avoiding a duplicate `.copy()` spelling.

Jet already uses `...` for expression spreads in lists (`[...a, x]`) and calls (`f(...xs)`), while `..` in expressions is the range operator (`a..b`). Keeping `...` for struct and record updates preserves one expression-spread sigil everywhere. Omitted stored fields move when `base` is a temporary, last use, or `...base.move()`, and copy when `base` stays live (`#Policy(copies: .Explicit)` requires `...base.copy()`); replaced fields drop without copying.
options.technical:
Reconciles `SIGIL_SPREAD` (`...`, `PackageFiles.jet:58`, `Expr.Spread` at `Expressions.jet:1231`) with `TOKEN_DOT_DOT` (`..`, `Spellings.jet:78,84-86`). Register `Type{field: value, ...base}` in `Spellings.jet`. The parser allows one trailing `...expr` only after at least one named or punned field, keeping `parser_literal_fields_ahead` (`Expressions.jet:726`) unambiguous.

Sema requires `base` to match the exact target struct or unnamed record type (enum payloads excluded) and checks `priv` visibility on every omitted stored field. Computed `name: T -> expr` fields are skipped (explicit overrides stay E0339), and `state { ... }` (`Spellings.jet:19`) carries over from `base`. `base` evaluates once under normal move/copy and `#Policy(copies: .Explicit)` rules.
options.code:
next: Config{port: 9090, ...base}
bounds2: {max: 100, ...bounds}

options.name: Trailing ..base spread
options.detail:
Allow one trailing `, ..base` after at least one explicit field or pun in a struct or unnamed record literal. Ownership, visibility, computed-field, and typestate rules match Option A.

This matches Rust's struct update syntax and rhymes visually with Jet's struct pattern rest (`Type{port: p, ..}`). However, it splits Jet's expression grammar into `...` for lists and calls versus `..` for structs and records, overloading the `..` range token.
options.technical: Same parser, sema, visibility, ownership, computed-field, and typestate rules as Option A. Uses `TOKEN_DOT_DOT` (`..`) instead of `SIGIL_SPREAD` (`...`) in trailing struct and record update position (probed on `c7b432d894`: currently fails with `Jet.InvalidStatement`).
options.code:
next: Config{port: 9090, ..base}
bounds2: {max: 100, ..bounds}

options.name: Keep explicit fields or mutable copy
options.detail:
Add no struct or record update syntax. Callers either list every field manually or mutate a copy (`next := base.copy()`, then assign `next.port = 9090`).

This adds zero grammar, but forces a mutable variable and copies overwritten fields too, wasting heap allocations and failing on structs with move-only fields.
options.technical: No parser, syntax registry, or sema changes; both `...` and `..` remain invalid inside struct and record literal expressions.
options.code:
next := base.copy()
next.port = 9090
bounds2 := bounds.copy()
bounds2.max = 100

comparisons.note: Trailing ..base struct update moves or copies only omitted fields; https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch05-01-defining-structs.html#creating-instances-from-other-instances-with-struct-update-syntax.
Object spread uses ...base matching array spread [...a], though JS allows leading and multiple spreads; https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/objects.html.
Gleam uses ..base inside record updates (Config(..base, port: 9090)); https://tour.gleam.run/data-types/record-updates/.

recommendation.why: Trailing ...base puts changed fields first, skips copying replaced fields, and keeps ... as Jet's one expression-spread mark across calls, lists, structs, and records.
gains: One expression-spread token (...) everywhere; .. stays exclusively ranges and pattern rests.
Requiring one explicit field avoids block ambiguity and prevents a duplicate .copy() spelling.

losses.loss: Differs by one dot from trailing .. in struct patterns.
losses.mitigation: The parser teaches `...base` when someone writes `..base` inside a struct or record literal.

whyNot.reason: B splits expression spreading across ... (lists and calls) and .. (structs and records).
C forces mutable copies or verbose field lists that copy overwritten fields.

recommendation.tradeoff: Struct updates use ... like every other expression spread instead of .. like struct patterns.

decisions.title: Field labels for Complex, Complex32, and Quaternion
decisions.situation: Complex and Complex32 in Core/Math/Math.jet currently spell their fields `real` and `imaginary`. Meanwhile, Color uses single letters (`r`, `g`, `b`, `a`), and D-ARRAY-QUAT1=A gives Quaternion `w`, `x`, `y`, and `z`. Writing `Complex{real: 3.0, imaginary: 4.0}` repeats long labels on every constructor and read. This vote picks one concise, consistent set of field labels across Complex, Complex32, and Quaternion. We recommend `re` and `im` on Complex and Complex32, keeping `w`, `x`, `y`, and `z` on Quaternion.
decisions.gist: Which field labels should Complex, Complex32, and Quaternion use?
decisions.lesson: Struct field labels serve both constructors (`Complex{...}`) and field reads (`z.re` or `z.r`). Short labels save tokens in numeric code, while avoiding confusion with polar radius `r` or 3D axes `x`, `y`, `z`, `w`.
decisions.story: Maya writes an FFT and 3D camera transform in Core math. She wants short field labels without mixing up real parts, polar radii, and 3D rotation axes.
decisions.detail: Provenance: owner comment on D-ARRAY-COMPLEXT1 (2026-11-17), tracked as #6177 c13. Verified in Core/Math/Math.jet (`Complex` and `Complex32` use `real` and `imaginary`). `Vec2`/`Vec3`/`Vec4` expose `x`, `y`, `z`, `w` accessors, swizzles, and `.new(...)` parameters over `lanes: [Float#N]`. `Color` and `LinearColor` use `r`, `g`, `b`, `a` (`Core/Color/Color.jet:33-44`). D-ARRAY-QUAT1=A specifies `Quaternion` with `w`, `x`, `y`, `z` and `q.xyz`, not yet landed in Core. D-LITCARRIER1=D ratifies `3 + 4i` and `1 + 2i + 3j + 4k` suffixes (not yet shipped).

options.name: `re` and `im` on Complex/Complex32; `w`, `x`, `y`, `z` on Quaternion
options.detail:
Rename `real` and `imaginary` to `re` and `im` on both `Complex` and `Complex32`. Keep `Quaternion`'s ratified `w`, `x`, `y`, `z` fields from D-ARRAY-QUAT1=A.

`re` and `im` shrink `imaginary` from nine characters to two. They stay unambiguous beside polar radius `r` (`r: z.abs()`, `z.re`, `z.im`). This matches Rust `num-complex`, Julia `Complex`, and standard math notation `Re(z)` and `Im(z)`.

options.name: `r` and `i` on Complex/Complex32; `w`, `x`, `y`, `z` on Quaternion
options.detail:
Rename `real` and `imaginary` to `r` and `i` on both `Complex` and `Complex32`. Keep `Quaternion`'s ratified `w`, `x`, `y`, `z` fields from D-ARRAY-QUAT1=A.

This gives the shortest character spelling on complex numbers, matching single-letter `Color{r, g, b, a}`. Its trade-off is that `r` also denotes polar radius (`r * exp(i * theta)`), so polar code can collide `r` with `z.r`.
options.technical: Greenfield cutover in `Core/Math/Math.jet` and all in-repo callers. Rename `Complex` and `Complex32` fields to `r` and `i`. Keep `Quaternion` fields `w`, `x`, `y`, `z` per D-ARRAY-QUAT1=A. Free scalar helpers `real(Float)` and `imag(Float)` stay unchanged.

options.name: `r`/`i` on Complex/Complex32 and `r`/`i`/`j`/`k` on Quaternion
options.detail:
Use one algebraic single-letter naming rule across all three types: `r` and `i` on `Complex` and `Complex32`, and `r`, `i`, `j`, `k` on `Quaternion`.

Every field matches the ratified `3 + 4i` and `1 + 2i + 3j + 4k` suffixes (D-LITCARRIER1=D, not yet shipped). This amends D-ARRAY-QUAT1=A, dropping 3D graphics coordinates (`q.x`, `q.y`, `q.z`, `q.w`) and changing vector swizzle `q.xyz` to `q.ijk`.

options.name: Keep `real`/`imaginary` on Complex/Complex32 and `w`, `x`, `y`, `z` on Quaternion

decisions.title: Marker for public enums that may grow across package releases
decisions.situation: Today every Jet enum is a closed set. Callers must cover every case (`Jet.NonExhaustiveDispatch`), and `Jet.ClosedSetElse` (`E0641`) forbids any `else` arm on a closed set, partial or complete. That makes adding a new case to any public enum a breaking change for downstream packages. This vote chooses the marker that lets a public enum add cases in minor releases by requiring an `else` arm outside its declaring package. We recommend `#Open`.
decisions.gist: How should a library mark a public enum that may add new cases without breaking callers?
decisions.lesson: Closed enums catch missing cases when you add a variant inside your own codebase. A growing public enum flips that contract across package boundaries: external matches must include `else -> ...`, while matches inside the declaring package remain exhaustive.
decisions.story: Sam ships an HTTP library with a public `StatusClass` enum. In v1.1 he wants to add a new case without breaking every downstream package that matched on it.
decisions.detail: Provenance: #6853 c7 (G1 open vocabularies). Verified in `Compiler/Prelude/Markers.jet` (`Open`, `Growing`, `NonExhaustive`, and `Closed` are unclaimed) and `Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Coverage.jet:994-1065` (`Jet.NonExhaustiveDispatch`, `Jet.ClosedSetElse`, `E0641`). Inside the declaring package, matches over a marked enum stay exhaustive without `else`. Outside the declaring package, dispatches and nested patterns require a catch-all (`else` or `_`), `E0641` is suppressed, single-arm guards (`if kind == .NotFound`) stay unaffected, and adding a case is a minor API change.

options.name: `#Open` marker on public enums
options.detail:
Declare `Open` in `Compiler/Prelude/Markers.jet` as a bare PascalCase marker on public (non-`priv`) enums (`#Open Status: enum { ... }`). Using `#Open` on a `struct` or `priv enum` is a compile error. Outside the declaring package, every dispatch or nested pattern over an `#Open` enum must include a catch-all (`else` or `_`), and `Jet.ClosedSetElse` (`E0641`) allows it. Inside the declaring package, matches stay exhaustive, and single-arm `if kind == .NotFound` guards stay unaffected.

`#Open` is one short word that pairs directly with Jet's `closed set` diagnostic wording (`Jet.ClosedSetElse`) and follows Jet's PascalCase marker convention.
options.technical: Add `Open: struct { impl Marker { sites: [.Type] } }` to `Compiler/Prelude/Markers.jet` (restricted in sema to public non-`priv` enums). In `Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Coverage.jet`, treat cross-package dispatches and nested patterns over `#Open` enums as open sets, requiring `else` or `_` and suppressing `E0641`. Preserve closed-set checking inside the declaring package. Record `#Open` in `PublicAPI.jet` (`E1218` publish / `#6860` check): adding cases is minor; adding or removing `#Open`, or removing cases, is major.

options.name: `#NonExhaustive` marker on public enums
options.detail:
Use `#NonExhaustive` instead of `#Open`, mirroring Rust's `#[non_exhaustive]` attribute with the exact same enum-only scope, cross-package catch-all rule, and same-package exhaustiveness.

Rust developers recognize the name immediately. However, `NonExhaustive` is a double-negative thirteen-character phrase that breaks from Jet's plain positive bare marker names (`#Scalar`, `#Error`, `#Local`, `#Shared`) and does not mirror `Jet.ClosedSetElse` (`closed set` vs `open`).
options.technical: Identical sema, coverage, `E0641`, and `PublicAPI.jet` rules as A, declaring `NonExhaustive` in `Compiler/Prelude/Markers.jet` with `sites: [.Type]` instead of `Open`.

options.name: `#Growing` marker on public enums
options.detail:
Use `#Growing` with the same enum-only scope, cross-package catch-all rule, and same-package exhaustiveness.

`#Growing` describes the author's intent directly (more cases may be added later) and avoids any confusion with file `open` or class inheritance `open` from Kotlin or Swift. Its trade-off is being slightly less paired with `closed set` than `#Open`.
options.technical: Identical sema, coverage, `E0641`, and `PublicAPI.jet` rules as A, declaring `Growing` in `Compiler/Prelude/Markers.jet` with `sites: [.Type]` instead of `Open`.

options.name: Open by default across packages, `#Closed` opt-in
options.detail:
Flip the default for all public enums across package boundaries (like Swift's library-evolution mode): external matches always require `else` unless the enum carries `#Closed`.

Library authors never forget to mark an evolving enum. However, every external match on small fixed enums (`Ordering`, AST kinds) would gain noisy `else` arms unless opted into `#Closed`, migrating existing exhaustive tests.
options.technical: Change `Coverage.jet` so cross-package enum dispatches are open by default unless marked `#Closed` (`sites: [.Type]`) in `Compiler/Prelude/Markers.jet`. Update existing Core and package exhaustive match tests, including `Tests/UI/core_enum_missing_case.jet`.

comparisons.note: `#[non_exhaustive]` requires a wildcard arm in downstream crates while keeping matches exhaustive inside the defining crate; https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/attributes/type_system.html#the-non_exhaustive-attribute.

Library-evolution mode makes public enums non-frozen by default (`@unknown default`), with `@frozen` opting into closed sets; https://docs.swift.org/swift-book/documentation/the-swift-programming-language/statements/#Switching-Over-Future-Enumeration-Cases.
comparisons.code: @frozen public enum ComparisonResult { case orderedAscending, orderedSame, orderedDescending }

comparisons.note: `sealed` marks closed hierarchies while ordinary public types remain open for extension; https://kotlinlang.org/docs/sealed-classes.html.
comparisons.code: sealed class Result { data object Ok : Result() }

recommendation.why: `#Open` is one plain word that pairs directly with Jet's existing `closed set` error wording while keeping closed enums the safe default.
gains: Pairs directly with `Jet.ClosedSetElse` (`closed set` vs `#Open`).
Keeps exhaustive checking by default on fixed enums across packages.
Matches Jet's short positive PascalCase marker style.

losses.loss: Library authors must remember to write `#Open` before v1.0.
losses.mitigation: `jet check` API-surface checks (`#6860`) and `jet registry publish` (`E1218`) flag adding a case to a closed enum.

whyNot.reason: `#NonExhaustive` is long, negative-phrased jargon unlike Jet's other markers.
Clean alternative, but slightly less crisp beside Jet's `closed set` terminology.
Forces noisy `else` arms on every fixed Core and library enum match.

recommendation.tradeoff: Opt-in `#Open` preserves exhaustive matching by default while requiring authors to mark evolving enums upfront.
