decisions.title: How a library declaration attaches its own build-time check and registered error to each call
decisions.situation: Some library calls need a check that types alone cannot make. A web route such as "/users/{id}" must follow the route grammar, and writing to a file opened for reading must fail. Today the compiler holds these checks itself: about 10,000 lines in eleven files that know Core functions by name. Each check prints its own registered error with a tested message. So a package author can never give their own library errors that good, and every Core change waits on a compiler change. You are asked how a declaration, in Core or in any package, attaches such a check and its error, so those files can go with every error unchanged. We recommend letting a marker rule also run at each call of the marked declaration and report its registered error there.
decisions.gist: How does a library function attach its own build-time check and registered error to each call of it?
decisions.lesson: A marker is a tag on a declaration, like `#RoutePath`. Its rule is a small function the library writes, and it runs while the program is built. Today a rule runs once, where the tag is written. This choice adds a second moment: every call of the tagged function. There the rule reads the call and can stop the build with the library's own error type.
decisions.explainer: Think of a post office counter. Today every special parcel rule is taped inside the sorting machine, so only the factory can add one. With call rules, each parcel type carries its own rule card, and the machine reads the card at the counter. A sender sees the same refusal slip either way, but anyone who makes a parcel type can now write its card.
decisions.story: Ana maintains the HTTP router in Core. To tighten the route grammar she must edit the compiler, wait for a new compiler build, and keep two copies of the rules in step. Ben writes a GraphQL package. He wants the same exact error for a bad query string, but no package can add a compiler check, so his users get a run-time failure instead.
decisions.detail:
Current code. Eleven files under Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Calls hold the checks. They are ProcessHandles, StreamHandles, UIHandles, TimeHandles, Hardware, Data, Geometry, Services, TaskGroups, HTTPRouting and the web-form part of HTTP. Together they are 10,390 lines and raise 45 distinct registered codes. The count was 49 until #6852 c7 moved the Args family into Core source and retired E1301 to E1304 into ordinary method arity errors. Card #6851 criteria c3 to c6 delete the files, and each remaining code must keep its UI snapshot (I4).

What is already built. Every diagnostic is a type with an `impl Diagnostic` (D-MARKER-DIAG1=A). A marker's `expand` rule raises one with `reject(Value)`, reported at the marker's use site; `reject` anywhere else is E0962. `#Pre(#run …)` decides a contract at each call while building, from the call's argument facts, and fails with E0180. A root build's `meta.events(watch: .Calls{to: f})` hears each call as a `CompilerCall`, under `jet build` alone today (#6846 c14). D-META-REG1=A keeps marker rules in one registration table.

What is missing. No rule runs at each call of a declaration and reports a registered type at a chosen argument. `#Pre(#run …)` alone falls short in three places. A call with the wrong argument count never binds, so no contract runs (E2911). A method the type lacks has no declaration to carry a contract (E2501). And a path known only at run time reports E0180, not the route's own E2805.

Edge cases for the recommendation. A value known only at run time reaches the rule as None. The rule then chooses: refuse it (a router path), or allow it and let the function check at run time (an App route). Ownership that spans statements, such as a DMA buffer held until `wait`, needs no rule: `start` borrows the buffer, and the ordinary check reports E0204.

Coordinate spaces (E2520, E2521) compare argument types in the rule. An asset check (E2822) reads the file as a recorded build input, so changing the file reruns it. Lint findings (E2930, E2931) keep `#Allow` by name. Where today's message and the registered wording differ, the error type gains the field its text varies on, so no snapshot changes.

options.name: Call rules: a marker rule also runs at each call
options.detail:
A marker's `impl Marker` block may add `check: fn(self, call: CompilerCall)`. While building, the compiler runs it once for each call of a function, method or type that carries the marker. The rule reads the call: each argument's type, its value when the build knows it, and the written name. It raises the library's own error with `reject(Finding{…}, at: …)`, underlining the call, its name or one argument. A rule that rejects nothing leaves the call to the ordinary checks.

A rule that rejects replaces that call's ordinary checks, so each bad call still shows one error, as today's snapshots do. Rules run with one meaning wherever Jet checks a program: `jet check`, `jet run`, `jet build` and the editor's language server.

Users write nothing new and see the same errors as today. A package author's first step stays `#Pre(cond, "message")`; a rule is the expert step.
options.technical:
The `Marker` trait gains `check: fn(self, call: CompilerCall)` beside `expand`. `CompilerCall`, the value call watches already hear, gains `name` (the written callee or member), `args: [CompilerArg]` in written order and `receiver: CompilerArg?`. A `CompilerArg` has `label`, `type` (a TypeId), `value` (a `Dyn?`, None when only the run knows it) and `function` (a `FunctionInfo?` for a function or lambda argument). `reject(value, at: part)` takes `call`, `call.name` or an argument, and `at:` defaults to the call.

A rule runs before argument binding, so a wrong-count call reaches it with its written arguments. A `.Type` rule also hears calls of members the type lacks, before E0311. A rejection ends that call's checking: no arity, type or E0311 report follows it. `#Pre(#run …)` becomes a Prelude marker whose `check` rejects E0180, so one mechanism checks calls while building.

Rules run under `jet check`, `jet run`, `jet build` and the language server with one meaning. This depends on #6846 c14, which makes `meta.events` call watches run under every command that checks; today they run under `jet build` alone.

Cost. Every package's rules, Core's included, are compiled into the one comptime child at O0, so no rule has a privileged path. A call watch today costs about 54 µs per heard call, one exchange with the child per call. In the review's probe, 20,000 calls added 1.09 s to a 0.80 s cold build of 21,211 lines.

Rule calls are therefore batched: every rule call of one checking wave goes to the child in one batch, settled once per wave. The budget is at most 1 µs per rule call, checked by rerunning that probe with a rule in place of the watch.

A rule runs only at calls of marked declarations. A rule that panics is E3010 at the call, and its steps count toward E0952.

options.name: Error contracts: `#Pre(#run …)` may name a registered error
options.detail: A `#run` contract keeps its condition, and its message slot may hold an error value instead of text. When the condition is false for a call, that error is reported, not E0180. It is the smallest change, but a contract only runs for a call that binds to a declaration. Wrong-count calls, methods a type lacks, and lambda shapes still need the compiler, so part of the eleven files stays.
options.technical: The `Pre` marker's `message` field accepts a `String` or a value whose type implements `Diagnostic`. The error underlines the call. A condition that cannot be decided while building still reports E0180. Kept in Sema: E2910, E2911, E2501 and the static-path form of E2805.

options.name: Retire the special errors into general ones
options.detail: Move every API to plain declarations and let the general checks report: E0104 for a wrong count, E0112 for a wrong type, E0180 for a false contract, E0311 for a missing method. The eleven files go with no new feature. Beginners lose the exact wording and fix for each API, and 45 tested messages change.
options.technical: The 45 codes become retired rows. Each UI snapshot is re-recorded with a general code, which breaks the rule that a moved check keeps its snapshot (I4).

options.name: Keep the checks in the compiler (today)
options.detail: Nothing changes. The compiler keeps about 10,000 lines that know Core functions by name. Each Core API change waits for a compiler change and a new compiler build. A package can never give its users errors as good as Core's, and criteria c3 to c6 of card #6851 stay open.
options.technical: The eleven Sema/Calls files stay, with their name lists in Tests/Guards/closed_lists/baseline.tsv. #6853 ("no compiler file recognizes a Core member by name") cannot close for these members.

options.name: Checked parameter types: a literal hook rejects a bad literal
options.detail:
A parameter takes a checking type such as `RoutePath` instead of `String`. A written literal becomes that type through its build-time literal hook, which may reject it with the library's registered error. The check runs once per literal, not once per call, which suits the literal-grammar family: routes, format strings, queries and asset paths.

It cannot see typestate, methods a type lacks or lambda shapes, so E2501 and its kin would stay in the compiler. Alone it is weaker than A. As a hybrid, it could carry the literals while A's `.Type` rules carry typestate, which lowers the number of calls that run a rule.
options.technical: Literal hooks exist for `Literal.Int` and `Literal.Float` (`#run from_literal`, run while building for each literal). E adds `Literal.String` and lets a hook call `reject(value)` with a registered type, which today is E0962 outside a marker's `expand`. A run-time String argument has no literal, so a checked parameter refuses it unless the API also takes the plain type. This is the C++ `consteval` and Zig `comptime` parameter shape.

comparisons.note: A `comptime` parameter plus `@compileError` lets any library check a literal while compiling, with its own text but no stable error code.
`#[diagnostic::on_unimplemented]` lets a library word the error for a missing trait, which is how typestate APIs teach. It changes text only and cannot check values.
comparisons.code:
#[diagnostic::on_unimplemented(message = "`{Self}` is not open for writing")]
trait Writable {}

comparisons.note: Roslyn analyzers ship in a NuGet package and run inside the compiler and the IDE. Each finding has the package's own stable ID, severity, suppression and code fix. Roslyn reports time per analyzer, because analyzers slow every build and keystroke.

A package's macro runs in a separate plugin process and can emit diagnostics with fix-its at chosen nodes. That is the same process boundary as Jet's comptime child, and Swift has had to tune its launch and message cost.

A C++20 `consteval` constructor checks a literal while compiling, as `std::format_string` does. The check rides on the parameter type, so no per-call hook exists, and an argument that is not a constant fails to compile.
Template-literal types let Hono and tRPC check route grammar and parameter names in the type system, with no user code running at all.

decisions.title: How build code gives each output its own setting values, and what the two cache-line facts mean
decisions.situation: A setting is a typed value a package declares, such as `fast_math: Bool = true`, that code reads while building. Today a setting can differ per profile in package.jet. But one `fn build` that makes an Arm and an x86 program from the same source cannot give the two programs different values. The hardware facts also blur two meanings. `#build.target.layout.cache_line` is the target triple's baseline, 128 bytes on Apple Arm. `#build.cpu.cache_line` should be the selected CPU's line, but it is a fixed 64 because no CPU can be selected yet. Game and embedded authors tune per machine, and today they split one build into several runs. You are asked how build code sets a setting for one output, and what the two cache-line facts mean. We recommend a labeled `options:` value for settings, and two fact families: the triple's baseline, and the selected CPU, which defaults to that baseline.
decisions.gist: How does one build give each output its own setting values, and what do the target and CPU cache-line facts mean?
decisions.lesson: An output is one thing a build makes, such as a program for Linux on x86 or the same program for Arm. A setting is a typed value the package declares and code reads while building as `#build.settings.name`. A target fact, read as `#build.target.…`, is what every machine of the output's triple guarantees. A CPU fact, read as `#build.cpu.…`, describes the one CPU chosen for the output. This choice decides where build code writes a per-output setting value and what the CPU facts answer.
decisions.explainer: Think of a bakery that bakes one recipe for two ovens. The recipe says how much sugar to use. Each oven model has a size on its label, and the oven you bought may be bigger. Today the baker changes the sugar only by printing a new recipe book, and a second size note always says the same small number. Under the recommendation each oven's order slip carries its own sugar amount. The label keeps the model's size, and the second note holds your oven's size, starting from the label.
decisions.story: Mira ships a game for x86 desktops and Apple Arm laptops from one `fn build`. The laptop build needs `max_particles: 2000` and the desktop `8000`, and her pool allocator aligns to the cache line. Today she keeps two profiles, runs `jet build` twice, and her alignment reads `#build.cpu.cache_line`, which is 64 even on Apple's chips, whose line is 128.
decisions.detail:
Current settings. Package.jet declares settings, as in `settings: { tls: Bool = true }`. Profiles override them, as in `build: { release: Build{ settings: { tls: false } } }`. Code reads `#build.settings.tls`, folded at build time (D-CONF-MODULE1=A, Examples/Modules/Packages/TypedSettings). An undeclared read is E0302 (sema_fact_build_setting_undeclared in Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Expressions/FactReads.jet).

Current outputs. `fn build` registers outputs with `b.add_executable(name, sources, actions, deps, probes, toolchain, signing)`, all positional (Compiler/JetBuildSession/Source/Declarations.jet). D-TARGET-ONE1=A and D-BUILD-CORE1=A ratified a labeled `options:` argument holding a `BuildOptions` value on every `b.add_*` call. It is ratified but not built. The slate card that ratified it, #5069, is closed, and no open card builds it. Under A, B and C, #5007 c7 builds `options:` first, and #5006 c1 reuses it.

Current target facts (sema_fact_build_value in FactReads.jet). `#build.target.layout.pointer_bits`, `.word_bits` and `.cache_line` come from the triple's layout table. Its cache line is 128 on `aarch64-apple-*` and 64 elsewhere (Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/Target/Layout.jet). `#build.target.cpu_features` lists the features every CPU of the triple has. `#build.cpu.cache_line` is the selected CPU's line (D-CACHE-CONTROL1=A). With no CPU selection it answers a constant 64, which is wrong on Apple Arm. It has 37 uses in 15 files.

Settings scope. An output's `options:` settings set the root package's declared settings only, the package whose `fn build` runs. A dependency keeps the values its own profile and the root's dependency entry give it, the same for every output. So a dependency library compiles once and is shared. Setting values join the instance fingerprint (D-CONF-MODULE1=A), so outputs with equal values share one compiled record.

Shared library. A root-package library that two outputs build with different values becomes two instances, one per distinct value set. The cost is one more compile of that library per extra value set. A setting may change a public type, such as an array length. That is sound, because each output links exactly one instance, so the two instances never meet in one program.

Feature list type. `cpu_features` stays `[String]`. Its names are the code generator's, an open set that differs per architecture and grows with each backend release. A typed set would need a closed enum per architecture, regenerated with the backend, while `contains("avx2")` already folds while building. A typed feature set belongs with CPU dispatch, D-CPU-DISPATCH1.

Out of scope. Host facts such as `#build.host.os` belong to D-JAI-CONFIG1=A. Which machine answers a per-OS Core call during preparation is D-BUILD-TOOLCHAIN1=A. Hardware requirements stay D-HOST-CAPS1. The card's draft wording used byte names such as `pointer_size`; the bit names are in use, and no option renames them.

Edge cases under A. An undeclared key in an output's `options:` settings is a registered error at the value. So is a value of the wrong type, and its message names the declared type (card c9). An unset key takes the profile's value, then the default. An output with no toolchain reads the build machine's facts, as today.

options.name: Per-output `options:` settings; the triple's baseline and the selected CPU as two fact families
options.detail:
Build code gives an output its own setting values in a labeled `options:` value on `b.add_executable` and the other `b.add_*` calls. Only the keys it names change; the others keep the profile's value. Each output's code reads its own value through `#build.settings.name`, folded while building, on every tier.

The facts keep two families with distinct meanings. `#build.target.*` is the triple's guaranteed baseline. `#build.cpu.cache_line` and a new `#build.cpu.features` describe the selected CPU, which defaults to that baseline until CPU selection exists. On Apple Arm `#build.cpu.cache_line` becomes 128, the chip's real line, with no rename.
options.technical:
`BuildOptions` gains no field, because `settings:` is already a profile field. `options: .{ settings: .{ max_particles: 2000 } }` layers the named keys over the selected profile's settings, for that output only. In D-SETTING-ORDER1's order, output options sit between the profile and entry-code pins. Keys and values are checked against the root package's declared settings while `fn build` runs.

`#build.cpu.cache_line` answers the output triple's layout cache line instead of a constant. `#build.cpu.features` answers `#build.target.cpu_features` until a CPU can be selected, which gives a future `--cpu` flag its home. Building `options:` itself is part of this work (#5007 c7).

options.name: Per-output `options:` settings; one merged cache-line fact
options.detail: Settings work as in A. The facts merge: `#build.cpu.cache_line` is removed, and its 37 uses in 15 files move to `#build.target.layout.cache_line` in one change, with no retired spelling kept. One name per fact is simpler today. But a future CPU flag has no fact to answer, and every aligned type on Apple Arm moves from 64 to 128 bytes in the same change.
options.technical: Same settings layer as A. The merge is one cutover: the spelling leaves the syntax registry, and every caller is rewritten in the same commit. `#build.target.layout.cache_line` keeps answering the triple's value.

options.name: A setter method on the output; facts as in A
options.detail: Build code calls a method on the output after adding it: `laptop.set("max_particles", 2000)`. The facts are as in A. It reads like a configuration script, but it is a second way to change an output beside `options:`, and the key is a string the editor cannot complete.
options.technical: `Output.set(key: String, value: Dyn)` checks the key against the declared settings while `fn build` runs. The call order matters: a `set` after the plan is sealed is an error. `options:` keeps its other fields, so an output's values come from two places.

options.name: Keep today
options.detail: One build gives every output the same setting values; a per-output value needs a separate `jet build --profile=…` run. Both cache-line facts stay, and `#build.cpu.cache_line` keeps answering 64 on every target, which is wrong on Apple Arm.
options.technical: No change. Card criteria c7 to c9 stay open.

comparisons.note: Each artifact gets its own options module from build.zig; code imports it. `std.atomic.cache_line` follows the selected CPU, and the target's `builtin` module gives the baseline.
Cargo has no per-artifact feature values in one build; a cross build is a separate `--target` run. `target_feature` follows `-C target-cpu`, which defaults to the triple's baseline.
Each workspace has its own Build_Options, set from the build program; code reads `#run` constants per workspace.

recommendation.why: A puts a per-output setting in the labeled `options:` value D-TARGET-ONE1 already ratified for every output. It keeps the triple's baseline and the selected CPU apart, as D-CACHE-CONTROL1 defined them, and fixes the Apple Arm value with no rename.
gains: One build makes outputs with different setting values, folded while building on every tier.
`#build.cpu.cache_line` gives the right value on Apple Arm, and a future CPU flag has a home.
No setter method and no rename of a fact in use.

losses.loss: `options:` on `b.add_*` is ratified but unbuilt, so A builds it first.
losses.mitigation: #5006 needs the same argument for several configurations, so the work serves both cards.

losses.loss: A root-package library built with two value sets compiles twice.
losses.mitigation: Outputs with equal values share one record, and dependencies never vary per output.

losses.loss: On Apple Arm, types aligned to `#build.cpu.cache_line` grow from 64 to 128 bytes.
losses.mitigation: 128 is that chip's real line, so the padding finally prevents false sharing there.

whyNot.reason: One name now, but the 64-to-128 change still happens, and a future CPU flag loses its fact.
A second way to change an output, with string keys the editor cannot complete.
Per-output values need separate runs, and the CPU cache line stays wrong on Apple Arm.

recommendation.tradeoff: Two cache-line facts stay, each with one meaning: the triple's baseline and the chosen CPU. Build authors write settings inside `options:`, the one place an output's changes live.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude. Adversarial model family: Claude. Fresh agent: Main. The review refuted merging the two cache-line facts, the retired spelling, and the unstated cost of the unbuilt `options:`. This draft keeps both fact families, states the settings scope and its compile cost, and names #5007 c7 as the builder of `options:`.

decisions.title: How a developer asks how the compiler knows a fact: one explain reader over the derivation records
decisions.situation:
The compiler keeps a derivation record for many facts it concludes. A record names the fact, who produced it, how, by which rule and from which premises. Checked definitions, frame schedules, proof rows, test outcomes and source imports make records today. The semantic index keeps the definition records, and evidence reports keep the rest. The frame schedule record is made and then dropped.

`jet inspect compiler check` prints the index records inside one large document. `jet explain "#build.settings.loud"` prints a build fact's writer chain, but that chain is not a record. No command answers 'how is this known?' for any other subject, and the editor never shows a record.

Card #6848 c8 joins all records into one checked relation that the CLI and the LSP read. This ballot decides only how a developer reads it.
decisions.gist: Which command and which editor view answer 'how does the compiler know this?' from the one derivation relation?
decisions.lesson: A derivation record is the compiler's receipt for a fact. It says what was concluded, by whom, by which rule, and from which other facts. Following the premises backwards gives the chain that led to the fact. Today most premises are hashes, so that chain stops after one step.
decisions.explainer: Think of a lab notebook. Each result sits next to the method that produced it and the earlier results it used. Today the pages sit in two binders, and one kind of page is thrown away after it is written. Build settings keep a separate logbook with its own front desk. The question is whether every page, and that logbook, gets one front desk.
decisions.story: Ana sees a frame schedule that puts two writes in order and wonders why. The compiler made a record of that schedule and then dropped it, so no command shows it. Asking `jet explain main.on_frame@412` today reaches the package explainer, which finds no package by that name. For `#build.settings.loud`, by contrast, `jet explain` already shows the writer chain. Her editor shows the type of a declaration, never how the compiler knows it.
decisions.detail:
Producers today: SemanticIndex.jet and SemIndex Build.jet (checked-definition), Frames.jet (checked-frame-accesses), ProveReport.jet (checked-proof-row) and ImportPlan.jet (foreign-source-import). EvidenceReport.jet's evidence-record rule covers test outcomes and comparison history. Records are defined in Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/Derivations.jet. Readers today: SemIndexJSON, EvidenceJSON, Review.jet and the Canvas reasoning view. The LSP's check already builds the index records, but no hover shows one.

BuildFactExplain.jet folds the writer chain while loading and prints it as an explanation, not as a record. A definition record's subject is a hash such as `def:…`. Its claim is a path such as `method:app.Point.area`. Premises today are hashes, operation names or evidence ids, never another record's subject.

`jet debug` answers a different question. Its `why <place>` command, run in a replay, finds the write that gave one runtime value its contents. A derivation record says why the compiler, or a recorded run, holds a claim. A reader uses `jet debug` for 'why does this variable hold 7' and explain for 'why does Jet believe this'.

options.name: One reader: `jet explain <subject> [file]` for record subjects, the build-fact chain included
options.detail:
`jet explain` keeps every subject it answers today and gains record subjects. A record subject is a declaration path such as `main.Shape.area`, a frame callback such as `main.on_frame@412`, or a build fact. It prints the record and its premises, and nests a premise that names another record.

Build-fact writer chains become records of a build-fact producer. The record keeps the ordered chain as its payload, so `jet explain "#build.settings.loud"` prints exactly today's text. `--json` keeps today's fields and adds one `derivation` field.

In the editor, hover adds a 'Known by' line only when a record says more than 'checked definition'. That means a frame schedule, a proof, test evidence, or a record that is no longer current.
options.technical:
Today's order stays and runs first (Front.jet `jet_cli_explain`). It covers flags such as `--cost`, codes and `Jet.` names, and the words `log`, `effects`, `strictness` and `marker`. Then come build facts, module values, policy keys, syntax words, registered facts, and `module.UpperCamel` Diagnostic types.

One new step comes before the package fallback. A dotted or `@` subject whose first segment names a module of the project is looked up by claim path. Anything else still reaches Jetpack's package explain, so `jet explain nixpkgs.ripgrep` and `jet explain ripgrep@14` keep working. `jetpack explain` stays the explicit package spelling.

Each subject is answered by the stage that makes it. Build facts and Diagnostic types need only the loaded program, as today, so they still answer after a failed check. Declarations and frame schedules need a Doc-mode check of the entry, about what `jet check` of that entry costs. Proof, test and import records are read from stored evidence reports, never re-run, and their disposition says when they are stale.

Without a file, the current directory's project entry is used, as build-fact explain does now. A miss inside a known module is a registered error that lists that module's closest subjects. `main.on_frame` alone answers when the module has one frame callback.

BuildFactExplain.jet and the Diagnostic-type explain become producers in one cutover, with no second print path. The ordered chain is a new DerivationPayload case beside FrameSchedule, because record premises are sorted and would lose the writer order.
options.code:
$ jet explain main.on_frame@412 app.jet
main.on_frame@412  checked frame resource schedule
  producer jet-sema · rule checked-frame-accesses · static_derivation · current
  premises
    draw@3
    update@1

$ jet explain "#build.settings.tls" run.jet --profile=release --set tls=true
Build.Settings.tls

What this means:
  Build.Settings.tls = true
  [shadowed] declaration / package true at package.jet:settings.tls (default):0..0
  [shadowed] optimization bundle / package false at package.jet:build.release.settings.tls:0..0
  [effective] command line / package true at command line:--set tls=true:0..0

The hover line is the same as in A. The build-fact explain keeps its own path, so 'how is this known' has two readers.

decisions.title: How you stop at a breakpoint in code that runs while Jet builds
decisions.situation: Some Jet code runs while the program is being built: prep blocks, the prep fn they call, marker bodies and `fn build`. None of it can be debugged today. `jet debug` runs the whole build first, in a separate process, and then debugs the finished program. A breakpoint on a prep block's line is refused as `No code on`. Prep code and `fn build` run as machine code in helper processes under a step limit. Marker bodies are expanded inside the compiler itself. The ratified D-PREP-FUEL1 counts steps, but the code times them, so a pause would spend them.
decisions.gist: How do you ask Jet to stop at a breakpoint inside prep code, a marker body or `fn build` while it builds, and what does a stop show?
decisions.lesson: Build-time code is Jet code the compiler runs while it builds: prep blocks, the prep fn they call, marker bodies and `fn build`. Each call runs under a step limit, 10,000,000 steps unless `#StepLimit(n)` sets another, so a runaway loop can't stall the build. A step is one evaluated expression or statement. A breakpoint pauses the code so you can read its local values and call stack.
decisions.explainer: Think of a bakery whose ovens count the turns of each mixer instead of watching a clock. Today you can only inspect a cake after it leaves the oven. The recommendation lets you open the oven door halfway through and use the same tools you use on finished cakes. While the door is open no mixer turns, so the cake gets exactly the same number of turns.
decisions.story: Ana's prep block fills a lookup table by calling a prep fn, and one entry comes out wrong. She runs `jet debug --break tables.jet:12`, but the build already ran before the session started, and the line never stops. She ends up printing every entry and building again.
decisions.detail:
Build-time code today. Each batch of compile-time items is compiled to x86-64 at O0 and loaded into a long-lived child of the compiler (Compiler/JetEval/Source/IR/Native.jet:1-21). `fn build`, `fn dev` and `jet eval` run in a second child. Marker bodies never reach either child. The compiler expands them itself, through the template engine derives use (JetSema Registration/UserTemplates.jet:702-716, Derives.jet:2100-2129).

The step limit. D-PREP-FUEL1 defines a step as one evaluated expression or statement, counted, never wall time. The native child times it instead: 2000 steps per millisecond of the compiler's wait (Native.jet:14-15, 102-104; SessionHost.jet:285-309, 391-393). That gap is a defect on its own card. This ballot only needs a pause never to spend steps.

Where a count can go. Every loop turn and every recursive entry in a batch already starts with a poll of one runtime word (JetIR Build.jet:3824-3858, X64Patch.jet:2867-2978). Jet's own plugin translator already counts fuel at each function entry and loop head (JetPlugin Translate.jet:9-10, 416-431).

The debugger today. `jet debug` runs `jet build -O0 --dead-code=keep` as a separate process, then traces the finished program (Debug.jet:333-350). Breakpoints resolve against that program's line table only, and a line with no code is left out (JetDebug Native.jet:708-746, 2671-2687). Batches carry no line table, only each function's range for `perf` (Native.jet:184-192, 585-613).

options.name: `jet debug --build` with counted steps
options.detail:
`jet debug --build [<file.jet>]` runs the same build `jet build` runs, with the same flags, behind the usual `(Jet)` console. A breakpoint in build-time code waits for its code and stops there with locals, call stack and the steps the call has used. The pause happens during that build, started from `jet debug` rather than typed as `jet build`.

Steps are counted, as D-PREP-FUEL1 says. A paused call runs no code, so it spends no steps by construction. The count at any stop is the same with or without the debugger, on every machine. `--dap` works with `--build`, so editors get the same stops.
options.technical:
The session runs the build in its own process. Both build-time children are its children, and marker bodies expand on its own threads, so the template engine can stop at a breakpoint directly. A marker body has no step limit, because its only loop walks a known list.

Each batch gets a line table and the places of its locals, carried by the listing already sent for `perf`. A breakpoint waits by file and line and is placed when its batch loads.

Each straight-line block adds its statement count to a word in the child. The limit is checked at the poll each loop turn and recursive entry already makes. Calls the debugger makes at a stop save and restore that word. Refused system calls arrive as a signal (ComptimeWire.jet:185, 268), which the session passes back unchanged.
options.code:
$ jet debug --build
(Jet) break tables.jet:12
Breakpoint 1 at tables.jet:12, placed when its code loads
(Jet) run
Stopped at tables.jet:12 in squares (build time)
  i = 7
  table = [0, 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36]
  #0 squares tables.jet:12
  #1 SQUARES tables.jet:20 (prep)
  steps: 1,204 of 10,000,000
(Jet) continue

options.name: `jet debug --build` with steps measured as processor time
options.detail: As A, but a step stays a slice of time, now the child's processor time instead of the compiler's wall-clock wait. A stopped child uses no processor time, so a pause spends nothing. The count still differs from machine to machine, so D-PREP-FUEL1 would have to be amended first. It reads "during `jet build`" as A does.
options.technical: No counter in build-time code. The compiler reads the child's processor clock each time its wait for a reply ends, and kills the child past the limit. That the clock can be read from the compiler is unprobed.
options.code: steps: 2,400 of 10,000,000 (measured as time)

options.name: `jet build --break=<place>`: the build stops and opens the console
options.detail: `jet build` takes `--break=<file:line|function>`, repeatable. The build runs as usual until build-time code reaches a breakpoint, then opens the `(Jet)` console there. This is the literal reading of "during `jet build`". The stop display and counted steps are as in A.
options.technical: The same compiler work as A, started from `jet build`'s argument parser. `jet build` gains an interactive mode and needs `jet debug`'s other flags, such as `--do`, `--stdin` and `--dap`, forwarded.
options.code:
$ jet build --break=tables.jet:12
Stopped at tables.jet:12 in squares (build time)
  i = 7
  steps: 1,204 of 10,000,000
(Jet) continue

options.name: Editor only: build-time stops through the debug adapter
options.detail: Build-time stops are reachable only through the editor adapter. Breakpoints set in the editor stop build-time code with locals, stack and the steps used in the Variables view. The pause happens during a build the editor starts, and there is no console form.
options.technical: The same compiler work as A without the console commands. Tests drive it through the adapter's case form.
options.code:
// .vscode/launch.json
{ "type": "jet", "request": "launch", "build": true }

options.name: An interpreter for debugged builds
options.detail: When debugged, build-time code runs in an interpreter instead of as machine code. Stepping moves by Jet expression, and the count is exact. The pause happens during a build, but not in the code a plain build runs.
options.technical: A second engine for all build-time Jet, whose results must equal the machine code's. The comptime child design review already rejected a second engine for drift and speed (Docs/Audits/2026-11-23-comptime-child-design.md:36).
options.code:
$ jet debug --build
Stopped at tables.jet:12 in squares
  steps: 1,204 of 10,000,000

options.name: Run one build-time call again outside the build: `jet debug --prep <place>`
options.detail: The build records each build-time call's arguments and the compiler's answers to it. `jet debug --prep tables.jet:20` runs that one call again in a fresh child under today's debugger. This is how Rust's build scripts and Roslyn's generators are debugged. Nothing pauses during any build.
options.technical: The build writes a small record per call, and the debugger runs the batch from it. Nothing traces a running build. `fn build` needs its build services answered from the record, and a marker body has no call to rerun.
options.code:
$ jet debug --prep tables.jet:20
Stopped at tables.jet:12 in squares (rerun of SQUARES)
  i = 7

comparisons.note: Setting `org.gradle.debug` to true makes the build wait for a remote debugger on port 5005. Breakpoints in build logic then stop inside the running build.
A build script is built as an ordinary program, which a debugger can run again by itself. Procedural macros run inside the compiler, and an endless loop in one hangs it.
Roslyn's cookbook debugs a source generator by driving it from a unit test with a generator driver. It runs outside the real build.
comparisons.code: CSharpGeneratorDriver.Create(generator).RunGeneratorsAndUpdateCompilation(input, out var output, out var diagnostics);

comparisons.note: `@compileLog` prints values at compile time and fails the build on purpose. `@setEvalBranchQuota` raises a limit counted in backward branches, not time.
`consume_fuel` instruments compiled code to count work deterministically. Its docs call that somewhat expensive and offer a cheaper time-based interrupt instead.
Macros are inspected with `dumpTree`, `treeRepr` and `expandMacros`. The compile-time VM's limit counts loop iterations.

recommendation.why: Build-time code is ordinary O0 Jet, so it should stop under the console and adapter people already use, as Gradle's build logic does. Counted steps keep D-PREP-FUEL1, and a pause spends none by construction.
gains: A breakpoint in a prep block, a prep fn, a marker body or `fn build` stops with locals and a call stack.
A stop shows an exact step count, the same on every machine and with or without the debugger.
The same console commands and editor adapter work for build-time code, and `jet build` stays non-interactive.

losses.loss: Build-time loops run slower: a probe measured at most 0.6 ns more per loop turn.
losses.mitigation: The count rides the poll each turn already makes, and real build-time code is measured before cutover.

losses.loss: Prep work above ten million counted steps fails until it carries `#StepLimit(n)`.
losses.mitigation: A count-only pass over the repository's builds lists those bindings before the limit is enforced.

losses.loss: Breakpoints in build-time code wait for code that loads later.
losses.mitigation: A breakpoint is placed when its batch loads, and one never placed is named when the build ends.

losses.loss: A stop holds the whole build until you continue.
losses.mitigation: Only `jet debug --build` stops, and a plain `jet build` never waits for a person.

losses.loss: Batches need line tables and local places, and marker bodies need a stop hook.
losses.mitigation: The `perf` listing carries the tables, and the hook is a call, because the build runs in the session.

whyNot.reason: Processor time still differs between machines, so it breaks ratified D-PREP-FUEL1 unless the owner amends it.
It adds an interactive mode to `jet build`, which scripts and CI call, and duplicates `jet debug`'s flags.
Terminal users and case tests lose the console form every other debugger feature has.
A second engine must match the machine code forever, and a debugged build would not run the code a plain build runs.
It reruns a call after the build instead of pausing during it, and marker bodies have no call to rerun.

recommendation.tradeoff: A keeps one debugger, one engine and D-PREP-FUEL1's counted steps, at the price of a counter in every build-time loop.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude. Adversarial model family: Claude. Fresh agent: DerivReadReview. The review found that pauses would spend timed steps, that marker bodies run in the compiler rather than a child, and that breakpoints can't wait for code. This draft runs the build in the session with counted steps, keeping D-PREP-FUEL1, after probing a counter's cost.

decisions.title: How a call check reads the type arguments of the types a call passes
decisions.situation: A marker's `check` rule hears each call of what it marks and sees each argument's type as a TypeId: its identity, its printed name and, for a function type, its signature. Coordinate spaces need more. `first.then(next)` is wrong when the first transform's destination space differs from the next one's source space, and a rule that reports it must compare those two type arguments. `T.reflect().generic_bindings` gives them for a type written in source, but a rule only holds TypeId values. Nothing turns a TypeId value into its arguments, so the Geometry checker can't move to Core.
decisions.gist: How does a call check read the type arguments of the types a call passes, such as the spaces of two transforms?
decisions.lesson: A marker can carry a `check` rule that runs at build time for each call of what it marks, and can reject the call with a registered error. The rule sees each argument's type as a TypeId, a small record that names one type. A generic type's arguments are the types written in its angle brackets: `Transform<Screen, World>` has `Screen` and `World`.
decisions.explainer: Think of a train ticket that only prints the route name, such as "Screen to World". The inspector can read it, but can't check that your connecting ticket starts where this one ends without reading the printed words. The recommendation prints the start and end stations as their own fields on every ticket. The inspector compares two fields, and nobody has to phone the office.
decisions.story: Mia writes a units library and wants `meters.add(seconds)` refused while building, with her own error. Her rule gets both argument types as TypeIds. It can print `Quantity<Meters>`, but it can't ask which unit `Quantity` was given without cutting the printed name apart, so she gives up and checks at run time.
decisions.detail:
Revised 2026-11-24 after the owner's question q0xapii2. Option A is now the interned-table design the owner proposed. Its design section is `$JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/tmp/orch/land/2026-11-23-d-rule-typeargs1-design.md`. It gives the file:symbol cutover with the copies it deletes, the other type tables, the sibling handles and the measured costs. A second adversarial review then repaired A's maker, its fn build tier and its site lists. Its audit is `$JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/tmp/orch/land/2026-11-24-d-rule-typeargs1-review2.md`.

What a rule holds today. CheckRules.jet builds each heard call's `CompilerCall` record in the compiler. Each argument's `type` is a TypeId made by sema_comptime_reflection_type_id_in (Reflection.jet:1519-1576, CheckRules.jet:275). A specialization's TypeId already names its arguments as text (`Pair<Int, String>`). The compiler holds the specialization as a structured type, and the parameter names come from the declaration, as TypeInfo's bindings do (Reflection.jet:2379-2389, 3066-3072).

Where rules run. A rule batch is compiled to x86-64 and run in the comptime child (JetEval IR/Native.jet). The driver runs every staged call of one rule in one batch, so the calls travel as one prepared list (CheckRules.jet:1-10). D-CORE-CHECK1=A set a budget of 1 µs per rule call. Two runs measured today's rule dispatch at about 46 to 50 µs per heard call before any type is read. That cost is the same under every option here.

What reflection can do today. `T.reflect()` is resolved by sema for a name it can see while checking, and becomes a constant. Its TypeInfo is rebuilt from the declarations at each reflect (Reflection.jet:3038-3100). Nothing maps a TypeId value to a TypeInfo: fn build's `b.program.types()` lists declarations, not specializations.

What the compiler already has. The compiler already has a type interner. Its `Interner` (JetFoundation Types/TypeIDs.jet:1-118) is the TypeID table that compiler-data.md:33-39 names. A row holds a kind and child ids. Today it keys a declared type by the name a module writes (TypeIDs.jet:906-917). So `Point` and `geo.Point` can be two rows for one type, and two modules' bare `Point` one row for two types. Reflection never reads this table: each TypeId is printed text (Reflection.jet:1519-1527).

What today's identity gets wrong. A review probe declares `Point` in an inline module `geo` (`$JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/tmp/TypeArgsReview2/identity/`). A field of that type reports the identity `main.M3GeoPoint`, a generated name. The same type as a generic argument reports `geo.Point`. So one type has two identities in one compile, against metaprogramming.md:748 and 888-890. A's one maker, keyed by the checker's canonical key, removes that split.

The channel the child already has. Compile-time code reaches the compiler through host routes (JetIR BuildTypes.jet:919-960). Kind 1 answers compiler value methods and `core.compiler` queries (JetEval IR/Host.jet:204-225). This review timed kind 1 routes in a `#run` loop: 43 µs per call with a FieldInfo receiver, and 229 µs when a TypeInfo crosses. The comptime child audit's 5.49 to 10.63 µs is a synthetic two-process benchmark, so it is a floor.

What the declaration already says. Core writes `then: fn<Next>(self, next: Transform<To, Next>)`, so a chain whose middle spaces differ already fails to type-check. The Geometry checker only words that failure as E2521 before inference runs (Expressions.jet:5001-5008).

The program each option is judged by. Core's `Transform.then` and `Transform2.then` refuse a chain whose middle spaces differ. They raise E2521 at `then`, keeping the UI snapshot `Tests/UI/coordinate_transform_mismatch.stderr` byte for byte. Options A to C differ only in the line that reads the spaces.

What A measured. These runs used the batch-12 compiler on a loaded 32-thread machine, at load 13 to 105, so they are upper bounds. In the comptime child, E2521's whole read costs 10 to 25 ns per call: two row reads and a handle compare. That is inside run-to-run noise. E2521's batch table holds 6 rows, each 17 bytes plus 4 per child and its text. The compiler's own interner already spends about 68 bytes per row.

What making a TypeId costs. Under A the maker interns the type: 0.67 to 1.1 µs on a cold 200,000-row table, and 0.22 to 0.35 µs on a warm 2,000-row one. Today's maker prints two strings for the same TypeId: 0.62 to 0.89 µs cold, and 0.45 to 0.91 µs warm. Both first resolve each declared type the same way. So A's compile cost is about today's.

options.name: A TypeId is a handle into one interned type table
options.detail:
TypeId becomes a small struct holding a handle into one interned type table. That table is the only store of type facts in a compile. One maker in sema makes every entry. It interns the resolved type, each declared type by the checker's canonical key, never by the spelling a module writes. So two TypeIds of one type are one handle within a compile, and two types never share one.

Every maker calls it: the reflection builders, the `TypeId{T}` literal, type_id_of, the derive templates, marker arguments, settings and variant payloads. fn build reads a frozen copy of the table that its program snapshot carries, stamped with that snapshot's SnapshotId. find_type reads it, add_struct appends a row, and the next compile interns that row again by `identity`.

Each entry holds a type's facts once: its kind, `generic_bindings` and a function type's `signature`. `identity` and `name` are printed from the row. `identity` names each declared type's package and path, so it is equal across compiles exactly when the type is. `name` uses leaf names, such as `Transform<Screen, World>`, and no longer echoes the module path a source wrote.

Each binding gives a parameter's `name` and the TypeId written for it. Every constructed type lists its arguments this way: declared generics, List, Option, Map, tuples, Result, function types and number-family sizes. Arguments are handles to other entries, so nothing is copied and recursion stops at the written type. A variant's named payload is a tuple row with field names.

Every record that holds a type holds a TypeId into this table instead of a copy. That covers TypeInfo, FieldInfo, ParamInfo, CallableSignature, AssociatedTypeInfo, SettingInfo, CaptureInfo and the error-domain facts. TypeInfo stays a declaration record, and only its type references become handles. It reads its `generic_bindings` through its `identity` entry, so the fact has one home.

Every reader uses the same table. That covers `T.reflect()` at check time, check rules in the comptime child, marker bodies and fn build. It also covers the retained runtime type catalog, the prelude `Type` value, `reflect.of`, `jet inspect`, the semantic index and its JSON, the LSP and the Canvas dev server. The comptime child receives the rows each batch reaches as static data, with no call back to the compiler.

The other compiler-issued handles follow the same pattern: SnapshotId, DeclarationHandle, ScopeId, NodeId and ValueHandle. Each is a struct holding a handle into one table per kind. SnapshotId stays a digest, since it must compare across compiles. Core's `SnapshotID` and `ScopeID` take the ratified spellings, together with the schema rows that name them.
options.technical:
Store. The table is the compilation's existing type interner (TypeIDs.jet:1-118, compiler-data.md:33-39), so A adds no store. What changes is its key. A declared type interns by the canonical key the checker already resolves (QualifiedTypes.jet), not by its spelling. `TypeId` becomes `{priv handle: U32, priv table: U32}`. Field reads such as `id.name` become row reads that sema answers.

Makers. sema_comptime_reflection_type_id (Reflection.jet:1519) resolves, interns and returns the handle. Its siblings at Reflection.jet:1531-1588 are deleted, with the unused written_signature (793-797) and the derive template maker (Derives.jet:2198-2203). The text makers at Reflection.jet:674, 1478, 2454-2459 and 2545 call it, and so does the `TypeId{T}` literal (Expressions.jet:8193-8209).

Its callers hold the registration graph. closure_info and CheckRules pass an optional one today (Statements.jet:6323, CheckRules.jet:275), and the cutover makes it required there. Handles come only from the merged compile interner, so a worker's delta ids are remapped at interner_merge first.

fn build. Today it answers find_type and add_struct from text rows of an earlier compile's ProgramInfo (BuildAdapter.jet:331-411, 639-651; Pipeline.jet:6715-6748). Under A that snapshot carries its own frozen table, and those text round trips are deleted.

Records. Each type field in CoreRecordRows becomes a handle: TypeInfo, FieldInfo, ParamInfo, CallableSignature, AssociatedTypeInfo, ConstantInfo, SettingInfo, CaptureInfo, LayoutField, MarkerArgInfo, the Compiler index records and the prepared values. TypeInfo's `generic_bindings`, `kind`, `base` and `numeric` are deleted and read through `identity`. The `failure_contract` text becomes `failure: TypeId?`.

Readers. The comptime child gets one table per batch, holding only the rows its values reach. Each row carries its compilation id for the way back. Running code gets one static table, and the prelude `Type` value and `reflect.of` names fold into it. Tools print from rows: SemIndexJSON.jet (118-204), JetSemIndex Build.jet and Symbols.jet, JetLSP Completion.jet and Navigation.jet, and the Canvas actions. Trait payload keys, DWARF and IR layout rows stay separate, for reasons the design section gives.

Stale handles. A table id is unique within a process, and each table records its SnapshotId. Only `identity` text leaves a compile. A handle read against another table is interned again by `identity`, or fails with `MetadataFailure.Stale`.

Cost. A row read is an array index, so E2521's read costs 10 to 25 ns. Making a TypeId costs about what today's two printed spellings cost, at compile time, never per call heard.

options.name: `id.reflect()` on a TypeId value, from a table sent with each batch
options.detail:
`.reflect()` on a TypeId value gives the TypeInfo of the type it names, the record `T.reflect()` gives for a written type. In a rule body it reads a table the compiler sends with the batch. The table holds one TypeInfo per distinct type the batch's calls pass as receiver or argument. A TypeId reached by walking, such as a binding's `type` or a field's `type`, is not in the table, and reflecting it fails.

One spelling, three answers. Marker bodies are expanded inside the compiler and answer directly. fn build answers over its host route. Rules answer from the table, so only top-level argument types reflect in a rule.

Beginner path: `first.type.reflect().generic_bindings`. Expert path: the whole TypeInfo of an argument's type, but nothing nested.
options.technical:
Sema accepts `.reflect()` on a TypeId-typed value. CheckRules adds the table to the batch's prepared list, built only when the rule body calls `.reflect()`, and JetIR lowers the call to a lookup by identity. No round trips.

Cost per batch: one full TypeInfo per distinct argument or receiver type. For `Transform2<Float, Screen, World>`, that is 8 fields and 8 method signatures today (Core/Math/Math.jet:44604-44695), with their effects, markers and locations. In this review's probe, such a TypeInfo held 28 TypeIds. Closing the table over nested TypeIds would grow it with every type each one mentions.
options.code:
to: bound(first.type.reflect().generic_bindings, "To") ?? return
            from: bound(next.type.reflect().generic_bindings, "From") ?? return

options.name: `id.reflect()` on a TypeId value, answered by the compiler over the host route
options.detail:
The same `.reflect()` as B, but every TypeId value reflects in every place, nested ones included. In a rule or `#run` code the child asks the compiler over the host route compile-time code already uses, and the compiler answers with the TypeInfo. Marker bodies answer directly and fn build over its own host route.

One meaning everywhere, with no table. A rule can read any fact of any type it reaches, such as an argument type's fields or traits.

Beginner path: `first.type.reflect().generic_bindings`. Expert path: walk from any TypeId to its TypeInfo and on.
options.technical:
Sema accepts `.reflect()` on a TypeId-typed value. JetIR lowers it to a host method route of kind 1. JetEval IR/Host.jet answers it by building the TypeInfo sema builds for `T.reflect()` and writing it into the child as a value. No new channel is needed.

Cost: one round trip and one TypeInfo copied into the child per reflect. This review measured kind 1 routes at 43 µs with a FieldInfo receiver and 229 µs when a TypeInfo crosses. So the E2521 rule's two reflects cost roughly 0.1 to 0.5 ms per heard call, against D-CORE-CHECK1's budget of 1 µs.

A memo by identity in the child would cut that to one round trip per distinct type per batch, at the price of a cache in compiled rule code.
options.code:
to: bound(first.type.reflect().generic_bindings, "To") ?? return
            from: bound(next.type.reflect().generic_bindings, "From") ?? return

options.name: The signature states the check, and a marker words its mismatch
options.detail:
The declaration already says what E2521 checks: `then` takes `next: Transform<To, Next>`, so differing middle spaces fail to type-check. D lets a parameter carry a marker naming the registered error for that failure. The compiler fills the error from the two types it compared and the pair of arguments that differ. No rule runs and no TypeId grows.

It covers only what a signature can say. A check such as "the spaces must differ" or "this unit must be a length" still needs a rule that reads type arguments. So D leaves this ballot's question open for packages.

Beginner path: write the constraint in the types, as today. Expert path: name the error a mismatch raises.
options.technical: Sema's argument check reaches E2521 today through the Geometry checker, before inference (Expressions.jet:5001-5008). Under D it reports a type mismatch at a marked parameter as that marker's error instead. The error's fields are filled from the compared types by a fixed convention. This is a second way to raise a registered error beside D-CORE-CHECK1's rules. It is Rust's shape: the bound checks, and `#[diagnostic::on_unimplemented]` words the error.

comparisons.note: P2996 reflection lists a specialization's arguments with `template_arguments_of`, each a reflection that can be queried in turn. It runs inside the compiler, and a `std::meta::info` can't reach run time, so it is never stale. A lets handles reach running code, so it ships a table and checks staleness where values cross.

A Roslyn analyzer reads `TypeArguments` off a constructed type's symbol, each itself a symbol, with no further query. Symbols belong to one Compilation. Across compilations Roslyn matches them by a stable id such as `DocumentationCommentId`, the split A makes between its handle and `identity`.

A macro reads a `TypeRepr`'s arguments with `typeArgs` and compares types with `=:=`. A TypeRepr is typed by its `Quotes` context, so the compiler stops it escaping its expansion. A refuses a stale handle when it crosses, not statically.
comparisons.code:
val List(_, to) = first.tpe.widen.typeArgs
if !(to =:= from) then report.error("spaces differ")

comparisons.note: A generic type is a function that returns a struct. `@typeInfo` lists that struct's fields and declarations but not the arguments it was made from, and the type's name is text such as `List(i32)`. A `type` is a comptime value compared with `==`, and it never reaches run time.

Inside rustc each type is an interned `Ty<'tcx>` compared by pointer, and `DefPathHash` names a definition across sessions: A's internal shape. A procedural macro sees only `syn` tokens, such as an unresolved `<Screen, World>`. Checks on resolved types are trait bounds, which `#[diagnostic::on_unimplemented]` words. That is D's shape.
comparisons.code: fn then<Next>(self, next: Transform<To, Next>) -> Transform<From, Next>

comparisons.note: A macro runs in a plugin process and receives syntax only. SE-0382 deferred type information to a later proposal, because its representation would have to stay stable.

recommendation.why: A type's arguments are part of the type, so they belong in the one record that names it. Interning stores each distinct type once, and every reader reads the same entry. That removes the first draft's duplication, uneven coverage and risk of divergent makers. The cost is static data per batch instead of a round trip measured at 43 µs or more.
gains: A rule compares type arguments directly, so E2521 and any package's own type-argument checks move to Core and packages.
One store and one maker: no copied type records, and TypeIds of one type can't disagree.
Every constructed type, built-in or declared, reads its arguments through the same field.
Every tier and tool reads the same entry, and the sibling handles share the same mechanism.

losses.loss: A rule still can't read an argument type's fields, methods or traits.
losses.mitigation: Today's checkers need only type arguments. A rule needing more is a later ballot, and C stays open for it.

losses.loss: TypeInfo's `generic_bindings`, `kind`, `base` and `numeric` move to its `identity`, so every reader of them changes.
losses.mitigation: One cutover changes them all. The design section lists each file and symbol, with the examples, cases and reference.

losses.loss: Making a TypeId resolves and interns it: 0.67 to 1.1 µs on a cold table and 0.22 to 0.35 µs on a warm one.
losses.mitigation: Today's maker prints two strings for 0.45 to 0.91 µs, so compile cost is about even. It is paid per TypeId made, never per call heard.

losses.loss: A value crossing into the comptime child or running code needs its rows shipped and its handles mapped.
losses.mitigation: A batch ships only the rows it reaches, 6 for E2521. Mapping back costs one array index per TypeId.

losses.loss: `name` stops echoing the module path a source writes: a field typed `geo.Point` prints `Point`.
losses.mitigation: `identity` still names the package and module. E2521's text is unchanged, since its types are local.

losses.loss: fn build reads its own frozen table per program snapshot, beside the compile's table.
losses.mitigation: It uses the same row format, stamped with its SnapshotId, and the next compile interns its rows again by `identity`.

losses.loss: Rule dispatch itself costs about 46 to 50 µs per heard call, so the 1 µs budget is not met yet.
losses.mitigation: That cost is D-CORE-CHECK1's machinery and the same under every option. A's own read costs 10 to 25 ns.

whyNot.reason: The table ships a whole TypeInfo per argument type to read one list, and a TypeId reached by walking can't reflect in a rule though it can elsewhere.
Each reflect is a host round trip measured at 43 to 229 µs. E2521's two reflects then cost about 90 to 460 times the 1 µs budget, unless rule code gains a cache.
It covers only what a signature can state, and it adds a second way to raise a registered error beside the rules D-CORE-CHECK1 made the one mechanism.

recommendation.tradeoff: A answers every constructed type's arguments from one table, cheaply and the same everywhere. The price is a cutover of every TypeId maker, record and reader, and a `name` that no longer echoes a written module path.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude. Adversarial model family: Claude. Fresh agent: TypeArgsReview2. A holds within limits: its interner was keyed by spelling, its fn build tier had no table and its site lists were short, and this revision repairs each.
