decisions.title: Where an impl for a built-in shape writes the bounds on its item types
decisions.situation: An impl gives a type the methods a trait asks for. Jet now has impls for built-in shapes: every list `[T]`, every fixed array `[T#N]`, every optional `T?` and every map `[K: V]`, all of them unbounded today. Some of these impls only make sense when the items qualify: a list can describe itself only when each of its items can. For a struct, Jet writes this condition in place, `impl Pair<T: Describe>.Describe`. The last draft recommended `impl [T]<T: Describe>.Describe`. You asked why that looks so odd and repetitive, and whether there is a better way. There is: write each name once, with its bound where the name stands. Under today's map syntax the bound needs angle brackets, `impl [<T: Describe>].Describe`, because `[T: Describe]` is a map.
decisions.gist: How does an impl for every list, array, optional or map say what its item types must support, writing each name once?
decisions.lesson: A trait names an ability, such as Describe. An impl gives one type that ability. A bound is a requirement on a type parameter, written `T: Describe`: only types with Describe meet it. A conditional impl applies only where its bounds hold, so `Pair<Int>` can describe itself while `Pair<String>` is refused. Every Jet bound is written where its name is declared: `fn<T: Describe>`, `impl Pair<T: Describe>`.
decisions.explainer: Think of a shop sign: "gift wrapping for any box, if what is inside is not fragile". The condition belongs next to the thing it is about. For a struct, Jet writes it inside the struct's own brackets, `Pair<T: Describe>`. For a list, the recommendation writes it inside the list's brackets, in its own small brackets so it is never mistaken for a map: `[<T: Describe>]`. If maps stop using `:`, those small brackets can go: `[T: Describe]`.
decisions.story: Ana writes a Describe trait for her report tool and implements it for Int. She wants `[1, 2].describe()` to print `[#1, #2]`, and `["x"].describe()` to be refused because String has no Describe. She writes `impl [T].Describe` and calls `item.describe()` inside it. The checker refuses the call with Jet.MissingGenericBound, and its edit rewrites the head to `impl [<T: Describe>].Describe`. Later she adds maps the same way: `impl [K: <V: Describe>].Describe`.
decisions.detail:
Today. Checked on the tip23 compiler (jet a0.0.46-dev, dev 45bbcdbd34). The probes are in `$JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/tmp/orch/ballot/structbound/owner-r1-probes` (p1-p5, q01-q21, r01-r13), with outputs in `outputs-tip23.txt`. The unbounded heads have landed. The spec documents them ("The head carries no bounds"), and r01 prints `list of 2`, `array of 2`, `some` and `map of 1`.

A body that calls the trait on an item is refused with Jet.MissingGenericBound (r02). Its fix says "Add `<T: Describe>` to the generic parameter list". A structural head has no such list, and the fix carries no edit.

What each spelling does today:

- `impl [T]<T: Describe>.Describe`, the last draft's A, stops at `<` with "Expected `.` and the trait after a structural `impl` head" (r09).

- `impl<T: Describe> [T].Describe` stops at `<` with "Expected a name after `impl`" (p2).

- `impl [T: Describe].Describe` is read as a map head whose value names a type. It is refused with "`impl [T: Describe]` names the type `Describe` in its head" (r10). As a type, `[String: Describe]{"a": 1}` is a valid map of trait values (p4).

- `[<T: Describe>]` is refused at `<` as a head and as a type: "Expected a type, found `<`" (r03, r04). `impl <T: Describe>?.Describe` and `impl [K: <V: Describe>].Describe` stop at the same `<` (r12, r13). So the slot form means nothing today.

- `(T: Int)` in a type position is not a named tuple. It is refused with "Expected `,` between tuple type members" (r08), so `(T: Describe)?` is free too.

- `impl Option<T: Describe>.Describe` is Jet.ImplOnBuiltinType (q19), though `Option<Int>` is the same type as `Int?` (q18). `List<Int>` is not a type (r05). `Map<String, Int>` is not the map type either (r05).

What changed since the last draft. The trait-value path now works: `Pair<Describe>{a: 1}.describe()` prints `pair #1` (q10). `[Describe]{1, 2}` passed to `fn<T: Describe>(xs: [T])` prints `[#1, #2]` (q13). A struct named `T` in scope no longer captures `impl Pair<T: Describe>`; both calls print (q15b).

Rule 1 is live: a head name that resolves to a type is refused with "`impl [T]` names the type `T` in its head" (r06). Its fix, "Rename the parameter, as in `T` or `Item`", suggests the very name it refused.

The one rule. Every bound in Jet is `Name: Bound`, written where the name is declared: `fn<T: Describe>`, `x: Int` and `impl Pair<T: Priced>`. In the last one, the bracket list belongs to Pair. A built-in shape has no bracket list of its own, so its slot needs one while `:` also spells a map.

New work under every option:

(a) Map keys. No generic `K` is a map key today: q09 and q09b give Jet.InvalidMapKeyType whatever its bound. Inside a `[K: V]` impl, `K` gets an implied key rule, as Swift implies `Key: Hashable`. The same rule extends to `fn<K, V>(m: [K: V])`.

(b) Fix edits. The MissingGenericBound fix (r02) carries an edit that writes the chosen bounded head. Rule 1's fix (r06) proposes a name that is not a type in scope. The r10 refusal of `[T: Describe]`, when `Describe` is a trait, offers the bounded head.

(c) The conformance table `sema_type_builtin_bound_satisfied` (TypeRelations.jet:2720). Its List, Option, FixedList and Map rows make `[1, 2]` Printable and `[[1]]` Equatable with no written bound (r11). They move to Core source impls in the chosen spelling, and the rows are deleted. Tuple rows stay; Result moves with its nominal head.

(d) Tooling. The chosen head reaches the tree-sitter `impl_block`, the VS Code and Zed grammars, the editor-grammar guard case and the formatter's head printer. It also reaches LSP hover and definition, `sema_type_conditional_impl_head` and the Spellings ledger.

Still open, owed on their own cards: `T` is not inferred from a `[Int#2]` argument to `fn<T, N: Int>(xs: [T#N])` (q02b). A `[T]` impl's methods do not reach a `[T#N]` value.

Considered and not offered:

- Nominal family names (`impl List<T: Describe>`) would add a second written name for every shape (r05). D-BUILTIN-METHOD1 chose the sigil heads.

- A trailing `where` clause is the shape you rejected for struct impls in D-IMPL-COND1.

- An anonymous slot bound, as in Swift's `[some Describe]`, leaves the body no name for the item type and adds a keyword.

Every option shows the same program: a Describe trait, an Int impl and bounded impls for all four shapes. Five calls follow, with the same results in each option. A sixth, refused call is a comment.

options.name: Bound in the slot, in angle brackets
options.detail:
Each name is written once. A bounded parameter is declared in its own slot, in angle brackets: `impl [<T: Describe>].Describe`. A parameter without a bound stays bare, so `impl [T].Describe` is unchanged, and so is `impl Pair<T: Priced>.Describe`.

The rule is the one every Jet bound already follows: `Name: Bound` inside `<…>`, where the name is declared. A struct's slot is already inside `Pair<…>`. A list's slot is inside `[…]`, where `[T: Describe]` is a map, so the slot gets its own brackets. Nothing in the head can be read as a map, because `<` cannot start a type (r03, r04).
options.technical:
Grammar. Inside a structural head, a slot is a bare name or a bounded slot `<Name: Bounds>`. Bounds are read by the reader `fn<…>` uses. Several bounds are `<T: [Describe, Encode]>`, and a parameterized trait closes with the existing `>>` splitter (`<T: Holds<Int>>`).

On an optional, a parameterized bound closes with `>>?.`, as in `impl <T: Holds<Int>>?.Describe`. The head parser splits it as it splits `?.` in the unbounded `impl T?.X` (r01). The four heads are `[<T: B>]`, `[<T: B>#N]`, `<T: B>?` and `[<K: B>: <V: B>]`, with either map slot bare. N is never bounded; it is a number by its `#` position, as in the unbounded head.

The optional's `<T: B>?.Describe` lexes as `>` followed by the optional-chain token `?.`, which the head parser already splits (Rule 2). It begins with `impl <`, the start of Rust's leading list. So the parser reads the token after the closing `>`: `?` makes it this slot form, and anything else is the C habit, refused with an edit.

Binding. A bounded slot declares its name, as `fn<T: …>` does. So a type named `T` in scope never turns `[<T: Describe>]` into a concrete head; inside the impl the parameter shadows it (q15b is the nominal analogue). Bare slots keep Rule 1.

Mechanism. The parser stores each slot's bounds in ImplDef.type_params, in head order, as it does for `Pair<T: …>`. Registration copies them onto the impl's conditions, and the checker reads them as it reads nominal conditions. Nothing new runs at run time, and each element type gets its own instance.

Refusals, each one error with an edit and no cascade:

- `[<T: Describe>]` outside an impl head gets the generic-function form `fn<T: Describe>(xs: [T])`.

- `impl [T]<T: Describe>.Describe` (D) and `impl<T: Describe> [T].Describe` (C) get `impl [<T: Describe>].Describe`.

- `impl Option<T: Describe>.Describe` gets `impl <T: Describe>?.Describe`.

- `impl [T: Describe].Describe`, when Describe is a trait, gets `impl [<T: Describe>].Describe` in place of r10's rename fix.

- A body that calls a trait method on a bare parameter is Jet.MissingGenericBound, whose edit rewrites that slot.

- `impl [T].Describe` beside `impl [<T: Describe>].Describe` is Jet.DuplicateTraitImpl, conditions or not.

- A nested head is Rule 3's refusal. `[[<T: Describe>]]` gets `[<T: Describe>]`, because the inner list then qualifies through the same impl.

Edge cases. `[[7]]` meets `T: Describe` because `[Int]` has Describe. Inside `fn<U: Describe>(items: [U])`, `items.describe()` meets the condition through U's declared bound. `[Describe]{1, 2}.describe()` qualifies, because a trait value has its trait (q13 is the generic-function analogue). An empty value still calls the impl, because the bound is checked on the type.

Beginner path: write `impl [T].Describe`, call `item.describe()` and accept the edit, which writes `[<T: Describe>]`. Expert path: several bounds, bounds on K and V, generic callers, and `[<T: Holds<Int>>#N]`.

options.name: Bounds inferred from the impl bodies
options.detail: Nothing is written: `impl [T].Describe` whose body calls `item.describe()` applies only to lists whose items have Describe. The checker reads the bounds off the bodies. It is the shortest form, but whether a list type has a trait then depends on what the impl's code happens to call, and Jet does not infer bounds anywhere else (r02).
options.technical:
Mechanism. Checking an impl's bodies collects every trait member called on a head parameter, including through generic helpers the body calls, and makes those traits the impl's conditions. A call site then checks them as it checks written conditions.

Costs that a redesign cannot remove:
- A body edit changes public conformance. Deleting the last `item.describe()` widens the impl to every list. Adding a call to `item.encode()` narrows it. Then code far away that passed a `[Opaque]` stops compiling, at a head that names no condition.

- Signatures depend on bodies. A module's interface (which list types have Describe) is known only after its impl bodies are checked. Every reader of interfaces needs them first: the semantic index, LSP hover, incremental rebuilds and separately checked packages.

- It reverses the ratified unbounded heads. The spec says "The head carries no bounds, so the methods ask nothing of `T` that every type does not offer". Under B, `impl [T].SequenceTools` would silently gain conditions from its bodies.

- Two rules. A generic function never infers its bounds: q06 and r02 refuse the call with Jet.MissingGenericBound. Under B, an impl infers and a function does not.

- Inference through helpers is transitive. A bound reached through `helper(item)` needs the helper's bounds, so a change to a helper in another module changes this impl's conformance.

Mitigation, kept under every other option: the refusal of `item.describe()` in an unbounded impl carries an edit that writes the bound. The edit gives B's convenience at writing time, and the head still states the condition.

Prior art. Haskell infers a function's context but requires an instance's context to be written, except `deriving`. Jet's derive rule ("derive when every field qualifies") is that exception, and it stays. Before C++20, a template's requirements were implicit in its body. Its errors surfaced deep inside instantiations, and C++20 added concepts so that a condition could be written in the head.

Beginner path: write the body and nothing else. Expert path: none, since conditions cannot be stated or narrowed beyond what the body calls.

options.name: A bound list right after `impl`
options.detail: The parameters are declared with their bounds right after `impl`, as Rust and Scala do: `impl<T: Describe> [T].Describe`. The bound is written once, but the name still appears twice, in the list and in the shape. Struct impls keep `impl Pair<T: Priced>` unless D-IMPL-COND1 is reopened, and reopening it turns them into `impl<T: Priced> Pair<T>.Describe`, which repeats the name too.
options.technical:
Grammar: `impl` List? Head `.` Trait, with the list read by the `fn<…>` reader (N written `N: Int`). The list declares the head's parameters, so a type named `T` in scope never collides with a bounded head.

Two ways to resolve the clash with struct impls, and the cost of each:
- Keep `impl Pair<T: Priced>.Describe` for structs. A bounded impl then has two places for its list, chosen by the head's kind.
- Make the prefix the only place. That reopens the ratified D-IMPL-COND1 and rewrites its seven test sites and spec paragraph. Every struct impl then reads `impl<T: Priced> Pair<T>.Describe`, naming T twice where it names it once today.

Either way, the repetition the owner asked about remains: the list names T, and the shape names it again.

Refusals: `impl [T]<T: Describe>.Describe`, `impl [<T: Describe>].Describe` and `impl [T: Describe].Describe` (when Describe is a trait) each get the prefix list as their edit. The tree-sitter impl block already admits a prefix type-parameter list.

Beginner path: as in A, with the edit writing the prefix. Expert path: as in A.

options.name: A bound list after the shape (the last draft)
options.detail: The last draft's recommendation, kept for comparison. The shape declares the names, then a list repeats them with their bounds, where `impl Pair<T: Priced>` puts its list: `impl [T]<T: Describe>.Describe`. Every name appears twice, and no other language does this. Today it stops at the `<` (r09).
options.technical:
Grammar: `impl` Head List? `.` Trait. The list names every head parameter in head order, T then `N: Int` for `[T#N]` and K then V for `[K: V]`, and each may carry bounds. Head and list are checked against each other, with an edit for a wrong name, order or count.

Why it was drafted: it puts the list after the type, where struct impls put theirs. But for `Pair` that list is the type's own argument list, so each name appears once. For a shape, the list is an extra list after the shape, so each name appears twice. A's slot form keeps the struct rule (the bound sits where the name is) without the repeat.

Refusals: the C habit and `impl Option<T: Describe>` get the D head as their edit. Beginner and expert paths are as in A, with longer heads.

comparisons.note: Parameters are declared in a list after `impl`, before use, so a head name is never a type in scope; `const N: usize` declares a number's kind. Each name appears twice, in the list and in the type, as in C. Rust also has `where`. Source: Rust Reference, Implementations and Generics (doc.rust-lang.org/reference/items/implementations.html).
comparisons.code:
impl<T: Describe> Describe for Vec<T> { … }
impl<T: Describe, const N: usize> Describe for [T; N] { … }

comparisons.note: Extensions name the library's declared parameters (Element, Wrapped, Key, Value) in a `where` clause, so nothing repeats, but the names are fixed by the library. Requirements the type states (`Key: Hashable`) are implied, the rule this ballot adopts for map keys. SE-0341 lets a parameter bound its slot anonymously, `[some Describe]`: the bound at the slot, as in A, but with no name for the body. Sources: SE-0143 Conditional conformances; SE-0341 Opaque parameter declarations.
comparisons.code:
extension Array: Describe where Element: Describe { … }
func describeAll(_ items: [some Describe]) -> String { … }

comparisons.note: Head variables are fresh because they are lower-case, and the context before `=>` repeats them. Haskell 2010 requires an instance head to be a constructor over distinct variables, the rule the unbounded heads adopt. Instance contexts are always written, never inferred, except by `deriving`. Source: Haskell 2010 Report, section 4.3.2.

A context bound sits on the declared name, `[T: Describe]`, once; Scala's maps never use `:`, so no clash arises. Source: Scala 3 Reference, Context Bounds (docs.scala-lang.org/scala3/reference/contextual/context-bounds.html).

Before concepts, a template's requirements were implicit in its body, close to B's model, and errors surfaced deep inside instantiations; concepts let the head state them. A constrained placeholder bounds a parameter at its slot (`Describe auto x`). Source: cppreference, Constraints and concepts.
comparisons.code:
template <Describe T> std::string describe(const std::vector<T>& items);
std::string one(Describe auto x);

recommendation.why: A writes each name once, with its bound where the name is declared, the rule `fn<T: Describe>` and `impl Pair<T: Priced>` already follow. The small brackets are what today's map syntax costs: `[T: Describe]` is a map, and `<` cannot start a type. B would let a body edit change which types qualify. C and D still name each parameter twice.
recommendation.tradeoff: Each name once and one bound rule for every impl, for a pair of brackets in each bounded slot while maps keep `:`.
gains: Each parameter name is written once, at its place in the shape.
One rule for every bound: `Name: Bound` inside `<…>` where the name is declared, as in `fn<T: …>` and `Pair<T: …>`.
No reading as a map: `<` cannot start a type, so the slot form means nothing else today (r03, r04, r12, r13).

losses.loss: Brackets inside brackets: `[<T: Describe>]` and `[K: <V: Describe>]` look busy.
losses.mitigation: Only bounded slots carry them, and unbounded heads stay `[T]`.

losses.loss: A bracketed slot is legal only in an impl head; `fn(xs: [<T: Describe>])` stays refused.

losses.loss: `impl <T: Describe>?.Describe` starts like Rust's leading list.
losses.mitigation: The token after the closing `>` decides: `?` is the slot form; anything else is refused, with an edit to the slot form.

whyNot.reason: Conformance would follow body edits, interfaces would need bodies, and it reverses the ratified unbounded heads; Jet infers no bounds anywhere else.
The name still appears twice, and one rule needs D-IMPL-COND1 reopened, which makes struct impls repeat too.
The repetition you asked about: every name appears twice.

surface.lesson: A bound like `T: Describe` lets only types with Describe in. Jet writes it where the name is declared: `fn<T: Describe>`, `impl Pair<T: Describe>`. In a list head the same place is the slot, but `[T: Describe]` means a map while maps use `:`.

decisions.title: How a byte list keeps its own encoding once list codecs are ordinary impls
decisions.situation: Core encodes a byte list (`[U8]`) as a byte string, never as a list of numbers. Decode takes `Dyn.Bytes` as is and reads text as base64; encode writes `Dyn.Bytes`. Today the compiler picks that route by type tests and by helper name. Card #6852 c8 asks that decode bind through public traits, with no Core helper named in CoreReach.jet. Its c9 asks that a user type implementing those traits works at O0, O1 and O2. So list, option and map codecs become ordinary impls such as `impl [T].Decode`, and impls may not overlap. This ballot decides how the byte rule survives the move. You asked that every downside be engineered away. This rework removes five of the last draft's seven costs by redesign and names the two that remain, with their mitigations.
decisions.gist: How should a byte list keep its own encoding once list codecs are ordinary impls, with no hidden compiler route?
decisions.lesson: The usual way is for the general impl to ask the element type how a list of it looks. Haskell's `Show` and the aeson JSON library work this way. The other way is specialization: a more specific impl wins. Rust has kept that unstable for public use since 2016 and uses it only inside its standard library. Jet can keep such a hook private to Core, because a `__` name is reserved for Jet.
decisions.explainer: Think of a post office that ships any box of items as a list of parcels. Letters are special: a stack of letters travels in one envelope. The office can ask each item how it ships in bulk, and letters answer 'one envelope'; only the post office can print that answer on the form. Or it can keep a special counter just for letter stacks. Or letters can become their own product, a letter pack.
decisions.story: Ana keeps a thumbnail as `[U8]` in a `#Codable` struct. Its JSON holds base64 text and its CBOR holds a byte string. That works today because the compiler tests for U8 and names `__decode_bytes`. Once list decoding is `impl [T].Decode` in Core, nothing in the language says `[U8]` still decodes that way. Her generic `load<T: Decode>` must also reach the byte rule when `T` is `[U8]`.
decisions.detail:
What changed since the last draft. Checked on the tip23 compiler (jet a0.0.46-dev, dev 45bbcdbd34). The probes are in `$JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/tmp/orch/ballot/concretehead/owner-r1-probes`, with outputs at O0, O1 and O2.

- The shared prerequisite is gone. One generic function at both `[U8]` and `[U8#2]` no longer collides. p4 prints `{"pixels":"AQI=","fixed":"AwQ="}`, then `[1, 2]` and `[3, 4]`, at O0, O1 and O2. p5, p6, p8 and p9 print correctly at every level too.

- Hooks can be Core-only by an existing rule plus #6851 c39. A source-written `__name` is lexer error E0067, Jet.ReservedDunderName: "`__dec_list` is reserved for Jet" (c02). Core source units are lexed with reserved names allowed (Loader.jet `jet_driver_core_source_unit`). 

- Template paste. A user marker template still pastes `__` names on tip23 (review probes d1, d3b), while the `#code` paste refuses them. #6851 c39 makes both paste doors refuse a `__` name outside Core's own templates. With that rule, a trait member named `__decode_list` can be declared and overridden only by Core, and user code cannot call it.

- A `priv` trait member is not a feature: c01 stops with "Expected a trait method, associated type or trait constant".

- The trait's module can already write the concrete type where a trait says `Self` or `[Self]`. c03 declares `dec: fn(tree: Dyn) -> Self` and `dec_list: fn(tree: Dyn) -> [Self]`. It implements them on U8 with `-> U8` and `-> [U8]`, and a generic call prints `[1, 2]` and `7` at O0 and O2. The last draft's prerequisite two is not needed.

- The streaming list read needs no generic trait member. `__Decoding.read_list` (Encoding.jet:462-482) reads an Array item by item. It decodes any other value through `reader.capture().decode<[Item]>()`, the tree route, which reaches the list impl. A byte string is never an Array, and an Array of numbers read item by item is exactly `__decode_bytes`' own Array fallback, `__decode_list<U8>`. So the byte exclusion at BuildDyn.jet:1084-1093 can be deleted with no hook, and the last draft's prerequisite four is not needed.

Still true. A default body that names `Self` is refused: q1 gives Jet.UnknownName for `Self`. q2 gives "`Self` does not implement `Decode`" and leaves `[Self]` unsubstituted. A `[T#N]` cannot be built from a `[T]` in generic code: c04's `[T#N].filled(…)` gives "`[T#N].filled` needs a known length". The spec has no other fixed-list builder.

Dispatch through an element hook works today (q3, `2 3 4` at every level). A static default that does not name `Self` is inherited and overridden correctly (q4). Core's auto-derived structs keep base64 bytes (q10, q13). A `distinct U8` list stays a number list (q9).

State of #6852 c8. The codec move is unlanded. `land/6852-c8-codec-seed-a.patch` is the compiler half. `land/6852-c8-codec-seed-b.patch` is the Core half, which declares `Encode` and `Decode` in core.encoding with `impl F32.Decode` and `impl Dyn.Decode`. On dev, `__decode_f32` and `__decode_dyn` are still live. Every option presupposes the pair.

Sites that carry the byte rule (dev lines). Decode, tree: BuildDyn.jet `ir_dyn_decode` 545-573 and `ir_codec_decode_helper` 707-724, with the U8 test at 711. Decode, streaming: `ir_decoding_read` 1063-1114, with its byte exclusion at 1084-1093. Encode: `ir_serde_encode` 783-850, with the byte test at 804.

Reach and Sema: CoreReach.jet `ir_codec_decode_helpers` 106-107 and `ir_decoding_reads` 212-213, and JetDriver Pipeline.jet `jet_driver_comptime_codec_refs` 1423-1446. TypeRelations.jet `sema_type_codec_structural_bound` 2807-2848 and Serde.jet `sema_serde_type_is_admissible_in` 278-319 disagree on `[U8: V]`. Runtime: `jet_rt_codec_decode_u8` (DynCodec.jet:530) is one of ten integer adapters over `codec_decode_integer`.

Map keys, under every option. `__decode_map` takes String keys only, and STRUCTBOUND Rule 1 refuses a head that names a type. So every option uses a key trait, as Swift SE-0320 and aeson's key classes do. PROPOSED: core.encoding declares `KeyText: trait { key_text: fn(self) -> String, from_key_text: fn(text: String) -> Self [FieldError]! }` and `impl String.KeyText`, writing `-> String` as c03 allows. A generic map key then needs the implied key rule that D-IMPL-STRUCTBOUND1 names as new work (q09).

Bound spelling. The code follows D-IMPL-STRUCTBOUND1's recommendation, `impl [<T: Decode>].Decode`. If that ballot picks B, read `impl [T: Decode].Decode`. Map types are written as D-MAP-ENTRY1 decides. Under its A they read `[String => [U8]]`, and the bounded head `impl [<K: KeyText> => <V: Decode>]`, or `[K: KeyText => V: Decode]` under STRUCTBOUND1's B. The key codec trait is named KeyText so it never reads as STRUCTBOUND1's key-eligibility bound.

Cases each option must pin at O0, O1 and O2: `[U8]`, `[U8#N]` and both in one struct and one generic function (p4, p9). Also `[[U8]]`, `[U8]?`, `[String: [U8]]`, `U8?` and `[I8]` (p1, p3), `[Level]` with `Level: distinct U8` (q9), and `load<[U8]>` and `load<[U8#2]>`. Also streaming JSON `"AQI="` and `[1,2]`, CBOR major type 2, CSV cells for `U8` and `[U8]`, comptime decode, and every error text with its framing.

Tooling, owed under every option. The q7 and q8 fixes say "only a map keyed by `String` has `Encode`"; they take the KeyText text. q5's overlap refusal now says "`impl Many<Small>.Name` singles out one instance of `Many`", which is right. It then cascades into Jet.DuplicateDefinition and a second Jet.DuplicateTraitImpl, which should go. q6's fix for `Bytes` says "no impl can add it", which changes under C.

Considered and not offered:

- One list impl that tests its element type in Core source, as `if T is U8` inside `impl [<T: Decode>].Decode`. It would avoid A's two remaining costs and keep impls from overlapping. Jet has no compile-time branch on a type parameter's identity in ordinary code; `#if` is template-only. Adding one is specialization under another name, and it puts back the per-type test that D removes from IR.

options.name: The list impl asks its element, through Core-only hooks
options.detail:
The general list impl asks its element how a list of it decodes and encodes. Decode gains a hook `__decode_list` and Encode gains `__encode_list`, each with a default body that reads or writes an Array item by item. U8's impl, in Core, overrides both: bytes in, bytes out. No two impls overlap, so the ratified no-overlap rule stands, and a generic call reaches the byte rule because it asks the same impl.

The hooks are Jet-reserved `__` names, so only Core can declare, override or call them (c02, plus the template-paste rule of #6851 c39). To a user, Decode and Encode look as they do today. A user type that implements them gets the default list form and works at every level.
options.technical:
Mechanism. `impl [<T: Decode>].Decode` is `T.__decode_list(tree)`. `impl [<T: Decode>#N].Decode` calls the same hook, checks the length and builds the fixed list. `impl [<T: Encode>].Encode` is `T.__encode_list(self)`. The fixed list passes `loop item in self -> item`, one copy, the copy `ir_list_operand` makes today. `impl <T: Decode>?.Decode` and the KeyText map impls take over `__decode_option` and `__decode_map`. Dispatch through an element hook already works at O0, O1 and O2 (q3).

How each of the last draft's costs is removed:

- "A public hook member on each trait." The hooks are reserved names. A user-written `__decode_list` is lexer error E0067 whether declared, overridden or called (c02), and Core is lexed with reserved names allowed.

A user marker template can still paste a `__` name today (review probes d1, d3b). It can declare and call a hidden hook, or call Core's `__cli_is_int`. #6851 c39 closes that door, so the guarantee is c02 plus the template-paste rule. As defense in depth, sema also refuses a non-Core impl that defines a Core trait's `__` member. Docs, hover and completion list no `__` member, which the Core doc pass must check.

- "A type's owner can change how lists of it encode." Only Core can write the hook (c02, plus the template-paste rule), and a user impl on a built-in is Jet.ImplOnBuiltinType. q9 pins today's IR route only. A' requires that the distinct codec derive writes `decode` and `encode` only. The hooks take the trait default, so a distinct element is never a byte string. `[Level]` stays `[1,2]` in the O0, O1 and O2 cases.

- "`-> Self` on builtin impls first." Not needed: the trait's module writes `-> U8` and `-> [U8]` for `Self` and `[Self]`, and generic calls reach them (c03).

- "Trait members with their own type parameters first." Not needed. The list impl's streaming `__read` calls the free generic `__Decoding.read_list<T, Source>`, as derived `__read` does today. Its non-Array branch tree-decodes `[T]`, which reaches `T.__decode_list`. So BuildDyn.jet:1084-1093 is deleted, and no generic trait member is called through a bound.

- "Fixed byte lists depend on the instance collision." Fixed on tip23 (p4, p5, p9 at every level).

What remains, each with its cost and mitigation:

- The template-paste rule (#6851 c39). Cost: one check where a template pastes a name, shared by both paste doors, and one UI test. Mitigation: it closes every reserved name, not just the codec hooks, and a pinned O0 probe shows that a user template declaring and calling `__decode_list` on a user type is refused.

- A default body that names `Self` and `[Self]`. Today q1 gives Jet.UnknownName and q2 leaves `[Self]` unsubstituted. Cost: Sema gives default bodies the `Self` scope that bound calls already have (spec: "`Self` reads as `T`"), about a day [INFERENCE]. Mitigation: it is general trait work, not codec work. If it slips, registration can write the missing hook into each impl with its concrete type, as c03 does by hand.

- Building `[T#N]` from a checked `[T]` in generic code. c04 refuses `[T#N].filled` without a known length. Cost: one fixed-list static, PROPOSED `[T#N].from_list(items) -> [T#N]?`, None on a length mismatch. Mitigation: the IR already makes this conversion for `__decode_fixed_list`. Options B and C need the same static; only D avoids it.

U8's scalar decode stays a host operation, `builtin.codec_decode_u8(tree)`, a jet_builtins row naming `jet_rt_codec_decode_u8`. So U8 keeps its Number lexemes, the CSV and environment text cells, and the error "expected U8, found out-of-range Int". Only the two hooks are new source.

Removed: the three IR byte tests (BuildDyn.jet 711, 804 and 1084-1093), every container decode helper, the CoreReach.jet helper names, and `through_elements` for these heads. The two Sema tables shrink to the impls' bounds, which ends their `[U8: V]` disagreement.

Edge cases. `[[U8]]` is a list of byte strings, because the outer list asks `[U8]`, whose hook is the default. `[U8]?` is an optional byte string. `U8?` is an optional number. `[String: [U8]]` maps to byte strings. `[I8]` stays numbers. `load<[U8]>` and a struct field reach the same impl, so generic and direct calls agree.

Beginner path: nothing changes; `[U8]` is a byte string and other lists are arrays. Expert path: a user who wants a packed list form wraps it in a struct with its own Decode and Encode impls.

options.name: A concrete Core impl narrows the list impl
options.detail: Core writes `impl [U8].Decode` and `impl [U8].Encode` beside the general list impls, and the narrower impl wins for `[U8]`. Overlap is allowed only in a narrow case: both impls sit in the Core module that declares the trait, and the narrow head names no parameter at all. Every other overlap stays refused, so no user and no other trait owner gains the power. Each generic instance knows its exact types, so `load<[U8]>` reaches the byte impl.
options.technical:
Rule. An impl may overlap a general impl only when three things hold. The trait is declared in Core, both impls are in that module, and the narrow head is fully concrete (`[U8]`, never `[U8#N]` or `[T]?`). The narrow impl must hold wherever the general one does (U8 is Decode), so deleting it never makes `[U8]` lose the trait. Instance selection prefers a matching concrete head.

How the last draft's costs are removed:

- "A specificity order on heads." Not needed. Concrete-beats-generic is the only comparison, so there is no partial order to define or review.

- "Every trait owner gains overlap." Only Core's traits, in their own modules, and only for concrete heads.

- "`[U8#N]` needs its own impl." Not needed. `impl [<T: Decode>#N].Decode` decodes through `[T].decode` and builds the fixed list, so its U8 instance reaches `impl [U8].Decode`. The encode side passes `loop item in self -> item` to `[T].encode`.

- "No `Self` work, no hooks." Kept: B′ adds no trait member and needs no `Self` in default bodies, which is its real advantage over A′.

What remains:

- It amends the ratified rule. D-BUILTIN-METHOD1 bans overlapping impls and concrete-head specialization. B′ makes a Core-only exception to both. Cost: a ratified clause gains a carve-out, and the overlap check, instance selection and trait-value tables learn a second impl per head. Mitigation: the carve-out is mechanical to check (same module, Core trait, no parameters).

- A generic and a direct call agree only if every route picks per instance. That covers the monomorphized code, the trait-value table for a `[U8]` held as `Decode`, comptime decode and the streaming read. Cost: each is a place to get wrong. Mitigation: pin all four at O0, O1 and O2 (p4 and p9 cases).

- Distinct element types. Today `[Level]` with `Level: distinct U8` encodes as `[1,2]` (q9), so the byte route does not see through the tag. B′ must match `[U8]` against the element exactly, never after stripping tags, to keep that.

- The fixed-list builder from a checked `[T]`, as in A′ (c04).

Edge cases follow A′: `[[U8]]` is a list of byte strings and `U8?` an optional number.

Beginner path: as in A′. Expert path: a user cannot specialize; a user who wants a packed list form wraps it in a struct.

options.name: Bytes get their own Codable type, with a migration
options.detail: `[U8]` becomes an ordinary list in codecs and encodes as numbers. The existing `Bytes` type becomes Codable and carries the byte rule through its own impls. A program that wants a byte string writes `Bytes`. A `jet fix` migration rewrites Codable `[U8]` fields to `Bytes`, and `Bytes` decode still accepts an Array of numbers, so data written before the change reads after it. This reverses the encoding spec's rule that a Codable `[U8]` is never an integer array.
options.technical:
Mechanism. `impl [<T: Decode>].Decode` covers every list with no overlap and no hook. `impl Bytes.Decode` takes `Dyn.Bytes`, base64 text and an Array of numbers. `impl Bytes.Encode` writes `Dyn.Bytes`. `Bytes` (spec.md:4936-4965) is a growable byte builder with a read cursor; its bytes are the wire value, and a decoded `Bytes` starts with its cursor at 0. It stays its own type, as D-BUILTIN-METHOD1 requires, and is not Codable today (q6).

How the last draft's costs are reduced:

- "Every Codable byte list changes on the wire." Programs: `jet fix` rewrites each `[U8]` field of a Codable struct to `Bytes`, so their wire form is unchanged. Core: its 28 auto-derived exported structs with a `[U8]` field (Digest256, Signature, UDPPacket, TLSCertificate, Image, JobPayload and others) switch their fields to `Bytes` in the same change. q10 and q13 pin Digest256's base64 round trip.

- "Old data no longer reads." `Bytes` decode accepts an Array of numbers too, so stored base64 and stored number arrays both read.

What remains:

- API churn. A field rewritten to `Bytes` loses list operations: indexing, `len()` on the list, `loop … in`, slicing, and every `[U8]` argument it was passed to. Cost: the migration must also rewrite those uses or add conversions. Every caller of the 28 Core structs sees the type change. Mitigation: `Bytes` gains list-like reads, but it then duplicates the list API.

- Generic and unmigrated code. `load<[U8]>`, a `[U8]` local encoded directly, and a `[U8]` inside a generic struct still change to numbers. `jet fix` cannot see intent there. Cost: silent wire changes in code the migration does not touch. Mitigation: a lint on encoding a `[U8]`, until programs settle.

- Fixed byte lists. `[U8#N]` (Go json v2's base64 case) becomes numbers too, unless `Bytes` gains a fixed form.

- The fixed-list builder from a checked `[T]`, as in A′ (c04).

Beginner path: write `Bytes` for binary data, `[U8]` for small numbers. Expert path: choose per field.

options.name: Keep the byte route in the compiler, behind a role
options.detail: The list, option and map helpers become ordinary impls, but `[U8]` keeps a compiler route. In its strongest form, from `land/6852-c8-decode-lines-r2.patch`, Core declares `#Builtin.Role(.DecodeBytes) __decode_bytes`, a visible declaration found through the ratified role door. CoreReach.jet then names no helper or Core path, so the card's proof grep passes. The exception is written down as a carve-out of D-BUILTIN-METHOD1.
options.technical:
Mechanism. Generic code at `[U8]` reaches the byte rule because IR picks the role-marked helper before any impl. `[U8#N]` follows `[U8]` as today. Go's encoding/json does this with a kind test. It needs no `Self` work and no fixed-list builder, because the IR keeps building fixed lists.

How the last draft's costs are reduced:

- "Hidden route." The role is declared in Core and shows in `jet inspect`, so the route is visible.

- "Hardcoded encode." An `EncodeBytes` role on a Core `__encode_bytes` moves the encode body into Core source.

What remains, and cannot be removed without becoming A′ or B′:

- The IR keeps three U8 type tests: BuildDyn.jet 711 (decode), 804 (encode) and 1086-1090 (streaming). They decide which role to call. Removing them means asking a trait (A′) or picking an impl (B′).

- #6852 c8 asks that decode "bind through public traits", and c9 that a user type implementing those traits works. Under D, no trait says how a list of a type encodes. c8's grep passes literally, and c9 holds for user types only because they never reach the byte route. Mitigation: none within D; the card text would need amending.

Beginner and expert paths are unchanged from today.

comparisons.note: `Show` has `showList` with a default, and `Char` overrides it. The Haskell 2010 Report (6.3.3) calls that "particularly useful for the Char type, where values of type String should be shown in double quotes". aeson does the same for JSON with `toJSONList` and `parseJSONList`, and binary with `putList`. aeson handles map keys with the separate ToJSONKey and FromJSONKey classes.
comparisons.code:
class FromJSON a where
  parseJSON     :: Value -> Parser a
  parseJSONList :: Value -> Parser [a]
instance FromJSON a => FromJSON [a] where
  parseJSON = parseJSONList

comparisons.note: encoding/json writes `[]byte` as base64 by a kind test in the encoder; an element type with its own Marshaler opts out. The json v1 package documentation lists the difference that its `FormatByteArrayAsArray` option controls: "In v1, a Go byte array is represented as a JSON array of JSON numbers. In contrast, in v2 a Go byte array is represented as a Base64-encoded JSON string." The v2 form is Jet's `[U8#N]` rule.

Specialization (RFC 1210) has been unstable for public use since 2016 over soundness, but std uses `min_specialization` internally. Serde cannot, so the serde_bytes README says: "Without specialization, Rust forces Serde to treat &[u8] just like any other slice and Vec<u8> just like any other vector."

`Data` is its own type, and JSONEncoder's `dataEncodingStrategy` defaults to base64, while `[UInt8]` encodes as numbers. Dictionary encoding tests whether its key is String or Int at run time. SE-0320, in Swift 5.6, added the `CodingKeyRepresentable` protocol as a key hook.
comparisons.code: extension Array: Codable where Element: Codable { }

comparisons.note: Partial specialization lets a template pick a narrower body. `std::vector<bool>` specializes into a packed form that breaks generic code expecting a real `bool&`.
comparisons.code:
template <class T> struct Codec { };
template <> struct Codec<std::vector<uint8_t>> { };

recommendation.why: A′ keeps the ratified rule that impls never overlap, and every generic instance still gets the byte rule because it asks the same impl. Its hooks are Jet-reserved names, so users see Decode and Encode unchanged. With #6851's paste rule, users cannot alter how a list of a type encodes. Five of the last draft's seven costs are gone (c02, c03, the streaming capture path, the fixed collision). Two remain, and both are general work: `Self` in default bodies, and a fixed-list builder that B′ and C′ need too.
recommendation.tradeoff: No overlap, no compiler byte route and no public hook, for `Self` in default trait bodies and one fixed-list static first.
gains: One impl per type, so a generic call and a direct call always agree.
`[U8]`, `[U8#N]`, streaming and encode follow one hook, so all three IR byte tests go.
The hooks are reserved names: users can neither override nor call them (c02, plus the template-paste rule of #6851 c39), and Decode and Encode look unchanged.
Decode binds through public traits for lists, fixed lists, options, maps and bytes, A′'s part of #6852 c8 and c9.
No `-> Self` work on builtin impls (c03) and no generic trait members (the streaming capture path).

losses.loss: Default trait bodies must name `Self` and `[Self]` (q1, q2).
losses.mitigation: General trait work the spec's `Self` rule already implies; if it slips, registration writes the hook into each impl with its concrete type, as c03 does by hand.

losses.loss: A `[T#N]` must be built from a checked `[T]` in generic code (c04).
losses.mitigation: One static, `[T#N].from_list(items) -> [T#N]?`, over a conversion the IR already makes; B′ and C′ need it too.

losses.loss: No user type can choose a non-default list form.
losses.mitigation: Deliberate: a packed form is a wrapper struct with its own impls, so the wire form of `[T]` never depends on who wrote T.

losses.loss: The reserved-name guarantee needs a template-paste rule first: a user template can paste a `__` name today.
losses.mitigation: #6851 c39 adds one check at the paste site for both paste doors, with a pinned O0 probe and a UI test.

whyNot.reason: It needs no `Self` work, but it carves an exception into the ratified no-overlap rule, and every dispatch route must pick per instance to keep generic and direct calls agreeing.
Even with `jet fix`, generic and unmigrated `[U8]` code silently changes wire form, and fields rewritten to `Bytes` lose the list API.
The IR keeps three U8 type tests, and no trait says how a list encodes, so #6852 c8's "bind through public traits" fails.

decisions.title: What `$/cancelRequest` means to `jet self lsp`, and when a cancelled request stops
decisions.situation: An editor sends `$/cancelRequest` when the answer to a request is no longer needed, for example after the user types again. `jet self lsp` reads one message, answers it, then reads the next. So it reads a cancel only after the request it names has been answered, and it ignores the cancel (Compiler/JetLSP/Source/LSP/Requests.jet: "Cancellation and tracing need no answer"). Card #6903 c1 asks that cancelled work return the -32800 response and never later publish a result as current. The card also says no public cancellation semantics may be chosen silently. You are asked when a cancel takes effect. We recommend that the server read every message already waiting before it answers a request, so a cancel for a waiting request answers -32800 and the request never runs. Requests still run one at a time, in arrival order. Every option first needs one fix: today the server stops when a long message reaches it in pieces.
decisions.gist: When the editor cancels a request, which work does `jet self lsp` drop, and how does it see the cancel in time?
decisions.lesson: An editor and its language server talk in numbered messages. A request asks for something, such as the outline of a file. A cancel says that one numbered request is no longer wanted. The answer to a cancelled request is error -32800. The question is how early the server notices a cancel. It can notice it only before the work starts, or also while the work runs.
decisions.explainer: Think of a print shop with one clerk. Customers drop order slips in a tray. Today the clerk takes one slip, finishes the job, then takes the next. A slip that says "cancel order 50" is read only after order 50 is printed. Under the recommendation, the clerk reads every slip in the tray before starting a job, so a cancelled order is never printed. Jobs still go in slip order. Stopping a job halfway needs more: a helper who watches the tray.
decisions.story: Mia opens a 3,000-line file in VS Code and types. Each keystroke sends the whole new text, and the outline pane asks for symbols again, cancelling its last request. Today `jet self lsp` stops with "input ended inside a message body" once such an edit reaches it in pieces. With that fixed, it answers every outline request in turn, cancelled ones included. When a check outlasts the gap between keystrokes, answers fall further behind. VS Code drops cancelled answers, so Mia sees a lagging outline, not an old one.
decisions.detail:
Current code. Compiler/JetLSP/Source/LSP/Loop.jet `lsp_serve` reads one framed message, handles it, and loops. `lsp_read_message` reads the header with `core.term.read_until` and the body with one `take(length)`. Before each request, `lsp_flush_dirty` checks and publishes the documents edited since their last publication (Loop.jet:96). `$/cancelRequest` falls through `lsp_handle_notification` with no effect. Requests read the stored check (Facts.jet:51), so the costly check before a request is that publishing step.

The case. Tests/Cases/LSP/lsp_canceled_costly_request_returns_32800_and_never_publishes.case is known-failing (Tests/known-failing.tsv:358, "answers requests in order and does not honor `$/cancelRequest`"). Its PENDING-SEAM(read_bytes) header names a need of the test harness, not of the server. It sends the edit, request 50 and the cancel as three separate writes. A read-ahead server passes only when the cancel is already waiting as request 50 is taken. So the case must send the three in one write to be deterministic.

A defect every option fixes first. `take` returns at most one read's worth of bytes (Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/RouteTerm.jet `jet_terminal8_take`: "One stdin read of up to `n` bytes"). `lsp_read_message` treats a short body as the end of input (Loop.jet:34-36). So a body that arrives in pieces stops the server with "input ended inside a message body".

Review probes p3 and p4 reproduce it with a 6,759-byte body written in two pieces, and with full-text edits of 1,000 to 3,000 lines. The fix reads until the body is complete. Card #6903 owns it.

What is missing for A and B. Core has no way to read standard input without waiting. `core.term` offers `read_until`, `read_all_input`, `binread` and the private `__take_bytes`, and each one waits for input. The runtime keeps one 64 KiB stdin buffer (TerminalInput.jet), and a burst usually lands in it in one read. So a check of the file descriptor alone would miss the messages already buffered.

The shape of the Core call. D-CORE-TERMRAW1=A chose a timed read for keys, `term.read_key_within(wait: Duration) -> Key?`: "A wait of zero checks without waiting". It dropped a separate poll-then-read call. D-TERM-INCREMENTAL1=A says every Core stdin reader takes bytes only from the runtime's one buffer. So A's call is a timed byte read in that shape, not a readiness flag.

Replay. Every stdin read is journaled for prove capture and `jet debug` replay (ProveJournal.jet `rt_prove_stdin_read`, RecordReplay.jet `replay_read`). A timed read that finds no bytes is an input event too, so it is journaled the same way. The runtime is the Linux pack today, and other packs get the call with their stdin code.

What the LSP specification says. A cancelled request still gets one answer, and an error answer should use -32800 (RequestCancelled). A server may also return a normal result. Servers "should therefore not decide by themselves to cancel requests simply due to that fact that a state change notification is detected in the queue" (LSP 3.17, Implementation Considerations).

Order. So under every option a request is answered on the text that the messages before it left. Edits queued after a request are applied after its answer. The passing case lsp_overlapping_edits_latest_checked_revision_wins pins this: request 2 answers marker_one while edits to versions 11 and 12 wait behind it (review probe p5).

What "never later publishes a result as current" means here. A cancelled request that never ran publishes nothing. Before a request, the publishing step still checks a document whose newer edit is queued, because the request reads that check, but it does not send those diagnostics. didOpen still publishes at once, as today. An edit that arrives while a check runs is seen at the next read.

Cancel matching. A cancel applies to the latest earlier unanswered request with the same id, matched as JSON, so 2 and "2" differ. A cancel for an answered id, an unknown id or a notification is ignored. A cancel never applies to `initialize` or `shutdown`, and the not-initialized and shutting-down errors keep precedence. The server sends no partial results and no progress, so neither needs a rule.

What each option catches. Review probe p4 types 20 full-text edits into a 100-line, 300-line or 1,000-line file. Each keystroke sends the edit, a cancel of the last outline request if it is unanswered, and a new outline request. When each check finished within the gap, no cancel was sent. At 30 ms between keystrokes, 16 of 19 and 18 of 19 cancels named a waiting request. With 1,000 lines at 300 ms, a check took about 270 ms, and 4 cancels met the running request.

Scope. This decides observable LSP behavior and the one Core call A and B need. Requests run one at a time in arrival order under every option, so no option chooses a count of workers that run requests. The card asks that no worker count or scheduling policy be chosen silently, and this ballot states each option's.

options.name: Read ahead: a cancel stops waiting requests only
options.detail: Before the server answers a request, it reads every byte already waiting on standard input, without waiting, and parses every complete message. Messages are still handled in arrival order. A `$/cancelRequest` for a queued request makes that request answer -32800 without running. A request that has started runs to the end and gets its normal answer, as the LSP specification allows. Before a request, the publishing step does not send diagnostics for a document whose newer edit is queued. The server stays single-threaded.
options.technical:
Core gains one call in D-CORE-TERMRAW1's shape: `core.term.take_within(n: Int, wait: Duration) -[IO, Time.Wait]> [U8]? IOError!`. It returns up to `n` bytes from the runtime's stdin buffer, or from one read if bytes arrive within `wait`. It returns None when no byte arrives in time, and an empty list at the end of input. A wait of zero checks without waiting.

The call is journaled like every stdin read, its None answers included, so prove capture and `jet debug` replay repeat it.

Loop.jet keeps a byte buffer and a queue of parsed messages. Before taking a request, it calls `take_within(65536, 0ms)` until None and frames every complete message. A partial message stays in the buffer and blocks nothing. When the queue is empty, the loop waits for more bytes. The same buffer fixes the short-body defect.

A queued cancel that matches the taken request, by the rule in the detail, answers `lsp_error_response(id, -32800, "the request was cancelled")`. The case lsp_late_cancel_does_not_poison_a_reused_request_id keeps passing, because its cancel for id 2 comes before any request 2.

options.name: Read ahead, and cancel a running check
options.detail: Everything in A. In addition, the check before a request runs as a task. While it runs, the loop keeps reading input with A's call. When the request that the check serves is cancelled, the loop cancels the task. The task stops at its next loop or call check (D-CANCELMODEL1=C). The request answers -32800, and nothing from the stopped check is stored or published. The driver needs no change.
options.technical:
The A call, plus a `task.group` around the check in `lsp_flush_dirty`. The check task sends its `LSPChecked` on a channel. The loop alternates `take_within(65536, 10ms)` with `try_receive()` on that channel. On a matching cancel it calls `cancel()` on the task.

Review probe p6 shows the language part works today. A computing task, canceled while another task waits on standard input, stops at once at O0, O1 and O2.

The checker keeps no state between checks (JetCLI LSP.jet `JetCLILSPChecker.check` returns an `LSPChecked`), so a stopped check leaves no server state behind. Whether a driver compile stopped mid-way leaves files or caches half-written is not yet audited.

options.name: A reader task reads input while work runs
options.detail: A reader task reads and frames messages with today's blocking reads and sends them on a channel. The loop takes them from the channel in arrival order. The check before a request runs as a task, as in B. A cancel for a queued or running request is seen as soon as it arrives. No new Core call is needed. Requests still run one at a time.
options.technical:
`lsp_serve` opens a `task.group` with the reader task and runs the loop. The reader uses `read_until` and `take`, with the short-body fix. The loop drains the channel with `try_receive()` before each request. While a check runs, it waits on the channel and the check's result.

Review probe p6 shows the parts work today. A reader task blocked in `read_until` gets its line while another task computes, and the cancel stops the computing task at once at O0, O1 and O2.

Costs: the server becomes concurrent. Replay must also repeat when each message reached the loop relative to the check, which is not yet shown. The reader owns standard input, so nothing else in the process may read it.

options.name: Keep in-order answers; cancel has no effect
options.detail: Keep today's behavior and record it: each request is answered in arrival order, and `$/cancelRequest` is ignored. The LSP specification allows this. A server "is free to ignore" `$/` notifications, and for a "single threaded synchronous" server "there is little a server can do" with a cancel. The -32800 criterion and its case are retired as not applicable to this server. The short-body defect is still fixed.
options.technical: No new Core call. Requests.jet's comment becomes the documented contract, and the known-failing case is deleted with a reason. Loop.jet reads until a body is complete.

comparisons.note: gopls cancels a request's context when `$/cancelRequest` arrives, matching integer and string ids separately. A reply sent after the cancel becomes RequestCancelled. Source: golang/tools gopls/internal/protocol/protocol.go, `CancelHandler`.

rust-analyzer reads messages on its own thread (lsp-server stdio.rs). A cancel answers -32800 at once for any pending request, and the late result is dropped (lsp-server req_queue.rs). Running queries unwind only when a change is applied to the database, and then answer ContentModified (-32801) or retry (handlers/dispatch.rs).

tsserver is single-threaded. Its client signals a cancel out of band by creating a named pipe whose existence tsserver checks, and long operations ask between steps. This is B's model without reading the message stream. Source: TypeScript src/tsserver/nodeServer.ts, `createCancellationToken`.

clangd keys running requests by their JSON id, and a cancel for an unknown id is ignored. "If a client reuses an ID, the last wins and the first cannot be canceled." Source: llvm-project clang-tools-extra/clangd/ClangdLSPServer.cpp, `onCancel`.

recommendation.why: When the server falls behind, most cancels name a request that is still waiting (review probe p4: 16 of 19 and 18 of 19 at 30 ms). Read-ahead catches those deterministically. It keeps the server single-threaded and needs no driver change, at the cost of one timed Core read in the shape already ratified for keys.
gains: A cancelled request that has not started answers -32800 and never runs, so the known-failing case can pass once it sends its burst in one write.

Requests keep arrival order, so passing cases such as lsp_overlapping_edits_latest_checked_revision_wins keep passing.
