decisions.title: How an editor hands the Jet regions of a host document to `jet self lsp`
decisions.situation: D-EMBED-REGION1=A (ratified) lets an HTML page or a Markdown file hold Jet. The host supplies the complete Jet source and its unchanged host segments, and Jet maps every result back through one position map. It did not fix how an editor sends that to the language server. Today JetLSP keeps no document whose languageId is not `jet`, answers `workspace/executeCommand` for two commands, and drops unknown notifications. You asked us to engineer away each option's downsides. This revision removes most of them and names the cost and mitigation of the rest. We still recommend a `jet/hostDocument` notification. Its modules now point at host ranges instead of copying them, and the client sends it in the same turn as the host's didChange.
decisions.gist: What message does an editor send so `jet self lsp` can check the Jet inside an HTML or Markdown file?
decisions.lesson: An editor tells a language server about a file with standard messages: didOpen gives the whole text, and didChange gives each edit. A host document is a file in another language, such as HTML, with Jet inside it. The editor extension knows where the Jet is and builds complete Jet modules from it. The question is which message carries those modules and their maps of shared text to the server.
decisions.explainer:
Think of a translator working on a bilingual letter. The post office already delivers the letter (didOpen and didChange). Someone must also hand over a slip that says "lines 3 to 4 are in Jet, and here is the Jet page they belong to".

The slip can follow the letter, ride stapled to the envelope, or go by registered mail. Each Jet passage can be cut out and sent alone, or the translator can guess which lines are Jet. A last choice files the letter as a scrapbook whose pages are the Jet passages.
decisions.story: Lin writes a Svelte-like page with two `<script lang="jet">` blocks. She types in the first block. Once her edit is checked, the editor shows the error in the second block at its new position. A quick fix must edit her page, never the hidden generated Jet module. Her Markdown notes hold ten independent Jet examples, and each is checked on its own.
decisions.detail:
Ratified ground. D-EMBED-REGION1=A (ratified 2026-09-10, not superseded) says this:
- Hosts "supply complete generated Jet source and its unchanged source segments" and "retain control of module scope and host syntax".
- "Jet validates UTF-8 boundaries and mappings".
- "Every result carries the external revision", and "the same checked maps serve diagnostics, completion, navigation, and edits".
- "Edits across unmapped generated text are rejected", and "generated-only locations stay labeled as generated".

It also says these:
- "Editor conversion uses UTF-16 units, not byte offsets".
- "Use one SourceDocument input for whole and mapped documents", migrating existing callers.
- The design pass "removed host-format parsing from the compiler proposal", and hosts "must identify their embedded regions".

D-LSP-CANCEL1=A (ratified) also bears on this. Before a request, the server reads every waiting byte without blocking and handles messages in arrival order. A queued cancel answers -32800, and diagnostics are not published for a document whose newer edit is queued.

What is built (dev 85d58ab042). JetDriver's SourceDocuments.jet holds `JetDriverSourceDocument{path, source, host}`. Its host side, `JetDriverHostDocument{identity, revision, text, mappings}`, keeps ordered UTF-8 byte mappings. `jet_driver_source_document_problem` refuses a mapping that is out of order, past its text, cuts a UTF-8 character, or changes the bytes it declares unchanged. The span, offset and edit maps are built. JetLSP's overlays are already `JetDriverSourceDocument`, but nothing in JetLSP builds a host side yet.

Today's server, probed on tip 22 and batch 23 (review probe p3, rerun):
- Server.jet `lsp_update_document` keeps no didOpen whose languageId is not `jet`. An HTML page opened as `html` gets no diagnostics and no answers.
- It answers `workspace/executeCommand` for `jet.impact` and `jet.reasoning`. Any other command gets -32602 "unknown command: …". The VS Code reasoning panel works.

More of today's server:
- It drops unknown notifications without a trace.
- After a didChange it publishes only when the next request arrives.
- It advertises no `experimental` capability and no `positionEncoding`, so positions are UTF-16.

What every option shares. A Jet module travels as an ordered list of parts. A part is `{"host": Range}`, a slice of the host text the module keeps unchanged, or `{"text": string}`, Jet the host generated. The server joins the parts into the complete Jet source, and each host part becomes one driver mapping.

Several things follow from that:
- This is the decision's "complete generated Jet source and its unchanged source segments", sent once instead of twice.
- A host part cannot differ from the host, so that class of refusal is gone.
- A keystroke outside the generated text resends no Jet text at all.

Host ranges are LSP ranges in the session's position encoding, UTF-16 by default, as the ratified clause on editor conversion asks. The server converts them with a strict converter. A character past its line's end is refused, not clamped as Position.jet's `lsp_checked_offset_bytes` clamps request positions. A position inside a surrogate pair is refused.

A host document carries zero or more modules, because Markdown examples are independent programs and the host owns module scope. A module's host parts run forward in the host. No two parts of any module share a host character. A host with zero modules has its results withdrawn.

Results for a host document are published on the host URI with the host version, in host ranges. Other results go elsewhere:
- A diagnostic that reaches generated text, or crosses parts, is published on the host URI at the module's nearest host part. Its message starts "In generated Jet: ", and its Jet range goes in the diagnostic's `data`, so it stays labeled as generated. No result is ever published on a module URI, which no editor can open.

Navigation, edits and requests outside the parts.
- A navigation target in generated text is dropped, because no editor can open it.
- An edit that reaches generated text is refused.
- A request at a host position outside every host part answers null.

Whole-document requests on a host, such as semantic tokens, document symbols, folding ranges, inlay hints and code lenses, cover the Jet parts only, in host ranges.

Formatting and range formatting on a host answer null. Formatting.jet returns one edit for a whole module or its lines, which a module of two or more parts can never map. So Jet inside a host is not formatted, a named cost, until edits are made per part. The extension registers formatting for `jet` documents only, so VS Code never offers Jet as an HTML or Markdown formatter.

A module URI must be a `file:` URI that names no file on disk, no open Jet document and no other host's module. Its directory decides the package, as for any Jet file.

Refusals are visible. A refused message is logged with `window/logMessage` (Warning). One diagnostic, code `Jet.HostRegionsRefused`, then sits on the host URI at the first bad part, or at line 0 when no part can be placed. Its message is "Jet could not use the Jet regions of this file: <reason>". The last good results stay on screen but are never published as current for a newer version.

The reasons for a bad part:
- "module 1 part 2 ends past the end of line 3".
- "module 1 part 2 starts inside a character".
- "module 1 part 2 runs backwards".
- "module 1 part 2 starts before part 1 ends".
- "module 2 part 1 shares host text with module 1 part 1".

The reasons for a bad module URI:
- "module 1 names file:///w/a.jet, a file on disk".
- "module 1 names file:///w/a.jet, an open Jet document".
- "module 1 names file:///w/b.html.jet, a module of file:///w/b.html".
- "module 1 names untitled:x, which is not a file: URI".

Modules belong to exactly one host version. Host parts are references, so the byte check that a part equals the host no longer guards against stale modules. Stale modules would validate silently. So a host didChange drops the host's modules. A host whose current version has no modules is never checked or published: it stays dirty, and its last results stay on screen. The cost: correctness rests on the version number alone.

Ordering. The client sends version N's modules in the same turn of its event loop as version N's didChange, before anything else it sends. Both first-party clients can, as their sources show.

vscode-languageclient 9.0.1 runs `middleware.didChange` synchronously (textSynchronization.ts 267-282). `sendNotification` and `sendRequest` both pass the same `await this.$start()` before writing (client.ts 715-765, 816-851). A notification the middleware sends right after `next(event)` is therefore written after that didChange and before any later request.

Neovim 0.11 accepts a function as `cmd` and uses the RPC client it returns (client.lua 459-461). The recipe's wrapper sends the modules right after each host didChange it writes. An `LspNotify` autocommand is easier to write but runs one tick later through `vim.schedule` (client.lua 769-778).

The server covers a client that is one tick late, and only option A needs it. A request on a host URI whose current version has no modules yet is held. This happens only if that host has had modules since it was opened. A notification with zero modules counts as that version's modules arriving.

While a request is held, the loop keeps reading for the rest of its 500 ms budget. It applies only notifications (didChange, didClose, jet/hostDocument and $/cancelRequest), in arrival order. Later requests stay queued behind the held one. So the one exception to CANCEL1's arrival order is exactly this: notifications may pass a held host request.

This rides on CANCEL1's queue and on the timed read `core.term.take_within`. Both arrive with #6903 c20, which has not landed yet, so A depends on it.

The set-aside request is answered by whichever comes first:
- That version's modules arrive: its normal answer.
- A newer didChange or a didClose of that host: -32801 "a newer version of this document arrived".
- Its cancel: -32800.
- 500 ms after it was set aside: -32801 "the Jet regions of this version did not arrive".

vscode-languageclient turns -32801 into an empty result for most requests (client.ts 1992-2034). Semantic tokens and the resolve calls get a quiet CancellationError instead. Either way a late client degrades to "no answer", never to a wrong one.

Host sync. The VS Code extension adds `html` and `markdown` to its document selector. Its middleware withholds the didOpen and didChanges of a host with no Jet region. When a withheld host gains a region, the extension sends didOpen with the current text, then the modules. When a host loses its last region, it sends zero modules and keeps the host open. Those zero modules count as that version's modules, so no request on the host waits. An HTML file with no Jet costs the server nothing.

Cutover inventory. These are the sites the recommended option touches:
- Requests.jet `lsp_handle_notification` and `lsp_initialize_response` take the new message and its capability.
- Server.jet `lsp_update_document` keeps a non-`jet` didOpen as a host, never checked as Jet. Hosts join the one document store as a host kind. A host didChange drops the host's modules, and a host without its current version's modules is never checked or published.
- Server.jet `overlays()` adds one `JetDriverSourceDocument` per module, with its host side built from the parts.

More sites:
- Diagnostics.jet `lsp_publish_document_diagnostics`, `lsp_document_group_json` and `lsp_close_document` carry the host version, publish generated-text diagnostics on the host URI, and clear it.

Positions. Every request provider converts host positions through the one driver map. Position.jet's UTF-16 counting (`lsp_utf16_length`, `lsp_checked_offset_bytes`) reuses the driver's counter (`jet_driver_utf16_offset`), so there is no second counter. The strict converter, which refuses a position past its line's end or inside a surrogate pair, is a new driver function, not the clamping one.

The last sites.
- Loop.jet holds a late host request as above, on the #6903 c20 queue.
- Formatting.jet answers null for a host, and the extension's formatting middleware skips hosts.
- Tools/Editors/Vscode/extension.js gains the host languages and the middleware. The Neovim recipe in Tools/Editors gains the `cmd` wrapper.

`jet check` of host files (item c4c) stays outside this ballot, because the CLI reads files, not editor versions.

Edge cases, answered under each option:
- E1. The host changes and its new modules have not arrived.
- E2. A part runs backwards, overlaps, cuts a character or ends past its line, or a module URI breaks the rule above.
- E3. Modules arrive for a URI the editor never opened.

More edge cases:
- E4. Modules name a host version other than the one the server holds.
- E5. The host closes.
- E6. The client never sends modules.
- E7. Generated Jet sits between host parts, such as a Markdown example wrapped in a `run` function.

Beginner path. Users never type any of this. In VS Code, installing the extension is enough. Errors appear inside the `<script lang="jet">` block, and a quick fix edits the page. In Neovim, the user copies the recipe, which wraps `cmd`. Emacs eglot runs one server per buffer, so pointing it at an HTML file replaces the HTML server. Zed and Helix cannot send any client-side message (option E answers them).

Expert path. A tool author whose host format embeds Jet sends the same message from their own client. They own region finding, generated parts and module scope. They can replay their output against `jet self lsp` from a JSON transcript, and a refusal names the bad part.

options.name: A `jet/hostDocument` notification in the same turn as each host version
options.detail:
The host document travels on the standard didOpen and didChange under its own URI and languageId, with incremental sync as usual. In the same turn, the client sends one `jet/hostDocument` notification with the host URI, the version and the modules as parts. The server checks each module and publishes on the host URI with that version.

The first draft listed six downsides. Four are removed.

- The request window is closed at the client by the ordering rule. The server covers a client one tick late by setting its request aside, with a 500 ms bound.
- The full text resent per keystroke is gone: host parts are references, so only generated parts travel as text. The price is that a stale module can't be caught by bytes, so a host didChange drops its modules and nothing is checked until that version's modules arrive.

Two more are gone.
- "The loop can't park" is gone, because CANCEL1=A's queue is the place a request waits, once #6903 c20 lands. Only notifications pass a held request.
- "Every HTML file is synced" is gone: the extension withholds hosts with no Jet region.

Two stay, with their mitigations:
- "Zed and Helix get nothing" cannot be removed inside A, because their clients cannot send it. Option E is the fix, and it feeds the same server entry.
- "The first `jet/` method" stays. It is versioned under `experimental`, and its params are the driver's own host document shape.

E1: with a same-turn client, no message ever lands in between. The didChange drops the old modules, so the host is never checked against the wrong version. Late clients are covered by the set-aside rule. The old diagnostics stay up for that hop, because CANCEL1 publishes nothing for a document whose newer edit is queued.

E2: the whole notification is refused, with the log and the `Jet.HostRegionsRefused` diagnostic. E3: ignored and logged as "jet/hostDocument for file:///w/x.html was ignored: the document is not open".

E4: an older version is dropped and logged as "… version 6 was ignored: version 7 is newer". A newer one is held, one per host, until that version's text arrives.

E5: didClose drops the host's text, modules, held notification and set-aside requests. It publishes empty diagnostics on the host URI.

E6: no results, and no request waits, because only a host that has had modules holds a request. The server logs once per host "no Jet regions arrived for file:///w/x.html; its Jet is not checked". E7: the generated text travels as a text part, has no host place, and its diagnostics go on the host URI, labeled generated.

options.name: A `jet` member inside didOpen and didChange
options.detail:
The same modules, as parts, ride on the standard messages: didOpen and every didChange of a host carry a `jet: {modules}` member for that version. Host text and modules arrive in one message, so E1, E3 and E4 cannot happen, and no request ever waits.

The first draft listed four downsides. One is removed.

- "VS Code may pair the member with newer text" is gone. The member is added in `middleware.sendNotification`, which receives the didChange params. It builds the modules from the live document only when `document.version` equals `params.textDocument.version`; otherwise it sends no member.

Why that holds, and where it fails.
- Between the change event and that middleware there are only promise continuations, and VS Code delivers each edit as a separate event, so the two versions match. That is [INFERENCE] from client.ts 816-851 and textSynchronization.ts 267-282, not run in an editor. It fails during client startup: there `$start()` is a pending promise, so other tasks can run between the event and the send. B then sends no member and withdraws that version's results.

Three stay:
- "Each client wraps its transport" remains for Neovim (the `cmd` wrapper) and Emacs (advice on `jsonrpc-connection-send`). Under A, Neovim takes the same wrapper to be same-turn. VS Code needs only its documented middleware.
- "A re-encoding tool may drop the member" remains: a proxy that rebuilds typed params withdraws the host's results, visibly and never wrongly.
- "Zed and Helix cannot add it" remains, and E answers it, as under A.

E1, E3, E4: impossible. E2: the server keeps the host text, refuses the modules, logs and shows `Jet.HostRegionsRefused` as in A. E5, E6, E7: as in A. A didChange without `jet` withdraws the host's results, as zero modules do.

options.name: An unlisted `workspace/executeCommand` named `jet.hostDocument`
options.detail:
A's params go through the standard `workspace/executeCommand` request as `jet.hostDocument`. typescript-language-server pushes state this way with `_typescript.configurePlugin`.

The first draft listed three downsides. Two are removed.

- "No working precedent" is false now. The server answers `jet.impact` and `jet.reasoning` (Commands.jet 53-58), and an unknown command gets -32602.
- "Helix offers it in its picker" is gone. The command is not listed in `executeCommandProvider.commands`; it is advertised as `experimental.jetHostDocument: {version: 1, via: "executeCommand"}`. Helix builds its `:lsp-workspace-command` picker from that list (helix-term typed.rs 1696-1702).
- vscode-languageclient registers only listed commands (executeCommand.ts 75-78) but still sends an unlisted one through `client.sendRequest`.

One stays, at a small cost:
- "A round trip per version" remains. The server answers `null` right after validating, before it checks, so the reply is a few bytes. The client does not wait for it, because the ordering rule is A's.

Its one remaining edge over A: a refusal comes back to the sender as an error response, and Neovim's `client:exec_cmd` can show it. A closes most of that gap with the `Jet.HostRegionsRefused` diagnostic.

E1, E5, E6 and E7 are answered as in A, including the set-aside rule. E2, E3 and E4 are answered as error responses, with the same messages as A's logs.
options.technical:
No new method name. `arguments: [{textDocument, modules}]`, the shape of A's params. The command joins Commands.jet's dispatch, not its listed commands.

Costs left:
- A request used as a state push, with a reply per version that no one waits for.
- The same set-aside exception to CANCEL1 as A.
- CANCEL1 makes a queued request cancellable, so a client that cancels one loses that version's modules.
- No Zed or Helix support until E.

options.name: Virtual Jet documents, mapped by each client
options.detail:
The client opens each region, or each module, as its own `jet` document under a virtual URI. It translates every position and edit between host and virtual documents itself. This is the request-forwarding shape of the VS Code embedded-languages guide, and of otter.nvim's hidden buffers. The server sees only ordinary Jet documents.

Ruled out by D-EMBED-REGION1=A, which chose "the same checked maps" and "Jet validates UTF-8 boundaries and mappings" over host-owned mapping, its option B. The downside cannot be engineered away inside D. A fix would let the server hold the map, and that fix is A. E1 to E7 stay each client's own problem.
options.technical: No server change beyond the languageId gate. Every first-party client carries a mapping layer for every feature. A virtual URI must still name a package directory for imports to resolve.

options.name: The server runs the workspace's own region finder
options.detail:
The first draft's E had the server parse HTML and Markdown itself, which D-EMBED-REGION1=A rules out. This revision engineers that away. The host still identifies its regions, but in Jet, as code the server runs.

A package declares a finder for a languageId, a pure function from host text to A's modules. The server calls it on each host version and feeds the result into A's handler. Jet ships finders for `<script lang="jet">` and Markdown `jet` fences as an ordinary package, not as compiler code.

Its gain is the one the draft gave E. Every client works with no client code, Zed, Helix and eglot included. Zed can list HTML among a server's `languages` (Zed extension docs, `language_servers.*.languages`), and Helix runs several servers per language (`language-servers = [...]`).

Running workspace code adds no new trust: tip 22's server already runs a workspace marker's `check` while it checks, and published its rejection (probe: `host.Refused` from a `#Always` marker).

E1, E3 and E4 cannot happen, because the server computes the modules from the text it holds. E2 becomes a finder's bug, refused and shown as in A. E5 as in A. E6 is a host with no finder for its languageId. E7 is the finder's generated parts.
options.technical:
This needs its own ballot before it is built. Its cost is a new declaration surface. A sketch:

```jet
#HostFinder("html")
find_jet: fn(text: String) -> [HostModule] { … }
```

Further costs:
- An evaluator call per host version, cached by host text hash.
- The owner must rule that a shipped finder package is not "host-format parsing in the compiler".
- A finder runs in the server, so a slow one slows every request on that host. It needs the comptime budget.

options.name: Notebook sync, one cell per Jet module
options.detail:
The client syncs each host as an LSP 3.17 notebook. `notebookDocument/didOpen` and `didChange` carry the host as the notebook and each Jet module as a cell. It is standard and atomic. All cells' structure and text change in one message under one notebook version, and several cells fit Markdown's independent examples.

The notebook model itself causes these downsides. None can be engineered away.

- Cells are documents with their own URIs and results come back on cell URIs, so the client maps cells to host positions as in D.
- vscode-languageclient syncs notebooks from `vscode.workspace.notebookDocuments` only (notebook.ts 440-465), which a text editor never creates.
- Neovim 0.11 names the notebook methods in protocol.lua, but its client never syncs a notebook.

E1, E3 and E4 cannot happen. E2 moves into cell metadata, and E6 is any client without notebook sync.
options.technical: No new method. The server advertises `notebookDocumentSync` for a `notebookType` such as `jet-host`. Each cell's host position would ride in cell metadata, which is a mapping again, kept by the client.

comparisons.note: The standard's own answer for one document holding several code parts. Cell structure and text change in one versioned message, and results go to cell URIs. That is option F; A borrows its rule that one version covers all the parts.
comparisons.code:
// https://microsoft.github.io/language-server-protocol/specifications/lsp/3.17/specification/#notebookDocument_synchronization
notebookDocument/didChange { notebookDocument: { version }, change: { cells: { structure, data, textContent } } }

comparisons.note: Volar language plugins run inside the language server; @vue/language-server and @astrojs/language-server depend on @volar/language-server. A plugin finds the regions and builds `VirtualCode` whose mappings carry per-feature flags. One server-side layer maps every result. The host format's own server finds the regions, the E shape, and one map serves every feature, as in A.
svelte-language-server parses `.svelte` files itself and generates TSX with a source map. The host format's own server finds the regions: the E shape.

It describes two shapes: language services inside the server, and request forwarding to `embedded-content://` virtual documents that the client maps. Request forwarding is D. The guide warns that renaming and formatting across regions are hard, and that escaping such as `</` must be handled.
Quarto's Neovim helper keeps hidden buffers such as `index.md.tmp.py` with every non-code line blanked, so line numbers match the host. That is client-side mapping, the D shape.

Custom capabilities go under `experimental`, and custom methods take an `experimental/` or `rust-analyzer/` prefix. Client-to-server notifications such as `rust-analyzer/runFlycheck` exist. A follows that convention.

Client-to-server actions go through `workspace/executeCommand`, including state pushes such as `_typescript.configurePlugin`. Its leading `_` follows VS Code's habit of marking internal commands. That is the C shape.

A middleware's `didChange` runs synchronously inside the change event. Notifications and requests pass the same `$start()` await before they are written, so a notification sent right after `next(event)` precedes any later request. A's ordering rule rests on this.
`Client:request` flushes pending didChanges first, and `cmd` may be a function returning a wrapped RPC client. `LspNotify` fires through `vim.schedule`, one tick after the message.

decisions.title: How a Core declaration attaches a value computed while building, such as a route's contract, to each call
decisions.situation: Card #6851 c3 deletes HTTPRouting.jet (1,482 lines) and HTTP.jet (590 lines). Their checks move into Core marker rules under D-CORE-CHECK1=A. A rule can only refuse a call, and `expand` runs once per marked declaration. But the checker also changes each call. It rewrites `router.post(p, h)` into `router.__route(verb, p, wrapped, contract)`, where the contract is JSON computed while building. It wraps a typed or zero-argument handler in a synthesized `fn(HTTPRequest)` lambda. This ballot asks how a Core declaration attaches such a value to each call. D-RULE-BODYFACTS1 decides how the contract learns the handler's body, and D-RULE-WRITTEN1 decides how a rule sees an interpolated literal. The two files go only when all three leave sema, with the route table, the App route path, the form methods, middleware and the shared lookups.
decisions.gist: How does a Core declaration attach a value computed while building, such as a route's contract, to each call?
decisions.lesson: Languages take one of two paths. Some let a library compute an extra argument at each call: C++ default arguments with `source_location::current()`, and Zig comptime parameters. Others let it replace the call: Swift expression macros, C# interceptors and Rust macros. The first keeps the call's meaning. The second can do anything.
decisions.explainer: A post office clerk staples a receipt to each registered parcel. The rule book can describe the receipt each parcel gets (A). It can let the clerk swap the parcel for a different one (B). The compiler's own clerk can keep the job (C). Or the receipt can be written when the parcel arrives (D).
decisions.story: Ana's `router.post("/orders", place)` must register place's contract, so `web.openapi(router)` lists POST /orders with an `Order` body and its 202 and 400 responses. A package router, `kit.router`, wants the same for its own `route` method. Today only `core.http`'s router and `web.App` get contracts, because the compiler knows their method names. Under the recommended answer, Ana's program and her diagnostics stay the same.
decisions.detail:
The program this ballot and its two siblings use, written as today's tests write it (Tests/UI/http_route_invalid_literal.jet, Tests/Run/Net/BackendBattery/run.jet). `web.openapi` is fallible, so the print handles its error. Without `?? …` the program fails with Jet.MissingErrorConversion (probe p4).

```
use {
    http: core.http
    server: core.http.server
    web: core.web
}

Order: struct { item: String, quantity: Int }
Receipt: struct { order_id: Int }

place: fn(req: HTTPRequest) -> HTTPResponse HTTPError! {
    order: req.json<Order>() ?? return Ok(server.response(400, "bad order"))
    Ok(server.json(202, Receipt{order_id: order.quantity}))
}

run: fn() {
    router := http.router()
    id: "42"
    router.get("/users/{id}", place)   // line 18: E2805, brace interpolation
    router.post("/orders", place)      // contract: body Order; 202 Receipt, 400
    print(web.openapi(router) ?? "openapi failed")
}
```

What sema does with `router.post` today. `sema_call_try_http_router` (HTTPRouting.jet:1170) checks the path literal (:466), the pattern grammar and the handler's shape (:1247). It binds each handler input to a path field, a query parameter or the body, and checks Decode admissibility. It wraps a typed or zero-argument handler in a `fn(HTTPRequest)` lambda (`sema_http_mux_route_handler`, :1345, :1452-1482). It checks the callback's middleware and ownership.

It reads the handler's body (:859, :1020) and renders JSON schemas of the input, body and response types (:535-614). It builds the contract JSON (`sema_http_route_contract`, :1107-1168) and records the route for E2804 (:1416-1427). Finally it emits `router.__route(verb, path, wrapped, contract)` (:1391-1411). For `App`, the targets are `__http_route`, `__http_route_dynamic` and `__http_route_custom` (Core/Web/Web.jet:496-512). All four targets take `at: SourceLocation{#caller}`, and a run-time App pattern's contract is completed when it registers.

`web.form(M, action: a)` becomes `core.web.forms.input("M", fields)` and then `core.web.forms.typed(input, "a")` (HTTP.jet:397-434). Its value depends only on the model type and the action's name. A `#Web.Form` marker's `expand` can emit the fields once per model type (D-META-LADDER1's second step). So web.form needs no per-call value under any option here.

Precedents in Jet, probed on the batch 20 compiler. A plain default may read an earlier parameter, and it is computed per call (`loud: String{shout(path)}`, probe p3b). `at: SourceLocation{#caller}` is computed per call, and a wrapper forwards it by declaring the same default (D-SITE-CALLER1). `#Pre(#run …)` is ratified to decide its predicate per call with the call's argument facts (D-JAI-GENERIC1, D-PRE-COMPILE1).

Today `#Pre(#run …)` does that only for a literal argument. A module constant or a forwarded parameter is Jet.CompileTimeReadsRuntimeValue, reported at the declaration rather than the call (p2b, p2c, p2g). D-PRE-COMPILE1 counts a constant as known. `#run` inside a larger value, a parameter default included, is Jet.UnsupportedCompileTimeValue (p1, p3). `.reflect()` on a function-typed parameter is Jet.UnknownMethod (p2). D-CORE-CHECK1's implementation decision M3 moves `#Pre` onto a check rule with a per-call self; it has not landed.

Ratified limits. D-META-LADDER1=A says Jet has no macros, and no call-site expansion is registered. D-META-RECONCILE1=A says written code means what its file says, and in standard code no rewrite happens. D-JAI-CODE1, as narrowed by D-META-COMPILER1=A, removed `#Expand` and `name!()`. A call-site rewrite in standard code needs those decisions reopened.

What the contract needs. The handler's parameters and types, which a heard argument's FunctionInfo carries once c30 lands, but only for a bare named function. A lambda, `mod.f` or a method value stays None (p8), although D-CORE-CHECK1=A promises a FunctionInfo for 'a function or lambda argument'. Nested type schemas need TypeId reflection (D-RULE-TYPEARGS1, c26). The body facts are D-RULE-BODYFACTS1's. The path, method and source line are in the route table when the route registers.

Sites that go under A, B or D: the lowering (:1391-1411), the handler wrap (:1345, :1452-1482) and the contract builder (:1107-1168) with its schema rendering (:535-614). So do the handler-shape and input-binding E2805s (:1170-1340) and HTTP.jet's `web.form` lowering (:274-437). Sites no option here moves: the E2804 route table (:1416-1427, Methods.jet:1506), which needs state across calls, and the App `route`/`page`/`layout` path (Methods.jet:1954-2035). HTTPMount.jet mounts structs only; it has no router variants.

c3 deletes all of HTTP.jet, not only `web.form`. `app.middleware(mw)` is lowered to `__http_middleware` (HTTP.jet:149-176, Methods.jet:1963) after a capture-crossing check that reads sema's ownership facts (:117-147). Under A it becomes an ordinary Core method, but the crossing check needs a declared crossing that no ballot here provides. `sema_call_http_mux_source_call` (:185-213) emits every lowered call and goes with the lowering.

The typed form's methods (:439-590) rename `form.validate(…)` and others to `core.web.forms.typed_*` members. They also lower a leading-dot selector `.email` to the String "email". The renames become ordinary Core methods, but the selector needs a per-model field type, which no ballot here settles. `server.json`'s E2411 admission (:74-93) waits on D-RULE-TYPEARGS1.

options.name: A per-call parameter, computed while building from the handler
options.detail:
A parameter's default may be `#run` over earlier parameters. At each call, the build evaluates it with those parameters bound to the call's argument facts, as `#Pre(#run …)` is ratified to work (D-JAI-GENERIC1). The route's default reads only the handler, so a run-time path, such as an App's dynamic route, needs nothing more.

The route table completes the path half of the contract when the route registers: canonical path, path or query placement, operation id, and provenance from `at`. `route_add_dynamic` already does this for App. The check rule hears both the path and the handler, so it keeps the input-binding E2805s for a static path while building. A handler that is neither a named function nor a lambda is refused at the call, as today (:1247).

A call may write the parameter only by forwarding its own caller's parameter that has the same default, as a `#caller` default is forwarded (D-SITE-CALLER1). Any other written value is refused, so a contract cannot be forged. `router.post("/orders", place)` stays a call of `post`, and `kit.router` declares and forwards the same parameter.
options.technical:
New: `#run` inside a parameter default, reading earlier parameters, decided per call with the call's facts. Today only `#Pre(#run …)` reaches that, and only for literals (p2b, p3). Spellings.jet's `#Pre(#run {{ … }}, "…")` row lists where `#run` around an expression is decided per call. It gains the parameter default (I7). It is the same `#run` meaning, so no spelling is added (I9). Also new: the forwarding rule and its refusal code.

Gates before A can land, each owned by card #6851. First, lambda and qualified-name handlers heard as FunctionInfo, as D-CORE-CHECK1=A states (c30; p8 shows None today). Second, `.reflect()` on a function-typed parameter (p2). Third, nested type schemas through TypeId (D-RULE-TYPEARGS1, c26). Fourth, the body facts D-RULE-BODYFACTS1 settles. Fifth, the handler adaptation below.

Sixth, the capture check every handler gets today (HTTPRouting.jet:1348, HTTP.jet:117-147). It refuses a lambda handler that captures state which cannot cross to request workers. No Core parameter can yet declare that crossing, which D-CONC-CROSS1=A's one prover checks. The same gap holds under B and D.

A default that cannot be computed reports at the call with the default's error type, so E2805 'no complete checked endpoint contract' keeps its text. Today a forwarded value is reported at the declaration instead (p2c), which M3 must fix. Hover and `jet inspect` must show the computed argument.

Costs. One comptime-child evaluation per distinct handler, cached by handler identity, not one per call. Rule dispatch costs about 46.5 µs per heard call today, against c22's 1 µs budget. Each reflect is a 43 to 229 µs host round trip (D-RULE-TYPEARGS1 review). So a handler with three nested types costs about 0.2 to 0.7 ms until c22 is met.

A does not remove the handler adaptation. Jet has no overloading (p11), so no Core spelling takes `fn()`, `fn(Int)` and `fn(Int, HTTPRequest)` under one name. A generic adapter needs one impl per input type (p10). Until D-RULE-TYPEARGS1's typed handler params land, sema keeps `sema_http_mux_route_handler` (about 30 lines) behind a declared role. The cross-call E2804 table also stays in sema.

options.name: A rule may replace its call
options.detail: A check rule may end by replacing the call it heard with a call of another function or method of the marking module. The new call passes the original arguments by position, plus values the rule computed. Sema checks the replacement as an ordinary call. `router.post("/orders", place)` becomes `router.__route("POST", "/orders", place, contract)`, one to one with today's lowering.
options.technical:
New: a `replace` result on CompilerCall, such as `call.replace(with: "__route", args: [...])`. Each arg is `.Arg(index)` or `.Value(dyn)`. The target must be declared by the module that declares the marker; without that limit, the rule could call anything. The replacement keeps the call's span. A failed check of the replacement reports at the call, with a note naming the rule. Two rules replacing one call is an error.

Ratified limits. D-META-LADDER1=A says 'no call-site expansion is registered'. D-META-RECONCILE1=A says that in standard code 'no rewrite happens'. B needs both reopened. B also cannot produce today's handler wrap: a replacement argument is an original argument or a computed value, never a synthesized lambda.

Costs. A call no longer means its callee. Go to definition, hover, `jet inspect`, coverage and stack traces must each say which rule replaced what. And this is a general rewrite power, which D-CORE-CHECK1 left out: rules hear and refuse.

options.name: Keep the lowering in sema, reached through declared roles
options.detail: Sema keeps computing the contract and lowering the call, as today. Core declares the targets as roles, for example `#Builtin.Role(.RouteRegister) __route`, so CoreReach.jet names no helper. Rules validate; sema lowers. This is the strongest form of keeping the checker.
options.technical:
The case at its strongest. The lowering already passes every route and form snapshot and every run test, with no new language surface. It runs in process, with no comptime-child round trip and no 46.5 µs per heard call. The contract is built from the handler's AST and sema's type tables, so D-RULE-BODYFACTS1 is moot for this route. The handler wrap stays where it is. Every tool already understands the call.

A library lowering is a bounded list the compiler owns, as Go's encoding/json special-cases `[]byte`. Costs: c3's criterion to delete HTTPRouting.jet (1,482 lines) and HTTP.jet (590 lines) is not met. The static-path rules still move. A package router cannot get contracts, so c7 (a user package gets the same checks) is not met for routes. Core keeps a privilege a package lacks.
options.code:
// Core/HTTP/Router.jet under C: a role, no new language form
#Builtin.Role(.RouteRegister) __route: fn(&self, method: String, path: String, handler: fn(HTTPRequest) -> HTTPResponse HTTPError!, contract: String) { … }

options.name: Compute the contract at run time; the rule only refuses
options.detail: The check rule refuses bad paths and handlers while building. `post` builds its contract at run time from the handler's retained reflection when it registers. No value crosses from build time to the call.
options.technical:
Needs the handler's FunctionInfo and its body facts retained in the binary for every route handler. Today they exist only while building. 'Complete contract' failures move from build errors to run-time panics, unless the rule also computes the contract while building. Then the work is done twice, once in the comptime child and once in the program.

The binary also grows by the retained facts. Only the path half is free at run time: the table already completes a run-time App pattern's contract when it registers.

comparisons.note: A default argument such as `std::source_location::current()` is evaluated at each call site, not at the declaration (C++20, [support.srcloc]). That is A's shape: the callee states what each call gets.
comparisons.code: void post(std::string_view path, Handler h, std::source_location at = std::source_location::current());

comparisons.note: Expression macros (SE-0382) replace the macro use with code the macro writes. The use is spelled `#name`, so a reader sees that it is rewritten. B's plain-looking call has no such mark.

C# 12 interceptors, shipped as an experimental feature (dotnet/roslyn docs/features/interceptors.md), let a source generator redirect one call site to another method. A reader of the call cannot see the redirect, which is B's cost.
comparisons.code:
[InterceptsLocation("Program.cs", line: 19, character: 12)]
static void Post(this Router r, string p, Handler h) { … }

recommendation.why: A keeps every call meaning its callee, which D-META-LADDER1=A and D-META-RECONCILE1=A require of standard code. It extends the per-call evaluation Jet already ratified for `#Pre(#run …)` and `#caller`. It gives a package router exactly what Core's router has. Because the default reads only the handler, run-time App paths keep working.
gains: HTTPRouting.jet's lowering and contract builder leave sema; `post` is an ordinary Core function.
A package router declares and forwards the same parameter.
No call is replaced, so tools need no rewrite tracking.
web.form needs no new form: its fields come once per model type from `#Web.Form`'s expand.

losses.loss: One new parameter form: a `#run` default over earlier parameters, which a call may write only by forwarding.
losses.mitigation: Plain defaults over earlier parameters and `#caller` forwarding already exist (p3b). Only `#run` in that place is new, and M3's per-call `#Pre` evaluation needs the same evaluator anyway.

losses.loss: Build cost: one comptime evaluation per distinct handler plus its reflects, about 0.2 to 0.7 ms per handler until c22's 1 µs dispatch budget is met.
losses.mitigation: Cached by handler identity, so a handler used on ten routes is computed once. c22 and the reflect cost are on card #6851, and A does not land before c22's measurement passes.

losses.loss: A cannot land before six gates: lambda FunctionInfo (c30), `.reflect()` on a function parameter, nested schemas through TypeId (c26), D-RULE-BODYFACTS1's body facts, the handler adaptation and a declared handler crossing.
losses.mitigation: Each gate is on card #6851. Until all hold, today's lowering stays and no program changes. The vote fixes the direction, not the landing date.

losses.loss: Typed and zero-argument handlers need an adaptation Core cannot spell yet. At least 17 test and example files pass typed lambdas and 32 pass `fn()`; Jet has no overloading (p11).
losses.mitigation: Sema keeps `sema_http_mux_route_handler` behind a declared role until D-RULE-TYPEARGS1's typed handler params replace it. No handler is rewritten.

losses.loss: E2804 across calls still needs the per-binding route table in sema.
losses.mitigation: The table also serves App pages, convention files and marked methods, so it moves with that mechanism on card #6851, not with this ballot. The run-time table already refuses a duplicate when a route registers.

whyNot.reason: A call-site rewrite in standard code, which D-META-LADDER1=A and D-META-RECONCILE1=A rule out. It needs both reopened, and every tool must track it.
About 2,000 lines stay in sema, Core keeps a privilege no package has, and c7 fails for routes.
Retains handler facts in every binary and turns build errors into run-time failures, or computes the contract twice.

recommendation.tradeoff: One new per-call parameter form with six landing gates, for no call rewriting and no Core privilege.

decisions.hybrid: This ballot is one of three for card #6851 c3. D-RULE-BODYFACTS1 decides how the contract learns a handler's body, and D-RULE-WRITTEN1 decides how a rule sees an interpolated literal. A plausible mixed answer is A here with C on D-RULE-BODYFACTS1: Core computes the contract per call from facts sema hands over. HTTPRouting.jet then keeps the body walk, about 370 lines, until it moves too.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude Opus. Adversarial model family: Claude Opus. Fresh agent: RewriteReview. The adversarial review attacked the recommendation. decisions.title: How a Core rule learns what a handler's body reads and returns
decisions.situation: A route's contract names its request body type and its responses. Today sema finds them by walking the handler's AST, not its checked tree. It looks for `json<T>()` on a receiver named as a request parameter (HTTPRouting.jet:928-1025). It reads the return paths whose value is a call named `response`, `json` or `empty_response`, following local aliases (:656-926). It matches the last name segment, not the callee's symbol, and drops other paths silently (probe p5). A router route is E2805 only when no path is recognized (:1165, :1387; p6). An App route is never refused, and its `web.openapi` then fails at run time (p7). FunctionInfo carries no fact about the calls a function makes. This ballot decides how a Core rule learns them, for the contract D-RULE-REWRITE1 attaches to each call.
decisions.gist: How does a Core rule learn what a handler's body reads and returns?
decisions.lesson: Web frameworks get a handler's contract from its signature (FastAPI's annotations, Axum's extractors, ASP.NET's typed results) or from its body (Jet today). Signature contracts need no body access. Body contracts need a compiler that shares what it saw.
decisions.explainer: To write the receipt, the clerk must know what is in the letter. The sender may list it on the envelope (B). The post office may mark the forms it cares about, so the clerk hears whenever a letter uses one (A). The compiler's clerk may keep reading letters and pass on a note (C). Or the clerk may open every letter (D).
decisions.story: Ana's `place` reads `req.json<Order>()` and returns `server.json(202, Receipt{…})` or `server.response(400, …)`. Her OpenAPI document must say exactly that. Today a 404 she returns through a helper is silently left out of it (p5).
decisions.detail:
The program is the one in D-RULE-REWRITE1's detail. What the contract reads today, exactly. The type argument of the first `json<T>()` call on a request parameter, anywhere in the body. For each recognized return path, the response call's status and its value's type, which the walk guesses from the syntax (:740-772), or its text. A path that ends in anything else is left out of the contract, and the build succeeds.

Probe p5 on batch 20: a 404 returned through a helper, a 400 returned through a helper and a body decoded in a helper are all missing from the OpenAPI document. A router route with no recognized path gets E2805 'HTTP route handler has no complete checked endpoint contract' (p6). Its Fix text asks for a typed `HTTPResponse` constructor on every handler path, but the rule needs only one.

An App route is never refused (p7). Its `web.openapi` then fails at run time with 'checked OpenAPI route contract has no responses' (Core/Web/Web.jet:4302).

What already exists. FunctionInfo has two body-derived facts, `reaches_panic` and `arithmetic: [ArithmeticOperationInfo]` (CoreRecordRows.jet:477-478). CompilerCall carries caller, callee, module, span, name, args and receiver (:250-256), but no type arguments. Sema publishes each checked body as a flat BodyTree (JetFoundation Facts/Body.jet).

D-JAI-CODE1, narrowed but still ratified, keeps `c.nodes()` over a `Code` value. It is 'a typed, read-only tree with kinds, children, locations and, after checking, types'. `meta.rewrite_body` already names a heard function's body as `#{f.body}`. `c.nodes()` has no row in Spellings.jet, so it is not built.

Sites that go if body facts leave sema: HTTPRouting.jet `sema_http_route_find_json_*` (:928-1025) and `sema_http_route_response_*` (:656-926), about 370 lines.

options.name: Recorded calls: calls of a marked callee are listed in their caller's FunctionInfo
options.detail:
Core marks the calls it cares about: `#Recorded` on `HTTPRequest.json`, `server.json`, `server.response` and `server.empty_response`. For each function, the build lists that function's calls of recorded callees in its FunctionInfo. Each is the `CompilerCall` value a check rule already hears: callee, name, arguments with their types and known values, and span.

A second list holds the recorded calls whose value a return path returns, following local aliases. The route contract reads `handler.recorded` and `handler.returns`. Ana's `place` is unchanged.
options.technical:
New: a `#Recorded` Prelude marker, registered in the syntax registry beside `#Pre` (I7). Two FunctionInfo fields, `recorded: [CompilerCall]` and `returns: [CompilerCall]`. One CompilerCall field, `type_args: [TypeId]`, since a call's explicit type arguments reach no field today. D-RULE-TYPEARGS1 covers a type's arguments, not a call's. Every heard call gets `type_args` too, empty for most calls.

No new record. A recorded call keeps the shape rules already hear, so no `RecordedCall` duplicates CompilerCall (I8). The fields follow `reaches_panic` and `arithmetic`: sema digests the checked body and Core reads the digest. It is a fact list, not a second tree view beside `c.nodes()`.

Sema fills both lists from the checked body and matches callees by symbol (`CompilerCall.callee`), so a user function named `json` no longer counts. Only the module that declares a callee can mark it. Behavior is kept: the rule rejects only when `returns` is empty on a router (today's :1165). Cost: one list per function that calls a recorded callee, filled during the walk sema already does. Only marked calls cross to the comptime child.

The alias and return-path search stays in sema. It becomes a generic digest that serves any marked callee, and the HTTP names leave. Gates: a lambda handler needs c30 to deliver the FunctionInfo D-CORE-CHECK1=A states (p8). A type argument's own arguments keep their identity only through D-RULE-TYPEARGS1 (c26). Gaps kept from today: a `json<T>()` call or a response made inside a helper is not seen (p5).

options.name: The handler's signature states its contract
options.detail: Typed handlers: the request body is a parameter and the responses are the return type. The contract reads `handler.signature` alone, which c30 provides for a named function once it lands. No body facts at all. Ana's `place` changes.
options.technical: New: parameter and return types the router recognizes, such as `Json<T>` and a response union, plus the router's adaptation from `HTTPRequest`. That adaptation is typed handler params, which wait on D-RULE-TYPEARGS1. Every handler in Tests and Examples that the contract walk reads today is rewritten. The 400 path becomes a response case and is no longer an early return. This is the FastAPI and Axum model, and it is the only option where the contract is visible at the declaration.

options.name: Keep the body walk in sema, handing Core the result
options.detail: Sema keeps reading handler bodies and hands Core the result as a fact on the heard argument, `CompilerArg.route: RouteFacts?`. It could also hand over the finished contract text. Rules and Core functions consume it. This is the strongest form of keeping the checker.
options.technical:
The case at its strongest. Exposing any part of a body to libraries turns compiler internals into language surface. Rust gives procedural macros only tokens and Swift gives macros only syntax. The walk is about 370 tested lines, and the contract is an HTTP notion, so a general mechanism serves one client.

Costs: HTTPRouting.jet's body walk stays, so the file is not deleted. The walk reads the AST and guesses local types from syntax (:740-772), so it keeps matching callees by name. The fact is HTTP-specific, so a package framework gets contracts only for `HTTPRequest.json` and Core's response helpers. And CompilerArg gains a domain field.

options.name: A general query over the checked body
options.detail: FunctionInfo gains `body: Code`, the heard function's checked body as the `Code` value D-JAI-CODE1 already defines and `#{f.body}` already names. The contract walks `handler.body.nodes()`, the typed read-only tree D-JAI-CODE1 keeps, for `json<T>()` calls and return paths.
options.technical:
The most general option, and the only one whose view is already ratified: D-JAI-CODE1's `c.nodes()` gives kinds, children, locations and types. D adds one field. Costs: `c.nodes()` is not built (no Spellings.jet row). Every heard handler's whole body crosses to the comptime child, at a 43 to 229 µs host round trip plus its size.

The rule re-implements alias following and return-path search, so about 370 lines move from sema into Core rather than going away. And a rule could depend on how a body is written, such as an alias or a helper call. Refactoring a handler could then change its contract in ways its signature does not show, as today.
options.code:
// PROPOSED
loop node in handler.body.nodes() { if node.kind == .MethodCall && node.name == "json" { … } }

comparisons.note: The handler's annotations are the contract; FastAPI reads them at startup and never reads the body (fastapi.tiangolo.com, 'Request Body' and 'Response Model').
Extractors in the signature say what the request yields; the return type says what is sent. OpenAPI crates such as utoipa add attributes on the handler (`#[utoipa::path(responses(...))]`).

Minimal APIs read `TypedResults` return types, such as `Results<Accepted<T>, BadRequest>`, for OpenAPI metadata. A handler returning a plain `IResult` gets none, as a Jet helper response gets none today.

recommendation.why: A keeps Ana's program as it is. It lets Core, and any package, declare exactly which calls it needs to hear about, and it exposes no other body detail. It follows the digest shape FunctionInfo already uses for `arithmetic`, and it reuses CompilerCall. D's tree view stays the general tool once it is built.
gains: The HTTP-only walk leaves sema; a generic digest replaces it.
A package framework marks its own request and response calls.
Callees match by symbol, not by name, and only marked calls become visible.

losses.loss: A new Prelude marker, two FunctionInfo fields and `CompilerCall.type_args`.
losses.mitigation: The FunctionInfo fields reuse CompilerCall, so no record is added, and follow `arithmetic`'s precedent. The marker is registered like `#Pre`. `type_args` is empty for calls with no type arguments, and any rule that checks a generic call needs it anyway.

losses.loss: A body type or a response made inside a helper is still not seen.
losses.mitigation: No worse than today (p5). A signature contract (B) stays open as a later addition, and `returns` could later follow a callee's own `returns` with no new surface.

losses.loss: Lambda handlers need a FunctionInfo for lambdas.
losses.mitigation: D-CORE-CHECK1=A already promises one; card #6851 c30 owns delivering it.

whyNot.reason: It rewrites every existing handler and waits on D-RULE-TYPEARGS1's typed handler params.
The body walk and an HTTP-only field stay in the compiler.
Its view is ratified but unbuilt, ships whole bodies to the comptime child, and moves the walk into Core instead of removing it.

recommendation.tradeoff: A marker, two FunctionInfo fields and one CompilerCall field, for unchanged handlers and no body API.

decisions.hybrid: This ballot is one of three for card #6851 c3. D-RULE-REWRITE1 decides how the contract reaches each call, and its option A reads these facts as a gate. A plausible mixed answer is C here with A on D-RULE-REWRITE1: sema keeps the walk and hands Core the result. HTTPRouting.jet then keeps about 370 lines.

decisions.title: Which field tells a check rule that an argument is an interpolated String literal, and what the rule can print from it
decisions.situation: A heard argument's `value` is the value the build knows, or None. `"/users/{id}"` interpolates a run-time `id`, so it is heard as None, like any String known only at run time (probe p1). Sema tells them apart by reading the AST (`sema_http_route_interpolated_source`, HTTPRouting.jet:430). So the snapshot `http_route_invalid_literal` reports 'Invalid HTTP route `/users/{id}`: brace interpolation is not allowed in route patterns'. Card #6851 c34 asks for this fact through D-CORE-CHECK1's CompilerCall surface, or a ballot. This is that ballot. It is independent of D-RULE-REWRITE1 and D-RULE-BODYFACTS1, but HTTPRouting.jet is deleted only when all three move their checks out of sema.
decisions.gist: Which field on CompilerArg tells a rule that an argument is an interpolated literal, and what can the rule print from it?
decisions.lesson: Checkers that refuse a format usually read the literal as written: Go vet's printf check, Roslyn analyzers over interpolated strings, Swift macros over string segments. A checker that sees only values cannot tell 'written with holes' from 'unknown'.
decisions.explainer: The clerk needs to know whether an address was handwritten with blanks to fill in, or is simply missing. Telling the clerk 'it had blanks' (B) lets him refuse it. Showing him the address as written, blanks marked (A), lets him quote it back in the refusal. Handing him a photocopy of the envelope (E) makes him read the handwriting himself.
decisions.story: Ana writes `router.get("/users/{id}", place)` meaning a route parameter. The error must quote her pattern, `/users/{id}`, and say braces are interpolation.
decisions.detail:
The program is the one in D-RULE-REWRITE1's detail; line 18 is Ana's. What E2805 needs, exactly. (1) That the argument is a String literal with at least one hole. (2) The literal rendered with each hole as `{name}` when the hole is a bare name, and `{…}` otherwise (probe p9). This is `sema_http_route_interpolated_source`'s rendering. (3) The argument's span, which CompilerArg already has.

A `#run "/teams/{{name}}"` value reaches the rule through `value` only when bound first, as `TEAM: #run …` or a local (p1, p1b). Written directly as the argument, batch 20 refuses it with Jet.UnsupportedCompileTimeValue before any rule runs.

I4 (card #6851) requires every remaining code to keep its UI snapshot. An option that cannot print (2) changes `http_route_invalid_literal` unless a separate decision changes its wording.

Callers of today's literal check, which would read the same field: router and mux registrations (HTTPRouting.jet:1189, :1202) and App `route`, `page` and `layout` (Methods.jet:1979). `app.mount`'s prefix (HTTPMount.jet:577) reads a constant string. Webhook paths and cron lines are marker arguments, which CompilerArg does not reach. Later SQL and format-string rules could read the field too.

options.name: `written: [CompilerWrittenPart]?`, an interpolated literal's parts
options.detail: CompilerArg gains `written`: when the argument is a String literal with at least one hole, its parts as written, text segments and holes. Otherwise it is None. A hole carries its name when it is a bare name, and its span. E2805 renders `/users/{id}` itself and keeps its snapshot exactly.
options.technical:
New: one Prelude enum, `CompilerWrittenPart: enum { Text(text: String), Hole(name: String?, span: SourceSpan) }`, and the field `written: [CompilerWrittenPart]?`. There is no wrapper struct. Sema fills it in `sema_rule_call_arg` (CheckRules.jet:268) from the argument's expression, only for an interpolated literal. Every other argument gets None, so a plain literal, a constant or a run-time value costs nothing. `sema_rule_call_arg` does not take the expression today; A adds that parameter at its callers.

Filling it only when there is a hole drops the draft's second use, telling a plain literal from a constant. No current check needs that. It would also let a rule refuse a spelling while accepting the same value written as a constant.

E2805: `written != None` is (1), and the parts joined with `{name}` or `{…}` are (2). It is exact. If Jet ever folds an interpolation over constant locals into a known `value` such as "/users/42", `written` still marks the argument, so the rule keeps refusing it.

options.name: `interpolated: Bool`
options.detail: CompilerArg gains `interpolated: Bool`, true when the argument is a String literal with at least one hole. The rule can refuse it, but cannot quote the pattern.
options.technical: The smallest field. For E2805 it gives (1) but not (2). The rule can say 'brace interpolation is not allowed in route patterns', but not 'Invalid HTTP route `/users/{id}`'. CompilerCall offers no way to read source text by span. So `http_route_invalid_literal`'s snapshot changes (I4 fails) unless its wording changes, for example to 'Invalid HTTP route: brace interpolation is not allowed in route patterns'. That wording change needs its own decision.
options.code:
// PROPOSED
if path.interpolated -> reject(InvalidRoute{pattern: "", reason: "brace interpolation is not allowed in route patterns"}, at: path)

options.name: `literal: CompilerLiteral?`, a literal-kind enum
options.detail: CompilerArg gains `literal`, the argument's literal kind: `.Plain`, `.Interpolated(pattern: String)`, `.Constant(name: String)` or `.Computed`. It is None when the argument is not a literal or a constant. `.Interpolated` carries the rendered pattern, so E2805 is exact.
options.technical: With `.Interpolated(pattern)`, E2805 gets (1) and (2). Without that payload, C is B. The compiler owns the rendering (`{name}` / `{…}`), so every rule quotes holes the same way and none can quote differently. `.Constant(name)` lets E2805 and E2808 name a constant in their text, which no current snapshot needs. Cost: a five-case enum whose cases mix syntax (interpolated) and provenance (constant).
options.code:
// PROPOSED
if path.literal == .Val(.Interpolated(pattern)) -> reject(InvalidRoute{pattern: pattern, reason: "brace interpolation is not allowed in route patterns"}, at: path)

options.name: Keep the interpolation check in sema
options.detail: Sema keeps `sema_http_route_check_literal`'s interpolation branch and reports it before any rule runs. The Core rule handles every other path problem. CompilerArg is unchanged.
options.technical:
The case at its strongest. Rules today hear values, not syntax, and a value check gives the same answer when `"/users/{id}"` is moved into a local. A syntax field invites rules that refuse a spelling and accept the same value written another way. D-CORE-CHECK1's text does not state this as a rule; it lists CompilerArg's fields, with no syntax field.

The check is about 20 lines and already exact. It covers router, mux and App paths with one function (HTTPRouting.jet:1189, :1202; Methods.jet:1979). Costs: HTTPRouting.jet is not deleted, since the literal check and its helper stay, so c3 is not met. The check is keyed to Core's route methods, so a package router cannot give the same message (c7).

options.name: `text: String`, the argument's source text
options.detail: CompilerArg gains `text`, the argument exactly as written in the source, for every argument. The rule looks for an unescaped `{` in a literal's text and quotes it.
options.technical:
The C# 10 `[CallerArgumentExpression]` and Rust `stringify!` shape: the source text of an argument. It is the most general field, and other rules could quote any argument. Costs: the rule must parse Jet's string syntax itself, including `{{` escapes, raw strings and multi-line literals, so the lexer's rules are duplicated in Core.

It quotes a non-bare hole in full (`/u/{id.len()}`), not as `{…}`, so the snapshot holds only for bare holes and p9's `/u/{…}` changes. Every heard argument carries a string, so a call heard 1,000 times copies 1,000 texts to the comptime child. And text is a spelling, not a meaning, so rules can depend on formatting.
options.code:
// PROPOSED
if path.text.starts_with("\"") && has_unescaped_brace(path.text) -> reject(InvalidRoute{pattern: unquote(path.text), …}, at: path)

comparisons.note: The printf analyzer checks a format string only when it is a literal or constant. Since Go 1.24, a call whose only argument is a computed format gets a separate 'non-constant format string' finding. So the analyzer tells 'as written' from 'unknown'.
comparisons.code:
fmt.Printf("%d", s) // vet: wrong type for %d
fmt.Printf(f)       // vet (Go 1.24+): non-constant format string

comparisons.note: An analyzer sees an interpolated string's `Contents`: text parts and interpolations, each with its expression and span (InterpolatedStringExpressionSyntax). That is A's shape.
comparisons.code: foreach (var part in node.Contents) { if (part is InterpolationSyntax hole) … }

comparisons.note: A macro sees `StringLiteralExprSyntax.segments`, string and expression segments (swift-syntax). A macro that refuses interpolation tests for an expression segment and quotes the literal.
comparisons.code: for segment in literal.segments { if case .expressionSegment = segment { … } }

comparisons.note: A parameter marked `[CallerArgumentExpression("value")]` receives another argument's source text as a string. That is E's shape, and the callee must parse the text itself.
comparisons.code: static void Check(bool value, [CallerArgumentExpression("value")] string? text = null)

recommendation.why: Only A and C keep E2805's snapshot exactly. A gives the rule the literal's parts and leaves the rendering to Core, as Roslyn and Swift macros do. Filled only for an interpolated literal, it adds no cost to other arguments and exposes no other spelling. C fixes one rendering in the compiler and mixes syntax with provenance. E duplicates the lexer in Core and misquotes non-bare holes.
gains: E2805's 'brace interpolation' snapshot holds exactly, so HTTPRouting.jet's literal check can go.
Router, mux, App and package routers use the same field.
If constant interpolations are ever folded into values, the rule still refuses them.

losses.loss: Rules can see that a String argument is an interpolated literal, and its parts.
losses.mitigation: Only interpolated literals are visible, never a local's initializer, a constant or a plain literal. Moving the literal into a local gives `written: None`, as today's sema check does.

losses.loss: One new Prelude enum and one CompilerArg field.
losses.mitigation: It is filled only for interpolated literals, from the expression sema already holds; every other argument gets None at no cost.

whyNot.reason: It cannot quote the pattern, so the snapshot changes without a wording decision.
It is exact only with a payload, and then it is A with the rendering fixed in the compiler.
A route check stays in sema, c3 is not met, and package routers cannot give the message.
Core must re-parse Jet's string syntax, a non-bare hole is quoted in full, and every argument carries its text.

recommendation.tradeoff: One enum that exposes an interpolated literal's parts, for an exact snapshot and no route code in sema.
