decisions.title: How a library's build-time check compares one call with the calls made before it, and points at both
decisions.situation: A route table is the list a web server keeps of which address goes to which handler. If you add the same address twice, for example `GET /users/:id` and then `GET /users/:login`, the second one can never answer. Today the compiler itself catches this while building and shows two places: the second registration as the error, and the first marked 'first registered here'. That check lives inside the compiler because a library's build-time check (a call rule) sees one call at a time and points at one place. So a package router cannot give the same error. You are asked how a call rule can relate a call to the earlier calls on the same table, and how its error can point at a second place. We recommend that a rule names the key of the row each call adds, the compiler pairs equal keys on one table, and `reject` may mark one more place with a label.
decisions.gist: How does a call rule relate a call to earlier calls on the same table, and point at both?
decisions.lesson: Linters that find duplicates name both sites. Roslyn analyzers report with extra locations, Go analyzers with related positions, and rustc labels the earlier span 'previous definition here'. Most keep a map while they walk the code, so finding a duplicate costs one lookup per call. A checker that sees one call at a time and one span cannot say 'this clashes with that'.
decisions.explainer:
Picture a clerk who stamps registration forms one at a time and forgets each form once it is stamped. So two forms for the same address both get through, and only the head office (the compiler) notices.

Option A has the clerk write one label on each form, such as 'GET /users/:'. The office files the forms by table and label, and hands the clerk the older form whenever a label repeats. Option B hands the clerk every older form for that table each time. Option C makes him read the whole pile at once. Option D gives him a notebook he keeps himself. Option E stops checking at the counter, and the office fails when it opens. Option F leaves the job with the head office.
decisions.story: Ana writes a small API. She registers `router.get("/users/:id", show_user)` and, ten lines later, `router.get("/users/:login", find_user)`. Both match `/users/anything`, so the second can never answer. She should see the error at the second call while building, with the first call underlined as 'first registered here'. Ben writes his own router package and wants the same error for his users, through the same rule mechanism Core uses.
decisions.detail:
What E2804 needs, per its six UI snapshots (listed in checkInstructions).

(1) Two registrations on one table: the same binding, the same builder chain, or the App's convention files and marked methods. (2) The same method and route shape (`:id` and `:login` are one shape), known while building. (3) The error at the later registration and a labeled second span at the earlier. The labels are 'first registered here' on a binding, and 'the other registration, by `builder`', '… `/x/:id` by `builder`' or '… by `dir/file.jet`' on a chain. The what line names the convention file a row comes from.

Where route rows and their pairing live today. `sema_http_route_table_record` (HTTPRouting.jet:1416-1427) keys a table by the receiver's root binding, method and shape. Its store is `SemaHTTPRouteIndex` in the check context (Scopes.jet:891, 1780-1791, 1809, 1957, 2052, 2177). `sema_app_check_route_registrations` and its helpers (Methods.jet:1501-1598, 1669-1683, 1689-1693) pair the rows of one App builder chain. `app.mount(value)` sends each marked method through the router path at its marker (HTTPMount.jet:747).

Run time checks again: `mux_register` (Core/HTTP/Server.jet:368-377) stops with E2804 and the other row's file and line. `jet explain --routes` builds its own list of rows (JetCLI WebGraph.jet:689-923) but pairs nothing. The E2804 text has three copies: Prelude's `AmbiguousRoute` (Diagnostics.jet:23257, no file variant), sema's `sema_http_route_duplicate` (HTTPRouting.jet:458) and Server.jet:372.

Today's pairing is wrong in four ways (probes p1, p2 and p4, on tip 21). It refuses a valid program three ways. Two exclusive `if` arms pair, as do two different routers in one struct (`pair.api`, `pair.admin`) and a binding reassigned to a new router. The chain uses a wider overlap test than the binding and the run time. So `web.app().get("/:a/b", h).get("/a/:b", g)` is refused, while the same two calls on a binding build and run.

What a rule has (spec.md:124-154, CheckRules.jet). `check: fn(self, call: CompilerCall)` runs at each call of a marked function or method, or each method call on a marked type. CompilerCall holds `caller`, `callee`, `module`, `span`, `name`, `args` and `receiver` (CoreRecordRows.jet:250-263). `reject(finding, at: part)` gives one CompilerRejection with one `span` (:264-269), and an `.Error` rejection replaces the call's own errors. Staged calls run in one batch per rule per pass, across bodies (CheckRules.jet:725-790).

No route rule is on dev yet. Core's `StaticRoutes` rule (E2808) is the submission land/6851-c3-static-routes-e2808-r2 for batch 23. Its r1 failed batch 21 because rules did not run in a module with other errors. Every E2804 snapshot has another error in its module, so that fix and rule-order-r2 come first.

This ballot covers E2804 only. D-RULE-REWRITE1's review left it in sema under every option (its finding F9). It does not decide how a route's contract is attached (D-RULE-REWRITE1) or how a body's calls are read (D-RULE-BODYFACTS1).

options.name: A row key the compiler pairs
options.detail: A rule may add `row: fn(self, call: CompilerCall) -> String?`: the key of the row this call adds to its receiver's table, or None. Its `check` then takes a second parameter, `first: CompilerCall?`: the earliest earlier call on the same table with an equal key. The compiler pairs keys with one map, so the rule holds no list and no memory. `reject` gains `also:` and `label:`. Core's route rule writes the key as the method and route shape. A package router writes the same two members.
options.technical:
New: the `row` member of `impl Marker` and the shape `check: fn(self, call: CompilerCall, first: CompilerCall?)`. E0907 accepts that shape only beside `row`, and `row` only beside it.

Same table. Two receivers are the same place: one binding and field path (`pair.api`), with no assignment to that place between them, or one builder chain. A binding made from a chain (`app: web.app().get(…)`) joins that chain. The earlier call must also sit in the later call's block or a block around it, so both always run. Calls in two `if` arms, or one in a loop and one after it, are not paired. That removes today's three wrong refusals (p1).

Order is the order the compiler meets the calls. A stand-in (below) takes the place of its `.routes` or `.mount` call, not of the marker or file it points at.

How it runs. The rule's batch gets one more list, each call's table. It runs `row` per call, keeps one map from table and key to the first call, and runs `check` with that call or None. That is one String and one map step per call, O(n). Keys of calls answered in an earlier pass stay with their answers, so a later pass pairs with them.

`reject(finding, at: part, also: other, label: text)`. `at:` and `also:` name the call, its name or an argument of `call` or of `first`. CompilerRejection gains `also: SourceSpan?` and `label: String`. A finding with `also:` is a clash between two calls that are each fine. So it is reported beside the call's own errors, not instead of them (p5). That narrows D-CORE-CHECK1=A's rule that a rejection replaces the call's checks, for two-call findings only.

Stand-ins. `.routes(from: dir)` is heard as written, then once per convention file as the `page(path, view)` it stands for, at the `.routes` name. `app.mount(value)` is heard once per marked route method as its verb call, at the marker. CompilerCall gains `source: String?`, the convention file a stand-in comes from. A stand-in's site key includes its registering call, so mounting one struct twice keeps two rows (p2).

What moves. Prelude's `AmbiguousRoute` gains `source: String{""}` and becomes E2804's one build text. One public rule marker, `#StaticRoutes`, is carried by `HTTPRouter` and by `App`, and a package router may carry it too. It replaces the binding table, its index and the App pairing. It uses the run time's test, equal route shapes (Server.jet:369-371), so a chain and a binding agree (p4).

The rule tells a chain from a binding by spans. On a chain, the later call's receiver span holds the earlier call, or both rows come from one `.routes` call. So it picks today's labels. When the earlier row is a convention file and the later a builder call, it reports at `first` (today's order).

Kept: the convention file walk (`sema_app_expand_route_root`, which also gives E2806), the run-time check and the `--routes` report.

Gates on #6851: the StaticRoutes landing with its rule-pass and order fixes, and c22's rule cost.

options.name: Every earlier call on the same table
options.detail: `check` may take `earlier: [CompilerCall]`: every call this rule heard before this one on the same table, in order. The rule loops over them and decides itself which ones clash. `reject` gains `also:` and `label:`, and 'same table', the stand-ins and the moves are as in A.
options.technical:
New: the shape `check: fn(self, call: CompilerCall, earlier: [CompilerCall])` and A's `also:` and `label:`. There is no `row` member.

Its strength is reach. A rule can test any relation between two calls, not only equal keys, such as an overlap test or 'no route after `serve()`'. Nothing in Sema/Calls needs that today: E2804 is the only check that labels a second call (`diagnostic_with_label` has one caller there), and equal shapes decide it.

Its cost is quadratic. With n calls on one table, call k gets k-1 calls, so the batch hands over n(n-1)/2 calls. That is 124,750 for 500 routes. A rule-heard call costs about 0.19 ms on this host today (p3, 1,600 to 3,200 calls). If a list item costs a tenth of that, 500 routes add about 2.4 s [INFERENCE]. The rule then compares each pair, so its own work grows the same way. D-CORE-CHECK1=A's budget is 1 µs per heard call.

options.name: A whole-body rule: `check_all`
options.detail: A marker may declare `check_all: fn(self, calls: [CompilerCall]) -> [CompilerRejection?]` instead of `check`. It runs once per function body with every call it hears there, in order, and answers each call by position. It finds the pairs itself, with its own map. Each CompilerArg gains `place`, which binding or chain a value comes from, so the rule can group calls by table. `reject` gains `also:` and `label:`.
options.technical:
New: the `check_all` member, `CompilerArg.place: CompilerPlace?` with `CompilerPlace: enum { Binding(name: String, declared: SourceSpan), Chain(start: SourceSpan) }`, and A's `also:` and `label:`. This is Go's analyzers and Roslyn's compilation-start actions: one pass over a unit, one map, O(n).

Answering by position keeps one answer per call, so no new verb is needed. But a rule builds each answer itself instead of with `reject`, so the body differs from every other rule's.

The rule must also decide 'same table' itself. `place` does not say whether one call always runs before another, whether the binding was reassigned, or which field path the receiver took. So each rule would repeat, or get wrong, what A computes once in the compiler (today's three wrong refusals, p1). Each fact it needs becomes more public record.

options.name: A notebook the rule keeps: rule memory
options.detail: `check` may take a third parameter, `memory: &[String: SourceSpan]`, a map the compiler keeps for this rule across one function body. The rule writes a key such as `"router GET /users/:"` and finds the earlier span when the same key comes again. CompilerArg gains C's `place` so the key can name the table. `reject` gains `also:` and `label:`.
options.technical:
New: the `memory` parameter, `CompilerArg.place` (as in C) and A's `also:` and `label:`. This is ESLint's closure and a Clippy lint pass's own fields: O(n), and familiar.

A call's answer then depends on state outside its inputs. The batch must run every call of a body in one pass, in order. A call staged in a later pass needs the memory rebuilt from calls already answered. Any reuse of an answer by its inputs is unsound, as Rust warns for state shared between procedural macro runs.

The key is the rule's own text, so the rule decides 'same table' alone, as in C. The label can quote only what the rule stored. A span alone cannot give 'the other registration, `/x/:id` by `builder`', so the memory must hold more than a span.

options.name: Check only when the program runs
options.detail: Delete the build-time E2804. Registering the second route stops the program at run time, as it already does for routes the build cannot see (`mux_register`, Core/HTTP/Server.jet:368). The stop names both places as file:line text. Rules stay as they are. Go's ServeMux, axum and Rocket work this way.
options.technical: Deleted: the binding table and its index, the App pairing, and sema's E2804 text. The six UI snapshots become run tests. `jet check` and editors no longer show the error. It appears on the first `jet run` or `jet test` that builds the table, and a table built only on a rare path may ship. The second place is a file:line in the message, not an underlined span. Nothing new is added to rules, and today's wrong refusals (p1, p4) go with the check.

options.name: Keep the check in the compiler (today)
options.detail: The compiler keeps its E2804 sites. Rules stay as they are. Core keeps a check a package cannot write.
options.technical:
The case at its strongest. The check is exact for its six snapshots. It pairs builder rows, convention files and marked methods in the table's order and costs one map per body. Its three wrong refusals and the chain's wider test (p1, p4) can be fixed in sema, with A's 'same table' facts.

Costs: HTTPRouting.jet and the App pairing keep route knowledge. Card #6851 c3 deletes HTTPRouting.jet whole, so c3 cannot close. Its goal, that Core use only what packages can use, is not met for routes. A package router (Ben) cannot give E2804 while building.

comparisons.note: An analyzer registers a start action per compilation, keeps a concurrent map, and reports per operation. `Diagnostic.Create` takes `additionalLocations`, a second place to show. That is C's or D's state with A's second place.
An analyzer's `run` sees one whole package at once, keeps its own maps, and reports with `Related` positions. That is C's whole-unit shape. Facts carry results across packages.
A rule's `create` returns visitors that share variables in a closure, so it remembers earlier nodes in the file. That is D's notebook. A report has one location.

The compiler labels the earlier span: 'previous definition of the value `x` here'. A Clippy late lint pass keeps fields across the crate and adds the second span with `span_note`. A procedural macro sees one item, so `#[get("/a")]` routers find clashes at launch (Rocket).
Go 1.22's ServeMux panics when a pattern conflicts and names where the other was registered; axum's `Router::route` panics on an overlapping route. Both check at start-up only, which is E.
comparisons.code:
mux.HandleFunc("GET /users/{id}", show)
mux.HandleFunc("GET /users/{login}", find) // panic: … conflicts with pattern "GET /users/{id}" (registered at main.go:12)

comparisons.note: A Hono app's type grows with each chained `.get()`, so a type-level check could refuse a repeated path along a chain. Calls on a binding lose that type, so Ana's case is out of reach. Hono itself does not check.
comparisons.code:
const app = new Hono().get("/users/:id", show).get("/users/:login", find) // typed chain
app.get("/users/:id", other) // a statement: the chain's type is not extended

recommendation.why:
A keeps all six E2804 snapshots and lets one rule in Core replace the compiler's pairing. The same rule is open to package routers. The compiler does the part every rule would get wrong alone: which calls share a table and always both run. So today's three wrong refusals and the chain's wider test go.

Each call still gets one answer from what it is handed: the call and at most one earlier call. So batching stays, and pairing costs one map step per call. B hands over every earlier call, which is quadratic. C and D make each rule rebuild 'same table' and keep its own state. E loses the build-time error. F keeps Core's privilege and c3 open.
gains: E2804's six snapshots hold, both places included, and the binding table, its index and the App pairing go.
A package router gives the same error the same way (Ben).
Programs refused today by mistake build: exclusive `if` arms, two routers in one struct, a reassigned binding, and chain pairs the run accepts (p1, p4).
`also:` and `label:` serve any rule that relates two places, not only routes.

losses.loss: A rule gains a `row` member and a second `check` shape.
losses.mitigation: Both are optional and come together; the one-parameter `check` stays the beginner path, and E0907's message lists both shapes.

losses.loss: Only relations an equal key expresses can be paired.
losses.mitigation: E2804, the only two-call check in Sema/Calls, is one. B's list can be added later, beside A, if a check needs another relation.

losses.loss: Convention files and marked methods are heard as the calls they stand for, so other rules on App hear them too.
losses.mitigation: Those rows are registrations in every other sense (`jet explain --routes` lists them). Each stand-in carries the `.routes` or marker span and its `source`, so findings land where today's do.

losses.loss: A pair split across functions, an alias (`other: router`), a parameter, a generic receiver or one call in a loop is not seen while building.
losses.mitigation: That is today's limit too, and run time E2804 names both places (Server.jet:372). A binding made from a chain is now paired with it, a case today misses.

losses.loss: A two-call finding keeps the call's own errors, a narrow exception to D-CORE-CHECK1=A's one error per call.
losses.mitigation: The call is valid alone; replacing its errors would hide a typo in the handler until the duplicate is fixed (p5).

losses.loss: Every method call on `App` becomes a rule-heard call, at c22's per-call cost.
losses.mitigation: An app makes tens of such calls, and `HTTPRouter` calls are already heard once StaticRoutes lands.

whyNot.reason: Every call gets every earlier call, so 500 routes hand over 124,750 calls and the rule compares each pair, against a 1 µs budget per call.
Each rule rebuilds 'same table' from new public place records and answers by position, so rules differ from every other rule and repeat today's mistakes.
Answers depend on state outside the call, so passes must replay it, and the rule still decides 'same table' alone.
The error moves from `jet check` and the editor to the first run, and the second place becomes text instead of an underline.
Route knowledge stays in the compiler, c3 cannot close, and package routers cannot give the error.

recommendation.tradeoff: One optional rule member and two `reject` labels, for an exact E2804 written in Core, open to packages, at one map step per call.

decisions.hybrid: B can join A later, as a second `check` shape, if a check needs a relation no equal key expresses. Nothing in Sema/Calls does today.

decisions.title: How a typed web form's `.validate(.carrier, on: .Blur, with: check)` names a field of its model without help from the compiler
decisions.situation: A typed web form is a form built from a struct: `web.form(ShipForm, action: submit)` gives one input per field. A program attaches a check to one field by naming it: `.validate(.carrier, on: .Blur, with: check_carrier)`. That spelling is already approved. Today the compiler turns `.carrier` into the text "carrier" before the library sees it. Nobody checks that name, so a typo such as `.carier` builds and runs, and the form shows `carier:invalid` forever. A library cannot write such a method, because nothing in the language says what `.carrier` means as an argument. You are asked what type that argument has, so the library can declare the form's methods itself and a typo fails the build. We recommend a small field-reference type, filled in from the form's model.
decisions.gist: What type does `.carrier` have in `form.validate(.carrier, on: .Blur, with: check)`, so Core can declare the method and a typo fails the build?
decisions.lesson: Languages that let a library name a field without a string give it a typed reference: Swift key paths (`\.carrier`), Kotlin property references (`ShipForm::carrier`), C# expression trees (`x => x.Carrier`). Each is checked against the type, so a misspelled field is a build error, and the library can still read the field's name.
decisions.explainer:
Think of a paper form with labeled boxes, and a clerk who checks one box when you leave it. Today you tell the clerk which box by writing its label on a sticky note. The head office (the compiler) copies the note over, and nobody checks the spelling. A note saying 'carier' points at no box, so the clerk marks it wrong forever.

Option A gives the clerk a pointer that can only be made from a real box on this form. Option B prints a menu of the form's boxes and you tick one. Option C hands the clerk a tiny instruction, 'read the carrier box', and the office works out which box it means. Option D keeps the head office copying notes, but has it check the spelling. Option E drops the dot and has you write the label as plain text.
decisions.story: Mia builds a shipping page. She writes `typed_form.validate(.carrier, on: .Blur, with: check_carrier).render()`. On a tired day she types `.carier`. Today the page builds and the field always shows as invalid, with no message saying why. She should get a build error at `.carier` that lists `id`, `carrier` and `tracking`. Leo writes his own form library and wants the same field selector for his forms, without compiler help.
decisions.detail:
The program every option keeps is in Examples/Apps/Web/JetWeb/run.jet (:41-46, :154-161, :258-260).

`#[Codable, Web.Form] ShipForm: struct { id: Int, carrier: String, tracking: String }`, then `web.form(ShipForm, action: submit_ship_order)`, `.validate(.carrier, on: .Blur, with: check_carrier)` and `.render()`. Before that, three `set("id", …)` calls fill the form.

What happens today. `sema_call_try_web_form_method` (Sema/Calls/HTTP.jet:469) takes over every method on `WebFormTyped`, a type the compiler owns. `sema_web_form_method_member` (:439-464) maps 14 method names to free functions in Core/Web/Forms.jet. For `validate` it binds the labels, and `sema_web_form_field_selector` (:566-590) turns `.carrier`, or `.Carrier`, into the String "carrier". `typed_validate_field` (Forms.jet:376-394) loops over the fields looking for it.

The typo. When no field matches, the loop does nothing, so `.render()` gives `carier:invalid` (probe f1). `.Carrier` does the same. The sibling methods already refuse an unknown name when run. `set("carier", …)` returns `WebFormError.Missing` (f1), as do `blur`, `focus` and `set_async_validator`. Only `validate` is silent, and fixing that needs no ballot.

Why no private typing works. The no-argument `validate()` is a second method under the same name, mapped to `typed_validate` (:368), with a different result. Jet has no overloading. The form's type does not carry its model (Forms.jet:96-100), so nothing at the `validate` call can check `.carrier` against `ShipForm`.

Other leading-dot field names. `devtools.publish(field: .selected, value: v)` lowers its selector the same way and checks it against the package's `#DevPanel` state (Sema/Calls/Devtools.jet:40-75). A marker body's `layout[.field]` is checked against the reflected type and reports Jet.UnknownField (Tests/UI/layout_unknown_selector). Elsewhere a lower-case `.name` means the subject shorthand, only where a one-argument function is expected (D-SUBJECT-CALL1=A). Inside a loop with no binding it means the loop's item, before any expected type (D-LOOP-SUBJECT1=A).

Hand-built forms. `forms.typed(input, action)` builds a typed form from any field list, and `input_exclude`, `input_group` and `input_rename` change that list (Forms.jet:247-302). Such a form has no model the build can check.

The `web.form` field derivation from `#Web.Form` is D-RULE-REWRITE1's matter, not this ballot's.

options.name: `FieldRef<Model, T>`: a typed field reference the form's model fills in
options.detail: Prelude gains `FieldRef<Model, T>`, a reference to one field of `Model` whose type is `T`. Where a `FieldRef<ShipForm, _>` is expected, `.carrier` means ShipForm's `carrier` field, and a name ShipForm lacks is a build error at the dot. `web.form(ShipForm, …)` gives a `WebFormTyped<ShipForm>`, so the form knows its model. Core declares the form's methods as ordinary methods. `validate`, `set`, `blur` and `focus` all take the field this way, so a form names its fields one way.
options.technical:
New: `FieldRef<Model, T>: struct { priv name: String }` in core.prelude, read through a `name()` method. Like Prelude's `Type` (Prelude.jet:168), only the compiler builds one, so no text becomes a `FieldRef`. One typing rule: where the expected type is `FieldRef<M, T>`, a bare `.name` checks `name` against M's stored fields visible at the call. It unifies `T` with the field's type. A computed field is refused, because `web.form` skips it (HTTP.jet:360).

This adds a context to D-SUBJECT-CALL1=A, which today sends every non-function context to the full lambda. D-LOOP-SUBJECT1=A's order stays: inside a loop with no binding, `.carrier` still reads the loop's item. So `loop ships -> form.validate(.carrier, …)`, which builds today (f3), is refused. The error says to name the loop binding.

An unknown name reports Jet.UnknownField at the selector, as `layout[.field]` does, listing M's fields. A longer chain (`.carrier.trim()`), a payload or an upper-case `.Carrier` is refused. Completion after the dot must list M's fields. A helper generic over the model takes a `FieldRef` from its caller, since `.carrier` needs a known model.

`WebFormTyped` gains the type parameter `Model`, as do the three records that hold a form (Forms.jet:114-128). `web.form` fills it, so nobody writes it. `forms.typed<Model>(input, action)` names it for a hand-built form. Its fields may differ from the model's, so `validate` also refuses an unknown name when run, with `WebFormError.Missing`. Its result becomes `WebFormValidationChain<Model> (E | WebFormError)!`, as `set_async_validator` has today.

The no-argument `validate()` method goes, so `validate` has one meaning. Nothing outside Core's conformance corpus calls it, `submit()` validates the whole form (Forms.jet:402), and `forms.typed_validate(form)` stays. The check still gets the field's text value, as the wire carries it.

Deleted: the whole method intercept, `sema_call_try_web_form_method` with `sema_web_form_method_member`, the selector helpers and their label binding (HTTP.jet:439-590). Also `WebFormTyped`'s compiler-owned type entry (Registration/Items.jet:2370) goes. The `WebFormTyped` rows in WebCoreSignatures.jet (:15, :60-72) gain the model.

Kept: devtools' selector, whose call has no state type to fill a `FieldRef` from, and Core's table, which names columns by text (a later user of `FieldRef`).

options.name: `#Web.Form` derives a field enum for each model
options.detail: The `#Web.Form` marker generates an enum of the model's fields, `ShipFormField { Id, Carrier, Tracking }`. `validate`, `set`, `blur` and `focus` take that enum, and the form's type names it, `WebFormTyped<ShipFormField>`. Enum cases are upper-case, so the selector is spelled `.Carrier`, a change from the approved `.carrier`. A typo is the ordinary 'no such case' build error.
options.technical:
New: an `expand` on `Web.Form` that writes the enum beside the model, and a generic `WebFormTyped<F>`. The enum is a real declaration, so it appears in docs, hover and `jet explain`. A field named `id` and one named `Id` would give the same case. Keeping `.carrier` lower-case instead needs a new rule letting a lower-case leading-dot name be an enum case when the expected type is an enum. That changes how every lower-case `.name` reads, since today it is always a member chain.

No typing rule is added, and D-SUBJECT-CALL1=A is untouched. Inside a loop with no binding, `.Carrier` is an enum case, so f3's program still builds. The no-argument `validate()` goes as in A, and hand-built forms are handled as in A. Devtools keeps its own intercept. Leo can write the same expand for his forms. Diesel's per-table column types are this shape in Rust.

options.name: The selector is a one-line function, and the build reads its field
options.detail: Jet already reads `.carrier` as a small function `fn(s: ShipForm) -> s.carrier` wherever a one-argument function is expected, as in `users.map(.name)`. `validate` takes such a function. A typo is the ordinary 'no field' error inside it. The library still needs the field's name for the form's state. So a build-time parameter, computed from the function's body at each call, supplies it.
options.technical:
Needs D-RULE-REWRITE1's option A: a parameter default `#run` per call, reading earlier parameters. It also needs a lambda argument heard as FunctionInfo (c30) and a body fact saying 'this function reads field `carrier`' (D-RULE-BODYFACTS1). None of these exist today.

The declaration would read `validate: fn<T, E>(self, field: fn(Model) -> T, name: String{#run field_read(field.reflect())}, on: …, with: …)`. A selector that is not a plain field read, such as `.carrier.trim()`, has no name and is refused at the call. No typing rule is added, but D-LOOP-SUBJECT1=A still makes `.carrier` the loop's item inside a loop with no binding (f3). The form must still know its model, and the no-argument `validate()` goes as in A. Elm's `.carrier` accessor functions are this shape.

options.name: Keep the compiler's lowering, and have it check the name
options.detail: The form's type names its model, `WebFormTyped<ShipForm>`, as in A. The compiler keeps turning `.carrier` into text, and now checks the name against the model's fields. A typo becomes a build error, and nothing else changes in what users write. This is the smallest change that catches the typo while building. Core keeps methods a library cannot declare, so Leo cannot offer the same selector.
options.technical:
`sema_web_form_field_selector` (HTTP.jet:566-590) reads the receiver's model argument and checks the name, with A's error. That is about 20 lines plus the generic `WebFormTyped<Model>` and its registry rows. The intercept, the label binding and the 14-method map stay (HTTP.jet:439-590).

The intercept reads the written selector before any typing, so D-SUBJECT-CALL1=A and D-LOOP-SUBJECT1=A are untouched, and f3's program still builds. `validate()` with no arguments may stay. Card #6851's goal, that Core use only what packages can use, is not met for forms.

options.name: Name the field with text: `validate("carrier", …)`
options.detail: `validate` takes the field's name as a String, like `set("carrier", …)` already does. Core declares it as an ordinary method with no new type. This replaces the approved `.carrier` spelling. A typo is caught when the program runs, where Core now reports it instead of the silent `carier:invalid`.
options.technical:
`validate: fn<E>(self, field: String, on: WebFormValidationTiming, with: fn(String) E!) -> WebFormValidationChain (E | WebFormError)!`, with the no-argument `validate()` gone as in A. The loop refuses an unknown name with `WebFormError.Missing`.

A call rule could catch the typo while building only if the form's type named its model and a rule could read that model's fields. A rule sees the receiver as a TypeId, which holds only `identity`, `name` and `signature` (CoreRecordRows.jet:616-618). So that needs both A's type change and a new reflection read. TypeScript's `Path<ShipForm>` checks such text through literal-string types, which Jet does not have. It reopens D-DX-FORM1's ratified spelling.

comparisons.note: A key path `\ShipForm.carrier` is a typed value `KeyPath<ShipForm, String>`. Where the root is known, `\.carrier` is enough. A misspelled field is a build error. That is A's shape, with Jet's existing leading dot in place of the backslash.
comparisons.code:
func validate<T>(_ field: KeyPath<ShipForm, T>, on: Timing, with: (String) throws -> Void)
form.validate(\.carrier, on: .blur, with: checkCarrier)

comparisons.note: A property reference `ShipForm::carrier` is a `KProperty1<ShipForm, String>` and carries `.name`. Libraries such as Exposed and Ktor validation use it to name a field without a string.
comparisons.code:
fun <T> validate(field: KProperty1<ShipForm, T>, on: Timing, with: (String) -> Unit)
form.validate(ShipForm::carrier, on = Timing.Blur, with = ::checkCarrier)

comparisons.note: `RuleFor(x => x.Carrier)` takes an expression tree, and the library reads the member name from it when run, which is C's shape. `nameof(ShipForm.Carrier)` is text the build checks, a narrower E.
`register("carrier")` takes a string, but its type is `Path<ShipForm>`, the union of the model's keys. A typo is a build error. That is E with checking only a type system of literal strings can give.
comparisons.code:
const { register } = useForm<ShipForm>();
<input {...register("carier")} />   // error: not assignable to Path<ShipForm>

comparisons.note: Elm's `.carrier` is an accessor function, so a form library still needs a separate name: C's gap. Diesel generates one column type per table field, B's shape with lower-case names in their own module.
comparisons.code:
-- Elm
List.map .carrier ships
// Rust, Diesel: generated by table!
ships.filter(ships::carrier.eq("Parcel"))

recommendation.why:
A keeps Mia's approved spelling and turns the silent typo into a build error that lists the real fields. Core declares the form's methods like any methods, and Leo's library can take the same parameter. It adds one small Prelude type and one typing rule beside the subject shorthand.

The form's model moves into its type, the only place a check at the call can find it. B changes the spelling and generates a type per model. C waits on three pending mechanisms. D is smaller but keeps Core's privilege. E reopens the approved spelling and catches typos only when run.
gains: `.carier` fails the build at the selector, listing `id`, `carrier` and `tracking`.
The typed-form intercept leaves the compiler whole (HTTP.jet:439-590), and the form names a field one way in every method.
A package's form or table library declares the same `FieldRef` parameter.
`T` is known at the call, so a later typed validator (`with: fn(T) E!`) needs no new mechanism.

losses.loss: One new Prelude type and one typing rule for a leading-dot name, a new context beside D-SUBJECT-CALL1=A's.
losses.mitigation: Users never write `FieldRef`; they write `.carrier` as today. The rule applies only where a `FieldRef` is expected, as the subject shorthand applies only where a function is expected.

losses.loss: Inside a loop with no binding, `.carrier` reads the loop's item, so a selector there is refused (f3).
losses.mitigation: D-LOOP-SUBJECT1=A keeps one meaning for `.name` in such a loop; the error says to name the binding (`loop ship in ships`).

losses.loss: The typed form's type gains its model: `WebFormTyped<ShipForm>`.
losses.mitigation: `web.form(ShipForm, …)` infers it, so only hover and explicit annotations show it. A hand-built form names its model once, at `forms.typed<Model>`.

losses.loss: `set("carrier", v)`, `blur` and `focus` take `.carrier` too, and the no-argument `validate()` method goes.
losses.mitigation: One way to name a field on a form. Three `set` lines in JetWeb change; nothing calls `validate()`, and `submit()` still validates the whole form.

whyNot.reason: It changes `.carrier` to `.Carrier` or changes what every lower-case `.name` means, and generates a public enum per model.
It needs D-RULE-REWRITE1 A, lambda FunctionInfo and body facts first, and refuses any selector that is not a plain field read.
It is the smallest fix, but Core keeps 14 methods no library can declare, and Leo cannot offer the selector.
It reopens the approved spelling and finds a typo only when the program runs.

recommendation.tradeoff: One small field-reference type and a visible model on the form's type, for the approved spelling, a build-time typo error and no compiler intercept.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude Opus. Adversarial model family: Claude Opus. Fresh agent: AcrossReview. The adversarial review attacked the recommendation. Probes on tip 21 showed A refused a selector in a loop with no binding, so A now names that and its D-SUBJECT-CALL1 change, covers every field method and drops `validate()`.

decisions.title: Write and take marks are spelled ^ and ^^
decisions.situation: Jet marks a parameter that a function may change with a write mark, and a parameter it keeps with a take mark. Until this change the marks were spelled `&T` and `&&T`. The same symbols are bitwise and and logical and between two values, so each carried two meanings told apart by position. The symbol `^` had no meaning in Jet, because infix `^` is a parse error and exclusive-or is `~`. The owner approved moving the marks to `^` and `^^`, and the cutover has shipped. This record states the alternatives, the costs a fresh review found, and the owner's ruling.
decisions.gist: Which symbols mark a write and a take: & and &&, or ^ and ^^?
decisions.lesson: A mark that shares its symbol with an operator costs every reader a second look. A free symbol costs nothing to give a job, but it can cost typing on keyboards where that symbol is a dead key.
decisions.explainer: Think of a shared notebook passed around a table. A small mark beside a name says this person may write in it, and a double mark says this person keeps it. Jet used to draw those marks with `&` and `&&`, which also mean bitwise and and logical and. Now it draws them with `^` and `^^`, which mean nothing else in Jet. The catch is that some keyboards treat `^` as an accent key, so typing it takes care.
decisions.story: Ana reads `fill: fn(values: ^[Int], n: Int)` and a few lines down `ready && count > 0`. Each symbol has one job, so she never stops to ask which one she is reading. Her colleague Jonas types the same code on a German keyboard, where `^` waits for the next letter. His `^^self` comes out as `^self`, and nothing tells him unless the body moves the receiver.
decisions.inWild:
Pascal and Odin write `^T` for a pointer type, and `p^` to read through it.
Go reads a prefix `^x` as bitwise complement, and C, Go, Rust and Swift read infix `^` as exclusive-or.
Swift marks a write with the word `inout` and a take with `consuming`; its call site writes `&values`.
Rust marks a write with `&mut T` and takes a plain `T` by value.
C++ writes `T&` for a reference and `T&&` for a value it may move from.
No common language uses `^^`.
decisions.detail:
Ruling. The owner ruled for A directly in session on 2026-11-24, in two statements quoted word for word. First: "I approve the & and && to ^ and ^^ conversion". Second: "Yes Im saying cancelling the ^ from @ conversion and use ^ in place of &". The first followed a side-by-side comparison of the old and the converted spelling over 24 excerpts from dev and five whole files.

Scope. The ruling amends the spelling of D-CALLSITE-MARK2=A and D-MOVE-SIGIL1=A only. What a write or a take means, and where a mark may appear, are unchanged. Because `^` now marks a write, links keep `@` (D-MEMREF1=A), and the drafted link move D-LINK-CARET1 is withdrawn. Infix `^` stays a parse error, and exclusive-or stays `~`. Prefix `&` and `&&` are now ordinary parse errors with no alias and no teaching diagnostic.

Registry. Spellings.jet holds the mark rows and the migration plan mark-caret1, shipped with toolchain a0.0.47. CoreSurface.jet sets SIGIL_WRITE to `^` and SIGIL_MOVE to `^^`. MathLayout.jet says OP_CARET is the write mark and never an operator, and OP_AMP is bitwise and only. Step B rewrote 2,921 files in one commit, and the cutover runs on card #6998.

Review, typing. On a dead-key layout, two presses of `^` compose to a single `^`. A probe wrote `redeem: fn(^self)` where `^^self` was meant, exactly as that collapse leaves it. It checked clean and redeemed the same ticket twice, printing `7 7`. The intended `^^self` program is refused with Jet.UseAfterMove. So a take can silently become a write, unless the body moves the receiver.

Review, composed letters. E0119 explains a composed letter only in a type name such as `Înt`, and a bogus Jet.ImmutableAssignment follows it. A parameter named `êntries` compiles silently. `ŝelf` gets the advice to write `ŝelf: Type`, and `ĉounts` gets only a spelling suggestion. A qualified type written `ĵson.Dyn` panics the compiler in sema_registration_unit_leaf_name, which slices characters by byte offsets.

Review, reading and tools. Go readers know a prefix `^x` as bitwise complement, so `edit: ^values[1..<3]` can read as a value. In Jet it opens a write window. `a ^= 3` is reported as a line that computes a value, because the lexer still makes a `^=` token. Regex and shell users must escape `^`. The diagnostic underline is also `^`, on its own gutter line under the marked code.

Review, verdicts. Separation from operators holds: `&` and `&&` now have one meaning each. Reading holds within limits. Typing fails on dead-key layouts for the take mark, and the help covers only type names. Diff noise holds within limits, since `git blame --ignore-rev` skips the one migration commit. Tooling holds within limits: the Zed query still colored `&&` as the take mark, and tree-sitter split `^^` into two tokens.

Follow-ups. The tree-sitter and Zed gaps, a README quote and a duplicated spec sentence are fixed in the criterion 4 patch. The compiler gaps go to the orchestrator: the `ĵson.Dyn` panic, the stale `^=` token, and the comptime token names operator.caret and operator.caret_caret. The proposed guard against the collapse flags a write-marked parameter or receiver that the body never writes. Jet.MutableNeverReassigned already does the same for a `:=` binding.

options.name: Marks use ^ and ^^
options.detail: A write is `^T` or `^self`, a take is `^^T` or `^^self`, and a write window is `^values[1..<3]`. A task capture that takes is `task ^^job`. `&` stays bitwise and and `&&` stays logical and, each with no other meaning. This is the shipped spelling, and the program below runs on today's toolchain.
options.technical: The lexer makes `^^` one token, TOKEN_CARET_CARET, as it makes `&&` one token. No grammar rule gives `^` an operator meaning, so a mark never needs position to tell it from an operator.

options.name: Marks keep & and &&
options.detail: No change from the former spelling: a write is `&T` or `&self`, and a take is `&&T` or `&&self`. `&` and `&&` keep two meanings each, a mark before a type or name and an operator between two values. The parser tells them apart by position.

options.name: Marks are words
options.detail: A write is `mut T` or `mut self`, and a take is `take T` or `take self`, close to Swift's `inout` and `consuming`. A write window is `mut values[1..<3]`, and a task capture is `task take job`. Jet once spelled marks with these words; the lexer still reserves them, and the tools teach the symbols instead.

options.name: Rust's split
options.detail: A read is `&T`, a write is `&mut T`, and a take is a plain `T`, as in Rust. This flips Jet's default: today a plain parameter is a read, and only a write or a take carries a mark. Every read of a value that does not copy would gain `&`.

comparisons.note: Rust writes through `&mut` and takes by plain value, so a read carries `&` and a take carries nothing.
Swift marks with words in the declaration and with `&` at the call site.
C++ shares `&` and `&&` between references and operators, the overlap B would keep.
Odin reads `^T` as a pointer type and `p^` as reading through it, a reading A's readers may bring.

recommendation.why: The owner ruled for A in two statements: "I approve the & and && to ^ and ^^ conversion" and "Yes Im saying cancelling the ^ from @ conversion and use ^ in place of &". A gives every symbol one job at the same width as before. It has shipped, with the registry, checker and editor grammars spelling `^` and `^^`.
gains: Each of `^`, `^^`, `&` and `&&` has one meaning.
Marks keep their width, so code stays aligned after the migration.
The marks were free, so no operator moved.

losses.loss: On dead-key layouts, two presses of `^` give one, so `^^self` can silently become `^self` and a take becomes a write.
losses.mitigation: Flag a write-marked parameter or receiver that the body never writes, as Jet.MutableNeverReassigned does for `:=`. This needs a new criterion.

losses.loss: Composed letters outside type names get no dead-key hint, and a composed qualified type crashed the compiler.
losses.mitigation: Card #6998 criterion 6 owns the hints, and the crash in sema_registration_unit_leaf_name goes to the orchestrator as a defect.

losses.loss: Readers from Go, Odin or Pascal bring other meanings for a prefix `^`, and `a ^= 3` gets a misleading message.
losses.mitigation: Jet has no `^` operator, the syntax dictionary explains both marks, and the stale `^=` token is reported for removal.

whyNot.reason: `&` and `&&` keep two meanings each, the overlap the owner chose to end. The Zed query even colored logical and as the take mark.
Words lengthen every marked parameter, and Jet already retired these words in favor of symbols.
It flips the default, so most parameters gain a mark, and `&` would still be both a mark and an operator.

recommendation.tradeoff: One clear meaning per symbol, paid for with typing risk on dead-key keyboards that the checker only partly catches today.

decisions.title: How a type says it never copies, stays on its thread, or must be used up
decisions.situation: The checker decides three facts about a type from lists of Core type names. Atomic, MutationPlan, ViewMut and the Cell guards never copy. Arena, Bump, Pool, Cell and the browser handles never leave the thread that made them. A Task must reach join or detach exactly once. Card #6852 c1 asks that these facts come from declarations, so the name lists in Ownership/Copy.jet, Ownership/Crossings.jet and Typestate.jet can go. Its c2 asks that a user type declared the same way gets the same facts. Jet already has three nearby markers. `#SingleUse` (D-LIN1) makes a type's values owe a consume on every path. `#MustUse` (E0419) refuses a result dropped as a bare statement. `#Local` (D-DATARACE1) rejects task, channel and parallel crossings, but only where a binding is declared. No ratified decision says how a type declares that it never copies or stays on its thread, or that Task is single-use.
decisions.gist: How should a type declare that it never copies, never leaves its thread, or must be used up, so a user type can say the same?
decisions.lesson: Three facts about a type change what the checker allows. A value that never copies can only move. A value bound to its thread never crosses to another. A value that must be used up has to reach a consuming call, such as a task's join or detach. Two facts are declared already: a Close type never copies and closes once, and a `#SingleUse` type is used up on every path. Never copying without being a resource, and staying on one thread, come only from Core type names.
decisions.explainer: Think of a library that lends out books. Some books are one of a kind and may never be photocopied. Some may never leave the reading room. Some must come back before the borrower leaves. Today only the librarian knows which books are which, from a private list. This ballot decides where the label goes, so anyone who adds a book can label it the same way.
decisions.story: Mia writes a `Pool` type for her game that hands out slots from memory her own thread owns. Core's `Arena` gets the same care for free: the checker refuses to copy it or send it to another task. Her `Pool` gets neither, because the checker finds `Arena` by name in a list. Nothing she can write on `Pool` puts it on that list.
decisions.detail:
Sites at origin/dev fd32fefaf1, unchanged from 2a09ee0e42. Copy.jet `sema_copy_named_is_builtin_resource` at 371-376 lists twelve Core resource types. Copy.jet `sema_copy_apply_is_noncloneable` at 392-398 lists ten types that never copy, and `sema_copy_apply_is_dynamic_loan` at 400-405 lists the two Cell guards. Copy.jet 1077-1078 tests for Task and ExpiringSecret, and 1410 and 1457 test SharedGuard, ProcessChild, TempDir and the guards by name.

Crossings.jet `sema_ownership_crossing_core_confined` at 144-157 names Arena, Bump, Pool, Fixed and seven browser handles by module and name. Crossings.jet 353, 363, 377 and 536 test Task, Receiver, Sender, Cell, the guards and Atomic. Typestate.jet 19-25 and 88-91 hold the Task states Running, Joined and Detached and the two methods that move between them. SingleUse.jet picks L1101 over E0140 for a bare task by name.

What is already declared. A type that implements Close is a resource: Copy.jet 857 reads the impl, and a generic `T: Close` bound counts too (582). A user Close type and any struct that holds one are move-only today. So the resource list can go once each Core resource type writes its Close impl. A `#SingleUse` type owes a consume on every path, through containers and fields too (D-LIN1, D-LIN-CONTAINER1, E0140-E0143).

A foreign handle carries `send` and `sync` facts from its binding (Registration/Items.jet 186-198). A runtime handle registered without `clone` already moves (RuntimeHandles.jet). Thread confinement already passes through fields: a struct that holds an Arena is refused at a task crossing (E1102).

What is not declared. Ten carriers have no Core declaration at all, so nothing can be written on them: Task, Atomic, ViewMut, ViewIter, SharedGuard, ProcessChild, Receiver, Sender, CellReadGuard and CellEditGuard. The checker matches each by its name, and Task even when a program declares its own `Task`.

What this ballot adds. One way to state the two missing facts on a type, which Core and packages write alike. Task's duty moves onto the existing `#SingleUse`. The checker then finds each fact by the declaration that carries it, not by a type name.

What the review changed. The review checked every cited site at fd32fefaf1, where they are unchanged from 2a09ee0e42, and ran nine probes on the tip23 compiler. It refuted four claims. First, the third fact is already declared: `#SingleUse` (D-LIN1, D-LIN-CONTAINER1) gives a user type the consume-on-every-path duty today (probe: an unconsumed user `#SingleUse` struct is Jet.SingleUseDropped). Second, Jet already has a `#MustUse` marker with another meaning: E0419, a result dropped as a bare statement (probe: Jet.MustUseIgnored on a user type).

So the draft's `#MustUse` would have given one spelling two meanings. Third, `#Local` (D-DATARACE1) already rejects task, channel and parallel crossings (E1102). It is allowed only at the Declaration site today (probe: on a type it is Jet.InvalidScopedPolicy), so a separate `#ThreadBound` would be a second word for one fact. Fourth, Task, Atomic, ViewMut, ViewIter, SharedGuard, ProcessChild, Receiver, Sender and both Cell guards have no Core declaration to write a marker on (Copy.jet 1075-1076 says so for Task).

This draft keeps option A but repairs it. It adds one marker, `#MoveOnly` (the spec's own word, used six times). It gives `#Local` the Type site and puts the existing `#SingleUse` on Task. It adds arity-only Core declarations for the undeclared carriers, following the precedent of `Arena: struct {}` in core.mem. It folds L1101 into E0140 through the registry's Retired status. It also corrects the spec line references and the reasons B and C lose.

It corrects the Cell-guard loan claim too: dynamic_loan is a borrow fact used at CheckProgram.jet 1610 and Checks.jet 4532, not only a copy and thread fact. Each loss is now engineered away or comes with a named mitigation.

options.name: Markers on the declaration
options.detail:
A type takes each fact by a marker in its header, and any package may write the same markers on its own types. `#MoveOnly` is the one new marker: the type moves and never copies. `#Local`, which a binding can already carry, may also be written on a type: its values never leave the thread that made them. The existing `#SingleUse` goes on Task, so a task must reach join or detach, as any single-use value must reach a consuming call.

A type that holds one of these facts in a field has the fact too, as fields already carry copy, crossing and single-use facts. Core writes the markers on Atomic, Arena, Cell, Task and every other listed type, and the name lists go.
options.technical:
`MoveOnly` joins the prelude marker registry (PreludeMarkers.jet) as a field-less struct implementing Marker with `sites: [.Type]`, beside `SingleUse`. The `Local` row gains the Type site. The checker reads a type's markers by the marker's declared identity, as it reads `#SingleUse` and `#MustUse` now.

The ten undeclared carriers get arity-only Core declarations, the form `Arena: struct {}` already uses in core.mem ('compiler-owned nominal surfaces'). The checker finds the builtin heads by those rows' Core identity, which also fixes the case where a program's own `Task` hides the builtin. Task declares `join: fn(&&self)` and `detach: fn(&&self)` under `#SingleUse`. A second join is then E0121 by ordinary move checking, and the Task rows in Typestate.jet go.

An unused task becomes E0140, whose text names the consuming methods the type declares ('owes `join` or `detach`'). L1101 takes the registry's Retired status, pointing to E0140. The Cell guards are `#MoveOnly #Local`. Their loan, which lives only as long as the Cell that lent it, stays a borrow rule on the Cell's guard methods, keyed by the guards' Core identity rather than their names. The existing `#MustUse` keeps its E0419 meaning.

options.name: Marker traits
options.detail: Core declares member-less traits such as `MoveOnly` and `Local`. A type takes a fact by implementing the trait, as a resource already implements Close. A generic function can then ask for the fact in a bound, such as `T: Local`.
options.technical:
Each trait is found by a D-CORE-ROLE1 role, not by its name. The impl can sit inside the struct body, so the fact can stay near the header. But these facts pass through fields: a struct that holds an Arena is thread-bound without writing any impl. A bound would answer no for that struct unless Jet gains Rust-style automatic traits, a new kind of trait. Without them a `T: Local` bound would give the wrong answer for such holders.

The used-up fact would duplicate `#SingleUse` as a third spelling.

options.name: Marker fields
options.detail: Core declares empty types such as `MoveMark` and `LocalMark`. A type takes a fact by holding a field of one of them, as Rust code holds a `PhantomData` field. The fields take no memory.
options.technical: The checker already passes copy and crossing facts from fields to the types that hold them, so only the leaf types are new. But every field list sees the extra field. Each struct literal has to write it or rely on a default, Codable and `#Layout(c)` have to skip it, and Core's runtime carriers each gain one. The facts never show in a type's header, only among its fields.

options.name: Keep the compiler lists
options.detail: The checker keeps its name lists, moved into one table with a role per fact. Core's types keep their facts, and a user type cannot take them.
options.technical: One closed table in jet_builtins replaces the four lists. #6852 c2 stays unmet, because no package can join the table.
options.code:
// Compiler table; a package cannot add a row
MOVE_ONLY_TYPES: [String]{"Atomic", "MutationPlan", "ViewMut"}

comparisons.note: Swift 5.9 lets a struct or enum opt out of copying with `~Copyable` in its own declaration (SE-0390). Thread crossing is the Sendable protocol, which a type adopts or is refused where it is declared.

Send and Sync are automatic traits. A type opts out with a marker field such as `PhantomData<*const ()>`, because negative impls are still unstable outside the standard library. `#[must_use]` on a type warns when a value is dropped unused.
A class forbids copying by deleting its copy constructor in its own declaration. Library and user classes write it the same way.

recommendation.why: A writes each fact where a reader looks for it, on the type, in the marker form `#SingleUse` and `#Error` already use. It adds only one new word, because thread confinement reuses `#Local` and the used-up duty reuses `#SingleUse`. Core and packages write the same markers, which is what #6852 c2 asks. It needs no new kind of trait.
gains: A reader sees a type's copy, thread and use facts in its header.
A user type gets exactly the facts a Core type gets.
The four name lists go, and so do the name tests for the ten undeclared carriers. Task's join and detach become ordinary consuming methods.
A program's own `Task` no longer collides with the builtin one.

losses.loss: One new marker, `#MoveOnly`, plus a new Type site for `#Local`.
losses.mitigation: `#MoveOnly` is the spec's own word for the fact. Most code never writes either. The copy and crossing errors name the marker and where it is written.

losses.loss: Ten builtin carriers need Core declarations before they can carry markers.
losses.mitigation: Engineered away in the same cutover. Each gets an arity-only declaration, as Arena already has, and the checker matches the builtin heads by those rows' identity.

losses.loss: L1101 folds into E0140, so one diagnostic code changes.
losses.mitigation: Engineered away. L1101 takes the registry's Retired status pointing to E0140, so `jet explain L1101` still answers. The message still says 'owes `join` or `detach`', from Task's declared consuming methods.

losses.loss: A generic function cannot ask that its type argument be thread-bound.
losses.mitigation: Not needed for soundness. Crossing and copy checks run on the instantiated type at each site, so a generic holder of an Arena is still refused (probe: E1102 on a struct that holds an Arena).

whyNot.reason: These facts pass through fields, so a trait bound needs automatic traits, a new kind of trait, or it gives the wrong answer for holders. It also adds a third spelling for the duty `#SingleUse` already declares.
Hidden fields bury the facts among the data. Every struct literal, Codable list and C layout has to account for them.
It keeps the facts closed to user types, so #6852 c2 stays unmet.

recommendation.tradeoff: One rarely written marker and a new site for `#Local`, in exchange for facts that any type can state and every reader can see.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude Opus. Adversarial model family: Claude Opus. Fresh agent: G1Facts-2. The review checked every cited site at fd32fefaf1 and ran nine probes on the tip23 compiler, refuting four claims of the earlier draft. It kept option A and repaired it, as the detail's last section shows.

decisions.title: How a stream whose close can fail also closes itself at the end of its scope
decisions.situation: The declared-facts ballot (ratified, option A) moves the copy and resource facts onto declarations so the compiler's name lists can go. In its cutover every Core resource gets an `impl Close`. Eight of them (Arena, Bump, Pool, Fixed, FileScope, FileLock, FileReader and FileWriter) take an empty one, because their runtime handle's drop already releases them. Four can't: TCPStream, UnixStream, TLSStream and WsConn each declare a public fallible `close`. A type can't hold a `close` method beside an `impl Close` whose method is also `close` (Jet.DuplicateDefinition, as Tests/UI/member_namespace_operator_hook_method.stderr shows). Until this ballot is decided, the four stay resources through one Core-identity row in Ownership/Copy.jet, the only resource name list left. This ballot decides how they leave it.
decisions.gist: TCPStream, UnixStream, TLSStream and WsConn each have a public `close` that can fail, so none of them can implement the infallible `Close`. How should they become resources declared like every other one?
decisions.lesson: A resource in Jet implements `Close`: it never copies and closes exactly once, by `close(x)` or at its scope end. `Close.close` can't fail, because a scope end has nowhere to send an error. Four Core streams also have a goodbye that can fail, and each calls it `close`, the name `Close` needs. For TCP and Unix streams that goodbye is a full shutdown. For TLS it is a close_notify alert, and for WebSocket a close frame.
decisions.explainer: Hotel key cards have to come back exactly once, and the hotel collects them when you leave even if you forget. Some guests also want a printed checkout receipt. Today the key-return desk and the receipt printer share one name, so the hotel can't put up a single sign saying 'every key comes back here'. This ballot decides which of the two gets the name.
decisions.story: Ravi writes `Conn`, a socket type for his game server. He gives it a `close` that reports whether the goodbye reached the client. He wants `Conn` to be a resource like Core's `TCPStream`, which never copies and always closes. But writing `impl Close` beside his `close` defines `close` twice. Core's `TCPStream` has the same clash, and it escapes only because the compiler keeps its name on a list. Ravi can't join that list.
decisions.detail:
Sites at 4f02506163e.

The trait. Compiler/Prelude/Traits.jet 250-255: `Close: trait { close: fn(^^self) Never! }`, described as 'Consuming, infallible cleanup'.

The four closes.

- Core/Net/Net.jet 132: `TCPStream.close: fn(self) -[Net]> NetError! { rt.tcp_close(self) }`. Its route, jet_net_tcp_close (JetRuntime NetHandleRoutes.jet 564-575), is `shutdown(fd, SHUT_RDWR)` plus a closed mark, and its only error is a failed shutdown other than ENOTCONN. TCPStream already has `shutdown(how: NetShutdown)` at Net.jet 120, so `close` is `shutdown(.Both)` under a second name.

- Net.jet 196: `UnixStream.close` is the same over jet_net_unix_close (NetUnix.jet 214).

- Core/Net/TLS.jet 184-192: `TLSStream.close: fn(self) -[Net, Time.Wait]> IOError!` sends close_notify, shuts the write side and releases the engine. Closing a closed stream succeeds.

- Core/Net/Ws.jet 41: `WsConn.close: fn(self, code: Int, reason: String) -[Net]> WsError!` sends a close frame, then shuts the connection.

- Free functions mirror three of them: `net.tcp_close` (Net.jet 509), `net.unix_close` (711) and `tls.close` (TLS.jet 426).

What the drop does today. At a scope end and at `close(x)`, the IR runs the type's Close glue and then its Drop (JetIR BuildExpr.jet 119-140). The Close method's receiver is lent to it, and the scope still owns the drop. Each of the four is a runtime handle registered without `clone`, so its drop releases the socket once.

No drop sends a goodbye:

- WsConn's drop (JetRuntime WsRoutes.jet 120-128) drops the stream and frees the buffers without a close frame, so the peer sees 1006, abnormal closure.

- TLSStream's state drop (TLS.jet 237-246) frees the engine and wipes the buffers without close_notify, so the peer can't tell a clean end from a truncation (RFC 8446 section 6.1).

- TCP and Unix drops close the fd.

The close routes are idempotent, so an explicit goodbye followed by the drop never closes twice (the TCP route checks its closed mark; Compiler/JetRuntime/Tests/TCPRoutesWitness.c 191-192 witnesses it).

Close glue carries no effects, since `Close.close` is `Never!` with an empty effect row, so a scope end needs no `Net` or `Time.Wait` authority.

The name `finish`. Core already uses `finish` for 'complete and flush, fallibly, consuming the work'. Examples are `Zstd.finish: fn(self) ZstdFileError!` (Core/Archive/Zstd.jet 378) and the CBOR and CBORStream encoders' `finish`. `Actor.finish` (Core/Actor/Actor.jet 113) is another.

Scale, with the commands in checkInstructions. 230 lines hold `impl Close`. 73 lines spell `tcp_close(` or `unix_close(` and 2 spell `tls.close(`. Method calls `.close()` on a stream are typed calls that grep can't separate from other `close` methods; 28 lines call a two-argument `.close(…, …)`, the WsConn form.

options.name: Delete the TCP and Unix closes; TLS and WebSocket rename theirs to `finish`
options.detail:
TCPStream and UnixStream lose their `close` method, because it is `shutdown(.Both)`, which both already spell. Their fallible goodbye is `shutdown(.Both)`, and the drop releases the fd. TLSStream and WsConn, the two with a protocol goodbye, rename theirs to `finish`. Then all four implement `Close` with an empty body, so `close(stream)` and the scope end release the stream and can't fail.

Beginner path: write nothing, and the stream closes when its scope ends, as a file does. Expert path: call `stream.shutdown(.Both)` on a TCP or Unix stream, or `finish()` on TLS (`finish(code, reason)` on WebSocket), and handle the error.
options.technical:
TCPStream and UnixStream add `impl Close { close: fn(^^self) {} }`, with a comment that the drop releases the fd. Their `close` methods and `net.tcp_close` and `net.unix_close` are deleted, and their callers write `shutdown(.Both)` or nothing. NetShutdown gains no new member. TLSStream and WsConn rename `close` to `finish` with unchanged signatures and bodies, `tls.close` becomes `tls.finish`, and both add the empty `impl Close`. The Core-identity row in Copy.jet goes.

Edge cases:
- A failed `shutdown` or `finish` leaves the handle open, and the drop still releases it once.
- `finish` on a finished TLS stream succeeds, as `close` does today.
- `close(x)` after `finish` is a move of a handle that is already closed.
- A stream held in a struct is released when the struct drops, with no goodbye. Code that needs the goodbye calls `finish` before the struct goes.

options.name: Rename all four goodbyes to `finish`
options.detail: Each of the four renames its fallible method to `finish`, so `close` is free for `impl Close`. `stream.finish()` performs the goodbye and reports its error. `close(stream)` and the scope end release the stream and can't fail.
options.technical: The same as A, except TCPStream and UnixStream keep a fallible goodbye under the name `finish`, beside `shutdown(how)`. `net.tcp_close` and `net.unix_close` become `net.tcp_finish` and `net.unix_finish`. On those two types `finish()` and `shutdown(.Both)` are then the same call under two names.

options.name: A Close whose close can fail
options.detail: `Close` takes an error type, so a stream implements `Close<NetError>` and keeps the name `close`. `close(stream)` returns the error. When the scope ends instead, the error is discarded, because a scope end has nowhere to send it.
options.technical:
Jet traits take type parameters (spec.md 1128) but have no associated types, so this is `Close<E>: trait { close: fn(^^self) E! }`, where today's Close is `Close<Never>`. Every `T: Close` bound has to accept any E: Calls/Direct.jet 488, Statements/Assignments.jet 785, Statements/Bindings.jet 313, and TypeRelations.jet 2605 and 2780.

The 230 `impl Close` sites either migrate or rely on a default. The close bodies also carry effects (`-[Net]`, `-[Net, Time.Wait]`). So either the glue a scope end runs needs those effects too, and every scope that drops a stream gains them. Or the scope end runs a different, effect-free release than `close(x)` runs, and the two paths differ. A discarded error at a scope end is silent unless the language adds a lint for it.

options.name: Close's method takes another name
options.detail: `Close`'s one method becomes `release`. The four streams keep their public fallible `close` and add `impl Close { release: fn(^^self) {} }`. Every other resource renames its Close method.
options.technical: Prelude/Traits.jet's `Close.close` becomes `Close.release`. All 230 `impl Close` sites and the FFI `#Close(close)` form (spec.md 5180) migrate. The builtin `close(x)` either becomes `release(x)` or keeps its name and calls `release`. In the second case `close(stream)` and `stream.close()` do different things on the same value: one releases infallibly, the other sends a fallible goodbye.

options.name: Keep the Core-identity row
options.detail: Nothing changes for callers. The four stay resources because the compiler finds them by their Core identity in one named row. A package type with a fallible `close` can't be a resource without renaming its method.
options.technical: Copy.jet keeps `sema_copy_fallible_close_stream`, which matches core.net's TCPStream, UnixStream, TLSStream and WsConn by declaring identity. It is the one resource name list left after the declared-facts cutover. The closed-list guard keeps it as a kernel row with a reason, and #6852 c1 is met for every list but this one. Under the greenfield cutover rule in AGENTS.md, migration cost counts for little against having one canonical form, which leaves the row's only argument weak.

comparisons.note: A Drop can't fail. BufWriter's Drop attempts a flush and loses its error, so code that needs the error calls `flush()` first. TcpStream has no close method: `shutdown(Both)` is its fallible goodbye, and the drop closes the fd and ignores errors, which is option A for TCP.
io.Closer's Close returns an error. A deferred Close usually throws it away, and code that cares calls Close explicitly and checks it.
comparisons.code:
defer conn.Close()      // error dropped
if err := w.Close(); err != nil { return err }

comparisons.note: A noncopyable type's deinit can't throw. Swift System's FileDescriptor has a separate throwing close() that the caller invokes.

recommendation.why:
A gives `close` one meaning: consume the value and release it, without failing, for every resource and at every scope end. Each fallible goodbye has exactly one name: `shutdown(.Both)`, which TCP and Unix already have, and `finish` for the two protocol goodbyes, the word Core already uses for a fallible flush-and-complete.

The four streams then declare `impl Close` like every other resource, the last resource name list goes, and a package stream can follow the same pattern. B does the same but leaves `finish` and `shutdown(.Both)` as two names for one call on TCP and Unix.
gains: Every resource, in Core or in a package, is declared by `impl Close`, and the last resource name list goes.
`close(x)` means the same thing on every resource and never needs an effect or an error path.
Every fallible goodbye stays, under one name each: `shutdown(.Both)` for TCP and Unix, and `finish` for TLS and WebSocket, matching Zstd, CBOR and Actor.
Only two types gain a new method name.

losses.loss: A WsConn that is never finished sends no close frame, so the peer sees 1006. A TLSStream that is never finished sends no close_notify, so the peer can't tell a clean end from a truncation.
losses.mitigation: This is today's behavior too: the drops skip both goodbyes now (WsRoutes.jet 120-128, TLS.jet 237-246), so A changes nothing at run time. The doc comments on TLSStream and WsConn say to call `finish` for a clean end. A later hint can flag a TLSStream or WsConn that reaches its scope end without `finish`.

losses.loss: Callers of the TCP and Unix closes and of `net.tcp_close` and `net.unix_close` migrate: 73 lines spell the free functions, and the method calls come on top.
losses.mitigation: The type checker finds every one, since the methods no longer exist. Each becomes `shutdown(.Both)`, keeping the error, or is deleted where the scope end already closes the stream.

losses.loss: `finish` is a new word on the net surface.
losses.mitigation: It is Core's existing word for a fallible flush-and-complete (Zstd, CBOR, Actor), and it appears only on the two types with a protocol goodbye.

whyNot.reason: It gives TCP and Unix two names for `shutdown(.Both)`.

A scope end has nowhere to send the error, and the close bodies carry `Net` and `Time.Wait` effects. So either every scope that drops a stream gains those effects, or the scope end and `close(x)` run different code. It also widens every `T: Close` bound.
It renames all 230 Close impls and the FFI form to spare four methods, and it leaves `close(x)` and `x.close()` doing different things on the same stream.
It keeps a name list the declared-facts ballot set out to remove, so a package type with a fallible goodbye still can't be a resource without renaming its method.

recommendation.tradeoff: Two types gain `finish`, two lose a duplicate `close`, and their callers migrate. In return, `close` has one meaning across every resource and each goodbye has one name.

decisions.title: When a ProcessSpec builder takes a named spec that is used again, is that an error, a silent copy, or a copy on every step
decisions.situation:
Card #6851 c5 asks that ProcessHandles.jet move to Core declarations and be deleted. The launch steps (`plan`, `run`, `run_checked`, `spawn`) already moved to `impl ProcessSpec` without a behavior change, since they only read the spec.

That leaves 22 receivers: the 21 builders such as `cwd`, `arg` and `env`, and `keep_open`'s receiver. Today the compiler checks them with Jet's law for an unmarked owning position (Ownership/Checks.jet:3701). A bare name there moves at its last use, and a later use becomes a share, materialized as a copy.

D-CALLSITE-MARK2=A rules the opposite for calls: a value passed to a take parameter and used again is an error, and a call never copies on its own. All 108 `fn(^^self` methods in Core obey it. A declared builder `fn(^^self, …)` therefore turns a later use into E0209, as a probe with a `^^ProcessSpec` parameter confirms.
decisions.gist: When a builder takes a named spec that is used again, what happens? A: E0209 with a `.copy()` fix. B: a silent copy for ProcessSpec only. C: a copy on every step. D: a silent copy for every take receiver. E: a change in place.
decisions.lesson: Rust's `Command` changes the command in place (`&mut self`), and Rust builders that take `self` need an explicit `.clone()` to keep the original. Swift value types copy only when a shared value is changed.
decisions.explainer: A recipe card: writing a change on it uses up the card. Today a clerk photocopies the card first whenever you look at the old one again, but only at the process desk. The shop has five choices. It can stop that clerk and ask you to photocopy on purpose (A), or keep the clerk at that desk only (B). It can always photocopy before every change (C), hire the clerk for every desk (D), or write the change on the card itself (E).
decisions.story:
Ana scripts a checkout of each branch:

```
base: process.cmd(["git"]).cwd(repo)
loop name in branches {
    base.arg("checkout").arg(name).run_checked() ?? return
}
```

Under A, `base.arg` is E0209 ("`ProcessSpec.arg` takes `base`, but `base` is used again later"), because the loop's next pass reads `base` again. The fix in the error is `base.copy().arg("checkout")`. Under B and D her loop stays, and each pass copies `base` without showing it. Under C it stays too, and each pass copies twice, once per builder. Under E the first pass runs `git checkout main`, and the second runs `git checkout main dev`, because the args pile up on `base`.
decisions.detail:
Census (git grep plus a scan, on 4b640637407). The scan walks every tracked .jet file and follows each name bound to a ProcessSpec. Such a name comes from `cmd(…)`, from one of the 78 functions that return ProcessSpec, from a ProcessSpec parameter, or from a builder on such a name. It reports a builder whose receiver is read again later in the function, or in a loop the name was bound outside of. It found 106 builder sites on a named spec.

99 of them are the rebinding form `spec = spec.env(…)`, which every option keeps. 5 sit on branches that never meet (TestReuse.jet:85/93, CacheEndpoints.jet:463/464, ShellEnv.jet:158/159, CensusSnap2.jet:196, Regression.jet:200/202).

Two read a spec again after a builder:
- Compiler/JetCLI/Source/CLI/NativeTests.jet:544 then :569, where `clean` feeds `alone` and then `batch_spec`.
- Core/Process/Process.jet:839 then :842, which is Core's own test of the share.

The loop case that the ProcessHandles comment names (`clean.env(…).run()` in a loop) is already written `alone.copy().env(…)` at NativeTests.jet:626 and :659. No Docs or guide sample reuses a spec; the two in core-library.md (:3102, :3333) chain on a fresh `process.cmd(…)`.

The 21 builders are `cwd`, `arg`, `args_extend`, `env`, `env_remove`, `env_clear`, `output_limit`, `memory_limit`, `memory_scope`, `open_file_limit` and `cpu_affinity`. The others are `io_priority`, `io_idle`, `detached`, `terminal`, `under`, `stdin`, `stdout`, `stderr`, `timeout` and `cpu_time_limit`. Their share calls sit at ProcessHandles.jet:233-236 and :339-342, and the 108 `fn(^^self` methods are in 43 Core files.

Beginner path: chain builders on `process.cmd(…)` and run. Every option keeps that form. A beginner meets the choice only when one base serves two runs, as in the story. Under A, E0209 names the call and the `.copy()` fix. Under B and D nothing is shown. Under E the mistake is silent.

Expert path: build one spec and launch it many times in a hot loop. Under A the copy is written at the one place it happens. Under B and D it is hidden. Under C it is paid on every step, also when the spec is never reused.

Whole mechanism: sema_ownership_mark_unmarked_move has nine callers. Six are owning positions under the general law: Checks.jet:3912 and :7378, CopySites.jet:631 and :684, Views.jet:31, and Calls/Checking.jet:1567 (a variadic list element). Every option keeps those.

Three are calls: ProcessHandles.jet:234 (the 21 builders), ProcessHandles.jet:340 (keep_open's receiver) and Calls/Static.jet:974. Static.jet:974 covers a builtin static with no declared conventions, `Shared.new(x)`; `Shared{x}` is a field position. A and C delete the two ProcessHandles calls. D replaces them with one general receiver rule. B keeps them. Static.jet:974 is outside c5 and follows the chosen law when `Shared` is declared in Core.

The runtime leaves (`rt.spec_cwd(spec: ^^ProcessSpec, …)`) take the spec, so a Core body that only reads `self` must copy before the leaf (C).

Related ratified decisions, checked: D-CORE-PROCFILE1 (`.stdout(.File(^stdout))`), D-CORE-PROCINHERIT1 (`.keep_open(^tool, at: 3)`), D-CORE-PROCGROUP1, D-CORE-PROCIDENT1 and D-CORE-PROCSIGNAL1. They fix builder and launch spellings, never the receiver or a reuse after a builder. Their samples chain on a fresh `process.cmd(…)` temporary, so A, B, C and D leave them unchanged. E breaks them unless its builders return a copy (see E). D-CALLSITE-MARK2=A ("a call never copies on its own") is the law that B keeps an exception to, and that D amends.

The two repository reuses (NativeTests.jet:569 and Core's Process test at :839) are migrated in the same patch. c5 is met.
