options.name: Every take receiver is an unmarked owning position
options.detail:
Builders are `fn(^^self, …)` as in A. The general receiver check then gives every `^^self` receiver on a bare name the owning-position law: it moves at its last use, and a later use shares, materialized as a copy. That covers ProcessSpec, the 108 other Core take receivers and every user one. Programs stay, a chain on a temporary copies nothing, and c5 is met because the law lives in the general receiver path.

A value that can't be copied (a resource with Close, a #SingleUse value) still fails at the later use, as at any owning position (CopySites.jet:334). But `buf.seal()` followed by a read of `buf` now copies the whole buffer without a word where it was an error. D-CALLSITE-MARK2's "a call never copies on its own" becomes "a call never copies an argument on its own".
options.technical: The method-receiver path of the ownership check calls sema_ownership_mark_unmarked_move for a bare-name `^^self` receiver instead of sema_ownership_mark_move. ProcessHandles.jet's builder path goes as in A. Every case that pins E0209 on a take receiver (Tests/UI and Tests/Cases) changes to a share.
options.code:
status: base.arg("status")  // copies base, read below
log: base.arg("log")

options.name: Builders change the spec in place (`fn(^self, …)`)
options.detail:
This is the shape of Rust's `Command`. Jet has no write borrow as a return value: no Core function returns `^T`, and Spellings has no form for one. A builder that changes `self` in place can't hand the same spec back for the next link of a chain.

It must either return nothing, which breaks every chain on `process.cmd(…)` in the five ratified samples, or return a copy, which copies on every step as in C. Either way, `status: base.arg("status")` followed by `log: base.arg("log")` silently runs `git status log`, because both args land on `base`.
options.technical: 22 builders become `fn(^self, …) Never!`, and every chain is respelled as statements on a `:=` binding.
options.code:
spec := process.cmd(["git"])
spec.arg("status")
spec.run()

comparisons.note: `std::process::Command` builders take `&mut self` and change the command in place (E's shape), so a base reused for two runs carries both runs' args unless the program clones it first. Builders that take `self`, such as `std::thread::Builder::name`, need an explicit `.clone()` to keep the original. That is A's shape.
Value types copy on write: changing a value that is still shared copies it first, without a mark. That is B's and D's behavior. Jet materializes the copy at the share site.

recommendation.why: A gives these 22 receivers the law D-CALLSITE-MARK2 ratified for every call and the 108 other Core take receivers follow: a call never copies on its own. It meets c5 by deleting the builder path and migrates the 2 repository reuses. E0209 names the beginner's one mistake and shows `.copy()`. D also gives one law and meets c5, but it adds hidden copies at every take receiver in Jet. That reverses a ratified decision for 108 Core methods and all user code, to spare 2 call sites.
gains: One law for every call: a take receiver never copies on its own.
ProcessHandles.jet's builder path and its two share calls are deleted (c5).
No copy unless the program writes one; chains on `process.cmd(…)` copy nothing.

losses.loss: A spec read again after a builder is E0209: 2 sites in the repository (NativeTests.jet:569, Core's Process test at :839) and any user script that reuses a base.
losses.mitigation: E0209 names the call and shows `base.copy().arg(…)`. The slice migrates both repository sites.

whyNot.reason: It keeps the only Core call receivers that copy on their own, as an exception to D-CALLSITE-MARK2, and it amends c5 to keep that exception in the compiler.
It copies the spec on every builder step, also on the common chain that never reuses it, and raises the copy ratchet by 22.

It amends D-CALLSITE-MARK2 for 108 Core take receivers and all user code: a read after `seal`, `close` or `finish` silently copies the value where today it is an error. All that to spare 2 sites in the repository.
Jet can't return the receiver as a write borrow, so either every ratified chain sample breaks or every step copies. A reused base also silently piles up args.

recommendation.tradeoff: An explicit `.copy()` at the 2 known reuse sites and in any user script that reuses a base, for one call law and no hidden copies.

decisions.title: How does card #6851 meet D-CORE-CHECK1's budget of 1 µs per heard call?
decisions.situation:
D-CORE-CHECK1 says rule calls go to the build-time process in batches, within 1 µs per call. Card #6851 criterion n=22 holds rule dispatch to that budget. One more heard call costs at most 1 µs, measured as (time with 20000 heard calls − time with one) / 19999. A module's first heard call, which builds and runs the rule program, costs at most 25 ms.

Measured on stage44e518, which carries all four c21 dispatch slices, one more heard call costs about 19.8 µs. That is the median of the paired per-run marginals; 7 interleaved runs and 8 quiet runs both give 19.4 to 19.8 µs. About 10 µs is sema hearing the call, and 9 to 10 µs is the rule run in the compile-time child. The rule body costs about 43 ns at O0. The first heard call's rule run takes 28 to 31 ms. So n=22 is not met at either bound, and the gap is dispatch, not the rule.

The work that reaches 1 µs is the compile-time child's: one warm child per compile, values through shared memory, no program compiled per batch. Card #6798 owns it; its c2 is open, and its burn-down estimate is weeks.
decisions.gist: Today's n=22 bounds are not met: one more heard call costs about 19.8 µs against 1 µs, and the first heard call 28 to 31 ms against 25 ms. B would relax the 25 ms first-call target to 35 ms. Should n=22 move unchanged to #6798 (A), close at 25 µs and 35 ms with steps on #6798 (B), or hold #6851 open (C)?
decisions.lesson: The rule's own work is about 43 ns per call at O0. The microseconds go to hearing the call and carrying it to the child and its answer back, and Jet's invariants fix that the child is a separate native process.
decisions.explainer: A post office promised to sort each letter in one second. Stamping takes a twentieth of a second. The rest is walking each sack to a back room. The building crew already plans a faster back room for every department. The office can hand the one-second promise itself to the crew (A), or count today's walk as done and add the promise to the crew's plan (B). It can wait for the crew (C), change the promise (D), or sort letters at the counter, which the office's rules forbid (E).
decisions.story: A package with 20000 calls to a `#Lit` function checks about 0.4 s slower than the same package with an unmarked function (19.8 µs × 20000). At 1 µs it would be 0.02 s slower. Its first heard call adds about 30 ms whatever the count.
decisions.detail:
Evidence. All runs use stage44e518 = $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/tmp/orch/stage44e518-chain/s1/jet, built from the tree $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/tmp/orch/stage44e518-exp. That tree carries the four c21 slices (`git apply --check -R` returns 0 for each). It also carries #6798's Pillar 3 fast-O0 stubs and shared-memory batch load, on dev bf843c6d0b6.

The probe is the n=22 rule-dispatch probe. It has a `priv Lit` Marker whose `check` rejects a computed first argument (E0635), `#Lit f: fn(x: Int) -> Int`, and a `main` of 20000 `t += …(i)` lines. n20k calls `f` on every line; n1 calls `f` once and an unmarked `g` on the rest; n0 is n1 without `#Lit`.

The files have the same 20028 lines, so line cost cancels. An unmarked control pair, n1 and n20k with the `#Lit` line removed, differs by −2.8 to 0 µs per call in 6 of 7 runs.

1. `jet perf run -A wrap.jet --out … -- $J <probe>/main.jet` and `jet perf compare`, 5 runs each at load 43 on 32 cores. Wall n0: 712 to 971 ms; n1: 813 to 896 ms; n20k: 1214 to 1354 ms. Paired marginal: 15.9, 18.1, 20.3, 20.8, 23.8 µs. `jet perf compare n1 n20k` reports wall 1064 → 1470 ms, a 3803 bp regression. The wrapper's samples don't see the child compiler's functions, so the split comes from spans.

2. `jet check --trace=FILE` spans, B/E events paired per thread. Eight quiet pairs earlier: marginal 14.0 to 22.0 µs, median 19.4 (two runs during load spikes read 59 and 62 and are left out). Seven interleaved runs today at load 26 to 28: paired marginal 16.9, 19.3, 19.3, 19.8, 25.4, 25.8, 32.9 µs, median 19.8.

Split of the marginal (medians): sema.bodies is about 10 to 11 µs, which is hearing the call. The marker's check span is about 9 to 10 µs. Of that, comptime.bodies is 8 to 8.4 µs and comptime.body.pending 1.2 to 1.4 µs. comptime.land.open is about 0.55 µs and sema.facts about 0.21 µs.

3. The fixed half, re-measured. On n1 the marker's check span takes 28 to 31 ms over the quiet runs (comptime.bodies 18 to 19 ms of it). The whole-run difference n1 − n0 has a median of about 16 ms over quiet pairs. But single pairs spread from −68 to +63 ms at load 26, wider than the bound itself, so only the span can prove a bound. Runs at load 65 to 98 were discarded.

Cost against the compile-speed target. #5479's target is 30M lines/s from cold, about 33 ns per line. 19.8 µs is about 600 lines' worth, a 25 µs bound about 760, and 1 µs about 30. At one heard call per 1000 lines, 19.8 µs adds about 20 ns per line, 60% of the whole budget; 1 µs adds 1 ns (3%). At one per 100 lines it is 198 ns per line (6× the budget) against 10 ns.

A 1000-line router with 200 heard route registrations [INFERENCE: each route line is a heard call] costs about 4 ms against its 33 µs budget (120×). At 1 µs it costs 0.2 ms (6×). The first heard call's 30 ms is about 900k lines' worth. A 100k-line program with one heard rule spends about 9× its whole budget on it, and 25 ms is still 7.6×. Rule-heavy programs (routers, services, data schemas) pay both halves.

Why only a child. AGENTS.md I9: compile-time code runs natively at O0 in a child of the compiler, and no interpreter or second code generator serves any tier. D-EXEC2=A makes the child live only for one compile. So the in-process shape of Zig's comptime or Rust's Clippy is not open to Jet without an I9 exception (option E). The path to 1 µs is the warm per-compile child #6798 c2 builds, plus cheaper hearing.

The r1 claim that the rule program is compiled at O1 or O2 and stays resident was wrong. Under I9 it runs at O0, and nothing survives the compile.

The steps to 1 µs, each with the span it removes today:
1. Hearing (sema.bodies, about 10 µs): sema hears each call into compact rows, with no probe, key text or source row per call.
2. Batch (comptime.bodies, about 8 µs): rows reach the warm child as bytes through #6798's shared region, with no data literal compiled and loaded per batch.

3. Program (part of the fixed 28 to 31 ms): one rule program per rule set is compiled once per compile at O0 on the copy-and-patch path (#6795). It stays in the warm child for that compile.
4. Landing (comptime.body.pending and comptime.land.open, about 1.9 µs): a batch lands as one value that its sites read by row.

Who carries the steps. Under A, n=22 itself moves to #6798 unchanged, and the four steps are the plan for meeting it. Under B the four steps and an end criterion become #6798 criteria. Owner-only choice inside B: the hearing step goes on #6798, not on #5479. It is paid only by heard calls and exists only to feed the child. #5479's sema.bodies phase root (c16) is measured on gate programs with no heard calls, so a #5479 criterion could not show it.

Owner order. A follow-up goes on the card that owns the area. The remaining n=22 work is the compile-time child's, which #6798 owns. A follows that order whole: the criterion moves with its bounds to the card that does the work and proves it. B splits it: #6851 keeps a relaxed bound, and #6798 gets five criteria that restate n=22's goal. So the owner order favors A.

A against B. B ships a bound that is enforced now: dispatch can't regress past 25 µs or 35 ms while #6798 works. A enforces nothing until #6798 lands its steps, but it weakens no bound. B also relaxes the 25 ms first-call target, which today's runs don't meet, to 35 ms.

Beginner path: nothing to write. A beginner meets rules only through markers a package ships, and sees the same errors under every option. Under A to D they pay about 20 µs per heard call until #6798 lands its steps; only E removes the cost without #6798.

Expert path: a package author who ships a `check` rule. Under A they see the 1 µs and 25 ms goal on #6798. Under B they see the bound #6851 proves, with 1 µs tracked on #6798. Under D, 25 µs becomes the language's promise, so a rule-heavy package plans around it.

options.name: Move n=22 unchanged to #6798
options.detail:
n=22 moves to #6798 with its bounds unchanged: at most 1 µs marginal per heard call and at most 25 ms for a module's first heard call, on the same probe. #6798 then owns both the work and the proof. #6851 closes with no bound weakened. No new criteria restate n=22's goal; the four steps in the detail are the plan for meeting it.

Until #6798 lands its steps, nothing enforces a dispatch bound: today's 19.8 µs and 28 to 31 ms are recorded, not held. D-CORE-CHECK1 keeps 1 µs.
options.technical: `tower card criteria 6851 --move 22 --to 6798`. No card text changes, and no code changes beyond the queued c21 slices.
options.code:
tower card criteria 6851 --move 22 --to 6798
// #6798 n=22: <= 1 µs marginal, <= 25 ms first heard call

options.name: Close n=22 at the measured bound; the 1 µs steps become criteria on #6798
options.detail:
n=22's bounds become the ones the c21 slices are measured to reach, with room for the measured spread. The marginal bound is at most 25 µs per heard call (measured 19.4 and 19.8). It is the median of the paired per-run marginals over 7 or more interleaved n1/n20k `jet check --trace` runs. The first-call bound is at most 35 ms for the first heard call's rule run (measured 28 to 31 ms). It is the marker's check span on n1, median over 7 or more runs.

Today's 25 ms first-call target is not met, and B relaxes it to 35 ms. If dev reads above either bound, n=22 stays open and the next #6798 step closes it.

D-CORE-CHECK1 keeps 1 µs. Card #6798 gains five criteria: the four steps in the detail, each proved by its span on the n=22 probe. The fifth is an end criterion that the n=22 probe reads at most 1 µs marginal and 25 ms first-call. No new card is filed.
options.technical: Card text of #6851 n=22 changes from 1 µs and 25 ms to 25 µs and 35 ms, with the measuring rule above. #6798 gains c6 to c10. No code changes beyond the queued c21 slices.

options.name: Keep n=22 at 1 µs and 25 ms; #6851 stays open until #6798 lands the steps
options.detail: The four steps land on #6798, as under B, and #6851 waits for them. On today's probe they must remove about 19 µs per call and 5 or more ms of first-call cost. #6798's c2 is open and its burn-down estimate is weeks, so G1's metaprogramming card stays open for compile-speed work that changes nothing rules can say.
options.technical: No text changes. #6798 gains the same step criteria as B; #6851 n=22 closes when its probe reads 1 µs.

// #6851 n=22: <= 1 µs, <= 25 ms

options.name: Restate D-CORE-CHECK1's budget as 25 µs per heard call
options.detail: The decision's budget changes from 1 µs to 25 µs per heard call, and n=22 closes on the same slices and bounds as B. No card carries 1 µs; #6798 keeps only its own criteria.

options.code:
marginal = median over runs of (t(n20k) - t(n1)) / 19999
// budget: <= 25 µs

options.name: Run check rules in the compiler, by an I9 exception
options.detail: An owner-ratified I9 exception lets check rules, and only they, run in-process in an evaluator inside the compiler, as Zig's comptime and Rust's Clippy do. A heard call becomes a function call with no child, batch or landing. The exception must name the tier it excludes: check rules would have a second meaning path besides the native O0 child every other compile-time function uses.
options.technical: New: an evaluator for the check-rule subset in JetSema or JetEval, with its own parity tests against the native child. #6798's child work stays for every other compile-time function.
options.code:
// a rule's check runs in the compiler's evaluator
// n=22: <= 1 µs reachable without #6798

comparisons.note: comptime code runs in the compiler's own interpreter, so a call's check is a function call. Jet's I9 forbids an interpreter, so this is option E's shape, not the child shape of A to D.
Lints run in-process over the checked HIR, with no process per call. Also option E's shape; not open under I9.
comparisons.code: impl LateLintPass for MyLint { fn check_expr(&mut self, cx: &LateContext, e: &Expr) { … } }

comparisons.note: Procedural macros run in a separate proc-macro server process that the IDE keeps for its session and sends requests to. That is the shape Jet allows: #6798's warm child, kept for one compile, with values through shared memory instead of serialized messages.
comparisons.code:
// rust-analyzer spawns `rust-analyzer proc-macro` once and sends
// ExpandMacro requests to it over a pipe for every macro call

recommendation.why: The owner order puts a follow-up on the card that owns the area, and the remaining n=22 work is the child work #6798 owns. A moves n=22 there unchanged, so #6798 owns both the work and the proof. #6851 closes now with no bound weakened and no criteria restating n=22's goal. B ships an enforced 25 µs bound, but it relaxes the unmet 25 ms target and splits one goal across two cards.
gains: The 1 µs and 25 ms bounds stay whole, on the card that owns the child.
#6851 closes now, so weeks of compile-speed work don't hold G1.
Each step has its span on the same probe, so progress shows per step.

losses.loss: Until #6798 lands the steps, a heard call costs about 20 µs (600 lines' worth at 30M lines/s). A module's first heard call costs about 30 ms. Rule-heavy programs such as routers pay that many times over the speed budget.
losses.mitigation: Only calls a marker's `check` rule hears pay it. #6798 cuts the cost in order of size: hearing (10 µs) and batch (8 µs) first.

losses.loss: No dispatch bound is enforced until #6798 lands its steps, so dispatch could regress unseen.
losses.mitigation: Today's 19.8 µs and 28 to 31 ms are recorded here. #6798 measures every step on the same n=22 probe, so a regression shows at its next step.

whyNot.reason: Its enforced bound is a real gain, but it relaxes the unmet 25 ms target to 35 ms and restates n=22's goal as five criteria on #6798. Its 25 µs margin is also thin: single runs read up to 32.9 µs under load. The owner order puts the whole criterion on the owning card.
It keeps G1 open for weeks on #6798's child work, which changes nothing rules can say.
It drops a goal the 43 ns rule body shows is reachable, and makes 600 lines' worth per heard call the language's promise against a 30M lines/s target.
It reverses I9 for one feature: check rules would get a second meaning path and their own parity tests, while #6798's child serves every other compile-time function anyway.

recommendation.tradeoff: About 20 µs per heard call and 30 ms per first heard call, with no enforced bound, until #6798 lands its steps. In return G1 closes now, and n=22 stays whole on the card that owns the work.

decisions.hybrid: A now, with E held back: if #6798's steps stall above a few µs, an I9 exception for check rules alone can be balloted then with #6798's measured floor in hand.

decisions.title: Who picks the form behind `tree.worker`, `tree.send` and `tree.call` when one name covers several Core functions
decisions.situation:
Card #6851 c4 asks that the compiler's service checker (Sema/Calls/Services.jet) move to Core declarations and be deleted. Five ratified decisions fix the spellings it serves. D-SERVICE-WORKER1 says `tree.worker` takes an ordinary function and returns `Endpoint<Email>`. D-SERVICE-REPLY1 says `tree.call(pricing, quote)` waits for the answer. D-SERVICE-KEEP1 puts `state:` on the worker line, and D-SERVICE-BATCH1 puts `batch:` and `wait:` there. D-SERVICE-CURRENT1 says a typed address reaches the current route on every call.

So one name, `tree.worker`, stands for seven Core functions: `worker` (the String mailbox, `fn()`), `typed_worker` (`fn(Q) -> R`), `stateful_worker` (`fn(^S, Q) -> R`) and `batched_worker` (`fn([Q])`). Each typed one has a durable form, taken when Q implements Decode. The handler's shape and the labels pick one. `tree.send` and `tree.send_durable` take a String address or a typed `Endpoint<Q, R>`, and the message type follows the address. Jet gives each name one declaration. A check rule can refuse a call but can't send it to another function.
decisions.gist: Does the compiler keep picking the service form behind one name, or do the ratified service spellings change, or does the language grow the features one generic Core worker would need?
decisions.lesson: Languages without overloading, such as Go, Zig and Rust, give each shape its own name or make the shape a type parameter. Languages with overloading, such as Swift, C++ and Kotlin, let one name cover several declarations. C++ also lets one template pick its form with `if constexpr`, because it checks each instance's taken branch separately. Jet checks a generic body once, both `#if` arms included.
decisions.explainer: A shop has one counter sign, Orders. Behind it, a clerk sends each customer to the right desk by what they carry. The shop can keep the clerk (A), put a sign on every desk (B), or merge the desks (C). It can teach the building to route people itself (D), or hire one clerk from the shop's own staff who can read every customer's parcel (E). That last clerk needs eyes the staff don't have yet.
decisions.story: Ana writes `pricing: tree.worker("pricing", price, capacity: 8)` and then `tree.call(pricing, 2)`, as the service guide shows. Ben writes `tree.worker("cart", add_item, state: Cart{}, capacity: 8)`. Under A, D and E their programs and errors stay the same. Under B both respell their worker lines, and Ana's call becomes `pricing.call(tree, 2)`. Under C Ben's line becomes `tree.stateful_worker(…)`.
decisions.detail:
Services.jet holds 616 lines. Each part left picks a callee or a result type by an argument's type. sema_services_typed_worker (:297) picks one of the six typed workers by the handler's shape, the labels, and whether the message type meets Decode (sema_services_type_meets, :383). It also writes the handler's name into the call as a String argument.

sema_services_typed_delivery (:398) sends a typed address to typed_send, call or typed_send_durable. sema_check_service_tree_method (:436) keeps the String `worker`. sema_call_try_job_queue_method (:561) does the same for #Job queues.

Why two declarations of `send` don't work. Batch 21's first cut of #6851 c4 (land/6851-c4-services-a.patch) made Core declare `ServiceTree.send(&self, endpoint: ServiceEndpoint, message: String)` and `send_durable(…, *, key: String)`. A declared method is checked before the special routes, so the typed route never ran.

Examples/Concurrency/ServiceWorkers and ServiceWorkersInMemory (O0/O1/O2) stopped on "Jet.ValueTypeMismatch: `send` wants `ServiceEndpoint` for argument 1, but this is `Endpoint<Email, Unit>`". So did the cases Concurrency/durable_typed_receipts_cross_a_handoff and typed_workers_take_the_worker_methods. `send_durable` failed the same way with `Endpoint<Int, Int>`. The UI tests service_send_wrong_message and service_send_replying_endpoint lost their texts.

One generic `send<E>(endpoint: E, message: …)` can't help either. Its message type would have to come from E, and Jet has no associated types, while a trait bound with a type-parameter argument is E0104. The r2 patch (land/6851-c4-services-a-r2.msg) therefore runs the typed route ahead of the declared method.

Why one generic Core worker doesn't work today (option E). G1 shipped compile-time `#if` over `T.reflect()` per generic instance (a79988747df, a5b846f8878, f0a643aec2d). So a generic Core `worker<H>(name, handler: H, *, state:, batch:, wait:, capacity:)` could in principle pick its form by reflecting on H. Probes in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/tmp/g1gen2/probe/svc, checked with the stage44e518 compiler, show where it stops.

1. p1: calling the handler in the taken arm, `#if is_function(TypeId{H}) { return handler(message) }`, fails with "Jet.CalledNonFunction: `handler` is H, not a function". Jet checks both arms against the generic H (metaprogramming.md section 2), and no bound makes H callable.

2. p2: a type table can't name a function-type arm, let alone bind Q and R from it. `if H == { fn(Q) -> R -> … }` fails with "Jet.InvalidStatement: Expected `{` to open the lambda body, found `->`". A parenthesized arm fails the same way.

3. p3: the result `Endpoint<Q, R>` can't come from H. A computed type alias over a type parameter, `MessageOf<H>: Message #run { if H == Int -> Quote else -> Order }`, fails with "Jet.UnsupportedCompileTimeValue: This condition isn't a `Bool` decided while building". A computed alias chooses only by its number parameters and the module's constants.

4. p4: one parameter type covering `fn(Q) -> R` and `fn(^S, Q) -> R` fails with "Jet.InvalidUnionMember: `fn(S, Q) -> R` can't be a union member". Anonymous unions hold no function types or type parameters.

5. p5: the ratified handler-name capture, `handler_name: String{#run handler.reflect().name}`, fails with "Jet.UnsupportedCompileTimeValue: `#run value` is used inside a larger value, which this compiler does not support yet". D-RULE-REWRITE1=A ratified it, but it is not built.

The labels themselves are expressible as optional parameters (`state: S?{None}`, `batch: Int?{None}`, `wait: Duration?{None}`). What can't be said is that S is the handler's first parameter type, which is item 2 again.

A pick works in Core today when the shape is fixed and only a type parameter inside it varies. p6, a generic `stamp_of<T>(row: Int, callback: fn(Int) -> T)` with `if T == { Int -> … Stamp -> … else -> 0 }`, runs and prints 5 and 4000. The worker and send picks vary the outer shape (one, two or a list of parameters, a String or a typed address), which is the case above.

Whole-mechanism inventory: every place the compiler picks one of several Core forms behind one name. There are three groups, and the language's own syntax is a fourth case that no option changes.

First group: the outer shape varies, and Core has no mechanism for it today.
- `tree.worker`: Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Calls/Services.jet: sema_check_service_tree_method (:436), sema_services_typed_worker (:297), sema_services_worker_shape (:237), sema_services_type_meets (:383). Calls/Core.jet:670 is the core.service `worker` route. In Core/Service/Service.jet: worker (:5249), typed_worker (:5328), stateful_worker (:5334), batched_worker (:5341), durable_worker (:5348), durable_stateful_worker (:5352), durable_batched_worker (:5356).

- `tree.send`, `tree.call`, `tree.send_durable`: Services.jet sema_services_typed_delivery (:398), called from Sema/Expressions.jet:5016 in sema_expr_check_method_on. In Service.jet: typed_send (:5573), call (:5583), typed_send_durable (:5594), ServiceTree.send (:678) and send_durable (:680).
- #Job queues: Services.jet sema_job_queue_function (:534) and sema_call_try_job_queue_method (:561), which write the handler's name as the worker path does.

- `data.query` over `[Row]`, `DataTracked<Row, Key>` or `DataStream<Row>`: Calls/Data.jet:1363-1391 (query_source role). Row sits inside a varying outer type, so it is the same case. This ballot decides only the service sites; `data.query` meets the same fence rule if its own criterion keeps its spelling.

Second group: a fixed shape with one varying type parameter. A type table serves it in Core today, as p6 shows, and A's fence does not cover these.
- grouped `sum` by its value's number type: Calls/Data.jet:624 and sema_data_group_sum_role (:708).
- `Stream.with_event_time` by the callback's result, Int or DateTime: Calls/Data.jet:657-701.

Third group: arity picks. One Core declaration with an optional parameter serves them, and A's fence does not cover these.
- `net.unix_connect` and `tls.client`: Calls/Core.jet sema_call_core_normalized_source_record (:1089) and :664-670.
- `ProcessSpec.terminal`: Calls/ProcessHandles.jet:266.
- the inline channel's new or bounded form: Calls/StreamHandles.jet:558.
- `live.invalidate` of one key or the whole source: Calls/Live.jet:178-182.

Language syntax, not Core forms: the task forms (JetFoundation AST/Expressions.jet TaskForm :625 and task_form_of :680; Sema/Ownership/TaskGroups.jet). They are named spellings of the language, as `#if` is, so no option here changes them.

Under A, the fence admits only the first group: a ratified spelling that puts several outer shapes under one name. The other two groups leave the compiler under the criteria that own their files, with a type table or an optional parameter. Under D or E the first group could leave as well.

Beginner path: write `tree.worker("name", handler, capacity: 8)` with any handler shape, then `tree.send` or `tree.call` with the address. That is unchanged under A, D and E. Under B the beginner must learn six worker names first, and under C two. Errors under A stay the ones the service guide shows.

Expert path: a package author who wants their own `worker`-like API with the same pick. Under A they can't write it today; they write one function per shape, as B does. Under D they declare an overload set. Under E they write one generic function with reflection.

options.name: Keep every ratified spelling; the compiler keeps the pick for outer-shape picks only
options.detail:
This amends no decision. It amends card #6851 c4, which isn't met as written: the service pick is language-owned under the five spelling decisions, as the task forms are. Services.jet moves out of Sema/Calls to a language-owned home, and the fence admits only picks whose outer shape varies under one ratified name (the first inventory group).

The shape refusals become Core check rules where a rule can say them: the worker name, the capacity, the batch size and the handler's identity, read through the argument's FunctionInfo. The rest of the pick stays in the compiler.

ServiceTree gains `#ServiceWorkerShape`, as `#ServiceGroupShape` exists. c4's text changes to: its refusals move to Core rules; its dispatch is language-owned. Fixed-shape and arity picks are not fenced and leave under their own criteria.

options.detail:
This amends D-SERVICE-KEEP1 and D-SERVICE-BATCH1. `tree.worker` keeps only the `fn(Q) -> R` shape and returns `Endpoint<Q, R>`. The old `fn()` worker that reads a String mailbox is retired, and its runtime moves onto the typed inbox, so one generic `send`, `call` and `send_durable` serve every address.

Workers that keep state or take batches still need their own names, so `state:` and `batch:` leave the worker line. The durable form still needs a pick on Q: Decode.

options.name: A language overload set picks the form
options.detail:
This keeps every ratified service spelling but adds a language feature that needs its own language ballot. A declaration may join an overload set. The call picks the one member whose parameters accept its arguments, and a bound such as `Q: Decode` ranks a member higher.

Every tool must learn overload sets: the language server, the formatter, docs, reflection and check rules. It reopens one declaration per name.
options.technical: New: overload sets with ranking by bounds. Needs D-RULE-REWRITE1=A built for `handler_name`.
options.code:
#Overload worker: fn<Q, R>(^self, name: String, handler: ^^fn(Q) -> R Err!, *, capacity: Int) -> Endpoint<Q, R> ServiceError!
#Overload worker: fn<S, Q, R>(^self, name: String, handler: ^^fn(^S, Q) -> R Err!, *, state: ^^S, capacity: Int) -> Endpoint<Q, R> ServiceError!

options.name: One generic Core worker that reflects on its handler
options.detail:
This keeps every ratified service spelling and one declaration per name. Core declares one `worker<H>` whose body picks the form with a compile-time `#if` over `H.reflect()`, as G1's per-instance `#if` allows, and one `send` and `call` likewise.

It needs three language features that Jet doesn't have, each its own language ballot (probes p1 to p4 in the detail). First, the taken arm of a generic `#if` is checked per instance, so it can call `handler` at its real type. Today both arms are checked against H (metaprogramming.md section 2).

Second, a type pattern binds Q, R and S from a function type. Third, a result type is computed from a type parameter, so the worker returns `Endpoint<Q, R>`. Today a computed alias reads only number parameters and constants. It also needs D-RULE-REWRITE1=A built for `handler_name`.
options.technical: Amends the spec rule that a generic `#if` checks both arms, and the computed-alias rule in Spellings.jet. Each instance's taken arm becomes a template-style check, which costs a check per instance.

comparisons.note: Overloads share a name and are picked by argument types. That is D's shape.
comparisons.code:
func worker<Q>(_ name: String, _ h: @escaping (Q) -> Void) -> Endpoint<Q>
func worker<S, Q>(_ name: String, _ h: @escaping (inout S, Q) -> Void, state: S) -> Endpoint<Q>

comparisons.note: Go has no overloading, so each shape has its own name. That is B's shape.
comparisons.code: func NewStatefulWorker[S, Q any](name string, h func(*S, Q), state S) *Endpoint[Q]

comparisons.note: One template picks its form with `if constexpr`, and only the taken branch is checked per instance; `std::invoke_result_t` computes the result type. That is E's shape, and it needs exactly the features E names.

recommendation.why: Five ratified decisions fix these spellings, and a ratified decision outranks a card criterion. A keeps every program, guide and error as it is and still moves the refusals into Core rules. The same-program route, one generic Core worker (E), was probed and stops at three missing language features. So every alternative today either changes a spelling (B, C) or adds a language feature (D, E).
gains: No user program, example, guide page or error text changes.
Services.jet leaves Sema/Calls, and its shape refusals become Core check rules.
The fence is narrow: fixed-shape and arity picks still leave the compiler, and D or E can still come later through a language ballot without changing a spelling.

losses.loss: The service pick stays a compiler privilege: a package can't declare its own `worker` with the same pick.
losses.mitigation: The privilege is fenced in one language-owned file and limited to outer-shape picks under a ratified name; D or E can remove it later.

whyNot.reason: It breaks the spellings of five ratified decisions, with their guide pages, examples and both beginner and expert paths, for a compiler cleanup.
It rewrites the String mailbox runtime and still breaks the KEEP1 and BATCH1 spellings, and the durable pick stays.
A new language feature that every tool must learn, which needs its own language ballot first.
Three missing language features (per-instance checking of a taken `#if` arm, function-type patterns, computed result types), each its own language ballot; probes p1 to p4 fail today.

recommendation.tradeoff: One narrow fenced compiler privilege kept, for no change to any ratified spelling and no new language feature.

decisions.hybrid: A now and D or E later is the natural mix: the refusals move to Core rules now, and a language ballot for overload sets (D) or for per-instance arm checking, function-type patterns and computed result types (E) can remove the compiler pick without changing a spelling.

decisions.title: Which of the two things called Pool keeps the name
decisions.situation: Jet has two different things called Pool. The first is a store of values, like a coat check. You hand in a value and get a ticket (an ID). The ticket gets the value back, and it stops working once the value is taken out. The second is a memory allocator, a box with a fixed number of slots that get reused. Sharing one name confuses readers, and one shared compiler entry for both crashes the compiler today. Beginners meet the store first, and only experts use the allocator. You are asked whether one of them gets a new name, or both keep it with separate entries. We recommend renaming the allocator to `mem.SlotPool`, because if both keep the name, importing the allocator hides the store.
decisions.gist: Jet has two different things named Pool: a store of values found by ID, and a memory allocator. One of them needs a new name.
decisions.lesson: `Pool<T>` is a store for many values of one type. You add a value and get back an ID ticket; the ticket finds the value later and goes stale once the value is removed. `mem.Pool.new(slots: N)` is something else: an allocator, a box with N slots. Each slot holds one value of any type and gets reused after a reset. The two share a name, a Core declaration and a compiler handle row.
decisions.explainer:
Today a program can use both, and both say Pool:

```jet
use core.mem

Player: struct { name: String, hp: Int }

run: fn() {
    world := Pool<Player>.new()          // the store: values found by ID
    kai: world.add(Player{name: "Kai", hp: 100})
    world[kai].hp -= 10

    scratch: mem.Pool.new(slots: 8)      // the allocator: 8 reusable slots
    hp: scratch.alloc(world[kai].hp)
    print(hp)
    close(scratch)
}
```

At the batch-44 tip this program stops with an internal compiler error, because the store picks up the allocator's close. Every option below writes this same program. A, B, C, D and E change the spelling of one Pool line, and F changes neither.
decisions.story: A beginner reads the spec chapter on pools and writes `world := Pool<Player>.new()`. Later they open the allocator example, see `pool: mem.Pool.new(slots: 8)`, and try `pool.add(...)`, which doesn't exist. Inside the compiler, the same mix-up is real: one Core declaration, `core.mem.Pool`, stands for the allocator but takes the store's type parameter. When that declaration gained an empty close, the store `Pool<T>` was treated as if it closed, and the build crashed.
decisions.inWild: Elsewhere, pool usually means an allocator that reuses slots. Examples are C++'s `std::pmr::unsynchronized_pool_resource`, Boost.Pool and Zig's `std.heap.MemoryPool`. A store of values reached by ticket is usually called a slot map or an arena. Examples are Rust's `slotmap::SlotMap` and the `generational_arena` crate's `Arena`. Game engines also say entity pool or object pool for the store.
decisions.detail:
Facts at the batch-44 tip 6cd78ce0aaf, which includes the #6852 p2a change that gave the allocators `impl Close`.

The store, `Pool<T>` and `ID<T>`, is specified in spec.md 2618-2646 (D-POOLID-API1). It is an ambient name that needs no `use`, from BuiltinStatics.jet 120 (owner Pool, method new, lowered as `jet_std.JetPool.new`). Nothing in Core declares it. IR knows it by name and lays it out as a list of entries (BuildPools.jet 1-63, `ir_pool_new`). Its inventory rows are CoreSurfaceInventory.rows 59-60.

The allocator, `mem.Pool.new(slots: N)`, is specified in spec.md 3813-3817 (Allocator families), 3869 and 4673-4676 (`#Context(allocator:)`). core-library.md 7409 also lists it, wrongly as `Pool.new<T>(slots: Int)`. Sema builds it in `sema_call_try_memory_static` (Sema/Calls/Memory.jet 196-314) and types it as the bare `Pool` (line 307). IR lowers it to `jet_pool_with_slots` (BuildCoreClosures.jet 428-483).

The allocator's runtime is MemStorage.jet 346-440. Its handle drop is `jet_rt_handle_drop_jet_pool`, and its exhaustion panic reads "Pool allocator exhausted its slab slots".

Where the two collide:
- Core/Mem/Mem.jet 51 declares `Pool: struct<T>` with an empty `impl Close`. It has the store's type parameter but stands for the allocator. Compiler/Prelude/Core.rows 163 exports it.
- RuntimeHandles.jet 238 (`<corelib>/core.mem.Pool`) and 491 (bare `Pool`) both map to the allocator's runtime handle `JetPool`.

The crash was probed with the batch-44 compiler, with the tip as toolchain root. `jet run` of the explainer program reports "ir.build unlowered: close [function:<corelib>/core.mem.type:<corelib>/core.mem.Pool.close]: method receiver type <corelib>/core.mem.Pool<T>". The queued p2b1 change works around it in `ir_close_method` by skipping an empty close on a bare generic row. That skip goes once each Pool has its own declaration.

Member imports were probed the same way. Start a file with `use core.mem.Pool` or `use core.mem.[Pool]`, and `Pool<Player>.new()` reports `Jet.UnknownMethod: Pool has no matching static method new`. The import binds `Pool` to the allocator and hides the store, and nothing reports it at the import.

Usage, lines/files at the tip:
- Store (`Pool<` or `ID<`): Core 0, Examples 14/7, Tests 66/30, Docs/Spec 11/3, Compiler 21/10.
- Allocator (`mem.Pool.new(slots:`): Core 0, Examples 1/1 (Memory/Allocation/Arena.jet 25), Tests 6/6, Compiler 2/2, plus the spec prose above.
- All four allocator constructors (`mem.Arena|Bump|Fixed|Pool.new|over`): Examples 16/8, Tests 139/96, Docs/Spec 6/3, Compiler 16/7.

Beginner path: the store, with no import, as in spec.md 2636. Expert path: `use core.mem`, then an allocator, optionally passed to `#Context(allocator:)`.

options.name: Rename the allocator to `mem.SlotPool`
options.detail:
The store keeps `Pool<T>` and `ID<T>`. The allocator becomes `mem.SlotPool.new(slots: N)`. The name still says what it is, a pool allocator of slots, as C++ and Zig use the word, and it no longer matches the store's name.

Beginner path: unchanged, `world := Pool<Player>.new()`. Expert path: `scratch: mem.SlotPool.new(slots: 8)`, and `#Context(allocator: scratch)` as before.
options.technical:
Core/Mem/Mem.jet 51 becomes `SlotPool: struct {}` without a type parameter, since it holds values of mixed types, and keeps the allocator's `impl Close`. Core.rows exports SlotPool instead of Pool. RuntimeHandles rows 238 and 491 become `<corelib>/core.mem.SlotPool` and `SlotPool`. The allocator name check (Memory.jet 81-89), its arity fix text, and the IR comment at BuildCoreClosures.jet 428 say SlotPool. The runtime panic says "SlotPool exhausted its slots".

The store gets one declaration of its own, as an ambient type with its own type parameter, and the queued `ir_close_method` bare-generic skip is deleted. Migration covers 1 example, 6 tests and the spec lines 3813-3817, 3869 and 4673-4676. It also covers core-library.md 7409, where the stray `<T>` is dropped.

Edge cases:
- `mem.Pool.new(slots: 8)` after the change is an unknown member of `core.mem`, reported the way any missing Core name is.
- `use core.mem.SlotPool` binds a name the store doesn't use, so no import can hide the store.
- `Pool<T>` without an import still means the store. With `use core.mem` in scope, `mem.Pool` names nothing.
- `#Context(allocator:)` accepts a SlotPool wherever it accepted the allocator Pool.
options.code:
use core.mem

Player: struct { name: String, hp: Int }

run: fn() {
    world := Pool<Player>.new()          // the store keeps its name
    kai: world.add(Player{name: "Kai", hp: 100})
    world[kai].hp -= 10

    scratch: mem.SlotPool.new(slots: 8)  // the allocator is renamed
    hp: scratch.alloc(world[kai].hp)
    print(hp)
    close(scratch)
}

options.name: Rename the store to `Slots<T>`
options.detail:
The allocator keeps `mem.Pool.new(slots: N)`. The store becomes `Slots<T>`, with `ID<T>` unchanged. This matches how C++ and Zig use pool, and it pairs with Core's `Rows<T>` table.

Beginner path: `world := Slots<Player>.new()`, still with no import. Expert path: unchanged, `scratch: mem.Pool.new(slots: 8)`.
options.technical:
The ambient static owner (BuiltinStatics.jet 120), the inventory rows, the IR pool routes and the spec chapter at 2618-2646 are renamed. The store gets a declaration of its own, `Slots: struct<T>`. Core/Mem's `Pool` loses its type parameter. Migration covers 7 examples, 30 test files, 3 spec files and 10 compiler files that name the store, including UI stderr goldens, the REPL transcript and pool_handle_word_cased_id.

Edge cases:
- `Pool<Player>.new()` after the change is an unknown name, with a rename hint.
- `Slots` and the allocator's `slots:` label share a word, so `mem.Pool.new(slots: 8)` and `Slots<T>` read alike in prose.
options.code:
use core.mem

Player: struct { name: String, hp: Int }

run: fn() {
    world := Slots<Player>.new()         // the store is renamed
    kai: world.add(Player{name: "Kai", hp: 100})
    world[kai].hp -= 10

    scratch: mem.Pool.new(slots: 8)      // the allocator keeps its name
    hp: scratch.alloc(world[kai].hp)
    print(hp)
    close(scratch)
}

options.name: Keep both names; move the allocators to `core.mem.alloc`
options.detail:
Both stay Pool, but in different modules. The store is `core.mem.Pool<T>`, still ambient. Arena, Bump, Pool and Fixed move to `core.mem.alloc`, so the allocator is `alloc.Pool`.

Beginner path: unchanged. Expert path: `use core.mem.alloc`, then `alloc.Pool.new(slots: 8)`.
options.technical:
A new Core module `core.mem.alloc` declares the four allocators. Sema's allocator check keys on that module instead of `core.mem`. `core.mem.Pool` becomes the store's declaration. Migration covers every allocator constructor: 16 lines in 8 examples, 139 lines in 96 test files, 6 spec lines and 16 compiler lines. The handle rows split by module path, but a bare `Pool` in an error message, a type display or the docs index still means either one.

Edge cases:
- A file that imports both `core.mem` and `core.mem.alloc` sees `Pool<T>` and `alloc.Pool` side by side.
- Diagnostics have to print the module path to tell the two apart.
options.code:
use core.mem.alloc

Player: struct { name: String, hp: Int }

run: fn() {
    world := Pool<Player>.new()          // the store, core.mem.Pool
    kai: world.add(Player{name: "Kai", hp: 100})
    world[kai].hp -= 10

    scratch: alloc.Pool.new(slots: 8)    // the allocator, core.mem.alloc.Pool
    hp: scratch.alloc(world[kai].hp)
    print(hp)
    close(scratch)
}

options.name: Rename the allocator to `mem.Slab`
options.detail:
Like A, but the allocator takes the systems name slab, which the runtime's panic text already uses ("slab slots"). No part of the name is shared with the store.

Beginner path: unchanged. Expert path: `scratch: mem.Slab.new(slots: 8)`.
options.technical:
Same changes as A, with `Slab` in place of `SlotPool`.

Edge cases:
- Rust's `slab::Slab<T>` is a store reached by key, which is the store's meaning, not the allocator's. Rust readers would expect `add` and indexing on it.
options.code:
use core.mem

Player: struct { name: String, hp: Int }

run: fn() {
    world := Pool<Player>.new()          // the store keeps its name
    kai: world.add(Player{name: "Kai", hp: 100})
    world[kai].hp -= 10

    scratch: mem.Slab.new(slots: 8)      // the allocator is renamed
    hp: scratch.alloc(world[kai].hp)
    print(hp)
    close(scratch)
}

options.name: Retire the slot allocator
options.detail:
Delete the allocator Pool. Its users switch to `mem.Bump`, which is also bounded but counts bytes instead of slots, or to `mem.Arena`. The store keeps `Pool<T>` alone.

Beginner path: unchanged. Expert path: `scratch: mem.Bump.new(capacity: 256)`.
options.technical:
The runtime pool storage (MemStorage.jet 346-440), its witness tests and routes, the `.Pool` allocator constructor case, and the spec and #Context rows for it are deleted. The 6 tests and the one example move to Bump.

Edge cases:
- Bounded reuse by count, where many resets and allocations fill the same slots, has no replacement. Bump bounds bytes and reuses nothing until reset.
options.code:
use core.mem

Player: struct { name: String, hp: Int }

run: fn() {
    world := Pool<Player>.new()          // the only Pool
    kai: world.add(Player{name: "Kai", hp: 100})
    world[kai].hp -= 10

    scratch: mem.Bump.new(capacity: 256) // no slot allocator any more
    hp: scratch.alloc(world[kai].hp)
    print(hp)
    close(scratch)
}

options.name: Keep both spellings; give each its own declaration
options.detail:
Nothing is renamed. The store `Pool<T>` and `ID<T>` get one declaration of their own as an ambient type, next to the other names a program can use without `use`. The allocator stays `core.mem.Pool`, with no type parameter. Each gets its own Core.rows and handle row. The crash came from one declaration and one handle row serving both, not from the spelling, so this fixes it, and nothing migrates.

Beginner path: unchanged, `world := Pool<Player>.new()`. Expert path: unchanged, `scratch: mem.Pool.new(slots: 8)`.
options.technical:
The store's ambient declaration takes over BuiltinStatics.jet 120 and the inventory rows. Core/Mem/Mem.jet 51 `Pool: struct<T>` drops its type parameter and stays the allocator. RuntimeHandles row 491 (bare `Pool`) goes, so a bare `Pool` inside the compiler no longer names the allocator.

The import F needs a rule for: spec.md 4067-4073 lets a file import one member, as `use core.mem.Pool` or `use core.mem.[Pool]`. That binds `Pool` to the allocator for the whole file and hides the store, with no diagnostic at the import. A probe at the batch-44 tip shows it. With `use core.mem.Pool` at the top, `world := Pool<Player>.new()` reports `Jet.UnknownMethod: Pool has no matching static method new`. `use core.mem.[Pool]` does the same.

spec.md 605-606 says language-owned built-in names stay reserved, but the probe shows `Pool` is not one of them. F therefore needs a new rule: a member import that would hide an ambient built-in name is an error whose fix is to write `mem.Pool`.

Edge cases:
- A program's own `Pool` declaration hides the store under every option, as any declaration hides an ambient name (probe: `Pool: struct { n: Int }` then `Pool<Player>.new()` is Jet.UnknownMethod). Only the import case is new to F.
- Messages and type displays have to print `mem.Pool` for the allocator to tell it from the store.
options.code:
use core.mem

Player: struct { name: String, hp: Int }

run: fn() {
    world := Pool<Player>.new()          // the store, its own declaration
    kai: world.add(Player{name: "Kai", hp: 100})
    world[kai].hp -= 10

    scratch: mem.Pool.new(slots: 8)      // the allocator, core.mem.Pool
    hp: scratch.alloc(world[kai].hp)
    print(hp)
    close(scratch)
}

comparisons.note: The standard library's pool is an allocator that keeps pools of blocks by size and reuses them, close to Jet's slot allocator. Value stores reached by handle aren't in the standard library.
comparisons.code:
std::pmr::unsynchronized_pool_resource pool;
std::pmr::vector<int> v{&pool};   // allocates from the pool

comparisons.note: MemoryPool(T) is a typed pool allocator: `create` hands out a slot, and `destroy` returns it for reuse.
The generational store is a crate, called SlotMap or Arena, not Pool. Its keys go stale on removal, like Jet's ID<T>.

recommendation.why: A renames the side with fewer users and keeps the word pool where other languages use it, as an allocator with slots. The store keeps the name beginners already learn from the spec and examples. One example and six tests migrate. F came close: it fixes the crash with no migration. But under F, importing the allocator by name hides the store, so F needs a new import rule. A needs no new rule.
gains: Each name has one meaning: `Pool<T>` is the store and `mem.SlotPool` is the allocator.
Core can declare each with its own shape: the store with a type parameter, the allocator without one.
Every import form stays safe: `use core.mem.SlotPool` binds a name that can't hide the store.
The compiler's special skip for an empty close on a bare generic type is deleted.
The beginner path doesn't change at all.

losses.loss: Seven call sites and the allocator spec text change spelling.
losses.mitigation: All seven move in the same change as the rename, and the allocator's arity error's fix text names `mem.SlotPool.new(slots: N)`.

losses.loss: C++ or Zig readers might take `Pool<T>` for an allocator.
losses.mitigation: `Pool<T>` takes a type and returns ID tickets, and the allocator next to it is named SlotPool, so the docs show the contrast at first sight.

whyNot.reason: It renames the beginner-facing side, about 50 files and a spec chapter, to spare 7 expert call sites.
Two types keep one bare name, so messages and docs stay ambiguous, and 111 files move to a new module.
Slab means a keyed store in Rust, which is the store's meaning, not the allocator's.
It removes bounded slot reuse that Bump and Arena don't provide.

A file that imports the allocator by name, `use core.mem.Pool`, hides the store, and today nothing reports it (probe p_member). F needs a new import rule for that one collision, and readers still meet two Pools.

recommendation.tradeoff: A changes 7 expert call sites to give each Pool one meaning. F changes none but needs a new import rule and keeps two Pools. B and C cost far more migration, D trades one ambiguity for another, and E drops a feature.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude Opus. Adversarial model family: Claude Opus. Fresh agent: Main. The review added option F and probed member imports, which hide the ambient store.

decisions.title: A function or lambda body written as fields builds the record, as an arm body already does
decisions.situation: After an arm's arrow, Jet already reads `{a: 1, b: 2}` as a record, because statements never form a comma-separated list of fields. After a function signature or a lambda head, the same braces are always code, by a rule ratified this month. So returning a struct takes two pairs of braces, and a lambda that returns fields is a syntax error, which data code meets whenever it maps rows to records. The vote decides whether body braces follow the arm rule; we recommend yes, with no type needed to decide.
decisions.gist: Should a function or lambda body written as fields build the record, as an arm body already does?
decisions.lesson: A record is a struct without a name, written `{x: 1, y: 2}`; where a struct type is expected the same braces build that struct. In a body, Jet tells a record from code by a top-level comma between fields. Arm bodies use that rule today; function and lambda bodies don't, so they need inner braces. After a declared result, one field is enough.
decisions.story: Priya turns sales rows into report lines: `rows.map(fn(r) { name: r.name, total: r.qty * r.price })`. Jet stops at the first comma with a syntax error. She adds a second pair of braces, then writes the same double braces in `new: fn(w: Float, h: Float) -> Rect { {width: w, height: h} }`. Her `if` arms took the single-brace form without complaint.
decisions.detail:
Sites are at dev 930090f78c8 (2026-11-25), probed with the installed compiler a0.0.46. Lists of sites are in the text blocks below.

D-RECORD-BRACE1=A (ratified 2026-11-06) set the brace rule that Spellings.jet row 78 records. Its detail says 'Function bodies always hold code. Returning a record needs inner braces, even for one member.' Arm bodies already read a comma record through parser_brace_record_value_at. S29-FLUSH (D-DOTCTOR3) makes a type name touching its brace, `Type{…}`, a construction. This ballot amends D-RECORD-BRACE1's function-body sentence. It narrows S29-FLUSH after a signature's arrow, where a touching `{` ends the result type and opens the body.

```text
Today
- Spellings.jet row 78: braces hold a record when every entry is a field or pun and a colon or
  comma appears; where a struct is expected they build it; braces after a signature, a control
  head or a block marker hold code.
- parser_brace_record_value_at: Compiler/JetParser/Source/Parser/Expressions.jet:1553-1601,
  called from DecisionTables.jet:507, ExpressionForms/Loops.jet:432, Expressions.jet:2594,
  Statements.jet:994 and 1013.
- S29-FLUSH: Docs/Spec/syntax-decisions.md:1692-1700.

Probes (a0.0.46)
- p: if c -> {a: 1, b: 2} else -> {a: 3, b: 4}          runs
- xs.map(fn(r) { n: r, sq: r * r })                     Jet.InvalidStatement at `,`
- xs.map(fn(r) { {n: r, sq: r * r} })                   runs
- mk: fn(w: Float, h: Float) -> Rect { width: w, height: h }   fails at `,`
- -> Rect { {width: w, height: h} }                     runs (Examples/Basics/Functions/NamedArgs.jet:11)
- mk: fn(v: Int) -> Box { value: v }                    Jet.MissingBlockValue
- X: #run { a: 1, b: 2 }                                fails at `,`; X: #run { {a: 1, b: 2} } runs
- sq: fn(n: Int) -> Int{n * n}, -> [Int]{[y]}           Jet.ArrowFunctionBody (E0080)
```

Two defects in this area are fixed whatever the vote. First, `jet fmt` applies E0080's fix to `sq: fn(n: Int) -> Int{n * n}` and writes `sq: fn(n: Int) { Int{n * n} }`. That is a function with no result, and its caller then fails because `print` can't show Unit. Second, `xs.each(fn(r) { {n: r, sq: r * r} })` passes `jet check` and stops with SIGSEGV at run time. A named function with the same body is Jet.ValueThrownAway.

Why no valid program changes meaning. Commas do appear at a block's top level, in generic arguments and loop headers. Yet a block is never read as a record, because every comma-separated member must be `name: value`, `name,` or `name}` (Expressions.jet:1577-1580). No statement list has that shape, so every body the rule reads as a record is an error today. The rule is syntactic and needs no types.

The one-field form is safe for the same reason. When the declared result carries a value, a body whose only line is `name: value` is an error today. The test is parser_return_type_has_value (Items.jet:1841-1847): not Unit and not a unit-fallible `E!`. The errors are Jet.MissingBlockValue, or NeverFunctionReachesEnd for `-> Never`. The exception is a labeled loop, `outer: loop { … }`, a binding-as-label under D-LOOPLABEL4=A, which stays code.

A gap in the shared helper. parser_brace_record_value_at doesn't skip a generic argument list. So `{a: 1, q: Pair<Int, Int>{first: 1, second: 2}}` fails after an arm today, and lambdas would spread the failure to data code such as `Group<K, V>{…}`. The helper learns to skip `<…>` where the parser's generic-head test holds: `<` touches the name and the matching `>` touches `{` or `(`.

Why braces never convert. `T{…}` converts in Jet: `U8{n}` stops at run time when `n` doesn't fit, `Int{t * 2.0}` stops on a fraction, and `[[Int]]{y}` wraps a list (D-ARRAY-CONVERT1). Body braces never take that role. The body's value is checked against the result type, so `-> U8 { n }` stays a compile error with its `checked(U8{value})` fix.

```text
Cutover list
1. Spellings.jet row 78 and its rendered copy at syntax-decisions.md:97: a value body (after a
   signature with a result, a lambda head, an arm's arrow, or a value-giving marker block such
   as #run) holds a record when a comma separates field or pun members at its top level, or when
   its declared result carries a value and its only line is `name: value` whose value does not
   start with `loop`; otherwise it holds code. Control heads keep code.
2. parser_parse_callable_body (Statements.jet:325) reads a record through
   parser_brace_record_value_at and returns it as the one value line. That covers its four
   callers: functions (Items.jet:1192), lambdas (Expressions.jet:1651), `impl A -> B`
   conversion bodies (Items.jet:3289) and collecting loops (Loops.jet:433), whose separate guard
   at Loops.jet:432 is deleted. The #run value block takes the same call. A second flag,
   one_field_record, admits the one-field form: functions pass
   parser_return_type_has_value(return_type), lambdas pass it for their declared result (false
   when none is declared), conversion bodies pass true, collecting loops and #run pass false.
3. parser_brace_record_value_at skips a `<…>` argument list only where the generic-head test
   holds (S29, syntax-decisions.md:1698-1700), so `{ok: MAX < n, big: m > LIMIT}` still reads
   as comparisons. Golden cases cover `Pair<Int, Int>{…}` fields, comparisons with capitalized
   constants, loop clauses, counted loops, and the unchanged bodies
   `-> Int { outer: loop { return n } }` and `fn() IOError! { x: n }`.
4. `-> T{`: parser_result_type_follows_arrow (Items.jet:1591) drops the gap test at 1613, so any
   result type touching `{` (Int, [Int], Box<T>, {a: Int}, after -> or -[E]>) ends there and the
   brace opens the body. Record result types keep their typed-member test at 1588-1597.
   Function-type defaults such as `f: fn(Int) -> Int{double}` use another path, unaffected.
   jet fmt prints the space.
5. E0080 then fires only for a real arrow body such as `-> n * n`. Its fix text (Items.jet:1681)
   says to write the result type and braces, and the formatter stops applying it:
   Compiler/Prelude/Diagnostics.jet:1369-1380 (structured_fix, fix_safety, fmt_applies_fix),
   the regenerated JetFoundation/Source/Registry/DiagnosticRows.jet:1392-1403,
   Formatter/Formatter.jet:2818, Formatter/Items.jet:2031-2034,
   Compiler/JetParser/Tests/Formatter/Teaching.jet:13.
6. A record body where no value is expected is Jet.ValueThrownAway in lambdas, as in functions;
   the SIGSEGV above is fixed first.
7. Jet.UnusedLocalBinding, which today does not fire for `xs.map(fn(r) { name: r })` (that
   program checks clean and builds a list of Unit), fires for a lambda whose only line binds a
   name it never reads, and shows `{ {name: value} }` as its fix.
8. The formatter prints a bare-record body without the inner braces: `{ {a: 1, b: 2} }`
   becomes `{ a: 1, b: 2 }`, about 130 sites.
9. Editors: the tree-sitter block already accepts `,` (Tools/Editors/TreeSitter/grammar.js:107-148
   and 372); corpus tests are added for comma bodies and `-> T{`; the grammar changes only if
   one fails.
10. Docs and examples: the record section of spec.md, Examples/Basics/Functions/NamedArgs.jet:11,
   and a new golden example with a function body, a one-field body, a lambda body, a #run body
   and an arm body that build records, run on every tier.

Edge cases
- `{x}` (one pun) and `{}` stay blocks, as row 78 says today.
- `{x, y}` builds a record from the locals x and y.
- `rows.map(fn(r) { name: r.name })`, a lambda with no declared result and one field, stays a
  binding; write `{ {name: r.name} }` or declare the result.
- `-> Int { x: 5 }` reads a record and fails the result type, as today it fails as a block.
- A decision table in braces (`{ a -> 1, b -> 2 }`) is not fields; the helper returns false at ->.
- Lists keep `[…]`.
```

Beginner path: write the fields, and Jet builds the struct the signature names. Expert path: unchanged, since `T{…}` still converts where a conversion is wanted.

Research. JavaScript's arrow function needs `({…})` to return an object, and without them returns undefined silently (MDN). Rust writes the type name inside the body braces. OCaml and F# write a record expression as the body, because their function bodies are expressions. Jet's rule matches the OCaml outcome without giving up braced bodies.

The adversarial review is Docs/Audits/2026-11-25-binding-and-body-syntax-review.md, section 'Idea 4'.

options.name: Fields build a record in every value body
options.detail: A value body (after a signature, a lambda head, an arm's arrow or `#run`) builds a record when a comma separates field members at its top level, the rule arms use today. After a declared result that carries a value, a body of one `name: value` line builds it too (a labeled loop, `outer: loop {…}`, stays code). The record builds the declared struct. `-> Int{n * n}` reads as the result type and a body, and the formatter adds the space. Braces never convert a value.
options.technical: parser_parse_callable_body calls parser_brace_record_value_at for all four of its callers. Purely syntactic: the declared result is already known at parse time and no type is inferred. Every program it reads as a record is an error today.

options.name: The expected type decides
options.detail: Body braces build the expected struct whenever it is a struct or record type. That includes a lambda whose result is only inferred from its call, so `rows.map(fn(r) { name: r.name })` builds a record too. Arm bodies keep their comma rule.
options.technical: For lambdas with an inferred result the parser keeps the braces unread until sema infers the type, then reads them as fields or code. Two rules: arms by comma, bodies by type.
options.code:
wrap: fn(v: Int) -> Box { value: v }
report: rows.map(fn(r) { name: r.name })   // inferred record

options.name: Keep the inner braces
options.detail: Function and lambda bodies stay code. A struct result is written `{ {…} }` or `{ T{…} }`, and a lambda that returns fields needs inner braces; forgetting them is a syntax error.
options.technical: No change to the rule. The two defects (the formatter dropping a result type, the lambda crash) are fixed anyway.
options.code:
new: fn(w: Float, h: Float) -> Rect { {width: w, height: h} }
report: rows.map(fn(r) { {name: r.name, total: r.qty * r.price} })

comparisons.note: An arrow body returning an object needs parentheses; without them the braces are a block and the result is undefined. MDN, Arrow functions, Function body.
comparisons.code:
rows.map(r => ({ name: r.name }))
rows.map(r => { name: r.name })   // returns undefined

comparisons.note: The struct literal names its type inside the body braces.
comparisons.code: fn new(w: f64, h: f64) -> Rect { Rect { width: w, height: h } }

comparisons.note: A function body is an expression, so a record is the body.
comparisons.code: let make w h = { width = w; height = h }

recommendation.why: A extends the rule arms already use, so the comma, or a declared result, decides every body before types, with no new meaning for any valid program. Lambdas get records too, the common case in data scripts.
gains: Struct results and record-returning lambdas need one pair of braces.
One comma rule for every body; a declared result also admits one field. Row 78 loses an exception.
`-> Int{n * n}` is accepted, and the formatter no longer drops the result type.

losses.loss: A one-field lambda with no declared result still needs inner braces.
losses.mitigation: A new warning for that lambda's unread binding shows the `{ {name: value} }` fix.

whyNot.reason: It makes parsing wait on inferred types and gives arms and bodies different rules, to save braces in one-field untyped lambdas.
It keeps two pairs of braces for every struct result and a syntax error for record lambdas.

recommendation.tradeoff: One-field untyped lambdas keep inner braces; every other field body loses a pair.

decisions.title: A semicolon separates statements on one line where a line break would end one, and means that line break
decisions.situation: Jet statements end at a line break, and a typed semicolon is an error in a file, yet `jet eval` turns semicolons into line breaks on its one line. So code can't move between a file and a one-line command unchanged, and anyone with C, Java or JavaScript habits fails a build on a harmless semicolon. One-line places such as a command, a shell script, a config value or a chat message can't hold two statements. The vote decides whether a semicolon becomes a line break everywhere; we recommend yes, while the formatter keeps stored files one statement per line.
decisions.gist: Should a semicolon between statements mean a line break everywhere, not only in `jet eval`?
decisions.lesson: A statement ends at a line break; Jet adds that end itself, so files never need semicolons. Today a typed semicolon is an error in a file but a line break in `jet eval`. Whichever option wins, stored files stay one statement per line, and semicolons stay errors inside records, arguments and loop headers.
decisions.story: Sam pastes `total: a + b; print(total)` from a `jet eval` command into a script and the build fails on the semicolon. Later an agent writes `count += 1;` from C habit, and the build fails again. Sam wonders why the same line works on the command line and not in a file.
decisions.detail:
Sites are at dev 930090f78c8 (2026-11-25), probed with the installed compiler a0.0.46. Lists of sites are in the text blocks below.

D-SEMI1=A (2026-09-02) enforces S6 with Jet.ExplicitSemicolon (E0373). Its rejected option C was 'accept; the formatter rewrites it', and it lost because a file that was never formatted keeps two spellings. This ballot reopens D-SEMI1 at the owner's request of 2026-11-25. Option A is close to that option C, and it answers C's lost point with the formatter check. D-CLI-EVAL1=A gave one-liners their own verb, which is where eval's semicolons live today.

```text
Today
- Spellings.jet row 92: ';' is the "retired explicit statement terminator; only a jet eval
  one-liner separates the statements on its one line with it".
- S6 (syntax-decisions.md:5067-5072): statements end at line end; the lexer inserts Go-style
  terminators. terminator_events (Compiler/JetLexer/Source/Lexer/Terminators.jet:383-407)
  decides each boundary: the previous token must pass ends_statement_at; suppresses_terminator
  lists continuing tokens (`.`, `?.`, binary operators, ...); scope_member_starts_at,
  dispatch_arm_starts_at, place_mark_starts_at, tuple_rename_starts_at and
  record_value_starts_at are its exceptions.
- Only jet eval turns each `;` into a line break before parsing (jet_cli_eval_lines,
  Compiler/JetCLI/Source/CLI/ScriptCache.jet:449-457). The REPL refuses semicolons and trims
  trailing ones for its echo (Repl.jet:235 and 893-897).
- The parser reports E0373 once per file from parser_bump
  (Compiler/JetParser/Source/Parser/State.jet:97-98 and 586).
- D-LOOP-SEMICOLON1=A (2026-06-29) once kept semicolons in counted loop headers; D-LOOP-COMMA1
  made header clauses use commas, and a `;` there is E0373
  (Tests/UI/loop_header_semicolon_retired.stderr).
- Struct, enum and record members end with a comma; a `;` there is E0373
  (Tests/UI/enum_case_semicolon.stderr).
- D-TAIL-RETURN1=A: a semicolon or statement tail yields unit;
  Compiler/JetParser/Source/Parser/ExpressionForms/DecisionTables.jet:471-481 reports a value
  branch ending `5; }` (E0114).
- D-FMTCOLLAPSE1=B stores a fitting braced block of one statement on one line.
- Canonical style is one statement per line (spec.md:5905-5910).
```

The rule that makes the meaning exact. A `;` is accepted only where a line break would end the statement, and there it means exactly that line break. The lexer's own line-break decision is the test. Where a line break would not end the statement, the `;` is refused, because a line break there would join the two lines or be an error. Examples are `x =; 5`, `a +; b`, `f(); .Red`, `a; ?.b`, `print(1); { … }` and a `;` before `)`.

So `{ note(); .Red }` is refused, and the fix is `Color.Red`. Every accepted program keeps its meaning when the formatter turns each `;` into a line break. Today eval has the opposite flaw: `jet eval 'x := 1; -1; print(x)'` prints 0, because the rewrite joins `-1` to the line above.

Arms. A one-line arm holds one statement, as in `if done -> save()`. With semicolons, `if done -> save(); exit()` could mean that both run when `done` holds, as Python reads it. It could also mean that `exit()` always runs, as C reads it and `jet eval` does today. Braceless bodies are the bug class behind Apple's 2014 'goto fail' flaw.

So A refuses a `;` right after a statement arm on the same line, and the fix shows the braced arm. A statement arm is an `if`, `else` or `loop` arm used as a statement. A `return`, `break` or `next` arm counts too, even in a value `if`. `v: if c -> 1 else -> return 0; print(v)` runs in eval today, and the two readings differ when `c` holds.

Inside a decision table a `;` ends a row, as a line break does, so `if x == { 1 -> "one"; 2 -> "two"; else -> "many" }` keeps working. An `if` used as a value ends with its expression, so `x: if c -> 1 else -> 2; print(x)` is two statements.

The trailing semicolon. `{ 5; }` means `{ 5 }`, as a line break would. The semicolon clause of D-TAIL-RETURN1 retires, and its statement-tail clause stays. Every such program is refused in a file today.

Why one statement per line stays the stored form. `jet debug` breakpoints and steps, `jet perf` line attribution, coverage, blame and diffs all address lines. Stored code already joins a header and one statement on a line (D-FMTCOLLAPSE1). A doesn't join two statements. B would, with coarser attribution until those tools address statements by column.

Gleam needs no separator at all, because its grammar never lets the next statement continue the last one. In Gleam `(` can't start an expression, there is no index syntax, tuples are `#(…)` and bindings start with `let`. Jet's `(` grouping, `[` indexing and lists, prefix `-`, `{`, a leading `.`, `^` and prefix `*` can each start a statement or continue one. So Jet needs either a line break or a separator.

```text
Cutover list
1. Spellings.jet row 92: ';' separates statements and items on one line where a line break
   would end one, with that meaning.
2. Lexer: the per-boundary decision of terminator_events (Terminators.jet:383-407) becomes one
   function that both the inserted terminator and an authored `;` call; where it would not end
   the statement, a new registered diagnostic refuses the `;`, with what, why and fix text and
   a UI snapshot.
3. Parser: E0373 moves out of parser_bump (State.jet:586, and the once-per-file flag at 97-98)
   into the places that keep it: records, argument lists, struct and enum bodies, types
   (Types.jet:152-159), loop headers, interpolation holes and struct and enum member lists
   (Items.jet:2610); the result-type speculation at Items.jet:1605-1617 keeps saving and
   restoring its flag. Between statements (Statements.jet:180 and 1293) and between items,
   including the method lists of impl, trait and module bodies, the boundary the parser already
   keeps is the separator. Foreign blocks (Foreign.jet:243-250) take the `;` as the terminator
   they expect after a path.
4. A second new diagnostic refuses a `;` right after a statement arm, or a return, break or
   next arm, on the same line; inside a decision table the `;` ends a row. It replaces the
   Jet.InvalidStatement that
   Tests/Cases/CLIPartsSurface/eval_final_value_is_any_final_expression.case:28-31 expects for
   `if 1 > 0 -> "a" else -> "b"; print(1)`.
5. DecisionTables.jet:471-481: the E0114 report for an authored `;` before `}` is deleted.
6. E0373's why and fix text say a semicolon only separates statements and items
   (Compiler/Prelude/Diagnostics.jet:6246, DiagnosticRows.jet:5501); the two UI snapshots are
   re-blessed.
7. A `;` before a line break, before `}` or after another `;` is accepted; jet fmt removes it.
8. Eval: jet_cli_eval_lines (ScriptCache.jet:449-457) is deleted. jet_cli_eval_line_starts and
   its callers jet_cli_eval_items (ScriptCache.jet:351-390) and jet_cli_eval_final_if (319-338)
   read statement starts from the parser's boundaries instead.
9. REPL: jet_cli_repl_trim_semicolons (Repl.jet:235) is deleted; the echo at 893-897 takes the
   last statement from the parser's boundaries, so `a(); b` echoes b.
10. Formatter: one statement per line, every `;` dropped. Tests:
   Compiler/JetParser/Tests/Formatter/Teaching.jet, Parser/BraceLayout.jet, GrammarSmoke.jet,
   Statements03.jet, ContractFixtures.jet:76-77, the eval case above, and new cases for each
   rule.
11. The agent primer line "No semicolons." at Compiler/JetCLI/Source/CLI/InspectB.jet:397.
12. Docs: spec.md:920-924 (members end with a comma) and 5905-5910, syntax-decisions.md S6 at
   5067-5072 and the stale lines 981 and 989, Docs/Spec/Reference/cli.md:886-889 and 905-909,
   Docs/Site. Editors: Tools/Editors/TreeSitter, Vscode, Zed and jet.tmGrammar.

Edge cases
- `if c { a() }; b()` is two statements.
- `if c -> a() else -> b(); c()` is refused; brace the arm or break the line.
- `S: struct { a: Int }; s: S{a: 1}` separates an item from a statement, as jet eval does today.
- `a(); // note` keeps the comment.
- A `;` inside a string or comment is text; inside an interpolation hole it is E0373.
- `}; else` is refused, because the semicolon ends the if, as `else` on its own line is.
```

Beginner path: write one statement per line. A semicolon typed from habit compiles, and `jet fmt` removes it. Expert path: `jet eval 'total: a + b; print(total)'`, shell one-liners, REPL lines and pasted snippets mean the same in files.

Research. Go keeps semicolons in the grammar, inserts them at line ends and has gofmt remove typed ones; that is A's shape. Python allows semicolons, and PEP 8 discourages several statements on one line. After `if x:` Python's joined statements all belong to the if, which is the reading A refuses rather than picks. Kotlin and Swift treat a semicolon as an optional separator.

JavaScript's automatic semicolon insertion lets a line starting with `(` or `[` join the line before. Jet's continuation rule decides that, and A refuses any `;` it would contradict.

The adversarial review is Docs/Audits/2026-11-25-binding-and-body-syntax-review.md, section 'Idea 5'.
