decisions.title: Changeable names carry Jet's write mark, `^count: 0` instead of `count := 0`, and write windows are made by `place.in_place()`
decisions.situation: Jet declares a fixed name with a colon, as in `total: 0`, and a changeable name with `:=`, as in `count := 0`, so changing state hides mid-line. Jet's write mark `^` already means writable in signatures, but plays no part in local names. A write window, `best: ^items[0]`, puts the mark after the colon, so moving it one place would silently turn a list-changing window into a changeable copy, or back. The vote decides where a changeable name's mark goes, and we recommend `^count: 0` with every write window made by `items[0].in_place()`.
decisions.gist: Should a changeable name be written `^count: 0` instead of `count := 0`, and where does the `^` go?
decisions.lesson: Jet has three binding events: a fixed name (`x: 1`), a changeable name (`x := 1`) and a write (`x = 2`). Three spellings let the compiler catch a misspelt write. This vote keeps the three events and respells the changeable one with the write mark `^`. Whichever wins, write windows get their own spelling, `place.in_place()`, so `^` never sits next to a binding's value.
decisions.story: Maya writes a loop that finds the largest score. She has met `^` in signatures, where it means the function may write a value, and looks for the same mark at the start of the line, where Rust puts `mut`. Today she must learn `:=` instead. Later she reads `best: ^scores[0]` beside `best := scores[0]`; the first silently rewrites the list as her loop runs, the second doesn't.
decisions.detail:
Sites are at dev 930090f78c8 (2026-11-25). Counts are pattern counts over the Jet sources in Compiler, Core, Examples, Tools, Jetpack and Tests, about 2.03 million lines. The installed a0.0.46 compiler predates dev's `^` window syntax, so window facts rest on source reads. Lists of sites are in the text blocks below.

This ballot amends three ratified decisions. D-BINDSIG-COUNT1 changes in spelling only: `x:`, `^x:` and `x =` keep their three jobs, with E0107 and E0118. D-MARK-CARET1 (ratified 2026-11-25) and D-SHAPE-PLACE1 change so that a window is made by a method instead of a mark on the place. It also retires the leading parameter mark that D-CALLSITE-MARK2 left readable.

```text
Today
- Spellings.jet row 13: `:=` mutable binding; row 14: `name := value` mutable module global;
  CoreSurface.jet:116 SIGIL_BIND_MUT.
- D-BINDSIG-COUNT1=A: three symbols for three events; a misspelt write is Jet.UnknownName (E0107).
- D-MUT-NEVER1=A: a changeable name that never changes is an error (card #6324, planning).
- D-MARK-CARET1=A: write and take marks are ^ and ^^; a named window is `edit: ^values[1..<3]`.
- D-SHAPE-PLACE1=A: an edit is marked at the selection.
- D-CALLSITE-MARK2=A: marks live in signatures and plain calls; #Policy(writes: .Explicit) is
  the opt-in that marks writing calls (`fill(^xs)`, `^buf.push(x)`).
- D-MAPSLOT-WINDOW1=A: a function returns a window onto one map value through a named window
  (`w: ^m[key]` then `w`).
- spec.md:2795-2797 lists the marks outside signatures: a named window, a writing match
  (`if ^shape == { … }`) and `task ^^name`. Writing loop sources (`loop x in ^items`) are also
  live (Statements.jet:1330).

Corpus
- 78,436 `:=` bindings (3,121 of them `_ :=`); 294,339 fixed bindings.
- 217 named windows `name: ^place`; 6 `name := ^place` (the same write-through alias,
  BuildExpr.jet:474); 193 writing matches (113 tables, 80 one-arm); 3 writing loop sources.
- 40 state loops (`loop i := 0, i < n {`); 7 destructuring `:=` lines.
```

Why windows get one new spelling in every option. Any changeable-name mark written with `^` sits one position from today's named window. `^best: scores[0]` would be a changeable copy, and `best: ^scores[0]` a window that writes into the list. Both would compile. The classic largest-value loop then either works or silently rewrites `scores[0]`.

So every explicit window maker moves to one method, `place.in_place()`. It is named like `x.copy()` and `x.move()` and lowered by the parser. A named window is `best: scores[0].in_place()`, a writing match is `if shape.in_place() == { … }` and a writing loop is `loop x in items.in_place()`. Matching or looping over a window binds windows, as the marked forms do today. In all, 419 sites change.

After the cutover, `^` before a place survives only as the opt-in audit mark of `#Policy(writes: .Explicit)` on a writing call. That mark makes no window, because the signature does. Outside that policy `best: ^scores[0]` is not Jet. By the owner's greenfield order of 2026-11-06, retired forms get no teaching diagnostic.

The method name. "In place" says the original, not a copy, which is the exact difference the hazard turns on. `lend` was rejected because Jet's own text uses it for read loans too. `edit` was rejected: Shared, Cell and CellEditGuard already have a compiler-owned `edit(body)`, input has an ambient `edit`, and records hold `edit` fields. `window` was rejected because App, KeyedStream, Files and core.mem define it.

`writable()` reads as a question, and `mut` is a reserved retired keyword (CoreSurface.jet:409). No method takes the name `in_place` today. One static function does, `NativeSwapRestartBoundary.in_place()` with one call, and it is renamed. Like `copy` and `move`, `in_place` becomes a name no member may take (E0436, Items.jet:1075).

Where `.in_place()` is resolved. The parser turns `place.in_place()` with no arguments into the window node that `^place` produces today. It does so only where `^place` makes a window today: a binding value, a match subject, a one-arm writing match and a loop source. So sema's window facts, E0213 and the IR keep their meaning, and the method-call cases for `copy` never see it. Elsewhere it is refused, as `^place` is. It ends the place: write `shape.inner.in_place()`, since `shape.in_place().inner` is refused.

```text
Cutover list (every option; B and C change only the mark's position)
1. Lexer: TOKEN_COLON_EQ retires (Compiler/JetLexer/Source/Lexer/Tokens.jet:330, Scan.jet:692,
   Terminators.jet:318). The statement-start tests at Terminators.jet:291-348
   (place_mark_starts_at, tuple_rename_starts_at, record_value_starts_at) learn that `^name:`
   and `{^name` start a statement, and keep the place-mark start for the policy's receiver marks
   and for `~name`. Lexer tests JetLexer/Tests/Entry.jet:18 and 503 follow.
2. Registry: Spellings.jet rows 13 and 14; CoreSurface.jet:116 SIGIL_BIND_MUT deleted and the
   marks comment at 362-368 rewritten; Highlights.jet:653, PackageFiles.jet:493, the jet syntax
   dictionary rows at Compiler/JetCLI/Source/CLI/SyntaxDictionaryData.jet:183 and 187, the
   comment at Jetpack/Foundation/Source/SyntaxRegistry.jet:1447, and
   Tests/Cases/ExplainSyntax/today-52-48.case.
3. Parser: the binding statement in Compiler/JetParser/Source/Parser/Statements.jet (132, 585,
   596, 1313, 1602, 1643, 1733-1735, 1777 where a window value is parsed, 2314); the writing
   match (Statements.jet:761, ExpressionForms/DecisionTables.jet:1038); the one-arm writing match
   (Parser/Expressions.jet:386-400, 428, 537); the loop source (Statements.jet:1330); the shared
   place-mark parse (Parser/Expressions.jet:2377-2384); module-level detection in Entry.jet (62,
   544-557, 1657, 1879); module globals and #Persist names in Items.jet (101, 2721, 2735, 2768);
   fenced names in FencedNames.jet (28, 350, 362); the state loop in ExpressionForms/Loops.jet
   (24, 320, 359, 368); Items.jet:2224, whose leftover read of a field default after `:=` retires.
4. Formatter: ` := ` at Formatter/Statements.jet:2181 and Formatter/Items.jet:2967 and 3003;
   window marks in Formatter/Expressions.jet.
5. Sema: machine fixes that insert `:=` (Ownership/Checks.jet:413 and 4899,
   Statements/Bindings.jet:1327 and 1380) insert `^` before the name; about 30 sema files quote
   `:=` in messages (Links.jet:130, Pins.jet:27, Checks.jet:2534, 2581 and 3579,
   Collections.jet:270, Game.jet:368, ...).
6. Code that writes Jet source: Registration/CLIEntry.jet:617-749, Calls/CheckRules.jet:1319,
   Driver/SchedulerProvider.jet:112, CLI/DebugCompile.jet:861 and 1530 (which then write
   `^_: {text}`), Host.jet:3664 scaffolds, Doctests.jet, ImportBindings.jet:531,
   ImportExpressions.jet:215 and 239, Repl.jet:1224, InspectB.jet:153 and 401, InspectFacts.jet,
   Codemod.jet:664, the LSP completion snippet at Completion.jet:80, and the token readers in
   FixCommands.jet:7 and 217, ScriptCache.jet:50 and 302, and
   Compiler/JetEval/Source/CompilerServices.jet:43 and 441.
7. Diagnostics: every row quoting `:=` in Compiler/Prelude/Diagnostics.jet (Jet.ImmutableAssignment
   E0111's fix becomes "add ^ before the name"; the uninitialized-binding fix at
   Statements.jet:1772), the window texts of E0213 and Jet.UnusedPlaceMark (E0225),
   D-MUT-NEVER1's fix ("remove the ^"), the regenerated
   JetFoundation/Source/Registry/DiagnosticRows.jet, and their UI snapshots.
8. The leading parameter mark (`fill: fn(^xs: [Int])`) retires: Items.jet:869-874 and the
   Jet.DuplicateAccessMarker (E0029) path at 940-948, the leading-mark case in
   Compiler/JetParser/Tests/CaretMarks.jet, Tests/UI/two_capability_markers.jet and
   spec.md:2783-2792. `^self` and `^^self` stay. #Policy(writes: .Explicit) and its call marks
   stay; `^buf.push(` differs from `^buf:` at its third token.
9. NativeSwapRestartBoundary.in_place (Compiler/JetDevServer/Source/NativeSwap.jet:457, call at
   840) is renamed; E0436 adds `in_place` for every member and module function, so the parser's lowering never captures a declared function.
10. The old migrations BitSigils1, LambdaShape1 and ParenTuple1 in Compiler/Migrations read
   TOKEN_COLON_EQ and follow.
11. Editors: Tools/Editors/TreeSitter (grammar.js, corpus tests colon_declarations.txt and
   editor_core.txt, generated parser.c, grammar.json, node-types.json, with a distinct highlight
   for a marked name), Vscode jet.tmLanguage.json, Zed highlights.scm, jet.tmGrammar.
12. Docs: the binding section of spec.md, the window text at spec.md:2242-2244 and the marks
   list at 2795-2797, Docs/Spec/Reference/core-library.md (13 lines),
   Reference/syntax-surface.jet:172, the stale state-loop example at syntax-decisions.md:981,
   and the 36 Docs/Site pages that show `:=`.
13. Migration: a jet fix migration in Compiler/Migrations rewrites, keeping meaning at every site:
   x := v                  ->  ^x: v
   _ := v                  ->  ^_: v   (keeps today's owned copy, Bindings.jet:854-877; `^_` is
                                        already exempt from the never-written check)
   {a, b} := v             ->  {^a, ^b}: v
   {left: a} := v          ->  {left: ^a}: v
   loop i := 0, ...        ->  loop ^i: 0, ...
   #Persist n := v         ->  #Persist ^n: v
   name: ^place            ->  name: place.in_place()
   name := ^place          ->  name: place.in_place()
   if ^shape == ...        ->  if shape.in_place() == ...
   loop x in ^items        ->  loop x in items.in_place()

Edge cases
- A `^x:` name that is never written stays an error (D-MUT-NEVER1); the fix removes the `^`.
- A second `^x:` in the same scope is Jet.NameAlreadyTaken (E0118), as today.
- A misspelt write is still Jet.UnknownName (E0107), because `=` still never declares.
- `^^x: v`, and `^` before a struct field, a call label, a record field, a pattern binding or a
  loop source binding, are not Jet.
- `{left: ^a}: v` marks the bound name `a`; inside the braces it is the name side, not a place.
- A window is bound with `:` only; `^w: xs[0].in_place()` is refused: a window can't be re-pointed.
- D-MAPSLOT-WINDOW1 reads `w: m[key].in_place()` then `w`.
- Typed values keep the type on the value: `^limit: U8{250}`, `^best: Int?{None}`.
```

Beginner path: write `^count: 0` for anything you will change. Writing to a fixed name says to add `^`, and a `^` you never use says to remove it. Expert path: `scores[0].in_place()` for a window, and `{^lo, hi}: bounds()` to make only some destructured names changeable.

Keeping `:=` is not an option on this ballot, because the owner asked to replace it. Its cost is stated here. Nothing would migrate, and the copy-or-window hazard would stay smaller, since `:=` doesn't use `^`. The changeable mark would stay mid-line, and `^` would keep two unrelated jobs: a signature's writable value and a place's window.

Research. Rust puts `mut` before the name and `&mut` on the borrowed value; this ballot keeps the same split. Swift and Kotlin use words (`var`/`let`, `var`/`val`), and a word would add a keyword. Odin and Jai use `:=` for a variable and `::` for a constant; Jet already dropped `::`. Go uses `:=` to declare and has no fixed locals.

The adversarial review is Docs/Audits/2026-11-25-binding-and-body-syntax-review.md, sections 'Idea 1' and 'Idea 1b'.

options.name: Mark before the name
options.detail: A changeable name is written `^count: 0`. The mark stands before the name, the thing that becomes writable, and the name is still found by searching `count:`. Destructuring chooses per name: `{^lo, hi}: bounds(values)`. Every write window is made by `place.in_place()`, so `^` never stands next to a binding's value.
options.technical: At the start of a statement, `^` followed by a name and `:` is a changeable binding; the AST mutable flag is set exactly as `:=` sets it today. Once the leading parameter mark retires, nothing else starts a statement that way; a writes-policy receiver mark `^buf.push(` differs at the third token. Every changeable name matches the pattern `(^\s*|[{,]\s*|loop |#Persist )\^\w+[:,}]`.

options.name: Mark after the name
options.detail: A changeable name is written `count^: 0`. Searching `^:` finds most changeable names, though not destructured ones (`{lo^, hi}`). Searching `count:` no longer finds the declaration, and this is the only Jet mark written after what it marks; it also looks like Pascal's pointer `p^`.
options.technical: After a name in a binding head, `^` is the changeable mark. Windows move to `.in_place()` as in A.
options.code:
best^: scores[0]
{lo^, hi}: bounds(values)
first: slots[0].in_place()

options.name: Mark glued to the colon
options.detail: A changeable name is written `count:^ 0`. Searching `:^` lists every changeable name, and searching `count:` still finds it. The mark sits in the column where a parameter's `^` means the caller's value (`p: ^Player`), with the opposite meaning, and destructuring can only make all names changeable or none.
options.technical: `:^` becomes one binding sigil, as `:=` is today. Windows move to `.in_place()` as in A.
options.code:
best:^ scores[0]
{lo, hi}:^ bounds(values)
first: slots[0].in_place()

comparisons.note: A changeable name is marked before the name with `mut`; a writable borrow is marked on the value with `&mut`. The Rust Book, chapter 3.1.
comparisons.code:

let first = &mut slots[0];

comparisons.note: A word chooses: `var` changes, `let` doesn't. A writable parameter is marked on its type with `inout`.
`:=` declares a variable and `::` a constant, the pair Jet's `:=` came from. Jet's fixed names are `:` now.

recommendation.why: A puts the mark on the name that becomes writable, at the line start where readers scan. It keeps name search and per-name destructuring, and never shares a position with a parameter's mark.
gains: Changeable state lines up at the left edge of every function.
`^` before a name means a writable name; `^` on a type means the caller's value.
Every declaration is found by `name:`, and destructuring chooses per name.
A copy and a window can no longer differ by where one mark sits.

losses.loss: Listing every changeable name needs a pattern search instead of a plain-text one.
losses.mitigation: Search `(^\s*|[{,]\s*|loop |#Persist )\^\w+[:,}]`; it finds them all, and editors highlight a marked name.

losses.loss: Write windows, writing matches and writing loops all change spelling, about 419 sites.
losses.mitigation: One `jet fix` migration rewrites every site with its meaning unchanged.

whyNot.reason: It gains a plain-text search but hides the declaration from a `name:` search and adds Jet's only trailing mark.
It puts a local's mark where a parameter's means the caller's value, and loses per-name destructuring.

recommendation.tradeoff: A plain-text `:=` search becomes a pattern search; in return the mark sits where readers look and means one thing.

decisions.title: Handles read like links and stale handles are a compile-time question; one shared object is a `Shared` cell; `@T` live links retire and prefix `@` is freed
decisions.situation: Jet has two ways for one value to refer to another. A live link, written `@Person`, is a counted pointer that every holder reads and writes. A handle, an `ID<Person>`, names a slot in a pool. Links share one object with no setup, but they are half built and put a count and a check word on every linked object. Handles are cheap plain numbers, but every lookup names the pool, and a removed slot stops the program at run time. The owner asked to retire links, free the `@` symbol, and keep both strengths with neither weakness.
decisions.gist: Should handles read like links, one shared object live in a `Shared` cell, and stale handles be caught, retiring `@T`?
decisions.lesson: A handle is a small number naming a slot in a store, plus a count that changes when the slot empties. A live link is a counted pointer to one object. A `Shared` cell is one object that many names can hold. This vote decides how handles read, how one object is shared without a store, and how stale handles are caught.
decisions.story: Maya builds a family tree and a small game. Under A she writes `ben.parent?.name`, and the tree saves as plain numbers. When she removes a cousin, the compiler makes her say what each possibly stale handle should do. Her hero is `hero: Shared{Player{…}}`, and `alias: hero` shares it with no store at all.
decisions.detail:
Sites are at dev 8f4309b5023 (2026-11-25). Every cited file is unchanged since 43951bb7788, and the earlier draft's 4b48f2bc485 sites were all re-read. Counts are pattern counts with comments and strings removed. Probes ran on the installed jet a0.0.46. Code uses the ratified spellings `^name: value` and `place.in_place()` (D-BIND-MARK1=A). Dev still spells them `name := value` (Spellings.jet:13) and `^place` (spec.md:2402-2404).

This ballot reopens D-MEMREF1=A, which made `@T` live links the way to share one value. The owner direction of 2026-11-25 binds it. Free `@`, keep the strengths of handles and links, and design out two downsides. Sharing must need no store first, and a stale handle must not be only a run-time stop.

```text
Built today (dev 8f4309b5023)
- `@` is the live-link sigil: Spellings.jet:31, CoreSurface.jet:373-374, Syntax Markers.jet:10-12.
- Link stack: JetSema Sema/Links.jet (304 lines; sema_link_classify at 57), JetIR
  BuildLinks.jet (427), JetRuntime Links.jet (163; a 24-byte header with count +0,
  exclusivity +8 and size +16, lines 3-10), 18 jet_rt_link_* exports (RuntimeCExports.jet:1666-1683).
- Examples/Memory/LiveLinks.jet:33-34 shares one object: `hero := @Player{…}` then `alias: hero`.
- The compiler holds two links: SemaBodyCheck.program and .environment (Scopes.jet:1188-1190),
  made by sema_body_check_init (Scopes.jet:1788-1789) at five sites: Calls/Checking.jet:1384,
  Expressions/Constructors.jet:545, FunctionCheck.jet:630, MarkerRules.jet:1270 and
  ComptimeItems.jet:1680. They are read with `.*` on 1,355 lines in 98 files. A pattern search
  for assignments, writing calls and `^` marks through them finds none.
- Link card #4500 has open criteria c1 and c5-c13. Two of them (c10, c11) record four ways
  safe code keeps a dangling link today. Card #4756 (stored sibling links) is open.
- Shared<T>: `Shared{value}`, one lock per field read or write, one lock per statement, and a
  clone shares the cell (spec.md:2513-2520). A write that could close a strong loop is refused
  with E0221, and Weak back edges break loops (spec.md:2521-2531). `same` and `downgrade`
  exist (SharedOwner.jet:506, 517).
- Probes on Shared: `hero: Shared{Player{…}}; alias: hero; alias.hp -= 1` runs, and hero
  shows the change. A parent pointer typed `Shared.Weak<Node>?` and set from downgrade() runs.
  Pushing one existing node into two parents (no loop) is refused with E0221, and so is
  moving a node from one parent to another.
- Probe on cost, at --release: 20 million `cell.hp += 1` writes through a Shared cell took
  about 1.1 s; the same writes through `pool[id].hp += 1` took about 20 ms. That is about
  55 ns against 1 ns per write.
- D-SHARED-CYCLE2=A (prove safe writes, through helpers and aliases) and D-GC-OPTIN1=A
  (`#Policy(gc)` on a module opts its types into a collector, and E0221 skips them) are
  ratified and unbuilt: with the opt-in the two-parent probe is still E0221.
- Pool<T> is a list of (generation I64, value T?) entries. ID<T> is (index I64, generation
  I64), 16 bytes, with no store stamp (BuildPools.jet:31-49). `add` always appends, so slots
  are never reused (BuildPools.jet:90-108). `remove` empties a slot and bumps its generation
  (140-162). `ids()` builds a new list of handles before a loop (164-195). `pool[id]` stops
  on a stale ID with "this ID no longer refers to a live value" (197-224). Methods are add,
  remove and ids only (SharedOwner.jet:453-495). `pool[id]` is the PoolSlot node, and a wrong
  index type is E0112 (Literals.jet:1268-1285).
- Probe: a loop over `ids()` that removes a later handle, then reads it, stops with that message.
- Rows<T>/Row<T>: add-only; Row<T> is a U32 with index() (Core Collections.jet:45-74). Only
  the row type is checked (spec.md:2682-2684, Literals.jet:1441).
- `?.` reads (S71): MathLayout.jet:769-771, syntax-decisions.md:1492-1496; a non-optional
  left side is E0047. A field read on T? is E0310 (spec.md:2050-2054).
- Probes: `x?.hp -= 1` is Jet.CompoundAssignNotPlace, `x?.hp = 1` is Jet.InvalidStatement,
  and `pool.has(id)` is Jet.UnknownFunction (D-POOL-HAS1 is unbuilt). Plain
  `xs[idx()] = val()` runs val() before idx(). A written match subject refuses even a read
  of its owner inside the arm (Jet.ReadDuringWriteWindow).
- Probe: `Ghost: distinct Person` type-checks, but no Ghost can be made: `Ghost(p)`,
  `Ghost{p}` and `Ghost.from(p)` all fail. The spec shows `distinct` only over Int
  (spec.md:1157-1158).
- Probe: a `View<T>` struct field cannot hold one table: storing it is a type mismatch, and
  `.count` through it is an unknown field. A plain value field filled from a read parameter
  works: 2,000 inits sharing one million-element list took 13-25 ms, so nothing was deep
  copied, and `jet audit copies` lists the store as one implicit read-view copy.
- Lambda captures: spec.md:1861-1888. Field footprints are inferred and published in the API
  snapshot (spec.md:2478-2484). View facts and their invalidation: spec.md:2438-2448.
- Markers that exist in Prelude Markers.jet: #Local (521-528), #Shared (530), #Transact (582),
  #Context (612) and #ContextKey (626).
Design (nothing below is built)
- The follow rule, liveness proofs, assignment through `?.`, the fixed 8-byte handle with slot
  reuse, `has`, the one-thread form of Shared cells, tracked reads of slots and cells, saving a
  store with its free list, and the compiler cutover. A also depends on D-SHARED-CYCLE2=A and
  D-GC-OPTIN1=A being built.
```

```text
The rule (A)
1. Follow. When h is a handle (ID<T>, Row<T>, or an index type of a `[T#IX]` list) or an
   optional of one, and the next step names a member of T, `h.m` means that member of h's
   entry in its store. A handle step follows again: who.parent?.parent?.name.
2. Store. The one Pool<T> (for ID<T>), Rows<T> (for Row<T>) or `[T#IX]` list (for IX) in
   reach: a parameter, a local, a captured name, or a field one level inside one of those
   (town.people). A Shared<Pool<T>> in those places counts. Context values and module
   statics are never searched.
3. Zero stores in reach: compile error; the fix adds the store parameter.
4. Two or more: compile error naming each; the fix writes `store[h].m`. Depth never decides.
5. Generic code resolves at its definition against declared types: a Pool<T> parameter
   serves ID<T>. An instantiation never changes the store and never adds an error.
6. Writes need the store writable, else E0205, as `store[h].m = v` does (spec.md:2652-2654).
7. Handle members and universal methods act on the handle: h.copy(), h.move(), r.index().
   Any other name that is both a handle member and a member of T is a compile error naming
   both; write store[h].m. jet fmt never rewrites store[h].copy() as h.copy().
8. A handle passed where a handle is expected stays a handle: hire(town, ben, mill).
9. Captures. A lambda that does not escape follows through a captured store under the
   capture rules: it reads its own copy, and a call after the store changed is E0204
   (spec.md:1863-1871). A lambda that escapes would own a copy of the store
   (spec.md:1871-1876), so a follow there is a compile error. The fix takes the store as a
   lambda parameter or captures a Shared<Pool<T>>. No follow silently reads a snapshot.
10. Lowering. One match becomes the existing PoolSlot node (Literals.jet:1277), so IR and
    backends reuse `pool[id]` code. A proven follow drops the generation compare.
11. One handle family. A `[T#IX]` list (D-ARRAY-INDEX1, unbuilt) has one slot per index
    value, so its follows are always proven and never checked. Game asset handles
    (D-GAME-ASSET1, unbuilt) are ID<T> into a store reached through `scene.assets`, so they
    follow, prove and go stale by this rule. No second handle kind exists.
```

**Downside 1: sharing needs no store.** One object with many holders is a `Shared` cell: `hero: Shared{Player{name: "Aria", hp: 10}}`, then `alias: hero`. Both names reach one object, and `alias.hp -= 1` shows through `hero`. This is built today, and the probe above ran it. It is the link example with `Shared{…}` in place of `@`, and no pool exists anywhere.

```text
Shared cells by case
- One object, many holders (a hero, a settings object): built and probed.
- A tree built in place with parent pointers: built. Children are Shared<Node>, and the parent
  is a Shared.Weak<Node>? from downgrade() (probed).
- Observers: the subject keeps Shared.Weak entries, so a dropped observer reads as gone and
  nothing keeps it alive.
- One child under two parents, or a node moved to a new parent: refused today with E0221 even
  when no loop forms (probed). D-SHARED-CYCLE2=A accepts such a write once its alias and call
  summaries prove no loop.
- Real loops (a graph with cycles, GUI nodes that point at each other): D-GC-OPTIN1=A lets
  `#Policy(gc)` on the module opt those types into a collector. Without the opt-in, the
  E0221 fixes are a Weak back edge, a handle, or the opt-in line, which `jet fix` writes.
- Across tasks: the cell takes its locked form (below).
No case needs a store first. A graph with many nodes and frequent removal still fits a store
better: a handle costs 8 bytes and no count.
```

**Cost of a cell.** Today every field read or write of a cell takes a lock. The probe above measured about 55 ns per write against about 1 ns through a pool slot. That fails the performance gate for games and GUI trees. So A moves D-MEMREF-TASK1=A's law from links to cells. If any cell of a type can reach another task, cells of that type use an atomic count and the lock. Otherwise they use a plain count and no lock.

`#Local` forbids crossing, `#Shared` forces the locked form, and `jet inspect` lists each switch, as D-DATARACE1=C already does for reactive boxes. Sendability is checked on concrete types at each generic use, so each type has one form. A paired two-program cell must show a one-thread cell write at plain field cost and the locked form still correct across tasks.

A second name for a place inside one function needs no cell: a write window, `edit: hero.in_place()`, is the place itself.

```text
Designs rejected for downside 1
- An implicit store per type: hides which store a function touches, loses no-alias facts,
  and leaves open when its slots are freed.
- An implicit store per function: fixes only the demo; a value that leaves the function
  needs a real store again.
- Generational references on every object, as Vale does: a check per use, and aliasing the
  optimizer cannot see.
- A collector for every object, as Java, Go and Pony do: every program pays for it, while
  D-GC-OPTIN1 makes only types with real loops pay.
- Regions with free pointers inside, as Verona has: a region is a store under another name,
  and its inner pointers still need a collector or a stale check.
```

**Downside 2: a stale handle is a compile-time question.** The compiler tracks which handles are proven live. That is the same kind of fact it keeps for windows, which an invalidating event ends (spec.md:2438-2448). A removal is one more such event. A plain `.` follows only a proven handle. Every other handle is followed with `?.`, checked with `has`, or indexed as `store[h]`. So the only run-time stop left is one the programmer writes.

```text
Stale handles (A)
A proof says: this handle is live in this one store place. With a proof, plain `.` compiles
and the follow skips the generation compare. The bounds compare stays, so a wrong proof can
never read outside the store. At a join, a handle is proven only if every path proved it.
Proven live:
- h from store.add(...) in this function.
- h bound by `loop h in store.ids()`, inside the body, when the body removes nothing from that
  store except h and calls nothing that may. ids() is a list made before the loop, so a handle
  removed earlier in the loop is still visited (probed).
- After store.has(h) is true: in the true branch, or after `if !store.has(h) -> return`.
- A handle a call returns proven in a store the caller passed, as in `e: spawn(world)`.
  "Returns proven" is inferred and published like may-remove.
- A handle parameter whose store is reached through another parameter. If the body follows it
  with plain `.` before any check, the function requires it live. That fact is inferred and
  published, and each caller must pass a handle proven in the same store it passes, else a
  compile error at the call. Function values and trait methods always require it.
A proof ends at:
- a `remove` on that store, unless the removed handle is proven different (another add, or
  checked != h);
- an assignment, move or replacement of the store or of any value that holds it;
- a call that takes the store, or a value holding it, writable and may remove or replace.
  "May remove" is inferred per function and published in the API snapshot, as field
  footprints are (spec.md:2478-2484). A call through a function value or trait method may;
- a call to a local lambda that captured the store writable;
- the end of the statement or #Transact block, for a store inside a Shared cell, a context or
  a static, since another holder may remove at any time.
After store.remove(h), h is known removed, and any follow of h is a compile error.
Unproven: a handle read from a field, list, map, file, channel, context or static, or one whose
proof ended. A plain `.` on it is a compile error whose fixes are `?.`, `has` or `store[h]`.
`h?.m` reads a removed slot as absent. On a non-optional handle it means "if live", which
extends E0047 to allow handles on the left.
`store[h]` keeps today's stop for a stale h, like list indexing. It is the explicit opt-in.
[INFERENCE] Compile cost: one flow pass per function over handle locals, as for moves, and one
published fact per store parameter; not measured.
```

```text
What remains after A, and its cost
- store[h] on a stale h stops, as today. It is written on purpose, like xs[i].
- h?.m on a removed slot is absent: a read falls back and a write is skipped. A logic error is
  still possible, as with a Swift weak reference that became nil.
- Walking handles kept in fields (tree children, graph edges) writes `?.` (skip) or `store[h]`
  (stop) at each step. No short form means "follow or stop".
- A handle from another store of the same type follows into the store in reach. The generation
  compare catches it unless that slot's generation happens to match. Today's 16-byte ID has no
  store stamp either (BuildPools.jet:42-49).
- A Row<T> from another table of the same row type reads another row; only bounds are checked.
- Across tasks proofs are one statement long, so code on a shared store mostly writes `?.`.
- Handles loaded from disk or received from a channel start unproven.
- A store deeper than one field inside a parameter is not searched; pass the inner value.
- ids() builds a list per loop (BuildPools.jet:164-195); the benchmark pair covers it.
- [INFERENCE] Code that removes often inside loops over other handles will write more `?.`.
```

**Handle layout.** `ID<T>` becomes 8 bytes for every T: a 32-bit slot and a 32-bit generation. The size never depends on how many stores a program makes, and no whole-program count exists. Today's ID is 16 bytes with no store stamp, so nothing that catches a wrong store today is lost.

Stores reuse emptied slots. A slot whose generation would reach the all-ones value is retired, so a generation never wraps. The all-ones generation is never live, so `ID<T>?` uses it for None and is also 8 bytes. A store holds at most 4,294,967,295 slots, retired ones included, and `add` past that stops, as Rows' add does (Core Collections.jet:61-65).

Rust slotmap keys are also 8 bytes, but a version wraps after 2^31 reuses of one slot, which its docs call a rare spurious match. Retiring the slot removes that case at the cost of one slot per about four billion reuses. A 16-byte stamped handle was rejected: handles sit in every record edge, so their size sets peak memory and cache use. A store saves its slots, generations and free list, and a handle saves as two numbers. Loaded handles start unproven, so no remap pass runs.

```text
Assignment through ?. (one new statement form for every optional place)
- Forms: `a?.b = v`, `a?.b op= v`, and a writing call such as `a?.items.push(x)`. Each `?.`
  step is a T? place or a handle. It is a statement and has no value.
- Order: the chain's tests run left to right. Each `?.` step tests its value: None, or a
  removed slot, is absent. If any step is absent, nothing more runs: the right side is not
  evaluated and nothing is written. Otherwise the right side runs, then the one write.
- Plain assignment runs the other way: `xs[idx()] = val()` runs val() first (probed). A `?.`
  write must test first to skip the right side, so the spec states both orders.
- The right side may read anything. It may not write a place the chain passes through, remove
  from a store the chain follows, or call something that may. That is a compile error whose
  fix binds the value on the line before, so no test goes stale before the write. A written
  match already guards its owner this way (Jet.ReadDuringWriteWindow, probed).
- Place: the base must be writable: a `^` binding, a `^` parameter, or a writable store.
- Today `x?.hp -= 1` is Jet.CompoundAssignNotPlace and `x?.hp = 1` is Jet.InvalidStatement.
- Swift skips the right side of `a?.b = f()` when a is nil; A matches that.
```

**A second store of one type.** A second `Pool<Person>` field in `Town` makes every bare `ID<Person>` follow that sees `Town` a compile error. Each error carries a machine fix that writes the store, so meaning never changes silently. The way to avoid it is a wrapper element type, `Ghost: struct { person: Person }`, so the second store's handles are `ID<Ghost>`. This builds today.

A `distinct` struct type cannot be made today (probed), so it is not offered. Rust slotmap solves the same case with a key type per map (`new_key_type!`). A Jet spelling for that would need its own ballot.

**Rows on the wrong table.** A `Row<T>` from another table of the same row type reads the wrong row with only a bounds check. That holds today and under A (Core Collections.jet:45-52, spec.md:2682-2684). Under A the follow uses the one table in reach, so the risk needs a row to cross between two tables of one type. The wrapper fix applies. Typed-index lists (D-ARRAY-INDEX1, unbuilt) let two lists share an index type, which is memory-safe because the index fits both.

**The compiler's own links.** `program` and `environment` become plain value fields, `program: SemaProgramTables` and `environment: SemaScopeEnvironment`. A `View<T>` field was tried and fails: it cannot hold one table (probed). A value field filled from a read parameter shares the tables instead of copying them (spec.md:2318-2330), and the probe above measured no deep copy.

The 1,355 reads drop `.*`, and the five init sites drop `@`. `jet audit copies` will list each init as an implicit read-view copy. [INFERENCE] Behavior is unchanged, since no write goes through the links; the compiler's own tests decide.

```text
Every downside, and what removes it
1. Sharing needs a store -> a Shared cell plus a second name, never a store. Built for one
   object, trees and Weak back edges; shared children, moves and real loops need
   D-SHARED-CYCLE2 and D-GC-OPTIN1 built.
2. Stale handle only stops at run time -> proofs make plain `.` safe; the rest is `?.`, `has`
   or an explicit store[h]. Remaining cost: the list above.
3. Lookups name the store -> the follow rule finds the one store in reach.
4. Handle size chosen by counting -> fixed 8 bytes for every T, `ID<T>?` included.
5. `?.` cannot write -> one new statement form with a fixed order and a guarded right side.
6. Two stores of one type -> compile error with a fix; a wrapper element type avoids it.
7. Member clashes -> handle members and copy/move win; other clashes are compile errors.
8. Generic code -> resolved at the definition, never per instantiation.
9. Escaping lambdas -> a follow through a captured plain store is a compile error.
10. Check cost in hot loops -> proven follows drop the generation compare; a benchmark pair
    against hand-written index code is still owed.
11. Hidden lookup -> hover names the store; signatures list every store.
12. Cycles -> handle cycles cost nothing; Shared loops use Weak, proven writes, or the
    opt-in collector.
13. FFI, intrusive and self-referential data -> mem.Ptr<T> under #Unsafe and Pin<T>, unchanged.
14. Cell cost -> the one-thread form for every type that never reaches a task.
15. Several handle kinds -> ID, Row, typed indexes and asset handles share one rule.
```

Peers split four ways. Swift, C#, Java and Go give stored references with counting or a collector. Rust slotmap, Bevy, Flecs and the Zig compiler use handles, and every lookup names the store. Pony and Verona share objects through reference capabilities, with a collector per actor or per region. Hylo and Austral forbid stored references and offer no short form. A is the handle model with a link-length reading, Swift's `?.` writes and weak-style absence, and counted cells that collect only types that opt in.

options.name: Follow handles through the one store in reach and share objects with Shared cells
options.detail:
Relationships are handles: an `ID<T>` into a `Pool<T>`, or a `Row<T>` into `Rows<T>`. Writing `who.parent?.name` follows the handle through the one store of that type the function can see. One object with many holders needs no store: `hero: Shared{Player{…}}`, then `alias: hero`. Trees use Weak parent pointers, and types with real loops opt into a collector. Live `@T` links retire, and prefix `@` is free.

The compiler tracks which handles are proven live. A handle from `add`, from a loop over `ids()` that removes nothing else, or after `has` follows with a plain `.` and no check. A handle read from a field follows with `?.`, which treats a removed slot as absent. A plain `.` on an unproven handle is a compile error, so no stale handle stops a program by surprise. Only an explicit `store[h]` keeps today's stop.
options.technical:
Sema resolves a member step on a handle type against the store types in reach and lowers one match to the existing pool-slot node. Liveness facts come from `add`, `ids` loops, `has`, published parameter and result facts, and end at a statement that may remove or replace the store. Each function's may-remove fact is inferred and published with its API, as field footprints are. Proven follows drop the generation compare and keep the bounds compare.

Handles are 8 bytes for every type, `ID<T>?` included. `?.` gains assignment for every optional place: tests first, then the right side, which may not write the chain. Shared cells take a one-thread form for every type that never reaches a task. The compiler's two links become value fields.

options.name: Name the store once per chain
options.detail:
Everything in A holds except the short form. Every chain starts at the store, as in `town.people[who].parent?.name`. Handle fields inside the chain follow within that store, or within its one sibling store of the right type.

Nothing is found by searching what is in reach, so each line shows its store. Every chain is longer than a link by the store name and brackets. Sharing uses `Shared` cells, and stale-handle proofs work as in A.
options.technical: Sema resolves handle fields inside a chain whose root is a `store[h]` place. A field of another handle type resolves to the one store of that type beside the root. Proofs, `?.` writes, layout, cells and the compiler cutover are as in A.

options.name: Keep live links as they are today
options.detail:
Keep `@Person` as the way to share one object, and finish building it. Links are partly built: they parse, check and run today, and the compiler itself holds two of them. Pools stay for games and graphs, with today's run-time stop on a stale handle.

The link work still owes runtime alias checks, counted lifetimes with cycle collection, and task-safe counting that costs no atomics in one-thread code. It also owes four safety fixes: today safe code can keep a dangling link in four ways (#4500 c10, c11). The `@` symbol stays taken. Retiring links later costs a migration of everything built on them by then.
options.technical: Keeps Sema/Links.jet, BuildLinks.jet and the runtime header with a count, an exclusivity word and a size. Every kept link pays a count change on copy and drop, atomic when shared. Any call that receives a link may write through an alias, so the optimizer loses no-alias facts at link uses. The `?.` writes, stale-handle proofs and one-thread cells of A could still be adopted on their own.

options.name: Search the context too
options.detail:
This is the starting idea as stated. It works as A, and a store set with `#Context(people: town.people) { }` is also searched. Deep call chains need no store parameter.

Context values are fixed for their block and kept by tasks started inside it. A store found there can be read but not written, and a task may keep reading it after the block ends. A signature no longer shows which stores a function reads, so may-remove facts and parameter proofs no longer cover every follow.
options.technical: Context reads are hidden inputs, so sema must add each followed store to the function facts that signatures used to show. Writes through a context store need a new writable context, which the context design does not have. Tasks inheriting a context store would share it without `Shared`. Handles followed through the context start unproven, so most follows there need `?.`.

comparisons.note: Versioned keys are a 32-bit index and a 32-bit version. The version wraps after 2^31 reuses of one slot, which may give a spurious match, and a key from another map is a logic error, not undefined behavior. A key type per map (`new_key_type!`) catches the wrong map. Source: docs.rs/slotmap, crate docs and KeyData.
A tree with parent pointers needs `Rc`, `RefCell` and `Weak`, and stored `&T` needs lifetime parameters. Source: The Rust Book, chapter 15.6.

An `Entity` is a 32-bit index plus a generation in 8 bytes, looked up through a query or the world; one from another world fails or reads the wrong entity. Source: docs.rs/bevy 0.15, bevy::ecs::entity::Entity and Parent.
Entity ids are 64-bit with a generation in the upper half; relationships such as ChildOf are pairs. Source: flecs.dev docs, Relationships manual.
comparisons.code:
ecs_entity_t parent = ecs_get_target(world, e, EcsChildOf, 0);
const Name *n = ecs_get(world, parent, Name);

comparisons.note: Classes are counted references; back edges are `weak` and read as nil once their object is gone. Optional chaining also assigns and skips the right side on nil. Source: The Swift Programming Language, Optional Chaining and Automatic Reference Counting.
comparisons.code:
class Person { weak var parent: Person?; var hp = 10 }
ben.parent?.hp -= 1   // skipped when parent is nil

comparisons.note: Objects are references under a tracing collector; `?.` follows a nullable reference. Source: Microsoft Learn, member access operators.
Every object is a reference under a tracing collector, so cycles cost nothing to write and every program pays for collection. Source: The Java Language Specification, chapter 4.3 and 12.6.
comparisons.code:
class Person { String name; Person parent; }
String name = ben.parent != null ? ben.parent.name : "nobody";

comparisons.note: Pointers under a tracing collector; cycles are fine and aliasing is unchecked. Source: The Go Programming Language Specification.
comparisons.code:
type Person struct { Name string; Parent *Person }
name := ben.Parent.Name

comparisons.note: Reference capabilities decide who may read or write an object, so objects are shared with no data races and no store; each actor has its own collector (ORCA). Source: Pony tutorial, Reference Capabilities; Clebsch et al., Orca, OOPSLA 2017.
comparisons.code:
class Person
  var name: String
  var parent: (Person ref | None) = None

comparisons.note: Objects live in regions; pointers inside a region are free, and each region picks its own memory manager (arena, counting or tracing). Source: Arvidsson et al., Reference Capabilities for Flexible Memory Management, OOPSLA 2023.
Raw optional pointers, and the Zig compiler stores its trees as 32-bit indices into arrays. Source: Andrew Kelley, Practical Data Oriented Design, Handmade Seattle 2021.
comparisons.code:
const Node = struct { parent: ?*Node, name: []const u8 };
const name = if (ben.parent) |p| p.name else "nobody";

comparisons.note: Raw pointers by default; handle maps are a common library pattern. Weissflog argues handles beat pointers for safety and memory layout. Source: floooh.github.io, Handles are the better pointers, 2018.
comparisons.code:
Person :: struct { name: string, parent: ^Person }
name := ben.parent.name if ben.parent != nil else "nobody"

comparisons.note: Every non-owning reference checks a generation; regions remove checks for data a pure call cannot change. Source: verdagon.dev, Generational References and Zero-Cost Borrowing with Vale Regions.
comparisons.code:
struct Person { name str; parent Opt<&Person>; }
// each use of a non-owning reference checks its generation

comparisons.note: Mutable value semantics: no stored references, access through projections that cannot escape. Source: Racordon et al., Implementation Strategies for Mutable Value Semantics, JOT 2022.
comparisons.code:
subscript person(_ i: Int): Person { yield people[i] }
inout p = &town.people[i]

comparisons.note: References carry an origin the compiler tracks; storing one in a struct needs an origin parameter. Source: Mojo manual, Lifetimes, origins and references.
comparisons.code:
struct View[origin: Origin]:
    var p: Pointer[Person, origin]

comparisons.note: Linear types and region borrows; a reference cannot be stored past its region. Source: Austral specification, Borrowing.

recommendation.why: A keeps the short reading and no-setup sharing of a link and the safety and speed of a handle. Stale handles become compile-time choices, cells cost a plain count unless they reach a task, signatures keep every store, and `@` is freed.
gains: `who.parent?.name` reads as short as a link.
One object, many holders, no store: a `Shared` cell and a second name.
A stale handle stops only where the code writes `store[h]`.
Handles are 8-byte plain numbers, optional ones too: they save, compare and cross tasks.
Prefix `@` is free, and about 900 lines of link machinery retire.

losses.loss: A function that follows handles must take their store.
losses.mitigation: One world value can carry every store, and the compiler offers the parameter as a fix.

losses.loss: Handles read from fields need `?.`, a `has` check or `store[h]` at each step.
losses.mitigation: The fix is one character or one line, and it replaces a surprise stop with a choice.

losses.loss: A `?.` on a removed slot silently does nothing.
losses.mitigation: Code that must not skip writes `store[h]`, which keeps today's stop and message.

losses.loss: A cell of a type that reaches a task pays a lock and an atomic count per step.
losses.mitigation: Every other type uses the one-thread form with a plain count and no lock, and hot data can live in stores.

losses.loss: Shared objects that form real loops need their module opted into a collector.
losses.mitigation: Trees, observers and shared children need no collector: Weak back edges and proven writes cover them, and `jet fix` writes the opt-in line.

whyNot.reason: It is A without the short form. Every chain repeats the store name, which is the friction the owner asked to remove.

Every link, even one to a local place, is a counted pointer the optimizer must treat as an alias. The link work still has four open ways to keep a dangling link in safe code, and `@` stays taken. A's cells give the same sharing only where a program asks for it.
Context stores cannot be written, stay readable by tasks after their block, and hide from signatures what a function reads.

recommendation.tradeoff: Each function that follows handles names its store once, and each unproven handle says what happens when its slot is gone. In return navigation reads like a link and costs what an index costs.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude Opus. Adversarial model family: Claude Opus. Fresh agent: ReviewHandleNav2. Probes found Shared refusing shared children and moves at 55 ns per write, five unsound proof gaps, a stale test in `?.` writes, and two fixes that could not build. All are repaired, and each claim holds within stated limits once D-SHARED-CYCLE2, D-GC-OPTIN1 and the benchmarks are built (Docs/Audits/2026-11-25-handle-navigation-review.md).

surface.lesson: A handle is a small number naming a slot in a store, plus a count that changes when the slot empties. A live link is a counted pointer to one object. A `Shared` cell is one object that many names can hold. This vote decides how handles read, how objects are shared, and how stale handles are caught.

decisions.title: Changeable module globals: what group workers, pure code, caches and tests may do with them
decisions.situation: A game keeps its score, its enemy list and its level in changeable values at the top of a file, and many functions use them. A ratified rule already lets every function read and change these values and keeps other tasks away from them. It left four things open or unsafe. Worker tasks in a group may not even read a global. Pure functions and caches can depend on one unseen, so a cache can return a stale answer. Each test gets its own copy only by slowing every access in test builds. We recommend A: group workers borrow globals as they borrow locals, pure code and caches may not read them, and each test restores the start values.
decisions.gist: Should group workers borrow changeable module globals, should pure code and caches be barred from reading them, and how should each test start fresh?
decisions.lesson: A module global is a changeable value declared at the top of a file, such as a game's score. A ratified rule already lets functions read and change one and keeps other tasks away from it. Three questions remain open: may worker tasks in a group use it, may pure functions and caches read it, and how does each test start fresh without slowing shipped code?
decisions.story: Sam is writing a small arcade game. The score, the enemy list and the current level sit at the top of the file, and a dozen functions use them. Sam adds worker tasks that plan each enemy's next move, a cached cost function, and a test that a hit adds five points. Sam should not need to copy the enemy list before each fan-out, see a cache return last level's answer, or chase a test that fails only when another test ran first.
decisions.detail:
What this decides. The ratified module-variable rule (D-MODULE-VAR1=A, 2026-11-10) already settles most of how a changeable global behaves. Card #6859 builds it, and its criteria C1-C11 hold every part this ballot does not reopen. This ballot decides only what that rule left open, and it says plainly where it amends the rule. The spelling stays `^score: 0` (D-BIND-MARK1=A, 2026-11-25); today's compiler still spells it `score := 0`.

```text
Already ratified and built under card #6859 (not reopened here)
- Functions, run included, read and write globals; the E0111 module branch goes (rule 1; C3).
- One touch fact per function, inferred through calls, closures, function values and trait
  dispatch, shown by hover, docs and jet inspect; the second read scan is deleted (rules 2, 4; C1, C9).
- The main task owns every global. A task whose work touches one is a build error naming the
  variable and the call path (rule 3; C2). #Persist globals follow the same rule (C8).
- No write behind a reader's back: a call that may write a global while the caller looks into
  it is refused (rule 5; C4).
- In-place edits (enemies.push(e), frame[i] = v, lending to a ^ parameter); E0223 retires (C7).
- A C callback that touches a global is refused, because C picks its thread (C10).
- A generic module gets one copy per instance; E0003 for it retires (C5).
- Each test starts with its own copy of every global and module Shared holder (rule 6; C6).
- The E0338 row text, docs of a public function's touches, a reference page (C11).
- Start values are baked while building (D-JAI-COMPTIME1=A); no code runs before run (E0643).
  jet dev restarts the program and keeps only #Persist values (D-DEV-STATE1=A, D-PERSIST-ONLY1=A).
```

```text
Decided here, and what each part amends
1 Group workers borrow globals: task.group children, task.all, task.race and task.any branches,
  and para_map, para_filter, para_partition and para_fold callbacks.
  Amends D-MODULE-VAR1 rule 3, which refuses any task "even to read".
2 Every other task stays refused, as ratified. A function exported to C joins the C callback
  rule, because a C host may call it on any thread. New.
3 A -[]> function may not read changeable module state. E3401 widens; amends spec.md:3075-3082.
4 A #Memo function may not read or write it. E0938 widens (card #7032 criterion 3).
5 How each test starts fresh: restore start values in one process, and run tests side by side
  in separate processes. Amends the mechanism of D-MODULE-VAR1 rule 6, one sentence of
  D-CORE-GLOBAL-STATE1, and what output checks see (Reference/cli.md:1169).
```

Worker tasks. A task.group joins every child at its closing brace, so a child may already borrow the opener's locals (spec.md:4923-4948). Under A a changeable global is borrowed the same way. Reads are free. A write needs a place no other child reaches: distinct fields and constant indexes are separate, and a dynamic index overlaps. A write made inside a called function holds the whole global. The global's type must be able to cross tasks, as a borrowed local's must.

Nesting and the opener. A child lends only what it holds, so a group inside a child follows the same rule. Code in the group body runs beside the children, so it joins the check as it does for locals (E1101). The branches of task.all, task.race and task.any borrow until the combinator returns. The parallel list adapters join before they return, so their callbacks may read globals. A callback that writes one is E1101, as an ordinary changeable capture is today (spec.md:4844-4847).

Other tasks. A handle task started outside a group body can outlive the function that started it, and a detached task outlives everything. A child spawned through a Group parameter joins in another frame, so the opener can't see what it touches. All three stay refused, as ratified. The task error gains a third fix: do the work in a task.group. On the web a browser refuses task groups (spec.md:4889-4891), so only the main task touches a global there.

Threads that C or Core chooses. A C callback that touches a global is refused (ratified, card #6859 C10). A function exported with #Export(c) is the same case, because a C host may call it on any thread. Under A it is refused with the same row unless every global it touches is a raw word. Core functions that run a callback on another thread, such as interrupt handlers and realtime audio callbacks, accept only functions that touch nothing, by ratified rule 4.

Pure code. A -[]> function already may not write changeable module state, because a later call would see the write. Under A it may not read that state either, because an earlier write would change its answer. The state is the list E3401 already names for writes: a global, a #Persist global, a module Shared holder's value and a module Cell. Context reads stay allowed, as today. A pure function that needs a global takes its value as a parameter.

Caches. A #Memo function may neither read nor write that state, so its cache can't go stale. Its key already holds every context value it reads (Examples/Concurrency/ContextReads.jet). Option C keeps the reads and keys the cache on a write count instead. Core's process-lifetime caches whose contents can't change an answer are not state for this rule; the sweep classes each of Core's 18 lifetime sites.

The debugger. The debugger checks a watched expression as a -[]> function and refuses only writes; jet eval --pure runs the same check. Both keep refusing writes only, so a watch on a global still works. The debugger's own call-graph walk (EvalProbe.jet:531-551) reads the touch fact instead and is deleted.

Tests, the mechanism. Ratified rule 6 reaches every global through the test's world, one extra load per access in test builds. A drops that load. A test build keeps a read-only copy of each changeable start value, including the data it points to. Before each test, rerun attempt and output check, the harness drops the live value of each global the test touches that an earlier test wrote. Then it copies the start value back.

The touch fact gives each test's set while building, and the harness knows the run order, so nothing is tracked while running. Module Shared holders and declared event points publish as World sites in test builds. After each test the harness calls the existing world-site reset, which nothing calls today. The reset also clears #Memo caches. A test ends when its tasks end: the harness cancels and joins any task the test left running before it restores.

Tests side by side. Under A one process runs one test at a time, because its tests share one copy. To run tests in parallel, the runner gives each core a child process and splits a file's tests between them. Today children start only for reruns, isolated tests and time limits, so this is new runner work. A child starts once and runs many tests. The ratified world pointer would also have needed new work to run tests in parallel.

What A amends in ratified text. D-CORE-GLOBAL-STATE1 says no process-wide clear before each test is allowed. A's restore is a compiler-built clear, so A amends that sentence for program globals and module holders. Core storage keeps its per-world tables. D-TEST-SCHEDULES1 runs reruns side by side on the profile's workers, and under A those workers are processes. A world made with testing.world shares its test's globals.

Output checks. Reference/cli.md:1169 says output checks run after the tests in the same process and see what they left. Once tests run in several processes there is no single batch state to see. So under A a check starts from start values and reads what the tests wrote to files. OutputCheckObservesTheJoinedBatchState.fixture reads a #Persist global today, so it is rewritten to read its events file.

Shipped builds. Group loans, purity and #Memo checks run while building. The start-value copy, the restore and the World sites exist only in test builds. A release, run or dev build pays nothing while running, which meets the performance gate. The compile cost is one more set per function, solved in the walk E3401 already does. The solver skips it when a program has no changeable global (Effects/Checks.jet:7069-7085).

```text
Edge cases
- A write in a function a child calls holds the whole global; a write in the child's own body
  holds just the field or constant index it names.
- A global whose type can't cross tasks, such as one holding a Cell, can't be lent to a child.
- Function values: a dynamic call touches every possible target's set (ratified).
- Raw words: a global whose every write sits inside #Unsafe skips the task check and the test
  restore, but purity and #Memo still see it. One plain write makes it tracked.
- #Persist: tests restore it like any global. jet dev keeps it across restarts, and an edited
  start value does not replace a kept one (D-DEV-STATE1=A).
- Hot reload: live code swap is retired, so a save restarts the program and plain globals start
  over. If a swap engine returns, a swap must wait until no group that lends a global is open.
- Shared holders build on first read and keep the first published cell (BuildSharedSites.jet:5-7),
  so two children reading one never race on its start.
- Packages: a library's touch facts travel in its published interface, as its effect rows do
  [inference; the package format was not read].
- Statement files: a top-level ^count: 0 among statements stays a local of that run
  (D-SCRIPT-HELPERS1=A).
- Plugins run in their own sandboxed memory and never see host globals
  [inference from D-PLUGIN-ENGINE1=A].
- Wasm and no-OS targets copy start values in before run (D-JAI-COMPTIME1=A); the rules are the same.
```

What A cannot remove. A program holds one copy of each global, so two independent games in one process need a struct; D buys many copies for a load on every access. A task that can outlive its starter can't touch a global. A pure function can't read one. Test builds carry a second copy of each start value, and running tests side by side costs one child process per core.

options.name: Group workers borrow globals; pure code and caches can't read them; tests restore start values
options.detail: Globals stay one line and read and write like locals, as ratified. Workers in a task.group, the branches of task.all, task.race and task.any, and the parallel list adapters borrow globals as they borrow the opener's locals. Every other task, and any function C may call, still may not touch one. Pure and memoised functions may not read changeable module state. Each test, rerun and output check starts from start values, restored in one process, and tests run side by side in separate processes.
options.technical: Group loans reuse the borrowed-capture rule (spec.md:4923-4948), with the touch fact naming each child's global places. E3401 adds reads of the state it already lists for writes, and E0938 adds any touch. The debugger and jet eval --pure keep a writes-only check. An #Export(c) function joins the C callback row. Test builds keep a read-only copy of each start value and restore touched globals an earlier test wrote. Holders and event points become World sites there. The runner splits a file's tests across per-core child processes.

options.name: The ratified rule as written, plus the cache fix
options.detail: Functions read and write globals, and the compiler refuses any task that touches one, even a group worker that only reads. Pure functions may still read a global. A #Memo function may not read one, because card #7032 requires a cache fix whatever wins. Each test gets its own copy through one extra load on every access in test builds, and tests run side by side in one process.
options.technical: D-MODULE-VAR1=A alone, as card #6859 builds it, plus E0938 widened to touches. The task row refuses group children, combinator branches and para adapter callbacks that touch a global. E3401 stays writes-only. Test builds reach every global through a world base pointer, and the harness runs tests in parallel inside one process, which is new runner work.

options.name: As A, but pure code may read globals and caches track their writes
options.detail: Group loans, task refusals and the test restore are A's. A pure function may read a changeable global, as it may read the task context. A #Memo function may read a global too: the program counts the writes to each global a cache reads, and the cache key holds those counts. Module Shared holders and Cells stay refused in a #Memo function, because writes reach them through copies the compiler can't follow.
options.technical: E3401 stays writes-only. Each := or #Persist global that some #Memo function reads gets a write counter. Every write site the touch fact lists adds one to it. A plain add is enough, because no two tasks write one global at once. A #Memo lookup compares one counter per global read. E0938 adds holder and Cell touches only. This extends how a #Memo key already holds context values (Examples/Concurrency/ContextReads.jet).

options.name: Every global lives in a world, and a program can make many worlds
options.detail: As A, but every global is reached through the current world in every build, not only in tests. A program can run several worlds at once, such as many matches on one server, and tests run side by side in one process with no restore. Every access to a global costs one extra load, in shipped builds too.
options.technical: A world base pointer in a register or thread slot, set by world.run. Each world copies all start values when it is made, so the baked no-copy start applies only to the first world. Group loans, task refusals, purity and #Memo rules are A's. Tests need no restore and no child processes.

comparisons.note: A `static mut` may be touched only in unsafe code, and since the 2024 edition a lint denies taking a reference to one by default. Safe code wraps a global in a `Mutex` or keeps one copy per thread. Scoped threads may borrow the caller's locals until they join, which is A's rule for group workers, but not a `static mut`. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/edition-guide/rust-2024/static-mut-references.html and https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/thread/fn.scope.html

Swift 6 refuses a plain global var as "not concurrency-safe" unless it belongs to a global actor such as the main actor, or is marked nonisolated(unsafe). That is close to Jet's main-task owner, but written on every declaration. Other code reaches it by awaiting a hop to the main actor. Source: https://www.swift.org/migration/documentation/swift-6-concurrency-migration-guide/commonproblems/
A pure function may not read or write a changeable global, and may read an immutable one. That is A's rule for -[]> code. Source: https://dlang.org/spec/function.html#pure-functions
comparisons.code:
int level = 1;
pure int cost(int x) { return x * level; }   // error: reading mutable global state

comparisons.note: The legacy memory manager confined top-level state to the main thread and checked it while running. The new memory manager, the default since Kotlin 1.7.20, lifted that limit, so any thread may change a top-level property. A keeps the confinement but checks it while building and lets group workers in. Source: https://kotlinlang.org/docs/native-migration-guide.html
comparisons.code: var score = 0   // legacy: only the main thread; since 1.7.20: any thread

comparisons.note: A container-level var is a plain global with no race or test check, and threadlocal gives each thread its own copy. Source: https://ziglang.org/documentation/master/#Container-Level-Variables
comparisons.code:
var score: i32 = 0;
threadlocal var scratch: [256]u8 = undefined;

comparisons.note: Package-level variables are plain globals, and the thread_local attribute gives each thread a copy. Nothing checks tasks or tests. Source: https://odin-lang.org/docs/overview/

Globals are plain and fast, and a global changed while compiling is copied into the program, as Jet bakes a start value. A hidden context carries the allocator and logger instead of globals. Sources: Jonathan Blow, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OHZwYYW9koI at 00:18:04; Docs/Audits/jai-parity-2026-10-16.md.
comparisons.code:
score: int;
#run { score = compute_start(); }   // kept in the executable

comparisons.note: Package variables are plain, and parallel tests share them. The race detector only finds races that happen while running, so it misses paths a test never takes. Source: https://go.dev/doc/articles/race_detector
comparisons.code:
var score int
func TestHit(t *testing.T) { t.Parallel(); hit(5) }   // shares score

comparisons.note: Each test runs in its own process, so singletons and globals separate per test with no coordination. The stated costs are slower process creation on Windows and harder sharing between tests. A runs many tests per child process and restores start values between them. Source: https://nexte.st/docs/design/why-process-per-test/
comparisons.code: cargo nextest run   # one process per test

comparisons.note: Static fields are one per process, and xUnit runs test classes in parallel by default, so shared statics need a collection that turns parallelism off. Source: https://xunit.net/docs/running-tests-in-parallel
comparisons.code:
static int score;
[Collection("serial")] public class HitTests { /* ... */ }

comparisons.note: A game-wide value is a resource. The scheduler runs systems in parallel unless they conflict, and a system that changes a resource runs alone. Jet's group loans give workers the same rule, checked while building. Source: https://bevy-cheatbook.github.io/programming/system-order.html
comparisons.code:
fn think(costs: Res<TileCosts>) { /* readers run together */ }
fn hit(mut score: ResMut<Score>) { score.0 += 5; }

comparisons.note: With domain reload off, static fields keep their values between Play mode runs, so scripts must reset them, by hand or with an attribute. That is the stale-state problem a test restore removes. Source: https://docs.unity3d.com/Manual/DomainReloading.html
comparisons.code:
static int score;
[RuntimeInitializeOnLoadMethod] static void Reset() { score = 0; }

recommendation.why: A keeps the one-line global that games want and removes each danger where the compiler can see it. Group workers borrow globals by the rule they already use for locals. Pure functions and caches can't depend on a changing global, and each test starts fresh with no cost in shipped builds.
recommendation.tradeoff: Checked sharing with group workers, honest caches and fresh tests. In return, tasks that can outlive their starter stay refused, a pure function takes a global as a parameter, and parallel tests need new runner work.
gains: Group workers, combinator branches and the parallel list adapters read globals and write separate places, checked while building.
A pure function's answer depends only on its arguments and context, so a #Memo cache can't go stale.
Each test, rerun and output check starts every global at its start value, with no cost per access.
Shipped builds pay nothing: every new check runs while building, and the restore exists only in test builds.

losses.loss: A task that can outlive the function that started it, or a function C may call on any thread, can't touch a global.
losses.mitigation: Group workers can. The error names the variable and the call path and offers a task.group, Shared, or passing the value in. The ratified rule refused every task, so A only loosens it.

losses.loss: A -[]> or #Memo function that needs a global must take its value as a parameter.
losses.mitigation: Context reads stay allowed, and option C shows the tracking alternative. No -[]> or #Memo function in the repository names a same-file global today; the built check finds the rest.

losses.loss: Tests run side by side only in separate processes, which is new runner work.
losses.mitigation: Each child process starts once and runs many tests, as cargo-nextest shows processes scale. The ratified world pointer also needed new work to run tests in parallel.

whyNot.reason: B refuses every worker task, even one that only reads, so a game copies its tables before each fan-out. Test builds pay one extra load on every global access, and parallel tests are still new runner work.

C lets a -[]> function give two answers for the same arguments, which breaks what pure means to a reader. Every write to a global a cache reads costs an add in shipped builds, and holders still can't be read in a cache.
D charges one extra load on every global access in shipped builds, the hot loops that games use globals for. A program that needs many matches can keep each match in a struct instead.

decisions.title: Effect classes: every effect Reads, Adds or Replaces, operations say whether they are repeatable, and irreversible stays its own fact
decisions.situation: A small notes server lists notes, saves a note, appends a line to a journal and sends a welcome email. Jet's effects say what each function touches, such as files or the network, but not what it does to data already there. One leaf, FS.Write, covers appending, overwriting and deleting alike. So nothing refuses a GET route that deletes a file, a retried job that sends a push twice, or an agent tool that claims to only read. Retries, previews, GET answers and route checks each guess with a list of their own today. We recommend A: every effect leaf says whether it Reads, Adds or Replaces, an operation that is safe to call twice says so with #Repeatable, and irreversible stays a separate fact.
decisions.gist: Should every effect say whether it reads, adds or replaces data, and whether calling it twice is safe, and where should those facts live?
decisions.lesson: An effect names what a function touches, such as files or the network, but not what it does to data already there. This ballot adds that answer as three plain facts. A call Reads, Adds or Replaces. It is repeatable when a second call leaves the kept data as one call would. It is irreversible, a fact Jet already has, when a rollback can't take it back. Retries, previews, transactions, route checks, agent tools, caches and docs then read the same facts instead of guessing.
decisions.story: Maya runs a notes service for her team and lets an AI agent use it as a set of tools. A GET link must never delete a note, even when a browser prefetches it. A failed job may run again only if running it twice is harmless. The agent may add notes but never overwrite or delete one, and its tool list should say which tools only read. She also wants a dry run that shows what a script would change.
decisions.detail:
What this decides. Card #7035 carries greenfield proposal item P7 as the owner reworded it on 2026-11-25. Every effect operation states what it does to data already there: it Reads, Adds or Replaces. Separately it states whether it is repeatable. The existing irreversible fact stays a third answer. This ballot decides where the three facts live, how they reach user code, and every site that reads them.

The proposal's older wording (read, idempotent write, destructive) is superseded. A fresh adversarial review repaired this text; its audit is Docs/Audits/2026-11-25-effect-access-review.md.

```text
The three facts, one question each                          MCP tool hint (2025-06-18 schema)
access        Reads     changes no data the program keeps    readOnlyHint: true
              Adds      puts new data beside the old          readOnlyHint: false, destructiveHint: false
              Replaces  changes or removes data already there readOnlyHint: false, destructiveHint: true
repeatable    a second call, even after a failed or lost      idempotentHint
              first one, leaves kept data as one call would
irreversible  a #Transact rollback can't take it back         (none; Jet's own fact, unchanged in meaning)
```

The questions are separate, and every combination occurs in one program. Sending an email Adds, is not repeatable and can't be undone. Deleting a database row Replaces, is repeatable and can be rolled back. Overwriting a file Replaces, is repeatable and can't be undone. Appending to a file Adds and is neither repeatable nor undoable.

A read is repeatable, since it changes no kept data, even when a second read of input returns other text. Returning the same result is a different fact, #Replayable's (E0725), and stays separate. MCP's fourth hint, openWorldHint, comes from the row too: a tool whose row reaches Net, Browser, Exec or FFI is open-world.

Kept data means files, databases, other services' records, the process environment and the program's code. The memory of the running process is not kept data, so Mem, GPU, Unsafe and Panic Read. State in memory is outside these facts; the edge cases below say what that leaves open.

Already settled and not reopened. An effect is a type that implements Effect (D-DECL-TYPES1=A), and a root covers its leaves (D-EFFTREE1=A). Irreversible is a declared fact the checker reads (D-RIGHTS1=C), and E0746 refuses it inside #Transact (D-BOUND-UNDO1=A, D-UNDOKW1=A).

A durable send needs a typed key, and at-least-once is the only retry path (D-SERVICE-DELIVERY1=D). The client retries on its own only a stale pooled connection, only for idempotent methods with replayable bodies, at most once (D-HTTP-CLIENT2=A). Run modes are card #7007. Effect scopes come from constant arguments (D-EFFECT-ARGS1=A). A marker setting is already named repeatable (D-MARK-REPEAT1, ratified).
