The recommended design, A. The access fact lives on the effect leaf, because that is where Jet already infers, checks and grants. Where one leaf mixes kinds of change today, it splits. Repeatable lives on the operation, because it is not a property of a leaf and does not survive composition. Irreversible stays on the leaf as today.

```text
A, part 1: access is a leaf fact, inferred like every effect
- New Prelude enum EffectAccess { Reads, Adds, Replaces }, and a third fact method in impl Effect,
  beside irreversible and expert:
    access: fn(self) -> EffectAccess { .Reads }
  Its body is one line: a case, or a chain that checks today, such as
    if self == .Read -> .Reads else if self == .Add -> .Adds else -> .Replaces
  A match table with else is refused on a closed enum (Jet.ClosedSetElse), so EffectVocabulary.jet
  learns this one chain, and E0633's text names access.
- No access method means .Replaces. A package effect with parent: takes its parent's access, as it
  takes its irreversibility (spec.md:3031). A bare root's access is the largest of its leaves.
- Leaves split where one mixes kinds: FS{Read, Add, Replace}, DB{Read, Add, Replace},
  Net{Read, Add, Replace}, Env{Read, Replace}. FS.Write and DB.Write are deleted. A bare Net, FS,
  DB or Env row stays valid as a root over its leaves and means Replaces. Scopes keep working:
  Net.Read("api.example.com"), FS.Add("notes/").
- Reads: Mem, GPU, Unsafe, Panic, Time, Rand, Secret, Exec.Args, Exec.Exit, Meta.Include and
  Meta.Host (host work keeps its own effects). IO and Log Read by a stated rule, the one RFC 9110
  9.2.1 gives for access logs: their output records the run and is not data the program keeps.
  Adds: Meta.Generate, Meta.Code.Types and Meta.Code.Raw. Replaces: running a program (bare Exec),
  FFI, Browser and Meta.Code.Rewrite.
- A function's access is the largest in its row: Reads < Adds < Replaces. A package effect counts
  at its declared access. That is the package's statement, as an MCP hint is a server's; the hard
  bound is the package's authority grant, which the runtime already enforces, and jet inspect
  rights prints each package effect's declared access beside the kernel effects it reaches.
- No argument value picks a leaf. An operation whose argument chooses between adding and replacing
  records Replaces, and the add-only case gets its own function, as Rust's File::create_new does:
  files.create_new(path) records FS.Add, files.create records FS.Replace, and CreateIfExists is
  deleted. The HTTP client gets one function per method: get, head and options record Net.Read,
  post records Net.Add, and put, patch and delete record Net.Replace. send of a built request, whose
  method is a run-time value, records bare Net.

A, part 2: repeatable is an operation fact
- New marker #Repeatable on a function or method, a marker struct in Compiler/Prelude/Markers.jet.
  #Repeatable(key: p) says the call is repeatable when parameter p carries a key that is the same on
  every try, as Stripe's Idempotency-Key does.
- Repeatable is about kept data, not the returned value: a second remove of one file reports
  NotFound and is still repeatable, as RFC 9110 9.2.2 lets a second DELETE answer differently.
- Every operation whose row only Reads is repeatable without a mark.
- Core marks: files.write, write_bytes, write_atomic, write_at, remove, remove_dir, remove_all,
  create_dir_all, set_mode, chown, rename and copy; Table add (#Repeatable(key: row), since a taken
  key is refused), put and delete; db migrate, which replays by checksum; client get, head, options,
  put and delete; send_durable(key:) and the jobs enqueue (key:). append, append_all, create_new,
  post, patch, send and execute stay unmarked.
- A user function is repeatable when it only Reads, or when it carries #Repeatable and reaches no
  call that is not repeatable, keyed or deferred until commit. A claim that reaches one is a new
  registered error naming the call path. The rest can't be proved: save(load(n) + 1) calls two
  repeatable operations and is not repeatable. A written #Repeatable is a promise the compiler can
  refute but never prove, like #Undo(inverse) on a foreign binding.
- A key counts only when it is built from the body's parameters and constants, which are the same
  on every try. A key built from Rand or Time is refused.

A, part 3: irreversible keeps its meaning and its one rule
- FS.Add, FS.Replace, Net.Add and Net.Replace are irreversible, as FS.Write and Net are. FS.Read
  and Net.Read are not, so E0746 stops refusing them in #Transact. Exec's fact becomes
  self == .Exit, so reading process.args() inside #Transact builds. DB stays reversible.
- Sema keeps one reader of the three facts. sema_effect_vocabulary_irreversible
  (Checks.jet:6871-6883) is deleted, and the hand leaf list in Calls.jet:494-532 is replaced by rows
  that Tools/Agent/CoreSourceRows.jet generates from Core's declared rows; no hand list stays.
```

```text
The notes service under A                                  access     repeatable  irreversible
list_notes    files.read("notes/index.txt")              Reads      yes         no
save_note     files.write("notes/42.txt", t)              Replaces   yes         yes
journal       files.append_all("journal.txt", line)       Adds       no          yes
welcome       client.post(mail_url, to)                   Adds       no          yes
rename_note   notes.put(row) in #Transact, then welcome   Replaces   no          yes
```

What each fact buys in this program. Safe retries: an HTTP client may resend GET /notes and PUT /notes/42 after a dropped connection, and the route checks make both harmless; nothing resends welcome's POST. An #App.Job that calls journal is refused until it sets retries: 0 or at_least_once: true, or journal takes a key. Previews: jet run --preview runs list_notes for real and records save_note, journal and welcome, with save_note marked as replacing.

Transactions: E0746 still refuses welcome inside #Transact, because it can't be undone, so rename_note calls it after the block. Caching: only a Reads method answers GET or keeps a cached reply. Docs: hover on save_note shows its three facts.

Agent tools: an MCP tool built from save_note gets destructiveHint true and idempotentHint true with no hand-written hints. Running the agent with --deny=FS.Replace,Exec,FFI lets it add notes but never overwrite or delete one. That grant holds for every call Jet makes. A program the agent starts is held by denying Exec, since Jet's kernel confinement covers reads only today (Compiler/JetBackend/Source/Image/Loader.jet:1958-1990).

```text
$ jet run --preview notes.jet        (format is card #7007's to settle; illustrative)
plan: notes.jet would
  replace  notes/42.txt                    save_note  notes.jet:27   repeatable, can't be undone
  add      journal.txt                     journal    notes.jet:31   can't be undone
  add      POST https://mail.example/send  welcome    notes.jet:35   can't be undone
ran for real: read notes/index.txt (list_notes)

hover on save_note
  save_note: fn(id: String, text: String) -[FS.Replace]> IOError!
  replaces files · repeatable · can't be undone

error: GET route `reset` replaces data          (new registered error)
  --> notes.jet:57
   | files.remove("notes/old.txt")              FS.Replace
   = browsers and proxies may send a GET again, prefetch it or cache it, so a GET may only read
   = fix: mark the route #Server.Post or #Server.Delete
```

The checks A adds, each a new registered error.

Routes. A #Server.Get, Head or Options handler that reaches Adds or Replaces is refused. A #Server.Put or Delete handler that isn't repeatable is refused, since HTTP lets a client resend those. The check reads the handler's row, so it covers marked methods, mounted values and closures passed to mux.get, because a function value's type carries its row.

RFC 9110 9.2.1 and 9.2.2 let a server log, count or charge on such a request. Log Reads, so logging needs nothing. Any other side record writes one field on the route marker, #Server.Get("/ads/:id", side_adds: true). The handler may then reach Adds that aren't repeatable, but a GET never reaches Replaces.

Retries. Core runs two kinds of body again that Jet can see. One is an #App.Job method after a failure, 5 tries by default; the other is an App endpoint or webhook body while the store is busy (Web.jet:3087-3104). In such a body every irreversible call must be repeatable, keyed, or deferred until commit with app.enqueue. Database work in the App store is rolled back with each try and needs nothing. Otherwise the body is refused, and the error names the call path.

A job that accepts doing its work twice says so with #App.Job(retries: 3, at_least_once: true), the delivery name Jobs.jet and D-SERVICE-DELIVERY1 already use. The client's own retry reads the method table while running, at most once (D-HTTP-CLIENT2).

Not checked, and said so on their reference pages: a core.jobs worker's code between claim and acknowledge, and a workflow activity named by a String. No function is registered for either, so there is no body to read; D-SERVICE-DELIVERY1's typed key stays their guard.

Claims. A #Repeatable claim that reaches a call that is not repeatable, keyed or deferred is refused.

App sites. An #App.Public method answers GET, or keeps a cached reply, only when it Reads; the cached .Public reply type stops standing in for that. #App.UploadCheck's method must Read, and its always-rolled-back transaction is deleted. A subscribe source may use Net.Read but not Net.Add or Net.Replace.

```text
Edge cases under A
- Adds and Replaces in one function: its row holds both leaves and its access is Replaces. A preview
  still lists each call with its own access.
- db.execute(sql) records DB.Replace whatever its SQL; typed Table add records DB.Add.
- Generic code: an open row (..E) takes each instance's leaves, and each instance is checked, as
  rows are today. Hover on the generic function says its access depends on E.
- Dynamic dispatch: a function value or trait call has its type's declared row, so its access is
  known. Its repeatable fact is not, so it counts as not repeatable unless its row only Reads.
- FFI: every FFI leaf Replaces and is irreversible. A binding may carry #Repeatable beside
  #Undo(inverse); its access stays Replaces. A package that wraps a foreign library in its own
  effect declares that effect's access, as Core's DB does.
- Partial failure: repeatable is defined over a failed or lost first call. write truncates and
  rewrites the whole file, so a second call fixes a half-written one; append_all can't.
- A call that removes what it reads, such as a queue claim, is not a read: Core's claim records DB,
  which is Replaces.
- State in memory: a write through a Shared handle is not an effect, so the route checks don't see
  it. A module variable write is seen once D-GLOBAL-SAFE1's touch fact (card #6859) lands, and the
  route checks count it as Replaces.
- Net.Read is not a secrecy boundary: a GET can carry data out in its URL. Host scopes and
  --deny=Net stay the secrecy controls.
- Browser stays one leaf, Replaces; splitting it is left to a later ballot if a need appears.
- Compile time: access is a maximum over a row the checker already holds. The claim, route and
  retry checks walk call edges the effect solver already built, once per marked body. The build
  card measures check time on Tests/Cases before and after (AGENTS.md performance gate).
- Beginners write nothing: rows are inferred, and hover, preview and errors speak the three words.
  Experts write --deny=FS.Replace, access in their own effects, and #Repeatable(key:) on their APIs.
```

```text
Amendments A states
- D-HONEST-SIG2=A: its "repeatable" and "not repeatable" labels, which mean #Replayable, become
  "replayable" and "not replayable", matching #Replayable and E0725. Not built, so no code moves.
- D-EFFDBREAD1=A: execute records DB.Replace, not DB.Write, and the Core-call table it extended is
  generated from Core's rows. Its note that user inference keeps only bare roots is stale: on

- D-HTTP-CLIENT2=A: the client gains head, options, put, patch and delete functions, and its
  retry reads the one method table.
- D-MARK-REPEAT1: the marker setting keeps the word. Both meanings say doing it twice is fine; one
  lives on MarkerInfo, the other on a function's reflection, and hover names which.
- Spec "Effects" and "Transactions": the root table (spec.md:3108-3126), the FS.Read and FS.Write
  text of #Transact (spec.md:2951-2968), and E0746 no longer refusing reads.
- Card #7007: a preview records Adds and Replaces calls, not "every write effect".
```

options.name: Access on the effect leaf, split where a leaf mixes kinds; repeatable on the operation; irreversible unchanged
options.detail:
Each effect declares whether it Reads, Adds or Replaces, beside its irreversible fact. FS.Write and DB.Write split into Add and Replace leaves, and Net gains Read, Add and Replace leaves, so a function's row already says what it does. The compiler infers it for user code exactly as it infers effects today, and --allow and --deny can grant adding without replacing.

Repeatable is marked on operations with #Repeatable, because it depends on the call, not the leaf. User code is repeatable when it only reads, or when it says #Repeatable and reaches nothing that isn't. Routes, retried bodies and claims are checked while building, and a route or job that means to do more says so in one field.
options.technical:
EffectAccess and the access fact method join irreversible and expert in impl Effect and in the vocabulary rows every reader uses; the scanner learns one one-line chain. Rows split FS, DB, Net and Env. One language rewrite moves FS.Write (736 hits) to FS.Add, FS.Replace and DB.Write (121 hits) likewise. The hand leaf list in Calls.jet and the second irreversible reader are deleted.

A function's access is the largest in its row, and a package effect counts at its declared access, bounded by its grant. An argument value never picks a leaf: files.create_new and one client function per method do that. #Repeatable and #Repeatable(key:) are marker structs; sema joins them over the call graph only to refute a claim.

New errors cover GET, HEAD and OPTIONS handlers that change data, PUT and DELETE handlers that aren't repeatable, retried #App.Job and endpoint bodies, and refuted claims. Route markers gain side_adds and #App.Job gains at_least_once.

Beginner path: nothing to write; hover, preview and errors use the three words. Expert path: grant FS.Add without FS.Replace, declare access in package effects, and put #Repeatable(key:) on keyed APIs. Costs: every FS.Write and DB.Write row is rewritten, and a true #Repeatable claim is trusted past what the compiler can see. A package's declared access is its own statement, and core.jobs workers and workflow activities stay unchecked.

options.name: Access and repeatable on each operation, inferred through user code beside the row; leaves unchanged
options.detail:
FS.Write and the other leaves stay as they are. Each Core operation carries two marks, its access and whether it is repeatable, and the compiler infers a function's access from the calls it reaches, beside its effect row. Nothing in existing rows changes.

The facts are as precise as A's for inference, but they live in a second plane that rows, scopes, manifests and --allow can't see. So a grant can't allow adding files without replacing them.
options.technical:
New markers #Access(.Adds) and #Repeatable on Core operations and foreign bindings. The effect walker carries a second inferred value per function, the largest access reached, which reflection and tools read. Repeatable is refuted as in A. Routes, retries, previews and tools read the new value.

Beginner path: same as A. Expert path: no add-only grant; a package effect declares access per operation instead of once. Costs: two parallel facts about one call, which every reader of rows must also learn to read (I8). Edge cases match A, but a function value's type has no access unless function types gain one, a new spelling this option would still need.

options.name: A leaf for every kind of change, with access and repeatable both declared on the leaf
options.detail:
Effects split further, one leaf per kind of change. FS gets Create, Append, Overwrite and Delete; Net gets Get, Post, Put and Delete; DB gets Insert, Update and Delete. Each leaf declares both its access and whether it is repeatable, so every fact is a leaf fact and grants are as fine as they can be.

Rows grow long, and repeatable still isn't a leaf property: an UPDATE that sets a value is repeatable and one that adds to it is not.
options.technical:
impl Effect gains access and repeatable fact methods. About fifteen new leaves; every Core row is rewritten by hand, since no rewrite can tell an append from an overwrite. A function is repeatable when all its leaves are, which is unsound for read-then-write code, so C either accepts wrong answers or adds A's refutation-only rule.

Beginner path: rows read like verbs but are long. Expert path: the finest grants, such as --allow=FS.Create. Costs: a leaf list per store that grows with every new kind of change, and a repeatable fact that is still wrong for DB.Update and FS.Rename.

options.name: Declared hints at boundaries only, as MCP does: routes, tools and jobs state them, nothing infers or checks them
options.detail:
Leaves stay as today. A route, a tool or a job states its own hints where it is declared, and tools copy them out, as MCP servers do. The compiler neither infers nor checks them.

This is the cheapest option and maps one to one onto MCP. A hint can be wrong, though, and nothing notices: a GET route marked read-only may still delete.
options.technical:
New fields on boundary markers, for example #App.Public(reads_only: true) and an MCP tool builder's hints argument. Retries, previews and caches read those fields where a boundary exists and the coarse leaves elsewhere. The retry lists in Client.jet and Web.jet stay.

Beginner path: write hints on each tool and route, or get MCP's pessimistic defaults. Expert path: none beyond the hints. Costs: hints duplicate what the code shows and drift from it, every boundary kind needs its own field (I8), and inner calls have no facts.

options.name: Keep today's state: one write leaf, irreversible as the only fact, and each site's own list
options.detail:
FS.Write and DB.Write keep covering every change. Irreversible stays the one fact, read by #Transact. The client keeps its fixed list of retryable methods, a GET keeps reading the cached reply type, and a preview counts every write as destructive.

Nothing changes, and nothing new is checked.
options.technical:
No work. The known gaps stay: RetryPolicy is stored but never read, and a .Public method that writes still answers GET. A subscribe source may POST, #App.Job reruns anything, and reading process.args() inside #Transact stays refused. MCP tools would need hand-written hints when D-MCP-SURFACE1 is built.

Beginner path: unchanged. Expert path: unchanged. Costs: the owner's three facts are not available to any tool, and card #7007's preview can't tell an append from a delete.

comparisons.note: Tool annotations carry readOnlyHint (default false), destructiveHint (default true, and false means the tool only adds), idempotentHint (default false) and openWorldHint (default true). The spec says a client must treat them as untrusted unless the server is trusted. A maps Reads to readOnlyHint, Adds to destructiveHint false, repeatable to idempotentHint, and a reached Net effect to openWorldHint, all derived from checked facts instead of written by hand. Sources: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18/server/tools and the 2025-06-18 schema.ts in the modelcontextprotocol GitHub repository.

RFC 9110 calls GET, HEAD, OPTIONS and TRACE safe, and PUT and DELETE idempotent as well. A safe method may still log, count or charge for a request, and an idempotent one may log each request separately. A client should not retry a request that isn't idempotent unless it knows the request is. A makes a Jet route keep those promises while building, treats logging as Reads, and lets a route that records a side row say side_adds. Source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#section-9.2
comparisons.code:
GET /notes        safe, idempotent
PUT /notes/42     idempotent
POST /journal     neither

comparisons.note: Any v1 POST may carry an Idempotency-Key. The server saves the status code and body of the first request with that key, even a 500 error, and answers a retry with the saved result. It refuses a retry whose parameters differ and may forget keys after 24 hours. That turns a call that isn't repeatable into one that is, which is A's #Repeatable(key:). Source: https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests

terraform plan prints what apply would add, change and destroy; a plan saved with -out is what apply performs. Its three counts are A's Adds and Replaces, which card #7007's preview reads. Source: https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/commands/plan
comparisons.code: Plan: 2 to add, 1 to change, 2 to destroy.

comparisons.note: Koka infers effect rows like Jet, and its heap effect is already split by what a call does: st<h> is read<h>, write<h> and alloc<h>. A function that only reads a reference has read<h> in its type. That is A's split on a leaf, with alloc as Adds; Koka has no repeatable fact. Source: https://koka-lang.github.io/koka/doc/std_core_types.html
comparisons.code:
alias st<h> = <read<h>, write<h>, alloc<h>>
fun peek(r : ref<h,int>) : read<h> int
  !r

comparisons.note: Haskell's runST runs a computation whose state no one else can see, so local changes are not effects at all; A's Mem Reads says the same about process memory. Rust gives creating a new file its own function, File::create_new, which fails if the file exists and is atomic. No argument picks the meaning, and A's files.create_new follows it. Sources: https://hackage.haskell.org/package/base/docs/Control-Monad-ST.html and https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/fs/struct.File.html#method.create_new
comparisons.code:
runST :: (forall s. ST s a) -> a

let f = File::create_new("notes/42.txt")?;

recommendation.why: A puts what a call does to data on the effect leaf, where Jet already infers, checks, grants and reports. User code writes nothing new, and --deny=FS.Replace becomes an add-only grant for Jet code. Repeatable stays on operations because it depends on the call and can't be inferred through composition. Irreversible keeps its meaning and its one rule. Every site that guesses today reads the same three facts instead, and the hand-kept lists in the compiler are deleted.
recommendation.tradeoff: Checked routes, safer retries, honest previews, add-only grants and MCP hints without hand-written hints. In return every FS.Write and DB.Write row is rewritten once, a true #Repeatable claim is a promise the compiler can only refute, and a package states its own effect's access.
gains: A GET, HEAD or OPTIONS route can't change data, and a PUT or DELETE route can't append twice.
A retried #App.Job or endpoint body is refused unless running it again is harmless, keyed, rolled back or accepted out loud.
jet run --preview runs reads for real and records adds and replaces, with replaces marked.
An agent can be allowed to add files or rows but never overwrite or delete them.
MCP tool hints, hover, jet doc and the run notice come from one checked fact, with no hand-written hints.

losses.loss: Every row that names FS.Write or DB.Write is rewritten, about 860 places in at most 431 files, and old --allow=FS.Write lines stop working.
losses.mitigation: One language rewrite turns FS.Write into FS.Add, FS.Replace, which covers the same calls, and the run notice says which rows can narrow. Bare FS, DB and Net rows stay valid.

losses.loss: A user function that changes data is repeatable only when marked, and a mark can't be fully proved.
losses.mitigation: The compiler refuses a mark that reaches any call that isn't repeatable, and keyed calls count as repeatable, so the common retry paths are checked.

losses.loss: A foreign call, a request sent with a method chosen at run time, or raw db.execute counts as Replaces even when it only reads.
losses.mitigation: Typed Table methods, one client function per HTTP method and files.create_new keep exact facts, and a package that wraps a foreign library declares its own effect's access.

losses.loss: A package's declared access and the bodies run by core.jobs workers and workflow activities are not checked.
losses.mitigation: The package's authority grant stays the hard limit, and inspect rights shows declared access beside the effects reached. Workers and activities keep D-SERVICE-DELIVERY1's typed key.

losses.loss: A GET that records a side row, and a job that may send twice, need one written field.
losses.mitigation: Logging needs nothing, since Log Reads. side_adds: true on the route or at_least_once: true on the job is one field, on the rare route or job that needs it.

losses.loss: Net.Read sounds safe but is no secrecy boundary, since a GET can carry data out.
losses.mitigation: Host scopes such as Net.Read("api.example.com") and --deny=Net stay the secrecy controls, and the reference page says so.

whyNot.reason: B keeps two parallel facts about one call. Rows, scopes, manifests and --allow can't see access, so an agent can't be allowed to add without replacing, and every row reader must learn a second plane.
C makes rows long and the leaf list grow with each new kind of change. Its repeatable leaf fact is still wrong for updates, renames and read-then-write code.
D's hints are unchecked and duplicate what the code shows. A GET marked read-only may still delete, and inner calls have no facts for retries or previews.
E leaves the owner's three facts unavailable. Retries, GET answers and previews keep guessing from their own lists, and the gaps found on dev stay open.

surface.gist: Should every effect say whether it reads, adds or replaces data, and whether a second call is safe?
surface.lesson: Effects say what a function touches, not what it does to data already there. Three facts answer that: a call Reads, Adds or Replaces; it may be repeatable; and it may be irreversible, as today. Routes, retries, previews, agent tools and docs then read the same facts.

decisions.title: How term.take and the stream forms of tls.client stop needing compiler rows
decisions.situation: Almost every Core call is now checked against the Core function that declares it. At this tree Core.rows still has four dispatcher rows: `core.term take`, `core.net.tls client`, `core.net sendfile` and `core.crypto.vault get`. A pending change deletes the sendfile and vault rows, so two are left, and this ballot is about them. `term.take(n)` reads up to n bytes from stdin, but `take` is a retired word that no declaration may use as its name. `tls.client` is one name with four shapes: `(host, port)`, `(stream, server_name)`, and two labeled forms over a stream with a deadline and an optional config. Jet has no overloading, so Core declares one of them and the compiler picks among three hidden role functions for the rest. You are asked how these two calls get a plain Core declaration. We recommend A: `tls.client` keeps the stream spelling the owner ratified, the host and port form becomes `tls.connect`, and stdin's read becomes `term.take_bytes`.
decisions.gist: Two Core calls still need a compiler table row, because Core can't declare them as written. Rename one of the TLS forms, read stdin another way, allow `take` as a member name, add a marker, or keep the rows.
decisions.lesson: Most Core calls are checked against their Core declaration, so a package that declares the same shape gets the same checks. Two calls can't be declared as they are spelled. `term.take(n)` is named with the retired word `take`, which Jet accepts after a dot but refuses as a declared name. `tls.client` has four shapes under one name, and Jet has no overloading. The compiler keeps one table row for each to pick the Core function that runs.
decisions.explainer:
Today both calls work, but only through compiler rows:

```jet
use {
    term: core.term
    net: core.net
    tls: core.net.tls
}

run: fn() -[IO, Net, Time.Wait]> {
    bytes: term.take(64) ?? return
    tcp: net.tcp_connect("example.org:443") ?? return
    secure: tls.client(tcp, server_name: "example.org", deadline: 5s) ?? return
    print(bytes.len())
}
```

The first call needs the Core.rows row `core.term take`, which points at the role TermTake. The third needs the row `core.net.tls client` and Sema's arity rule in Sema/Calls/Core.jet `sema_call_core_arity_source_record`, which points at TLSClientStream, TLSClientDeadline or TLSClientConfigDeadline.
decisions.story: A contributor reads Core/Term/Term.jet to see what `term.take(64)` does. There is no `take` in the file, only a private `__take_bytes` with a role marker. The link between the two is a row in Compiler/Prelude/Core.rows. For `tls.client(tcp, server_name: "x", deadline: 1s)` the trail is longer. Sema counts the arguments and checks whether the first is moved. Then it picks one of three private role functions in Core/Net/TLS.jet.
decisions.inWild:
Most languages solve a keyword clash with a raw name, such as Rust's `r#match` or Kotlin's backquoted `when`, or by picking another word.
Overloads by arity are common in C++, Java and Swift. Rust and Go have none, and name each form instead.
Go's crypto/tls names the dialing form `Dial` and the wrapping form `Client`.
Rust's native-tls has only the wrapping form, `TlsConnector::connect(domain, stream)`, and the caller dials the TCP stream first.
decisions.detail:
Facts at the batch-48 tree 08d2eae9774. The cited lines are the same at dev 35cc4235d3b.

Rows: Core.rows 304 maps `core.term take` to the role TermTake. Core.rows 305 keeps `core.net.tls client` as source-owned, with arity 2 up to 4. Rows 307 `core.net sendfile` and 308 `core.crypto.vault get` are native dispatcher rows too. The pending change 6851-n18-p11-r2-s2-b48 deletes rows 307 and 308. Every claim below that the dispatcher table empties holds only once that change lands.

`term.take`: Core/Term/Term.jet 272 declares `#Builtin.Role(.TermTake) priv __take_bytes: fn(n: Int) -[IO, Time.Wait]> [U8] IOError!`. Inside Term.jet, the stdin Reader's `read_bytes` (line 72) and a test (line 866) call it directly. Its neighbour `take_within(n, wait)` at 286 is a plain declaration.

`take` is a retired keyword that the lexer still reserves. Compiler/JetLexer/Source/Lexer/KeywordSpans.jet 116-121 lists it, and Compiler/JetFoundation/Data/Syntax/CoreSurface.jet 411-413 names it KW_MOVE. The parser refuses it as a declared function name, at module level or in a struct, and as a bare call. It accepts it after a dot, as in `reader.take(n)`, and as a struct field name, as in Core/App/App.jet 2071.

Six calls use `term.take`. One is in an example: Examples/Systems/IOSurface.jet 30 calls `io.take(0)` through `use io: core.term`, and IOSurface.out 8 pins its output. One is Compiler/JetLSP/Source/LSP/Loop.jet 52.

Three are in Jetpack/CLI: HangarArchiveCommands.jet 90, BuildPluginHost.jet 44 and CompilerExtensionHost.jet 19. The sixth is Tests/Conformance/Corpus/Core/Term/take.jet 5, which calls `take(0)`. The spec rows are core-library.md 192-195 and the `take(n)` table row at 2664.

`tls.client`: Core/Net/TLS.jet 316 declares `client(host: String, port: Int) -[Net, Time.Wait]> TLSStream IOError!`. Lines 335, 340 and 344 declare the role entries TLSClientStream, TLSClientDeadline and TLSClientConfigDeadline over a moved `TCPStream`. Core/HTTP/Client.jet 815 and 2005 call two of them by name: `build_tls.__client_deadline_entry` and `build_tls.__client_config_deadline_entry`.

TLS.jet 516 declares a second dial form, `connect_host(cfg, port)`, which takes its host from `ClientConfig.host` (line 33). It has 2 callers: the CoreLib fixture CoreTLSConfigurationCarriersPreservePolicy and the conformance file Net/TLS/connect_host.jet. Another Core module already exports a bare `connect`: `ws.connect(url)` at Core/Net/Ws.jet 66.

Sema picks a TLS role in Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Calls/Core.jet `sema_call_core_arity_source_record` (1100-1113), by argument count and by whether the first argument is moved. Its caller is Core.jet 1463. `sema_call_core_configured_client` and `sema_call_core_native_resource_consumer` (622-629) special-case `tls.client` too.

Their `configured_client` flag runs through three route resolvers, fed from Core.jet 1536, Expressions.jet 4275 and Direct.jet 1230. A test at Core.jet 1696-1705 checks the consumer rule. `sema_call_core_has_explicit_source_target` (631-634) is true only for row 304, the one row with a source role.

`git grep 'tls\.client('` over `*.jet` finds 14 lines, but three are not calls. One is a comment at Sema/Calls/Core.jet 622, and two are strings in Tools/Agent/CoreSurfaceLedger.jet 1075-1076. Six `.template` fixtures also call the stream form. The stream form has 11 call lines: 2 examples, 3 `.jet` fixtures and 6 templates. The host and port form has 5 calls and one label-error fixture.

Conformance witnesses are keyed by their path (Tools/Hardening/Manifest.jet 142-148). Corpus/Core/Term/take.jet witnesses `core.term.take`. Corpus/Core/Net/TLS/client.jet witnesses `core.net.tls.client` with a host and port call.

The TLS spec rows are core-library.md 7895 (stream form), 7896 (host and port form) and 7916-7917. Docs/Spec/syntax-decisions.md 5977-5983 records D-NETTLSSTREAM1=A. That decision ratified the labeled stream spelling `tls.client(stream, server_name:, config:, deadline:)`. CoreSurfaceLedger.jet 1075-1076 record D-CORESURF-SMALL1's note that TLS start ships as `tls.client()`.

Expected output names the spelling too. Tests/Cases/CoreNetTLS/configured_tls_client_keeps_native_builder_identity_and_exact_labels.case 9 expects "`tls.client` has no parameter labeled `host`", and Tests/known-failing.tsv 116 lists that case. Tests/Cases/CoreLib/core_net_ratified_named_forms_require_exact_labels.case 57 expects a fix naming `host:` for the host and port form.

Name-keyed stores outside the rows: Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/CoreDeclarations/Calls.jet keys effects by module and member at 464, 504, 518 and 521-522. Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/Target/TargetMachine.jet 788 lists `take` among core.term reads. Core.rows 184-185 and 220-221 list `client` and `take` in the export and ownership lines. Core/Builtins/Builtins.jet holds the four RoleKind cases at 381-383 and 430, and its comment at 77-79 names them.

The row table has readers in every tier. Foundation has Registry/CoreCallRows.jet, Registry/CoreCalls.jet, CoreDeclarations/Declarations.jet and Sources.jet. JetIR has Lint.jet `ir_lint_core_routes` and CoreRecords.jet. Driver has CoreReach.jet 772. JetCLI has InspectStructure.jet 102-154 and ProveReplay.jet 2842. Sema has Taint.jet 486, Scheduling/FrameCalls.jet 122 and Calls/ReactiveHandles.jet 101. Tools and guards have DeadRowSweep.jet, RuntimeEffectRows.jet, Tools/Hardening/Facts.jet and Tests/Guards/runtime_leaf_exports.jet.

`CoreCallRecord` has two makers that need no row. `core_call_role_receiver` (Registry/CoreCalls.jet 174) serves data-query roles from Sema/Calls/Data.jet 612. `core_call_source_function` (183) serves Sema/Calls/Core.jet 1255. So the record type outlives every option here. Card criterion 18 deletes Registry/CoreCalls.jet, so those makers need their own move. Card criteria 4 and 6 move the Services.jet and Data.jet checkers that call them.

options.name: Keep `tls.client` for the stream, rename the dial form to `tls.connect`
options.detail:
`tls.client(tcp, server_name:, config:, deadline:)` becomes one plain declaration, so the spelling D-NETTLSSTREAM1 ratified stays. Its `config` defaults to `ClientConfig{}` and its `deadline` to none, which means no deadline. Core already declares `net.unix_connect(path, /, *, deadline: Duration?{None})` in this shape (Core/Net/Net.jet 655). A probe on the batch-48 seed declares this shape and checks all three stream calls clean.

The host and port convenience becomes `tls.connect(host, port)`. `term.take(n)` becomes `term.take_bytes(n)`, a plain Core function next to `take_within`. Both rows and the arity rule go.

This is Go's split: `tls.Dial` dials and `tls.Client` wraps a connection. It also uses Core's dial verb. `ws.connect(url)` is already a bare `connect` in a sibling module, and `net.tcp_connect` and `net.unix_connect` carry the verb in their names.

Beginner path: `tls.connect("example.org", 443)` and `term.take_bytes(64)`. Expert path: `tls.client(tcp, server_name: "example.org", config: cfg, deadline: 5s)`, unchanged.
options.technical:
Core/Net/TLS.jet renames `client(host, port)` at 316 to `connect`, which keeps `IOError!`. Its `tls_error` operation text "client" at 318, 321 and 326, and the test of that text at 562, become "connect". The comments at 313-315 and 332-334 go.

In place of the role entries at 335-346 it declares `client: fn(stream: ^^TCPStream, /, *, server_name: String, config: ClientConfig{ClientConfig{}}, deadline: Duration?{None}) -[Net, Time.Wait]> TLSStream NetError!`. A None deadline calls `client_connect` with `forever()`. Core/HTTP/Client.jet 815 and 2005 call `build_tls.client(…)` in place of the two role entries they name.

Core/Term/Term.jet renames `__take_bytes` to the public `take_bytes` and drops its role marker; lines 72 and 866 call the new name. Core/Builtins/Builtins.jet drops RoleKind TermTake, TLSClientStream, TLSClientDeadline and TLSClientConfigDeadline, and their comment at 77-79. Core.rows drops rows 304 and 305.

Core.rows also adds `connect` to the core.net.tls lines (184-185) and renames `take` in the core.term lines (220-221). CoreDeclarations/Calls.jet renames `take` at 518 and adds `connect` at 522. TargetMachine.jet 788 renames `take`.

Sema/Calls/Core.jet deletes `sema_call_core_arity_source_record` and its call at 1463. decisions.title: An effect is its provider trait: one name per service in rows, manifests, contexts and tests
decisions.situation: Jet names each outside service twice. Effect rows, manifests and the run flags say FS, Net or Time, while the code that does the work, and any test fake, is a separate type with its own name. Few services have a provider type at all: the allocator, the task queue, the database driver and the compute device do, and the clock is a plain struct. A fake reached through a trait still counts as touching the disk, so a test with a fake file store can't deny file access. The ratified provider plan would add Clock, Files and Transport traits beside the effects, keeping two names. This ballot decides whether each service is declared once, as a trait that is also its effect. The row, the grant, the context slot and the fake would then share one name.
decisions.gist: Should each service, such as files or the clock, be declared once as a trait whose name is also its effect, context slot and fake's target?
decisions.lesson: An effect says which outside service a function uses. A provider is the code that does that service's work: the real disk, or a fake one in a test. When the two share one declaration, the row, the grant, the context slot and the fake all use one name, and installing a fake removes the effect it replaces.
decisions.explainer:
Today a function that writes a file says -[FS.Write]> in its signature. A test that wants a fake disk has nowhere to put one. There is no files slot in #Context, and a fake reached through a trait still counts as writing to the disk.

Under the recommended design FS is a trait of the disk's basic operations. The real disk and every fake implement it, and #Context(fs: testing.MemoryFS{}) swaps one in for a block. Rows, --allow and package.jet keep the names they use today.
decisions.story:
Ravi writes a small tool that stamps a note with the time and saves it. His test should check the saved text without touching his disk or depending on the clock. He wants his test's helper to say -[!FS]>, so a slip that reaches his real files fails the build.

Today he can't. The clock is a struct he has to pass into every function by hand. There is no slot for a fake file store, and the compiler rejects #Context(clock: …). If he writes his own Store trait and a memory fake, a call through the trait still charges its -[FS.Write]> bound.

Under A he writes #Context(fs: testing.MemoryFS{}, time: testing.FixedTime{unix_ms: 0}) around the call. The block's file and clock calls reach only the fakes, so its row holds neither FS nor Time, and the -[!FS]> helper builds. His production code is unchanged: files.write and time.now_utc call whatever provider the context holds.

A program that installs nothing calls the real disk and clock directly, as today. The denial covers Core's file functions. A child process he starts is checked as Exec, and foreign code as FFI.
decisions.detail:
What this decides. Card #7030 carries greenfield proposal item P3 (Docs/Proposals/2026-11-24-greenfield-language.md, Part 2 lines 279-296 and Part 3.6). Every outside service has one effect name in rows, manifests, --allow and --deny, and a separate provider type for the work and for test fakes. This ballot decides whether the provider trait becomes the effect, so one declaration holds the operations, the effect name, its leaves and facts, its fakes' target and its context slot.

Four Core traits already pair a provider with an effect under a second name. The Prelude's Driver (Compiler/Prelude/Traits.jet:267-276) is the database driver for DB. Accelerator (Core/Compute/Compute.jet:472-481) is the compute device for GPU. mem.Allocator serves Mem.Alloc, and Scheduler (Core/Tasks/Tasks.jet:100-114) is the run queue, which needs no effect.

Time already has three provider stores besides Clock. The runtime World (Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/World.jet:1-110) supplies a virtual clock, seeded random numbers and environment. testing.world and DeterministicWorld drive it (Core/Testing/Testing.jet:1685-1708).

A controlled monotonic clock sits on thread-local state (World.jet:88-100). Wall-time and replay overrides come from the environment (Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/HostTime.jet:183-200 and Compiler/JetCLI/Source/CLI/ProveReplay.jet:153-164). Core/Time/Time.jet:2771-2791 consults them all before the host clock.

Fault injection is another store. The runtime schedule (Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/FaultSchedule.jet) is keyed by strings such as "FS.Write" and "Net.Accept". Its hooks appear 98 times in 29 files across the runtime, Core/Files, Core/Term and Core/Crypto/Random.jet. Core/Files/Sealed.jet:282-323 also injects short reads, early ends and interruptions.

The gap shows on jet a0.0.46. A static call charges the implementation's own row, so a concrete fake written -[]> passes a -[!FS]> caller today. The gap is calls through the trait. A generic <S: Store> call, or a call on a Store value, charges the trait's -[FS.Write]> bound even when the fake writes nothing (E0749).

A fake that prints is refused against the bound (E0742). #Context(clock: …) is refused as an unknown context field (E0761), while a #ContextKey of a struct works. A trait operation with a default body and a wrapper holding an inner Store both check and run. The CLI prints these as Jet.ProhibitedEffectReached, Jet.ImplEffectBoundExceeded and Jet.UnknownContextField.

The recommended design, in two paragraphs. A service effect is a trait that implements Effect. Its body lists its leaves as an enum lists cases, then its basic operations, each with a row naming the leaf it performs, then its impl Effect facts. The real provider and every fake implement the trait, and each must fit every operation's row (E0742).

context.fs reads the current provider, and #Context(fs: v) installs one for a block. Inside the block a call that reaches the fs slot is charged v's own row, so a memory fake removes FS. Every other path keeps its effect. A target profile names each machine's provider by the same slot name. Effects that are facts, not services, stay structs and enums.

What does not change. Every effect row, package.jet authority list, grant line, --allow and --deny value and run notice keeps its spelling. A function's row still names FS.Read or Time. Core's public functions keep their names and rows: files.read stays files.read. Only the line inside it changes, from a direct runtime call to a call on context.fs. Deny-only effects, effect scopes such as FS.Read("assets/"), and the runtime's path checks stay where they are.

Counts are git-tracked .jet matches in the dev tree. The word Clock has 358 matches in 107 files; Clock.new has 91 in 60 files and Clock.system 26 in 24. fake_clock has 23, fake_rng 15, #Context(logger 8 and context.logger 6. testing.world( has 12. How it combines with D-EFFECT-CLASS1. That ballot puts an access fact (Reads, Adds or Replaces) on each leaf and splits FS, DB, Net and Env leaves to match. If both are ratified, the split leaves are the cases at the top of those traits. Each operation's row names the one split leaf that ballot gives the Core function calling it. Its access and irreversible facts sit unchanged in each trait's impl Effect block.

#Repeatable stays on Core's public functions, as that ballot writes, and also sits on each trait operation they call. A provider's version of a #Repeatable operation is checked as a #Repeatable function is. The Net trait has one exchange operation per access leaf beside its socket operations, so client.get calls a Net.Read operation and E0742 stops a fake from widening it.

If only this ballot is ratified, the leaves stay Read and Write. If only that one is, the enums take its split exactly as it writes them.

Decisions this amends, each by name. D-CORE-PROVIDER1 keeps its outcome but loses its stated reason that effects stay separate: its Clock, Files, Transport and LogSink traits become Time, FS, Net and Log. D-EFFECT-HANDLE1 keeps one task-local slot per service. Its keys http, fs and process become net, fs and exec, and its traits become Net, FS and Exec.

D-EFFECT-HANDLE1's rule that authority stays orthogonal to providers changes: an install now narrows the block's row. Its reason that leaves are permission names, not operations, still holds, since several operations name FS.Read. D-JAI-CONTEXT1's logger field becomes the Log effect's log slot. D-DECL-TYPES1 gains the trait form.

D-EFF3 changes for effect traits only: inside an install, a slot call is charged the installed provider's row. D-DET1's injected Clock becomes an installed Time provider. D-FREESTAND-FACTS1 keeps its typed fact menu, but its service rows are generated from the effect traits. The spec's sentence that declarations have no runtime representation (spec.md:2982) gains the slot as its exception. Nothing else is re-decided.

Not decided here: the full list of operations in each trait, which the build card writes from today's runtime rows. Plain-word descriptions stay in Authority.jet's table, which covers every effect, not only services; moving them is outside this ballot.

options.name: One declaration: a service effect is a trait whose implementations are its providers
options.detail:
A service effect is declared once, as a trait that implements Effect. Its leaves are listed at the top like enum cases. Its basic operations follow, each row naming the leaf it performs, then the impl Effect facts. Every effect name stays as it is. The real provider for each machine, every fake, and the failing provider a #Test(faults:) list installs all implement that trait. Each must fit every operation's row (E0742).

The context slot is the effect's name in snake case: context.fs, context.time, context.net. #Context(fs: v) installs a provider for a block and the tasks it starts, and nested blocks restore the outer one. Inside the block a file call is charged v's own row, so a memory fake removes FS and a -[!FS]> row passes. A read-only wrapper leaves FS.Read, and a provider that forwards everything keeps FS.

Services with many live instances, such as databases and compute devices, have no ambient slot. Their handles are values of the effect trait, passed as today: DB replaces Driver, and GPU replaces Accelerator. Effects that are facts about code (Panic, Mem, Unsafe) or calls across a language bridge (FFI, Browser) keep their struct or enum declarations and have no operations or slot. The allocator stays a context field that is not an effect, because allocation needs no grant.

Beginners write nothing new: files.read, rows and --allow are unchanged, and their first fake is one #Context line. Experts implement a trait to write a provider, wrap one to narrow it, pass one as a generic value, or declare a library service effect with a default provider.
options.technical:
Grammar and registry (I7). Two forms are new, and both fail to parse on a0.0.46: case lines at the top of a trait body, and an impl Effect block inside one. Both are allowed only in a trait that implements Effect. This ballot ratifies them as syntax rows in Compiler/JetFoundation/Data/Syntax/Spellings.jet beside the trait rows (line 83). No keyword or marker is added, and recognition stays D-DECL-TYPES1's rule: an impl Effect block.

Slots. A machine effect's slot default comes from the target profile. A library effect trait gets a slot when its impl Effect names a default provider, as provider: StripePay, the same shape as parent:. Without one, its providers are passed as values, as DB handles are. The scanner must learn that fact, since Registry/EffectVocabulary.jet:264-462 refuses other bodies today (E3010).

Slot names follow the snake_case rule for context keys (Spellings.jet:280) and join the reserved context names (spec.md:4704-4706), and E0761's text names them. CoreSurface.jet:906-918 drops its CTX_FIELD_LOGGER row. The allocator stays a field, and #Context(allocator:) keeps today's runtime call.

One list. The vocabulary scanner learns the trait form. From it the build generates the context slot names, the Context marker's fields (Prelude/Markers.jet:612-619 and Sema/Statements/ContextBlocks.jet:31-117) and the target profile's service keys. The service rows of Prelude/Facts.jet:358-504 and Target/TargetMachine.jet:7-43 come from it too, and so does the failing provider #Test(faults:) installs. A trait's leaf cases and operation rows are the only home of which operation needs which leaf.

Rows. Each provider's operation fits that operation's declared row (E0742 stays), counting a service effect's #FX list inside it (spec.md:2944-2949). Inside #Context(fs: v), a call that reaches the fs slot is charged the row of v's own operation. That row fits the bound, so an install can only narrow. Any other path keeps its effect: a direct runtime call, FFI, an open-world call, or a call through an unknown function value.

When v is a trait value, such as a parameter of type FS, its calls count with each operation's declared row (spec.md:3518-3522), so FS stays. A static call on a provider value charges that type's own row, as it does on a0.0.46. A call through a trait value or a generic bound charges the trait's bound, also as today. Generic code bounded by a trait is unchanged.

Keeping E0742 is what makes the narrowing sound. files.write declares -[FS.Write]>, and every check made on its row assumes it, including !IO rows, #Transact bodies and access checks. A provider that also printed would break those checks wherever it is installed. A fake that serves recorded files reads them before the block. A file system over the network is passed as a value of its own trait, as Go code passes an fs.FS.

Denials. A function's own denial is checked without knowing its caller's install. So a slot call there counts every provider the build can put in that slot: the target's, plus each type installed there anywhere in the program. That is the sealed set an executable build already uses for trait calls (spec.md:2698-2704). A -[!FS]> function that calls log.info keeps building, as it does today.

Summaries record slot calls as slot calls, so an executable build resolves a dependency's slot calls with its own sealed set and rechecks the denials they reach. An install that breaks a denial elsewhere is an error that names the install.

Binding (performance gate). Prelude and Core are compiled once per Jet version (D-EXEC1), so Core cannot be specialized per program. Each slot operation in Core calls one hook symbol that the static link binds, as Compiler/JetDriver/Source/Driver/SchedulerProvider.jet binds the scheduler's weak hooks today. With no install of that slot in the image, the hook is the target provider's function: the same direct call files.write makes now.

With an install, the hook is a generated dispatcher. It loads the context record's provider word and calls the current provider: two loads and one indirect call more per operation. The task record grows by that one word, which points to a shared, unchanging provider set, so spawn copies one word. Each install pushes and restores the word, as deadline blocks do.

Release profiles can refuse installs under D-EFFECT-HANDLE1's .Deny policy, so their hooks are always direct. Two builds always use the dispatcher: --linkage dynamic (D-LINK-MODEL1), and jet dev, whose live replacement can add an install later. WASM plugins are their own images with their own providers: a host install never reaches into one, and a call into a plugin keeps its effects.

The build card adds a paired two-program cell, direct against installed, for the files and time operations. The peer-floor cells must not move, since they install nothing.

Forwarding. A provider's operations may not reach their own effect's slot, and the build refuses one that does. A wrapper holds the provider it forwards to, read before the block, as ReadOnlyFS{inner: context.fs}. So a dispatched call needs no slot swap around it, and a provider can never call itself through the slot.

State. context.fs returns a copy of the current provider value, as context.get does (spec.md:4697). Operations take self, so a fake keeps what it records in a Shared cell, and the copy the block installs shares it with the test's value (spec.md:2513-2520). Providers are not lent by reference as allocators are, because tasks keep their provider after the block ends.

Edges. A task started inside an install keeps its provider, and its body is charged as the block is. A closure called after the block sees the provider current at the call and is charged where it is called. A C callback reads no context, so it can't reach a provider (E3218, E3203 unchanged). Code run while building reads the build host's providers, as Core calls do today.

Host reads keep their rows. The reads Docs/Spec/Reference/host-reads.md lists under another effect, such as name resolution reading /etc/hosts under Net, stay with that effect's provider. A denial covers what Core's file functions do. A child process is checked as Exec, and foreign code as FFI.

Target profiles. MachineFacts (Core/Target/Target.jet:29-84) names one provider per effect slot: fs, net, io, time, rand, env, exec. It names them as it names its scheduler today, so one link-time binding serves the scheduler, the allocator and every slot. Panic, ffi and browser remain facts. The hand map row() (62-83) is deleted: an absent slot denies its root, and a provider that lacks a leaf lists it.

Second stores. testing.world and DeterministicWorld install Time, Rand and Env providers, and the runtime World keeps only the timer and idle hooks those providers call. The controlled monotonic clock and the replay and wall overrides become providers the harness installs, so now_utc keeps one path. Slot faults, including Sealed.jet's short reads and interruptions, become modes of the generated failing provider. Allocation faults stay with the allocator.

Operations may have default bodies, as trait members can today (Spellings.jet:83). Each defaults to failing with its error, so a fake writes only the operations its test reaches.

options.name: Two names, linked by one declared fact
options.detail:
Effects stay as today's structs and enums, and D-CORE-PROVIDER1's provider traits are built as ratified: Clock, Files, Transport, LogSink and the rest. Each provider trait names its effect once, in a trait constant, so the compiler can check the link and generate the key list. The context key is the provider's name in snake case (clock, files, transport), while rows, manifests and --allow keep the effect's name (Time, FS, Net).

Installing a fake can still remove its effect from a block's row, because the link tells the compiler which effect a provider serves. Beginners see two words for one service: they grant FS and install files. Experts read two declarations to learn one service.
options.technical: A trait constant (Spellings.jet:89, name: Type{default}) such as effect: Effect{FS} sits on each provider trait. The scanner reads it, and the same generated list that A builds feeds #Context fields, target keys and fault providers. Leaves come from each provider operation's row, as in A. The same row, cost and target rules as A apply, so the performance and soundness work is the same. The difference is the second declaration and the second name in every test and profile.

options.name: The proposal's literal form: #Effect on any trait, called through the trait name
options.detail:
Any trait marked #Effect is an effect. Rows name the trait, such as -[Clock]>, and code calls an operation through the trait's name, Clock.now(), which reaches the provider the context holds. #Context(Clock: FixedClock{…}) installs one. Leaves become sub-traits, and the effect names become the provider names the proposal's examples use, such as Clock.

It reads well in small examples. It adds a second way to say a type is an effect, a context label in the type's casing, and a new meaning for a call on a trait name. Every operation goes through the context at run time.
options.technical:
The #Effect marker sits beside D-DECL-TYPES1's impl Effect recognition, so there are two ways to declare an effect (I8).

A PascalCase #Context label breaks the registry's snake_case rule for context keys (Spellings.jet:280). Leaves as sub-traits have no spelling: a dotted declaration is not Jet syntax (Spellings.jet:18), and a user module that could hold them must be snake_case. Its compile table (proposal lines 1521-1530) makes a runtime-chosen handler one indirect call, with no program-wide check that keeps today's direct calls when nothing is installed. Renaming Time to Clock reopens D-EFFECT-ROOT-WORDS1.

options.name: Keep today's two names and build D-CORE-PROVIDER1 as ratified
options.detail:
Nothing about effects changes. The provider traits D-CORE-PROVIDER1 ratified are added beside them with their own names and keys, and each place that relates a provider to an effect keeps its own hand-written copy. That covers the target profile's denial map, the target capability lists, the world, replay and fault stores, and the plain words.

It costs least now. A fake reached through its trait keeps charging the effect it replaces, so a test can't deny the disk it never touches. Two words stay for one service, and every new service adds entries to several hand maps.
options.technical:
The probe in the detail is this option on a0.0.46. A memory Store called through the trait, generically or as a Store value, still charges FS.Write to a -[!FS]> caller (E0749). Called on its own type, it is charged its own row. The closest working spelling for a context-held service is a #ContextKey of a struct, which checks and runs today. A key's value has one fixed type, so a fake must be the same type as the real provider.

MachineFacts.row(), the Facts.jet and TargetMachine.jet capability lists, the fault strings, the world and replay checks in Time.jet, and Authority.jet's words stay hand-kept copies.

options.name: Capabilities as values only, with no ambient services
options.detail:
Every function that uses a service takes it as a parameter, as Go and Swift code does with dependency injection, Rust with generics, or Scala ZIO with an environment. A function's effects are the provider types it receives, so rows follow from parameters. There is no context slot and no #Context install.

It makes every dependency visible and every fake a plain argument. It also makes files.read(path) need an fs argument at every call, threaded through every caller up to run. That is the opposite of a small beginner surface.
options.technical: Each Core service function gains a provider parameter, and every call chain threads it. D-EFFECT-HANDLE1's ratified service slots lose their role. D-CONTEXT-EFFECT1's implicit context stays, but it carries no services. Static dispatch through generics is free, as in Rust, but a dynamic provider costs one indirect call. Rows and grants still need effect names, so a provider type would still map to an effect, which brings back B's link.

options.name: One declaration, but an install leaves the row unchanged
options.detail:
Effects become traits as in A, with the same names, slots, generated lists, binding and second-store cutover. An install swaps the provider at run time but leaves the block's row as it was. That is D-EFFECT-HANDLE1's ratified rule that authority stays orthogonal to providers.

It needs no new row rule and no sealed set for slot denials. A test with a memory fake still counts as writing files, so it can't deny the disk, which is the gap the card names.
options.technical: A's grammar, one list, slots, binding, forwarding, state, edges and target sections all apply. A's Rows and Denials sections drop: a slot call is charged its operation's declared row everywhere, and E0742 still bounds providers. Code that must prove it touches no disk passes a fake of a concrete type as a value, whose own row a static call charges, as E does.

comparisons.note: Flix's standard library declares Fs.FileSystem, Time.Clock, Net.Http and others as effects with operations, each with a default handler, so main needs no setup. withInMemoryFS fully handles FileSystem and drops it from the signature, though it adds Clock for timestamps. Middleware such as withReadOnly and withChroot forward to the real effect. Flix is the closest peer to A; Jet adds grants and denials over the same names. Sources: https://doc.flix.dev/filesystem.html and https://doc.flix.dev/library-effects.html

An effect declares its operations, and a handler gives them meaning. A function's type lists the effects it may perform, and a handler removes its effect from the type of the code it wraps. Evidence passing compiles common handlers to fast calls (Xie and Leijen, ICFP 2021). A follows this: the trait is the effect, a provider is the handler, and an install drops the effect from the block's row. Source: https://koka-lang.github.io/koka/doc/book.html#sec-handlers

Effects are interfaces, and a try block with a handler supplies an implementation; the compiler passes handlers as capabilities. Brachthaeuser and others, Effects as Capabilities, OOPSLA 2020. Effekt shows an effect can be an interface with operations, handled lexically and compiled without a global lookup. Source: https://effekt-lang.org/docs/

An ability declares operations; a function's type lists the abilities it needs, and a handler interprets them. IO and Exception are built-in abilities the runtime handles. Unison has no ability hierarchy, so a partial grant like read-only files has to be a separate ability. Source: https://www.unison-lang.org/docs/fundamentals/abilities/
comparisons.code:
unique ability Clock where now : {Clock} Nat
stamp : '{Clock} Text
stamp _ = "t=" ++ Nat.toText Clock.now

comparisons.note: Effects are declared operations with deep and shallow handlers, but the type system does not track them. An effect nobody handles fails at run time with Effect.Unhandled. Handlers there are a control mechanism, not a permission system; Jet keeps rows checked while building. Source: https://ocaml.org/manual/5.2/effects.html
comparisons.code:
type _ Effect.t += Now : int Effect.t
let stamp () = "t=" ^ string_of_int (Effect.perform Now)

comparisons.note: ZIO's ZIO[R, E, A] lists required services in R, and services are traits provided by layers. ZIO 2 took its built-in Clock, Console, Random and System out of R; ZIO.withClock overrides one for a scope, much as A's install does, and TestClock replaces it in tests. Those built-ins are no longer tracked in the type, while A keeps them in rows. Kyo tracks pending effects in a type and handles them one by one. Sources: https://zio.dev/guides/migrate/zio-2.x-migration-guide/ and https://getkyo.io

mtl uses type classes such as MonadReader; effectful lists effects in Eff es a and interprets a dynamic effect by a handler, with static effects for speed. Both make the effect and its interface one declaration, as A does. Source: https://hackage.haskell.org/package/effectful
comparisons.code:
data Clock :: Effect where Now :: Clock m Int
type instance DispatchOf Clock = Dynamic
stamp :: Clock :> es => Eff es String
stamp = ("t=" ++) . show <$> send Now

comparisons.note: A trait with a generic parameter gives a static, monomorphized provider; dyn Trait gives one indirect call. Rust does not track effects, and cap-std removes ambient file access by passing directory handles. E follows Rust; A keeps Rust's static calls when nothing is installed. Source: https://docs.rs/cap-std
comparisons.code:
trait Clock { fn now(&self) -> u64; }
fn stamp<C: Clock>(c: &C) -> String { format!("t={}", c.now()) }

comparisons.note: Protocols with dependency injection; Point-Free's swift-dependencies keeps one key per dependency and overrides it for a scope with withDependencies, close to A's #Context install. Nothing tracks which code uses a dependency. Source: https://github.com/pointfreeco/swift-dependencies
comparisons.code:
@Dependency(\.continuousClock) var clock
withDependencies { $0.continuousClock = ImmediateClock() } operation: { model.start() }

comparisons.note: io/fs.FS is a one-method interface (Open), os.DirFS is the real disk and testing/fstest.MapFS is the fake. Code that wants a fake must take an fs.FS argument, which is E's model; os.ReadFile ignores it. Sources: https://pkg.go.dev/io/fs and https://pkg.go.dev/testing/fstest
comparisons.code:
func stamp(fsys fs.FS) ([]byte, error) { return fs.ReadFile(fsys, "note.txt") }
stamp(fstest.MapFS{"note.txt": {Data: []byte("hi")}})

recommendation.why: A gives each service one declaration and one name, and the row, the grant, the context slot, the target profile and the fake all read it. It fixes the real gap: a fake no longer charges the effect it replaces, so a test can deny the disk. Keeping E0742 makes that sound, since an install can only narrow a row. It changes no row, manifest or flag spelling. A program that installs nothing keeps today's direct calls, because the static link binds each operation's hook as it binds the scheduler's.
recommendation.tradeoff: One name, honest fakes and generated lists. The price is a new trait-body form, a Core rewrite of each service and its second stores, and a dispatcher per operation in builds that install a provider.
gains: One declaration per service holds its operations, effect name, leaves, facts and context slot.
Installing a fake narrows its effect, so a test helper can say -[!FS]> and build.
Target denials, capability rows, #Context fields and fault providers are generated, deleting the hand maps.
The world, replay and override stores become providers, so the clock has one path.
No effect row, manifest, grant or flag changes spelling.

losses.loss: Effects get a second declaration shape: a trait with leaf cases and operations, beside struct and enum effects. Both parts are new syntax rows.
losses.mitigation: One rule covers both: an effect is a type that implements Effect, and a trait effect is one with operations. Only Core and library authors declare effects, and the registry rows land before the parser accepts the form.

losses.loss: Core is rewritten once. Service functions call their slots, every Clock use (358 matches in 107 files) moves to Time providers, and the world, replay and fault stores become providers. Driver, Accelerator and the logger key are renamed.
losses.mitigation: One language rewrite moves them together. Public Core function names and rows stay, so user programs that call files.read or time.now_utc are untouched.

losses.loss: A build that installs a provider pays two loads and an indirect call per operation of that service, and every task record grows by one word.
losses.mitigation: Only builds with an install pay, mostly tests. The others bind each hook to the real provider at link time. A paired two-program cell measures both, and the peer-floor cells install nothing.

losses.loss: A provider must fit each operation's row, so a fake can't read fixtures from disk inside the block, and a network file system can't be installed as fs.
losses.mitigation: A fake loads its fixtures before the block. A network file system is passed as a value of its own trait, as Go passes an fs.FS.

losses.loss: A denial on code that calls a slot counts every provider the program installs there, so adding an install can fail a denial elsewhere.
losses.mitigation: This is the sealed-set rule executable builds already use for trait calls, and the error names the install.

losses.loss: A test with fakes no longer exercises the real grant checks for the effects it replaces.
losses.mitigation: That is the point of a fake, and a fake that forwards to the real provider keeps the effect. A direct runtime call, FFI, an open-world call or an unknown function value keeps its effect even inside an install.

losses.loss: Seven ratified decisions are amended: D-CORE-PROVIDER1, D-EFFECT-HANDLE1, D-JAI-CONTEXT1, D-DECL-TYPES1, D-EFF3, D-DET1 and D-FREESTAND-FACTS1. D-EFFECT-HANDLE1 loses its rule that authority stays orthogonal to providers.
losses.mitigation: Each keeps its outcome except the parts the detail names. The ballot lists every amendment, so the owner votes them together.

whyNot.reason: B gets A's generated keys and narrowing but keeps two names for one service. A user grants FS and installs files, and a reader must find two declarations to learn one service. It saves no work, since the link fact needs the same scanner and rules.

C adds a second way to declare an effect, a context label against the snake_case rule, and leaves with no spelling. It renames Time to Clock against D-EFFECT-ROOT-WORDS1. It also sends every operation through the context with no rule that keeps today's direct calls.

D leaves the gap the probe shows: a fake reached through its trait still charges the effect it replaces. It also keeps two names per service and the hand maps in MachineFacts.row(), the capability lists, the fault strings, the clock's second stores and the context field menu.

E makes every file read take a provider argument threaded from run, which fails the small beginner surface. It drops the ratified context slot, and it still needs effect names for grants, which brings back the link B writes.

F gets A's one name and generated lists but keeps the gap the card names: a fake still charges the effect it replaces, so a test can't deny the disk. The row rule it avoids is the part that makes fakes honest, and A keeps that rule sound by keeping E0742.
