decisions.title: Calls write ^ before each named argument they change
decisions.situation: Today a Jet call is written plain, and only the signature says that it changes an argument (D-CALLSITE-MARK2=A, ratified 2026-11-06). A reader of grow(xs) cannot tell from that line that xs changes, and a diff or a web page shows no editor hints. The answers were an opt-in policy, an audit command and editor hints; only four test files use the policy. On 2026-11-25 you ruled that a call writes ^ before every named argument it changes, that receivers stay unmarked, and that jet fmt inserts every required mark. This ballot settles the mechanism around that ruling: the error and its fix, cheap mark placement in fmt, the editor, and the cutover of about 105,000 call sites.
decisions.gist: Should a call write ^ before each named argument it changes, with jet fmt and the editor writing every mark for you?
decisions.lesson: A signature says what a function does to each input: a plain parameter reads it, ^ changes it and ^^ takes it. A call-site mark repeats that fact where the call is written, so a reader of grow(^xs) sees the change without opening grow. The compiler checks each mark against the signature, so a mark can never claim a change that does not happen.
decisions.explainer:
## Read the example

`grow: fn(xs: ^[Int])` declares that `grow` changes the list it gets. Today the call reads `grow(xs)`, exactly like a call that only reads. Under A the call reads `grow(^xs)`, and the compiler refuses `grow(xs)` with a fix that writes the mark.

## What stays as it is

Signatures keep their marks. A method's receiver stays plain, as in Swift, Rust and C#: `xs.push(4)`. A move at a name's last use needs no mark, though `seal(^^buf)` may be written there and is checked.

## Who types the marks

Nobody has to. `jet fmt` and `jet fix` write every missing mark from the checked program. In the editor, the error's quick fix and fix-on-save write the same marks, and completion offers `^xs` in a slot that changes its argument.
decisions.story:
Mira reviews a teammate's change. One line says `apply_discount(order, code)`. Today she must open `apply_discount` to learn that it changes `order`, because the review page shows no editor hints. Under A the line reads `apply_discount(^order, code)`, so the change is visible in the diff itself.

Her teammate never typed the mark. He wrote the plain call, the editor underlined `order` with the missing-mark error, and saving the file applied the fix. Had he been on the command line, `jet fmt` would have written it.
decisions.detail:
## What the ruling fixes and what this ballot settles

Your 2026-11-25 ruling fixes the rule itself. A call writes `^` before every named argument it changes, including one that is already a `^` parameter. Receivers are never marked. A take at a last use needs no mark, but a written `^^` there is accepted and checked, and fmt leaves it as written. `jet fmt` inserts every required mark. `#Policy(writes: .Explicit)` is deleted, and UFCS stays rejected (D-UFCS1=B); pipes give chaining.

Option A is that ruling. This ballot settles the mechanism around it: which arguments count, how wrong marks are refused and fixed, how fmt places marks cheaply, what the editor does, and what is deleted. Options B, C and D record the alternatives the ruling set aside, so the record states their costs. They are not open questions.

## The rule, exactly

A named argument is a place rooted at a name: a name, `self`, or either followed by fields, indexes or ranges. That is the place `sema_receiver_mark_place_root` already recognizes (Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Ownership/Checks.jet:4765-4773). A literal, a call result, `x.copy()` or a lambda is fresh, so it never takes a mark.


- A named argument bound to a `^` parameter must be written `^place`. A missing mark is E0228 `Jet.CallMarkRequired`, now a default error with no policy.

- The mark sits before the root of the place: `sort_part(^xs[0..2])`, `grow(^st.items)`. A labeled argument writes the label first: `copy(to: ^dst, from: src)`.

- A whole name bound to a `^^` parameter may be written plain or `^^name`. Either way, a later use is E0209 naming the call.

- `^` where the parameter takes, or `^^` where it only changes, is E0228 with a Safe replacement.

- A mark on a receiver, on a read argument or on a fresh value is E0225 `Jet.UnusedPlaceMark` with a Safe removal. `^xs.push(4)` is therefore refused, and the fix writes `xs.push(4)`.

- `^^` on a name whose type copies, or on a function item, is E0225 with a Safe removal. The call copies, so the name stays usable and a take mark would be false.

- `^^` on a field, as in `seal(^^st.buf)`, is E0225 with a Safe rewrite to `seal(st.buf.move())`. A field take keeps `owner.field.move()` (Docs/Spec/spec.md:2282-2283).

- Operators are never marked. `xs[i] = v`, `n += 1` and `a == b` have no argument slot to hold a mark, as in C#.

- One rule here goes beyond the ruling. `name.move()` written straight into a `^^` parameter is E0225 with a Safe rewrite to `^^name`, so a call take has one spelling. It amends D-MOVE-SIGIL1's `x.move()` for call arguments only.

- A constructor or a variant payload is no `^^` parameter, so `Dyn.Text(text.move())` keeps its spelling (spec.md:2213-2214). Every other value position keeps `x.move()` too.

## Edge cases


- Generic and trait-bound calls take marks from the bound's signature: `put_one(^xs, 9)` and `use_filler(Ones{n: 2}, ^xs)` checked on a0.0.46 in the old spelling.

- A stored function value takes marks from its function type: `st.action(^m)`. This amends D-FNVAL-WRITE1's "called plainly".

- A method call marks its arguments, never its receiver: `st.add_into(^xs)`.

- A closure that captures `xs` and changes it marks the write inside its body. Calling the closure is plain, because the call passes no argument.

- A task call follows the same rule. `task ^^name { … }` keeps its capture mark, and `t.join()` is a receiver, so it stays plain.

- A function that writes only on some branches is still a `^` parameter, so the call is marked. The signature decides, never the body.

- A call resolves to one declaration before marks are checked, so the mark follows that declaration. Dynamic dispatch through a trait value uses the trait method's signature.

- Two marks on one name in one call stay E0204, unchanged.

## Pipes

A pipe whose head is a name lets its first step change that name in place, written `^<>`: `xs |> grow(^<>)`. Today such a step already changes `xs` in place; a probe printed the grown length.

That contradicts ratified D-PIPE1=A. Its text says a first step that also writes the name keeps the hidden binding, which is immutable (Docs/Spec/syntax-decisions.md:949-953). A takes your words "pipes give chaining" as the authority to amend D-PIPE1, so the in-place write becomes the rule.

The `<>` of a computed head or of a later step stays a hidden read-only value, as D-PIPE1 lowers it. A writing step there is refused, as today. Today's message leaks a hidden name: "Cannot edit through `__jet_pipe_174`". Under A it names `<>` and offers binding the head to a name first.

`^<>` gives a registered token a new use. So the `<>` row (Compiler/JetFoundation/Data/Syntax/Spellings.jet:71) and the sigil table (Tests/Guards/SigilMeaningTable/sigil_meaning_table.jet:209) gain it.

## How fmt places the marks, and what that costs

Today plain layout never compiles (Compiler/JetCLI/Source/CLI/Host.jet:4275-4302), and editor formatting is text-only (Compiler/JetLSP/Source/LSP/Formatting.jet:24-31). The compiling fmt passes are `--explicit-copies` and `--explicit-failures` (Front.jet:358-361).

Those two share `jet_cli_fmt_policy_marks` (Host.jet:4199-4269), which compiles each file twice. The first compile refuses on any other error (Host.jet:4205-4208), and the second prepends a policy (Host.jet:4213). No fmt pass writes call marks today; under the writes policy only `jet fix` does.

The design removes each cost:


- Layout never waits for a check. A file that parses is laid out exactly as today.

- Marks come from one compile per package. The ordinary check already carries every E0228 Safe edit, so no policy is prepended.

- The shared machinery becomes one checked-insertion pass for call marks, copies and failures alike. So the two compiles per file go for all three.

- An error blocks only the marks it touches. An error in a declaration, such as an unknown type in a signature, blocks the mark at every call that resolves through it, in any body.

- An error inside a body blocks only the calls whose callee or argument place did not resolve. fmt names each blocked call and its error.

- A file that does not parse gets no marks and keeps its text. fmt prints one line naming the parse error.

- fmt inserts marks only. It never removes or adds an optional `^^`, never applies another fix, and re-parses the result under the structure guard (Host.jet:4292).

- `jet fmt --check` runs the same path, so CI reports a missing mark as a dirty file.

- `--stdin-path` checks the buffer against its package. Editor fix-on-save takes the marks from the server's last check instead, so it never compiles again.

The cost is real today. On a0.0.46, `jet fmt --check` of Examples/Systems/Files/CompressZstdStream.jet at c137227f92 took 18 to 56 ms. `jet check` of the same file took 1.4 to 2.3 s, and a nine-line file checked in about 27 ms.

So a marking fmt costs one package check. The build card measures that on the repository and on single files, and owns making it cheap.

## The editor and the beginner path

A beginner writes `grow(xs)`. The editor shows E0228 with its preferred quick fix, which comes from the Safe edit (Compiler/JetLSP/Source/LSP/CodeActions.jet:28-80). A new `source.fixAll` code action applies every Safe mark insert from the editor's last check. Today the server offers only quickfix, refactor.rewrite and source.organizeImports (Requests.jet:123).

Completion inside a `^` slot inserts `^name`, and signature help shows the `^T` parameter. On the command line, `jet run` prints "Fix: write `^xs`", and `jet fix` applies it.

Inlay hints drop the argument `^`, which the text now shows. Today one hint label joins the parameter name and its mark (Compiler/JetLSP/Source/LSP/Hints.jet:132-175), so A splits it and keeps the name. Receiver `^` and `^^` hints stay, and a `^^` hint shows only where no `^^` is written. The underline of changed names stays (Tokens.jet:120-127).

## Diagnostics


- E0228 `Jet.CallMarkRequired` (Compiler/Prelude/Diagnostics.jet:4327-4350) loses its policy wording at 4331, 4332, 4339 and 4343. It names the whole place, for example "write `^st.items`", and its fix names `jet fmt` and `jet fix`. It stays Opinion with a Safe edit, and its UI snapshot is replaced.

- The edit must sit before the place root. Today it sits at `expr_source_start` of the argument (Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Ownership/CallMarks.jet:122). That function has no arm for a slice, so a slice falls to the default arm (Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/AST/Expressions.jet:816).

- So on a0.0.46 the fix for `sort_part(xs[0..2])` wrote `xs&[0..2]`, which then failed with "This operator works on integer values only". An index is placed right: `bump(xs[0])` became `bump(&xs[0])`.

- `jet fix` still reported "applied 1 fix", for a file or a package, and `--dry-run` said "would apply 1 fix". Its rollback check (Compiler/JetCLI/Source/CLI/FixCommands.jet:427-456) missed the new error. Both defects are fixed with A, each with a regression case.

- E0225 (Diagnostics.jet:4279-4301) today means a place mark sits where nothing writes or takes a named place. A receiver mark on a writing method does write, so its meaning, message, why and safety text are all rewritten.

- Each new E0225 case gets a UI snapshot: receiver, read argument, fresh value, `.move()` argument, field `^^`, and `^^` on a copied type.

- Today's extra-mark text is false for takes. On a0.0.46, `seal(&&st.buf)` and `take_n(&&n)` with an `Int` both say the callee reads this input (CallMarks.jet:115 and 184-185). The E0225 cases above replace it.

- E0003 "expected a value, found `^`" no longer fires for an argument mark (CallMarks.jet:191-193).

- A dead-key layout types `^s` as `ŝ`. The dead-key fixes already planned on card #6998 apply to an unknown name such as `ŝtate` and offer `^state`.

## What is deleted or rewritten, and where the old fact lives

The fact "calls carry no marks" lives in many places, and each changes in the same cutover.


- Policy: `writes:` in Compiler/JetParser/Source/Parser/Declarations/Policies.jet:205 and 216, and Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/Policy/Policy.jet:30, 59, 67, 222, 319, 409 and 480. Also SyntaxCodec.jet:4278 and 4308, and Formatter/Statements.jet:181.

- Sema: the policy gate in CallMarks.jet:97-156 and the `writes_explicit` flag in Scopes.jet (1209, 1246-1248, 1338, 2392, 2428, 2493, 2793, 2821, 3389 and 3455). Also Statements.jet:1431, Checks.jet:4125, 4700 and 4971, FunctionMemory.jet:656, and AuditCopies.jet:48 and 77-78.

- Kept and generalized: Host.jet:4159-4164 and 4199-4269 hold the copies and failures policies and their shared mark pass. They serve `--explicit-copies` and `--explicit-failures`, so they are not deleted.

- `jet audit writes`: Compiler/JetCLI/Source/CLI/AuditWrites.jet works only by prepending the policy (line 18), so it goes. So does cli.md:1428-1438, which still shows the stale `mark=<&|&&>`.

- Its plan arm goes too: Front.jet:141 and 326 with its other `.AuditWrites` arms, and Host.jet:4973, 4998 and 5166-5168. So do CheckReceipt.jet:295, Entry.jet:1557, Publish.jet:678, RemoteRun.jet:188 and TestSettingLayers.jet:401.

- Also InspectB.jet:993-1004, hot-text.list:5765 and 8971, and the audit rows in six Compiler/JetCLI/Tests files. The audit also listed changed receivers and unwritten takes. Under A that listing lives only in editor hints.

- Registry and syntax data: Spellings.jet:71-74 and CoreSurface.jet:362-371 in Compiler/JetFoundation/Data/Syntax. Also SyntaxDictionaryData.jet:187-188 and DiagnosticRows.jet:3862-3871.

- The sigil table row at sigil_meaning_table.jet:174 teaches `^items.push(x)`, which A refuses, so its example changes. Its `f(^^xs)` row at line 176 stays.

- Compiler code: Formatter/Expressions.jet:2950-2951, Parser/Expressions.jet:2503 and 2576-2584, and AST/Expressions.jet:140, where `CallArg.mark` already exists. Sema notes sit at Checks.jet:519 and 4877, WindowFacts.jet:7, Scopes.jet:1246 and FunctionMemory.jet:647.

- Editor: Hints.jet:132 says "since calls carry no marks", and Tokens.jet:120. In Tools/Editors, the TreeSitter grammar.js:25-26, 69, 198 and 222, with its generated src files rebuilt. Also Zed highlights.scm:100, 109 and 126-130, jet.tmGrammar:203 and Highlights.jet:669-676.

- Docs: spec.md:2187-2201, 2227-2237, 2259-2273 and 2277-2287. Also syntax-decisions.md:91-93, 949-953, 2246, 3686 and 3728-3745, core-library.md:892 and 4101, and syntax-surface.jet:551. Plus the memory-marks proposal at lines 26, 124 and 264.

- Prose outside Docs: Examples/Text/README.md:29, Tools/AgentEval/jet-context-capsule.md:97 and Tools/Editors/Vscode/README.md:152. The generated page Docs/Site/Dist/e/Jet.CallMarkRequired is rebuilt.

- Tests that use the policy: four `.jet` files and their outputs, among them Tests/UI/writes_policy_call_marks, Tests/Cases/Fmt/FmtKeepsCallMarksUnderWritesPolicy and Tests/Cases/Migrations/MarkCaret1RewritesEveryMark.

- Also the writes-audit case in Tests/Cases/Ownership, two inspect-guarantees outputs, Tests/UI/policy_conflicting_module.stderr, Tests/diagnostics_census.tsv and the E0225 snapshots Tests/UI/move_mark_*.

- Migration: a `call-mark3` row in LANGUAGE_REWRITES (Spellings.jet:111-122). It runs the checked insertion, because a text rewrite cannot see signatures. It also applies the `.move()` rewrite above, which fmt never does.

## Code that no compile checks

No manual work also covers Jet that no compile reaches. The repository holds 853 Jet fences in Markdown, 433 `.template` files (427 under Tests/Cases), Jet inside test strings, and about 3,059 `.stderr` snapshots that quote source lines.

The migration runs the checked insertion on every runnable fence, checked the way Tests/Guards/doc_blocks.jet checks them, and the snapshots are regenerated. Compiler/Migrations/MarkCaret1.jet shows the earlier text migration covering fences and snapshots.

A fragment that does not check is listed by the migration with its path. That residue is counted when the row is built; it is not measured yet.

## How many call sites gain a mark

Method: a script lists the tracked `.jet` files under Core, Compiler, Jetpack, Tools, Examples and Tests. It blanks comments and string text and collects every `name: fn(…)` declaration with each parameter's mark. Then it maps each call's arguments by label or position and counts named arguments bound to a `^` parameter.

A site counts as "certain" when every declaration with that name agrees the slot changes. The looser "possible" count needs only one such declaration.

Calibration: at `5ef77a52ad^`, the last tree where every changing argument carried a written `&`, the code holds 67,629 such marks. The certain count marked 67,003 slots, 65,448 of them right.

So the certain count has precision 65,448 / 67,003 = 0.977 and recall 65,448 / 67,629 = 0.968. The script's printed line, precision 0.840 and recall 0.979, belongs to the looser count.

Today, on dev at `de8a554abe1`, 22,953 files hold 1,050,119 calls. The certain count is 104,619 sites in 1,616 files: Compiler 82,909, Core 16,266, Tests 2,312, Jetpack 2,002, Tools 995 and Examples 135.

Scaled by recall over precision, that is about 105,600, so about 105,000 sites change. The possible count is 126,336. About two in three of those pass on a name that is already a `^` parameter, and the ruling marks those too.

For comparison, D-CALLSITE-MARK2 counted 69,758 argument marks and about 29,800 receiver marks on dev `b486d6c09a` (2026-11-05). That was a raw text count. The same text pattern finds 69,817 at `5ef77a52ad^`, including comments, strings, fixtures and Docs.

The cutover commit `5ef77a52ad` changed 4,097 files, but it also changed other spellings, so that is no count of marked files. Since `5ef77a52ad^`, calls grew from 680,361 to 1,050,119, and certain sites grew in Compiler from 60,524 and in Core from 1,325.

Under A no receiver gains a mark. The script found 909 arguments written as a whole-name `x.move()`. Of those, 408 certainly reach a `^^` parameter and 610 possibly do; each becomes `^^x`.

## Probes

The installed jet is a0.0.46, which still spells the marks `&` and `&&`. Every probe used that spelling under `#Policy(writes: .Explicit)`, the nearest thing to A that runs.

- The same-program example checks and prints 2. The policy reports five E0228 sites with fixes, and `jet fix` inserted every mark.

- Generic, trait-bound, trait-value, function-value, field, labeled and index arguments all got the right mark.

- A pipe step `xs |> grow(<>)` changed `xs` in place, and the fix wrote `grow(&<>)`. With a computed head, `make() |> grow(<>)` was refused with the leaked `__jet_pipe_174` name.

- An unknown type in one function's signature removed the mark at its call in another body. `jet fix` then also rewrote that argument's `k := 2` to `k: 2`, a binding the call may change.

- A type error inside one body left the marks in that body in place.

- A file with a parse error got "no changes made" with no line naming the error.

## Decisions this amends


- D-CALLSITE-MARK2=A: its call half is reversed. Calls mark changed arguments; the policy, `jet audit writes` and argument hints go. Its signature rules, receiver rule and its law that a call never copies on its own stand.

- D-MOVE-SIGIL1=A and D-MARK-CARET1: "calls stay unmarked" becomes "calls mark changed arguments; a `^^` take mark is optional". A whole-name `x.move()` argument into a `^^` slot becomes `^^x`.

- D-PIPE1=A: a first step on a named head changes it in place through `^<>`, and syntax-decisions.md:949-953 is rewritten. A computed head stays read-only.

- D-BIND-MARK1=A: its text on `^` surviving only as the policy's audit mark changes. `^buf.push(` versus `^buf:` stays, now as E0225.

- D-FNVAL-WRITE1=A: a stored function value is called with marks, `st.action(^m)`, as that decision first said.

- D-COPY-DEFAULT1=A and D-CAP-RECEIVER1=D: the historical notes point here.

- D-RECEIVER-MARK1=A (2026-10-30) stands: receivers are plain and changed arguments are marked. A returns to that rule in the `^` spelling, with tools writing the marks.

- Card #6418 criterion c9 (inlay hints) narrows to receivers and unwritten takes.

options.name: Mark every changed named argument; fmt and the editor write the marks
options.detail:
A call writes `^` before every named argument it changes, and the compiler refuses a missing or wrong mark with a Safe fix. Receivers stay plain, and `^^` at a last-use take is optional and checked. `jet fmt`, `jet fix`, the editor's quick fix and fix-on-save write the marks.

Beginner path: write `grow(xs)`, see the error, apply the fix or save. Expert path: type `grow(^xs)` directly, and add `^^` where a take should stand out.
options.technical: E0228 becomes a default error whose Safe edit inserts the mark before the place root. E0225 refuses receiver, read, fresh, field-take and copied-take marks, and rewrites a whole-name .move() argument to ^^name. fmt lays out at once, then inserts marks from one compile per package, shared with the copies and failures passes. The writes policy, its audit and the argument hint are deleted.

options.name: Keep today's plain calls (D-CALLSITE-MARK2=A)
options.detail:
Calls stay plain and the signature alone says what happens. A module can opt into marks with `#Policy(writes: .Explicit)`, `jet audit writes` lists every changing call, and editor hints show the marks.

Beginner path: nothing to write. Expert path: read signatures, the audit or the hints to see changes.
options.technical: No compiler change. Under the policy only jet fix writes marks, and it marks receivers too, which your ruling rejects. The misplaced slice edit (Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/AST/Expressions.jet:816), the unchecked rollback in jet fix and the stale audit text still need fixing.

options.name: Show marks only as editor hints
options.detail:
The source stays plain, and the editor draws `^` and `^^` before changed and taken arguments and underlines them. The policy and the audit are deleted.

Beginner path: nothing to write; the editor shows the change. Expert path: the same, but reviews in a browser, a terminal or a diff show nothing.
options.technical: Delete the policy, E0228 and jet audit writes. Hints.jet already draws per-argument hints from the checked index, so the editor needs no new work.

options.name: Require marks only in package library code
options.detail:
Library source that `jet publish` ships must mark changed arguments, and fmt inserts the marks there. Apps, scripts and tests may write them or leave them out, and a written mark is still checked.

Beginner path: nothing to write until code becomes a library. Expert path: library authors work as in A.
options.technical: E0228 fires only in files the formatter already classifies as library source (Host.jet:4291). Two dialects of call syntax coexist, and moving a function between a library and an app changes which spelling is required.

comparisons.note: An inout argument is written &xs at every call, including when the caller forwards its own inout parameter. A mutating method receiver is plain.
ref and out are repeated at the call, including when forwarding a ref parameter. Receivers are plain.
comparisons.code:
static void Load(ref Buffer buf) { Fill(ref buf); }
Load(ref buf);

comparisons.note: A fresh mutable borrow is written &mut xs, but a caller forwards its own &mut parameter plainly. Receivers borrow automatically.
mut sits only in the signature, and its call is plain. A var parameter takes ownership; the caller moves with a postfix ^, and without it the value is copied.
An inout argument is written &x at the call, and so are mutating receivers and operators. Only Hylo marks receivers.

recommendation.why: A is your ruling, made cheap: the change is visible in every diff and page, the compiler checks each mark, and fmt, fix and the editor write all of them. It matches Swift and C#, and D-RECEIVER-MARK1.
recommendation.tradeoff: Visible changes in plain text, for about 105,000 marks in one cutover and a compile inside fmt.
gains: Every changed argument is visible in diffs, reviews and pages.
One rule with no policy, audit command or second compile.
No one has to type a mark: fmt, fix and the editor write them.

losses.mitigation: One checked fmt run writes them in a mark-only commit that blame can skip.

losses.mitigation: One compile per package, shared with the copies and failures passes; layout never waits, and fix-on-save reuses the editor's last check.

losses.mitigation: Changed arguments now show in the text, and editor hints still show receivers and takes.

A printed 0.840 and 0.979 belong to the looser count.

To check the 69,758 figure, read D-CALLSITE-MARK2: it was a raw text count on b486d6c09a. A text search for an & argument mark finds 69,817 at 5ef77a52ad^.

To check the mechanism, read Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Ownership/CallMarks.jet:97-193 and Checks.jet:4765-4773. Then read Compiler/Prelude/Diagnostics.jet:4279-4350 and Compiler/JetCLI/Source/CLI/Host.jet:4159-4302. Host.jet:4199-4269 serves the copies and failures passes, which A keeps.

Also read Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/AST/Expressions.jet:809-818 for the slice defect and Compiler/JetCLI/Source/CLI/FixCommands.jet:427-456 for the rollback. Read AuditWrites.jet, Compiler/JetLSP/Source/LSP/Hints.jet:132-244, CodeActions.jet:28-80 and Formatting.jet:24-31.

To reproduce the probes, use jet a0.0.46 with & for ^ and && for ^^. Put #Policy(writes: .Explicit) on the same-program example. Expect E0228 at the load and fill calls and at the receiver, and expect jet fix to insert every mark.

Then probe sort_part(xs[0..2]): the fix writes xs&[0..2], the result fails to check, and jet fix still reports one fix applied. Probe xs |> grow(<>) to see xs change, and make() |> grow(<>) to see the refusal that names __jet_pipe_N.

decisions.title: Calls that pass a failure up are written with ?, and jet fmt writes the marks
decisions.situation: A Jet call that fails passes the failure up, and the function holding it returns early, with nothing written at the call. Only the editor's faint `?`, `jet review` and an opt-in setting show those exits, so a pull request on the web and a model reading files see none. On 2026-11-25 you ruled for call marks that `jet fmt` writes every required mark, and asked that failures be weighed under the same rule. The old case against required marks was the work of writing one every 12 to 17 lines, and under your rule tools do that work. We recommend that every call that can pass a failure up is written `call()?`, inserted by the same checked fmt pass as the call marks.
decisions.gist: Should every call that can pass a failure up be written with `?`, with `jet fmt` writing the marks?
decisions.lesson: A call that fails passes the failure up, so the function holding it returns early too. Today nothing is written there. Under A the call reads `files.read(path)?`, the compiler checks every mark, and `jet fmt` and the editor write them. A marked call runs exactly like an unmarked one; the mark only shows the exit.
decisions.explainer:
## Read the example

`files.read(path)` can fail. Today the call reads `files.read(path)`, and nothing in the text says the function may stop there. Under A it reads `files.read(path)?`, and the compiler refuses the plain call with a fix that writes the mark.

## What needs no mark

A call whose failure is handled, with `??`, a match or `.drop(…)`, needs no mark, because the failure never leaves. Neither does a call that cannot fail, a call the compiler wrote, or a call whose only failure is a refused allocation.

## Who types the marks

Nobody has to. `jet fmt`, `jet fix`, the editor's quick fix and fix-on-save write every missing mark from the checked program. They also delete a `?` on a call that can no longer fail, so every mark stays true.
decisions.story:
Sam reviews a pull request on a web page. Between two ledger edits sits `save(order)`, and today nothing shows that it can return early and leave the second edit undone. Under A the line reads `save(order)?`, so the early exit is in the diff.

The author never typed the mark. Saving the file in the editor wrote it, and `jet fmt` would have too. A week later `price(item)` starts reading a file, and the same change gains a `?` at each caller that now passes that failure up.
decisions.detail:
## What changed, and what this ballot settles

Your 2026-11-25 ruling on call marks (D-CALLSITE-MARK3=A) set one rule: `jet fmt` inserts every required mark from the checked compile. Nobody writes a mark by hand at an existing call. You asked that proposal P36, which reopens D-FAIL-VISIBLE1, be weighed under that rule.

The earlier draft kept marks optional mainly because writing them is work: a mark every 12 to 17 lines in code that can fail. Under the rule that work moves to tools, so this ballot rebuilds the recommendation from what remains. Option A requires the mark and shares the call marks' checked fmt pass, quick fix and fix-on-save. It designs no second pass (I8).

Option B is today's rule, kept as a fair choice with its unbuilt tools finished. Option C mirrors the call-mark ballot's library-only option. The letters follow the recommendation, so the flip P36 describes is A.

Cited lines are at dev e3bf920e00a (2026-11-25). Probes used the installed jet a0.0.46, built from c137227f924, in a scratch directory since deleted.

## The rule under A, exactly

- A call that can pass a failure up is written `call()?`, or `call()?(text)` to add one context frame (S7, D-FAIL-CTX1). Both are the mark; the second also adds text to the report.

- A missing mark is E0434 `Jet.FailureMarkRequired`, a default error whose Safe edit writes the mark. `#Policy(failures: .Explicit)` is deleted, so nothing turns the rule on or off.

- A call used as a receiver is written `(call()?).field`, because `call()?.field` is an optional chain. The Safe edit writes the parentheses, as it does today. A probe of `files.read(p)?.count_bytes()` gave E0047, and the fix wrapped the call.

- A call whose failure is handled owes no mark: `call() ?? fallback`, a match with an `.Err` arm, an `== .Ok(…)` test, or `.drop("reason")`. The failure never leaves the function there.

- A call of a function that cannot fail owes no mark. Which calls can fail is the failure solve's answer, the same fact E0434 reads today (Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/FailureMarks.jet:119-145).

- A marked call checks and runs exactly as an unmarked one, as now (Docs/Spec/spec.md:2058-2065). Marks show exits; they never change them. Failures still pass up by themselves under D-FAILURE-FOUNDATION1.

## Each remaining downside, and how A removes it

Stale marks. Today a mark on a call that cannot fail is accepted (spec.md:2063-2064). A probe confirmed it: `twice(2)?` on a function that cannot fail checks clean under the setting. Under A a bare `?` there is a new warning, `Jet.UnusedFailureMark`, whose Safe edit deletes it. The shared fmt pass applies that edit, so when a callee stops failing, the next fmt removes the marks at its callers.

A `?(text)` on a call that cannot fail warns too, but fmt keeps it, because it holds words someone wrote. `jet fix` and the quick fix delete it. Both are warnings, not errors, so a callee that stops failing never breaks its callers' build.

Churn up the call chain. When a leaf newly can fail, every function above it whose failures are inferred can fail too, and each call on the way owes a mark. The next `jet fmt`, fix-on-save or `jet fix` writes all of them in the same change, from one compile per package. So the diff shows exactly the new exits, which is the point of the rule.

The chain stops at a call that handles the failure, and at a function whose written contract excludes it; there the compiler already demands handling. `jet review` keeps its `newly can fail` flag (Compiler/JetCLI/Source/CLI/Review.jet:1590-1682), so a reviewer sees which leaf caused the added marks.

A published package also needs acknowledgment before a public function newly fails (D-FAIL-PUBSIG1). A dependent package that upgrades gets E0434 until its own fmt runs, which is one command, not work at each call.

Allocation failure. D-ALLOC-FAIL1=C (ratified 2026-11-11, not built) makes a refused allocation an ordinary failure, `AllocError`, that passes up by itself. If it counted, nearly every call that builds a list or a string would need a mark. So E0434 leaves `AllocError` out when it asks whether a call can fail, and a call that can fail only that way owes no mark.

A mark written on such a call is accepted and is not stale, because the call can still leave the function. So the stale-mark warning fires only where a call cannot fail at all, `AllocError` included, and fmt never deletes a mark that shows a real exit.

That is an honest limit: a refused allocation can still leave a function with no mark in the text. Swift's design note says the same of any language whose allocation failures are recoverable (swift/docs/ErrorHandlingRationale.md). Literals and string building allocate with no call to mark, so no spelling could cover them. A call that can also fail some other way is marked, and its mark covers the allocation too.

Loop headers. Under D-ITERATOR-FAIL1=A, `loop x in source` calls `next` at each step, and a failure from `next` leaves the function from the header. Today that path skips E0434. The header's `next` is a generated method call (Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Statements/ForIn.jet:241-298, node id `AST_NODE_GENERATED` at 284), and FailureMarks.jet:124 exempts generated nodes.

A `?` after the source cannot mark the step, because it marks the source's own call. So A adds one spelling: `loop? x in source` marks a header whose step can fail, as Swift writes `for try await x in sequence`. E0434 reports at the header with a Safe edit that writes `loop?`, and a `loop?` whose step cannot fail is the stale-mark warning.

`loop?` gets a registry row beside `loop` (Compiler/JetFoundation/Data/Syntax/CoreSurface.jet:503-505, I7), and the editor grammars are regenerated from it. `results()` keeps per-item recovery and needs no mark, because its step does not fail.

Style selectors. Under D-FORMAT-TRAIT1=A, `{x:Hex(2)}` calls a style trait method. A user implementation that can fail passes its failure up (Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Expressions.jet:2993-2999), and today the string has no place for a mark. A lets `?` or `?(text)` follow the selector inside the braces: `{x:Hex(2)?}`.

The selector parser (Compiler/JetParser/Source/Parser/Expressions.jet:1450-1482) accepts the mark, and the Safe edit lands after the selector. The selector rail's registry row (Compiler/JetFoundation/Data/Syntax/EffectsSurface.jet:173-181) gains the trailing mark. A plain call inside braces needs no new rule: `"{load(p)?}"` is an ordinary marked call.

These are the only call roots that pass a failure up. Operators, indexing and fields never do (Expressions/Control.jet:526-537), so no other spelling is needed.

Generated calls. The `#CLI` entry wraps the user's `run(args: T)` in a generated function whose source is parsed at Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Registration/CLIEntry.jet:165. Only items with an `external_type` get `compiler_generated` (CLIEntry.jet:174-176), so the wrapper's call of `run` reaches E0434.

On a0.0.46 that call got E0434 with no edit, at a line past the end of the file. The count saw it in 7 Examples/Network/Browser programs and 15 Tools/Gauntlet entries, and a 12-line probe reproduced it.

Under A a call the compiler wrote owes no mark, because nobody reads it. The test cannot live in `parse_generated_source`: it also parses embedded Core (Compiler/JetParser/Source/Parser/Entry.jet:164-170), so a bit set there would excuse every Core call.

JetIR already names the generated functions: `__jet_cli_run` and the synthetic decode, merge and enum bodies (Compiler/JetIR/Source/BuildExpr.jet:7115-7119). That test moves to one shared place, and E0434 and `jet review` skip calls in those functions. It cannot reuse `compiler_generated`, which also stops automatic propagation (Expressions/Control.jet:1440-1444). The user's own `run` body is marked like any body.

Lambdas. A lambda's own calls are marked like any body's, and the call that runs a failing lambda is marked too: `paths.map(fn(p: String) { size(p)? })?`. Today `jet review` skips every point inside a lambda (Review.jet:1520-1537). Under A those points are in the text, and the review lists them under the lambda.

Scripts and `jet eval`. `run: fn()` can fail by default (D-FAIL-EXIT1), and a script's lines are its run body, so they carry marks too. The error prints the marked line, and `jet fmt` fixes a script file.

Targets. A callee can fail on one target and not on another, through a `#Target` impl or an `#if #build.target.os` arm (spec.md:1451-1471). If marks followed one machine's check, fmt on Linux could add a mark that fmt on Windows deletes. So a call owes a mark when its callee can fail on any target the package builds for, and a mark is stale only when it fails on none.

Whether the failure solve joins the targets today was not checked [inference]; the build card proves it with a two-target case.

Code that no compile checks is covered by the migration below.

## How fmt and the editor write the marks

A designs no pass of its own. D-CALLSITE-MARK3=A turns the shared `jet_cli_fmt_policy_marks` machinery (Compiler/JetCLI/Source/CLI/Host.jet:4199-4269) into one checked-insertion pass for call marks, copies and failures. That pass lays out first without compiling, then inserts marks from one compile per package; an error blocks only the marks it touches.

Today failure marks come only from `jet fmt --explicit-failures` (Host.jet:4286-4290). It prepends the setting and compiles each file twice (Host.jet:4205-4213). Under A, failures are a default part of plain `jet fmt` and the flag goes. The ordinary check already carries every E0434 Safe edit, so nothing is prepended.

The pass gains one thing for failures: it also applies the Safe deletion of a stale bare `?` or `loop?`. That amends D-CALLSITE-MARK3's sentence that fmt inserts marks only, for failure marks alone; its `^` rule is unchanged. `jet fmt --check` runs the same path, so CI reports a missing or stale mark as a dirty file.

In the editor, E0434's quick fix comes from its Safe edit (Compiler/JetLSP/Source/LSP/CodeActions.jet:28-80). D-CALLSITE-MARK3's new `source.fixAll` applies every Safe mark edit from the server's last check, and fix-on-save uses that check, so it never compiles again.

The faint `?` hints and their second compile are deleted, because the text now shows the marks. They live in Compiler/JetCLI/Source/CLI/LSP.jet:91-132, and in JetLSP Check.jet:74-81, Server.jet:71-72 and Hints.jet:40-44.

Mark placement must be exact before any of this runs. The tree keeps no `)`, so FailureMarks.jet:147-195 guesses a call's end from its last argument. On a0.0.46, `each_size([String]{"a.txt"})` became `each_size([?String]{"a.txt"})`, and a `map(fn(p: String) {…})` call got `fn?(`. The parser records each call's `)`, and the edit lands after it.

## Code that no compile checks

The repository holds 853 Jet fences in Markdown, 433 `.template` files and about 3,059 `.stderr` snapshots that quote source. Test strings hold Jet too. Those counts were taken for D-CALLSITE-MARK3. A adds a `fail-mark2` row to LANGUAGE_REWRITES (Compiler/JetFoundation/Data/Syntax/Spellings.jet:112) beside the call marks' row.

The row runs the checked insertion on every runnable fence, checked the way Tests/Guards/doc_blocks.jet checks them, and on each template as the case runner instantiates it. Snapshots are regenerated. A fragment that does not check is listed with its path; that residue is counted when the row is built, not measured yet.

The seed compiler accepts a call's `?` only under the setting, and the compiler builds itself with the seed. So the cutover first writes `#Policy(failures: .Explicit)` into each package and lone file, inserts the marks, and then flips the default. The setting lines are deleted once a seed with the new default is published.

## How many calls gain a mark

Two methods, each reproducible with a script kept beside this ballot: D-FAIL-VISIBLE2.count-compiled.mjs and D-FAIL-VISIBLE2.count-static.mjs.

Measured. The installed a0.0.46 checks only its own syntax, so the measurement uses Examples, Tools and Tests at c137227f924, the commit it was built from. Each file is checked as written, and a file with any error is left out. Then the setting goes on its own line after a leading `#!` line or an inline `package:` header, else at the top. Each E0434 in that file is one call A marks.

Each check ran alone in a 4 GiB memory scope. Tests were sampled: the 400 paths with the smallest SHA-1 of their path, of 14,484 files.

```text
Measured with a0.0.46 at c137227f924
tree      checked files   lines    marks  per 1,000 lines  files with a mark      receiver  no edit
Examples  992 of 1,058   40,976    1,054       25.7        242 (one per 12.4 lines)    23        7
Tools     707 of 894    122,726    2,250       18.3        168 (one per 33.5 lines)   154       15
Tests     254 of 400      4,833      103       21.3         33 (one per 8.6 lines)      0        0

receiver: the edit wraps the call as (call()?).  no edit: the generated run(args: T) call.
left out: files with errors as written (Tests holds many on purpose) and 2 Examples files
that gained other errors under the setting.
```

Why the earlier figures differ. The draft's 785 came from 726 Examples files. The stopped review's 311 came from 902 files, with the setting placed above `package:` headers, which broke every file that opens with one. Placed after the header, 992 files check and give 1,054, close to the draft's 1.08 marks per file. The card's 311-454 range is superseded.

Estimated. a0.0.46 cannot check today's syntax, nor Compiler, Core or Jetpack one file at a time. So a static script counts every tree on dev 72bd6f6904c. It blanks comments and string text, keeps interpolations, and classes each `name: fn(…)` by its written contract: `Never!`, another `E!`, or none.

It solves the inferred contracts to a fixed point: a body that builds `Err(…)` or holds an unhandled failing call can fail. A call counts as certain when every visible declaration of its name can fail and nothing handles it. A method call weighs every method of that name; `alias.f(` on a Core module alias weighs that module.

Calibration. On the measured files, the certain count found 2,545 of the 3,407 measured marks and predicted 3,378, so precision is 0.753 and recall 0.747. By tree: Examples 0.794 and 0.649, Tools 0.737 and 0.802, Tests 0.851 and 0.553. Predicted and measured totals agree within 1 percent, so the totals below need no scaling.

```text
Estimated on dev 72bd6f6904c (.jet files except package.jet)
tree      files     lines     certain  per 1,000 lines  possible  receiver  ?("text") now  ?? now
Compiler  1,905    984,342     9,323        9.5          33,350      197          0      22,524
Core        306    318,082     2,933        9.2           7,021       13          2       7,744
Jetpack     774    237,172     7,818       33.0          13,268       68          0      12,799
Tools       916    144,742     2,734       18.9           8,487       80         14       8,512
Examples  1,084     44,376       921       20.8           2,466       28          3       2,631
Tests    14,844    299,860     3,172       10.6          16,633       46         47      14,660
total    19,829  2,028,574    26,901                     81,225      432         66      68,870

possible: one visible declaration of the name can fail (precision about 0.3, not a bound).
?("text") now and ?? now: plain text counts of written context marks and fallbacks.
```

Read about 27,000 as the size of the cutover. Calibrated trees are good to roughly a quarter either way. Compiler, Core and Jetpack are not calibrated, because a per-file check cannot reach them; their method names collide most, so the Compiler figure could be off by half [inference]. Most Compiler helpers are written `Never!`, which is why its rate is low.

The review reran the static script and got 26,901 again. It also measured 18 fresh files, 12 from Examples and 6 from Tools: 260 marks, of which the script predicted 254.

The earlier draft extrapolated 36,000 to 53,000 from 2 percent of the lines, assuming every tree failed like Examples. For scale, the call marks changed about 105,000 sites.

## Probes on a0.0.46

- Option A's code and option B's code, each under the setting where it marks, check clean and print 12 with a six-byte a.txt.

- `twice(2)?` and `twice(3)?("doubling")` on a function that cannot fail check clean under the setting. Outside it, the `?(text)` form is accepted too.

- `files.read(p)?.count_bytes()` is E0047, the optional chain; the E0434 edit for a receiver writes `(` and `?)`.

- `jet fmt --explicit-failures` on `each_size([String]{"a.txt"})` and on a `map(fn(p: String) {…})` call wrote `?` inside the literal and the lambda, and the output failed to parse.

- A `#CLI` program whose `run(args)` body can fail got E0434 on `run` at line 12 of an 11-line file, with no edit.

- Read from code only: a0.0.46's `next` cannot fail (Compiler/Prelude/Traits.jet:302 at c137227f924), and it predates user style selectors (E0914 on `{n:Shout}`). Loop headers and selectors follow today's dev code.

## Card #7034

Criterion c3 (placement inside a typed literal or lambda) holds under every option, through the recorded `)`.

Criterion c4 says `jet review` and `jet diff` list points inside lambdas and loop headers, and E0434 covers a loop header. The earlier draft left headers unmarked, which contradicted that clause. This ballot withdraws that rule: under A, and under B's setting, E0434 covers a failing loop header and its mark is `loop?`. The clause stands as written.

Criterion c5 asks for pull-request annotations, as D-FAIL-VISIBLE1=A promised, and no E0434 without a fix on a generated `run(args: T)` call. Under A the marks are in the diff, so the annotation half is dropped and the generated-call half stands. Under B both halves stand. Criteria c1, c2 and c6 stand.

## Decisions this amends if A wins

- D-FAIL-VISIBLE1=A (2026-09-30) is reversed: marks are required, tools write them, and the setting, the flag and the faint hints go.

- D-FAILURE-FOUNDATION1=A: failures still pass up by themselves, but the call is marked. Its bare call `?`, kept as a diagnostic only, becomes the mark.

- S7 and D-FAIL-CTX1=A: `?(text)` is still no second propagation operator; it becomes the framed form of the required mark.

- D-ITERATOR-FAIL1=A: a header whose step can fail is written `loop?`.

- D-FORMAT-TRAIT1=A: a selector whose method can fail takes `?` inside the braces.

- D-ALLOC-FAIL1=C keeps its behavior and gains one sentence: a failure that is only `AllocError` owes no mark, and a mark written there stays.

- D-CALLSITE-MARK3=A: its shared pass applies failure marks in plain fmt, and deletes a stale bare `?` or `loop?`. Its sentence that fmt inserts marks only gains that exception, and its note that `--explicit-failures` is kept no longer holds.

- D-FAIL-PUBSIG1=A and D-FAIL-EXIT1 stand.

## History and what was left out

Jet once required `?` at every call that passed a failure up. D-FAILURE-FOUNDATION1=A (2026-08-25) made plain calls propagate. D-FAIL-VISIBLE1=A (2026-09-30) chose tools plus an opt-in setting, because required marks add a mark to one of the most common operations and collide with `?.`.

The first reason is the typing cost your ruling removes. The second remains as the receiver form `(f()?).x`, which fmt writes: 23 of 1,054 measured marks in Examples and 154 of 2,250 in Tools. No code in Core, Examples, Tools or Jetpack opts into the setting today.

Considered and left out. Marks only where a failure leaves a public function: declarations are public by default (spec.md:4052), so this is nearly A, and `priv` would silently drop marks. Marks only on calls into another package still mark every Core I/O call. Hints only, as the call-mark ballot's C, is B without the setting.

What a mark does not buy. A mark changes no behavior, and a half-done update like the story's is still possible. `#Transact` checks that case: it rolls back `Shared` writes on every exit, including a passed-up failure, and refuses irreversible effects inside (spec.md:2592-2600, E0746).

Research. Rust, Swift and Zig require a mark at each call that passes an error up, and Swift marks a loop whose step can throw. Go writes the check out by hand. Kotlin and Java mark nothing at the call. Gleam deprecated its `try` keyword in 2023 for `use` with `result.try`. The comparisons give sources.

comparisons.note: The `?` operator returns an `Err` early and is required at each call that passes one up; `f()?.x` chains on the success. Source: The Rust Book, chapter 9.2.

comparisons.note: `try` is required before an expression that can throw and covers the whole expression. A loop over an asynchronous sequence whose step can throw is written `for try await` (SE-0298). The design note calls this marked propagation. It adds that a language whose allocation failures are recoverable cannot claim it fully. Sources: The Swift Programming Language, Error Handling; swift/docs/ErrorHandlingRationale.md.
comparisons.code:
let n = try String(contentsOfFile: path).count
for try await line in url.lines { print(line) }

comparisons.note: `try x` means `x catch |err| return err`, written at every call; error return traces show the path. Source: Zig language reference, try and Error Return Traces.

The check is written out after every call. In June 2025 the Go team stopped pursuing shorter syntax after three proposals, and mentioned editor support for reading them. Source: go.dev/blog/error-syntax.

Exceptions pass up with nothing at the call. Kotlin has no checked exceptions; Java lists checked ones in `throws`, still unmarked at the call. Sources: kotlinlang.org/docs/exceptions.html; Hejlsberg, "The Trouble with Checked Exceptions", artima.com.

questions.text: How do other languages handle this? What are the tradeoffs for each approach?
questions.answer: Most modern toolchains use Option A — one binary, tool subcommands: Deno (deno fmt/lint/lsp), Gleam (gleam format/lsp), Ruff (ruff format/check/server), Bun. The recurring exception is the LSP, shipped as a separate artifact by Zig (ZLS), Go (gopls), and Rust (rust-analyzer) because editors spawn it long-lived on its own cadence. Rust's fmt/clippy are separate binaries (B) but hidden behind cargo subcommands and version-locked via rustup. Pure plugin (C) has no real precedent for compiled-language toolchains. Tradeoffs: A = one install, tooling can never disagree with the compiler, bigger binary, no independent patch cadence; B = independent releases + smaller core but version-skew risk and N artifacts; C = max flexibility, runtime ABI surface, no prior art, fights one-source-of-truth. Jet-specific: fmt/lint/lsp all need the real lexer/parser/sema (I2/I3), so under B/C they must link the same front end as a shared lib and stay version-locked anyway — getting separation's costs without its benefits. Prior art + that constraint both point at A, reserving the LSP as the one piece that could become a separate artifact later. Full table added to the D-TOOL-SPLIT card in docs/ballots/decision-ballots.md.

C (a defer keyword) adds a second cleanup mechanism plus the Go leak-by-omission bug class S63 was chosen to avoid; its only unique win is errdefer-style partial rollback, not yet proven. B doesn't foreclose C — add the keyword later on evidence. defer (C) stays declined (D-SUGAR5); user-definable Drop remains the long-term roadmap item.

questions.text: 1) Isnt sharing not supportable with the borrow checker? Wouldnt that be a mutable borrow which can only have 1, but immutable can have many? I dont get the point, refresh me on the memory capability model. How does it play into the borrow checker system? What is auto inferred for beginners but can be specified for experts?
questions.answer: `share` is shared *ownership* (Rc/Arc), not a shared mutable borrow — so the borrow-checker rule still holds: mutable XOR shared. The four capabilities map onto it directly: `view` = `&T` (many readers ok), `edit` = `&mut T` (exactly one, exclusive), `take` = move (ownership transfer), `share` = `Rc<T>`/`Arc<T>` (many owners, READ-only — no mutation, so no conflict with the one-mutable rule). `share` exists for graph/tree shapes where a single owner is awkward; it buys multiple readers by giving up mutation, exactly mirroring &T. Beginners write none of this — the compiler infers the narrowest capability from how the value is used; experts annotate it to pin intent or widen sharing. Full capability↔borrow-checker table is on the D-CAP2 card.

questions.text: How is a supportive of the experts? That is one of the major points for jet -> a beginner friendly automagical side & an expert exposed full control side
questions.answer: Reframed so it serves experts directly: ship BOTH. A (scope-inferred regions) is the beginner default — the compiler places allocations automatically. B (`region r { … }`) is the explicit expert tier — you name a region and allocate into it deliberately, e.g. two arenas live side by side and you choose which one each value lands in. The beginner never sees a region; the expert gets full manual placement. Now RATIFIED (D-REGION1 = A+B together, 2026-06-21). Worked two-arena example is on the card.

questions.text: I'm leaning towards A, but how is bloat/buildup addressed? For large codebases, how will users be able to avoid 3k lines of code that are just migrations?

So a large codebase with a few published types stays tiny. Now RATIFIED (D-MIGRATE1 = A) and the rename-only slice is implemented end-to-end + verified green; the squash/baseline tooling and other ops are tracked as follow-on D-MIGRATE2.

questions.text: How does this interplay with experts that will want to use low level memory controls like references and pointers?
questions.answer: The tiers compose rather than conflict. `view`/`edit` ARE the safe references an expert wants (`&T`/`&mut T`) — capabilities are the safe-reference surface, not a wall in front of it. The drop below that layer is a raw `Ptr<T>` via `use core.mem` inside a `#Unsafe`/`#Audit` region, where the guarantees are explicitly suspended. The two bridge at the function boundary: public params stay safe capabilities, and the raw-pointer work is a localized `#Unsafe` block inside. Worked `checksum(buf: view [U8])` example added to the D-CAP3/D-CAP2 card. Decision still open.

questions.text: How is this affected when no type is written (inferred type)?
questions.answer: Capabilities are a parameter concept and parameters carry types, so an omitted capability is simply inferred — there is no token to place when no type is written, and the capability rides the type. Rule: no type written ⇒ capability inferred too; you never get a dangling capability. This reinforces option A (type + capability written together in one place). The only spot you'd write an inferred-type parameter is a lambda, where you write the type alongside precisely to pin a capability. Decision still open.

questions.text: I think the $ is fine for me, but what about people trying to use the language globally? Is having such a commonly needed symbol an issue? What if people dont have that symbol? How likely is that? Is it a reasonable concern or not a big deal

Programmers type `$` constantly (shell/PHP/JS) and no mainstream language uses it as a binding operator, so no conflicting habit. Answered in the D-BIND2 card; rec stands at A (`$=`); decision stays open for your pick.

questions.text: I dont understand the downside. Please explain more precisely why we shouldn't just allow all core calls.
questions.answer: Updated D-CTCORE1 with the precise downside: allowing all Core at comptime turns pure compile-time evaluation into running a second runtime during compilation. That harms reproducibility, allows ambient side effects during builds (fs/env/process/net/secrets), forces the comptime interpreter to duplicate runtime behavior, complicates supply-chain policy, and creates machine-dependent compile failures. questions.text: What are the downsides of recommendation A? In practice does this cause friction? How do new users know what to do? Will this make it harder to use the system for simpler projects or beginner projects?
questions.answer: Honest answer: A's only real cost is key custody, and it lands entirely on PUBLISHERS — never on consumers, never on beginners, never on simple projects. (1) Consuming a package (the common case + every beginner): zero friction — `jet add` verifies the signature silently and only ever speaks on a MISMATCH (a normal Jet diagnostic, not crypto). Strictly better than checksum-only for the same effort. (2) Simpler/local/unpublished projects: nothing changes — signing is only on the registry-publish path; path/git/unpublished deps are never signed or asked about. (3) Publishing (the one place friction exists): mitigated by the dual-facet rule — `jet publish` auto-generates+stores a keypair on first publish (no separate keygen on the magic path), then prints one line nudging `jet key backup`. The beginner's required action is the command they were already running. What stays genuinely hard is key LOSS/THEFT/ROTATION — the inherent cost of authenticity. Prior art is a warning: PyPI REMOVED GPG signing in 2023 (nobody verified, so publisher pain bought nothing); npm/Go/crates.io all moved authenticity OFF author-managed keys; Maven Central's mandatory GPG is the canonical 'publishing is painful' complaint. Lesson: never make key management mandatory or visible on the magic path. Bearing on the decision: this argues for A as an OPT-IN / non-blocking layer with SHA-256 checksum (B) as the always-on floor — `require_signed` stays an org policy, OFF by default — not a hard gate that refuses unsigned packages. That keeps A's unique win (offline authorship proof) while spending friction only on publishers who opt in. Full Owner Q&A block added to the D-PKGSIGN1 card.

questions.text: What is really the issue with full jai? Build systems allow arbitrary code execution, but this just keeps it within the language. Play devil's advocate & tell me what we would lose out on by going with option a vs full jai. Consider every level of use case (beginner/college student/enterprise/etc.)
questions.answer: Full writeup is on the D-METADEPTH1 ballot card as Owner Q5. Steel-manning C: one language/debugger/syntax (no second toolchain) and a genuinely higher ceiling — rewrite decls, schema-driven codegen, DSLs — that A (read + derive) gives up. BUT 'inside the language' only removes a TOOLCHAIN seam, not Jai's two real costs: (1) local reasoning dies — if any macro can rewrite any decl you can't read code and know what it does; grep/go-to-def/'what did it expand to' all degrade (the proc-macro tax), bending I3/I8 and D-CTCODEGEN1=A (generated code re-enters sema, never injected). (2) It's still arbitrary build-time code execution + non-reproducibility — identical whether in-language or in build.rs; keeping it in-language removes the very seam you'd sandbox/audit it through, so it makes supply-chain RISK worse, not better. By use case: BEGINNER loses ~nothing (and C only adds footguns — a struct no longer trustworthy at face value); LEARNER trades metaprogramming exercises for the guarantee that reading code = understanding it (A wins for learning the language, C only for learning metaprogramming); POWER USER loses custom rules/DSLs/schema-codegen — the genuine cost, mitigated by S56 derives + blessed first-class rules (#(net) effects enforce 'no panic in net', typestate enforces state rules) + the B rung (rejection-lint); ENTERPRISE flips entirely — frictionless idiomatic compile-time exec is exactly the xz/SolarWinds/npm-postinstall attack surface, so a Jai-style Jet gets banned or heavily sandboxed and reproducibility (D-CTEFFECT1) dies. Decisive point: A⊂B⊂C is a LADDER. A is the floor, not the ceiling — we can vote UP later (B for rejection rules, C only post-self-host) with no redesign, because nothing in A forecloses them; the reverse is impossible (you can't un-ship macros — the ecosystem locks you in, see Rust). So A is the only rung that is safe-by-default for beginners, auditable-by-default for enterprise, AND forward-compatible. Recommendation stays A; the live decision is how far up the ladder v1 goes (Owner Q1/Q2: ship B's rejection-lint now or defer).

questions.text: How does jai handle this? Show me a detailed comparison between jet & c3 so I can see what this looks like in practice. What about jai's "#run" directive? How do we do that in jet? How can we scope to a code block?
questions.answer: Full writeup on the D-CTMARKER1 ballot card as Owner Q3 (with a Jet↔C3 table and the Jai #run breakdown). Jai's #run does two jobs: (a) bake a compile-time value into the binary (X :: #run f();), and (b) a free-standing #run { … } block of arbitrary build-time statements that can even generate source via add_build_string — and it is UNGATED (any I/O, no reproducibility wall). Jet already has (a): a `comptime` binding IS #run-for-a-value (`comptime ICONS = pack(@embed("icons/"))`), but GATED — comptime runs only the curated pure-Core whitelist (D-CTCORE1), and world-touching effects are hashed-reproducible (Tier 1 @embed/find/fetch(…,sha256:)) or behind #Impure (Tier 2) per D-CTEFFECT1. Jai's source-generating add_build_string is exactly what D-CTCODEGEN1=A (generated code re-enters lexer→parser→sema, never injected) and D-METADEPTH1=A (reflection/derives only, no user macros) deliberately fence off — so Jet gives you #run's POWER (compute at build time, derive code) without #run's FOOTGUNS (ungated RCE + post-sema injection). C3 vs Jet in practice = the same program with C3's `$` sigil vs Jet's `comptime` keyword: $crc/comptime crc, $if/comptime if, $foreach/comptime loop — identical for everything EXCEPT a build-time statement BLOCK, which Jet does NOT have today (only comptime bindings + comptime if; 'no comptime blocks'). That is the genuine gap and the real thing to add. Sharpened recommendation: add a keyword-spelled `comptime { … }` block (Jet's gated equivalent of Jai's free-standing #run {}, consistent with comptime if) and reserve `$` for the metaprogramming SPLICE site only (rec C: $name = a comptime value woven into runtime/generated code) — Jai's full reach behind Jet's reproducible-by-default wall, no $if/comptime-if I8 fork. Added Owner Q4 to the card to pick the block form. Decision stays open.

questions.text:
1) This was more a request for comprehensive and native builtin support for inline assembly and easy way to see generated assembly from jet source
2) too many downsides, must design away negatives
questions.answer:
Final integration: D-CODE-INSPECT2 recommends A: direct source assembly emission while preserving the ratified explicit capture workflow. B is the explicit alternative that removes retained capture. Fresh review found that capture was already ratified, not merely a new proposal; removing it must be an honest owner amendment.

The earlier Astra recommendation is preserved below as attributed design advice, not the final recommendation or ratification. The final source-view and three native-assembly ballots have completed independent beginner/adversarial review and pass the ballot readiness checker. They remain owner choices, not implemented features.

Astra answer — openai-codex/gpt-6-astra. This is a design recommendation, not a claim that the proposed commands already ship.

1. Native inline assembly and generated assembly viewing are separate needs. Keep the ratified #FFI(asm), core.mem and audited #Unsafe gates. Complete typed operands/results, register directions/classes, constants, symbols, local control flow, machine effects, target facts and applicable native execution modes through that one compiler contract. Do not add a competing asm! or mem.asm API. Existing ratified defects remain on #3017; the additional expressiveness is on #3042.

For ordinary Jet, propose jet emit --asm FILE: compile current source when needed and show compiler-emitted assembly without starting the application or requiring a prior recording. Propose jet inspect code for exact existing artifacts or identified live code. Source compilation may still perform its authorized compile-time/build work. #3016 owns this viewer.

2. The earlier ballot put recording infrastructure in the way. Remove the proposed --capture-code, --run and --generation workflow from this revision. Use one source-linked code representation for the simple view, exact inspection and export. Do not reconstruct vanished historical code and label it original; report unavailable/missing-code. An optimized function may have no standalone instructions, and mappings must come from real producer facts.

The remaining constraints are real: new source needs compilation, exact old code requires retained bytes, and hand-written instructions still require an audited unsafe promise and compatible hardware. Full ballot revisions are being reviewed separately; this answer neither ratifies them nor claims implementation or benchmark proof.

questions.text: I think parallel default wouldn't be a terrible idea with magic for beginners but it could make debugging difficult and make things less predictable with effective data races. So we would need a non default version as well for full expert control.
questions.answer:
Agree, and parallel by default does not create data races here. The scheduler (ResourceSchedule) only runs systems together when their checked access sets do not overlap: reads with reads, writes on disjoint resources or regions. Unknown aliases are treated as conflicts, and a system that needs parallel access with unknown or conflicting writes is rejected. Tests cover read/read, overlap, unknown alias, conflicting writes, and disjoint regions.

What can still vary: which system finishes first, the order of emitted commands, events, and logs, and float sums that combine in a different order. Fix these by merging commands and events in a fixed order (system declaration order) at the end of each stage.

Expert control, using the choose-explain-pin rule: Auto groups disjoint systems; `jet inspect` or `schedule.explain()` shows why; a Serial pin runs one at a time for debugging and fully repeatable runs; a Parallel pin fails compilation when facts become incomplete or conflicting. Bevy offers similar ambiguity reports.

Note: game callbacks still run directly today; D-SYSSCHED1 is open.

Evidence: crates/jet-foundation/src/ResourceSchedule.rs:62-114,289-306,772-829,1377-1497,1941-2017; crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib/Top/Game.rs:303-352; Docs/proposals/memory-model-foundations-2026-09-27.md:376-392; https://docs.rs/bevy/latest/bevy/ecs/schedule/.

questions.text: I want to support both reactive & timed, please update accordingly
questions.answer:
Done. Option A is now both, sharing one key queue.

Timed: term.read_key_within(wait) returns a key, or None when the wait runs out. Closed input is an error, so a loop cannot spin.
Reactive: term.keys() returns a Receiver<Key> that joins the wait table beside process.signals and after arms. This is the same shape as the ratified D-CORE-PROCSIGNAL1=A.

Both calls take keys from one queue that #Live owns. A receiver reads input only while the program waits on it, so each key goes to exactly one reader and none is lost. That removes a trap in Rust crossterm, which offers both styles but forbids mixing them. It also keeps one mechanism (I8): the timed call is the beginner path, and the receiver is the expert path.

Options are re-lettered. B is receiver only, where a time limit is an after arm. C is the earlier timed-only option. The earlier poll-then-read option is dropped, because the timed call already returns the key in one step. Recommendation: A. Its one loss is that two spellings can wait for a key with a time limit.

questions.text: we should be able to produce web assembly, but my bigger point is that our goal is to REPLACE docker and webassembly with a perfected system for running sandboxed code similar to the potential of unison, eyg, etc. you fundamentally misunderstood the request. We want a new fundamental sandbox that REPLACES docker and wasm
questions.answer:
# D-PORTABLE1 — answer

**Owner (verbatim):** "we should be able to produce web assembly, but my bigger
point is that our goal is to REPLACE docker and webassembly with a perfected
system for running sandboxed code similar to the potential of unison, eyg, etc.
you fundamentally misunderstood the request. We want a new fundamental sandbox
that REPLACES docker and wasm"

You're right; the old ballot misread the goal. It treated WebAssembly as the
sandbox and only designed a file format around it. I withdrew that design and
rewrote the ballot around **Jet's own sandbox**.

**What the sandbox is (options A and B).** You ship one file of checked Jet
code. Before it runs, the machine that runs it:

1. **verifies the code itself:** types, memory safety, control flow. It never
   trusts what the builder claimed, so a file that fails verification never
   runs. A changed file that still verifies is a new program with a new hash,
   and it must ask for its grants again;
2. **compares the powers it needs with what you granted.** These use the
   effect names Jet already has (`--allow=FS.Write,IO`), plus a prompt;
3. **runs it with no ambient access.** Files, network, and clock are reached
   only through handles the host hands in, and a handle cannot be forged. A
   handle can be narrowed to one directory; the flag spelling for that waits
   on the open D-AUTH-NARROW1, so today's examples grant all files.

It starts at once in the interpreter and compiles native code on that machine,
so later runs are fast. A pure Jet app runs on any CPU and OS that has Jet.
Libraries inside are named by content hash, as in Unison, so a machine checks
and stores each one once. Memory, CPU, disk, and task limits apply per run.

```jet
SHIP :: Output.Bundle{name: "notes", of: APP, form: .Portable}
```
```
$ jet run notes.jetapp
notes wants FS.Write, IO. Run it? [Y/n/always]
$ jet run --allow=FS.Write,IO notes.jetapp     // any machine: same output
```

**WebAssembly** stays as an export (`jet build --target=wasm32-wasip2`) for
WASI hosts such as Wasmtime; browsers still need a separate adapter. It is no
longer how Jet sandboxes its own programs.

**The real question left for you: foreign code.** Docker is often used to run
C libraries and other programs, and that code cannot be verified.

- **A (recommended):** foreign code runs in a separate helper process walled
  off by the operating system. The app talks to it only through a typed
  interface; raw C pointers and callbacks cannot cross. Helpers are native, so
  they need a build for each CPU and OS, and if the walls are unavailable the
  app stops rather than running unconfined. The sandbox still covers the apps
  people use Docker for.
- **B:** a portable app cannot contain foreign code. Apps that need it ship as
  ordinary native programs, labeled TRUSTED.
- **C:** no Jet verifier. Native builds run behind OS walls only, like a typed
  Docker. Unlisted CPUs cannot run the app.

**One honest limit.** No sandbox is "perfect": each one trusts its own checker.
Docker trusts the kernel, and WebAssembly trusts its engine. Here Jet trusts its
verifier, runtime, and compiler. The ballot names that trusted base and lists
the checks that must pass before release. Those are: a denied write stops
before running, a file that fails verification is rejected, a helper without
its OS walls does not start, and the same pure Jet file gives the same output
on two CPU types.

Review note for Main: full rewrite, and the design changed. Run fresh beginner
and adversarial passes before marking it ready. The stored passes are labeled as
belonging to the earlier draft. The rewrite reverses D-DEP-WASM1's choice of
WebAssembly over a Jet virtual machine and changes what `--target=sandbox`
emits. Both are listed in the detail. SolBallotAdvisor's note
(advisor/D-PORTABLE1.md) shaped the verifier-first design, fail-closed loading,
the trusted-base statement, and the foreign-code axis.

- Only a lone Escape press waits, and only when that Escape byte is the last byte available. Whole keys that arrive together (the normal case, including arrows, F-keys and pastes) decode instantly. A pending Escape never blocks timers or messages in an `if` table.
- Modern terminals (kitty, foot, WezTerm, Ghostty, Alacritty, iTerm2): Jet asks once whether the terminal can send Escape as its own code (the same query Neovim sends). If it can, Escape waits 0 ms. Jet turns the mode on only while a receive is waiting and turns it off before your program runs again, so Ctrl-C still stops a busy program.
- Older terminals: the default drops from 35 ms to 10 ms (tmux's default since 3.5, less than one 60 Hz frame; the REPL waits 100 ms today).
- Expert control stays: `term.set_escape_wait` now ranges from 0 ms to 1 s.

All three options share the same decoder and key mode. Ballot updated.

questions.text: Can we expand this further by having effectively an extensible api to feed the compiler hw info for a target, almost like how nix has hardware configuration files that feed the config.nix files? That way we have an EXTENSIBLE way that is future proofed, can be tailored to individual targets, and if an expert requires it, they can require certain HW to run the code, like "requires a gpu, 4gb ram, etc"
questions.answer: Yes. The redraft makes that option A, built from parts Jet already ratified rather than a new configuration system. A target's hardware is a typed Jet description file. The hardware scan JetOS already uses writes it for the machine you're on, the way nixos-generate-config writes hardware-configuration.nix. For other machines you write it by hand or pull in a shared hardware profile package. It feeds build facts that code reads as $build.hardware, and a target in package.jet selects its description. It is extensible: Core ships CPU, GPU, Memory, Storage, Display and Network as typed kinds, and any package can add a new kind (say, a vendor NPU) with no compiler release. Experts can write requires: [GPU.any(), Memory.at_least(4GiB)] and uses: [GPU.feature(.TensorCores)]. A native program checks these at build time and again once at start-up on the real machine. A portable bundle is checked at install and at every launch, and recompiles if the hardware changed. A machine that lacks the hardware refuses the program with the missing item named. Free GPU memory stays with the existing check just before each GPU job, and hardware facts never grant powers. The old fixed-list design is now option B, and asking at run time is C. (The redrafted ballot is with fresh beginner and adversarial readers now; it replaces the posted text as soon as they pass.)
